Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Vinayapiṭake

In the Vinaya Piṭaka

Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā (tatiyo bhāgo)

The Sāratthadīpanī Sub-commentary (Third Part)

5. Pācittiyakaṇḍaṃ

5. The Section on Pācittiya

1. Musāvādavaggo

1. The Chapter on False Speech

1. Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on False Speech

1. Musāvādavaggassa [M 3.0001][V 3.0001] paṭhamasikkhāpade khuddakānanti ettha “khuddaka-saddo bahu-saddapariyāyo[V 3.0002]. Bahubhāvato imāni khuddakāni nāma jātānī”ti vadanti. Tatthāti tesu navasu vaggesu, tesu vā khuddakesu. Kāraṇena kāraṇantarapaṭicchādanameva vibhāvetuṃ “rūpaṃ anicca”ntiādimāha. Rūpaṃ aniccanti paṭijānitvā tattha kāraṇaṃ vadanto “jānitabbato”ti āha. “Yadi evaṃ nibbānassapi aniccatā āpajjatī”ti parena vutto taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicchādetuṃ puna “jātidhammato”ti aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ vadati.

1. In the first training rule of the Chapter on False Speech, regarding 'khuddakāni,' they say: 'The term "khuddaka" is a synonym for "bahu" (many). Because of their multiplicity, these have come to be called "khuddaka."' 'There' means in those nine chapters, or among those minor rules. To explain the concealment of one reason by another, the Teacher stated, 'Form is impermanent,' and so on. Having declared, 'Form is impermanent,' when stating the reason for it, he said, 'because it is knowable.' When told by another, 'If so, then even Nibbāna would become impermanent,' to conceal that reason, he states another reason, saying, 'because it is subject to origination.'

“Sampajānaṃ musā bhāsatī”ti vattabbe sampajāna musā bhāsatīti anunāsikalopena niddesoti āha “jānanto musā bhāsatī”ti.

When it should be said, 'He speaks false speech knowingly' (sampajānaṃ musā bhāsati), the indication is made with the elision of the nasal as 'sampajāna musā bhāsati.' Therefore, the Teacher said: 'Knowing, he speaks a lie.'

2. Jānitvā jānantassa ca musā bhaṇaneti pubbabhāgepi jānitvā vacanakkhaṇepi jānantassa musā bhaṇane. Bhaṇanañca nāma idha abhūtassa vā bhūtataṃ bhūtassa vā abhūtataṃ katvā kāyena vā vācāya vā viññāpanapayogo. Sampajānamusāvādeti ca nimittatthe bhummavacanaṃ, tasmā [M 3.0002] yo sampajāna musā vadati, tassa taṃnimittaṃ taṃhetu tappaccayā pācittiyaṃ hotīti evamettha aññesu ca īdisesu attho veditabbo.

2. Regarding 'having known and for one who is knowing, speaking falsely': this means speaking falsely having known beforehand and also knowing at the moment of speaking. And 'speaking' here is the application of making known, by body or by speech, having presented what is not true as true, or what is true as not true. And 'in intentional false speech' (sampajānamusāvāde) is a locative expression in the sense of a cause. Therefore, for one who knowingly speaks falsely, a pācittiya offense is incurred on account of that cause, for that reason, and through that condition. Thus the meaning should be understood here and in other similar cases.

3. Visaṃvādenti etenāti visaṃvādanaṃ, vañcanādhippāyavasappavattaṃ cittaṃ. Tenāha “visaṃvādanacittaṃ purato katvā vadantassā”ti. Vadati etāyāti vācā, vacanasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā. Tenāha “micchāvācā…pe… cetanā”ti. Pabhedagatā vācāti anekabhedabhinnā. Evaṃ paṭhamapadena suddhacetanā…pe… kathitāti veditabbāti iminā imaṃ dīpeti – suddhacetanā vā suddhasaddo vā suddhaviññatti vā musāvādo nāma na hoti, viññattiyā saddena ca sahitā taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādoti. Cakkhuvasena aggahitārammaṇanti cakkhusannissitena viññāṇena aggahitamārammaṇaṃ. Ghānādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ indriyānaṃ sampattavisayaggāhakattā vuttaṃ “tīhi indriyehi ekābaddhaṃ viya katvā”ti. “Dhanunā vijjhatī”tiādīsu viya “cakkhunā diṭṭha”nti ayaṃ vohāro loke pākaṭoti āha “oḷārikeneva nayenā”ti.

3. They deceive by means of this; thus, it is 'deception'—a mind operating with the intention to deceive. Therefore, he said: 'For one who speaks having made the deceptive mind foremost.' One speaks by this, thus it is 'speech'; it is the volition that produces speech. Therefore, he said: 'Wrong speech... the volition.' 'Speech that has gone to division' means speech divided into many kinds. Thus, by this, he clarifies the following point: neither pure volition, nor pure sound, nor pure intimation is called false speech; rather, it is the volition that originates them, co-arisen with the intimation and the sound, that is false speech. 'An object not grasped by means of the eye' means an object not grasped by consciousness dependent on the eye. Because the three faculties of the nose and so on grasp objects that have come into their range, it was said: 'as if having made them bound together as one by the three faculties.' Just as in expressions like 'He shoots with a bow,' this worldly convention 'seen with the eye' is well-known; therefore, he said: 'only by the coarse method.'

11. Avīmaṃsitvāti anupaparikkhitvā. Anupadhāretvāti avinicchinitvā. Jaḷattāti aññāṇatāya. Dārusakaṭaṃ yojetvā gatoti dārusakaṭaṃ yojetvā tattha nisīditvā gatoti adhippāyo. Gato bhavissatīti tatheva sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā vuttattā musāvādo jāto. Keci pana “keḷiṃ kurumānoti vuttattā evaṃ vadanto dubbhāsitaṃ āpajjatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ[V 3.0003]. Jātiādīhiyeva hi dasahi akkosavatthūhi davakamyatāya vadantassa dubbhāsitaṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

11. 'Not having reflected' (avīmaṃsitvā) means not having investigated. 'Not having considered' (anupadhāretvā) means not having ascertained. 'Due to dullness' (jaḷattā) means due to ignorance. 'Having yoked a wooden cart, he went' means: having yoked a wooden cart, having sat in it, he went; this is the intended meaning. Because it was said after making the conclusion in that very way, 'He must have gone,' false speech arose. Some, however, say, 'Because it was said, "making a joke," one speaking thus incurs a wrong speech offense'; that should not be accepted. For a wrong speech offense is stated for one who speaks out of a desire to jest concerning the ten grounds for abuse, beginning with birth. For this has been said:

“Hīnukkaṭṭhehi ukkaṭṭhaṃ, hīnaṃ vā jātiādihi;

Ujuṃ vāññāpadesena, vade dubbhāsitaṃ davā”ti.

'If one, in jest, speaks of a superior person or an inferior person by means of inferior and superior classifications like birth, or speaks of an upright person by way of pretext, it is wrong speech.'

Cittena thokatarabhāvaṃyeva aggahetvā bahubhāvaṃyeva gahetvā vuttattā “gāmo ekatelo”tiādināpi musāvādo jāto. Cāresunti upanesuṃ. Visaṃvādanapurekkhāratā, visaṃvādanacittena yamatthaṃ vattukāmo, tassa puggalassa viññāpanapayogo cāti imānettha dve aṅgāni[M 3.0003]. Uttarimanussadhammārocanatthaṃ musā bhaṇantassa pārājikaṃ, amūlakena pārājikena anuddhaṃsanatthaṃ saṅghādiseso, saṅghādisesena anuddhaṃsanatthaṃ pācittiyaṃ, ācāravipattiyā dukkaṭaṃ, “yo te vihāre vasatī”tiādipariyāyena uttarimanussadhammārocanatthaṃ paṭivijānantassa musā bhaṇite thullaccayaṃ, appaṭivijānantassa dukkaṭaṃ, kevalaṃ musā bhaṇantassa idha pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Because it was said by the mind not grasping the lesser aspect but grasping only the greater aspect, false speech arose even by saying, 'The village has only one sesame seed,' and so on. 'They presented' (cāresuṃ) means they offered. Here, there are two factors: having deception as foremost, and the application of communication to that person, with a deceptive mind, regarding the matter one wishes to convey. For one who speaks falsely for the purpose of declaring a superhuman state, it is a pārājika offense. For the purpose of accusing another with a groundless pārājika offense, it is a saṅghādisesa. For the purpose of accusing another with a saṅghādisesa, it is a pācittiya. For a breach of conduct, it is a dukkaṭa. In the case of speaking falsely for the purpose of declaring a superhuman state by way of an insinuation such as, 'He who dwells in your monastery,' it is a thullaccaya offense if the other person understands, and a dukkaṭa if they do not. For one who merely speaks falsely, a pācittiya offense is stated here.

Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on false speech is finished.

2. Omasavādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Deprecatory Speech

12. Dutiye kaṇṇakaṭukatāya amanāpaṃ vadantā kaṇṇesu vijjhantā viya hontīti āha “omasantīti ovijjhantī”ti. Padhaṃsentīti abhibhavanti.

12. In the second training rule: because of being harsh to the ear, those who speak unpleasant words are as if piercing the ears; therefore, he said, 'They deprecate (omasanti) means they pierce (ovijjhanti).' 'They assail' (padhaṃsenti) means they overpower.

13. Bodhisatto tena samayena hotīti tena samayena bodhisatto nandivisālo nāma ahosīti attho. Atītatthe vattamānavacanaṃ, kiriyākālavacanicchāya vā vattamānappayogo saddantarasannidhānena bhūtatāvagamo siyāti. Paccesīti “amanāpaṃ ida”nti aññāsi. Heṭṭhārukkhe datvāti upatthambhake datvā. Pubbe patiṭṭhitārappadesaṃ puna are patteti pubbe ujukaṃ heṭṭhāmukhaṃ patiṭṭhitaarassa bhūmippadesaṃ puna tasmiṃyeva are parivattetvā heṭṭhāmukhabhāvena sampatte, paṭhamaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitanemippadese parivattetvā puna bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhiteti vuttaṃ hoti. Sithilakaraṇanti sithilakiriyā.

13. 'The Bodhisatta is at that time' means that at that time the Bodhisatta was named Nandivisāla. This is a present-tense expression used for a past meaning, or it is a present-tense usage due to the desire to speak of the time of the action, whereby the understanding of a past event may occur through the proximity of other words. 'He went back' (paccesi) means he knew, 'This is unpleasant.' 'Having placed supports underneath' (heṭṭhārukkhe datvā) means having given props. 'He brings the previously established part of the spoke back to the spoke' (pubbe patiṭṭhitārappadesaṃ puna are patteti) means: when the part of the spoke that was previously established straight and facing downwards towards the ground is turned again on that same spoke and arrives with its downward-facing part, it is said that the part of the rim first established on the ground, having been turned, is established on the ground again. 'The act of loosening' (sithilakaraṇa) means the action of loosening.

15. Pubbeti aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ. Tacchakakammanti vaḍḍhakīkammaṃ. Koṭṭakakammanti vā pāsāṇakoṭṭakakammaṃ[V 3.0004]. Hatthamuddāgaṇanāti aṅgulisaṅkoceneva gaṇanā. Pādasikamilakkhakādayo viya navantavasena gaṇanā acchiddakagaṇanā. Ādi-saddena saṅkalanapaṭuppādanavoklanabhāgahārādivasena pavattā piṇḍagaṇanā gahitā. Yassa sā paguṇā hoti, so rukkhampi disvā “ettakāni ettha paṇṇānī”ti jānāti. Yabha methuneti vacanato ya-kāra bha-kāre ekato yojite asaddhammavacanaṃ hoti.

15. 'Formerly' (pubbe) means in the origin story. 'The work of a plane-maker' (tacchakakamma) means carpentry. Or 'the work of a storehouse-builder' (koṭṭakakamma) means the work of a stone mason. 'Counting by hand-gestures' (hatthamuddāgaṇanā) is counting by the mere bending of the fingers. Like the Pādasikas, Milakkhas, and others, counting up to nine is 'unbroken counting.' By the word 'etc.' (ādi), aggregate calculation is included, which proceeds by way of addition, production, subtraction, division, and so on. One for whom this is fluent, on seeing even a tree, knows, 'There are this many leaves on it.' From the saying, 'Yabha is sexual intercourse,' when the letters 'ya' and 'bha' are joined together, it becomes unvirtuous speech.

16-26. Āpattiyā [M 3.0004] kāretabboti pācittiyena kāretabbo upasaggādimattavisiṭṭhānaṃ aticaṇḍālādipadānaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatesuyeva saṅgahitattā. Corosītiādīnaṃ pana kenaci pariyāyena pāḷiyaṃ anāgatattā dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Hasādhippāyatāti purimapadassa atthavivaraṇaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ avuttepi “jātiādīhi akkosavatthūhi parammukhā akkosantassa vatthūnaṃ anaññabhāvato yathā dukkaṭaṃ, tathā davakamyatāya parammukhā vadantassapi dubbhāsitamevā”ti ācariyā vadanti. Sabbasattāti ettha vacanatthavijānanapakatikā tiracchānagatāpi gahetabbā.

'He should be dealt with according to the offense' means he should be dealt with by a pācittiya offense, because terms such as 'extreme outcaste,' which are distinguished merely by prefixes and so on, are included only when they appear in the Pāḷi canon. However, for terms such as 'You are a thief,' because they do not appear in the Pāḷi canon in any way, a dukkaṭa offense is stated. 'Having the intention to jest' is an explanation of the meaning of the preceding term. Even if not stated in the Pāḷi canon, the teachers say: 'Just as for one who insults someone in their absence with the grounds for abuse such as birth, it is a dukkaṭa offense because the objects of abuse are not different, so too for one who speaks in another's absence with the desire to jest, it is indeed wrong speech.' Here, by 'all beings,' even animals who are by nature capable of understanding the meaning of what is said should be included.

35. Anusāsanipurekkhāratāya ṭhatvā vadantassa cittassa lahuparivattibhāvato antarā kope uppannepi anāpatti. Yaṃ akkosati, tassa upasampannatā, anaññāpadesena jātiādīhi akkosanaṃ, “maṃ akkosatī”ti jānanā, atthapurekkhāratādīnaṃ abhāvatāti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

35. If one speaks while standing with the intention of giving instruction, there is no offense even if anger should arise in the meantime, due to the quick-changing nature of the mind. The four factors for the offense are: (1) the one who is reviled is an ordained person; (2) the reviling is done with reference to birth and so on, without using an alias; (3) knowing, ‘He is reviling me’; and (4) the absence of having benefit as the foremost aim.

Omasavādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Deprecatory Speech is finished.

3. Pesuññasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Divisive Speech

36. Tatiye bhaṇḍanaṃ jātaṃ etesanti bhaṇḍanajātā. Sammantananti raho saṃsandanaṃ. Hatthaparāmāsādivasena matthakaṃ patto kalaho jāto etesanti kalahajātā. Anāpattigāmikaṃ viruddhavādabhūtaṃ vivādaṃ āpannāti vivādāpannā. Viggahasaṃvattanikā kathā viggāhikakathā. Pisatīti pisuṇā, vācā, samagge satte avayavabhūte vagge bhinne karotīti attho. Pisuṇā eva pesuññaṃ. Tāya vācāya vā samannāgato pisuṇo, tassa kammaṃ pesuññaṃ. Piyabhāvassa suññakaraṇavācanti iminā pana “piyasuññakaraṇato pisuṇā”ti niruttinayena atthaṃ vadati.

36. In the third, ‘bhaṇḍanajātā’ (those in whom quarreling has arisen) means ‘quarreling has arisen in them.’ ‘Sammantananti’ means secret consultation. ‘Kalahajātā’ (those in whom conflict has arisen) means ‘conflict has arisen in them, reaching its climax through physical contact and the like.’ ‘Vivādāpannā’ (those who have entered into disputes) means ‘they have entered into a dispute characterized by opposing viewpoints, which does not lead to an offense.’ ‘Viggahasaṃvattanikā kathā’ is contentious speech. ‘Pisuṇā’ (divisive speech) is so called because it grinds (pisati); the meaning is that it divides harmonious beings into separate factions. ‘Pesuñña’ is simply divisive speech. One endowed with that speech is a divisive person (pisuṇo); his action is divisive speech (pesuññaṃ). Furthermore, with the phrase ‘speech that makes affection empty,’ it states the meaning according to the etymological method: ‘pisuṇā because it makes affection empty (piyasuññakaraṇato).’

Idhāpi “dasahākārehi pesuññaṃ upasaṃharatī”ti vacanato dasavidhaakkosavatthuvaseneva pesuññaṃ upasaṃharantassa pācittiyaṃ. Pāḷimuttakānaṃ corotiādīnaṃ vasena pana dukkaṭamevāti veditabbaṃ[V 3.0005]. “Anakkosavatthubhūtaṃ [M 3.0005] pana pesuññakaraṃ tassa kiriyaṃ vacanaṃ vā piyakamyatāya upasaṃharantassa kiñcāpi iminā sikkhāpadena āpatti na dissati, tathāpi dukkaṭenettha bhavitabba”nti vadanti. Jātiādīhi anaññāpadesena akkosantassa bhikkhuno sutvā bhikkhussa upasaṃharaṇaṃ, piyakamyatābhedādhippāyesu aññataratā, tassa vijānanāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

Here too, in accordance with the statement, ‘One engages in divisive speech in ten ways,’ a pācittiya offense is incurred by one who engages in divisive speech based on the ten kinds of grounds for abuse. However, it should be understood that for grounds outside the Pāli text, such as calling someone a thief, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. Some say: ‘Moreover, for one who engages in divisive speech that is not a ground for abuse out of a desire to be liked, although no offense is apparent under this training rule, there should still be a dukkaṭa offense here.’ The three factors here are: reporting to a bhikkhu after having heard another bhikkhu revile him with reference to birth and so on without using an alias; having one of two intentions, either to endear oneself or to cause division; and being aware of it.

Pesuññasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Divisive Speech is finished.

4. Padasodhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Reciting Dhamma Word by Word

45. Catutthe ekatoti anupasampannena saddhiṃ. Purimabyañjanena sadisaṃ pacchābyañjananti “rūpaṃ anicca”nti ettha anicca-saddena sadisaṃ “vedanā aniccā”ti ettha anicca-saddaṃ vadati. Akkharasamūhoti avibhattiko akkharasamūho. Akkharānubyañjanasamūho padanti vibhattiantaṃ padamāha. Vibhattiantameva padaṃ gahetvā “paṭhamapadaṃ padameva, dutiyaṃ anupada”nti vuttaṃ.

45. In the fourth, ‘ekato’ means ‘together with one who is not fully ordained.’ ‘The latter consonant is similar to the former consonant’ refers to the word ‘anicca’ in ‘vedanā aniccā’ being similar to the word ‘anicca’ in ‘rūpaṃ aniccaṃ.’ ‘Akkharasamūho’ (a collection of syllables) means an uninflected collection of syllables. ‘Akkharānubyañjanasamūho’ (a collection of syllables and consonants) is called a ‘pada’ (word); it refers to a word ending with an inflection. Taking only the inflected word as a ‘pada,’ it is said: ‘The first word is a pada, the second is an anupada.’

Ekaṃ padanti gāthāpadaṃ sandhāya vadati. Padagaṇanāyāti gāthāpadagaṇanāya. Apāpuṇitvāti saddhiṃ akathetvā. Runti opātetīti ettha anunāsiko āgamavasena vutto, saṃyogapubbassa rassattaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “rū-kāramattamevā”ti. Ettha ca “rūpaṃ aniccanti bhaṇa sāmaṇerā”ti vuccamāno sace rū-kāraṃ avatvā ru-iti rassaṃ katvā vadati, aññaṃ bhaṇitaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā anāpatti. Evañca katvā “vedanā aniccā”ti etthāpi anicca-saddamatteneva āpatti hotīti veditabbaṃ. Esa nayoti ekamevakkharaṃ vatvā ṭhānaṃ. “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti vuccamāno hi ma-kāramattameva vatvā tiṭṭhati. “Evaṃ me suta”ntiādisuttaṃ bhaṇāpiyamāno e-kāraṃ vatvā tiṭṭhati ce, anvakkharena pācittiyaṃ, aparipuṇṇapadaṃ vatvā ṭhite anubyañjanena. Padesu ekaṃ paṭhamapadaṃ virajjhati, dutiyena anupadena pācittiyaṃ.

‘Ekaṃ padaṃ’ (one word) refers to a line of a verse. ‘Padagaṇanāya’ (by counting words) means by counting the lines of a verse. ‘Apāpuṇitvā’ (without reaching) means without speaking together. In ‘runti opātetīti’ (he drops it), the nasal sound is said to be an augment; it should be understood that the vowel preceding the conjunct has been shortened. Therefore, it is said, ‘only the syllable “rū”.’ And here, if, when told, ‘Say, “Form is impermanent,” novice,’ one says ‘ru-’ having shortened it, without uttering the syllable ‘rū’, it is considered to be saying something else; therefore, there is no offense. And so, it should be understood that even in ‘vedanā aniccā,’ an offense occurs merely by the word ‘anicca.’ This is the method: stopping after speaking a single syllable. For instance, if, when told, ‘Mind precedes all phenomena,’ one stops after saying only the syllable ‘ma.’ If, while being instructed to recite a sutta such as ‘Thus have I heard,’ one stops after saying the syllable ‘e,’ there is a pācittiya offense for each syllable. If one stops after speaking an incomplete word, there is an offense by the following syllable. In the case of words, if one fails on the first word, a pācittiya offense is incurred by the second, the following word.

Anaṅgaṇasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.57 ādayo) sammādiṭṭhisuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.89 ādayo) mahāvedallañca (ma. ni. 1.449 ādayo) dhammasenāpatinā bhāsitaṃ, anumānasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.181 ādayo) mahāmoggallānattherena, cūḷavedallasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.460 ādayo) dhammadinnāya [M 3.0006] theriyā bhāsitaṃ. Paccekabuddhabhāsitampi buddhabhāsiteyeva saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Aṭṭhakathānissitoti [V 3.0006] pubbe magadhabhāsāya vuttaṃ dhammasaṅgahāruḷhaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ sandhāya vadati. Idānipi “yathāpi dīpiko nāma, nilīyitvā gaṇhate mige”ti (mi. pa. 6.1.5) evamādikaṃ saṅgahāruḷhaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ gahetabbanti vadanti. Pāḷinissitoti “makkaṭī vajjiputtā cā”tievamādinā (pārā. 66) pāḷiyaṃyeva āgato. Vivaṭṭūpanissitanti nibbānupanissitaṃ. Vivaṭṭanissitaṃ pana sāmaññato gahetabbanti āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Therassāti nāgasenattherassa. Maggakathādīni pakaraṇāni. “Akkharena vāceti, akkharakkhare āpatti pācittiyassā”ti vattabbe “akkharāya vāceti, akkharakkharāya āpatti pācittiyassā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

The Anaṅgaṇasutta, the Sammādiṭṭhisutta, and the Mahāvedallasutta were spoken by the General of the Dhamma. The Anumānasutta was spoken by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. The Cūḷavedallasutta was spoken by the Elderess Dhammadinnā. Even what is spoken by Paccekabuddhas is included in what is spoken by the Buddha. ‘Aṭṭhakathānissita’ (dependent on the commentary) refers to the commentary previously spoken in the Magadhan language and included in the Dhamma collection. Even now, they say that commentary passages included in the collection, such as ‘Just as a panther, having hidden, captures the deer,’ should be taken. ‘Pāḷinissita’ (dependent on the Pāli) refers to what appears in the Pāli itself, such as ‘The female monkey and the Vajjiputta.’ ‘Vivaṭṭūpanissita’ (dependent on the unfolding) means dependent on Nibbāna. But what is dependent on the unfolding should be taken in a general sense, as stated in the passage beginning ‘kiñcāpi.’ ‘Therassa’ (of the Elder) refers to the Elder Nāgasena. The treatises on the path and so on are such works. Where it should be said, ‘He teaches by the letter; for each letter, there is a pācittiya offense,’ in the Pāli it is stated, ‘He teaches by the letter; for each letter, there is a pācittiya offense,’ using the dative case for parallelism.

48. Anupasampannena saddhiṃ gaṇhantassa anāpattīti anupasampannena saha nisīditvā uddesaṃ gaṇhantassa anāpatti vuttā. Daharabhikkhu nisinno…pe… bhaṇato anāpattīti ettha dvīsupi ṭhitesu nisinnesu vā upasampannassa bhaṇāmīti bhaṇantassa anāpattiyeva. Upacāraṃ muñcitvāti parisapariyantato dvādasahatthaṃ muñcitvā. “Nisinne vācemī”ti bhaṇantassapi upacāraṃ muñcitvā nisinnattā anāpatti. Sace pana dūre nisinnampi vācemīti visuṃ sallakkhetvā bhaṇati, āpattiyeva. Eko pādo na āgacchatīti pubbe paguṇoyeva pacchā asarantassa na āgacchati, taṃ “evaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti ekato bhaṇantassa anāpatti. Opātetīti saddhiṃ katheti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Anupasampannatā, vuttalakkhaṇadhammaṃ padaso vācanatā, ekato bhaṇanañcāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

48. ‘There is no offense for one who learns together with one not fully ordained’—this refers to the stated non-offense for one who, sitting together with one not fully ordained, learns a passage. In the case of ‘a young monk sitting… while speaking, there is no offense’—here, whether both are standing or both are sitting, for one who speaks thinking, ‘I am speaking to the ordained one,’ there is indeed no offense. ‘Releasing proximity’ means releasing a space of twelve cubits from the boundary of the assembly. For one who says, ‘I will teach while seated,’ there is no offense because of being seated having released the proximity. However, if one deliberately speaks, having specifically noted even one seated at a distance and thinking, ‘I will teach,’ there is indeed an offense. ‘One line of verse does not come’ means that what was previously fluent does not come to one who does not remember it later. For one who recites it together, saying, ‘Recite it like this,’ there is no offense. ‘Opātetī’ means to speak together. The rest here is self-evident. The state of one being unordained; the act of reciting word-by-word the Dhamma with the aforementioned characteristics; and reciting together—these are the three factors here.

Padasodhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Reciting Dhamma Word by Word is finished.

5. Sahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Sleeping in the Same Lodging

49-50. Pañcame vikūjamānāti nitthunantā. Kākacchamānāti rodantā. Tatridaṃ vatthunidassanaṃ vā. Tena nu kho pātitanti pucchāvasena kathitattā natthi musāvādo. Keci pana “sandehavasena vacanaṃ musā nāma [M 3.0007] na hoti, tasmā evaṃ vutta”nti vadanti. Santikaṃ agantvāti “yaṃ etesaṃ na kappati, taṃ tesampi na kappatī”ti adhippāyena agantvā.

In the fifth, ‘vikūjamānā’ means wailing. ‘Kākacchamānā’ means lamenting. Here, this is an illustration of the case. Since ‘Tena nu kho pātitanti’ is stated in the manner of a question, there is no false speech. Some, however, say, ‘A statement made out of doubt is not called false speech; therefore, it is stated thus.’ ‘Santikaṃ agantvā’ means not going to their presence, with the intention that ‘what is unsuitable for them is also unsuitable for these others.’

51. Dirattatirattanti ettha vacanasiliṭṭhatāmattena diratta-ggahaṇaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Tirattañhi sahavāse labbhamāne diratte vattabbameva natthīti dirattaggahaṇaṃ visuṃ na yojeti. Tenevāha [V 3.0007] “uttaridirattatirattanti bhagavā sāmaṇerānaṃ saṅgahakaraṇatthāya tirattaparihāraṃ adāsī”ti. Nirantaraṃ tirattadassanatthaṃ vā dirattaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Kevalañhi tirattanti vutte aññattha vāsena antarikampi tirattaṃ gaṇheyya, dirattavisiṭṭhaṃ pana tirattaṃ vuccamānaṃ tena anantarikameva tirattaṃ dīpeti. Sayanaṃ seyyā, sayanti etthātipi seyyāti āha “kāyappasāraṇasaṅkhāta”ntiādi. Tasmāti yasmā ubhayampi pariggahitaṃ, tasmā. Pañcahi chadanehīti iṭṭhakasilāsudhātiṇapaṇṇasaṅkhaātehi pañcahi chadanehi. Vācuggatavasenāti paguṇavasena. Diyaḍḍhahatthubbedho vaḍḍhakīhatthena gahetabbo. Ekūpacāroti vaḷañjanadvārassa ekattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Satagabbhaṃ vā catussālaṃ ekūpacāraṃ hotīti sambandho.

51. Regarding 'For two or three nights' (Dirattatirattaṃ): here, it should be understood that the inclusion of 'two nights' (diratta) is made merely for the elegance of the phrasing. For when co-residence for three nights is obtainable, there is nothing to be said about two nights; thus, the inclusion of 'two nights' is not applied separately. It is for this reason that he said, 'Further, for two or three nights... the Blessed One, for the sake of accommodating the novices, granted the allowance of three nights.' Alternatively, the inclusion of 'two nights' is made to show three consecutive nights. For if it were merely said 'for three nights,' one might take it as three nights even with an intervening stay elsewhere; but when 'three nights' is specified by 'two nights,' it indicates three nights that are indeed consecutive. Lying down (sayanaṃ) is a lodging (seyyā); and because 'they lie down' (sayanti) in it (ettha), it is also a lodging (seyyā). Thus he said, 'designated as the stretching out of the body,' and so on. Regarding 'Therefore' (tasmā): because (yasmā) both are included, therefore (tasmā). By 'with five kinds of roofing': with the five kinds of roofing designated as bricks, stone, plaster, grass, and leaves. By 'by way of being learned by heart' (vācuggatavasena): by way of being proficient. 'One and a half cubits in height' should be taken according to the carpenter's cubit. 'Having a single approach' (ekūpacāroti) is said with reference to the singleness of the door for use. The connection is: 'A four-gabled building with a hundred cells has a single approach'.

Uparimatalena saddhiṃ asambaddhabhittikassāti idaṃ tulāya abbhantare sayitvā puna teneva susirena nikkhamitvā bhittiantarena heṭṭhimatalaṃ pavisituṃ yoggepi uparimatalena asambaddhabhittike senāsane anāpattiyā vuttāya tathā pavisituṃ asakkuṇeyye sambaddhabhittike vattabbameva natthīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana sambaddhabhittike āpattīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhāpāsāde sayitabhikkhussa anāpattīti idampi tādise senāsane heṭṭhimatale sayitasseva āpattippasaṅkā siyāti taṃnivāraṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana uparimatale sayitassa āpattīti dassanatthaṃ. Nānūpacāreti yattha bahi nisseṇiṃ katvā uparimatalaṃ ārohanti, tādisaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Uparimatalepi ākāsaṅgaṇe nipajjantassa āpattiyā abhāvato “chadanabbhantare”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'of one with walls not connected with the upper floor': this is said to show that, since no offense is stated for a dwelling with walls not connected to the upper floor—even when it is possible to lie inside a loft, exit through the same opening, and enter the lower floor through the space within the wall—there is no need to speak of a dwelling with connected walls where it is not possible to enter in such a way. It is not said, however, to show that there is an offense in the case of connected walls. The statement 'There is no offense for a monk sleeping in the lower part of a storied building' is also said to prevent the contingency of an offense for one sleeping on the lower floor in such a dwelling; it is not said to show that there is an offense for one sleeping on the upper floor. 'Having different approaches' refers to a dwelling where they ascend to the upper floor by having built a staircase outside; it is said with reference to such a case. Because there is no offense for one lying down in the open-air terrace even on the upper floor, the phrase 'within the roofed area' is stated.

Sabhāsaṅkhepenāti sabhākārena. Aḍḍhakuṭṭake senāsaneti ettha “aḍḍhakuṭṭakaṃ nāma yattha ekaṃ passaṃ muñcitvā tīsu passesu bhittiyo baddhā [M 3.0008] honti, yattha vā ekasmiṃ passe bhittiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā ubhosu passesu upaḍḍhaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ katvā bhittiyo uṭṭhāpenti, tādisaṃ senāsana”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Gaṇṭhipade pana “aḍḍhakuṭṭaketi chadanaṃ aḍḍhena asampattakuṭṭake”ti vuttaṃ, tampi no na yuttaṃ. “Vāḷasaṅghāṭo nāma thambhānaṃ upari vāḷarūpehi katasaṅghāṭo vuccatī”ti vadanti. Parikkhepassa bahigateti ettha yasmiṃ passe parikkhepo natthi, tatthāpi parikkhepārahappadesato bahigate anāpattiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aparicchinnagabbhūpacāreti ettha majjhe vivaṭaṅgaṇavantāsu pamukhamahācatussālāsu yathā ākāsaṅgaṇaṃ anotaritvā pamukheneva gantvā sabbagabbhe pavisituṃ na sakkā hoti, evaṃ ekekagabbhassa dvīsu passesu kuṭṭaṃ nīharitvā kataṃ paricchinnagabbhūpacāraṃ nāma, idaṃ pana tādisaṃ na hotīti “aparicchinnagabbhūpacāre”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbagabbhe pavisantīti gabbhūpacārassa aparicchinnattā ākāsaṅgaṇaṃ anotaritvā pamukheneva gantvā taṃ taṃ gabbhaṃ pavisanti. Atha kuto tassa parikkhepoyeva sabbaparicchannattāti [V 3.0008] vuttanti āha “gabbhaparikkhepoyeva hissa parikkhepo”ti. Idañca samantā gabbhabhittiyo sandhāya vuttaṃ. Catussālavasena sanniviṭṭhepi senāsane gabbhapamukhaṃ visuṃ aparikkhittampi samantā ṭhitagabbhabhittīnaṃ vasena parikkhittaṃ nāma hoti.

By 'in the summary form of an assembly hall': in the manner of an assembly hall. Regarding 'in a dwelling with half-walls' (aḍḍhakuṭṭake senāsane): here, it is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipada texts: 'An aḍḍhakuṭṭaka is a dwelling where, leaving one side open, walls are constructed on three sides; or where, having erected a wall on one side, they erect walls on both sides having made them half and half. Such is a dwelling called aḍḍhakuṭṭaka.' In a Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: 'Aḍḍhakuṭṭaka is where the roof does not reach the wall by half.' That too is not unsuitable. They say: 'A vāḷasaṅghāṭa is the name for a structure made with figures of beasts on top of the pillars.' Regarding 'gone outside of the enclosure': here, it should be seen that even on a side where there is no enclosure, if one has gone outside the area that is fit for an enclosure, there is no offense. Regarding 'in one with an unrestricted approach to the cells': here, in large four-gabled halls with an open courtyard in the middle, just as it is not possible to go by the main entrance and enter all the cells without descending into the open courtyard, so too a structure made by extending a wall on two sides of each cell is called 'one with a restricted approach to the cells.' But this one is not like that, therefore it is called 'one with an unrestricted approach to the cells.' 'They enter all the cells': because the approach to the cells is unrestricted, they go by the main entrance without descending into the open courtyard and enter this or that cell. Then how does it have an enclosure? He said: 'The enclosure of the cells themselves is its enclosure.' And this is said with reference to the cell walls on all sides. Even in a dwelling arranged as a four-gabled hall, the entrance to the cells, though not separately enclosed, is called 'enclosed' by means of the cell walls standing on all sides.

“Nanu ca ‘aparikkhitte pamukhe anāpattī’ti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ avisesena vuttaṃ, tasmā catussālavasena sanniviṭṭhepi senāsane visuṃ aparikkhitte pamukhe anāpattiyevā”ti yo vadeyya, tassa vādaparimocanatthaṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ “yaṃ pana…pe… pāṭekkasannivesā ekacchadanā gabbhapāḷiyo sandhāya vutta”nti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “aparikkhitte pamukhe anāpattīti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ na catussālavasena sanniviṭṭhā gabbhapāḷiyo sandhāya vuttaṃ, kiñcarahi visuṃ sanniviṭṭhaṃ ekameva gabbhapāḷiṃ sandhāya. Tādisāya hi gabbhapāḷiyā aparikkhitte pamukhe anāpatti, na catussālavasena sanniviṭṭhāyā”ti. Ekāya ca gabbhapāḷiyā tassa tassa gabbhassa upacāraṃ paricchinditvā antamaso ubhosu passesu khuddakabhittīnaṃ uṭṭhāpanamattenapi pamukhaṃ parikkhittaṃ nāma hoti, catussālavasena sanniviṭṭhāsu pana gabbhapāḷīsu ubhosu passesu gabbhabhittīnaṃ vasenapi pamukhaṃ parikkhittaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmā [M 3.0009] yaṃ iminā lakkhaṇena parikkhittaṃ pamukhaṃ, tattha āpatti, itarattha anāpattīti idamettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ.

Should someone say: 'But is it not said in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā without distinction, "In an unenclosed entrance hall, there is no offense"? Therefore, even in a dwelling arranged as a four-gabled hall, if the entrance hall is separately unenclosed, there is indeed no offense.'—to release him from that view, this was said: 'But that which... was said with reference to rows of cells that are single-roofed and individually arranged.' This is what is meant: The statement, 'In an unenclosed entrance hall, there is no offense,' was not said with reference to rows of cells arranged as a four-gabled hall. Rather, what was it said with reference to? A single row of cells, arranged separately. For in such a row of cells, there is no offense in an unenclosed entrance hall; but not so for one arranged as a four-gabled hall. And for a single row of cells, having defined the approach for each cell, the entrance hall is called 'enclosed' even by the mere erection of small walls on both sides. But in rows of cells arranged as a four-gabled hall, the entrance hall is called 'enclosed' by means of the cell walls on both sides. Therefore, whichever entrance hall is enclosed according to this characteristic, in that case there is an offense; in the other case, there is no offense. This is the conclusion here.

Idāni “aparikkhitte pamukhe anāpattī”ti vatvā tasseva vacanassa adhippāyaṃ pakāsentena yaṃ vuttaṃ “bhūmiyaṃ vinā jagatiyā pamukhaṃ sandhāya kathita”nti, tassa ayuttatāvibhāvanatthaṃ “yañca tatthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Bhūmiyaṃ vinā jagatiyā pamukhaṃ sandhāya kathitanti hi imassa vacanassa ayamadhippāyo – “aparikkhitte pamukhe anāpattī”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ vinā vatthuṃ bhūmiyaṃ katagehassa pamukhaṃ sandhāya kathitaṃ. Sace pana uccavatthukaṃ pamukhaṃ hoti, parikkhittasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchatīti. Tenevāha “dasahatthubbedhāpi hi jagati parikkhepasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchatī”ti. Heṭṭhāpi idameva manasi sannidhāya vuttaṃ “uccavatthukaṃ cepi hoti, pamukhe sayito gabbhe sayitānaṃ āpattiṃ na karotī”ti. Tatthāti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Jagatiyā pamāṇaṃ vatvāti “sace jagatiyā otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ sayito, jagatiyā upari sayitaṃ na passatī”ti evaṃ jagatiyā ubbedhena pamāṇaṃ vatvā. Ekasālādīsu ujukameva dīghaṃ katvā sannivesito pāsādo ekasālasanniveso. Dvisālasannivesādayopi vuttānusārato veditabbā. Sālappabhedadīpanameva cettha heṭṭhā vuttato viseso.

Now, having said, 'In an unenclosed entrance hall, there is no offense,' the passage beginning 'And what there...' was undertaken to demonstrate the unsuitability of what was said by one clarifying the meaning of that very statement, namely: 'It was spoken with reference to an entrance hall on a terrace, without being on the ground.' For the meaning of this statement is as follows: what was said as 'In an unenclosed entrance hall, there is no offense' was spoken with reference to the entrance hall of a house built on the ground without a foundation. But if the entrance hall has a high foundation, it does not count as an enclosure. For this reason he said: 'For even a terrace ten cubits high does not count as an enclosure.' Below, too, this very point was stated, keeping it in mind: 'And even if it has a high foundation, one sleeping in the entrance hall does not cause an offense for those sleeping in the inner chamber.' 'There' means in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā. 'Having stated the measure of the terrace' means: having stated the measure by way of the terrace's height, thus: 'If, having descended from the terrace, one sleeps on the ground, one does not see a person sleeping on top of the terrace.' Among single-hall buildings and so on, a storied building arranged by being made long and straight is a single-hall arrangement. Double-hall arrangements and so on should also be understood according to what has been said. The only difference here from what was said below is the explanation of the different types of halls.

Majjhepākāraṃ karontīti etthāpi parikkhepassa heṭṭhimaparicchedena diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhattā diyaḍḍhahatthaṃ cepi [V 3.0009] majjhe pākāraṃ karonti, nānūpacārameva hotīti veditabbaṃ. Na hi chiddena gehaṃ ekūpacāraṃ nāma hotīti ettha sace ubbedhena diyaḍḍhahatthabbhantare manussānaṃ sañcārappahonakaṃ chiddaṃ hoti, tampi dvāramevāti ekūpacāraṃ hoti. Kiṃ parikkhepoviddhastoti pamukhassa parikkhepaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sabbattha pañcannaṃyeva chadanānaṃ āgatattā vadati “pañcannaṃ aññatarena chadanena channā”ti.

Regarding 'they build a wall in the middle,' here too, because the lower boundary of the enclosure is one and a half cubits in height, even if they build a wall one and a half cubits high in the middle, it should be understood that it does not have a single approach-area. For a house with a gap is not called a single approach-area. Here, if within a height of one and a half cubits there is a gap sufficient for the passage of people, that too is a door, thus it has a single approach-area. The question 'Is the enclosure breached?' refers to the enclosure of the entrance-hall. Since it is stated everywhere for the five kinds of roofing, he says, 'covered by any one of the five kinds of roofing.'

53. Pāḷiyaṃ “seyyā nāma sabbacchannā sabbaparicchannā yebhuyyenacchannā yebhuyyenaparicchannā”ti vadantena yebhuyyenacchannayebhuyyenaparicchannasenāsanaṃ pācittiyassa avasānaṃ viya katvā dassitaṃ, “upaḍḍhacchanne upaḍḍhaparicchanne āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vadantena ca upaḍḍhacchannaupaḍḍhaparicchannasenāsanaṃ dukkaṭassa ādiṃ katvā dassitaṃ, ubhinnamantarā kena bhavitabbaṃ [M 3.0010] pācittiyena, udāhu dukkaṭenāti? Lokavajjasikkhāpadasseva anavasesaṃ katvā paññāpanato imassa ca paṇṇattivajjattā yebhuyyenacchannayebhuyyenaparicchannassa upaḍḍhacchannaupaḍḍhaparicchannassa ca antarā pācittiyaṃ anivāritameva, tasmā vinayavinicchaye ca garukeyeva ṭhātabbattā aṭṭhakathāyampi pācittiyameva dassitaṃ. Satta pācittiyānīti pāḷiyaṃ vuttapācittiyaṃ sāmaññato ekattena gahetvā vuttaṃ. Visuṃ pana gayhamāne “sabbacchanne sabbaparicchanne pācittiyaṃ, yebhuyyenacchanne yebhuyyenaparicchanne pācittiya”nti aṭṭheva pācittiyāni honti.

53. In the Pāli, when it is said, 'A lodging is called fully covered, fully enclosed, mostly covered, mostly enclosed,' a mostly covered and mostly enclosed lodging is presented as if it were the final case for a pācittiya offense. And when it is said, 'In a half-covered, half-enclosed lodging, there is a dukkaṭa offense,' a half-covered and half-enclosed lodging is presented as the initial case for a dukkaṭa offense. Between these two, what should it be, a pācittiya or a dukkaṭa? Since this training rule concerning a worldly fault is laid down exhaustively, and because this is an offense by designation, a pācittiya offense between a mostly covered and mostly enclosed lodging and a half-covered and half-enclosed one is certainly not precluded. Therefore, in a Vinaya decision, because one should stand on the weighty side, in the commentary as well, only a pācittiya offense is shown. The phrase 'seven pācittiyas' is stated by taking the pācittiya mentioned in the Pāli generally as one. But when taken separately, 'in a fully covered, fully enclosed lodging, a pācittiya; in a mostly covered, mostly enclosed lodging, a pācittiya,' there are indeed eight pācittiyas.

Senambamaṇḍapavaṇṇaṃ hotīti sīhaḷadīpe kira uccavatthuko sabbacchanno sabbaaparicchanno evaṃnāmako sannipātamaṇḍapo atthi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yadi jagatiparikkhepasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, uccavatthukattā maṇḍapassa sabbaaparicchannatā na yujjatīti āha “imināpetaṃ veditabba”ntiādi. Cūḷakacchannādīni cettha evaṃ veditabbāni – yassa catūsu bhāgesu eko channo, sesā acchannā, idaṃ cūḷakacchannaṃ. Yassa tīsu bhāgesu dve channā, eko acchanno, idaṃ yebhuyyenacchannaṃ. Yassa dvīsu bhāgesu eko channo, eko acchanno, idaṃ upaḍḍhacchannaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ. Cūḷakaparicchannādīnipi imināva nayena veditabbāni. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Pācittiyavatthukasenāsanaṃ, tattha tattha anupasampannena saha nipajjanaṃ, catutthadivase sūriyatthaṅgamananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

Regarding 'it has the description of a Senamba pavilion': in the island of Sīhaḷa, it is said, there is an assembly pavilion of that name which is on a high base, fully covered, and completely unenclosed; this is stated in reference to that. If the terrace is counted as an enclosure, then due to its high base, the pavilion's being completely unenclosed is not suitable. He says, 'by this, it should be understood,' etc. Here, 'partially covered' and so on should be understood as follows: that of which one of four parts is covered and the rest are uncovered, this is 'partially covered.' That of which two of three parts are covered and one is uncovered, this is 'mostly covered.' That of which one of two parts is covered and one is uncovered, this lodging is called 'half-covered.' 'Partially enclosed' and so on should also be understood in this same way. The rest is clear. A lodging that is the basis for a pācittiya offense, lying down there with one who is not fully ordained, and the setting of the sun on the fourth day—these are the three factors here.

Sahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on sharing a lodging is concluded.

6. Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The explanation of the second training rule on sharing a lodging

55. Chaṭṭhe “paṭhamasikkhāpade ‘bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā avaseso anupasampanno nāmā’ti vuttattā [V 3.0010] ‘mātugāmopi anupasampannaggahaṇena gahitoyevā’ti catutthadivase mātugāmena saddhiṃ sayantassa dvīhi sikkhāpadehi dve pācittiyāni hontī”ti vadanti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana tīsupi “imasmiṃ sikkhāpade mātugāmassa visuṃ vuccamānattā paṭhamasikkhāpade ‘bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā avaseso anupasampanno nāmā’ti purisasseva gahaṇaṃ anucchavika”nti vuttaṃ, tadeva ca yuttataraṃ.

55. In the sixth, some say: 'Because it is stated in the first training rule, “Except for a bhikkhu, the rest are called unordained,” a woman is also included by the term ‘unordained’; therefore, for one sleeping with a woman on the fourth day, two pācittiya offenses arise from two training rules.' In the three Gaṇṭhipadas, however, it is said: 'In this training rule, since a woman is mentioned separately, the statement in the first training rule, “Except for a bhikkhu, the rest are called unordained,” should suitably be taken as referring only to a man.' And that is indeed more appropriate.

Yañca [M 3.0011] idha “paṭhamadivasepīti pi-saddena catutthadivasepīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti kāraṇaṃ vadanti, tampi akāraṇaṃ pi-saddo sampiṇḍanatthoyevāti niyamābhāvato avadhāraṇatthassa ca sambhavato. Sambhāvane vā pi-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Tena idha paṭhamadivasepi tāva āpatti, dutiyādidivase kimeva vattabbanti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Sampiṇḍanatthepi pi-sadde gayhamāne imināva sikkhāpadena āpajjitabbāpattiyā aññasmimpi divase āpajjanaṃ dīpeti, na paṭhamasikkhāpadena āpajjitabbāpattiyāti akāraṇameva tanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Matitthī pārājikavatthubhūtāpi anupādinnapakkhe ṭhitattā sahaseyyāpattiṃ na janetī”ti vadanti. “Atthaṅgate sūriye mātugāme nipanne bhikkhu nipajjatī”ti vacanato divā sayantassa sahaseyyāpatti na hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pācittiyavatthukasenāsanaṃ, tattha mātugāmena saha nipajjanaṃ, sūriyatthaṅgamananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

And the reason stated here, that 'by the word 'pi' in 'on the first day too,' it means 'on the fourth day too,'' is also no reason, for there is no rule that the word 'pi' is only for the purpose of inclusion, and because the meaning of emphasis is also possible. Or, the word 'pi' should be seen in the sense of possibility. By that, it indicates this meaning: here, there is an offense on the first day at least; what then needs to be said about the second and following days? Even when the word 'pi' is taken in the sense of inclusion, it indicates the incurring of an offense on another day by this very training rule, not an offense to be incurred by the first training rule. Thus, that reasoning should be seen as unfounded. They say: 'A dead woman, though she is the basis for a pārājika offense, does not give rise to the offense of sharing a lodging, because she is in the category of the unappropriated.' From the statement, 'When the sun has set, if a woman is lying down, a bhikkhu lies down,' it should be understood that for one who lies down during the day, the offense of sharing a lodging does not occur at all. A lodging that is the basis for a pācittiya offense, lying down there with a woman, and the setting of the sun—these are the three factors here.

Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule on sharing a lodging is concluded.

7. Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The explanation of the training rule on teaching the Dhamma

60-64. Sattame gharaṃ nayatīti gharaṇī, gharanāyikā. Tenāha “gharasāminī”ti. Suṇhāti suṇisā. Na yakkhenātiādīnaṃ “aññatrā”ti iminā sambandho. Purisaviggahaṃ gahetvā ṭhitena yakkhena vā petena vā tiracchānena vā saddhiṃ ṭhitāyapi desetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Akkharāya desetīti ettha “chappañcavācato uttari ‘imaṃ padaṃ bhāsissāmī’ti ekampi akkharaṃ vatvā tiṭṭhati, āpattiyevā”ti vadanti.

In the seventh: 'She who leads the household' (gharaṃ nayati) is a 'housewife' (gharaṇī), a 'mistress of the house' (gharanāyikā). Therefore he said 'lady of the house' (gharasāminī). 'Suṇisā' (daughter-in-law) comes from 'suṇāti' (she listens). The phrase 'by a yakkha,' etc., is not to be connected with this word 'except.' It is not permissible to teach even if she is standing with a yakkha, a peta, or an animal that has assumed a male form. Regarding 'teaching syllable by syllable,' here they say: 'If, after more than five or six words, one stops after uttering even a single syllable with the thought, “I will say this phrase,” it is an offense.'

66. “Eko gāthāpādoti idaṃ gāthābandhameva sandhāya vuttaṃ, aññattha pana vibhattiantapadameva gahetabba”nti vadanti. “Aṭṭhakathaṃ dhammapadaṃ jātakādivatthuṃ vāti imināpi porāṇaṃ saṅgītiāruḷhameva aṭṭhakathādi vutta”nti vadanti. Aṭṭhakathādipāṭhaṃ ṭhapetvā damiḷādibhāsantarena [V 3.0011] yathāruci kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Padasodhamme vuttappabhedoti iminā aññattha anāpattīti dīpeti. Uṭṭhahitvā puna nisīditvāti iriyāpathaparivattananayena nānāiriyāpathenapi [M 3.0012] anāpattīti dīpeti. Sabbaṃ cepi dīghanikāyaṃ kathetīti yāva na niṭṭhāti, tāva punadivasepi katheti.

66. They say: 'The phrase “one verse-foot” is stated with reference to the verse-structure itself, but elsewhere it should be taken as referring only to a word ending in an inflection.' They say: 'By “commentary, Dhammapada, Jātaka stories, etc.,” it is meant that only the ancient commentaries and so forth that have been included in the recitations are referred to.' Apart from the text of the commentary and so forth, it is permissible to speak in Damiḷa or other languages as one pleases. By 'the distinctions stated in the word-by-word analysis of the Dhamma,' it is indicated that there is no offense elsewhere. By 'rising up and sitting down again,' it is indicated that there is no offense even with various postures, by way of changing one's deportment. Even if one recites the entire Dīghanikāya, as long as it is not finished, one may continue reciting it on the following day.

Dutiyassa viññūpurisassa aggahaṇaṃ akiriyā. Mātugāmena saddhiṃ ṭhitassa ca viññūpurisassa ca upacāro aniyatesu vuttanayeneva gahetabbo. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Vuttalakkhaṇassa dhammassa channaṃ vācānaṃ upari desanā, vuttalakkhaṇo mātugāmo, iriyāpathapaavattanābhāvo, viññūpurisābhāvo, apañhavissajjanāti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

The non-inclusion of a second wise person is not a relevant action. The procedure concerning a woman standing with a wise person should be understood in the same way as stated in the Aniyata (undetermined) cases. The rest is clear. Teaching the Dhamma with the stated characteristics for more than six utterances; a woman with the stated characteristics; the absence of a change of deportment; the absence of a wise person; and not answering a question—these are the five factors here.

Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on teaching the Dhamma is concluded.

8. Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The explanation of the training rule on declaring a true attainment

77. Aṭṭhame antarāti parinibbānasamayato aññasmiṃ kāle. Atikaḍḍhiyamānenāti “vadatha, bhante, kiṃ tumhehi adhigata”nti evaṃ nippīḷiyamānena. Anatikaḍḍhiyamānenapi pucchite vā apucchite vā tathārūpe kāraṇe sati ārocetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Teneva aññatarena daharabhikkhunā upavadito aññataro thero “āvuso, uparimaggatthāya vāyāmaṃ mā akāsi, khīṇāsavo tayā upavadito”ti āha. Therena ca “atthi te, āvuso, imasmiṃ sāsane patiṭṭhā”ti vutto daharabhikkhu “āma, bhante, sotāpanno aha”nti avoca. “Kārako aya”nti ñatvāpi paṭipattiyā amoghabhāvadassanena samuttejanāya sampahaṃsanāya ca ariyā attānaṃ pakāsentiyeva. Sutapariyattisīlaguṇanti sutaguṇaṃ pariyattiguṇaṃ sīlaguṇañca. Ummattakassa idha avacane kāraṇaṃ vadantena khittacittavedanaṭṭānampi avacane kāraṇaṃ vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iti-saddena vā ādiatthena khittacittavedanaṭṭe saṅgaṇhāti. Teneva vadati “cittakkhepassa vā abhāvā”ti. Diṭṭhisampannānanti maggaphaladiṭṭhiyā samannāgatānaṃ. Ariyānameva hi ummattakādibhāvo natthi. Jhānalābhino pana tasmiṃ sati jhānā parihāyanti, tasmā tesaṃ abhūtārocanapaccayā anāpatti vattabbā, na bhūtārocanapaccayā. Tenevāha “bhūtārocanapaccayā anāpatti na vattabbā”ti.

77. In the eighth: 'interval' means a time other than the time of final Parinibbāna. 'Being excessively pressed' means being urged thus: “Speak, venerable sir, what have you attained?” Even if not excessively pressed, whether asked or unasked, when there is a suitable reason, it is indeed proper to declare. For this reason, a certain elder, having been reproached by a certain young monk, said, “Friend, do not strive for the higher path; you have reproached one who is an Arahant.” And when the elder said, “Friend, do you have a footing in this dispensation?” the young monk replied, “Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer.” Even knowing, “This one is a practitioner,” the noble ones do indeed reveal themselves for the sake of showing the unfailing nature of the practice, for encouragement, and for gladdening. 'Qualities of learning, scripture, and virtue' means the quality of learning, the quality of scripture, and the quality of virtue. It should be understood that by stating the reason for not mentioning the insane here, the reason for not mentioning those with deranged minds or those afflicted by painful feeling has also been stated. Or, the word 'iti', in the sense of 'and so on', includes those with deranged minds and those afflicted by painful feeling. Therefore, he says, “or due to the absence of mental derangement.” 'Those accomplished in view' means those endowed with the vision of the path and fruition. For it is only for the noble ones that there is no state of insanity and so on. But those who have attained jhāna, when in that state, fall away from their jhāna. Therefore, for them, 'no offense' should be stated on account of declaring what is not true, but not on account of declaring what is true. Therefore, he said, “'No offense' should not be stated on account of declaring what is true.”

Pubbe avuttehīti catutthapārājike avuttehi. Idañca sikkhāpadaṃ paṇṇattiajānanavasena acittakasamuṭṭhānaṃ [V 3.0012] hoti. Ariyā cettha paṇṇattiṃ jānantā [M 3.0013] vītikkamaṃ na karonti, puthujjanā pana paṇṇattiṃ jānitvāpi vītikkamaṃ karonti, te ca satthuno āṇāvītikkamacetanāya balavaakusalabhāvato jhānā parihāyantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ, ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena ariyapuggale eva sandhāya “kusalābyākatacittehi dvicitta”nti vuttaṃ. Paṇṇattiṃ ajānantā pana jhānalābhī puthujjanā vatthumhi lobhavasena akusalacittenapi na ārocentīti natthi. Idha dukkhavedanāya abhāvato “dvivedana”nti imassa anurūpaṃ katvā dvicittanti idaṃ vuttanti evaṃ vā ettha adhippāyo gahetabbo. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Uttarimanussadhammassa bhūtatā, anupasampannassa ārocanaṃ, taṅkhaṇavijānanā, anaññappadesoti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

‘By those not mentioned before’ means by those not mentioned in the fourth Pārājika. And this training rule has an unintentional origin, by way of not knowing the regulation. Herein, noble ones, knowing the regulation, do not transgress; but ordinary people, even knowing the regulation, do transgress. And it should be understood that they fall away from jhāna due to the powerful unwholesome state of the intention to transgress the Teacher's command. It is said, “two mind-moments, with wholesome and indeterminate minds,” referring only to noble persons by way of the highest distinction. Moreover, it is not the case that ordinary people who have attained jhāna and do not know the regulation would refrain from declaring, even with an unwholesome mind, out of greed for the object. Or, the meaning here should be understood thus: here, due to the absence of painful feeling, this “two mind-moments” is stated, having made it correspond to “two feelings.” The rest is clear. The four factors here are: the reality of a superhuman state, declaring it to one not fully ordained, understanding it at that moment, and not indicating another person.

Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on declaring a true attainment is concluded.

9. Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Training Rule on Revealing Grave Offenses

78. Navame duṭṭhullasaddatthadassanatthanti duṭṭhullasaddassa atthadassanatthaṃ. Atthe hi dassite saddopi “ayaṃ etesu atthesu vattatī”ti dassitoyeva hoti. “Yaṃ yaṃ duṭṭhullasaddena abhidhīyati, taṃ sabbaṃ dassetuṃ pārājikāni vuttānī”ti ayañhettha adhippāyo. Tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇāti tatra pāḷiyaṃ ayaṃ vicāraṇā, tatra pāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu vā ayaṃ vicāraṇā. Tattha bhaveyyāti tattha kassaci vimati evaṃ bhaveyya. Anupasampannassa duṭṭhullārocane viya dukkaṭena bhavitabbanti āha “dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatī”ti. Akkosantopi dukkaṭaṃ āpajjeyyāti omasavādena dukkaṭaṃ āpajjeyya. Adhippāyaṃ ajānantenapi aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ vacaneyeva ṭhātabbanti dīpanatthaṃ “aṭṭhakathācariyāva ettha pamāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Punapi aṭṭhakathāvacanameva upapattito daḷhaṃ katvā patiṭṭhapento “imināpi ceta”ntiādimāha.

9. In the ninth: 'for the purpose of showing the meaning of the word duṭṭhulla' means for the purpose of showing the meaning of the term 'duṭṭhulla'. For when the meaning is shown, the word itself is also thereby shown as 'this is used in these meanings'. The intention here is this: “The Pārājika rules have been stated in order to show everything that is expressed by the word duṭṭhulla.” 'Herein is this investigation' means this is the investigation in the Pāḷi text, or this is the investigation in the Pāḷi text and the commentaries. 'There it might be' means someone's doubt there might be thus: “Just as in revealing a grave offense to an unordained person, it should be a dukkaṭa offense.” Therefore, he says, “one incurs a dukkaṭa offense.” 'Even one who insults would incur a dukkaṭa' means one would incur a dukkaṭa through disparaging speech. To clarify that even one who does not know the intention should stand by the word of the commentary teachers alone, it is said, “Here, the commentary teachers are the authority.” Again, establishing the word of the commentary firmly through reasoning, he says, “And by this…” and so on.

80. “Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā”ti vuttattā sammuti atthīti gahetabbāti āha “idha vuttattāyevā”tiādi.

78. Because it is said, “Except by the consent of the bhikkhus,” it should be understood that consent exists; therefore, he says, “just because it is stated here,” and so on.

82. Ādito pañca sikkhāpadānīti pāṇātipātādīni pañca sikkhāpadāni. “Sesānīti vikālabhojanādīni pañcā”ti vadanti. Keci pana [M 3.0014] “ādito paṭṭhāya pañca sikkhāpadānīti sukkavissaṭṭhiādīni pañcā”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Pāṇātipātādīni hi daseva sikkhāpadāni sāmaṇerānaṃ paññattāni. Vuttañhetaṃ –

80. ‘The five training rules from the beginning’ means the five training rules beginning with the abstention from killing living beings. They say that ‘the remaining’ means the five beginning with abstention from untimely meals. However, some say that ‘the five training rules from the beginning’ means the five beginning with seminal emission and so on. That should not be accepted. For indeed, only the ten training rules beginning with the abstention from killing living beings are prescribed for novices. For this has been said:

“Atha [V 3.0013] kho sāmaṇerānaṃ etadahosi ‘kati nu kho amhākaṃ sikkhāpadāni, kattha ca amhehi sikkhitabba’nti? Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sāmaṇerānaṃ dasa sikkhāpadāni, tesu ca sāmaṇerehi sikkhituṃ, pāṇātipātā veramaṇī adinnādānā veramaṇī”tiādi (mahāva. 106).

82. Then it occurred to the novices: ‘How many training rules do we have, and in what should we train?’ They reported this matter to the Blessed One. ‘Bhikkhus, I allow ten training rules for novices, and that novices should train in them: abstention from killing living beings, abstention from taking what is not given,’ and so on (Mahāvagga 106).

Tesaṃ paññattesuyeva sikkhāpadesu duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullavicāraṇā kātabbā, na ca sukkavissaṭṭhiādīni visuṃ tesaṃ paññattāni atthīti. Atha bhikkhuno duṭṭhullasaṅkhātāni sukkavissaṭṭhiādīni anupasampannassa kiṃ nāma hontīti āha “sukkavissaṭṭhi…pe… ajjhācāro nāmāti vutta”nti. Imināpi cetaṃ siddhaṃ “anupasampannassa sukkavissaṭṭhiādi duṭṭhullaṃ nāma na hotī”ti. Ajjhācāro nāmāti hi vadanto anupasampannassa sukkavissaṭṭhiādi kevalaṃ ajjhācāro nāma hoti, na pana duṭṭhullo nāma ajjhācāroti dīpeti. “Ajjhācāro nāmāti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā akattabbarūpattā ca anupasampannassa sukkavissaṭṭhiādīni daṇḍakammavatthupakkhaṃ bhajanti, tāni ca aññassa anupasampannassa avaṇṇakāmatāya ārocento bhikkhu dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatī”ti vadanti. Idha pana anupasampannaggahaṇena sāmaṇerasāmaṇerīsikkhamānānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Antimavatthuṃ anajjhāpannassa bhikkhuno savatthuko saṅghādiseso, anupasampannassa ārocanaṃ, bhikkhusammutiyā abhāvoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

The investigation of grave and non-grave offenses should be made only within the training rules prescribed for them, and there are no separate precepts concerning seminal emission and the like prescribed for them. Then, as to what those things reckoned as a grave offense for a bhikkhu—such as seminal emission and the like—are called for one who is not fully ordained, it is said: ‘Seminal emission… is called misconduct.’ By this, too, it is established that ‘for one not fully ordained, seminal emission and the like are not called a grave offense.’ For by saying ‘it is called misconduct,’ he clarifies that for one not fully ordained, seminal emission and the like are merely called misconduct, but not misconduct that is called grave. And because it is stated in the commentary as ‘it is called misconduct,’ and because it is of the nature of something that should not be done, for one not fully ordained, seminal emission and the like fall into the category of a basis for disciplinary action. And they say that a bhikkhu who reports these things about another unordained person out of a desire to disparage him incurs a dukkaṭa offense. Here, however, by the taking of ‘unordained person,’ the taking of male novices, female novices, and female probationers should be understood. The rest here is clear. The final case: for a bhikkhu who has not committed the offense, a Saṅghādisesa offense with its basis; declaring it to an unordained person; and the absence of the bhikkhus' consent—these are the three factors here.

Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on revealing grave offenses is concluded.

10. Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Digging the Earth

84-86. Dasame ekindriyanti “kāyindriyaṃ atthī”ti maññamānā vadanti. Muṭṭhippamāṇāti muṭṭhinā saṅgahetabbappamāṇā. Ettha kiñcāpi yebhuyyapaṃsuṃ appapaṃsuñca [M 3.0015] pathaviṃ vatvā upaḍḍhapaṃsukā pathavī na vuttā, tathāpi paṇṇattivajjasikkhāpadesu sāvasesapaññattiyāpi sambhavato upaḍḍhapaṃsukāyapi pathaviyā pācittiyamevāti gahetabbaṃ. Keci pana “sabbacchannādīsu upaḍḍhe dukkaṭassa vuttattā idhāpi dukkaṭaṃ yutta”nti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ pācittiyavatthukañca anāpattivatthukañca duvidhaṃ pathaviṃ ṭhapetvā aññissā dukkaṭavatthukāya tatiyāya pathaviyā abhāvato. Dveyeva hi pathaviyo vuttā “jātā ca pathavī ajātā ca pathavī”ti. Tasmā dvīsu aññatarāya pathaviyā bhavitabbaṃ, vinayavinicchaye ca sampatte garukeyeva ṭhātabbattā na sakkā [V 3.0014] ettha anāpattiyā bhavituṃ. Sabbacchannādīsu pana upaḍḍhe dukkaṭaṃ yuttaṃ tattha tādisassa dukkaṭavatthuno sabbhāvā.

84-86. In the tenth, concerning 'one sense faculty,' they say this, thinking, 'There is the body faculty.' 'Fist-measure' means a measure that can be gathered with a fist. Here, although after speaking of earth with much soil and earth with little soil, earth with half soil was not mentioned, nevertheless, because in the training rules concerning offenses by designation the possibility of a partial designation also exists, it should be understood that for earth with half soil as well, it is indeed an offense entailing confession. Some, however, say, 'Since in cases like "fully covered," etc., an offense of wrong-doing is stated for half, here too an offense of wrong-doing is appropriate.' That is not correct, because, having set aside the two kinds of earth—that which is a ground for an offense entailing confession and that which is a ground for no offense—there is no third kind of earth that is a ground for an offense of wrong-doing. For indeed, only two kinds of earth are mentioned: 'earth that is produced and earth that is not produced.' Therefore, it must be one of these two kinds of earth, and since in a Vinaya determination, when a serious matter is encountered, one must adhere to the more serious side, it is not possible for there to be no offense here. But in cases like 'fully covered,' etc., an offense of wrong-doing for half is appropriate, because there exists a ground for such an offense of wrong-doing.

“Pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇā”ti vadati, vaṭṭatīti “imasmiṃ okāse”ti aniyametvā vuttattā vaṭṭati. “Imaṃ valliṃ khaṇā”ti vuttepi pathavīkhaṇanaṃ sandhāya pavattavohārattā imināva sikkhāpadena āpatti, na bhūtagāmapātabyatāya. Kuṭehīti ghaṭehi. Tanukakaddamoti udakamissakakaddamo. So ca udakagatikattā vaṭṭati. Omakacātumāsanti ūnacātumāsaṃ. Ovaṭṭhanti devena ovaṭṭhaṃ. Akatapabbhāreti avaḷañjanaṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tādise hi vammikassa sabbhāvoti. Mūsikukkuraṃ nāma mūsikāhi khaṇitvā bahi katapaṃsurāsi. Eseva nayoti omakacātumāsaovaṭṭhoyeva vaṭṭatīti attho.

When one says, 'Dig a pond,' it is permissible; because it is said without specifying 'in this place,' it is permissible. Even when it is said, 'Dig up this vine,' because this is common speech that proceeds with reference to digging the earth, an offense is incurred under this very training rule, not for destroying plant life. 'With pots' means with jars. 'Thin mud' is mud mixed with water. And that is permissible because it has the nature of water. 'Less than four months' means fewer than four months. 'Rain-soaked' means soaked by rain. 'Without making an embankment' is said to show a place that is not to be used. For in such a place there is the existence of an anthill. 'Rat-dug-earth' refers to a pile of soil dug up by rats and brought outside. This is the principle: the meaning is that only what is less than four months old and rain-soaked is permissible.

Ekadivasampi na vaṭṭatīti ovaṭṭhaekadivasātikkantopi vikopetuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Heṭṭhābhūmisambandhepi ca gokaṇṭake bhūmito chinditvā uddhaṃ ṭhitattā accuggatamatthakato chinditvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Sakaṭṭhāne atiṭṭhamānaṃ katvā pādehi madditvā chinditvā āloḷitakaddamampi gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tatoti tato purāṇasenāsanato. Iṭṭhakaṃ gaṇhāmītiādi suddhacittaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Udakenāti ujukaṃ ākāsatoyeva patanakaudakena. “Sace pana aññattha paharitvā patitena udakena temitaṃ hoti, vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Uccāletvāti ukkhipitvā. Tena apadesenāti tena lesena.

'Not permissible even for a single day' means it is not permissible to disturb it even if one day has passed since it was rain-soaked. Some say, 'Even if a gokaṇṭaka is connected to the ground below, because it has been cut from the ground and stands upright, it is permissible to take it by cutting it from its very top.' It is also permissible to take even stirred-up mud, having made it not stand in its own place, trampled it with the feet, and broken it up. 'From there' means from that old dwelling place. 'I take a brick,' etc., is said with reference to a pure intention. 'With water' means with water falling directly from the sky. They say, 'But if it is moistened by water that has fallen after striking elsewhere, it is permissible.' 'Having lifted' means having raised up. 'By that pretext' means by that excuse.

87-88. Avisayattā [M 3.0016] anāpattīti ettha sacepi nibbāpetuṃ sakkā hoti, paṭhamaṃ suddhacittena dinnattā “dahatū”ti sallakkhetvāpi tiṭṭhati, anāpatti. Ovaṭṭhaṃ channanti paṭhamaṃ ovaṭṭhaṃ pacchā channaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Jātapathavī, pathavīsaññitā, khaṇanakhaṇāpanānaṃ aññataranti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

87-88. 'No offense because it is not within the scope'—here, even if it is possible to extinguish it, since it was first given with a pure mind, if one stands by even after considering, 'Let it burn,' there is no offense. 'Rain-soaked and covered' means first rain-soaked, afterwards covered. The rest is clear. 'Naturally formed earth,' 'perception of it as earth,' and 'one of either digging or causing to dig'—these are the three factors here.

Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on digging the earth is concluded.

Niṭṭhito musāvādavaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter, on false speech, is concluded.

2. Bhūtagāmavaggo

2. The Chapter on Plant Life

1. Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Plant Life

89. Senāsanavaggassa [V 3.0015] paṭhame niggahetuṃ asakkontoti sandhāretuṃ asakkonto. Iminā pana vacanena dārakassa tattha upanītabhāvo tena ca diṭṭhabhāvo vuttoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tena hi bhikkhunā taṃ rukkhaṃ chindituṃ āraddhe tattha nibbattā ekā taruṇaputtā devadhītā puttaṃ aṅkenādāya ṭhitā taṃ yāci “mā me sāmi vimānaṃ chindi, na sakkhissāmi puttakaṃ ādāya anāvāsā vicaritu”nti. So “ahaṃ aññattha īdisaṃ rukkhaṃ na labhissāmī”ti tassā vacanaṃ nādiyi. Sā “imampi tāva dārakaṃ oloketvā oramissatī”ti puttaṃ rukkhasākhāya ṭhapesi. So bhikkhu ukkhittaṃ pharasuṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto dārakassa bāhaṃ chindi. Evañca sayito vimāne sayito nāma hotīti katvā vuttaṃ “rukkhaṭṭhakadibbavimāne nipannassā”ti.

2. In the first of the Chapter on Lodgings, 'unable to restrain' means unable to hold back. By this statement, it should be understood that it is indeed stated that the child was brought there and was seen by him. For when that monk began to cut down that tree, a celestial maiden with a young son who dwelt there, holding her son in her arms, stood and pleaded with him, 'Sir, do not destroy my celestial mansion; I will not be able to wander without a dwelling while holding my child.' But he, thinking, 'I will not find such a tree elsewhere,' did not heed her words. She then thought, 'At least he will desist after seeing this child,' and placed the child on a branch of the tree. The monk, unable to restrain the raised axe, cut off the child’s arm. And because one who lies in a mansion is called 'one who lies in a mansion,' it was said: 'of one lying in the tree-abiding divine mansion'.

Rukkhaṭṭhakadibbavimāneti ca sākhaṭṭhakavimānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Rukkhassa upari nibbattañhi vimānaṃ rukkhapaṭibaddhattā “rukkhaṭṭhakavimāna”nti vuccati. Sākhaṭṭhakavimānaṃ pana sabbasākhāsannissitaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Tattha yaṃ rukkhaṭṭhakavimānaṃ hoti, taṃ yāva rukkhassa mūlamattampi tiṭṭhati, tāva na nassati. Sākhaṭṭhakavimānaṃ pana sākhāsu bhijjamānāsu tattha tattheva bhijjitvā sabbasākhāsu bhinnāsu sabbaṃ bhijjati, idampi ca vimānaṃ sākhaṭṭhakaṃ, tasmā rukkhe chinne taṃ vimānaṃ sabbaso vinaṭṭhaṃ, teneva sā devatā bhagavato santikā laddhe aññasmiṃ vimāne vasi. Bāhuṃ thanamūleyeva chindīti aṃsena saddhiṃ [M 3.0017] bāhaṃ chindi. Iminā ca rukkhadevatānaṃ gattāni chijjanti, na cātumahārājikādīnaṃ viya acchejjānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rukkhadhammeti rukkhapakatiyaṃ, rukkhasabhāveti attho. Rukkhānaṃ viya chedanādīsu akuppanañhi rukkhadhammo nāma.

1. And 'the tree-abiding divine mansion' is said with reference to a branch-abiding mansion. For a mansion that has arisen on top of a tree is called a 'tree-abiding mansion' because it is connected to the tree. A branch-abiding mansion, however, stands supported by all the branches. Therein, a tree-abiding mansion does not perish as long as even the mere root of the tree remains. But a branch-abiding mansion, when the branches are breaking, breaks in those very places, and when all the branches are broken, the entire mansion is broken. This mansion, too, was a branch-abiding one; therefore, when the tree was cut, that mansion was completely destroyed. For that very reason, that deity dwelt in another mansion obtained from the Blessed One. 'He cut the arm at the very root of the breast' means he severed the arm together with the shoulder. And by this it should be understood that the limbs of tree deities are cut, and are not unbreakable like those of the Four Great Kings and others. 'The nature of a tree' means the natural condition of a tree; the meaning is the inherent state of a tree. For the nature of a tree is indeed not to be angered by cutting and so on, just like a tree.

Uppatitanti uppannaṃ. Bhantanti dhāvantaṃ. Vārayeti niggaṇheyya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nāma cheko sārathi ativegena dhāvantaṃ rathaṃ niggahetvā yathicchakaṃ peseti, evaṃ yo puggalo uppannaṃ [V 3.0016] kodhaṃ vāraye niggaṇhituṃ sakkoti, tamahaṃ sārathiṃ brūmi. Itaro pana rājauparājādīnaṃ rathasārathijano rasmiggāho nāma hoti, na uttamasārathīti.

89. 'Uppatitaṃ' means 'arisen.' 'Bhantaṃ' means 'running.' 'Vāraye' means 'one should restrain.' This is what is said: Just as a skilled charioteer, restraining a chariot running with great speed, directs it as desired, so too, the person who is able to restrain arisen anger—that one I call a charioteer. The other, the chariot driver of kings, viceroys, and the like, is merely called a rein-holder, not a supreme charioteer.

Dutiyagāthāya pana ayamattho – yoti (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1) yo yādiso khattiyakulā vā pabbajito brāhmaṇakulā vā pabbajito navo vā majjhimo vā thero vā. Uppatitanti uddhamuddhaṃ patitaṃ, gataṃ pavattanti attho, uppannanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kodhanti “anatthaṃ me caratīti āghāto jāyatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.340; a. ni. 9.29) nayena sutte vuttānaṃ navannaṃ, “atthaṃ me na caratī”tiādīnañca tappaṭipakkhato siddhānaṃ navannamevāti aṭṭhārasannaṃ khāṇukaṇṭakādinā aṭṭhānena saddhiṃ ekūnavīsatiyā āghātavatthūnaṃ aññatarāghātavatthusambhavaṃ āghātaṃ. Visaṭanti vitthataṃ. Sappavisanti sappassa visaṃ. Ivāti opammavacanaṃ. I-kāralopaṃ katvā va-icceva vuttaṃ. Osadhehīti agadehi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā visatikicchako vejjo sappena daṭṭho sabbaṃ kāyaṃ pharitvā ṭhitaṃ visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃ mūlakhandhatacapattapupphādīnaṃ aññatarehi, nānābhesajjehi payojetvā katehi vā osadhehi khippameva vineyya, evameva yo yathāvuttena āghātavatthunā uppatitaṃ cittasantānaṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ kodhaṃ vinayanupāyesu tadaṅgavinayādīsu yena kenaci upāyena vineti nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantiṃ karoti, so bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṃ. So evaṃ kodhaṃ vinento bhikkhu yasmā kodho tatiyamaggena sabbaso pahīyati, tasmā orapārasaññitāni pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni jahātīti. Avisesena hi pāranti tīrassa nāmaṃ, tasmā orāni ca tāni saṃsārasāgarassa pārabhūtāni cāti katvā “orapāra”nti vuccati.

Now, this is the meaning of the second verse: ‘Yo’ (as in Su. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1) refers to whosoever—whether one gone forth from a khattiya family or a brahmin family, whether new, middle, or an elder. ‘Uppatitaṃ’ means fallen upwards, gone, occurred; ‘arisen’ is what is said. ‘Kodhaṃ’ refers to resentment arising from one or another of the nineteen grounds for resentment, which are: the nine spoken of in the Suttas by the method beginning, “Resentment is born, thinking, ‘He has acted to my detriment’” (Dī. Ni. 3.340; A. Ni. 9.29); the nine established by way of their opposites, beginning, “He does not act to my benefit,” thus making eighteen; together with the unreasonable ground such as stumbling on a stump or thorn. ‘Visaṭaṃ’ means spread out. ‘Sappavisaṃ’ means a snake’s venom. ‘Iva’ is a word of comparison; it is stated as just ‘va’ after eliding the letter ‘i’. ‘Osadhehi’ means with antidotes. This is what is said: Just as a physician skilled in treating venom, when bitten by a snake, would quickly dispel the snake’s venom that has spread and pervades the entire body with one or another of remedies from roots, trunks, bark, leaves, flowers, and so on, or with medicines prepared by compounding various medicinal substances; even so, that bhikkhu who, by some means or other among the methods for dispelling such as dispelling by substitution, dispels the anger that has arisen from a ground for resentment as described and pervades the stream of consciousness—he does not tolerate it, abandons it, gets rid of it, makes an end of it—that bhikkhu abandons the near and far. Since for a bhikkhu thus dispelling anger, anger is completely abandoned by the third path, he therefore abandons the five lower fetters, which are designated as the near and far. For, in a general sense, ‘pāra’ is a name for a shore; therefore, because they are both the near shores (orāni) and they are the far shores (pārabhūtāni) of the ocean of saṃsāra, they are called ‘orapāra’.

Atha [M 3.0018] vā yo uppatitaṃ vineti kodhaṃ visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃva osadhehi, so tatiyamaggena sabbaso kodhaṃ vinetvā anāgāmiphale ṭhito bhikkhu jahāti orapāraṃ. Tattha oranti sakattabhāvo. Pāranti parattabhāvo. Oraṃ vā cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, pāraṃ cha bāhirāyatanāni. Tathā oraṃ manussaloko, pāraṃ devaloko. Oraṃ kāmadhātu, pāraṃ rūpārūpadhātu. Oraṃ kāmarūpabhavo, pāraṃ arūpabhavo. Oraṃ attabhāvo, pāraṃ attabhāvasukhupakaraṇāni. Evametasmiṃ orapāre catutthamaggena chandarāgaṃ pajahanto “jahāti orapāra”nti vuccati. Ettha ca kiñcāpi anāgāmino kāmarāgassa pahīnattā idhattabhāvādīsu chandarāgo eva natthi, apica kho panassa vaṇṇappakāsanatthaṃ sabbametaṃ orapārabhedaṃ saṅgahetvā tattha chandarāgappahānena “jahāti orapāra”nti vuttaṃ.

Alternatively, a bhikkhu who dispels arisen anger—like spreading snake’s venom with antidotes—having completely dispelled anger by the third path and being established in the fruit of non-returning, abandons the near and far. Therein, ‘ora’ (near) is one’s own existence; ‘pāra’ (far) is another’s existence. Or, the near is the six internal sense bases; the far, the six external sense bases. Likewise, the near is the human world; the far, the world of the devas. The near is the sense-sphere realm; the far, the form and formless realms. The near is sense-sphere and form existence; the far, formless existence. The near is one’s own being; the far, the requisites for the comfort of one’s being. Thus, by abandoning sensual passion for this near and far with the fourth path, he is said to ‘abandon the near and far’. And here, although for a non-returner, since sensual passion is abandoned, there is no sensual passion at all with regard to one’s own existence and so on in this life, nevertheless, for the sake of proclaiming his quality, all these distinctions of near and far are gathered together, and with reference to the abandonment of sensual passion for them, it is said, ‘he abandons the near and far’.

Idāni [V 3.0017] tassatthassa vibhāvanatthāya upamaṃ āha “urago jiṇṇamivattacaṃ purāṇa”nti. Tattha urena gacchatīti urago, sappassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. So duvidho kāmarūpī ca akāmarūpī ca. Kāmarūpīpi duvidho jalajo thalajo ca. Jalajo jale eva kāmarūpaṃ labhati, na thale saṅkhapālajātake (jā. 2.17.143 ādayo) saṅkhapālanāgarājā viya. Thalajo thale eva, na jale. So jajjarabhāvena jiṇṇaṃ, cirakālatāya purāṇañcāti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ tacaṃ jahanto catubbidhena jahati sajātiyaṃ ṭhito jigucchanto nissāya thāmenāti. Sajāti nāma sappajāti dīghattabhāvo. Uragā hi pañcasu ṭhānesu sajātiṃ nātivattanti upapattiyaṃ cutiyaṃ vissaṭṭhaniddokkamane sajātiyā methunapaṭisevane jiṇṇatacāpanayane cāti. Tasmā yadā tacaṃ jahati, tadā sajātiyaṃyeva ṭhatvā jahati. Sajātiyaṃ ṭhitopi ca jigucchanto jahati. Jigucchanto nāma yadā upaḍḍhaṭṭhāne mutto hoti, upaḍḍhaṭṭhāne amutto olambati, tadā naṃ aṭṭīyanto jahati, evaṃ jigucchantopi ca daṇḍantaraṃ vā mūlantaraṃ vā pāsāṇantaraṃ vā nissāya jahati. Nissāya jahantopi ca thāmaṃ janetvā ussāhaṃ karitvā vīriyena vaṅkaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ katvā passasantova phaṇaṃ karitvā jahati. Evaṃ jahitvā yenakāmaṃ pakkamati.

Now, to clarify that meaning, He stated the simile: ‘Like a snake its old, worn-out skin.’ Therein, ‘urago’ is one that goes on its chest; this is a designation for a snake. It is of two kinds: one that can assume forms at will and one that cannot. The one that can assume forms at will is also of two kinds: aquatic and terrestrial. The aquatic one can assume forms at will only in water, not on land, like the nāga king Saṅkhapāla in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka (Jā. 2.17.143 ff.). The terrestrial one can do so only on land, not in water. When shedding its skin—which is called ‘worn-out’ (jiṇṇa) due to decay and ‘old’ (purāṇa) due to its long duration—it sheds it in four ways: while remaining in its own kind, with disgust, by relying on something, and with strength. ‘Its own kind’ (sajāti) means the snake species, its elongated form. For snakes do not transgress their own kind in five situations: at birth, at death, when casting off their slough, when mating with their own kind, and when removing their old skin. Therefore, when it sheds its skin, it does so while remaining in its own kind. And even while remaining in its own kind, it sheds it with disgust. ‘With disgust’ means that when it is free in one half, but in the other half it is not free and the skin hangs down, then, being vexed by it, it sheds it. And even while shedding it with disgust, it does so by relying on the space between sticks, between roots, or between rocks.
