And even while shedding it by relying on something, it does so by generating strength, making an effort, and with energy making its tail crooked and, as if breathing out, making a hood. Having shed it thus, it departs wherever it wishes.

Evameva ayampi bhikkhu orapāraṃ jahitukāmo catubbidhena jahati sajātiyaṃ ṭhito jigucchanto nissāya thāmenāti. Sajāti nāma bhikkhuno “ariyāya jātiyā jāto”ti (ma. ni. 2.351) vacanato sīlaṃ. Tenevāha “sīle patiṭṭhāya [M 3.0019] naro sapañño”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192). Evametissaṃ sajātiyaṃ ṭhito bhikkhu taṃ sakattabhāvādibhedaṃ orapāraṃ jiṇṇapurāṇattacamiva taṃ dukkhaṃ janentaṃ tattha tattha ādīnavadassanena jigucchanto kalyāṇamitte nissāya adhimattasammāvāyāmasaṅkhātaṃ thāmaṃ janetvā “divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetī”ti (a. ni. 3.16; 4.37) vuttanayena rattindivaṃ chadhā vibhajitvā ghaṭento vāyamanto urago viya vaṅkaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā urago viya passasanto ayampi asithilaparakkamatāya vāyamanto uragova phaṇaṃ karitvā ayampi ñāṇavipphāraṃ janetvā uragova tacaṃ orapāraṃ jahati, jahitvā ca urago viya ohitataco yenakāmaṃ pakkamati, ayampi ohitabhāro anupādisesanibbānadhātudisaṃ pakkamatīti.

In the very same way, this bhikkhu, wishing to abandon the near and far, abandons it in four ways: standing in his own kind, with disgust, by relying on something, and with strength. For a bhikkhu, ‘his own kind’ is virtue, according to the saying, ‘born of the noble birth’ (MN 2.351). For that reason it was said: ‘A wise person, established in virtue…’ (SN 1.23, 192). Thus, this bhikkhu, standing in this ‘own kind,’ becomes disgusted with that near and far—differentiated as one’s own existence and so on, which generates suffering like an old, worn-out skin—by seeing the danger in it here and there. Relying on spiritual friends, he generates the strength known as supreme right effort. Striving and exerting himself day and night, divided into six parts, according to the method stated, ‘During the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states’ (AN 3.16; 4.37), he folds his legs crosswise like a snake making its tail crooked; like a snake breathing out, he too strives with unslackened effort; like a snake making a hood, he too generates the radiance of knowledge; and just as a snake sheds its skin, he abandons the near and far. And having abandoned it, just as a snake with its skin cast off departs wherever it wishes, he too, with his burden laid down, proceeds towards the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining.

90. Bhavantīti iminā viruḷhamūle nīlabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā vaḍḍhamānake taruṇagacche dasseti. Ahuvunti iminā pana vaḍḍhitvā ṭhite mahante rukkhagacchādike dasseti. Bhavantīti imassa vivaraṇaṃ “jāyanti vaḍḍhantī”ti, ahuvunti imassa “jātā vaḍḍhitā”ti. Rāsīti suddhaṭṭhakadhammasamūho. Bhūtānanti tathāladdhasamaññānaṃ aṭṭhadhammānaṃ. “Bhūtānaṃ gāmo”ti vuttepi avayavavinimuttassa [V 3.0018] samudāyassa abhāvato bhūtasaññitā teyeva tiṇarukkhalatādayo gayhanti. “Bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā haritabhāvamāpannā rukkhagacchādayo devatāhi pariggayhanti, tasmā bhūtānaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānatāya bhūtānaṃ gāmo”tipi vadanti. Rukkhādīnanti ādi-saddena osadhigacchalatādayo veditabbā.

90. By ‘bhavanti’ (they come to be), it indicates young plants that are growing, having become green from a well-established root. By ‘ahuvuṃ’ (they were), on the other hand, it indicates great trees, shrubs, and so on, that have grown and are standing. The explanation of ‘bhavanti’ is ‘they are born and grow’; of ‘ahuvuṃ’, ‘they were born and have grown.’ ‘A mass’ (rāsi) is a collection of the pure octad of phenomena. ‘Of beings’ (bhūtānaṃ) refers to those eight phenomena that have received that designation. Even when ‘a village of beings’ is said, since there is no collection separate from its components, those very grasses, trees, creepers, and so on, which are designated as ‘beings’ (bhūtā), are what is meant. Some also say: ‘Trees, shrubs, and so on, that are established on the earth and have become green are taken possession of by deities (devatā); therefore, because it is a dwelling place for beings (bhūtā, i.e., deities), it is a “village of beings”.’ By ‘trees and so on’ (rukkhādīnaṃ), the word ‘so on’ should be understood to include medicinal herbs, shrubs, creepers, and the like.

Nanu ca rukkhādayo cittarahitatāya na jīvā, cittarahitatā ca paripphandābhāvato chinnepi ruhanato visadisajātikabhāvato catuyoniapariyāpannato ca veditabbā, vuḍḍhi pana pavāḷasilālavaṇānampi vijjatīti na tesaṃ jīvabhāve kāraṇaṃ, visayaggahaṇañca nesaṃ parikappanāmattaṃ supanaṃ viya ciñcādīnaṃ, tathā dohaḷādayo, tattha kasmā bhūtagāmassa chedanādipaccayā pācittiyaṃ vuttanti? Samaṇasāruppato taṃnivāsasattānurakkhaṇato [M 3.0020] ca. Tenevāha “jīvasaññino hi moghapurisā manussā rukkhasmi”ntiādi.

But are not trees and so on without life, because they are without consciousness? And their being without consciousness should be understood from their lack of thrashing movements, from their regrowing when cut, from the absence of a dissimilar nature, and from their not being included among the four kinds of birth. Moreover, growth is also found in coral, rock, and salt, so that is no reason for them to be considered living beings. Their perception of objects is merely conceptual, like the dream of a tamarind tree, and similarly with cravings and the like. So why is a Pācittiya offense stated for cutting or harming plant life? It is because of what is suitable for an ascetic and for protecting the beings dwelling in them. Hence it was said, “For, foolish men, humans perceive a tree as living,” and so on.

91. “Mūle jāyantī”tiādīsu attho upari attanā vuccamānappakārena sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttoti āha “evaṃ santepi…pe… na samentī”ti. Vijāta-saddo idha vi-saddalopaṃ katvā niddiṭṭhoti āha “vijātānī”ti. Vijāta-saddo ca “vijātā itthī”tiādīsu viya pasūtavacanoti āha “pasūtānī”ti. Pasūti ca nāmettha nibbattapaṇṇamūlatāti āha “nibbattapaṇṇamūlānī”ti. Iminā imaṃ dīpeti “nibbattapaṇṇamūlāni bījāni bhūtagāmasaṅkhameva gacchanti, tesu ca vattamāno bījajāta-saddo ruḷhīvasena rukkhādīsupi vattatī”ti. Purimasmiṃ atthavikappe pana bījehi jātānaṃ rukkhalatādīnaṃyeva bhūtagāmatā vuttā.

91. In 'mūle jāyantī,' etc., the meaning is stated in the Sinhala commentary in a manner to be explained by the author himself; therefore, he says, 'Even so... they do not cease.' The word 'vijāta' here is indicated by the elision of the syllable 'vi,' thus he says 'vijātāni.' And the word 'vijāta' is a term for 'having given birth,' as in 'a woman who has given birth,' etc., thus he says 'pasūtāni.' And 'pasūti' here is the state of having produced leaves and roots, thus he says 'nibbattapaṇṇamūlāni' (having produced leaves and roots). By this, he explains the following: 'Seeds that have produced leaves and roots are classified as plant life, and the term 'bījajāta' (seed-born), which applies to them, also applies conventionally to trees, etc.' In the former alternative interpretation, however, being plant life was spoken of only in relation to trees, creepers, etc., born from seeds.

Tāni dassentoti tāni bījāni dassento. Mūlabījantiādīsu mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Phaḷubījanti pabbabījaṃ. Paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato viruhanasamatthe sāraphale niruḷho bīja-saddo. Tadatthasaṃsiddhiyā mūlādīsupi kesuci pavattatīti mūlādito nivattanatthaṃ ekena bījasaddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “bījabīja”nti “rūparūpaṃ, dukkhadukkha”nti ca yathā. Bījato nibbattena bījaṃ dassitanti kāriyopacārena kāraṇaṃ dassitanti dīpeti.

To show them means showing those seeds. In 'root-seed,' etc., the root itself is the seed, hence 'root-seed.' The same method applies to the rest. Phaḷubīja means a node-seed. The word 'seed' is established in the essential fruit capable of sprouting, due to its being a special cause for the arising of similar fruit when other conditions combine. For the accomplishment of that meaning, it also occurs in some roots, etc.; therefore, in order to distinguish it from roots, etc., it is stated by specifying with the word 'seed' as 'seed-seed,' just as 'form-form' and 'suffering-suffering.' He explains that by the phrase 'the seed is shown by what is produced from it,' the cause is shown by a figurative use of the effect.

92. Bīje bījasaññīti ettha kāraṇūpacārena kāriyaṃ vuttanti dassento “tattha yathā”tiādimāha. Bhūtagāmaparimocanaṃ katvāti bhūtagāmato mocetvā, viyojetvāti attho. Yaṃ bījaṃ bhūtagāmo nāma hotīti bījāni ca tāni jātāni cāti vuttamatthaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tattha [V 3.0019] yaṃ bījanti yaṃ nibbattapaṇṇamūlaṃ bījaṃ. Tasmiṃ bījeti tasmiṃ bhūtagāmasaññite bīje. Ettha ca bījajāta-saddassa viya ruḷhīvasena rukkhādīsu bīja-saddassapi pavatti veditabbā. Yathārutanti yathāpāḷi.

92. 'In the seed, perceiving it as a seed'—showing that here the effect is stated by a figurative use of the cause, he says 'therein, as follows,' and so on. 'Having freed it from plant life' means having released it from plant life, having separated it. He says 'That seed which is called plant life' with reference to the meaning stated as 'both those seeds and those that have sprouted.' Therein, 'that which is a seed' means that seed which has produced leaves and roots. 'In that seed' means in that seed perceived as plant life. And here, just as the word 'seed-born' applies conventionally to trees and so on, so too the application of the word 'seed' to trees and so on should be understood by conventional usage. 'As heard' means according to the Pāli text.

Yattha katthacīti mūle agge majjhe vā. Sañcicca ukkhipituṃ na vaṭṭatīti ettha sacepi sarīre laggabhāvaṃ jānantova udakato uṭṭhahati, “taṃ uddharissāmī”ti saññāya abhāvato vaṭṭati. Uppāṭitānīti uddhaṭāni. Bījagāme saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti bhūtagāmato parimocitattā vuttaṃ. Anantaka-ggahaṇena sāsapamattikā gahitā. Nāmañhetaṃ tassā sevālajātiyā[M 3.0021]. Mūlapaṇṇānaṃ asampuṇṇattā “asampuṇṇabhūtagāmo nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Abhūtagāmamūlattāti ettha bhūtagāmo mūlaṃ kāraṇaṃ etassāti bhūtagāmamūlo, bhūtagāmassa vā mūlaṃ kāraṇanti bhūtagāmamūlaṃ. Bījagāmo hi nāma bhūtagāmato sambhavati, bhūtagāmassa ca kāraṇaṃ hoti, ayaṃ pana tādiso na hotīti “abhūtagāmamūlattā”ti vuttaṃ. Tatraṭṭhakattā vuttaṃ “so bījagāmena saṅgahito”ti. Idañca “abhūtagāmamūlattā”ti ettha paṭhamaṃ vuttaatthasambhavato vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi tālanāḷikerādīnaṃ khāṇu uddhaṃ avaḍḍhanato bhūtagāmassa kāraṇaṃ na hoti, tathāpi bhūtagāmasaṅkhyupagatanibbattapaṇṇamūlabījato sambhūtattā bhūtagāmato uppanno nāma hotīti bījagāmena saṅgahaṃ gacchati.

'Wherever it may be' means at the root, the tip, or the middle. 'It is not proper to intentionally lift it'—here, even if one rises from the water knowing it is attached to the body, it is permissible because there is no intention of 'I will remove it.' 'Uprooted' means pulled out. 'It goes to inclusion in seed-plants'—this is said because it is freed from the plant kingdom. By the term 'anantaka', algae the size of a mustard seed is included. This is indeed the name of that kind of algae. Because the roots and leaves are incomplete, it is called 'the incomplete plant kingdom.' Regarding 'because it has no root in the plant kingdom'—here, 'bhūtagāmamūla' means 'the plant kingdom is its root or cause,' or 'the root or cause of the plant kingdom.' For the seed-plant indeed arises from the plant kingdom and is the cause of the plant kingdom, but this is not so here—thus it is said, 'because it has no root in the plant kingdom.' Because it is situated there, it is said, 'it is included among seed-plants.' And this is stated here from the possibility of the meaning stated first in 'because it has no root in the plant kingdom.' For although the stump of palms and coconuts does not grow upward and thus is not a cause of the plant kingdom, nevertheless, because it has arisen from seeds that have produced leaves and roots, which are counted as belonging to the plant kingdom, it is said to have originated from the plant kingdom—thus it is included among seed-plants.

“Aṅkure harite”ti vatvā tameva vibhāveti “nīlapaṇṇavaṇṇe jāte”ti, nīlapaṇṇassa vaṇṇasadise vaṇṇe jāteti attho. “Nīlavaṇṇe jāte”ti vā pāṭho gahetabbo. Amūlakabhūtagāme saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti nāḷikerassa āveṇikaṃ katvā vadati. “Pānīyaghaṭādīnaṃ bahi sevālo udake aṭṭhitattā bījagāmānulomattā ca dukkaṭavatthū”ti vadanti. Kaṇṇakampi abbohārikamevāti nīlavaṇṇampi abbohārikameva. Seleyyakaṃ nāma silāya sambhūtā ekā sugandhajāti. “Rukkhattacaṃ vikopetīti vuttattā rukkhe jātaṃ yaṃ kiñci chattakaṃ rukkhattacaṃ avikopetvā matthakato chinditvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Rukkhato muccitvā tiṭṭhatīti ettha “yadipi kiñcimattaṃ rukkhe allīnā hutvā tiṭṭhati, rukkhato gayhamāno pana rukkhacchaviṃ na vikopeti, vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Allarukkhato na vaṭṭatīti etthāpi rukkhattacaṃ avikopetvā matthakato tacchetvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Hatthakukkuccenāti hatthānaṃ asaṃyatabhāvena, hatthacāpallenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pānīyaṃ na vāsetabbanti idaṃ attano atthāya nāmitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kevalaṃ anupasampannassa atthāya nāmite pana pacchā tato labhitvā na vāsetabbanti [V 3.0020] natthi. “Yesaṃ rukkhānaṃ sākhā ruhatīti vuttattā yesaṃ sākhā na ruhati, tattha kappiyakaraṇakiccaṃ natthī”ti vadanti.

Having said 'in a green shoot,' he explains it as 'when they turn the color of dark green leaves,' meaning they take on a hue resembling the color of dark green leaves. Alternatively, the reading 'when they turn dark green' may be adopted. He speaks of including the rootless plant community, making the coconut palm a special case. They say that moss growing outside water pots and the like, because it is not established in water and conforms to seed-plants, constitutes an object for a dukkaṭa offence. Even kaṇṇaka is not to be dealt with, just as the dark green kind is not to be dealt with. Seleyyaka refers to a fragrant variety that grows on rocks. Because it is said 'it damages the tree bark,' they state that any mushroom born on a tree is permissible to take by cutting it from the top without harming the tree bark. Regarding 'what stands detached from the tree,' they say that even if something clings slightly to the tree, as long as it does not damage the bark when taken, it is permissible. Concerning 'not from a living tree,' here too, it should be understood that one may take it by shaving it from the top without harming the tree bark. By 'hand-scruple' is meant the unrestrained nature of the hands, that is to say, due to hand-fidgeting. 'Water should not be perfumed'—this is said with reference to a branch bent down for one's own use. However, if it is a branch bent down for the sake of an unordained person, there is no prohibition against perfuming it later after obtaining it from them. They say that since it is stated 'for trees whose branches grow,' there is no need for the act of making it allowable for trees whose branches do not grow.

93. Pañcahi [M 3.0022] samaṇakappehīti pañcahi samaṇavohārehi. Kiñcāpi hi bījānaṃ agginā phuṭṭhamattena nakhādīhi vilikhanamattena ca aviruḷhīdhammatā na hoti, tathāpi evaṃ kateyeva samaṇānaṃ kappatīti aggiparijitādayo samaṇavohārā nāma jātā, tasmā tehi samaṇavohārehi karaṇabhūtehi phalaṃ paribhuñjituṃ anujānāmīti adhippāyo. Abījanibbaṭṭabījānipi samaṇānaṃ kappantīti paññattapaṇṇattibhāvato samaṇavohārāicceva saṅkhaṃ gatāni. Atha vā aggiparijitādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ kappiyabhāvatoyeva pañcahi samaṇakappiyabhāvasaṅkhātehi kāraṇehi phalaṃ paribhuñjituṃ anujānāmīti evamettha adhippāyo veditabbo. Aggiparijitantiādīsu “paricita”ntipi paṭhanti. Abījaṃ nāma taruṇambaphalādi. Nibbaṭṭabījaṃ nāma ambapanasādi, yaṃ bījaṃ nibbaṭṭetvā visuṃ katvā paribhuñjituṃ sakkā hoti. “Kappiya”nti vatvāva kātabbanti yo kappiyaṃ karoti, tena kattabbākārasseva vuttattā bhikkhunā avuttepi kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti na gahetabbaṃ. Puna “kappiyaṃ kāretabba”nti kārāpanassa paṭhamameva kathitattā bhikkhunā “kappiyaṃ karohī”ti vutteyeva anupasampannena “kappiya”nti vatvā aggiparijitādi kātabbanti gahetabbaṃ. “Kappiyanti vacanaṃ pana yāya kāyaci bhāsāya vattuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. “Kappiyanti vatvāva kātabba”nti vacanato paṭhamaṃ “kappiya”nti vatvā pacchā aggiādinā phusanādi kātabbanti veditabbaṃ. “Paṭhamaṃ aggiṃ nikkhipitvā nakhādinā vā vijjhitvā taṃ anuddharitvāva ‘kappiya’nti vattumpi vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti.

93. 'By five things allowable for ascetics' means by five ascetic conventions. For although seeds do not lose their ability to sprout merely by being touched by fire or scraped by nails and so forth, still, only when this is done does it become allowable for ascetics. Thus, 'touched by fire' and so forth have come to be called 'ascetic conventions.' Therefore, the intended meaning is: 'I permit the eating of fruit by means of these ascetic conventions which are the cause.' Even fruits that are seedless or from which the seed has been removed are allowable for ascetics; thus, by virtue of being designated as such, they are counted as 'ascetic conventions.' Alternatively, because the five, such as 'touched by fire,' are allowable, the intended meaning here should be understood thus: 'I permit the eating of fruit by means of these five causes, which are designated as things allowable for ascetics.' In 'touched by fire' and so forth, some also read 'paricita.' 'Seedless' refers to young fruit such as unripe mangoes. 'Seed-removed' refers to fruits like mango or jackfruit, from which the seed can be taken out and set apart before eating. Regarding the statement, 'It must be done only after saying "allowable,"' it should not be understood that it is permissible to act even without being instructed by the monk, because what is stated is only the manner in which it is to be done by the one who makes it allowable. Furthermore, since 'it should be caused to be made allowable' is stated first, it should be understood that only when a monk has said, 'Make it allowable,' should an unordained person, having said 'allowable,' perform the act of touching with fire and so forth. Some say, 'The word "allowable" may be spoken in any language.' In accordance with the statement, 'It must be done only after saying "allowable,"' it should be understood that first one says 'allowable,' and afterwards one performs the act of touching with fire and so forth. Some also say, 'It is permissible to first apply fire or pierce with a nail and so forth, and then, without removing that implement, to say "allowable."'

Ekasmiṃ bīje vātiādīsu “ekaṃyeva kāremīti adhippāye satipi ekābaddhattā sabbaṃ katameva hotī”ti vadanti. Dāruṃ vijjhatīti ettha “jānitvāpi vijjhati vā vijjhāpeti vā, vaṭṭatiyevā”ti vadanti. Bhattasitthe vijjhatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. “Taṃ vijjhati, na vaṭṭatīti rajjuādīnaṃ bhājanagatikattā”ti vadanti. Maricapakkādīhi missetvāti ettha bhattasitthasambandhavasena ekābaddhatā veditabbā, na phalānaṃyeva aññamaññaṃ sambandhavasena. Bhindāpetvā kappiyaṃ kārāpetabbanti bījato muttassa kaṭāhassa bhājanagatikattā vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'on one seed,' and so forth, they say: 'Even if one has the intention, "I will make only one allowable," because they are bound as one, the whole is considered to have been made allowable.' Regarding 'pierces wood,' they say: 'Even if one knowingly pierces it or causes it to be pierced, it is indeed allowable.' The same principle applies to 'pierces a lump of cooked rice.' Regarding 'pierces that, it is not allowable,' they say this is because ropes and so forth have the nature of a container. Regarding 'having mixed with pepper powder and so forth,' the state of being bound as one should be understood by way of its connection with the lump of cooked rice, not merely by way of the connection of the fruits themselves with one another. The statement 'having caused it to be broken and made allowable' is said because the shell, once freed from the seed, has the nature of a container.

Nikkhāmetunti taṃ bhikkhuṃ nikkhāmetuṃ. “Sace etassa anuloma”nti senāsanarakkhaṇatthāya anuññātampi paṭaggidānādiṃ attanāpi kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti [M 3.0023] ettakeneva idampi etassa anulomanti evamadhippāyo siyā. Paṭaggidānaṃ parittakaraṇañca attano parassa vā [V 3.0021] senāsanarakkhaṇatthāya vaṭṭatiyeva. Tasmā sace tassa suttassa etaṃ anulomaṃ siyā, attano na vaṭṭati, aññassa vaṭṭatīti ayaṃ viseso kuto labbhatīti āha “attano na vaṭṭati…pe… na sakkā laddhu”nti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Bhūtagāmo, bhūtagāmasaññitā, vikopanaṃ vā vikopāpanaṃ vāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

'To make him leave' means to make that monk leave. Regarding 'If it is suitable for this one': it is permissible for one to do for oneself even such things as giving a firebrand, which is permitted for the sake of protecting the lodging. By just this much, this too is suitable for this one—such might be the intention. Giving a firebrand and digging a protective trench are indeed permissible for the sake of protecting one's own or another's lodging. Therefore, if this is suitable for that rule, from where is this distinction obtained, that for oneself it is not allowable, but for another it is allowable? Thus, he said: 'For oneself it is not allowable... it cannot be obtained.' The rest here is self-evident. A living plant, perception of it as a living plant, and either destroying it or causing it to be destroyed—these are the three factors here.

Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning living plants is concluded.

2. Aññavādakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Equivocation

94-98. Dutiye aññaṃ vacananti yaṃ codakena cuditakassa dosavibhāvanavacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ tato aññeneva vacanena paṭicarati. Atha vā aññenaññaṃ paṭicaratīti aññena kāraṇena aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicaratīti evamettha attho veditabbo, yaṃ codakena cuditakassa dosavibhāvanakāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tato aññena codanāya amūlakabhāvadīpakena kāraṇena paṭicaratīti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṭicaratīti ca paṭicchādanavasena carati, pavattatīti attho. Paṭicchādanattho eva vā carati-saddo anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ. Tenāha “paṭicchādetī”ti. Ko āpannotiādinā pāḷiyaṃ codanaṃ avissajjetvā vikkhepāpajjanavasena aññena aññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Aparampi pana codanaṃ vissajjetvā bahiddhā kathāapanāmavasena pavattaṃ pāḷimuttakaṃ aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti puṭṭho “pāṭaliputtaṃ gatomhī”ti vatvā puna “na tava pāṭaliputtagamanaṃ pucchāma, āpattiṃ pucchāmā”ti vutte “tato rājagahaṃ gatomhī”ti vatvā “rājagahaṃ vā yāhi brāhmaṇagahaṃ vā, āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti vutte “tattha me sūkaramaṃsaṃ laddha”ntiādīni vatvāva kathaṃ bahiddhā vikkhipantopi hi “aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati”cceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

94-98. In the second training rule, 'a different statement' means that when the accuser has stated a fault-revealing statement to the accused, the latter evades it with a different statement. Alternatively, 'he evades one thing with another' means he evades one reason with another reason; thus should the meaning here be understood. When the accuser has stated the reason revealing the fault of the accused, it is said that the latter evades it with a different reason, one that indicates the baselessness of the accusation. And 'he evades' (paṭicarati) means he acts, he proceeds, by way of concealment. Or, the root 'car' itself has the meaning of concealment, due to the multiple meanings of verbal roots. Therefore, he said, 'he conceals.' In the Pāḷi text, beginning with 'Who has committed an offense?', evading one thing with another is shown by way of resorting to distraction without answering the accusation. Furthermore, another kind of evading one thing with another, which is outside the Pāḷi text, should be understood as that which occurs by way of leading the conversation astray after having answered the accusation. For example, when asked, 'Have you committed such-and-such an offense?', he says, 'I went to Pāṭaliputta.' When told again, 'We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta; we are asking about the offense,' he says, 'From there, I went to Rājagaha.' When told, 'Go to Rājagaha or to a brahmin's house, but have you committed the offense?', he says, 'There I received pork,' and so on. Even by distracting the conversation to external matters in this way, one is still counted as 'evading one thing with another.'

Yadetaṃ aññena aññaṃ paṭicaraṇavasena pavattavacanaṃ, tadeva pucchitamatthaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ vadatīti aññavādakanti āha “aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇassetaṃ nāma”nti. Tuṇhībhūtassetaṃ nāmanti tuṇhībhāvassetaṃ nāmaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Aññavādakaṃ āropetūti aññavādakakammaṃ āropetu, aññavādakattaṃ [M 3.0024] vā idāni kariyamānena kammena āropetūti attho. Vihesakaṃ āropetūti etthāpi vihesakakammaṃ vihesakabhāvaṃ vā āropetūti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

That statement which proceeds by way of evading one thing with another, because it sets aside the matter asked about and speaks of something else, is called 'equivocation.' Thus, he said: 'This is the name for evading one thing with another.' 'This is the name for one who has become silent' means this is the name for the state of silence, or this is the reading itself. 'Let him impose equivocation' means let him impose the formal act of equivocation, or, by means of the formal act now being performed, let him impose the state of being an equivocator; this is the meaning. In 'Let him impose harassment' as well, the meaning should be understood as: let him impose the formal act of harassment or the state of being a harasser.

Anāropite aññavādake vuttadukkaṭaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgataaññenaññaṃpaṭicaraṇavasena yujjati[V 3.0022]. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatena pana pāḷimuttakaaññenaññaṃpaṭicaraṇavasena anāropite aññavādake musāvādena pācittiyaṃ, āropite imināva pācittiyanti veditabbaṃ. Keci pana “āropite aññavādake musāvādena iminā ca pācittiyadvayaṃ hotī”ti vadanti, taṃ vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Yā sā ādikammikassa anāpatti vuttā, sāpi pāḷiyaṃ āgataaññenaññaṃpaṭicaraṇavasena vuttāti daṭṭhabbā, iminā sikkhāpadena anāpattidassanatthaṃ vā. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Dhammakammena āropitatā, āpattiyā vā vatthunā vā anuyuñjiyamānatā, chādetukāmatāya aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ vā tuṇhībhāvo vāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

When the formal act of equivocation has not been imposed, the stated dukkaṭa offense is applicable by way of the 'evading one thing with another' that is found in the Pāḷi. However, by way of the 'evading one thing with another' that is outside the Pāḷi, which is found in the commentary, it should be understood that when the formal act of equivocation has not been imposed, there is a pācittiya offense for false speech; when it has been imposed, there is a pācittiya offense by this very rule. Some, however, say: 'When the formal act of equivocation has been imposed, there are two pācittiya offenses: one for false speech and one by this rule.' This should be investigated before being accepted. The non-offense that is stated for the first-time offender should also be seen as stated by way of the 'evading one thing with another' found in the Pāḷi, or for the purpose of showing non-offense in regard to this training rule. The rest is self-evident. Being charged through a formal act of the Dhamma, being questioned about an offense or its basis, and, with the desire to conceal, either evading one thing with another or remaining silent—these are the three factors here.

Aññavādakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning equivocation is concluded.

3. Ujjhāpanakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Fault-Finding

103. Tatiye dhātupāṭhe jhe-saddo cintāyaṃ paṭhitoti āha “lāmakato vā cintāpentī”tiādi. Ayameva ca anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ olokanatthopi hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Akkharāya vācetī”tiādīsu (pāci. 46) viya “chandāyā”ti liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttanti āha “chandenā”ti.

103. In the third Dhātupāṭha, the word 'jhe' is recited in the sense of thinking, as stated in 'or causing to think meanly,' and so on. And this same root, because roots have multiple meanings, should be understood as also having the meaning of looking. As in 'He recites (the text) by means of the letters,' and so on (Pāc. 46), it is said 'chandāya' by way of gender displacement; hence it is stated as 'chandena'.

105. Yena vacanenāti yena “chandāya itthannāmo idaṃ nāma karotī”tiādivacanena. Yena ca khiyyantīti yena “chandāya itthannāmo”tiādivacanena tattha tattha bhikkhūnaṃ savanūpacāre ṭhatvā avaṇṇaṃ pakāsenti.

105. "By which speech" means by speech such as, "Driven by desire, so-and-so does such-and-such." "And by which they are disparaged" means by speech such as, "Driven by desire, so-and-so," standing here and there within earshot of the monks, they proclaim his dispraise.

106. Aññaṃ anupasampannaṃ ujjhāpetīti aññena anupasampannena ujjhāpeti. Tassa vā taṃ santike khiyyatīti tassa anupasampannassa santike [M 3.0025] taṃ saṅghena sammataṃ upasampannaṃ khiyyati, avaṇṇaṃ vadanto vā pakāseti. Anupasampannaṃ saṅghena sammatanti ettha sammatapubbo sammatoti vutto. Tenāha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Yasmā ujjhāpanaṃ khiyyanañca musāvādavaseneva pavattaṃ, tasmā ādikammikassa anāpattīti pācittiyaṭṭhāne dukkaṭaṭṭhāne ca imināva anāpattidassanatthaṃ vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Evañca katvā ujjhāpentassa khiyyantassa ca ekakkhaṇe dve dve āpattiyo hontīti āpannaṃ. Atha vā īdisaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ musāvādato paṭhamaṃ paññattanti gahetabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Dhammakammena sammatatā, upasampannatā, agatigamanābhāvo[V 3.0023], tassa avaṇṇakāmatā, yassa santike vadati, tassa upasampannatā, ujjhāpanaṃ vā khiyyanaṃ vāti imāni panettha cha aṅgāni.

106. ‘To cause another unordained person to find fault’ means to cause fault-finding by means of another unordained person. Or, ‘to disparage him in the presence of that person’ means that he disparages one who has been approved by the Saṅgha and is ordained in the presence of that unordained person, or speaking ill of him, he makes it known. ‘An unordained person approved by the Saṅgha’ here refers to one who has been previously approved. Hence it is said, “even though,” etc. Since causing fault-finding and disparaging arise by way of false speech, therefore, for the first offender, there is no offense—this should be understood as stated by this very means to show non-offense in the cases of pācittiya and dukkaṭa. And so, for one who causes fault-finding and who disparages, two offenses each are incurred in a single moment. Alternatively, it should be understood that this training rule was established before that concerning false speech. The rest here is clear. In this case, there are these six factors: approval by a formal act; being ordained; absence of going to a wrong course; the desire for his dispraise; the ordained status of the one in whose presence one speaks; and causing fault-finding or disparaging.

Ujjhāpanakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on causing fault-finding is concluded.

4. Paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the First Training Rule on Lodgings

108-110. Catutthe himavassenāti himameva vuttaṃ. Apaññāteti appatīte, appasiddheti attho. “Maṇḍape vā rukkhamūle vāti vacanato vivaṭaṅgaṇepi nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Gocarappasutāti gocaraṭṭhānaṃ paṭipannā. “Aṭṭha māse”ti iminā vassānaṃ cātumāsaṃ cepi devo na vassati, paṭikkhittamevāti āha “aṭṭha māseti vacanato…pe… nikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭatiyevā”ti. Tattha cattāro māseti vassānassa cattāro māse. Avassikasaṅketeti iminā anuññātepi aṭṭha māse yattha hemante devo vassati, tattha aparepi cattāro māsā paṭikkhittāti āha “avassikasaṅketeti vacanato”tiādi. Iminā imaṃ dīpeti “yasmiṃ dese hemante devo vassati, tattha aṭṭha māse paṭikkhipitvā cattāro māsā anuññātā. Yattha pana vassāneyeva vassati, tattha cattāro māse paṭikkhipitvā aṭṭha māsā anuññātā”ti.

In the fourth, “during the snow season” means that only “snow” is stated. “Not declared” means not apparent, unresolved—this is the meaning. From the statement, “whether in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree,” it is permissible to place them even in an open courtyard—this is mentioned in all three sub-commentaries. “Devoted to the alms-resort” means one who has gone to the alms-resort. “For eight months”—by this, even if it does not rain during the four months of the rainy season, it is indeed prohibited. It is stated, “the phrase ‘for eight months’…it is not permissible to place them at all.” Here, “four months” refers to the four months of the rainy season. “Without a rainy-season agreement”—by this, even if eight months are permitted, in a place where it rains in the winter, the other four months are prohibited. It is stated, “by the phrase ‘without a rainy-season agreement,’ etc.” This elucidates the following: “In a region where it rains in winter, after prohibiting for eight months, four months are permitted. But where it rains only in the rainy season, after prohibiting for four months, eight months are permitted.”

Imināva nayena majjhimapadese yattha hemante himavassaṃ vassati, tatthāpi aṭṭheva māsā paṭikkhittāti veditabbā. Tasmā vassānakāle pakatiajjhokāse ovassakamaṇḍape rukkhamūle ca santharituṃ na vaṭṭati, hemantakāle pakatiajjhokāse ovassakamaṇḍapādīsupi vaṭṭati. Tañca [M 3.0026] kho yattha himavassena senāsanaṃ na temati, gimhakālepi pakatiajjhokāsādīsu vaṭṭatiyeva, tañca kho akālameghādassane, kākādīnaṃ nibaddhavāsarukkhamūle pana kadācipi na vaṭṭatīti evamettha vinicchayo veditabbo.

By this same method, it should be understood that in the middle region where snow falls in winter, eight months are also prohibited. Therefore, during the rainy season, it is not permissible to spread bedding in a natural open space, in a pavilion exposed to rain, or at the foot of a tree; but in the winter, it is permissible even in a natural open space, in pavilions exposed to rain, and so on. And that is only where the lodging is not dampened by snowfall. Even in the hot season, it is permissible in natural open spaces and so on, provided there is no appearance of untimely clouds. But at the foot of a tree where crows and others habitually roost, it is never permissible. Thus, the determination here should be understood.

Imañca pana atthavisesaṃ gahetvā bhagavatā paṭhamameva sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti visuṃ anupaññatti na vuttā. Teneva hi mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “iti yattha ca yadā ca santharituṃ na vaṭṭati, taṃ sabbamidha ajjhokāsasaṅkhameva gata”nti. Atha vā avisesena ajjhokāse santharaṇasantharāpanāni paṭikkhipitvā “īdise kāle īdise ca padese ṭhapethā”ti anujānanamatteneva alanti na sikkhāpade [V 3.0024] visuṃ anupaññatti uddhaṭāti veditabbā. Parivāre (pari. 65-67) pana imasseva sikkhāpadassa anurūpavasena paññattattā “ekā anupaññattī”ti vuttaṃ.

Moreover, taking into account this special meaning, the Blessed One laid down the training rule at the very beginning, and so a separate supplementary rule was not stated. For this very reason, it is said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: “Thus, wherever and whenever it is not suitable to spread bedding, all of that is included here under the term ‘open air.’” Alternatively, it should be understood that having prohibited spreading and having bedding spread in the open air without distinction, it is sufficient merely to grant permission by saying, “In such a season and in such a place, you may place them,” and so a separate supplementary rule was not extracted in the training rule. In the Parivāra, however, because it was laid down in accordance with this same training rule, it is said, “There is one supplementary rule.”

Navavāyimo sīghaṃ na nassatīti āha “navavāyimo vā”ti. Onaddhakoti cammena onaddho. Ukkaṭṭhaabbhokāsikoti idaṃ tassa parivitakkadassanamattaṃ, ukkaṭṭhaabbhokāsikassa pana cīvarakuṭi na vaṭṭatīti natthi. Kāyānugatikattāti bhikkhuno tattheva sannihitabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Iminā ca tasmiṃyeva kāle anāpatti vuttā, cīvarakuṭito nikkhamitvā pana aññattha gacchantassa piṇḍāya pavisantassapi āpattiyeva. “Yasmā pana dāyakehi dānakāleyeva sahassagghanakampi kambalaṃ ‘pādapuñchaniṃ katvā paribhuñjathā’ti dinnaṃ tatheva paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā ‘imaṃ mañcapīṭhādisenāsanaṃ abbhokāsepi yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjathā’ti dāyakehi dinnaṃ ce, sabbasmimpi kāle abbhokāse nikkhipituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Pesetvā gantabbanti ettha “yo bhikkhu imaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgantvā vasati, tassa dethā”ti vatvā pesetabbaṃ.

A newly woven item does not quickly perish, hence it is said, “or a newly woven item.” ‘Covered’ means covered with leather. ‘An extreme open-air dweller’—this is merely to show his reflection; it is not the case that a robe-hut is not permissible for an extreme open-air dweller. ‘Because it follows the body’ is said in reference to the monk being present right there. And by this, non-offense is stated only for that time. But for one who leaves the robe-hut and goes elsewhere, or enters a village for alms, there is indeed an offense. Some say: “However, since when donors at the time of giving a blanket worth even a thousand say, ‘Use it as a foot-wiper,’ it is permissible to use it just so, therefore, if donors give a bed, bench, or other lodging, saying, ‘Use this in the open air as you please,’ then it is permissible to place it in the open air at all times.” ‘Having it sent, one should go’ means here that it should be sent after saying, ‘Give this to whichever monk comes and stays in this place.’

Valāhakānaṃ anuṭṭhitabhāvaṃ sallakkhetvāti iminā ca gimhānepi meghe uṭṭhite mañcapīṭhādiṃ yaṃkiñci senāsanaṃ ajjhokāse nikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭatīti dīpitanti veditabbaṃ. “Pādaṭṭhānābhimukhāti nisīdantānaṃ pādapatanaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti keci. “Sammajjantassa pādaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti apare. “Bahi vālukāya agamananimittaṃ pādaṭṭhānābhimukhā vālikā haritabbāti vutta”nti eke[M 3.0027]. Kacavaraṃ hatthehi gahetvā bahi chaṭṭetabbanti iminā kacavaraṃ chaḍḍessāmīti vālikā na chaḍḍetabbāti dīpeti.

“Having observed that clouds have not arisen”—by this it should be understood that it is indicated that even in the summer, if clouds have arisen, it is not permissible to leave any lodging such as a bed or bench in the open. Some say that “facing the place of the feet” means “facing the spot where the feet of those sitting would fall.” Others say, “facing the place of the feet of one who is sweeping.” Some say it is stated that “sand should be moved facing the place of the feet, so that it does not go outside.” “Rubbish should be taken by hand and discarded outside”—by this it is shown that sand should not be discarded with the thought, “I will discard rubbish.”

111. Anto saṃveṭhetvā baddhanti erakapattādīhi veṇiṃ katvā tāya veṇiyā ubhosu passesu vitthataṭṭhānesu bahuṃ veṭhetvā tato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhaṭṭhānaṃ, tāva anto ākaḍḍhanavasena veṭhetvā majjhe saṅkhipitvā tiriyaṃ tattha tattha bandhitvā kataṃ. Kappaṃ labhitvāti gacchāti vuttavacanena kappaṃ labhitvā. Therassa hi āṇattiyā gacchantassa anāpatti. Purimanayenevāti “nisīditvā sayaṃ gacchanto”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayeneva. Aññattha gacchatīti taṃ maggaṃ atikkamitvā aññattha gacchati. Leḍḍupātupacārato bahi ṭhitattā “pāduddhārena kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ, aññattha gacchantassa paṭhamapāduddhāre dukkaṭaṃ, dutiyapāduddhāre pācittiyanti attho. Pākatikaṃ akatvāti appaṭisāmetvā. Antarasannipāteti antarantarā sannipāte.

111. Having wrapped it inside, they bind it: this means having made a braid with leaves of eraka grass or the like, and with that braid, having wrapped it extensively in the spread-out places on both sides, then from there, having wrapped it inwards by pulling as far as the middle section, having gathered it in the middle, and having tied it crosswise here and there. 'Having obtained authorization': this means having obtained authorization by the spoken word, 'Go!' For one who goes by the command of an elder, there is no offense. 'By the previous method': this means by the method previously stated, beginning with 'having sat down, he goes himself.' 'He goes elsewhere': this means having passed that path, he goes to another place. Because he stands outside the vicinity of a clod's throw, it is said, 'it is to be done by the lifting of the foot.' For one going elsewhere, there is a dukkaṭa offense at the first lifting of the foot, and a pācittiya offense at the second lifting of the foot; this is the meaning. 'Without making it as it was': this means without putting it back. 'In gatherings in between': this means in gatherings at various intervals.

Āvāsikānaṃyeva palibodhoti ettha āgantukehi āgantvā kiñci avatvā tattha nisinnepi [V 3.0025] āvāsikānaṃyeva palibodhoti adhippāyo. Mahāpaccarivāde pana “aññesu āgantvā nisinnesū”ti idaṃ amhākanti vatvā vā avatvā vā nisinnesūti adhippāyo. Mahāaṭṭhakathāvāde “āpattī”ti pācittiyameva vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana santharaṇasantharāpane sati pācittiyena bhavitabbanti anāṇattiyā paññattattā dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ ussārakassa, idaṃ dhammakathikassā”ti visuṃ paññattattā anāṇattiyā paññattepi pācittiyeneva bhavitabbanti adhippāyena “tasmiṃ āgantvā nisinne tassa palibodho”ti vuttaṃ. Keci pana vadanti “anāṇattiyā paññattepi dhammakathikassa anuṭṭhāpanīyattā pācittiyena bhavitabbaṃ, āgantukassa pana pacchā āgatehi vuḍḍhatarehi uṭṭhāpetabbattā dukkaṭaṃ vutta”nti.

'The impediment is only for the residents': here, the intention is that even if visitors arrive and sit there without saying anything, the impediment is only for the residents. In the Mahāpaccarī, however, the intention of 'when others have arrived and sat down' is that this applies whether they have said, 'This is ours,' or not. In the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, when it says 'an offense,' only a pācittiya is meant. But in the Mahāpaccarī, it is said that although when there is a spreading or causing to be spread it should be a pācittiya offense, a dukkaṭa offense is stated because it was laid out without authorization. With the intention that because it was laid out separately—'This is for the arranger, this is for the Dhamma speaker'—even when laid out without authorization, it should be a pācittiya offense, it is said, 'When someone arrives and sits on it, it is an impediment for that person.' Some, however, say: 'Even when laid out without authorization, it should be a pācittiya offense because the Dhamma speaker is not to be made to get up; but for a visitor, a dukkaṭa offense is stated because they are to be made to get up by more senior monks who arrive later.'

112. Bhūmiyaṃ attharitabbāti cimilikāya sati tassā upari, asati suddhabhūmiyaṃ attharitabbā. Sīhacammādīnaṃ pariharaṇeyeva paṭikkhepo veditabboti iminā –

112. 'It should be spread on the ground': this means if there is a floor-spread, it should be spread on top of it; if there is not, it should be spread on the clean ground. By this, it should be understood that the prohibition on lion skins and so forth is only in the carrying of them around:

“Na[M 3.0028], bhikkhave, mahācammāni dhāretabbāni sīhacammaṃ byagghacammaṃ dīpicammaṃ, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 255) –

'Bhikkhus, large skins are not to be used: lion skin, tiger skin, leopard skin. Whoever should use one, commits an offense of wrong-doing.'

Evaṃ vuttāya khandhakapāḷiyā adhippāyaṃ vibhāveti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “antopi mañce paññattāni honti, bahipi mañce paññattāni hontī”ti imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ sikkhāpadassa paññattattā mañcapīṭhesu attharitvā paribhogoyeva paṭikkhitto, bhūmattharaṇavasena paribhogo pana appaṭikkhittoti. Yadi evaṃ “pariharaṇeyeva paṭikkhepo”ti idaṃ kasmā vuttanti? Yathā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ pāsādaparibhoga”nti (cūḷava. 320) vacanato puggalikepi senāsane senāsanaparibhogavasena niyamitaṃ suvaṇṇaghaṭādikaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭamānampi kevalaṃ attano santakaṃ katvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati, evamidaṃ bhūmattharaṇavasena paribhuñjiyamānampi attano santakaṃ katvā taṃ taṃ vihāraṃ haritvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatīti dassanatthaṃ “pariharaṇeyeva paṭikkhepo veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Dārumayapīṭhanti phalakamayameva pīṭhaṃ vuttaṃ. Pādakathalikanti adhotapādaṭṭhapanakaṃ. Ajjhokāse rajanaṃ pacitvā…pe… paṭisāmetabbanti ettha theve asati rajanakamme niṭṭhite paṭisāmetabbaṃ.

He clarifies the intention of the Pāḷi of the Khandhaka thus stated. This is what is said: 'They are spread even on a bed, and they are spread even off a bed.' Because the training rule was established in this case, the use by spreading them on beds and benches is prohibited, but their use as a ground-covering is not prohibited. If so, why is it said, 'The prohibition is only in the carrying of them around'? Just as, in accordance with the saying, 'I allow, bhikkhus, all use of monastery furnishings,' even in a personal lodging, it is permissible to use items such as a golden pot designated for use as lodging-furnishings, but it is not permissible to make them one's own property and use them; so too, even when this is being used as a ground-covering, it is not permissible to make it one's own property and, having carried it to this or that monastery, to use it. To show this, it is said, 'The prohibition is to be understood as being only in the carrying of it around.' 'A wooden bench' means a bench made of planks. 'A foot-mat': this means a place for putting unwashed feet. 'Having prepared dye in the open... it should be put away': here, this means that when there is no rain, and the work of dyeing is finished, it should be put away.

113. “Bhikkhu vā sāmaṇero vā ārāmiko vā lajjī hotīti vuttattā alajjiṃ āpucchitvā gantuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Otāpento gacchatīti ettha “kiñcāpi ‘ettakaṃ dūraṃ gantabba’nti paricchedo natthi, tathāpi leḍḍupātaṃ atikkamma nātidūraṃ gantabba”nti vadanti. Sesamettha [V 3.0026] uttānameva. Mañcādīnaṃ saṅghikatā, vuttalakkhaṇe dese santharaṇaṃ vā santharāpanaṃ vā, apalibuddhatā, āpadāya abhāvo, leḍḍupātātikkamoti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

113. They say, 'Because it is said, "A bhikkhu or a novice or a monastery attendant is a conscientious one," it is not proper to go after asking an unscrupulous one.' Regarding 'goes while sunning it,' they say, 'Although there is no limit stating, "One should go this far," still, having crossed the distance of a clod's throw, one should not go too far.' The rest here is clear. The five factors here are: that the beds and so forth belong to the Sangha; the spreading or causing to be spread in a place with the stated characteristics; being unencumbered; the absence of danger; and the exceeding of a clod's throw.

Mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) pana anāpucchaṃ vā gaccheyyāti ettha “yo bhikkhu vā sāmaṇero vā ārāmiko vā lajjī hoti, attano palibodhaṃ viya maññati, tathārūpaṃ anāpucchitvā taṃ senāsanaṃ tassa aniyyātetvā nirapekkho gacchati, thāmamajjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupātaṃ atikkameyya, ekena pādena leḍḍupātātikkame dukkaṭaṃ, dutiyapādātikkame pācittiya”nti vatvā aṅgesupi nirapekkhatāya saddhiṃ cha aṅgāni [M 3.0029] vuttāni. Pāḷiyaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāyañca “nirapekkho gacchatī”ti ayaṃ viseso na dissati. “Otāpento gacchatī”ti ca otāpanavisaye eva sāpekkhagamane anāpatti vuttā. Yadi aññatthāpi sāpekkhagamane anāpatti siyā, “anāpatti sāpekkho gacchatī”ti avisesena vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, tasmā vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbanti.

In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, however, regarding 'or should go without asking,' it is said: 'Whatever bhikkhu, novice, or monastery attendant is conscientious and considers it like an impediment for himself—if one goes away indifferent without asking such a person and without entrusting that lodging to him, and should cross the distance of a clod's throw of a man of medium strength, there is a dukkaṭa offense in crossing the clod's-throw distance with one foot, and a pācittiya offense in crossing with the second foot.' Having said this, among the factors, six factors are stated including indifference. However, in the Pāḷi and the commentary, this specific detail 'goes away indifferent' is not seen. And regarding 'goes while sunning it,' an exception from offense is stated for going with concern only in the case of sunning. If there were an exception from offense for going with concern in other cases too, it should have been stated without distinction, 'There is no offense for one who goes with concern.' Therefore, having investigated, the more suitable interpretation should be adopted.

Paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the First Training Rule concerning Lodgings is concluded.

5. Dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Second Training Rule concerning Lodgings.

116. Dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpade ettakameva vuttanti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. “Idañca aṭṭhakathāsu tathāvuttabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, aññampi tādisaṃ mañcapīṭhesu attharitaṃ paccattharaṇamevā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “paccattharaṇaṃ nāma pāvāro kojavoti ettakamevā”ti niyametvā vuttaṃ, tasmā gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ iminā na sameti, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Senāsanatoti sabbapacchimasenāsanato. Yo kocīti tassa ñātako vā aññātako vā yo koci.

116. In the commentaries it is said, 'In the Second Training Rule concerning Lodgings, only this much is stated.' In all three Gaṇṭhipadas it is said: 'And this is stated to show that it was said thus in the commentaries; and any other such thing spread on beds and benches is just a covering.' In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is stated with the specification: 'A covering means only a cloak or a woolen rug.' Therefore, what is said in the Gaṇṭhipadas does not agree with this; it should be examined and then adopted. 'From the lodging' means from the very last lodging. 'Whoever' means anyone, whether a relative of his or not.

117. Pariveṇanti ekekassa vihārassa parikkhepabbhantaraṃ. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttamevatthaṃ savisesaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “kiñcāpi vutto”tiādi āraddhaṃ. “Aparicchanne maṇḍape”ti visuṃ yojetabbaṃ. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “aparicchannamaṇḍape vā paricchanne vāpi bahūnaṃ sannipātabhūte”ti vuttaṃ. Bhojanasālāyampi ayaṃ viseso labbhatiyeva. Vattabbaṃ natthīti visesetvā kiñci vattabbaṃ natthi. Palujjatīti vinassati. Nasseyyāti corādīhi vinasseyya.

117. 'A monastic compound' means the area inside the enclosure of each monastery. To show the very meaning stated in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, having presented it with its distinctions, the passage beginning 'Although it is said...' is commenced. 'In an unenclosed pavilion' should be construed separately. For that reason, in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā it is said: '...in an unenclosed pavilion, or in an enclosed one that is a place where many gather.' This distinction is indeed also found regarding the dining hall. 'There is nothing to be said' means there is nothing further to specify. 'It perishes' means it is destroyed. 'It might be lost' means it might be destroyed by thieves and so on.

118. Yena [V 3.0027] mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā vinanti, taṃ mañcapīṭhakavānaṃ. Siluccayaleṇanti siluccaye leṇaṃ, pabbataguhāti attho. “Senāsanaṃ upacikāhi khāyita”nti imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ paññattattā vatthuanurūpavasena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ upacikāsaṅkāya abhāve anāpatti vuttā. Vattakkhandhake gamikavattaṃ paññapentena [M 3.0030] “senāsanaṃ āpucchitabba”nti vuttattā kevalaṃ itikattabbākāramattadassanatthaṃ “āpucchanaṃ pana vatta”nti vuttaṃ, na pana vattabhedena dukkaṭanti dassanatthaṃ. Teneva andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “senāsanaṃ āpucchitabba”nti ettha “yaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ vā pāsāṇatthambhesu vā katasenāsanaṃ yattha upacikā nārohanti, taṃ anāpucchantassapi anāpattī”ti vakkhati, tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ gaṇṭhipade “tādise senāsane anāpucchā gacchantassa pācittiyaṃ natthi, gamikavattavasena pana anāpucchā gacchato vattabhedo hoti, tasmā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatī”ti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

118. That which is used to weave a bed or a chair is called ‘mañcapīṭhakavāna’. ‘Siluccayaleṇa’ means a dwelling in a rock pile, that is, a mountain cave. Because it was prescribed in the case of ‘a lodging eaten by termites,’ the commentary states that there is no offense in the absence of suspicion of termites, according to the specifics of the case. Because it was stated ‘one should ask permission for a lodging’ by the one who laid down the traveler's duties in the Vattakkhandhaka, the statement ‘but asking permission is a duty’ is said merely to show the procedure, not to indicate a dukkaṭa offense through a breach of duty. Therefore, in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, regarding ‘one should ask permission for a lodging,’ it will be said: ‘that lodging which is made on a stone surface or stone pillars, where termites do not climb, there is no offense even for one not asking permission’; therefore, that which is said in the Gaṇṭhipada—‘for one going from such a lodging without asking permission, there is no pācittiya, but for one who travels without asking permission regarding the traveler's duty, there is a breach of duty, therefore he incurs a dukkaṭa’—that should not be taken as authoritative.

Pacchimassa ābhogena mutti natthīti tassa pacchato gacchantassa aññassa abhāvato vuttaṃ. Ekaṃ vā pesetvā āpucchitabbanti ettha gamanacittassa uppannaṭṭhānato anāpucchitvā gacchato dutiyapāduddhāre pācittiyaṃ. Kiñcāpi mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā ajjhokāse nikkhipitvā gacchantassa idha visuṃ āpatti na vuttā, tathāpi akāle ajjhokāse mañcapīṭhāni paññapetvā gacchantassa leḍḍupātātikkame purimasikkhāpadena pācittiyaṃ, parikkhepātikkame iminā dukkaṭanti veditabbaṃ. “Maṇḍape vā rukkhamūle vā”ti iminā ajjhokāsopi saṅgahitoyevāti tatthāpi dukkaṭaṃ idha vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Seyyaṃ pana ajjhokāse santharitvā gacchantassa ubhayenapi dukkaṭameva. “Saṅghike vihāre saṅghikaṃyeva seyyaṃ santharitvā pakkamantassa pācittiyaṃ vuttanti ubhosu ekekasmiṃ saṅghike dukkaṭa”nti vadanti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Vuttalakkhaṇaseyyā, tassā saṅghikatā, vuttalakkhaṇe vihāre santharaṇaṃ vā santharāpanaṃ vā, apalibuddhatā, āpadāya abhāvo, anapekkhassa disāpakkamanaṃ, upacārasīmātikkamoti imāni panettha satta aṅgāni.

Regarding the statement, 'For the last person, there is no exemption through informing another,' this is said because there is no one else going after him. Regarding 'Or having sent someone, one should ask permission,' for one who departs without asking permission from the place where the thought of going has arisen, a pācittiya offense is incurred at the lifting of the second foot. Although no separate offense is stated here for one who leaves after placing a bed or a chair in an open space, nevertheless, it should be understood that for one who sets out beds or chairs in an open space at an inappropriate time and then departs, there is a pācittiya offense under the previous training rule upon transgressing the distance of a clod's throw, and a dukkaṭa offense under this rule upon transgressing the enclosure. By the phrase ‘in a pavilion or at the root of a tree,’ an open space is also included; therefore, it should be understood that a dukkaṭa offense in that case is also spoken of here. For one who, however, spreads out bedding in an open space and departs, there is a dukkaṭa offense under both rules. They say, 'It is said that for one who departs after spreading out a Sangha-owned sleeping place in a Sangha-owned dwelling, a pācittiya offense is incurred; therefore, for each of the two Sangha-owned items, a dukkaṭa is incurred.' The rest here is clear. The sleeping place with the stated characteristics, its being Sangha-owned, the spreading or having it spread in a dwelling with the stated characteristics, not being bound by an obligation, the absence of an emergency, the departure of one who is unconcerned, and the transgression of the boundary of the environs—these are the seven factors here.

Dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule concerning lodgings is finished.

6. Anupakhajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Encroaching

119-121. Chaṭṭhe anupavisitvāti samīpaṃ pavisitvā. Bahūpakārataṃ guṇavisiṭṭhatañca sallakkhentoti [V 3.0028] bhaṇḍāgārikassa bahūpakārataṃ dhammakathikādīnaṃ guṇavisiṭṭhatañca sallakkhento. Samantā diyaḍḍho hatthoti majjhe paññattamañcapīṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

In the sixth rule, 'having entered' means having approached. 'Considering the great assistance and the distinguished qualities' refers to considering the great assistance of the storekeeper and the distinguished qualities of the Dhamma preachers and others. 'One and a half cubits all around' is said in reference to the bed or chair set up in the middle.

122. Upacāraṃ [M 3.0031] ṭhapetvāti vuttalakkhaṇaṃ upacāraṃ ṭhapetvā. Ekavihāreti ekasmiṃ senāsane. Ekapariveṇeti tassa vihārassa parikkhepabbhantare. “Gilāno pavisatītiādīsu anāpattikāraṇasabbhāvato gilānāditāya pavisissāmīti upacāraṃ pavisantassa satipi sambādhetukāmatāya anāpatti vuttāyevā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Evañca sati agilānādibhāvopi visuṃ aṅgesu vattabbo siyā, mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. anupakhajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) pana “saṅghikavihāratā, anuṭṭhāpanīyabhāvajānanaṃ, sambādhetukāmatā, upacāre nisīdanaṃ vā nipajjanaṃ vāti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgānī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ, tasmā vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

122. 'Having set aside the environs' means having set aside the environs with the stated characteristics. 'In a single dwelling' means in a single lodging. 'In a single compound' means within the enclosure of that dwelling. It is said in all three Gaṇṭhipadas: 'In cases such as "a sick person enters," because there exist reasons for no offense, for one entering the environs with the thought "I will enter on account of being sick, etc.," no offense is stated even if there is a desire to cause crowding.' This being the case, the state of not being sick and so on should also be included as a separate factor. In the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, however, only this much is said: 'Being a Sangha dwelling, knowing that the person is not to be made to get up, the desire to cause crowding, and sitting or lying down in the environs—these are the four factors here.' Therefore, this should be investigated.

Anupakhajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on encroaching is finished.

7. Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Expulsion

126. Sattame koṭṭhakānīti dvārakoṭṭhakāni. “Nikkhamāti vacanaṃ sutvāpi attano ruciyā nikkhamati, anāpattī”ti vadanti.

126. In the seventh, 'compartments' refers to door frames. They say, "Even after hearing the words 'Leave,' if one leaves according to one's own inclination, there is no offense."

128. Alajjiṃ nikkaḍḍhatītiādīsu paṭhamaṃ alajjīādibhāvena nikkaḍḍhissāmīti cintetvā nikkaḍḍhantassa cittassa lahuparivattitāya kope uppannepi anāpatti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Saṅghikavihāro, upasampannassa bhaṇḍanakārakabhāvādivinimuttatā, kopena nikkaḍḍhanaṃ vā nikkaḍḍhāpanaṃ vāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

128. In cases such as 'he expels a shameless one,' for one who expels after first thinking, 'I will expel him for being shameless, etc.,' there is no offense even if anger arises, due to the quick-changing nature of the mind. The rest here is clear. A Sangha dwelling; the ordained person being free from being a maker of quarrels, etc.; expelling or causing to be expelled out of anger—these are the three factors here.

Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on expulsion is finished.

8. Vehāsakuṭisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Vehāsakuṭi Training Rule

129-131. Aṭṭhame uparimatale padarānaṃ asantharitattā “upariacchannatalāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Pubbe vuttanayenevāti anupakhajjasikkhāpade vuttanayeneva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Saṅghiko vihāro[V 3.0029], asīsaghaṭṭā vehāsakuṭi[M 3.0032], heṭṭhā saparibhogatā, apaṭāṇidinne āhaccapādake nisīdanaṃ vā nipajjanaṃ vāti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

In the eighth rule, because the floorboards on the upper level were not laid, it is called 'having an uncovered upper floor.' 'In the way previously stated' means in the way stated in the Anupakhajja training rule. The rest is easily understood. A Sangha dwelling; a high-level hut that is not head-bumping; the lower part having things for use; sitting or lying on a bed with removable legs that has not been given a stand—these are the four factors here.

Vehāsakuṭisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Vehāsakuṭi training rule is finished.

9. Mahallakavihārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Training Rule on a Large Dwelling

135. Navame “mahallako nāma vihāro sasāmiko”ti vuttattā saññācikāya kuṭiyā anāpatti. “Aḍḍhateyyahatthampī”ti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena vuttavacanaṃ pāḷiyā sametīti āha “taṃ suvutta”nti. “Pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇassa okāsassa dassitattā kavāṭaṃ aḍḍhateyyahatthavitthārato ūnakaṃ vā hotu adhikaṃ vā, aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇaṃyeva okāso”ti vadanti.

135. In the ninth rule, because it is said, 'A large dwelling is one with an owner,' there is no offense in the case of a hut obtained by begging. The statement 'Even two and a half cubits' is said as the maximum limit and agrees with the Pāḷi; therefore, he said, 'That is well said.' They say, "Because in the Pāḷi and the commentary the space of two and a half cubits is shown as the maximum limit, whether the door is less or more than two and a half cubits in width, the space is just two and a half cubits."

Yassa vemajjheti yassa vihārassa vemajjhe. Sā aparipūraupacārāpi hotīti vivariyamānaṃ kavāṭaṃ yaṃ bhittiṃ āhanati, sā samantā kavāṭavitthārappamāṇaupacārarahitāpi hotīti attho. Ālokaṃ sandheti pidhetīti ālokasandhi. “Punappunaṃ chādāpesi, punappunaṃ limpāpesīti imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ uppannadosena sikkhāpadassa paññattattā lepaṃ anujānantena ca dvārabandhassa samantā aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇeyeva padese punappunaṃ lepassa anuññātattā tato aññattha punappunaṃ limpentassa vā limpāpentassa vā bhittiyaṃ mattikāya kattabbakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā puna catutthalepe dinne pācittiyena bhavitabba”nti vadanti. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana tīsupi “punappunaṃ lepadānassa vuttappamāṇato aññattha paṭikkhittamattaṃ ṭhapetvā pācittiyassa avuttattā dukkaṭaṃ anurūpa”nti vuttaṃ.

'In the middle of which' means in the middle of which dwelling. 'It has an incomplete precinct' means that when the opening door strikes a wall, that wall is also without a precinct all around of the same measure as the door's width. It joins and closes off the light, hence it is a light-opening. Because the training rule was established due to a fault that arose in this story, 'He had it repeatedly roofed, he had it repeatedly plastered,' and because the one who permitted plastering allowed repeated plastering only in the area measuring two and a half cubits around the doorframe, they say: 'Therefore, for one who repeatedly plasters or has plastered elsewhere, after the work to be done on the wall with clay has been finished, a pācittiya offense should be incurred when the fourth coat of plaster is applied.' In the Gaṇṭhipadas, however, in all three it is said: 'Since, apart from the mere prohibition of repeated application of plaster elsewhere than the stated measure, a pācittiya offense is not mentioned, a dukkaṭa offense is appropriate.'

Adhiṭṭhātabbanti saṃvidhātabbaṃ. Appahariteti ettha appa-saddo “appiccho”tiādīsu viya abhāvatthoti āha “aharite”ti. Patanokāsoti patanokāsattā tatra ṭhitassa bhikkhuno upari pateyyāti adhippāyo. Sace harite ṭhito adhiṭṭheti, āpatti dukkaṭassāti vacanena imamatthaṃ dīpeti – sace vihārassa samantā vuttappamāṇe paricchede pubbaṇṇādīni na santi, tattha vihāro kāretabbo. Yattha pana santi, tattha kārāpentassa dukkaṭanti.

“It should be determined” means it should be arranged. In “with little foliage,” the word “little” (appa) here signifies absence, as in “one of few wishes,” and so forth. Therefore, it says “without foliage.” “A place where things may fall” means that because it is a place where things may fall, the intention is that something might fall upon a bhikkhu standing there. The statement, “If one determines while standing in a place with foliage, it is an offense of wrong-doing,” clarifies this meaning: if, around the monastery within the specified boundary, there are no crops such as early grain, then a monastery should be caused to be built there. But where they do exist, for one who causes it to be built, it is an offense of wrong-doing.

136. Ekekaṃ [M 3.0033] maggaṃ ujukameva uṭṭhapetvā chādanaṃ maggena chādanaṃ nāma hotīti dassetuṃ [V 3.0030] “maggena chādentassā”ti vuttaṃ. Iminā pana nayena sabbasmiṃ vihāre ekavāraṃ chādite taṃ chadanaṃ ekamagganti gahetvā “dve magge”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Pariyāyena chādanepi imināva nayena yojetabba”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ, taṃ “punappunaṃ chādāpesī”ti imāya pāḷiyā “sabbampi cetaṃ chadanaṃ chadanūpari veditabba”nti iminā aṭṭhakathāvacanena ca sameti, tasmā dve magge adhiṭṭhahitvā tatiyāya maggaṃ āṇāpetvā pakkamitabbanti ettha dve chadanāni adhiṭṭhahitvā tatiyaṃ chadanaṃ “evaṃ chādehī”ti āṇāpetvā pakkamitabbanti evamattho gahetabbo.

136. To show that covering by setting up each course straight is called “covering by a course,” it is said, “for one who covers by a course.” By this method, when the entire monastery is covered once, that covering is taken as one course, and thus “two courses,” and so on, is said. “Even when covering in rotation, it should be applied by this same method”—this is said in all three knot-passages. This accords with the Pāli text “he had it covered again and again” and with this commentary statement, “and all this covering should be understood as being upon the previous covering.” Therefore, in the phrase “having determined two courses, one should depart after giving an order for the third course,” the meaning should be understood thus: having determined two coverings, one should depart after giving the order for a third covering, saying, “Cover it in this way.”

Keci pana “paṭhamaṃ tāva ekavāraṃ aparisesaṃ chādetvā puna chadanadaṇḍake bandhitvā dutiyavāraṃ tatheva chādetabbaṃ, tatiyavāracatutthavāre sampatte dve magge adhiṭṭhahitvā āṇāpetvā pakkamitabba”nti vadanti. Apare pana “paṭhamavāreyeva tayopi magge adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati, catutthato paṭṭhāya āpatti pācittiya”nti vadanti. Tadubhayampi pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca na sameti. Tatiyāya magganti ettha tatiyāyāti upayogatthe sampadānavacanaṃ, tatiyaṃ magganti attho. Tiṇṇaṃ maggānanti maggavasena chāditānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ chadanānaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ pariyāyānanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Catutthe magge vā pariyāye vāti ca tathā chādentānaṃ catutthaṃ chādanameva vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Mahallakavihāratā, attano vāsāgāratā, uttari adhiṭṭhānanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

Some, however, say: “First, one should cover it completely one time, then, having tied the covering-poles, one should cover it in the same way a second time. When the third and fourth times are reached, one should determine two courses, give the order, and then depart.” Others, however, say: “It is permissible to determine all three courses on the very first occasion; from the fourth onwards, it is a pācittiya offense.” Both of these views do not accord with the Pāli text and the commentary. In the phrase “for the third course” (tatiyāya maggaṃ), the word “tatiyāya” is a dative used in the sense of purpose, meaning “the third course” (tatiyaṃ maggaṃ). “Of three courses” means of the three coverings which have been covered by way of courses. “Of three rotations”—here too, this is the method. And “on the fourth course or rotation” refers to the fourth covering itself for those who are covering in such a way. The rest is self-evident. The fact of it being a large monastery, the fact of it being one's own dwelling, and determining beyond the limit—these are the three factors here.

Mahallakavihārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning a large monastery is concluded.

10. Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Water Containing Living Beings

140. Dasame imassa sikkhāpadassa “siñceyya vā siñcāpeyya vā”ti bāhiraparibhogavasena paṭhamaṃ paññattattā “sappāṇakaṃ udakaṃ paribhuñjeyyā”ti sikkhāpadaṃ attano nahānapānādiparibhogavasena paññattanti veditabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ vā paṭhamaṃ paññattepi attano paribhogavaseneva paññattattā [M 3.0034] puna imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ bāhiraparibhogavaseneva paññattanti gahetabbaṃ.

10. In the tenth training rule: because in this training rule “one might sprinkle or cause to be sprinkled” was first laid down with regard to external use, it should be understood that the training rule “one might use water containing living beings” was laid down with regard to one's own use, such as for bathing and drinking. Or, even if that latter rule was laid down first, since it was laid down with regard to one's own use, it should be understood that this training rule was laid down again with regard to external use.

Sappāṇakasaññissa “paribhogena pāṇakā marissantī”ti pubbabhāge jānantassapi siñcanasiñcāpanaṃ “padīpe nipatitvā paṭaṅgādipāṇakā marissantī”ti jānantassa padīpujjalanaṃ viya vināpi vadhakacetanāya hotīti āha “paṇṇattivajja”nti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva[V 3.0031]. Udakassa sappāṇakatā, “siñcanena pāṇakā marissantī”ti jānanaṃ, tādisameva ca udakaṃ, vinā vadhakacetanāya kenacideva karaṇīyena tiṇādīnaṃ siñcananti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

140. For one who perceives it as containing living beings, even when knowing beforehand “living beings will die through its use,” the act of sprinkling or causing to be sprinkled occurs even without an intention to kill—like the lighting of a lamp by one who knows “moths and other creatures will die by falling into it.” Therefore, it is said to be “an offense by regulation” (paṇṇattivajja). The rest is of clear meaning. The fact that the water contains living beings; the knowledge that “living beings will die through the sprinkling”; the water being of such a nature; and the sprinkling of grass and so forth for some necessary purpose without an intention to kill—these are the four factors here.

Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning water with living beings is concluded.

Niṭṭhito senāsanavaggo dutiyo.

The second chapter, the Section on Lodgings, is concluded.

Bhūtagāmavaggotipi imasseva nāmaṃ.

The Section on Plant Life (Bhūtagāmavagga) is also a name for this same chapter.

3. Ovādavaggo

3. The Chapter on Exhortation

1. Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Exhortation

144. Bhikkhunivaggassa paṭhamasikkhāpade kathānusārenāti “so thero kiṃsīlo kiṃsamācāro katarakulā pabbajito”tiādinā pucchantānaṃ pucchākathānusārena. Kathetuṃ vaṭṭantīti nirāmiseneva cittena kathetuṃ vaṭṭanti. Aniyyānikattā saggamokkhamaggānaṃ tiracchānabhūtā kathā tiracchānakathāti āha “saggamaggagamanepī”tiādi. Api-saddena pageva mokkhamaggagamaneti dīpeti. Tiracchānabhūtanti tirokaraṇabhūtaṃ, bādhikanti vuttaṃ hoti. Laddhāsevanā hi tiracchānakathā saggamokkhānaṃ bādhikāva hoti. Samiddhoti paripuṇṇo. Sahitatthoti yuttattho. Atthagambhīratādiyogato gambhīro. Bahurasoti attharasādibahuraso. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhasaṃyuttoti aniccādilakkhaṇapaṭivedharasaāvahanato lakkhaṇapaṭivedhasaṃyutto.

In the first training rule of the Section on Nuns: “According to the discussion” means according to the sequence of the questioning, such as, “What is that elder's virtue? What is his conduct? From what family did he go forth?” and so on. “It is proper to speak” means it is proper to speak with a disinterested mind. Because it is not conducive to release, talk that is an obstruction to the paths to heaven and liberation is called “animal talk”; thus it says, “even in going on the path to heaven,” and so on. By the word “even” (api), it shows how much more so in going on the path to liberation. “Being an obstruction” (tiracchānabhūtaṃ) means that which causes concealment (tirokaraṇabhūtaṃ); “a hindrance” is what is said. For animal talk, when habitually practiced, is indeed a hindrance to heaven and liberation. “Rich” (samiddha) means complete. “Coherent in meaning” (sahitattha) means having a suitable meaning. It is “profound” (gambhīra) due to its connection with profundity of meaning and so forth. “Of many flavors” (bahurasa) means having many flavors, such as the flavor of the meaning. “Connected with the penetration of the characteristics” (lakkhaṇapaṭivedhasaṃyutta) is so called because it conveys the flavor of the penetration of the characteristics of impermanence and so on.

145-147. Paratoti parattha, uttarinti attho. Karontovāti paribāhire karontoyeva. Pātimokkhoti cārittavārittappabhedaṃ sikkhāpadasīlaṃ[M 3.0035]. Tañhi yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehi, tasmā “pātimokkha”nti vuccati. Saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro, kāyavacīdvārānaṃ pidahanaṃ. Yena hi te saṃvutā pihitā honti, so saṃvaro, kāyikavācasikassa avītikkamassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarena saṃvutoti pātimokkhasaṃvarena pihitakāyavacīdvāro. Tathābhūto ca yasmā tena samaṅgī nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “samannāgato”ti[V 3.0032]. Vattatīti attabhāvaṃ pavatteti. Viharatīti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle ṭhitassa bhikkhuno iriyāpathavihāro dassito.

3. “Further” (parato) means in another place, beyond. “While doing” (karontova) means while doing so externally. “Pātimokkha” is the virtue of the training rules, distinguished as observances and avoidances. For it protects (pāti) one who guards it, and it liberates (mokkheti), frees, him from sufferings such as those of the states of deprivation; therefore, it is called “Pātimokkha.” Restraining is restraint (saṃvaro), the closing of the doors of body and speech. For that by which these are restrained and closed is restraint; this is a name for the non-transgression of bodily and verbal actions. “Restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint” means one whose doors of body and speech are closed by the Pātimokkha restraint. And because one who is so becomes endowed with it, it is said “endowed” (samannāgato). “He conducts himself” (vattati) means he carries on his individual existence. By “he dwells” (viharati), the abiding in the four postures of a bhikkhu established in the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint is shown.

Saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato pāḷiyā vibhāvetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha vibhaṅgeti jhānavibhaṅge. Sīlaṃ patiṭṭhātiādīni pātimokkhasseva vevacanāni. Tattha (vibha. aṭṭha. 511) sīlanti kāmañcetaṃ saha kammavācāpariyosānena ijjhanakassa pātimokkhasseva vevacanaṃ, evaṃ santepi dhammato etaṃ sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanādayo dhammā veditabbā. Yasmā pana pātimokkhasīlena bhikkhu sāsane patiṭṭhāti nāma, tasmā taṃ “patiṭṭhā”ti vuttaṃ. Patiṭṭhahati vā ettha bhikkhu, kusaladhammā eva vā ettha patiṭṭhahantīti patiṭṭhā. Ayamattho “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192) ca “patiṭṭhā, mahārāja, sīlaṃ sabbesaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammāna”nti (mi. pa. 2.1.9) ca “sīle patiṭṭhitassa kho, mahārāja, sabbe kusalā dhammā na parihāyantī”ti ca ādisuttavasena veditabbo.

1. To clarify in detail by means of the Pāli text the meaning stated briefly, the passage beginning “For it has been said...” is introduced. Therein, “in the Vibhaṅga” means in the Jhānavibhaṅga. “Virtue,” “foundation,” and so on are synonyms for the Pātimokkha itself. Therein, “virtue”—although this is a synonym for the Pātimokkha which is accomplished together with the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā)—even so, in terms of its nature, this “virtue” should be understood as the mental factors, such as volition, of one who is abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who is fulfilling the duties and observances. And because a bhikkhu is said to be established in the Dispensation by means of the Pātimokkha virtue, it is therefore called “foundation” (patiṭṭhā). Or, a bhikkhu is established herein, or wholesome states are established herein; therefore, it is a “foundation.” This meaning should be understood by way of suttas such as: “A wise person established in virtue” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.23, 192), “Virtue, great king, is the foundation of all wholesome states” (Mi. Pa. 2.1.9), and “For one established in virtue, great king, all wholesome states do not decline,” and so on.

Tadetaṃ pubbuppattiatthena ādi. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

144. This same virtue is the “beginning” in the sense of prior arising. And this has also been said:

“Tasmātiha tvaṃ, uttiya, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ diṭṭhi ca ujukā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.382).

Therefore, Uttiya, here purify the very beginning in wholesome qualities. And what is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Well-purified virtue and a straight view.

Yathā hi nagaravaḍḍhakī nagaraṃ māpetukāmo paṭhamaṃ nagaraṭṭhānaṃ sodheti, tato aparabhāge vīthicatukkasiṅghāṭakādiparicchedena vibhajitvā nagaraṃ māpeti, evameva yogāvacaro ādimhi sīlaṃ sodheti, tato aparabhāge [M 3.0036] samādhivipassanāmaggaphalanibbānāni sacchikaroti. Yathā vā pana rajako paṭhamaṃ tīhi khārehi vatthaṃ dhovitvā parisuddhe vatthe yadicchakaṃ raṅgajātaṃ upaneti, yathā vā pana cheko cittakāro rūpaṃ likhitukāmo ādito bhittiparikammaṃ karoti, tato aparabhāge rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, evameva yogāvacaro āditova sīlaṃ visodhetvā aparabhāge samathavipassanādayo dhamme sacchikaroti. Tasmā sīlaṃ “ādī”ti vuttaṃ.

Just as a city architect, wishing to build a city, first clears the city site, then later divides it with sections such as streets, squares, and crossroads before constructing the city, so too does a yogi first purify virtue, and later realizes concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Or, just as a dyer first washes a cloth with three kinds of alkali, and only when the cloth is purified does he apply the desired color, or just as a skilled artist, wishing to paint a picture, first prepares the wall, and only later creates the image, so too does a yogi first purify virtue and later realizes the qualities of serenity, insight, and so on. Therefore, virtue is called the 'beginning.'

Tadetaṃ caraṇasarikkhatāya caraṇaṃ. “Caraṇā”ti pādā vuccanti. Yathā hi chinnacaraṇassa purisassa disaṃgamanābhisaṅkhāro na jāyati, paripuṇṇapādasseva jāyati, evameva yassa sīlaṃ bhinnaṃ [V 3.0033] hoti khaṇḍaṃ aparipuṇṇaṃ, tassa nibbānagamanāya ñāṇagamanaṃ na sampajjati. Yassa pana taṃ abhinnaṃ hoti akhaṇḍaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, tassa nibbānagamanāya ñāṇagamanaṃ sampajjati. Tasmā sīlaṃ “caraṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

This is called 'conduct' (caraṇa) because it is similar to a foot. 'Feet' are called 'caraṇa'. Just as a person whose feet are cut off cannot generate the intention to travel to a destination, while one with intact feet can, so too, for one whose virtue is broken, flawed, or incomplete, the progression of knowledge towards Nibbāna is not accomplished. But for one whose virtue is unbroken, unflawed, and complete, the progression of knowledge towards Nibbāna is accomplished. Therefore, virtue is called 'conduct.'

Tadetaṃ saṃyamanavasena saṃyamo, saṃvaraṇavasena saṃvaroti ubhayenapi sīlasaṃyamo ceva sīlasaṃvaro ca kathito. Vacanattho panettha saṃyameti vītikkamavipphandanaṃ, puggalaṃ vā saṃyameti vītikkamavasena tassa vipphandituṃ na detīti saṃyamo, vītikkamassa pavesanadvāraṃ saṃvarati pidahatīti saṃvaro. Mokkhanti uttamaṃ mukhabhūtaṃ vā. Yathā hi sattānaṃ catubbidho āhāro mukhena pavisitvā aṅgamaṅgāni pharati, evaṃ yoginopi catubhūmakakusalaṃ sīlamukhena pavisitvā atthasiddhiṃ sampādeti. Tena vuttaṃ “mokkha”nti. Pamukhe sādhūti pamokkhaṃ, pubbaṅgamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ padhānanti attho. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyāti catubhūmakakusalānaṃ paṭilābhatthāya pamokkhaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ padhānanti veditabbaṃ.

This is called 'restraint' (saṃyama) by way of restraining, and 'guarding' (saṃvara) by way of guarding; thus, in both ways, it is spoken of as 'virtuous restraint' (sīlasaṃyama) and 'virtuous guarding' (sīlasaṃvara). Herein, the meaning is: 'it restrains' (saṃyameti), meaning it restrains the agitation from transgression, or it restrains a person, not allowing them to become agitated through transgression—thus it is 'restraint' (saṃyama). 'It guards' (saṃvarati), meaning it closes or shuts the door of entry for transgression—thus it is 'guarding' (saṃvara). 'Mokkha' means supreme, or it is that which is a mouth (mukha).
