Gaṇavasena vā [V 3.0050] nimantitattā te bhikkhū apakataññutāya kukkuccāyantā na paṭiggaṇhiṃsūti ayaṃ amhākaṃ khanti, vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Since this training rule was laid down in the case of eating after making a request, a group meal by request is evident by the very nature of the case. Without stating that, in the word-analysis, 'a group meal is where… (etc.) …those invited eat,' a group meal is spoken of in terms of an invitation. Lest some might have the doubt, 'Could some training rule be inconsistent with its subject matter? Does a group meal occur solely by way of invitation, according to the method stated in the word-analysis?', to dispel that, it is said: 'But this group meal arises in two ways.' Here, regarding 'having taken the name of the five foods,' some say, 'Even when it is said, "Take food," it is still a group meal.' In all three difficult passages it is said: 'Previously, in the case of a journey and the case of embarking on a boat, when it was said, "Venerable sirs, eat right here," because, being scrupulous, they did not accept, therefore, even when it is said, "Eat," it is not a group meal.' However, since it is said, 'Having taken the name of the five foods, one invites,' a group meal occurs only when it is said having taken the name of a food, such as 'Eat rice' or 'Eat a meal,' but not otherwise. Even in the case of 'Venerable sirs, eat right here,' it should be understood that they invited them only after saying 'rice' or 'a meal.' Or, because they were invited as a group, those monks, being unskilled in the discipline, were scrupulous and did not accept—this is our view. Having investigated, the more suitable interpretation should be adopted.

Ekato gaṇhantīti ettha aññamaññassa dvādasahatthaṃ amuñcitvā ṭhitā ekato gaṇhanti nāmāti gahetabbaṃ. “Amhākaṃ catunnampi bhattaṃ dehīti vā viññāpeyyu”nti vacanato heṭṭhā “tvaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno bhattaṃ dehi, tvaṃ dvinnanti evaṃ viññāpetvā”ti vacanato ca attano atthāya aññehi viññattampi sādiyantassa gaṇabhojanaṃ hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ viññattito pasavatīti ettha viññattiyā sati gaṇhantassa ekato hutvā gahaṇe iminā sikkhāpadena āpatti, visuṃ gahaṇe paṇītabhojanasūpodanaviññattīhi āpatti veditabbā.

Here, regarding 'they receive together,' it should be understood that those standing without leaving a twelve-cubit distance from one another are said to 'receive together.' From the passage, 'They might request, "Give a meal to the four of us,"' and from the passage below, 'Having requested thus: "You give a meal to one monk, you to two,"' it should be seen that it is indeed a group meal for one who consents to what is requested by others for one's own benefit. Here, regarding 'it arises from a request': when there is a request, for one who receives, if the receiving is done together, there is an offense under this training rule; if receiving separately, an offense should be understood through the rules on requesting choice food, soup, and rice.

Vicāretīti pañcakhaṇḍādivasena saṃvidahati. Ghaṭṭetīti anuvātaṃ chinditvā hatthena daṇḍakena vā ghaṭṭeti. Suttaṃ karotīti suttaṃ vaṭṭeti. Valetīti daṇḍake vā hatthe vā āvaṭṭeti. “Abhinavasseva cīvarassa karaṇaṃ idha cīvarakammaṃ nāma, purāṇacīvare sūcikammaṃ nāma na hotī”ti vadanti. “Catutthe āgate na yāpentīti vacanato sace añño koci āgacchanto natthi, cattāroyeva ca tattha nisinnā yāpetuṃ na sakkonti, na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti.

`Vicāreti` means: he arranges it by way of five sections, etc. `Ghaṭṭeti` means: having cut the nap, he rubs it with his hand or a stick. `Suttaṃ karoti` means: he twists the thread. `Valeti` means: he winds it on a stick or his hand. They say: 'Here, the making of a new robe is called robe-work; needlework on an old robe is not called robe-work.' They say: 'From the passage "When a fourth arrives, they do not carry on," if there is no one else coming, and the four seated there are unable to carry on, it is not allowable.'

220. Gaṇabhojanāpattijanakanimantanabhāvato “akappiyanimantana”nti vuttaṃ. Sampavesetvāti nisīdāpetvā. Gaṇo bhijjatīti gaṇo āpattiṃ na āpajjatīti adhippāyo. “Yattha cattāro bhikkhū…pe… bhuñjantī”ti imāya pāḷiyā saṃsandanato “itaresaṃ pana gaṇapūrako hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Avisesenāti “gilāno vā cīvarakārako vā”ti avisesetvā sabbasādhāraṇavacanena. Tasmāti avisesitattā. Bhutvā gatesūti ettha agatesupi bhojanakicce niṭṭhite gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati[M 3.0056]. Tāni ca tehi ekato na gahitānīti yehi bhojanehi visaṅketo natthi, tāni bhojanāni tehi bhikkhūhi ekato na gahitāni ekena pacchā gahitattā. Mahāthereti bhikkhū sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dūtassa puna paṭipathaṃ āgantvā “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vacanabhayena “gāmadvāre aṭṭhatvāvā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha tattha gantvāti antaravīthiādīsu tattha tattha ṭhitānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā. Bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya gharadvāre ṭhapetvā diyyamānepi eseva nayo. Nivattathāti vuttapade nivattituṃ vaṭṭatīti “nivattathā”ti vicchinditvā pacchā “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttattā vaṭṭati. Sesamettha uttānameva. Gaṇabhojanatā, samayābhāvo, ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

220. Because it is an invitation that generates an offense of group-eating, it is called an 'unallowable invitation.' `Sampavesetvā` means: having made them sit down. `Gaṇo bhijjati` (the group is broken) means: the group does not fall into an offense. From its connection with this Pāli text, 'Where four monks… (etc.) …eat,' it is said, 'but for the others, he is a group-completer.' `Avisesena` means: by a general statement, without making a distinction such as 'is sick or is a robe-maker.' Therefore: because no distinction was made. Here, regarding 'after they have eaten and gone,' even if they have not gone, it is allowable to receive when the business of the meal is finished. And 'those were not received by them together' means: those foods about which there was no prior agreement were not received together by those monks, because they were received later by one. The term `Mahāthera` is said referring to the monks. For fear that the messenger might come back along the path and say, 'Receive the meal,' it is said, 'or having stood at the village gate.' 'Going here and there' means: going to the vicinity of those standing here and there in the inner streets and so on. Even when it is placed at a house door and given for the sake of the monks, this is the same method. Regarding the spoken word 'Turn back,' it is allowable to turn back; because 'Turn back' was said, and after an interruption, 'Receive the meal' was said, it is allowable. The rest here is self-evident. Being a group meal, absence of a proper occasion, and consumption—these are the three factors here.

Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Explanation of the Training Rule on Group Meals is concluded.

3. Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Consecutive Meals

221. Tatiye [V 3.0051] kulapaṭipāṭiyā abbocchinnaṃ katvā nirantaraṃ diyyamānattā “bhattapaṭipāṭi aṭṭhitā hotī”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, antarā aṭṭhatvā nirantaraṃ pavattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upacāravasenāti vohāravasena. Na hi so badaramattameva deti, upacāravasena pana evaṃ vadati. Badaracuṇṇasakkharādīhi payojitaṃ “badarasāḷava”nti vuccati.

In the third case, because it is given continuously according to the order of families, having been made uninterrupted, it is said in the Pāli text, 'a sequence of meals is established.' This means it is said that it proceeds continuously without stopping in between. `Upacāravasena` means: by way of common usage. For he does not give just the measure of a jujube fruit, but he speaks thus by way of convention. What is prepared with jujube powder, sugar, and so on, is called 'jujube congee'.

226. Vikappanāvaseneva taṃ bhattaṃ asantaṃ nāma hotīti anupaññattivasena vikappanaṃ aṭṭhapetvā yathāpaññattaṃ sikkhāpadameva ṭhapitaṃ. Parivāre pana vikappanāya anujānanampi anupaññattisamānanti katvā “catasso anupaññattiyo”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariādīsu vuttanayaṃ pacchā vadanto pāḷiyā saṃsandanato parammukhāvikappanameva patiṭṭhāpesi. Keci pana “tadā attano santike ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ aññassa abhāvato thero sammukhāvikappanaṃ nākāsi, bhagavatā ca visuṃ sammukhāvikappanā na vuttā, tathāpi sammukhāvikappanāpi vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Teneva mātikāaṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “yo bhikkhu pañcasu sahadhammikesu aññatarassa ‘mayhaṃ bhattapaccāsaṃ tuyhaṃ dammī’ti vā ‘vikappemī’ti vā evaṃ sammukhā vā ‘itthannāmassa dammī’ti [M 3.0057] vā ‘vikappemī’ti vā evaṃ parammukhā vā paṭhamanimantanaṃ avikappetvā pacchā nimantitakule laddhabhikkhato ekasitthampi ajjhoharati, pācittiya”nti vuttaṃ.

3. That meal becomes what is called 'non-existent' solely by means of allocation. Therefore, setting aside allocation by way of a supplementary regulation, the training rule itself was established just as it was laid down. In the Parivāra, however, treating the permission for allocation as similar to a supplementary regulation, it is said, 'There are four supplementary regulations.' Later, when stating the method mentioned in the Mahāpaccarī and other texts, by way of comparison with the Pāli, he established only allocation in absence. Some, however, say: 'At that time, apart from the Blessed One in his presence, there being no one else, the Elder did not perform a face-to-face allocation; and the Blessed One did not separately state a face-to-face allocation, yet a face-to-face allocation is still allowable.' For this reason, in the Mātikā Commentary it is also said: 'Whatever monk, without having allocated the first invitation to one of the five co-religionists—either face-to-face, saying, "I give my leftover meal to you," or "I allocate it," or in absence, saying, "I give it to one with such-and-such a name," or "I allocate it"—should later consume even a single lump of rice from what was received in the invited household, it is a pācittiya offense.'

229. Pañcahi bhojanehi nimantitassa yena yena paṭhamaṃ nimantito, tassa tassa bhojanato uppaṭipāṭiyā avikappetvā vā parassa parassa bhojanaṃ paramparabhojananti āha “sace pana mūlanimantanaṃ heṭṭhā hoti, pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ upari, taṃ uparito paṭṭhāya bhuñjantassa āpattī”ti. Hatthaṃ anto pavesetvā sabbaheṭṭhimaṃ gaṇhantassa majjhe ṭhitampi antohatthagataṃ hotīti āha “hatthaṃ pana…pe… yathā tathā vā bhuñjantassa anāpattī”ti. Khīrassa rasassa ca bhattena amissaṃ hutvā upari ṭhitattā “khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vā pivato anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ.

229. For one invited with five kinds of foods, eating the food of a later donor out of sequence from the food of the one by whom he was first invited, or without having allocated it, is called 'eating in succession.' Thus, it is said: 'But if the food from the original invitation is at the bottom and that from a later one is on top, for one who eats starting from the top, there is an offense.' When one inserts a hand and takes the very bottom portion, even that which is in the middle is considered to have come into the hand; thus, it is said: 'But for one who inserts a hand... and eats in whatever way, there is no offense.' Because milk and juice, being unmixed with the rice, are on top, it is said: 'There is no offense for one who drinks milk or juice.'

Mahāupāsakoti gehasāmiko. “Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘āpattī’ti vacanena kurundiyaṃ ‘vaṭṭatī’ti vacanaṃ viruddhaṃ viya dissati, dvinnampi adhippāyo mahāpaccariyaṃ vibhāvito”ti mahāgaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Sabbe nimantentīti akappiyanimantanena nimantenti. “Paramparabhojanaṃ nāma [V 3.0052] pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena bhojanena nimantito, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjati, etaṃ paramparabhojanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttattā satipi bhikkhācariyāya paṭhamaṃ laddhabhāve “piṇḍāya caritvā laddhabhattaṃ bhuñjati, āpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Avikappavasena “vacīkamma”nti vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Paramparabhojanatā, samayābhāvo, ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

A great lay devotee is a householder. In the Mahāgaṇṭhipadas it is said: 'In the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, the statement, “it is an offense,” appears to contradict the statement in the Kurundī, “it is allowable”; the intention of both is clarified in the Mahāpaccarī.' 'All invite' means they invite with an improper invitation. Because it is said, 'Successive eating is when one has been invited to one of the five kinds of foods, and setting that aside, one eats another of the five kinds of foods; this is called successive eating,' it is therefore stated, 'Even if it was first obtained through the practice of going for alms, if one eats food obtained by going for alms, it is an offense.' On account of not having allocated it, it is called a 'verbal act.' The rest here is self-evident. The fact of it being a successive meal, the absence of a valid occasion, and the act of swallowing—these are the three factors here.

Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on successive eating is concluded.

4. Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Kāṇamātā

230-231. Catutthe kāṇāya mātāti kāṇāti laddhanāmāya dārikāya mātā. Kasmā panesā kāṇā nāma jātāti āha “sā kirassā”tiādi. Imissā daharakāle mātāpitaro sinehavasena “amma kāṇe, amma kāṇe”ti vohariṃsu, sā tadupādāya kāṇā nāma jātā, tassā ca mātā “kāṇamātā”ti pākaṭā ahosīti [M 3.0058] evamettha kāraṇaṃ vadanti. Paṭiyālokanti pacchimaṃ disaṃ, paccādiccanti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the fourth, 'mother of Kāṇā' means the mother of the girl who had acquired the name Kāṇā. As to why this girl came to be named Kāṇā, he says, 'She, it is said...' and so on. When she was a child, her parents, out of affection, would address her, saying, 'Dear Kāṇā, dear Kāṇā.' On account of this, she came to be named Kāṇā, and her mother became well-known as 'Kāṇamātā.' Thus they state the reason here. 'Looking back' means the western direction; this is to say, 'towards the setting sun.'

233. Pūvagaṇanāya pācittiyanti mukhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimalekhato upariṭṭhitapūvagaṇanāya pācittiyaṃ. “Dvattipattapūrā paṭiggahetabbā”ti hi vacanato mukhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimalekhaṃ anatikkante dve vā tayo vā pattapūre gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

233. A pācittiya offense for the number of cakes means a pācittiya for the number of cakes placed above the lower line of the bowl's rim. For, according to the saying, 'Two or three bowlfuls are to be accepted,' it is proper to accept two or three bowlfuls, provided they do not go beyond the lower line of the bowl's rim.

235. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana…pe… vuttanti idaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu tathā āgatabhāvamattadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana tassa vādassa patiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu vuttañhi pāḷiyā na sameti. Tatuttarigahaṇe anāpattidassanatthañhi “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti vuttaṃ. Aññathā “anāpatti dvattipattapūre paṭiggaṇhātī”ti imināva pamāṇayuttaggahaṇe anāpattisiddhito “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti visuṃ na vattabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “taṃ pāḷiyā na sametī”ti kasmā na vuttanti? Heṭṭhā tatuttarisikkhāpade vuttanayeneva sakkā viññātunti na vuttaṃ. Vuttañhi tattha (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.526) “aṭṭhakathāsu pana ñātakapavāritaṭṭhāne pakatiyāva bahumpi vaṭṭati, acchinnakāraṇā pamāṇameva vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ, taṃ pāḷiyā na sametī”ti. “Apātheyyādiatthāya paṭiyādita”nti saññāya gaṇhantassapi āpattiyeva acittakattā sikkhāpadassa. Attanoyeva gahaṇatthaṃ “imassa hatthe dehī”ti vacanenapi āpajjanato “vacīkamma”nti vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva[V 3.0053]. Vuttalakkhaṇapūvamanthatā, asesakatā, apaṭippassaddhagamanatā, na ñātakāditā, atirekapaṭiggahaṇanti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

235. 'But in the commentaries... it is said'—this is stated merely to show that it has come down thus in the commentaries, not to establish that view. For what is stated in the commentaries does not accord with the Pāḷi. Indeed, the phrase 'for relatives and for those who have invited' was stated to show there is no offense in receiving more than that. Otherwise, since non-offense when taking the proper amount is already established by 'there is no offense if one accepts two or three bowlfuls,' the separate phrase 'for relatives and for those who have invited' would not need to be stated. If so, why was it not said, 'That does not accord with the Pāḷi'? It was not said because it can be understood by the method stated below in the training rule on receiving more than that. For it is said there: 'But in the commentaries it is said that in the case of relatives and those who have invited, even a large amount is normally allowable, but when the reason is uninterrupted, only the specified amount is allowable—this does not accord with the Pāḷi.' Even for one who accepts with the perception that 'it is prepared for the purpose of provisions, etc.,' there is still an offense, because the training rule is one that does not depend on intention. Since one incurs an offense even by the words, 'Give it into this person's hand,' for the purpose of taking it for oneself, it is called a 'verbal act.' The rest is self-evident. Here, there are these five factors: the cakes or meal-cakes having the stated characteristics, their being without remainder, the departure not having ceased, the donors not being relatives and so on, and the receiving of an excessive amount.

Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is concluded.

5. Paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule

236. Pañcame bhuttāvīti bhuttāvino bhuttavanto, katabhattakiccāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pavāritāti ettha catūsu pavāraṇāsu yāvadatthapavāraṇā paṭikkhepapavāraṇā ca labbhatīti āha “brāhmaṇena…pe… paṭikkhepapavāraṇāya pavāritā”ti. Catubbidhā hi pavāraṇā vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā, paccayapavāraṇā[M 3.0059], paṭikkhepapavāraṇā, yāvadatthapavāraṇāti. Tattha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vassaṃvutthānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tīhi ṭhānehi pavāretu”nti (mahāva. 209) ayaṃ vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā. Pakārehi diṭṭhādīhi vāreti saṅghādike bhajāpeti bhatte karoti etāyāti pavāraṇā, āpattivisodhanāya attavossaggokāsadānaṃ. Sā pana yasmā yebhuyyena vassaṃvutthehi kātabbā vuttā, tasmā “vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā”ti vuccati. “Icchāmahaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ cātumāsaṃ bhesajjena pavāretu”nti (pāci. 303) ca, “aññatra puna pavāraṇāya aññatra niccapavāraṇāyā”ti (pāci. 306) ca ayaṃ paccayapavāraṇā pavāreti paccaye icchāpeti etāyāti katvā, cīvarādīhi upanimantanāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Pavārito nāma asanaṃ paññāyati, bhojanaṃ paññāyati, hatthapāse ṭhito abhiharati, paṭikkhepo paññāyati, eso pavārito nāmā”ti (pāci. 239) ayaṃ paṭikkhepapavāraṇā. Vippakatabhojanatādipañcaṅgasahito bhojanapaṭikkhepoyeva hettha pakārayuttā vāraṇāti pavāraṇā. “Paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresī”ti (ma. ni. 1.363) ayaṃ yāvadatthapavāraṇā. Yāvadatthaṃ bhojanassa pavāraṇā yāvadatthapavāraṇā.

236. In the fifth, `bhuttāvī` means 'those who have eaten,' 'those who are done eating'; that is to say, 'those who have completed the business of the meal.' As for `pavāritā`, here, among the four kinds of pavāraṇā, the `yāvadatthapavāraṇā` and the `paṭikkhepapavāraṇā` are applicable; thus, it is said: 'by the brahmin... they were invited by means of a `paṭikkhepapavāraṇā`.' Indeed, there are four kinds of pavāraṇā: the `vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā` (pavāraṇā after the rains residence), the `paccayapavāraṇā` (pavāraṇā of requisites), the `paṭikkhepapavāraṇā` (pavāraṇā of refusal), and the `yāvadatthapavāraṇā` (pavāraṇā to satisfaction). Among these, 'I allow, monks, for monks who have completed the rains residence to perform pavāraṇā on three grounds'—this is the `vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā`. By this, one invites (`vāreti`) through various means such as what has been seen; one causes them to attend upon the Sangha and so on; one makes them devoted—hence, it is `pavāraṇā`. It is the granting of an opportunity for self-surrender for the purification of offenses. And since it is said that this should mostly be performed by those who have completed the rains residence, it is called `vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā`. 'Venerable sirs, I wish to invite the Sangha with medicines for four months,' and 'apart from a further invitation, apart from a standing invitation'—this is the `paccayapavāraṇā`. It is so called because by this one invites (`pavāreti`) or causes a wish for requisites; this is a term for an invitation with robes and so on. 'One is called `pavārita` when food is available, when a meal is available, when one stands within arm's reach offering it, when a refusal is indicated—this is what is called `pavārita`'—this is the `paṭikkhepapavāraṇā`. Here, the refusal of food itself, accompanied by the five factors beginning with the meal being unfinished, is the prevention (`vāraṇā`) connected with a specific manner; hence, `pavāraṇā`. 'With excellent hard and soft food, he satisfied them with his own hands and invited them to take their fill'—this is the `yāvadatthapavāraṇā`. The invitation regarding food to one's satisfaction is the `yāvadatthapavāraṇā`.

237. Ti-kāraṃ avatvā…pe… vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti idaṃ vattabbākāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Ti-kāre pana vuttepi akataṃ nāma na hotī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

237. 'Without saying the syllable `ti`... it is proper to say'—this was stated to show the manner of what should be said. 'But even if the syllable `ti` is said, it is not considered as not done'—this is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas.

238-239. Pavāritoti paṭikkhepito. Yo hi bhuñjanto parivesakena upanītaṃ bhojanaṃ anicchanto paṭikkhipati, so tena pavārito paṭikkhepito nāma hoti. Byañjanaṃ pana anādiyitvā atthamattameva dassetuṃ “katapavāraṇo katapaṭikkhepo”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā “asana”nti [V 3.0054] imināva padena “bhuttāvī”ti imassa attho vutto, tasmā na tassa kiñci payojanaṃ visuṃ upalabbhati. Yadi hi upalabbheyya, pavāraṇā chaḷaṅgasamannāgatā āpajjeyyāti manasi katvā pañcasamannāgatattaṃyeva dassetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādinā pāḷiṃ āharati. Keci pana “hatthapāse ṭhito abhiharatī”ti ekameva aṅgaṃ katvā “caturaṅgasamannāgatā pavāraṇā”tipi vadanti.

238-239. 'Pavārita' means 'one who has refused.' For when a bhikkhu who is eating refuses food offered by an attendant, not wishing for it, he is called 'pavārita,' that is, 'one who has refused' by that act. However, without taking the phrasing into account and only to show the meaning, it is stated: 'one who has made the pavāraṇā, one who has made the refusal.' Since the meaning of 'bhuttāvī' (one who has eaten) is conveyed by the word 'asana' (staple food) itself, no separate purpose is found for it. For if a purpose were found, the pavāraṇā would become one endowed with six factors; bearing this in mind, to show that it is endowed with only five factors, the Pāḷi is cited with the words 'vuttampi ceta...' and so on. Some, however, taking 'standing within arm's reach and offering' as a single factor, also say, 'the pavāraṇā is one endowed with four factors.'

Ambilapāyāsādīsūti [M 3.0060] ādi-saddena khīrapāyāsādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha ambilapāyāsaggahaṇena takkādiambilasaṃyuttā ghanayāgu vuttā. Khīrapāyāsaggahaṇena khīrasaṃyuttā yāgu saṅgayhati. Pavāraṇaṃ na janetīti anatirittabhojanāpattinibandhanaṃ paṭikkhepaṃ na sādheti. Katopi paṭikkhepo anatirittabhojanāpattinibandhano na hotīti akataṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhatīti āha “pavāraṇaṃ na janetī”ti. “Yāgu-saddassa pavāraṇajanakayāguyāpi sādhāraṇattā ‘yāguṃ gaṇhathā’ti vuttepi pavāraṇā hotīti pavāraṇaṃ janetiyevāti vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ, taṃ parato tattheva “bhattamissakaṃ yāguṃ āharitvā”ti ettha vuttakāraṇena na sameti. Vuttañhi tattha “heṭṭhā ayāguke nimantane udakakañjikakhīrādīhi saddhiṃ madditaṃ bhattameva sandhāya ‘yāguṃ gaṇhathā’ti vuttattā pavāraṇā hoti, ‘bhattamissakaṃ yāguṃ āharitvā’ti ettha pana visuṃ yāguyā vijjamānattā pavāraṇā na hotī”ti. Tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva khīrādīhi saṃmadditaṃ bhattameva sandhāya “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttattā yāguyā ca tattha abhāvato pavāraṇā hotīti evamettha kāraṇaṃ vattabbaṃ. Evañhi sati parato “yenāpucchito, tassa atthitāyā”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttakāraṇenapi saṃsandati, aññathā gaṇṭhipadesuyeva pubbāparavirodho āpajjati. Aṭṭhakathāvacanena ca na sameti. Sace…pe… paññāyatīti iminā vuttappamāṇassa macchamaṃsakhaṇḍassa nahāruno vā sabbhāvamattaṃ dasseti. Tāhīti puthukāhi.

'In the case of sour gruel and so on'—the word 'ādi' (and so on) includes milk-gruel and so on. Therein, by the term 'sour gruel,' thick gruel mixed with sour substances such as buttermilk is meant. By the term 'milk-gruel,' gruel mixed with milk is included. 'It does not generate pavāraṇā' means it does not accomplish a refusal that is the basis for the offense of eating non-leftover food. Even if a refusal is made, it does not become a basis for the offense of eating non-leftover food, so it remains as if not done—thus it is said, 'it does not generate pavāraṇā.' 'Since the word 'yāgu' (gruel) is also a term common to gruel that does generate pavāraṇā, even when 'take the gruel' is said, pavāraṇā occurs—thus it is said that it does indeed generate pavāraṇā'—this is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas, but it does not accord with the reason stated later in the same texts in the context of 'having brought gruel mixed with rice.' For it is stated there: 'In the section below, regarding an invitation without gruel, since rice itself mixed with water-gruel, milk, etc., is intended when it is said, 'take the gruel,' pavāraṇā occurs. But in the case of 'having brought gruel mixed with rice,' since gruel is present separately, pavāraṇā does not occur.' Therefore, in accordance with the method stated there, since rice mixed with milk, etc., is intended when it is said, 'take the gruel,' and since gruel itself is absent there, pavāraṇā occurs. Thus, this reason should be stated here. This being so, it also accords with the reason stated later in the commentary: 'because of its existence for the one who was asked.' Otherwise, a contradiction between earlier and later statements arises within the Gaṇṭhipadas themselves, and it does not accord with the statement of the commentary. 'If... it appears'—this indicates the mere existence of a piece of fish or meat of the stated size, or of a tendon. 'Tāhi' means 'with flattened rice.'

Sālivīhiyavehi katasattūti yebhuyyanayena vuttaṃ, satta dhaññāni pana bhajjitvā katopi sattuyeva. Tenevāha “kaṅguvaraka…pe… sattusaṅgahameva gacchatī”ti. Sattumodakoti sattuyo piṇḍetvā kato apakko sattuguḷo. Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataravasena vippakatabhojanabhāvassa upacchinnattā “mukhe sāsapamattampi…pe… na pavāretī”ti vuttaṃ. “Akappiyamaṃsaṃ paṭikkhipati, na pavāretī”ti vacanato sace saṅghikaṃ lābhaṃ attano apāpuṇantaṃ jānitvā vā ajānitvā vā paṭikkhipati, na pavāreti paṭikkhipitabbasseva paṭikkhittattā. Alajjisantakaṃ paṭikkhipantopi na pavāreti. Avatthutāyāti anatirittāpattisādhikāya pavāraṇāya avatthubhāvato. Etena paṭikkhipitabbasseva paṭikkhittabhāvaṃ dīpeti[M 3.0061]. Yañhi paṭikkhipitabbaṃ [V 3.0055] hoti, tassa paṭikkhepo āpattiaṅgaṃ na hotīti taṃ “pavāraṇāya avatthū”ti vuccati.

'Sattu made from sāli rice, vīhi rice, and barley'—this is stated by way of generality; for sattu made by roasting any of the seven kinds of grain is still sattu. For that reason, it is said, 'Kaṅgu, varaka... it is included under sattu.' 'Sattumodaka' means an uncooked ball of sattu, made by kneading sattu meal. Because the state of being an unfinished meal, in the sense of one of the five kinds of staple foods, has been interrupted, it is said, 'Even a mustard seed's worth in the mouth... one does not make pavāraṇā.' In accordance with the statement, 'One who refuses unsuitable meat does not make pavāraṇā,' if one refuses a communal gain, whether knowing or not knowing that it will not reach oneself, one does not make pavāraṇā, because what ought to be refused has been refused. Even one who refuses something belonging to a shameless person does not make pavāraṇā. 'Due to being without a basis' means because it is not a basis for a pavāraṇā that establishes an offense regarding non-leftover food. By this, it shows that what ought to be refused has simply been refused. For when something ought to be refused, its refusal is not a factor of an offense, and thus it is called 'not a basis for pavāraṇā.'

Upanāmetīti iminā kāyābhihāraṃ dasseti. Hatthapāsato bahi ṭhitassa satipi dātukāmābhihāre paṭikkhipantassa dūrabhāveneva pavāraṇāya abhāvato therassapi dūrabhāvamattaṃ gahetvā pavāraṇāya abhāvaṃ dassento “therassa dūrabhāvato”ti āha, na pana therassa abhihārasabbhāvato. Sacepi gahetvā gato hatthapāse ṭhito hoti, kiñci pana avatvā ādhārakaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā abhihāro nāma na hotīti “dūtassa ca anabhiharaṇato”ti vuttaṃ. “Gahetvā gatena ‘bhattaṃ gaṇhathā’ti vutte abhihāro nāma hotīti ‘sace pana gahetvā āgato bhikkhu…pe… pavāraṇā hotī’ti vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “pattaṃ kiñci upanāmetvā ‘imaṃ bhattaṃ gaṇhathā’ti vuttanti gahetabba”nti vadanti, taṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati vācābhihārassa idha anadhippetattā.

'He presents'—by this, a physical offering is shown. For one standing outside arm's reach, even if there is an offering with the intention to give, when one refuses, the absence of pavāraṇā is due to the distance alone. Thus, showing the absence of pavāraṇā by taking into account merely the elder's distance, it is said, 'because of the elder's distance,' and not because of the existence of an offering from the elder. Even if one who has taken something and gone stands within arm's reach, if one stands at the place of the bowl-stand without saying anything, it is not called an offering. Hence, it is said, 'and because of the messenger's non-offering.' 'If one who has taken it and gone says, 'Take this meal,' it is called an offering. Therefore, it is said, 'But if a bhikkhu who has taken it comes... pavāraṇā occurs''—this is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas. Some, however, say, 'It should be understood as: having brought a bowl or something near and said, 'Take this meal.'' This seems reasonable, since a verbal offering is not intended here.

Parivesanāyāti bhattagge. Abhihaṭāva hotīti parivesakeneva abhihaṭā hoti. Tato dātukāmatāya gaṇhantaṃ paṭikkhipantassa pavāraṇā hotīti ettha agaṇhantampi paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hotiyeva. Kasmā? Dātukāmatāya abhihaṭattā. “Tasmā sā abhihaṭāva hotī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Teneva tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu “dātukāmābhihāre sati kevalaṃ ‘dassāmī’ti gahaṇameva abhihāro nāma na hoti, ‘dassāmī’ti gaṇhantepi agaṇhantepi dātukāmābhihārova abhihāro nāma hoti, tasmā gahaṇasamaye vā aggahaṇasamaye vā taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni asati tassa dātukāmābhihāre gahaṇasamayepi paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā na hotīti dassetuṃ “sace panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'At the serving' means in the dining hall. 'It is indeed brought forward' means it is brought forward by the server. Then, when one refuses what is being offered with the desire to give, pavāraṇā occurs. Here, even if one refuses without taking it, pavāraṇā still occurs. Why? Because it has been brought forward with the desire to give. For it is said, 'Therefore, it is indeed brought forward.' For this reason, in all three Gaṇṭhipadas, it is stated: 'When there is an offering with the desire to give, merely grasping it with the thought, 'I will give,' is not what is called an offering. Whether one takes it or not, it is the offering with the desire to give that is called an offering. Therefore, when one refuses it, whether at the time of taking or not taking, pavāraṇā occurs.' Now, to show that if there is no such offering with the desire to give, pavāraṇā does not occur for one who refuses, even at the time of taking, the passage beginning with 'But if...' is stated.

“Rasaṃ gaṇhathā”ti apavāraṇajanakassa nāmaṃ gahetvā vuttattā “taṃ sutvā paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Maccharasaṃ maṃsarasanti ettha pana na kevalaṃ macchassa rasaṃ maccharasamicceva viññāyati, atha kho maccho ca maccharasañca maccharasanti evaṃ pavāraṇajanakasādhāraṇanāmavasenapi viññāyamānattā [M 3.0062] taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇāva hoti. Parato macchasūpanti etthāpi eseva nayo. “Idaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttepīti ettha evaṃ avatvāpi pavāraṇapahonakaṃ yaṃkiñci abhihaṭaṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Karambakoti missakādhivacanametaṃ. Yañhi aññenaññena missetvā karonti, so “karambako”ti vuccati. So sacepi maṃsena missetvā katova hoti, “karambakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti apavāraṇārahassa nāmena vuttattā [V 3.0056] paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā na hoti. “Maṃsakarambakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vutte pana maṃsamissakaṃ gaṇhathāti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā pavāraṇāva hoti.

'Take the juice'—since this is said using the name of something that does not generate pavāraṇā, it is stated, 'for one who hears that and refuses, there is no pavāraṇā.' But here, in the case of 'fish-juice' or 'meat-juice,' it is not understood merely that the juice of fish is 'fish-juice'; rather, it is understood that 'fish and fish-juice are "fish-juice."' Thus, since it is understood by way of a name common to what does generate pavāraṇā, for one who refuses it, pavāraṇā does indeed occur. Later, in the case of 'fish-soup,' this same principle applies. 'Even when "Take this" is said'—here, it should be understood that even without saying this, for one who refuses anything brought forward that is suitable for pavāraṇā, pavāraṇā does indeed occur. 'Karambaka' is a term for a mixture. For whatever is made by mixing one thing with another is called 'karambaka.' Even if it is made mixed with meat, if it is said, 'take the karambaka,' since this is said using the name of something not liable to pavāraṇā, for one who refuses it, pavāraṇā does not occur. However, when 'Take the meat-karambaka' is said, it means 'take what is mixed with meat' has been said; therefore, pavāraṇā does indeed occur.

“Uddissakata”nti maññamānoti ettha “vatthuno kappiyattā akappiyasaññāya paṭikkhipatopi acittakattā imassa sikkhāpadassa pavāraṇā hotī”ti vadanti. “Heṭṭhā ayāguke nimantane udakakañjikakhīrādīhi saddhiṃ madditaṃ bhattameva sandhāya ‘yāguṃ gaṇhathā’ti vuttattā pavāraṇā hoti, ‘bhattamissakaṃ yāguṃ āharitvā’ti ettha pana visuṃ yāguyā vijjamānattā pavāraṇā na hotī”ti vadanti. Ayamettha adhippāyoti “yenāpucchito”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ sandhāya vadati. Kāraṇaṃ panettha duddasanti ettha eke tāva vadanti “yasmā yāgumissakaṃ nāma bhattameva na hoti, khīrādikampi hotiyeva, tasmā karambake viya pavāraṇāya na bhavitabbaṃ. Evañca sati yāgu bahutarā vā hoti samasamā vā, na pavāreti. ‘Yāgu mandā, bhattaṃ bahutaraṃ, pavāretī’ti ettha kāraṇaṃ duddasa”nti. Keci pana vadanti “yāgumissakaṃ nāma bhattaṃ, tasmā taṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇāya eva bhavitabbaṃ. Evañca sati ‘idha pavāraṇā hoti na hotī’ti ettha kāraṇaṃ duddasa”nti.

Here, regarding 'considering it as prepared for distribution,' they say that because the item is allowable, even if one rejects it due to perceiving it as unallowable or due to it being unintentional, the declaration (pavāraṇā) for this training rule occurs. Below, in an invitation without gruel, when it is said, 'Take the gruel,' referring to rice mixed with water-gruel, milk, and so forth, the declaration occurs. But here, in the case of 'having brought gruel mixed with rice,' since the gruel exists separately, the declaration does not occur—so they say. This is the intended meaning here; it refers to the matter already stated with 'by whom asked,' and so on. The reason here is hard to discern. Regarding this, some say: 'Because what is called "gruel-mixed" is not just rice—milk and so forth are also present—therefore, as in the case of a mixed dish (karambaka), the declaration should not occur. And if this is so, whether the gruel is more abundant or equal in amount, one does not declare. In the case of "The gruel is little, the rice is more abundant, so one declares," the reason is hard to discern.' Others, however, say: 'What is called "gruel-mixed" is rice; therefore, for one who rejects it, the declaration must indeed occur. And if this is so, in the case of "Here the declaration occurs, here it does not," the reason is hard to discern.'

Yathā cettha kāraṇaṃ duddasaṃ, evaṃ parato “missakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti etthāpi kāraṇaṃ duddasamevāti veditabbaṃ. Na hi pavāraṇappahonakassa appabahubhāvo pavāraṇāya bhāvābhāvanimittaṃ, kiñcarahi pavāraṇajanakassa nāmaggahaṇamevettha pamāṇaṃ, tasmā “idañca karambakena na samānetabba”ntiādinā yampi kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi pubbe vuttena saṃsandiyamānaṃ na sameti. Yadi hi “missaka”nti bhattamissakeyeva ruḷhaṃ siyā, evaṃ sati yathā “bhattamissakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vutte bhattaṃ bahutaraṃ vā samaṃ vā appataraṃ vā hoti, pavāretiyeva, evaṃ “missakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttepi appatarepi [M 3.0063] bhatte pavāraṇāya bhavitabbaṃ missakanti bhattamissakeyeva ruḷhattā. Tathā hi “missakanti bhattamissakeyeva ruḷhavohārattā idaṃ pana ‘bhattamissakamevā’ti vutta”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Atha “missaka”nti bhattamissake ruḷhaṃ na hoti, missakabhattaṃ pana sandhāya “missakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttanti. Evampi yathā ayāguke nimantane khīrādīhi saddhiṃ madditaṃ bhattameva sandhāya “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti vutte pavāraṇā hoti, evamidhāpi missakabhattameva sandhāya “missakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vutte bhattaṃ appaṃ vā hotu bahu vā, pavāraṇā eva siyā. Tasmā “missaka”nti bhattamissake ruḷhaṃ vā hotu sandhāyabhāsitaṃ vā, ubhayatthāpi pubbenāparaṃ na sametīti kimettha kāraṇacintāya, īdisesu pana ṭhānesu aṭṭhakathāpamāṇeneva gantabbanti ayaṃ amhākaṃ khanti.

And just as the reason here is hard to discern, so it should be understood that further on, in the case of 'Take the mixed food,' the reason is also hard to discern. For the abundance or scarcity of that which is sufficient for the declaration is not the cause for the declaration's occurrence or non-occurrence. Rather, the very mention of the name of that which generates the declaration is the standard here. Therefore, the reason that is given, beginning with 'And this should not be equated with a karambaka,' does not align when compared with what was previously stated. For if 'mixed' were established in usage as referring only to 'rice-mixed,' then, just as when it is said, 'Take the rice-mixed food,' one declares whether the rice is more, equal, or less, so too when it is said, 'Take the mixed food,' the declaration should occur even if the rice is less, because 'mixed' is established as referring only to 'rice-mixed.' Indeed, it is stated in all three sub-commentaries: 'Because "mixed" is established in common usage as referring only to "rice-mixed," this is said to be "rice-mixed" itself.' If, however, 'mixed' is not established as referring to 'rice-mixed,' but 'Take the mixed food' is said with reference to mixed rice, even so, just as in an invitation without gruel, when 'Take the gruel' is said with reference to rice mixed with milk and so forth, the declaration occurs, so too here, when 'Take the mixed food' is said with reference to mixed rice, the declaration should indeed occur whether the rice is little or much. Therefore, whether 'mixed' is established as referring to 'rice-mixed' or is spoken with reference to it, in both cases the latter does not align with the former. So what is the use of pondering the reason here? In such instances, one should proceed by the authority of the commentary alone—this is our conviction.

“Visuṃ [V 3.0057] katvā detīti bhattassa upari ṭhitaṃ rasādiṃ visuṃ gahetvā detī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Kenaci pana “yathā bhattasitthaṃ na patati, tathā gāḷhaṃ hatthena pīḷetvā parissāvetvā detī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathāpi kāraṇaṃ na dissati. Yathā hi bhattamissakaṃ yāguṃ āharitvā “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā yāgumissakaṃ bhattampi dentaṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā na hoti, evamidhāpi bahukhīrarasādīsu bhattesu “khīraṃ gaṇhathā”tiādīni vatvā khīrādīni vā detu khīrādimissakabhattaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi pavāraṇāya na bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā “visuṃ katvā detī”ti tenākārena dentaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana bhattamissakaṃ katvā diyyamānaṃ paṭikkhipato pavāraṇā hotīti dassanatthanti gahetabbaṃ. Yadi pana bhattamissakaṃ katvā diyyamāne pavāraṇā hotīti adhippāyena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “visuṃ katvā detī”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati aṭṭhakathāyevettha pamāṇanti gahetabbaṃ, na pana kāraṇantaraṃ gavesitabbaṃ.

In all three sub-commentaries, it is stated: '“Gives after separating” means taking the juice and so forth that is on top of the rice and giving it separately.' By someone, however, it has been said: 'One gives it after pressing firmly with the hand and straining it so that not a grain of rice falls through.' Even so, a reason is not apparent. For just as when, having brought gruel mixed with rice and having said, 'Take the gruel,' for one who rejects the rice given mixed with gruel, the declaration does not occur; so too here, in the case of rice with much milk, juice, and so forth, whether one says, 'Take the milk,' and so on, and gives the milk or gives the rice mixed with milk, in either case the declaration should not occur. Therefore, it should be understood that 'gives after separating' was said with reference to one who gives in that manner, and not for the purpose of showing that a declaration occurs for one who rejects what is given having been mixed with rice. If, however, 'gives after separating' was said in the commentary with the intention that a declaration does occur when it is given having been mixed with rice, in that case, it should be understood that the commentary itself is the authority here, and no other reason should be sought.

Sace ukkuṭikaṃ nisinno pāde amuñcitvāpi bhūmiyaṃ nisīdati, iriyāpathaṃ vikopento nāma hotīti ukkuṭikāsanaṃ avikopetvāva sukhena nisīdituṃ “tassa pana heṭṭhā…pe… nisīdanakaṃ dātabba”nti vuttaṃ. “Āsanaṃ acāletvāti pīṭhe phuṭṭhokāsato ānisadamaṃsaṃ amocetvā, anuṭṭhahitvāti vuttaṃ hoti, adinnādāne viya ṭhānācāvanaṃ na gahetabba”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

If one who is sitting in a squatting position then sits on the ground, even without releasing the feet, one is said to be disrupting the posture. Therefore, so that one may sit comfortably without disrupting the squatting posture, it was said, 'For him, below… a sitting cloth should be given.' In all three sub-commentaries, it is stated: '“Without moving from the seat” means not lifting the flesh of the buttocks from its point of contact with the stool; that is to say, not getting up. It should not be taken as moving from a place, as in the case of theft.'

Akappiyakatanti [M 3.0064] ettha akappiyakatasseva anatirittabhāvato kappiyaṃ akārāpetvā tasmiṃ patte pakkhittamūlaphalādiyeva atirittaṃ na hoti, sesaṃ pana pattapariyāpannaṃ atirittameva hoti, paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Taṃ pana mūlaphalādiṃ paribhuñjitukāmena tato nīharitvā kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā aññasmiṃ bhājane ṭhapetvā atirittaṃ kārāpetvā bhuñjitabbaṃ.

Here, regarding 'made unallowable': because only that which has been made unallowable has the status of not being leftover, only the roots, fruits, and so forth that were placed in that bowl without having been made allowable are not leftover. The rest, however, contained in the bowl, is indeed leftover and is allowable to consume. But one who wishes to consume those roots, fruits, and so forth should remove them from there, have them made allowable, place them in another vessel, have them made leftover, and then consume them.

So puna kātuṃ na labhatīti tasmiṃyeva bhājane kariyamānaṃ paṭhamaṃ katena saddhiṃ kataṃ hotīti puna soyeva kātuṃ na labhati, añño labhati. Aññasmiṃ pana bhājane tena vā aññena vā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāha “yena akataṃ, tena kātabbaṃ. Yañca akataṃ, taṃ kātabba”nti. Tenapīti ettha pi-saddo na kevalaṃ aññena vāti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Evaṃ katanti aññasmiṃ bhājane kataṃ. Pesetvāti anupasampannassa hatthe pesetvā. Imassa vinayakammabhāvato “anupasampannassa hatthe ṭhitaṃ na kāretabba”nti vuttaṃ.

“He cannot do it again” means that because what is being done in the same vessel becomes one with what was done first, he himself cannot do it again, but another can. In a different vessel, however, it is allowable for him or for another to do it. Therefore, He said: 'By whom it was not done, by him it should be done. And what was not done, that should be done.' Here, in 'by him also' (tenapi), the particle 'pi' indicates this meaning: not only by another is it allowable. 'Done in this way' means done in another vessel. 'Having sent' means having sent it into the hand of one who is not fully ordained. Because this is a formal Vinaya act, it was said, 'It should not be done while it is in the hand of one who is not fully ordained.'

Sace pana āmisasaṃsaṭṭhānīti ettha sace mukhagatenapi anatirittena āmisena saṃsaṭṭhāni honti[V 3.0058], pācittiyamevāti veditabbaṃ. Tasmā pavāritena bhojanaṃ atirittaṃ kārāpetvā bhuñjantenapi yathā akatena missaṃ na hoti, evaṃ mukhañca hatthañca suddhaṃ katvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Kiñcāpi appavāritassa purebhattaṃ yāmakālikādīni āhāratthāya paribhuñjatopi anāpatti, pavāritassa pana pavāraṇamūlakaṃ dukkaṭaṃ hotiyevāti “yāmakālikaṃ…pe… ajjhohāre āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Here, regarding 'if they are mixed with food': it should be understood that if they are mixed with food that is not leftover, even with that which has entered the mouth, it is indeed a pācittiya offense. Therefore, one who has been satisfied, even when eating after having had food made leftover, should eat after making both mouth and hand clean, so that it does not mix with what has not been made leftover. And although for one who has not been satisfied there is no offense even when consuming, for the sake of sustenance, time-limited items and so forth before the main meal, for one who has been satisfied there is indeed a dukkaṭa offense rooted in that satisfaction. Thus it is said in the Pāli text: 'In swallowing a time-limited item… and so on… there is an offense of wrong-doing.'

241. Kāyena bhuñjanato vācāya āṇāpetvā atirittaṃ akārāpanato ca āpajjatīti “kāyavācato”ti vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Pavāritabhāvo, āmisassa anatirittatā, kāle ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

241. One incurs an offense by consuming it with the body, and by not having it made leftover after ordering it by speech; therefore, it was said 'by body and speech.' The rest here is self-evident. The state of having been satisfied, the food's status as not-leftover, and consuming it within the prescribed time—these are the three factors here.

Paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first training rule concerning invitation is concluded.

6. Dutiyapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Second Training Rule concerning Invitation

243. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0065] sādhāraṇamevāti “handa bhikkhu khāda vā”tiādinā vuttapavāraṇāya sādhāraṇaṃ. “Bhuttasmiṃ pācittiya”nti mātikāyaṃ vuttattā bhojanapariyosāne āpatti, na ajjhohāre ajjhohāre. Abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreti, āpatti pācittiyassāti idañca bhojanapariyosānaṃyeva sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Pavāritatā, pavāritasaññitā, āsādanāpekkhatā, anatirittena abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāraṇā, bhojanapariyosānanti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

243. In the sixth (rule), it is common, meaning it is common to the invitation spoken with 'Here, monk, eat or...' and so forth. Since 'when one has eaten, it is an offense entailing expiation' is stated in the Mātikā, the offense occurs at the end of the meal, not with each mouthful. And 'one invites to bring more, there is an offense entailing expiation'—this too should be understood as referring only to the end of the meal. The rest here is clear. The state of having been invited, the perception of having been invited, the desire to find fault, the invitation to bring what is not leftover, and the end of the meal—these are the five factors here.

Dutiyapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second training rule concerning invitation is concluded.

7. Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Untimely Meals

247. Sattame aggasamajjoti uttamaṃ naccaṃ. Taṃ kira pabbatamatthake ṭhatvā ekaṃ devataṃ uddissa karonti. Naṭānaṃ nāṭakāni naṭanāṭakāni, sītāharaṇādīni. Apaññatte sikkhāpadeti ūnavīsativassasikkhāpade apaññatte. Adaṃsūti “vihāraṃ netvā khādissathā”ti adaṃsu.

247. In the seventh (rule), 'agga-samajja' means the highest dance. It is said that they perform it on a mountaintop, dedicating it to a single deity. The dramatic performances of the dancers are the 'naṭanāṭakāni', such as the abduction of Sītā and others. Regarding 'when the training rule was not yet laid down,' it refers to the training rule for those under twenty years of age not yet having been laid down. 'They gave' means they gave, saying, 'Take it to the monastery and eat it.'

248-249. Mūlakamūlādīni upadesatoyeva veditabbāni. Na hi tāni pariyāyantarena vuccamānānipi [V 3.0059] sakkā viññātuṃ. Pariyāyantarepi hi vuccamāne taṃ taṃ nāmaṃ ajānantānaṃ sammohoyeva siyā, tasmā tattha na kiñci vakkhāma. Khādanīyatthanti khādanīyena kattabbakiccaṃ. Neva pharantīti na nipphādenti. Tesu tesu janapadesūti ettha “ekasmiṃ janapade āhārakiccaṃ sādhentaṃ sesajanapadesupi na kappatī”ti vadanti. Rukkhavalliādīnanti heṭṭhā vuttameva sampiṇḍetvā vuttaṃ. Antopathavīgatoti sālakalyāṇīkhandhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sabbakappiyānīti mūlakhandhatacapattādivasena sabbaso kappiyāni. Tesampi nāmavasena na sakkā pariyantaṃ dassetunti sambandho. Acchivādīnaṃ aparipakkāneva phalāni yāvajīvikānīti dassetuṃ “aparipakkānī”ti vuttaṃ.

Roots and similar things should be understood only by the given designation. For even when described by another method, they cannot be truly understood. For even when described by another method, it would only cause confusion for those who do not know those names. Therefore, we will say nothing further on that matter. 'For the purpose of edibles' means the function to be performed with edibles. 'They do not fulfill' means they do not produce. 'In various countries' here refers to the statement that 'what serves the purpose of food in one country is not allowable in other countries.' 'Trees, vines, etc.' is a condensed version of what was previously stated. 'Underground' refers to the trunk of the Sālakalyāṇī tree. 'All allowable things' means allowable in every way by means of roots, trunks, bark, leaves, etc. It is impossible to show the limit of even these by a list of names—this is the connection. 'Unripe' is said to show that the fruits of the acchivā and others are allowable for a lifetime only when they are unripe.

Harītakādīnaṃ aṭṭhīnīti ettha miñjaṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitakapālāni yāvajīvikānīti ācariyā. Miñjampi yāvajīvikanti eke. Hiṅgūti hiṅgurukkhato paggharitaniyyāso. Hiṅgujatuādayopi hiṅguvikatiyo eva. Tattha hiṅgujatu [M 3.0066] nāma hiṅgurukkhassa daṇḍapattāni pacitvā kataniyyāso, hiṅgusipāṭikaṃ nāma hiṅgupattāni pacitvā kataniyyāso. “Aññena missetvā kato”tipi vadanti. Takanti aggakoṭiyā nikkhantasileso. Takapattinti pattato nikkhantasileso. Takapaṇṇinti palāse bhajjitvā katasileso. “Daṇḍato nikkhantasileso tipi vadanti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Vikālatā, yāvakālikatā, ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

'The pits of harītakī and the like': here, the teachers say that the shells that remain covering the kernel are allowable for a lifetime. Some say the kernel is also allowable for a lifetime. 'Asafoetida' is the sap exuding from the asafoetida tree. Asafoetida gum and other such products are also varieties of asafoetida. Of these, 'asafoetida gum' is sap made by boiling the stems and leaves of the asafoetida tree, while 'asafoetida sipāṭika' is sap made by boiling the leaves of the asafoetida tree. Some also say, 'It is made by mixing with other things.' 'Taka' refers to the secretion coming from the tip of a branch. 'Takapatti' is secretion coming from a leaf. 'Takapaṇṇi' is secretion made by frying palāsa leaves. Some also say, 'It is secretion coming from a stem.' The rest here is straightforward. Untimeliness, being a short-term allowable, and consumption—these are the three factors here.

Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning untimely meals is concluded.

8. Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Storing

252-3. Aṭṭhame tādisanti asūpabyañjanaṃ. Yaṃkiñci yāvakālikaṃ vā yāmakālikaṃ vāti ettha “yāmakālika”nti iminā na kevalaṃ yāvakālike eva sannidhipaccayā pācittiyaṃ, atha kho yāmakālikepīti dasseti. Nanu ca yāmakālikaṃ neva khādanīyesu antogadhaṃ, na bhojanīyesu. Teneva padabhājanīye “khādanīyaṃ nāma pañca bhojanāni yāmakālikaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ khādanīyaṃ nāma. Bhojanīyaṃ nāma pañca bhojanānī”ti vuttaṃ, “yo pana bhikkhu sannidhikārakaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā khādeyya vā bhuñjeyya vā, pācittiya”nti ca vuttaṃ, tasmā yāmakālike pācittiyena bhavitabbanti kathaṃ viññāyatīti? Vuccate – padabhājane khādanīya-saddassa atthadassanatthaṃ “yāmakālikaṃ [V 3.0060] ṭhapetvā”ti vuttaṃ, na pana sannidhipaccayā anāpattidassanatthaṃ. Khāditabbañhi yaṃkiñci khādanīyanti adhippetaṃ, na ca yāmakālikesu kiñci khāditabbaṃ atthi pātabyabhāvato. Tasmā kiñcāpi yāmakālikaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyehi na saṅgahitaṃ, tathāpi anāpattiṃ dassentena “anāpatti yāmakālikaṃ yāme nidahitvā bhuñjatī”ti vacanato yāmātikkame sannidhipaccayā pācittiyena bhavitabbanti viññāyati. “Yāmakālikena, bhikkhave, sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ yāme kappati, yāmātikkante na kappatī”ti (mahāva. 305) imināpi [M 3.0067] cāyamattho siddho. Teneva bhagavato adhippāyaññūhi aṭṭhakathācariyehi yāmakālike pācittiyameva vuttaṃ.

In the eighth (rule), 'such as' refers to what is without broth or condiments. Regarding the phrase 'whatever is for a limited time or for a watch period,' the term 'for a watch period' here indicates that an offense entailing expiation arises due to storing not only in the case of what is for a limited time, but also in the case of what is for a watch period. But is not what is for a watch period included neither among edibles nor among staple foods? Precisely for this reason, in the word-analysis, it is said: '“Edible” means: having set aside the five staple foods, what is for a watch period, what is for seven days, and what is for a lifetime, the remainder is called “edible.” “Staple food” means the five staple foods.' And it is also said: 'Whatever monk should eat or consume an edible or a staple food that has been stored, it is an offense entailing expiation.' Therefore, how is it understood that there must be an offense entailing expiation for what is for a watch period? It is said: In the word-analysis, the phrase 'excluding what is for a watch period' is stated to clarify the meaning of the word 'edible,' not to indicate non-offense due to storing. For the intention is that whatever is to be eaten is 'edible,' but nothing among what is for a watch period is to be eaten, because it is to be drunk. Thus, although what is for a watch period is not included among edibles or staple foods, from the statement showing non-offense, 'there is no offense if one consumes what is for a watch period, having stored it, within the watch period', it is understood that an offense entailing expiation arises due to storing if the watch period is exceeded. This meaning is also established by the passage: 'Monks, what is for a watch period, what is for seven days, or what is for a lifetime, received that day, is allowable for a watch period; when the watch period is exceeded, it is not allowable' (Mahāvagga 305). Therefore, the commentators, who understood the Blessed One’s intention, stated that there is indeed an offense entailing expiation for what is for a watch period.

Paṭiggahaṇeti gahaṇameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paṭiggahitameva hi taṃ, puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Teneva “ajjhoharitukāmatāya gaṇhantassa paṭiggahaṇe”ti vuttaṃ. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) pana “ajjhoharissāmīti gaṇhantassa paṭiggahaṇe”icceva vuttaṃ. Yanti yaṃ pattaṃ. Sandissatīti yāguyā upari sandissati. Telavaṇṇe patte satipi nisnehabhāve aṅguliyā ghaṃsantassa vaṇṇavaseneva lekhā paññāyati, tasmā tattha anāpattīti dassanatthaṃ “sā abbohārikā”ti vuttaṃ. Sayaṃ paṭiggahetvā apariccattameva hi dutiyadivase na vaṭṭatīti ettha paṭiggahaṇe anapekkhavissajjanena anupasampannassa nirapekkhadānena vā vijahitapaṭiggahaṇaṃ pariccattameva hotīti “apariccatta”nti iminā ubhayathāpi avijahitapaṭiggahaṇameva vuttaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ parassa pariccajitvā adinnampi sace paṭiggahaṇe nirapekkhavissajjanena vijahitapaṭiggahaṇaṃ hoti, tampi dutiyadivase vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ.

'Receiving' is said referring simply to taking. For it is indeed already received; there is no further act of receiving. Hence, it is said, 'in the receiving of one who takes with the desire to consume.' However, in the Mātikā Commentary, it is stated thus: 'in the receiving of one who takes with the thought, “I will consume.”' The word 'which' refers to 'which bowl.' 'It is visible' means it is visible on the surface of the gruel. In a bowl with an oily appearance, even though there is no greasiness, when one rubs it with a finger, a line appears due to the color itself. Therefore, to show there is no offense in that case, it is said, 'That is not to be reckoned.' For what one has received oneself and not relinquished is indeed not allowable on the second day. Here, the reception is considered relinquished if it is abandoned by relinquishing without concern or by giving without concern to an unordained person. Therefore, by 'not relinquished,' it is meant that in both these ways the reception has not been abandoned. Thus, it should be understood that if something, having been relinquished to another and not given back, is nevertheless an abandoned reception due to being relinquished without concern, it is also allowable on the second day.

Yadi evaṃ “patto duddhoto hotī”tiādīsu kasmā āpatti vuttāti? “Paṭiggahaṇaṃ avissajjetvāva sayaṃ vā aññena vā tucchaṃ katvā na sammā dhovitvā niṭṭhāpite patte laggampi avijahitapaṭiggahaṇameva hotīti tattha āpattī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “sāmaṇerānaṃ pariccajantīti imasmiṃ adhikāre ṭhatvā ‘apariccattamevā’ti vuttattā anupasampannassa pariccattameva vaṭṭati, apariccattaṃ na vaṭṭatīti āpannaṃ, tasmā nirālayabhāvena paṭiggahaṇe vijahitepi anupasampannassa apariccattaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ yuttaṃ viya na dissati. Yadaggena hi paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati, tadaggena sannidhimpi na karoti vijahitapaṭiggahaṇassa appaṭiggahitasadisattā. Paṭiggahetvā nidahiteyeva ca sannidhipaccayā āpatti vuttā. “Paṭiggahetvā ekarattaṃ vītināmitassetaṃ adhivacana”nti hi vuttaṃ.

If so, why is an offense stated in cases such as, 'the bowl is improperly washed'? 'Because what remains stuck in a bowl that has been emptied by oneself or another and not properly washed and finished—without having relinquished the reception—is indeed unabandoned reception, and thus there is an offense.' This is stated in all three glossaries. Some, however, argue: 'Standing in the context of "they relinquish for novices," and because it is stated "it is only what is unrelinquished," it follows that for an unordained person, only what is relinquished is allowable; what is not relinquished is not allowable. Therefore, even if the reception is abandoned through a state of non-attachment, what is not relinquished is not allowable for an unordained person.' This does not seem correct. For by the same principle that one abandons the reception, one also does not store it up, since an abandoned reception is like something not received. Moreover, an offense due to storing is stated only for that which has been received and then stored away. For it is said: 'This is a term for that which has been received and kept for one night.'

Pāḷiyaṃ [V 3.0061] “sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ āhāratthāya paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādinā sannihitesu sattāhakālikayāvajīvikesu purebhattampi āhāratthāya ajjhoharaṇepi dukkaṭassa vuttattā [M 3.0068] yāmakālikepi āhāratthāya ajjhoharaṇe visuṃ dukkaṭenapi bhavitabbanti āha “āhāratthāya ajjhoharato dukkaṭena saddhiṃ pācittiya”nti. Pakatiāmiseti odanādikappiyāmise. Yāmakālikaṃ sati paccaye sāmisena mukhena ajjhoharato dveti hiyyo paṭiggahitayāmakālikaṃ ajja purebhattaṃ sāmisena mukhena bhuñjato sannihitayāmakālikapaccayā ekaṃ pācittiyaṃ, sannihitena saṃsaṭṭhaāmisapaccayā ekanti dve pācittiyāni. Vikappadvayepīti sāmisena nirāmisenāti vuttavidhānadvaye. Dukkaṭaṃ vaḍḍhatīti āhāratthāya ajjhoharaṇapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ vaḍḍhati. Thullaccayañca dukkaṭañca vaḍḍhatīti manussamaṃse thullaccayaṃ, sesaakappiyamaṃsesu dukkaṭaṃ vaḍḍhati.

In the Pāli, by the text beginning, 'If one accepts a seven-day or lifetime requisite for the purpose of food, it is an offense of dukkaṭa,' it is stated that for consuming stored seven-day or lifetime requisites for the purpose of food even before the main meal, there is a dukkaṭa. Therefore, since for a yāmakālika item too, when consumed for the purpose of food, there should be a separate dukkaṭa, it is said: 'For one who consumes for the purpose of food, there is a pācittiya along with a dukkaṭa.' 'Ordinary food' (pakatiāmisa) means permissible food such as cooked rice. 'Two (offenses) for one who consumes a yāmakālika item with food in the mouth when there is a condition' means: for one who consumes a yāmakālika item received yesterday, today before the main meal with food in the mouth, there is one pācittiya offense on account of the stored yāmakālika item, and one on account of the food mixed with the stored item—thus there are two pācittiya offenses. 'In the two alternatives' (vikappadvaye) refers to the two methods stated: with food and without food. 'A dukkaṭa accrues' means a dukkaṭa accrues on account of consuming for the purpose of food. 'A thullaccaya and a dukkaṭa accrue' means a thullaccaya accrues in the case of human flesh, and a dukkaṭa accrues in the case of other impermissible meats.

255. Paṭiggahaṇapaccayā tāva dukkaṭanti ettha sannihitattā purebhattampi dukkaṭameva. Sati paccaye pana sannihitampi sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ bhesajjatthāya gaṇhantassa paribhuñjantassa ca anāpattiyeva. Sesamettha uttānameva. Yāvakālikayāmakālikatā, sannidhibhāvo, tassa ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

255. Regarding the statement, 'Firstly, a dukkaṭa offense on account of receiving': here, because it is stored, it is a dukkaṭa even before the main meal. However, when there is a condition, there is no offense for one who takes and consumes a stored seven-day or lifetime requisite for the purpose of medicine. The rest here is self-evident. The three factors here are: (1) its being a yāvakālika or yāmakālika item, (2) the state of being stored, and (3) its consumption.

Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on storing is concluded.

9. Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Choice Foods

257-259. Navame paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni bhojanāni paṇītabhojanāni. Yathā hi ājaññayutto ratho “ājaññaratho”ti vuccati, evamidhāpi paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni sattadhaññanibbattāni bhojanāni “paṇītabhojanānī”ti vuttāni. Yehi pana paṇītehi saṃsaṭṭhāni, tāni “paṇītabhojanānī”ti vuccanti, tesaṃ pabhedadassanatthaṃ “seyyathidaṃ, sappi navanīta”ntiādi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappatī”ti idañca pācittiyavatthuparicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana kappiyavatthuparicchedadassanatthaṃ. Na hi akappiyamaṃsasattānaṃ sappiādīni na kappanti. Ekañhi manussavasātelaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbesaṃ khīrasappinavanītavasātelesu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Sappibhattanti ettha kiñcāpi sappisaṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattaṃ sappibhattaṃ, sappi ca bhattañca sappibhattantipi viññāyati, aṭṭhakathāsu pana “sālibhattaṃ viya sappibhattaṃ nāma natthī”ti kāraṇaṃ vatvā dukkaṭasseva [V 3.0062] daḷhataraṃ [M 3.0069] katvā vuttattā na sakkā aññaṃ vattuṃ. Aṭṭhakathācariyā eva hi īdisesu ṭhānesu pamāṇaṃ.

In the ninth (sikkhāpada), foods mixed with choice items are 'choice foods'. Just as a chariot yoked with thoroughbreds is called a 'thoroughbred chariot,' so too here, foods produced from the seven kinds of grain that are mixed with choice items are called 'choice foods.' Furthermore, those choice items with which they are mixed are also called 'choice foods.' To show the varieties of these, it is stated in the Pāli, 'namely, ghee, fresh butter,' and so on. The phrase 'those whose flesh is permissible' is stated to show the delimitation of the object for a pācittiya offense, not to show the delimitation of what is permissible. For the ghee, etc., of beings whose flesh is impermissible are not themselves impermissible. Indeed, setting aside oil from human fat, there is nothing called 'impermissible' among the milk, ghee, fresh butter, fat, and oil of any beings. Regarding 'ghee-rice' (sappibhatta), although 'ghee-rice' can be understood as rice mixed with ghee, or as ghee and rice, since the commentaries, stating the reason that 'there is no such thing as ghee-rice in the way there is sāli-rice,' have spoken, making it firmly only a dukkaṭa, it is not possible to say otherwise. For in such places, the commentary masters are the authority.

Mūlanti kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Anāpattīti visaṅketattā sabbāhiyeva āpattīhi anāpatti. Keci pana “pācittiyeneva anāpatti vuttā, sūpodanaviññattidukkaṭaṃ pana hotiyevā”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Kappiyasappinā akappiyasappināti ca idaṃ kappiyākappiyamaṃsānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, tasmā kappiyamaṃsasappinā akappiyamaṃsasappināti evamettha attho gahetabbo. Nānāvatthukānīti sappinavanītādīnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ.

The term 'root' (mūla) is stated with reference to a permissible article. 'No offense' (anāpatti) means there is no offense from any of the offenses because of a misunderstanding. Some, however, say, 'No offense is stated only for the pācittiya, but the dukkaṭa for requesting curry and rice still occurs.' This should not be accepted. The phrase 'with permissible ghee, with impermissible ghee' is stated by way of permissible and impermissible meats. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'with ghee from permissible meat' and 'with ghee from impermissible meat.' 'Of various kinds' is stated by way of ghee, fresh butter, and so on.

261. Mahānāmasikkhāpadena kāretabboti ettha –

261. In the phrase, 'He should be dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule':

“Agilānena bhikkhunā catumāsapaccayapavāraṇā sāditabbā aññatra punapavāraṇāya aññatra niccapavāraṇāya, tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 306) –

'A bhikkhu who is not ill may consent to an invitation for requisites for four months, unless it is a renewed invitation or a standing invitation. If he should consent to more than that, it is a pācittiya offense.'

Idaṃ mahānāmasikkhāpadaṃ nāma. Iminā ca sikkhāpadena saṅghavasena gilānapaccayapavāraṇāya pavāritaṭṭhāne sace tattha rattīhi vā bhesajjehi vā paricchedo kato hoti, ettakāyeva rattiyo ettakāni vā bhesajjāni viññāpetabbānīti. Atha tato rattipariyantato vā bhesajjapariyantato vā uttari na bhesajjakaraṇīyena vā bhesajjaṃ aññabhesajjakaraṇīyena vā aññaṃ bhesajjaṃ viññāpentassa pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā agilāno gilānasaññī hutvā pañca bhesajjāni viññāpento na bhesajjakaraṇīyena bhesajjaṃ viññāpento nāma hotīti “mahānāmasikkhāpadena kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Etāni pāṭidesanīyavatthūnīti pāḷiyaṃ āgatasappiādīni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ anāgatāni pana akappiyasappiādīni bhikkhunīnampi dukkaṭavatthūnīti veditabbaṃ. Sūpodanaviññattiyanti bhikkhūnaṃ pācittiyavatthūni bhikkhunīnaṃ pāṭidesanīyavatthūni ca ṭhapetvā avasesaviññattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Paṇītabhojanatā, agilānatā, akataviññattiyā paṭilābho, ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

This is called the Mahānāma training rule. And by this training rule, in a case where an invitation for requisites for the sick has been made on behalf of the Saṅgha, if a limit has been set there either by nights or by medicines, then only that many nights or that many medicines should be requested. Then, if one requests medicine beyond that limit of nights or medicines, or when there is no need for medicine, or requests a different medicine when there is a need for another, a pācittiya offense is stated. Therefore, one who is not ill, but having the perception of being ill, requests the five medicines, is called one who requests medicine without a medicinal need; thus it is said, 'he should be dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule.' The phrase 'These are items to be confessed' is stated with reference to ghee and so on that are mentioned in the Pāli. However, it should be understood that items not mentioned in the Pāli, such as impermissible ghee, are grounds for a dukkaṭa offense for bhikkhunīs as well. The phrase 'in the case of requesting curry and rice' is stated with reference to the remaining kinds of requests, setting aside the grounds for a pācittiya for bhikkhus and the grounds for a pāṭidesanīya for bhikkhunīs. The rest here is self-evident. The four factors here are: (1) its being a choice food, (2) the state of not being ill, (3) its obtainment without a request having been made, and (4) its consumption.

Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on choice foods is concluded.

10. Dantaponasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Tooth-Cleaner

263. Dasame [M 3.0070][V 3.0063] ayyavosāṭitakānīti pitupiṇḍassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ummāreti susāne katagehassa attano gehassa vā ummāre. Ghanabaddhoti ghanamaṃsena sambaddho, kathinasaṃhatasarīroti vuttaṃ hoti.

263. In the tenth, 'ayyavosāṭitakāni' is a term for the ancestral offering. 'On the threshold' (ummāre) means on the threshold of a dwelling made in a charnel ground, or of one's own dwelling. 'Of solid build' (ghanabaddha) means endowed with dense flesh; that is to say, having a hard and compact body.

264. Mukhadvāranti galanāḷikaṃ. Āhāranti ajjhoharitabbaṃ yaṃkiñci yāvakālikādiṃ. Āhareyyāti mukhadvāraṃ paveseyya. Mukhena vā paviṭṭhaṃ hotu nāsikāya vā, galena ajjhoharaṇīyattā sabbampi taṃ mukhadvāraṃ pavesitameva hoti. Yasmā pana te bhikkhū anāhārepi udake āhārasaññāya dantapone ca mukhadvāraṃ āhaṭaṃ idanti saññāya kukkuccāyiṃsu, tasmā vuttaṃ “te bhikkhū adinnaṃ…pe… sammā atthaṃ asallakkhetvā kukkuccāyiṃsū”ti. Udakañhi yathāsukhaṃ pātuṃ dantakaṭṭhañca dantaponaparibhogena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, tassa pana rasaṃ gilituṃ na vaṭṭati. Sacepi dantakaṭṭharaso ajānantassa anto pavisati, pācittiyameva. Anajjhoharantena pana dantakaṭṭhaṃ vā hotu aññaṃ vā, kiñci mukhe pakkhipituṃ vaṭṭati.

264. 'The mouth-door' means the throat passage. 'Food' means anything that is to be swallowed, such as yāvakālika items and so on. 'One might bring' means one might cause it to enter the mouth-door. Whether it has entered through the mouth or through the nose, since it is to be swallowed by means of the throat, all of it is considered to have been made to enter the mouth-door. And since those monks, even regarding water which is not food, had the perception of food, and regarding a tooth-cleaner, had the perception 'this has been brought to the mouth-door,' they became scrupulous. Therefore it was said: 'Those monks... not given... became scrupulous.' Indeed, it is permissible to drink water as one likes and to use a tooth-stick for the purpose of cleaning the teeth, but it is not permissible to swallow its flavor. If the flavor of the tooth-stick enters inside without one's knowledge, it is a pācittiya offense. But for one who is not swallowing, it is permissible to place a tooth-stick or anything else in the mouth.

265. Akallakoti gilāno sahatthā paribhuñjituṃ asakkonto mukhena paṭiggaṇhāti. Uccāraṇamattanti ukkhipanamattaṃ. Ekadesenapīti aṅguliyāpi phuṭṭhamattena. Taṃ ce paṭiggaṇhāti, sabbaṃ paṭiggahitamevāti veṇukoṭiyā bandhitvā ṭhapitattā. Sacepi bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitameva ghaṭaṃ dāyakena hatthapāse ṭhatvā ghaṭaṃ dassāmīti dinnaveṇukoṭiggahaṇavasena paṭiggaṇhāti, ubhayakoṭibaddhaṃ sabbampi paṭiggahitameva hoti. Bhikkhussa atthāya apīḷetvā pakatiyā pīḷiyamānaucchurasaṃ sandhāya “gaṇhathā”ti vuttattā “abhihāro na paññāyatī”ti vuttaṃ. Hatthapāse ṭhitassa pana bhikkhussa atthāya pīḷiyamānā ucchuto paggharantaṃ rasaṃ gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati, doṇikāya sayaṃ paggharantaṃ ucchurasaṃ majjhe āvaritvā āvaritvā vissajjitampi gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Katthaci aṭṭhakathāsu.

265. 'Not well' means: a sick person, being unable to partake with his own hand, receives with his mouth. 'Mere lifting' means just lifting up. 'Even by a part' means even by the mere touch of a finger. If he receives it, the whole is considered received; this is because it was tied and placed by the end of a bamboo stick. Even if a monk receives a pot that is just standing on the ground by means of taking hold of the end of a bamboo stick given by a donor who is standing within hand's reach and says, 'I will give the pot,' everything tied to both ends is considered received. Referring to sugarcane juice being pressed naturally, not specially pressed for the sake of a monk, because it was said, 'Take it,' it is said, 'An offering is not apparent.' But for a monk standing within hand's reach, it is permissible to take the juice dripping from sugarcane being pressed for his sake. It is also permissible to take sugarcane juice flowing naturally into a trough, even that which is released after having been blocked in the middle. (This is found) in some commentaries.

Asaṃhārimeti thāmamajjhimena purisena asaṃhāriye. “Tintiṇikādipaṇṇesū”ti vacanato sākhāsu paṭiggahaṇaṃ ruhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Puñchitvā paṭiggahetvāti ettha “puñchite paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi, tasmā puñchitvā gahetvāti [M 3.0071] evamattho gahetabbo”ti vadanti. Puñchitvā paṭiggahetvā vāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Patte patitarajanacuṇṇañhi abbhantaraparibhogatthāya [V 3.0064] aparihaṭabhāvato paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Pubbābhogassa anurūpena “anupasampannassa datvā…pe… vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ “aññassa dassāmī”ti cittuppādamattena parasantakaṃ nāma na hoti, tasmā tassa adatvāpi paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

'Immovable' means that which cannot be moved by a man of average strength. From the statement 'on tamarind leaves, etc.,' it should be understood that receiving on branches is valid. Regarding 'having wiped and received,' some say, 'For a wiped bowl, there is no act of receiving; therefore, the meaning should be taken as "having wiped and taken."' Or the meaning here should be understood thus: 'having wiped or having received.' Indeed, regarding dust or powder that has fallen into a bowl, because it has not been brought for the purpose of internal use, it is permissible to receive and consume it. In accordance with a prior intention, it was said, 'Having given to one not fully ordained... it is permissible.' And since, by the mere arising of the thought, 'I will give this to another,' it does not become the property of another, therefore, even without giving it to him, it is permissible to receive and consume it.

Bhikkhussa detīti aññassa bhikkhussa deti. Kañjikanti khīrarasādiṃ yaṃkiñci dravaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Hatthato mocetvā puna gaṇhāti, uggahitakaṃ hotīti āha “hatthato amocentenevā”ti. Ālulentānanti ālolentānaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Āharitvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitattā abhihāro natthīti āha “patto paṭiggahetabbo”ti. Paṭhamataraṃ uḷuṅkato thevā patte patantīti ettha “yathā paṭhamataraṃ patitatheve doso natthi, tathā ākiritvā apanentānaṃ pacchā patitathevepi abhihaṭattā nevatthi doso”ti vadanti. Carukenāti khuddakabhājanena. Mukhavaṭṭiyāpi gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti mukhavaṭṭiṃ ukkhipitvā hatthe phusāpite gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Esa nayoti kāyapaṭibaddhapaṭibaddhampi kāyapaṭibaddhamevāti ayaṃ nayo. Tathā ca tattha kāyapaṭibaddhe taṃpaṭibaddhe ca thullaccayameva vuttaṃ.

'He gives to a bhikkhu' means he gives to another bhikkhu. 'Kañjika' is said referring to any liquid such as milk-juice and so on. If he releases it from his hand and takes it again, it becomes 'taken up'; therefore, it was said, 'by not releasing it from the hand.' 'Ālulentānaṃ' means 'of those who are stirring'; or this itself is the reading. Because it was brought and placed on the ground, there is no offering; therefore, it was said, 'the bowl should be received.' Regarding 'drops from a ladle falling into the bowl for the first time,' some say: 'Just as there is no fault in the drop that falls first, so too, for those who pour and then remove it, even if a drop falls afterwards, because it has been offered, there is no fault.' 'Carukena' means with a small vessel. 'It is permissible to take it even with the rim of the mouth' means it is permissible to take it by lifting the rim of the mouth and causing it to touch the hand. 'Some' means the residents of Abhayagiri. 'This is the method' means this is the principle: that which is connected to what is connected to the body is itself connected to the body. And so, in that case, for what is connected to the body and for what is connected to that, only a grave offense is stated.

Tenāti yassa bhikkhuno santikaṃ gataṃ, tena. Tasmāti yasmā mūlaṭṭhasseva paribhogo anuññāto, tasmā. Taṃ divasaṃ hatthena gahetvā dutiyadivase paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa uggahitakapaṭiggahitaṃ hotīti āha “anāmasitvā”ti. Appaṭiggahitattā “sannidhipaccayā anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ. Appaṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa adinnamukhadvārāpatti hotīti āha “paṭiggahetvā pana paribhuñjitabba”nti. “Taṃ divasaṃ…pe… na tato para”nti vacanato taṃ divasaṃ hatthena gahetvā vā aggahetvā vā ṭhapitaṃ dutiyadivase appaṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa adinnamukhadvārāpatti hoti, hatthena gahetvā ṭhapitaṃ dutiyadivase paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa pana uggahitakapaṭiggahitaṃ hoti. Appaṭiggahitameva hi hatthena gahetvā ṭhapitaṃ. “Sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjitu”nti hi vacanato appaṭiggahitasseva tasmiṃ divase paribhogo anuññāto. Tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ gaṇṭhipade “taṃ diyyamānaṃ patatīti ettha yathā gaṇabhojanādīsu gilānādīnaṃ [M 3.0072] kukkuccāyantānaṃ gaṇabhojanaṃ anuññātaṃ, evamidhāpi bhagavatā paṭiggahitameva kukkuccavinodanatthaṃ anuññāta”nti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. “Taṃ diyyamānaṃ patatī”ti avisesena vuttattā catūsupi kālikesu ayaṃ nayo veditabbo.

'By him' means by that monk to whose presence it has gone. 'Therefore' means: because use is permitted only for the one at the original place, therefore... For one who takes it by hand that day and consumes it on the second day after receiving it, it becomes 'taken up and received'; therefore, it was said, 'without touching.' Because it has not been formally received, it was said, 'There is no offense on account of storing.' For one who consumes it without having received it, there is the offense of taking what is not given through the mouth-door; therefore, it was said, 'But it should be consumed after having received it.' According to the statement, 'That day... and not beyond': if something placed on that day—whether taken by hand or not—is consumed on the second day without being received, there is the offense of taking what is not given through the mouth-door. But for one who consumes on the second day, after receiving it, something that was taken by hand and placed, it becomes 'taken up and received.' For it was indeed something not formally received that was taken by hand and placed. Indeed, according to the statement 'to take and consume it oneself,' use on that day is permitted only for what has not been formally received. Therefore, what was said in the gloss—'Regarding "while it is being given, it falls": just as in cases like group meals, an allowance for group meals was made for the sick and the scrupulous, so too here the Blessed One, to dispel scrupulosity, allowed only what had already been received'—that should not be accepted. Because 'while it is being given, it falls' was stated without distinction, this principle should be understood for all four kinds of time-limited items.

Satthakenāti paṭiggahitasatthakena. Kasmā panettha uggahitapaccayā sannidhipaccayā vā doso [V 3.0065] na siyāti āha “na hi taṃ paribhogatthāya pariharantī”ti. Imināva bāhiraparibhogatthaṃ sāmaṃ gahetvā anupasampannena dinnaṃ vā gahetvā pariharituṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Tasmā pattasammakkhanādiatthaṃ sāmaṃ gahetvā parihaṭatelādiṃ sace paribhuñjitukāmo hoti, paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa anāpatti. Abbhantaraparibhogatthaṃ pana sāmaṃ gahitaṃ paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa uggahitakapaṭiggahitaṃ hoti, appaṭiggahetvā paribhuñjantassa adinnamukhadvārāpatti hoti, abbhantaraparibhogatthameva anupasampannena dinnaṃ gahetvā pariharantassa siṅgīloṇakappo viya sannidhipaccayā āpatti hoti.
