Keci pana “thāmamajjhimassa purisassa uccāraṇamattaṃ hotītiādinā vuttapañcaṅgasampattiyā paṭiggahaṇassa ruhanato bāhiraparibhogatthampi sace anupasampannena dinnaṃ gaṇhāti, paṭiggahitamevā”ti vadanti. Evaṃ sati idha bāhiraparibhogatthaṃ anupasampannena dinnaṃ gahetvā pariharantassa sannidhipaccayā āpatti vattabbā siyā, “na hi taṃ paribhogatthāya pariharantī”ti ca na vattabbaṃ, tasmā bāhiraparibhogatthaṃ gahitaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ nāma na hotīti veditabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ pañcasu paṭiggahaṇaṅgesu “paribhogatthāyā”ti visesanaṃ vattabbanti? Na vattabbaṃ. Paṭiggahaṇañhi paribhogatthameva hotīti “paribhogatthāyā”ti visuṃ avatvā “tañce bhikkhu kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā paṭiggaṇhātī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Apare pana “satipi paṭiggahaṇe ‘na hi taṃ paribhogatthāya pariharantī’ti idha aparibhogatthāya pariharaṇe anāpatti vuttā”ti vadanti. Udukkhalamusalāni khiyyantīti ettha udukkhalamusalānaṃ khayena pisitakoṭṭitabhesajjesu sace āgantukavaṇṇo paññāyati, na vaṭṭati.

‘With a knife’ means with a formally received knife. Why is there no offense here on account of the ‘taken up’ condition or the ‘storage’ condition? It is said, ‘For they do not carry it for the purpose of consumption.’ By this, it is shown that it is permissible to take something oneself for external use, or to take and carry what is given by an unordained person. Therefore, if one takes oil, etc., oneself for the purpose of anointing a bowl, etc., and carries it, and if one wishes to consume it, there is no offense for one who consumes it after having formally received it. However, for something taken oneself for internal consumption, if one consumes it after having formally received it, it becomes ‘taken up and formally received.’ If one consumes it without having formally received it, there is an offense of taking what is not given through the mouth-door. If one takes and carries what is given by an unordained person for internal consumption, there is an offense on account of storage, like the case of horn-salt. Some, however, say, ‘Because the receiving is established by the fulfillment of the five factors stated in the passage beginning, “it is a mere lifting by a man of average strength,” even if one takes what is given by an unordained person for external use, it is indeed formally received.’ If this is so, then in this case, for one who takes and carries what is given by an unordained person for external use, an offense on account of storage would have to be stated, and the statement ‘for they do not carry it for the purpose of consumption’ should not be said. Therefore, it should be understood that something taken for external use is not called ‘formally received.’ If so, should the qualification ‘for the purpose of consumption’ be stated among the five factors of formal receiving? It should not be stated. For formal receiving is indeed for the purpose of consumption, and thus, without stating it separately, only this much is said: ‘if a monk formally receives it with his body or with what is attached to his body.’ Others, however, say, ‘Even when there is a formal receiving, here, in the statement “for they do not carry it for the purpose of consumption,” no offense is stated for carrying it for a purpose other than consumption.’ Regarding ‘the mortar and pestle wear out’—if, due to the wearing out of the mortar and pestle, a foreign color is discernible in medicines that have been pounded and ground, it is not permissible.

Suddhaṃ udakaṃ hotīti rukkhasākhādīhi gaḷitvā patanaudakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Patto vāssa paṭiggahetabboti etthāpi pattagataṃ chupitvā dentassa hatthalaggena [M 3.0073] āmisena dosābhāvatthaṃ pattapaṭiggahaṇanti abbhantaraparibhogatthameva paṭiggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ sāmaṇerassa patte patati…pe… paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahatīti ettha punappunaṃ gaṇhantassa attano patte pakkhittameva “attano santaka”nti sanniṭṭhānakaraṇato hatthagataṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahati, paricchinditvā dinnaṃ pana gaṇhantassa gahaṇasamayeyeva “attano santaka”nti sanniṭṭhānassa katattā hatthagataṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati. Kesañci atthāya odanaṃ pakkhipatīti ettha anupasampannassa atthāya pakkhipantepi “āgantvā gaṇhissatī”ti sayameva pakkhipitvā ṭhapanato paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahati, anupasampannassa hatthe pakkhittaṃ pana anupasampanneneva ṭhapitaṃ nāma hotīti paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati pariccattabhāvato. Tena vuttaṃ “sāmaṇera…pe… pariccattattā”ti.

‘It becomes pure water’ is said with reference to water that falls after dripping from tree branches and the like. Regarding ‘Or the bowl should be formally received by him,’ here too, the formal receiving of the bowl is for the purpose of avoiding a fault from the food clinging to the hand of the one who gives after touching what is in the bowl; thus, the formal receiving should be understood as being only for internal consumption. Regarding ‘Whatever falls into the novice’s bowl… the formal receiving is not relinquished,’ here, for one who repeatedly takes what has been placed in one's own bowl, because of making the determination ‘it is my own possession,’ the formal receiving by hand is not relinquished. However, for one who takes what has been given after being demarcated, because the determination ‘it is my own possession’ was made at the very moment of taking, the formal receiving by hand is relinquished. Regarding ‘He places rice for the sake of some,’ here, even when placing it for the sake of an unordained person, because one places it oneself and sets it down with the thought, ‘He will come and take it,’ the formal receiving is not relinquished. But what is placed in the hand of an unordained person is considered as having been placed by the unordained person himself, and thus the formal receiving is relinquished due to its having been given up. Therefore, it is said, ‘A novice… because it has been relinquished.’

Paṭiggahaṇūpagaṃ bhāraṃ nāma thāmamajjhimassa purisassa ukkhepārahaṃ. Kiñcāpi avissajjetvāva [V 3.0066] aññena hatthena pidahantassa doso natthi, tathāpi na pidahitabbanti aṭṭhakathāpamāṇeneva gahetabbaṃ. Macchikavāraṇatthanti ettha “sacepi sākhāya laggarajaṃ patte patati, sukhena paribhuñjituṃ sakkāti sākhāya paṭiggahitattā abbhantaraparibhogatthamevidha paṭiggahaṇanti mūlapaṭiggahaṇameva vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Apare pana “macchikavāraṇatthanti ettha vacanamattaṃ gahetvā bāhiraparibhogatthaṃ gahita”nti vadanti. Tasmimpi asatīti cāṭiyā vā kuṇḍake vā asati. Anupasampannaṃ gāhāpetvāti taṃyeva ajjhoharaṇīyabhaṇḍaṃ anupasampannena gāhāpetvā. Therassa pattaṃ anutherassāti therassa pattaṃ attanā gahetvā anutherassa deti. Tuyhaṃ yāguṃ mayhaṃ dehīti ettha evaṃ vatvā sāmaṇerassa pattaṃ gahetvā attanopi pattaṃ tassa deti. Ettha panāti paṇḍito sāmaṇerotiādipattaparivattanakathāya. Kāraṇaṃ upaparikkhitabbanti yathā mātuādīnaṃ telādīni haranto tathārūpe kicce anupasampannena aparivattetvāva paribhuñjituṃ labhati, evamidha pattaparivattanaṃ akatvā paribhuñjituṃ na labhatīti ettha kāraṇaṃ vīmaṃsitabbanti attho.

‘A load suitable for formal receiving’ is a load that can be lifted by a man of average strength. Although there is no offense for one who covers it with the other hand without having released it, nevertheless, the statement ‘it should not be covered’ should be taken on the authority of the commentary. Regarding ‘for the purpose of warding off flies,’ here it is said: ‘Even if dust clinging to the branch falls into the bowl, it can be consumed with ease because the branch has been formally received. Therefore, the formal receiving here is for internal consumption, and so only the initial formal receiving is valid.’ Others, however, say: ‘Regarding “for the purpose of warding off flies,” taking this as a mere phrase, it was taken for external use.’ ‘When that is not present’ means when a pot or a small vessel is not present. ‘Having an unordained person take it’ means having that very consumable item taken by an unordained person. ‘The elder’s bowl to the junior elder’ means he takes the elder’s bowl himself and gives it to the junior elder. Regarding ‘Give me your gruel,’ here, having said this, he takes the novice’s bowl and also gives his own bowl to him. ‘Here, however’ refers to the discussion on exchanging bowls, beginning with ‘a wise novice.’ The meaning of ‘The reason should be examined’ is this: just as one who is carrying oil, etc., for one’s mother and others, in such a situation, is able to consume it without having exchanged it with an unordained person, so here one is not able to consume it without an exchange of bowls. The reason for this should be investigated.

Ettha pana “sāmaṇerehi gahitataṇḍulesu parikkhīṇesu avassaṃ amhākaṃ sāmaṇerā saṅgahaṃ karontīti vitakkuppatti sambhavati, tasmā taṃ parivattetvāva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Mātāpitūnaṃ atthāya pana chāyatthāya vā gahaṇe [M 3.0074] paribhogāsā natthi, tasmā taṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kāraṇaṃ vadanti. Teneva ācariyabuddhadattattherenapi vuttaṃ –

Here, however, they state the reason: ‘When the rice taken by the novices is exhausted, the arising of the thought, “Our novices will certainly make a collection,” is possible. Therefore, it should be consumed only after having been exchanged. However, in the case of taking something for the sake of one’s parents or for the sake of shade, there is no expectation of consumption; therefore, that is permissible.’ For that very reason, it was also said by the Elder Ācariya Buddhādatta:

“Mātāpitūnamatthāya, telādiharatopi ca;

Sākhaṃ chāyādiatthāya, imesaṃ na visesati.

“For the sake of mother and father, and when carrying oil and such; for a branch for the sake of shade and so on—for these there is no distinction.

“Tasmā hissa visesassa, cintetabbaṃ tu kāraṇaṃ;

Tassa sālayabhāvaṃ tu, visesaṃ takkayāma ta”nti.

“Therefore, the reason for this difference should indeed be considered; we reckon that difference to be its state of having attachment.”

Idamevettha yuttataraṃ avassaṃ tathāvidhavitakkuppattiyā sambhavato. Na sakkā hi ettha vitakkaṃ sodhetunti. Mātādīnaṃ atthāya haraṇe pana nāvassaṃ tathāvidhavitakkuppattīti sakkā vitakkaṃ sodhetuṃ. Yattha hi vitakkaṃ sodhetuṃ sakkā, tattha nevatthi doso. Teneva vakkhati “sace pana sakkoti vitakkaṃ sodhetuṃ, tato laddhaṃ khāditumpi vaṭṭatī”ti.

This itself is more suitable here, because the arising of such a thought is certainly possible. For it is not possible here to purify the thought. But when carrying for the sake of one’s mother and others, the arising of such a thought is not certain, so it is possible to purify the thought. For wherever it is possible to purify the thought, there is no fault. For that very reason, he will say, ‘But if one is able to purify the thought, then it is permissible even to eat what is obtained from that.’”

Niccāletuṃ na sakkotīti niccāletvā sakkharā apanetuṃ na sakkoti. Ādhārake patto ṭhapito [V 3.0067] hotīti paṭiggahetabbapattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Cāletīti vinā kāraṇaṃ cāleti. Satipi kāraṇe bhikkhūnaṃ paribhogārahaṃ cāletuṃ na vaṭṭati. Kiñcāpi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, amanussikābādhe āmakamaṃsaṃ āmakalohita”nti (mahāva. 264) tādise ābādhe attano atthāya āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇaṃ anuññātaṃ, “āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hotī”ti ca sāmaññato paṭikkhittaṃ, tathāpi attano aññassa vā bhikkhuno atthāya aggahitattā “sīhavighāsādiṃ…pe… vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Sakkoti vitakkaṃ sodhetunti mayhampi detīti vitakkassa anuppannabhāvaṃ sallakkhetuṃ sakkoti, sāmaṇerassa dassāmīti suddhacittena mayā gahitanti vā sallakkhetuṃ sakkoti.

“It cannot be moved” means it is not possible to remove the gravel after moving it. “The bowl is placed on a stand” refers to a bowl that is to be received. “To move it” means to move it without a reason. Even if there is a reason, it is not proper to move what is suitable for bhikkhus’ use. Although it is stated, “Bhikkhus, I allow raw meat and raw blood in the case of diseases caused by non-human beings” (Mahāvagga 264), and in such a disease the acceptance of raw meat for one’s own benefit is permitted, and although it is generally prohibited by the statement, “he abstains from accepting raw meat,” nevertheless, because it is not taken for oneself or for the benefit of another bhikkhu, it is said, “lion’s leavings, etc., are permissible.” “He is able to purify the thought” means he is able to note the non-arising of the thought, “He will give it to me too,” or he is able to note, “It was taken by me with a pure mind, thinking, ‘I will give it to the novice.’”

Sace pana mūlepi paṭiggahitaṃ hotīti ettha “gahetvā gate mayhampi dadeyyunti saññāya sace paṭiggahitaṃ hotī”ti vadanti. Koṭṭhāse karotīti bhikkhusāmaṇerā ca attano attano abhirucitaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ gaṇhantūti sabbesaṃ samake koṭṭhāse karoti. Gahitāvasesanti [M 3.0075] sāmaṇerehi gahitakoṭṭhāsato avasesaṃ. Gaṇhitvāti “mayhaṃ idaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti gahetvā. Idha gahitāvasesaṃ nāma tena gaṇhitvā puna ṭhapitaṃ. Paṭiggahetvāti tadahu paṭiggahetvā. Teneva “yāvakālikena yāvajīvikasaṃsagge doso natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Sace pana purimadivase paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitā hoti, sāmisena mukhena tassā vaṭṭiyā dhūmaṃ pivituṃ na vaṭṭati. Samuddodakenāti appaṭiggahitasamuddodakena. Yasmā katakaṭṭhi udakaṃ pasādetvā visuṃ tiṭṭhati, tasmā “abbohārika”nti vuttaṃ. Laggatīti mukhe hatthe ca udake sukkhe setavaṇṇaṃ dassentaṃ laggati. Pānīyaṃ gahetvāti attanoyeva atthāya gahetvā. Sace pana pītāvasesaṃ tattheva ākirissāmīti gaṇhāti, puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Vikkhambhetvāti viyūhitvā, apanetvāti attho.

Regarding “But if it is received even at the root,” here they say, “If it is received with the perception, ‘Having taken it and gone, they might give some to me too.’” “He makes portions” means he makes equal portions for all, so that the bhikkhus and novices may take the portion they each prefer. “What remains after being taken” means what is left from the portion taken by the novices. “Having taken” means taking with the thought, “I will take this for myself.” Here, “what remains after being taken” refers to what was taken by him and then put down again. “Having received” means having received it on that very day. Therefore, it is said, “There is no fault when a temporary requisite is mixed with a lifelong one.” But if it was received on the previous day and set aside, it is not allowable to inhale the smoke from that roll with a mouth that contains food. “With seawater” means with unreceived seawater. Because a clearing nut, after clarifying the water, remains separate, it is therefore called “not for consumption.” “It sticks” means when the water dries on the mouth or hands, it sticks, showing a white color. “Having taken drinking water” means taking it for one’s own sake. But if one takes it with the thought, “I will discard what remains after drinking right here,” there is no further need for receiving. “Having dispersed” means having pushed away or having removed—that is the meaning.

Mahābhūtesūti sarīranissitesu mahābhūtesu. Patatīti vicchinditvā patati. Vicchinditvā patitameva hi paṭiggahetabbaṃ, na itaraṃ. Alladāruṃ rukkhato chinditvāpi kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti ettha mattikatthāya pathaviṃ khaṇitumpi vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Sappadaṭṭhakkhaṇeyeva vaṭṭatīti asati kappiyakārake sāmaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, aññadā paṭiggahāpetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Appaṭiggahitatā, ananuññātatā, dhūmādiabbohārikābhāvo, ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

“In the great elements” means in the great elements dependent on the body. “It falls” means it falls after being severed. Indeed, only what has fallen after being severed is to be accepted, not anything else. Regarding “It is allowable to make it even by cutting fresh wood from a tree,” here it should be understood that it is also allowable to dig the earth for clay. “It is allowable only at the moment of a snakebite” means when there is no one to make it allowable, it is permissible to take and use it oneself; at other times, it should be used after having it made allowable. The rest here is clear. The factors here are four: not having been received, not having been permitted, its being a consumable item (i.e., not something unusable like smoke), and the act of swallowing.

Dantaponasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on tooth-sticks is finished.

Niṭṭhito bhojanavaggo catuttho.

The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Meals, is finished.

5. Acelakavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics

1. Acelakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Naked Ascetics

273. Acelakavaggassa [V 3.0068] paṭhamasikkhāpade tesanti titthiyānaṃ. Tatthāti bhājane. Itoti pattato. Sace titthiyo vadatīti “paṭhamameva maṃ sandhāya abhiharitvā ṭhapitaṃ mayhaṃ santakaṃ hoti, imasmiṃ bhājane ākirathā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati. Sesamettha uttānameva. Aññatitthiyatā, ajjhoharaṇīyatā[M 3.0076], ajjhoharaṇatthāya sahatthā anikkhittabhājane dānanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

5. In the first training rule of the Acelaka Chapter, `tesaṃ` refers to the sectarians. `Tattha` means in a vessel. `Ito` means from the bowl. If a sectarian says, “What was brought and set aside for my sake from the very beginning becomes my property; pour it into this vessel,” it is allowable. The rest here is clear. The factors here are three: the person being a sectarian, the item being consumable, and the giving with one's own hand from a vessel that has not been put down, for the purpose of consumption.

Acelakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

1. The explanation of the training rule concerning naked ascetics is finished.

2. Uyyojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Dismissal

274. Dutiyaṃ uttānatthameva. Anācāraṃ ācaritukāmatā, tadatthameva upasampannassa uyyojanā, evaṃ uyyojentassa upacārātikkamoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

273. The second has a clear meaning. The factors here are three: the desire to engage in misconduct, the dismissal of one who has been ordained for that very purpose, and the transgression of the boundary by one who dismisses in such a way.

Uyyojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning dismissal is finished.

3. Sabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Training Rule on a House with Food

280. Tatiye piṭṭhasaṅghāṭoti dvārabāhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Khuddakaṃ nāma sayanigharaṃ vitthārato pañcahatthappamāṇaṃ hoti, tassa ca majjhimaṭṭhānaṃ piṭṭhasaṅghāṭato aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇameva hoti, tasmā tādise sayanighare piṭṭhasaṅghāṭato hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā nisinno piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā nisinno nāma hoti. Evaṃ nisinno ca majjhaṃ atikkamitvā nisinno nāma hotīti āha “iminā majjhātikkamaṃ dassetī”ti. Yathā vā tathā vā katassāti piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ āropetvā vā anāropetvā vā katassa. Sacittakanti anupavisitvā nisīdanacittena sacittakaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Pariyuṭṭhitarāgajāyampatikānaṃ sannihitatā, sayanigharatā, dutiyassa bhikkhuno abhāvo, anupakhajja nisīdananti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

2. In the third, `piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa` is a term for a door-post. A small sleeping chamber is five cubits in width, and its midpoint is only two and a half cubits from the door-post. Therefore, in such a sleeping chamber, one sitting having left a hand's reach from the door-post is said to be one who sits having passed the central beam. And one sitting thus is said to be one who sits having passed the middle; thus he said, “By this he shows the passing of the middle.” “Of one made in whatever way” means of one made either with a central beam installed or without one installed. “With intention” means it is with intention through the thought of sitting down after entering. The rest here is clear. The factors here are four: the presence of a husband and wife whose passion is aroused, it being a sleeping chamber, the absence of a second bhikkhu, and intruding and sitting down.

Sabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

274. The explanation of the training rule concerning eating together is finished.

284-289. Catutthapañcamesu [V 3.0069] natthi kiñci vattabbaṃ.

In the fourth and fifth, there is nothing that needs to be said.

6. Cārittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Conduct

298. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0077] pakativacanenāti ettha yaṃ dvādasahatthabbhantare ṭhitena sotuṃ sakkā bhaveyya, taṃ pakativacanaṃ nāma. Āpucchitabboti “ahaṃ itthannāmassa gharaṃ gacchāmī”ti vā “cārittaṃ āpajjāmī”ti vā īdisena vacanena āpucchitabbo. Sesamettha uttānameva. Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena nimantanasādiyanaṃ, santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchanā, bhattiyagharato aññagharappavesanaṃ, majjhanhikānatikkamo, samayassa vā āpadānaṃ vā abhāvoti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

3. In the sixth, regarding “by a normal utterance”: here, whatever could be heard by one standing within twelve cubits, that is called a “normal utterance.” “One should ask leave” means one should ask leave with such words as, “I am going to the house of so-and-so,” or “I am going on my rounds.” The rest here is clear. The five factors here are: accepting an invitation for one of the five kinds of food, not asking leave of a bhikkhu who is present, entering a house other than the one where the meal is offered, the time being before midday has passed, and the absence of a suitable occasion or an emergency.

Cārittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

280. The explanation of the training rule on going about is finished.

7. Mahānāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Mahānāma Training Rule

303. Sattame mahānāmo nāmāti anuruddhattherassa bhātā bhagavato cūḷapitu putto. Suddhodano sakkodano sukkodano dhotodano amitodanoti ime hi pañca janā bhātaro. Amitā nāma devī tesaṃ bhaginī, tissatthero tassā putto. Tathāgato ca nandatthero ca suddhodanassa puttā, mahānāmo ca anuruddhatthero ca sukkodanassa, ānandatthero amitodanassa. So bhagavato kaniṭṭho, mahānāmo mahallakataro sakadāgāmī ariyasāvako. Tena vuttaṃ “mahānāmo nāma…pe… ariyasāvako”ti.

In the seventh, the one named Mahānāma was the brother of the Elder Anuruddha, the son of the Blessed One’s younger paternal uncle. Indeed, these five persons were brothers: Suddhodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana. Their sister was the lady named Amitā, and the Elder Tissa was her son. The Tathāgata and the Elder Nanda were the sons of Suddhodana; Mahānāma and the Elder Anuruddha were the sons of Sukkodana; and the Elder Ānanda was the son of Amitodana. He was younger than the Blessed One, while Mahānāma was older, a once-returner and a noble disciple. Therefore, it is said: “Mahānāma by name… a noble disciple.”

305-306. Pāḷiyaṃ ajjaṇhoti ajja ekadivasanti attho, “ajjano”ti vā attho gahetabbo, no amhākaṃ. Kālaṃ āharissathāti sve harissatha. Tato ce uttari sādiyeyyāti sace tattha rattīhi vā bhesajjehi vā paricchedo kato hoti “ettakāyeva vā rattiyo ettakāni vā bhesajjāni viññāpetabbānī”ti, tato rattipariyantato vā bhesajjapariyantato vā uttari viññāpento sādiyeyya. “Imehi tayā bhesajjehi pavāritamha, amhākañca imināva bhesajjena attho”ti ācikkhitvā viññāpetumpi gilānova labhati.

In the Pāḷi, 'ajjaṇho' means 'today,' that is, 'one day'; or the meaning 'of today' (ajjano) should be taken, but 'of us' is not our preferred reading. 'Kālaṃ āharissatha' means 'you will bring it tomorrow.' 'If he should accept more than that' means: if a limit has been set there by nights or by medicines, such as, 'Only this many nights or only this many medicines are to be requested,' then if he, requesting, should go beyond that limit of nights or that limit of medicines, he accepts it. A sick person is also permitted to request after stating, 'We have been invited by you with these medicines, and we have need of this very medicine.'

310. Yasmā saṅghapavāraṇāyamevāyaṃ vidhi, tasmā “ye attano puggalikāya pavāraṇāya pavāritā”ti [V 3.0070] vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Saṅghapavāraṇatā[M 3.0078], bhesajjaviññatti, agilānatā, pariyantātikkamoti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

310. Because this procedure is only for an invitation by the Saṅgha, it is therefore said, 'those who have been invited by an individual invitation…'. The rest is clear in meaning. The state of being an invitation by the Saṅgha, the request for medicine, not being ill, and transgressing the limit—these are the four factors here.

Mahānāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mahānāma Training Rule is concluded.

8. Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Deployed Army

311. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānatthameva. Uyyuttasenā, dassanatthāya gamanaṃ, anuññātokāsato aññatra dassanaṃ, tathārūpapaccayassa āpadāya vā abhāvoti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

311. The eighth is clear in meaning. A deployed army, going for the purpose of seeing, seeing in a place other than one permitted, and the absence of a suitable reason or a calamity—these are the four factors here.

Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Deployed Army is concluded.

9. Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Dwelling in a Military Encampment

317. Navamasikkhāpadampi uttānameva. Tirattātikkamo, senāya sūriyassa atthaṅgamo, gilānatādīnaṃ abhāvoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

317. The ninth training rule is also clear in meaning. Exceeding three nights, the sun setting while one is in the military encampment, and the absence of illness and so forth—these are the three factors here.

Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Dwelling in a Military Encampment is concluded.

10. Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Military Spectacle

322. Dasame kati te lakkhāni laddhānīti tava sarappahārassa lakkhaṇabhūtā kittakā janā tayā laddhāti attho, kittakā tayā viddhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Uyyodhikādidassanatthāya gamanaṃ, anuññātokāsato aññatra dassanaṃ, tathārūpapaccayassa āpadāya vā abhāvoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

322. In the tenth, 'How many targets have you gained?' means: 'How many people, having become the mark of your arrow's strike, have been hit by you?' This is the meaning. It is also said, 'How many have you pierced?' The rest here is clear in meaning. Going for the purpose of seeing a military spectacle or the like, seeing in a place other than one permitted, and the absence of a suitable reason or a calamity—these are the three factors here.

Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Military Spectacle is concluded.

Niṭṭhito acelakavaggo pañcamo.

The fifth chapter, the Chapter on Naked Ascetics, is concluded.

6. Surāpānavaggo

6. The Sixth Chapter: On Drinking Intoxicants

1. Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Drinking Intoxicants

326-328. Surāpānavaggassa [M 3.0079][V 3.0071] paṭhamasikkhāpade vatiyāti gāmaparikkhepavatiyā. Pāḷiyaṃ piṭṭhasurādīsu piṭṭhaṃ bhājane pakkhipitvā tajjaṃ udakaṃ datvā madditvā katā piṭṭhasurā. Evaṃ pūve odane ca bhājane pakkhipitvā tajjaṃ udakaṃ datvā madditvā katā pūvasurā odanasurāti ca vuccati. “Kiṇṇā”ti pana tassā surāya bījaṃ vuccati. Ye surāmodakātipi vuccanti, te pakkhipitvā katā kiṇṇapakkhittā. Harītakīsāsapādinānāsambhārehi saṃyojitā sambhārasaṃyuttā.

In the first training rule of the Chapter on Drinking Intoxicants, 'within the boundary' means within the village enclosure. In the Pāḷi, regarding flour-liquor and so forth: flour-liquor is made by putting flour in a vessel, adding suitable water, and kneading it. Similarly, when cakes or rice are put in a vessel, suitable water is added, and it is kneaded, it is called cake-liquor or rice-liquor. 'Kiṇṇa' refers to the starter for that liquor. That which is made by adding what are also called 'liquor-cakes' is 'that to which a starter has been added.' That which is combined with various ingredients such as myrobalan and mustard seeds is 'that which is combined with ingredients.'

Madhukatālanāḷikerādipuppharaso ciraparivāsito pupphāsavo. Panasādiphalaraso phalāsavo. Muddikāraso madhvāsavo. Ucchuraso guḷāsavo. Harītakāmalakakaṭukabhaṇḍādinānāsambhārānaṃ raso ciraparivāsito sambhārasaṃyutto. Bījato paṭṭhāyāti sambhāre paṭiyādetvā cāṭiyaṃ pakkhittakālato, tālanāḷikerādīnaṃ puppharasassa gahitaabhinavakālatoyeva ca paṭṭhāya.

The juice from the flowers of the madhuca tree, palmyra palm, coconut tree, and so forth, when left to stand for a long time, is flower-liquor. The juice from fruits such as jackfruit is fruit-liquor. Grape juice is grape-liquor. Sugarcane juice is jaggery-liquor. The juice of various ingredients such as harītakī, āmalaka, and pungent spices, when left to stand for a long time, is 'that which is combined with ingredients.' 'From the seed onwards' means from the time the ingredients are prepared and put into a pot, and from the very time the fresh juice of flowers from the palmyra palm, coconut tree, and so forth is taken.

329. Loṇasovīrakaṃ suttañca anekehi bhesajjehi abhisaṅkhato amajjabhūto āsavaviseso. Vāsaggāhāpanatthanti sugandhibhāvaggāhāpanatthaṃ. Acittakaṃ lokavajjanti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Majjabhāvo, tassa pānañcāti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

329. Salt-vinegar is a special kind of fermented drink prepared with many medicines that has become non-intoxicating. 'For the purpose of imparting a scent' means for the purpose of imparting the quality of fragrance. Regarding 'unintentional, a worldly offense,' what is to be said here should be understood according to the method stated in the explanation of the first Pārājika. The rest here is clear in meaning. The state of being an intoxicant, and the drinking of it—these are the two factors here.

Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Drinking Intoxicants is concluded.

2. Aṅgulipatodakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Poking with a Finger

330. Dutiye bhikkhunīpi anupasampannaṭṭhāne ṭhitāti ettha bhikkhupi bhikkhuniyā anupasampannaṭṭhāne [V 3.0072] ṭhitoti veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānameva. Hasādhippāyatā, upasampannassa kāyena kāyāmasananti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

330. In the second, regarding 'a bhikkhunī also stands in the position of one not fully ordained,' it should be understood here that a bhikkhu also stands in the position of one not fully ordained in relation to a bhikkhunī. The rest here is clear in meaning. The intention of amusement, and bodily contact with one who is fully ordained—these are the two factors here.

Aṅgulipatodakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Poking with a Finger is concluded.

3. Hasadhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sport

335. Tatiyaṃ [M 3.0080] uttānatthameva. Uparigopphakatā, hasādhippāyena kīḷananti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

335. The third is clear in meaning. The water being above the ankles, and playing with the intention of amusement—these are the two factors here.

Hasadhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sport is concluded.

4. Anādariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Disrespect

344. Catutthe gārayho ācariyuggaho na gahetabboti yasmā ucchuraso sattāhakāliko, tassa kasaṭo yāvajīviko, dvinnaṃyeva samavāyo ucchuyaṭṭhi, tasmā vikāle ucchuyaṭṭhiṃ khādituṃ vaṭṭati guḷaharītakaṃ viyāti evamādiko gārayhācariyavādo na gahetabbo. Lokavajje ācariyuggaho na vaṭṭatīti lokavajjasikkhāpade āpattiṭṭhāne yo ācariyavādo, so na gahetabbo, lokavajjaṃ atikkamitvā “idaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyuggaho”ti vadantassa uggaho na vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Suttānulomaṃ nāma aṭṭhakathā. Paveṇiyā āgatasamodhānaṃ gacchatīti “paveṇiyā āgato ācariyuggahova gahetabbo”ti evaṃ vutte mahāaṭṭhakathāvādeyeva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti adhippāyo. Sesamettha uttānameva. Upasampannassa paññattena vacanaṃ, anādariyakaraṇanti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

344. In the fourth, a blameworthy teaching from a master should not be accepted. Because sugarcane juice is allowable for seven days and its dregs are allowable for life, and a sugarcane stalk is a combination of the two, therefore a blameworthy teaching from a master such as, 'It is allowable to chew a sugarcane stalk at the wrong time, like jaggery and myrobalan,' should not be accepted. 'In a worldly fault, a teaching from a master is not allowable' means that in a training rule concerning a worldly fault, a teaching from a master that constitutes a ground for an offense should not be accepted. The intention is that the teaching is not allowable for one who, having transgressed a worldly fault, says, 'This is our master's teaching.' The Suttānuloma is a commentary. 'It is included in what has come down by tradition' means that when it is said, 'Only a master's teaching that has come down by lineage should be accepted,' the intention is that it is included only in the view of the Great Commentary. The rest here is clear in meaning. A statement made by one who is fully ordained, and the act of disrespect—these are the two factors here.

Anādariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Disrespect is concluded.

5. Bhiṃsāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Frightening

345. Pañcamaṃ uttānatthameva. Upasampannatā, tassa dassanasavanavisaye bhiṃsāpetukāmatāya vāyamananti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

345. The fifth is clear in meaning. The other being fully ordained, and making an effort with the desire to frighten him within the range of sight and hearing—these are the two factors here.

Bhiṃsāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Frightening is concluded.

6. Jotisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Fire

350. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0081][V 3.0073] bhaggā nāma janapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīsaddena “bhaggā”ti vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ “bhaggāti janapadassa nāma”nti. Susumāragireti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tassa kira nagarassa māpanatthaṃ vatthuvijjācariyena nagaraṭṭhānassa pariggaṇhanadivase avidūre susumāro saddamakāsi giraṃ nicchāresi. Atha anantarāyena nagare māpite tameva susumāragiraṇaṃ subhanimittaṃ katvā susumāragiraṃtvevassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Keci pana “susumārasaṇṭhānattā susumāro nāma eko giri, so tassa nagarassa samīpe, tasmā taṃ susumāragiri etassa atthīti ‘susumāragirī’ti vuccatī”ti vadanti. Tathā vā hotu aññathā vā, nāmametaṃ tassa nagarassāti āha “susumāragiranti nagarassa nāma”nti. Bhesakaḷāti ghampaṇḍanāmako gacchaviseso. Keci “setarukkho”tipi vadanti. Tesaṃ bahulatāya pana taṃ vanaṃ bhesakaḷāvanantveva paññāyittha. “Bhesagaḷāvane”tipi pāṭho. “Bheso nāma eko yakkho ayuttakārī, tassa tato gaḷitaṭṭhānatāya taṃ vanaṃ bhesagaḷāvanaṃ nāma jāta”nti hi keci.

350. In the sixth, the Bhaggas are royal princes of a country. Their residence, even a single country, is known by the established term 'Bhaggā.' Hence it is said, 'Bhaggā is the name of the country.' Susumāragiri is the name of a city. It is said that for the founding of this city, on the day the master of architecture was surveying the city's location, a crocodile nearby made a sound, uttering a roar. Then, when the city was established without any obstacle, they took that very roar of the crocodile as a good omen and gave it the name Susumāragira. Some, however, say, 'Because there was a mountain shaped like a crocodile, named Susumāra, near that city, it is therefore called Susumāragiri, meaning it has the Susumāra mountain.' Whether it is so or otherwise, this is the name of that city; thus he says, 'Susumāragiri is the name of the city.' Bhesakaḷā is a type of tree called ghampaṇḍa. Some also say it is the 'white tree.' Due to their abundance, that forest became known as Bhesakaḷāvana. There is also the reading 'Bhesagaḷāvana.' For some say, 'There was a mischievous yakkha named Bhesa, and because that was the place where he was driven out, the forest became known as Bhesagaḷāvana.'

352. Jotikaraṇeti aggikaraṇe. Sesamettha uttānameva. Agilānatā, anuññātakaraṇābhāvo, visibbetukāmatā, samādahananti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

352. Jotikaraṇe means kindling a fire. The rest here is straightforward. Herein, these are the four factors: not being ill, the absence of an allowable reason, the desire to warm oneself, and the act of kindling.

Jotisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Fire is concluded.

7. Nahānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Bathing

357. Sattamasikkhāpadassa pāḷiyaṃ asambhinnenāti amakkhitena, anaṭṭhenāti attho. Orenaddhamāsaṃ nahāyeyyāti nahātadivasato paṭṭhāya addhamāse aparipuṇṇe nahāyeyya. Sesamettha uttānameva. Majjhimadeso, ūnakaddhamāse nahānaṃ, samayānaṃ vā nadīpāragamanassa vā āpadānaṃ vā abhāvoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

357. In the Pāli of the seventh training rule, asambhinnena means not smeared, that is, not for the purpose of adornment. Orenaddhamāsaṃ nahāyeyya means one should bathe before half a month has passed from the day of the previous bath. The rest here is straightforward. The three factors here are: (1) being in the Middle Country; (2) bathing when less than half a month has passed; and (3) the absence of a valid reason, such as an occasion of travel, crossing a river, or a calamity.

Nahānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Bathing is concluded.

8. Dubbaṇṇakaraṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Making a Displeasing Color

368. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0082][V 3.0074] “cammakāranīlaṃ nāma pakatinīla”nti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Gaṇṭhipade pana “cammakārā udake tipumalaṃ ayagūthañca pakkhipitvā cammaṃ kāḷaṃ karonti, taṃ cammakāranīla”nti vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Vuttappakārassa cīvarassa akatakappatā, anaṭṭhacīvarāditā, nivāsanaṃ vā pārupanaṃ vāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

368. In the eighth, 'cammakāranīlaṃ means natural blue' is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas. In a Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said, 'Tanners make leather black by putting tin dross and iron rust into water; that is cammakāranīla.' The rest here is straightforward. The three factors here are: (1) the robe of the said kind not having been made allowable; (2) the robe not being lost or destroyed; and (3) it being a lower robe or an upper robe.

Dubbaṇṇakaraṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Making a Displeasing Color is concluded.

9. Vikappanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Training Rule on Assignment

374. Navame apaccuddhāraṇanti “mayhaṃ santakaṃ paribhuñja vā vissajjehi vā”tiādinā akatapaccuddhāraṃ. Yena vinayakammaṃ katanti yena saddhiṃ vinayakammaṃ kataṃ. Tiṃsakavaṇṇanāyanti nissaggiyavaṇṇanāyaṃ. Paribhogena kāyakammaṃ, apaccuddhārāpanena vacīkammaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Sāmaṃ vikappitassa apaccuddhāro, vikappanupagacīvaratā, paribhogoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

374. In the ninth, apaccuddhāraṇaṃ (not withdrawn) means that the withdrawal has not been made from the person to whom the item was assigned with a statement such as, 'Use or dispose of what is mine.' Yena vinayakammaṃ kataṃ means with whom the formal act of the Vinaya was performed. Tiṃsakavaṇṇanāyanti means in the commentary on the thirty [Nissaggiya rules]. Through use, it is a bodily action; by not having it withdrawn, it is a verbal action. The rest here is straightforward. The three factors here are: (1) non-withdrawal of what one has assigned oneself; (2) the state of a robe being subject to assignment; and (3) use.

Vikappanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Assignment is concluded.

10. Cīvaraapanidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Concealing a Robe

377. Dasamaṃ uttānatthameva. Upasampannassa santakānaṃ pattādīnaṃ apanidhānaṃ, vihesetukāmatā vā hasādhippāyatā vāti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

377. The tenth is straightforward in meaning. The two factors here are: (1) the concealing of the belongings of an ordained person, such as a bowl; and (2) the intention to harass or the intention to joke.

Cīvaraapanidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Concealing a Robe is concluded.

Niṭṭhito surāpānavaggo chaṭṭho.

The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Liquor, is concluded.

7. Sappāṇakavaggo

7. The Chapter on Living Beings

1. Sañciccasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Intention

382. Sappāṇakavaggassa [M 3.0083][V 3.0075] paṭhamasikkhāpade usuṃ saraṃ assati khipatīti issāso, dhanusippakusaloti āha “dhanuggahācariyo”ti. Paṭisattuvidhamanatthaṃ dhanuṃ gaṇhantīti dhanuggahā, tesaṃ ācariyo dhanuggahācariyo. Appamattena vattaṃ kātabbanti yathā te pāṇā na maranti, evaṃ sūpaṭṭhitassatinā senāsane vattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Aṅgānipi manussaviggahe vuttanayena veditabbānīti.

382. In the first training rule of the Chapter on Living Beings, issāso (an archer) is one who shoots or throws an arrow (usuṃ saraṃ). Since he is skilled in the art of the bow, he is called a 'teacher of archers' (dhanuggahācariyo). Dhanuggahā (bowmen) are those who take up a bow for the purpose of destroying their enemies; their teacher is a dhanuggahācariyo. 'One should act with heedfulness' means that one should perform one's duties in the dwelling place with well-established mindfulness so that those living beings do not die. The rest here is straightforward. The factors, too, should be understood in the way explained in the case of a human being.

Sañciccasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Intention is concluded.

2. Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Living Beings

387. Dutiye udakasaṇṭhānakappadeseti yattha bhūmibhāge udakaṃ nikkhittaṃ santiṭṭhati, na sahasā parikkhayaṃ gacchati, tādise padese. Sesamettha uttānameva. Aṅgāni siñcanasikkhāpade vuttanayāneva.

387. In the second, 'a place suitable for water to remain' means a place on the ground where water, when poured, remains and does not quickly disappear. The rest here is straightforward. The factors are the same as explained in the training rule on sprinkling.

Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Living Beings is concluded.

3. Ukkoṭanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Revoking

392. Tatiye yathāpatiṭṭhitabhāvena patiṭṭhātuṃ na dentīti tesaṃ pavattiākāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana dhammena adhikaraṇaṃ nihataṃ, taṃ sunihatameva. Sace vippakate kamme paṭikkosati, taṃ saññāpetvāva kātabbaṃ. Itarathā kammañca kuppati, kārakānañca āpatti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Yathādhammaṃ nihatabhāvo, jānanā, ukkoṭanāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

392. In the third, the phrase 'they do not allow it to stand as established' is stated to show the manner of their proceeding. A legal question that has been settled according to the Dhamma is indeed well-settled. If one objects while the formal act is still incomplete, it should only be done after informing them. Otherwise, the formal act is invalidated, and those who performed it incur an offense. The rest here is straightforward. The three factors here are: (1) the state of being settled according to the Dhamma; (2) knowing this; and (3) revoking it.

Ukkoṭanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Revoking is concluded.

4. Duṭṭhullasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Training Rule on a Gross Offense

399. Catutthe [M 3.0084][V 3.0076] tassevāti yo āpanno, tasseva. Ārocetīti paṭicchādanatthameva mā kassaci ārocesīti vadati. Vatthupuggaloti āpannapuggalo. Yenassa ārocitanti yena dutiyena assa tatiyassa ārocitaṃ. Koṭi chinnā hotīti yasmā paṭicchādanapaccayā āpattiṃ āpajjitvāva dutiyena tatiyassa ārocitaṃ, tasmā tappaccayā puna tena āpajjitabbāpattiyā abhāvato āpattiyā koṭi chinnā nāma hoti.

399. In the fourth, tasseva (of that very one) means: of that very one who has committed the offense. Āroceti (he informs) means that for the very purpose of concealment, he says, 'Do not inform anyone.' Vatthupuggalo means the person who has committed the offense. Yenassa ārocitaṃ means: by which second person it was reported to this third person. Koṭi chinnā hoti (the end is cut off) means that since the second person, having already incurred an offense because of concealment, reported it to the third, there is therefore no further offense to be incurred by him on that account. Thus, the end of the offense is said to be cut off.

400. “Anupasampannassa sukkavissaṭṭhi ca kāyasaṃsaggo cāti ayaṃ duṭṭhullaajjhācāro nāmā”ti idaṃ duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāya na sameti. Vuttañhi tattha (pāci. aṭṭha. 82) “anupasampannassa duṭṭhullaṃ vā aduṭṭhullaṃ vā ajjhācāranti ettha ādito pañca sikkhāpadāni duṭṭhullo nāma ajjhācāro, sesāni aduṭṭhullo, sukkavissaṭṭhikāyasaṃsaggaduṭṭhullaattakāmā panassa ajjhācāro nāmā”ti. “Ārocane anupasampannassa duṭṭhullaṃ aññathā adhippetaṃ, paṭicchādane aññathā”ti etthāpi visesakāraṇaṃ na dissati, tasmā aṭṭhakathāya pubbenāparaṃ na sameti. Avirodhaṃ icchantena pana vīmaṃsitabbamettha kāraṇaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Upasampannassa duṭṭhullāpattijānanaṃ, paṭicchādetukāmatāya nārocessāmīti dhuranikkhepoti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

400. The statement, 'For one who is not fully ordained, emission of semen and physical contact are called gross misconduct,' does not agree with the commentary on the training rule about reporting a gross offense. For it is stated there: 'For one who is not fully ordained, misconduct may be gross or not gross. Herein, the first five training rules are called gross misconduct, the rest are not gross. But for him, emission of semen, physical contact, and gross offenses related to sensual gratification are called misconduct.' As for the suggestion that 'in the case of reporting, what is gross for one not fully ordained is intended in one way, and in the case of concealment, in another,' no specific reason for this is seen here either. Therefore, the earlier part of the commentary does not agree with the later part. However, one who desires consistency should investigate the reason here. The rest here is straightforward. The two factors here are: (1) knowing the gross offense of one who is fully ordained; and (2) laying aside the responsibility with the thought, 'I will not report it,' out of a desire to conceal.

Duṭṭhullasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on a Gross Offense is concluded.

5. Ūnavīsativassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning One Under Twenty Years of Age

402. Pañcame rūpasuttanti heraññikānaṃ suttaṃ. Duruttānanti akkosavasena duruttānaṃ, duruttattāyeva durāgatānaṃ. Vacanapathānanti ettha vacanameva tadatthaṃ ñātukāmānaṃ ñāpetukāmānañca pathoti vacanapatho. Dukkhamānanti dukkhena khamitabbānaṃ.

402. In the fifth, `rūpasutta` means the craft of goldsmiths. `Duruttānaṃ` means of those with harsh words by way of abuse, and of those whose speech is ill-come precisely because it is harsh. `Vacanapatha` means that here, speech itself is the path for those who wish to know its meaning and for those who wish to make it known. `Dukkhamānaṃ` means of those things which must be endured with difficulty.

404. Gabbhe [M 3.0085] sayitakālena saddhiṃ vīsatimaṃ vassaṃ assāti gabbhavīso. Hāyanavaḍḍhananti gabbhamāsesu adhikesu uttarihāyanaṃ, ūnesu vaḍḍhananti veditabbaṃ. Ekūnavīsativassanti dvādasamāse mātukucchismiṃ vasitvā mahāpavāraṇāya jātakālato paṭṭhāya ekūnavīsativassaṃ. Pāṭipadadivaseti pacchimikāya vassūpagamanadivase. “Tiṃsarattidivo māso”ti [V 3.0077] (a. ni. 3.71; 8.43; vibha. 1023) vacanato “cattāro māsā parihāyantī”ti vuttaṃ. Vassaṃ ukkaḍḍhantīti vassaṃ uddhaṃ kaḍḍhanti, tatiye saṃvacchare ekamāsaṃ adhikamāsavasena pariccajantā vassaṃ uddhaṃ kaḍḍhantīti attho, tasmā tatiyo saṃvaccharo terasamāsiko hoti, saṃvaccharassa pana dvādasamāsikattā aṭṭhārasasu vassesu adhikamāse visuṃ gahetvā “cha māsā vaḍḍhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tatoti chamāsato. Nikkaṅkhā hutvāti adhikamāsehi saddhiṃ paripuṇṇavīsativassattā nibbematikā hutvā. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ tīsu gaṇṭhipadesu “aṭṭhārasannaṃyeva vassānaṃ adhikamāse gahetvā gaṇitattā sesavassadvayassapi adhikāni divasāni honteva, tāni adhikadivasāni sandhāya ‘nikkaṅkhā hutvā’ti vutta”nti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi dvīsu vassesu adhikadivasāni nāma visuṃ upalabbhanti tatiye vasse vassukkaḍḍhanavasena adhikamāse pariccatteyeva atirekamāsasambhavato. Tasmā dvīsu vassesu atirekadivasāni nāma visuṃ na sambhavanti.

404. `Gabbhavīso` means one for whom the twentieth year is reckoned together with the time spent in the womb. `Hāyanavaḍḍhanaṃ` means it should be understood that when there are more months in the womb, there is a further decrease, and when there are fewer, an increase. `Ekūnavīsativassaṃ` means nineteen years counting from the time of birth on the Mahāpavāraṇā day, after having dwelt for twelve months in the mother's womb. `Pāṭipadadivase` means on the day of entering the rains retreat of the later period. According to the statement, 'A month is thirty days and nights,' it is said, 'four months are reduced.' `Vassaṃ ukkaḍḍhanti` means they draw the year upwards. The meaning is that in the third year, by adding one month as an intercalary month, they draw the year upwards. Therefore, the third year has thirteen months. Since a year has twelve months, it is said that in eighteen years, by taking the intercalary months separately, 'six months are added.' `Tato` means from those six months. `Nikkaṅkhā hutvā` means having become free from doubt, because the full twenty years are completed together with the intercalary months. However, what was said in the three knot-points—'Because the intercalary months of only eighteen years were taken in the calculation, the remaining two years also have extra days, and it is with reference to those extra days that “having become free from doubt” was said'—that should not be accepted. For in two years, extra days are not found separately, since an extra month can arise only when an intercalary month is added by way of extending the year in the third year. Therefore, extra days do not arise separately in two years.

Nanu ca “te dve māse gahetvā vīsativassāni paripuṇṇāni hontī”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, ekūnavīsativassamhi puna aparasmiṃ vasse pakkhitte vīsativassāni paripuṇṇāni hontīti āha “ettha pana…pe… vutta”nti. Anekatthattā nipātānaṃ pana-saddo hi-saddatthe, ettha hīti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañhi vuttassevatthassa samatthanavasena vuttaṃ. Iminā ca imaṃ dīpeti “yaṃ vuttaṃ ‘ekūnavīsativassaṃ sāmaṇeraṃ nikkhamanīyapuṇṇamāsiṃ atikkamma pāṭipadadivase upasampādentī’ti, tattha gabbhamāsepi aggahetvā dvīhi māsehi aparipuṇṇavīsativassaṃ sandhāya ‘ekūnavīsativassa’nti vuttaṃ, tasmā adhikamāsesu dvīsu gahitesu vīsativassāni paripuṇṇāni nāma hontī”ti. Tasmāti yasmā gabbhamāsāpi gaṇanūpagā honti, tasmā. Ekavīsativasso hotīti jātadivasato paṭṭhāya vīsativasso samāno gabbhamāsehi saddhiṃ ekavīsativasso hoti.

Surely, why was it said, 'Taking those two months, twenty years are completed'? Because when another year is added to the nineteenth year, twenty years are completed; he states this with the words, 'Here, pana...pe... it is said.' Because particles have many meanings, the word `pana` is used here in the sense of `hi`; thus, it is as if `ettha hi` was said. Indeed, this is said by way of supporting the meaning that has already been stated. And by this, he explains the following: 'Regarding what was said—'They give higher ordination to a novice who is nineteen years old, having passed the full moon day of going forth, on the first day of the fortnight'—there, 'nineteen years old' was said with reference to someone who is twenty years old but incomplete by two months, without taking the months in the womb into account. Therefore, when the two additional months are taken, twenty years are indeed completed.' `Tasmā` means: because the months in the womb are also fit for calculation, therefore. `Ekavīsativasso hoti` means: being twenty years old counting from the day of birth, he becomes twenty-one years old together with the months in the womb.

406. Aññaṃ [M 3.0086] upasampādetīti upajjhāyo kammavācācariyo vā hutvā upasampādeti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Ūnavīsativassatā, ūnakasaññitā, upasampādananti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

406. `Aññaṃ upasampādeti` means that the preceptor or the teacher who recites the formal act performs the higher ordination. The rest here is self-evident. Being under twenty years of age, the perception of him being underage, and the act of higher ordination—these are the three factors here.

Ūnavīsativassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning one under twenty years of age is concluded.

6. Theyyasatthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Exposition of the Training Rule on a Caravan of Thieves

407. Chaṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ [V 3.0078] uttānatthameva. Theyyasatthakabhāvo, jānanaṃ, saṃvidhānaṃ, avisaṅketena gamananti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

407. The sixth training rule is self-evident in meaning. The four factors here are: the fact of it being a caravan of thieves, knowing it to be so, making an arrangement, and going according to the arrangement without fail.

Theyyasatthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the training rule on a caravan of thieves is concluded.

412. Sattame natthi kiñci vattabbaṃ.

412. In the seventh, there is nothing to be said.

8. Ariṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Exposition of the Ariṭṭha Training Rule

417. Aṭṭhame bādhayiṃsūti haniṃsu. Taṃtaṃsampattiyā vibandhanavasena sattasantānassa antare vemajjhe eti āgacchatīti antarāyo, diṭṭhadhammikādianattho. Anatikkamanaṭṭhena tasmiṃ antarāye niyuttā, antarāyaṃ vā phalaṃ arahanti, antarāyassa vā karaṇasīlāti antarāyikā. Tenāha “antarāyaṃ karontīti antarāyikā”ti. Ānantariyadhammāti ānantarikasabhāvā cetanādhammā. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – cutianantaraphalaṃ anantaraṃ nāma, tasmiṃ anantare niyuttā, taṃnibbattanena anantarakaraṇasīlā, anantarappayojanāti vā ānantarikā, te eva ānantariyāti vuttā. Kammāni eva antarāyikāti kammantarāyikā. Mokkhasseva antarāyaṃ karoti, na saggassāti micchācāralakkhaṇābhāvato vuttaṃ. Na hi bhikkhuniyā dhammarakkhitabhāvo atthi. Pākatikabhikkhunīvasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ariyāya pana pavattaṃ apāyasaṃvattanikameva, nandamāṇavako cettha nidassanaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ samānacchandatāvasena vā na saggantarāyikatā[M 3.0087], mokkhantarāyikatā pana mokkhatthāya paṭipattiyā vidūsanato. Abhibhavitvā pana pavattiyaṃ saggantarāyikatāpi na sakkā nivāretunti.

417. In the eighth, `bādhayiṃsu` means they killed. That which comes into being in the midst of a being's continuity by way of obstructing various attainments is an obstacle (`antarāya`), namely, harm in this very life and so on. Because they are engaged in that obstacle in the sense of not overcoming it, or because they deserve the result that is an obstacle, or because they are disposed to create an obstacle, they are called `antarāyikā` (obstructive). Hence it is said, 'They create an obstacle, thus they are obstructive.' `Ānantariyadhammā` means volitional states that have an immediate nature. Herein, this is the word-meaning: the result immediately following death is called 'immediate' (`anantara`); because they are engaged in that immediacy, or because they are disposed to create the immediate by producing it, or because they have immediacy as their purpose, they are called `ānantarikā`; these very things are called `ānantariya`. Actions themselves are obstructive, thus they are `kammantarāyikā`. It is said, 'It creates an obstacle only to liberation, not to heaven,' because of the absence of the characteristic of sexual misconduct. For a bhikkhunī does not have the status of being protected by the Dhamma. And this is said with reference to an ordinary bhikkhunī. But in the case of a noble one, the act leads only to the lower realms; Nanda the youth is the example here. Alternatively, because of the similar consent of both, it is not an obstacle to heaven; but it is an obstacle to liberation because it corrupts the practice for the sake of liberation. However, in the case of an act occurring through coercion, even its being an obstacle to heaven cannot be prevented.

Ahetukadiṭṭhiakiriyadiṭṭhinatthikadiṭṭhiyova niyatabhāvaṃ pattā niyatamicchādiṭṭhidhammā. Paṭisandhidhammāti paṭisandhicittuppādamāha. Paṇḍakādiggahaṇañcettha nidassanamattaṃ sabbāyapi ahetukapaṭisandhiyā vipākantarāyikabhāvato. Yāhi ariye upavadati, tā cetanā ariyūpavādā jātā. Tato paranti khamāpanato upari. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ dibbacakkhukathāyaṃ vuttameva. Sañcicca āpannā āpattiyoti sañcicca vītikkantā satta āpattikkhandhā. Sañcicca vītikkantañhi antamaso dukkaṭadubbhāsitampi saggamaggaphalānaṃ antarāyaṃ [V 3.0079] karoti. Yāva bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānāti pārājikaṃ āpanno, na vuṭṭhāti sesagarukāpattiṃ āpanno, na deseti lahukāpattiṃ āpanno.

The very views of causelessness, inaction, and nihilism, having attained a fixed nature, are states of fixed wrong view. The term `paṭisandhidhammā` refers to the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness. The inclusion of eunuchs and so on here is merely an example, because all causeless rebirth-linking has the nature of being an obstacle to the fruition. Those volitions by which one slanders noble ones become 'slandering of noble ones.' `Tato paraṃ` means after asking for forgiveness. Whatever should be said here has already been said in the discourse on the divine eye. `Sañcicca āpannā āpattiyo` means the seven classes of offenses that are intentionally transgressed. For an intentionally transgressed offense, even down to a wrong-doing or wrong speech, creates an obstacle to heaven, the path, and the fruits. This is the case as long as one who has committed a `pārājika` offense continues to profess to be a bhikkhu; as long as one who has committed another serious offense does not arise from it; and as long as one who has committed a light offense does not confess it.

Ayaṃ bhikkhūti ariṭṭho bhikkhu. Rasena rasaṃ saṃsanditvāti anavajjena paccayaparibhuñjanarasena sāvajjakāmaguṇaparibhogarasaṃ samānetvā. Yoniso paccavekkhaṇena natthi ettha chandarāgoti nicchandarāgo, paccayaparibhogo. Upanento viyāti bandhanaṃ upanento viya. “Ghaṭento viyā”tipi pāṭho. Upasaṃharanto viyāti sadisataṃ upasaṃharanto viya ekantasāvajje anavajjabhāvapakkhepanato. Pāpakanti lāmakaṭṭhena duggatisampāpanaṭṭhena ca pāpakaṃ. Mahāsamuddaṃ bandhantena viyāti setukaraṇavasena mahāsāgaraṃ bandhantena viya. Sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhantoti sabbaññutaññāṇena “sāvajja”nti diṭṭhaṃ “anavajja”nti gahaṇena tena saha paṭivirujjhanto. Āṇācakketi paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpadasaṅkhāte, “abrahmacariyaṃ pahāyā”tiādidesanāsaṅkhāte ca āṇācakke.

This monk means the monk Ariṭṭha. 'By mixing taste with taste' means equating the taste of enjoying blameless requisites with the taste of enjoying blameworthy sensual pleasures. 'Through wise reflection, there is no sensual desire here' means the enjoyment of requisites is without sensual desire. 'Like one who fastens' means like one who fastens a bond. There is also the reading, 'like one who joins.' 'Like one who equates' means like one who equates to what is similar, by superimposing a blameless quality onto what is entirely blameworthy. 'Evil' means evil in the sense of being inferior and in the sense of leading to a bad destination. 'Like one who binds the great ocean' means like one who binds the great ocean by means of building a bridge. 'Contradicting the knowledge of omniscience' means contradicting it by taking what is seen as 'blameworthy' by the knowledge of omniscience to be 'blameless'. 'In the wheel of command' refers to the wheel of command designated as the first Pārājika training rule, and also designated as the teaching beginning with 'abandoning the unholy life,' and so forth.

Aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ nāma uraṭṭhi vā piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ vā sīsaṭṭhi vā. Tañhi nimmaṃsattā “kaṅkala”nti vuccati. Vigatamaṃsāya hi aṭṭhisaṅkhalikāya ekaṭṭhimhi vā kaṅkala-saddo niruḷho. Anudahanaṭṭhenāti anupāyapaṭipattiyā sampati āyatiñca anudahanaṭṭhena. Mahābhitāpanaṭṭhena anavaṭṭhitasabhāvatāya, ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhena [M 3.0088] muhuttakaraṇīyatāya, tāvakālikaṭṭhena parehi abhibhavanatāya, sabbaṅgapaccaṅgapalibhañjanaṭṭhena bhedanādiadhikaraṇabhāvena, ugghāṭasadisatāya adhikuṭṭanaṭṭhena, avaṇe vaṇaṃ uppādetvā anto anupavisanabhāvatāya vinivijjhanaṭṭhena, diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaanatthanimittatāya sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayaṭṭhena.

'A skeleton' means the breastbone, the spine, or the skull. Because it is fleshless, it is called a 'kaṅkala.' Indeed, the term 'kaṅkala' is established in reference to a chain of bones or a single bone that is devoid of flesh. 'By the meaning of burning up' means by the meaning of burning up both in the present and in the future through improper practice. By the meaning of great torment, due to its unstable nature; by the meaning of appearing as trifling; by the meaning of being temporary, due to being overpowered by others; by the meaning of breaking all major and minor limbs, due to being a basis for breaking and so on; by its resemblance to being uprooted and by the meaning of excessive pounding; by the meaning of piercing through, due to creating a wound where there was none and then entering inside; by the meaning of being dangerous and fearful, due to being a sign of misfortune in this life and the next.

Pāḷiyaṃ “thāmasā parāmāsā”tiādīsu evamattho veditabbo. Thāmasāti diṭṭhithāmena, tassā diṭṭhiyā thāmagatabhāvenāti attho. Parāmāsāti diṭṭhiparāmāsena, diṭṭhisaṅkhātaparāmāsenāti attho. Diṭṭhiyeva hi dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato āmasanena parāmāso. Abhinivissāti taṇhābhinivesapubbaṅgamena diṭṭhābhinivesena “idamettha sacca”nti abhinivisitvā. Voharatīti katheti. Yato ca kho te bhikkhūti yadā te bhikkhū. Evaṃbyākho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatāti idaṃ esa attano laddhiṃ nigūhitukāmatāya natthīti vattukāmopi bhagavato ānubhāvena sampaṭicchati. Buddhānaṃ kira sammukhā dve kathā kathetuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Kassa nu kho nāma tvaṃ moghapurisāti tvaṃ moghapurisa kassa khattiyassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā vessassa vā suddassa vā gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā devassa vā manussassa vā mayā evaṃ [V 3.0080] dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāsi. Sesamettha uttānameva. Dhammakammatā, samanubhāsanā, appaṭinissajjananti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

In the Pāli, in such phrases as 'thāmasā parāmāsā,' the meaning should be understood thus. 'Thāmasā' means with the firmness of view; that is, due to the state of having become firm in that view. 'Parāmāsā' means with the clinging to view; that is, with the misapprehension designated as view. For it is by wrongly grasping, after having transgressed the true nature of phenomena, that a view becomes a 'clinging.' 'Abhinivissāti' means having adhered with the adherence to view, which is preceded by adherence to craving, thinking, 'This alone is true here.' 'Voharatīti' means he speaks. 'Yato ca kho te bhikkhūti' means when those monks. 'Thus was it declared by the Blessed One, venerable sir'—this he accepts due to the Blessed One’s power, even though, wishing to conceal his own tenet, he wanted to say, 'It is not so.' For it is said that no one is able to make two different statements in the presence of the Buddhas. 'Foolish man, from whom—be it a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, a worker, a householder, a renunciant, a god, or a human—do you know the Dhamma to have been taught by me in this way?' The rest here is self-evident. The three factors here are: the act being in accordance with the Dhamma, the formal admonition, and the non-relinquishing of the view.

Ariṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Ariṭṭha Training Rule is concluded.

9. Ukkhittasambhogasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Commingling with a Suspended Monk

424. Navame payogagaṇanāyāti dānaggahaṇappayogagaṇanāya. Saṃvāse kammapariyosānavasena, sahaseyyāya ekasmiṃ nipanne itarassa nipajjanapayogavasena āpattiparicchedo veditabbo. Ettha ca padabhājane “ekacchanne”ti avisesena vuttattā nānūpacārepi ekacchanne nipajjantassa āpatti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. ukkhittasambhogasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ “saha [M 3.0089] vā seyyaṃ kappeyyāti nānūpacārepi ekacchanne nipajjeyyā”ti. Paṇṇattiṃ ajānantena arahatāpi kiriyābyākatacittena āpajjitabbattā “ticitta”nti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana kenaci vuttaṃ “ticittanti ettha vipākābyākatacittena saha vā seyyaṃ kappeyyāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo, aññathā sacittakattā sikkhāpadassa kiriyābyākataṃ sandhāya na yujjatī”ti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi sacittakasikkhāpadavītikkamo arahato na sambhavati. Teneva pathavīkhaṇanādīsu sacittakasikkhāpadesu ticittameva vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Akatānudhammatā, jānanā, sambhogādikaraṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

424. In the ninth rule, 'by counting the applications' means by counting the applications of giving and taking. In the case of communion, the determination of the offense should be understood as based on the conclusion of the formal act; in the case of sleeping together, it is based on the act of the other lying down when one has already lain down. And here, in the analysis of the terms, since 'under one roof' is stated without distinction, there is an offense for one lying down under one roof even without close proximity. For that reason, it is said in the commentary to the Mātikā: 'Or should he share a bed' means he might lie down under one roof even without close proximity. Because an offense can be incurred even by an Arahant who is unaware of the regulation, with a functionally indeterminate mind, it is said to be 'of three minds.' But what has been said by some—'Here, in "of three minds," the meaning should be understood thus: "or should he share a bed" along with a resultant indeterminate mind; otherwise, since the training rule is intentional, it would not be logical to refer to the functionally indeterminate'—that should not be accepted. For a transgression of an intentional training rule is not impossible for an Arahant. For that very reason, in intentional training rules such as digging the earth, it is simply stated as 'of three minds.' The rest here is self-evident. The three factors here are: non-performance of the corresponding duties, knowing, and engaging in communion, etc.

Ukkhittasambhogasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Commingling with a Suspended Monk is concluded.

10. Kaṇṭakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule.

428. Dasame pireti nipātapadaṃ. Sambodhane vattamānaṃ para-saddena samānatthaṃ vadantīti āha “para amāmakā”ti, amhākaṃ anajjhattikabhūtāti attho. Pireti vā “parato”ti iminā samānatthaṃ nipātapadaṃ, tasmā cara pireti parato gaccha, mā idha tiṭṭhāti evampettha attho veditabbo. Sesamettha purimasikkhāpadadvaye vuttanayameva.

428. In the tenth rule, 'pire' is a particle. They say that when it occurs in the vocative, it has the same meaning as the word 'para,' hence he said, 'para amāmakā,' meaning, 'you who are other, not our own,' that is, 'those who are not internal to us.' Alternatively, 'pire' is a particle with the same meaning as 'parato' (away); therefore, 'cara pire' should be understood here to mean, 'Go away; do not stand here.' The rest here follows the same method as stated in the previous two training rules.

Kaṇṭakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule is concluded.

Niṭṭhito sappāṇakavaggo sattamo.

The Seventh Chapter, the Section on Living Beings, is concluded.

8. Sahadhammikavaggo

8. The Chapter on What is in Accordance with the Dhamma

1. Sahadhammikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on What is in Accordance with the Dhamma

434. Sahadhammikavaggassa [V 3.0081] paṭhamasikkhāpade vācāya vācāya āpattīti anādariyabhayā lesena evaṃ vadantassa āpatti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Upasampannassa paññattena vacanaṃ, asikkhitukāmatāya evaṃ vacananti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

434. In the first training rule of the Sahadhammika chapter: 'An offense for every word' means that an offense is incurred by one who speaks thus with pretense out of disrespect. The rest here is self-evident. The two factors here are: the statement being one prescribed for the fully ordained, and speaking thus with a desire not to train.

Sahadhammikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on What is in Accordance with the Dhamma is concluded.

2. Vilekhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Vexing

438. Dutiye [M 3.0090] vinayassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ vinayapariyattīti āha “vinayaṃ pariyāpuṇantāna”ntiādi. Suguttoti yathā karaṇḍake pakkhittamaṇikkhandho viya na nassati vipattiṃ na pāpuṇāti, evaṃ suṭṭhu gopito. Surakkhitoti tasseva pariyāyavacanaṃ. Yathā hi kilesacorehi avilumpanīyo hoti, evaṃ sabbadā sūpaṭṭhitassatitāya suṭṭhu rakkhito. Kukkuccapakatānanti kappiyākappiyaṃ nissāya uppannakukkuccena abhibhūtānaṃ. Sārajjanaṃ sārado, byāmohabhayaṃ. Vigato sārado etassāti visārado. Sahadhammenāti sakāraṇena vacanena. Suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhātīti yathā na puna sīsaṃ ukkhipanti, atha kho appaṭibhānā maṅkubhūtāyeva honti, evaṃ suṭṭhu niggaṇhāti.

438. In the second rule, the learning of the Discipline is 'Vinaya learning'; thus he said, 'for those learning the Vinaya,' and so on. 'Well-guarded' means well-protected, so that it does not perish or come to ruin, like a heap of jewels placed in a casket. 'Well-protected' is a synonym for that. Just as it is not to be plundered by the thieves of the defilements, so it is well-protected by constantly well-established mindfulness. 'Of those beset by scruples' means of those who are overwhelmed by scruples that have arisen concerning what is allowable and what is not. Timidity is `sārada`, which is fear born of delusion. One for whom that timidity is gone is 'undaunted' (`visārado`). 'In accordance with the Dhamma' means with a statement that is well-reasoned. 'He restrains them well' means he restrains them in such a way that they do not raise their heads again, but rather become speechless and downcast.

Alajjitāti ya-kāralopena niddeso, alajjitāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññāṇatātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Mando momūhoti aññāṇabhāvena mando, avisayato momūho, mahāmūḷhoti attho.

The term 'alajjitā' is an indication through the elision of the letter 'ya'; it means that 'alajjitāya' (through shamelessness) is stated. This same method applies to 'aññāṇatā' (through ignorance) and so on. 'Dull and deluded' means dull due to ignorance and deluded from having no proper domain, the meaning being 'greatly deluded'.

Attapaccatthikāti attano paccatthikā. Vajjiputtakā dasavatthudīpakā. Parūpahāraaññāṇakaṅkhāparavitāraṇādivādāti ettha ye arahattaṃ paṭijānantānaṃ appatte pattasaññīnaṃ adhimānikānaṃ kuhakānaṃ vā arahattaṃ paṭijānantānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ disvā mārakāyikā devatā “arahato asuciṃ [V 3.0082] upasaṃharantī”ti maññanti seyyathāpi pubbaseliyā aparaseliyā ca, te parūpahāravādā. Yesaṃ pana arahato itthipurisādīnaṃ nāmagottādīsu ñāṇappavattiyā abhāvena atthi arahato aññāṇaṃ, tattheva sanniṭṭhānābhāvena atthi arahato kaṅkhā, yasmā cassa tāni vatthūni pare vitārenti pakāsenti ācikkhanti, tasmā atthi arahato paravitāraṇāti imā tisso laddhiyo seyyathāpi etarahi pubbaseliyānaṃ, te aññāṇakaṅkhāparavitāraṇavādā. Niggaho pana nesaṃ kathāvatthuppakaraṇe vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

'Attapaccatthikā' means one's own adversaries. The Vajjiputtakas are the proponents of the ten points. Regarding the views of 'parūpahāra, aññāṇa, kaṅkhā, and paravitāraṇa': Here, those who falsely claim arahantship—whether mistakenly believing they have attained it, being conceited, or deceitful—and upon seeing the emission of semen, the Māra-bodied deities think, 'They are offering impurity to the arahant.' This is like the views of the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas; these are the 'parūpahāra-vādins.' For those who, due to the absence of the arising of knowledge regarding names, clans, etc., of men and women, believe there is ignorance in an arahant; or who, due to the absence of firm conviction, believe there is doubt in an arahant; and because others clarify, explain, or reveal these matters for the arahant, there is 'paravitāraṇa' (clarification by others) for an arahant. These three views are held, for example, by the present-day Pubbaseliyas; they are the 'aññāṇa-kaṅkhā-paravitāraṇa-vādins.' Their refutation, however, should be understood in the manner explained in the Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa.

Cattāro maggā ca phalāni cāti ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena vuttaṃ, catasso paṭisambhidā tisso vijjā cha abhiññāti ayampi adhigamasaddhammoyeva. Ca-kāro [M 3.0091] vā avuttasampiṇḍanattho daṭṭhabbo. Keci therāti dhammakathikā. Āhaṃsūti paṃsukūlikattherā evaṃ āhaṃsu.

The four paths and four fruits are mentioned by way of the designation of excellence; and also the four analytical knowledges, the three true knowledges, and the six direct knowledges—these too are the noble Dhamma of attainment. Or, the particle 'ca' should be understood as having the purpose of including what has not been stated. 'Some elders' (keci therā) refers to the Dhamma preachers. 'They said' (āhaṃsu) means the rag-robe-wearing elders spoke thus.

Kadā panāyaṃ kathā udapādīti? Ayañhettha anupubbikathā (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.130) – imasmiṃ kira dīpe caṇḍālatissamahābhaye sakko devarājā mahāuḷumpaṃ māpetvā bhikkhūnaṃ ārocāpesi “mahantaṃ bhayaṃ bhavissati, na sammā devo vassissati, bhikkhū paccayehi kilamantā pariyattiṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkhissanti, paratīraṃ gantvā ayyehi jīvitaṃ rakkhituṃ vaṭṭati. Imaṃ mahāuḷumpaṃ āruyha gacchatha bhante, yesaṃ ettha nisajjaṭṭhānaṃ nappahoti, te kaṭṭhakhaṇḍepi uraṃ ṭhapetvā gacchantu, sabbesaṃ bhayaṃ na bhavissatī”ti. Tadā samuddatīraṃ patvā saṭṭhi bhikkhū katikaṃ katvā “amhākaṃ ettha gamanakiccaṃ natthi, mayaṃ idheva hutvā tepiṭakaṃ rakkhissāmā”ti tato nivattitvā dakkhiṇamalayajanapadaṃ gantvā kandamūlapaṇṇehi jīvikaṃ kappentā vasiṃsu, kāye vahante nisīditvā sajjhāyaṃ karonti, avahante vālikaṃ ussāretvā parivāretvā sīsāni ekaṭṭhāne katvā pariyattiṃ sammasanti. Iminā niyāmena dvādasa saṃvaccharāni sāṭṭhakathaṃ tepiṭakaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā dhārayiṃsu.

When did this discussion arise? This is the sequential account: It is said that on this island, during the great terror of Caṇḍālatissa, Sakka, the king of the devas, had a great raft made and announced to the bhikkhus: 'A great danger will arise; the deva will not rain properly. The bhikkhus, struggling with requisites, will not be able to maintain the scriptures. It is fitting, venerable sirs, to go to the other shore and preserve your lives. Board this great raft and depart. Those for whom there is insufficient seating space here, let them go even placing their chests on pieces of wood. There will be no danger for any of you.' Then, reaching the seashore, sixty bhikkhus made an agreement: 'We have no need to go from here. We will stay right here and protect the Tipiṭaka.' Turning back from there, they went to the southern Malayajanapada and lived, sustaining their lives with roots, tubers, and leaves. When their bodies were able, they would sit and recite. When they were unable, they would make a mound of sand, surround it, place their heads together in one place, and review the scriptures. In this manner, for twelve years, they completely mastered and preserved the Tipiṭaka along with its commentaries.

Bhaye vūpasante sattasatā bhikkhū attano gataṭṭhāne sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake ekakkharampi ekabyañjanampi avināsetvā imameva dīpamāgamma kallagāmajanapade maṇḍalārāmavihāraṃ pavisiṃsu. Therānaṃ āgatapavattiṃ sutvā imasmiṃ dīpe ohīnā saṭṭhi bhikkhū “there passissāmā”ti gantvā therehi saddhiṃ tepiṭakaṃ sodhentā ekakkharampi ekabyañjanampi asamentaṃ nāma na passiṃsu. Tasmiṃ ṭhāne therānaṃ ayaṃ kathā udapādi “pariyatti nu kho sāsanassa mūlaṃ, udāhu paṭipattī”ti. Paṃsukūlikattherā “paṭipatti mūla”nti āhaṃsu, dhammakathikā “pariyattī”ti[V 3.0083]. Atha ne therā “tumhākaṃ dvinnampi janānaṃ vacanamatteneva na sakkā viññātuṃ, jinabhāsitaṃ suttaṃ āharathā”ti āhaṃsu. Suttaṃ āharituṃ na bhāroti –

When the fear had subsided, seven hundred bhikkhus, without losing even a single letter or syllable of the Tipiṭaka with its commentary in the place they had gone, returned to this very island and entered the Maṇḍalārāma monastery in the Kallagāma district. Having heard the account of the elders' arrival, the sixty bhikkhus who had been left behind on this island went, thinking, 'We shall see the elders.' While collating the Tipiṭaka with the elders, they did not find even a single letter or syllable that was discrepant. At that place, this discussion arose among the elders: 'Is the foundation of the Dispensation scriptural learning (pariyatti), or is it the practice (paṭipatti)?' The rag-robe-wearing elders said, 'Practice is the foundation,' while the Dhamma preachers said, 'Scriptural learning is.' Then the elders said to them, 'It is not possible to know the view of either of you by mere words alone. Bring forth a discourse spoken by the Jina.' They replied, 'It is no burden to bring forth a sutta.'

“Ime ca, subhadda, bhikkhū sammā vihareyyuṃ, asuñño loko arahantehi assā”ti (dī. ni. 2.214). “Paṭipattimūlakaṃ, mahārāja, satthusāsanaṃ[M 3.0092], paṭipattisārakaṃ, mahārāja, satthusāsanaṃ, paṭipatti tiṭṭhantī tiṭṭhatī”ti (mi. pa. 4.1.7) –

'And Subhadda, if these bhikkhus were to live rightly, the world would not be devoid of arahants.' (Dī. Ni. 2.214). 'Great king, the Teacher's Dispensation is rooted in practice; great king, the Teacher's Dispensation has practice as its essence. When practice endures, the Dispensation endures.' (Mi. Pa. 4.1.7)

Suttaṃ āhariṃsu.

They brought forth the discourse.

Imaṃ suttaṃ sutvā dhammakathikā attano vādaṭṭhapanatthāya imaṃ suttaṃ āhariṃsu –

Having heard this discourse, the Dhamma preachers, for the purpose of establishing their own view, brought forth this discourse:

“Yāva tiṭṭhanti suttantā, vinayo yāva dippati;

Tāva dakkhanti ālokaṃ, sūriye abbhuṭṭhite yathā.

'As long as the Discourses endure, as long as the Discipline shines; so long will they see the light, as when the sun has risen.'

“Suttantesu asantesu, pamuṭṭhe vinayamhi ca;

Tamo bhavissati loke, sūriye atthaṅgate yathā.

'When the Discourses are absent, and the Discipline is forgotten; darkness will be in the world, as when the sun has set.'

“Suttante rakkhite sante, paṭipatti hoti rakkhitā;

Paṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito dhīro, yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatī”ti.

'When the Discourses are protected, practice is protected; the wise, established in practice, do not fall away from security from the yoke.'

Imasmiṃ sutte āhaṭe paṃsukūlikattherā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Dhammakathikattherānaṃyeva vacanaṃ purato ahosi. Yathā hi gavasatassa gavasahassassa vā antare paveṇipālikāya dhenuyā asati so vaṃso sā paveṇī na ghaṭīyati, evameva āraddhavipassakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ satepi sahassepi vijjamāne pariyattiyā asati ariyamaggapaṭivedho nāma na hoti. Yathā ca nidhikumbhiyā jānanatthāya pāsāṇapiṭṭhe akkharesu upanibaddhesu yāva akkharāni dharanti, tāva nidhikumbhī naṭṭhā nāma na hoti, evameva pariyattiyā dharamānāya sāsanaṃ antarahitaṃ nāma na hotīti. Tassādheyyoti tassāyatto.

When this discourse was brought forth, the rag-robe-wearing elders were silent. The words of the Dhamma-preaching elders alone were foremost. For just as, among a herd of a hundred or a thousand cows, if there is no lineage-keeping cow, that lineage is not maintained, so too, even if there are a hundred or a thousand bhikkhus who have undertaken insight meditation, without scriptural learning, there is no such thing as the penetration of the noble path. And just as, for the purpose of knowing a pot of treasure, letters are inscribed on a stone slab; as long as the letters endure, the pot of treasure is not considered lost, so too, as long as scriptural learning endures, the Dispensation is not considered to have disappeared. 'Tassādheyya' means dependent on it.

439. So [V 3.0084] panāti so pātimokkho. Sesamettha uttānameva. Garahitukāmatā, upasampannassa santike sikkhāpadavivaṇṇanañcāti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

439. 'So pana' means 'that Pātimokkha.' The rest here is straightforward. The two factors here are: the desire to censure, and the disparagement of a training rule in the presence of one who is fully ordained.

Vilekhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
