For her, indeed, who is striving to engage in bodily contact, which is the preliminary part of the sexual act, there is a cutting off on account of the sexual act. Cutting off itself is ‘chejjaṃ’.

Methunadhammassa pubbabhāgattāti iminā methunadhammassa pubbabhāgabhūto kāyasaṃsaggoyeva tattha methunadhamma-saddena vutto, na dvayaṃdvayasamāpattīti dīpeti. Vaṇṇāvaṇṇoti dvīhi sukkavissaṭṭhi vuttā. Gamanuppādananti sañcarittaṃ. Sabbapadesūti “saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahaṇaṃ sādiyeyyā”tiādīsu. Sesamettha uttānameva. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgo, saussāhatā, aṭṭhamassa vatthussa pūraṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

By the phrase “because it is the preliminary part of the sexual act,” it is shown that in that context, by the word “sexual act,” only bodily contact, which is the preliminary part of the sexual act, is spoken of, not the attainment of coupling. By “praise and dispraise” (vaṇṇāvaṇṇa), the two kinds of seminal emission are meant. “Causing to go” (gamanuppādana) means acting as a go-between. “In all phrases” refers to such instances as “one might consent to the taking of the corner of the outer robe,” and so on. The rest here is self-evident. Lust for bodily contact, exertion, and the fulfillment of the eighth basis—these are the three factors here.

Catutthapārājikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Fourth Pārājika Training Rule is concluded.

Bhikkhunīvibhaṅge pārājikakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pārājika section in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga is concluded.

Pārājikakaṇḍaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Pārājika section is concluded.

2. Saṅghādisesakaṇḍaṃ (bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)

2. The Chapter on Saṅghādisesa (Explanation of the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga)

1. Paṭhamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

679. Saṅghādisesakaṇḍassa [M 3.0116][V 3.0107] paṭhamasikkhāpade dvīsu janesūti aḍḍakārakesu dvīsu janesu. Yo kocīti tesuyeva dvīsu yo koci, añño vā tehi āṇatto. Dutiyassa ārocetīti etthāpi dvīsu janesu yassa kassaci dutiyassa kathaṃ yo koci ārocetīti evamattho gahetabboti āha “dutiyassa ārocetīti etthāpi eseva nayo”ti. Gatigatanti cirakālapavattaṃ.

679. In the first training rule of the Saṅghādisesa section, “among two people” means among the two people who are litigants. “Whoever” means any one of those two, or another person instructed by them. Regarding “informs the second party,” here too the meaning should be understood in this way: among the two people, whoever informs the companion of either one. Thus he says, “Regarding ‘informs the second party,’ here too the same method applies.” “Having gone again and again” (gatigataṃ) means long-standing.

Āpattīti āpajjanaṃ. Saha vatthujjhācārāti vatthuvītikkamena saha. Sahayoge karaṇavacanappasaṅge idaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ. Yanti yaṃ dhammaṃ. Nissāretīti āpannaṃ bhikkhunisaṅghamhā nissāreti. Hetumhi cāyaṃ kattuvohāro. Nissāraṇahetubhūto hi dhammo nissāraṇīyoti vutto. Gīvāyeva hoti, na pārājikaṃ anāṇattiyā gahitattā. Yathā dāsadāsīvāpīādīni sampaṭicchituṃ na vaṭṭati, evaṃ tesaṃ atthāya aḍḍakaraṇampi na vaṭṭatīti āha “ayaṃ akappiyaaḍḍo nāma, na vaṭṭatī”ti.

“Offense” (āpatti) means the act of offending. “Together with the basis of misconduct” means together with the transgression of the basis. In connection with the word saha, when the instrumental case is applicable, this is an ablative expression. “Which” (yaṃ) means which rule (dhamma). “To expel” (nissāreti) means to expel the offending bhikkhunī from the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. And this is a usage of the agent in the sense of cause. For the rule that is the cause for expulsion is called “that which causes expulsion” (nissāraṇīya). It is only a grave offense (gīvā), not a Pārājika, because it was undertaken without being instructed. Just as it is not permissible to accept male slaves, female slaves, reservoirs, and so on, so too it is not permissible to undertake a lawsuit for their sake. Thus he says, “This is called an improper lawsuit; it is not permissible.”

Ettha ca sace adhikaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “amhākaṃ eso dāso, dāsī, vāpī, khettaṃ, ārāmo, ārāmavatthu, gāvo, ajā, kukkuṭā”tiādinā voharati, akappiyaṃ. “Ayaṃ amhākaṃ ārāmiko, ayaṃ vāpī itthannāmena saṅghassa bhaṇḍadhovanatthāya dinnā, ito khettato ārāmato uppajjanakacatupaccayā ito gāvito mahiṃsito ajāto uppajjanakagorasā itthannāmena saṅghassa dinnāti pucchite vā apucchite vā vattuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Anākaḍḍhitāya aḍḍakaraṇaṃ, aḍḍapariyosānanti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

And here, if one goes to the place of the legal dispute and declares, “This is our male slave, female slave, reservoir, field, monastery, monastery land, cows, goats, chickens,” and so on, it is improper. They say it is permissible, whether asked or unasked, to say: “This is our monastery attendant; this reservoir was given to the Saṅgha by someone of such-and-such a name for the purpose of washing bowls; the four requisites arising from this field or monastery, and the milk-products arising from these cows, buffaloes, or goats were given to the Saṅgha by someone of such-and-such a name.” The rest here is self-evident. Undertaking a lawsuit for one who is not being compelled, and the conclusion of the lawsuit—these are the two factors here.

Paṭhamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

2. Dutiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

683. Dutiye [M 3.0117][V 3.0108] mallagaṇabhaṭiputtagaṇādikantiādīsu mallagaṇo nāma nārāyanabhattiko tattha tattha pānīyaṭṭhapanapokkharaṇīkhaṇanādipuññakammakārako gaṇo, bhaṭiputtagaṇo nāma kumārabhattikagaṇo. Dhammagaṇoti sāsanabhattigaṇo anekappakārapuññakammakārakagaṇo vuccati. Gandhikaseṇīti anekappakārasugandhivikatikārako gaṇo. Dussikaseṇīti pesakārakagaṇo. Kappagatikanti kappiyabhāvaṃ gataṃ.

683. In the second rule, regarding “the group of wrestlers, the group of Bhaṭiputtas, etc.”: A “group of wrestlers” (mallagaṇa) is a group devoted to Nārāyaṇa that performs meritorious deeds in various places, such as establishing drinking water, digging ponds, and so on. A “group of Bhaṭiputtas” (bhaṭiputtagaṇa) is a group devoted to Kumāra. A “Dhamma group” (dhammagaṇa) is said to be a group devoted to the Dispensation, a group that performs various kinds of meritorious deeds. A “guild of perfumers” (gandhikaseṇī) is a group that makes various kinds of fragrant substances. A “guild of cloth-makers” (dussikaseṇī) is a group of weavers. “One who has gone to what is allowable” (kappagatika) means one who has reached a state of being allowable.

Vuṭṭhāpentiyāti upasampādentiyā. “Coriṃ vuttanayena anāpucchā pabbājentiyā dukkaṭa”nti vadanti. Paṇṇattiṃ ajānantā ariyāpi vuṭṭhāpentīti vā kammavācāpariyosāne āpattikkhaṇe vipākābyākatasamaṅgitāvasena vā “ticitta”nti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Coritā, corisaññā, aññatra anuññātakāraṇā vuṭṭhāpananti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

“For one giving the higher ordination” (vuṭṭhāpentiyā) means for one conferring the higher ordination (upasampādentiyā). They say, “For one who gives the going forth to a thief without asking, according to the stated method, there is a dukkaṭa offense.” It should be understood that it is called “three-minded” (ticitta) either because even noble ones, not knowing the regulation, might give the higher ordination, or because of being endowed with an indeterminate resultant consciousness at the moment of the offense at the conclusion of the formal act. The rest here is self-evident. The state of being a thief, the perception of her as a thief, and giving the higher ordination for a reason other than one that is permitted—these are the three factors here.

Dutiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Second Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

3. Tatiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Third Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

692. Tatiye parikkhepaṃ atikkāmentiyāti sakagāmato aññassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkāmentiyā. “Gāmantaraṃ gaccheyyā”ti hi vacanato aññassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkāmentiyā eva āpatti, na sakagāmassa. Añño hi gāmo gāmantaraṃ. Aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāranti ettha upacāra-saddena gharūpacārato paṭhamaleḍḍupātasaṅkhātaṃ parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ gahitaṃ, na tato dutiyaleḍḍupātasaṅkhāto upacāroti āha “parikkhepārahaṭṭhāna”nti. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ “upacāraṃ atikkāmentiyā”ti vuttaṃ. Aññathā yathā vikālagāmappavisanasikkhāpade “parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkamantassa, aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantassā”ti (pāci. 513) vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi “parikkhittassa gāmassa parikkhepaṃ atikkāmentiyā aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantiyā”ti vadeyya. Saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vibhajitvā dassento “apicetthā”tiādimāha. Vihārassa [M 3.0118] catugāmasādhāraṇattāti iminā “vihārato ekaṃ gāmaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ettha [V 3.0109] kāraṇamāha. Vihārassa catugāmasādhāraṇattāyeva hi catūsu gāmesu yaṃkiñci ekaṃ gāmaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati.

692. In the third [rule], 'crossing the boundary' means crossing the boundary of another village from one's own village. For according to the statement 'she should go to another village,' an offense is incurred only by crossing the boundary of another village, not of one's own village. Indeed, another village is a 'gāmantara' (another village). Regarding 'the vicinity of an unenclosed village,' here by the word 'vicinity' is taken the place suitable for a boundary, reckoned as the first stone's throw from the vicinity of the houses, and not the vicinity reckoned as the second stone's throw from there; therefore, he said 'a place suitable for a boundary.' For that very reason, in the Pāli it is said, 'crossing the vicinity.' Otherwise, just as in the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time it is said, 'for crossing the boundary of an enclosed village, or for entering the vicinity of an unenclosed village' (Pāc. 513), so too here one would say, 'for crossing the boundary of an enclosed village, or for entering the vicinity of an unenclosed village.' To analyze and show the meaning stated concisely, he says 'Moreover, here…' and so on. By this, 'because the monastery is common to four villages,' he states the reason here for 'It is permissible to go to one village from the monastery.' For it is precisely because the monastery is common to four villages that it is permissible to go to any one of the four villages.

Yatthāti yassaṃ nadiyaṃ. “Paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ uttārentiyā āpatti thullaccayassa, dutiyaṃ pādaṃ uttārentiyā āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti vacanato nadiṃ otaritvā padasā uttarantiyā eva āpattīti āha “setunā gacchati, anāpattī”tiādi. Paratīrameva akkamantiyā anāpattīti nadiṃ anotaritvā yānanāvādīsu aññatarena gantvā paratīrameva akkamantiyā anāpatti. Ubhayatīresu vicaranti, vaṭṭatīti idaṃ asatipi nadīpāragamane upari vakkhamānassa vinicchayassa phalamattadassanatthaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Orimatīrameva āgacchati, āpattīti paratīraṃ gantukāmatāya otiṇṇattā vuttaṃ. Tameva tīranti tameva orimatīraṃ. Anāpattīti paratīraṃ gantukāmatāya abhāvato anāpatti.

Where: that is, in whatever river. For according to the statement, 'For bringing the first foot across, there is an offense of thullaccaya; for bringing the second foot across, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa,' he says 'one who goes by a bridge incurs no offense,' and so on, because an offense is incurred only by one who enters the river and crosses on foot. 'There is no offense for one who steps directly onto the opposite bank' means there is no offense for one who, without entering the river, goes by some means such as a vehicle or boat and steps directly onto the opposite bank. It should be understood that this, 'wandering on both banks is allowable,' is said for the purpose of showing merely the result of the ruling that will be stated further on, even when there is no crossing to the far bank of the river. 'If she comes only to the near bank, there is an offense' is said because she entered the water with the intention of going to the far bank. 'That same bank' means that same near bank. 'No offense' means there is no offense due to the absence of the intention to go to the far bank.

Tādise araññeti “bahiindakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇe araññe. Atha tādisasseva araññassa gahitabhāvo kathaṃ viññāyatīti āha “tenevā”tiādi. Iminā hi aṭṭhakathāvacanena īdisepi gāmasamīpe dassanūpacāre vijahite satipi savanūpacāre āpatti hotīti viññāyati. Maggamūḷhā uccāsaddaṃ karontīti āha “maggamūḷhasaddena viyā”ti. Saddāyantiyāti saddaṃ karontiyā. Purimāyoti puretaraṃ gacchantiyo. Aññaṃ maggaṃ gaṇhātīti maggamūḷhattā, na ohātuṃ, tasmā dvinnampi anāpatti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Anantarāyena ekabhāvo, gāmantaragamanādīsu aññataratāpajjanaṃ, āpadāya abhāvoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

In such a wilderness: that is, in a wilderness with the characteristics stated thus, 'outside the city-post, all this is wilderness' (Vibh. 529). Then how is it known that such a wilderness is meant? He says 'by that very…' and so on. For by this commentary statement, it is understood that even in such a place near a village, although the range of sight is left behind, if one is within the range of hearing, an offense occurs. He says 'like by the word for one lost on the path' because those who are lost on the path make a loud noise. 'Making a noise' means for one who is making a sound. 'Of the one in front' means those going ahead. 'She takes another path' because of being lost on the path, not in order to be left behind; therefore, there is no offense for both. The rest here is clear. Being alone without danger, the undertaking of one of the [acts] such as going to another village, and the absence of an emergency—these are the three factors here.

Tatiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third Saṅghādisesa training rule is concluded.

4. Catutthasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

694. Catutthe kārakagaṇassāti ukkhepanīyakammakārakagaṇassa. Tecattālīsappabhedaṃ vattaṃ khandhake āvi bhavissati. Netthāravatteti nittharaṇahetumhi [M 3.0119] vatte. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Dhammena kammena ukkhittatā, aññatra anuññātakāraṇā osāraṇanti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

694. In the fourth, 'of the group of perpetrators' means of the group that performs the act of suspension. The forty-three-fold observance will become clear in the Khandhaka. 'In the observance for rehabilitation' means in the observance that is a cause for rehabilitation. The rest is clear. Being suspended by a formal act in accordance with the Dhamma, and reinstatement for a reason other than one that is permitted—these are the two factors here.

Catutthasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

5. Pañcamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

701. Pañcame [V 3.0110] etaṃ na vuttanti “bhikkhuniyā avassutabhāvo daṭṭhabbo”ti etaṃ niyamanaṃ na vuttaṃ. Tanti taṃ niyametvā avacanaṃ. Pāḷiyā sametīti “ekato avassute”ti avisesetvā vuttapāḷiyā “anavassutoti jānantī paṭiggaṇhātī”ti imāya ca pāḷiyā sameti. Yadi hi puggalassa avassutabhāvo nappamāṇaṃ, kiṃ “anavassutoti jānantī”ti iminā vacanena, “anāpatti ubhatoanavassutā honti, anavassutā paṭiggaṇhātī”ti ettakameva vattabbaṃ siyā. “Ubhatoanavassutā honti, anavassutoti jānantī paṭiggaṇhātī”ti imassa ca anāpattivārassa ayamattho. Ubho ce anavassutā, sabbathāpi anāpatti. Atha bhikkhunī anavassutā samānā avassutampi “anavassuto”ti saññāya tassa hatthato paṭiggaṇhāti, evampi anāpatti. Atha sayaṃ anavassutāpi aññaṃ anavassutaṃ vā avassutaṃ vā “avassuto”ti jānāti, dukkaṭameva. Vuttañhetaṃ anantarasikkhāpade “kissa tvaṃ ayye na paṭiggaṇhāsīti. Avassutā ayyeti. Tvaṃ pana ayye avassutāti. Nāhaṃ ayye avassutā”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Udakadantaponato aññaṃ ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ, ubhatoavassutatā, sahatthā gahaṇaṃ, ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

701. In the fifth, this is not stated, meaning this stipulation—'the bhikkhunī's state of being lustful should be seen'—is not stated. That is, it is not stated by way of stipulation. It accords with the Pāli, both with the Pāli that is stated without specification, 'if one of them is lustful,' and with this Pāli passage: 'knowing he is not lustful, she receives it.' For if a person's state of being lustful is not the standard, what is the use of this statement, 'knowing he is not lustful'? It would be enough to say just this: 'There is no offense if both are not lustful; she receives from one who is not lustful.' And this is the meaning of this no-offense clause, 'If both are not lustful, knowing he is not lustful, she receives it': If both are not lustful, there is no offense in any case. Or if a bhikkhunī, being not lustful herself, receives from his hand even a lustful man, perceiving him as 'not lustful,' even so there is no offense. Or if she, though not lustful herself, knows another—whether not lustful or lustful—as 'lustful,' it is only a dukkaṭa offense. For this is stated in the immediately preceding training rule: '“Why do you not receive it, venerable lady?” “The venerable one is lustful.” “But are you, venerable lady, lustful?” “I am not lustful, venerable sir.”' The rest here is clear. Something to be consumed other than water and a tooth-cleaner; the state of both being not lustful; receiving with one's own hand; and consuming—these are the four factors here.

Pañcamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

6. Chaṭṭhasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sixth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

705. Chaṭṭhe parivāragāthāya ayamattho. Na deti na paṭiggaṇhātīti (pari. aṭṭha. 481) na uyyojikā deti, nāpi uyyojitā tassā hatthato gaṇhāti[M 3.0120]. Paṭiggaho tena na vijjatīti teneva kāraṇena uyyojikāya hatthato uyyojitāya paṭiggaho na vijjati. Āpajjati garukanti evaṃ santepi avassutassa hatthato piṇḍaggahaṇe uyyojentī saṅghādisesāpattiṃ āpajjati. Tañca paribhogapaccayāti tañca pana āpattiṃ āpajjamānā tassā uyyojitāya paribhogapaccayā āpajjati. Tassā hi bhojanapariyosāne uyyojikāya saṅghādiseso hoti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Manussapurisatā, aññatra anuññātakāraṇā khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ gahetvā bhuñjāti uyyojanā, tena vacanena gahetvā itarissā bhojanapariyosānanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

705. In the sixth, the meaning of the Parivāra verse is this. 'She does not give, nor does she receive' (Parivāra Aṭṭhakathā 481) means the instigating bhikkhunī does not give, nor does the instigated bhikkhunī take from her hand. 'There is no acceptance by her' means for that very reason, there is no acceptance by the instigated one from the hand of the instigating one. 'She incurs a grave offense' means even so, one who instigates the taking of almsfood from the hand of a lustful man incurs a Saṅghādisesa offense. 'And that is on account of consumption' means, moreover, while incurring that offense, she incurs it on account of the consumption by that instigated bhikkhunī. For at the conclusion of her meal, a Saṅghādisesa is incurred by the instigating bhikkhunī. The rest here is clear. The state of being a human male; instigation, saying, 'Take and eat hard or soft food, except for a permitted reason'; and the other one taking it in accordance with that word and the conclusion of her meal—these are the three factors here.

Chaṭṭhasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Commentary on the Sixth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

7. Sattamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

709. Sattame [V 3.0111] kinnumāva samaṇiyoti kiṃ nu imā eva samaṇiyo. Tāsāhanti tāsaṃ ahaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

709. In the seventh [rule]: 'Kinnumāva samaṇiyo' means 'Are these indeed female ascetics?' 'Tāsāhaṃ' means 'I am of them.' The rest is clear.

Sattamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Commentary on the Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

715. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānatthameva.

715. The eighth is clear in meaning.

9. Navamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Ninth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

721. Navame vajjappaṭicchādikāti khuddānukhuddakavajjassa paṭicchādikā. Samanubhāsanakammakāle cettha dve tisso ekato samanubhāsitabbā.

721. In the ninth [rule]: 'Vajjappaṭicchādikā' means 'one who conceals an offense,' that is, one who conceals a minor and lesser offense. And here, at the time of the act of formal inquiry, two or three should be formally inquired into together.

Navamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Commentary on the Ninth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

727. Dasamaṃ uttānatthameva.

727. The tenth is clear in meaning.

Bhikkhunīvibhaṅge saṅghādisesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Saṅghādisesa in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is concluded.

Saṅghādisesakaṇḍaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Saṅghādisesa Section is concluded.

3. Nissaggiyakaṇḍaṃ (bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)

3. The Nissaggiya Section (Explanation of the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga)

733. Nissaggiyesu [M 3.0121][V 3.0112] paṭhamaṃ uttānameva.

733. Among the Nissaggiyas, the first is simply clear.

740. Dutiye “ayyāya dammīti evaṃ paṭiladdhanti nissaṭṭhapaṭiladdhaṃ. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi “nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvāpi yathādāneyeva upanetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Yathādāneyeva upanetabbanti yathā dāyakena dinnaṃ, tathā upanetabbaṃ, akālacīvarapakkheyeva ṭhapetabbanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ca bhājāpitāya laddhacīvarameva nissaggiyaṃ hoti, taṃ vinayakammaṃ katvāpi attanā na labhati. Sesamettha uttānameva. Akālacīvaratā, tathāsaññitā, kālacīvaranti adhiṭṭhāya lesena bhājāpanaṃ, paṭilābhoti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

740. In the second, 'I give this to the lady,' thus obtained means obtained after relinquishment. For that reason, it is also said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, 'Even having relinquished it and obtained it back, it should be presented just as it was given.' 'It should be presented just as it was given' means it should be presented as it was given by the donor, and it is said that it should be kept only in the category of out-of-season robes. Here, only a robe obtained by having it distributed becomes subject to forfeiture. Even after performing that Vinaya act, one does not obtain it for oneself. The rest here is clear. The four factors here are: it being an out-of-season robe; perceiving it as such; having it distributed by a pretext after determining it as an in-season robe; and the obtaining of it.

743. Tatiye metanti me etaṃ. Sakasaññāya gahitattā pācittiyaṃ dukkaṭañca vuttaṃ. Itarathā bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbaṃ. Upasampannatā, parivattitacīvarassa vikappanupagatā, sakasaññāya acchindanaṃ vā acchindāpanaṃ vāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

743. In the third, `metanti` is `me etaṃ`, meaning 'this is mine'. Because it was taken with the perception that it was one's own, a Pācittiya and a Dukkaṭa are stated. Otherwise, it should be dealt with according to the value of the goods. The three factors here are: being fully ordained; the exchanged robe not having been made over to another; and seizing or causing to seize with the perception that it is one's own.

748-752. Catutthe āhaṭasappiṃ datvāti attano datvā. Yamakaṃ pacitabbanti sappiñca telañca ekato katvā pacitabbaṃ. Lesena gahetukāmatā, aññassa viññāpanaṃ, paṭilābhoti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

In the fourth, 'having given brought ghee' means having given of one's own. 'A pair should be cooked' means ghee and oil should be put together and cooked. The three factors here are: the desire to obtain by a pretext, requesting from another, and the obtaining.

753. Pañcame sāti thullanandā. Ayanti ayaṃ sikkhamānā. Cetāpetvāti jānāpetvā icceva atthoti idha vuttaṃ, mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. aññacetāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) pana “aññaṃ cetāpetvāti attano kappiyabhaṇḍena idaṃ nāma āharāti aññaṃ parivattāpetvā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā “cetāpetvā”ti imassa parivattāpetvātipi attho daṭṭhabbo. Aññaṃ cetāpeyyāti “evaṃ me idaṃ datvā aññampi āharissatī”ti maññamānā “na me iminā attho, idaṃ nāma me āharā”ti tato aññaṃ cetāpeyya.

753. In the fifth, 'she' refers to Thullanandā. 'The one coming' refers to this female trainee. 'Having caused to acquire' means 'having made known'—this is the meaning stated here. In the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: '“Having caused another to be acquired” means having caused another thing to be exchanged for one's own suitable goods, saying, “Bring this particular thing.”' Therefore, for 'having caused to acquire,' the meaning 'having caused to exchange' should also be understood. 'She might cause another to be exchanged' means: thinking, 'Having given this to me, she will also bring something else,' she might say, 'I have no need for this; bring me this particular thing,' and thereby cause another thing to be exchanged for that.

758. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0122][V 3.0113] dhammakiccanti puññakammaṃ. Pāvārikassāti dussavāṇijakassa. Yāya cetāpitaṃ, tassāyeva nissaggiyaṃ nissaṭṭhapaṭilābho ca, tasmā tāya bhikkhuniyā nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvā yathādāne upanetabbaṃ, na attanā gahetabbaṃ. Aññassatthāyāti cīvarādīsu aññatarassatthāya. Aññuddisikenāti purimassevatthadīpanaṃ. Parikkhārenāti kappiyabhaṇḍena.

758. In the sixth, 'a Dhamma-duty' means a meritorious act. 'Of a weaver' means of a cloth merchant. For her by whom it was caused to be acquired, for her alone is it subject to forfeiture and is there the re-obtaining of the forfeited item. Therefore, that bhikkhunī, having re-obtained the forfeited item, should present it as it was given; it should not be taken for herself. 'For the sake of another' means for the sake of one among robes and so on. 'Intended for another' is an explanation of the meaning of the preceding. 'With a requisite' means with suitable goods.

764. Sattame sayaṃ yācitakenāti sayaṃ yācitakenāpīti attho. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ “tena ca parikkhārena sayampi yācitvā”ti vuttaṃ, tatoyeva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saññācikenāti sayaṃ yācitakenāpī”ti attho vutto.

764. In the seventh, `sayaṃ yācitakena` means 'even by one who has requested it oneself'. For that reason, it is said in the Pāli text: '...and having oneself requested with that requisite...'. For that very reason, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, the meaning is stated thus: '`saññācikena` means “even by one who has requested it oneself”.'

768-773. Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāni uttānatthāneva.

The eighth, ninth, and tenth are simply clear in meaning.

784. Ekādasame yasmā pavāritaṭṭhāne viññatti nāma na paṭisedhetabbā, tasmā bhagavā dhammanimantanavasena pavāritaṭṭhāne “vadeyyāsi yenattho”ti vuttāya “catukkaṃsaparamaṃ viññāpetabba”nti paricchedaṃ dassetīti veditabbaṃ. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. garupāvuraṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “cetāpetabbanti ṭhapetvā sahadhammike ca ñātakapavārite ca aññena kismiñcideva guṇe parituṭṭhena vadeyyāsi yenatthoti vuttāya viññāpetabba”nti vuttaṃ.

784. In the eleventh, it should be understood that since a request is not to be refused at a place of invitation, the Blessed One, at a place of invitation by way of a Dhamma invitation, when it was said, 'You may say what you need,' showed the limit: 'A request may be made up to a maximum of four kaṃsas.' For that reason, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā it is said: 'Excluding “to have it acquired,” a request may be made when it is said, “You may say what you need,” by a fellow practitioner, by an invited relative, or by another person who is pleased with some quality.'

788. Dvādasamaṃ uttānatthameva.

788. The twelfth is simply clear in meaning.

Bhikkhunīvibhaṅge nissaggiyapācittiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rules in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga is concluded.

Nissaggiyakaṇḍaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Nissaggiya Section is concluded.

4. Pācittiyakaṇḍaṃ (bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)

4. The Section on Pācittiya (Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Commentary)

1. Lasuṇavaggavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Garlic Chapter

793-797. Pācittiyesu [M 3.0123][V 3.0114] lasuṇavaggassa paṭhame jātiṃ saratīti jātissaro. Sabhāvenevāti sūpasampākādiṃ vināva. Badarasāḷavaṃ nāma badaraphalāni sukkhāpetvā cuṇṇetvā kattabbā khādanīyavikati. Sesamettha uttānameva. Āmakalasuṇañceva ajjhoharaṇañcāti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

In the Pācittiya rules, in the first of the Garlic Chapter, `jātissaro` means 'one who remembers birth'. 'By its very nature' means without things like curry or proper cooking. `Badarasāḷava` is the name of an edible preparation to be made by drying and powdering jujube fruits. The rest here is clear. The two factors here are: raw garlic and swallowing it.

798-802. Dutiyatatiyacatutthāni uttānatthāneva.

The second, third, and fourth are simply clear in meaning.

812. Pañcame dvinnaṃ pabbānaṃ uparīti ettha dvinnaṃ aṅgulīnaṃ saha pavesane ekekāya aṅguliyā ekekaṃ pabbaṃ katvā dvinnaṃ pabbānaṃ upari. Ekaṅgulipavesane dvinnaṃ pabbānaṃ upari na vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Mahāpaccariyampi ayameva nayo dassito. Udakasuddhipaccayena pana satipi phassasādiyane yathāvuttaparicchede anāpatti.

812. In the fifth, regarding 'above two joints,' here, when two fingers are inserted together, counting one joint for each finger, it is 'above two joints'. It should be understood that in the case of inserting one finger, it is not allowable to go beyond two joints. In the Mahāpaccariya too, this very same method is shown. However, on account of purification with water, even if there is enjoyment of contact, there is no offense within the aforementioned limit.

815-817. Chaṭṭhe āsumbhitvāti pātetvā. Dadhimatthūti dadhimaṇḍaṃ dadhimhi pasannodakaṃ. Bhuñjantassa bhikkhuno hatthapāse ṭhānaṃ, pānīyassa vā vidhūpanassa vā gahaṇanti imāni panettha dve aṅgāni.

In the sixth, `āsumbhitvā` means having dropped. `Dadhimatthu` means the scum of curds, the clear water on curds. The two factors here are: standing within arm's reach of a monk who is eating, and taking either drinking water or a fan.

822. Sattame “paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti idaṃ pubbapayogadukkaṭassa nidassanamattanti āha “na kevalaṃ paṭiggahaṇeyeva hotī”tiādi. Pamāṇanti pācittiyāpattiyā pamāṇaṃ. Imehiyeva dvīhi pācittiyaṃ hoti, nāññehi bhajjanādīhīti attho. Vuttamevatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādimāha. Taṃ pubbāparaviruddhanti punapi vuttanti vuttavādaṃ sandhāyāha. Aññāya viññattiyā laddhampi hi anāṇattiyā viññattiyā imissā [V 3.0115] aviññattiyā laddhapakkhaṃ bhajati, tasmā heṭṭhā aviññattiyā laddhe karaṇakārāpanesu visesaṃ avatvā idha visesavacanaṃ pubbāparaviruddhaṃ. Yadi cettha karaṇe pācittiyaṃ, kārāpanepi pācittiyeneva bhavitabbaṃ. Atha kārāpane dukkaṭaṃ, karaṇepi dukkaṭeneva bhavitabbaṃ. Na hi karaṇe vā kārāpane vā viseso atthi, tasmā aññāya viññattiyā [M 3.0124] laddhaṃ sayaṃ bhajjanādīni katvāpi kārāpetvāpi bhuñjantiyā dukkaṭamevāti idamettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Avisesena vuttanti karaṇakārāpanānaṃ sāmaññato vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ aññatarassa viññāpanaṃ vā viññāpāpanaṃ vā, paṭilābho, bhajjanādīni katvā vā kāretvā vā ajjhoharaṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

822. In the seventh, regarding 'if one accepts, it is an offense of wrong conduct,' this is merely an indication of the dukkaṭa offense in the preliminary stage, hence it is said, 'it does not occur only in the act of receiving,' and so on. 'Measure' refers to the measure for a pācittiya offense. The meaning is that a pācittiya occurs only through these two, not through others like frying, and so on. To show the stated meaning in detail, he says 'therefore,' and so on. Referring to the repeated statement, he says that this is contradictory to what was said before and after. For what is obtained even by another's request, if it is by an unauthorized request, it falls into the category of being obtained without a request for this person. Therefore, having not stated a distinction below regarding doing and causing to do for what was obtained without a request, the statement of a distinction here is contradictory to what was said before and after. If there is a pācittiya for doing it oneself here, there must also be a pācittiya for causing it to be done. If there is a dukkaṭa for causing it to be done, there must also be a dukkaṭa for doing it oneself. For there is no distinction between doing and causing to do. Therefore, for one who, having obtained something through another's request, eats it after preparing it herself or having it prepared, there is only a dukkaṭa offense—this is the conclusion here. 'Stated without distinction' means stated generally regarding doing and causing to do. The rest here is clear. The three factors here are: requesting or causing to request one of the seven kinds of grain, obtaining it, and swallowing it after having prepared it oneself or having had it prepared.

824. Aṭṭhame nibbiṭṭhoti patiṭṭhāpito. Keṇīti rañño dātabbassa āyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ṭhānantaranti gāmajanapadādiṭhānantaraṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Uccārādibhāvo, anavalokanaṃ, vaḷañjanaṭṭhānaṃ, tirokuṭṭapākāratā, chaḍḍanaṃ vā chaḍḍāpanaṃ vāti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

824. In the eighth, `nibbiṭṭha` means established. `Keṇī` is a term for the revenue to be given to the king. 'Another place' means another place such as a village or a country. The rest here is clear. The five factors here are: being excrement, etc.; not looking; a place of use; being beyond a wall or fence; and discarding or causing to be discarded.

830. Navame sabbesanti bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā ca. Idha khettapālakā ārāmādigopakā ca sāmikā eva.

830. In the ninth, 'for all' means for a bhikkhu and a bhikkhunī. Here, the field-keepers, park-keepers, and so forth, are themselves the owners.

836. Dasame ekapayogenāti ekadisāvalokanapayogena. Tesaṃyevāti yesaṃ naccaṃ passati. Kiñcāpi sayaṃ naccanādīsu pācittiyaṃ pāḷiyaṃ na vuttaṃ, tathāpi aṭṭhakathāpamāṇena gahetabbanti dassetuṃ “sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu vutta”nti āha. “Ārāme ṭhatvāti na kevalaṃ ṭhatvā, tato tato gantvāpi sabbiriyāpathehi labhati, ‘ārāme ṭhitā’ti pana ārāmapariyāpannabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Itarathā nisinnāpi na labheyyā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Naccādīnaṃ aññataratā, aññatra anuññātakāraṇā gamanaṃ, dassanaṃ vā savanaṃ vāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

836. In the tenth, 'by one application' means by the application of looking in one direction. 'Of those' refers to those whose dancing one sees. Although a pācittiya offense for oneself in dancing and so on is not stated in the Pāli text, to show that it should be understood according to the authority of the commentaries, it is said, 'as stated in all the commentaries.' Regarding 'standing in the monastery,' it is not only by standing, but one also incurs the offense by going from place to place in any posture. The phrase 'standing in the monastery' is used to show inclusion within the monastery’s boundaries. Otherwise, one would not incur the offense even when sitting. This is stated in all three Gaṇṭhipadas. The rest here is clear. The factors here are these three: any one of dancing and so on; going, except for a permitted reason; and seeing or hearing.

Lasuṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Garlic Chapter is concluded.

2. Andhakāravaggavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Darkness Chapter

841. Andhakāravaggassa paṭhame dāne vā pūjāya vāti dānanimittaṃ vā pūjānimittaṃ vā. [V 3.0116] Mantetīti katheti. Rattandhakāratā, purisassa hatthapāse ṭhānaṃ vā sallapanaṃ vā, sahāyābhāvo, rahopekkhatāti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

841. In the first of the Darkness Chapter, 'by a gift or by worship' means on an occasion for a gift or on an occasion for worship. 'Converses' means speaks. The four factors here are: the darkness of night, a man being within arm’s reach for standing or conversing, the absence of a companion, and the desire for seclusion.

842-846. Dutiyatatiyacatutthāni uttānatthāneva.

The second, third, and fourth are clear in meaning.

856-857. Pañcame [M 3.0125] anovassakaṃ atikkāmentiyāti channassa anto nisīditvā pakkamantiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Upacāro dvādasahattho”ti vadanti. Pallaṅkassa anokāseti ūrubaddhāsanassa anokāse appahonte. Purebhattatā, antaraghare nisajjā, āsanassa pallaṅkokāsatā, aññatra anuññātakāraṇā anāpucchanaṃ, vuttaparicchedātikkamoti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

In the fifth, 'in a place sheltered from the rain, as she is departing' is said in reference to one who, having sat inside a covered place, is departing. They say, 'The vicinity is twelve hands.' 'In a place not allowing for a cross-legged posture' means in a space insufficient for a seat with bound thighs. The five factors here are: being before the main meal, sitting inside a house, the seat having space for a cross-legged posture, not asking leave except for a permitted reason, and exceeding the stated limit.

859-864. Chaṭṭhasattamādīni uttānatthāneva.

The sixth and seventh are clear.

Andhakāravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Darkness Chapter is concluded.

3. Naggavaggavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Chapter on the Naked

883-887. Naggavaggassa paṭhamadutiyāni uttānatthāneva.

The first and second of the Chapter on the Naked are clear in meaning.

893. Tatiye visibbetvāti dussibbitaṃ puna sibbanatthāya visibbetvā vijaṭetvā. Aññatra catūhapañcāhāti visibbitadivasato pañca divase atikkamitvā. Nivāsanapāvuraṇūpagacīvaratā, upasampannāya santakatā, sibbanatthāya visibbanaṃ vā visibbāpanaṃ vā, aññatra anuññātakāraṇā pañcāhātikkamo, dhuranikkhepoti imāni panettha pañca aṅgāni.

893. In the third, 'having unsewn' means having unsewn and unraveled a poorly sewn robe in order to sew it again. 'Except for four or five days' means having exceeded five days from the day of unsewing. The five factors here are: its being a robe suitable for an under-robe or an outer-robe; its being the property of a fully ordained nun; unsewing it or having it unsewn for the purpose of sewing; exceeding five days without a permitted reason; and abandoning the responsibility.

898. Catutthe pañcannaṃ cīvarānanti ticīvaraṃ udakasāṭikā saṅkaccikāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ cīvarānaṃ. Pañcannaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataratā, pañcāhātikkamo, anuññātakāraṇābhāvo, aparivattananti imāni panettha cattāri aṅgāni.

898. In the fourth, 'of the five robes' refers to these five robes: the three robes, the bathing cloth, and the breast-band. The four factors here are: its being any one of the five robes, exceeding five days, the absence of a permitted reason, and not exchanging it.

902. Pañcamaṃ uttānatthameva.

902. The fifth is clear in meaning.

907. Chaṭṭhe [V 3.0117] cīvaralābhanti labhitabbacīvaraṃ. Vikappanupagapacchimatā, saṅghassa pariṇatabhāvo, vinā ānisaṃsadassanena antarāyakaraṇanti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

907. In the sixth, 'acquisition of a robe' means a robe to be received. The three factors here are: its being the last robe suitable for formal disposal (vikappana), its having been turned over to the Sangha, and creating an obstacle without showing the benefit.

911. Sattamaṃ uttānatthameva.

911. The seventh is clear in meaning.

916. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0126] kumbhathūṇaṃ nāma kumbhasaddo, tena caranti kīḷanti, taṃ vā sippaṃ etesanti kumbhathūṇikā. Tenāha “ghaṭakena kīḷanakā”ti. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.13) pana “kumbhathūṇaṃ nāma caturassaambaṇakatāḷa”nti vuttaṃ. Caturassaambaṇakatāḷaṃ nāma rukkhasāradantādīsu yena kenaci caturassaambaṇaṃ katvā catūsu passesu cammena onandhitvā katavāditabhaṇḍaṃ. Bimbisakantipi tasseva vevacanaṃ, taṃ vādenti, taṃ vā sippaṃ etesanti kumbhathūṇikā. Tenāha “bimbisakavādakātipi vadantī”ti. Samaṇacīvaratā, ṭhapetvā sahadhammike mātāpitaro ca aññesaṃ dānaṃ, atāvakālikatāti imāni panettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

916. In the eighth, the term 'kumbhathūṇa' means the sound of a pot; they wander and play with it, or that is their skill, hence they are called 'kumbhathūṇikā.' Therefore it is said, 'those who play with a small pot.' However, in the commentary to the Dīghanikāya it is said, 'kumbhathūṇa means a four-sided ambaṇa instrument.' A 'four-sided ambaṇa instrument' is a musical instrument made by crafting a four-sided ambaṇa from heartwood, ivory, or any other such material, and covering it with leather on four sides. 'Bimbisaka' is also a synonym for it; they play it, or that is their skill, hence they are called 'kumbhathūṇikā.' Therefore it is said, 'they are also called players of the bimbisaka.' The three factors here are: its being a recluse's robe, giving it to others—except for co-religionists and parents—and its not being a temporary item (atāvakālika).

920. Navamaṃ uttānatthameva.

920. The ninth is clear in meaning.

927. Dasame dhammikaṃ kathinuddhāranti sabbāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ akālacīvaraṃ dātukāmena upāsakena yattako atthāramūlako ānisaṃso, tato adhikaṃ vā samakaṃ vā datvā yācitakena samaggena bhikkhunisaṅghena yaṃ kathinaṃ ñattidutiyena kammena antarā uddharīyati, tassa so uddhāro dhammikoti vuccati, evarūpaṃ kathinuddhāranti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

927. In the tenth, a 'lawful Kathina withdrawal' means the following: when a lay devotee, wishing to give out-of-season robes to all the bhikkhunīs, gives a gift equal to or exceeding the benefit derived from the spreading of the Kathina cloth, and upon his request the unified Bhikkhunī Sangha withdraws the Kathina privilege mid-season by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement. This withdrawal is called 'lawful.' This is the meaning of 'lawful Kathina withdrawal.' The rest is clear in meaning.

Naggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on the Naked is concluded.

932. Tuvaṭṭavagge sabbaṃ uttānameva.

932. In the Tuvaṭṭavagga, everything is clear.

5. Cittāgāravaggavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Picture Gallery Chapter

978. Cittāgāravaggassa paṭhame kīḷanaupavananti antonagare ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, kīḷanuyyānanti bahinagare ṭhitaṃ sandhāya. Pāṭekkā āpattiyoti gīvāya parivaṭṭanappayogagaṇanāya āpattiyo, na ummīlanagaṇanāya. “Ajjhārāme rājāgārādīni karonti[V 3.0118], tāni passantiyā anāpattī”ti vacanato “antoārāme tattha tattha gantvā naccādīni passituṃ labhatī”tipi siddhaṃ.

978. In the first of the Picture Gallery Chapter, 'pleasure grove' refers to one situated inside the city, while 'pleasure park' refers to one situated outside the city. 'Separate offenses' means offenses are counted according to the number of times one turns one's neck, not by the number of times one opens one's eyes. Because it is said, 'There is no offense for one who sees royal buildings and so on that they are constructing within the monastery,' it is therefore established that 'one is allowed to go to various places within the monastery to see dancing and so on.'

982. Dutiyādīni [M 3.0127] uttānatthāneva.

982. The second and following are clear in meaning.

1015. Navame hatthiādīsu sippa-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo, tathā āthabbaṇādīsu manta-saddo. Tattha āthabbaṇamanto nāma āthabbaṇavedavihito parūpaghātakaro manto, khīlanamanto nāma dārusārakhīlaṃ mantetvā pathaviyaṃ pavesetvā māraṇamanto, agadappayogo visayojanaṃ. Nāgamaṇḍalanti sappānaṃ pavesanivāraṇatthaṃ maṇḍalabaddhamanto.

1015. In the ninth, the word 'skill' should be applied individually to 'elephant skill' and so on; likewise, the word 'spell' should be applied to 'Atharvan spell' and so on. Therein, an 'Atharvan spell' is a spell prescribed in the Atharva Veda that harms others. A 'peg spell' is a killing spell whereby one enchants a hardwood peg and drives it into the ground. The 'application of an antidote' is the counteracting of poison. A 'snake-circle' is a spell that binds a circle to prevent the entry of snakes.

1018. Dasamaṃ uttānatthameva.

1018. The tenth is clear in meaning.

Cittāgāravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Picture Gallery Chapter is concluded.

1021. Ārāmavagge sabbaṃ uttānatthameva.

1021. In the Ārāmavagga, everything is clear in meaning.

1067. Gabbhinivaggepi sabbaṃ suviññeyyameva.

1067. In the Gabbhinīvagga also, everything is easily understood.

8. Kumāribhūtavaggavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Chapter on Young Women

1119. Kumāribhūtavaggassa paṭhame sabbapaṭhamā dve mahāsikkhamānāti gabbhinivagge sabbapaṭhamaṃ vuttā dve sikkhamānā. Sikkhamānā icceva vattabbāti sammutikammādīsu evaṃ vattabbā. Gihigatāti vā kumāribhūtāti vā na vattabbāti sace vadanti, kammaṃ kuppatīti adhippāyo. Ito paraṃ navamapariyosānaṃ uttānatthameva.

1119. In the first of the Kumāribhūtavagga, 'the very first two great probationers' means the two probationers mentioned at the very beginning of the Gabbhinīvagga. 'They should be called "probationers"' means they should be addressed thus in formal acts of the Sangha, such as giving consent. 'They should not be called "a married woman" or "a maiden"' means that if they are so called, the formal act is invalid; this is the intention. From here until the end of the ninth, the meaning is clear.

1163. Dasame apubbasamuṭṭhānasīsanti paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānādīsu terasasu samuṭṭhānesu ananuññātasamuṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi ito pubbe tādisassa samuṭṭhānasīsassa anāgatattā “apubbasamuṭṭhānasīsa”nti vuttaṃ.

1163. In the tenth, 'a heading of unprecedented origin' refers to an unpermitted origin among the thirteen origins beginning with that of the first pārājika. Because such a heading of origin had not occurred before this, it is called 'a heading of unprecedented origin.'

1166. Ekādasamādīni [V 3.0119] uttānatthāneva.

1166. The eleventh and following are clear in meaning.

Kumāribhūtavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Chapter on Young Women, the Eighth.

9. Chattupāhanavaggavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear

1214. Chattupāhanavaggassa [M 3.0128] ekādasame upacāraṃ sandhāyāti samantā dvādasahatthupacāraṃ sandhāya. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

1214. In the eleventh of the Chattupāhanavagga, 'with reference to the precinct' means with reference to the surrounding precinct of twelve hands. The rest is clear in all respects.

Chattupāhanavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear is concluded.

Giraggasamajjādīni acittakāni lokavajjānīti vuttattā naccanti vā vaṇṇakanti vā ajānitvāva passantiyā vā nahāyantiyā vā āpattisambhavato vatthuajānanacittena acittakāni, naccanti vā vaṇṇakanti vā jānitvā passantiyā vā nahāyantiyā vā akusaleneva āpajjanato lokavajjānīti veditabbāni. Corīvuṭṭhāpanādīni corītiādinā vatthuṃ jānitvā karaṇe eva āpattisambhavato sacittakāni, upasampadādīnaṃ ekantaakusalacitteneva akattabbattā paṇṇattivajjāni. “Idha sacittakācittakatā paṇṇattijānanājānanatāya aggahetvā vatthujānanājānanatāya gahetabbā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

The training rules beginning with the Giraggasamajja are 'mindless' (acittaka) and 'worldly faults' (lokavajja). Because it is said that an offense can occur for one who sees or bathes without knowing that dancing or singing is taking place, due to a mind that is unaware of the object, they are called 'mindless'. Because an offense is incurred purely through an unwholesome mind if one knows that dancing or singing is happening and sees or bathes, they are to be understood as 'worldly faults'. The training rules beginning with the raising up of a thief are 'intentional' (sacittaka) because an offense can occur only when the act is performed with knowledge of the object, such as knowing 'she is a thief'. Ordination and the like are 'faults by regulation' (paṇṇattivajja) because they are not to be performed except with a purely wholesome mind. 'Here, the state of being intentional or mindless should be understood by means of knowing or not knowing the object, not by means of knowing or not knowing the regulation,' as stated in all three difficult passages. The rest here has a plain meaning.

Bhikkhunīvibhaṅge khuddakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Minor Matters in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is concluded.

Pācittiyakaṇḍaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Pācittiya Section is concluded.

5. Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍaṃ (bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)

5. Pāṭidesanīya Section (Explanation of the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga)

Pāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule

1228. Pāṭidesanīyā [M 3.0129][V 3.0120] nāma ye aṭṭha dhammā saṅkhepeneva saṅgahaṃ āruḷhāti sambandho. Pāḷivinimuttakesūti pāḷiyaṃ anāgatesu sappiādīsu.

1228. 'Pāṭidesanīya' refers to those eight matters that have been included in the collection only in brief—this is the connection. 'In what is apart from the Pāḷi' means regarding matters not mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as ghee and so on.

Pāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is concluded.

Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Pāṭidesanīya Section is concluded.

Ye pana pañcasattati sekhiyā dhammā uddiṭṭhā, ye ca tesaṃ anantarā sattādhikaraṇavhayā dhammā uddiṭṭhāti sambandho. Tattha tesanti tesaṃ sekhiyānaṃ. Sattādhikaraṇavhayāti sattādhikaraṇasamathasaṅkhātā. Taṃ atthavinicchayaṃ tādisaṃyeva yasmā vidū vadantīti attho.

Now, the seventy-five Sekhiya rules that have been set forth, and the rules called the seven Adhikaraṇa that immediately follow them have been set forth—this is the connection. Therein, 'tesaṃ' refers to those Sekhiya rules. 'Called the seven Adhikaraṇa' means those designated as the seven settlements of legal issues. Because the wise speak of that determination of meaning as being just so, this is the meaning.

Yathā niṭṭhitāti sambandho. Sabbāsavapahaṃ magganti sabbāsavavighātakaṃ arahattamaggaṃ patvā sasantāne uppādetvā. Passantu nibbutinti maggañāṇalocanena nibbānaṃ sacchikarontu, pappontūti vā pāṭho. Tattha nibbutinti khandhaparinibbānaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

'As it is finished'—this is the connection. 'The path that abandons all taints' means: having attained the path of Arahantship which destroys all taints, and having produced it in one's own mental continuum. 'May they see quenching' means: may they realize Nibbāna with the eye of path-knowledge; or the reading is 'may they attain'. Therein, by 'quenching' the final quenching of the aggregates should be understood.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ.

Thus in the Sāratthadīpanī, on the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā.

Bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is concluded.

Ubhatovibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Commentary on the Two Vibhaṅgas is concluded.

Pācittiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Pācittiya is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Mahāvagga-ṭīkā

The Mahāvagga Subcommentary

1. Mahākhandhakaṃ

1. The Great Section

Bodhikathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Bodhi Discourse

Idāni [M 3.0131][V 3.0121] ubhatovibhaṅgānantaraṃ saṅgahamāropitassa mahāvaggacūḷavaggasaṅgahitassa khandhakassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ ārabhitukāmo “ubhinnaṃ pātimokkhāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha ubhinnaṃ pātimokkhānanti ubhinnaṃ pātimokkhavibhaṅgānaṃ. Pātimokkhaggahaṇena hettha tesaṃ vibhaṅgo abhedena gahito. Yaṃ khandhakaṃ saṅgāyiṃsūti sambandho. Khandhānaṃ samūho khandhako, khandhānaṃ vā pakāsanato dīpanato khandhako. “Khandhā”ti cettha pabbajjupasampadādivinayakammasaṅkhātā cārittavārittasikkhāpadasaṅkhātā ca paññattiyo adhippetā. Pabbajjādīni hi bhagavatā paññattattā “paññattiyo”ti vuccanti. Paññattiyañca khandhasaddo dissati “dārukkhandho aggikkhandho”tiādīsu viya. Apica bhāgarāsaṭṭhatāpettha yujjatiyeva tāsaṃ paññattīnaṃ bhāgato rāsito ca vibhattattā. Khandhakovidāti paññattibhāgarāsaṭṭhavasena khandhaṭṭhe kovidā.

Now, after the two Vibhaṅgas, wishing to begin the explanation of the meaning of the Khandhaka, which was brought into the collection and is comprised of the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga, he said the words beginning with 'of the two Pātimokkhas'. Therein, 'of the two Pātimokkhas' means of the two Pātimokkha-vibhaṅgas. For here, by the taking of 'Pātimokkha', their Vibhaṅga is taken without distinction. 'Which Khandhaka they recited'—this is the connection. A collection of 'khandhas' is a 'khandhaka', or because it proclaims or illuminates the 'khandhas', it is a 'khandhaka'. And here by 'khandhas' are intended the regulations designated as Vinaya acts such as going forth and ordination, and the training rules designated as proper conduct and what is to be avoided. For going forth and so on are called 'regulations' because they were regulated by the Blessed One. And the word 'khandha' is seen in the sense of a regulation, as in 'a log of wood', 'a mass of fire', and so on. Moreover, the meaning of 'portion' or 'mass' is indeed suitable here, because those regulations are divided by portion and by mass. 'Skilled in the Khandhakas' means skilled in the meaning of 'khandha' in the sense of portions and masses of regulations.

Padabhājanīye [V 3.0122] yesaṃ padānaṃ atthā yehi aṭṭhakathānayehi pakāsitāti yojetabbaṃ. Te ce puna vadeyyāmāti te ce aṭṭhakathānaye punapi vadeyyāma. Atha vā padabhājanīye yesaṃ padānaṃ ye atthā heṭṭhā pakāsitā, te ce atthe puna vadeyyāmāti yojetabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ pakkhe hi-saddo padapūraṇe daṭṭhabbo. Pariyosānanti saṃvaṇṇanāpariyosānaṃ. Uttānā ceva ye atthāti ye atthā pubbe apakāsitāpi uttānā agambhīrā.

In the Padabhājanīya, it should be connected thus: 'the meanings of which words have been explained by which commentarial methods'. 'If we were to speak them again' means 'if we were to speak those commentarial methods again'. Or alternatively, it should be connected thus: 'in the Padabhājanīya, if we were to speak again those meanings of which words have been explained below'. In this alternative, the word 'hi' should be seen as a particle filling out the line. 'Conclusion' means the conclusion of the explanation. 'And those meanings which are plain' means 'those meanings which, even if not explained before, are plain, not profound'.

1. Visesakāraṇaṃ natthīti “yena samayena āyasmato sāriputtattherassa sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanahetubhūto parivitakko udapādi, tena [M 3.0132] samayenā”tiādinā vuttakāraṇaṃ viya idha visesakāraṇaṃ natthi. Ayamabhilāpoti “tena samayenā”ti ayamabhilāpo. Kiṃ panetassa vacane payojananti yadi visesakāraṇaṃ natthi, etassa vacane kiṃ payojananti adhippāyo. Nidānadassanaṃ payojananti yojetabbaṃ. Tameva vibhāvetuṃ “yā hi bhagavatā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

1. 'There is no special reason' means: just as there was a reason stated in the words beginning 'at the time when the reflection that was the cause for the request for the laying down of a training rule arose for the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, at that time...', here there is no special reason. 'This is the expression' means: 'at that time' is this expression. 'But what is the purpose in this statement?' means: 'if there is no special reason, what is the purpose in this statement?'—this is the intention. It should be connected thus: 'showing the occasion is the purpose'. To clarify that very point, the words beginning 'for what by the Blessed One...' were said.

Mahāvelā viya mahāvelā, vipulavālukapuñjatāya mahanto velātaṭo viyāti attho. Tenāha “mahante vālikarāsimhīti attho”ti. Uru maru sikatā vālukā vaṇṇu vālikāti ime saddā samānatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Tenāha “urūti vālikā vuccatī”ti.

'Like a great shore' (mahāvelā viya mahāvelā): the meaning is 'like a great seashore' on account of its being a vast heap of sand. Therefore, it is said, 'the meaning is "on a great heap of sand"'. The words 'uru', 'maru', 'sikatā', 'vālukā', 'vaṇṇu', and 'vālikā' have the same meaning; only the expression is different. Therefore, it is said, ''uru' is called 'vālikā' (sand)'.

Ito paṭṭhāya ca –

And from here on—

Yasmā suttantapāḷīnaṃ, attho saṅkhepavaṇṇito;

Tasmā mayaṃ karissāma, tāsaṃ atthassa dīpanaṃ.

Because the meaning of the Suttanta Pāḷis has been explained in brief, therefore we will make an illumination of their meaning.

Najjāti (udā. aṭṭha. 1) nadati sandatīti nadī, tassā najjā, nadiyā ninnagāyāti attho. Nerañjarāyāti “nelañjalāyā”ti vattabbe la-kārassa ra-kāraṃ katvā “nerañjarāyā”ti vuttaṃ, kaddamasevālapaṇakādidosarahitasalilāyāti attho. Keci “nīlaṃjalāyāti vattabbe nerañjarāyāti vutta”nti vadanti, nāmameva vā etaṃ tassā nadiyāti veditabbaṃ. Tassā nadiyā tīre yattha bhagavā vihāsi, taṃ dassetuṃ “bodhirukkhamūle”ti vuttaṃ. “Bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”nti (cūḷava. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121) ettha maggañāṇaṃ bodhīti vuttaṃ, “pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso”ti (dī. ni. 3.217) ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Tadubhayampi bodhiṃ bhagavā ettha pattoti rukkhopi “bodhirukkho”tveva nāmaṃ labhi. Atha vā satta bojjhaṅge bujjhatīti bhagavā bodhi. Tena bujjhantena sannissitattā so rukkho [V 3.0123] “bodhirukkho”ti nāmaṃ labhi. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ekadeseneva atthaṃ dassetuṃ “bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Mūleti samīpe. Paṭhamābhisambuddhoti anunāsikalopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho”ti. Paṭhamanti ca bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, tasmā abhisambuddho hutvā sabbapaṭhamaṃ bodhirukkhamūle viharatīti evamettha sambandho veditabbo.

Regarding 'Of the river' (najjā): a river (nadī) is so called because it sounds (nadati) and flows (sandati). 'Najjā' means of the river (nadiyā), of the downward-flowing one (ninnagāya). Regarding 'Of the Nerañjarā' (nerañjarāya): when 'Nelañjalā' should be said, 'Nerañjarā' is said, having made the letter 'l' into the letter 'r'. The meaning is 'of the one whose water is free from faults such as mud, moss, and water-plants'. Some say that when 'Nīlañjalā' should be said, 'Nerañjarā' is said. Or it should be known that this is just the name of that river. To show where on the bank of that river the Blessed One dwelled, 'at the foot of the Bodhi tree' was said. In 'Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths', 'bodhi' refers to path-knowledge. In 'He attains bodhi, the supreme and vast wisdom', it refers to omniscient knowledge. The Blessed One attained both these kinds of bodhi here, thus the tree also received the name 'Bodhi tree'. Or, the Blessed One is 'bodhi' because he awakens to the seven factors of awakening (bojjhaṅga). Because it was resorted to by him while awakening, that tree received the name 'Bodhi tree'. In the commentary, however, to show the meaning only in part, the words beginning 'Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths' were said. 'At the foot' (mūle) means nearby. Regarding 'First-enlightened' (paṭhamābhisambuddho): this is a directive with the elision of the nasal, thus he says 'first enlightened'. And 'first' (paṭhamaṃ) is a neuter adverbial directive, therefore the connection here should be understood thus: having become enlightened, he dwelled at the foot of the Bodhi tree first of all.

Atha [M 3.0133] kho bhagavāti ettha athāti tasmiṃ samayeti evamattho gahetabbo anekatthattā nipātānaṃ, yasmiṃ samaye abhisambuddho hutvā bodhirukkhamūle viharati, tasmiṃ samayeti attho. Teneva udānapāḷiyaṃ (udā. 2) “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinno hoti vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedī”ti vuttaṃ. Athāti vā pacchāti imasmiṃ atthe nipāto, tasmā abhisambodhito pacchāti evamattho gahetabbo. Khoti padapūraṇe nipāto. Satta ahāni sattāhaṃ. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Yasmā bhagavā taṃ sattāhaṃ nirantaratāya accantameva phalasamāpattisukhena vihāsi, tasmā “sattāha”nti accantasaṃyogavasena upayogavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekapallaṅkenāti visākhapuṇṇamāya anatthaṅgateyeva sūriye aparājitapallaṅkavasena vajirāsane nisinnakālato paṭṭhāya sakimpi anuṭṭhahitvā yathābhujitena ekeneva pallaṅkena.

Regarding 'Atha kho bhagavā': here, the word 'atha' should be understood as 'at that time' (tasmiṃ samaye), due to the multiple meanings of particles, meaning 'at the time when, having become perfectly enlightened, he dwelt at the foot of the Bodhi tree'—that is the meaning. For that reason, in the Udāna Pāḷi (Ud. 2), it is said: 'At that time, the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation.' Alternatively, 'atha' is a particle in the sense of 'after,' so in this context, it should be understood as 'after the perfect enlightenment.' The word 'kho' is an expletive particle. 'Seven days' (satta ahāni) is 'sattāhaṃ.' This is an expression of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoge). Because the Blessed One dwelt uninterruptedly for those seven days, entirely in the bliss of fruition attainment, therefore 'sattāhaṃ' is used as an expression of absolute continuity. 'In a single posture' (ekapallaṅkena) means from the time he sat on the diamond seat in the unconquered posture, even before the sun had set on the Visākha full moon day, without rising even once, remaining in the same single posture as he had initially assumed.

Vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedīti ettha tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttīsu pañcasu paṭippassaddhivimuttisaṅkhātā bhagavato phalavimutti adhippetāti āha “vimuttisukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedayamāno”ti. Vimuttīti ca upakkilesehi paṭippassaddhivasena cittassa vimuttabhāvo, cittameva vā tathā vimuttaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tāya vimuttiyā jātaṃ, sampayuttaṃ vā sukhaṃ vimuttisukhaṃ. “Yāyaṃ, bhante, upekkhā sante sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti (ma. ni. 2.88) vacanato upekkhāpi cettha sukhamicceva veditabbā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 232) “upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā”ti. Bhagavā hi catutthajjhānikaṃ arahattaphalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, na itaraṃ. Atha vā “tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.221, 272) yathā saṅkhāradukkhavūpasamo “sukho”ti vuccati, evaṃ sakalakilesadukkhūpasamabhāvato aggaphale labbhamānā paṭippassaddhivimutti eva idha “sukha”nti veditabbā.

'Experiencing the bliss of liberation': here, among the five liberations—liberation by substitution of opposites, liberation by suppression, liberation by cutting off, liberation by subsidence, and liberation by escape—the Blessed One’s fruition liberation, known as the liberation by subsidence, is intended. Thus it is said, 'experiencing the bliss of liberation, the bliss of fruition attainment.' And 'liberation' should be understood either as the mind’s state of being freed through the subsidence of defilements, or simply as the mind itself being thus liberated. The bliss born of that liberation, or associated with it, is the bliss of liberation. From the statement, 'Venerable sir, this equanimity is spoken of by the Blessed One as peaceful bliss,' equanimity too should be understood here as bliss. For it is said in the Sammohavinodanī: 'Equanimity, being peaceful, is indeed called bliss.' Indeed, the Blessed One attains the fruition attainment of arahantship based on the fourth jhāna, not any other. Alternatively, just as in passages like 'their cessation is bliss,' the cessation of conditioned suffering is called 'bliss,' so too the liberation by subsidence, obtained in the supreme fruition due to the cessation of all suffering of defilements, should here be understood as 'bliss.'

Athāti adhikāratthe nipāto, khoti padapūraṇe. Tesu adhikāratthena “athā”ti iminā vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedanato [V 3.0124] aññaṃ adhikāraṃ dasseti. Ko panesoti? Paṭiccasamauppādamanasikāro. Rattiyāti avayavasambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Paṭhamanti accantasaṃyogatthe upayogavacanaṃ[M 3.0134]. Bhagavā hi tassā rattiyā sakalampi paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ teneva manasikārena yutto ahosīti.

The particle 'atha' is in the sense of introducing a new topic, and 'kho' is an expletive particle. Among these, by 'atha' in the sense of introducing a new topic, a different topic from the experiencing of the bliss of liberation is shown. And what is that? It is reflection on dependent origination. 'Rattiyā' is a genitive case denoting a part-whole relationship. 'Paṭhamaṃ' is a term used in the sense of continuous connection. For the Blessed One was indeed engaged in that very reflection throughout the entire first watch of that night.

Paccayākāranti avijjādipaccayadhammaṃ. Paṭiccāti paṭimukhaṃ gantvā, kāraṇasāmaggiṃ apaṭikkhipitvāti attho. Paṭimukhagamanañca paccayassa kāraṇasāmaggiyā aṅgabhāvena phalassa uppādanameva. Apaṭikkhipitvāti pana vinā tāya kāraṇasāmaggiyā aṅgabhāvaṃ agantvā sayameva na uppādetīti attho. Etena kāraṇabahutā dassitā. Avijjādiekekahetusīsena hi hetusamūho niddiṭṭho. Sahiteti samudite, avinibbhutteti attho. Avijjādiko hi paccayadhammo sahiteyeva aññamaññaṃ avinibbhogavuttidhamme uppādeti. Iminā paccayuppannadhammabahutā dassitā. Ubhayenapi “ekaṃ na ekato”tiādinayo (vibha. aṭṭha. 226 saṅkhārapadaniddesa; visuddhi. 2.617) dīpito hoti. Ekato hi kāraṇato na idha kiñci ekaṃ phalamatthi, na anekaṃ, nāpi anekehi kāraṇehi ekaṃ, anekehi pana kāraṇehi anekameva hoti. Tathā hi anekehi utupathavībījasalilasaṅkhātehi kāraṇehi anekameva rūpagandharasādiaṅkurasaṅkhātaṃ phalamuppajjamānaṃ dissati. Yaṃ panetaṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti ekekahetuphaladīpanaṃ kataṃ, tattha payojanaṃ na vijjati.

'The mode of conditionality' refers to the conditional phenomena beginning with ignorance. 'Dependent on' means approaching directly, not rejecting the causal assemblage—this is the meaning. And approaching directly is precisely the production of the result, with the condition being a factor in the causal assemblage. 'Not rejecting' means that without becoming a factor in that causal assemblage, it does not produce the result by itself—this is the meaning. By this, the multiplicity of causes is shown. For the mass of causes is described with ignorance, etc., as individual chief causes. 'Together' means assembled, inseparable—this is the meaning. For the conditional phenomena, beginning with ignorance, when assembled, give rise to other phenomena that exist inseparably from each other. By this, the multiplicity of conditionally arisen phenomena is shown. Through both, the principle 'not one from one,' etc., (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 226, Saṅkhārapadaniddesa; Visuddhimagga 2.617) is illuminated. For here, from a single cause there is not any single result, nor many; nor from many causes is there a single result; but rather, from many causes, many results arise. Thus, it is seen that multiple results—such as sprouts characterized by form, scent, taste, etc.—arise from multiple causes, such as season, earth, seed, and water. However, as for this illustration of a single cause and a single result that has been made, there is no purpose to be found in it.

Bhagavā hi katthaci padhānattā katthaci pākaṭattā katthaci asādhāraṇattā desanāvilāsassa ca veneyyānañca anurūpato ekameva hetuṃ vā phalaṃ vā dīpeti. “Phassapaccayā vedanā”ti hi ekameva hetuṃ phalañcāha. Phasso hi vedanāya padhānahetu yathāphassaṃ vedanāvavatthānato. Vedanā ca phassassa padhānaphalaṃ yathāvedanaṃ phassavavatthānato. “Semhasamuṭṭhānā ābādhā”ti (mahāni. 5) pākaṭattā ekaṃ hetuṃ āha. Pākaṭo hi ettha semho, na kammādayo. “Ye keci, bhikkhave, akusalā dhammā, sabbete ayonisomanasikāramūlakā”ti asādhāraṇattā ekaṃ hetuṃ āha. Asādhāraṇo hi ayonisomanasikāro akusalānaṃ, sādhāraṇāni vatthārammaṇādīnīti. Tasmā avijjā tāvettha vijjamānesupi aññesu vatthārammaṇasahajātadhammādīsu saṅkhārakāraṇesu “assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.52) ca “avijjāsamudayā āsavasamudayo”ti [M 3.0135] (ma. ni. 1.104) ca vacanato aññesampi taṇhādīnaṃ saṅkhārahetūnaṃ hetūti padhānattā, “avidvā, bhikkhave, avijjāgato puññābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharotī”ti pākaṭattā asādhāraṇattā ca saṅkhārānaṃ hetubhāvena dīpitāti [V 3.0125] veditabbā. Evaṃ sabbattha ekekahetuphaladīpane yathāsambhavaṃ nayo netabbo. Tenāhu porāṇā –

For the Blessed One, in some cases due to prominence, in some due to obviousness, and in some due to uniqueness, as well as in accordance with the elegance of the teaching and the suitability of the disciples, reveals only one cause or result. For example, he states, 'With contact as condition, feeling,' revealing only one cause and one result. Here, contact is the prominent cause of feeling, as feeling is established according to contact. Feeling, in turn, is the prominent result of contact, as contact is established according to feeling. In the statement, 'Illnesses arising from phlegm' (Mahāni. 5), due to obviousness, he mentions only one cause. Here, phlegm is obvious, not kamma or other factors. In the statement, 'Monks, whatever unwholesome states there are, they are all rooted in unwise attention,' due to uniqueness, he mentions only one cause. For unwise attention is unique to unwholesome states, whereas other factors like the basis and object are common. Therefore, it should be understood that although other causes for formations exist here, such as basis, object, and co-arisen phenomena, ignorance is shown as the cause of formations due to its prominence—as it is the cause of other causes of formations like craving, as stated in 'For one who dwells contemplating gratification, craving grows' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.52) and 'With the arising of ignorance, the taints arise' (Ma. Ni. 1.104)—and due to its obviousness and uniqueness, as stated in 'Monks, an ignorant person, having gone to ignorance, generates even meritorious formations.' Thus, in all cases of revealing a single cause and result, the method should be applied as is appropriate. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Ekaṃ na ekato idha, nānekamanekatopi no ekaṃ;

Phalamatthi atthi pana eka-hetuphaladīpane attho”ti.

Here, one is not from one, nor many from many, nor one from many; but a result exists, and there is a purpose in the illustration of a single cause and result.

Paccetumarahatīti paṭicco. Yo hi naṃ pacceti abhisameti, tassa accantameva dukkhavūpasamāya saṃvattati. Sammā saha ca uppādetīti samuppādo. Paccayadhammo hi attano phalaṃ uppādento sampuṇṇameva uppādeti, na vikalaṃ. Ye ca dhamme uppādeti, te sabbe saheva uppādeti, na ekekaṃ. Iti paṭicco ca so samuppādo cāti paṭiccasamuppādoti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Vitthāroti paṭiccasamuppādapadavaṇṇanāpapañco. Mayampi taṃ atipapañcabhayā idha na dassayissāma, evaṃ parato vakkhamānampi vitthāraṃ. Anulomapaṭilomanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Svevāti so eva paccayākāro. Purimanayena vā vuttoti “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena vutto paccayākāro. Pavattiyāti saṃsārappavattiyā. Manasi akāsīti yo yo paccayadhammo yassa yassa paccayuppannadhammassa yathā yathā hetupaccayādinā paccayabhāvena paccayo hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ aviparītaṃ aparihāpetvā anavasesato paccavekkhaṇavasena citte akāsīti attho.

Paṭicca means ‘that which is to be realized.’ For whoever realizes and comprehends it, that leads ultimately to the cessation of suffering. Samuppāda means ‘that which arises rightly and together.’ For a causal condition, while producing its own fruit, produces it fully, not incompletely. And whatever phenomena it produces, it produces all together, not one by one. Thus, being both ‘that which is to be realized’ and ‘that which arises rightly and together’—hence ‘dependent origination’—in this way, the meaning should be understood here. ‘Elaboration’ refers to the detailed explanation and expansion of the term ‘dependent origination.’ We too, fearing excessive elaboration, will not present it here. Likewise, the detailed explanation to be given elsewhere should be understood. ‘Forward and reverse’ is an adverbial neuter designation, as in ‘the moon and sun revolve unevenly’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.70) and similar passages. ‘Just that’ means that very mode of conditionality. ‘Or as stated by the previous method’ means the mode of conditionality stated in the way of ‘with ignorance as condition, formations’ and so on. ‘In the course of existence’ means in the cycle of saṃsāra. ‘He placed in mind’ means that whatever causal condition, in whatever way it serves as a condition—whether as root condition, supporting condition, etc.—for whatever causally originated phenomenon, he reflected on all of it without distortion, without omission, and without remainder, placing it fully in his mind. This is the meaning.

Avijjāpaccayātiādīsu (vibha. aṭṭha. 225; visuddhi. 2.586-587; udā. aṭṭha. 1) avindiyaṃ kāyaduccaritādiṃ vindatīti avijjā, vindiyaṃ kāyasucaritādiṃ na vindatīti avijjā, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvaṃ aviditaṃ karotīti avijjā, antavirahite saṃsāre bhavādīsu satte javāpetīti avijjā, avijjamānesu javati, vijjamānesu na javatīti avijjā, vijjāpaṭipakkhāti vā avijjā. Sā “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā catubbidhā veditabbā. Paṭicca naṃ na vinā phalaṃ eti uppajjati ceva pavattati cāti paccayo, upakāraṭṭho vā paccayo. Avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo[M 3.0136], tasmā avijjāpaccayā. Saṅkharontīti saṅkhārā, lokiyā kusalākusalacetanā. Te puññāpuññāneñcābhisaṅkhāravasena tividhā veditabbā. Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ, taṃ lokiyavipākaviññāṇavasena bāttiṃsavidhaṃ. Namatīti nāmaṃ, vedanādikkhandhattayaṃ. Ruppatīti rūpaṃ, bhūtarūpaṃ cakkhādiupādārūpañca. Āyatanti, āyatañca saṃsāradukkhaṃ nayatīti āyatanaṃ[V 3.0126]. Phusatīti phasso. Vedayatīti vedanā. Idampi dvayaṃ dvāravasena chabbidhaṃ, vipākavasena gahaṇe bāttiṃsavidhaṃ. Tassati paritassatīti taṇhā, sā kāmataṇhādivasena saṅkhepato tividhā, vitthārato aṭṭhasatavidhā ca. Upādiyatīti upādānaṃ, taṃ kāmupādānādivasaena catubbidhaṃ.

Regarding 'dependent on ignorance' and so on (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 225; Visuddhimagga 2.586-587; Udāna Aṭṭhakathā 1): Ignorance (avijjā) is that which finds unwholesome bodily conduct, etc.; it is that which does not find wholesome bodily conduct, etc.; it makes the true nature of phenomena unknown; it drives beings in the endless cycle of existence toward becoming, etc.; it rushes toward what does not exist and does not rush toward what exists; or it is the opposite of knowledge. It should be understood as fourfold, beginning with 'ignorance of suffering.' A condition (paccaya) is that without which the result does not come to be, but with which it arises and continues to exist; or it is a condition in the sense of assistance. Ignorance itself is the condition, thus 'dependent on ignorance.' They construct, thus they are volitional formations (saṅkhārā), namely, worldly wholesome and unwholesome volitions. They should be understood as threefold: meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable formations. It cognizes, thus it is consciousness (viññāṇa), which is thirty-twofold as mundane resultant consciousness. It bends, thus it is name (nāma), namely, the three aggregates of feeling, etc. It is afflicted, thus it is form (rūpa), namely, the primary elements and the derived forms such as the eye. They stretch, and they lead to the suffering of the cycle, thus they are sense bases (āyatana). It contacts, thus it is contact (phassa). It feels, thus it is feeling (vedanā). These two are sixfold by way of the doors, and thirty-twofold when taken as resultant. It thirsts and intensely thirsts, thus it is craving (taṇhā), which is briefly threefold as sensual craving, etc., and in detail as one hundred and eight kinds. It clings, thus it is clinging (upādāna), which is fourfold as sensual clinging, etc.

Bhavati bhāvayati cāti bhavo, so kammopapattibhedato duvidho. Jananaṃ jāti. Jīraṇaṃ jarā. Maranti tenāti maraṇaṃ. Socanaṃ soko. Paridevanaṃ paridevo. Dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ. Uppādaṭṭhitivasena dvedhā khanatīti vā dukkhaṃ. Dummanassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Bhuso āyāso upāyāso. Sambhavantīti nibbattanti. Na kevalañca sokādīheva, atha kho sabbapadehi “sambhavantī”ti padassa yojanā kātabbā. Evañhi avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantīti paccayapaccayuppannavavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tenevāha “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantīti iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo”ti. Evametassa…pe… samudayo hotīti ettha pana ayamattho. Evanti niddiṭṭhanayanidassanaṃ. Tena avijjādīheva kāraṇehi, na issaranimmānādīhīti dasseti. Etassāti yathāvuttassa. Kevalassāti asammissassa, sakalassa vā. Dukkhakkhandhassāti dukkhasamūhassa, na sattassa nāpi subhasukhādīnaṃ. Samudayo hotīti nibbatti sambhavati.

It comes to be and causes to be, thus it is becoming (bhava), which is twofold by way of kamma and rebirth. Generation is birth (jāti). Decay is aging (jarā). They die by it, thus it is death (maraṇa). Sorrowing is sorrow (soka). Lamenting is lamentation (parideva). It afflicts, thus it is suffering (dukkha). Or it wears away in two ways, by way of arising and persisting, thus it is suffering. The state of mental distress is dejection (domanassa). Great anxiety is distress (upāyāsa). They come to be, that is, they arise. And the connection of the word 'they come to be' should be made not only with sorrow and the like, but with all terms. For thus, 'with ignorance as condition, formations come to be'—this shows the establishment of conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena. Therefore, it is said: 'With ignorance as condition, formations come to be—in this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.' Now, regarding 'Thus, this… the origin comes to be'—here, this is the meaning. 'Thus' (evaṃ) indicates the method of explanation. By that, it shows that ignorance and the like are the causes, not a creator or the like. 'Of this' (etassa) means as stated. 'Entirely' (kevalassa) means unmixed or complete. 'Of the mass of suffering' (dukkhakkhandhassa) means of the aggregate of suffering, not of a being nor of auspiciousness, pleasure, and the like. 'The origin comes to be' (samudayo hoti) means it arises, it comes into existence.

Accantameva saṅkhārehi virajjati etenāti virāgo, ariyamaggoti āha “virāgasaṅkhātena maggenā”ti. Asesaṃ nirodhā asesanirodhā, asesetvā nissesetvā nirodhā samucchindanā anusayappahānavasena aggamaggena avijjāya accantasamugghātatoti attho. Yadipi heṭṭhimamaggehipi pahīyamānā avijjā accantasamugghātavaseneva pahīyati, tathāpi na anavasesato pahīyati. Apāyagamanīyā hi avijjā paṭhamamaggena pahīyati, tathā sakideva imasmiṃ loke sabbattha ca anariyabhūmiyaṃ upapattiyā paccayabhūtā avijjā yathākkamaṃ dutiyatatiyamaggehi pahīyati, na itarāti, arahattamaggeneva pana sā anavasesaṃ [M 3.0137] pahīyatīti. Anuppādanirodho hotīti sabbesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ anavasesaṃ anuppādanirodho hoti. Heṭṭhimena hi maggattayena keci saṅkhārā nirujjhanti, keci na nirujjhanti avijjāya sāvasesanirodhā, aggamaggena panassā anavasesanirodhā na keci saṅkhārā na nirujjhantīti. Evaṃ niruddhānanti evaṃ anuppādanirodhena niruddhānaṃ. Kevala-saddo niravasesavācako ca hoti “kevalā aṅgamagadhā”tiādīsu. Asammissavācako ca “kevalā sālayo”tiādīsu. Tasmā ubhayathāpi [V 3.0127] atthaṃ vadati “sakalassa, suddhassa vā”ti. Tattha sakalassāti anavasesassa sabbabhavādigatassa. Sattavirahitassāti paraparikappitajīvarahitassa.

One is utterly disenchanted with formations by means of it, thus it is dispassion (virāga). It is the Noble Path, as it is said: 'by the path called dispassion.' Complete cessation (asesanirodha) means cessation without remainder, cutting off entirely, uprooting; the meaning is that ignorance is utterly eradicated by the supreme path by way of abandoning the latent tendencies. Although ignorance, when abandoned even by the lower paths, is abandoned by way of utter eradication, still it is not abandoned without remainder. For ignorance leading to rebirth in the lower realms is abandoned by the first path; likewise, ignorance that is a condition for rebirth in this world and in all non-noble realms is abandoned respectively by the second and third paths, but not the other kinds. However, by the path of arahantship alone is it abandoned without remainder. 'Non-arising cessation occurs' means the non-arising cessation of all formations without remainder. For by the three lower paths, some formations cease, and some do not cease, because ignorance ceases with remainder. But by the supreme path, since ignorance ceases without remainder, no formations fail to cease. 'Thus ceased' (evaṃ niruddhānaṃ) means ceased by such non-arising cessation. The word 'kevala' is used to mean 'without remainder,' as in 'the entire Aṅga and Magadha,' etc., and also to mean 'unmixed,' as in 'only sal trees,' etc. Therefore, it conveys the meaning in both ways: 'whole' or 'pure.' Here, 'whole' (sakalassa) means without remainder, pertaining to all states of existence, etc. 'Devoid of beings' (sattavirahitassa) means free from the living entity imagined and conceived by others.
