Apicettha kiñcāpi “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho”ti ettāvatāpi sakalassa dukkhakkhandhassa anavasesato nirodho vutto hoti, tathāpi yathā anulome yassa yassa paccayadhammassa atthitāya yo yo paccayuppannadhammo na nirujjhati pavattati evāti imassa atthassa dassanatthaṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… samudayo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ tappaṭipakkhato tassa tassa paccayassa abhāve so so paccayuppannadhammo nirujjhati na pavattatīti dassanatthaṃ idha “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho, viññāṇanirodhā nāmarūpanirodho…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti vuttaṃ, na pana anulome viya kālattayapariyāpannassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodhadassanatthaṃ. Anāgatasseva hi ariyamaggabhāvanāya asati uppajjanārahassa dukkhakkhandhassa ariyamaggabhāvanāya nirodho icchitoti ayampi viseso veditabbo.

Moreover, here, although by the statement, ‘With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness,’ the cessation of the entire mass of suffering without remainder is stated, nevertheless, just as in the forward order it is said, ‘With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations… this is the origin,’ to show that due to the existence of a particular conditional phenomenon, a particular conditioned phenomenon does not cease but continues to occur, so too, in the opposite way, it is said here, ‘With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations… this is the cessation of the mass of suffering,’ to show that in the absence of that particular condition, that particular conditioned phenomenon ceases and does not continue to occur. This, however, is not for the purpose of showing the cessation of the mass of suffering pertaining to the three periods of time, as in the forward order. For the cessation intended through the development of the noble path is only of the future mass of suffering, which is liable to arise when the noble path is not developed. This distinction should also be understood.

Yadā haveti ettha haveti byattanti imasmiṃ atthe nipāto. Keci pana “haveti āhave yuddhe”ti atthaṃ vadanti, “yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhenā”ti (dha. pa. 40) hi vacanato kilesamārena yujjhanasamayeti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Ārammaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇenāti ārammaṇūpanijjhānasabhāvena. Lakkhaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇenāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tattha ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṃ nāma aṭṭha samāpattiyo kasiṇārammaṇassa upanijjhāyanato. Lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ nāma vipassanāmaggaphalāni. Vipassanā hi tīṇi lakkhaṇāni upanijjhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ, maggo [M 3.0138] vipassanāya āgatakiccaṃ sādhetīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ, phalaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ upanijjhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. No kallo pañhoti ayutto pañho, duppañho esoti attho. Ādisaddena –

Regarding 'yadā haveti,' here 'haveti' is a particle in the sense of 'manifest.' Some, however, say that 'haveti' means 'in battle, in war,' their intention being that it refers to the time of battling with the Māra of defilements, according to the saying, 'Fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom' (Dhp 40). 'By the characteristic of contemplating the object' means by the nature of contemplating the object. 'By the characteristic of contemplating the characteristics'—here too, the same method applies. Herein, 'contemplating the object' refers to the eight attainments, due to their contemplating the kasiṇa object. 'Contemplating the characteristics' refers to insight, the path, and the fruits. For insight contemplates the three characteristics, thus it is 'contemplating the characteristics.' The path accomplishes the task brought about by insight, thus it is 'contemplating the characteristics.' The fruit contemplates the truth of cessation, which has such a characteristic, thus it is 'contemplating the characteristics.' 'Not a fitting question' means an unsuitable question; the meaning is, 'This is an ill-posed question.' By the word 'ādi' (etc.) is meant:

“Phusatīti ahaṃ na vadāmi. Phusatīti cāhaṃ vadeyyaṃ, tatrassa kallo pañho ‘ko nu kho, bhante, phusatī’ti? Evañcāhaṃ na vadāmi, evaṃ maṃ avadantaṃ yo evaṃ puccheyya ‘kiṃpaccayā nu kho, bhante, phasso’ti, esa kallo pañho. Tatra kallaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ ‘saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā’ti. Ko nu kho, bhante, vedayatīti? No kallo pañhoti bhagavā avoca, vedayatīti ahaṃ na vadāmi, vedayatīti cāhaṃ vadeyyaṃ, tatrassa kallo pañho ‘ko nu kho, bhante, vedayatī’ti? Evañcāhaṃ [V 3.0128] na vadāmi. Evaṃ maṃ avadantaṃ yo evaṃ puccheyya ‘kiṃpaccayā nu kho, bhante, vedanā’ti, esa kallo pañho. Tatra kallaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ ‘phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā’”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.12) –

‘I do not say, “One makes contact.” If I were to say, “One makes contact,” then it would be a fitting question to ask, “Who, venerable sir, makes contact?” But I do not say that. Since I do not say that, if someone were to ask me, “With what as condition, venerable sir, is there contact?”—that is a fitting question. To that, the fitting explanation is: “With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling.”’ ‘Who, venerable sir, feels?’ ‘That is not a fitting question,’ the Blessed One said. ‘I do not say, “One feels.” If I were to say, “One feels,” then it would be a fitting question to ask, “Who, venerable sir, feels?” But I do not say that. Since I do not say that, if someone were to ask me, “With what as condition, venerable sir, is there feeling?”—that is a fitting question. To that, the fitting explanation is: “With contact as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving.”’ (SN 2.12)

Evamādiṃ pāḷisesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Thus, it includes the remainder of the Pāli text.

Ādinā ca nayenāti ettha ādi-saddena pana “katamā nu kho, bhante, jāti, kassa ca panāyaṃ jātīti. ‘No kallo pañho’ti bhagavā avocā”ti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Nanu cettha “katamaṃ nu kho, bhante, jarāmaraṇa”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.35) idaṃ supucchitanti? Kiñcāpi supucchitaṃ, yathā pana satasahassagghanake suvaṇṇathālake vaḍḍhitassa subhojanassa matthake āmalakamatte gūthapiṇḍe ṭhapite sabbaṃ bhojanaṃ dubbhojanaṃ hoti chaḍḍetabbaṃ, evameva “kassa ca panidaṃ jarāmaraṇa”nti iminā sattūpaladdhivādapadena gūthapiṇḍena taṃ bhojanaṃ dubbhojanaṃ viya ayampi sabbo duppañho jātoti.

Regarding 'And by the initial method': here, by the word 'ādi' (etc.) is included such as: ‘“But, venerable sir, what is birth, and to whom does this birth belong?” “That is not a fitting question,” the Blessed One said.’ But is not the question, ‘What, venerable sir, is aging-and-death?’ (SN 2.35) well-asked here? Although it is well-asked, just as when a lump of excrement the size of a myrobalan fruit is placed on top of excellent food served on a golden platter worth a hundred thousand, all the food becomes unfit to eat and must be thrown away, so too, because of this lump of excrement which is the phrase based on the view of apprehending a being—namely, ‘And to whom does this aging-and-death belong?’—this entire question, like that food, has become ill-posed.

Soḷasa kaṅkhāti “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho ahosiṃ, kiṃ nu kho ahosiṃ, kathaṃ nu kho ahosiṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho bhavissāmi, kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmi, kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmi, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, ahaṃ [M 3.0139] nu khosmi, no nu khosmi, kiṃ nu khosmi, kathaṃ nu khosmi, ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.20; ma. ni. 1.18) evamāgatā atītānāgatapaccuppannavisayā soḷasavidhā kaṅkhā.

The sixteen doubts are: “Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?” And now in the present: “Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? This being, from where has it come? Where will it go?” Thus are the sixteen kinds of doubt concerning the past, future, and present set forth. (SN 2.20; MN 1.18)

Tattha (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.18; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.20) ahosiṃ nu kho, na nu khoti sassatākārañca adhiccasamuppattiākārañca nissāya atīte attano vijjamānatañca avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati, kiṃ kāraṇanti na vattabbaṃ. Ummattako viya hi bālaputhujjano yathā tathā vā pavattati. Apica ayonisomanasikāroyevettha kāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ ayonisomanasikārassa pana kiṃ kāraṇanti? Sveva puthujjanabhāvo ariyānaṃ adassanādīni vā. Nanu ca puthujjanopi yoniso manasi karotīti. Ko vā evamāha “na manasi karotī”ti. Na pana tattha puthujjanabhāvo kāraṇaṃ, saddhammasavanakalyāṇamittādīni tattha kāraṇāni[V 3.0129]. Na hi macchamaṃsādīni attano pakatiyā sugandhāni, abhisaṅkhārapaccayā pana sugandhānipi honti.

Therein (MA 1.18; SA 2.2.20), regarding ‘Was I? Was I not?,’ one doubts about one’s own existence and non-existence in the past, relying on the mode of eternalism and the mode of accidental origination. It should not be asked, ‘What is the cause?’ For the foolish worldling behaves this way and that, like a madman. Moreover, unwise attention is indeed the cause here. But what is the cause for such unwise attention? It is that very state of being a worldling, or not seeing the noble ones, and so on. ‘But does not a worldling also attend wisely?’ Who says, ‘He does not attend wisely’? But in that case, the state of being a worldling is not the cause; the causes there are listening to the good Dhamma, spiritual friends, and so on. For fish, meat, and the like are not fragrant by their own nature, but through the condition of preparation, they can become fragrant.

Kiṃ nu kho ahosinti jātiliṅgupapattiyo nissāya “khattiyo nu kho ahosiṃ, brāhmaṇavessasuddagahaṭṭhapabbajitadevamanussānaṃ aññataro”ti kaṅkhati.

Regarding ‘What was I?,’ relying on birth, characteristics, and rebirths, one doubts: 'Was I a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, a sudda, a householder, a renunciant, or one among devas or humans?'

Kathaṃ nu khoti saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya “dīgho nu kho ahosiṃ, rassaodātakaṇhappamāṇikaappamāṇikādīnaṃ aññataro”ti kaṅkhati. Keci pana “issaranimmānādiṃ nissāya ‘kena nu kho kāraṇena ahosi’nti hetuto kaṅkhatī”ti vadanti.

Regarding ‘How was I?,’ relying on the mode of bodily configuration, one doubts: 'Was I tall, short, fair, dark, of limited measure, or immeasurable, or one of these?' But some say: 'Relying on creation by a lord, etc., one doubts about the cause, thinking, “By what cause was I?”'

Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosinti jātiādīni nissāya “khattiyo hutvā nu kho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ…pe… devo hutvā manusso”ti attano paramparaṃ kaṅkhati. Sabbattheva pana addhānanti kālādhivacanametaṃ, tañca bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding ‘Having been what, what was I?,’ relying on birth, etc., one doubts one's own succession: 'Having been a khattiya, did I become a brahmin... or having been a deva, a human?' But everywhere, 'addhāna' is a term denoting time, and it should be understood as a word used in the locative sense.

Bhavissāmi nu kho, na nu khoti sassatākārañca ucchedākārañca nissāya anāgate attano vijjamānatañca avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

Regarding ‘Shall I be? Shall I not be?,’ relying on the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilationism, one doubts one's own existence and non-existence in the future. The rest here is just as has been stated.

Ahaṃ [M 3.0140] nu khosmīti attano atthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Yuttaṃ panetanti? Yuttaṃ ayuttanti kā ettha cintā. Apicettha idaṃ vatthumpi udāharanti, cūḷamātāya kira putto muṇḍo, mahāmātāya putto amuṇḍo. Taṃ suttaṃ muṇḍesuṃ. So uṭṭhāya “ahaṃ nu kho cūḷamātāya putto”ti cintesi. Evaṃ “ahaṃ nu khosmī”ti kaṅkhā hoti.

Am I? One doubts one's own existence. But is this fitting? What thought is there here about whether it is fitting or unfitting? Moreover, they also cite this story here: Cūḷamātā's son, it is said, was bald, while Mahāmātā's son was not bald. They shaved him while he was asleep. He got up and thought, 'Am I Cūḷamātā's son?' Thus, the doubt 'Am I?' arises.

No nu khosmīti attano natthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Tatrāpi idaṃ vatthu – eko kira macche gaṇhanto udake ciraṭṭhānena sītibhūtaṃ attano ūruṃ “maccho”ti cintetvā pahari. Aparo susānapasse khettaṃ rakkhanto bhīto saṅkuṭito sayi. So paṭibujjhitvā attano jaṇṇukāni “dve yakkhā”ti cintetvā pahari, evaṃ “no nu khosmī”ti kaṅkhati.

Am I not? One doubts one's own non-existence. Here too is this story: A man, it is said, while catching fish, struck his own thigh, which had become chilled from standing long in the water, thinking, 'It is a fish.' Another, guarding a field near a charnel ground, lay down frightened and curled up. Awakening, he struck his own knees, thinking, 'They are two demons.' Thus, one doubts, 'Am I not?'

Kiṃ nu khosmīti khattiyova samāno attano khattiyabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati kaṇṇo viya sūtaputtasaññī. Esa nayo sesesu. Devo pana samāno devabhāvaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi. Sopi pana “ahaṃ rūpī nu kho arūpī nu kho”tiādinā nayena kaṅkhati. Khattiyādayo kasmā [V 3.0130] na jānantīti ce? Appaccakkhā tesaṃ tattha tattha kule uppatti. Gahaṭṭhāpi ca pātalikādayo pabbajitasaññino. Pabbajitāpi “kuppaṃ nu kho me kamma”ntiādinā nayena gahaṭṭhasaññino. Manussāpi ca ekacce rājāno viya attani devasaññino honti.

What am I? Being a khattiya, one doubts one's own khattiya-nature, like Kaṇṇa, who thought himself the son of a charioteer. The same applies to the others. But there is no god who, being a god, does not know his divine nature. Yet he too doubts according to the method, 'Am I with form or without form?' etc. If it is asked, 'Why do khattiyas and others not know?'—their birth in those respective families is not directly perceived. And householders, like Pāṭalika and others, may think themselves renunciants; while renunciants may think themselves householders, wondering, 'Is my action subject to corruption?' etc. And some humans, like certain kings, consider themselves gods.

Kathaṃ nu khosmīti vuttanayameva. Kevalañhettha abbhantare jīvo nāma atthīti gahetvā tassa saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya “dīgho nu khosmi, rassacaturassachaḷaṃsaaṭṭhaṃsasoḷasaṃsādīnaṃ aññatarappakāro”ti kaṅkhanto “kathaṃ nu khosmī”ti kaṅkhatīti veditabbo. Sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ pana paccuppannaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi.

How am I? This is just as stated. Only here, taking hold of the idea that there is an inner living principle, relying on its mode of bodily configuration, one doubts: 'Am I long, short, square, six-sided, eight-sided, sixteen-sided, or of some other kind?' Thus, it should be understood that one doubts 'How am I?' But there is no one who does not know the present bodily configuration.

Kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti attabhāvassa āgatigatiṭṭhānaṃ kaṅkhati.

From where has this being come? Where will it go? One doubts the origin, destination, and state of one's existence.

Vapayantīti viapayanti, ikāralopenāyaṃ niddeso. Byapayantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “vapayanti apagacchantī”ti. Apagamanañca anuppattinirodhavasenāti āha “nirujjhantī”ti.

'Vapayanti' means 'vi-apayanti'; this is a designation by way of the elision of the 'i' sound. The meaning is 'byapayanti'. Therefore, it is said, 'Vapayanti means departing, vanishing.' And departing is in the sense of cessation by way of non-recurrence; therefore, it is said, 'They cease.'

3. Kadā [M 3.0141] panassa bodhipakkhiyadhammā catusaccadhammā vā pātubhavanti uppajjanti pakāsantīti? Vipassanāmaggañāṇesu pavattamānesu. Tattha vipassanāñāṇe tāva vipassanāñāṇasampayuttā satiādayo vipassanāñāṇañca yathārahaṃ attano attano visayesu tadaṅgappahānavasena subhasaññādike pajahantā kāyānupassanādivasena visuṃ visuṃ uppajjanti. Maggakkhaṇe pana te nibbānamālambitvā samucchedavasena paṭipakkhe pajahantā catūsupi ariyasaccesu asammohapaṭivedhasādhanavasena sakideva uppajjanti. Evaṃ tāvettha bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ uppajjanaṭṭhena pātubhāvo veditabbo. Ariyasaccadhammānaṃ pana lokiyānaṃ vipassanākkhaṇe vipassanāya ārammaṇakaraṇavasena lokuttarānaṃ tadadhimuttatāvasena maggakkhaṇe nirodhasaccassa ārammaṇābhisamayavasena sabbesampi kiccābhisamayavasena pākaṭabhāvato pakāsanaṭṭhena pātubhāvo veditabbo.

3. But when do the factors of enlightenment or the four noble truths become manifest, arise, and appear? When insight knowledges and path knowledge are progressing. There, in insight knowledge, mindfulness and other factors associated with insight knowledge, as well as insight knowledge itself, arise separately, each in their respective domains, abandoning perceptions of beauty and the like by way of abandonment by substitution of opposites, by way of contemplation of the body, etc. At the moment of the path, however, those factors, taking Nibbāna as their object, abandon the opposing factors through eradication and arise all at once, by way of the accomplishment of penetration without confusion into all four noble truths. Thus, the manifestation of the enlightenment factors should be understood here in terms of their arising. As for the four noble truths, the mundane ones become manifest at the moment of insight by serving as objects for insight; the supramundane ones become manifest at the moment of the path by way of their being resolved upon that Nibbāna and by way of the direct comprehension of the truth of cessation as an object; and for all of them, by way of the direct comprehension of their functions, their manifestation should be understood as their becoming evident.

Iti bhagavā satipi sabbākārena sabbadhammānaṃ attano ñāṇassa pākaṭabhāve paṭiccasamuppādamukhena vipassanābhinivesassa katattā nipuṇagambhīrasududdasatāya paccayākārassa taṃ paccavekkhitvā uppannabalavasomanasso paṭipakkhasamucchedavibhāvanena saddhiṃ attano tadabhisamayānubhāvadīpakamevettha udānaṃ udānesi.

Thus, even though the Blessed One's knowledge of all phenomena was fully manifest in every respect, because he had established a strong dedication to insight meditation by way of dependent origination, and having reflected on that mode of conditions, which is subtle, profound, and extremely difficult to see, strong joy arose in him. Together with the manifestation of the destruction of opposing forces, he uttered here this inspired utterance, illuminating the power of his own realization.

“Kāmā [V 3.0131] te paṭhamā senā”tiādinā nayena vuttappakāraṃ mārasenanti –

The army of Māra, described in the manner beginning with 'Desires are your first army'—

“Kāmā te paṭhamā senā, dutiyā arati vuccati;

Tatiyā khuppipāsā te, catutthī taṇhā pavuccati.

"Desires are your first army, the second is called discontent; your third is hunger and thirst, the fourth is called craving.

“Pañcamī thinamiddhaṃ te, chaṭṭhā bhīrū pavuccati;

Sattamī vicikicchā te, makkho thambho ca aṭṭhamā.

"Fifth is sloth and torpor, the sixth is called cowardice; your seventh is doubt, and the eighth is hypocrisy and obstinacy."

“Lābho siloko sakkāro, micchāladdho ca yo yaso;

Yo cattānaṃ samukkaṃse, pare ca avajānati.

"Gain, fame, honor, and whatever ill-gotten renown; whoever exalts himself and disparages others—

“Esā [M 3.0142] namuci te senā, kaṇhassābhippahārinī;

Na naṃ asūro jināti, jetvā ca labhate sukha”nti. (su. ni. 438-441; mahāni. 28) –

"This, Namuci, is your army, the Dark One's assailing host; no non-hero conquers it, but having conquered, one gains bliss."

Iminā nayena vuttappakāraṃ mārasenaṃ.

The army of Māra, described in this manner.

Tattha (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.439-41; mahāni. aṭṭha. 28) yasmā āditova agāriyabhūte satte vatthukāmesu kilesakāmā mohayanti, te abhibhuyya anagāriyabhāvaṃ upagatānaṃ pantesu vā senāsanesu aññataraññataresu vā adhikusalesu dhammesu arati uppajjati. Vuttampi cetaṃ “pabbajitena kho, āvuso, abhirati dukkarā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.331). Tato te parapaṭibaddhajīvikattā khuppipāsā bādhati, tāya bādhitānaṃ pariyesana taṇhā cittaṃ kilamayati, atha nesaṃ kilantacittānaṃ thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, tato visesamanadhigacchantānaṃ durabhisambhavesu araññavanapatthesu senāsanesu viharataṃ utrāsasaññitā bhīru jāyati, tesaṃ ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitānaṃ dīgharattaṃ vivekarasamanassādayamānānaṃ viharataṃ “na siyā nu kho esa maggo”ti paṭipattiyaṃ vicikicchā uppajjati, taṃ vinodetvā viharataṃ appamattakena visesādhigamena mānamakkhathambhā jāyanti, tepi vinodetvā viharataṃ tato adhikataraṃ visesādhigamaṃ nissāya lābhasakkārasilokā uppajjanti, lābhādimucchitā dhammapatirūpakāni pakāsentā micchāyasaṃ adhigantvā tattha ṭhitā jātiādīhi attānaṃ ukkaṃsenti paraṃ vambhenti, tasmā kāmādīnaṃ paṭhamasenādibhāvo veditabbo.

Here, because from the very beginning, defilement-sensual pleasures delude beings who are in household life regarding material sensual pleasures. Having overcome these, discontent arises in those who have entered the homeless life, in remote lodgings or in various lodgings, or regarding certain higher wholesome qualities. And it has been said: 'Friend, for one gone forth, contentment is hard to achieve.' Then, because their livelihood depends on others, hunger and thirst afflict them. Afflicted by these, craving for seeking wearies the mind. Then, sloth and torpor overcome those whose minds are weary. Failing to attain distinction, dwelling in forest and woodland lodgings that are difficult to access, fear, called terror, arises in them. Being suspicious and apprehensive for a long time, and not experiencing the taste of seclusion, doubt arises in them regarding their practice: 'Could this be the correct path?' Having dispelled this, when dwelling with a slight attainment of distinction, conceit, hypocrisy, and obstinacy arise. Having dispelled these too, when dwelling based on a greater attainment of distinction, gain, honor, and praise arise. Infatuated with gain and the like, displaying semblances of the Dhamma, they achieve wrong reputation and, remaining there, praise themselves due to birth and other qualities while disparaging others. Therefore, it should be understood that sensual pleasures and the like are the first division of the army of Māra.

Evametaṃ [V 3.0132] dasavidhaṃ senaṃ uddisitvā yasmā sā kaṇhadhammasamannāgatattā kaṇhassa namucino upakārāya saṃvattati, tasmā naṃ “tava senā”ti niddisantena “esā namuci te senā, kaṇhassābhippahārinī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha abhippahārinīti samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ghātanī nippothanī, antarāyakarīti attho. Na naṃ asūro jināti, jetvā ca labhate sukhanti evaṃ tava senaṃ asūro kāye ca jīvite ca sāpekkho puriso na jināti, sūro pana jināti, jetvā ca maggasukhaṃ phalasukhañca adhigacchatīti attho. Sopi brāhmaṇoti sopi khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo.

Having thus described this tenfold army, because it is endowed with dark qualities and conduces to the benefit of the dark one, Namuci, therefore, when indicating it as 'your army', it is said: 'This, Namuci, is your army, assailing on behalf of the Dark One.' Here, 'assailing' means it is a slayer and destroyer of ascetics and brahmins, causing obstruction. 'No non-hero conquers it, but having conquered, one attains happiness'—thus, a person attached to body and life, being a non-hero, does not conquer your army. But the hero conquers it, and having conquered, attains the happiness of the path and the happiness of the fruit—this is the meaning. 'Even he is a brahmin'—that is, he is the brahmin whose defilements are destroyed.

Idāni [M 3.0143] “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinno hoti vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedī. Atha kho bhagavā tassa sattāhassa accayena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ anulomaṃ sādhukaṃ manasākāsi. Rattiyā majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ paṭilomaṃ sādhukaṃ manasākāsi. Rattiyā pacchimaṃ yāmaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ sādhukaṃ manasākāsī”ti evaṃ vuttāya udānapāḷiyā (udā. 1) imissā ca khandhakapāḷiyā avirodhaṃ dassetuṃ “udāne panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Ettha tassa vasenāti tassa paccayākārapajānanassa paccayakkhayādhigamassa ca vasena. Ekekameva koṭṭhāsanti anulomapaṭilomesu ekekameva koṭṭhāsaṃ. Pāṭipadarattiyā evaṃ manasākāsīti rattiyā tīsupi yāmesu anulomapaṭilomaṃyeva manasākāsi. Bhagavā kira ṭhapetvā ratanagharasattāhaṃ sesesu chasu sattāhesu antarantarā dhammaṃ paccavekkhitvā yebhuyyena vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedī vihāsi, ratanagharasattāhe pana abhidhammapavicayavaseneva vihāsi. Tasmā antarantarā dhammapaccavekkhaṇavasena uppāditamanasikāresu pāṭipadarattiyā uppāditaṃ manasikāraṃ sandhāya imissaṃ khandhakapāḷiyaṃ evaṃ vuttanti adhippāyo.

Now, to show that there is no contradiction between the Udāna passage (Ud. 1)—'At that time, the Blessed One sat for seven days in one cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation. Then, at the end of those seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and thoroughly contemplated dependent origination in forward order during the first watch of the night. During the middle watch of the night, he thoroughly contemplated dependent origination in reverse order. During the last watch of the night, he thoroughly contemplated dependent origination in both forward and reverse order'—and this Khandhaka passage, the phrase 'but in the Udāna' and so on is introduced. Here, 'by means of that' refers to that understanding of the mode of conditions and the attainment of the destruction of conditions. 'Each section separately' means each section in the forward and reverse orders. 'He contemplated thus on the night of the first day' means that he contemplated dependent origination in both forward and reverse order during all three watches of that night. It is said that the Blessed One, except for the seven days at the Jeweled House, spent most of the other six weeks experiencing the bliss of liberation, occasionally reflecting on the Dhamma in between. However, during the seven days at the Jeweled House, he dwelt primarily engaged in the analysis of the Abhidhamma. Therefore, the intention in this Khandhaka passage is to refer to the attention aroused by reflecting on the Dhamma intermittently, specifically the attention aroused on the night of the first day.

Bodhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bodhi Story is concluded.

Ajapālakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Ajapāla Story

4. Tassa sattāhassa accayenāti pallaṅkasattāhassa apagamanena. Tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvāti tato arahattaphalasamāpattisamādhito yathākālaparicchedaṃ vuṭṭhahitvā. Aññepi buddhattakarāti visākhapuṇṇamito paṭṭhāya rattindivaṃ evaṃ niccasamāhitabhāvahetubhūtānaṃ buddhaguṇānaṃ upari aññepi buddhattasādhakā. “Ayaṃ buddho”ti buddhabhāvassa paresaṃ vibhāvanā dhammā kiṃ nu kho santīti yojanā. Ekaccānaṃ devatānanti yā adhigatamaggā sacchikatanirodhā ekapadesena [V 3.0133] buddhaguṇe jānanti, tā ṭhapetvā tadaññāsaṃ devatānaṃ. Animisehīti dhammapītivipphāravasena [M 3.0144] pasādavibhāvaniccaladalatāya nimesarahitehi. Ratanacaṅkameti devatāhi māpite ratanamayacaṅkame. “Ratanabhūtānaṃ sattannaṃ pakaraṇānaṃ tattha ca anuttarassa dhammaratanassa sammasanena taṃ ṭhānaṃ ratanagharacetiyaṃ nāma jāta”ntipi vadanti. Teneva aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) “ratanagharaṃ nāma na ratanamayaṃ gehaṃ, sattannaṃ pana pakaraṇānaṃ sammasitaṭṭhānaṃ ratanagharanti veditabba”nti vuttaṃ.

4. 'After seven days had passed' means after the ending of the seven days of sitting cross-legged. 'Having emerged from that concentration' means having risen from that concentration, the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, at the determined time. The phrase 'and other qualities that make one a Buddha' is to be construed as the question of whether there are other qualities—beyond the Buddha's qualities that are the cause of his constant concentration day and night since the Visākhā full moon—that establish his Buddhahood and reveal it to others, so they think, 'This is the Buddha.' 'Some deities' refers to those deities other than the ones who have attained the path, realized cessation, and know the Buddha's qualities in part. 'With unblinking eyes' means with eyes that do not blink, due to the unwavering state of their pupils, which reveals their delight, owing to the diffusion of joy in the Dhamma. 'The jeweled walk' refers to the jeweled walk created by the deities. They also say: 'Because of the reflection on the seven jewel-like treatises there, and especially on the unsurpassed Dhamma-jewel, that place became known as the Jeweled House Shrine.' Therefore, in the Aṭṭhasālinī (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary, Nidānakathā), it is stated: 'The Jeweled House is not a house made of jewels, but the place where the seven treatises are reflected upon should be understood as the Jeweled House.'

Kasmā panāyaṃ ajapālanigrodho nāma jātoti āha “tassa kirā”tiādi. Keci pana “yasmā tattha vede sajjhāyituṃ asamatthā mahallakabrāhmaṇā pākāraparikkhepayuttāni nivesanāni katvā sabbe vasiṃsu, tasmāssa ‘ajapālanigrodho’ti nāmaṃ jāta”nti vadanti. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – na japantīti ajapā, mantānaṃ anajjhāyakāti attho. Ajapā lanti ādiyanti nivāsaṃ etthāti ajapāloti. Apare pana vadanti “yasmā majjhanhike samaye anto paviṭṭhe aje attano chāyāya pāleti rakkhati, tasmā ‘ajapālo’tissa nāmaṃ ruḷha”nti. Sabbathāpi nāmametaṃ tassa rukkhassa.

To the question, 'Why is this called the Ajapāla banyan tree?' the answer begins, 'It is said that...' and so on. Some, however, say: 'Because elderly brahmins, unable to recite the Vedas, built dwellings enclosed by walls and all lived there, it was named the “Ajapāla banyan tree.”' Herein, this is the etymology: 'They do not chant' (na japanti), thus they are 'non-chanters' (ajapā); the meaning is 'non-reciters of mantras.' The non-chanters (ajapā) take up (lanti) residence here, thus it is 'Ajapāla.' Others, however, say: 'Because at midday it protects with its shade the goats that have come under it, therefore the name “Goatherd” (Ajapālo) became established for it.' In any case, this is the name of that tree.

Vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentoti dhammaṃ vicinantoyeva antarantarā vimuttisukhañca paṭisaṃvedento. “Dhammaṃ vicinanto vimuttisukhañca paṭisaṃvedento”ti evaṃ vā ettha pāṭho gahetabbo. Udānaṭṭhakathāyampi (udā. aṭṭha. 4) hi ayameva pāṭho. Dhammaṃ vicinanto cettha evaṃ abhidhamme nayamaggaṃ sammasi paṭhamaṃ dhammasaṅgaṇīpakaraṇaṃ nāma, tato vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ, dhātukathāpakaraṇaṃ, puggalapaññattippakaraṇaṃ, kathāvatthuṃ nāma, yamakaṃ nāma, tato mahāpakaraṇaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti. Tatthassa saṇhasukhumaṭṭhānamhi citte otiṇṇe pīti uppajji, pītiyā uppannāya lohitaṃ pasīdi, lohite pasanne chavi pasīdi, chaviyā pasannāya puratthimakāyato kūṭāgārādippamāṇā rasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā ākāse pakkhandaṃ chaddantanāgakulaṃ viya pācīnadisāya anantāni cakkavāḷāni pakkhandā. Pacchimakāyato uṭṭhahitvā pacchimadisāya, dakkhiṇaṃsakūṭato uṭṭhahitvā dakkhiṇadisāya, vāmaṃsakūṭato uṭṭhahitvā uttaradisāya anantāni cakkavāḷāni pakkhandā. Pādatalehi [M 3.0145] pavāḷaṅkuravaṇṇā rasmiyo nikkhamitvā mahāpathaviṃ vinibbijjha udakaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā vātakkhandhaṃ padāletvā ajaṭākāsaṃ pakkhandā. Sīsato saṃparivattiyamānaṃ maṇidāmaṃ viya nīlavaṇṇarasmivaṭṭi uṭṭhahitvā cha devaloke vinivijjhitvā nava brahmaloke atikkamma ajaṭākāsaṃ pakkhandā. Tasmiṃ divase aparimāṇesu cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇā sattā sabbe suvaṇṇavaṇṇāva ahesuṃ. Taṃ divasañca pana bhagavato sarīrā nikkhantā [V 3.0134] yāvajjadivasāpi kira tā rasmiyo anantalokadhātuyo gacchantiyeva. Na kevalañca imasmiṃyeva sattāhe dhammaṃ vicinantassa sarīrato rasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu, atha kho ratanagharasattāhepi paṭṭhānaṃ sammasantassa evameva sarīrato rasmiyo nikkhantā evāti veditabbaṃ.

'Experiencing the bliss of liberation' means experiencing the bliss of liberation intermittently while investigating the Dhamma. Or this reading should be adopted here: 'Investigating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation,' for this very reading is also found in the Udāna Commentary (Ud.A. 4). Here, 'investigating the Dhamma' refers to comprehending in this way the method of the Abhidhamma path, beginning first with the Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, then the Vibhaṅga treatise, the Dhātukathā treatise, the Puggalapaññatti treatise, the Kathāvatthu treatise, the Yamaka treatise, and finally the great treatise, the Paṭṭhāna. At that time, when his mind was immersed in the subtle and refined state, joy arose in him. With the arising of joy, his blood became clear. With the clarity of blood, his skin became radiant. With the radiance of his skin, beams of light, the size of a gabled house, arose from the front of his body and leapt into the sky, like a herd of Chaddanta elephants rushing forth, and pervaded the infinite world-systems in the eastern direction. From the back of his body, they arose and pervaded the western direction. From his right shoulder-blade, they arose and pervaded the southern direction. From his left shoulder-blade, they arose and pervaded the northern direction with infinite world-systems. From the soles of his feet, rays the color of coral sprouts emerged, piercing the great earth, splitting the water in two, shattering the mass of wind, and leaping into the unobstructed sky. From his head, a circle of blue rays, like a revolving wreath of jewels, arose, piercing the six celestial worlds, surpassing the nine Brahmā worlds, and leaping into the unobstructed sky. On that day, in countless world-systems, countless beings all appeared golden in color. And it is said that the rays that emerged from the Blessed One’s body on that day continue to travel through infinite world-systems even to this very day. Not only during this week did rays emerge from his body while he was investigating the Dhamma, but it should be understood that also during the week in the Jeweled House, while he was comprehending the Paṭṭhāna, rays emerged from his body in the very same way.

Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) –

For this has been said in the Aṭṭhasālinī (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary, Nidānakathā):

“Imesu ca ekavīsatiyā divasesu ekadivasepi satthu sarīrato rasmiyo na nikkhantā, catutthe pana sattāhe pacchimuttarāya disāya ratanaghare nisīdi. Tattha dhammasaṅgaṇiṃ sammasantassapi sarīrato rasmiyo na nikkhantā. Vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ, dhātukathaṃ, puggalapaññattiṃ, kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ, yamakappakaraṇaṃ sammasantassapi rasmiyo na nikkhantā. Yadā pana mahāpakaraṇaṃ oruyha ‘hetupaccayo ārammaṇapaccayo…pe… avigatapaccayo’ti sammasanaṃ ārabhi, athassa catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānaṃ sammasantassa ekantato sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ mahāpakaraṇe okāsaṃ labhi. Yathā hi timirapiṅgalamahāmaccho caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīre mahāsamuddeyeva okāsaṃ labhati, evameva sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ekantato mahāpakaraṇeyeva okāsaṃ labhi.

“During these twenty-one days, not even on a single day did rays emerge from the Teacher’s body. However, in the fourth week, he sat in the jeweled house in the northwest direction. Even while contemplating the Dhammasaṅgaṇī there, no rays emerged from his body. Similarly, while reflecting on the Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, and Yamaka, no rays emerged. But when he descended into the Great Treatise and began contemplating, ‘The condition of root, the condition of object… up to the condition of non-disappearance,’ then, as he contemplated the twenty-four universal conditions of the Paṭṭhāna, the knowledge of omniscience unequivocally found its opportunity in the Great Treatise. Just as the great Timirapiṅgala fish finds its opportunity only in the great ocean eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, so too did the knowledge of omniscience unequivocally find its opportunity exclusively in the Great Treatise.”

“Satthu evaṃ laddhokāsena sabbaññutaññāṇena yathāsukhaṃ saṇhasukhumadhammaṃ sammasantassa sarīrato nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassaravasena chabbaṇṇarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu. Kesamassūhi ceva akkhīnañca nīlaṭṭhānehi nīlarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu, yāsaṃ vasena gaganatalaṃ añjanacuṇṇasamokiṇṇaṃ viya umāpupphanīluppaladalasañchannaṃ viya vītipatantamaṇitālavaṇṭaṃ viya sampasāritamecakapaṭaṃ [M 3.0146] viya ca ahosi. Chavito ceva akkhīnañca pītaṭṭhānehi pītarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu, yāsaṃ vasena disābhāgā suvaṇṇarasanisiñcamānā viya suvaṇṇapaṭapasāritā viya kuṅkumacuṇṇakaṇikārapupphasamparikiṇṇā viya ca virociṃsu. Maṃsalohitehi ceva akkhīnañca rattaṭṭhānehi lohitarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu, yāsaṃ vasena disābhāgā cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇarañjitā viya supakkalākhārasanisiñcamānā viya rattakambalaparikkhittā viya jayasumanapāribaddhakabandhujīvakakusumasamparikiṇṇā viya ca virociṃsu. Aṭṭhīhi ceva dantehi ca akkhīnañca setaṭṭhānehi odātarasmiyo nikkhamiṃsu, yāsaṃ vasena disābhāgā rajatakuṭehi āsiñcamānakhīradhārāsamparikiṇṇā viya pasāritarajatapaṭavitānā viya vītipatantarajatatālavaṇṭā [V 3.0135] viya kundakumudasindhuvārasumanamallikādikusumasañchannā viya ca virociṃsu. Mañjiṭṭhapabhassarā pana tamhā tamhā sarīrappadesā nikkhamiṃsu. Iti tā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo nikkhamitvā ghanamahāpathaviṃ gaṇhiṃsu.

“With his omniscient knowledge having thus found its opportunity, as the Teacher contemplated the subtle and refined Dhamma at will, six-colored rays—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and radiant—emerged from his body. From his hair, beard, and the blue parts of his eyes, blue rays emerged, by which the expanse of the sky became as if strewn with antimony powder, as if covered with petals of blue lotuses and Umā flowers, as if a fanning sapphire palm-leaf, or as if a stretched-out dark-blue cloth. From his skin and the yellow parts of his eyes, yellow rays emerged, by which the quarters of the world shone as if anointed with liquid gold, as if spread with golden cloth, or as if scattered with saffron powder and Kaṇikāra flowers. From his flesh, blood, and the red parts of his eyes, red rays emerged, by which the quarters of the world shone as if dyed with Chinese powder, as if anointed with the juice of ripe lac, as if draped with red blankets, or as if scattered with Jayasumanā, Pāribaddhaka, and Bandhujīvaka flowers. From his bones, teeth, and the white parts of his eyes, white rays emerged, by which the quarters of the world shone as if scattered with streams of milk poured from silver pitchers, as if with canopies of silver cloth spread out, as if a fanning silver palm-leaf, or as if covered with Kunda, Kumuda, Sindhuvāra, Sumanā, Mallikā, and other flowers. Crimson and radiant rays, however, emerged from various parts of his body. Thus, these six-colored rays emerged and seized the solid great earth.”

“Catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalā mahāpathavī niddhantasuvaṇṇapiṇḍi viya ahosi. Pathaviṃ bhinditvā heṭṭhā udakaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Pathavīsandhārakaṃ aṭṭhanahutādhikacatuyojanasatasahassabahalaṃ udakaṃ suvaṇṇakalasehi āsiñcamānavilīnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ahosi. Udakaṃ vinivijjhitvā vātaṃ aggahesuṃ. Channavutādhikanavayojanasatasahassabahalo vāto samussitasuvaṇṇakkhandho viya ahosi. Vātaṃ vinivijjhitvā heṭṭhā ajaṭākāsaṃ pakkhandiṃsu. Uparibhāgena uggantvāpi catumahārājike gaṇhiṃsu. Te vinivijjhitvā tāvatiṃse, tato yāme, tato tusite, tato nimmānaratī, tato paranimmitavasavattī, tato nava brahmaloke, tato vehapphale, tato pañca suddhāvāse vinivijjhitvā cattāro āruppe gaṇhiṃsu. Cattāro ca āruppe vinivijjhitvā ajaṭākāsaṃ pakkhandiṃsu.

“The great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, appeared like a lump of purified gold. Breaking through the earth, they seized the water below. The water supporting the earth, four hundred and eighty thousand yojanas thick, was like molten gold being poured from golden jars. Having pierced the water, they seized the wind. The wind, nine hundred and ninety-six thousand yojanas thick, resembled a mass of piled-up gold. Having pierced the wind, they plunged into the unobstructed space below. Rising upward, they grasped the realm of the Four Great Kings. Having pierced that, they reached the Tāvatiṃsa realm, then the Yāma realm, then the Tusita realm, then the Nimmānaratī realm, then the Paranimmitavasavattī realm, then the nine Brahma worlds, then the Vehapphala realm, then the five Pure Abodes. Having pierced all these, they grasped the four formless realms. And having pierced the four formless realms, they plunged into the unobstructed space.”

“Tiriyabhāgehi [M 3.0147] anantā lokadhātuyo pakkhandiṃsu, ettake ṭhāne candamhi candappabhā natthi, sūriye sūriyappabhā natthi, tārakarūpesu tārakarūpappabhā natthi, devatānaṃ uyyānavimānakapparukkhesu sarīre ābharaṇesūti sabbattha pabhā natthi. Tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuyā ālokapharaṇasamattho mahābrahmāpi sūriyuggamane khajjopanako viya ahosi, candasūriyatārakarūpadevatuyyānavimānakapparukkhānaṃ paricchedamattakameva paññāyittha. Ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ buddharasmīhiyeva ajjhotthaṭaṃ ahosi. Ayañca neva buddhānaṃ adhiṭṭhāniddhi, na bhāvanāmayiddhi. Saṇhasukhumadhammaṃ pana sammasato lokanāthassa lohitaṃ pasīdi, vatthurūpaṃ pasīdi, chavivaṇṇo pasīdi. Cittasamuṭṭhānā vaṇṇadhātu samantā asītihatthamatte padese niccalā aṭṭhāsī”ti.

“The rays plunged into countless world-systems in the transverse directions. In that space, the moon had no moonlight, the sun had no sunlight, the stars had no starlight; and in the gardens, mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, bodies, and ornaments of the devas, radiance was absent everywhere. Even the Great Brahmā, capable of illuminating the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system, became like a firefly at sunrise, and only the mere outline of the moon, sun, stars, devas, gardens, mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees was discernible. That entire space was pervaded by the Buddha’s rays. And this was neither the Buddha’s power of determination, nor the power born of meditation. But as the Lord of the World contemplated the subtle and refined Dhamma, his blood became clear, his physical form became clear, and the color of his skin became clear. The element of color, born of his mind, stood motionless in a space of eighty cubits all around.”

Evaṃ nisinneti tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā nisinne. Eko brāhmaṇoti nāmagottavasena anabhiññāto apākaṭo eko brāhmaṇo. “Huṃ hu”nti karonto vicaratīti sabbaṃ acokkhajātikaṃ passitvā jigucchanto “huṃ hu”nti karonto vicarati. Etadavocāti (udā. aṭṭha. 4) etaṃ idāni vattabbaṃ “kittāvatā nu kho”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha kittāvatāti kittakena pamāṇena. Nu-ti saṃsayatthe nipāto, kho-ti padapūraṇe. Bho-ti [V 3.0136] brāhmaṇānaṃ jātisamudāgataṃ ālapanaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “bhovādi nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano”ti (dha. pa. 396; su. ni. 625). Gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ brāhmaṇo sampati samāgato bhagavato gottaṃ jānātīti? Nāyaṃ sampati samāgato, chabbassāni padhānakaraṇakāle upaṭṭhahantehi pañcavaggiyehi saddhiṃ caramāno aparabhāge taṃ vataṃ chaḍḍetvā uruvelāyaṃ senanigame eko adutiyo hutvā piṇḍāya caramānopi tena brāhmaṇena diṭṭhapubbo ceva sallapitapubbo ca, tena so pubbe pañcavaggiyehi gayhamānaṃ bhagavato gottaṃ anussaranto “bho gotamā”ti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Yato paṭṭhāya vā bhagavā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto anomānadītīre pabbaji, tato pabhuti “samaṇo [M 3.0148] gotamo”ti cando viya sūriyo viya pākaṭo paññāto hoti, na ca tassa gottajānane kāraṇaṃ gavesitabbaṃ. Brāhmaṇakaraṇāti brāhmaṇaṃ karontīti brāhmaṇakaraṇā, brāhmaṇabhāvakarāti attho. Ettha ca “kittāvatā”ti etena yehi dhammehi brāhmaṇo hoti, tesaṃ dhammānaṃ parimāṇaṃ pucchati. “Katame”ti pana iminā tesaṃ sarūpaṃ pucchati.

Having risen from that concentration, he was seated. A certain brahmin—unknown and unrenowned by name and clan—was wandering around, making the sound 'huṃ huṃ,' seeing everything as impure and feeling disgust. He spoke thus—that is, he spoke the words now to be spoken, “To what extent…” and so on (Ud-a 4). Here, 'to what extent' means by what measure. Nu is a particle indicating a question or doubt; kho is an expletive particle. 'Sir' (bho)—this is a form of address common among brahmins by virtue of their birth. As it has been said: “He is called a 'bho'-sayer if he has possessions” (Dhp 396; Snp 625). 'Gotama'—he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. But how did this brahmin, having just arrived, know the Blessed One's clan name? It is not that he met him just now. During the six years of striving, when he was living with the group of five, and later, after abandoning that practice, he lived alone in Uruvelā, in the village of Senā, wandering for alms. Even then, that brahmin had seen and conversed with him before. Thus, recalling the Blessed One's clan name from when he was associated with the group of five, he addresses him as “Sir Gotama.” Or, from the time the Blessed One set out on the Great Renunciation and was ordained on the bank of the river Anomā, from that time onwards he became renowned as “the ascetic Gotama,” like the moon or the sun. Thus, no reason need be sought for the knowing of his clan name. 'Brahmin-making qualities'—those which make one a brahmin, meaning those which create the state of being a brahmin. Here, 'to what extent' asks for the measure of the qualities by which one becomes a brahmin. 'Which' asks for the nature of those qualities.

Udānaṃ udānesīti “yo brāhmaṇo”tiādikaṃ udānaṃ udānesi, na pana tassa brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desesi. Kasmā? Dhammadesanāya abhājanabhāvato. Tathā hi tassa brāhmaṇassa imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā na saccābhisamayo ahosi. Yathā ca imassa, evaṃ upakassa ājīvakassa buddhaguṇappakāsanaṃ sutvā. Dhammacakkappavattanato hi pubbabhāge bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ paresaṃ suṇantānampi tapussabhallikānaṃ saraṇadānaṃ viya vāsanābhāgiyameva jātaṃ, na asekkhabhāgiyaṃ vā nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ vā. Esā hi dhammatāti. Vedehi vā antanti ettha antaṃ nāma sabbasaṅkhārapariyosānaṃ nibbānaṃ. Ime ussadā natthīti sabbaso ime pahīnattā na santi.

He uttered an inspired utterance: he uttered the inspired utterance beginning with “that brahmin,” but he did not teach the Dhamma to that brahmin. Why? Because he was not a suitable vessel for the teaching of the Dhamma. For indeed, that brahmin, upon hearing this verse, did not attain realization of the truth. And just as with him, so too with Upaka the Ājīvaka upon hearing the proclamation of the Buddha's virtues. For, in the preliminary stage before the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, what was spoken by the Blessed One, even when heard by others like Tapussa and Bhallika, only gave rise to a share in the disposition, not to a share in the state of an adept or a share in penetration. Such is the nature of things. By ‘know the end,’ here ‘end’ means Nibbāna, the complete cessation of all formations. By ‘these upsurges are no more,’ it means that because they are completely abandoned, they do not exist.

Ajapālakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Ajapāla story is concluded.

Mucalindakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mucalinda Story

5. Mucalindamūleti (udā. aṭṭha. 11) ettha mucalindo vuccati nīparukkho, yo “niculo”tipi vuccati, tassa samīpeti attho. Keci pana “mucaloti tassa rukkhassa nāmaṃ, vanajeṭṭhakatāya pana mucalindoti vutta”nti vadanti. Udapādīti sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ pūrento mahāmegho udapādi. Evarūpo kira megho dvīsuyeva kālesu vassati cakkavattimhi vā uppanne buddhe vā, idha buddhuppādakāle udapādi. Pokkharaṇiyā nibbattoti pokkharaṇiyā heṭṭhā [V 3.0137] nāgabhavanaṃ atthi, tattha nibbatto. Sakabhavanāti attano nāgabhavanato. Evaṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvāti satta vāre attano sarīrabhogehi bhagavato kāyaṃ parivāretvā. Uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ [M 3.0149] vihaccāti bhagavato muddhappadesassa upari attano mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ pasāretvā. “Phaṇaṃ karitvā”tipi pāṭho, soyevattho.

5. ‘At the foot of the Mucalinda tree’ (Udāna Commentary 11): here ‘Mucalinda’ refers to the Nīpa tree, also called ‘Nicula’; the meaning is ‘near it’. Some say, “Mucala is the name of that tree; however, because it is the chief of the forest, it is called Mucalinda.” ‘Arose’: a great cloud arose, filling the entire world-sphere. Such a cloud, it is said, rains only on two occasions: when a wheel-turning monarch arises or when a Buddha arises; here it arose at the time of the Buddha’s appearance. ‘Born in a lotus pond’: below the lotus pond there is the abode of the Nāga, where he was born. ‘From his own abode’: from his own Nāga abode. ‘Having thus surrounded with his coils’: having encircled the Blessed One’s body seven times with the coils of his own body. ‘Spreading a large hood above the head’: having spread his large hood above the Blessed One’s head-region. There is also a reading, ‘having made a hood’; the meaning is the same.

Tassa kira nāgarājassa etadahosi “bhagavā ca mayhaṃ bhavanasamīpe rukkhamūle nisinno, ayañca sattāhavaddalikā vattati, vāsāgāramassa laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So sattaratanamayaṃ pāsādaṃ nimminituṃ sakkontopi “evaṃ kate kāyasāro gahito na bhavissati, dasabalassa kāyaveyyāvaccaṃ karissāmī”ti mahantaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā satthāraṃ sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā upari phaṇaṃ dhāresi. “Tassa parikkhepabbhantaraṃ lohapāsāde bhaṇḍāgāragabbhappamāṇaṃ ahosī”ti idha vuttaṃ. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.284) pana –

It is said that the Nāga king had this thought: “The Blessed One is seated at the foot of a tree near my abode, and this seven-day storm is raging; it is fitting that a dwelling be found for him.” Although he was able to construct a seven-jeweled palace, thinking, “If I do so, no physical service will be involved; I will perform personal service for the Ten-Powered One,” he manifested a large form and surrounded the Teacher seven times with his coils, holding his hood above. “The space within his coils was the size of a storeroom in the Bronze Palace,” it is said here. But in the Majjhima Nikāya commentary (MA 1.284), it says—

“Parikkhepassa anto okāso heṭṭhā lohapāsādappamāṇo ahosi, ‘icchiticchitena iriyāpathena satthā viharissatī’ti nāgarājassa ajjhāsayo ahosi, tasmā evaṃ mahantaṃ okāsaṃ parikkhipi, majjhe ratanapallaṅko paññatto hoti, upari suvaṇṇatārakavicittaṃ samosaritagandhadāmakusumacelavitānaṃ ahosi, catūsu koṇesu gandhatelena dīpā jalitā, catūsu disāsu vivaritvā candanakaraṇḍakā ṭhapitā”ti –

“The inner space of the enclosure was as large as the lower Bronze Palace. The Nāga king’s intention was, ‘The Teacher will dwell here in whatever posture he desires.’ Therefore, he enclosed such a vast space. In the middle, a jeweled couch was arranged. Above, a cloth canopy adorned with golden stars and hung with fragrant garlands and flowers was spread. In the four corners, lamps fueled with fragrant oil were burning. In the four directions, sandalwood caskets were placed open.”

Vuttaṃ. Icchiticchitena iriyāpathena viharissatīti ca nāgarājassa ajjhāsayamattametaṃ, bhagavā pana yathānisinnova sattāhaṃ vītināmesi.

So it was said. And that the Nāga king merely intended, “He will dwell in whatever posture he wishes.” However, the Blessed One passed those seven days seated in that very same posture.

Kiñcāpi…pe… cintetuṃ yuttanti ettha keci vadanti “uṇhaggahaṇaṃ bhogaparikkhepassa vipulabhāvakaraṇe kāraṇakittanaṃ. Khuddake hi tasmiṃ bhagavantaṃ nāgarājassa sarīrasambhūtā usmā bādheyya, vipulabhāvakaraṇena pana tādisaṃ mā uṇhaṃ bādhayitthā”ti. Saupasaggapadassa attho upasaggena vināpi viññāyatīti āha “viddhanti ubbiddha”nti, sā cassa ubbiddhatā upakkilesavigamena dūrabhāvena upaṭṭhānanti āha “meghavigamena dūrībhūta”nti. Indanīlamaṇi viya dibbati jotatīti devo, ākāso. Viditvāti “idāni vigatavalāhako ākāso, natthi bhagavato sītādiupaddavo”ti ñatvā. Viniveṭhetvāti apanetvā. Attano [M 3.0150] rūpanti attano nāgarūpaṃ. Paṭisaṃharitvāti antaradhāpetvā. Māṇavakavaṇṇanti kumārakarūpaṃ.

Regarding ‘Although… it is fitting to consider,’ some here say: “The mention of heat is stated as the reason for making the coils spacious. For in a small space, the heat arising from the Nāga king’s body might have troubled the Blessed One, but by making it spacious, such heat would not trouble him.” He says that the meaning of a word with a prefix is understood even without the prefix, as in ‘viddha’ meaning ‘ubbiddha’ (pierced through). And its being ‘pierced through’ is understood as being far due to the removal of defilements; hence he says, ‘made distant by the departure of the clouds’. ‘Devo’ means it shines brilliantly like an Indranīla gem; it refers to the sky. ‘Viditvā’ (having known): having known, ‘Now the sky is free of clouds, there is no trouble from cold, etc., for the Blessed One.’ ‘Viniveṭhetvā’ (having unwound): having removed. ‘Attano rūpaṃ’ (his own form): his own Nāga form. ‘Paṭisaṃharitvā’ (having withdrawn): having made it disappear. ‘Māṇavakavaṇṇaṃ’ (the form of a young man): the form of a young boy.

Etamatthaṃ [V 3.0138] viditvāti “vivekasukhapaṭisaṃvedino yattha katthaci sukhameva hotī”ti etaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārena jānitvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ vivekasukhānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Sutadhammassāti vissutadhammassa. Tenāha “pakāsitadhammassā”ti. Akuppanabhāvoti akuppanasabhāvo.

‘Having known this meaning’: having known this meaning in all respects, that ‘for one who experiences the bliss of seclusion, there is only happiness wherever they may be’. ‘This inspired utterance’: he uttered this inspired utterance illuminating the experience of the bliss of seclusion. ‘Of one whose Dhamma is heard’: of one whose Dhamma is well-known. Therefore he says, ‘of one who has proclaimed the Dhamma’. ‘The state of being unshakeable’: the nature of being unshakeable.

Mucalindakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Mucalinda Story is concluded.

Rājāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Rājāyatana Story

6. Osadhaharītakaṃ upanesīti na kevalaṃ osadhaharītakameva, dantakaṭṭhampi upanesi. Paccaggheti ettha purimaṃ atthavikappaṃ keci na icchanti, teneva ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ “paccaggheti abhinave. Paccekaṃ mahagghatāya paccaggheti keci, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Na hi buddhā bhagavanto mahagghaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti paribhuñjanti vā”ti.

6. “He offered medicinal herbs”—not only medicinal herbs but also a tooth-stick. ‘Paccaggheti’—here, some do not accept the previous interpretation. Therefore, the elder Ācariya Dhammapāla said, “‘Paccaggheti’ means ‘newly’. Some say it means ‘individually precious’ because of its great value, but that is not proper. For the Blessed Buddhas do not accept or use what is of great value.”

Rājāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Rājāyatana Story is concluded.

Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story of Brahmā's Request

7. Āciṇṇasamāciṇṇoti ācarito ceva ācarantehi ca sammadeva ācaritoti attho. Etena ayaṃ parivitakko sabbabuddhānaṃ paṭhamābhisambodhiyaṃ uppajjatevāti ayamettha dhammatāti dasseti. Gambhīropi dhammo paṭipakkhavidhamanena supākaṭo bhaveyya, paṭipakkhavidhamanaṃ pana sammāpaṭipattipaṭibaddhaṃ, sā saddhammasavanādhīnā, taṃ satthari dhamme ca pasādāyattaṃ. So visesato loke sambhāvanīyassa garukātabbassa abhipatthanāhetukoti paramparāya sattānaṃ dhammasampaṭipattiyā brahmuno yācanānimittanti taṃ dassento “brahmunā yācite desetukāmatāyā”tiādimāha.

7. “Āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo” means both practiced and well-practiced by those who practice. This shows that it is the nature of things that this reflection invariably arises in all Buddhas at the time of their supreme enlightenment. Even a profound Dhamma can become clear through the removal of obstacles, but the removal of obstacles depends on right practice, which in turn relies on hearing the true Dhamma. That depends on faith in the Teacher and the Dhamma. Showing that this faith is especially caused by the aspiration for one in the world worthy of esteem and respect, and that Brahmā's request is the cause for beings to attain the Dhamma in succession, he said, 'out of the desire to teach when requested by Brahmā,' and so on.

Adhigatoti [M 3.0151] paṭividdho, sayambhūñāṇena “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā yathābhūtaṃ avabuddhoti attho. Dhammoti catusaccadhammo tabbinimuttassa paṭivijjhitabbadhammassa abhāvato. Gambhīroti mahāsamuddo viya makasatuṇḍasūciyā aññatra samupacitaparipakkañāṇasambhārehi aññesaṃ ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho. Gambhīrattāva duddaso dukkhena daṭṭhabbo, na sakkā sukhena daṭṭhuṃ. Yo [V 3.0139] hi alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭho, so ogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya sarūpato ca visesato ca sukhena passituṃ na sakkā, atha kho kicchena kenaci kadācideva daṭṭhabbo. Duddasattāva duranubodho dukkhena avabujjhitabbo, na sakkā sukhena avabujjhituṃ. Yañhi daṭṭhumeva na sakkā, tassa ogāhetvā anubujjhane kathā eva natthi avabodhassa dukkarabhāvato. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1115) suttapadaṃ vattabbaṃ.

“Adhigato” means penetrated, comprehended through self-awakened knowledge as “this is suffering,” etc., in accordance with reality. “Dhamma” refers to the Four Noble Truths, since there is no other Dhamma apart from them to be penetrated. “Gambhīro” means profound, like the great ocean, whose foundation is unattainable by the knowledge of others—except for those with the provisions of accumulated and matured wisdom—and cannot be reached even by a needle as fine as a mosquito's proboscis. Because of its profundity, it is hard to see—it must be seen with difficulty, not easily. What has an unattainable foundation cannot be easily seen in its true nature, either generally or specifically, because it cannot be fathomed. It can only be seen with great effort, occasionally, by some. Because it is hard to see, it is also hard to comprehend—it must be understood with difficulty, not easily. For what cannot even be seen, there is no question of penetrating and comprehending it, due to the difficulty of comprehension. In this context, the sutta passage should be recalled: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more difficult or harder to fully understand?” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1115).

Santoti anupasantasabhāvānaṃ kilesānaṃ saṅkhārānañca abhāvato vūpasantasabbapariḷāhatāya santo nibbuto, santārammaṇatāya vā santo. Ettha ca nirodhasaccaṃ santaṃ ārammaṇanti santārammaṇaṃ, maggasaccaṃ santaṃ santārammaṇañcāti santārammaṇaṃ. Padhānabhāvaṃ nītoti paṇīto. Atha vā paṇītoti atittikaraṇaṭṭhena atappako sādurasabhojanaṃ viya. Santapaṇītabhāveneva cettha asecanakatāya atappakatā daṭṭhabbā. Idañhi dvayaṃ lokuttarameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atakkāvacaroti uttamañāṇavisayattā takkena avacaritabbo ogāhitabbo na hoti, ñāṇeneva avacaritabbo. Tato eva nipuṇañāṇagocaratāya saṇhasukhumasabhāvattā ca nipuṇo saṇho. Paṇḍitavedanīyoti bālānaṃ avisayattā sammāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipannehi paṇḍitehi eva veditabbo.

Peaceful because of the absence of defilements and formations whose nature is restless, and because it is the cessation of all burning distress. Or, peaceful because its object is peace. Here, the truth of cessation is a peaceful object, and the truth of the path is peaceful and has a peaceful object—thus, it is called “having a peaceful object.” Exalted because it is brought to the state of excellence. Or, exalted because, in the sense of not causing satiety, it is insatiable, like food of excellent taste. And in this context, its insatiability should be seen due to its not needing to be sprinkled [with anything else to enhance it]. For these two are spoken referring exclusively to the supramundane. Beyond the sphere of thought because, being the domain of supreme knowledge, it cannot be approached or entered into by thought; it can only be approached by knowledge. Therefore, because it is the sphere of subtle knowledge and because of its subtle and refined nature, it is subtle and refined. To be experienced by the wise because, being a domain inaccessible to fools, it can only be known by the wise who have embarked on the right path.

Allīyanti abhiramitabbaṭṭhena seviyantīti ālayā, pañca kāmaguṇāti āha “sattā pañcakāmaguṇe allīyanti, tasmā te ālayāti vuccantī”ti. Tattha pañcakāmaguṇe allīyantīti pañcakāmaguṇe sevantīti attho. Teti pañca kāmaguṇā. Ramantīti ratiṃ vindanti kīḷanti laḷanti. Ālīyanti abhiramaṇavasena sevantīti ālayā, aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritāni, tehi ālayehi ramantīti ālayarāmāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ime hi sattā yathā kāmaguṇe, evaṃ rāgampi assādenti [M 3.0152] abhinandantiyeva. Yatheva hi susajjitapupphaphalabharitarukkhādisampannaṃ uyyānaṃ paviṭṭho rājā tāya tāya sampattiyā ramati, sammudito āmoditapamodito hoti, na ukkaṇṭhati, sāyampi nikkhamituṃ na icchati, evamimehi kāmālayataṇhālayehi sattā ramanti, saṃsāravaṭṭe sammoditā anukkaṇṭhitā vasanti. Tena nesaṃ bhagavā duvidhampi ālayaṃ uyyānabhūmiṃ viya dassento “ālayarāmā”tiādimāha. Ratāti niratā. Suṭṭhu muditāti ativiya muditā anukkaṇṭhanato.

They are called “ālaya” because they are clung to, delighted in, and indulged in. The five strands of sensual pleasure are referred to as such: “Beings cling to the five strands of sensual pleasure; therefore, they are called ‘ālaya’ (attachments).” Here, “clinging to the five strands of sensual pleasure” means indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure. These are the five strands of sensual pleasure. “They delight” means they find enjoyment, play, and revel. “They cling” means they indulge through delight—thus, they are called “ālaya.” These are the one hundred and eight workings of craving; delighting in these attachments, they are called “delighting in attachments.” Thus, the meaning should be understood here. Indeed, just as beings delight in the strands of sensual pleasure, so too do they relish and rejoice in lust. For example, when a king enters a park adorned with well-arranged flowers and trees laden with fruit, he delights in its various pleasures, becomes joyful, elated, and happy, and does not grow weary. Even in the evening, he does not wish to leave. Similarly, beings delight in these attachments to sensual pleasures and cravings, rejoicing in the cycle of existence without discontent. Thus, the Blessed One, showing these two kinds of attachments like a pleasure ground, declares: “delighting in attachments,” and so on. “Delighted” means thoroughly engrossed. “Greatly joyful” means exceedingly delighted, due to being free from discontent.

Ṭhānaṃ sandhāyāti ṭhānasaddaṃ sandhāya. Atthato pana ṭhānanti ca paṭiccasamuppādo eva adhippeto[V 3.0140]. Tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayabhūtā avijjādayo. Imesaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayāti idappaccayā, avijjādayova. Idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā yathā devo eva devatā. Idappaccayānaṃ vā avijjādīnaṃ attano phalaṃ paṭicca paccayabhāvo uppādanasamatthatā idappaccayatā. Tena samatthapaccayalakkhaṇo paṭiccasamuppādo dassito hoti. Paṭicca samuppajjati phalaṃ etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādo. Padadvayenapi dhammānaṃ paccayaṭṭho eva vibhāvito. Saṅkhārādipaccayānañhi avijjādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādoti. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbaṃ atthato nibbānameva. Yasmā hi taṃ āgamma paṭicca ariyamaggassa ārammaṇapaccayabhāvahetu sabbasaṅkhāravipphanditāni sammanti vūpasammanti, tasmā “sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti vuccati. Sabbasaṅkhatavisaṃyutte hi nibbāne saṅkhāravūpasamapariyāyo ñāyāgatoyevāti. Idaṃ panettha nibbacanaṃ – sabbe saṅkhārā sammanti etthāti sabbasaṅkhārasamathoti.

It refers to the term ‘ṭhāna’ (condition) by mentioning the word ‘ṭhāna.’ In meaning, however, ‘ṭhāna’ is intended as dependent origination. A condition (ṭhāna) is where the fruit remains, dependent on it for its existence—that is, ignorance and other factors serving as conditions for formations and so on. These formations and so on depend on conditions—meaning these very dependent conditions are ignorance and the rest. Dependent conditions themselves are dependent conditionality, just as a god is a deity. Or, the dependent conditionality of ignorance and the like is their capacity to produce their own results by serving as a condition. Thus, dependent origination is shown to have the characteristic of being an effective condition. Dependent origination means that the fruit arises dependent on this. Even through these two terms, the nature of conditionality among phenomena is clarified. For this is a designation for ignorance and the like, which are the conditions of formations and other things, namely, dependent conditionality or dependent origination. “Stillness of all formations” and so on—all of these, in meaning, refer solely to Nibbāna. For it is by relying on it, as the object condition for the Noble Path, that all the agitations of formations cease and subside. Thus, it is called “the stillness of all formations.” Since Nibbāna is devoid of all conditioned things, the concept of cessation of formations is a well-established expression. Here, this is the analysis: “All formations cease here”—hence, “the stillness of all formations.”

Yasmā ca taṃ āgamma sabbe upadhayo paṭinissaṭṭhā samucchedavasena pariccattā honti, aṭṭhasatappabhedā sabbāpi taṇhā khīyanti, sabbe kilesarāgā virajjanti, jarāmaraṇādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ nirujjhati, tasmā “sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho”ti vuccati, yā panesā taṇhā tena tena bhavena bhavantaraṃ bhavanikantibhāvena vinati saṃsibbati, phalena vā saddhiṃ kammaṃ vinati saṃsibbatīti katvā vānanti vuccati, tato nikkhantaṃ vānatoti nibbānaṃ. Kilamathoti kāyakilamatho. Vihesāpi kāyavihesāyeva, citte pana ubhayampetaṃ buddhānaṃ natthi bodhimūleyeva samucchinnattā. Ettha ca ciranisajjācirabhāsanehi [M 3.0153] piṭṭhiāgilāyanatālugalasosādivasena kāyakilamatho ceva kāyavihesā ca veditabbā, sā ca kho desanāya atthaṃ ajānantānañca appaṭipajjantānañca vasena. Jānantānaṃ pana paṭipajjantānañca desanāya kāyaparissamopi satthu aparissamova, tenāha bhagavā “na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ vihesetī”ti. Teneva vuttaṃ “yā ajānantānaṃ desanā nāma, so mama kilamatho assā”ti.

Because by relying on it, all acquisitions are relinquished, given up through complete destruction; all one hundred and eight kinds of craving are entirely exhausted, all defilement-lusts fade away, and all suffering of the round of existence, such as aging and death, ceases. Therefore, it is called “the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation.” Moreover, this craving, by binding and weaving from one existence to another through the inclination towards rebirth, or by binding and weaving kamma together with its result, is called “vāna.” That which has gone out from that is called “nibbāna.” “Fatigue” refers to bodily fatigue. “Affliction” is also bodily affliction, but for the Buddhas, neither of these exists in their minds, as they have been completely uprooted at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Here, bodily fatigue and affliction should be understood as arising from prolonged sitting and prolonged speaking, leading to back-aching, throat-drying, and so on—but only with respect to those who do not understand the purpose of the teaching or do not practice accordingly. For those who understand and practice, however, even the bodily exertion of the Teacher in teaching is no exertion at all. Thus, the Blessed One said, “And a matter concerning the Dhamma does not afflict me.” For this reason, it is said, “Teaching those who do not know—that would be my fatigue.”

Apissūti sampiṇḍanatthe nipāto. So na kevalaṃ etadahosi, imāpi gāthā paṭibhaṃsūti dīpeti. Bhagavantanti paṭisaddayogena sāmiatthe upayogavacananti āha “bhagavato”ti. Vuddhippattā acchariyā vā anacchariyā. Vuddhiatthopi hi a-kāro hoti yathā “asekkhā dhammā”ti. Kappānaṃ cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni satasahassañca sadevakassa lokassa dhammasaṃvibhāgakaraṇatthameva pāramiyo pūretvā idāni samadhigatadhammarajjassa tattha appossukkatāpattidīpanattā gāthātthassa [V 3.0141] anuacchariyatā tassa vuddhippatti ca veditabbā. Atthadvārena hi gāthānaṃ anacchariyatā. Gocarā ahesunti upaṭṭhahaṃsu, upaṭṭhānañca vitakkayitabbatāti āha “parivitakkayitabbabhāvaṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti.

'Apissūti' is a particle used in the sense of combination. It indicates that not only did this occur, but also that these verses arose spontaneously. The word 'Bhagavantam' (accusative) is used in the sense of ownership by connection with a correlative word; therefore, it is explained as 'Bhagavato' (genitive). The verses are 'vuddhippattā' (having attained growth), and they are 'acchariyā vā anacchariyā' (wonderful or not wonderful). Indeed, the letter 'a' can have a negative sense, as in 'asekkhā dhammā' (qualities of one beyond training). Having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons solely for the purpose of distributing the Dhamma to the world with its deities, now, for him who has attained sovereignty of the Dhamma, the not-wonderful nature of the meaning of the verses and its attainment of growth should be understood, due to the revelation of his disinclination in that regard. For the not-wonderful nature of the verses is by way of their meaning. 'Gocarā ahesuṃ' means they arose, and that arising is something to be considered; therefore, it is said, "they attained a state fit for reflection."

Kicchenāti na dukkhappaṭipadāya. Buddhānañhi cattāropi maggā sukhappaṭipadāva honti. Pāramīpūraṇakāle pana sarāgasadosasamohasseva sato āgatāgatānaṃ yācakānaṃ alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ sīsaṃ kantitvā galalohitaṃ nīharitvā suañjitāni akkhīni uppāṭetvā kulavaṃsappadīpaṃ puttaṃ manāpacāriniṃ bhariyanti evamādīni dentassa aññāni ca khantivādisadisesu attabhāvesu chejjabhejjādīni pāpuṇantassa āgamanīyapaṭipadaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ha-iti vā byattanti etasmiṃ atthe nipāto. Ekaṃsattheti keci. Ha byattaṃ ekaṃsena vā alaṃ nippayojanaṃ evaṃ kicchena adhigataṃ dhammaṃ desetunti yojanā. Halanti vā alanti iminā samānatthaṃ padaṃ “halanti vadāmī”tiādīsu viya. “Pakāsita”ntipi paṭhanti, desitanti attho. Evaṃ kicchena adhigatassa dhammassa alaṃ desitaṃ pariyattaṃ desitaṃ, ko attho desitenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rāgadosaparetehīti rāgadosaphuṭṭhehi, phuṭṭhavisena viya sappena rāgena dosena ca samphuṭṭhehi abhibhūtehīti [M 3.0154] attho. Atha vā rāgadosaparetehīti rāgadosānugatehi, rāgena ca dosena ca anubandhehīti attho.

'With difficulty' (kicchena) does not mean by a painful practice. For with Buddhas, all four paths are indeed practices of ease. Rather, this was said with reference to the path undertaken at the time of fulfilling the perfections, when, while still having lust, hatred, and delusion, one gives to the beggars who come again and again things like one's own adorned and prepared head after cutting it off, blood from the neck after drawing it out, well-anointed eyes after plucking them out, a son who is the lamp of the family lineage, and a beloved wife; and when in other existences, such as that of the Khantivādī, one endures being cut and dismembered. 'Ha' is a particle in the sense of 'clearly' (byattaṃ). Some say it is in the sense of 'certainly' (ekaṃsa). The construction is: 'Ha—clearly, or certainly—it is enough, it is useless to teach the Dhamma attained with such difficulty.' Or, 'halaṃ' is a word with the same meaning as 'alaṃ' (enough), as in such phrases as 'I say halaṃ'. Some also read 'pakāsitaṃ', meaning 'taught'. Thus, it is said: 'Enough has been taught of the Dhamma attained with difficulty, sufficiently has it been taught; what is the use of teaching it?' 'By those overcome by lust and hatred' (rāgadosaparetehi) means by those affected by lust and hatred; that is, affected and overwhelmed by lust and hatred as if by a serpent with pervasive venom. Alternatively, 'by those overcome by lust and hatred' means by those followed by lust and hatred; that is, pursued by lust and hatred.

Paṭisotagāminti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.65; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.281; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.172) niccagāhādīnaṃ paṭisotaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā asubhanti evaṃ gataṃ pavattaṃ catusaccadhammanti attho. Rāgarattāti kāmarāgena bhavarāgena diṭṭhirāgena ca rattā. Na dakkhantīti aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā asubhanti iminā sabhāvena na passissanti, te apassante ko sakkhissati aniccantiādinā sabhāvena yāthāvato dhammaṃ jānāpetunti adhippāyo. Rāgadosaparetatāpi nesaṃ sammuḷhabhāvenevāti āha “tamokhandhena āvuṭā”ti, avijjārāsinā ajjhotthaṭāti attho.

'Going against the stream' (paṭisotagāmi) means the Dhamma of the Four Truths, which proceeds against the stream of grasping at permanence and so on, being characterized as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and unattractive. 'Impassioned by lust' (rāgarattā) means impassioned by sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. 'They will not see' means they will not see by way of this nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and unattractiveness. The intention is: when they do not see, who will be able to make them know the Dhamma as it really is, by way of its nature as impermanent and so on? And their being overcome by lust and hatred is precisely due to their state of delusion; therefore, it is said, "enveloped by a mass of darkness," meaning overwhelmed by the heap of ignorance.

Appossukkatāya cittaṃ namatīti kasmā panassa evaṃ cittaṃ nami, nanu esa “muttohaṃ mocessāmi, tiṇṇohaṃ tāressāmi,

Regarding the words, "his mind inclines to disinclination": why did his mind incline thus? For surely he had resolved:

Kiṃ me aññātavesena, dhammaṃ sacchikatenidha;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, tārayissaṃ sadevaka”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.55) –

"What use is it for me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown guise? Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world with its gods."

Patthanaṃ [V 3.0142] katvā pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ pattoti? Saccameva, tadeva paccavekkhaṇānubhāvena panassa evaṃ cittaṃ nami. Tassa hi sabbaññutaṃ patvā sattānaṃ kilesagahanataṃ dhammassa ca gambhīrataṃ paccavekkhantassa sattānaṃ kilesagahanatā ca dhammagambhīratā ca sabbākārena pākaṭā jātā. Athassa “ime sattā kañjiyapuṇṇalābu viya takkabharitacāṭi viya vasātelapītapilotikā viya añjanamakkhitahattho viya ca kilesabharitā atisaṃkiliṭṭhā rāgarattā dosaduṭṭhā mohamuḷhā, te kiṃ nāma paṭivijjhissantī”ti cintayato kilesagahanapaccavekkhaṇānubhāvenapi evaṃ cittaṃ nami.

Having made the aspiration and fulfilled the perfections, did he attain omniscience? Indeed, he did. Yet it was precisely through the power of reflection that his mind inclined thus. For when he attained omniscience and reflected on the density of beings' defilements and the profundity of the Dhamma, the density of beings' defilements and the profundity of the Dhamma became manifest to him in every way. Then, as he thought, "These beings are filled with defilements like a gourd full of rice-gruel, like a pot filled with buttermilk, like a cloth soaked in fat and oil, like a hand smeared with collyrium—they are utterly defiled, impassioned by lust, corrupted by hatred, bewildered by delusion. How will they ever penetrate this?" his mind inclined thus also through the power of reflecting on the density of defilements.

“Ayaṃ dhammo pathavīsandhārakaudakakkhandho viya gambhīro, pabbatena paṭicchādetvā ṭhapito sāsapo viya duddaso, satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭi viya aṇu. Mayā hi imaṃ dhammaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ vāyamantena adinnaṃ dānaṃ nāma natthi, arakkhitaṃ sīlaṃ nāma natthi, aparipūritā kāci pāramī nāma natthi, tassa me nirussāhaṃ viya mārabalaṃ vidhamantassapi pathavī [M 3.0155] na kampittha, paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantassapi na kampittha, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhentassapi na kampittha, pacchimayāme pana paṭiccasamuppādaṃ paṭivijjhantasseva me dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha. Iti mādisenapi tikkhañāṇena kicchenevāyaṃ dhammo paṭividdho, taṃ lokiyamahājanā kathaṃ paṭivijjhissantī”ti dhammagambhīratāya paccavekkhaṇānubhāvenapi evaṃ cittaṃ namīti veditabbaṃ.

"This Dhamma is as profound as the great mass of water that supports the earth, as hard to see as a mustard seed placed and covered by a mountain, as subtle as the tip of a hair split a hundred times. While I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift I did not give, no virtue I did not guard, no perfection I did not fulfill. Yet for me, even when dispelling the army of Māra as if without effort, the earth did not tremble. In the first watch, when recollecting past lives, it did not tremble. In the middle watch, when purifying the divine eye, it did not tremble. But in the last watch, just as I was penetrating dependent origination, this ten-thousandfold world-system trembled. Thus, this Dhamma was penetrated with difficulty even by one such as me with keen wisdom; how then will the ordinary people of the world penetrate it?" It should be understood that his mind inclined thus also through the power of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma.

Apica brahmunā yācite desetukāmatāyapissa evaṃ cittaṃ nami. Jānāti hi bhagavā “mama appossukkatāya citte namamāne mahābrahmā dhammadesanaṃ yācissati, ime ca sattā brahmagarukā, te ‘satthā kira dhammaṃ na desetukāmo ahosi, atha naṃ mahābrahmā yācitvā desāpeti, santo vata bho dhammo paṇīto’ti maññamānā sussūsissantī”ti. Idampissa kāraṇaṃ paṭicca appossukkatāya cittaṃ nami, no dhammadesanāyāti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, his mind also inclined thus from a desire to teach only upon being requested by Brahmā. For the Blessed One knew: "When my mind is inclining to disinclination, Mahābrahmā will request the teaching of the Dhamma. And these beings hold Brahmā in high esteem. Thinking, 'It seems the Teacher was unwilling to teach the Dhamma, but then Mahābrahmā requested it and had him teach. Oh, how excellent, how sublime is the Dhamma!' they will be eager to listen." It should be understood that for this reason too his mind inclined to disinclination, and not to teaching the Dhamma.

8. Sahampatissāti so kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane sahako nāma thero paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ kappāyukabrahmā hutvā nibbatto, tatra naṃ sahampati brahmāti sañjānanti. Taṃ sandhāyāha “brahmuno sahampatissā”ti. Nassati vatāti so kira imaṃ saddaṃ tathā nicchāreti, yathā dasasahassilokadhātubrahmāno sutvā sabbe sannipatiṃsu. Apparajakkhajātikāti paññāmaye akkhimhi appaṃ parittaṃ rāgadosamoharajaṃ etesaṃ evaṃsabhāvāti apparajakkhajātikā. Appaṃ rāgādirajaṃ yesaṃ te sabhāvā apparajakkhajātikāti [V 3.0143] evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Assavanatāti “sayaṃ abhiññā”tiādīsu viya karaṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ, assavanatāyāti attho. Bhavissantīti purimabuddhesu dasapuññakiriyavasena katādhikārā paripākagatapadumāni viya sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ dhammadesanaṃyeva ākaṅkhamānā catuppadikagāthāvasāne ariyabhūmiṃ okkamanārahā na eko, na dve, anekasatasahassā dhammassa aññātāro bhavissantīti dasseti.

8. "Of Sahampati" — It is said that Sahaka, a senior monk, a companion in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, having developed the first jhāna, was reborn as a Brahmā with a lifespan of an eon in the realm of the first jhāna. There, they recognized him as Brahmā Sahampati. Referring to him, it is said, "of Brahmā Sahampati." "Alas, the world perishes!" — It is said that he uttered this sound in such a way that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system heard it and all gathered together. "A generation with little dust in their eyes" — In the eye of wisdom, there is little, slight dust of greed, hatred, and delusion in them. Being of such a nature, they are called "a generation with little dust in their eyes." The meaning here should be understood thus: those whose nature has little dust of greed and so forth are "a generation with little dust in their eyes." "Through not hearing" — The dative/genitive case here signifies the means, as in phrases like "by direct knowledge," so the meaning is "by not hearing." "There will be" — Just as lotuses, ripened by the merit done through the ten meritorious deeds in the time of previous Buddhas, long only for the touch of the sun's rays, that is, the teaching of the Dhamma, so too, at the end of the four-line verse, not one, not two, but many hundreds of thousands will become those who have understood the Dhamma, worthy of entering the noble plane. This is what is shown.

Pāturahosīti pātubhavi. Samalehi cintitoti samalehi pūraṇakassapādīhi chahi satthārehi cintito. Te hi puretaraṃ uppajjitvā sakalajambudīpe kaṇṭake pattharamānā viya visaṃ siñcamānā viya [M 3.0156] ca samalaṃ micchādiṭṭhidhammaṃ desayiṃsu. Te kira buddhakolāhalānussavena sañjātakutūhalā lokaṃ vañcetvā kohaññe ṭhatvā sabbaññutaṃ paṭijānantā yaṃ kiñci adhammaṃyeva dhammoti dīpesuṃ. Apāpuretanti vivara etaṃ. Amatassa dvāranti amatassa nibbānassa dvārabhūtaṃ ariyamaggaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – etaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato pabhuti pihitaṃ nibbānanagarassa mahādvāraṃ ariyamaggaṃ saddhammadesanāhatthena apāpura vivara ugghāṭehīti.
