Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhanti ime sattā rāgādimalānaṃ abhāvato vimalena sammāsambuddhena anubuddhaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ suṇantu tāva bhagavāti yācati.

"He has appeared" means he has become manifest. "Conceived by the defiled" means conceived by the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, who were defiled. For they, having arisen earlier, spread their defiled, wrong-viewed teachings throughout the whole of Jambudīpa like scattering thorns or pouring poison. It is said that, their curiosity stirred by the uproar about the Buddha, they became eager to deceive the world, establishing themselves in deceit, claiming omniscience and proclaiming whatever was non-Dhamma as Dhamma. "Open" means to uncover this. "The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path, which serves as the door to the Deathless, Nibbāna. This is what is meant: "Since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation, this great door to the city of Nibbāna—the Noble Path—has been closed. With the hand of teaching the true Dhamma, open it, uncover it, unfasten it!" "May they hear the Dhamma realized by the Stainless One"—he entreats the Blessed One, saying, "May these beings first listen to the Dhamma of the Four Truths, realized by the Fully Enlightened One, who is stainless due to the absence of stains such as lust."

Selapabbato ucco hoti thiro ca, na paṃsupabbato missakapabbato vāti āha “sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito”ti. Tassattho “selamaye ekagghane pabbatamuddhani yathāṭhitova. Na hi tattha ṭhitassa dassanatthaṃ gīvukkhipanapasāraṇādikiccaṃ atthī”ti. Tathūpamanti tappaṭibhāgaṃ selapabbatūpamaṃ. Dhammamayaṃ pāsādanti lokuttaradhammamāha. So hi sabbaso pasādāvaho sabbadhamme atikkamma abbhuggataṭṭhena pāsādasadiso ca, paññāpariyāyo vā idha dhamma-saddo. Paññā hi abbhuggataṭṭhena pāsādoti abhidhamme niddiṭṭhā. Tathā cāha –

"The rock mountain is high and firm, not like a dust mountain or a mixed mountain," he said, "as if standing on the summit of a rock mountain." The meaning of that is, "just as one stands on the summit of a solid rock mountain. For one standing there, there is no need to crane the neck or stretch to see." "Like that" means comparable, similar to the rock mountain. "The palace made of Dhamma" refers to the supramundane Dhamma. For it is entirely inspiring, surpassing all things by its elevated nature, and thus resembles a palace. Alternatively, here the word "Dhamma" is a term for wisdom. Indeed, wisdom, due to its elevated nature, is called a palace, as explained in the Abhidhamma. And so it is said:

“Paññāpāsādamāruyha, asoko sokiniṃ pajaṃ;

Pabbataṭṭhova bhūmaṭṭhe, dhīro bāle avekkhatī”ti. (dha. pa. 28);

"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the sorrowless one surveys the sorrowing crowd; as one on a mountain peak surveys those on the ground, so the wise one surveys the foolish."

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yathā selapabbatamuddhani yathāṭhitova cakkhumā puriso samantato janataṃ passeyya, tathā tvampi sumedha sundarapañña sabbaññutaññāṇena samantacakkhu bhagavā dhammamayaṃ paññāmayaṃ pāsādamāruyha sayaṃ apetasoko sokāvatiṇṇaṃ jātijarābhibhūtaṃ janataṃ avekkhassu [V 3.0144] upadhāraya upaparikkhāti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yathā hi pabbatapāde samantā mahantaṃ khettaṃ katvā tattha kedārapāḷīsu kuṭikāyo katvā rattiṃ aggiṃ jāleyyuṃ, caturaṅgasamannāgatañca andhakāraṃ assa, atha tassa pabbatassa matthake ṭhatvā cakkhumato purisassa bhūmiṃ olokayato neva khettaṃ, na kedārapāḷiyo, na kuṭiyo, na tattha sayitamanussā paññāyeyyuṃ anujjalabhāvato, kuṭikāsu pana aggijālāmattameva [M 3.0157] paññāyeyya ujjalabhāvato, evaṃ dhammapāsādaṃ āruyha sattanikāyaṃ olokayato tathāgatassa ye te akatakalyāṇā sattā, te ekavihāre dakkhiṇajāṇupasse nisinnāpi buddhacakkhussa āpāthaṃ nāgacchanti ñāṇagginā anujjalabhāvato anuḷārabhāvato ca, rattiṃ khittā sarā viya honti. Ye pana katakalyāṇā veneyyapuggalā, te evassa dūrepi ṭhitā āpāthamāgacchanti paripakkañāṇaggitāya samujjalabhāvato uḷārasantānatāya ca, so aggi viya himavantapabbato viya ca. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Here is the concise meaning—just as a man with good eyesight standing on the peak of a rock mountain would see the people all around, so too, O Wise One of beautiful wisdom, O Blessed One with the all-seeing eye of omniscience, having ascended the palace of Dhamma and wisdom, yourself free from sorrow, look upon the people sunk in sorrow, overcome by birth and aging; observe and examine them. This is the intended meaning—just as if, having made a large field around the foot of a mountain, one were to build huts in the rice-paddy rows there and light fires at night, and there was a fourfold darkness, then a man with good eyesight standing on the peak of that mountain, looking down at the ground, would see neither the field, nor the paddy-rows, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping there, because they are not luminous; only the flames of the fires in the huts would be visible, because they are luminous. Similarly, having ascended the palace of Dhamma and looking upon the host of beings, to the Tathāgata, those beings who have not done good deeds do not come into the range of the Buddha’s vision, even if seated in the same dwelling with their right knee beside him, because they are not luminous with the fire of knowledge and because they are not eminent; they are like arrows shot at night. But those who have done good deeds, the individuals who can be taught, even if standing far away, come into his range due to being luminous with the fire of their mature knowledge and due to their eminent nature, like a fire or like the Himālaya mountain. And this has been said:

“Dūre santo pakāsenti, himavantova pabbato;

Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṃ khittā yathā sarā”ti. (dha. pa. 304);

"The good are visible from afar, like the Himālaya mountains; the bad are not seen here, like arrows shot at night."

Uṭṭhehīti bhagavato dhammadesanatthaṃ cārikacaraṇaṃ yācanto bhaṇati. Uṭṭhehīti vā dhammadesanāya appossukkatāsaṅkhātasaṅkocāpattito kilāsubhāvato uṭṭhaha. Vīrātiādīsu bhagavā sātisayacatubbidhasammappadhānavīriyavantatāya vīro, devaputtamaccukilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ vijitattā vijitasaṅgāmo, jātikantārādito veneyyasatthaṃ vāhanasamatthatāya nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ khemappadesaṃ sampāpanasamatthatāya satthavāho, kāmacchandaiṇassa abhāvato aṇaṇoti veditabbo. Yo hi paresaṃ iṇaṃ gahetvā vināseti, so tehi “iṇaṃ dehī”ti tajjamānopi pharusaṃ vuccamānopi vambhamānopi vadhiyamānopi kiñci paṭippaharituṃ na sakkoti, sabbaṃ titikkhati. Titikkhakāraṇañhissa taṃ iṇaṃ hoti, evameva yo yamhi kāmacchandena rajjati, taṇhāgahaṇena taṃ vatthuṃ gaṇhāti, so tena pharusaṃ vuccamānopi vambhamānopi vadhiyamānopi kiñci paṭippaharituṃ na sakkoti, sabbaṃ titikkhati. Titikkhakāraṇañhissa so kāmacchando hoti gharasāmikehi viheṭhiyamānānaṃ itthīnaṃ viya. Kasmā? Iṇasadisattā kāmacchandassa.

He says "Arise," requesting that the Blessed One set out on a journey for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Or, 'Arise' means: arise from the state of weariness and from the contraction known as a lack of zeal for teaching the Dhamma. In "hero" and so on, the Blessed One is a hero because of his surpassing energy of the fourfold right striving; a conqueror of the battle because he has conquered the Māras of the gods, death, defilements, and formations; a caravan leader because he is capable of conveying the caravan of trainees from the wilderness of birth and so on, and capable of leading them to the safe place called Nibbāna; he should be known as debt-free because of the absence of the debt of sensual desire. For whoever takes a loan from others and wastes it, even when pressed by them saying, "Pay the debt!", even when spoken to harshly, ridiculed, or beaten, he cannot retaliate in any way but endures everything. The reason for his endurance is that debt. Just so, whoever is impassioned for anything through sensual desire, grasping that object with the grip of craving, even when spoken to harshly, ridiculed, or beaten by it, he cannot retaliate in any way but endures everything. The reason for his endurance is that sensual desire, just like women harassed by the masters of the house. Why? Because sensual desire is like a debt.

9. Ajjhesananti garuṭṭhānīyaṃ payirupāsitvā garutaraṃ payojanaṃ uddissa abhipatthanā ajjhesanā, sāpi atthato yācanā eva. Buddhacakkhunāti indriyaparopariyattañāṇena ca āsayānusayañāṇena ca. Imesañhi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ buddhacakkhūti nāmaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇassa samantacakkhūti[V 3.0145]. Heṭṭhimānaṃ [M 3.0158] tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānaṃ dhammacakkhūti. Apparajakkhetiādīsu yesaṃ vuttanayeneva paññācakkhumhi rāgādirajaṃ appaṃ, te apparajakkhā. Yesaṃ taṃ mahantaṃ, te mahārajakkhā. Yesaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni tikkhāni, te tikkhindriyā. Yesaṃ tāni mudūni, te mudindriyā. Yesaṃ teyeva saddhādayo ākārā sundarā, te svākārā. Ye kathitakāraṇaṃ sallakkhenti, sukhena sakkā honti viññāpetuṃ, te suviññāpayā. Ye paralokañceva vajjañca bhayato passanti, te paralokavajjabhayadassāvino nāma.

9. A request (ajjhesanā) is an aspiration for a more significant purpose, made after having attended upon one worthy of respect; in essence, it is also a plea. The Buddha's eye (buddhacakkhu) refers to the knowledge of the maturity of faculties (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa) and the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusayañāṇa). For these two knowledges, the term 'Buddha's eye' is used, while the knowledge of omniscience is called the 'all-around eye' (samantacakkhu). The lower three path knowledges are termed the 'eye of Dhamma' (dhammacakkhu). In the phrases 'those with little dust' and so forth, 'those with little dust' (apparajakkhā) are those in whom, as explained regarding the eye of wisdom, the dust of passion and so forth is slight. 'Those with much dust' (mahārajakkhā) are those in whom it is great. 'Those with sharp faculties' (tikkhindriyā) are those whose faculties of faith and so forth are keen. 'Those with dull faculties' (mudindriyā) are those whose faculties are dull. 'Those with beautiful qualities' (svākārā) are those whose very qualities, such as faith, are beautiful. 'Easy to instruct' (suviññāpayā) are those who consider the stated reasons and can easily be made to understand. 'Those who see danger in the other world and in blameworthy actions' (paralokavajjabhayadassāvino) are those who see the other world and blameworthy actions as fearful.

Uppalāni ettha santīti uppalinī, gacchopi jalāsayopi, idha pana jalāsayo adhippeto, tasmā uppaliniyanti uppalavaneti evamattho gahetabbo. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Antonimuggaposīnīti yāni udakassa anto nimuggāneva hutvā pussanti vaḍḍhanti, tāni antonimuggaposīni. Udakaṃ accuggamma tiṭṭhantīti udakaṃ atikkamitvā tiṭṭhanti. Tattha yāni accuggamma ṭhitāni sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ āgamayamānāni, tāni ajja pupphanakāni. Yāni samodakaṃ ṭhitāni, tāni sve pupphanakāni. Yāni udakā anuggatāni antonimuggaposīni, tāni tatiyadivase pupphanakāni. Udakā pana anuggatāni aññānipi sarogauppalādīni nāma atthi, yāni neva pupphissanti macchakacchapabhakkhāneva bhavissanti, tāni pāḷiṃ nāruḷhāni, āharitvā pana dīpetabbānīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pakāsitāni. Yatheva hi tāni catubbidhāni pupphāni, evameva ugghaṭitaññū vipañcitaññū neyyo padaparamoti cattāro puggalā.

Because there are lotuses here, it is called Uppalinī, which can refer to a plant or a water reservoir. Here, however, a water reservoir is intended, so 'uppalini' should be understood as 'lotus pond' in this sense. The same method applies to the rest as well. 'Antonimuggaposīni' refers to those that, being submerged in water, grow and thrive. 'Standing above the water' means they stand having risen above the water. Among them, those that stand having risen above the water and receive the touch of the sun's rays will bloom today. Those that remain level with the water will bloom tomorrow. Those that have not risen from the water, the antonimuggaposīni, will bloom on the third day. There are also other lotuses that have not risen from the water, such as diseased lotuses and so forth, which will not bloom but will instead be eaten by fish and turtles. These are not mentioned in the Pāli text but are explained in the commentary when brought up for clarification. Just as there are four types of flowers, so too are there four types of individuals: the one who understands immediately (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands after explanation (vipaṇcitaññū), the one who needs guidance (neyya), and the one for whom the words are the limit (padaparama).

Tattha yassa puggalassa saha udāhaṭavelāya dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā nayena saṅkhittena mātikāya ṭhapiyamānāya desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhituṃ samattho puggalo ugghaṭitaññūti vuccati. Yassa puggalassa saṅkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo vipañcitaññū. Yassa puggalassa uddesato paripucchato yoniso manasikaroto kalyāṇamitte sevato bhajato payirupāsato anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo neyyo. Yassa puggalassa bahumpi suṇato bahumpi bhaṇato bahumpi dhārayato [M 3.0159] bahumpi vācayato na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hoti, tena attabhāvena maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā antamaso jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamo. Tattha bhagavā uppalavanādisadisaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ olokento ajja pupphanakāni viya ugghaṭitaññū, sve pupphanakāni viya vipañcitaññū, tatiyadivase pupphanakāni viya neyye, macchakacchapabhakkhapupphāni [V 3.0146] viya padaparame ca addasa, passanto ca “ettakā apparajakkhā, ettakā mahārajakkhā, tatrāpi ettakā ugghaṭitaññū”ti evaṃ sabbākāratova addasa.

Here, the person who attains understanding of the Dhamma at the very moment it is proclaimed—this person, by means of the concise outline such as 'the four foundations of mindfulness,' and following the method of teaching, is able to send forth knowledge and attain arahantship. Such a person is called one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū). The person who attains understanding of the Dhamma when what was spoken concisely is explained in detail—this person is called one who understands after elaboration (vipaṇcitaññū). The person who gradually attains understanding of the Dhamma through recitation, questioning, wise reflection, and by serving, frequenting, and attending upon virtuous friends—this person is called one to be guided (neyya). The person who, despite much listening, much speaking, much memorizing, and much recitation, does not attain understanding of the Dhamma in that lifetime—who cannot, in that very existence, produce the path, the fruit, or even jhāna or insight—this person is called one for whom the words are the limit (padaparama). There, the Blessed One, surveying the ten-thousandfold world-system like a lotus pond and so forth, saw those like today’s flowers as the quick-understanding ones, those like tomorrow’s flowers as those who understand after elaboration, those like the flowers of the third day as those to be guided, and those like the flowers eaten by fish and turtles as those for whom the words are the limit. Seeing thus, he discerned fully: 'So many are of little dust, so many are of great dust; among them, so many are of quick understanding.' Thus, he saw everything in all its aspects.

Tattha tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ imasmiññeva attabhāve bhagavato dhammadesanā atthaṃ sādheti. Padaparamānaṃ anāgatatthāya vāsanā hoti. Atha bhagavā imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ atthāvahaṃ dhammadesanaṃ viditvā desetukamyataṃ uppādetvā puna sabbepi tīsu bhavesu satte bhabbābhabbavasena dve koṭṭhāse akāsi. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ “ye te sattā kammāvaraṇena samannāgatā vipākāvaraṇena samannāgatā kilesāvaraṇena samannāgatā assaddhā acchandikā duppaññā abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ, ime te sattā abhabbā. Katame te sattā bhabbā? Ye te sattā na kammāvaraṇena…pe… ime te sattā bhabbā”ti (vibha. 826-827). Tattha sabbepi abhabbapuggale pahāya bhabbapuggaleyeva ñāṇena pariggahetvā “ettakā rāgacaritā, ettakā dosa, moha, vitakka, saddhā, buddhicaritā”ti cha koṭṭhāse akāsi, evaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desessāmīti cintesi. Ettha ca apparajakkhādibhabbādivasena āvajjentassa bhagavato te sattā puñjapuñjāva hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, na ekekāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, the Blessed One's teaching achieves its purpose for three types of individuals in this very existence. For those for whom the words are the limit, it becomes a basis for the future. Then, knowing the teaching that brings benefit to these four types of individuals, the Blessed One, wanting to teach, further divided all beings in the three existences into two groups based on capability and incapability. Regarding this, it was said: 'Those beings who are endowed with the obstruction of kamma, endowed with the obstruction of results, endowed with the obstruction of defilements, faithless, without desire, unwise, incapable of entering the fixed course, of rightness in wholesome qualities—these beings are incapable. Which beings are capable? Those beings who are not obstructed by kamma... these beings are capable' (Vibh. 826-827). Here, having abandoned all incapable individuals, the Blessed One encompassed only the capable individuals with his knowledge, dividing them into six groups: 'So many are of lustful character, so many of hateful, deluded, speculative, faithful, and intelligent character.' Having done so, he thought, 'Thus will I teach the Dhamma.' Here, it should be seen that when the Blessed One reflects on those beings based on their capability, such as having little dust, etc., they appear to him in clusters, not individually.

Paccabhāsīti patiabhāsi. Apārutāti vivaṭā. Amatassa dvārāti ariyamaggo. So hi amatasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa dvāraṃ, so mayā vivaritvā ṭhapito mahākaruṇūpanissayena sayambhūñāṇena adhigatattāti dasseti. “Apārutaṃ tesaṃ amatassa dvāra”nti keci paṭhanti. Pamuñcantu saddhanti sabbe attano saddhaṃ muñcantu vissajjentu pavedentu, mayā desite dhamme mayi ca attano saddahanākāraṃ uṭṭhāpentūti attho. Pacchimapadadvaye ayamattho – ahañhi attano paguṇaṃ suppavattitampi imaṃ paṇītaṃ [M 3.0160] uttamaṃ dhammaṃ kāyavācākilamathasaññī hutvā na bhāsiṃ, na bhāsissāmīti cintesiṃ, idāni pana sabbo jano saddhābhājanaṃ upanetu, pūressāmi nesaṃ saṅkappanti. Antaradhāyīti satthāraṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā antarahito, sakaṭṭhānameva gatoti attho. Satthusantikañhi upagatānaṃ devānaṃ brahmānañca tassa purato antaradhānaṃ nāma sakaṭṭhānagamanameva.

'Responded' means replied. 'Open' means unveiled. 'The door to the Deathless' refers to the Noble Path. For it is the door to Nibbāna, known as the Deathless, which I have opened and established out of great compassion, having realized it through self-awakened knowledge. Some read, 'Open is the door to the Deathless for them.' 'Let them release their faith' means let all release, send forth, and declare their faith, arousing their confidence in me and in the Dhamma I have taught. The meaning of the last two lines is this: 'Though I had fully mastered and could smoothly expound this excellent, supreme Dhamma, I refrained from teaching it, being one who perceived weariness of body and speech, thinking, "I will not teach." But now, let all people bring forth their vessel of faith; I will fulfill their aspirations.' 'Disappeared' means that having honored the Teacher with garlands, perfumes, and so forth, he vanished; the meaning is that he went to his own place. For the disappearance of devas and brahmās who approach the presence of the Teacher is simply their return to their own abodes.

Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of the Brahmā's Request is concluded.

Pañcavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Group of Five.

10. Etadahosīti [V 3.0147] etaṃ ahosi, “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya”nti ayaṃ dhammadesanāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko udapādīti attho. Āḷāroti tassa nāmaṃ. Dīghapiṅgalo kiresa. So hi tuṅgasarīratāya dīgho, piṅgalacakkhutāya piṅgalo, tenassa “āḷāro”ti nāmaṃ ahosi. Kālāmoti gottaṃ. Paṇḍitoti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.284) paṇḍiccena samannāgato, samāpattipaṭilābhasaṃsiddhena adhigamabāhusaccasaṅkhātena paṇḍitabhāvena samannāgatoti attho. Byattoti veyyattiyena samannāgato, samāpattipaṭilābhapaccayena pārihārikapaññāsaṅkhātena byattabhāvena samannāgatoti attho. Medhāvīti ṭhānuppattiyā paññāya samannāgato. Atha vā medhāvīti tihetukapaṭisandhipaññāsaṅkhātāya taṃtaṃitikattabbatāpaññāsaṅkhātāya ca medhāya samannāgatoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Apparajakkhajātikoti samāpattiyā vikkhambhitattā nikkilesajātiko visuddhasatto. Ājānissatīti sallakkhessati paṭivijjhissati.

10. ‘This occurred to him’ means ‘this happened,’ that is, the thought arose, ‘To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?’ This is the meaning connected with the deliberation about teaching the Dhamma. Āḷāra was his name. It is said he was Dīghapiṅgala. For he was ‘long’ because of his tall body, and ‘tawny’ because of his tawny eyes; hence his name was Āḷāra. Kālāma was his clan name. ‘Paṇḍita’ means endowed with wisdom, that is, endowed with the quality of a wise person, which consists of extensive learning perfected through the acquisition of attainments. ‘Byatta’ means endowed with skill, that is, endowed with the quality of being skilled, which consists of practical wisdom due to the acquisition of attainments. ‘Medhāvī’ means endowed with wisdom that arises on the spot. Or, ‘medhāvī’ means endowed with intelligence (medhā) consisting of triple-rooted rebirth-linking wisdom and with intelligence consisting of wisdom for discerning particular functions; thus, the meaning here should be understood. ‘Apparajakkhajātiko’ means of undefiled nature, a pure being, because defilements have been suppressed by attainment. ‘Ājānissati’ means he will discern, he will penetrate.

Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādīti bhagavatopi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ uppajji. Bhagavā kira devatāya kathiteneva niṭṭhaṃ agantvā sayampi sabbaññutaññāṇena olokento ito sattamadivasamatthake kālaṃ katvā ākiñcaññāyatane nibbattoti addasa. Taṃ sandhāyāha “bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādī”ti. Mahājāniyoti sattadivasabbhantare pattabbamaggaphalato [M 3.0161] parihīnattā mahatī jāni parihāni assāti mahājāniyo. Akkhaṇe nibbattatthā idha dhammadesanaṭṭhānaṃ āgamanapādāpi natthi, athāhaṃ tattha gaccheyyaṃ, gantvā desiyamānaṃ dhammampissa sotuṃ sotapasādopi natthi, evaṃ mahājāniyo jātoti dasseti. Kiṃ pana bhagavatā taṃ attano buddhānubhāvena dhammaṃ ñāpetuṃ na sakkāti? Āma na sakkā, na hi paratoghosamantarena sāvakānaṃ dhammābhisamayo sambhavati, aññathā itarapaccayarahitassapi dhammābhisamayena bhavitabbaṃ, na ca taṃ atthi. Vuttañhetaṃ – “dveme, bhikkhave, paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāya parato ca ghoso ajjhattañca yonisomanasikāro”ti (a. ni. 2.127).

‘Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One’ means the knowledge of omniscience arose in the Blessed One. It is said that the Blessed One, not having come to a conclusion based solely on what the deity had said, himself surveyed with the knowledge of omniscience and saw that, having passed away on the seventh day from then, he had been reborn in the base of nothingness. Referring to this, it is said, ‘Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One.’ ‘Mahājāniyo’ (one who has suffered a great loss) means he was one who had suffered a great loss, a great falling away, because he was deprived of the path and fruit that could have been attained within seven days. Because he had been reborn at an inopportune time, there was no way for him to come here to a place where the Dhamma is taught. And even if I were to go there, having gone, he would not have the faculty of hearing to listen to the Dhamma being taught. Thus, it is shown that he had suffered a great loss. But could not the Blessed One make him understand the Dhamma by his own Buddha-power? Indeed, he could not. For the realization of the Dhamma by disciples does not occur without the voice of another. Otherwise, even one devoid of other conditions would have to attain Dhamma-realization, but that is not the case. For it has been said: ‘Monks, there are these two conditions for the arising of right view: the voice of another and wise attention internally’ (AN 2.127).

Udakoti tassa nāmaṃ, rāmassa pana puttatāya rāmaputto. Abhidosakālakatoti aḍḍharatte kālakato. Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādīti idhāpi kira bhagavā devatāya kathitavacanena sanniṭṭhānaṃ akatvā sabbaññutaññāṇena olokento “hiyyo aḍḍharatte kālaṃ katvā udako rāmaputto [V 3.0148] nevasaññānāsaññāyatane nibbatto”ti addasa, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

Udaka was his name; but as he was the son of Rāma, he was called Rāmaputta. ‘Abhidosakālakato’ means he passed away at midnight. ‘Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One’—here too, it is said, the Blessed One, without making a determination based solely on the words spoken by the deity, surveyed with his knowledge of omniscience and saw, ‘Yesterday at midnight Udaka Rāmaputta passed away and was reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ Therefore, it is stated thus. The rest is just as in the previous account.

Bahūpakārāti bahuupakārā. Padhānapahitattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsūti padhānatthāya pesitattabhāvaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne pariveṇasammajjanena pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā anubandhanena mukhodakadantakaṭṭhadānādinā ca upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Ke panete pañcavaggiyā nāma? Ye te –

‘Bahūpakārā’ means very supportive. ‘They supported him in his commitment to striving’ means they supported his state of having committed himself to striving by sweeping his dwelling place and monastic cell, by following him carrying his bowl and robe, and by providing water for his mouth, tooth-sticks, and so on. And who were these of the group of five? They were—

Rāmo dhajo lakkhaṇo cāpi mantī;

Koṇḍañño ca bhojo suyāmo sudatto;

Ete tadā aṭṭha ahesuṃ brāhmaṇā;

Chaḷaṅgavā mantaṃ viyākariṃsūti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.284; jā. aṭṭha. 1.nidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.avidūrenidānakathā);

Rāma, Dhaja, Lakkhaṇa, and also Mantī; Koṇḍañña, Bhoja, Suyāma, and Sudatta; These eight were brahmins at that time; They expounded the six-limbed Veda with its mantras.

Bodhisattassa jātakāle supinapaṭiggāhakā ceva lakkhaṇapaṭiggāhakā ca aṭṭha brāhmaṇā. Tesu tayo dvedhā byākariṃsu “imehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato agāraṃ ajjhāvasamāno rājā hohiti cakkavattī, pabbajamāno buddho”ti. Pañca brāhmaṇā ekaṃsabyākaraṇā ahesuṃ [M 3.0162] “imehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato agāre na tiṭṭhati, buddhova hotī”ti. Tesu purimā tayo yathāmantapadaṃ gatā. Ete hi lakkhaṇamantasaṅkhātavedavacanānurūpaṃ paṭipannā dve gatiyo bhavanti anaññāti vuttaniyāmena nicchinituṃ asakkontā vuttameva paṭipajjiṃsu, na mahāpurisassa buddhabhāvappattiṃ paccāsīsiṃsu. Ime pana koṇḍaññādayo pañca “ekaṃsato buddho bhavissatī”ti jātanicchayattā mantapadaṃ atikkantā. Te attanā laddhaṃ tuṭṭhidānaṃ ñātakānaṃ vissajjetvā “ayaṃ mahāpuriso agāre na ajjhāvasissati, ekantena buddho bhavissatī”ti nibbematikā bodhisattaṃ uddissa samaṇapabbajjaṃ pabbajitā, tesaṃ puttātipi vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ. Ete kira daharakāleva bahū mante jāniṃsu, tasmā ne brāhmaṇā ācariyaṭṭhāne ṭhapayiṃsu. Te “pacchā amhehi puttadārajaṭaṃ chinditvā na sakkā bhavissati pabbajitu”nti daharakāleyeva pabbajitvā ramaṇīyāni senāsanāni paribhuñjantā vicariṃsu. Kālena kālaṃ pana “kiṃ bho mahāpuriso mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto”ti pucchanti. Manussā “kuhiṃ tumhe mahāpurisaṃ passissatha, tīsu pāsādesu vividhanāṭakamajjhe devo viya sampattiṃ anubhotī”ti vadanti. Te sutvā “na tāva mahāpurisassa ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gacchatī”ti appossukkā vihariṃsuyeva.

At the time of the Bodhisatta’s birth, there were eight brahmins who received and interpreted dreams and marks. Among them, three gave a twofold prediction: ‘Endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, he will become a universal monarch; if he goes forth, he will become a Buddha.’ Five brahmins gave a definitive prediction: ‘Endowed with these marks, he will not remain in the household life—he will certainly become a Buddha.’ Of these, the first three followed the traditional interpretation of the mantras. For these, acting in accordance with the Vedic pronouncements consisting of marks and mantras, and being unable to decisively determine otherwise according to the stated principle that ‘there are two destinies, not another,’ adhered to what was stated. They did not anticipate the Great Being’s attainment of Buddhahood. But these five, beginning with Koṇḍañña, having come to the firm conclusion that ‘he will undoubtedly become a Buddha,’ transcended the traditional interpretation of the mantras. They, having distributed to their relatives the gifts they had received with delight, and being convinced that ‘this Great Being will not remain in the household life—he will certainly become a Buddha,’ went forth into the ascetic life for the sake of the Bodhisatta. Some say they were their sons, but this is refuted in the commentary. It is said that these five, even in their youth, mastered many mantras, and thus the brahmins placed them in the position of teachers. Thinking, ‘Later, it will not be possible for us to go forth after cutting off the tangle of wives and children,’ they renounced while still young and wandered, enjoying pleasant dwellings. From time to time, they would ask, ‘Has the Great Being gone forth in the great renunciation?’ People would reply, ‘Where would you see the Great Being? He enjoys splendor like a god amidst the three palaces, surrounded by various entertainments.’ Hearing this, they would say, ‘The Great Being’s wisdom has not yet matured,’ and they remained unconcerned.

Kasmā [V 3.0149] panettha bhagavā “bahukārā kho me pañcavaggiyā”ti āha. Kiṃ upakārakānaṃyeva esa dhammaṃ deseti, anupakārakānaṃ na desetīti? No na deseti. Paricayavasena hesa āḷārañceva kālāmaṃ udakañca rāmaputtaṃ olokesi. Etasmiṃ pana buddhakkhette ṭhapetvā aññāsikoṇḍaññaṃ añño paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ sacchikātuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Kasmā? Tathāvidhaupanissayattā. Pubbe kira puññakaraṇakāle dve bhātaro ahesuṃ. Te ca ekato sassaṃ akaṃsu. Tattha jeṭṭhassa “ekasmiṃ sasse nava vāre aggasassadānaṃ mayā dātabba”nti ahosi. So vappakāle bījaggaṃ nāma datvā gabbhakāle kaniṭṭhena saddhiṃ mantesi “gabbhakāle gabbhaṃ phāletvā dassāmī”ti. Kaniṭṭho “taruṇasassaṃ nāsetukāmosī”ti āha. Jeṭṭho kaniṭṭhassa ananuvattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā khettaṃ vibhajitvā attano koṭṭhāsato gabbhaṃ phāletvā khīraṃ nīharitvā sappiphāṇitena yojetvā adāsi, puthukakāle puthukaṃ kāretvā adāsi[M 3.0163], lāyane lāyanaggaṃ, veṇikaraṇe veṇaggaṃ, veṇiyo purisabhāravasena bandhitvā kalāpakaraṇe kalāpaggaṃ, khale kalāpānaṃ ṭhapanadivase khalaggaṃ, madditvā vīhīnaṃ rāsikaraṇadivase khalabhaṇḍaggaṃ, koṭṭhāgāre dhaññassa pakkhipanadivase koṭṭhagganti evaṃ ekasmiṃ sasse nava vāre aggadānaṃ adāsi. Kaniṭṭho pana khalato dhaññaṃ uddharitvā gahaṇadivase adāsi. Tesu jeṭṭho aññāsikoṇḍaññatthero jāto, kaniṭṭho subhaddaparibbājako. Iti ekasmiṃ sasse navannaṃ aggadānānaṃ dinnattā ṭhapetvā theraṃ añño paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ sacchikātuṃ samattho nāma natthi. “Navannaṃ aggadānānaṃ dinnattā”ti idañca tassa rattaññūnaṃ aggabhāvatthāya katābhinīhārānurūpaṃ pavattitasāvakapāramiyā ciṇṇante pavattitattā vuttaṃ. Tiṇṇampi hi bodhisattānaṃ taṃtaṃpāramiyā sikhāppattakāle pavattitaṃ puññaṃ apuññaṃ vā garutaravipākameva hoti, dhammassa ca sabbapaṭhamaṃ sacchikiriyāya vinā kathaṃ rattaññūnaṃ aggabhāvasiddhīti? “Bahukārā kho me pañcavaggiyā”ti idaṃ pana upakārānussaraṇamattakeneva vuttaṃ.

But why did the Blessed One say here, "The group of five monks has been very helpful to me"? Does he teach the Dhamma only to those who are helpful and not to those who are not? No, he does not fail to teach. It was out of familiarity that he considered both Āḷāra Kālāma and Udaka Rāmaputta. However, in this Buddha-field, apart from Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, there is no one else capable of realizing the Dhamma first. Why is that? Because of such supporting conditions. In the past, during the time of making merit, there were two brothers. They cultivated crops together. The elder brother thought, "In one harvest, I should give the choicest portion of the crop nine times." At the time of sowing, he gave the choicest seeds. When the grain was forming in the ear, he consulted with the younger brother, saying, "When the grain is forming in the ear, I will break it open and give it." The younger brother said, "Do you wish to destroy the young crop?" Knowing that the younger brother would not agree, the elder divided the field. From his own portion, he broke open the grain ears, extracted the milky sap, mixed it with ghee and molasses, and gave it. At the time of making flattened rice, he made and gave the choicest flattened rice. At the time of reaping, the choicest of the reaping. At the time of making sheaves, the choicest sheaf. He bound the sheaves according to a man's load and gave the choicest bundle. At the threshing floor, on the day of placing the bundles, he gave the choicest portion of the threshing floor. After threshing, on the day of heaping the grain, he gave the choicest portion of the heap. When the grain was stored in the granary, on the day of putting it in the granary, he gave the choicest portion of the granary. Thus, in one harvest, he gave the choicest portion nine times. The younger brother, however, took the grain from the threshing floor and gave it on the day of gathering. Of those two, the elder became the Venerable Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, and the younger became the wanderer Subhadda. Because of giving the choicest portions nine times in one harvest, apart from the elder, there is no one else capable of realizing the Dhamma first. The statement, "Because of giving the choicest portions nine times," was made because it accords with his aspiration for the foremost among those of long-standing, and because it was performed in the course of his disciple-perfection, which was developed in accordance with that aspiration. For all three Bodhisattas, at the time of reaching the peak of their respective perfections, the merit or demerit performed produces a very weighty result. And how could the foremost status among those of long-standing be achieved without the very first realization of the Dhamma? The statement, "The group of five monks has been very helpful to me," was said merely as a recollection of their help.

Isipatane migadāyeti tasmiṃ kira padese anuppanne buddhe paccekasambuddhā gandhamādanapabbate sattāhaṃ nirodhasamāpattiyā vītināmetvā nirodhā vuṭṭhāya nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā anotattadahe mukhaṃ dhovitvā pattacīvaramādāya ākāsena āgantvā nipatanti. Tattha cīvaraṃ pārupitvā nagare piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakiccā gamanakālepi tatoyeva uppatitvā gacchanti. Iti isayo ettha nipatanti uppatanti cāti taṃ ṭhānaṃ “isipatana”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ, migānaṃ pana abhayatthāya dinnattā “migadāyo”ti vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ “isipatane migadāye”ti. Aññe buddhā paṭhamaṃ dhammadesanatthāya gacchantā ākāsena gantvā tattheva otaranti, amhākaṃ pana bhagavā upakassa ājīvakassa upanissayaṃ disvā “upako imaṃ addhānaṃ [V 3.0150] paṭipanno, so maṃ disvā sallapitvā gamissati, atha puna nibbinno āgamma arahattaṃ sacchikarissatī”ti ñatvā aṭṭhārasayojanaṃ maggaṃ padasāva agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “yena bārāṇasī, tena cārikaṃ pakkāmī”ti.

At Isipatana in the Migadāya—it is said that in that place, before the appearance of a Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, after spending seven days in the attainment of cessation on the Gandhamādana mountain, would emerge from that attainment. Then, having chewed on a tooth-stick of nāga creeper, washed their mouths in Anotatta Lake, and taken their robes and bowls, they would come through the air to alight there. Having put on their robes, they would go for alms in the city. After completing their meal duties, at the time of departure, they would rise up from that very spot and depart. Thus, because sages alight and rise up here, that place came to be known as "Isipatana." And because it was given as a sanctuary for deer, it was called "Migadāya." Hence it is said, "at Isipatana in the Migadāya." Other Buddhas, when going to deliver their first teaching, would travel through the air and descend right there. But our Blessed One, seeing the supporting condition of Upaka the Ajīvaka, thought, "Upaka has entered upon this path; seeing me, he will converse and go on his way; then, later, becoming disenchanted, he will come back and realize arahantship." Knowing this, he went the eighteen-yojana path on foot. Hence it is said, "he set out on tour towards Bārāṇasī."

11. Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhinti gayāya ca bodhissa ca vivare tigāvutantare ṭhāne. Bodhimaṇḍato hi gayā tīṇi gāvutāni, bārāṇasī [M 3.0164] aṭṭhārasa yojanāni. Upako bodhimaṇḍassa ca gayāya ca antare bhagavantaṃ addasa. Antarā-saddena pana yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kataṃ. Īdisesu ca ṭhānesu akkharacintakā “antarā gāmañca nadiñca yātī”ti evaṃ ekameva antarā-saddaṃ payujjanti, so dutiyapadenapi yojetabbo hoti, ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti sāmivacanassa pasaṅge antarā-saddayogena upayogavacanassa icchitattā. Idha pana yojetvā eva vutto. Addhānamagganti addhānasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ, dīghamagganti attho. Addhānagamanasamayassa vibhaṅge “addhayojanaṃ gacchissāmīti bhuñjitabba”ntiādivacanato (pāci. 218) addhayojanampi addhānamaggo hoti. Bodhimaṇḍato pana gayā tigāvutaṃ. Vippasannānīti suṭṭhu pasannāni. Indriyānīti manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni. Parisuddhoti niddoso. Pariyodātoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Nirupakkilesatāyeva hi esa “pariyodāto”ti vutto, na setabhāvena. Etassa pariyodātataṃ disvāva indriyānaṃ vippasannataṃ aññāsi, nayaggāhīpaññā kiresā tassa ājīvakassa.

11. Between Gayā and the Bodhi tree: in the space of three gāvutas between Gayā and the Bodhi tree. For from the Bodhi seat, Gayā is three gāvutas away, and Bārāṇasī is eighteen yojanas. Upaka saw the Blessed One between the Bodhi seat and Gayā. But because the word "antarā" is connected with the two terms, the accusative case is used. In such places, grammarians use "antarā" only once, as in, "he goes between the village and the river," but it should be connected with the second term as well; if not connected, the accusative case is not obtained, because the accusative case is desired by the use of the word "antarā" in place of the genitive. Here, however, it is stated with connection. The path called 'addhāna' means a path reckoned as a journey, meaning a long path. In the analysis of the time for a journey, it is said, "One should eat thinking, 'I will go half a yojana,'" and so on (Pāc. 218); therefore, even half a yojana is a journey-path. From the Bodhi seat, Gayā is three gāvutas. "Vippasannāni" means 'very clear'. "Indriyāni" means the faculties with mind as the sixth. "Parisuddho" means 'faultless'. "Pariyodāto" is a synonym for that. Indeed, it is said to be "pariyodāto" because of its freedom from defilements, not because of whiteness. Having seen this purity, he recognized the clarity of his faculties; indeed, that Ajīvaka's wisdom was one that grasped the essence.

Sabbābhibhūti sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ abhibhavitvā ṭhito. Sabbavidūti sabbaṃ catubhūmakadhammaṃ avediṃ aññāsiṃ sabbaso ñeyyāvaraṇassa pahīnattā. Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalittoti sabbesu tebhūmakadhammesu rajjanadussanamuyhanādinā kilesalepena alitto. Sabbañjahoti sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ jahitvā ṭhito. Appahātabbampi hi kusalābyākataṃ tappaṭibaddhakilesappahānena pahīnattā na hotīti jahitameva hoti. Taṇhakkhaye vimuttoti taṇhakkhaye nibbāne ārammaṇakaraṇavasena vimutto. Sayaṃ abhiññāyāti sabbaṃ catubhūmakadhammaṃ attanāva jānitvā. Kamuddiseyyanti kaṃ aññaṃ “ayaṃ me ācariyo”ti uddiseyyaṃ.

Sabbābhibhū means 'having overcome all'; he stands having overcome all phenomena of the three realms. Sabbavidū means 'all-knowing'; I have fully understood and known all phenomena of the four realms because the obstruction to what is knowable has been entirely abandoned. Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitto means 'unstained in all things'; he is unstained by the defilement-stain of lust, aversion, delusion, and so on, in all phenomena of the three realms. Sabbañjaho means 'having relinquished all'; he stands having relinquished all phenomena of the three realms. Indeed, even the wholesome and indeterminate, which should not be abandoned, are considered abandoned because the defilements connected to them have been abandoned; therefore, they are indeed relinquished. Taṇhakkhaye vimutto means 'liberated through the destruction of craving'; he is liberated by making Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, his object. Sayaṃ abhiññāya means 'having realized by himself'; having known all phenomena of the four realms by himself. Kamuddiseyyaṃ means 'whom should I point out?'; whom else should I designate, saying, "This is my teacher?"

Na me ācariyo atthīti lokuttaradhamme mayhaṃ ācariyo nāma natthi. Kiñcāpi hi lokiyadhammānampi yādiso lokanāthassa adhigamo, na tādiso adhigamo parūpadeso atthi, lokuttaradhamme panassa lesopi natthi. Natthi me paṭipuggaloti mayhaṃ sīlādīhi guṇehi paṭinidhibhūto puggalo nāma natthi. Sammāsambuddhoti hetunā nayena cattāri saccāni sayaṃ buddho[V 3.0151]. Sītibhūtoti sabbakilesagginibbāpanena sītibhūto, kilesānaṃ yeva nibbutattā nibbuto.

Na me ācariyo atthi means 'I have no teacher'; in the supramundane Dhamma, there is no one who is my teacher. Indeed, although even in worldly matters, the attainment of the Lord of the World is not such as can be gained from another's instruction, in the supramundane Dhamma there is not even a trace of such instruction for him. Natthi me paṭipuggalo means 'there is no one equal to me'; there is no individual who could be my counterpart in virtues such as morality. Sammāsambuddho means 'the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One'; he is awakened to the four truths by himself by means of cause and method. Sītibhūto means 'cooled'; he is cooled by the extinguishing of all the fires of defilements, and because the defilements themselves are extinguished, he is extinguished.

Kāsinaṃ [M 3.0165] puranti kāsiraṭṭhe nagaraṃ. Āhañchanti āhanissāmi. Amatadundubhinti veneyyānaṃ amatādhigamāya ugghosanādiṃ katvā satthu dhammadesanā “amatadundubhī”ti vuttā, dhammacakkapaṭilābhāya taṃ amatabheriṃ paharissāmīti gacchāmīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Kāsinaṃ puranti means 'the city of the Kāsīs.' Āhañchanti means 'I will strike.' Amatadundubhinti means 'the drum of the Deathless'; the Teacher's teaching is called "the drum of the Deathless," having made a proclamation for the attainment of the Deathless by those capable of being guided. It is said, "I will go," meaning, "I will strike that drum of the Deathless in order to obtain the Wheel of Dhamma."

Arahasi anantajinoti anantajinopi bhavituṃ yuttoti attho. Anantañāṇo jitakilesoti anantajino. Hupeyyapāvusoti āvuso evampi nāma bhaveyya, evaṃvidhe nāma rūparatane īdisena ñāṇena bhavitabbanti adhippāyo. Ayañhissa pabbajjāya paccayo jāto. Katādhikāro hesa. Tathā hi bhagavā tena samāgamanatthaṃ padasāva taṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Pakkāmīti vaṅkahārajanapadaṃ nāma agamāsi.

Arahasi anantajinoti means 'it is fitting for you to be the Conqueror of the Infinite.' The Conqueror of the Infinite is one whose knowledge is infinite and who has conquered defilements. Hupeyyapāvusoti means: “Friend, it could indeed be so; in such a jewel of form, such wisdom should exist.” This was the cause for his going forth. For he had made a resolution. Indeed, the Blessed One himself set out on that path on foot to meet him. Pakkāmīti means he went to the country called Vaṅkahāra.

Tatthekaṃ migaluddakagāmakaṃ nissāya vāsaṃ kappesi, jeṭṭhakaluddako taṃ upaṭṭhāsi. Tasmiñca janapade caṇḍā makkhikā honti. Atha naṃ ekāya cāṭiyā vasāpesuṃ. Migaluddako dūraṃ migavaṃ gacchanto “amhākaṃ arahante mā pamajjī”ti cāpaṃ nāma dhītaraṃ āṇāpetvā agamāsi saddhiṃ puttabhātukehi. Sā cassa dhītā dassanīyā hoti koṭṭhāsasampannā. Dutiyadivase upako gharaṃ āgato taṃ dārikaṃ sabbaṃ upacāraṃ katvā parivisituṃ upagataṃ disvā rāgena abhibhūto bhuñjitumpi asakkonto bhājanena bhattaṃ ādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā bhattaṃ ekamantaṃ nikkhipitvā “sace cāpaṃ labhāmi, jīvāmi. No ce, marāmī”ti nirāhāro sayi. Sattame divase māgaviko āgantvā dhītaraṃ upakassa pavattiṃ pucchi. Sā “ekadivasameva āgantvā puna nāgatapubbo”ti āha.

There he took up residence dependent on a village of deer hunters, and the chief hunter attended to him. In that region, there were fierce flies. Then they made him dwell in a hut. The deer hunter, going far to hunt deer, instructed his daughter named Cāpā, saying, “Do not be negligent regarding our Arahant,” and left with his sons and brothers. His daughter was beautiful and well-proportioned. The next day, Upaka came to the house. Seeing the girl performing all the services and approaching to serve him, he was overcome by lust. Unable even to eat, he took the food in a bowl, went to his dwelling place, set the food aside, and lay down without eating, thinking, “If I obtain Cāpā, I will live. If not, I will die.” On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter about Upaka’s situation. She replied, “He came only one day and has not come again since.”

Māgaviko āgataveseneva naṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchissāmīti taṅkhaṇaṃyeva gantvā “kiṃ, bhante, aphāsuka”nti pāde parāmasanto pucchi. Upako nitthunanto parivattatiyeva. So “vada bhante, yaṃ mayā sakkā kātuṃ, sabbaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Upako “sace cāpaṃ labhāmi, jīvāmi, no ce, mayhameva maraṇaṃ seyyo”ti āha. Jānāsi kira, bhante, kiñci sippanti? Na jānāmīti. Na, bhante, kiñci sippaṃ ajānantena sakkā gharāvāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātunti. So āha “nāhaṃ kiñci sippaṃ jānāmi, apica [M 3.0166] tumhākaṃ maṃsahārako bhavissāmi, maṃsañca vikkiṇissāmī”ti. Māgaviko “amhākampi etadeva ruccatī”ti uttarasāṭakaṃ [V 3.0152] datvā gharaṃ ānetvā dhītaraṃ adāsi. Tesaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya putto vijāyi, “subhaddo”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Cāpā tassa rodanakāle “maṃsahārakassa putta migaluddakassa putta mā rodi mā rodī”tiādīni vadamānā puttatosanagītena upakaṃ uppaṇḍesi. “Bhadde tvaṃ maṃ anāthoti maññasi, atthi me anantajino nāma sahāyo, tassāhaṃ santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti āha. Cāpā “evamayaṃ aṭṭīyatī”ti ñatvā punappunaṃ kathesi. So ekadivasaṃ anārocetvāva majjhimadesābhimukho pakkāmi.

The hunter, thinking, “I will approach him in the guise of one just arrived and ask,” went up to him at once and, touching his feet, asked, “What is it, venerable sir, are you unwell?” Upaka groaned and just turned over. The hunter said, “Speak, venerable sir, whatever I can do, I will do it all.” Upaka replied, “If I obtain Cāpā, I will live; if not, death would be better for me.” “Do you know any craft, venerable sir?” “I know nothing.” “No, venerable sir, without knowing any craft, how can one maintain a household?” He said, “I know no craft, but I will become your meat-carrier and sell meat.” The hunter said, “That suits us too,” and gave him an upper garment, took him home, and gave him his daughter. Through their living together, a son was born, and they named him “Subhadda.” When the child cried, Cāpā would tease Upaka by saying, “Meat-carrier’s son, hunter’s son, don’t cry, don’t cry,” and so on; using a song to soothe the child, she mocked Upaka. “Good woman,” he said, “you think I am helpless, but I have a friend named Anantajina; I will go to him.” Cāpā, realizing that this troubled him, said it again and again. One day, without informing anyone, he set out toward the Middle Country.

Bhagavā ca tena samayena sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane, atha kho bhagavā paṭikacceva bhikkhū āṇāpesi “yo, bhikkhave, anantajinoti pucchamāno āgacchati, tassa maṃ dasseyyāthā”ti. Upakopi kho “kuhiṃ anantajino vasatī”ti pucchanto anupubbena sāvatthiṃ āgantvā vihāramajjhe ṭhatvā “kuhiṃ anantajino”ti pucchi. Taṃ bhikkhū bhagavato santikaṃ nayiṃsu. So ca bhagavantaṃ disvā “sañjānātha maṃ bhagavā”ti āha. Āma upaka sañjānāmi, kuhiṃ pana tvaṃ vasitthāti. Vaṅkahārajanapade, bhanteti. Upaka mahallakosi jāto, pabbajituṃ sakkhissasīti. Pabbajissāmi, bhanteti. Bhagavā pabbājetvā tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So kammaṭṭhāne kammaṃ karonto anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāya kālaṃ katvā avihesu nibbatto, nibbattikkhaṇeyeva ca arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Avihe nibbattamattā hi satta janā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, tesaṃ so aññataro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove. Then the Blessed One, beforehand, instructed the bhikkhus, saying, “Bhikkhus, if someone comes asking for Anantajina, you should show him to me.” Upaka, while asking, “Where does Anantajina dwell?” gradually arrived in Sāvatthī. Standing in the middle of the monastery, he asked, “Where is Anantajina?” The bhikkhus led him to the presence of the Blessed One. Upon seeing the Blessed One, he said, “Blessed One, do you recognize me?” “Yes, Upaka, I recognize you. But where have you been dwelling?” “In the Vaṅkahāra country, venerable sir.” “Upaka, you have grown old. Will you be able to go forth?” “I will go forth, venerable sir.” The Blessed One ordained him and gave him a meditation subject. Practicing the meditation subject, he became established in the fruit of non-returning and passed away. He was reborn in the Aviha realm, and at the very moment of rebirth, he attained arahantship. Indeed, seven beings who were reborn in Aviha attained arahantship immediately upon rebirth—he was one of them. And this was said:

“Avihaṃ upapannāse, vimuttā satta bhikkhavo;

Rāgadosaparikkhīṇā, tiṇṇā loke visattikaṃ.

“Seven bhikkhus reborn in Aviha are liberated; with lust and hatred utterly destroyed, they have crossed over attachment in the world.”

“Upako palagaṇḍo ca, pukkusāti ca te tayo;

Bhaddiyo khaṇḍadevo ca, bāhuraggi ca saṅgiyo;

Te hitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, dibbayogaṃ upaccagu”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.50, 105);

“Upaka, Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti, those three; Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi, and Saṅgiya; they, having abandoned the human body, went to the divine state.”

12. Saṇṭhapesunti “neva abhivādetabbo”tiādinā katikaṃ akaṃsu. Bāhullikoti cīvarabāhullādīnaṃ atthāya paṭipanno. Padhānavibbhantoti [M 3.0167] padhānato pubbe anuṭṭhitadukkaracaraṇato vibbhanto bhaṭṭho parihīno. Āvatto bāhullāyāti cīvarādibahubhāvatthāya āvatto. Apica kho āsanaṃ ṭhapetabbanti apica kho panassa uccakule nibbattassa āsanamattaṃ [V 3.0153] ṭhapetabbanti vadiṃsu. Asaṇṭhahantāti buddhānubhāvena buddhatejena abhibhūtā attano katikāya ṭhātuṃ asakkontā. Nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācarantīti “gotamā”ti ca “āvuso”ti ca vadanti, “āvuso gotama, mayaṃ uruvelāyaṃ padhānakāle tuyhaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vicarimha, mukhodakaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ adamha, vutthapariveṇaṃ sammajjimha, pacchā te ko vattapaṭipattiṃ akāsi, kacci amhesu pakkantesu na cintayitthā”ti evarūpaṃ kathaṃ kathentīti attho.

12. Saṇṭhapesunti means they made an agreement, beginning with, ‘He should not be greeted.’ Bāhullikoti means one who has undertaken the practice for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth. Padhānavibbhantoti means one who has strayed, fallen, or become deficient from striving, from the difficult practice not undertaken before. Āvatto bāhullāyāti means he has turned back for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth. Apica kho āsanaṃ ṭhapetabbanti means they said that at least a seat should be prepared for him, who was born into a high family. Asaṇṭhahantāti means that, being overpowered by the Buddha’s majesty and power, they were unable to stand by their own agreement. Nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācarantīti means they addressed him by name and with the term ‘friend,’ saying ‘Gotama’ and ‘friend,’ and speaking such words as: ‘Friend Gotama, at the time of striving in Uruvelā, we carried your bowl and robe, provided mouth-rinsing water and tooth-sticks, and swept the dwelling you had used. Later, who performed the services for you? Surely you were not troubled after we departed?’—this is the meaning.

Na cirassevāti acireneva. Kulaputtāti duvidhā kulaputtā jātikulaputtā ācārakulaputtā ca, ete pana ubhayathāpi kulaputtāyeva. Agārasmāti gharā. Agārāya hitaṃ agāriyaṃ, kasigorakkhādi kuṭumbaposanakammaṃ vuccati. Natthi ettha agāriyanti anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pabbajantīti upagacchanti upasaṅkamanti. Tadanuttaranti taṃ anuttaraṃ. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyassa pariyosānaṃ, arahattaphalanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa hi atthāya kulaputtā pabbajanti. Diṭṭheva dhammeti tasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanoyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā, aparappaccayaṃ katvāti attho. Upasampajja viharissathāti pāpuṇitvā sampādetvā viharissatha.

Na cirassevāti means 'in a short time.' Kulaputtāti: there are two kinds of sons of good family, sons of good family by birth and sons of good family by conduct; but these are both sons of good family. Agārasmāti means 'from the house.' Agāriyaṃ means 'what pertains to a house,' which is called household work such as farming and cattle-breeding for maintaining the family. Natthi ettha agāriyanti means anagāriyaṃ, 'the homeless life.' This is a designation for going forth. Pabbajantīti means 'they approach, they draw near.' Tadanuttaranti means 'that unsurpassed.' Brahmacariyapariyosānanti means 'the culmination of the holy life'; the culmination of the holy life of the path, that is, the fruit of arahantship, is meant. For this purpose, sons of good family go forth. Diṭṭheva dhammeti means 'in that very existence.' Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti means having realized it directly for oneself through higher knowledge, that is, having personally experienced it through one’s own wisdom, without reliance on another—this is the meaning. Upasampajja viharissathāti means 'having attained and accomplished it, you will abide.'

Iriyāyāti dukkarairiyāya. Paṭipadāyāti dukkarapaṭipattiyā. Dukkarakārikāyāti pasatapasatamuggayūsādiāharaṇādinā dukkarakaraṇena. Uttari manussadhammāti manussadhammato upari. Alaṃ ariyaṃ kātunti alamariyo, ariyabhāvāya samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti, ñāṇadassanameva ñāṇadassanaviseso, alamariyo ca so ñāṇadassanaviseso cāti alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso. Ñāṇadassananti ca dibbacakkhupi vipassanāpi maggopi phalampi paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi sabbaññutaññāṇampi vuccati. “Appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādhetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.311) hi ettha dibbacakkhu ñāṇadassanaṃ nāma. “Ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmetī”ti (dī. ni. 1.235) ettha [M 3.0168] vipassanāñāṇaṃ. “Abhabbā te ñāṇadassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāyā”ti (a. ni. 4.196) ettha maggo. “Ayamañño uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso adhigato phāsuvihāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.328) ettha phalaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi ‘akuppā me cetovimutti, ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo’”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 16) ettha paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi ‘sattāhakālakato āḷāro kālāmo’”ti (ma. ni. 1.284; 2.340; mahāva. 10) [V 3.0154] ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Idha pana sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhāno ariyamaggo sabbaññutaññāṇameva vā adhippetaṃ.

By 'conduct' (iriyāya) is meant difficult conduct. By 'practice' (paṭipadā) is meant difficult practice. By 'performing what is hard' (dukkarakārikāya) is meant the performance of difficult deeds such as consuming gruel made of parched grains and mung beans. By 'beyond human states' (uttari manussadhammā) is meant above the human state. By 'able to make noble' (alaṃ ariyaṃ kātuṃ) is meant 'noble-making' (alamariyo), that is, capable of nobility. 'Knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassana) is itself a special kind of knowledge and vision; and since that special kind is noble-making, it is called 'the noble-making special kind of knowledge and vision' (alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso). The term 'knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassana) is also used for the divine eye, insight, the path, the fruit, reviewing knowledge, and omniscient knowledge. For instance, in 'By being diligent, one develops knowledge and vision' (MN 1.311), 'knowledge and vision' refers to the divine eye. In 'He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision' (DN 1.235), it refers to insight knowledge. In 'They are incapable of the unsurpassed knowledge and vision for supreme awakening' (AN 4.196), it refers to the path. In 'This is another superhuman state, the noble-making special kind of knowledge and vision attained, a pleasant abiding' (MN 1.328), it refers to the fruit. In 'And then knowledge and vision arose in me: “My mind’s liberation is unshakeable; this is my last birth; now there is no more rebirth”' (SN 5.1081; Mhv. 16), it refers to reviewing knowledge. In 'And then knowledge and vision arose in me: “Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago”' (MN 1.284; 2.340; Mhv. 10), it refers to omniscient knowledge. Here, however, the Noble Path, which is the basis for omniscient knowledge, is intended, or else omniscient knowledge itself.

Abhijānātha me noti abhijānātha nu me. Evarūpaṃ pabhāvitametanti ettha evarūpaṃ vākyabhedanti attho, api nu ahaṃ uruvelāyaṃ padhāne tumhākaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ anukkaṇṭhanatthaṃ rattiṃ vā divā vā āgantvā “āvuso, mayaṃ yattha katthaci gamissāmāti mā vitakkayittha, mayhaṃ obhāso vā kammaṭṭhānanimittaṃ vā paññāyatī”ti evarūpaṃ kañci vacanabhedaṃ akāsinti adhippāyo. Te ekapadeneva satiṃ labhitvā uppannagāravā “addhā esa buddho jāto”ti saddahitvā “no hetaṃ bhante”ti āhaṃsu. Asakkhi kho bhagavā pañcavaggiye bhikkhū saññāpetunti bhagavā pañcavaggiye bhikkhū “buddho aha”nti jānāpetuṃ asakkhi. Aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhāpesunti aññāya arahattappattiyā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapesuṃ abhinīhariṃsu.

By 'Do you acknowledge me or not?' (abhijānātha me no) is meant 'Do you acknowledge me?' (abhijānātha nu me). Here, by 'Has such a thing been manifested by me?' (evarūpaṃ pabhāvitametaṃ) is meant 'Has such a kind of utterance been made?' The intention is: 'Did I, while striving at Uruvelā, come day or night for the sake of keeping you together and preventing your discouragement, and make any such utterance as, “Friends, do not think, ‘We will go somewhere else’; my radiance or a sign of my meditation object is appearing”?' They, gaining mindfulness with a single word and with reverence arisen, believed, 'Surely, this one has become a Buddha,' and replied, 'No, venerable sir.' By 'Indeed, the Blessed One was able to make the group of five monks understand' (asakkhi kho bhagavā pañcavaggiye bhikkhū saññāpetuṃ) is meant that the Blessed One was able to make the group of five monks know, 'I am the Buddha.' By 'They established their minds for final knowledge' (aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhāpesuṃ) is meant they directed their minds towards the attainment of arahantship.

Dhammacakkappavattanasuttavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion

13. Dveme, bhikkhave, antāti dve ime, bhikkhave, koṭṭhāsā, dve bhāgāti attho. Bhāgavacano hettha anta-saddo “pubbante ñāṇaṃ aparante ñāṇa”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. 1063) viya. Imassa pana padassa uccāraṇasamakālaṃ pavattanigghoso buddhānubhāvena heṭṭhā avīciṃ upari bhavaggaṃ patvā dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃyeva samaye paripakkakusalamūlā saccābhisambodhāya katādhikārā aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhā brahmāno samāgacchiṃsu. Pacchimadisāya sūriyo atthameti, pācīnadisāya āsāḷhanakkhattena yutto puṇṇacando uggacchati. Tasmiṃ samaye bhagavā [M 3.0169] dhammacakkappavattanasuttaṃ ārabhanto “dveme, bhikkhave, antā”tiādimāha.

13. By 'These two extremes, monks' (dveme, bhikkhave, antā) is meant 'these two divisions, monks, these two portions.' Here, the word 'extreme' (anta) is used in the sense of a portion, as in 'knowledge of the prior end, knowledge of the posterior end,' etc. (Dhs. 1063). However, at the very moment this phrase was uttered, a sound generated by the Buddha’s power, reaching downward to Avīci and upward to the peak of existence, pervading the ten-thousandfold world-system, stood firm. At that very time, eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, whose roots of merit were fully matured and who had made their aspiration for the realization of the truths, assembled. The sun was setting in the western direction, while in the eastern direction, the full moon, conjoined with the Āsāḷha constellation, was rising. At that time, the Blessed One, beginning the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, said, 'These two extremes, monks,' and so on.

Tattha pabbajitenāti gihibandhanaṃ chetvā pabbajjupagatena. Na sevitabbāti na vaḷañjetabbā nānuyuñjitabbā. Yo cāyaṃ kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogoti yo ca ayaṃ vatthukāmesu kilesakāmasukhassa anuyogo, kilesakāmasaṃyuttassa sukhassa anugatoti attho. Hīnoti lāmako. Gammoti gāmavāsīnaṃ santako tehi sevitabbatāya. Pothujjanikoti puthujjanena andhabālajanena āciṇṇo. Anariyoti na ariyo na visuddho na uttamo, na vā ariyānaṃ santako. Anatthasaṃhitoti na atthasaṃhito, hitasukhāvahakāraṇaṃ anissitoti attho. Attakilamathānuyogoti attano kilamathassa anuyogo, dukkhakaraṇaṃ dukkhuppādananti attho. Dukkhoti [V 3.0155] kaṇṭakāpassayaseyyādīhi attabādhanehi dukkhāvaho. Majjhimā paṭipadāti ariyamaggaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Maggo hi kāmasukhallikānuyogo eko anto, attakilamathānuyogo eko anto, ete dve ante na upeti na upagacchati, vimutto etehi antehi, tasmā “majjhimā paṭipadā”ti vuccati. Etesaṃ majjhe bhavattā majjhimā, vaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthikehi paṭipajjitabbato ca paṭipadāti, tathā lobho eko anto, doso eko anto. Sassataṃ ekaṃ antaṃ, ucchedo eko antoti purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

Here, by 'one who has gone forth' (pabbajitena) is meant one who has cut off the bonds of household life and embraced the homeless state. By 'not to be indulged in' (na sevitabbā) is meant not to be cultivated, not to be engaged in. By 'and this pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasures' (yo cāyaṃ kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogo) is meant this pursuit of pleasure connected with defilements in regard to material sensual objects, that is, the following after pleasure associated with the defilement of sensual desire. By 'low' (hīna) is meant inferior. By 'vulgar' (gamma) is meant belonging to village dwellers, because it is indulged in by them. By 'worldly' (pothujjanika) is meant practiced by ordinary folk, by the blind and foolish. By 'ignoble' (anariya) is meant not noble, not purified, not supreme, nor belonging to the noble ones. By 'unbeneficial' (anatthasaṃhita) is meant not connected to welfare, that is, not based on what is beneficial and conducive to happiness. By 'the pursuit of self-mortification' (attakilamathānuyogo) is meant the pursuit of one's own affliction, that is, causing suffering and producing pain. By 'painful' (dukkha) is meant bringing suffering through self-torments such as lying on a bed of thorns. The 'Middle Path' (majjhimā paṭipadā) is stated with reference to the Noble Path. For the path does not approach or go to these two extremes—the pursuit of sensual indulgence being one extreme, and the pursuit of self-mortification being the other extreme; it is free from these extremes. Therefore, it is called 'the Middle Path.' Because it exists in the middle of these, it is the middle; and because it is to be practiced by those seeking escape from the suffering of the round of rebirth, it is called the path. Similarly, greed is one extreme, hatred is another. Eternalism is one extreme, annihilationism is another—this should be elaborated in the same manner as before.

Cakkhukaraṇītiādīhi tameva paṭipadaṃ thometi. Paññācakkhuṃ karotīti cakkhukaraṇī. Sā hi catunnaṃ saccānaṃ dassanāya saṃvattati pariññābhisamayādibhedassa dassanassa pavattanaṭṭhenāti “cakkhukaraṇī”ti vuccati. Tayidaṃ satipi paṭipadāya anaññatte avayavavasena sijjhamāno attho samudāyena kato nāma hotīti upacāravasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dutiyapadaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Upasamāyāti kilesupasamatthāya. Abhiññāyāti catunnaṃ saccānaṃ abhijānanatthāya. Sambodhāyāti tesaṃyeva sambujjhanatthāya. Nibbānāyāti nibbānasacchikiriyāya. Atha vā nibbānāyāti anupādisesanibbānāya. “Upasamāyā”ti hi iminā saupādisesanibbānaṃ gahitaṃ.

With the phrase 'vision-producing' (cakkhukaraṇī), etc., that same path is praised. It is 'vision-producing' because it produces the eye of wisdom. For it conduces to the seeing of the four truths, in the sense of bringing about seeing which is differentiated as full understanding, penetration, etc.; hence, it is called 'vision-producing.' Although there is no otherness from the path itself, the meaning here is accomplished by way of its components, and thus it should be seen as spoken of figuratively, as if the whole is made up of its parts. The second term is a synonym for this. By 'for the sake of peace' (upasamāya) is meant for the pacification of defilements. By 'for direct knowledge' (abhiññāya) is meant for the thorough knowledge of the four truths. By 'for awakening' (sambodhāya) is meant for the awakening to those very truths. By 'for Nibbāna' (nibbānāya) is meant for the realization of Nibbāna. Alternatively, by 'for Nibbāna' is meant Nibbāna without residue. For with 'for the sake of peace,' Nibbāna with residue is taken.

Idāni [M 3.0170] taṃ majjhimappaṭipadaṃ sarūpato dassetukāmo “katamā ca sā”ti pucchitvā “ayamevā”tiādinā nayena vissajjesi. Tattha ayamevāti avadhāraṇavacanaṃ aññassa nibbānagāmimaggassa atthibhāvapaṭisedhanatthaṃ. Sattāpaṭikkhepo hi idha paṭisedhanaṃ alabbhamānattā aññassa maggassa. Ariyoti kilesānaṃ ārakattā ariyo niruttinayena. Aripahānāya saṃvattatītipi ariyo arayo pāpadhammā yanti apagacchanti etenāti katvā. Ariyena bhagavatā desitattā ariyassa ayantipi ariyo, ariyabhāvappaṭilābhāya saṃvattatītipi ariyo. Ettha pana ariyakaro ariyotipi uttarapadalopena ariya-saddasiddhi veditabbā. Aṭṭhahi aṅgehi upetattā aṭṭhaṅgiko. Maggaṅgasamudāye hi maggavohāro, samudāyo ca samudāyīhi samannāgato nāma hoti. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – attano avayavabhūtāni aṭṭhaṅgāni etassa santīti aṭṭhaṅgikoti. Paramatthato pana aṅgāniyeva maggo pañcaṅgikatūriyādīni viya, na ca aṅgavinimutto chaḷaṅgo vedo viya. Kilese mārento gacchatīti maggo niruttinayena, nibbānaṃ maggati gavesatīti vā maggo. Ariyamaggo hi nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karonto gavesanto viya hoti. Nibbānatthikehi maggīyatīti vā maggo vivaṭṭūpanissayapuññakaraṇato [V 3.0156] paṭṭhāya tadatthapaṭipattito. Gammati vā tehi paṭipajjīyatīti maggo. Ettha pana ādiantavipariyāyena saddasiddhi veditabbā.

Now, wishing to show that middle path in its true form, he asked, “What is that?” and then answered, “This very one,” and so on. Here, the word 'this very one' is a term of determination for the purpose of denying the existence of any other path leading to Nibbāna. For here, the denial is not a rejection of something existent, since another path is not found. It is noble (ariya) because it is far from defilements, according to etymology. It is also noble because it conduces to the abandoning of enemies (ari), meaning that evil states depart by means of it. Or, it is noble because it was taught by the Noble One, the Blessed One, and because it belongs to the noble one; it is also noble because it leads to the attainment of nobility. Here, however, the formation of the word 'ariya' should be understood as from 'ariyakaro' (making one noble), by the elision of the latter part. It is eight-factored (aṭṭhaṅgiko) because it is endowed with eight factors. Indeed, the designation 'path' applies to the collection of path-factors, and a collection is said to be possessed of its constituents. Here, the meaning of the word is: 'This possesses its own eight constituent parts,' hence it is 'eight-factored.' Ultimately, however, the factors themselves are the path, like a five-factored musical instrument, and not something devoid of factors like the Veda with its six auxiliaries. Etymologically, it is called a path (maggo) because it goes while destroying defilements, or because it seeks Nibbāna. Indeed, the Noble Path, taking Nibbāna as its object, is as if seeking it. Alternatively, it is called a path because it is sought by those who aim for Nibbāna, starting from the performance of merit that serves as a support for turning away from the round of existence and from the practice directed toward that goal. Or, it is a path because it is travelled by them, because it is practiced by them. Here, however, the formation of the word should be understood by the reversal of beginning and end.

Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa katamo so iti ceti attho, katamāni vā tāni aṭṭhaṅgānīti. Sabbaliṅgavibhattivacanasādhāraṇo hi ayaṃ nipāto. Ekamekampi aṅgaṃ maggoyeva. Yathāha “sammādiṭṭhi maggo ceva hetu cā”ti (dha. sa. 1039). Porāṇāpi bhaṇanti “dassanamaggo sammādiṭṭhi, abhiniropanamaggo sammāsaṅkappo…pe… avikkhepamaggo sammāsamādhī”ti. Nanu ca aṅgāni samuditāni maggo antamaso sattaṅgavikalassa ariyamaggassa abhāvatoti? Saccametaṃ saccasampaṭivedhe, maggappaccayatāya pana yathāsakaṃ kiccakaraṇena paccekampi tāni maggoyeva, aññathā samuditānampi tesaṃ maggakiccaṃ na sambhaveyyāti. Sammādiṭṭhiādīsu sammā passatīti sammādiṭṭhi, sammā saṅkappeti sampayuttadhamme [M 3.0171] nibbānasaṅkhāte ārammaṇe abhiniropetīti sammāsaṅkappo, sammā vadati etāyāti sammāvācā, sammā karoti etenāti sammākammaṃ, tadeva sammākammanto, sammā ājīvati etenāti sammāājīvo, sammā vāyamati ussahatīti sammāvāyāmo, sammā sarati anussaratīti sammāsati, sammā samādhiyati cittaṃ etenāti sammāsamādhīti evaṃ nibbacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Idāni ayaṃ kho sā bhikkhaveti tameva paṭipadaṃ nigamento āha. Tassattho – yvāyaṃ cattāropi lokuttaramagge ekato katvā kathito aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, ayaṃ kho sā bhikkhave…pe… nibbānāya saṃvattatīti.

The particle 'seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable. Its meaning is 'what is that?' or 'what are those eight factors?' Indeed, this indeclinable is common to all genders, cases, and numbers. Each individual factor is itself the path. As it is said: 'Right view is both the path and a cause' (Dhs. 1039). The ancients also say: 'The path of seeing is right view, the path of application is right intention… and so on… the path of non-distraction is right concentration.' But is it not so that the factors, when combined, form the path, since the Noble Path does not exist if it is deficient by even one factor? This is indeed true in the penetration of the truths. However, in terms of being conditions for the path, each one individually is itself the path by performing its own function; otherwise, even when combined, their path-function would not be possible. In the case of right view and so on, the derivation of these terms should be understood thus: one sees rightly, hence right view; one intends rightly, applying the associated states to the object called Nibbāna, hence right intention; one speaks rightly by means of this, hence right speech; one acts rightly by means of this, hence right action (sammākammaṃ), and that itself is right action (sammākammanto); one lives rightly by means of this, hence right livelihood; one strives rightly and endeavors, hence right effort; one is rightly mindful and recollects, hence right mindfulness; the mind is rightly concentrated by means of this, hence right concentration. Now, the phrase 'This, bhikkhus, is that...' was spoken to conclude concerning that very path. Its meaning is: 'That very eight-factored path, which has been spoken of by combining all four supramundane paths, is the one, bhikkhus… leading to Nibbāna.'

14. Evaṃ majjhimapaṭipadaṃ sarūpato dassetvā idāni cattāri ariyasaccāni dassetuṃ “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha (visuddhi. 2.530) dukkhanti ettha du-iti ayaṃ saddo kucchite dissati. Kucchitañhi puttaṃ “duputto”ti vadanti, khaṃ-saddo pana tucche. Tucchañhi ākāsaṃ “kha”nti vuccati. Idañca paṭhamasaccaṃ kucchitaṃ anekaupaddavādhiṭṭhānato, tucchaṃ bālajanaparikappitadhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitato, tasmā kucchitattā tucchattā ca “dukkha”nti vuccati. Yasmā panetaṃ buddhādayo ariyā paṭivijjhanti, tasmā “ariyasacca”nti vuccati. Ariyapaṭivijjhitabbañhi saccaṃ purimapade uttarapadalopena “ariyasacca”nti vuttaṃ. Ariyassa tathāgatassa saccantipi ariyasaccaṃ. Tathāgatena hi sayaṃ adhigatattā paveditattā tato eva ca aññehi adhigamanīyattā taṃ tassa hotīti. Atha vā etassa abhisambuddhattā ariyabhāvasiddhito ariyasādhakaṃ saccantipi ariyasaccaṃ pubbe viya uttarapadalopena[V 3.0157]. Avitathabhāvena vā araṇīyattā adhigantabbattā ariyaṃ saccantipi ariyasaccaṃ. Saccatthaṃ pana catunnampi saccānaṃ parato ekajjhaṃ dassayissāma.

14. Having thus shown the Middle Way in its true nature, he now spoke beginning with 'Now this, bhikkhus' (idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave) in order to present the Four Noble Truths. Herein (Visuddhimagga 2.530), regarding 'dukkha': here the syllable 'du-' is seen in the sense of 'despicable.' For a despicable son is called 'duputta' (bad son), and the syllable 'kha' means 'void.' For the void sky is called 'kha.' And this first truth is despicable because it is the ground of many troubles, and void because it is devoid of the lasting, beautiful, and happy nature imagined by foolish people. Therefore, because it is despicable and void, it is called 'dukkha.' But because this is penetrated by the noble ones such as the Buddhas, it is called 'ariyasacca' (Noble Truth). For the truth to be penetrated by the noble ones is called 'ariyasacca' by the elision of the latter part of the preceding member in the compound. Or, 'ariyasacca' is the truth of the noble Tathāgata. For because the Tathāgata has realized it himself, declared it, and because others can realize it through him, it belongs to him. Or alternatively, because of his full enlightenment of it, and because it establishes the noble state, it is called 'ariyasacca' (truth that establishes nobility), as before, by the elision of the latter part. Or, because it is true in an undeniable way, and because it is to be attained, it is called 'ariyasacca' (noble truth). As for the meaning of truth, however, we will explain the four truths together later.

Idāni taṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “jātipi dukkhā”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ jāti-saddo anekattho. Tathā hesa “ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo”ti (dī. ni. 1.31; ma. ni. 1.148) ettha bhave āgato. “Atthi, visākhe, nigaṇṭhā nāma samaṇajātī”ti (a. ni. 3.71) ettha nikāye. “Jāti dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahitā”ti (dhātu. 71) ettha saṅkhatalakkhaṇe. “Yaṃ mātukucchismiṃ paṭhamaṃ cittaṃ [M 3.0172] uppannaṃ paṭhamaṃ viññāṇaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, tadupādāya sāvassa jātī”ti (mahāva. 124) ettha paṭisandhiyaṃ. “Sampatijāto, ānanda, bodhisatto”ti (dī. ni. 2.31; ma. ni. 3.207) ettha pasūtiyaṃ. “Akkhitto anupakuṭṭho jātivādenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.303) ettha kule. Svāyamidha gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya yāva mātukucchimhā nikkhamanaṃ, tāva pavattesu khandhesu, itaresaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇesvevāti daṭṭhabbo. Ayampi ca pariyāyakathāva, nippariyāyato pana tattha tattha nibbattamānānaṃ sattānaṃ ye khandhā pātubhavanti, tesaṃ paṭhamapātubhāvo jāti nāma.

Now, to show that Noble Truth of suffering in its true nature, he spoke beginning with 'Birth is suffering' (jātipi dukkhā). Herein, the word 'jāti' has many meanings. Thus, in 'one birth or two births' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.31; Majjhima Nikāya 1.148), it refers to existence. In 'There is, Visākha, a class of ascetics called Nigaṇṭhas' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.71), it refers to a group. In 'Jāti is included by two aggregates' (Dhātukathā 71), it refers to the characteristic of the conditioned. In 'The first mind arisen in the mother’s womb, the first consciousness manifested, from that the being's birth arises' (Mahāvagga 124), it refers to rebirth-linking. In 'The Bodhisatta is just born, Ānanda' (Dīgha Nikāya 2.31; Majjhima Nikāya 3.207), it refers to parturition. In 'Not reviled, not reproached on account of birth' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.303), it refers to family. Here, for those lying in the womb, it should be understood as referring to the aggregates that occur from rebirth-linking until emerging from the mother’s womb; while for others, it is only at the moment of rebirth-linking. This, however, is a figurative explanation; in a direct sense, the first manifestation of the aggregates that appear for beings being born in this or that state is called 'jāti' (birth).

Kasmā panesā dukkhāti ce? Anekesaṃ dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvato. Anekāni hi dukkhāni. Seyyathidaṃ – dukkhadukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ saṅkhāradukkhaṃ paṭicchannadukkhaṃ appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ pariyāyadukkhaṃ nippariyāyadukkhanti. Tattha kāyikacetasikā dukkhā vedanā sabhāvato ca nāmato ca dukkhattā dukkhadukkhanti vuccati. Sukhā vedanā vipariṇāmadukkhuppattihetuto vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ. Upekkhā vedanā ceva sesā ca tebhūmakā saṅkhārā udayabbayapīḷitattā saṅkhāradukkhaṃ. Kaṇṇasūladantasūlarāgajapariḷāhadosajapariḷāhādikāyikacetasikā ābādhā pucchitvā jānitabbato upakkamassa ca apākaṭabhāvato paṭicchannadukkhaṃ. Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇādisamuṭṭhāno ābādho apucchitvāva jānitabbato upakkamassa ca pākaṭabhāvato appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ. Ṭhapetvā dukkhadukkhaṃ sesadukkhaṃ saccavibhaṅge āgataṃ jātiādi sabbampi tassa tassa dukkhassa vatthubhāvato pariyāyadukkhaṃ. Dukkhadukkhaṃ pana nippariyāyadukkhanti vuccati. Tatrāyaṃ jāti yaṃ taṃ bālapaṇḍitasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 3.246 ādayo) bhagavatāpi upamāvasena pakāsitaṃ āpāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yañca sugatiyampi manussaloke gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tassa vatthubhāvato dukkhā. Tenāhu porāṇā –

But why is it called suffering? Because it is the basis for many kinds of suffering. Indeed, there are many kinds of suffering. Namely: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, the suffering of formations, concealed suffering, unconcealed suffering, indirect suffering, and direct suffering. Herein, bodily and mental painful feelings are called the suffering of suffering because they are suffering by nature and by name. Pleasant feelings are the suffering of change because they are the cause for the arising of suffering upon their change. Neutral feelings and all other formations in the three realms are the suffering of formations because they are oppressed by arising and passing away. Bodily and mental afflictions such as earache, toothache, the fever of lust, the fever of hatred, and so on, are concealed suffering because they must be known by asking and because the means of remedy is not obvious. Afflictions arising from the thirty-two kinds of torture and so forth are unconcealed suffering because they are known without asking and the means of remedy is obvious. Except for the suffering of suffering, all other suffering mentioned in the Analysis of the Truths—such as birth and so on—are indirect suffering because they are the basis for each respective suffering. However, the suffering of suffering is called direct suffering. Herein, this birth is suffering because it is the basis for that suffering in the lower realms, which the Blessed One has also explained by way of simile in the Sutta on the Foolish and the Wise and others, and for the suffering that arises even in happy destinations, in the human world, such as that rooted in conception. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Jāyetha [V 3.0158] no ce narakesu satto;

Tatthaggidāhādikamappasayhaṃ;

Labhetha dukkhaṃ na kuhiṃ patiṭṭhaṃ;

Iccāha dukkhāti munīdha jātiṃ.

“If a being were not born in the hells, they would not there obtain unbearable suffering such as burning by fire, nor find a foothold anywhere. Thus the Sage here declares birth to be suffering.”

“Dukkhaṃ [M 3.0173] tiracchesu kasāpatoda-

Daṇḍābhighātādibhavaṃ anekaṃ;

Yaṃ taṃ kathaṃ tattha bhaveyya jātiṃ;

Vinā tahiṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā.

“That manifold suffering among animals, arising from whips, goads, blows with sticks, and the like—how could it exist there without birth? Therefore, on that account also, birth is suffering.”

“Petesu dukkhaṃ pana khuppipāsā-

Vātātapādippabhavaṃ vicittaṃ;

Yasmā ajātassa na tattha atthi;

Tasmāpi dukkhaṃ muni jātimāha.

“Among the departed, suffering arises in various forms—from hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and the like. Since for one who is unborn, none of that exists there, therefore, the Sage declares birth to be suffering.”

“Tibbandhakāre ca asayha sīte;

Lokantare yaṃ asuresu dukkhaṃ;

Na taṃ bhave tattha na cassa jāti;

Yato ayaṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā.

“And that suffering among the asuras in the world-interstice, in thick darkness and unbearable cold—that would not exist there if there were no birth for them. Since there is this birth, on that account also it is suffering.”

“Yañcāpi gūthanarake viya mātu gabbhe;

Satto vasaṃ ciramato bahi nikkhamañca;

Pappoti dukkhamatighoramidampi natthi;

Jātiṃ vinā itipi jāti ayañhi dukkhā.
