“And also, just as in a hell of excrement, so in the mother's womb, a being dwells long, and then comes forth from it. He encounters most terrible suffering, and this too would not exist without birth. Therefore, this birth is indeed suffering.”

“Kiṃ bhāsitena bahunā nanu yaṃ kuhiñci;

Atthīdha kiñcidapi dukkhamidaṃ kadāci;

Nevatthi jātivirahena yato mahesi;

Dukkhāti sabbapaṭhamaṃ imamāha jāti”nti. (visuddhi. 2.541; vibha. aṭṭha. 191; mahāni. aṭṭha. 5; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.32-33);

“What use is much speaking? Surely, whatever suffering exists here anywhere, at any time, none of it exists in the absence of birth. Therefore, O Great Sage, you declared this birth to be suffering first of all.”

Jarāpi [V 3.0159] dukkhāti ettha pana duvidhā jarā saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca khaṇḍiccādisammato santatiyaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannakkhandhapurāṇabhāvo ca, sā idha adhippetā. Sā panesā jarā saṅkhāradukkhabhāvato ceva dukkhavatthuto ca dukkhā. Yañhi aṅgapaccaṅgasithilabhāvaindriyavikāravirūpatāyobbanavināsavīriyāvisādasatimativippavāsaparaparibhavādianekapaccayaṃ kāyikacetasikaṃ dukkhamuppajjati, jarā tassa vatthu. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Herein, regarding ‘Old age, too, is suffering,’ old age is twofold: the characteristic of the conditioned, and the state of becoming old of the aggregates pertaining to a single existence in the continuity, which is manifest as brokenness of teeth, etc. It is the latter that is intended here. This old age is suffering both because it is the suffering of formations and because it is a basis for suffering. For old age is the basis for the bodily and mental suffering that arises from many causes, such as the slackening of the major and minor limbs, the impairment of the faculties, disfigurement, the destruction of youth, the decline of energy, the fading of memory and intelligence, and contempt from others. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Aṅgānaṃ sithilībhāvā, indriyānaṃ vikārato;

Yobbanassa vināsena, balassa upaghātato.

“From the slackening of the limbs, from the impairment of the faculties; from the destruction of youth, from the decline of strength.”

“Vippavāsā [M 3.0174] satādīnaṃ, puttadārehi attano;

Appasādanīyato ceva, bhiyyo bālattapattiyā.

“From the fading of memory and so on, from being unpleasing to one’s own sons and wives, and further, from the attainment of senility.”

“Pappoti dukkhaṃ yaṃ macco, kāyikaṃ mānasaṃ tathā;

Sabbametaṃ jarāhetu, yasmā tasmā jarā dukhā”ti. (visuddhi. 2.542; vibha. aṭṭha. 192; mahāni. aṭṭha. 5; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.32-33);

“Whatever suffering a mortal experiences, whether physical or mental, all of this has old age as its cause; therefore, old age is suffering.”

Byādhipi dukkhoti idaṃ padaṃ vibhaṅge dukkhasaccaniddesapāḷiyaṃ na āgataṃ, teneva visuddhimaggepi dukkhasaccaniddese taṃ na uddhaṭaṃ, dhammacakkapavattanasuttantapāḷiyaṃyeva pana upalabbhati, tasmā tatthevimassa vacane aññattha ca avacane kāraṇaṃ vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

‘Illness, too, is suffering’—this phrase is not found in the Pāli text of the Vibhaṅga's exposition on the truth of suffering. For that same reason, it is not cited in the Visuddhimagga's exposition on the truth of suffering either. However, it is found only in the Pāli text of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Therefore, the reason for its inclusion there and its exclusion elsewhere should be investigated.

Maraṇampi dukkhanti etthāpi duvidhaṃ maraṇaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “jarāmaraṇaṃ dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahita”nti (dhātu. 71). Ekabhavapariyāpannajīvitindriyappabandhavicchedo ca. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “niccaṃ maraṇato bhaya”nti (su. ni. 581; jā. 1.11.88), taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Jātipaccayamaraṇaṃ upakkamamaraṇaṃ sarasamaraṇaṃ āyukkhayamaraṇaṃ puññakkhayamaraṇantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Tayidaṃ dukkhassa vatthubhāvato dukkhanti veditabbaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Herein, regarding ‘Death, too, is suffering,’ death is twofold. There is the characteristic of the conditioned, regarding which it is said: “Aging and death are included in two aggregates.” And there is the cutting off of the continuity of the life faculty pertaining to a single existence, regarding which it is said: “There is constant fear of death.” It is the latter that is intended here. Death conditioned by birth, death by external means, natural death, death by the exhaustion of lifespan, and death by the exhaustion of merit are also names for this. This should be understood as suffering because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Pāpassa [V 3.0160] pāpakammādi-nimittamanupassato;

Bhaddassāpasahantassa, viyogaṃ piyavatthukaṃ;

Mīyamānassa yaṃ dukkhaṃ, mānasaṃ avisesato.

“The mental suffering, especially, of one who is dying—whether of a wicked person seeing the sign of their evil deeds and so on, or of a good person who cannot bear separation from beloved things.”

“Sabbesañcāpi yaṃ sandhi-bandhanacchedanādikaṃ;

Vitujjamānamammānaṃ, hoti dukkhaṃ sarīrajaṃ.

“And for all, the bodily suffering that arises from the cutting of joints and ligaments and so on, as the vital spots are being pierced.”

“Asayhamappaṭikāraṃ, dukkhassetassidaṃ yato;

Maraṇaṃ vatthu tenetaṃ, dukkhamicceva bhāsita”nti. (visuddhi. 2.543; vibha. aṭṭha. 193; mahāni. aṭṭha. 5; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.32-33);

“Since death is the basis of this unbearable and irremediable suffering, therefore it is declared to be suffering.”

Imasmiñca ṭhāne “sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsāpi dukkhā”ti vibhaṅge dukkhasaccaniddese āgataṃ, idha pana taṃ natthi, tatthāpi kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ.

In this place, the phrase “Sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair are also suffering” is found in the Vibhaṅga's exposition on the truth of suffering. Here, however, it is absent, and the reason for that also should be sought.

Appiyehi sampayogo dukkhoti ettha appiyasampayogo nāma amanāpehi sattasaṅkhārehi samodhānaṃ. Sopi dukkhavatthuto dukkho. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Herein, regarding ‘Association with the disliked is suffering,’ ‘association with the disliked’ means union with disagreeable beings and formations. That too is suffering because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Disvāva [M 3.0175] appiye dukkhaṃ, paṭhamaṃ hoti cetasi;

Tadupakkamasambhūta-matha kāye yato idha.

“Upon seeing the unpleasant, suffering first arises in the mind; then, born from that affliction, it arises here in the body.”

“Tato dukkhadvayassāpi, vatthuto so mahesinā;

Dukkho vuttoti viññeyyo, appiyehi samāgamo”ti.

“Therefore, that association with the unpleasant is to be understood as declared by the Great Seer as suffering, because it is the basis for both kinds of suffering.”

Piyehi vippayogo dukkhoti ettha pana piyavippayogo nāma manāpehi sattasaṅkhārehi vinābhāvo. Sopi sokadukkhassa vatthuto dukkho. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Herein, regarding ‘Separation from the beloved is suffering,’ ‘separation from the beloved’ means being parted from agreeable beings and formations. That too is suffering because it is a basis for the suffering of sorrow. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Ñātidhanādiviyogā;

Sokasarasamappitā vitujjanti;

Bālā [V 3.0161] yato tatoyaṃ;

Dukkhoti mato piyavippayogo”ti.

“Because fools are pierced by the arrow of grief due to separation from relatives, wealth, and so on, therefore, this separation from the beloved is considered suffering.”

Yampicchaṃ na labhatīti ettha “aho vata mayaṃ na jātidhammā assāmā”tiādīsu alabbhaneyyavatthūsu icchāva “yampicchaṃ na labhati, tampi dukkha”nti vuttā, sāpi dukkhavatthuto dukkhā. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Herein, regarding ‘Not getting what one desires,’ in cases such as “Oh, if only we were not subject to birth!” and so on, regarding unattainable things, the desire itself is called “Not getting what one desires, that too is suffering.” That too is suffering because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Taṃ taṃ patthayamānānaṃ, tassa tassa alābhato;

Yaṃ vighātamayaṃ dukkhaṃ, sattānaṃ idha jāyati.

“For beings longing for this and that, due to not obtaining each respective thing, whatever suffering of frustration arises here.”

“Alabbhaneyyavatthūnaṃ, patthanā tassa kāraṇaṃ;

Yasmā tasmā jino dukkhaṃ, icchitālābhamabravī”ti.

“The longing for unattainable things is its cause. Therefore, the Conqueror declared the non-obtaining of what is desired as suffering.”

Saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhāti ettha pana yasmā indhanamiva pāvako, lakkhamiva paharaṇāni, gorūpaṃ viya ḍaṃsamakasādayo, khettamiva lāyakā, gāmaṃ viya gāmaghātakā, upādānakkhandhapañcakameva jātiādayo nānappakārehi vibādhentā tiṇalatādīni viya bhūmiyaṃ, pupphaphalapallavāni viya rukkhesu upādānakkhandhesuyeva nibbattanti, upādānakkhandhānañca ādidukkhaṃ jāti, majjhedukkhaṃ jarā, pariyosānadukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ, manorathavighātappattānañca icchāvighātadukkhaṃ icchitālābhoti evaṃ nānappakārato upaparikkhiyamānā upādānakkhandhāva dukkhāti yadetaṃ ekamekaṃ dassetvā vuccamānaṃ anekehipi kappehi na sakkā anavasesato vattuṃ, tasmā taṃ sabbampi dukkhaṃ ekajalabindumhi sakalasamuddajalarasaṃ viya yesu kesuci pañcupādānakkhandhesu saṅkhipitvā dassetuṃ “saṃkhittena [M 3.0176] pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti bhagavā avoca. Tenāhu porāṇā –

“In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.” Here, just as fire is sustained by fuel, blows by a target, gadflies and mosquitoes by cattle, reapers by a field, and raiders by a village—so too, it is on the five aggregates subject to clinging themselves that birth and so on arise, harassing in various ways, just as grass and creepers arise on the earth, or flowers, fruits, and leaves arise on trees. Within the aggregates subject to clinging, birth is the initial suffering, aging the middle suffering, and death the final suffering; and for those whose wishes are thwarted, the non-attainment of what is desired is the suffering of frustrated desire. Thus, when examined in many ways, the aggregates subject to clinging are indeed suffering. Even if one were to explain each aspect individually, it could not be fully expressed even over countless eons. Therefore, all this suffering—just as a single drop of water contains the taste of the entire ocean—is summarized and shown in relation to any of the five aggregates subject to clinging, as when the Blessed One declared: “In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.” Thus spoke the ancients:

“Jātippabhutikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ vuttamidha tādinā;

Avuttaṃ yañca taṃ sabbaṃ, vinā ete na vijjati.

“The suffering that originates with birth, as was spoken of here by the Such-a-One, and all that was unspoken—none of it exists apart from these.”

“Yasmā tasmā upādāna-kkhandhā saṅkhepato ime;

Dukkhāti vuttā dukkhanta-desakena mahesinā”ti.

“Therefore, these aggregates of clinging are, in brief, called suffering by the Great Sage, the teacher of the end of suffering.”

Evaṃ [V 3.0162] sarūpato dukkhasaccaṃ dassetvā idāni samudayasaccaṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhasamudaya”ntiādimāha. Tattha saṃ-iti ayaṃ saddo “samāgamo sameta”ntiādīsu saṃyogaṃ dīpeti, u-iti ayaṃ “uppannaṃ udita”ntiādīsu uppattiṃ. Aya-saddo pana kāraṇaṃ dīpeti. Idañcāpi dutiyasaccaṃ avasesapaccayasamāyoge sati dukkhassuppattikāraṇanti dukkhassa saṃyoge uppattikāraṇattā “dukkhasamudaya”nti vuccati. Yāyaṃ taṇhāti yā ayaṃ taṇhā. Ponobbhavikāti punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punabbhavo uttarapadalopena, punabbhavo sīlametissāti ponobbhavikā. Nandīrāgena sahagatāti nandīrāgasahagatā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “nandanato rajjanato ca nandīrāgabhāvaṃ sabbāsu avatthāsu appaccakkhāya vuttiyā nandīrāgasahagatā”ti. Tatratatrābhinandinīti yatra yatra attabhāvo nibbattati, tatratatrābhinandinī.

Having thus shown the truth of suffering in its own nature, now to show the truth of the origin of suffering, he begins with “Now this, bhikkhus, is the origin of suffering.” Here, the prefix ‘saṃ-’ conveys connection, as in ‘coming together’ or ‘meeting,’ while ‘u-’ signifies arising, as in ‘arisen’ or ‘appeared.’ The word ‘aya’ indicates cause. This second truth, because it is the cause of suffering’s arising when combined with the remaining conditions, and due to its role in connecting and producing suffering, is called the ‘origin of suffering’. “This very craving” refers to that same craving. “Leading to renewed existence” means causing renewed existence, having renewed existence as its nature. “Accompanied by delight and lust” means associated with delight and lust. This is said to mean: “Because of delighting and lusting, and due to its nature of operating without being directly perceived in all states, it is accompanied by delight and lust.” “Finding delight here and there” means finding delight wherever a renewed existence arises.

Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa sā katamāti ceti ayamattho. Rūpataṇhādibhedena chabbidhāyeva taṇhā pavattiākārabhedato kāmataṇhādivasena tividhā vuttā. Rūpataṇhāyeva hi yadā cakkhussa āpāthamāgataṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ kāmassādavasena assādayamānā pavattati, tadā kāmataṇhā nāma hoti. Yadā tadevārammaṇaṃ dhuvaṃ sassatanti pavattāya sassatadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ pavattati, tadā bhavataṇhā nāma hoti. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagato hi rāgo “bhavataṇhā”ti vuccati. Yadā pana tadevārammaṇaṃ ucchijjati vinassatīti pavattāya ucchedadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ pavattati, tadā vibhavataṇhā nāma hoti. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato hi rāgo “vibhavataṇhā”ti vuccati. Esa nayo saddataṇhādīsupi.

The particle ‘seyyathidaṃ’ has the meaning ‘that is to say, which?’ Craving, which is sixfold by way of form-craving and so on, is spoken of as threefold—sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—based on its modes of occurrence. For when form-craving arises, delighting in a visible form that has come into the range of the eye as a source of sensual pleasure, it is called “sensual craving.” When that same object is regarded as permanent and eternal, and craving arises together with the view of eternalism, it is called “craving for existence.” For lust accompanied by the view of eternalism is called “craving for existence.” But when that same object is regarded as being cut off and destroyed, and craving arises together with the view of annihilationism, it is called “craving for non-existence.” For lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism is called “craving for non-existence.” The same principle applies to sound-craving and the rest.

Kasmā [M 3.0177] panettha taṇhāva samudayasaccaṃ vuttāti? Visesahetubhāvato. Avijjā hi bhavesu ādīnavaṃ paṭicchādentī diṭṭhiādiupādānañca tattha tattha abhinivisamānaṃ taṇhaṃ abhivaḍḍheti, dosādayopi kammassa kāraṇaṃ honti, taṇhā pana taṃtaṃbhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāāvāsasattanikāyakulabhogissariyādivicittataṃ abhipatthentī kammavicittatāya upanissayataṃ kammassa ca sahāyabhāvaṃ upagacchantī bhavādivicittataṃ niyameti, tasmā dukkhassa visesahetubhāvato aññesupi avijjāupādānakammādīsu sutte abhidhamme ca avasesakilesākusalamūlādīsu vuttesu dukkhahetūsu vijjamānesu taṇhāva “samudayasacca”nti vuttāti veditabbaṃ.

Why then is craving alone declared as the truth of the origin of suffering? Because it is the specific cause. Ignorance, by concealing the dangers in states of existence, and clinging to views and so forth by adhering to them in various ways, fosters craving. Hatred and other defilements are also a cause of kamma. But craving, by aspiring for diverse forms of existence, rebirth destinations, states of consciousness, abodes of beings, classes of beings, families, wealth, dominion, and so on, determines the diversity of existence by serving as a decisive support for the diversity of kamma and by assisting kamma. Therefore, since craving is the specific cause of suffering, even though other causes of suffering—such as ignorance, clinging, and kamma, as well as the remaining defilements and unwholesome roots mentioned in the Suttas and Abhidhamma—are present, it is craving alone that is declared as the “truth of the origin.” This should be understood.

Idāni dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodha”ntiādimāha. Tattha yasmā ni-saddo abhāvaṃ, rodha-saddo ca cārakaṃ dīpeti, tasmā abhāvo ettha saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa sabbagatisuññattā, samadhigate vā tasmiṃ saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa [V 3.0163] dukkharodhassa abhāvo hoti tappaṭipakkhattātipi “dukkhanirodha”nti vuccati. Dukkhassa vā anuppādanirodhapaccayattā dukkhanirodhaṃ. Dukkhanirodhaṃ dassentena cettha “yo tassāyeva taṇhāyā”tiādinā nayena samudayanirodho vutto, so kasmā vuttoti ce? Samudayanirodhena dukkhanirodho. Byādhinimittavūpasamena byādhivūpasamo viya hi hetunirodhena phalanirodho, tasmā samudayanirodheneva dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, na aññathā. Tenāha –

Now, to present the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, he says, “Now, bhikkhus, this is the cessation of suffering,” and so on. Here, because the prefix ‘ni-’ denotes absence, and the word ‘rodha’ signifies a prison, it is called ‘dukkhanirodha’ because it is the absence of the prison of suffering known as the prison of saṃsāra, due to its being empty of all destinations. Or, alternatively, when that (Nibbāna) is attained, there is the absence of the prison of suffering known as the prison of saṃsāra, because it is the opposite of it. Or, because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering, it is called the cessation of suffering. In explaining the cessation of suffering here, why is the cessation of the origin stated in the phrase, “the remainderless fading and cessation of that very craving,” and so on? Because the cessation of suffering occurs through the cessation of the origin. Just as the calming of a disease occurs through the calming of its cause, so too does the cessation of the effect occur through the cessation of the cause. Therefore, suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin, not otherwise. Thus he said:

“Yathāpi mūle anupaddave daḷhe;

Chinnopi rukkho punareva rūhati;

Evampi taṇhānusaye anūhate;

Nibbattatī dukkhamidaṃ punappuna”nti. (dha. pa. 338);

“Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again if its root remains unharmed and firm, so too, while the underlying tendency to craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again.” (Dhp. 338)

Iti yasmā samudayanirodheneva dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, tasmā bhagavā dukkhanirodhaṃ dassento samudayanirodhena desesi. Sīhasamānavuttino hi tathāgatā. Te dukkhaṃ nirodhentā dukkhanirodhañca desentā hetumhi paṭipajjanti, na phale. Yathā hi sīho yenattani saro khitto, tattheva attano [M 3.0178] balaṃ dasseti, na sare, tathā buddhānaṃ kāraṇe paṭipatti, na phale. Titthiyā pana suvānavuttino. Te dukkhaṃ nirodhentā dukkhanirodhañca desentā attakilamathānuyogadesanādīhi phale paṭipajjanti, na hetumhi. Yathā hi sunakhā kenaci leḍḍuppahāre dinne bhussantā leḍḍuṃ khādanti, na pahāradāyake uṭṭhahanti, evaṃ aññatitthiyā dukkhaṃ nirodhetukāmā kāyakhedamanuyujjanti, na kilesanirodhanaṃ, evaṃ tāva dukkhanirodhassa samudayanirodhavasena desanāya payojanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Thus, because suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin, the Blessed One, in pointing out the cessation of suffering, taught through the cessation of its origin. For the Tathāgatas have the conduct of a lion. When ceasing suffering and teaching the cessation of suffering, they address the cause, not the effect. Just as a lion, when shot with an arrow, displays his strength against the shooter, not against the arrow, so too the Buddhas’ practice is with regard to the cause, not the effect. The sectarians, however, have the conduct of a dog. When ceasing suffering and teaching the cessation of suffering, they address the effect through teachings of self-mortification and the like, not the cause. Just as dogs, when someone throws a clod at them, bark and chew the clod, not rising up against the thrower, so too other sectarians, wishing to cease suffering, engage in exhausting the body, not in ceasing the defilements. Thus, the purpose of teaching the cessation of suffering by way of the cessation of its origin should be understood.

Ayaṃ panettha attho. Tassāyeva taṇhāyāti tassā “ponobbhavikā”ti vatvā kāmataṇhādivasena vibhattataṇhāya. Virāgo vuccati maggo. “Virāgā vimuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.245; saṃ. ni. 3.12, 59) hi vuttaṃ. Virāgena nirodho virāganirodho, anusayasamugghātato aseso virāganirodho asesavirāganirodho. Atha vā virāgoti pahānaṃ vuccati, tasmā anusayasamugghātato aseso virāgo aseso nirodhoti evampettha yojanā daṭṭhabbā, atthato pana sabbāneva etāni nibbānassa vevacanāni. Paramatthato hi dukkhanirodho ariyasaccanti nibbānaṃ vuccati. Yasmā pana taṃ āgamma taṇhā virajjati ceva nirujjhati ca, tasmā “virāgo”ti ca “nirodho”ti ca vuccati. Yasmā ca tadeva āgamma tassā cāgādayo [V 3.0164] honti, kāmaguṇālayādīsu cettha ekopi ālayo natthi, tasmā cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayoti vuccati.

Herein, this is the meaning. ‘Of that very craving’: having stated that it is ‘leading to renewed existence,’ this refers to craving divided according to sensual craving and so forth. Dispassion is called the path. For it is said: ‘Through dispassion one is liberated’ (MN 1.245; SN 3.12, 59). Cessation through dispassion is dispassion-cessation; from the uprooting of latent tendencies, complete dispassion-cessation is total dispassion-cessation. Or alternatively, dispassion is called abandonment; therefore, from the uprooting of latent tendencies, complete dispassion is complete cessation. Thus, the interpretation here should be understood. But in meaning, all these are synonyms for Nibbāna. For, in the ultimate sense, the cessation of suffering, as a noble truth, is called Nibbāna. And because craving fades away and ceases by resorting to it, it is called ‘dispassion’ and ‘cessation’. And because by resorting to that very thing, giving up, relinquishment, release, and non-clinging occur—and here, not even one instance of clinging to sensual qualities and the like remains—it is called ‘giving up,’ ‘relinquishment,’ ‘release,’ and ‘non-clinging’.

Idāni dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadāariyasaccaṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhagāminī”tiādimāha. Yasmā panetaṃ ariyasaccaṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati ārammaṇavasaena tadabhimukhabhūtattā, paṭipadā ca hoti dukkhanirodhappattiyā, tasmā “dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti vuccati. Sesamettha vuttanayameva. Ko pana nesaṃ dukkhādīnaṃ saccaṭṭhoti? Yo paññācakkhunā upaparikkhiyamānānaṃ māyāva viparīto, marīciva visaṃvādako, titthiyānaṃ attā viya anupalabbhasabhāvo ca na hoti, atha kho bādhanappabhavasantiniyyānappakārena tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvena ariyañāṇassa gocaro hotiyeva, esa aggilakkhaṇaṃ viya lokapakati viya ca tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvo saccaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Ettha ca aggilakkhaṇaṃ nāma uṇhattaṃ. Tañhi katthaci kaṭṭhādiupādānabhede visaṃvādakaṃ viparītaṃ [M 3.0179] abhūtaṃ vā kadācipi na hoti, “jātidhammā jarādhammā, atho maraṇadhammino”ti (a. ni. 5.57) evaṃ vuttajātiādikā lokapakatīti veditabbā. “Ekaccānaṃ tiracchānānaṃ tiriyaṃ dīghatā, manussādīnaṃ uddhaṃ dīghatā, vuddhiniṭṭhappattānaṃ puna avaḍḍhananti evamādikā ca lokapakatī”ti vadanti.

Now, to show the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, he said, ‘And this, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and so on. Because this Noble Truth leads to the cessation of suffering by way of being its object and facing towards it, and because the path is for attaining the cessation of suffering, it is therefore called ‘the path leading to the cessation of suffering’. The rest here is in accordance with the method already stated. But what is the meaning of truth for these—suffering and so forth? When examined with the eye of wisdom, it is not perverted like an illusion, deceptive like a mirage, or like the self of the sectarians, which has an unreal nature. But rather, in the manner of oppression, origination, peace, and escape, it is indeed the domain of noble knowledge, being true and unperverted. This state of being true and unperverted should be understood as the meaning of truth, like the characteristic of fire and like the natural course of the world. Here, the characteristic of fire is heat. For heat, in whatever variety of fuel and so forth, is never deceptive, perverted, or unreal. The natural course of the world, as stated, ‘Subject to birth, subject to aging, and also subject to death’ (AN 5.57), should be understood as birth and so forth. Some say: ‘For some animals, length is horizontal; for humans and others, it is vertical; for those who have reached full growth, there is no further growth—such is the natural course of the world.’

Apica –

Furthermore:

Nābādhakaṃ yato dukkhaṃ, dukkhā aññaṃ na bādhakaṃ;

Bādhakattaniyāmena, tato saccamidaṃ mataṃ.

Since suffering is not afflicted, and nothing other than suffering afflicts; by the principle of being an afflicter, therefore this is considered a truth.

Taṃ vinā nāññato dukkhaṃ, na hoti na ca taṃ tato;

Dukkhahetuniyāmena, iti saccaṃ visattikā.

Without it, suffering does not arise from another source, nor does that (origin) arise from that (suffering); by the principle of being the cause of suffering, thus is the truth of clinging.

Nāññā nibbānato santi, santaṃ na ca na taṃ yato;

Santabhāvaniyāmena, tato saccamidaṃ mataṃ.

There is no peace other than Nibbāna, and since that is not un-peaceful; by the principle of its peaceful nature, therefore this is considered a truth.

Maggā aññaṃ na niyyānaṃ, aniyyāno na cāpi so;

Tacchaniyyānabhāvattā, iti so saccasammato.

There is no egress other than the path, nor is it not an egress; because it has the nature of true egress, thus it is regarded as a truth.

Iti [V 3.0165] tacchāvipallāsa-bhūtabhāvaṃ catūsupi;

Dukkhādīsvavisesena, saccaṭṭhaṃ āhu paṇḍitāti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 189);

Thus, the wise declare the meaning of truth, without distinction, in all four—suffering and so forth—to be the state of being true, unperverted, and real. (Vibha. aṭṭha. 189)

15. Pubbe ananussutesūti ito pubbe “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā na anussutesu assutapubbesu catusaccadhammesu. Cakkhuntiādīni ñāṇavevacanāneva. Ñāṇameva hettha paccakkhato dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu viyāti cakkhu, ñāṇaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, pakārato jānanaṭṭhena paññā, paṭivijjhanaṭṭhena vijjā, saccappaṭicchādakassa mohandhakārassa vidhamanato obhāsanaṭṭhena ālokoti vuttaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ catūsu saccesu lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ.

15. ‘Previously unheard’: this means the Four Truths, such as ‘This is suffering,’ had not been heard or learned before. ‘Eye’ and so forth are simply synonyms for knowledge. Here, knowledge itself is called ‘eye’ because, like an eye, it sees directly; ‘knowledge’ because of its knowing nature; ‘wisdom’ because of its thorough comprehension; ‘true knowledge’ because of its penetration; and ‘light’ because it dispels the darkness of delusion that conceals the truth and illuminates. However, it should be understood that this knowledge is described as a mixture of mundane and supramundane in relation to the Four Truths.

16. Yāvakīvañcāti yattakaṃ kālaṃ. Tiparivaṭṭanti saccañāṇakiccañāṇakatañāṇasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ parivaṭṭānaṃ vasena tiparivaṭṭaṃ. Saccañāṇādivasena hi tayo parivaṭṭā etassāti tiparivaṭṭanti vuccati ñāṇadassanaṃ. Ettha ca “idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, idaṃ dukkhasamudaya”nti evaṃ catūsu saccesu yathābhūtañāṇaṃ saccañāṇaṃ nāma. Tesuyeva “pariññeyyaṃ [M 3.0180] pahātabbaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ bhāvetabba”nti evaṃ kattabbakiccajānanañāṇaṃ kiccañāṇaṃ nāma. “Pariññātaṃ pahīnaṃ sacchikataṃ bhāvita”nti evaṃ tassa katabhāvajānanañāṇaṃ katañāṇaṃ nāma. Dvādasākāranti tesaṃyeva ekekasmiṃ sacce tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena dvādasākāraṃ. Ñāṇadassananti etesaṃ tiparivaṭṭānaṃ dvādasannaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena uppannañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ dassanaṃ.

16. ‘As long as’ means for that much time. ‘Threefold turning’ refers to the threefold turning consisting of knowledge of the truth, knowledge of the task, and knowledge of accomplishment. For knowledge and vision is called ‘threefold turning’ because it has these three turnings, namely, knowledge of the truth and so forth. Here, the knowledge that understands the Four Truths as they truly are—‘This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering’—is called knowledge of the truth. The knowledge that discerns the task to be done in those very truths—‘it is to be fully understood, it is to be abandoned, it is to be realized, it is to be developed’—is called knowledge of the task. The knowledge that recognizes the accomplished state of that—‘it has been fully understood, it has been abandoned, it has been realized, it has been developed’—is called knowledge of accomplishment. ‘Twelve aspects’ refers to the twelve aspects, namely, three aspects for each of the four truths. ‘Knowledge and vision’ is the vision consisting of the knowledge that arises from these three turnings and twelve aspects.

Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhinti uttaravirahitaṃ sabbaseṭṭhaṃ sammā sāmañca bodhiṃ. Atha vā pasatthaṃ sundarañca bodhiṃ. Bodhīti ca bhagavato arahattamaggo idhādhippeto. Sāvakānaṃ arahattamaggo anuttarā bodhi hoti, na hotīti? Na hoti. Kasmā? Asabbaguṇadāyakattā. Tesañhi kassaci arahattamaggo arahattaphalameva deti, kassaci tisso vijjā, kassaci cha abhiññā, kassaci catasso paṭisambhidā, kassaci sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ. Paccekabuddhānampi paccekabodhiñāṇameva deti, buddhānaṃ pana sabbaguṇasampattiṃ deti abhiseko viya rañño sabbalokissariyabhāvaṃ. Tasmā aññassa kassacipi anuttarā bodhi na hotīti. Abhisambuddhoti paccaññāsinti abhisambuddho ahaṃ patto paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitoti evaṃ paṭijāniṃ. Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādīti adhigataguṇānaṃ yāthāvato dassanasamatthaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇañca pana me udapādi. Akuppā me vimuttīti ayaṃ mayhaṃ arahattaphalavimutti akuppā paṭipakkhehi na kopetabbāti evaṃ ñāṇaṃ udapādi. Tattha dvīhākārehi akuppatā veditabbā maggasaṅkhātakāraṇato ca ārammaṇato ca. Sā hi catūhi maggehi samucchinnakilesānaṃ [V 3.0166] puna anivattanatāya kāraṇatopi akuppā, akuppadhammaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattatāya ārammaṇatopi akuppā anākuppārammaṇānaṃ lokiyasamāpattīnaṃ tadabhāvato. Antimāti pacchimā. Natthi dāni punabbhavoti idāni puna añño bhavo nāma natthīti.

‘Unsurpassed perfect self-awakening’ means awakening that is without superior, the best of all, and perfectly self-awakened. Alternatively, it is awakening that is praised and beautiful. Here, ‘awakening’ is intended to mean the Arahant path of the Blessed One. Is the Arahant path of disciples unsurpassed awakening? No, it is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities. For the Arahant path of some gives only the fruit of Arahantship; of some, the three knowledges; of some, the six higher knowledges; of some, the four analytical insights; and of some, the knowledge of a disciple’s perfections. Even for Paccekabuddhas, it gives only the Paccekabodhi knowledge. But for Buddhas, it gives the accomplishment of all qualities, like an anointing that grants a king sovereignty over the entire world. Therefore, the unsurpassed awakening belongs to no one else. ‘I have fully awakened’ means ‘I have attained, penetrated, and stand having realized,’ thus I declared. ‘And knowledge and vision arose in me’ means the knowledge of reviewing, capable of truly seeing the qualities attained, arose in me. ‘My liberation is unshakeable’ means the knowledge arose that this liberation of mine, the fruit of Arahantship, is unshakeable, not to be shaken by opposing forces. Here, its unshakeability should be understood in two ways: by way of cause, namely the path, and by way of object. For it is unshakeable by way of cause because the defilements eradicated by the four paths do not return, and it is unshakeable by way of object because it proceeds by taking the unshakeable Nibbāna as its object—unlike mundane attainments, which lack such an unshakeable object. ‘The last’ means the final. ‘There is no further becoming now’ means there is no other becoming now.

Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasminti imasmiṃ niggāthake sutte. Niggāthakañhi suttaṃ pucchāvissajjanasahitaṃ “veyyākaraṇa”nti vuccati. Bhaññamāneti bhaṇiyamāne, desiyamāneti attho. Virajanti apāyagamanīyarāgarajādīnaṃ vigamena virajaṃ. Vītamalanti anavasesadiṭṭhivicikicchāmalāpagamena vītamalaṃ[M 3.0181]. Paṭhamamaggavajjhakilesarajābhāvena vā virajaṃ, pañcavidhadussīlyamalāpagamena vītamalaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti brahmāyusutte (ma. ni. 2.383 ādayo) heṭṭhimā tayo maggā vuttā, cūḷarāhulovāde (ma. ni. 3.416 ādayo) āsavakkhayo, idha pana sotāpattimaggo adhippeto. Catusaccasaṅkhātesu dhammesu tesaṃ dassanaṭṭhena cakkhūti dhammacakkhu, heṭṭhimesu vā tīsu maggadhammesu ekaṃ sotāpattimaggasaṅkhātaṃ cakkhūti dhammacakkhu, samathavipassanādhammanibbattatāya sīlāditividhadhammakkhandhabhūtatāya vā dhammamayaṃ cakkhūtipi dhammacakkhu, tassa uppattiākāradassanatthaṃ “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti āha. Nanu ca maggañāṇaṃ asaṅkhatadhammārammaṇaṃ, na saṅkhatadhammārammaṇanti? Saccametaṃ, yasmā taṃ nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccavasena sabbasaṅkhataṃ asammohappaṭivedhavasena paṭivijjhantaṃ uppajjati, tasmā tathā vuttaṃ.

And in this exposition, “in this discourse” refers to this verse-less discourse. For a discourse that includes questions and answers is called an “exposition.” “Being spoken” (bhaññamāne) means “being recited,” that is, “being taught” or “being expounded.” “Free from dust” (virajaṃ) means free from the dust of lust and other defilements that lead to the lower realms, by their elimination. “Free from stain” (vītamalaṃ) means free from stain by the complete elimination of the stains of wrong view and doubt. Alternatively, “free from dust” refers to the absence of the dust-like defilements to be abandoned by the first path, and “free from stain” means free from stain by the elimination of the five kinds of stains of immorality. “The eye of Dhamma” (dhammacakkhu)—in the Brahmāyu Sutta (MN 2.383ff.) the three lower paths are mentioned; in the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta (MN 3.416ff.) the destruction of the taints is discussed. Here, however, the path of stream-entry is intended. The “eye of Dhamma” is an eye in the sense of seeing the truths, which are the Dhamma consisting of the Four Noble Truths; or it is the eye, meaning one of the three lower path-dhammas, specifically the path called stream-entry. Or it is the eye made of Dhamma because it is produced by the Dhamma of serenity and insight, or because it consists of the threefold aggregate of Dhamma beginning with virtue. To show the manner of its arising, it is said: “Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.” But is not path-knowledge taking the unconditioned Dhamma as its object, not the conditioned Dhamma? This is true, because it arises by taking cessation as its object, penetrating all conditioned phenomena by way of its function of undeluded comprehension. Therefore, it is so stated.

17. Dhammacakketi paṭivedhañāṇañceva desanāñāṇañca pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ. Bodhipallaṅke nisinnassa hi catūsu saccesu uppannaṃ dvādasākāraṃ paṭivedhañāṇampi, isipatane nisinnassa dvādasākārāya saccadesanāya pavattakaṃ desanāñāṇampi dhammacakkaṃ nāma. Ubhayampi hetaṃ dasabalassa ure pavattañāṇameva. Tadubhayaṃ imāya desanāya pakāsentena bhagavatā dhammacakkaṃ pavattitaṃ nāma. Taṃ panetaṃ dhammacakkaṃ yāva aññāsikoṇḍaññatthero aṭṭhārasahi brahmakoṭīhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāti, tāva bhagavā pavatteti nāma pavattanakiccassa aniṭṭhitattā. Patiṭṭhite pavattitaṃ nāma kassapasammāsambuddhassa sāsanantaradhānato paṭṭhāya yāva buddhuppādo, ettakaṃ kālaṃ appavattapubbassa pavattitattā. Taṃ sandhāya “pavattite ca pana bhagavatā dhammacakke bhummā devā saddamanussāvesu”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bhummāti bhūmaṭṭhakadevatā. Saddamanussāvesunti ekappahāreneva sādhukāraṃ datvā “etaṃ bhagavatā”tiādīni vadantā anussāvayiṃsu. Obhāsoti sabbaññutaññāṇānubhāvena pavatto cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhāno obhāso. So hi tadā devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ atikkamitvā virocittha. Aññāsi vata bho koṇḍaññoti [V 3.0167] imassapi udānassa udāharaṇaghoso dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavato hi dhammacakkappavattanassa ārambhe viya parisamāpanepi ativiya uḷāratamaṃ pītisomanassaṃ udapādi.

17. “The Dhamma-wheel” (dhammacakkaṃ) is called a “wheel” in the sense of its setting in motion, referring to both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. For the twelve-faceted knowledge of penetration that arose regarding the four truths for the one seated on the seat of enlightenment, and the knowledge of teaching that set in motion the twelve-faceted proclamation of the truths for the one seated at Isipatana—both are called the Dhamma-wheel. Indeed, both these are knowledge that arose in the breast of the Ten-Powered One. By proclaiming both through this teaching, the Blessed One is said to have set in motion the Dhamma-wheel. This Dhamma-wheel, the Blessed One is said to have set in motion until the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, along with eighteen crore brahmas, was established in the fruit of stream-entry, because the function of setting it in motion was not yet completed. Once he was established, it is called “set in motion” because, from the time of the disappearance of the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa until the arising of the present Buddha, for such a long time, it had not been set in motion before. Regarding this, it is said: “When the Dhamma-wheel had been set in motion by the Blessed One, the earth-dwelling deities raised a cry…” and so forth. Here, “earth-dwelling” (bhummā) refers to the deities residing on the earth. “Raised a cry” (saddamanussāvesu) means they gave a single shout of approval and, proclaiming “This is by the Blessed One,” and so forth, made it known abroad. “The radiance” (obhāso) refers to the light that arose, produced by the power of omniscient knowledge, originating from mind-produced and temperature-originated phenomena. At that time, it surpassed even the splendor of the gods and shone forth. “Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood!”—the resounding echo of this inspired utterance filled the ten-thousandfold world-system. For at the beginning of the Blessed One’s turning of the Dhamma-wheel, as well as at its conclusion, an exceedingly sublime joy and gladness arose.

18. Diṭṭho [M 3.0182] ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Ettha ca dassanaṃ nāma ñāṇadassanato aññampi atthīti taṃnivattanatthaṃ “pattadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Patti ca ñāṇasampattito aññāpi vijjatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “viditadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Sā panesā viditadhammatā ekadesatopi hotīti nippadesato viditabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “pariyogāḷhadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Tenassa saccābhisambodhiṃyeva dīpeti. Maggañāṇañhi ekābhisamayavasena pariññādikiccaṃ sādhentaṃ nippadesena catusaccadhammaṃ samantato ogāḷhaṃ nāma hoti. Sappaṭibhayakantārasadisā soḷasavatthukā aṭṭhavatthukā ca tiṇṇā vicikicchā anenāti tiṇṇavicikiccho. Pavattiādīsu “evaṃ nukho na nukho”ti evaṃ pavattikā vigatā samucchinnā kathaṃkathā assāti vigatakathaṃkatho. Vesārajjappattoti sārajjakarānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahīnattā tappaṭipakkhesu ca sīlādīsu guṇesu suppatiṭṭhitattā visāradabhāvaṃ veyyattiyaṃ patto adhigato. Svāyaṃ vesārajjappattisuppatiṭṭhitabhāvo katthāti āha “satthusāsane”ti. Attanā paccakkhato adhigatattā na paraṃ pacceti, parassa saddhāya ettha nappavattati, na tassa paro paccetabbo atthīti aparappaccayo.

18. “The Dhamma of the Noble Truths is seen by him”; thus, he is called “one who has seen the Dhamma” (diṭṭhadhammo). This method applies to the remaining terms as well. Here, “seeing” (dassanaṃ) can also mean something other than seeing by knowledge, so to exclude that, it is said “one who has attained the Dhamma” (pattadhammo). And attainment (patti) can also exist apart from the attainment of knowledge, so to distinguish it further, it is said “one who has understood the Dhamma” (viditadhammo). However, this state of understanding the Dhamma can be partial, so to show that it is understood completely, it is said “one who has thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma” (pariyogāḷhadhammo). By this, his full realization of the truths is indicated. For path-knowledge, fulfilling the tasks of full understanding and so on by way of a single moment of realization, is said to have thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths completely and entirely. The sixteen-factored and eight-factored doubts, which are like a dangerous wilderness, have been crossed by him; thus, he is called “one who has crossed doubt” (tiṇṇavicikiccho). His uncertainty (kathaṃkathā), which arises as “Is it so or not so?” in the course of existence and so forth, has vanished and been eradicated; thus, he is called “one free from uncertainty” (vigatakathaṃkatho). “He has attained fearlessness” (vesārajjappatto) because unwholesome qualities that cause fear have been abandoned, and he is well-established in virtuous qualities like morality, which are their antithesis. Thus, he has reached a state of confidence and mastery. Where is this attainment of fearlessness and well-established state found? It is said, “in the Teacher’s dispensation” (satthusāsane). Since it is directly realized by oneself, one does not depend on others; faith in another does not operate here, nor is there anyone else on whom to depend; thus, he is called “independent of others” (aparappaccayo).

Labheyyāhanti labheyyaṃ ahaṃ, āyācanavacanametaṃ. Ehīti āyācitānaṃ pabbajjūpasampadānaṃ anumatabhāvappakāsanavacanaṃ, tasmā ehi sampaṭicchāhi yathāyācitaṃ pabbajjūpasampadavisesanti attho. Iti-saddo tassa ehibhikkhūpasampadāpaṭilābhanimittavacanapariyosānadassano. Tadavasāno hi tassa bhikkhubhāvo. Tenevāha “ehi bhikkhūti bhagavato vacanena abhinipphannā sāva tassa āyasmato ehibhikkhūpasampadā ahosī”ti. Cara brahmacariyanti uparimaggattayasaṅkhātaṃ brahmacariyaṃ samadhigaccha. Kimatthaṃ? Sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya. Idhāpi “avocā”ti sambandhitabbaṃ. “Nava koṭisahassānī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.20; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.37) vuttappabhedānaṃ anekasahassānaṃ saṃvaravinayānaṃ samādiyitvā vattanena uparibhūtā aggabhūtā sampadāti upasampadā.

“May I attain” (labheyyāhaṃ) means “may I attain”; this is an expression of entreaty. “Come” (ehi) is a word expressing permission, indicating approval for those who have requested ordination and higher ordination. Therefore, it means “come, accept the special ordination and higher ordination as requested.” The word “iti” (thus) indicates the conclusion of the statement marking the occasion of his receiving the “Come, monk” ordination. For his state of being a monk was accomplished with that. Hence it is said, “Through the Blessed One’s words, the ordination as ‘Come, monk’ was instantly accomplished for that venerable one.” “Practice the holy life” (cara brahmacariyaṃ) means “attain the holy life, which consists of the three higher paths.” For what purpose? For the complete ending of suffering. Here too, “he said” should be connected. Higher ordination (upasampadā) is a supreme (upari-) and excellent (agga-) accomplishment (sampadā) achieved by undertaking and practicing the many thousands of kinds of restraint and discipline, such as those mentioned in the passage beginning, “Nine thousand crores…” (Vism 1.20; Paṭis-a 1.1.37).

19. Nīhārabhattoti nīhaṭabhatto, gāmato bhikkhaṃ nīharitvā bhikkhūhi dinnabhattoti attho[V 3.0168]. Bhagavā hi daharakumārake viya te bhikkhū [M 3.0183] pariharanto pāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya piṇḍapātatthāyapi gāmaṃ apavisitvā antovihāreyeva vasi.

19. “Nīhārabhatta” means “food brought out” (nīhaṭabhatta); that is, it means almsfood brought out from the village and given by the monks. For the Blessed One, looking after those monks as if they were young boys, from the very first day, did not even enter the village for alms but stayed within the monastery.

Dhammacakkappavattanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is concluded.

Anattalakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta

20. Āmantesīti āsāḷhīpuṇṇamadivase dhammacakkappavattanato paṭṭhāya anukkamena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhite aññāsikoṇḍaññappamukhe pañcavaggiye “idāni tesaṃ āsavakkhayāya dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti pañcamiyā pakkhassa āmantesi. Anattāti avasavattanaṭṭhena asāmikaṭṭhena suññataṭṭhena attapaṭikkhepaṭṭhenāti evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi anattā. Tattha “uppannaṃ rūpaṃ ṭhitiṃ mā pāpuṇātu, ṭhānappattaṃ mā jīratu, jarappattaṃ mā bhijjatu, udayabbayehi mā kilamayatū”ti na ettha kassaci vasībhāvo atthi, svāyamassa avasavattanaṭṭho. Sāmibhūtassa kassaci abhāvo asāmikaṭṭho. Nivāsīkārakavedakaadhiṭṭhāyakavirahena tato suññatā suññataṭṭho. Paraparikappitaattasabhāvābhāvo eva attapaṭikkhepaṭṭho. Idāni anattataṃyeva vibhāvetuṃ “rūpañca hidaṃ bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha attā abhavissāti kārako vedako sayaṃvasīti evaṃbhūto attā abhavissāti adhippāyo. Evañhi sati rūpassa ābādhāya saṃvattanaṃ ayujjamānakaṃ siyā. Kāmañcettha “yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ anattā, tasmā rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvattatī”ti rūpassa anattatāya dukkhatā vibhāvitā viya dissati, tathāpi “yasmā rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvattati, tasmā anattā”ti pākaṭāya sābādhatāya rūpassa attasārābhāvo vibhāvito, tato eva ca “na ca labbhati rūpe ‘evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī’ti” rūpe kassaci anissaratā tassa ca avasavattanākāro dassito. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo.

20. He addressed them: On the full-moon day of Āsāḷhī, starting from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and gradually establishing the group of five monks headed by Aññāsi Koṇḍañña in the fruit of stream-entry, he addressed them on the fifth day of the fortnight, thinking, “Now I will teach them the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.” Not-self: It is not-self in four ways—by way of its being ungovernable, by way of its being without an owner, by way of its being empty, and by way of rejecting the notion of self. Here, regarding its being ungovernable: “Let arisen form not reach stability, let what has reached stability not age, let what has aged not break apart, let it not be afflicted by rise and fall”—in this, no one has mastery; this is its being ungovernable. Its being without an owner is the absence of anyone who owns it. Its emptiness is due to its lack of an inhabitant, a doer, an experiencer, or a director. Rejecting the notion of self is simply the absence of any self-nature conceived by others. Now, to clarify this very not-self nature, he says, “And this, monks, form…” Here, the meaning is: “If there were a self, it would be an agent, an experiencer, self-controlled.” For if that were so, form’s being subject to affliction would be untenable. Although here it seems that the suffering nature of form is shown through its being not-self, as in, “Because, monks, form is not-self, therefore form leads to affliction,” still, through the evident affliction of form, the absence of any essence of self is clarified, and therefore, “And it is not possible to obtain in form ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus’”—this shows the lack of control in form and its being ungovernable. The same method applies to feeling and so on.

21. Taṃ kiṃmaññatha bhikkhaveti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Ettakena ṭhānena anattalakkhaṇameva kathitaṃ, na aniccadukkhalakkhaṇāni, idāni tāni dassetvā [M 3.0184] samodhānetvā tīṇipi lakkhaṇāni dassetuṃ idamāraddhanti veditabbaṃ. Aniccaṃ bhanteti bhante yasmā hutvā na hoti, tasmā aniccaṃ. Yasmā pubbe asantaṃ paccayasamavāyena hutvā uppajjitvā puna bhaṅgupagamanena na hoti, tasmā na niccanti aniccaṃ, addhuvanti adhippāyo. Atha vā uppādavayavantatāya tāvakālikatāya vipariṇāmakoṭiyā niccappaṭikkhepatoti imehipi kāraṇehi [V 3.0169] aniccaṃ. Ettha khaṇe khaṇe uppajjanavasena nirujjhanavasena ca pavattanato uppādavayavantatā. Taṅkhaṇikatāya tāvakālikatā. Vipariṇāmavantatāya vipariṇāmakoṭi. Rūpañhi uppādādivikārāpajjanena vipariṇāmantaṃ vināsaṃ pāpuṇāti. Niccasabhāvābhāvo eva niccapaṭikkhepo. Aniccā hi dhammā, teneva attano aniccabhāvena atthato niccataṃ paṭikkhipanti nāma.

21. “What do you think, monks?” Why has this been begun? Up to this point, only the characteristic of not-self has been explained, not the characteristics of impermanence and suffering. Now, it should be understood that this has been begun in order to show those characteristics, combine them, and then show all three characteristics together. “It is impermanent, venerable sir.” Venerable sir, because what comes into being does not endure, therefore it is impermanent. Because what did not exist before arises through the coming together of conditions, and, having arisen, ceases again due to its nature of dissolution, therefore it is not permanent—thus it is impermanent. The meaning is “unstable.” Or, because of its nature of arising and passing away, because of its momentariness, because of its ending in change, it is impermanent, thus rejecting permanence. By these reasons too, it is impermanent. Here, its nature of arising and passing away is due to occurring through arising and ceasing moment by moment. Its momentariness is its temporality. Its ending in change is due to being subject to change. For form, by undergoing transformations such as arising, etc., it reaches destruction through transformation. The absence of a permanent nature is simply the rejection of permanence. For impermanent phenomena, by their very impermanent nature, they inherently reject permanence.

Dukkhaṃ bhanteti bhante paṭipīḷanākārena dukkhaṃ. Uppādajarābhaṅgavasena hi rūpassa nirantaraṃ bādhati, paṭipīḷanākārenassa dukkhatā. Atha vā santāpaṭṭhena dukkhamaṭṭhena dukkhavatthukaṭṭhena sukhapaṭikkhepaṭṭhena cāti catūhi kāraṇehi dukkhaṃ. Ettha ca santāpo nāma dukkhadukkhatādivasena santāpanaṃ paridahanaṃ. Tato evassa dussahatāya dukkhamatā. Tissannaṃ dukkhatānaṃ saṃsāradukkhassa ca adhiṭṭhānatāya dukkhavatthukatā. Sukhasabhāvābhāvo eva sukhapaṭikkhepo. Vipariṇāmadhammanti jarāya maraṇena ca vipariṇāmasabhāvaṃ. Kallaṃ nūti yuttaṃ nu. Tanti evaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ rūpaṃ. Etaṃ mamāti taṇhāgāho mamaṅkārabhāvato. Esohamasmīti mānagāho ahaṅkārabhāvato. Eso me attāti diṭṭhigāho attabhāvavipallāsaggāhato. Taṇhāgāho cettha aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritavasena, mānagāho navavidhamānavasena, diṭṭhigāho dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhivasena veditabbo. Imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhigāhānaṃ vasena yuttaṃ nu taṃ samanupassitunti vuttaṃ hoti.

“It is suffering, venerable sir.” Venerable sir, it is suffering in the sense of being oppressive. Suffering continuously afflicts form through arising, aging, and disintegration—hence its oppressive nature. Alternatively, suffering is defined by four aspects: burning (torment), the nature of suffering, being the basis of suffering, and the rejection of pleasure. Here, “burning” refers to the scorching and tormenting through suffering of suffering itself, and so on. From that, because of its unbearable nature, is the nature of suffering. It serves as the foundation for the three types of suffering and the suffering of saṃsāra; thus, being the basis of suffering. The absence of a pleasurable nature is itself the rejection of pleasure. “Subject to change” means its nature is changed by aging and death. “Is this fitting?”—Is this appropriate? Thus, form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. “This is mine”—this is the grip of craving, due to the sense of “mine-making.” “I am this”—this is the grip of conceit, due to the sense of “I-making.” “This is my self”—this is the grip of wrong view, the taking of self-identity through distortion. Here, the grip of craving should be understood through the one hundred and eight modes of craving, the grip of conceit through the ninefold conceit, and the grip of wrong view through the sixty-two views. “Is it fitting to regard it thus under the influence of these three—craving, conceit, and wrong view?”—this is what is meant.

Iti bhagavā aniccadukkhavasena anattalakkhaṇaṃyeva dassesi. Bhagavā hi katthaci aniccavasena anattataṃ dasseti, katthaci dukkhavasena, katthaci ubhayavasena. Tathā hi “cakkhu attāti yo vadeyya, taṃ na upapajjati, cakkhussa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ceva veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ na upapajjati. ‘Cakkhu attā’ti [M 3.0185] yo vadeyya, iti cakkhu anattā”ti imasmiñca chachakkasutte (ma. ni. 3.422) aniccavasena anattataṃ dassesi. “Rūpañca hidaṃ, bhikkhave, attā abhavissa…pe… evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī”ti imasmiṃyeva anattalakkhaṇasutte dukkhavasena anattataṃ dassesi. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā, yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na me so attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabba”nti imasmiṃ arahantasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.76-77) ubhayavasena anattataṃ dassesi. Kasmā? Aniccaṃ dukkhañca pākaṭaṃ, anattā apākaṭaṃ. Paribhogabhājanādīsu hi bhinnesu “aho anicca”nti vadanti, “aho anattā”ti [V 3.0170] pana vattā nāma natthi. Sarīre gaṇḍapiḷakāsu vā uṭṭhitāsu kaṇṭakena vā viddhā “aho dukkha”nti vadanti, “aho anattā”ti pana vattā nāma natthi. Kasmā? Idañhi anattalakkhaṇaṃ nāma avibhūtaṃ duddasaṃ duppaññāpanaṃ. Tathā hi sarabhaṅgādayopi satthāro nāddasaṃsu, kuto paññāpanā, tena naṃ bhagavā aniccavasena vā dukkhavasena vā ubhayavasena vā dassesi. Tayidaṃ imasmimpi teparivaṭṭe aniccadukkhavaseneva dassitaṃ. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo.

Thus, the Blessed One showed the characteristic of not-self through impermanence and suffering. For the Blessed One sometimes reveals not-self through impermanence, sometimes through suffering, and sometimes through both. For example, in the Chachakka Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 3.422), he shows not-self through impermanence: “If someone were to say, ‘The eye is self,’ that would not be tenable. The arising and passing away of the eye are evident. But for that which has evident arising and passing away, it would follow that ‘My self arises and ceases.’ Therefore, that is not tenable. If someone were to say, ‘The eye is self,’ thus the eye is not-self.” In this very Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, he shows not-self by way of suffering: 'And this form, monks, if it were self, it would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible to have it of form: “Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.”' In the Arahanta Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.76-77), he shows not-self through both: “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it truly is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’” Why? Because impermanence and suffering are evident, but not-self is not evident. For when vessels or utensils break, people say, “Alas, impermanent!” But no one says, “Alas, not-self!” When boils or abscesses arise on the body, or when one is pierced by a thorn, people say, “Alas, suffering!” But no one says, “Alas, not-self!” Why? Because this characteristic of not-self is unmanifest, hard to see, and difficult to explain. Even teachers like Sarabhaṅga and others did not see it—how much less explain it? Therefore, the Blessed One revealed it through impermanence, suffering, or both. In this threefold round, too, it is shown only through impermanence and suffering. The same method applies to feeling and the rest.

22. Tasmātihāti tasmā icceva vuttaṃ. Ti-kāra ha-kārā nipātā, yasmā ime pañcakkhandhā aniccā dukkhā anattā, tasmāti attho. Yaṃ kiñcīti anavasesapariyādānametaṃ. Yanti hi sāmaññena aniyamadassanaṃ, kiñcīti pakārato bhedaṃ āmasitvā aniyamadassanaṃ. Ubhayenapi atītaṃ vā…pe… santike vā appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā yādisaṃ vā tādisaṃ vā napuṃsakaniddesārahaṃ sabbaṃ byāpetvā saṅgaṇhāti, tasmā anavasesapariyādānametaṃ “yaṃ kiñcī”ti. Evañca sati aññesupi napuṃsakaniddesārahesu pasaṅgaṃ disvā tattha adhippetatthaṃ adhicca pavattanato atippasaṅgassa niyamanatthaṃ “rūpa”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ padadvayenapi rūpassa asesapariggaho kato hoti. Athassa atītādivibhāgaṃ ārabhati “atītānāgatapaccuppanna”ntiādinā. Tañhi kiñci atītaṃ kiñci anāgatādibhedanti. Esa nayo vedanādīsupi.

22. The word 'tasmātihā' is said to mean 'therefore'. The syllables 'ti' and 'ha' are particles, and the meaning is: because these five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and not-self, therefore. 'Whatever' is a term for complete inclusion without residue. 'Yaṃ' indicates generality, a non-specific reference, while 'kiñci' touches upon distinctions of kind, a non-specific reference. By both, it encompasses everything—past, future, present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near; little or much, of whatever kind or suchlike—everything that can be designated in the neuter gender, thus making it a term for complete inclusion without residue: 'whatever.' And seeing the possibility of extension to other things that can be designated in the neuter gender, the word 'form' is used to restrict over-extension to the intended meaning there. In this way, the pair of words brings about the complete inclusion of form without residue. Then, its division into past, future, etc., begins with 'past, future, present,' and so on. For some is past, some is future, and so on. This method applies to feeling and the others as well.

Tattha rūpaṃ tāva addhāsantatisamayakhaṇavasena catudhā atītaṃ nāma hoti, tathā anāgatapaccuppannaṃ. Tattha addhāvasena tāva ekassa ekasmiṃ [M 3.0186] bhave paṭisandhito pubbe atītaṃ, cutito uddhamanāgataṃ, ubhinnamantare paccuppannaṃ. Santativasena sabhāgekautusamuṭṭhānaekāhārasamauṭṭhānañca pubbāpariyavasena vattamānampi paccuppannaṃ, tato pubbe visabhāgautuāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Cittajaṃ ekavīthiekajavanaekasamāpattisamuṭṭhānaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Kammasamuṭṭhānassa pāṭiyekkaṃ santativasena atītādibhedo natthi. Tesaṃyeva pana utuāhāracittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ upatthambhakavasena tassa atītādibhāvo veditabbo. Samayavasena ekamuhuttapubbaṇhasāyanharattidivādīsu samayesu santānavasena pavattamānaṃ taṃtaṃsamayavantaṃ rūpaṃ paccuppannaṃ nāma, tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Khaṇavasena uppādādikkhaṇattayapariyāpannaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ, idamevettha nippariyāyaṃ, sesā pariyāyakathā.

Here, material form is past, future, and present in four ways, based on periods (addhā), continuity (santati), occasions (samaya), and moments (khaṇa). Regarding periods, in a single existence, what precedes rebirth-linking is called past, what follows death is future, and what lies between these two is present. Regarding continuity, material form arising from homogeneous temperature or homogeneous nutriment, even if occurring in sequence, is present. What arises from heterogeneous temperature or nutriment before that is past; what arises after is future. Mind-produced material form arising within a single cognitive process, a single javana-impulse, or a single attainment is present. What arises before that is past; what arises after is future. For kamma-originated material form, there is no classification into past, etc., based on continuity alone. However, the past, etc., nature of these kamma-originated forms should be understood in terms of the support provided by temperature, nutriment, or mind. Regarding occasions, material form persisting in a continuum during specific times—such as a single moment, forenoon, afternoon, night, or day—is called present as the material form belonging to that particular time. What occurs before is past; what occurs after is future. Regarding moments, material form included within the three moments—arising, presence, and dissolution—is present. What precedes them is past; what follows is future. This alone here is the direct explanation; the rest is conventional speech.

Ajjhattaṃ [V 3.0171] vā bahiddhā vāti cakkhādipañcavidhaṃ rūpaṃ attabhāvaṃ adhikicca pavattattā ajjhattaṃ, sesaṃ tato bāhirattā bahiddhā. Apica niyakajjhattampi idha ajjhattaṃ, parapuggalikampi ca bahiddhāti veditabbaṃ. Oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vāti cakkhādīni nava, āpodhātuvajjā tisso dhātuyo cāti dvādasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ ghaṭṭanavasena gahetabbato oḷārikaṃ, sesaṃ tato viparītattā sukhumaṃ. Hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vāti ettha hīnapaṇītabhāvo pariyāyato nippariyāyato ca. Tattha akaniṭṭhānaṃ rūpato sudassīnaṃ rūpaṃ hīnaṃ, tadeva sudassānaṃ rūpato paṇītaṃ. Evaṃ yāva narakasattānaṃ rūpaṃ, tāva pariyāyato hīnapaṇītatā veditabbā. Nippariyāyato pana yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā akusalavipākaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, taṃ hīnaṃ aniṭṭhabhāvato. Yaṃ pana ārammaṇaṃ katvā kusalavipākaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, taṃ paṇītaṃ iṭṭhabhāvato. Yathā hi akusalavipāko sayaṃ aniṭṭho aniṭṭhe eva uppajjati, na iṭṭhe, evaṃ kusalavipākopi sayaṃ iṭṭho iṭṭheyeva uppajjati, na aniṭṭhe. Yaṃ dūre santike vāti yaṃ sukhumaṃ, tadeva duppaṭivijjhasabhāvattā dūre, itaraṃ suppaṭivijjhasabhāvattā santike. Apicettha okāsatopi upādāyupādāya dūrasantikatā veditabbā. Taṃ sabbanti taṃ atītādīhi padehi visuṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ. Sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbanti sahavipassanāya maggapaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Internally or externally: The five kinds of material form pertaining to the eye, etc., are internal because they occur based on one's own individual existence. The remainder, being external to that, is external. Furthermore, one's own internal is here called internal, and what belongs to another person is called external. Coarse or subtle: The nine kinds of material form beginning with the eye, and the three elements excluding the water element—these twelve kinds of material form are coarse because they are apprehended by impact. The remainder, being the opposite of that, are subtle. Inferior or superior: Here, inferiority and superiority are to be understood in a figurative sense and a literal sense. Figuratively, the form of the Sudassī gods is inferior to the form of the Akaniṭṭha gods, and that same form of the Sudassī gods is superior to the form of the Sudassa gods. Thus, as far as the form of hell beings, inferiority and superiority are to be understood relatively. Literally, whatever object conditions unwholesome resultant consciousness to arise is inferior because of being undesirable. But whatever object conditions wholesome resultant consciousness to arise is superior because of being desirable. Just as an unwholesome result is itself undesirable and arises only in the undesirable, not in the desirable, so too a wholesome result is itself desirable and arises only in the desirable, not in the undesirable. Far or near: That which is subtle, being of a nature difficult to penetrate, is far, while the other, being of a nature easy to penetrate, is near. Furthermore, here nearness and distance are to be understood also in terms of location. All that: All that material form separately designated by the terms past, etc. Should be seen with right wisdom: It should be seen by path-wisdom together with insight.

Yā [M 3.0187] kāci vedanātiādīsu pana santativasena ca khaṇavasena ca vedanāya atītānāgatapaccuppannabhāvo veditabbo. Tattha (visuddhi. 2.497 ādayo) santativasena ekavīthiekajavanaekasamāpattipariyāpannā ekavidhavisayasamāyogappavattā ca divasampi buddharūpaṃ passantassa dhammaṃ suṇantassa pavattasaddhādisahitavedanā paccuppannā, tato pubbe atītā, pacchā anāgatā. Khaṇavasena khaṇattayapariyāpannā paccuppannā, tato pubbe atītā, pacchā anāgatā. Ajjhattabahiddhābhedo niyakajjhattavasena veditabbo. Oḷārikasukhumabhedo “akusalā vedanā oḷārikā, kusalābyākatā vedanā sukhumā”tiādinā nayena vibhaṅge (vibha. 11) vuttena jātisabhāvapuggalalokiyalokuttaravasena veditabbo. Jātivasena tāva akusalavedanā sāvajjakiriyahetuto kilesasantāpasabhāvato ca avūpasantavuttīti kusalavedanāya oḷārikā, sabyāpārato saussāhato savipākato kilesasantāpasabhāvato sāvajjato ca vipākābyākatāya oḷārikā, savipākato kilesasantāpasabhāvato sabyāpajjato sāvajjato ca kiriyābyākatāya oḷārikā, kusalābyākatā pana vuttavipariyāyato akusalāya sukhumā. Dvepi kusalākusalavedanā sabyāpārato saussāhato savipākato ca yathāyogaṃ duvidhāyapi abyākatāya oḷārikā, vuttavipariyāyena duvidhāpi abyākatā tāhi sukhumā. Evaṃ tāva jātivasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā.

In the case of 'Whatever feelings there are,' the past, future, and present nature of feeling should be understood both in terms of continuity and momentariness. In this regard, by continuity, a feeling that is included in a single cognitive process, a single impulsion, or a single attainment, and that occurs in conjunction with a single kind of object—such as the feeling accompanied by faith, etc., that arises even for one seeing the Buddha’s form or hearing the Dhamma for a day—is present. What precedes it is past, and what follows is future. By momentariness, what is included in the three moments (arising, presence, and dissolution) is present. What precedes it is past, and what follows is future. The distinction between internal and external should be understood by way of one's own internal experience. The distinction between gross and subtle is explained in the Vibhaṅga in such terms as: 'Unwholesome feeling is gross, wholesome and indeterminate feelings are subtle.' This should be understood in terms of class, nature, person, worldly, and supramundane aspects. By class, unwholesome feeling is gross compared to wholesome feeling because it is the cause of blameworthy action, characterized by defilement and distress, and its activity is not stilled. It is also gross compared to resultant indeterminate feeling because it is active, energetic, productive of results, characterized by defilement and distress, and blameworthy. It is also gross compared to functional indeterminate feeling because it produces results, is characterized by defilement and distress, is active, and blameworthy. On the other hand, wholesome and indeterminate feelings are subtle compared to unwholesome feeling due to the opposite of the aforementioned reasons. Both wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross compared to the two types of indeterminate feelings, as appropriate, because they are active, energetic, and productive of results. Conversely, both types of indeterminate feelings are subtle compared to them, due to the opposite of the aforementioned reasons. Thus, grossness and subtlety should first be understood in terms of class.

Sabhāvavasena [V 3.0172] pana dukkhavedanā nirassādato savipphārato ubbejanīyato abhibhavanato ca itarāhi dvīhi oḷārikā, itarā pana dve sātato santato paṇītato manāpato majjhattato ca yathāyogaṃ dukkhāya sukhumā. Ubho pana sukhadukkhā savipphārato khobhakaraṇato pākaṭato ca adukkhamasukhāya oḷārikā, sā vuttavipariyāyena tadubhayato sukhumā. Evaṃ sabhāvavasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā. Puggalavasena pana asamāpannassa vedanā nānārammaṇavikkhittabhāvato samāpannassa vedanāya oḷārikā, vipariyāyena itarā sukhumā. Evaṃ puggalavasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā. Lokiyalokuttaravasena pana sāsavā vedanā lokiyā. Sā āsavuppattihetuto [M 3.0188] oghaniyato yoganiyato ganthaniyato nīvaraṇiyato upādāniyato saṃkilesikato puthujjanasādhāraṇato ca anāsavāya oḷārikā, sā vipariyāyena sāsavāya sukhumā. Evaṃ lokiyalokuttaravasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā.

By nature, painful feeling is grosser than the other two because it is without relish, accompanied by agitation, alarming, and overwhelming. The other two, however, are subtle compared to painful feeling, because they are agreeable, tranquil, refined, pleasing, and, as is appropriate, neutral. Both pleasant and painful feelings, however, are grosser than neutral feeling because they are accompanied by agitation, cause disturbance, and are obvious; the latter, by the reverse of what has been stated, is subtle compared to both of them. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by nature. By way of individuals, the feeling of one who has not attained absorption is grosser than the feeling of one who has attained absorption, because it is scattered among various objects; conversely, the other is subtle. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of individuals. By way of worldly and supramundane, tainted feelings are worldly. They are grosser than untainted feeling because they are a cause for the arising of taints, bound by floods, bound by yokes, bound by bonds, bound by hindrances, bound by clinging, defiling, and common to ordinary people; the latter, conversely, is subtle compared to tainted feeling. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of worldly and supramundane.

Tattha jātiādivasena sambhedo pariharitabbo. Akusalavipākakāyaviññāṇasampayuttā hi vedanā jātivasena abyākatattā sukhumāpi samānā sabhāvādivasena oḷārikā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ “abyākatā vedanā sukhumā, dukkhā vedanā oḷārikā. Asamāpannassa vedanā oḷārikā, sāsavā vedanā oḷārikā”ti (vibha. 11). Yathā ca dukkhavedanā, evaṃ sukhādayopi jātivasena oḷārikā, sabhāvādivasena sukhumā honti. Tasmā yathā jātiādivasena sambhedo na hoti, tathā vedanānaṃ oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā. Seyyathidaṃ – abyākatā jātivasena kusalākusalāhi sukhumā. Na tattha “katamā abyākatā, kiṃ dukkhā, kiṃ sukhā, kiṃ samāpannassa, kiṃ asamāpannassa, kiṃ sāsavā, kiṃ anāsavā”ti evaṃ sabhāvādibhedo parāmasitabbo. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Here, confusion based on birth, etc., should be avoided. For feeling associated with unwholesome resultant body-consciousness, though subtle by way of its being indeterminate by birth, is gross by way of nature, etc. For this was said: “Indeterminate feeling is subtle, painful feeling is gross. The feeling of one not in absorption is gross, tainted feeling is gross” (Vibh. 11). And just as painful feeling, so too pleasant and other feelings are gross by way of birth, but are subtle by way of nature, etc. Therefore, the grossness and subtlety of feelings should be understood in such a way that there is no confusion by way of birth, etc. That is to say: indeterminate feeling is subtle by way of birth compared to wholesome and unwholesome feelings. There, one should not consider distinctions by way of nature, etc., such as: “Which is indeterminate? Which is painful? Which is pleasant? Which is of one in absorption? Which is of one not in absorption? Which is tainted? Which is untainted?” This is the method everywhere.

Apica “taṃ taṃ vā pana vedanaṃ upādāyupādāya vedanā oḷārikā sukhumā daṭṭhabbā”ti vacanato akusalādīsupi lobhasahagatāya dosasahagatavedanā aggi viya attano nissayadahanato oḷārikā, lobhasahagatā sukhumā. Dosasahagatāpi niyatā oḷārikā, aniyatā sukhumā. Niyatāpi kappaṭṭhitikā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Kappaṭṭhitikāsupi asaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Lobhasahagatā pana diṭṭhisampayuttā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Sāpi niyatā kappaṭṭhitikā asaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā, avisesena akusalā bahuvipākā oḷārikā, appavipākā sukhumā. Kusalā pana appavipākā oḷārikā, bahuvipākā sukhumā.

Moreover, from the statement, “depending on this or that feeling, feelings should be seen as gross or subtle,” even among unwholesome states, feeling associated with hatred is gross compared to that associated with greed, like fire burning its own support, while feeling associated with greed is subtle. Even feeling associated with hatred, when determined, is gross; when undetermined, it is subtle. Even among the determined, that which is long-lasting is gross; the other is subtle. Even among the long-lasting, the unprompted is gross; the other is subtle. However, feeling associated with greed and connected with wrong view is gross; the other is subtle. Even that, when determined, long-lasting, and unprompted, is gross; the other is subtle. In general, unwholesome states with many results are gross; those with few results are subtle. Wholesome states, however, with few results are gross; those with many results are subtle.

Apica [V 3.0173] kāmāvacarakusalā oḷārikā, rūpāvacarā sukhumā, tato arūpāvacarā, tato lokuttarā. Kāmāvacarā ca dānamayā oḷārikā, sīlamayā sukhumā, tato bhāvanāmayā. Bhāvanāmayāpi duhetukā oḷārikā[M 3.0189], tihetukā sukhumā. Tihetukāpi sasaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, asaṅkhārikā sukhumā. Rūpāvacarā paṭhamajjhānikā oḷārikā…pe… pañcamajjhānikā sukhumāva. Arūpāvacarā ākāsānañcāyatanasampayuttā oḷārikā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasampayuttā sukhumāva. Lokuttarā ca sotāpattimaggasampayuttā oḷārikā…pe… arahattamaggasampayuttā sukhumāva. Esa nayo taṃtaṃbhūmivipākakiriyavedanāsu dukkhādiasamāpannādisāsavādivasena vuttavedanāsu ca.

Furthermore, wholesome states of the sense-sphere are gross; those of the form-sphere are subtle; then those of the formless-sphere; then the supramundane. And among the sense-sphere wholesome states, those based on giving are gross; those based on virtue are subtle; then those based on meditation. Even among those based on meditation, the two-rooted are gross; the three-rooted are subtle. Even among the three-rooted, those with prompting are gross; those without prompting are subtle. Form-sphere states associated with the first jhāna are gross...up to... those associated with the fifth jhāna are subtle. Formless-sphere states associated with the base of infinite space are gross...up to... those associated with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are subtle. And supramundane states associated with the path of stream-entry are gross...up to... those associated with the path of arahantship are subtle. This is the method for the resultant and functional feelings of each plane, and for the feelings described as painful, etc., as of one not in absorption, etc., and as tainted, etc.

Okāsavasena cāpi niraye dukkhā oḷārikā, tiracchānayoniyaṃ sukhumā…pe… paranimmitavasavattī sukhumāva. Yathā ca dukkhā, evaṃ sukhāpi sabbattha yathānurūpaṃ yojetabbā. Vatthuvasena cāpi hīnavatthukā yā kāci vedanā oḷārikā, paṇītavatthukā sukhumā. Hīnappaṇītabhede yā oḷārikā, sā hīnā. Yā ca sukhumā, sā paṇītāti veditabbā. Dūrapadaṃ pana akusalā vedanā kusalābyākatāhi vedanāhi dūre, santikapadaṃ akusalā vedanā akusalāya vedanāya santiketiādinā nayena vibhattaṃ. Tasmā akusalā vedanā visabhāgato asaṃsaṭṭhato asarikkhato ca kusalābyākatāhi dūre, tathā kusalābyākatā akusalāya. Esa nayo sabbavāresu. Akusalā pana vedanā sabhāgato ca saṃsaṭṭhato ca sarikkhato ca akusalāya santiketi. Taṃtaṃvedanāsampayuttānaṃ pana saññādīnampi evameva veditabbaṃ.

And by way of location, painful feeling in hell is gross; in the animal realm it is subtle...up to... in the realm of the Paranimmitavasavattī gods it is subtle. And just as with painful feeling, so too should pleasant feeling be applied everywhere as appropriate. And by way of object, any feeling with an inferior object is gross; one with a refined object is subtle. In the distinction between inferior and refined, that which is gross is inferior, and that which is subtle is to be understood as refined. The term 'distant' is distinguished by the method that unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings, and the term 'near' is distinguished by the method that unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling, and so on. Therefore, unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings due to dissimilarity, non-association, and non-likeness; and wholesome and indeterminate feelings are distant from unwholesome feeling in the same way. This principle applies in all instances. However, unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling due to similarity, association, and likeness. The same should be understood for perceptions and other mental factors associated with those respective feelings.

23. Sutavāti āgamādhigamasaṅkhātena bāhusaccena samannāgatattā sutavā. Nibbindatīti ukkaṇṭhati. Ettha ca nibbidāti vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanā adhippetā. Nibbindaṃ virajjatīti ettha virāgavasena cattāro maggā kathitā. Virāgā vimuccatīti virāgena maggeneva hetubhūtena paṭippassaddhivimuttivasena vimuccati. Iminā cattāri sāmaññaphalāni kathitāni. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hotīti iminā pana paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ kathitaṃ. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmi. Tena hi ñāṇena ariyasāvako paccavekkhanto “khīṇā jātī”tiādīni pajānāti. Katamā panassa jāti khīṇā, kathañca naṃ pajānātīti? Na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā anāgate vāyāmābhāvato, na paccuppannā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ [M 3.0190] āpajjanena khīṇā, taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese [V 3.0174] paccavekkhitvā kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ hotīti jānanto pajānāti.

23. ‘Learned’ (sutavā) means one endowed with extensive learning, consisting of scriptural knowledge and penetrative realization. ‘Becomes disenchanted’ means one becomes disgusted. Here, disenchantment is intended as insight leading to emergence. ‘Disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate’—here, the four paths are stated by way of dispassion. ‘Through dispassion, one is liberated’—one is liberated by means of the path itself, which is the cause, through liberation by way of subsidence. By this, the four fruits of recluseship are stated. ‘When liberated, there arises the knowledge “I am liberated”’—by this, reviewing knowledge is stated. ‘Destroyed is birth,’ etc.—these are its grounds. For with that knowledge, the noble disciple, reviewing, understands ‘Destroyed is birth,’ etc. But what birth is destroyed for him, and how does he understand it? Not his past birth, for it was already destroyed before; not the future, because there is no effort in the future; not the present. Rather, the birth that would arise in one-, four-, or five-constituent existences—the birth differentiated into one, four, or five aggregates—due to the undeveloped path, is destroyed by the path’s development, having attained the state of non-arising. Having reviewed the defilements abandoned through path-development, he understands, in the absence of defilements, that even existing kamma does not lead to future rebirth, and thus he knows.

Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā maggabrahmacariyaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso, tasmā ariyasāvako attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto “vusitaṃ brahmacariya”nti pajānāti. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā ariyasāvako attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto “kataṃ karaṇīya”nti pajānāti. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃsoḷasakiccabhāvāya, kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti pajānāti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvā imasmā evaṃpakārā idāni vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi, ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā rukkhā viya. Te carimakaviññāṇanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissantīti pajānāti.

“The holy life has been lived” (vusitaṃ) means that it has been lived, fully lived, done, practiced, and finished—this is the meaning. “The holy life” (brahmacariyaṃ) refers to the holy life of the Path. For along with a virtuous worldling, seven trainees indeed live the holy life of the Path; the one whose taints are destroyed has lived the life. Therefore, the noble disciple, reflecting on his own living of the holy life, understands, “The holy life has been lived.” “What had to be done has been done” (kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ) means that the sixteenfold task—comprising full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development in relation to the Four Noble Truths by means of the Four Paths—has been accomplished—this is the meaning. The virtuous worldling and others indeed do that task, while the one whose taints are destroyed has done what had to be done. Therefore, the noble disciple, reflecting on his own duty, understands, “What had to be done has been done.” “There is no further for this state” (nāparaṃ itthattāya) means he understands: “Now there is no further task of developing the Path for the sake of such a sixteenfold task or for the destruction of taints.” Alternatively, “for this state” means he understands: “From this present state of being, this present continuum of aggregates, there will be no further continuum of aggregates for me. These five aggregates remain fully understood, like trees with severed roots. They, like a fire without fuel, will be extinguished with the cessation of the final consciousness.”

24.
