Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti te bhikkhū sakamanā tuṭṭhamanā, pītisomanassehi vā samattamanā hutvā karavīkarutamañjunā kaṇṇasukhena paṇḍitajanahadayānaṃ amatābhisekasadisena brahmassarena bhāsato bhagavato vacanaṃ sukathitaṃ sulapitaṃ “evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”ti matthakena sampaṭicchantā anumodiṃsu ceva sampaṭicchiṃsu cāti attho. Ayañhi abhinanda-saddo “abhinandati abhivadatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.114, 118) taṇhāyapi āgato. “Annamevābhinandanti, ubhaye devamānusā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.43) upagamanepi.

24. ‘Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words’ means that those monks, being joyful, pleased, and filled with rapture and gladness, having become fully delighted, received the Blessed One’s well-spoken, well-declared words—spoken with a Brahma-like voice, which were as sweet as the karavīka bird’s cry, pleasing to the ear, and like an immortal anointing for the hearts of the wise—with their heads, saying, ‘So it is, Blessed One, so it is, Fortunate One,’ and they both approved and accepted—this is the meaning. For this term ‘rejoice’ (abhinanda) is also found in contexts like ‘rejoices, greets’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.5; 4.114, 118) in the sense of craving. It is also used in contexts like ‘Both devas and humans rejoice in food’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.43), in the sense of ‘approaches.’

“Cirappavāsiṃ purisaṃ, dūrato sotthimāgataṃ;

Ñātimittā suhajjā ca, abhinandanti āgata”nti. (dha. pa. 219; vi. va. 861) –

“A man long absent, returning safe from afar, his relatives, friends, and companions rejoice at his coming.” (Dhammapada 219; Vimānavatthu 861)

Ādīsu [M 3.0191] sampaṭicchanepi. “Abhinanditvā anumoditvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.205) anumodanepi. Svāyamidha anumodanasampaṭicchanesu yujjati. Tena vuttaṃ “anumodiṃsu ceva sampaṭicchiṃsu [V 3.0175] cā”ti. Anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsūti anuppādanirodhena nirujjhamānehi āsavehi anupādāya aggahetvā kañci dhammaṃ “ahaṃ mamā”ti anādiyitvāva cittāni vimucciṃsu. Cha arahantoti bhagavatā saddhiṃ cha janā arahanto. Aññesaṃ pana devabrahmānampi arahattappattisambhavato idaṃ manussaarahanteyeva sandhāya vuttanti āha “cha manussā arahanto hontī”ti.

And so forth, also in the sense of receiving. In phrases like “having rejoiced, having appreciated” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.205), it is also in the sense of appreciation. Thus, here it is used in the sense of both appreciation and reception. Therefore, it is said, “they approved and accepted.” “Their minds were liberated without clinging from the taints” means that their minds were liberated without clinging, without grasping any phenomenon as “I” or “mine,” as the taints ceased through non-arising and cessation. “Six arahants” means six individuals, including the Blessed One, were arahants. However, since the attainment of arahantship is possible even for devas and brahmās, it is said, “six humans were arahants,” referring specifically to human arahants.

Anattalakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta is concluded.

Pañcavaggiyakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Group of Five is concluded.

Yasassa pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of Yasa's Going Forth

25. Idāni yasassa pabbajjaṃ dassetuṃ “tena kho pana samayenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – hemantikotiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.42; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.39) yattha sukhaṃ hoti hemantakāle vasituṃ, ayaṃ hemantiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – hemante vāso hemantaṃ uttarapadalopena, hemantaṃ arahatīti hemantiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Tattha vassiko pāsādo nātiucco hoti nātinīco, dvāravātapānānipissa nātibahūni nātitanūni, bhūmattharaṇapaccattharaṇakhajjabhojjānipettha missakāneva vaṭṭanti. Hemantike thambhāpi bhittiyopi nīcā honti, dvāravātapānāni tanukāni sukhumachiddāni, uṇhappavesanatthāya bhittiniyyūhāni hariyanti, bhūmattharaṇapaccattharaṇanivāsanapārupanāni panettha uṇhavikiriyāni kambalādīni vaṭṭanti, khajjabhojjaṃ siniddhaṃ kaṭukasannissitañca. Gimhike thambhāpi bhittiyopi uccā honti, dvāravātapānāni panettha bahūni vipulajātāni honti, bhūmattharaṇāni sītavikiriyāni dukūlamayāni vaṭṭanti, khajjabhojjāni madhurarasasītavikiriyāni, vātapānasamīpesu cettha navā cāṭiyo ṭhapetvā udakassa pūretvā nīluppalādīhi sañchādenti, tesu tesu padesesu udakayantāni karonti, yehi deve vassante viya udakadhārā nikkhamanti.

25. Now, in order to show Yasa's going forth, the passage beginning 'Then on that occasion...' has been commenced. Herein is the explanation of the terms that are not obvious—regarding 'hemantika' and so on (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.42; A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.3.39)—that place where it is pleasant to dwell in the winter season is called 'hemantika.' The same method applies to the others. Herein is the meaning of the word: 'dwelling in winter' is 'hemanta' by elision of the latter part of the compound; that which is suitable for winter is 'hemantika.' The same method applies to the others. There, the rainy-season residence is neither too high nor too low; its doors and windows are neither too many nor too few. Floor coverings, spread coverings, and food and drink are all suitable there in a mixed variety. In the winter residence, the pillars and walls are low; the doors and windows are narrow with fine holes. Wall projections are made to let in warmth. Floor coverings, spread coverings, bedding, and wraps there are warm-radiating, such as blankets. The food and drink are rich and oily, and mixed with pungent flavors. In the summer residence, the pillars and walls are high; the doors and windows there are many and of wide variety. The floor coverings are cool-radiating, made of fine linen. The food and drink are sweet-tasting and cool-radiating. Near the windows, new water jars are placed, filled with water and covered with blue lotuses and the like. In those various places, they construct water mechanisms from which streams of water issue forth as if a god were raining.

Nippurisehīti [M 3.0192] purisavirahitehi. Na kevalañcettha tūriyāneva nippurisāni, sabbaṭṭhānānipi nippurisāneva. Dovārikāpi itthiyova, nahāpanādiparikammakarāpi itthiyova. Pitā kira “tathārūpaṃ issariyasukhasampattiṃ anubhavamānassa purisaṃ disvā parisaṅkā uppajjati, sā me puttassa mā ahosī”ti sabbakiccesu itthiyova ṭhapāpesi. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehīti [V 3.0176] rūpasaddādīhi pañcahi kāmakoṭṭhāsehi. Samappitassāti sammā appitassa, upetassāti attho. Samaṅgībhūtassāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Paricārayamānassāti parito cārayamānassa, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāmaguṇe indriyāni cārayamānassāti attho. Āḷambaranti paṇavaṃ. Vikesikanti muttakesaṃ, vippakiṇṇakesanti attho. Vikkheḷikanti vissandamānalālaṃ. Vippalapantiyoti viruddhaṃ palapantiyo vā rudantiyo vā. Susānaṃ maññeti āmakasusānaṃ viya addasa sakaṃ parijananti sambandho. Udānaṃ udānesīti saṃvegavasena udānaṃ udānesi, saṃvegavasappavattaṃ vācaṃ nicchāresīti attho.

'Devoid of men' means empty of men. Not only were the musical instruments here devoid of men, but all the places were indeed devoid of men. Even the gatekeepers were women, and those who performed tasks like bathing and other services were also women. It is said that the father, thinking, 'Seeing a man enjoying such royal pleasures might give rise to suspicion, lest that should happen to my son,' appointed only women for all duties. 'By the five strands of sensual pleasure' means by the five aspects of sensual enjoyment, such as sights and sounds. 'To one who is well-provided' means to one who is properly provided, that is, 'endowed with.' 'Being well-equipped' is another term for the same. 'Entertaining himself' means thoroughly entertaining himself, that is, moving his senses among the various strands of sensual pleasure. 'Āḷambara' refers to a hand-drum. 'Vikesika' means with loose hair, that is, 'with disheveled hair.' 'Vikkheḷika' refers to flowing saliva. 'Vippalapantiyo' means either speaking incoherently or weeping. 'He thought it was a charnel ground'—this is the connection: he saw his own retinue as if it were a fresh charnel ground. 'He uttered an inspired utterance' means he uttered an inspired utterance out of a sense of spiritual urgency, that is, he expressed words arising from that agitation.

26. Idaṃ kho yasāti bhagavā nibbānaṃ sandhāyāha. Tañhi taṇhādīhi kilesehi anupaddutaṃ anupassaṭṭhañca. Anupubbiṃ kathanti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.75; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.69) dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ, sīlānantaraṃ saggaṃ, saggānantaraṃ magganti evamanupaṭipāṭikathaṃ. Tattha dānakathā nāma “idaṃ dānaṃ nāma sukhānaṃ nidānaṃ, sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ, bhogānaṃ patiṭṭhā, visamagatassa tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ, idhalokaparalokesu dānasadiso avassayo patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi. Idañhi avassayaṭṭhena ratanamayasīhāsanasadisaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena mahāpathavīsadisaṃ, ārammaṇaṭṭhena ālambanarajjusadisaṃ, idañhi dukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhena nāvā, samassāsanaṭṭhena saṅgāmasūro, bhayaparittāṇaṭṭhena susaṅkhatanagaraṃ, maccheramalādīhi anupalittaṭṭhena padumaṃ, tesaṃ nidahanaṭṭhena aggi, durāsadaṭṭhena āsīviso, asantāsanaṭṭhena sīho, balavantaṭṭhena hatthī, abhimaṅgalasammataṭṭhena setausabho, khemantabhūmisampāpanaṭṭhena valāhako assarājā. Dānaṃ nāmetaṃ mayā gatamaggo, mayheveso vaṃso, mayā dasa pāramiyo pūrentena velāmamahāyaññā mahāgovindamahāyaññā mahāsudassanamahāyaññā vessantaramahāyaññāti aneke mahāyaññā pavattitā, sasabhūtena jalite [M 3.0193] aggikkhandhe attānaṃ niyyātentena sampattayācakānaṃ cittaṃ gahitaṃ. Dānañhi loke sakkasampattiṃ deti, mārasampattiṃ brahmasampattiṃ cakkavattisampattiṃ sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ abhisambodhiñāṇaṃ detī”ti evamādinā dānaguṇappaṭisaṃyuttakathā.

26. 'This, O Yasa' – the Blessed One said this with reference to Nibbāna. For it is untroubled by defilements such as craving, and is tranquil. 'The gradual discourse' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.75; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.69) means a discourse in due order, thus: after generosity, virtue; after virtue, heaven; after heaven, the path. Herein, the discourse on generosity is as follows: 'This generosity is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, the foundation of wealth, a refuge, a shelter, a destination, and a final resort for one who has gone astray. In this world and the next, there is no other support, foundation, reliance, refuge, shelter, destination, or final resort like generosity. For by its nature as a support, it is like a jeweled lion-throne; by its nature as a foundation, it is like the great earth; by its nature as a reliance, it is like a rope for clinging. This, by its nature as a crossing over suffering, is a boat; by its nature as a consolation, a hero in battle; by its nature as protection from fear, a well-fortified city; by its nature as being unstained by the impurities of stinginess, a lotus; by its nature as burning them (defilements), fire; by its nature as being hard to approach, a venomous snake; by its nature as fearlessness, a lion; by its nature as strength, an elephant; by its nature as being regarded as auspicious, a white bull; by its nature as leading to the land of safety, a rain-cloud, the king of horses. Generosity, indeed, is the path I have traveled; this is my lineage. By me, fulfilling the ten perfections, many great sacrifices such as the Velāma great sacrifice, the Mahāgovinda great sacrifice, the Mahāsudassana great sacrifice, and the Vessantara great sacrifice were set in motion. By offering myself, as a hare, into a blazing mass of fire, the hearts of those who sought prosperity were captivated. For generosity in this world grants the attainment of Sakka’s prosperity, Māra’s prosperity, Brahmā’s prosperity, the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch, the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection, the knowledge of a paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of supreme enlightenment.' Such is the discourse connected with the virtues of generosity.

Yasmā pana dānaṃ dadanto sīlaṃ samādātuṃ sakkoti, tasmā tadanantaraṃ sīlakathaṃ kathesi. Dānañhi nāma dakkhiṇeyyesu hitajjhāsayena pūjanajjhāsayena vā attano santakassa paresaṃ pariccajanaṃ, tasmā dāyako sattesu ekantahitajjhāsayo purisapuggalo, paresaṃ vā santakaṃ haratīti aṭṭhānametaṃ. Tasmā dānaṃ dadanto sīlaṃ samādātuṃ sakkotīti dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Apica dānakathā tāva pacurajanesupi pavattiyā sabbasādhāraṇattā sukarattā sīle patiṭṭhānassa [V 3.0177] upāyabhāvato ca ādito kathitā. Pariccāgasīlo hi puggalo pariggahavatthūsu nissaṅgabhāvato sukheneva sīlāni samādiyati, tattha ca suppatiṭṭhito hoti. Sīlena dāyakapaṭiggāhakavisuddhito parānuggahaṃ vatvā parapīḷānivattivacanato kiriyadhammaṃ vatvā akiriyadhammavacanato bhogayasasampattihetuṃ vatvā bhavasampattihetuvacanato ca dānakathānantaraṃ sīlakathā kathitā.

Since one who gives gifts is able to undertake virtue, therefore, immediately after that, he spoke the discourse on virtue. For giving is indeed the relinquishing of one’s own possessions to those worthy of offerings, with the intention of benefiting them or honoring them. Therefore, it is impossible for a donor—a person whose sole intention is the welfare of beings—to take what belongs to others; this is untenable. Thus, it is said that one who gives gifts is able to undertake virtue, and so virtue was spoken of after giving. Moreover, the discourse on giving was spoken first because it is common and easy to practice among many people, and serves as a means for establishing oneself in virtue. For a person whose nature is generosity, being unattached to objects of acquisition, easily undertakes the precepts and becomes well-established in them. The discourse on virtue was given after the discourse on giving because it explains the purification of both the giver and the recipient through virtue, speaks of benefiting others, speaks of the cessation of harming others, teaches active wholesome deeds while rejecting doctrines of inaction, and speaks of the cause of attaining wealth and fame as well as the cause of prosperity in future existences.

Sīlakathā nāma “sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ avassayo patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ. Sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ mama vaṃso, ahaṃ saṅkhapālanāgarājakāle bhūridattanāgarājakāle campeyyanāgarājakāle sīlavarājakāle mātuposakahatthirājakāle chaddantahatthirājakāleti anantesu attabhāvesu sīlaṃ paripūresiṃ. Idhalokaparalokasampattīnañhi sīlasadiso avassayo sīlasadisā patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi, sīlālaṅkārasadiso alaṅkāro natthi, sīlapupphasadisaṃ pupphaṃ natthi, sīlagandhasadiso gandho natthi. Sīlālaṅkārena hi alaṅkataṃ sīlakusumapiḷandhanaṃ sīlagandhānulittaṃ sadevakopi loko olokento tittiṃ na gacchatī”ti evamādisīlaguṇappaṭisaṃyuttakathā.

The discourse on virtue is a discourse connected with the qualities of virtue, such as: "Virtue is indeed a reliance, a foundation, a support, a refuge, a shelter, a destination, a final resort. Virtue is my lineage. In countless existences—such as when I was the Nāga king Saṅkhapāla, the Nāga king Bhūridatta, the Nāga king Campeyya, the virtuous king, the elephant king Mātuposaka, and the six-tusked elephant king Chaddanta—I perfected virtue. For the attainments of this world and the next, there is no reliance, foundation, support, refuge, shelter, destination, or final resort equal to virtue. There is no ornament like the adornment of virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue. Even the world with the gods, gazing upon one adorned with the ornament of virtue, wearing the garland of virtue-flowers, and anointed with the perfume of virtue, is not satiated."

Idaṃ pana sīlaṃ nissāya ayaṃ saggo labbhatīti dassanatthaṃ sīlānantaraṃ saggakathaṃ kathesi. Saggakathā nāma “ayaṃ saggo nāma iṭṭho kanto manāpo[M 3.0194], niccamettha kīḷā, niccaṃ sampattiyo labbhanti, cātumahārājikā devā navutivassasatasahassāni dibbasukhaṃ dibbasampattiṃ paṭilabhanti, tāvatiṃsā tisso ca vassakoṭiyo saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassānī”ti evamādisaggaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttakathā. Saggasampattiṃ kathayantānañhi buddhānaṃ mukhaṃ nappahoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “anekapariyāyena kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, saggakathaṃ katheyya”ntiādi.

Now, to show that by relying on this virtue, this heaven is attained, he gave the discourse on heaven after the discourse on virtue. The discourse on heaven is a discourse connected with the qualities of heaven, such as: "This heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; here there is constant play; constant attainments are gained; the Cātumahārājika gods obtain divine happiness and divine prosperity for nine million years; the Tāvatiṃsa gods, for thirty-six million years." Indeed, the mouths of the Buddhas are not sufficient to describe the prosperity of heaven. And this too was said: "In many ways, monks, I would speak of the discourse on heaven," and so on.

Evaṃ saggakathāya palobhetvā puna hatthiṃ alaṅkaritvā tassa soṇḍaṃ chindanto viya ayampi saggo anicco addhuvo, na ettha chandarāgo kātabboti dassanatthaṃ “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.177; pāci. 417) nayena kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ kathesi. Tattha ādīnavoti doso, aniccatādinā appassādatādinā ca dūsitabhāvoti attho. Atha vā ādīnaṃ vāti pavattatīti ādīnavo, paramakapaṇatā. Tathā ca kāmā yathābhūtaṃ paccavekkhantānaṃ paccupatiṭṭhanti. Okāroti lāmakabhāvo nihīnabhāvo aseṭṭhehi sevitabbatā seṭṭhehi na sevitabbatā ca. Saṃkilesoti tehi sattānaṃ saṃkilissanaṃ, vibādhetabbatā upatāpetabbatāti attho.

Having thus enticed with the discourse on heaven, then again, like one who, having adorned an elephant, cuts off its trunk, to show that this heaven too is impermanent and unstable, and that no desire or lust should be formed for it, he spoke of the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, in accordance with the method beginning: "Sensual pleasures give little satisfaction, are full of suffering, full of despair; the danger in them is greater," and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.177; Pācittiya 417). Therein, 'danger' (ādīnava) means fault; the meaning is the state of being corrupted by impermanence and the like, and by giving little satisfaction and the like. Alternatively, 'danger' (ādīnava) is so called because it proceeds to misery, meaning extreme wretchedness. And thus do sensual pleasures appear to those who examine them as they truly are. 'Degradation' (okāra) means inferiority, baseness—being resorted to by the ignoble and not by the noble. 'Defilement' (saṃkilesa) refers to the defiling of beings by them, meaning they are a cause of vexation and torment.

Evaṃ [V 3.0178] kāmādīnavena tajjetvā nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesi. Yattakā ca kāmesu ādīnavā, paṭipakkhato tattakāva nekkhamme ānisaṃsā. Apica “nekkhammaṃ nāmetaṃ asambādhaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ, nikkhantaṃ kāmehi, nikkhantaṃ kāmasaññāya, nikkhantaṃ kāmavitakkehi, nikkhantaṃ kāmapariḷāhehi, nikkhantaṃ byāpārato”tiādinā nayena nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesi, pabbajjāya jhānādīsu ca guṇe vibhāvesi vaṇṇesi. Ettha ca saggaṃ kathetvā svāyaṃ saggo rāgādīhi upakkiliṭṭho, sabbathāpi anupakkiliṭṭho ariyamaggoti dassanatthaṃ saggānantaraṃ maggo kathetabbo. Maggañca kathentena tadadhigamupāyasandassanatthaṃ saggapariyāpannāpi pageva itare sabbepi kāmā nāma bahvādīnavā aniccā addhuvā vipariṇāmadhammāti kāmānaṃ ādīnavo, hīnā gammā pothujjanikā anariyā anatthasañhitāti tesaṃ okāro lāmakabhāvo, sabbepi bhavā kilesānaṃ vatthubhūtāti tattha saṃkileso, sabbasaṃkilesavippamuttaṃ nibbānanti nekkhamme ānisaṃso [M 3.0195] ca kathetabboti kāmesu ādīnavo okāro saṃkileso nekkhamme ca ānisaṃso pakāsitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Having thus warned with the danger of sensual pleasures, he proclaimed the advantages of renunciation. And as many dangers as there are in sensual pleasures, so many advantages are there in renunciation, by way of opposition. Moreover, he proclaimed the benefits of renunciation in this way: "Renunciation is indeed unconfined, undefiled, free from sensual pleasures, free from perceptions of sensuality, free from thoughts of sensuality, free from the fever of sensuality, and free from vexation," and so on. He further explained and praised the virtues in going forth, in the jhānas, and so on. And here, having spoken of heaven, the Path should be spoken of after heaven, to show that this heaven is tainted by lust and so on, but the Noble Path is utterly untainted. And by speaking of the Path, to show the means of its attainment, the dangers of sensual pleasures should also be spoken of: even the sensual pleasures included in heaven, and even more so all other sensual pleasures, are indeed full of dangers, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change—thus, the danger of sensual pleasures. They are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not connected with benefit—thus, their degradation, their baseness. All existences are the basis for defilements—thus, the defilement therein. Nibbāna is completely free from all defilements—thus, the advantage in renunciation should be spoken of. Thus, it should be understood that the danger, degradation, and defilement in sensual pleasures, and the advantage in renunciation, are revealed.

Kallacittanti kammaniyacittaṃ, heṭṭhā pavattitadesanāya assaddhiyādīnaṃ cittadosānaṃ vigatattā uparidesanāya bhājanabhāvūpagamanena kammakkhamacittanti attho. Assaddhiyādayo vā yasmā cittassa rogabhūtā tadā tassa vigatā, tasmā kallacittaṃ arogacittanti attho. Diṭṭhimānādikilesavigamena muducittaṃ, kāmacchandādivigamena vinīvaraṇacittaṃ, sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ uḷārapītipāmojjayogena udaggacittaṃ. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā pasannacittaṃ yadā bhagavā aññāsīti sambandho. Atha vā kallacittanti kāmacchandavigamena arogacittaṃ. Muducittanti byāpādavigamena mettāvasena akaṭhinacittaṃ. Vinīvaraṇacittanti uddhaccakukkuccavigamena vikkhepassa vigatattā tena apihitacittaṃ. Udaggacittanti thinamiddhavigamena sampaggahavasena alīnacittaṃ. Pasannacittanti vicikicchāvigamena sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ adhimuttacittanti evampettha attho veditabbo. Sāmukkaṃsikāti sāmaṃ ukkaṃsikā, attanāyeva uddharitvā gahitā, sayambhūñāṇena diṭṭhā asādhāraṇā aññesanti attho. Kā ca pana sāti? Ariyasaccadesanā. Tenevāha “dukkhaṃ samudayaṃ nirodhaṃ magga”nti.

"Kallacitta (pliant mind) means a workable mind; the meaning is that because, through the preceding discourse, the mental faults such as disbelief have vanished, it has become a mind fit for work, having become a receptacle for the higher teaching. Or, since disbelief and the like are diseases of the mind, and they have vanished at that time, therefore kallacitta means a healthy mind. Muducitta (soft mind) means a mind free from defilements such as wrong views and pride. Vinīvaraṇacitta (mind free from hindrances) means a mind free from sensual desire and other obstructions. Udaggacitta (uplifted mind) means a mind filled with great joy and delight through proper practice. Here, the connection is that the Blessed One knew when the mind was confident through the attainment of faith. Alternatively, kallacitta means a healthy mind, free from sensual desire. Muducitta means a mind free from ill will, not hardened by means of loving-kindness. Vinīvaraṇacitta means a mind free from restlessness and remorse, unhindered by distraction due to its absence. Udaggacitta means a mind free from sloth and torpor, not drooping due to energetic exertion. Pasannacitta (confident mind) means a mind free from doubt, resolved on the right practice—this is how the meaning should be understood here. Sāmukkaṃsikā means self-elevated, grasped by oneself, seen by the knowledge of the self-awakened, not common to others—this is the meaning. And what is it? The teaching of the Noble Truths. Therefore, he said: 'Suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path.'"

Seyyathāpītiādinā upamāvasena tassa kilesappahānaṃ ariyamagguppādañca dasseti. Apagatakāḷakanti vigatakāḷakaṃ. Sammadevāti suṭṭhu eva. Rajananti nīlapītādiraṅgajātaṃ. Paṭiggaṇheyyāti gaṇheyya, pabhassaraṃ bhaveyya. Tasmiṃyeva āsaneti tassaṃyeva nisajjāyaṃ. Etenassa lahuvipassakatā tikkhapaññatā sukhapaṭipadakhippābhiññatā ca dassitā hoti. Virajantiādi [V 3.0179] vuttanayameva. Tatridaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ – vatthaṃ viya cittaṃ, vatthassa āgantukamalehi kiliṭṭhabhāvo viya cittassa rāgādimalehi saṃkiliṭṭhabhāvo, dhovanasilā viya anupubbikathā, udakaṃ viya saddhā, udakena temetvā temetvā ūsagomayachārikakhārakehi kāḷakapadese sammadditvā vatthassa dhovanapayogo viya saddhāsinehena temetvā temetvā satisamādhipaññāhi dose sithile katvā sīlasutādividhinā cittassa sodhane vīriyārambho, tena payogena vatthe kāḷakāpagamo viya vīriyārambhena kilesavikkhambhanaṃ, raṅgajātaṃ [M 3.0196] viya ariyamaggo, tena suddhassa vatthassa pabhassarabhāvo viya vikkhambhitakilesassa cittassa maggena pariyodapananti.

By 'Just as,' etc., through the simile, it shows the abandoning of defilements and the arising of the noble path. 'Apagatakāḷaka' (Free from blackness) means devoid of blackness. 'Sammadevā' (Properly) means very well indeed. 'Rajana' (Dye) refers to the kinds of color produced, such as blue and yellow. 'Paṭiggaṇheyya' (Would accept) means would take, would become radiant. 'Tasmiṃyeva āsane' (On that very seat) means in that very sitting. By this, his quick insight, sharp wisdom, ease of practice, and swift attainment of higher knowledge are shown. 'Viraja' (Free from defilements), etc., follows the same method as explained. Here is the application of the simile: The mind is like the cloth; the defiled state of the cloth by adventitious stains is like the defiled state of the mind by stains such as lust; the washing stone is like gradual instruction; water is like faith; the effort of washing the cloth by wetting it repeatedly with water and scrubbing the black areas with saline earth, cow-dung, ash, and lye is like the effort of purifying the mind by wetting it repeatedly with the moisture of faith and loosening the defilements with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, following the method of virtue, learning, etc.; the removal of blackness from the cloth by that effort is like the suppression of defilements by the exertion of energy; the dye is like the noble path; the radiant state of the purified cloth is like the complete purification of the mind, whose defilements have been suppressed, by the path.

27. Assadūteti āruḷhaasse dūte. Iddhābhisaṅkhāranti iddhikiriyaṃ. Abhisaṅkharesīti abhisaṅkhari, akāsīti attho. Kimatthanti ce? Ubhinnaṃ paṭilabhitabbavisesantarāyanisedhanatthaṃ. Yadi hi so puttaṃ passeyya, puttassapi arahattappatti seṭṭhissapi dhammacakkhupaṭilābho na siyā. Adiṭṭhasaccopi hi “dehi te mātuyā jīvita”nti yācanto kathañhi nāma vikkhepaṃ paṭibāhitvā bhagavato dhammadesanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā dhammacakkhuṃ paṭilabheyya, yaso ca evaṃ tena yāciyamāno kathaṃ taṃ vikkhepaṃ paṭibāhitvā arahatte patiṭṭhaheyya.

27. 'Assadūta' means a messenger mounted on a horse. 'Iddhābhisaṅkhāra' refers to the exercise of psychic power. 'Abhisaṅkharesi' means he performed, he did; this is the meaning. If it is asked, 'For what purpose?' To prevent an impediment to the attainment of a particular distinction for both of them. For if he were to see his son, the son's attainment of arahantship and the merchant's acquisition of the Dhamma-eye would not occur. Indeed, one who has not seen the truth, begging with the words, "Give your mother life," how could he, having warded off distraction and directed knowledge in accordance with the Blessed One's teaching, acquire the Dhamma-eye? And Yasa, being begged in this way, how could he, having warded off that distraction, become established in arahantship?

Etadavocāti bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ abbhanumodamāno etaṃ “abhikkantaṃ bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Abhikkanta-saddo cāyamidha abbhanumodane, tasmā sādhu sādhu bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Etadavoca' (He said this) — approving of the Blessed One's teaching, he spoke these words beginning with, "Excellent, venerable sir." The word 'abhikkanta' here signifies approval; therefore, it means: "Good, good, venerable sir."

“Bhaye kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite kotūhalacchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budho”ti. –

"In fear, anger, praise, and haste, In excitement, curiosity, and wonder, In laughter, sorrow, and delight, the wise repeat."

Imināva lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Seyyathāpītiādinā catūhi upamāhi bhagavato desanaṃ thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti uparimukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādichāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā “esa maggo”ti vadeyya. Andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasī aḍḍharatti ghanavanasaṇḍameghapaṭalehi caturaṅgatame.

By this very characteristic, it should be understood that here, by way of devotion and praise, this has been stated twice. By the words 'Just as,' etc., with these four similes, he praises the teaching of the Blessed One. There, 'nikkujjita' means placed face-down, or turned to have the face downward. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to turn it face-up. 'Paṭicchanna' means covered with grass, leaves, or the like. 'Vivareyya' means to uncover it. 'Mūḷhassa' means one who is lost in direction. 'Maggaṃ ācikkheyya' means to take them by the hand and say, "This is the path." 'Andhakāra' refers to the dark fortnight, the fourteenth night, midnight, dense forests, thick cloud masses—fourfold darkness.

Evaṃ [V 3.0180] desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattaye pasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto “esāha”ntiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretūti maṃ bhagavā “upāsako aya”nti evaṃ dhāretu, jānātūti attho. Ajjataggeti etthāyaṃ agga-saddo ādiatthe, tasmā ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvāti [M 3.0197] evamattho veditabbo. Ajjatanti ajjabhāvaṃ. “Ajjadagge”ti vā pāṭho, da-kāro padasandhikaro, ajja aggaṃ katvāti attho. Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ. Yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ, anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu jānātu. Ahañhi sacepi me tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindeyya, neva buddhaṃ “na buddho”ti vā, dhammaṃ “na dhammo”ti vā, saṅghaṃ “na saṅgho”ti vā vadeyyanti evaṃ attasanniyyātanena saraṇaṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ “abhikkanta”ntiādīnaṃ anuttānapadattho veditabbo, vitthāro pana heṭṭhā verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ āgatoyevāti idha na dassito.

Having praised this teaching, with a heart devoted to the Three Jewels through this discourse, he expressed his devotion by saying, 'Esāhaṃ...' (I am this...). Herein, 'esāhaṃ' means 'eso ahaṃ' (this I am). 'Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu' means 'May the Blessed One regard me as a lay follower,' that is, may the Blessed One know me as 'this is a lay follower,' such is the meaning. 'Ajjatagge' — here the word 'agga' is used in the sense of beginning. Therefore, 'ajjatagge' should be understood as meaning 'having made today the beginning.' 'Ajjata' means the present state. Alternatively, the reading is 'Ajjadagge,' the 'da' sound being a euphonic link; the meaning is 'having made today the foremost.' 'Pāṇupeta' means endowed with life. As long as my life continues, so long am I endowed, not seeking another teacher, having gone for refuge with the threefold refuge. May the Blessed One recognize me as a lay follower. For even if someone were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, "He is not the Buddha," nor of the Dhamma, "It is not the Dhamma," nor of the Sangha, "They are not the Sangha." Thus, with this self-surrender, he went for refuge. In this way, the meaning of the words 'abhikkanta' and so on should be understood as not elaborated here. The detailed explanation, however, is found in the commentary on the Verañja section, and thus is not shown here.

28. Bhūmiṃ paccavekkhantassāti attanā diṭṭhamatthaṃ paccavekkhantassa. Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ paṭippassambhesīti yathā taṃ seṭṭhi gahapati tattha nisinnova yasaṃ kulaputtaṃ passati, tathā adhiṭṭhāsīti attho. Adhivāsetūti sampaṭicchatu. Ajjatanāyāti yaṃ me tumhesu sakkāraṃ karoto ajja bhavissati puññañca pītipāmojjañca, tadatthāya. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvenāti bhagavā kāyaṅgaṃ vā vācaṅgaṃ vā acopetvā abbhantareyeva khantiṃ karonto tuṇhībhāvena adhivāsesi, seṭṭhissa anuggahatthaṃ manasāva sampaṭicchīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Ehi bhikkhū”ti bhagavā avocāti tassa kira iddhimayapattacīvarassa upanissayaṃ olokento anekāsu jātīsu cīvarādiaṭṭhaparikkhāradānaṃ disvā “ehi bhikkhū”ti avoca. So tāvadeva bhaṇḍu kāsāvavasano aṭṭhahi bhikkhuparikkhārehi sarīre paṭimukkeheva vassasaṭṭhikatthero viya bhagavantaṃ namassamānova nisīdi. Yo hi cīvarādike aṭṭha parikkhāre pattacīvarameva vā sotāpannādiariyassa puthujjanasseva vā sīlasampannassa datvā “idaṃ parikkhāradānaṃ anāgate ehibhikkhubhāvāya paccayo hotū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapeti, tassa taṃ sati adhikārasampattiyaṃ buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve iddhimayaparikkhāralābhāya saṃvattatīti veditabbaṃ.

28. 'Bhūmiṃ paccavekkhantassa' means reflecting on the state one has realized. 'Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ paṭippassambhesi' means he resolved so that the merchant householder, while sitting there, would see the young man Yasa. 'Adhivāsetu' means 'may he consent.' 'Ajjatanāya' means for the sake of the merit and joy that will arise for me today by honoring you. 'Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena' (The Blessed One accepted by silence) means the Blessed One, without moving his body or speech, enduring inwardly, accepted by silence—it is said that he consented mentally for the merchant's benefit. 'Ehi bhikkhu'ti bhagavā avoca' (The Blessed One said, 'Come, monk') — it is said that while observing the potential for the miraculous robe and bowl, he saw the giving of robes and other requisites in many past lives and said, 'Come, monk.' Immediately, he became shaven-headed, wearing the saffron robe, adorned with the eight monastic requisites as if they were fastened to his body, like a sixty-year elder, and sat down, paying homage to the Blessed One. For whoever gives the eight requisites, such as robes and bowls, or even just a robe and bowl, to a noble one like a stream-enterer or to a virtuous ordinary person, and makes the aspiration, "May this gift of requisites become a condition for the 'ehi bhikkhu' ordination in the future," it should be understood that when there is the accomplishment of the aspiration, in the presence of the Buddhas, it leads to the attainment of miraculous requisites.

29. Paṇītenāti uttamena. Sahatthāti sahatthena. Santappetvāti suṭṭhu tappetvā, paripuṇṇaṃ suhitaṃ yāvadatthaṃ katvā. Sampavāretvāti suṭṭhu pavāretvā, alaṃ alanti hatthasaññāya paṭikkhipāpetvā. Bhuttāvinti bhuttavantaṃ[M 3.0198]. Onītapattapāṇinti pattato onītapāṇiṃ, apanītahatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. “Onittapattapāṇi”ntipi pāṭho, tassattho – onittaṃ nānābhūtaṃ vinābhūtaṃ [V 3.0181] pattaṃ pāṇito assāti onittapattapāṇi, taṃ onittapattapāṇiṃ, hatthe ca pattañca dhovitvā ekamantaṃ pattaṃ nikkhipitvā nisinnanti attho. Ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsūti bhagavantaṃ evaṃbhūtaṃ ñatvā ekasmiṃ okāse nisīdiṃsūti attho. Dhammiyā kathāyātiādīsu taṅkhaṇānurūpāya dhammiyā kathāya diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaatthaṃ sandassetvā kusale ca dhamme samādapetvā tattha ca naṃ samuttejetvā saussāhaṃ katvā tāya ca saussāhatāya aññehi ca vijjamānaguṇehi sampahaṃsetvā dhammaratanavassaṃ vassitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi.

29. 'Paṇītena' means with the excellent. 'Sahatthā' means with his own hand. 'Santappetvā' means having thoroughly satisfied, making them fully content, satiated to their heart's desire. 'Sampavāretvā' means having fully invited them to take more, causing them to refuse by a gesture of the hand, saying 'enough, enough.' 'Bhuttāvī' means one who has eaten. 'Onītapattapāṇi' means having withdrawn the hand from the bowl, meaning the hand has been removed. The reading 'Onittapattapāṇi' is also found, its meaning being—the bowl is distinct and separate from the hand, thus 'onittapattapāṇi,' that is, one who has washed both hand and bowl, set the bowl aside, and sat down. 'Ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu' means, knowing the Blessed One to be in such a state, they sat down in a suitable place. In 'dhammiyā kathāya,' etc., it refers to a Dhamma talk suitable for the occasion, pointing out the benefits in this life and the next, establishing them in wholesome qualities, inspiring them in that, making them enthusiastic, gladdening them with existing virtues, showering them with the rain of the jewel of Dhamma, and then rising from their seat and departing.

Yasassa pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Yasa's going forth is finished.

Catugihisahāyapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Going Forth of the Four Householder Friends.

30. Idāni tassa sahāyānaṃ pabbajjaṃ dassento “assosuṃ kho”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – seṭṭhino ca anuseṭṭhino ca yesaṃ kulānaṃ tāni seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīni kulāni, tesaṃ seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīnaṃ kulānaṃ, paveṇivasena āgatehi seṭṭhīhi ca anuseṭṭhīhi ca samannāgatānaṃ kulānanti attho. Vimalotiādīni tesaṃ puttānaṃ nāmāni. Kesamassuṃ ohāretvāti kesañca massuñca oropetvā. Kāsāyāni vatthānīti kasāyarasapītāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni. Orakoti ūnako lāmako. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

30. Now, to show the going forth of his friends, he begins with "they heard," and so on. Here is the explanation of terms that are not clear: seṭṭhino ca anuseṭṭhino ca refers to the families of the bankers and the sub-bankers; seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīni kulāni means the families endowed with bankers and sub-bankers, who have come in succession. Vimalo, and so on, are the names of their sons. Kesamassuṃ ohāretvā means having shaved off hair and beard. Kāsāyāni vatthāni means robes dyed with astringent juice, suitable for those leading the holy life. Orako means deficient, inferior. The rest here is as stated previously.

Catugihisahāyapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Going Forth of the Four Householder Friends is concluded.

Paññāsagihisahāyapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Going Forth of the Fifty Householder Friends.

31. Paññāsamattānaṃ gihisahāyānaṃ pabbajjāyapi yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vuttameva. Imesaṃ pana sabbesaṃ pubbayogo vattabboti taṃ dassetuṃ “yasaādīnaṃ [M 3.0199] kulaputtānaṃ ayaṃ pubbayogo”tiādimāha. Tattha vaggabandhanenāti gaṇabandhanena, ekībhūtāti vuttaṃ hoti. Anāthasarīrānīti anāthāni matakaḷevarāni. Paṭijaggantāti bahi nīharitvā jhāpentā.

31. Regarding the going forth of the fifty householder friends, what needed to be said has already been said. However, the past karma of all of them should be told; so to show this, it begins with "this was the past karma of the clansmen like Yasa," and so on. Here, vaggabandhanena means by group bond, which means united. Anāthasarīrāni means helpless corpses. Paṭijaggantā means taking them outside and cremating them.

Paññāsagihisahāyapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Going Forth of the Fifty Householder Friends is concluded.

Mārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Māra Story.

32. Idāni [V 3.0182] saraṇagamanūpasampadaṃ dassetuṃ “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbapadavaṇṇanā (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.141) – muttāhanti mutto ahaṃ. Cārikanti anupubbagamanacārikaṃ, gāmanigamarājadhānīsu anukkamena gamanasaṅkhātaṃ cārikanti attho. Carathāti divasaṃ yojanaparamaṃ gacchantā caratha. Mā ekena dve agamitthāti ekena maggena dvīsu gatesu ekasmiṃ dhammaṃ desente ekena tuṇhībhūtena ṭhātabbaṃ hoti, tasmā evamāha. Ādikalyāṇanti ādimhi kalyāṇaṃ sundaraṃ bhaddakaṃ, tathā majjhapariyosānesu. Ādimajjhapariyosānañca nāmetaṃ sāsanassa ca desanāya ca vasena dubbidhaṃ. Tattha sāsanassa sīlaṃ ādi, samathavipassanāmaggā majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ. Sīlasamādhayo vā ādi, vipassanāmaggā majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ. Sīlasamādhivipassanā vā ādi, maggo majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ. Desanāya pana catuppadikagāthāya tāva paṭhamapādo ādi, dutiyatatiyā majjhaṃ, catuttho pariyosānaṃ. Pañcapadachappadānaṃ paṭhamapādo ādi, avasānapādo pariyosānaṃ, sesā majjhaṃ. Ekānusandhikassa suttassa nidānaṃ ādi, idamavocāti pariyosānaṃ, sesaṃ majjhaṃ. Anekānusandhikassa suttassa majjhe bahukampi anusandhi majjhameva, nidānaṃ ādi, idamavocāti pariyosānaṃ. Sātthanti sātthakaṃ katvā desetha. Sabyañjananti byañjanehi ceva padehi ca paripūraṃ katvā desetha. Kevalaparipuṇṇanti sakalaparipuṇṇaṃ. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ. Pakāsethāti āvi karotha.

32. Now, to show the going for refuge and the higher ordination, the text begins with "Then the Blessed One," and so on. Here is the sequential explanation of the terms (Saṃ. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.141):

Muttāhaṃ means "I am freed."

Cārikaṃ refers to the gradual journey, the act of traveling successively through villages, towns, and royal cities.

Caratha means "travel," traveling about a league per day.

Mā ekena dve agamittha means that if two go by one path, when one is teaching the Dhamma, the other should remain silent. Hence, it is said thus.

Ādikalyāṇaṃ means excellent, beautiful, and auspicious in the beginning, likewise in the middle and the end.

The beginning, middle, and end are twofold—by way of the Dispensation and the teaching.

Therein, for the Dispensation:

Virtue is the beginning,

Serenity, insight, and the path are the middle,

Fruition and Nibbāna are the end.

Or:

Virtue and concentration are the beginning,

Insight and the path are the middle,

Fruition and Nibbāna are the end.

Or:

Virtue, concentration, and insight are the beginning,

The path is the middle,

Fruition and Nibbāna are the end.

For the teaching:

In a four-line verse, the first line is the beginning,

The second and third are the middle,

The fourth is the end.

In five- or six-line verses, the first line is the beginning, the last line is the end, and the rest are the middle.

For a discourse with a single connection:

The introduction is the beginning,

"idamavocāti" is the end,

The rest is the middle.

For a discourse with multiple connections, even the many connecting sections in the middle are just the middle; the introduction is the beginning, and 'idamavocāti' is the end.

Sātthaṃ means teach with meaning.

Sabyañjanaṃ means teach completely with phrases and syllables.

Kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ means wholly complete.

Parisuddhaṃ means perfectly pure, free from defilements.

Brahmacariyaṃ refers to the holy life, the Dispensation's holy life, comprising the threefold training.

Pakāsetha means make it clear.

Apparajakkhajātikāti paññācakkhumhi appakilesarajasabhāvā, dukūlasāṇiyā paṭicchannā viya catuppadikagāthāpariyosāne arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthā [M 3.0200] sattā santīti attho. Parihāyantīti alābhaparihāniyā dhammato parihāyanti. Tenevāha “anadhigataṃ nādhigacchantā visesādhigamato parihāyantī”ti. Senānigamoti senāya nigamo. Paṭhamakappikānaṃ kira tasmiṃ ṭhāne senāniveso ahosi, tasmā so padeso “senānigamo”ti vuccati. “Senānigāmo”tipi pāṭho, senāni nāma sujātāya pitā, tassa gāmoti attho. Tenupasaṅkamissāmīti nāhaṃ tumhe uyyojetvā pariveṇādīni kāretvā upaṭṭhākādīhi paricariyamāno viharissāmi, tiṇṇaṃ pana jaṭilānaṃ aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni dassetvā dhammameva desetuṃ upasaṅkamissāmi.

Apparajakkhajātikā means that, in the eye of wisdom, beings with little defilement-dust, like those covered by fine cloth or hemp, are capable of attaining arahantship by the end of a four-line verse—this is the meaning. Parihāyanti means they decline from the Dhamma through the loss that is non-attainment. Therefore, it is said, "They decline from attaining what they have not attained, declining from higher distinctions." Senānigamo means an army settlement. It is said that in that place, there was an army encampment of the first inhabitants, hence that area is called Senānigamo. There is also a variant reading, Senānigāmo, meaning the village of Senāni, Sujātā’s father—that is the meaning. Tenupasaṅkamissāmi means: "I will not send you away to build monasteries or live being attended to by supporters. Instead, I will approach after showing the three matted-hair ascetics two and a half thousand miracles, solely to teach the Dhamma."

33. Māro pāpimāti attano visayaṃ atikkamituṃ paṭipanne satte māretīti māro, pare [V 3.0183] pāpe niyojeti, sayaṃ vā pāpe niyuttoti pāpimā. Aññānipissa kaṇho adhipati vasavattī antako namuci pamattabandhūtiādīni bahūni nāmāni, idha pana nāmadvayameva gahitaṃ. Upasaṅkamīti “ayaṃ samaṇo gotamo mahāyuddhaṃ vicārento viya ‘mā ekena dve agamittha, dhammaṃ desethā’ti saṭṭhi jane uyyojeti, imasmiṃ pana ekasmimpi dhammaṃ desente mayhaṃ cittassa sātaṃ natthi, evaṃ bahūsu desentesu kuto bhavissati, paṭibāhāmi na”nti cintetvā upasaṅkami.

33. Māra is called Māra because he kills beings who have transgressed his realm. He is called Pāpimā because he incites others to evil or is himself addicted to evil. He has many other names, such as the Dark One, the Overlord, the Possessor of Power, the Ender, Namuci, the Kinsman of the Negligent, but here only two names are taken. Upasaṅkamī means he approached thinking, "This ascetic Gotama, as if preparing for a great battle, sends forth sixty people with the words, 'Do not go two by one, teach the Dhamma.' But even when this one teaches the Dhamma to a single person, my mind finds no pleasure. How then will it be when many are teaching? I will thwart him." Thus, he approached.

Sabbapāsehīti sabbehi kilesapāsehi. Ye dibbā ye ca mānusāti ye dibbakāmaguṇasaṅkhātā mānusakakāmaguṇasaṅkhātā ca kilesapāsā nāma atthi, sabbehi tehi tvaṃ baddhoti vadati. Mahābandhanabaddhoti mahatā kilesabandhanena baddho, mahati vā bandhane baddho, kilesabandhanassa ṭhānabhūte bhavacārake baddhoti attho. Na me samaṇa mokkhasīti samaṇa tvaṃ mama visayato na muccissasi. “Na me samaṇa mokkhasī”ti ca idaṃ māro “muttāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbapāsehī”ti bhagavato vacanaṃ asaddahanto vadati, saddahantopi vā “evamayaṃ paresaṃ sattānaṃ mokkhāya ussāhaṃ na kareyyā”ti santajjento kohaññe ṭhatvā vadati.

Sabbapāsehi means by all the snares of defilements. Ye dibbā ye ca mānusā refers to the snares of defilements known as the divine strands of sensual pleasure and the human strands of sensual pleasure. "You are bound by all of them," he says. Mahābandhanabaddho means bound by the great bondage of defilements, or bound in a great bondage; the meaning is bound in the prison of existence, which is the ground for the bondage of defilements. Na me samaṇa mokkhasī means: "Ascetic, you will not escape from my domain." And this phrase, "O ascetic, you will not escape me," is spoken by Māra either because he does not believe the Blessed One’s statement, "Monks, I am freed from all snares," or, even if he believes it, he speaks thus deceitfully, intending to frighten him, thinking: "In this way, this one might not make an effort for the liberation of other beings."

Nihatoti tvaṃ mayā nihato, nibbisevanabhāvaṃ gamito parājitoti attho. Antalikkhe carante pañcābhiññepi bandhatīti antalikkhacaro. Rāgapāso hi antalikkhacaresupi kiccasādhanato “antalikkhacaro”ti [M 3.0201] vuccati, teneva naṃ māropi antalikkhacaroti maññati. Manasi jātoti mānaso, manasampayuttoti attho. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

Nihata means "You are struck down by me," rendered powerless, meaning defeated. Antalikkhacaro means one who moves in the sky, because he binds even those with the five supernormal knowledges who move in the sky. Indeed, the snare of lust is called "sky-wanderer" because it accomplishes its purpose even among those who wander in the sky; for that reason Māra also considers himself a sky-wanderer. Mānaso means born in the mind, that is, associated with the mind. The rest here is of obvious meaning.

Mārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Māra Story is concluded.

Pabbajjūpasampadākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Going Forth and Higher Ordination

34. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave”tiādikāya pana pāḷiyā yo pabbajjūpasampadāvinicchayo vattabbo, taṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “pabbajjāpekkhaṃ kulaputtaṃ pabbājentenā”tiādimāha. Tattha ye puggalā paṭikkhittāti sambandho. Sayaṃ pabbājetabboti kesacchedanādīni sayaṃ karontena pabbājetabbo. Kesacchedanaṃ kāsāyacchādanaṃ saraṇadānanti hi imāni tīṇi karonto “pabbājetī”ti vuccati. Etesu ekaṃ dve vāpi karonto tathā voharīyatiyeva, tasmā etaṃ pabbājehīti kesacchedanaṃ kāsāyacchādanañca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Upajjhāyaṃ [V 3.0184] uddissa pabbājetīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Khaṇḍasīmaṃ netvāti bhaṇḍukammārocanapariharaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena sabhikkhuke vihāre aññampi “etassa kese chindā”ti vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pabbājetvāti kesacchedanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Bhikkhuto añño pabbājetuṃ na labhatīti saraṇadānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “sāmaṇero panā”tiādi. Bhabbarūpoti bhabbasabhāvo. Tamevatthaṃ pariyāyantarena vibhāveti “sahetuko”ti. Ñātoti pākaṭo. Yasassīti parivārasampattiyā samannāgato.

34. Regarding the Pāli passage beginning, “I allow, monks,” the ruling on going forth and higher ordination is to be stated. To show this in detail, it is said, beginning with, “By one ordaining a clansman who desires to go forth…” Here, the connection is to those individuals who are rejected. “He is to be ordained by oneself” means he is to be ordained by one who himself performs the cutting of the hair and so on. For one who performs these three acts—cutting the hair, putting on the ochre robes, and giving the refuges—is called “one who ordains.” Even one who performs one or two of these is still referred to in this way. Therefore, the statement “Ordain this one” is said with reference to cutting the hair and putting on the ochre robes. In the phrase “one ordains having designated a preceptor,” this same principle applies. “Having led him to a partial boundary” is said for the purpose of avoiding the announcement and procedure for the shaving. For that reason, in a monastery with monks, it is not proper for even another to say, “Cut this one’s hair.” “Having ordained” is said with reference to cutting the hair. “No one other than a monk may ordain” is said with reference to giving the refuges. For that reason, it is said, “But a novice…” and so on. Bhabbarūpo means of a suitable nature. It clarifies this same meaning with another term: sahetuko, “having a cause.” Ñāto means manifest. Yasassī means endowed with the asset of a retinue.

Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena asucijegucchapaṭikūlabhāvaṃ pākaṭaṃ karontenāti sambandho. Tattha kesā nāmete vaṇṇatopi paṭikūlā, saṇṭhānatopi gandhatopi āsayatopi okāsatopi paṭikūlā. Manuññepi (visuddhi. 1.183; vibha. aṭṭha. 356; sārattha. ṭī. pārājikakaṇḍa 2.162) hi yāgupatte vā bhattapatte vā kesavaṇṇaṃ kiñci disvā “kesamissakamidaṃ, haratha na”nti jigucchanti, evaṃ kesā vaṇṇato paṭikūlā. Rattiṃ bhuñjantāpi kesasaṇṭhānaṃ akkavākaṃ vā makacivākaṃ vā chupitvā [M 3.0202] tatheva jigucchanti, evaṃ saṇṭhānato paṭikūlā. Telamakkhanapupphadhūmādisaṅkhāravirahitānañca kesānaṃ gandho paramajeguccho hoti, tato jegucchataro aggimhi pakkhittānaṃ. Kesā hi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikūlāpi siyuṃ, gandhena pana paṭikūlāyeva. Yathā hi daharassa kumārakassa vaccaṃ vaṇṇato haliddivaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānatopi haliddipiṇḍisaṇṭhānaṃ. Saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍitañca uddhumātakakāḷasunakhasarīraṃ vaṇṇato tālapakkavaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānato vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamudiṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ, dāṭhāpissa sumanamakuḷasadisā, taṃ ubhayampi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato siyā appaṭikūlaṃ, gandhena pana paṭikūlameva, evaṃ kesāpi siyuṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikūlā, gandhena pana paṭikūlāyevāti. Yathā pana asuciṭṭhāne gāmanissandena jātāni sūpeyyapaṇṇāni nāgarikamanussānaṃ jegucchāni honti aparibhogāni, evaṃ kesāpi pubbalohitamuttakarīsapittasemhādinissandena jātattā paramajegucchāti evaṃ āsayato paṭikūlā. Ime ca kesā nāma gūtharāsimhi uṭṭhitakaṇṇakaṃ viya ekatiṃsakoṭṭhāsarāsimhi jātā, te susānasaṅkāraṭṭhānādīsu jātasākaṃ viya parikhādīsu jātakamalakuvalayādipupphaṃ viya ca asuciṭṭhāne jātattā paramajegucchāti evaṃ okāsato paṭikūlātiādinā nayena tacapañcakassa vaṇṇādivasena paṭikūlabhāvaṃ pakāsentenāti attho.

The connection is: "by one who makes manifest the state of being impure, disgusting, and repulsive by way of color, shape, smell, origin, and location." Herein, these things called hairs are repulsive by color, repulsive by shape, by smell, by origin, and by location. For even in a pleasant bowl of gruel or a bowl of rice, upon seeing something the color of a hair, people are disgusted, saying, "This is mixed with hair, take it away!" Thus, hairs are repulsive by color. Even when eating at night, if they touch the shape of a hair, or the fibre of an akka plant, or a bug's leg, they are disgusted in the same way. Thus, hairs are repulsive by shape. And the smell of hairs that are without preparations such as oiling, flowers, and incense is extremely disgusting; even more disgusting is the smell of those thrown on a fire. Hairs might not be repulsive by color and shape, but by smell they are certainly repulsive. For example, a young child’s excrement is the color of turmeric and has the shape of a lump of turmeric. And a bloated, black dog’s corpse discarded in a refuse heap is the color of a ripe palm fruit and, when rolled up and cast aside, has the shape of a drum; its teeth are like jasmine buds. Both of these might not be repulsive by color and shape, but by smell they are certainly repulsive. In the same way, hairs might not be repulsive by color and shape, but by smell they are certainly repulsive. Just as curry-leaves grown in a filthy place from the runoff of a village are disgusting and unfit for consumption by city-dwellers, so too hairs, being born from the runoff of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so on, are extremely disgusting. Thus, they are repulsive by origin. And these things called hairs are born in the heap of the thirty-one body parts like a mushroom that has sprung up on a dung-heap. Because they are born in a filthy place—like vegetables grown in a charnel ground or a rubbish heap, or like flowers such as lotuses and water lilies grown in a moat—they are extremely disgusting. Thus, they are repulsive by location. By this method, the meaning is: "by one who reveals the repulsive nature of the pentad ending in skin by way of color and so on."

Nijjīvanissattabhāvaṃ vā pākaṭaṃ karontenāti ime kesā nāma sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacamme jātā. Tattha yathā vammikamatthake jātesu kunthatiṇesu na vammikamatthako jānāti “mayi kunthatiṇāni jātānī”ti, nāpi kunthatiṇāni jānanti “mayaṃ vammikamatthake jātānī”ti, evameva [V 3.0185] na sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacammaṃ jānāti “mayi kesā jātā”ti, nāpi kesā jānanti “mayaṃ sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacamme jātā”ti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti kesā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūtiādinā nayena nijjīvanissattabhāvaṃ pakāsentena. Pubbeti purimabuddhānaṃ santike. Madditasaṅkhāroti nāmarūpavavatthānena ceva paccayapariggahavasena ca ñāṇena parimadditasaṅkhāro. Bhāvitabhāvanoti kalāpasammasanādinā sabbaso kusalabhāvanāya pūraṇena bhāvitabhāvano.

Or: "by one who makes manifest the state of being lifeless and without a being." These things called hairs are born on the skin that wraps the bowl of the skull. Herein, just as when kuntha grass grows on the top of a termite mound, the top of the termite mound does not know, "Kuntha grass has grown on me," nor does the kuntha grass know, "We have grown on the top of a termite mound," so too, the skin that wraps the bowl of the skull does not know, "Hairs have grown on me," nor do the hairs know, "We have grown on the skin that wraps the bowl of the skull." These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, by the method beginning, "Hairs are a separate part in this body, non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, without a being, rigid, the earth element," one reveals the state of being lifeless and without a being. Pubbe means in the presence of former Buddhas. Madditasaṅkhāro means one whose formations have been thoroughly ground by knowledge, by way of the determination of name-and-form and the comprehension of conditions. Bhāvitabhāvano means one whose cultivation has been developed by the fulfillment of wholesome cultivation in every way, by means of the comprehension of groups and so on.

Adinnaṃ [M 3.0203] na vaṭṭatīti ettha pabbajjā na ruhatīti vadanti. Anuññātaupasampadāti ñatticatutthakammena anuññātaupasampadā. Ṭhānakaraṇasampadanti ettha urādīni ṭhānāni, saṃvutādīni karaṇānīti veditabbāni. Anunāsikantaṃ katvā dānakāle antarā vicchedaṃ akatvā dātabbānīti dassetuṃ “ekasambandhānī”ti vuttaṃ. Vicchinditvāti ma-kārantaṃ katvā dānasamaye vicchedaṃ katvā. Sabbamassa kappiyākappiyaṃ ācikkhitabbanti dasasikkhāpadavinimuttaṃ parāmāsāparāmāsādibhedaṃ kappiyākappiyaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Ābhisamācārikesu vinetabboti iminā sekhiyaupajjhāyavattādiābhisamācārikasīlamanena pūretabbaṃ, tattha ca kattabbassa akaraṇe akattabbassa ca karaṇe daṇḍakammāraho hotīti dīpeti.

Regarding "what is not given is not allowable," here they say that the going forth does not take root. "Authorized higher ordination" means the higher ordination authorized by a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements. "The accomplishment of basis and means"—here, the bases are the chest and so on, and the means are closure and so on; thus it should be understood. To show that it should be given at the time of giving by making it end with a nasal and without making an interruption in between, it is said, "connected as one." "Having interrupted" means having made it end with the letter 'm' and having made an interruption at the time of giving. "All that is allowable or unallowable should be explained to him" means the allowable and unallowable, which is separate from the ten training rules, with distinctions such as touching and not touching, should be explained. "He should be trained in the customary observances"—by this it is indicated that the good conduct of the customary observances, such as the rules of training, the duties to a preceptor, and so on, should be fulfilled by him, and that therein, for not doing what should be done and for doing what should not be done, he is liable to a disciplinary action.

Pabbajjūpasampadākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Going Forth and Higher Ordination is concluded.

Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on Māra.

35. Atha kho bhagavā vassaṃvuṭṭhotiādikāya pana pāḷiyā ayaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā. Yonisomanasikārāti upāyamanasikārena, aniccādīsu aniccādito manasikaraṇenāti attho. Yoniso sammappadhānāti upāyavīriyena, anuppannākusalānuppādanādividhinā pavattavīriyenāti attho. Vimuttīti ukkaṭṭhaniddesena arahattaphalavimutti vuttā. Ajjhabhāsīti “ayaṃ attanā vīriyaṃ katvā arahattaṃ patvāpi na tussati, idāni aññesampi ‘pāpuṇāthā’ti ussāhaṃ karoti, paṭibāhessāmi na”nti cintetvā abhāsi. Mārapāsenāti kilesapāsena. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

35. Now, this is the commentary on the unprecedented passage in the Pāli text beginning with 'Atha kho bhagavā vassaṃvuṭṭho' (Then the Blessed One, having completed the rains residence). ‘Yonisomanasikāra’ (wise attention) means attention with skill, that is, attending to impermanence and so forth from the aspect of impermanence. ‘Yoniso sammappadhāna’ (right effort with wisdom) means effort with skill, that is, effort that proceeds in the manner of preventing unarisen unwholesome states from arising and so forth. ‘Vimutti’ (liberation) refers to the liberation of arahantship, stated by way of the highest designation. ‘Ajjhabhāsī’ (addressed) means he spoke, thinking: ‘Even though he has striven and attained arahantship himself, he is not content; now he encourages others, saying, “Attain!” I will obstruct him.’ ‘Mārapāsena’ (Māra’s snare) means the snare of defilements. The rest here is to be understood in the same way as previously stated.

Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on Māra is concluded.

Bhaddavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of the Bhaddavaggiyā.

36. Tiṃsabhaddavaggiyavatthumhi [V 3.0186] yathābhirantaṃ viharitvāti yathāajjhāsayaṃ viharitvā. Buddhānañhi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ chāyūdakādīnaṃ vipattiṃ vā aphāsukasenāsanaṃ vā manussānaṃ assaddhādibhāvaṃ vā āgamma [M 3.0204] anabhirati nāma natthi, tesaṃ sampattiyā “idha phāsuṃ viharāmā”ti abhiramitvā ciravihāropi natthi. Yattha pana tathāgate viharante sattā saraṇesu vā tīsu patiṭṭhahanti, sīlāni vā samādiyanti, pabbajanti vā, sotāpattimaggādīnaṃ vā paresaṃ upanissayo hoti, tattha buddhā satte tāsu sampattīsu patiṭṭhāpanaajjhāsayena vasanti, tāsaṃ abhāve pakkamanti. Tena vuttaṃ “yathāajjhāsayaṃ viharitvā”ti. Ajjhogāhetvāti pavisitvā. Tiṃsamattāti tiṃsapamāṇā. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

36. In the account of the thirty Bhaddavaggiyā, ‘yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā’ (having dwelt as long as he pleased) means having dwelt according to his inclination. For when Buddhas dwell in one place, discontent never arises on account of a lack of shade, water, and so forth, or unsuitable lodging, or the lack of faith and so forth among people. Nor, due to the abundance of these things, do they delight in dwelling long, thinking, ‘Here we dwell at ease.’ But where, while the Tathāgata dwells, beings establish themselves in the three refuges, or undertake precepts, or go forth, or where there is a basis for others to attain the path of stream-entry and so forth, there the Buddhas dwell with the intention of establishing beings in those attainments; in their absence, they depart. Therefore, it is said, ‘yathāajjhāsayaṃ viharitvā’ (having dwelt according to his inclination). ‘Ajjhogāhetvā’ (having plunged into) means having entered. ‘Tiṃsamattā’ (about thirty) means numbering thirty. The rest here is to be understood in the same way as previously stated.

Bhaddavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Account of the Bhaddavaggiyā is concluded.

Uruvelapāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of the Miracle at Uruvelā.

37-38. Uruvelakassapavatthumhi jaṭiloti jaṭādharo. Jaṭā assa atthīti hi jaṭilo. Netīti nāyako, sāmaṃ vineti attano laddhiṃ sikkhāpetīti vināyako. Sace te kassapa agarūti kassapa sace tuyhaṃ bhāriyaṃ aphāsukaṃ kiñci natthi. Agyāgāreti aggisālāyaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ sajotibhūtānanti ubhosu sajotibhūtesu pajjalitesu. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma.

37-38. In the account of Uruvelā Kassapa, ‘jaṭila’ (the matted-hair ascetic) means one who has matted locks. Indeed, because he has matted locks, he is called a jaṭila. ‘Neti’ (leads) means a guide (nāyako); because he himself trains (vineti) and teaches his own doctrine, he is called a trainer (vināyako). ‘Sace te kassapa agarū’ (if, Kassapa, you have no objection) means, Kassapa, if there is nothing weighty or uncomfortable for you. ‘Agyāgāre’ (in the fire chamber) means in the fire hall. ‘Ubhinnaṃ sajotibhūtānaṃ’ (both blazing) means both were blazing, being endowed with light. ‘Yatra hi nāma’ (where indeed) means which indeed.

39. Ajjaṇhoti ajja ekadivasaṃ. Aggisālamhīti agyāgāre. Sumanamanasoti sundaracittasaṅkhātamano. Tejodhātūsu kusaloti tejokasiṇasamāpattīsu kusalo. Udicchareti ullokesuṃ, parivāresunti vā attho. Pattamhi odahitvāti patte pakkhipitvā. Dhuvabhattenāti niccabhattena.

39. ‘Ajjaṇho’ (today) means this one day. ‘Aggisālamhi’ (in the fire hall) means in the fire hall (agyāgāre). ‘Sumanamanaso’ (with a joyful mind) means a mind reckoned as a beautiful thought. ‘Tejodhātūsu kusalo’ (skilled in the fire element) means skilled in the attainments of the fire kasiṇa. ‘Udicchare’ (they looked up) means they looked up, or it also means they surrounded. ‘Pattamhi odahitvā’ (having placed in the bowl) means having put into the bowl. ‘Dhuvabhattena’ (with regular alms-food) means with constant alms-food.

40. Abhikkantāya rattiyāti ettha abhikkanta-saddo khaye vattati, tena parikkhīṇāyarattiyāti attho. Ete hi cattāro mahārājāno majjhimayāmasamanantare āgatā. Niyāmo kiresa devatānaṃ, yadidaṃ buddhānaṃ vā buddhasāvakānaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantā majjhimayāmasamanantare āgacchanti. Abhikkantavaṇṇāti abhirūpachavivaṇṇā, iṭṭhavaṇṇā manāpavaṇṇāti [V 3.0187] vuttaṃ hoti. Devatā hi manussalokaṃ āgacchamānā pakativaṇṇaṃ pakatiiddhiṃ [M 3.0205] jahitvā oḷārikaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā atirekavaṇṇavatthālaṅkārakāyādīhi obhāsaṃ muñcamānādivasena ca dibbaṃ iddhānubhāvañca nimminitvā naṭasamajjādīni gacchantā manussā viya abhisaṅkhatena kāyena āgacchanti. Tattha kāmāvacarā anabhisaṅkhatenapi āgantuṃ sakkonti oḷārikarūpattā. Tathā hi te kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhā, rūpāvacarā pana anabhisaṅkhatena kāyena āgantuṃ na sakkonti sukhumatararūpattā. Tesañhi atisukhumova attabhāvo, na tena iriyāpathakappanaṃ hoti. Tasmā brahmalokepi brahmāno yebhuyyena nimmitarūpeneva pavattanti. Mūlapaṭisandhirūpañhi nesaṃ ativiya sukhumamahārūpaṃ, kevalaṃ taṃ cittuppādassa nissayādhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ saṇṭhānavantaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati.

40. ‘Abhikkantāya rattiyā’ (when the night was far advanced)—here, the word ‘abhikkanta’ is used in the sense of passing away, meaning the night had fully passed. Indeed, these four great kings arrived just after the middle watch. For it is a fixed rule for deities that when they come to attend upon the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddhas, they arrive just after the middle watch. ‘Abhikkantavaṇṇā’ (of surpassing beauty) means they had a beautiful complexion and appearance; it is said that they had a pleasing and delightful appearance. For when deities come to the human world, they abandon their natural form and natural power, assume a coarser existence, and manifest extraordinary beauty, clothing, ornaments, and radiance, appearing to emit light and displaying divine power. Like humans going to a performance or festival, they come with artificially fashioned bodies. In this regard, the deities of the sense-sphere realm can come even without artificial fashioning due to their relatively coarse form. Indeed, they consume solid food. However, the deities of the form realm cannot come without an artificially fashioned body because their forms are more subtle. For their existence is extremely refined; the physical postures cannot be maintained by means of it. Therefore, even in the Brahma realms, the Brahmas mostly function through created forms. Their fundamental rebirth-linking form is exceedingly subtle, a great form, serving merely as a basis and support for the arising of consciousness, remaining stable and endowed with a configuration.

Kevalakappanti ettha kevala-saddassa anavasesattaṃ attho, kappa-saddassa samantabhāvo, tasmā kevalakappaṃ vanasaṇḍanti anavasesaṃ samantato vanasaṇḍanti attho. Anavasesaṃ pharituṃ samatthassapi hi obhāsassa kenaci kāraṇena ekadesapharaṇampi siyā, ayaṃ pana sabbaso pharatīti dassetuṃ samantattho kappa-saddo gahito. Atha vā īsaṃ asamatthaṃ kevalakappaṃ. Bhagavato pabhāya anobhāsitameva hi padesaṃ devatā attano pabhāya obhāsenti. Na hi bhagavato pabhā kāyaci pabhāya abhibhūyati, sūriyādīnampi pana pabhaṃ sā abhibhuyya tiṭṭhatīti. Obhāsetvāti vatthālaṅkārasarīrasamuṭṭhitāya ābhāya pharitvā, cando viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekapajjotaṃ karitvāti attho. Devatānañhi sarīrābhā dasadvādasayojanamattaṭṭhānaṃ tato bhiyyopi pharitvā tiṭṭhati, tathā vatthābharaṇādīsu samuṭṭhitā pabhā. Catuddisāti catūsu disāsu. Yatra hi nāmāti yaṃ nāma.

‘Kevalakappaṃ’ (entirely)—here, the word ‘kevala’ means without remainder, and the word ‘kappa’ means all-embracing. Therefore, ‘kevalakappaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ’ (the entire forest grove) means the forest grove without remainder, all around. Indeed, even a light capable of spreading everywhere might, for some reason, illuminate only a part. But here, the word ‘kappa’ is taken with the meaning of ‘all-embracing’ to show that it spreads completely in every direction. Alternatively, ‘kevalakappaṃ’ implies it is slightly incomplete. Indeed, the deities illuminate with their own radiance only a place unilluminated by the radiance of the Blessed One. For the radiance of the Blessed One is never overpowered by any other light; rather, it surpasses even the light of the sun and other sources. ‘Obhāsetvā’ (having illuminated) means having spread the radiance that arises from the body, garments, and ornaments, making a single radiance, a single illumination, like the moon or the sun. Indeed, the radiance of the deities’ bodies extends up to ten or twelve yojanas and even beyond, as does the light arising from their garments and ornaments. ‘Catuddisā’ means in the four directions. ‘Yatra hi nāma’ (where indeed) means which indeed.

43. Aṅgamagadhāti ubho aṅgamagadharaṭṭhavāsino. Iddhipāṭihāriyanti iddhibhūtaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ, na ādesanānusāsanīpāṭihāriyanti attho. Tividhañhi pāṭihāriyaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ ādesanāpāṭihāriyaṃ anusāsanīpāṭihāriyanti. Tattha “idha bhikkhu ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāva”ntiādinayappavattaṃ (dī. ni. 1.238-239; ma. ni. 1.147; saṃ. ni. 2.70; 5.834) iddhividhameva [M 3.0206] iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ. “Idha bhikkhu parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cittampi ādisati, cetasikampi ādisati, vitakkitampi ādisati, vicāritampi ādisati ‘evampi te mano, itthampi te mano’”tiādinayappavattaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.30) parassa cittaṃ ñatvā kathanaṃ ādesanāpāṭihāriyaṃ. “Idha bhikkhu evamanusāsati ‘evaṃ vitakketha, mā evaṃ vitakkayittha, evaṃ [V 3.0188] manasi karotha, mā evaṃ mānasā karittha, idaṃ pajahatha, idaṃ upasampajja viharathā’”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.30) evamādinayappavattā sāvakānaṃ buddhānañca sabbakālaṃ desetabbadhammadesanā anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ.

43. ‘Aṅgamagadhā’ means the residents of both the Aṅga and Magadha countries. ‘Iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ’ means a marvel that is psychic power; it does not mean the miracle of revelation or the miracle of instruction. For there are three kinds of miracles: the miracle of psychic power, the miracle of revelation, and the miracle of instruction. Of these, the miracle of psychic power is simply the manifestation of psychic power, such as, ‘Here, a bhikkhu, being one becomes many; being many becomes one; he appears; he disappears,’ and so forth, which proceeds in that way (Dī. Ni. 1.238-239; Ma. Ni. 1.147; Saṃ. Ni. 2.70; 5.834). The miracle of revelation is the telling, having known the mind of another, which proceeds in the manner of a bhikkhu declaring the mind of other beings and other persons, their mental factors, what they have thought, and what they have deliberated, saying, ‘Such is your mind, in this way is your mind,’ and so forth (Paṭi. Ma. 3.30). The miracle of instruction is the teaching of the Dhamma to be taught at all times to disciples and Buddhas, which proceeds in the manner of a bhikkhu instructing thus: ‘Think in this way, do not think in that way; apply your mind to this, do not apply your mind to that; abandon this, having attained this, dwell in it,’ and so forth (Paṭi. Ma. 3.30).

Tattha (udā. aṭṭha. 1) pāṭihāriyapadassa vacanatthaṃ paṭipakkhaharaṇato rāgādikilesāpanayanato pāṭihāriyanti vadanti. Bhagavato pana paṭipakkhā rāgādayo na santi ye haritabbā, puthujjanānampi vigatūpakkilese aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgate citte hatapaṭipakkhe iddhividhaṃ vattati, tasmā tattha pavattavohārena ca na sakkā idha pāṭihāriyanti vattuṃ. Sace pana mahākāruṇikassa bhagavato veneyyagatā ca kilesā paṭipakkhā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyanti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati yuttametaṃ. Atha vā bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyaṃ. Te hi diṭṭhiharaṇavasena diṭṭhippakāsane asamatthabhāvena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīhi haritā apanītā hontīti. Paṭīti vā ayaṃ saddo pacchāti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (cūḷani. vatthugāthā 4) viya, tasmā samāhite citte vigatūpakkilesena katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ, attano vā upakkilesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchā haraṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ, iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo ca vigatūpakkilesena katakiccena sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, haritesu ca attano upakkilesesu parasattānaṃ upakkilesaharaṇāni hontīti paṭihāriyāni bhavanti, paṭihāriyameva pāṭihāriyaṃ. Paṭihāriye vā iddhiādesanānusāsanīsamudāye bhavaṃ ekekaṃ pāṭihāriyanti vuccati. Paṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato, tattha jātaṃ nimittabhūte, tato vā āgatanti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Svātanāyāti sve dātabbassa atthāya.

Here, at Udāna Commentary, p. 1, the meaning of the term "pāṭihāriya" is explained as the removal of opposing factors, or the removal of defilements such as lust and so forth; hence it is called "pāṭihāriya." However, the Blessed One has no opposing factors like lust to be removed. Even in ordinary beings, when the mind is free from impurities and endowed with the eight qualities, psychic powers arise, their opposing factors being overcome. Therefore, by conventional usage there, it cannot be called "pāṭihāriya" here. But if it is said that the defilements inherent in those receptive to training are the opposing factors for the greatly compassionate Blessed One, and their removal constitutes "pāṭihāriya," then this is appropriate. Alternatively, the opponents of the Blessed One and his dispensation are the heretics. Their removal constitutes "pāṭihāriya," for they are removed and dispelled through the destruction of wrong views, their inability to establish their teachings, and through psychic power, revelation, and instruction. Or, the term "paṭīti" suggests the meaning of "afterwards," as in the phrase, "When he had entered there, another brahmin arrived" (Cūḷaniddesa, Vatthugāthā 4). Therefore, what is to be enacted afterwards by a mind that is concentrated, free from impurities, and has fulfilled its duty is called "paṭihāriya." Alternatively, when one’s own defilements are removed by the fourth jhāna and the path, the subsequent removal is "paṭihāriya." The psychic power, revelation, and instruction are to be manifested again by one free from impurities and who has fulfilled their duty, for the welfare of beings. When one’s own defilements are removed, the removal of others’ defilements also occurs—these are called "pāṭihāriyas." "Paṭihāriya" itself is "pāṭihāriya." Alternatively, each instance in the collection of psychic power, revelation, and instruction is called a "pāṭihāriya." Or, "pāṭihāriya" refers to the fourth jhāna and the path, which arise from the removal of opposing factors; or to what is born therein as a sign; or to what comes from them. "Svātanāyāti" means 'for the sake of what is to be given tomorrow.'

44. Paṃsukūlaṃ [M 3.0207] uppannaṃ hotīti pariyesamānassa paṭilābhavasena uppannaṃ hoti. Vicittapāṭihāriyadassanatthāva sā pariyesanā. Yasmā pāṇinā phuṭṭhamatte sā pokkharaṇī nimmitā ahosi, tasmā vuttaṃ “pāṇinā pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇitvā”ti.

44. A rag-robe arises: it arises for one who is seeking, by way of obtaining it. That search is merely for the purpose of displaying a wondrous feat. Because the pond was created the moment it was touched by the hand, therefore it is said, "having dug the pond with his hand."

46-49. Jaṭilāti tāpasā. Te hi jaṭādhāritāya idha “jaṭilā”ti vuttā. Antaraṭṭhakāsu himapātasamayeti hemantassa utuno abbhantarabhūte māghamāsassa avasāne catasso, phagguṇamāsassa ādimhi catassoti evaṃ ubhinnamantare aṭṭharattīsu himapatanakāle. Nerañjarāya ummujjantīti keci tasmiṃ titthasammate udake paṭhamaṃ nimuggasakalasarīrā tato ummujjantā vuṭṭhahanti [V 3.0189] uppilavanti. Nimujjantīti sasīsaṃ udake osīdanti. Ummujjananimujjanampi karontīti punappunaṃ ummujjananimujjanānipi karonti. Tattha hi keci “ekummujjaneneva pāpasuddhi hotī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhikā, te ummujjanameva katvā gacchanti. Ummujjanaṃ pana nimujjanamantarena natthīti avinābhāvato nimujjanampi te karontiyeva. Yepi “ekanimujjaneneva pāpasuddhi hotī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhikā, tepi ekavārameva nimujjitvā vuttanayeneva avinābhāvato ummujjanampi katvā pakkamanti. Apare “punappunaṃ ummujjananimujjanāni katvā nahāte pāpasuddhi hotī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhikā, te kālena kālaṃ ummujjananimujjanāni karonti. Te sabbepi sandhāya vuttaṃ “ummujjantipi nimujjantipi ummujjananimujjanampi karontī”ti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi nimujjanapubbakaṃ ummujjanaṃ, nimujjanameva pana karontā katipayā, ummujjanaṃ tadubhayañca karontā bahūti tesaṃ yebhuyyabhāvadassanatthaṃ ummujjanaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ.

46-49. "Jaṭilā" refers to ascetics. They are called "Jaṭilā" here because they wear matted hair. "During the Antaraṭṭhaka period, at the time of snowfall" means during the winter season, in the middle of it, at the end of the month of Māgha for four nights and at the beginning of the month of Phagguna for four nights—thus, during the eight nights between these two when snowfall occurs. "Emerging from the Nerañjarā" means that some, in that water considered sacred, first submerge their entire bodies and then emerge, rise up, and float. "Submerging" means sinking into the water headfirst. "Performing both emerging and submerging" means repeatedly performing both actions. There, some hold the view that "purification from evil is achieved by a single emergence," and so they only emerge and then leave. However, since emergence cannot occur without a prior submersion, they inevitably perform a submersion as well. Others believe that "purification from evil is achieved by a single submersion," and so they submerge once and, by the same logic, inevitably perform an emergence before departing. Still others think that "purification from evil is achieved by bathing with repeated emergences and submersions," and so they perform emergences and submersions from time to time. All of these are referred to in the statement: "emerging, submerging, and performing both emergence and submersion." Here, although emergence follows submersion, some perform only submersion, while many perform emergence and both. To show the predominance of the latter, emergence is mentioned first.

50-51. Udakavāhakoti udakogho. Reṇuhatāyāti rajogatāya, rajokiṇṇāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Neva ca kho tvaṃ kassapa arahāti etena tadā kassapassa asekkhabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati, nāpi arahattamaggasamāpannoti etena sekkhabhāvaṃ. Ubhayenapissa anariyabhāvameva dīpeti. Sāpi te paṭipadā natthi, yāya tvaṃ arahā vā assasi arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannoti iminā panassa kalyāṇaputhujjanabhāvampi paṭikkhipati. Tattha paṭipadāti sīlavisuddhiādayo cha visuddhiyo. Paṭipajjati etāya ariyamaggoti paṭipadā. Assasīti [M 3.0208] bhaveyyāsi. Cirapaṭikāti cirakālato paṭṭhāya, nāgadamanato paṭṭhāyāti attho. Khārikājamissanti ettha khārīti araṇīkamaṇḍalusūciādayo tāpasaparikkhārā, taṃ haraṇakājaṃ khārikājaṃ. Aggihutamissanti dabbiādiaggipūjopakaraṇaṃ.

50-51. "Udakavāhako" means a flood of water. "Reṇuhatāya" means covered with dust; it is said to be "rajokiṇṇāya." "Nor are you, Kassapa, an arahant"—by this, he rejects Kassapa's state of being beyond training; "nor one attaining the path to arahantship"—by this, he rejects the state of a trainee. By both, he only reveals his non-noble state. "That path too is not yours, by which you might become an arahant or attain the path to arahantship"—by this, he also rejects his state as a virtuous ordinary person. Therein, "path" refers to the six purifications, beginning with purification of virtue. The Noble Path is attained by it, therefore it is the Path. "Assasi" means you might be. "Cirapaṭikā" means from a long time ago, starting from the taming of the Nāga; that is the meaning. "Khārikājamissanti"—here, "khārī" refers to ascetic implements like fire-drills, water pots, needles, etc.; the work of carrying those is "khārikāja." "Aggihutamissanti" means implements for fire worship, such as sacrificial ladles and the like.

52-53. Upasaggoti upaddavo. Idāni aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni ekato gaṇetvā dassetuṃ “bhagavato adhiṭṭhānena pañca kaṭṭhasatāni na phāliyiṃsū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Nāgadamanādīni pana soḷasa pāṭihāriyāni idha na gaṇitāni, tehi saddhiṃ soḷasātirekaaḍḍhuḍḍhapāṭihāriyasahassānīti veditabbaṃ.

52-53. "Upasagga" means misfortune. Now, to demonstrate by counting together the three and a half thousand miracles, the account beginning "By the Blessed One’s resolve, five hundred pieces of wood did not split," and so on, was begun. However, the sixteen miracles such as the taming of the Nāga are not counted here; together with them, three thousand five hundred and sixteen miracles should be understood.

Ādittapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Fire Discourse

54. Idāni tassa bhikkhusahassassa ādittapariyāyadesanāya arahattappattiṃ dassetuṃ “atha kho [V 3.0190] bhagavā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.
