Tattha gayāyaṃ viharati gayāsīseti gayānāmikāya nadiyā avidūre bhavattā gāmo gayā nāma, tassaṃ gayāyaṃ viharati. Samīpatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Gayāgāmassa hi avidūre gayāti ekā pokkharaṇīpi atthi nadīpi gayāsīsanāmako hatthikumbhasadiso piṭṭhipāsāṇopi. Yattha bhikkhusahassassa okāso pahoti, bhagavā tattha viharati. Tena vuttaṃ “gayāsīse”ti, gayāgāmassa āsanne gayāsīsanāmake piṭṭhipāsāṇe viharatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhikkhū āmantesīti tesaṃ sappāyadhammadesanaṃ vicinitvā taṃ desessāmīti āmantesi. Bhagavā hi taṃ iddhimayapattacīvaradharaṃ samaṇasahassaṃ ādāya gayāsīsaṃ gantvā tena parivārito nisīditvā “katarā nu kho etesaṃ dhammakathā sappāyā”ti cintento “ime sāyaṃ pātaṃ aggiṃ paricaranti, imesaṃ dvādasāyatanāni ādittāni sampajjalitāni viya katvā dassessāmi, evaṃ ime arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ sakkhissantī”ti sanniṭṭhānamakāsi. Atha nesaṃ tathā desetuṃ “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, āditta”ntiādinā imaṃ ādittapariyāyaṃ abhāsi.

54. Now, to show the attainment of arahantship by that thousand bhikkhus through the Fire Sermon, the passage beginning 'Then the Blessed One...' is introduced. Therein, 'dwells at Gayāsīsa' means he dwells in Gayā, a village so named because it is not far from the river named Gayā. This is a locative case indicating proximity. For not far from the village of Gayā there is also a pond called Gayā, a river, and a back-rock resembling an elephant's forehead called Gayāsīsa. The Blessed One dwelt there, where there was sufficient space for the thousand bhikkhus. Therefore it is said 'at Gayāsīsa,' meaning he dwelt on the back-rock named Gayāsīsa, near the village of Gayā. He addressed the bhikkhus, having discerned a suitable teaching for them, intending to teach it. For the Blessed One, having taken that thousand ascetics who bore bowls and robes created by psychic power, went to Gayāsīsa and sat down surrounded by them. Reflecting, 'What kind of Dhamma talk would be suitable for these?' he resolved, 'These ones attend to fire morning and evening; I will show them the twelve sense bases as if burning and blazing. Thus, they will be able to attain arahantship.' Then, to teach them accordingly, he spoke this Fire Sermon, beginning 'All is aflame, bhikkhus.'

Tattha (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.23) sabbaṃ nāma catubbidhaṃ sabbasabbaṃ āyatanasabbaṃ sakkāyasabbaṃ padesasabbanti. Tattha –

Herein, 'all' is of four kinds: the all-inclusive all, the all of the sense bases, the all of identity, and the partial all. Therein:

“Na [M 3.0209] tassa addiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñci;

Atho aviññātamajānitabbaṃ;

Sabbaṃ abhiññāsi yadatthi neyyaṃ;

Tathāgato tena samantacakkhū”ti (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32; paṭi. ma. 1.121) –

"Nothing here is unseen by him;

Atho aviññātamajānitabbaṃ;

Sabbaṃ abhiññāsi yadatthi neyyaṃ;

Tathāgato tena samantacakkhū’’ti (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32; paṭi. ma. 1.121) –

Idaṃ sabbasabbaṃ nāma. “Sabbaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi, taṃ suṇāthā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.23) idaṃ āyatanasabbaṃ nāma. “Sabbadhammamūlapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.1) idaṃ sakkāyasabbaṃ nāma. “Sabbadhammesu vā paṭhamasamannāhāro uppajjati cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ tajjā manoviññāṇadhātū”ti idaṃ padesasabbaṃ nāma. Iti pañcārammaṇamattaṃ padesasabbaṃ, tebhūmakā dhammā sakkāyasabbaṃ, catubhūmakā dhammā āyatanasabbaṃ, yaṃ kiñci neyyaṃ sabbasabbaṃ. Padesasabbaṃ sakkāyasabbaṃ na pāpuṇāti tassa tebhūmakadhammesupi ekadesassa asaṅgaṇhanato. Sakkāyasabbaṃ āyatanasabbaṃ na pāpuṇāti lokuttaradhammānaṃ asaṅgaṇhanato. Āyatanasabbaṃ sabbasabbaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Kasmā? Yasmā āyatanasabbena catubhūmakadhammāva pariggahitā[V 3.0191], na lakkhaṇapaññattiyoti. Imasmiṃ pana sutte āyatanasabbaṃ adhippetaṃ, tatthāpi idha vipassanupagadhammāva gahetabbā.

This is called the all-inclusive all. 'I will teach you, bhikkhus, the All; listen to it,' (saṃ. ni. 4.23) this is called the all of the sense bases. 'I will explain to you, bhikkhus, the Root of All Phenomena,' (ma. ni. 1.1) this is called the all of identity. 'In all phenomena, the first mental engagement arises—mind, thought, intellect, and the element of mind-consciousness,' this is called the partial all. Thus, the partial all is merely five objects; the all of identity includes phenomena of the three planes of existence; the all of the sense bases includes phenomena of the four planes of existence; and whatever is knowable is the all-inclusive all. The partial all does not reach the all of identity because it does not encompass even a portion of the phenomena of the three planes of existence. The all of identity does not reach the all of the sense bases because it does not include the supramundane phenomena. The all of the sense bases does not reach the all-inclusive all. Why? Because the all of the sense bases only encompasses phenomena of the four planes of existence, not conceptual designations. In this discourse, however, the all of the sense bases is intended, and here too, only the phenomena suitable for insight should be taken.

Cakkhūti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 596; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.1) dve cakkhūni ñāṇacakkhu ceva maṃsacakkhu ca. Tattha ñāṇacakkhu pañcavidhaṃ buddhacakkhu dhammacakkhu samantacakkhu dibbacakkhu paññācakkhūti. Tesu buddhacakkhu nāma āsayānusayañāṇañceva indriyaparopariyattañāṇañca, yaṃ “buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento”ti (dī. ni. 2.69; ma. ni. 1.283) āgataṃ. Dhammacakkhu nāma heṭṭhimā tayo maggā tīṇi ca phalāni, yaṃ “virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādī”ti (dī. ni. 1.355; saṃ. ni. 5.1081) āgataṃ. Samantacakkhu nāma sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, yaṃ “pāsādamāruyha samantacakkhū”ti (dī. ni. 2.70; ma. ni. 1.282) āgataṃ. Dibbacakkhu nāma ālokavaḍḍhanena uppannañāṇaṃ, yaṃ “dibbena cakkhunā visuddhenā”ti (ma. ni. 1.148, 284) āgataṃ. Paññācakkhu nāma catusaccaparicchedakañāṇaṃ, yaṃ “cakkhuṃ udapādī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 15) āgataṃ. Maṃsacakkhupi duvidhaṃ sasambhāracakkhu pasādacakkhūti. Tesu yvāyaṃ akkhikūpake akkhipaṭalehi parivārito maṃsapiṇḍo, yattha catasso dhātuyo vaṇṇagandharasojā sambhavo jīvitaṃ [M 3.0210] bhāvo cakkhuppasādo kāyappasādoti saṅkhepato terasa sambhārā honti, vitthārato pana catasso dhātuyo vaṇṇagandharasojā sambhavoti ime nava catusamuṭṭhānavasena chattiṃsa, jīvitaṃ bhāvo cakkhuppasādo kāyappasādoti ime kammasamuṭṭhānā tāva cattāroti cattālīsa sambhārā honti, idaṃ sasambhāracakkhu nāma. Yaṃ panettha setamaṇḍalaparicchinnena kaṇhamaṇḍalena parivārite diṭṭhimaṇḍale sanniviṭṭhaṃ rūpadassanasamatthaṃ pasādamattaṃ, idaṃ pasādacakkhu nāma. Tassa tato paresañca sotādīnaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.436) vuttāva.

The eye (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 596; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.1) is twofold: the knowledge-eye and the flesh-eye. Among these, the knowledge-eye is fivefold: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the all-seeing eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom-eye. Among these, the Buddha-eye is the knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies, and the knowledge of the superiority or inferiority of faculties, as stated: 'Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye' (dī. ni. 2.69; ma. ni. 1.283). The Dhamma-eye is the three lower paths and the three fruits, as stated: 'The stainless, immaculate Dhamma-eye arose' (dī. ni. 1.355; saṃ. ni. 5.1081). The all-seeing eye is omniscient knowledge, as stated: 'Having ascended the palace, with the all-seeing eye' (dī. ni. 2.70; ma. ni. 1.282). The divine eye is the knowledge that arises from the increase of light, as stated: 'With the divine eye, purified' (ma. ni. 1.148, 284). The wisdom-eye is the knowledge that distinguishes the four truths, as stated: 'The eye arose' (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 15). The flesh-eye is also twofold: the eye with its constituents and the sensitive eye. Among these, the lump of flesh enclosed by the eye socket and the eyelids, where four elements—color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence—along with origination, vitality, existence, eye-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity, briefly there are thirteen constituents. But in detail, the four elements—color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence—along with origination, these nine, with their fourfold arising, make thirty-six; vitality, existence, eye-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity, these four arising from kamma, make forty constituents in total. This is called the eye with its constituents. But here, that mere sensitivity which is enclosed by the white circle and surrounded by the black circle, settled in the visual field, capable of seeing forms—this is called the sensitive eye. The detailed explanation of this and the others beginning with the ear is already stated in the Visuddhimagga (visuddhi. 2.436).

Tattha yadidaṃ pasādacakkhu, tañca gahetvā bhagavā “cakkhu āditta”ntiādimāha. Tattha ādittanti padittaṃ, sampajjalitaṃ ekādasahi aggīhi ekajālībhūtanti attho. Cakkhusannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, cakkhussa vā kāraṇabhūtassa viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Kāmaṃ rūpālokamanasikārādayopi tassa viññāṇassa kāraṇaṃ, te pana sādhāraṇakāraṇaṃ, cakkhu asādhāraṇanti asādhāraṇakāraṇenāyaṃ niddeso yathā “yavaṅkuro”ti. Sotaviññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Cakkhusannissito phasso cakkhusamphasso, cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttaphassassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sotasamphassādīsupi eseva nayo. Cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati [V 3.0192] vedayitanti cakkhusamphassaṃ mūlapaccayaṃ katvā uppannā sampaṭicchanasantīraṇavoṭṭhabbanajavanavedanā. Cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttāya pana vedanāya cakkhusamphassassa paccayabhāve vattabbameva natthi. Cakkhusamphasso hi sahajātāya vedanāya sahajātādivasena, asahajātāya upanissayādivasena paccayo hoti. Teneva “cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Sotadvāravedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha pana manoti bhavaṅgacittaṃ manodvārassa adhippetattā. Dhammāti dhammārammaṇaṃ. Manoviññāṇanti sahāvajjanakaṃ javanaṃ. Manosamphassoti bhavaṅgasahajāto phasso. Vedayitanti āvajjanavedanāya saddhiṃ javanavedanā. Bhavaṅgasampayuttāya pana vedanāya gahaṇe vattabbameva natthi. Āvajjanaṃ vā bhavaṅgato amocetvā manoti sāvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dhammāti dhammārammaṇameva. Manoviññāṇanti javanaviññāṇaṃ. Manosamphassoti [M 3.0211] bhavaṅgāvajjanasahajāto phasso. Vedayitanti javanasahajātā vedanā, bhavaṅgāvajjanasahajātāpi vaṭṭatiyeva.

Here, the Blessed One takes up the term 'sensitive eye' and declares, 'The eye is burning,' and so on. Herein, 'burning' means ablaze, fiercely burning, having become a single flame with the eleven fires—this is the meaning. Consciousness dependent on the eye is eye-consciousness; or, it is the consciousness for which the eye is the cause. Though forms, light, attention, and the like are also causes for that consciousness, they are common causes, whereas the eye is the uncommon cause—hence this designation is by way of the uncommon cause, as in the phrase 'barley sprout.' The same applies to ear-consciousness and so on. Contact dependent on the eye is eye-contact; this is a term for contact associated with eye-consciousness. The same applies to ear-contact and so on. 'Conditioned by eye-contact, feeling arises' means that, with eye-contact as the root condition, the receiving, investigating, determining, and javana feelings arise. However, regarding the feeling associated with eye-consciousness, there is nothing to be said about eye-contact being its condition. For eye-contact is a condition for co-arisen feeling by way of co-arising, etc., and for non-co-arisen feeling by way of dependence, etc. Therefore it is said: 'Conditioned by eye-contact, feeling arises—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.' The same applies to feeling arising at the ear-door and so on. Here, 'mind' refers to the life-continuum consciousness, as the mind-door is intended. 'Dhammas' means a mental object. 'Mind-consciousness' is javana along with adverting. 'Mind-contact' is contact co-arisen with the life-continuum. 'Feeling' refers to the feeling of adverting together with the javana feeling. However, regarding the inclusion of the feeling associated with the life-continuum, there is nothing to be said. Alternatively, 'mind' should be understood as the life-continuum with adverting, without separating adverting from the life-continuum. 'Dhammas' means simply a mental object. 'Mind-consciousness' is javana consciousness. 'Mind-contact' is contact co-arisen with the life-continuum and adverting. 'Feeling' is the feeling co-arisen with javana, and the feeling co-arisen with the life-continuum and adverting is also suitable.

Rāgagginātiādīsu rāgova anudahanaṭṭhena aggīti rāgaggi. Rāgo hi tikhiṇaṃ hutvā uppajjamāno satte anudahati jhāpeti, tasmā “aggī”ti vuccati. Itaresupi dvīsu eseva nayo. Tatrimāni vatthūni (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305; vibha. aṭṭha. 924) – ekā daharabhikkhunī cittalapabbatavihāre uposathāgāraṃ gantvā dvārapālarūpaṃ olokayamānā ṭhitā. Athassā anto rāgo tikhiṇataro hutvā uppanno, tasmā taṃsamuṭṭhānā tejodhātu ativiya tikhiṇabhāvena saddhiṃ attanā sahajātadhammehi hadayapadesaṃ jhāpesi yathā taṃ bāhirā tejodhātu sannissayaṃ, tena sā bhikkhunī jhāyitvā kālamakāsi. Bhikkhuniyo gacchamānā “ayaṃ daharā ṭhitā, pakkosatha na”nti āhaṃsu. Ekā gantvā “kasmā ṭhitāsī”ti hatthe gaṇhi. Gahitamattā parivattitvā papatā. Idaṃ tāva rāgassa anudahanatāya vatthu.

In the phrase 'by the fire of lust' and so on, lust itself is 'fire' in the sense of burning. For lust, arising intensely, scorches and burns beings—hence it is called 'fire.' The same principle applies to the other two. Here are the accounts: Once, a young bhikkhunī, while staying at Cittalapabbata Monastery, went to the Uposatha hall and stood there gazing at the form of a doorkeeper. Then, a more intense lust arose within her, and due to that, the heat element born from it, along with the phenomena co-arisen with it, burned her heart region with extreme intensity—just as external heat burns its support. Consequently, that bhikkhunī, having been burned, passed away. Other bhikkhunīs, passing by, said, 'This young one is standing—call her!' One went and, taking her hand, asked, 'Why are you standing?' The moment she was touched, she collapsed and fell. This, then, is an instance illustrating the burning nature of lust.

Dosassa pana anudahanatāya manopadosikā devā daṭṭhabbā. Tesu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.47-48) kira eko devaputto “nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti saparivāro rathena vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Athañño nikkhamanto taṃ purato gacchantaṃ disvā “bho ayaṃ kapaṇo adiṭṭhapubbaṃ viya etaṃ disvā pītiyā uddhumāto viya bhijjamāno viya ca gacchatī”ti kujjhati. Purato gacchantopi nivattitvā taṃ kuddhaṃ disvā kuddhā nāma suvijānā hontīti kuddhabhāvamassa ñatvā “tvaṃ kuddho mayhaṃ kiṃ karissasi, ayaṃ sampatti mayā dānasīlādīnaṃ vasena laddhā, na tuyhaṃ vasenā”ti paṭikujjhati. Ekasmiñhi kuddhe itaro akuddho rakkhati. Kuddhassa hi so kodho itarasmiṃ akujjhante anupādāno ekavārameva uppattiyā anāsevano [V 3.0193] cāvetuṃ na sakkoti, udakaṃ patvā aggi viya nibbāyati, tasmā akuddho taṃ cavanato rakkhati. Ubhosu pana kuddhesu ekassa kodho itarassa paccayo hoti, tassapi kodho itarassa paccayo hotīti ubho kandantānaṃyeva orodhānaṃ cavanti. Ubhosu hi kuddhesu bhiyyo bhiyyo aññamaññamhi parivaḍḍhanavasena tikhiṇasamudācāro nissayadahanaraso [M 3.0212] kodho uppajjamāno hadayavatthuṃ niddahanto accantasukhumālaṃ karajakāyaṃ vināseti, tato sakalopi attabhāvo antaradhāyati. Idaṃ dosassa anudahanatāya vatthu.

As for the burning nature of hatred, the mind-corrupted deities should be considered. Among them, it is said that a certain young deity, thinking, 'I will enjoy the festival,' proceeded along the road in a chariot with his retinue. Then another, coming out, saw him going ahead and became angry, thinking, 'This wretch, as if seeing such a thing for the first time, goes about as if puffed up with joy and about to burst.' The one going ahead, upon turning back and seeing the angry one, recognized his angry state—for angry beings are easily recognized—and retorted, 'You are angry—what can you do to me? This prosperity of mine has been attained through generosity, virtue, and so on, not through your power.' When one is angry and the other is not, the one who is not angry protects him. For the anger of the angry one, when the other does not get angry in return, becomes without fuel; being uncultivated by even a single arising, it is unable to cause a fall. Like fire that has reached water, it is extinguished. Thus, the one who is not angry protects him from falling away. But when both are angry, one's anger becomes a condition for the other, and the other's anger becomes a condition for the first. Both fall away, just like the weeping women of the inner quarters. For when both are angry, anger—with its sharp conduct and its nature of burning its support—arises by way of mutual increase, burns the heart-base, and destroys the extremely delicate kamma-born body. Then the entire individual existence vanishes. This is the account illustrating the burning nature of hatred.

Mohassa pana anudahanatāya khiḍḍāpadosikā devā daṭṭhabbā. Mohavasena hi tesaṃ satisammoso hoti, tasmā khiḍḍāvasena āhārakālaṃ ativattetvā kālaṃ karonti. Te (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.45-46) kira puññavisesādhigatena mahantena attano sirivibhavena nakkhattaṃ kīḷantā tāya sampattimahantatāya “āhāraṃ paribhuñjimha, na paribhuñjimhā”tipi na jānanti. Atha ekāhārātikkamanato paṭṭhāya nirantaraṃ khādantāpi pivantāpi cavantiyeva na tiṭṭhanti. Kasmā? Kammajatejassa balavatāya. Manussānañhi kammajatejo mando, karajakāyo balavā. Tesaṃ tejassa mandatāya karajakāyassa balavatāya sattāhampi atikkamitvā uṇhodakaacchayāguādīhi sakkā vatthuṃ upatthambhetuṃ. Devānaṃ pana tejo balavā hoti uḷārapuññanibbattattā uḷāragarusiniddhasudhāhārajiraṇato ca, karajaṃ mandaṃ mudusukhumālabhāvato. Teneva hi bhagavā indasālaguhāyaṃ pakatipathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkontaṃ sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ “oḷārikakāyaṃ adhiṭṭhāhī”ti āha, tasmā te ekaṃ āhāravelaṃ atikkamitvā saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Yathā nāma gimhānaṃ majjhanhike tattapāsāṇe ṭhapitaṃ padumaṃ vā uppalaṃ vā sāyanhasamaye ghaṭasatenapi siñciyamānaṃ pākatikaṃ na hoti vinassatiyeva, evameva pacchā nirantaraṃ khādantāpi pivantāpi cavantiyeva na tiṭṭhanti.

As for the burning nature of delusion, the Khiḍḍāpadosikā deities should be considered. For through delusion, they lose their mindfulness, and so they neglect the time for food in play and die. They, it is said, having attained great prosperity through their exceptional merit, revel in their own grand splendor during festivals. Due to the vastness of their good fortune, they do not even know whether they have eaten or not. Then, from the moment they miss a single meal, even if they continuously eat and drink, they still die and do not remain. Why? Because of the strength of their kamma-born energy. For humans, the kamma-born energy is weak, while the kamma-born body is strong. Due to the weakness of their energy and the strength of their kamma-born body, they can be sustained even after seven days with warm water, rice gruel, and the like. But for the deities, their energy is strong because of their immense merit and the digestion of their sublime, heavy, rich, and succulent ambrosial food, while their kamma-born body is weak, being delicate and subtle. Indeed, the Blessed One told Sakka, the king of gods, who was unable to stand on the natural ground of Indasāla Cave, 'Resolve on a coarse body.' Therefore, they cannot endure even beyond a single mealtime. Just as a lotus or water lily placed on a scorching stone at midday in the summer, even if sprinkled with a hundred pots of water in the evening, does not return to its natural state but perishes, so too, even if they later eat and drink continuously, they die and do not remain.

Ko pana tesaṃ āhāro, kā āhāravelāti? Sabbesampi kāmāvacaradevānaṃ sudhā āhāro, so heṭṭhimehi heṭṭhimehi uparimānaṃ uparimānaṃ paṇītatamo hoti. Taṃ yathāsakaṃ divasavasena divase divase bhuñjanti. Keci pana “biḷārapadappamāṇaṃ sudhāhāraṃ bhuñjanti. So jivhāya ṭhapitamatto yāva kesagganakhaggā kāyaṃ pharati, tesaṃyeva divasavasena sattadivasaṃ yāpanasamatthova hotī”ti vadanti.

What is their food, and what is the time for eating? For all the sense-sphere deities, ambrosia is their food, and it becomes more refined for the higher deities than for the lower ones. They consume it day by day, according to their respective days. Some say, "They eat an amount of ambrosia the size of a cat's paw. Placed on the tongue, it suffuses the body right up to the tips of the hair and nails and is sufficient to sustain them for seven of their days."

Ke pana te khiḍḍāpadosikā nāma devāti? Ime nāmāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vicāraṇā natthi, “kammajatejo balavā hoti, karajaṃ manda”nti avisesena [M 3.0213] vuttattā pana ye keci kabaḷīkārāhārūpajīvino [V 3.0194] evaṃ karonti, te evaṃ cavantīti veditabbā. Keci panāhu “nimmānaratiparanimmitavasavattino te devā. Khiḍḍāya padussanamatteneva hete khiḍḍāpadosikāti vuttā”ti. Manopadosikā pana cātumahārājikāti aṭṭhakathāyameva vuttaṃ. Keci pana “khiḍḍāpadosikāpi cātumahārājikāyevā”ti vadanti. Evaṃ tāva rāgādayo tayo anudahanaṭṭhena “aggī”ti veditabbā. Jātiādittayaṃ pana nānappakāradukkhavatthubhāvena anudahanato aggi. Sokādīnaṃ anudahanatā pākaṭāyeva. Sesamettha vuttanayameva. Iti imasmiṃ sutte dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ kathitaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ ekādasahi aggīhi ādittabhāvena dukkhamatāya dukkhabhāvassa kathitattā.

And who are the deities called 'Khiḍḍāpadosikā'? There is no detailed analysis of these by name in the commentary. However, since it is stated without distinction that 'the kamma-born energy is strong, while the physical body is weak,' it should be understood that any beings who sustain themselves on solid food and act in such a way will pass away accordingly. Some, however, say: 'These deities are the Nimmānaratī and Paranimmitavasavattī deities. They are called 'Khiḍḍāpadosikā' merely because they become corrupted by play.' Regarding the 'Manopadosikā,' it is stated explicitly in the commentary itself that they belong to the Cātumahārājikā realm. But some say the 'Khiḍḍāpadosikā' also belong to the Cātumahārājikā realm. Thus, the three—lust, hatred, and delusion—should be understood as 'fire' due to their burning nature. Birth and the triad beginning with it, however, are fire because they burn by being the basis for various kinds of suffering. The burning nature of sorrow and the rest is quite evident. The remainder here follows the method already stated. Thus, in this sutta, the characteristic of suffering is explained, as the state of suffering is declared through the eye and the others being aflame with the eleven fires, and through their nature as suffering.

Ādittapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ādittapariyāya Sutta is concluded.

Uruvelapāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the story of the miracles at Uruvelā is concluded.

Bimbisārasamāgamakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Meeting with Bimbisāra

55. Idāni “atha kho bhagavā gayāsīse yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā”tiādīsu yā sā anuttānapadavaṇṇanā, taṃ dassetuṃ “laṭṭhivaneti tāluyyāne”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tāluyyāneti tālarukkhānaṃ bahubhāvato evaṃladdhanāme uyyāne. Appekacce yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvātiādīsu añjaliṃ paṇāmetvāti ye ubhatopakkhikā, te sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Te kira evaṃ cintayiṃsu “sace no micchādiṭṭhikā codessanti ‘kasmā tumhe samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vanditthā’ti, tesaṃ ‘kiṃ añjalimattakaraṇenapi vanditaṃ hotī’ti vakkhāma. Sace no sammādiṭṭhikā codessanti ‘kasmā bhagavantaṃ na vanditthā’ti, ‘kiṃ sīsena bhūmiṃ paharanteneva vanditaṃ hoti, nanu añjalikammampi vandanā evā’ti vakkhāmā”ti. Nāmagottaṃ sāvetvāti “bho gotama, ahaṃ asukassa putto datto nāma mitto nāma idha āgato”ti vadantā nāmaṃ sāventi nāma, “bho gotama, ahaṃ vāseṭṭho nāma kaccāno nāma idhāgato”ti vadantā gottaṃ sāventi nāma. Ete kira daliddā jiṇṇakulaputtā parisamajjhe nāmagottavasena pākaṭā bhavissāmāti evaṃ [M 3.0214] akaṃsu. Ye pana tuṇhībhūtā nisīdiṃsu, te kerāṭikā ceva andhabālā ca. Tattha kerāṭikā “ekaṃ dve kathāsallāpe karonte vissāsiko hoti, atha vissāse sati ekaṃ dve bhikkhā adātuṃ na yutta”nti tato attānaṃ mocentā tuṇhī nisīdanti. Andhabālā aññāṇatāyeva avakkhittā mattikāpiṇḍo viya yattha katthaci tuṇhībhūtā nisīdanti.

55. Now, to explain the obscure terms in phrases like “Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Gayāsīsa as long as he pleased,” the commentary begins with “Laṭṭhivana, meaning a palm grove.” Here, “in a palm grove” refers to a park so named due to the abundance of palm trees. Regarding the passage “some, approaching the Blessed One, paid homage with hands in añjali,” this refers to those who were on both sides. They thought thus: “If those of wrong view reproach us, asking, ‘Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?’, we will reply, ‘Is merely making the añjali gesture considered homage?’ If those of right view reproach us, asking, ‘Why did you not pay homage to the Blessed One?’, we will reply, ‘Must one strike one’s head on the ground to pay homage? Is not the act of añjali itself a form of homage?’” Regarding “announcing name and clan”: some announce their name, saying, “Venerable Gotama, I am the son of so-and-so, named Datta or Mitta, and I have come here.” Others announce their clan, saying, “Venerable Gotama, I am of the Vāseṭṭha clan, named Kaccāna, and I have come here.” These, it is said, were poor, aged men of good families who did this, thinking, “We will become known in the assembly by name and clan.” But those who sat down silently were either crafty or blind fools. Among them, the crafty ones, thinking, “If one engages in a bit of conversation, familiarity arises. Once there is familiarity, it is not right not to give an alms or two,” remained silent to free themselves from this. The blind fools, out of sheer ignorance, sat down silently wherever they were, like a discarded lump of clay.

Kisakovadānoti [V 3.0195] ettha kisakānaṃ ovadāno kisakovadānoti imaṃ tāva atthavikappaṃ dassetuṃ “tāpasacariyāya kisasarīrattā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aggihuttanti aggiparicaraṇaṃ. Rūpādayova idha kāmanīyaṭṭhena “kāmā”ti vuttāti āha “ete rūpādayo kāme”ti. Yaññā abhivadantīti yāgahetu ijjhantīti vadanti. Upadhīsūti ettha cattāro upadhī kāmupadhi khandhupadhi kilesupadhi abhisaṅkhārupadhīti. Kāmāpi hi “yaṃ pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo”ti (ma. ni. 1.167) evaṃ vuttassa sukhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato upadhīyati ettha sukhanti iminā vacanatthena “upadhī”ti vuccanti. Khandhāpi khandhamūlakassa dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, kilesāpi apāyadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, abhisaṅkhārāpi bhavadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato “upadhī”ti vuccanti, tesu khandhupadhi idhādhippetoti āha “khandhupadhīsu malanti ñatvā”ti. Yaññā malameva vadantīti yāgahetu malameva ijjhatīti vadanti. Yiṭṭheti mahāyāge. Huteti divase divase kattabbaaggiparicaraṇe. Kāmabhave asattanti kāmabhave alaggaṃ, tabbinimuttanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Regarding 'Kisakovadāna,' to show the alternative meaning 'an exhortation to the lean is Kisakovadāna,' it is said, “due to having a lean body from ascetic practice,” and so on. 'Aggihutta' means the tending of the fire. Here, forms and so on are called 'kāma' in the sense of being desirable; thus it says, “these forms, etc., as sensual pleasures.” 'Yaññā abhivadanti' means they say that sacrifices succeed on account of the offering. 'Upadhīsu' refers to the four substrates: the substrate of sensual pleasures, the substrate of the aggregates, the substrate of the defilements, and the substrate of volitional formations. Sensual pleasures are called 'upadhi' because they are the basis for the happiness spoken of thus: “Whatever happiness and joy arise in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures” (MN 13). Happiness is supported (upadhīyati) by them; from this verbal sense, they are called 'upadhi.' The aggregates are also called 'upadhi' because they are the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates; the defilements, because they are the basis for suffering in the lower realms; and volitional formations, because they are the basis for the suffering of existence. Among these, the substrate of the aggregates is intended here; thus it says, “having known it as a stain in the substrates of the aggregates.” 'Yaññā malameva vadanti' means they say that only a stain succeeds on account of sacrifice. 'Yiṭṭhe' means in a great sacrifice. 'Hute' means in the daily fire-tending that is to be performed. 'Kāmabhave asattaṃ' means not attached to the desire realm, that is to say, liberated from it.

57-58. Āsīsanāti patthanā. Dibbasuvaṇṇesupi siṅgīsuvaṇṇassa sabbaseṭṭhattā “siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo”ti vuttaṃ. Yatheva hi manussaparibhoge suvaṇṇe yuttikataṃ hīnaṃ, tato rasaviddhaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, rasaviddhato ākaruppannaṃ, tato yaṃ kiñci dibbaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, evaṃ dibbasuvaṇṇesupi cāmīkarato sātakumbhaṃ, sātakumbhato jambunadaṃ, jambunadato siṅgīsuvaṇṇaṃ, tasmā taṃ sabbaseṭṭhaṃ. Siṅgīnikkhanti ca nikkhaparimāṇena siṅgīsuvaṇṇena kataṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ. Ūnakanikkhena katañhi ghaṭṭanamajjanakkhamaṃ na hoti, atirekena kataṃ ghaṭṭanamajjanaṃ khamati, vaṇṇavantaṃ pana na hoti, pharusadhātukaṃ khāyati, nikkhena kataṃ ghaṭṭanamajjanañceva khamati vaṇṇavantañca hoti. Nikkhaṃ pana vīsatisuvaṇṇanti keci[M 3.0215]. Pañcavīsatisuvaṇṇanti apare. Majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “nikkhaṃ nāma pañcasuvaṇṇā”ti vuttaṃ. Suvaṇṇo nāma catudharaṇanti vadanti.

57-58. 'Āsīsanā' means aspiration. Among divine golds, siṅgī gold is the best, hence the term 'siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo' (the color of a siṅgī-nikkha) is used. Just as among gold for human use, manufactured gold is inferior; superior to that is alchemical gold; superior to alchemical gold is gold produced from a mine; and superior to that is any kind of divine gold. Similarly, among divine golds, sātakumbha is superior to cāmīkara, jambunada is superior to sātakumbha, and siṅgī gold is superior to jambunada; therefore, it is the very best. A 'siṅgīnikkha' is a gold plate made of siṅgī gold to the measure of one nikkha. If made with less than a nikkha, it cannot withstand rubbing and polishing. If made with more, it can withstand rubbing and polishing but is not lustrous and appears coarse in texture. When made with exactly a nikkha, it both withstands rubbing and polishing and is lustrous. Some say a nikkha is twenty suvaṇṇas; others, twenty-five. In the Majjhima Nikāya commentary, however, it is said: “A nikkha is five suvaṇṇas.” They say a suvaṇṇa is four dharaṇas.

Dasasu ariyavāsesu vutthavāsoti –

One who has fulfilled the dwelling in the ten noble dwellings:

“Idha, (dī. ni. 3.348; a. ni. 10.20) bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti chaḷaṅgasamannāgato ekārakkho caturāpasseno panuṇṇapaccekasacco samavayasaṭṭhesano anāvilasaṅkappo passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro suvimuttacitto suvimuttapañño.

“Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has dispelled individual truths, has utterly stilled quests, has untroubled intentions, has tranquilized the bodily formation, is well-liberated in mind, and is well-liberated in wisdom.”

“Kathañca[V 3.0196], bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno kāmacchando pahīno hoti, byāpādo pahīno hoti, thinamiddhaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, vicikicchā pahīnā hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti.

“And how, monks, has a monk abandoned five factors? Here, monks, a monk’s sensual desire is abandoned, ill will is abandoned, sloth and torpor are abandoned, restlessness and remorse are abandoned, and doubt is abandoned. It is in this way, monks, that a monk has abandoned five factors.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk endowed with six factors? Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having felt a tactile object with the body... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Thus, monks, a monk is endowed with six factors.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satārakkhena cetasā samannāgato hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk one who has a single protection? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with a mind protected by mindfulness. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has a single protection.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodeti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk one with four supports? Here, monks, a monk uses after considering, endures after considering, avoids after considering, and dispels after considering. Thus, monks, a monk is one with four supports.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu panuṇṇapaccekasacco hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yāni tāni puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ puthupaccekasaccāni[M 3.0216], sabbāni tāni nuṇṇāni honti panuṇṇāni cattāni vantāni muttāni pahīnāni paṭinissaṭṭhāni. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu panuṇṇapaccekasacco hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk one who has rejected individual truths? Here, monks, all those various individual truths of the diverse ascetics and brahmins have been driven out, rejected, discarded, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has rejected individual truths.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno kāmesanā pahīnā hoti, bhavesanā pahīnā hoti, brahmacariyesanā paṭippassaddhā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk one whose quests are completely abandoned? Here, monks, a monk’s quest for sensual pleasures has been abandoned, his quest for existence has been abandoned, and the quest for the holy life has been stilled. Thus, monks, a monk is one whose quests are completely abandoned.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappo hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno [V 3.0197] kāmasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, byāpādasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, vihiṃsāsaṅkappo pahīno hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappo hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk of unclouded intention? Here, monks, a monk’s sensual intention has been abandoned, his intention of ill will has been abandoned, and his intention of harmfulness has been abandoned. Thus, monks, a monk is of unclouded intention.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk one with tranquil bodily formation? Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the prior passing away of joy and sorrow, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Thus, monks, a monk is one with tranquil bodily formation.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno rāgācittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk of well-liberated mind? Here, monks, a monk’s mind is liberated from greed, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion. Thus, monks, a monk is of well-liberated mind.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘rāgo me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti, ‘doso me pahīno…pe… moho me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hotī”ti (dī. ni. 3.348; a. ni. 10.20) –

“And how, monks, is a monk one whose wisdom is well-liberated? Here, monks, a monk understands: ‘Lust in me has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered nonexistent, not liable to future arising.’ He understands: ‘Hatred in me has been abandoned… delusion in me has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered nonexistent, not liable to future arising.’ Thus, monks, a monk is one whose wisdom is well-liberated.”

Evamāgatesu dasasu ariyavāsesu vutthavāso.

He is one who has thus dwelt in these ten noble dwellings.

Tattha vasanti etthāti vāsā, ariyānaṃ eva vāsāti ariyavāsā anariyānaṃ tādisānaṃ vāsānaṃ asambhavato. Ariyāti cettha ukkaṭṭhaniddesena [M 3.0217] khīṇāsavā gahitā. Ekārakkhoti ekā satisaṅkhātā ārakkhā etassāti ekārakkho. Khīṇāsavassa (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.348; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.10.20) hi tīsu dvāresu sabbakāle sati ārakkhakiccaṃ sādheti. Tenevassa carato ca tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hotīti vuccati.

They dwell therein, thus they are ‘dwellings’ (vāsā). They are the dwellings of the noble ones, thus ‘noble dwellings’ (ariyavāsā), because such dwellings are impossible for the ignoble. Here, by ‘noble’ are meant those with cankers destroyed (khīṇāsavā), by way of a superior designation. ‘One with a single protection’ (ekārakkho) means ‘one whose single protection is that designated as mindfulness (sati).’ For one with cankers destroyed, mindfulness fulfills the function of protection at all times at the three doors. Therefore, it is said that for him, whether walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present.

Caturāpassenoti cattāri apassenāni apassayā etassāti caturāpasseno. Saṅkhāyāti ñāṇena (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.308). Paṭisevatīti ñāṇena ñatvā sevitabbayuttakameva sevati. Tassa vitthāro “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paribhuñjatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) nayena veditabbo. Saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāsetīti ñāṇena ñatvā adhivāsetabbayuttakameva adhivāseti. Vitthāro panettha “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso khamo hoti sītassā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.24) nayena [V 3.0198] veditabbo. Parivajjetīti ñāṇena ñatvā parivajjetabbayuttakameva parivajjeti. Tassa vitthāro “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjetī”tiādinā nayena veditabbo. Vinodetīti ñāṇena ñatvā vinodetabbameva vinodeti nudati nīharati anto vasituṃ na deti. Tassa vitthāro “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā nayena veditabbo.

‘One with four supports’ (caturāpasseno) means one who has four supports (apassenāni), things to be relied upon (apassayā). ‘After considering’ (saṅkhāya) means with knowledge (ñāṇena). ‘Uses’ (paṭisevati) means that one uses only what is fit to be used, having known it with knowledge. Its elaboration should be understood according to the method beginning with ‘Reflecting wisely, one uses the robe’ (MN 2; AN 6.58). ‘Endures after considering’ (saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti) means that one endures only what is fit to be endured, having known it with knowledge. Its elaboration here should be understood according to the method beginning with ‘Reflecting wisely, one is patient with cold’ (MN 2). ‘Avoids’ (parivajjeti) means that one avoids only what is fit to be avoided, having known it with knowledge. Its elaboration should be understood according to the method beginning with ‘Reflecting wisely, one avoids a fierce elephant’ (MN 2). ‘Dispels’ (vinodeti) means that one dispels only what is fit to be dispelled, having known it with knowledge—one pushes it away, removes it, does not allow it to dwell within. Its elaboration should be understood according to the method beginning with ‘One does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual pleasure’ (MN 2).

Panuṇṇapaccekasaccoti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.38; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.348) “idameva dassanaṃ saccaṃ, idameva sacca”nti evaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ gahitattā paccekasaṅkhātāni diṭṭhisaccāni panuṇṇāni nīhaṭāni pahīnāni assāti panuṇṇapaccekasacco. Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānanti bahūnaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ. Ettha ca samaṇāti pabbajjupagatā. Brāhmaṇāti bhovādino. Puthupaccekasaccānīti bahūni pāṭekkasaccāni, “idameva dassanaṃ saccaṃ, idameva sacca”nti pāṭiyekkaṃ gahitāni bahūni saccānīti attho. Nuṇṇānīti nīhaṭāni. Panuṇṇānīti suṭṭhu nīhatāni. Cattānīti vissaṭṭhāni. Vantānīti vamitāni. Muttānīti chinnabandhanāni katāni. Pahīnānīti pajahitāni. Paṭinissaṭṭhānīti yathā na puna cittaṃ ārohanti, evaṃ paṭivissajjitāni. Sabbāneva cetāni ariyamaggādhigamato pubbe gahitassa diṭṭhiggāhassa vissaṭṭhabhāvavevacanāni.

‘One who has rejected individual truths’ (panuṇṇapaccekasacco) means one for whom the truths of views (diṭṭhisaccāni), designated as ‘individual’ because they are grasped individually with the thought ‘This view alone is true, this alone is the truth,’ have been rejected (panuṇṇāni), removed (nīhaṭāni), and abandoned (pahīnāni). ‘Of the diverse ascetics and brahmins’ (puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ) means of many ascetics and brahmins. Here, ‘ascetics’ (samaṇā) are those who have gone forth into homelessness. ‘Brahmins’ (brāhmaṇā) are those who address others as ‘bho.’ ‘Various individual truths’ (puthupaccekasaccāni) means many individual truths; that is, many truths grasped individually with the thought ‘This view alone is true, this alone is the truth.’ ‘Driven out’ (nuṇṇāni) means removed (nīhaṭāni). ‘Rejected’ (panuṇṇāni) means well-removed. ‘Discarded’ (cattāni) means relinquished (vissaṭṭhāni). ‘Vomited out’ (vantāni) means vomited. ‘Released’ (muttāni) means made with severed bonds. ‘Abandoned’ (pahīnāni) means given up (pajahitāni). ‘Relinquished’ (paṭinissaṭṭhāni) means given back in such a way that they do not arise in the mind again. All these are synonyms for the state of having relinquished the clinging to views (diṭṭhiggāha) that was held before the attainment of the noble path.

Samavayasaṭṭhesanoti [M 3.0218] (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.348; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.10.20) ettha avayāti anūnā. Saṭṭhāti nissaṭṭhā. Sammā avayā saṭṭhā esanā assāti samavayasaṭṭhesano, sammā vissaṭṭhasabbaesanoti attho. “Rāgā cittaṃ vimutta”ntiādīhi maggassa kiccanipphatti kathitā rāgādīnaṃ pahīnabhāvadīpanato. “Rāgo me pahīno”tiādīhi paccavekkhaṇāmukhena ariyaphalaṃ kathitaṃ. Adhigate hi aggaphale sabbaso rāgādīnaṃ anuppādadhammataṃ pajānāti, tañca pajānanaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇanti. Tattha pañcaṅgavippahānapaccekasaccāpanodanaesanāsamavayasajjanāni “saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati adhivāseti parivajjeti vinodetī”ti vuttesu apassenesu vinodanā ca maggakiccāneva, itare ca maggeneva samijjhanti.

Samavayasaṭṭhesano means ‘one whose seeking is harmoniously relinquished.’ Here, avayā means ‘not deficient.’ Saṭṭhā means ‘completely relinquished.’ Samavayasaṭṭhesano means ‘one whose seeking is rightly, not deficiently, relinquished,’ that is, one whose every seeking is rightly relinquished. Through phrases like ‘the mind is liberated from lust,’ the accomplishment of the path’s function is described by indicating the abandoned state of lust and other defilements. Through statements like ‘Lust has been abandoned by me,’ the noble fruit is described by way of reviewing. For when the highest fruit is attained, one fully understands the nature of lust and other defilements not arising again, and that understanding is called the knowledge of reviewing. In this context, the abandonment of the five factors, the dispelling of individual truths, and the harmonious relinquishment of seeking—among the supports mentioned as ‘one uses after reflection, endures, avoids, and dispels’—the dispelling (vinodanā) is indeed a function of the path, while the others are accomplished by the path itself.

Dasabaloti kāyabalasaṅkhātāni ñāṇabalasaṅkhātāni ca dasa balāni etassāti dasabalo. Duvidhañhi [V 3.0199] tathāgatassa balaṃ kāyabalaṃ ñāṇabalañca. Tesu kāyabalaṃ hatthikulānusārena veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

Dasabalo means ‘one who possesses ten powers,’ because these are the ten powers reckoned as bodily powers and knowledge powers. For the Tathāgata has two kinds of power: bodily power and power of knowledge. Among these, bodily power should be understood according to the families of elephants. For this was said by the ancients:

“Kāḷāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandhamaṅgalahemañca, uposathachaddantime dasā”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.148; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.22; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.10.21; vibha. aṭṭha 76; udā. aṭṭha. 75; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 1.39; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.2.44; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 81);

“Kāḷāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, and Piṅgala; Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema; Uposatha and Chaddanta—these are the ten.”

Imāni hi dasa hatthikulāni. Tattha kāḷāvakanti pakatihatthikulaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ kāyabalaṃ, taṃ ekassa kāḷāvakassa hatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ kāḷāvakānaṃ balaṃ, taṃ ekassa gaṅgeyyassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gaṅgeyyānaṃ, taṃ ekassa paṇḍarassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ paṇḍarānaṃ, taṃ ekassa tambassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ tambānaṃ, taṃ ekassa piṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ piṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa gandhahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gandhahatthīnaṃ, taṃ ekassa maṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ maṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa hemavatassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ hemavatānaṃ, taṃ ekassa uposathassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ uposathānaṃ, taṃ ekassa chaddantassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ, taṃ ekassa tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ. Nārāyanasaṅghātabalantipi idameva vuccati. Tattha nārā vuccanti rasmiyo, tā bahū nānāvidhā tato uppajjantīti nārāyanaṃ, vajiraṃ, tasmā vajirasaṅghātabalanti attho. Tadetaṃ pakatihatthigaṇanāya hatthīnaṃ koṭisahassānaṃ, purisagaṇanāya dasannaṃ [M 3.0219] purisakoṭisahassānaṃ balaṃ hoti. Idaṃ tāva tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ.

These are indeed the ten elephant families. Among them, the Kāḷāvaka should be understood as the ordinary elephant family. The bodily strength of ten men is that of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants is that of one Gaṅgeyya. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyya elephants is that of one Paṇḍara. The strength of ten Paṇḍara elephants is that of one Tamba. The strength of ten Tamba elephants is that of one Piṅgala. The strength of ten Piṅgala elephants is that of one Gandhahatthi. The strength of ten Gandhahatthi elephants is that of one Maṅgala. The strength of ten Maṅgala elephants is that of one Hemavata. The strength of ten Hemavata elephants is that of one Uposatha. The strength of ten Uposatha elephants is that of one Chaddanta. The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is the bodily strength of one Tathāgata. This is also called the strength of the Nārāyana aggregate. Here, nārā are called rays; since many diverse ones arise from it, it is Nārāyana, the thunderbolt. Therefore, it means the strength of the thunderbolt aggregate. This strength, by the reckoning of ordinary elephants, is that of a thousand koṭis of elephants; by the reckoning of men, it is the strength of ten thousand koṭis of men. This, then, is the bodily strength of the Tathāgata.

Ñāṇabalaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi (ma. ni. 1.148; a. ni. 10.21) –

As for the power of knowledge, that is already found in the Pāli. Here is the passage:

“Dasa kho panimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalāni, yehi balehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti. Katamāni dasa? Idha, sāriputta, tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti, yaṃ balaṃ āgamma [V 3.0200] tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti. (1)

“Sāriputta, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the foremost place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. What are the ten? Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it actually is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. And this, Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata understands as it actually is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—this, Sāriputta, is a power of the Tathāgata, relying on which the Tathāgata claims the foremost place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. (1)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ kammasamādānānaṃ ṭhānaso hetuso vipākaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe…. (2)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it actually is the result of past, future, and present undertakings of action, in terms of their basis and cause... (2)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato sabbatthagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe…. (3)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it actually is the path leading to all destinations... (3)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato anekadhātuṃ nānādhātuṃ lokaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe…. (4)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it actually is the world with its many and diverse elements... (4)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikataṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe…. (5)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as they actually are the diverse inclinations of beings... (5)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe…. (6)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it actually is the state of the faculties of other beings and other individuals... (6)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe…. (7)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it actually is the defilement, cleansing, and emergence of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments... (7)

“Puna [M 3.0220] caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathidaṃ? Ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati…pe…. (8)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars... (8)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate, yathākammūpage satte pajānāti…pe…. (9)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and understands beings faring according to their actions... (9)

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ [V 3.0201] diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati…pe… idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti, yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti. Imāni kho, sāriputta, dasa tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī”ti. (10)

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge and entered upon the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life... This too, Sāriputta, is a power of the Tathāgata, relying on which the Tathāgata claims the foremost place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of the Tathāgata.” (10)

Tattha (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.148; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.10.21; vibha. aṭṭha. 760) ṭhānañca ṭhānatoti kāraṇañca kāraṇato. “Ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ hetū paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ. Ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ na hetū na paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ aṭṭhāna”nti pajānanto ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampīti yena ñāṇena.

Here, “possibility as possibility” means “cause as cause.” “Those phenomena that are causes and conditions for the arising of certain other phenomena—that is a possibility. Those phenomena that are not causes or conditions for the arising of certain other phenomena—that is an impossibility.” Thus, by understanding this, one knows possibility as possibility and impossibility as impossibility, as it actually is. “Yampi” means: by which knowledge.

Kammasamādānānanti samādiyitvā katānaṃ kusalākusalakammānaṃ, kammameva vā kammasamādānaṃ. Ṭhānaso hetusoti paccayato ceva hetuto ca. Tattha gatiupadhikālapayogā vipākassa ṭhānaṃ, kammaṃ hetu.

‘Undertakings of actions’ refers to wholesome and unwholesome actions done after having undertaken them, or it is simply the action itself. ‘In terms of their basis and cause’ means in terms of their condition and in terms of their root cause. Herein, destination, substratum, time, and effort are the basis for the result, while action is the root cause.

Sabbatthagāmininti sabbagatigāminiñca agatigāminiñca. Paṭipadanti maggaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti bahūsupi manussesu ekameva pāṇaṃ ghātentesu kāmaṃ sabbesampi cetanā tassevekassa jīvitindriyārammaṇā, taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ nānākāraṃ. Tesu hi eko ādarena chandajāto karoti, eko “ehi tvampi karohī”ti parehi nippīḷito karoti, eko samānacchando [M 3.0221] viya hutvā appaṭibāhiyamāno vicarati, tasmā tesu eko teneva kammena niraye nibbattati, eko tiracchānayoniyaṃ, eko pettivisaye. Taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva “iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa niraye nibbattissati, esa tiracchānayoniyaṃ, esa pettivisaye”ti jānāti. Niraye nibbattamānampi “esa mahāniraye nibbattissati, esa ussadaniraye”ti jānāti. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattamānampi “esa apādako bhavissati, esa dvipādako, esa catuppādo, esa bahuppādo”ti jānāti. Pettivisaye nibbattamānampi “esa nijjhāmataṇhiko bhavissati, esa khuppipāsiko, esa paradattūpajīvī”ti jānāti. Tesu ca kammesu “idaṃ kammaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhissati, etaṃ aññena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkaṃ bhavissatī”ti jānāti.

'Going everywhere' means going to all destinations and to no destination. 'The practice' means the path. 'He understands as it truly is': Even among many people killing a single living being, though the intention of all is focused on that one life faculty, their kamma is of various kinds. For among them, one acts out of eager desire; another is pressured by others, saying, “Come, you too do it”; another wanders about as if sharing the same desire, not resisting. Therefore, among them, one is reborn in hell because of that very kamma, another in the animal realm, another in the sphere of spirits. The Tathāgata knows at the very moment of accumulation: “Because it was accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in hell, this one in the animal realm, this one in the sphere of spirits.” Even when one is being reborn in hell, he knows: “This one will be reborn in a great hell, this one in a subsidiary hell.” When one is being reborn in the animal realm, he knows: “This one will be footless, this one two-footed, this one four-footed, this one many-footed.” When one is being reborn in the sphere of spirits, he knows: “This one will be tormented by thirst, this one afflicted by hunger and thirst, this one will live on what is given by others.” And among those kammas, he knows: “This kamma will bring about rebirth-linking; this one will ripen during the course of existence after rebirth-linking has been given by another kamma.”

Tathā sakalagāmavāsikesu ekato piṇḍapātaṃ dadamānesu kāmaṃ sabbesampi cetanā piṇḍapātārammaṇāva, [V 3.0202] taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ nānākāraṃ. Tesu hi eko ādarena karotīti sabbaṃ purimasadisaṃ. Tasmā tesu ca keci devaloke nibbattanti, keci manussaloke. Taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva jānāti. “Iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa manussaloke nibbattissati, esa devaloke, tatthāpi esa khattiyakule, esa brāhmaṇakule, esa vessakule, esa suddakule, esa paranimmitavasavattīsu, esa nimmānaratīsu, esa tusitesu, esa yāmesu, esa tāvatiṃsesu, esa cātumahārājikesu, esa bhummadevesū”tiādinā tattha tattha hīnapaṇītasuvaṇṇadubbaṇṇaappaparivāramahāparivāratādibhedaṃ taṃ taṃ visesaṃ āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva jānāti.

Similarly, when all the villagers give alms-food together, though the intention of all is focused on the alms-food, their kamma is of various kinds. For among them, one acts with eagerness—and so on, all as before. Therefore, some are reborn in the deva world, some in the human world. The Tathāgata knows this at the very moment of accumulation: “Because it was accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in the human world, this one in the deva world—and there, this one in a khattiya family, this one in a brahmin family, this one in a vessa family, this one in a sudda family; or this one among the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, this one among the Nimmānaratī devas, this one among the Tusita devas, this one among the Yāma devas, this one among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, this one among the Cātumahārājika devas, this one among the earth-dwelling devas.” In this way, he knows at the very moment of accumulation each particular distinction, such as the differences in being inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly, having a small or large retinue, and so forth.

Tathā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapentesuyeva “iminā nīhārena esa kiñci sallakkhetuṃ na sakkhissati, esa mahābhūtamattameva vavatthapessati, esa rūpapariggahe eva ṭhassati, esa arūpapariggaheyeva, esa nāmarūpapariggaheyeva, esa paccayapariggaheyeva, esa lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāyameva, esa paṭhamaphaleyeva, esa dutiyaphale eva, esa tatiyaphale eva, esa arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti jānāti. Kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontesupi “imassa parikammamattameva bhavissati, esa nimittaṃ uppādessati, esa appanaṃ eva pāpuṇissati, esa jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti jānāti.

Likewise, among those establishing insight, he knows: ‘By this approach, this one will not be able to discern anything; this one will only determine the mere great elements; this one will stop at the comprehension of form; this one, at the comprehension of the formless; this one, at the comprehension of name-and-form; this one, at the comprehension of conditions; this one, at insight that takes characteristics as its object; this one will attain only the first fruit; this one, only the second fruit; this one, only the third fruit; this one will attain arahantship.’ And among those performing the kasiṇa preliminary work, he knows: ‘For this one, there will only be the preliminary work; this one will produce the sign; this one will attain only absorption; this one, having made jhāna the basis and established insight, will attain arahantship.’

Anekadhātunti [M 3.0222] cakkhudhātuādīhi, kāmadhātuādīhi vā dhātūhi bahudhātuṃ. Nānādhātunti tāsaṃyeva dhātūnaṃ vilakkhaṇattā nānappakāradhātuṃ. Lokanti khandhāyatanadhātulokaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti tāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ aviparītato sabhāvaṃ paṭivijjhati.

“Manifold elements” refers to the many elements, such as the eye-element and so on, or the elements such as the desire realm and so on. “Diverse elements” means that those same elements are of various kinds due to their distinct characteristics. “The world” means the world of aggregates, sense-bases, and elements. “He understands as it truly is” means that he penetrates the inherent nature of those elements without distortion.

Nānādhimuttikatanti hīnādīhi adhimuttīhi nānādhimuttikabhāvaṃ. Parasattānanti padhānasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti tato paresaṃ hīnasattānaṃ. Ekatthameva vā etaṃ padadvayaṃ, veneyyavasena pana dvedhā vuttaṃ. Indriyaparopariyattanti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ parabhāvañca aparabhāvañca, vuddhiñca hāniñcāti attho.

“The diversity of inclinations” means the state of having diverse inclinations, such as inferior and so on. “Of other beings” means of superior beings. “Of other persons” means of beings inferior to them. Or, these two terms have the same meaning but are stated in two ways with respect to those who are to be guided. “The superiority and inferiority of the faculties” means the superiority and inferiority, the increase and decrease, of the faculties such as faith and so on; this is the meaning.

Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnanti paṭhamādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ, “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ, savitakkasavicārādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnaṃ, paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiādīnañca navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnaṃ. Saṃkilesanti hānabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vodānanti visesabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vuṭṭhānanti “vodānampi vuṭṭhānaṃ, tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti (vibha. 828) evaṃ vuttaṃ paguṇajjhānañceva bhavaṅgaphalasamāpattiyo ca. Heṭṭhimaṃ [V 3.0203] heṭṭhimañhi paguṇajjhānaṃ uparimassa uparimassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmā “vodānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Bhavaṅgena sabbajhānehi vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, phalasamāpattiyā nirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tametaṃ sandhāya “tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Sabbañāṇānañca vitthārakathāya vinicchayo sammohavinodaniyaṃ vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 760) vutto. Pubbenivāsānussatidibbacakkhuāsavakkhayañāṇakathā pana verañjakaṇḍe (pārā. 12) vitthāritāyeva.

“Of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments” refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with ‘one with form sees forms’; the three concentrations beginning with that with initial and sustained thought; and the nine successive attainments beginning with the first jhāna attainment. “Defilement” means states conducive to decline. “Purification” means states conducive to distinction. “Emergence” refers to what is stated thus: ‘Purification is also emergence, and emerging from this or that concentration is also emergence’ (Vibhaṅga 828), which includes both proficient jhānas and the life-continuum and the attainment of fruition. For each lower proficient jhāna serves as a basis for the one immediately higher; hence it is said, ‘Purification is also emergence.’ Emerging from all jhānas occurs through the life-continuum, and emerging from the attainment of cessation occurs through the attainment of fruition. It is with reference to this that it is said, ‘and emerging from this or that concentration is also emergence.’ The detailed discussion and analysis of all the knowledges is given in the Sammohavinodanī, the commentary to the Vibhaṅga (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 760). The discussion of the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, however, is already elaborated in the Verañja section (Pārājika 12).

Imāni kho sāriputtāti yāni pubbe “dasa kho panimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī”ti avocaṃ, imāni tānīti appanaṃ karoti. Tattha paravādikathā hoti “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ natthi, sabbaññutaññāṇassevāyaṃ pabhedo”ti, taṃ na tathā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññameva hi dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Dasabalañāṇaṃ sakasakakiccameva jānāti, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ tampi tato avasesampi pajānāti. Dasabalañāṇesu hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti, dutiyaṃ kammantaravipākantarameva, tatiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva, catutthaṃ dhātunānattakāraṇameva[M 3.0223], pañcamaṃ sattānaṃ ajjhāsayādhimuttimeva, chaṭṭhaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva, sattamaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva, aṭṭhamaṃ pubbenivutthakkhandhasantatimeva, navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhimeva, dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttariñca pajānāti, etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ na sabbaṃ karoti. Tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti, iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkoti, maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti. Iti yathāvuttakāyabalena ceva ñāṇabalena ca samannāgatattā bhagavā “dasabalo”ti vuccati.

He makes the concluding statement thus: ‘These, Sāriputta,’ are those of which I previously said, ‘Sāriputta, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata.’ Here, there is the argument of other schools: ‘There is no separate knowledge of the ten powers; this is just a division of omniscience.’ This should not be seen in that way. For the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another. The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective function, whereas the knowledge of omniscience knows that and what is beyond it. For, among the knowledges of the ten powers: the first knows only cause and non-cause; the second, only the diversity of kamma and the diversity of its results; the third, only the determination of the path; the fourth, only the cause for the diversity of elements; the fifth, only the inclinations and dispositions of beings; the sixth, only the keenness and dullness of the faculties; the seventh, only the defilement and so on associated with the jhānas and so on; the eighth, only the continuity of aggregates previously inhabited; the ninth, only the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings; the tenth, only the determination of the truths. The knowledge of omniscience, however, understands what is to be known by these and what is beyond that, but it does not perform all of their functions. For it cannot become jhāna and attain absorption; it cannot become psychic power and perform transformations; it cannot become the path and destroy the defilements. Thus, because the Blessed One is endowed with both the bodily power and the knowledge power as described, he is called ‘the One with Ten Powers.’

Dasahi asekkhehi aṅgehi upetoti “asekkhā sammādiṭṭhi, asekkho sammāsaṅkappo, asekkhā sammāvācā, asekkho sammākammanto, asekkho sammāājīvo, asekkho sammāvāyāmo, asekkhā sammāsati, asekkho sammāsamādhi, asekkhaṃ sammāñāṇaṃ, asekkhā sammāvimuttī”ti (dī. ni. 3.348, 360) evaṃ vuttehi dasahi asekkhadhammehi samannāgato. Asekkhā sammādiṭṭhiādayo ca sabbe phalasampayuttadhammā eva. Ettha ca sammādiṭṭhi sammāñāṇanti dvīsu ṭhānesu paññāva kathitā “sammā dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi, sammā pajānanaṭṭhena sammāñāṇa”nti. Atthi hi dassanajānanānaṃ visaye pavattiākāraviseso. Sammāvimuttīti iminā pana padena vuttāvasesā phalasamāpattisahagatadhammā saṅgahitāti veditabbā[V 3.0204]. Ariyaphalasampayuttadhammāpi hi sabbaso paṭipakkhato vimuttataṃ upādāya vimuttīti vattabbataṃ labhanti.

He is endowed with ten qualities of the non-learner, as stated: 'Non-learner's right view, non-learner's right intention, non-learner's right speech, non-learner's right action, non-learner's right livelihood, non-learner's right effort, non-learner's right mindfulness, non-learner's right concentration, non-learner's right knowledge, non-learner's right liberation' (Dī. Ni. 3.348, 360). Thus he is endowed with the ten states of a non-learner so described. The non-learner's right view and the others are all states associated with the fruit. Here, in the two instances of right view and right knowledge, wisdom alone is spoken of: 'Right view in the sense of seeing rightly; right knowledge in the sense of understanding rightly.' For there is indeed a distinction in the mode of their occurrence regarding their respective objects of seeing and knowing. By the term 'right liberation,' it should be understood that the remaining states associated with the attainment of fruition are included. For the states associated with the noble fruit also attain the designation 'liberation' on account of being entirely freed from their opponents.

59. Vacanasaddena appasaddanti ārāmupacārena gacchato addhikajanassapi vacanasaddena appasaddaṃ. Nagaranigghosasaddenāti avibhāvitatthena nagare manussānaṃ nigghosasaddena. Manussehi samāgamma ekajjhaṃ pavattitasaddo hi nigghoso. Anusañcaraṇajanassāti antosañcārino janassa. Manussānaṃ rahassakiriyaṭṭhāniyanti manussānaṃ rahassakaraṇassa yuttaṃ anucchavikaṃ. Vivekānurūpanti ekībhāvassa anurūpaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

59. 'With little noise by utterance' means with little noise from the speech even of travelers passing by in the vicinity of the monastery. 'With the noise of the city' means with the indistinct noise of people in the city. For 'noise' is a sound produced by people gathering together. 'Of the people who wander about' means of the people moving about inside. 'A place for people's secret activities' means suitable and fitting for people's secret doings. 'Suitable for seclusion' means fitting for being alone. The rest here is clear.

Bimbisārasamāgamakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the account of the meeting with Bimbisāra is concluded.

Sāriputtamoggallānapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna

60. Idāni [M 3.0224] “tena kho pana samayena sañcayo paribbājako”tiādīsu apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ dassento “sāriputtamoggallānā”tiādimāha. Tattha sārībrāhmaṇiyā putto sāriputto, moggallībrāhmaṇiyā putto moggallāno. Amhākaṃ kira (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.189-190; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.10 sāriputtattheravatthu) bhagavato nibbattito puretarameva sāriputto rājagahanagarassa avidūre upatissagāme sārībrāhmaṇiyā nāma kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Taṃdivasamevassa sahāyopi rājagahasseva avidūre kolitagāme moggallībrāhmaṇiyā kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tāni kira dvepi kulāni yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā ābaddhapaṭibaddhasahāyāneva. Tesaṃ dvinnaṃ ekadivasameva gabbhaparihāraṃ adaṃsu. Dasamāsaccayena jātānampi tesaṃ chasaṭṭhi dhātiyo upanayiṃsu. Nāmaggahaṇadivase sārībrāhmaṇiyā puttassa upatissagāme jeṭṭhakulassa puttattā “upatisso”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu, itarassa kolitagāme jeṭṭhakulassa puttattā “kolito”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “gihikāle upatisso kolitoti evaṃ paññāyamānanāmā”ti.

60. Now, to provide an explanation for words not previously explained in the passage beginning, 'At that time, the wanderer Sañcaya,' etc., the commentary states, 'Sāriputta and Moggallāna,' etc. Herein, Sāriputta was the son of the brahmin woman Sārī, and Moggallāna was the son of the brahmin woman Moggallī. It is said that, according to our tradition, even before the Blessed One arose, Sāriputta took conception in the womb of the brahmin woman named Sārī in the village of Upatissa, not far from the city of Rājagaha. On that very same day, his friend also took conception in the womb of the brahmin woman Moggallī in the village of Kolita, also not far from Rājagaha. It is said that these two families had been close, bound friends for seven generations. For both of them, pregnancy care was given on the same day. When they were born after the passing of ten months, sixty-six nurses were appointed for them. On the naming day, the son of the brahmin woman Sārī, being the son of the leading family in Upatissa village, was given the name 'Upatissa,' while the other, being the son of the leading family in Kolita village, was named 'Kolita.' Hence it is said, 'In their household days, they were known by the names Upatissa and Kolita.'

Aḍḍhateyyasatamāṇavakaparivārāti ettha pañcapañcasatamāṇavakaparivārātipi vadanti. Vuttañhetaṃ aṅguttaranikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.189-190) –

Regarding the phrase 'with a retinue of two hundred and fifty young men,' here some also say 'with a retinue of five hundred young men each.' For this is stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya commentary:

“Upatissamāṇavakassa kīḷanatthāya nadiṃ vā uyyānaṃ vā gamanakāle pañca suvaṇṇasivikāsatāni [V 3.0205] parivārāni honti, kolitamāṇavakassa pañca ājaññarathasatāni. Dvepi janā pañcapañcamāṇavakasataparivārā hontī”ti.

“When the young man Upatissa went to the river or the park for amusement, his retinue consisted of five hundred golden palanquins, and the young man Kolita's consisted of five hundred thoroughbred chariots. Both persons had retinues of five hundred young men each.”

Rājagahe ca anusaṃvaccharaṃ giraggasamajjaṃ nāma hoti. Tesaṃ dvinnampi ekaṭṭhāneyeva mañcakaṃ bandhanti. Dvepi ekatova nisīditvā samajjaṃ passitvā hasitabbaṭṭhāne hasanti, saṃvegaṭṭhāne saṃvijjanti, dāyaṃ dātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne dāyaṃ denti. Tesaṃ imināva niyāmena ekadivasaṃ samajjaṃ passantānaṃ paripākagatattā ñāṇassa purimadivasesu viya hasitabbaṭṭhāne hāso vā saṃvegaṭṭhāne saṃvijjanaṃ vā dāyaṃ dātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne dāyadānaṃ vā nāhosi. Dvepi [M 3.0225] pana janā evaṃ cintayiṃsu “kiṃ ettha oloketabbaṃ atthi, sabbepime appatte vassasate apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gamissanti, amhehi pana ekaṃ mokkhadhammaṃ gavesituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā nisīdiṃsu. Tato kolito upatissaṃ āha “samma upatissa, na tvaṃ aññadivasesu viya haṭṭhapahaṭṭho, anattamanadhātukosi, kiṃ te sallakkhita”nti. “Samma kolita, etesaṃ olokane sāro natthi, niratthakametaṃ, attano mokkhadhammaṃ gavesituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ cintayanto nisinnomhīti. Tvaṃ pana kasmā anattamanoti. Sopi tatheva āha. Athassa attanā saddhiṃ ekajjhāsayataṃ ñatvā upatisso evamāha “amhākaṃ ubhinnaṃ sucintitaṃ, mokkhadhammaṃ pana gavesantehi ekā pabbajjā laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, kassa santike pabbajāmā”ti.

In Rājagaha, there was an annual festival called the Mountain-Top Festival. For both of them, a single couch was set up in one place. The two sat together and, watching the festival, laughed where it was laughable, were moved where it was moving, and gave gifts where it was proper to give. As they were watching the festival one day in this way, because their knowledge had matured, there was no laughter where it was laughable, no being moved where it was moving, and no giving of gifts where it was proper to give, unlike on previous days. Then the two men thought thus: “What is there to see here? All these people will become unidentifiable before a hundred years have passed. It is right for us to seek a teaching of liberation.” Taking this as their object of mind, they sat down. Then Kolita said to Upatissa: “Friend Upatissa, you are not joyful and delighted as on other days; you seem dispirited. What have you noticed?” “Friend Kolita, there is no substance in watching these things. This is meaningless. I am sitting here thinking, 'It is right for us to seek a teaching of liberation for ourselves.' But why are you dispirited?” He replied in the same way. Then, realizing they were of one mind, Upatissa said: “We have both thought well. For those seeking a teaching of liberation, it is right to obtain the going forth. Under whom shall we go forth?”

Tena kho pana samayena sañcayo paribbājako rājagahe paṭivasati mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ. Te “tassa santike pabbajissāmā”ti pañcahi māṇavakasatehi saddhiṃ sañcayassa santike pabbajiṃsu. Tesaṃ pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya sañcayo atirekalābhaggayasaggappatto ahosi. Te katipāheneva sabbaṃ sañcayassa samayaṃ parimadditvā “ācariya, tumhākaṃ jānanasamayo ettakova, udāhu uttaripi atthī”ti pucchiṃsu. Sañcayo “ettakova, sabbaṃ tumhehi ñāta”nti āha. Tassa kathaṃ sutvā cintayiṃsu “evaṃ sati imassa santike brahmacariyavāso niratthako, mayaṃ mokkhadhammaṃ gavesituṃ nikkhantā, so imassa santike uppādetuṃ na sakkā, mahā kho pana jambudīpo, gāmanigamarājadhāniyo carantā avassaṃ mokkhadhammadesakaṃ ācariyaṃ labhissāmā”ti. Te tato paṭṭhāya “yattha yattha paṇḍitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā atthī”ti suṇanti, tattha tattha gantvā pañhasākacchaṃ karonti, tehi puṭṭhaṃ pañhaṃ añño kathetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, te pana tesaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjenti. Evaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ pariggaṇhitvā nivattitvā sakaṭṭhānameva āgantvā “samma kolita, yo paṭhamaṃ amataṃ adhigacchati[V 3.0206], so ārocetū”ti katikaṃ akaṃsu. Imameva vatthuṃ saṅkhipitvā dassento “tatra nesaṃ mahājanaṃ disvā…pe… katikaṃ akaṃsū”ti āha.

At that time, the wanderer Sañcaya was residing in Rājagaha with a large assembly of wanderers. Thinking, “We will go forth under him,” they, together with five hundred young men, went forth under Sañcaya. From the time of their going forth, Sañcaya attained an excess of gain, honor, and fame. Within just a few days, they had thoroughly mastered all of Sañcaya’s doctrine and asked him, “Teacher, is this the extent of your doctrine, or is there anything further?” Sañcaya replied, “This is all; you have understood everything.” Hearing his words, they thought, “If that is so, living the holy life under him is pointless. We went forth to seek a teaching of liberation, and that cannot be produced under him. Jambudīpa is vast; traveling through villages, towns, and royal cities, we will surely find a teacher who can teach the doctrine of liberation.” From then on, wherever they heard that there were wise ascetics or brahmins, they went there and held discussions. No one was able to answer the questions put by them, but they answered the questions of those others. Having thus traversed the whole of Jambudīpa, they returned to their own place and made an agreement: “Friend Kolita, whoever first attains the Deathless should inform the other.” Explaining this very account in brief, the commentary states: “There, seeing the great crowd of people… and so on… they made an agreement.”

Tattha channaparibbājakassāti setapaṭadharassa paribbājakassa. Tena nāyaṃ naggaparibbājakoti dasseti. Pāsādikena abhikkantenātiādīsu pāsādikenāti pasādāvahena sāruppena samaṇānucchavikena. Abhikkantenāti [M 3.0226] gamanena. Paṭikkantenāti nivattanena. Ālokitenāti purato dassanena. Vilokitenāti ito cito dassanena. Samiñjitenāti pabbasaṅkocanena. Pasāritenāti tesaṃyeva pasāraṇena. Sabbattha itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ, tasmā satisampajaññakehi vabhisaṅkhatattā pāsādikaabhikkantapaṭikkantaālokitavilokitasamiñjitapasārito hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Okkhittacakkhūti heṭṭhākhittacakkhu. Iriyāpathasampannoti tāya pāsādikaabhikkantāditāya sampannairiyāpatho. Atthikehi upaññātanti “maraṇe sati amatenapi bhavitabba”nti evaṃ anumānañāṇena “atthī”ti upagataṃ nibbānaṃ nāma, taṃ magganto pariyesanto yannūnāhaṃ imaṃ bhikkhuṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandheyyanti sambandho. Sudinnakaṇḍe vuttappakāranti “dānapatīnaṃ gharesu sālā honti, āsanāni cettha paññattāni honti, upaṭṭhāpitaṃ udakakañjiyaṃ, tattha pabbajitā piṇḍāya caritvā nisīditvā bhuñjanti. Sace icchanti, dānapatīnampi santakaṃ gaṇhanti, tasmā tampi aññatarassa kulassa īdisāya sālāya aññataraṃ kuṭṭamūlanti veditabba”nti evaṃ vuttappakāraṃ.

Herein, “Channa the wanderer” refers to a wanderer wearing a white robe. Thereby it shows that he was not a naked ascetic. In the phrases “with graceful approach,” and so on, “graceful” means inspiring confidence, seemly, and befitting for a renunciate. “Approach” refers to going forward. “Departure” refers to turning back. “Looking ahead” means seeing in front. “Looking around” means seeing here and there. “Drawing in” means contracting the limbs. “Extending” means stretching them out. In all these cases, the instrumental case indicates the characteristic of the action; therefore, because these actions were performed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, it is said that he was one who was graceful in his approaching, departing, looking ahead, looking around, drawing in, and extending. “With downcast eyes” means with eyes cast downwards. “Perfect in deportment” means possessing a deportment endowed with that graceful approach, departure, and so on. “‘Known by those who seek the essence’ refers to Nibbāna, which is understood to exist through inferential knowledge thus: ‘If there is death, there must also be the Deathless.’ Seeking and searching for that, one thinks, ‘Let me follow this monk from behind.’ This is the connection. The manner described in the Sudinnakaṇḍa is as follows: “In the houses of donors, there are halls where seats are arranged and water and gruel are prepared. Having wandered for alms, renunciates sit and eat there. If they wish, they may also take what belongs to the donors.” Therefore, it should be understood that this also occurred at the foot of a wall in such a hall belonging to a certain family. Thus, the manner is as described.

Appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā bhāsassūti paribbājako “ahaṃ upatisso nāma, tvaṃ yathāsattiyā appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā pāvada, etaṃ nayasatena nayasahassena paṭivijjhituṃ mayhaṃ bhāro”ti cintetvā evamāha. Nirodho ca nirodhupāyo ca ekadesasarūpekasesanayena “nirodho”ti vuttoti dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Paṭipādentoti nigamento.
