Imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādīti ettha paribbājako paṭhamapadadvayameva sutvā sahassanayasampanne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Itarapadadvayaṃ sotāpannakāle niṭṭhāsīti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding “Speak little or much,” the wanderer, thinking, “I am Upatissa by name. You speak according to your ability, whether little or much. It is my task to penetrate this with a hundred or a thousand methods,” said this. Showing that cessation and the path to cessation are spoken of as “cessation” by the method of one remaining due to partial similarity of nature, he said “or else,” and so forth. “Paṭipādenti” means “concluding.” Regarding “Having heard this Dhamma discourse, the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose,” herein, the wanderer, having heard just the first two lines, was established in the fruit of stream-entry, which is endowed with a thousand methods. The remaining two lines should be understood as having been comprehended at the time he became a stream-enterer.

Bahukehi kappanahutehīti ettha dasa dasakāni sataṃ, dasa satāni sahassaṃ, sahassānaṃ sataṃ satasahassaṃ, satasahassānaṃ sataṃ koṭi, koṭisatasahassānaṃ sataṃ pakoṭi, pakoṭisatasahassānaṃ sataṃ koṭipakoṭi, koṭipakoṭisatasahassānaṃ sataṃ ekanahutanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding “for many nahutas of eons”—here, it should be understood that ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand; a hundred thousands make a hundred thousand; a hundred hundred-thousands make a koṭi; a hundred hundred-thousands of koṭis make a pakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousands of pakoṭis make a koṭipakoṭi; and a hundred hundred-thousands of koṭipakoṭis make one nahuta.

61. Atha [M 3.0227][V 3.0207] kho sāriputto paribbājako yena moggallāno paribbājako tenupasaṅkamīti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.189-190; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.10 sāriputtattheravatthu) sotāpanno hutvā uparivisese appavattante “bhavissati ettha kāraṇa”nti sallakkhetvā theraṃ āha “bhante, mā upari dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍhayittha, ettakameva hotu, kahaṃ amhākaṃ satthā vasatī”ti. Veḷuvane paribbājakāti. “Bhante, tumhe purato yātha, mayhaṃ eko sahāyako atthi, amhehi ca aññamaññaṃ katikā katā ‘yo paṭhamaṃ amataṃ adhigacchati, so ārocetū’ti, ahaṃ taṃ paṭiññaṃ mocetvā sahāyakaṃ gahetvā tumhākaṃ gatamaggeneva satthu santikaṃ āgamissāmī”ti pañcapatiṭṭhitena therassa pādesu nipatitvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā theraṃ uyyojetvā paribbājakārāmābhimukho agamāsi.

61. Regarding “Then the wanderer Sāriputta approached the wanderer Moggallāna”: Having become a stream-enterer, and as higher attainments were not yet arising, he considered, “There must be a reason for this.” So he said to the elder: “Venerable sir, do not extend the Dhamma teaching further; let it be just this much. Where does our Teacher reside?” “In the Bamboo Grove, wanderer.” “Venerable sir, you go ahead. I have a friend, and we have made a mutual agreement: ‘Whoever first attains the Deathless should inform the other.’ I must fulfill that promise, take my friend, and come to the Teacher’s presence by the same path you took.” Having prostrated at the elder’s feet with the five points of contact, circumambulated him three times, and sent the elder on his way, he set out toward the wanderers’ park.

62. Sāriputtaṃ paribbājakaṃ etadavocāti “ajja mayhaṃ sahāyassa mukhavaṇṇo na aññadivasesu viya, addhā anena amataṃ adhigataṃ bhavissatī”ti amatādhigamaṃ pucchanto etadavoca. Sopissa “āmāvuso, amataṃ adhigata”nti paṭijānitvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā tameva gāthaṃ abhāsi. Gāthāpariyosāne moggallāno paribbājako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho moggallānassa paribbājakassa…pe… dhammacakkhuṃ udapādī”ti. Gacchāma mayaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato santiketi “kahaṃ samma satthā vasatī”ti pucchitvā “veḷuvane kira samma, evaṃ no ācariyena assajittherena kathita”nti vutte evamāha.

62. Regarding the words, 'He said this to the wanderer Sāriputta': Moggallāna, asking about the attainment of the Deathless, said this, thinking: 'Today my friend's complexion is not as on other days. Surely, he must have attained the Deathless.' And Sāriputta admitted to him, 'Yes, friend, the Deathless has been attained,' and after recounting the entire event, he recited that same verse. At the end of the verse, the wanderer Moggallāna was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Therefore it is said: 'Then for the wanderer Moggallāna… the Dhamma-eye arose.' Regarding the words, 'Let us go, friend, to the presence of the Blessed One': Moggallāna said this after asking, 'Friend, where does the Teacher reside?' and Sāriputta replied, 'In the Bamboo Grove, friend; so our teacher, the elder Assaji, has told us.'

Sāriputtatthero ca nāmesa sadāpi ācariyapūjakova, tasmā sahāyaṃ moggallānaṃ paribbājakaṃ evamāha “amhehi adhigataṃ amataṃ amhākaṃ ācariyassa sañcayaparibbājakassapi kathessāma, bujjhamāno paṭivijjhissati, appaṭivijjhanto amhākaṃ saddahitvā satthu santikaṃ gamissati, buddhānaṃ desanaṃ sutvā maggaphalappaṭivedhaṃ karissatī”ti. Tato dvepi janā sañcayassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho sāriputtamoggallānā yena sañcayo paribbājako tenupasaṅkamiṃsū”ti. Upasaṅkamitvā ca “ācariya, tvaṃ kiṃ karosi, loke buddho [M 3.0228] uppanno, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho, āyāma dasabalaṃ passissāmā”ti. So “kiṃ vadatha tātā”ti tepi vāretvā lābhaggayasaggappavattimeva nesaṃ dīpeti. Te “amhākaṃ evarūpo antevāsikavāso niccameva hotu, tumhākaṃ pana gamanaṃ vā agamanaṃ vā jānāthā”ti āhaṃsu. Sañcayo “ime ettakaṃ jānantā mama vacanaṃ na karissantī”ti ñatvā “gacchatha tumhe tātā, ahaṃ mahallakakāle antevāsikavāsaṃ vasituṃ na sakkomī”ti [V 3.0208] āha. Te anekehipi kāraṇasatehi taṃ bodhetuṃ asakkontā attano ovāde vattamānaṃ janaṃ ādāya veḷuvanaṃ agamaṃsu. Pañcasu antevāsikasatesu aḍḍhateyyasatā nivattiṃsu, aḍḍhateyyasatā tehi saddhiṃ agamaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho sāriputtamoggallānā tāni aḍḍhateyyāni paribbājakasatāni ādāya yena veḷuvanaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsū”ti.

The Elder Sāriputta was, by nature, always one who revered his teacher. Therefore, he said to his companion, the wanderer Moggallāna: “We have attained the Deathless. Let us tell our teacher, the wanderer Sañcaya. If he understands, he will penetrate it. If he does not penetrate it, he will trust us and go to the Teacher. Having heard the teaching of the Buddhas, he will realize the path and its fruits.” Then both men went to Sañcaya. Thus it is said: “Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached the wanderer Sañcaya.” Having approached, they said: “Teacher, what are you doing? A Buddha has arisen in the world, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, and the Saṅgha is practicing rightly. Come, let us go see the One of Ten Powers.” He replied: “What are you saying, my dears?” and trying to dissuade them, he merely pointed out to them the prospect of the highest gains, fame, and heavenly birth. They said: “May our discipleship of this kind be constant. But as for you, decide for yourself whether to go or not.” Knowing, 'They, who know so much, will not follow my word,' Sañcaya said: “Go, my dears. I am too old to live as a disciple now.” Unable to persuade him despite many hundreds of reasons, they took those people who followed their advice and went to the Bamboo Grove. Out of five hundred disciples, two hundred and fifty turned back, while two hundred and fifty went with them. Thus it is said: “Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna, taking those two hundred and fifty wanderers, approached the Bamboo Grove.”

Vimutteti yathāvuttalakkhaṇe nibbāne tadārammaṇāya phalavimuttiyā adhimutte ne sāriputtamoggallāne byākāsīti sambandho.

Regarding the word 'liberated' (`vimutte`): He declared them, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who were intent upon Nibbāna, characterized as stated, and upon the fruit-liberation which has that as its object. This is the connection.

Evaṃ byākaritvā ca satthā catuparisamajjhe dhammaṃ desento nesaṃ parisāya cariyavasena dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍhesi, ṭhapetvā dve aggasāvake sabbepi aḍḍhateyyasatā paribbājakā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthā “etha bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi, sabbesaṃ kesamassu antaradhāyi, iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ ahosi. Aggasāvakānampi iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ āgataṃ, uparimaggattayakiccaṃ pana na niṭṭhāti. Kasmā? Sāvakapāramīñāṇassa mahantatāya. Athāyasmā mahāmoggallāno pabbajitadivasato sattame divase magadharaṭṭhe kallavāḷagāmakaṃ upanissāya samaṇadhammaṃ karonto thinamiddhaṃ okkamanto satthārā saṃvejito thinamiddhaṃ vinodetvā tathāgatena dinnaṃ dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ suṇantova uparimaggattayakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā sāvakapāramīñāṇassa matthakaṃ patto. Sāriputtattheropi pabbajitadivasato addhamāsaṃ atikkamitvā satthārā saddhiṃ tameva rājagahaṃ upanissāya sūkarakhataleṇe viharanto attano bhāgineyyassa dīghanakhaparibbājakassa vedanāpariggahasuttante desiyamāne suttānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā parassa vaḍḍhitabhattaṃ bhuñjanto viya sāvakapāramīñāṇassa matthakaṃ patto. Tenevāha “mahāmoggallānatthero sattahi divasehi arahatte patiṭṭhito, sāriputtatthero addhamāsenā”ti.

Having thus declared, the Teacher, while teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, developed the Dhamma discourse in accordance with the disposition of that assembly. Except for the two chief disciples, all two hundred and fifty wandering ascetics attained arahantship. The Teacher extended his hand, saying, “Come, monks,” and the hair and beards of all vanished, while robes and bowls created by psychic power appeared attached to their bodies. Even for the chief disciples, robes and bowls created by psychic power appeared, but the task of the three higher paths was not yet completed. Why? Due to the greatness of the knowledge of the disciples’ perfections. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, on the seventh day after his ordination, while practicing the recluse's duties near the village of Kallavāḷa in the Magadha country, being overcome by sloth and torpor, was stirred by the Teacher. Having dispelled his sloth and torpor, and while listening to the meditation subject on the elements given by the Tathāgata, he completed the task of the three higher paths and reached the summit of the knowledge of the disciples’ perfections. The Venerable Sāriputta, too, after half a month had passed since his ordination, dwelling with the Teacher near Rājagaha in the Sūkarakhata Cave, while the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being taught to his nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, directed his knowledge in accordance with the sutta and, like one eating a meal served by another, reached the summit of the knowledge of the disciples’ perfections. Therefore it is said: “The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was established in arahantship in seven days, and the Venerable Sāriputta in half a month.”

Yadipi [M 3.0229] mahāmoggallānatthero na cirasseva arahattaṃ patto, dhammasenāpati tato cirena, evaṃ santepi sāriputtattherova mahāpaññataro. Mahāmoggallānatthero hi sāvakānaṃ sammasanacāraṃ yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷento viya ekadesameva sammasanto satta divase vāyamitvā arahattaṃ patto. Sāriputtatthero ṭhapetvā buddhānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca sammasanacāraṃ sāvakānaṃ sammasanacāraṃ nippadesaṃ sammasi, evaṃ sammasanto addhamāsaṃ vāyami. Ukkaṃsagatassa sāvakānaṃ sammasanacārassa nippadesena pavattiyamānattā sāvakapāramīñāṇassa ca tathā paripācetabbattā. Yathā hi puriso “veṇuyaṭṭhiṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti mahājaṭaṃ veṇuṃ disvā “jaṭaṃ chindantassa papañco bhavissatī”ti antarena hatthaṃ pavesetvā sampattameva yaṭṭhiṃ mūle ca agge ca chinditvā ādāya pakkameyya, so [V 3.0209] kiñcāpi paṭhamataraṃ gacchati, yaṭṭhiṃ pana sāraṃ vā ujuṃ vā na labhati. Aparo tathārūpameva veṇuṃ disvā sace sampattayaṭṭhiṃ gaṇhissāmi, sāraṃ vā ujuṃ vā na labhissāmīti kacchaṃ bandhitvā mahantena satthena veṇujaṭaṃ chinditvā sārā ceva ujū ca yaṭṭhiyo uccinitvā ādāya pakkameyya, ayaṃ kiñcāpi pacchā gacchati, yaṭṭhiyo pana sārā ceva ujū ca labhati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ therānaṃ padhānaṃ.

Although the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained arahantship very soon, and the General of the Dhamma later than that, even so, the Venerable Sāriputta was the one with greater wisdom. For the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, as if pressing upon the disciples' field of comprehension with the tip of a staff, comprehended only a part of it, and having striven for seven days, attained arahantship. The Venerable Sāriputta, however, setting aside the field of comprehension of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, comprehended the disciples' field of comprehension completely, without remainder. Striving thus, he took half a month. This was because the disciples' field of comprehension, having reached its highest point, proceeds without remainder, and because the knowledge of a disciple's perfections must be matured in such a way. It is like a man who, thinking, “I will get a bamboo staff,” sees a dense bamboo thicket and thinks, “Cutting through the thicket will be a complication.” He thrusts his hand in, takes the very staff he has reached, cuts it at the base and the tip, and departs. Although he leaves first, he does not get a staff that is strong or straight. Another man, seeing a similar bamboo thicket, thinks, “If I take the staff I can reach, I will not get one that is strong or straight.” So he girds his waist, cuts through the bamboo thicket with a large blade, selects staffs that are both strong and straight, and departs. Although this one leaves later, he gets staffs that are both strong and straight. Of such a nature was the striving of these two elders.

Sammasanacāro ca nāmettha vipassanābhūmi veditabbā sammasanaṃ carati etthāti sammasanacāroti katvā. Tattha buddhānaṃ sammasanacāro dasasahassalokadhātuyaṃ sattasantānagatā anindriyabaddhā ca saṅkhārāti vadanti. Koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesūti apare. Tathā hi attaniyavasena paṭiccasamuppādanayaṃ otaritvā chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhena buddhānaṃ mahāvajirañāṇaṃ pavattaṃ. Paccekabuddhānaṃ sasantānagatehi saddhiṃ majjhimadesavāsīsattasantānagatā anindriyabaddhā ca saṅkhārā sammasanacāroti vadanti. Jambudīpavāsīsantānagatāti keci. Sasantānagate sabbadhamme parasantānagate ca santānavibhāgaṃ akatvā bahiddhābhāvasāmaññato sammasanaṃ, ayaṃ sāvakānaṃ sammasanacāro. Moggallānatthero pana bahiddhā dhammepi sasantānavibhāgena keci keci uddharitvā sammasi, tañca kho ñāṇena phuṭṭhamattaṃ katvā. Tena vuttaṃ “yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷento viya ekadesameva sammasanto”ti. Tattha ñāṇena nāma yāvatā neyyaṃ vattitabbaṃ, tāvatā avattanato “yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷento [M 3.0230] viyā”ti vuttaṃ, anupadadhammavipassanāya abhāvato “ekadesameva sammasanto”ti vuttaṃ. Dhammasenāpatinopi yathāvuttasāvakānaṃ vipassanāya bhūmiyeva sammasanacāro. Tattha pana thero sātisayaṃ niravasesaṃ anupadañca sammā vipassi. Tena vuttaṃ “sāvakānaṃ sammasanacāraṃ nippadesaṃ sammasī”ti.

And here, the field of comprehension should be understood as the ground for insight, because one 'moves in comprehension' (sammasanaṃ carati) therein. In this regard, some say the field of comprehension for the Buddhas consists of the formations, both those included in the continuity of beings and those not bound to the sense faculties, throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system. Others say it extends to a hundred thousand koṭis of world-spheres. For, having penetrated the principle of dependent origination in relation to himself, the great diamond-like knowledge of the Buddhas proceeds through thirty-six hundred thousand koṭi doorways. For Paccekabuddhas, some say their field of comprehension consists of the formations included in the continuity of beings dwelling in the Middle Country, and those not bound to the sense faculties, along with those in their own continuity. Others say it includes the continuity of beings dwelling in Jambudīpa. For disciples, the field of comprehension is the examination of all phenomena in one's own continuity and in the continuity of others without making a distinction between continuities, based on the generality of their external nature. The Elder Moggallāna, however, with regard to external phenomena, examined them by extracting certain ones, distinguishing them from his own continuity, and doing so only to the extent that they were touched by his knowledge. Therefore it was said: “like pressing with the tip of a staff, comprehending only a part.” Herein, it is said “like pressing with the tip of a staff” because his knowledge did not extend as far as the knowable extends; and it is said “comprehending only a part” because of the absence of insight into phenomena moment by moment. For the General of the Dhamma, too, the field of comprehension was the very ground for insight as described for the disciples. Therein, however, the Elder practiced insight perfectly, pre-eminently, without remainder, and moment by moment. Therefore it was said: “He comprehended the disciples' field of comprehension completely.”

Ettha ca sukkhavipassakā lokiyābhiññappattā pakatisāvakā mahāsāvakā aggasāvakā paccekabuddhā sammāsambuddhāti chasu janesu sukkhavipassakānaṃ jhānābhiññāhi anadhigatapaññānepuññattā andhānaṃ viya icchitapadesokkamanaṃ vipassanākāle icchiticchitadhammabhāvanā natthi, te yathāpariggahitadhammamatteyeva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhenti. Lokiyābhiññappattā pana pakatisāvakā yena mukhena vipassanaṃ ārabhanti, tato aññenapi vipassanaṃ vitthārikaṃ kātuṃ sakkonti vipulañāṇattā. Mahāsāvakā abhinīhārasampannattā tato sātisayaṃ vipassanaṃ vitthārikaṃ kātuṃ sakkonti. Aggasāvakesu dutiyo abhinīhārasampattiyā samādhānassa sātisayattā vipassanaṃ tatopi vitthārikaṃ karoti. Paṭhamo pana tatopi mahāpaññatāya sāvakehi asādhāraṇaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vitthārikaṃ karoti. Paccekabuddhā tehipi [V 3.0210] mahābhinīhāratāya attano abhinīhārānurūpaṃ tatopi vitthārikaṃ vipassanaṃ karonti. Buddhānaṃ sammadeva paripūritapaññāpāramīpabhāvitā sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamassa anurūpā yathā nāma katavālavedhaparicayena sarabhaṅgasadisena dhanuggahena khitto saro antarā rukkhalatādīsu asajjamāno lakkheyeva patati, na sajjati na virajjati, evaṃ antarā asajjamānā avirajjamānā vipassanā sammasanīyadhammesu yāthāvato nānānayehi pavattati, yaṃ “mahāvajirañāṇa”nti vuccati.

Herein, among these six kinds of individuals—dry-insight meditators, ordinary disciples who have attained mundane direct knowledge, great disciples, chief disciples, Paccekabuddhas, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas—for dry-insight meditators, due to their lack of proficiency in wisdom, not having attained the jhānas and direct knowledges, there is no development of whatever phenomena they wish during insight meditation, like a blind person trying to reach a desired place. They develop insight only within the scope of the phenomena they have grasped. Ordinary disciples who have attained mundane direct knowledge, however, due to their vast knowledge, are able to expand their insight from whatever approach they began with to another as well. Great disciples, being endowed with a past aspiration, are able to expand their insight even more excellently. Among the chief disciples, the second one expands his insight even further, due to the excellence of his concentration and the fulfillment of his aspiration. The first one, however, due to his great wisdom, expands his insight even further still, in a way uncommon among disciples. Paccekabuddhas, due to their great aspiration, develop an even more expansive insight in accordance with their own resolve. For the Buddhas, their insight—developed through the perfectly fulfilled perfection of wisdom and suited to the attainment of omniscient knowledge—proceeds through the phenomena to be comprehended accurately and in various ways, without getting stuck or wavering, just as an arrow, shot by an archer like Sarabhaṅga skilled in the practice of splitting a hair, flies without getting stuck in trees or vines in its path and hits the target exactly, neither sticking nor falling short. This is called the 'Great Diamond Knowledge.'

Etesu ca sukkhavipassakānaṃ vipassanācāro khajjotappabhāsadiso, abhiññappattapakatisāvakānaṃ dīpappabhāsadiso, mahāsāvakānaṃ ukkāppabhāsadiso, aggasāvakānaṃ osadhitārakappabhāsadiso, paccekabuddhānaṃ candappabhāsadiso, sammāsambuddhānaṃ rasmisahassapaṭimaṇḍitasaradasūriyamaṇḍalasadiso hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Tathā sukkhavipassakānaṃ vipassanācāro andhānaṃ [M 3.0231] yaṭṭhikoṭiyā gamanasadiso, lokiyābhiññappattapakatisāvakānaṃ daṇḍakasetugamanasadiso, mahāsāvakānaṃ jaṅghasetugamanasadiso, aggasāvakānaṃ sakaṭasetugamanasadiso, paccekabuddhānaṃ mahājaṅghamaggagamanasadiso, sammāsambuddhānaṃ mahāsakaṭamaggagamanasadiso. Tathā buddhānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca vipassanā cintāmayañāṇasaṃvaḍḍhitattā sayambhūñāṇabhūtā, itaresaṃ sutamayañāṇasaṃvaḍḍhitattā paropadesasambhūtāti veditabbā.

Among these, the practice of insight for dry-insight meditators is like the light of a firefly. For ordinary disciples who have attained higher knowledge, it is like the light of a lamp. For great disciples, it is like the light of a torch. For the foremost disciples, it is like the light of the morning star. For Paccekabuddhas, it is like the light of the moon. For Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, it appears like the disc of the autumn sun adorned with a thousand rays. Similarly, the practice of insight of dry-insight practitioners is like a blind person's going with the tip of a stick. For ordinary disciples who have attained mundane higher knowledge, it is like going across a log bridge. For great disciples, it is like going across a footbridge. For the foremost disciples, it is like going across a cart bridge. For Paccekabuddhas, it is like going on a great footpath. For Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, it is like going on a great cart road. Furthermore, it should be known that the insight of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, being developed through knowledge acquired by reflection, is self-arisen knowledge; for others, being developed through knowledge acquired by learning, it arises from the instruction of another.

Idāni ubhinnampi therānaṃ pubbayogaṃ dassetuṃ “atīte kirā”tiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthameva.

Now, to show the prior connection of both elders, it begins with "in the past, indeed," and so forth. All of that is clear in meaning.

63. Giribbajanagaranti samantā pabbataparikkhittaṃ vajasadisaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhatīti giribbajanti evaṃladdhanāmaṃ rājagahanagaraṃ. Usūyanakiriyāya kammabhāvaṃ sandhāya “upayogatthe vā”ti vuttaṃ.

63. "The city of Giribbaja" means the city of Rājagaha, which, being surrounded by mountains, stands like a cattle pen, and thus obtained the name Giribbaja. With reference to the object of the act of envying, it is said, "or in the sense of application."

Sāriputtamoggallānapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the account of Sāriputta and Moggallāna's going forth is finished.

Upajjhāyavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Account of the Duties toward the Preceptor.

64. Vajjāvajjaṃ upanijjhāyatīti upajjhāyo, natthi upajjhāyo etesanti anupajjhāyakā. Tenāha “vajjāvajjaṃ upanijjhāyakena garunā virahitā”ti. Tattha vajjāvajjanti khuddakaṃ [V 3.0211] mahantañca vajjaṃ. Vuddhiattho hi ayamakāro “phalāphala”ntiādīsu viya. Uttiṭṭhapattanti ettha ucchiṭṭha-saddasamānattho uttiṭṭha-saddo. Tenevāha “tasmiñhi manussā ucchiṭṭhasaññino, tasmā uttiṭṭhapattanti vutta”nti. Piṇḍāya caraṇakapattanti iminā pana pattassa sarūpadassanamukhena ucchiṭṭhakappanāya kāraṇaṃ vibhāvitaṃ. Tasminti tasmiṃ piṇḍāya caraṇakapatte.

64. One who reflects upon what is a fault and what is not a fault is a preceptor; those for whom there is no preceptor are 'without a preceptor.' Therefore it is said: "devoid of a teacher who reflects on what is a fault and what is not a fault." Herein, "what is a fault and what is not a fault" refers to minor and major faults. This 'a' is indeed for the purpose of augmentation, as in 'fruits and non-fruits' and so forth. The word 'uttiṭṭha' here, in 'uttiṭṭhapattanti', has a meaning similar to the word 'ucchiṭṭha'. Therefore it is said: "For people perceive it as 'ucchiṭṭha' (leftovers), hence it is called 'uttiṭṭhapattanti'." However, by means of 'the bowl used for alms-gathering', the reason for the concept of 'ucchiṭṭha' is clarified through the presentation of the bowl's nature. 'Tasminti' means 'in that bowl used for alms-gathering'.

65. Sagāravā sappatissāti ettha garubhāvo gāravaṃ, pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garukaraṇīyatā. Saha gāravenāti sagāravā. Garunā kismiñci vutte gāravavasena patissavanaṃ patisso, patissavabhūtaṃ taṃsabhāgañca yaṃkiñci gāravanti attho. Saha patissenāti sappatissā, ovādaṃ sampaṭicchantāti attho[M 3.0232]. Patissīyatīti vā patisso, garukātabbo. Tena saha patissenāti sappatissā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana byañjanavicāraṃ akatvā atthamattameva dassetuṃ “garukabhāvañceva jeṭṭhakabhāvañca upaṭṭhapetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Sāhūti sādhu. Lahūti agaru, mama tuyhaṃ upajjhāyabhāve bhāriyaṃ nāma natthīti attho. Opāyikanti upāyapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ te upajjhāyaggahaṇaṃ iminā upāyena tvaṃ me ito paṭṭhāya bhāro jātosīti vuttaṃ hoti. Patirūpanti anurūpaṃ tava upajjhāyaggahaṇanti attho. Pāsādikenāti pasādāvahena kāyavacīpayogena. Sampādehīti tividhasikkhaṃ nipphādehīti attho. Kāyena vāti hatthamuddādiṃ dassento kāyena vā viññāpeti. Gahito tayā…pe… viññāpetīti “sāhū”tiādīsu ekaṃ vadantoyeva imamatthaṃ viññāpetīti vuccati. Tenevāha “idameva hī”tiādi. Sādhūti sampaṭicchanaṃ sandhāyāti upajjhāyena “sāhū”ti vutte saddhivihārikassa “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchanavacanaṃ sandhāya. Kasmā nappamāṇanti āha “āyācanadānamattena hī”tiādi, saddhivihārikassa “upajjhāyo me, bhante, hohī”ti āyācanamattena, upajjhāyassa ca “sāhū”tiādinā dānavacanamattenāti attho. Na ettha sampaṭicchanaṃ aṅganti saddhivihārikassa sampaṭicchanavacanaṃ ettha upajjhāyaggahaṇe aṅgaṃ na hoti.

65. Regarding 'respectful and compliant,' herein, 'gāravaṃ' is the state of being venerable, the quality of being revered like a stone parasol. 'Sagāravā' means 'with respect.' When something is said by the teacher, 'patisso' is the act of responding out of respect; the meaning is reverence for anything that is of the nature of compliance and partakes of that. 'Sappatissā' means 'with compliance,' meaning accepting advice. Or, 'patisso' means 'that which is to be revered' (from 'patissīyati'), that which should be treated with reverence. Therefore, 'sappatissā' means 'with him who is to be revered.' However, in the Commentary, without analyzing the phrasing, it is stated, merely to show the meaning: 'establishing both the state of being venerable and the state of being senior.' 'Sāhu' means 'good.' 'Lahu' means 'not heavy,' meaning there is no heavy burden for me in being your preceptor. 'Opāyikaṃ' means 'connected with a means.' It means your taking of a preceptor is suitable. By this means it is said, 'From now on, you have become my responsibility.' 'Patirūpaṃ' means 'appropriate,' meaning your taking of a preceptor is fitting. By 'pāsādikena' is meant 'by means of bodily and verbal application that inspires confidence.' 'Sampādehi' means 'accomplish,' meaning 'bring to completion the threefold training.' By 'kāyena vā' (or with the body), it means he makes it known with the body, showing gestures such as a hand-seal. The phrase 'Gahito tayā…pe… viññāpetīti' means that by merely saying one of the words like 'sāhu,' this meaning is conveyed. Therefore it is said: 'This alone is…' and so forth. 'Sādhūti sampaṭicchanaṃ sandhāya' means 'referring to the acceptance.' It refers to the co-resident's word of acceptance, 'sādhu,' when the preceptor has said 'sāhu.' 'Why is it not a requirement?' it is said: 'Because it is merely by the act of requesting and granting,' and so forth. This means that it is merely by the co-resident's request, 'Venerable sir, be my preceptor,' and by the preceptor's word of granting, such as 'sāhu.' Here, the co-resident's word of acceptance is not a factor in the taking of a preceptor.

66. Sammāvattanāti sammāpavatti. Assāti saddhivihārikassa. Tādisameva mukhadhovanodakaṃ dātabbanti utumhi sarīrasabhāve ca ekākāre tādisameva dātabbaṃ. Dve cīvarānīti pārupanaṃ saṅghāṭiñca sandhāya vadati. Yadi evaṃ “saṅghāṭiyo”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “sabbañhi cīvaraṃ saṅghaṭitattā saṅghāṭīti vuccatī”ti. Padavītihārehīti ettha padaṃ vītiharati etthāti padavītihāro, padavītiharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ dūtavilambitaṃ akatvā samagamane dvinnaṃ padānaṃ antare muṭṭhiratanamattaṃ. Padānaṃ vā vītiharaṇaṃ abhimukhaṃ haritvā nikkhepo padavītihāroti [V 3.0212] evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ito paṭṭhāyāti “na upajjhāyassa bhaṇamānassā”ti ettha vutta na-kārato paṭṭhāya. Sabbattha dukkaṭāpatti veditabbāti “īdisesu gilānopi na muccatī”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Aññampi hi yathāvuttaṃ upajjhāyavattaṃ anādariyena akarontassa agilānassa vattabhede sabbattha dukkaṭameva. Teneva vakkhati “agilānena hi saddhivihārikena saṭṭhivassenapi sabbaṃ upajjhāyavattaṃ [M 3.0233] kātabbaṃ, anādarena akarontassa vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ. Na-kārapaṭisaṃyuttesu pana padesu gilānassapi paṭikkhittakiriyaṃ karontassa dukkaṭamevā”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 64). Āpattiyā āsannavācanti āpattijanakameva vacanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yāya hi vācāya āpattiṃ āpajjati, sā vācā tassā āpattiyā āsannāti vuccati.

66. 'Sammāvattanā' means 'proper conduct.' 'Assa' refers to the co-resident. 'Water for washing the face should be given in the same way' means that according to the season and the nature of the body, it should be given in a uniform manner. By 'two robes' is meant the upper robe and the outer robe (saṅghāṭi). If so, why is it said 'saṅghāṭiyo'? It is said: 'Because all robes are stitched together, every robe is called "saṅghāṭi".' Here, 'padavītihārehi' means 'where a step is taken.' The place of taking steps is the distance of about a fist's length between two steps when walking together without causing delay to a messenger. Alternatively, 'padavītihāro' means the lifting and placing of the feet forward. This is how the meaning should be understood here. 'From this point onward' means starting from the negation 'na' stated in 'na upajjhāyassa bhaṇamānassa.' 'It should be understood that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred everywhere' is stated to show that 'even the sick are not exempt in such cases.' Indeed, for any other duty toward the preceptor as stated, if a healthy co-resident does not perform it out of disrespect, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred in every instance of breaching the duty. Therefore it will be said: 'Indeed, a healthy co-resident, even one of sixty years, must perform all duties toward the preceptor; not doing so out of disrespect incurs a dukkaṭa offense for breaching the duty. However, in passages connected with the negation "na", even a sick person who performs the prohibited action incurs a dukkaṭa offense' (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 64). 'Āpattiyā āsannavāca' refers to speech that generates an offense. For the speech by which one incurs an offense is called 'speech proximate to that offense'.

Cīvarena pattaṃ veṭhetvāti ettha “uttarāsaṅgassa ekena kaṇṇena veṭhetvā”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Gāmeti gāmapariyāpanne tādise kismiñci padese. Antaraghareti antogehe. Paṭikkamaneti āsanasālāyaṃ. Tikkhattuṃ pānīyena pucchitabboti sambandho, ādimhi majjhe anteti evaṃ tikkhattuṃ pucchitabboti attho. Upakaṭṭhoti āsanno. Dhotavālikāyāti nirajāya parisuddhavālikāya. Sace pahotīti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “na kenaci gelaññena abhibhūto hotī”ti. Pariveṇaṃ gantvāti upajjhāyassa pariveṇaṃ gantvā.

'Wrapping the bowl with the robe' here refers to 'wrapping with one corner of the upper robe,' as stated in the sections on knots. By 'gāme' is meant in some such place within the village boundary. By 'antaraghare' is meant 'in the inner house.' By 'paṭikkamane' is meant 'in the assembly hall.' The phrase 'should be asked for water three times' is connected, meaning one should ask three times: at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. 'Upakaṭṭho' means 'nearby.' By 'dhotavālikāya' is meant 'with washed sand,' that is, with pure sand free from dust. 'Sace pahoti' elucidates the meaning already stated, namely, 'he is not overcome by any sickness.' By 'pariveṇaṃ gantvā' is meant 'going to the preceptor's residence'.

Upajjhāyavattakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Account of the Duties toward the Preceptor is concluded.

67. Saddhivihārikavattakathā uttānatthāyeva.

67. The Account of the Duties of the Co-resident is clear in meaning.

Nasammāvattanādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Account of Improper Conduct and So Forth

68. Nasammāvattanādikathāyaṃ gehassitapemanti “pitā me aya”nti evaṃ uppannapemaṃ. Upajjhāyamhi pitucittupaṭṭhānameva hi idha gehassitapemaṃ nāma. Na hi idaṃ akusalapakkhiyaṃ gehassitapemaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ paṭividdhasaccānaṃ pahīnānugedhānaṃ tadasambhavato, na ca bhagavā bhikkhū saṃkilese niyojeti, gehassitapemasadisattā pana pemamukhena mettāsineho idha vuttoti veditabbaṃ. “Tesu eko vattasampanno bhikkhu…pe… tesaṃ anāpattī”ti vacanato sace eko vattasampanno bhikkhu “bhante, tumhe appossukkā hotha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ saddhivihārikaṃ antevāsikaṃ vā gilānaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmi, ovaditabbaṃ ovadissāmi, iti karaṇīyesu ussukkaṃ āpajjissāmī”ti vadati, te eva vā saddhivihārikādayo “bhante, tumhe kevalaṃ appossukkā [V 3.0213] hothā”ti vadanti, vattaṃ vā na sādiyanti[M 3.0234], tato paṭṭhāya ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ anāpattīti vadanti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

68. In the discussion on improper conduct and so forth, 'affection rooted in the household' refers to the affection that arises by thinking, 'This is my father.' Indeed, here, establishing the thought of a father towards one's preceptor is what is called 'household-rooted affection.' This is not said with reference to unwholesome household-rooted affection, for it is impossible for those who have penetrated the truths and abandoned longing to have such. Nor does the Blessed One engage monks in defilements. Rather, it should be understood that here, loving-kindness and affection are spoken of by way of affection, because of their similarity to household-rooted affection. From the statement, 'Among them, one monk accomplished in duty... there is no offense for them,' it is said that if one monk accomplished in duty says, 'Venerable sir, you should be free from concern; I will attend to your sick student or novice, I will advise as should be advised, and I will undertake the necessary duties,' or if those students themselves say, 'Venerable sir, you should be entirely free from concern,' or if they do not consent to the duty, then from that point onwards, there is no offense for the teachers and preceptors. The rest here is self-evident.

Nasammāvattanādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Improper Conduct and So Forth is concluded.

Rādhabrāhmaṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of Rādha the Brahmin

69. Rādhabrāhmaṇavatthumhi kiso ahosīti khādituṃ vā bhuñjituṃ vā asakkonto tanuko ahosi appamaṃsalohito. Uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātoti sañjātuppaṇḍuppaṇḍukabhāvo paṇḍupalāsappaṭibhāgo. Dhamanisanthatagattoti pariyādinnamaṃsalohitattā sirājāleneva santharitagatto. Adhikāranti adhikiriyaṃ, sakkāranti vuttaṃ hoti. Kataṃ jānantīti kataññuno, kataṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā jānantīti katavedino. Kiṃ pana thero bhagavatā bārāṇasiyaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi anuññātaṃ pabbajjaṃ upasampadañca na jānātīti? No na jānāti. Yadi evaṃ “kathāhaṃ, bhante, taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pabbājemi upasampādemī”ti kasmā āhāti imaṃ anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “kiñcāpi āyasmā sāriputto”tiādi. Parimaṇḍalehīti paripuṇṇehi. Aññathā vā vattabbaṃ aññathā vadatīti “bhante”ti vattabbaṃ “bandhe”ti vadati.

69. In the story of Rādha the brahmin, 'he was thin' means that being unable to chew or eat, he was emaciated, with little flesh and blood. 'Having become pale-yellow' means having become pale-yellow in complexion, resembling a withered leaf. 'His body was covered with veins' means his body was covered with a network of veins because his flesh and blood were exhausted. 'A service rendered' means a good deed done; it is said to be 'honor.' 'Grateful' means knowing what has been done; 'one who shows gratitude' means knowing what has been done by making it evident. But did the Elder not know that the going forth and full ordination had been authorized by the Blessed One in Bārāṇasī by means of the three refuges? It is not that he did not know. If so, why did he say, 'How, venerable sir, shall I give that brahmin the going forth and full ordination?' With reference to this inquiry, it is said, 'Although the Venerable Sāriputta...' and so forth. 'Well-rounded' means complete. 'He speaks otherwise than should be spoken' means that when 'bhante' (venerable sir) should be said, he says 'bandhe'.

71-73. Samanantarāti anantaraṃ. Paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ karotīti sikkhāpadavītikkamaṃ karoti. Attabhāvapariharaṇatthaṃ nissīyantīti nissayā, piṇḍiyālopabhojanādikā cattāro paccayā. Tattha piṇḍiyālopabhojananti jaṅghapiṇḍiyabalena caritvā ālopamattaṃ laddhabhojanaṃ. Atirekalābhoti “piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāyā”ti evaṃ vuttabhikkhāhāralābhato adhikalābho saṅghabhattādi. Tattha sakalassa saṅghassa dātabbabhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ. Katipaye bhikkhū uddisitvā dātabbabhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ. Nimantetvā dātabbabhattaṃ nimantanaṃ. Salākaṃ gāhāpetvā dātabbabhattaṃ salākabhattaṃ. Ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekadivasaṃ dātabbabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ. Uposathe dātabbabhattaṃ uposathikaṃ. Pāṭipadadivase dātabbabhattaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ. Vitthārakathā nesaṃ senāsanakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ āvi bhavissati.

71-73. 'Immediately after' means subsequently. 'He transgresses a regulation' means he transgresses a training rule. 'Supports' are so called because they are relied upon for the maintenance of one's person; they are the four requisites, beginning with almsfood. Here, 'almsfood' means food obtained by wandering on the strength of one's shanks, amounting to a mere lump. 'Extra gain' means a gain over and above the gain of almsfood spoken of as 'relying on almsfood,' such as a meal for the Sangha and so forth. Among these, a 'Sangha meal' is a meal to be given to the entire Sangha. A 'designated meal' is a meal to be given by designating a few monks. An 'invitation' is a meal to be given after an invitation. A 'ticket meal' is a meal to be given by having them draw tickets. A 'fortnightly meal' is a meal to be given on one day of a fortnight. An 'Uposatha meal' is a meal to be given on the Uposatha day. A 'first-day meal' is a meal to be given on the first day of the fortnight. The detailed account of these will become evident in the commentary on the chapter on lodgings.

Vihāroti [M 3.0235] pākāraparicchinno sakalo āvāso. Aḍḍhayogoti

'Monastery' means the entire residence enclosed by a wall. 'A gabled building' means...

Dīghapāsādo. Garuḷasaṇṭhānapāsādotipi vadanti. Pāsādoti caturassapāsādo. Hammiyanti muṇḍacchadanapāsādo. Apare pana bhaṇanti “vihāro nāma dīghamukhapāsādo, aḍḍhayogo ekapassacchadanakasenāsanaṃ[V 3.0214], tassa kira ekapasse bhitti uccatarā hoti, itarapasse nīcā, tena taṃ ekapassacchadanakaṃ hoti, pāsādo āyatacaturassapāsādo, hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanaṃ candikaṅgaṇayutta”nti. Guhāti pabbataguhā. Pūtimuttanti yaṃ kiñci muttaṃ. Yathā suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kāyo “pūtikāyo”ti vuccati, evaṃ abhinavampi muttaṃ pūtimuttameva. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

a long mansion. Some also call it a mansion shaped like a Garuḍa. 'Mansion' means a four-sided mansion. 'A flat-roofed house' means a mansion with a flat roof. But others say: 'A monastery is a long-fronted mansion; a gabled building is a lodging with a one-sided roof; it is said that one side of its wall is higher and the other side lower, and thus it has a one-sided roof. A mansion is an elongated four-sided mansion; a flat-roofed house is a flat-roofed building with a moonlit terrace.' 'Cave' means a mountain cave. 'Foul urine' means any kind of urine. Just as even a golden-colored body is called a 'foul body,' so too even fresh urine is 'foul urine.' The rest here is self-evident in meaning.

Rādhabrāhmaṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of Rādha the Brahmin is concluded.

Ācariyavattakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Teacher's Duties

75. Upasenavatthumhi āciṇṇanti caritaṃ vattaṃ anudhammatā. Kacci bhikkhu khamanīyanti bhikkhu kacci tuyhaṃ idaṃ catucakkaṃ navadvāraṃ sarīrayantaṃ khamanīyaṃ sakkā khamituṃ sahituṃ pariharituṃ, na kiñci dukkhaṃ uppādetīti. Kacci yāpanīyanti kacci sabbakiccesu yāpetuṃ sakkā, na kiñci antarāyaṃ dassetīti. Jānantāpi tathāgatātievamādi yaṃ parato “kati vassosi tvaṃ bhikkhū”tiādinā pucchi, tassa parihāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – tathāgatā nāma jānantāpi sace tādisaṃ pucchākāraṇaṃ hoti, pucchanti. Sace pana tādisaṃ pucchākāraṇaṃ natthi, jānantāpi na pucchanti. Yasmā pana buddhānaṃ ajānanaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā “ajānantāpī”ti na vuttaṃ. Kālaṃ viditvā pucchantīti sace tassā pucchāya so kālo hoti, evaṃ taṃ kālaṃ viditvā pucchanti. Sace na hoti, evampi kālaṃ viditvāva na pucchanti. Evaṃ pucchantāpi ca atthasaṃhitaṃ tathāgatā pucchanti, yaṃ atthanissitaṃ kāraṇanissitaṃ, tadeva pucchanti, no anatthasaṃhitaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā anatthasaṃhite setughāto tathāgatānaṃ. Setu vuccati maggo, maggeneva tādisassa vacanassa ghāto samucchedoti vuttaṃ hoti.

75. In the story of Upasena, 'practiced' means conduct, duty, and conformity to the Dhamma. 'I hope the bhikkhu is well,' means, 'Bhikkhu, I hope this four-wheeled, nine-doored body-frame of yours is tolerable, capable of being endured, borne, and maintained without causing any suffering.' 'I hope it is sustainable,' means, 'I hope you can manage all duties without presenting any hindrance.' Even the Tathāgatas, though knowing, ask in this way—such as when they inquire from another, 'How many years have you been a bhikkhu?'—this was said to illustrate the point. Here is the condensed meaning: the Tathāgatas, though knowing, ask if there is a cause for such a question. But if there is no such cause, though knowing, they do not ask. Since there is no such thing as not knowing for the Buddhas, it is therefore not said 'though not knowing.' They ask knowing the right time—if it is the right time for that question, they ask knowing that time. If it is not, even then, knowing the time, they do not ask. And when they ask, the Tathāgatas ask what is connected with the goal, which is grounded in purpose and reason—they ask only what is associated with benefit, not what is associated with non-benefit. Why? Because for the Tathāgatas, what is not connected with the goal is a destruction of the bridge. The bridge is called the path; by means of the path itself, it is said, such speech is destroyed, cut off.

Idāni atthasaṃhitanti ettha yaṃ atthanissitaṃ vacanaṃ tathāgatā pucchanti, taṃ dassento “dvīhi ākārehī”tiādimāha. Tattha ākārehīti kāraṇehi[M 3.0236]. Dhammaṃ vā desessāmāti aṭṭhuppattiyuttaṃ suttaṃ vā pubbacaritakāraṇayuttaṃ jātakaṃ vā kathayissāma. Sāvakānaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmāti sāvakānaṃ vā tāya pucchāya vītikkamaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā garukaṃ vā lahukaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāma āṇaṃ ṭhapessāma. Atilahunti atisīghaṃ.

Now, regarding 'connected with the goal,' to show what speech based on the goal the Tathāgatas ask about, it is said, 'for two reasons,' and so on. Here, 'reasons' means 'causes.' 'We will teach the Dhamma' means: we will relate a sutta connected with the occasion of its arising or a Jātaka connected with the reason of previous conduct. 'Or we will lay down a training rule for the disciples' means: by means of that question, having made a transgression by the disciples evident, we will lay down a heavy or light training rule—we will establish a command. 'Too quickly' means too hastily.

76. Aññatitthiyavatthumhi aññatitthiyapubboti pubbe aññatitthiyo bhūtoti aññatitthiyapubbo. Ettha (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.62) ca titthaṃ jānitabbaṃ, titthakaro jānitabbo[V 3.0215], titthiyā jānitabbā, titthiyasāvakā jānitabbā. Tattha titthaṃ nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo. Ettha hi sattā taranti uppilavanti ummujjanimujjaṃ karonti, tasmā “tittha”nti vuccanti. Tāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ uppādetā titthakaro nāma pūraṇakassapādiko. Tassa laddhiṃ gahetvā pabbajitā titthiyā nāma. Te hi titthe jātāti titthiyā, yathāvuttaṃ vā diṭṭhigatasaṅkhātaṃ titthaṃ etesaṃ atthīti titthikā, titthikā eva titthiyā. Tesaṃ paccayadāyakā titthiyasāvakāti veditabbā. Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamānoti sahadhammikena vuccamāno, karaṇatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Pañcahi sahadhammikehi sikkhitabbattā, tesaṃ vā santakattā “sahadhammika”nti laddhanāmena buddhapaññattena sikkhāpadena vuccamānoti attho. Pasūroti tassa nāmaṃ. Paribbājakoti gihibandhanaṃ pahāya pabbajjupagato.

76. In the case of a matter concerning another sect, one who was formerly of another sect is called 'aññatitthiyapubbo,' meaning one who previously was a follower of another sect. Here, 'tittha' should be understood, the 'titthakaro' should be understood, the 'titthiyā' should be understood, and the 'titthiyasāvakā' should be understood. In this context, 'tittha' means the sixty-two views. For here, beings cross over, float, and plunge up and down; thus they are called 'tittha.' The originator of these views is called 'titthakaro,' such as Pūraṇakassapa and others. Those who have gone forth adopting his doctrine are called 'titthiyā.' They are called 'titthiyā' because they are born in the tittha, or because they possess the tittha, as described, which is designated as a collection of views. 'Titthikā' are simply 'titthiyā.' Their supporters are to be understood as 'titthiyasāvakā.' 'Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno' means being spoken to by a fellow practitioner; the locative case is used here in the sense of the instrumental. Because one should train by means of the five sahadhammikas, or because they belong to them, the training rule established by the Buddha is given the name 'sahadhammika,' and it means being spoken to by this rule. 'Pasūro' is his name. 'Paribbājako' means one who has gone forth, having abandoned the bonds of household life.

Taṃyeva titthāyatananti ettha dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhisaṅkhātaṃ titthameva āyatananti titthāyatanaṃ, titthaṃ vā etesaṃ atthīti titthino, titthiyā, tesaṃ āyatanantipi titthāyatanaṃ. Āyatananti ca “assānaṃ kambojo āyatanaṃ, gunnaṃ dakkhiṇapatho āyatana”nti ettha sañjātiṭṭhānaṃ āyatanaṃ nāma.

'That very sectarian ground': Here, the sect designated as the sixty-two views is itself the ground, thus 'titthāyatana' (sectarian ground). Or, because these people possess a sect, they are 'titthino' or 'titthiyā' (sectarians), and their ground is also 'titthāyatana'. And 'āyatana' here means a place of origin, as in 'Kamboja is the place of origin for horses, the southern region is the place of origin for cattle.'

“Manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā;

Chāyaṃ chāyatthino yanti, phalatthaṃ phalabhojino”ti. (a. ni. 5.38) –

'In a delightful abode, birds frequent it; those seeking shade go to the shade, and fruit-eaters go for fruit.'

Ettha samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, vimuttāyatanānī”ti (a. ni. 5.26) ettha kāraṇaṃ, taṃ idha sabbampi labbhati. Sabbepi hi diṭṭhigatikā sañjāyamānā imāsuyeva dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīsu sañjāyanti, samosaramānāpi etāsuyeva samosaranti sannipatanti, diṭṭhigatikabhāve ca nesaṃ imāyeva dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo [M 3.0237] kāraṇaṃ, tasmā yathāvuttaṃ titthameva sañjātiādinā atthena āyatananti titthāyatanaṃ, tenevatthena titthīnaṃ āyatanantipi titthāyatanaṃ.

Here, it means a place of convergence. In the phrase, 'Monks, there are these five bases of liberation,' (A. Ni. 5.26) it means cause. All of these meanings are found here. Indeed, all those who hold to views, when they arise, arise within these very sixty-two views; when converging, they also converge and assemble within these. And in their state as holders of views, these very sixty-two views are the cause. Therefore, as stated, the sect itself is a 'ground' in the sense of origin and so forth, thus 'sectarian ground'; and by that same meaning, it is also the 'ground' of the sectarians, thus 'sectarian ground'.

Āyasmato nissāya vacchāmīti ettha āyasmatoti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, āyasmantaṃ nissāya vasissāmīti attho. Byatto…pe… vuttalakkhaṇoyevāti parisupaṭṭhāpakabahussutaṃ sandhāya vadati. Pañcahupāli aṅgehītiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati.

'Relying on the Venerable One, I shall live'—here, 'āyasmato' is the genitive case used in the sense of the locative, meaning 'I shall live relying on the Venerable One.' 'Skilled… and so on… having the very characteristics stated'—this is said in reference to one who is learned and an attendant of the assembly. In 'With five factors, Upāli,' and so on, whatever is to be said will become clear later.

Ācariyavattakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Duties toward a Teacher is concluded.

Paṇāmanākhamāpanākathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discussion on Salutation and Not Asking for Forgiveness.

80. Yaṃ [V 3.0216] pubbe lakkhaṇaṃ vuttanti sambandho, “teneva lakkhaṇena nissayantevāsikassa āpatti veditabbā”ti potthakesu pāṭho dissati, “na teneva lakkhaṇena nissayantevāsikassa āpatti veditabbā”ti evaṃ panettha pāṭho veditabbo. Saddhivihārikassa vuttalakkhaṇena nissayantevāsikassa āpatti na veditabbāti evaṃ panettha atthopi veditabbo. Aññathā “nissayantevāsikena hi yāva ācariyaṃ nissāya vasati, tāva sabbaṃ ācariyavattaṃ kātabba”nti idaṃ virujjheyya. Idañhi vacanaṃ nissayantevāsikassa amuttanissayasseva vattaṃ akarontassa āpattīti dīpeti. Tasmā saddhivihārikassa yathāvuttavattaṃ akarontassa nissayamuttakassa amuttakassapi āpatti, nissayantevāsikassa pana amuttanissayasseva āpattīti gahetabbaṃ. Teneva visuddhimaggepi (visuddhi. 1.41) ñātipalibodhakathāyaṃ –

80. The connection is with the characteristic previously stated. The reading, 'By that very characteristic, the offense of a student under dependence should be understood,' is found in the manuscripts. However, here the reading should be understood as: 'Not by that very characteristic should the offense of a student under dependence be understood.' Moreover, the meaning here should be understood as: The offense of a student under dependence should not be understood by the characteristic stated for a resident pupil. Otherwise, the statement, 'For as long as a student under dependence lives relying on the teacher, all the duties toward the teacher must be performed,' would be contradicted. For this statement clarifies that an offense is incurred by a student under dependence who does not perform the duties only while he is not released from dependence. Therefore, it should be understood that for a resident pupil who does not perform the duties as stated, there is an offense whether released from dependence or not, but for a student under dependence, an offense is incurred only while he is not released from dependence. For this reason, in the Visuddhimagga as well (Vism. 1.41), in the discussion on the obstacle of relatives, it is said:

“Ñātīti vihāre ācariyupajjhāyasaddhivihārikaantevāsikasamānupajjhāyakasamānācariyakā, ghare mātā pitā bhaginī bhātāti evamādikā. Te gilānā imassa palibodhā honti, tasmā so palibodho upaṭṭhahitvā tesaṃ pākatikakaraṇena upacchinditabbo. Tattha upajjhāyo tāva gilāno sace lahuṃ na vuṭṭhāti, yāvajīvaṃ paṭijaggitabbo. Tathā [M 3.0238] pabbajjācariyo upasampadācariyo saddhivihāriko upasampāditapabbājitaantevāsikasamānupajjhāyakā ca. Nissayācariya uddesācariya nissayantevāsika uddesantevāsikasamānācariyakā pana yāva nissayauddesā anupacchinnā, tāva paṭijaggitabbā”ti –

'Relatives'—in the monastery, they are the teacher, preceptor, resident pupil, student, fellow preceptee, and fellow student of the same teacher; at home, they are mother, father, sister, brother, and so on. If they are sick, they become an impediment for this monk. Therefore, that impediment should be severed by attending to them and restoring them to their normal state. Therein, if the preceptor is sick and does not recover quickly, he should be cared for as long as he lives. Likewise, the teacher who gave the going forth, the teacher who gave the higher ordination, the resident pupil, the student to whom one has given the higher ordination or the going forth, and fellow preceptees. But the teacher of dependence, the teacher of instruction, the student under dependence, the student under instruction, and fellow students of the same teacher should be cared for only as long as the dependence or instruction has not been terminated.'

Vibhāgena vuttaṃ. Ayañca vibhāgo “teneva lakkhaṇena nissayantevāsikassa āpatti veditabbā”ti evaṃ pāṭhe sati na yujjeyya. Ayañhi pāṭho saddhivihārikassa viya nissayantevāsikassapi yathāvuttavattaṃ akarontassa nissayamuttakassa amuttakassapi āpattīti imamatthaṃ dīpeti, tasmā vuttanayenevettha pāṭho gahetabbo.

It is stated with a distinction. And this distinction would not be fitting if the reading were: 'By that very characteristic, the offense of a student under dependence should be understood.' For this reading indicates that, just as for a resident pupil, so too for a student under dependence who does not perform the stated duties, there is an offense whether released from dependence or not. Therefore, the reading here should be taken according to the method stated.

Pabbajjaupasampadadhammantevāsikehi pana…pe… tāva vattaṃ kātabbanti pabbajjācariyaupasampadācariyadhammācariyānaṃ

But by the students of the going forth, higher ordination, and the Dhamma… and so on… the duties should be performed for as long as… towards the teacher of the going forth, the teacher of the higher ordination, and the teacher of the Dhamma.

Etehi yathāvuttavattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tattha yena sikkhāpadāni dinnāni, ayaṃ [V 3.0217] pabbajjācariyo. Yena upasampadakammavācā vuttā, ayaṃ upasampadācariyo. Yo uddesaṃ paripucchaṃ vā deti, ayaṃ dhammācariyoti veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

By these students, the aforementioned duties should be performed. Herein, the one by whom the training rules are given is the teacher of the going forth. The one by whom the formal act of higher ordination is recited is the teacher of the higher ordination. The one who gives instruction or questioning is to be understood as the teacher of the Dhamma. The rest here is self-evident.

Paṇāmanākhamāpanākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Salutation and Not Asking for Forgiveness is concluded.

Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Relinquishment of Dependence.

83. Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāyaṃ disaṃ gatoti puna āgantukāmo anāgantukāmo vā hutvā vāsatthāya kañci disaṃ gato. Bhikkhuno sabhāgatanti pesalabhāvaṃ. Oloketvāti upaparikkhitvā. Vibbhante…pe… tattha gantabbanti ettha sace kenaci karaṇīyena tadaheva gantuṃ asakkonto katipāhena gamissāmīti gamane saussāho hoti, rakkhatīti vadanti. Mā idha paṭikkamīti mā idha pavisi. Tatreva vasitabbanti tattheva nissayaṃ gahetvā vasitabbaṃ. Taṃyeva vihāraṃ…pe… vasituṃ vaṭṭatīti ettha upajjhāyena pariccattattā upajjhāyasamodhānaparihāro natthi, tasmā upajjhāyena samodhānagatassapi ācariyassa santike gahitanissayo na paṭippassambhati.

83. In the Discussion on the Relinquishment of Dependence, 'gone to a region' means having gone to some region for the sake of dwelling, whether with the intention to return or not. 'A suitable monk' means one of virtuous character. 'Having looked' means having investigated. In 'When they have left… and so on… one should go there,' if, due to some duty, one is unable to go on that very day but is zealous to go, thinking, 'I will go in a few days,' they say 'he is protecting it.' 'Do not return here' means do not enter here. 'One should dwell right there' means one should take dependence there and dwell. In 'That very monastery… and so on… it is proper to dwell,' because he has been abandoned by the preceptor, there is no avoidance of meeting with the preceptor. Therefore, even for one who has met with the preceptor, the dependence taken in the presence of a teacher is not relinquished.

Ācariyamhā [M 3.0239] nissayapaṭippassaddhīsu ācariyo pakkanto vā hotīti ettha “pakkantoti disaṃ gato”tiādinā upajjhāyassa pakkamane yo vinicchayo vutto, so tattha vuttanayeneva idhāpi sakkā viññātunti taṃ avatvā “koci ācariyo āpucchitvā pakkamatī”tiādinā aññoyeva nayo āraddho, ayañca nayo upajjhāyapakkamanepi veditabboyeva. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu ekattha vuttalakkhaṇaṃ aññatthāpi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sace dve leḍḍupāte atikkamitvā nivattati, paṭippassaddho hotīti ettha ettāvatā disāpakkanto nāma hotīti antevāsike anikkhittadhurepi nissayo paṭippassambhati. Ācariyupajjhāyā dve leḍḍupāte atikkamma aññasmiṃ vihāre vasantīti bahiupacārasīmāyaṃ antevāsikasaddhivihārikānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānato dve leḍḍupāte atikkamma aññasmiṃ senāsane vasanti, antoupacārasīmāyaṃ pana dve leḍḍupāte atikkamitvāpi vasato nissayo na paṭippassambhati. “Sacepi ācariyo muñcitukāmova hutvā nissayapaṇāmanāya paṇāmetī”tiādi sabbaṃ upajjhāyassa āṇattiyampi veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

In the sections on the relinquishment of dependence from a teacher, regarding the phrase ‘the teacher has departed or…,’ the legal decision given concerning the preceptor’s departure—‘departed means gone to a region,’ and so on—can be understood here in the same way as stated there. Without repeating that, another method is introduced: ‘some teacher departs after asking leave,’ and so on. This method should also be understood in the case of the preceptor’s departure. For in such cases, a characteristic stated in one place should be seen in another as well. Regarding the phrase ‘If, having gone beyond two clod-throws, he turns back, it is relinquished’—here, by this much he is called ‘departed to a region,’ so even if the pupil has not laid down his duties, the dependence is relinquished. Regarding the phrase ‘The teachers and preceptors dwell in another monastery beyond two clod-throws’—this means that outside the boundary of proximity, they dwell in another lodging beyond two clod-throws from the dwelling place of the pupils and co-residents. But within the boundary of proximity, even if one dwells beyond two clod-throws, the dependence is not relinquished. The entire section beginning with ‘Even if the teacher, wishing to release him, dismisses him by way of dismissing from dependence,’ should be understood as applying also to the dismissal by a preceptor. The rest here is clear.

Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section concerning the relinquishment of dependence is concluded.

Upasampādetabbapañcakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section of the Five Who Should Not Be Ordained.

84. Pañcahi[V 3.0218], bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgatenātiādīsu na sāmaṇero upaṭṭhāpetabboti upajjhāyena hutvā sāmaṇero na gahetabbo. Ayamattho aṅguttaranikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.251-253) vuttoyeva.

84. In the passages beginning with ‘Monks, one endowed with five factors,’ and so on, the meaning is that a novice should not be taken on for attendance, and that having become a preceptor, a novice should not be accepted. This meaning is indeed stated in the Commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya (A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.5.251-253).

“Attānameva paṭhamaṃ, patirūpe nivesaye;

Athaññamanusāseyya, na kilisseyya paṇḍito”ti. (dha. pa. 158) –

‘First, one should establish oneself in what is proper; then one may instruct others. The wise one will not be defiled.’ (Dhp. 158)

Imassa anurūpavasena paṭhamaṃ tāva attasampattiyaṃ niyojetuṃ “na asekkhena sīlakkhandhenā”tiādi vuttaṃ, na āpattiaṅgavasena. Tattha asekkhena sīlakkhandhenāti asekkhassa sīlakkhandho asekkho sīlakkhandho nāma. Asekkhassa ayanti hi asekkho, sīlakkhandho. Evaṃ [M 3.0240] sabbattha. Evañca katvā vimuttiñāṇadassanasaṅkhātassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇassapi asekkhatā upapannā. Asekkhasīlanti ca na maggaphalameva adhippetaṃ, atha kho yaṃkiñci asekkhasantāne pavattasīlaṃ lokiyalokuttaramissakassa sīlassa idhādhippetattā. Samādhikkhandhādīsupi vimuttikkhandhapariyosānesu ayameva nayo. Tasmā yathā sīlasamādhipaññakkhandhā missakā adhippetā, evaṃ vimuttikkhandhopīti tadaṅgavimuttiādayopi veditabbā, na paṭippassaddhivimutti eva. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ pana lokiyameva. Teneva saṃyuttanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.135) vuttaṃ “purimehi catūhi padehi lokiyalokuttarasīlasamādhipaññāvimuttiyo kathitā, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ hoti, taṃ lokiyamevā”ti.

In accordance with this, it is first said ‘not by the virtue aggregate of a non-learner,’ and so on, in order to direct one towards personal attainment, not in terms of the factors of offenses. Herein, ‘by the virtue aggregate of a non-learner’ means the virtue aggregate that belongs to a non-learner; it is called the ‘non-learner virtue aggregate.’ For ‘non-learner’ means ‘of a non-learner’; thus, it is the virtue aggregate of a non-learner. So it is in all cases. And in this way, the quality of being ‘non-learner’ is also established for the reviewing knowledge, which is designated as the knowledge and vision of liberation. And by ‘non-learner virtue’ is not meant only the path and fruition, but rather any virtue occurring in the continuum of a non-learner, because it is mixed virtue, both mundane and supramundane, that is intended here. This same method applies to the concentration aggregate and so on, up to the liberation aggregate. Therefore, just as the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom are intended in a mixed sense, so too is the liberation aggregate to be understood, including liberation by substitution of opposites and so on, not just liberation by tranquillization. The knowledge and vision of liberation, however, is purely mundane. Thus, it is stated in the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya (Saṃ. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.135): ‘By the first four terms, mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are discussed. The knowledge and vision of liberation is the reviewing knowledge, which is purely mundane.’

Assaddhotiādīsu tīsu vatthūsu saddhā etassa natthīti assaddho. Sukkapakkhe saddahatīti saddho, saddhā vā etassa atthītipi saddho. Natthi etassa hirīti ahiriko, akusalasamāpattiyā ajigucchamānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Hirī etassa atthīti hirimā. Na ottappatīti anottappī, akusalasamāpattiyā na bhāyatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tabbiparīto ottappī. Kucchitaṃ sīdatīti kusīto, hīnavīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Āraddhaṃ vīriyaṃ etassāti āraddhavīriyo, sammappadhānayuttassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Muṭṭhā sati etassāti muṭṭhassati, naṭṭhassatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Upaṭṭhitā sati etassāti upaṭṭhitassati, niccaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhappavattasatissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Regarding the items beginning with ‘faithless,’ one who has no faith is ‘faithless’ (assaddho). One who has faith in the wholesome side is ‘faithful’ (saddho), or one who possesses faith is also ‘faithful.’ One who has no moral shame is ‘shameless’ (ahiriko); this is a designation for one who feels no disgust at undertaking unwholesome states. One who possesses moral shame is ‘conscientious’ (hirimā). One who has no moral dread is ‘reckless’ (anottappī); this means one does not fear undertaking unwholesome states. The opposite of that is ‘scrupulous’ (ottappī). One who sinks in a blameworthy way is ‘lazy’ (kusīto); this is a designation for one of weak energy. One whose energy is aroused is ‘energetic’ (āraddhavīriyo); this is a designation for one engaged in the right exertions. One whose mindfulness is muddled is ‘unmindful’ (muṭṭhassati); this means one's mindfulness is lost. One whose mindfulness is established is ‘mindful’ (upaṭṭhitassati); this is a designation for one whose mindfulness is constantly directed towards its object.

Adhisīle [V 3.0219] sīlavipanno ca ajjhācāre ācāravipanno ca āpajjitvā avuṭṭhito. Sassatucchedasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ gaṇhāti gāhayatīti vā antaggāhikā, micchādiṭṭhi. Purimāni dve padānīti “na paṭibalo hoti antevāsiṃ vā saddhivihāriṃ vā gilānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ vā upaṭṭhāpetuṃ vā, anabhirataṃ vūpakāsetuṃ vā vūpakāsāpetuṃ vā”ti imāni dve padāni.

One who is deficient in virtue with regard to higher virtue, and deficient in conduct with regard to behavior, and who, having fallen into an offense, has not been rehabilitated from it. ‘An adherent to extremes’ (antaggāhikā) means one who holds or causes others to hold to the extremes designated as eternalism and annihilationism; this is wrong view. ‘The former two terms’ refers to these two phrases: ‘He is not able to attend to or have attended to a sick pupil or co-resident, nor to appease or have appeased one who is discontent.’

Abhivisiṭṭho uttamo samācāroti abhisamācāro, abhisamācārova sikkhitabbato sikkhāti ābhisamācārikā sikkhā, abhisamācāraṃ vā ārabbha paññattā sikkhā ābhisamācārikā. Maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtāti [M 3.0241] ādibrahmacariyakā, ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannasikkhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Teneva “ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannaṃ ādibrahmacariyakaṃ, khandhakavattapariyāpannaṃ ābhisamācārika”nti visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.11) vuttaṃ. Tasmā sekkhapaṇṇattiyanti ettha sikkhitabbato sabbāpi ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannā paṇṇattīti gahetabbā. Teneva gaṇṭhipadepi vuttaṃ “sekkhapaṇṇattiyanti pārājikamādiṃ katvā sikkhitabbasikkhāpadapaññattiya”nti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

‘Refined conduct’ (abhisamācāra) is conduct that is especially distinguished and excellent. Because this refined conduct is to be trained in (sikkhitabbato), it is called ‘training in refined conduct’ (ābhisamācārikā sikkhā). Or, the training prescribed concerning refined conduct is ābhisamācārikā. ‘Pertaining to the beginning of the holy life’ (ādibrahmacariyakā) is so called because it is the beginning of the holy life of the path; this is a designation for the training included in both Vibhaṅgas. For this reason it is said in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. I, 11): ‘What is included in both Vibhaṅgas pertains to the beginning of the holy life; what is included in the Khandhakas pertains to refined conduct.’ Therefore, in the phrase ‘in the ordinances for a trainee,’ all the ordinances included in both Vibhaṅgas are to be understood as what is to be trained in. For this reason it is also stated in the Gaṇṭhipada: ‘“In the ordinances for a trainee” means in the ordinances of the training rules to be trained in, beginning with the Pārājikas.’ The rest here is clear in meaning.

Upasampādetabbapañcakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section of the Five Who Should Not Be Ordained is concluded.

Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section Concerning the Case of Former Adherents of Other Sects.

86. Aññatitthiyavatthumhi ājīvako acelakoti duvidho naggaparibbājakoti āha “naggaparibbājakasseva ājīvakassa vā”tiādi. Tattha ājīvako upari ekameva vatthaṃ upakacchake pavesetvā paridahati, heṭṭhā naggo. Acelako sabbena sabbaṃ naggoyeva.

86. In the account of the former adherent of another sect, it is said that the Ājīvaka and the Acelaka are two kinds of naked wanderers, hence the text says ‘of a naked wanderer or of an Ājīvaka,’ and so on. Therein, the Ājīvaka wears only a single garment on his upper body, tucking it under his armpit, while being naked below. The Acelaka is completely and entirely naked.

87. Āmisakiñcikkhasampadānaṃ nāma appamattakasseva deyyadhammassa anuppadānaṃ. Rūpūpajīvikāti attano rūpaṃyeva nissāya jīvantiyo. Vesiyā gocaro mittasanthavavasena upasaṅkamitabbaṭṭhānaṃ assāti vesiyāgocaro. Esa nayo sabbattha. Yobbanappattā yobbanātītā vāti ubhayenapi mahallikā anividdhakumāriyova vadati. Bhikkhuniyo nāma ussannabrahmacariyā, tathā bhikkhūpi. Tesaṃ aññamaññavisabhāgavatthubhāvato santhavavasena upasaṅkamane katipāheneva brahmacariyantarāyo siyāti āha “tāhi saddhiṃ khippameva vissāso hoti, tato sīlaṃ bhijjatī”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

87. ‘The giving of some trifle’ means the giving of even a small gift. ‘Those who live by their beauty’ are women who live depending solely on their physical appearance. ‘One who resorts to prostitutes’ is one for whom there is a place to be approached by way of friendly intimacy with prostitutes. This method applies in all cases. ‘Whether having reached youth or passed beyond youth’—in both cases, it refers to elderly women who speak as if they were untouched maidens. ‘Nuns’ refers to those for whom the holy life is pre-eminent, and likewise for monks. Because they are of a mutually dissimilar physical nature, if they associate through intimacy, an obstacle to the holy life could arise within a few days. Thus it is said: ‘Familiarity with them arises quickly, and then one’s virtue is broken.’ The rest here is clear.

Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section Concerning the Case of Former Adherents of Other Sects is concluded.

Pañcābādhavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section Concerning the Case of the Five Diseases.

88. Pañcābādhavatthumhi [V 3.0220] nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇanti ettha “kaniṭṭhaṅgulinakhapiṭṭhi adhippetā”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. “Tañce nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇampi vaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitaṃ [M 3.0242] hoti, na pabbājetabbo”ti iminā sāmaññato lakkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ, tasmā yattha katthaci sarīrāvayavesu nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ vaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitañce, na vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Evañca sati nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇampi avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitañce, sabbattha vaṭṭatīti āpannaṃ, tañca na sāmaññato adhippetanti padesaviseseyeva niyametvā dassento “sace panā”tiādimāha. Sace hi avisesena nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitaṃ vaṭṭeyya, “nivāsanapārupanehi pakatipaacchanne ṭhāne”ti padesaniyamaṃ na kareyya, tasmā nivāsanapārupanehi pakatipaṭicchannaṭṭhānato aññattha nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitampi na vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ, nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇato khuddakataraṃ pana avaḍḍhanakapakkhe vaḍḍhanakapakkhe vā ṭhitaṃ hotu, vaṭṭati nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇato khuddakatarassa vaḍḍhanakapakkhe avaḍḍhanakapakkhe vā ṭhitassa mukhādīsuyeva paṭikkhittattā.

88. In the account of the five impediments, regarding 'the size of the back of a nail,' it is stated in all three commentaries that 'the back of the nail of the little finger is intended.' By the statement, 'If it is even the size of the back of a nail and is in a state of growth, he should not be ordained,' the general characteristic is shown. Therefore, it is established that wherever on the parts of the body there is something the size of the back of a nail in a state of growth, it is not permissible. This being the case, if something the size of the back of a nail is in a state of non-growth, it would follow that it is permissible everywhere. But this is not intended generally. To show this by restricting it to particular places, he said, 'But if…' and so on. For if, without distinction, something the size of the back of a nail in a state of non-growth were permissible, he would not have made the restriction of place by saying, 'in a place naturally covered by the lower and upper robes.' Therefore, it is established that something the size of the back of a nail, even if in a state of non-growth, is not permissible elsewhere than in a place naturally covered by the lower and upper robes. However, something smaller than the size of the back of a nail, whether it be in a state of growth or non-growth, is permissible, because something smaller than the size of the back of a nail is prohibited only on the face and so on.

Gaṇḍepi imināva nayena vinicchayo veditabbo. Tattha pana mukhādīsu kolaṭṭhimattato khuddakataropi gaṇḍo na vaṭṭatīti visuṃ na dassito. “Mukhādike appaṭicchannaṭṭhāne avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitopi na vaṭṭatī”ti ettakameva hi tattha vuttaṃ, tathāpi kuṭṭhe vuttanayena mukhādīsu kolaṭṭhippamāṇato khuddakataropi gaṇḍo na vaṭṭatīti viññāyati, tasmā avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitopīti ettha pi-saddo avuttasampiṇḍanattho. Tena kolaṭṭhimattato khuddakataropi na vaṭṭatīti ayamattho dassitoyevāti ayamamhākaṃ khanti. Pakativaṇṇe jāteti rogahetukassa vikāravaṇṇassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kolaṭṭhimattakoti badaraṭṭhippamāṇo. Suchaviṃ kāretvāti sañjātachaviṃ kāretvā. “Sañchaviṃ kāretvā”tipi pāṭho, vijjamānachaviṃ kāretvāti attho. Padumapuṇḍarīkapattavaṇṇanti rattapadumasetapadumavasena padumapattavaṇṇaṃ. Sosabyādhīti khayarogo.

In the case of a boil, the determination should be understood in this same way. However, it is not separately shown that in the case of the mouth and other areas, a boil even smaller than the size of a jujube seed is not permissible. For it is only said there: 'Even if it is located in an unconcealed place like the mouth and is in a state of non-growth, it is not permissible.' Nevertheless, by the method stated for leprosy, it is understood that in the case of the mouth and other areas, a boil even smaller than the size of a jujube seed is not permissible. Therefore, the particle 'pi' (even) in the phrase 'even if it is in a state of non-growth' has the meaning of including what is unstated. By this, the meaning is shown that even one smaller than the size of a jujube seed is not permissible—this is our view. 'Born with a natural color' is said with reference to the absence of a discolored appearance caused by disease. 'The size of a jujube seed' means the size of a jujube stone. 'Having caused good skin to form' means having caused skin to grow back. There is also the reading 'sañchaviṃ kāretvā,' which means having caused the existing skin to be restored. 'The color of a paduma or puṇḍarīka petal' means the color of a lotus petal, by way of the red lotus and the white lotus. 'The wasting disease' is consumption.

Pañcābādhavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the account of the five impediments is concluded.

Rājabhaṭādivatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of Royal Servants and So Forth

90-96. Rājabhaṭādivatthūsu [M 3.0243] āhaṃsūti manussā vadiṃsu. Tasmā…pe… evamāhāti yasmā sayaṃ dhammassāmī, tasmā bhikkhūhi apabbājitabbaṃ coraṃ aṅgulimālaṃ pabbājetvā āyatiṃ [V 3.0221] akaraṇatthāya bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapento “na, bhikkhave, dhajabandho coro pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti āha. Uparamantīti viramanti nivattanti. Bhinditvāti andubandhanaṃ bhinditvā. Chinditvāti saṅkhalikabandhanaṃ chinditvā. Muñcitvāti rajjubandhanaṃ muñcitvā. Vivaritvāti gāmabandhanādīsu gāmadvārādīni vivaritvā. Apassamānānaṃ vā palāyatīti purisaguttiyaṃ purisānaṃ apassamānānaṃ palāyati. Upaḍḍhupaḍḍhanti thokaṃ thokaṃ.

90-96. In the accounts of royal servants and so forth, 'they said' means people spoke. 'Therefore… he said thus' means: because he himself is the master of the Dhamma, therefore, after the robber Aṅgulimāla who should not have been ordained by bhikkhus was ordained, in order to prevent this in the future, he laid down a training rule for the bhikkhus, saying: 'Bhikkhus, a proclaimed robber should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain one, commits an offense of wrong conduct.' 'They desist' means they abstain, they turn back. 'Having broken' means having broken fetters. 'Having cut' means having cut chains. 'Having released' means having released from rope bonds. 'Having opened' means having opened village gates and so on in cases of village confinement. 'Or fleeing when they are not watching' means he flees when the men on guard are not watching. 'Bit by bit' means little by little.

97. Abhisekādīsu bandhanāgārādīni sodhenti, taṃ sandhāyāha “sabbasādhāraṇena vā nayenā”ti. Sace sayameva paṇṇaṃ āropenti, na vaṭṭatīti tā bhujissitthiyo “mayampi dāsiyo homā”ti sayameva dāsipaṇṇaṃ likhāpenti, na vaṭṭati. Takkaṃ sīse āsittakasadisāva hontīti yathā adāse karontā takkena sīsaṃ dhovitvā adāsaṃ karonti, evaṃ ārāmikavacanena dinnattā adāsāva teti adhippāyo. Takkāsiñcanaṃ pana sīhaḷadīpe cārittanti vadanti. Neva pabbājetabboti vuttanti kappiyavacanena dinnepi saṅghassa ārāmikadāsattā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Nissāmikadāso nāma yassa sāmikā saputtadārādayo matā honti, na koci tassa pariggāhako, sopi pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati, taṃ pana attanāpi bhujissaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Ye vā pana tasmiṃ raṭṭhe sāmino, tehipi kārāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Devadāsiputtaṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tīsu gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Dāsassa pabbajitvā attano sāmike disvā palāyantassa āpatti natthīti vadanti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

97. During coronations and so forth, they clear out the prisons; referring to this, it is said, 'or by a general method.' If they themselves draw up the deed, it is not permissible. Thus, those free women say, 'We too shall be slaves,' and themselves have a slave-deed written, but it is not permissible. 'They are like one whose head has been sprinkled with buttermilk' means: just as when making someone a non-slave, they wash their head with buttermilk and make them a non-slave, in the same way, the meaning is that because they are given by the word of a monastery attendant, they are indeed non-slaves. They say, however, that the sprinkling of buttermilk is a custom on the island of Sri Lanka. 'He should not be ordained' is said because, even though given by a valid statement, he is a monastery-attendant slave of the Saṅgha. A masterless slave is one whose masters—with their sons, wives, and so on—have died, and there is no one to claim him. He too is not to be ordained. But it is permissible to make him a free person oneself. Or it is permissible to have it done by those who are masters in that country. 'It is permissible to ordain the son of a temple slave,' is stated in the three glosses. They say there is no offense for a slave who, having been ordained, sees his masters and flees. The rest is clear everywhere.

Rājabhaṭādivatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Account of Royal Servants and So Forth is concluded.

Nissayamuccanakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of Release from Dependence

103. Nissayamuccanakassa [M 3.0244] vattesu pañcakachakkesu pana ubhayāni kho pana…pe… anubyañjanasoti ettha “sabbopi cāyaṃ pabhedo mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ ñātāyaṃ ñāto hotī”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Āpattiṃ jānātītiādīsu ca “pāṭhe avattamānepi ‘idaṃ nāma katvā idaṃ āpajjatī’ti jānāti ce, vaṭṭatī”ti tattheva vuttaṃ. Tañca kho pubbe pāṭhe paguṇe kateti gahetabbanti ca ācariyupajjhāyānampi eseva nayoti ca keci vadanti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

103. Now, regarding the duties for one released from dependence, in the sections of fives and sixes, 'both… and so on… the minor characteristics'—here it is said in all three glosses: 'And all these distinctions are known when the commentary on the matrix is known.' And concerning 'knows an offense' and so on, it is stated in that same place: 'Even if it is not in the text, if one knows, "Having done such-and-such, one incurs this offense," it is permissible.' And some say that this should be understood as being after one has first become proficient in the text, and that this is the same method for teachers and preceptors. The rest here is clear.

Nissayamuccanakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Account of Release from Dependence is concluded.

Rāhulavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of Rāhula

105. Rāhulavatthumhi [V 3.0222] tattheva vihariṃsūti sabbepi te arahattaṃ pattakālato paṭṭhāya ariyā nāma majjhattāva hontīti rañño pahitasāsanaṃ dasabalassa anārocetvāva tattha vihariṃsu. Ekadivasaṃ jātaṃ kāḷudāyiṃ nāma amaccanti ayaṃ kira (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.225) padumuttarabuddhakāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ kulappasādakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā adhikārakammaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthesi. So yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bodhisattassa mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase kapilavatthusmiṃyeva amaccagehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Jātadivase bodhisattena saddhiṃyeva jātoti taṃ divasaṃyeva dukūlacumbaṭake nipajjāpetvā bodhisattassa upaṭṭhānatthāya nayiṃsu. Bodhisattena hi saddhiṃ bodhirukkho rāhulamātā catasso nidhikumbhiyo ārohaniyahatthī kaṇḍako channo kāḷudāyīti ime satta ekadivase jātattā sahajātā nāma ahesuṃ. Athassa nāmaggahaṇadivase sakalanagarassa udaggacittadivase jātoti udāyītveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Thokaṃ kāḷadhātukattā pana kāḷudāyī nāma jāto. So bodhisattena saddhiṃ kumārakīḷaṃ kīḷanto vuddhiṃ agamāsi.

105. In the account of Rāhula, the phrase 'they remained right there' means this: from the time they attained arahantship, they were all noble ones and thus neutral, so they remained there without informing the One of Ten Powers of the king’s message. Now, the minister named Kāḷudāyī was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta. It is said that in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born in a family household in the city of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Teacher’s teaching, he saw the Teacher appointing a monk to the foremost position among those who inspire faith in families.
