He performed a deed of aspiration and longed for that position. After performing wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering among gods and humans, on the day our Bodhisatta took rebirth-linking in his mother’s womb, he took rebirth in the household of a minister in Kapilavatthu itself. Being born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, on that very day, they laid him on a roll of fine cloth and brought him to attend upon the Bodhisatta. For with the Bodhisatta, the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four pots of treasure, the state elephant, Kaṇḍaka, Channa, and Kāḷudāyī were born on the same day; these seven were called the 'co-natals.' On the day of his naming, since he was born on the day the entire city was filled with joy, they named him Udāyī. But because he had a slightly dark complexion, he came to be known as Kāḷudāyī. He grew up playing childhood games with the Bodhisatta.

Saṭṭhimattāhi [M 3.0245] gāthāhīti –

By about sixty verses:

“Aṅgārino dāni dumā bhadante;

Phalesino chadanaṃ vippahāya;

Te accimantova pabhāsayanti;

Samayo mahāvīra bhāgīrasānaṃ. (theragā. 527)

“Now, venerable sir, the trees are like glowing embers; having shed their foliage, they are eager for fruit. They shine forth as if aflame. It is time, O Great Hero, for the Bhāgīrathas.”

“Nātisītaṃ nātiuṇhaṃ, nātidubbhikkhachātakaṃ;

Saddalā haritā bhūmi, esa kālo mahāmunī”ti. –

“Not too cold, not too hot, not too much famine or hunger; the earth is lush with grass and green. This is the time, Great Sage.”

Ādikāhi saṭṭhimattāhi gāthāhi. “Pokkharavassanti pokkharapattavaṇṇamudaka”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Pokkharapattappamāṇaṃ majjhe uṭṭhahitvā anukkamena satapaṭalaṃ sahassapaṭalaṃ hutvā vassanakavassantipi vadanti. Tasmiṃ kira vassante temetukāmāva tementi, na itare. Ekopi rājā vā…pe… gato natthīti dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pakkantesu ñātīsu ekopi rājā vā rājamahāmatto [V 3.0223] vā “sve amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantetvā gato natthi. Pitāpissa suddhodanamahārājā “mayhaṃ putto mama gehaṃ anāgantvā kahaṃ gamissatī”ti animantetvāva agamāsi, gantvā pana gehe vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassānaṃ yāguādīni paṭiyādāpetvā āsanāni paññāpesi.

With about sixty initial verses. 'Pokkharavassa means water the color of a lotus leaf'—so it is stated in the glosses. They say that it arises in the middle to the size of a lotus leaf and, gradually forming a hundred layers, a thousand layers, it rains down. Some even call it 'the rain of rains.' Indeed, when that rain falls, only those who wish to be moistened get moistened, not others. When his relatives had heard the Dhamma teaching and departed, not a single king or royal minister invited him, saying, 'Tomorrow, accept alms from us,' before leaving. His father, King Suddhodana, thinking, 'Where else will my son go if not to my house?' departed without inviting him. But upon arriving home, he had rice gruel and other provisions prepared for twenty thousand monks and had seats arranged.

Kulanagareti ñātikulassa nagare. Uṇhīsato paṭṭhāyāti sīsato paṭṭhāya. Uṇhīsanti hi uṇhīsasadisattā bhagavato paripuṇṇanalāṭassa paripuṇṇasīsassa ca etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhagavato hi dakkhiṇakaṇṇacūḷikato paṭṭhāya maṃsapaṭalaṃ uṭṭhahitvā sakalanalāṭaṃ chādayamānaṃ pūrayamānaṃ gantvā vāmakaṇṇacūḷikāya patiṭṭhitaṃ saṇhatamatāya suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya pabhassaratāya paripuṇṇatāya ca rañño baddhauṇhīsapaṭṭo viya virocati. Bhagavato kira imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ disvā rājūnaṃ uṇhīsapaṭṭaṃ akaṃsu. Aññe pana janā aparipuṇṇasīsā honti, keci kappasīsā, keci phalasīsā, keci aṭṭhisīsā, keci tumbasīsā, keci kumbhasīsā, keci pabbhārasīsā, bhagavato pana āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitaṃ viya suparipuṇṇaṃ udakapubbuḷasadisampi hoti. Teneva uṇhīsaveṭhitasīsasadisattā uṇhīsaṃ viya sabbattha parimaṇḍalasīsattā ca uṇhīsasīsoti bhagavā vuccati.

'In the city of his clan' means in the city of his family. 'Starting from the turban' means from the top of the head. 'Turban' is a term for the Blessed One’s perfectly rounded forehead and head, because it resembles a turban. Indeed, for the Blessed One, a layer of flesh, rising from the tip of the right ear, covering and filling the entire forehead, extends to and rests at the tip of the left ear; it shines like a king’s bound turban cloth due to its extreme smoothness, golden color, radiance, and fullness. It is said that kings made turbans for themselves after seeing this mark of the Blessed One. Other people, however, have heads that are not perfectly rounded—some are like a bowl, some like a fruit, some like a skeleton, some like a gourd, some like a pot, some like a cliff. But the Blessed One’s head is perfectly rounded, like a water bubble, as if shaped by a lathe. Therefore, because his head resembles one wrapped in a turban and is perfectly round in every way, the Blessed One is called 'One with a Turban-like Head.'

Narasīhagāthāhi [M 3.0246] nāma aṭṭhahi gāthāhīti –

By the eight verses called the 'Verses on the Lion of Men':

“Siniddhanīlamudukuñcitakeso;

Sūriyanimmalatalābhinalāṭo;

Yuttatuṅgamudukāyatanāso;

Raṃsijālavitato narasīho”ti. (jā. aṭṭha. 1.santikenidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.santikenidānakathā) –

“With hair smooth, dark blue, soft, and curling; a forehead bright as the spotless surface of the sun; a nose well-proportioned, prominent, soft, and long; radiant with a net of rays—the Lion among Men.”

Evamādikāhi aṭṭhahi gāthāhi. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana –

With these eight verses and others like them. But in the glosses:

“Cakkavaraṅkitarattasupādo;

Lakkhaṇamaṇḍitaāyatapaṇhi;

Cāmarachattavibhūsitapādo;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“With excellent red feet marked by the supreme wheel; with long heels adorned with auspicious signs; with feet decorated with marks of the yak-tail whisk and parasol—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Sakyakumāravaro [V 3.0224] sukhumālo;

Lakkhaṇacittikapuṇṇasarīro;

Lokahitāya gato naravīro;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“The excellent Sakyan prince, so delicate; his full body adorned with auspicious marks; the hero of men, gone for the welfare of the world—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Puṇṇasasaṅkanibho mukhavaṇṇo;

Devanarāna piyo naranāgo;

Mattagajindavilāsitagāmī;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“His facial complexion is like the full moon; a great man, beloved of gods and men; he walks with the grace of a mighty tusker in rut—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Khattiyasambhavaaggakulīno;

Devamanussanamassitapādo;

Sīlasamādhipatiṭṭhitacitto;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“Of foremost lineage, born of Khattiyas; his feet revered by gods and humans; his mind firmly established in virtue and concentration—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Āyatayuttasusaṇṭhitanāso;

Gopakhumo abhinīlasunetto;

Indadhanūabhinīlabhamūko;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“His nose is long, well-proportioned, and well-formed; he has eyelashes like a cow's and beautiful, very dark blue eyes; his eyebrows are very dark blue like Indra's bow—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Vaṭṭasuvaṭṭasusaṇṭhitagīvo[M 3.0247];

Sīhahanū migarājasarīro;

Kañcanasucchaviuttamavaṇṇo;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“His neck is round, well-rounded, and well-formed; his jaws are like a lion’s, his torso like the king of beasts’; his complexion is of the finest hue, his skin like refined gold—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Siniddhasugambhiramañjusaghoso;

Hiṅgulabandhukarattasujivho;

Vīsativīsatisetasudanto;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“His voice is smooth, very deep, and sweet; his beautiful tongue is red like cinnabar and the bandhuka flower; he has beautiful white teeth, twenty and twenty—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Añjanavaṇṇasunīlasukeso[V 3.0225];

Kañcanapaṭṭavisuddhanalāṭo;

Osadhipaṇḍarasuddhasuuṇṇo;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho.

“His beautiful hair is a lovely dark blue, the color of collyrium; his forehead is perfectly pure, like a golden plate; his beautiful uṇṇā-hair is pure white like the Osadhi star—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.

“Gacchatinilapathe viya cando;

Tāragaṇāpariveṭhitarūpo;

Sāvakamajjhagato samaṇindo;

Esa hi tuyha pitā narasīho”ti. (jā. aṭṭha. 1.santikenidānakathā) –

“Like the moon moving on its blue path, his form is surrounded by a host of stars; the lord of ascetics, amidst his disciples—this, indeed, is your father, the Lion among Men.”

Imā nava gāthāyopi ettha dassitā, tā pana “aṭṭhahi gāthāhī”ti vacanena na samenti. Uṇhīsato paṭṭhāya yāva pādatalāti vuttānukkamopi tattha na dissati. Bhikkhāya caratīti bhikkhācāro.

These nine verses are also shown here, but they do not agree with the statement 'by eight verses.' Also, the stated sequence, 'from the turban down to the soles of the feet,' is not found there. 'Bhikkhācāro' means one who wanders for alms.

Uttiṭṭheti uttiṭṭhitvā paresaṃ gharadvāre ṭhatvā gahetabbapiṇḍe. Nappamajjheyyāti piṇḍacārikavattaṃ hāpetvā paṇītabhojanāni pariyesanto uttiṭṭhe pamajjati nāma, sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caranto pana nappamajjati nāma, evaṃ karonto uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya. Dhammanti anesanaṃ pahāya sapadānaṃ caranto tameva bhikkhācariyadhammaṃ sucaritaṃ care. Sukhaṃ setīti desanāmattametaṃ, evaṃ panetaṃ bhikkhāya cariyadhammaṃ caranto dhammacārī idhaloke ca paraloke ca catūhipi iriyāpathehi sukhaṃ viharatīti attho.

'One should rise up' refers to the alms-food to be received by having risen and standing at the doorsteps of others' houses. 'One should not be negligent' means that one who abandons the practice of the alms-round and seeks delicious food is called 'negligent in rising up.' But one who goes for alms in due order is called 'not negligent.' Doing so, one should not be negligent in rising up. 'Dhamma' means that, abandoning improper seeking and walking in due order, one should practice that very Dhamma of alms-faring well. 'One sleeps happily' is merely a manner of teaching; the meaning is that one who practices this Dhamma of alms-faring, a Dhamma-farer, dwells happily in this world and the next in all four postures.

Dutiyagāthāya [M 3.0248] na naṃ duccaritanti vesiyādibhede agocare caranto naṃ bhikkhācariyadhammaṃ duccaritaṃ carati nāma, evaṃ acaritvā taṃ dhammaṃ care sucaritaṃ, na naṃ duccaritaṃ care. Sesamettha vuttatthameva. Imaṃ pana dutiyagāthaṃ pitu nivesanaṃ gantvā abhāsīti veditabbaṃ. Teneva theragāthāsaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (theragā. aṭṭha. 1.156 nandattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ “dutiyadivase piṇḍāya paviṭṭho ‘uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā’ti gāthāya pitaraṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā nivesanaṃ gantvā ‘dhammaṃ care sucarita’nti gāthāya mahāpajāpatiṃ sotāpattiphale rājānañca sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāpesī”ti. Dhammapadaṭṭhakathāyampi (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.12 nandattheravatthu) vuttaṃ “punadivase piṇḍāya paviṭṭho ‘uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā’ti gāthāya pitaraṃ sotāpattiphale [V 3.0226] patiṭṭhāpetvā ‘dhammaṃ care’ti gāthāya mahāpajāpatiṃ sotāpattiphale rājānañca sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāpesī”ti.

In the second verse, concerning 'na naṃ duccaritaṃ' (do not practice it as misconduct): By wandering in improper resorts such as brothels, one practices the alms-round as misconduct. Thus, not acting in that way, one should practice that Dhamma as good conduct, not practicing it as misconduct. The rest here is as previously explained. This second verse, however, should be understood as spoken after going to his father’s residence. As stated in the commentary to the Theragāthā (Theragāthā Aṭṭhakathā 1.156, Nandattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) by the elder Ācariya Dhammapāla: "On the second day, having entered for alms, with the verse ‘One should rise and not be heedless,’ he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, going to the residence, with the verse ‘Practice the Dhamma as good conduct,’ he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the king in the fruit of once-returning." Similarly, in the Dhammapadaṭṭhakathā (Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā 1.12, Nandattheravatthu), it is said: "On the following day, having entered for alms, with the verse ‘One should rise and not be heedless,’ he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, with the verse ‘Practice the Dhamma,’ he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the king in the fruit of once-returning."

Dhammapālajātakaṃ sutvā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsīti punekadivasaṃ rājanivesane katapātarāso ekamantaṃ nisinnena raññā “bhante, tumhākaṃ dukkarakārikakāle ekā devatā maṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘putto te kālakato’ti āha. Ahaṃ tassā vacanaṃ asaddahanto ‘na mayhaṃ putto bodhiṃ appatvā kālaṃ karotī’ti paṭikkhipinti vutte idāni kathaṃ saddahissatha, pubbepi aṭṭhikāni dassetvā ‘putto te mato’ti vutte na saddahitthā”ti imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā mahādhammapālajātakaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi.

Having heard the Dhammapāla Jātaka, he was established in the fruit of non-return. Then, one day, after the morning meal at the royal residence, while the king was sitting to one side, he said: "Venerable sir, during the time when you were performing difficult ascetic practices, a certain deity approached me and said, 'Your son is dead.' I, not believing her words, replied, 'My son will not die without attaining awakening.'" When this was said, the Teacher replied: "Now how will you believe? Even in the past, when bones were shown to you and you were told, 'Your son is dead,' you did not believe." In connection with this origin of the story, he narrated the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka. Hearing it, the king was established in the fruit of non-return.

Kesavissajjananti kulamariyādavasena kesoropanaṃ. Paṭṭabandhoti yuvarājapaṭṭabandho. Abhinavagharappavesanamaho gharamaṅgalaṃ, vivāhakaraṇamaho āvāhamaṅgalaṃ. Chattamaṅgalanti yuvarājachattamaṅgalaṃ. Janapadakalyāṇīti (udā. aṭṭha. 22) janapadamhi kalyāṇī uttamā chasarīradosarahitā pañcakalyāṇasamannāgatā. Sā hi yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷā nāccodātāti atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇaṃ, appattā dibbaṃ vaṇṇaṃ, tasmā chasarīradosarahitā. Chavikalyāṇaṃ maṃsakalyāṇaṃ nahārukalyāṇaṃ aṭṭhikalyāṇaṃ vayakalyāṇanti imehi pana pañcahi kalyāṇehi samannāgatattā pañcakalyāṇasamannāgatā nāma. Tassā hi āgantukobhāsakiccaṃ natthi. Attano sarīrobhāseneva dvādasahatthaṭṭhāne [M 3.0249] ālokaṃ karoti, piyaṅgusāmā vā hoti suvaṇṇasāmā vā, ayamassā chavikalyāṇatā. Cattāro panassā hatthapādā mukhapariyosānañca lākhārasaparikammakataṃ viya rattapavāḷarattakambalasadisaṃ hoti, ayamassā maṃsakalyāṇatā. Vīsati pana nakhapattāni maṃsato amuttaṭṭhāne lākhārasapūritāni viya muttaṭṭhāne khīradhārāsadisāni honti, ayamassā nahārukalyāṇatā. Dvattiṃsa dantā suphusitā sudhotavajirapanti viya khāyanti, ayamassā aṭṭhikalyāṇatā. Vīsativassasatikāpi samānā soḷasavassuddesikā viya hoti nivalipalitā, ayamassā vayakalyāṇatā. Iti imehi pañcahi kalyāṇehi samannāgatattā janapadakalyāṇīti vuccati.

`Kesavissajjana` means the cutting of hair according to family tradition. `Paṭṭabandha` refers to the crown prince's consecration. The auspicious house-entering ceremony is the house-blessing, and the auspicious marriage ceremony is the wedding-blessing. The umbrella ceremony refers to the crown prince's umbrella-blessing. 'The beauty of the realm' (as mentioned in Udāna Aṭṭhakathā 22) is the most excellent woman in the realm, free from six bodily defects and endowed with five beauties. For she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too pale—thus surpassing human beauty but not yet attaining divine beauty. Therefore, she is free from six bodily defects. She is endowed with five beauties: beauty of skin, beauty of flesh, beauty of sinews, beauty of bones, and beauty of youth. Hence, she is called 'endowed with five beauties.' For her, there is no need for applying external radiance. By the radiance of her own body, she illuminates a space of twelve cubits. Her complexion is like gold or the piyaṅgu flower—this is her beauty of skin. Her four limbs and the area around her mouth appear as if polished with lacquer, resembling red coral or a red blanket—this is her beauty of flesh. Her twenty nails appear as if filled with lacquer where they are attached to the flesh, and where they are free, they resemble streams of milk—this is her beauty of sinews. Her thirty-two teeth are well-set and shine like a row of well-washed diamonds—this is her beauty of bones. Though she may be a hundred and twenty years old, she appears like a maiden of sixteen, free from wrinkles and gray hair—this is her beauty of youth. Thus, because she is endowed with these five beauties, she is called 'the beauty of the realm.'

Tuvaṭanti sīghaṃ. Sopi bhagavantaṃ “pattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vattuṃ avisahamāno vihāraṃyeva agamāsīti. So kira tathāgate gāravena “pattaṃ vo bhante gaṇhathā”ti vattuṃ nāsakkhi. Evaṃ pana cintesi “sopānasīse pattaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti. Satthā tasmimpi ṭhāne na gaṇhi. Itaro “sopānapādamūle gaṇhissatī”ti cintesi. Satthā tatthāpi na gaṇhi. Itaro “rājaṅgaṇe gaṇhissatī”ti [V 3.0227] cintesi. Satthā tatthāpi na gaṇhi. Kumāro nivattitukāmo aruciyā gacchanto satthu gāravena “pattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vattumpi asakkonto “idha gaṇhissati, ettha gaṇhissatī”ti cintento gacchati. Janapadakalyāṇiyā ca vuttavacanaṃ tassa hadaye tiriyaṃ patitvā viya ṭhitaṃ. Nandakumārañhi abhisekamaṅgalaṃ na tathā pīḷesi, yathā janapadakalyāṇiyā vuttavacanaṃ, tenassa cittasantāpo balavā ahosi. Atha naṃ “imasmiṃ ṭhāne nivattissati, imasmiṃ ṭhāne nivattissatī”ti cintentameva satthā vihāraṃ netvā “pabbajissasi nandā”ti āha. So buddhagāravena “na pabbajissāmī”ti avatvā “āma pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Satthā “tena hi nandaṃ pabbājethā”ti vatvā pabbājesi. Tena vuttaṃ “anicchamānaṃyeva bhagavā pabbājesī”ti. “Satthā kapilapuraṃ gantvā tatiyadivase nandaṃ pabbājesī”ti dhammapadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.12 nandattheravatthu) vuttaṃ, aṅguttaranikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.230) pana –

`Tuvaṭaṃ` means quickly. Unable to bring himself to tell the Blessed One, "Take the bowl," he went right to the monastery. It is said that due to reverence for the Tathāgata, he could not say, "Venerable sir, please take your bowl." Then he thought, "He will take it at the top of the stairs." But the Teacher did not take it in that place. The other thought, "He will take it at the foot of the stairs." The Teacher did not take it there either. The other thought, "He will take it in the royal courtyard." Still, the Teacher did not take it there. The prince, wishing to turn back but going on reluctantly, unable even to say, out of reverence for the Teacher, "Take the bowl," kept thinking, "He will take it here, he will take it there," as he walked. And the words of Janapadakalyāṇī had struck his heart sideways, as it were, and remained there. For the consecration ceremony did not distress Prince Nanda as much as the words of Janapadakalyāṇī did, so his mental anguish was intense. Then, while he was still thinking, "He will turn back in this place, he will turn back in that place," the Teacher led him to the monastery and said, "Nanda, will you go forth?" Out of reverence for the Buddha, instead of saying, "I will not go forth," he said, "Yes, I will go forth." The Teacher said, "Then ordain Nanda," and had him ordained. Hence it is said, "The Blessed One made him go forth even though he was unwilling." In the Dhammapada Commentary (DhpA. 1.12, Nandattheravatthu), it is said, "The Teacher went to Kapilapura and on the third day had Nanda go forth." But in the Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary (AN.A. 1.1.230), it is said—

“Mahāsattopi sabbaññutaṃ patvā pavattitavaradhammacakko lokānuggahaṃ karonto rājagahato kapilavatthuṃ gantvā paṭhamadassaneneva [M 3.0250] pitaraṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesi, punadivase pitu nivesanaṃ gantvā rāhulamātāya ovādaṃ katvā sesajanassapi dhammaṃ kathesi, punadivase nandakumārassa abhisekagehappavesanaāvāhamaṅgalesu vattamānesu tassa nivesanaṃ gantvā kumāraṃ pattaṃ gāhāpetvā pabbājetuṃ vihārābhimukho pāyāsī”ti –

"The Great Being, having attained omniscience and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, acting for the welfare of the world, went from Rājagaha to Kapilavatthu. At the very first sight, he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry. The next day, he went to his father's residence, gave an exhortation to Rāhula's mother, and also taught the Dhamma to the other people. On the following day, while the ceremonies of Prince Nanda's consecration, house-entry, and marriage were taking place, he went to his residence, had the prince take up the bowl, and set out toward the monastery to ordain him."

Vuttaṃ, idha pana “bhagavā kapilapuraṃ āgantvā dutiyadivase nandaṃ pabbājesī”ti vuttaṃ, sabbampetaṃ ācariyena taṃtaṃbhāṇakānaṃ tathā tathā anussavavasena pariharitvā āgatabhāvato tattha tattha tathā tathā vuttanti natthettha ācariyavacane pubbāparavirodho.

While that has been stated, here it is said: 'The Blessed One, having arrived at Kapilapura, ordained Nanda on the second day.' All this has been stated in such and such a way in various places, as it has been handed down by the teacher in accordance with the respective oral traditions of the various reciters. Therefore, there is no contradiction between earlier and later statements in the teacher's words.

Brahmarūpavaṇṇanti brahmarūpasamānarūpaṃ. Tyassāti te assa. Vaṭṭānugatanti vaṭṭapariyāpannaṃ. Savighātanti dukkhasahitattā savighātaṃ, sadukkhanti attho. Sattavidhaṃ ariyadhananti –

`Brahmarūpavaṇṇa` means a form similar to that of a Brahmā. `Tyassa` means 'his.' `Vaṭṭānugata` means included in the cycle. `Savighāta` means 'with vexation,' because it is accompanied by suffering; 'with suffering' is the meaning. `Sattavidhaṃ ariyadhana` means the sevenfold noble wealth:

“Saddhādhanaṃ sīladhanaṃ, hiriottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ;

Sutadhanañca cāgo ca, paññā ve sattamaṃ dhana”nti. (a. ni. 7.5-6) –

"The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of conscience and prudence; the wealth of learning and generosity, and wisdom is indeed the seventh wealth."

Evaṃ vuttaṃ sattavidhaṃ ariyadhanaṃ. Uñchācariyāyāti bhikkhācariyāya. Puttasineho uppajjamāno sakalasarīraṃ [V 3.0228] khobhetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhatīti āha “puttapemaṃ bhante…pe… aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhatī”ti. Puttasineho hi balavabhāvato sahajātapītivegassa savipphāratāya taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpadhammehi pharaṇavasena sakalasarīraṃ āloḷetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Thus was spoken the sevenfold noble wealth. 'By the practice of gleaning' means by the practice of alms-seeking. 'Affection for a child, arising, agitates the entire body and, striking the marrow, it stands'—thus it was said, 'Affection for a child, venerable sir... striking the marrow, it stands.' For affection for a child, due to its strong nature and the pervasive force of its co-nascent joy, agitates the entire body by pervading it with the material phenomena that arise together with it and, striking the marrow, it stands. 'Yatra hi nāma' means 'who indeed.' The rest here is self-explanatory.

Rāhulavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Rāhula is concluded.

Sikkhāpadadaṇḍakammavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of the Subject of Penal Actions regarding the Training Rules.

106. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sāmaṇerānaṃ dasa sikkhāpadānītiādīsu sikkhitabbāni padāni sikkhāpadāni, sikkhākoṭṭhāsāti attho. Sikkhāya vā padāni sikkhāpadāni, adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāsikkhāya adhigamupāyāti [M 3.0251] attho. Atthato pana kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayuttā viratiyo, taṃsampayuttadhammā panettha taggahaṇeneva gahetabbā. Saraseneva patanasabhāvassa antarā eva atipātanaṃ atipāto, saṇikaṃ patituṃ adatvā sīghaṃ pātananti attho. Atikkamma vā satthādīhi abhibhavitvā pātanaṃ atipāto, pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇavadho pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññatarappavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto, tato pāṇātipātā.

106. “I allow, bhikkhus, the ten training rules for novices,” and so forth. The items in which one should train are the training rules; this is the meaning of 'a section of training.' Or, the foundations of training are the training rules; this is the meaning of 'a means of attainment' for the training in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. In terms of meaning, however, these are the abstinences associated with wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere. The states associated with them here should be understood simply by their inclusion. 'Killing' (atipāto) is the act of causing something to fall (atipātanaṃ) before its natural tendency to fall on its own; the meaning is to cause it to fall quickly without allowing it to fall slowly. Or, 'killing' is causing something to fall by overcoming or overpowering it with weapons and so forth. The killing of a living being is 'destruction of life' (pāṇātipāto); it is said to be 'slaying a living being' (pāṇavadho) or 'killing a living being' (pāṇaghāto). Here, 'living being' (pāṇa) conventionally means a sentient being, but in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty. With regard to that living being, when one perceives it as a living being, the destructive volition that arises from an endeavor to cut off the life faculty, manifested through either the bodily or verbal door, is the destruction of life.

Veramaṇīti verahetutāya verasaññitaṃ pāṇātipātādipāpadhammaṃ maṇati, “mayi idha ṭhitāya kathamāgacchasī”ti vā tajjentī viya nīharatīti veramaṇī. Viramati etāyāti vā viramaṇīti vattabbe niruttinayena “veramaṇī”ti vuttaṃ. Atthato pana veramaṇīti kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayuttā viratiyo. Sā “pāṇātipātādiṃ viramantassa yā tasmiṃ samaye pāṇātipātā ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī akiriyā akaraṇaṃ anajjhāpatti velānatikkamo setughāto”ti evamādinā nayena vibhaṅge (vibha. 704) vuttā. Kāmañcesā veramaṇī nāma lokuttarāpi atthi, idha pana samādānavasappavattā virati adhippetāti lokuttarāya viratiyā samādānavasena pavattiasambhavato kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayuttā viratiyo gahetabbā.

‘Abstinence’ (veramaṇī) is so called because it keeps away (maṇati) evil states such as the destruction of life, which are designated as hostile (vera) due to being causes of hostility. Or, it is as if it scolds them, saying, “How can you come near while I stand here?” and thus drives them away. Or, it should be called ‘viramaṇī’ because one abstains (viramati) by means of it, but according to the rule of etymology, it is called ‘veramaṇī.’ In terms of meaning, however, ‘veramaṇī’ refers to abstinences associated with wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere. This is stated in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 704) in this and other ways: “For one who abstains from the destruction of life and so forth, at that time there is cessation from the destruction of life, abstinence, restraint, avoidance, non-action, non-doing, non-transgression, not overstepping the boundary, and breaking the bridge.” Although this ‘veramaṇī’ can also be supramundane, here the intended meaning is the abstinence that arises through undertaking. Since supramundane abstinence cannot arise through undertaking, only the abstinences associated with wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere should be taken.

Adinnādānā veramaṇītiādīsu adinnassa ādānaṃ adinnādānaṃ, parassaharaṇaṃ, theyyaṃ corikāti [V 3.0229] vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ. Yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo ca hoti, tasmiṃ pana parapariggahite parapariggahitasaañano tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ.

Regarding “abstinence from taking what is not given” and so forth: The taking of what is not given is “taking what is not given” (adinnādānaṃ); it is said to be seizing another’s property, theft, or stealing. Here, “what is not given” means what is possessed by another. With regard to that which is possessed by another—over which its owner may act as they please without being liable to punishment or deserving of reproach—the thievish volition that arises from an endeavor to take it, while perceiving it as possessed by another, is “taking what is not given.”

Abrahmacariyaṃ nāma aseṭṭhacariyaṃ dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti. Sā hi “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.177; 2.42) hīḷitattā aseṭṭhā appasatthā cariyāti vā aseṭṭhānaṃ nihīnānaṃ itthipurisānaṃ cariyāti vā aseṭṭhacariyaṃ, aseṭṭhacariyattā abrahmacariyanti ca vuccati[M 3.0252], atthato pana asaddhammasevanādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā maggenamaggappaṭipattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā abrahmacariyaṃ.

“Non-celibacy” (abrahmacariyaṃ) is ignoble conduct, the union of two by two. For it is despised by such statements as “Sensual pleasures are of little enjoyment, much suffering, much despair, and greater danger here” (MN 1.177; 2.42), and thus it is ignoble and unpraiseworthy conduct. Or, it is the conduct of ignoble, inferior men and women, hence it is ignoble conduct. Because it is ignoble conduct, it is also called “non-celibacy.” In terms of meaning, however, “non-celibacy” is the volition, arising through the bodily door with the intention of engaging in that wrong practice, which gives rise to the practice of the wrong path by means of the bodily path.

Musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu, vādoti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo musā vadīyati vuccati etāyāti katvā.

“False” (musā) is an untrue, unreal matter. “Speech” (vāda) is the communication of that matter as true and real. By characteristic, however, “false speech” (musāvādo) is the volition that arises in one who desires to communicate an untrue matter as true to another, bringing about that communication. It is called “false speech” because one speaks falsely by means of it.

Surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānāti ettha surāti pūvasurā piṭṭhasurā odanasurā kiṇṇapakkhittā sambhārasaṃyuttāti pañca surā. Merayanti pupphāsavo phalāsavo madhvāsavo guḷāsavo sambhārasaṃyuttoti pañca āsavā. Tattha pūve bhājane pakkhipitvā tajjaṃ udakaṃ datvā madditvā katā pūvasurā. Evaṃ sesasurāpi. Kiṇṇāti pana tassā surāya bījaṃ vuccati, ye surāmodakāti vuccanti, te pakkhipitvā katā kiṇṇapakkhittā. Harītakīsāsapādinānāsambhārehi saṃyojitā sambhārasaṃyuttā. Madhukatālanāḷikerādipuppharaso ciraparivāsito pupphāsavo. Panasādiphalaraso phalāsavo. Muddikāraso madhvāsavo. Ucchuraso guḷāsavo. Harītakaāmalakakaṭukabhaṇḍādinānāsambhārānaṃ raso ciraparivāsito sambhārasaṃyutto. Taṃ sabbampi madakaraṇavasena majjaṃ pivantaṃ madayatīti katvā. Pamādaṭṭhānanti pamādakāraṇaṃ. Yāya cetanāya taṃ majjaṃ pivanti, tassā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Surāmerayamajje pamādaṭṭhānaṃ surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā.

Here, in the phrase “grounds for heedlessness due to fermented drinks, distilled liquors, and intoxicants” (surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā), “surā” refers to five types of fermented drinks: cake-fermented liquor, flour-fermented liquor, rice-fermented liquor, yeast-infused liquor, and mixed-ingredient liquor. “Meraya” refers to five types of distilled liquors: flower-distilled liquor, fruit-distilled liquor, honey-distilled liquor, molasses-distilled liquor, and mixed-ingredient distilled liquor. Among these, “cake-fermented liquor” (pūvasurā) is made by placing cakes in a vessel, adding the appropriate water, and mashing it. The other types of surā are made similarly. “Kiṇṇa” is said to be the starter culture for that surā; the yeast-infused liquor is made by adding what are called “surāmodakā” (liquor cakes). “Mixed-ingredient liquor” (sambhārasaṃyuttā) is prepared by combining various ingredients such as harītakī and mustard seeds. “Flower-distilled liquor” (pupphāsavo) is the juice of flowers such as madhuka, tāla, and coconut, long fermented. “Fruit-distilled liquor” (phalāsavo) is the juice of fruits such as jackfruit. “Honey-distilled liquor” (madhvāsavo) is the juice of grapes. “Molasses-distilled liquor” (guḷāsavo) is the juice of sugarcane. “Mixed-ingredient distilled liquor” (sambhārasaṃyutto) is the long-fermented juice of various mixed ingredients such as harītakī, āmalaka, and kaṭuka. All of these are called “intoxicants” (majja) because, by their intoxicating nature, they intoxicate one who drinks them. “Grounds for heedlessness” (pamādaṭṭhānaṃ) means a cause of heedlessness. This is a designation for the volition with which one drinks that intoxicant. The grounds for heedlessness due to fermented drinks, distilled liquors, and intoxicants is “surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānaṃ.” From that comes the precept “surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā.”

Vikālabhojanāti aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhanhikā. Ayaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo bhojanassa kālo nāma, tadañño vikālo. Bhuñjitabbaṭṭhena bhojanaṃ, yāgubhattādi sabbaṃ yāvakālikavatthu. Yathā ca “rattūparato”ti (dī. 1.10, 194; ma. ni. 1.293; 3.14) ettha [V 3.0230] rattiyā bhojanaṃ rattīti uttarapadalopena vuccati, evamettha bhojanajjhoharaṇaṃ bhojananti. Vikāle bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ, tato vikālabhojanā, vikāle yāvakālikavatthussa ajjhoharaṇāti attho. Atha vā na ettha kammasādhano bhuñjitabbatthavācako bhojanasaddo, atha kho bhāvasādhano ajjhoharaṇatthavācako gahetabbo[M 3.0253], tasmā vikāle bhojanaṃ ajjhoharaṇaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ. Kassa pana ajjhoharaṇanti? Yāmakālikādīnaṃ anuññātattā vikālabhojana-saddassa vā yāvakālikajjhoharaṇe niruḷhattā yāvakālikassāti viññāyati, atthato pana kāyadvārappavattā vikāle yāvakālikajjhoharaṇacetanā “vikālabhojana”nti veditabbā.

Regarding “eating at the wrong time” (vikālabhojana): The proper time for eating is from the rising of the dawn until midday. This is the time for eating customarily observed by the noble ones such as the Buddha. Any other time is the wrong time. “Bhojana” (food) means that which is to be eaten, that is, all things allowable for the period of a day, such as rice gruel and cooked rice. Just as in the phrase “abstaining at night” (rattūparato) (DN 1.10, 194; MN 1.293; 3.14), “night” (ratti) is used by the elision of a subsequent word to mean eating at night, so here too, “bhojana” means the act of consuming food. Eating at the wrong time is “vikālabhojana.” From that comes the precept “vikālabhojanā,” which means the consumption of things allowable for the period of a day at the wrong time. Alternatively, here the word “bhojana” is not a kamma-sādhana denoting the object to be eaten, but rather a bhāva-sādhana denoting the act of consuming. Therefore, “vikālabhojana” means the act of consuming at the wrong time. But the consumption of what? Since things allowable for a watch (yāmakālika) and so forth are permitted, and since the word “vikālabhojana” is conventionally established for the consumption of things allowable for the period of a day, it is understood to refer to things allowable for the period of a day. In essence, the volition arising through the bodily door to consume things allowable for the period of a day at the wrong time is what should be understood as “vikālabhojana.”

Naccagītavāditavisūkadassanāti ettha sāsanassa ananulomattā visūkaṃ paṭāṇībhūtaṃ dassananti visūkadassanaṃ. Naccādīnañhi dassanaṃ sachandarāgappavattito saṅkhepato “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”ntiādinayappavattaṃ (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183) bhagavato sāsanaṃ na anulometi. Naccañca gītañca vāditañca visūkadassanañca naccagītavāditavisūkadassanaṃ. Attanā payojiyamānaṃ parehi payojāpiyamānañcettha naccaṃ naccabhāvasāmaññato pāḷiyaṃ ekeneva nacca-saddena gahitaṃ, tathā gītavādita-saddehi gāyanagāyāpanavādanavādāpanāni, tasmā attanā naccananaccāpanādivasena naccā ca gītā ca vāditā ca antamaso mayūranaccādivasenapi pavattānaṃ naccādīnaṃ visūkabhūtā dassanā ca veramaṇīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Naccādīni attanā payojetuṃ vā parehi payojāpetuṃ vā payuttāni passituṃ vā neva bhikkhūnaṃ na bhikkhunīnaṃ vaṭṭati. Dassanena cettha savanampi saṅgahitaṃ virūpekasesanayena. Yathā sakaṃ visayaālocanasabhāvatāya vā pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ savanakiriyāyapi dassanasaṅkhepasambhavato “dassanā” icceva vuttaṃ. Teneva vuttaṃ “pañcahi viññāṇehi na kañci dhammaṃ paṭivijānāti aññatra abhinipātamattā”ti. Dassanakamyatāya upasaṅkamitvā passato eva cettha vītikkamo hoti, ṭhitanisinnasayanokāse pana āgataṃ gacchantassa vā āpāthagataṃ passato siyā saṃkileso, na vītikkamo.

Regarding 'dancing, singing, music, and watching shows,' herein 'watching shows' (visūkadassana) is a viewing that is frivolous (visūka) and antagonistic (paṭāṇībhūta), because it is contrary to the teaching. Indeed, watching dancing and the like, which proceeds from desire and lust, does not conform to the Blessed One's teaching, which is set forth by the principle beginning with 'the non-doing of all evil' (Dī. Ni. 2.90; Dha. Pa. 183). Dancing, singing, music, and watching shows together constitute 'dancing, singing, music, and watching shows.' Herein, dancing performed by oneself and that caused to be performed by others are included by the single word 'dancing' in the Pāli, due to the general nature of the act of dancing. Similarly, the words 'singing' and 'music' include singing and causing to sing, and playing and causing to play. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as abstinence from dancing, singing, and music, and also from the viewing of such frivolous performances, even those such as a peacock's dance, whether performed by oneself or caused to be performed by others. It is not proper for either monks or nuns to perform dancing and the like, to have others perform them, or to watch them being performed. Herein, by 'watching,' hearing is also included, by the method of including dissimilar items (virūpekasesa). Just as, either due to the nature of perceiving its own object, or due to the possibility of summarizing the act of hearing among the five consciousnesses under the term 'seeing,' it is simply called 'seeing.' For this reason, it is said: 'One does not fully cognize any phenomenon by means of the five consciousnesses, except for mere impact.' Here, a transgression occurs only when one approaches with the desire to see and then sees. But if one sees something that comes into range while one is standing, sitting, or lying down, or while one is coming or going, there may be defilement, but no transgression.

Mālāgandhavilepanadhāraṇamaṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhānāti ettha mālāti yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi mālā-saddo loke baddhamālavācako, sāsane pana ruḷhiyā pupphesupi vutto, tasmā yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ baddhamabaddhaṃ vā, taṃ sabbaṃ “mālā”ti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gandhanti vāsacuṇṇadhūmādikaṃ vilepanato aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci gandhajātaṃ. Vilepananti vilepanatthaṃ pisitvā paṭiyattaṃ yaṃ kiñci chavirāgakaraṇaṃ. Piḷandhanaṃ dhāraṇaṃ, ūnaṭṭhānapūraṇaṃ maṇḍanaṃ, gandhavasena chavirāgavasena ca sādiyanaṃ [M 3.0254][V 3.0231] vibhūsanaṃ. Teneva dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.10) majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāyañca (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.293) “piḷandhanto dhāreti nāma, ūnaṭṭhānaṃ pūrento maṇḍeti nāma, gandhavasena chavirāgavasena ca sādiyanto vibhūseti nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Paramatthajotikāyaṃ pana khuddakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 2.pacchimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “mālādīsu dhāraṇādīni yathāsaṅkhyaṃ yojetabbānī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Ṭhānaṃ vuccati kāraṇaṃ, tasmā yāya dussīlyacetanāya tāni mālādhāraṇādīni mahājano karoti, sā dhāraṇamaṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhānaṃ.

Regarding 'the basis for wearing, adorning, and beautifying with garlands, perfumes, and ointments,' herein 'garland' refers to any kind of flower. Although in the world the word 'garland' denotes strung flowers, in the teaching, by convention, it is also used for flowers in general. Therefore, any flower, whether strung or unstrung, should be regarded as 'garland.' 'Perfume' refers to scented powders, incense, and the like—any kind of fragrant substance other than ointments. 'Ointment' refers to anything ground and prepared for the purpose of anointing, which beautifies the skin. The wearing of ornaments is 'wearing' (dhāraṇa); filling a deficiency is 'adornment' (maṇḍana); and enjoying by means of fragrance or by means of beautifying the skin is 'beautification' (vibhūsana). Thus, in the Commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya (Dī. Ni. A. 1.10) and the Commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya (Ma. Ni. A. 1.293), it is said: 'One who puts on an ornament is said to "wear"; one who fills a deficiency is said to "adorn"; and one who enjoys by means of fragrance or by means of beautifying the skin is said to "beautify."' In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary to the Khuddakapāṭha (Khu. Pā. A. 2. Pacchimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā), however, it is only stated: 'In the case of garlands and so on, "wearing" and so on are to be applied respectively.' 'Basis' (ṭhāna) is said to mean 'cause' (kāraṇa). Therefore, that immoral volition by which the populace wears garlands and so on, that is the 'basis for wearing, adornment, and beautification.'

Uccāsayanamahāsayanāti ettha uccāti ucca-saddena samānatthaṃ ekaṃ saddantaraṃ. Seti etthāti sayanaṃ, uccāsayanañca mahāsayanañca uccāsayanamahāsayanaṃ. Uccāsayanaṃ vuccati pamāṇātikkantaṃ mañcādi. Mahāsayanaṃ akappiyattharaṇehi atthataṃ āsandādi. Āsanañcettha sayaneneva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā pana ādhāre paṭikkhitte tadādhārā kiriyā paṭikkhittāva hoti, tasmā “uccāsayanamahāsayanā” icceva vuttaṃ, atthato pana tadupabhogabhūtanisajjānipajjanehi virati dassitāti daṭṭhabbā. Atha vā uccāsayanamahāsayanasayanāti etasmiṃ atthe ekasesanayena ayaṃ niddeso kato yathā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti, āsanakiriyāpubbakattā sayanakiriyāya sayanaggahaṇeneva āsanampi gahitanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'high and great beds,' herein `uccā` is another word synonymous with `ucca`. That on which one lies (seti) is a bed (sayana); a high bed and a great bed are 'high and great beds.' A 'high bed' is said to be a couch or the like that exceeds the proper measure. A 'great bed' is a high chair or the like, spread with unsuitable coverings. It should be understood that a seat (āsana) is also included herein by 'bed' (sayana). For when the support is rejected, the action dependent on that support is also rejected. Therefore, it is stated simply as 'from high and great beds.' In meaning, however, abstinence from the use of them for sitting and lying down is shown. Alternatively, this exposition is made by the method of elision (ekasesa), as in 'from name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.' Because the act of sitting precedes the act of lying down, it should be understood that 'seat' is also included by the taking up of 'bed.'

Jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Rajatanti kahāpaṇo lohamāsako jatumāsako dārumāsakoti ye vohāraṃ gacchanti, tassa ubhayassapi paṭiggahaṇaṃ jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇaṃ. Tividhañcettha paṭiggahaṇaṃ kāyena vācāya manasāti. Tattha kāyena paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggaṇhanaṃ, vācāya paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggahāpanaṃ, manasā paṭiggahaṇaṃ sādiyanaṃ. Tividhampi paṭiggahaṇaṃ sāmaññaniddesena ekasesanayena vā gahetvā “paṭiggahaṇā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā neva uggahetuṃ na uggahāpetuṃ na upanikkhittaṃ vā sādituṃ vaṭṭati. Imāni pana dasa sikkhāpadāni gahaṭṭhānampi sādhāraṇāni. Vuttañhetaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 13) “upāsakaupāsikānaṃ niccasīlavasena pañca sikkhāpadāni, sati vā ussāhe dasa, uposathaṅgavasena aṭṭhāti idaṃ gahaṭṭhasīla”nti. Ettha hi dasāti sāmaṇerehi rakkhitabbasīlamāha [M 3.0255] ghaṭikārādīnaṃ viya. Paramatthajotikāyaṃ pana khuddakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 2.sādhāraṇavisesavavatthāna) “ādito dve catutthapañcamāni upāsakānaṃ sāmaṇerānañca sādhāraṇāni niccasīlavasena, uposathasīlavasena pana upāsakānaṃ sattamaṭṭhamaṃ cekaṃ aṅgaṃ katvā sabbapacchimavajjāni sabbānipi sāmaṇerehi sādhāraṇāni, pacchimaṃ pana sāmaṇerānameva visesabhūta”nti [V 3.0232] vuttaṃ, taṃ “sati vā ussāhe dasā”ti iminā na sameti. Nāsanavatthūti liṅganāsanāya vatthu, adhiṭṭhānaṃ kāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Regarding 'the acceptance of gold and silver,' herein 'jātarūpa' means gold. 'Rajata' means kahāpaṇas, metal māsalas, lac māsalas, or wooden māsalas—whatever is used in commerce. The acceptance of both of these is 'the acceptance of gold and silver.' Herein, acceptance is threefold: by body, by speech, and by mind. Therein, acceptance by body is taking; acceptance by speech is causing to take; acceptance by mind is consenting. All three types of acceptance are referred to as 'acceptance' either by way of a general statement or by the method of elision (ekasesa). Therefore, it is not proper to take, to cause to take, or to consent to what has been deposited. These ten training rules are also common to householders. For it is said in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 13): 'For male and female lay followers, there are five training rules as constant morality; or, if there is energy, ten; and eight as the factors of the Uposatha—this is the householder's morality.' Here, 'ten' refers to the morality to be observed by novices, as in the case of Ghaṭikāra and others. In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary to the Khuddakapāṭha (Khu. Pā. A. 2. Sādhāraṇavisesavavatthāna), however, it is stated: 'The first two, the fourth, and the fifth are common to lay followers and novices as constant morality. As for the Uposatha precepts for lay followers, by combining the seventh and eighth into a single factor, all precepts except the very last one are common with those of novices. The last one, however, is specific to novices alone.' This does not accord with the statement 'or, if there is energy, ten.' 'A ground for expulsion' (nāsanavatthu) means a ground for the destruction of the monastic sign; that is to say, it is the basis, the cause.

107. Kintīti kena nu kho upāyena. “Attano pariveṇanti idaṃ puggalikaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Ayamettha gaṇṭhipadakārānaṃ adhippāyo – “vassaggena pattasenāsana”nti iminā tassa vassaggena pattaṃ saṅghikasenāsanaṃ vuttaṃ, “attano pariveṇa”nti imināpi tasseva puggalikasenāsanaṃ vuttanti. Ayaṃ panettha amhākaṃ khanti – “yattha vā vasatī”ti iminā saṅghikaṃ vā hotu puggalikaṃ vā, tassa nibaddhavasanakasenāsanaṃ vuttaṃ. “Yattha vā paṭikkamatī”ti iminā pana yaṃ ācariyassa upajjhāyassa vā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ upaṭṭhānādinimittaṃ nibaddhaṃ pavisati, taṃ ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “ubhayenapi attano pariveṇañca vassaggena pattasenāsanañca vutta”nti āha. Tattha attano pariveṇanti iminā ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ, vassaggena pattasenāsananti iminā pana tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ. Tadubhayampi saṅghikaṃ vā hotu puggalikaṃ vā, āvaraṇaṃ kātabbamevāti. Mukhadvārikanti mukhadvārena bhuñjitabbaṃ. Daṇḍakammaṃ katvāti daṇḍakammaṃ yojetvā. Daṇḍenti vinenti etenāti daṇḍo, soyeva kātabbattā kammanti daṇḍakammaṃ, āvaraṇādi.

107. How is this? By what means indeed? 'One's own dwelling' refers to individual quarters, it is said in the Gaṇṭhipadas (textual glosses). This is the intention of the Gaṇṭhipada authors here: 'the lodging obtained by seniority' is said to refer to the communal lodging obtained by that person through seniority, and 'one's own dwelling' is also said to refer to that same person's individual lodging. Our position here is this: by 'wherever he resides' is meant his regularly inhabited lodging, whether communal or individual. By 'wherever he frequents', however, is meant the residence of the teacher or preceptor which he regularly enters for the purpose of attendance, and so forth; that is said to be the residence of the teacher or preceptor. Therefore, to show both, it is said: 'Both one's own dwelling and the lodging obtained by seniority are mentioned.' Therein, by 'one's own dwelling' is indicated the residence of the teacher or preceptor; by 'the lodging obtained by seniority', however, is indicated his own residence. Both of these, whether communal or individual, must be enclosed. 'Through the main door' means it is to be eaten through the main door. 'Having performed a penalty action' means having applied a penalty action. They punish, they train by means of it—thus it is a penalty (daṇḍa); and because it is to be performed, it is an action (kamma), thus 'penalty action' (daṇḍakamma), such as enclosure, and so forth.

Sikkhāpadadaṇḍakammavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discussion of the case for the penalty action concerning the training rule is concluded.

Anāpucchāvaraṇavatthuādikathāvaṇṇanā

The commentary on the discussion of the cases beginning with enclosure without permission.

108. Daṇḍakammamassa karothāti assa daṇḍakammaṃ yojetha āṇāpetha. Daṇḍakammanti vā niggahakammaṃ, tasmā niggahamassa karothāti vuttaṃ [M 3.0256] hoti. Esa nayo sabbattha īdisesu ṭhānesu. Senāsanaggāho ca paṭippassambhatīti iminā ca chinnavasso ca hotīti dīpeti. Sace ākiṇṇadosova hoti, āyatiṃ saṃvare na tiṭṭhati, nikkaḍḍhitabboti ettha sace yāvatatiyaṃ vuccamāno na oramati, saṅghaṃ apaloketvā nāsetabbo. Puna pabbajjaṃ yācamānopi apaloketvā pabbājetabboti vadanti. Pacchimikāya vassāvāsikaṃ lacchatīti pacchimikāya puna vassaṃ upagatattā lacchati. Apaloketvā lābho dātabboti chinnavassatāya vuttaṃ. Itarāni pañca sikkhāpadānīti vikālabhojanādīni pañca. Accayaṃ desāpetabboti “accayo maṃ, bhante, accagamā”tiādinā nayena desāpetabbo.

108. "Perform a penalty action on him" means assign or command a penalty action for him. "Penalty action" here refers to disciplinary action; therefore, it means "perform disciplinary action on him." This is the method in all such similar instances. "And the taking of lodging is calmed" indicates that he also becomes one whose rains-residence is broken. If he is constantly full of faults and does not stand firm in future restraint, he should be expelled. Here, if he does not desist even after being told up to three times, he should be deprived of his monastic status after informing the Sangha. Even when he asks for ordination again, some say he should be ordained after informing the Sangha. "He will receive the rains-residence allowance for the latter period" means he will receive it because he has undertaken the rains-residence again in the latter period. That the benefit "should be given after informing" is said because of his broken rains-residence. The other five training rules are the five, beginning with eating at the wrong time. "He should be made to confess the transgression" means he should be made to confess according to the method beginning with, "Venerable sir, a transgression overcame me," and so forth.

Anāpucchāvaraṇavatthuādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discussion of the cases beginning with enclosure without permission is concluded.

Paṇḍakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The commentary on the discussion of the case of the paṇḍaka.

109. Paṇḍakavatthumhi [V 3.0233] “yo kāḷapakkhe itthī hoti, juṇhapakkhe puriso, ayaṃ pakkhapaṇḍako”ti keci vadanti, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “kāḷapakkhe paṇḍako hoti, juṇhapakkhe panassa pariḷāho vūpasammatī”ti apaṇḍakapakkhe pariḷāhavūpasamasseva vuttattā paṇḍakapakkhe ussannapariḷāhatā paṇḍakabhāvāpattīti viññāyati, tasmā idamevettha sārato paccetabbaṃ. Itthibhāvo pumbhāvo vā natthi etassāti abhāvako. Tasmiṃ yevassa pakkhe pabbajjā vāritāti ettha “apaṇḍakapakkhe pabbājetvā paṇḍakapakkhe nāsetabbo”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “apaṇḍakapakkhe pabbajito sace kilesakkhayaṃ pāpuṇāti, na nāsetabbo”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ paṇḍakassa kilesakkhayāsambhavato khīṇakilesassa ca paṇḍakabhāvānupapattito. Ahetukapaṭisandhikathāyañhi avisesena paṇḍakassa ahetukapaṭisandhitā vuttā. Āsittausūyapakkhapaṇḍakānañca paṭisandhito paṭṭhāyeva paṇḍakasabhāvo, na pavattiyaṃyevāti vadanti. Teneva ahetukapaṭisandhiniddese jaccandhabadhirādayo viya paṇḍako jātisaddena visesetvā na niddiṭṭho. Idhāpi [M 3.0257] catutthapārājikasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.233) “abhabbapuggale dassentena paṇḍakatiracchānagataubhatobyañjanakā tayo vatthuvipannā ahetukapaṭisandhikā, tesaṃ saggo avārito, maggo pana vārito”ti avisesena vuttaṃ.

109. Regarding the case of a paṇḍaka: Some say, "One who is a woman during the dark fortnight and a man during the bright fortnight—this is a pakkhapaṇḍaka." However, in the commentary, it is stated, "During the dark fortnight, one is a paṇḍaka, but during the bright fortnight, their affliction subsides." Since, in the non-paṇḍaka phase, it is stated only that the affliction subsides, it is understood that in the paṇḍaka phase, heightened affliction leads to the attainment of paṇḍaka status. Therefore, this is the essential point to be understood here. There is neither female nor male nature in them—this is the meaning of abhāvako. For this reason, ordination is prohibited during that very phase of theirs. Here, it is said in all three Gaṇṭhipadas: "Having ordained them during the non-paṇḍaka phase, one should deprive them of their monastic status during the paṇḍaka phase." Some, however, say, "If one ordained during the non-paṇḍaka phase attains the destruction of defilements, they should not be deprived of their monastic status." That is merely their opinion, because the destruction of defilements is impossible for a paṇḍaka, and the status of a paṇḍaka is untenable for one whose defilements are destroyed. In the discussion of rootless rebirth-linking, it is generally stated that a paṇḍaka has a rootless rebirth-linking without distinction. And the āsittaka, usūyaka, and pakkhapaṇḍakas are said to have the nature of a paṇḍaka from the very moment of rebirth-linking, not merely during the course of existence. For this reason, in the exposition of rootless rebirth-linking, the paṇḍaka is not specifically designated with the word "by birth," like those born blind or deaf. Here too, in the explanation of the fourth pārājika (Vin. Aṭṭha. 2.233), it is generally stated: "When illustrating incapable persons, the three—paṇḍakas, animals, and hermaphrodites—are those with defective bases and rootless rebirth-linking; heaven is not barred for them, but the path is barred."

Paṇḍakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discussion of the case of the paṇḍaka is concluded.

Theyyasaṃvāsakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The commentary on the discussion of the case of the fraudulent co-resident.

110. Theyyasaṃvāsakavatthumhi kolaññāti mātuvaṃse pituvaṃse ca jātā mātāpituppabhutisabbañātayo. Theyyāya saṃvāso etassāti theyyasaṃvāsako. So ca na saṃvāsamattasseva thenako idhādhippeto, atha kho liṅgassa tadubhayassa ca thenakopīti āha “tayo theyyasaṃvāsakā”tiādi. Na yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyatīti yathāvuḍḍhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vā sāmaṇerānaṃ vā vandanaṃ na sādiyati. Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyatīti attanā musāvādaṃ katvā dassitavassānurūpaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyati. Bhikkhuvassagaṇanādikoti iminā na ekakammādikova idha saṃvāso nāmāti dasseti.

110. In the case of the fraudulent co-resident, 'of good family' means all relatives, beginning with mother and father, born in the lineage of both mother and father. 'Fraudulent co-resident' means one whose cohabitation is for theft. Here, it is not merely the theft of cohabitation that is intended, but also the theft of the monastic sign, and of both. Thus, it is said, 'There are three fraudulent co-residents,' and so on. 'He does not approve of respect according to seniority' means he does not approve of the respect shown to monks or novices according to their seniority. 'He approves of respect according to seniority' means, having spoken falsely, he approves of respect according to the number of years he has declared. By 'calculation of a monk's years, and so forth,' it is shown that 'cohabitation' here does not mean just a single formal act and so forth.

Rāja…pe… bhayenāti ettha bhaya-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo “rājabhayena dubbhikkhabhayenā”tiādinā[V 3.0234]. Saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, yāva so suddhamānasoti rājabhayādīhi gahitaliṅgatāya so suddhamānaso yāva saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāsetīti attho. Yo hi rājabhayādiṃ vinā kevalaṃ bhikkhū vañcetvā tehi saddhiṃ saṃvasitukāmatāya liṅgaṃ gaṇhāti, so asuddhacittatāya liṅgaggahaṇeneva theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hoti. Ayaṃ pana tādisena asuddhacittena bhikkhū vañcetukāmatāya abhāvato yāva saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, tāva theyyasaṃvāsako nāma na hoti. Teneva “rājabhayādīhi gahitaliṅgānaṃ ‘gihī maṃ samaṇoti jānantū’ti vañcanācitte satipi bhikkhūnaṃ vañcetukāmatāya abhāvā doso na jāto”ti tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “vūpasantabhayatā [M 3.0258] idha suddhacittatā”ti vadanti, evañca sati so vūpasantabhayo yāva saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, tāva theyyasaṃvāsako na hotīti ayamattho viññāyati. Imasmiñca atthe viññāyamāne avūpasantabhayassa saṃvāsasādiyanepi theyyasaṃvāsakatā na hotīti āpajjeyya, na ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ avūpasantabhayassa saṃvāsasādiyanepi atheyyasaṃvāsakatā dassitā. Sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni bhuñjantoti ca iminā avūpasantatayenapi saṃvāsaṃ asādiyanteneva vasitabbanti dīpeti. Teneva tīsupi gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ “yasmā vihāraṃ āgantvā saṅghikaṃ gaṇhantassa saṃvāsaṃ pariharituṃ dukkaraṃ, tasmā sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni bhuñjantoti idaṃ vutta”nti, tasmā rājabhayādīhi gahitaliṅgatāyevettha suddhacittatāti gahetabbaṃ.

Here, the word 'fear' in 'from fear of the king...etc.' should be applied individually, as in 'from fear of the king, from fear of famine,' and so on. 'He does not consent to cohabitation, for as long as he is of pure mind'—the meaning is that he, being of pure mind on account of having taken the sign out of fear of the king and the like, does not consent to cohabitation. For one who, without fear of the king or such, takes the sign merely desiring to deceive the monks and cohabit with them, is called a fraudulent resident by the very act of taking the sign, due to his impure mind. This one, however, because he lacks the desire to deceive the monks with such an impure mind, is not called a fraudulent resident as long as he does not consent to cohabitation. Therefore, it is stated in all three 'knotty points' (gaṇṭhipadas): 'For those who have taken the sign due to fear of the king and the like, even if there is a deceptive thought, "Let householders know me as an ascetic," no fault arises due to the absence of a desire to deceive the monks.' Some, however, say, 'Here, purity of mind means the subsidence of fear.' If that is so, then this meaning is understood: as long as he whose fear has subsided does not consent to cohabitation, he is not a fraudulent resident. And if this meaning is understood, it would follow that even if one whose fear has not subsided consents to cohabitation, he would not be a fraudulent resident. But the commentary does not indicate that one whose fear has not subsided is not a fraudulent resident even if he consents to cohabitation. Moreover, by 'he eats the food of all sectarians,' it is shown that even one whose fear has not subsided must live without consenting to cohabitation. Therefore, it is stated in all three 'knotty points': 'Since it is difficult for one who comes to the monastery and takes what belongs to the Sangha to avoid cohabitation, this is why "he eats the food of all sectarians" was said.' Thus, here, 'purity of mind' should be understood precisely as having taken the sign due to fear of the king and the like.

Sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattānīti sabbasāmayikānaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ katvā vīthicatukkādīsu ṭhapetvā dātabbabhattāni. Kāyaparihāriyānīti kāyena pariharitabbāni. Abbhuggacchantīti abhimukhaṃ gacchanti. Kammantānuṭṭhānenāti kasigorakkhādikammakaraṇena. Tadeva pattacīvaraṃ ādāya vihāraṃ gacchatīti cīvarāni nivāsanapārupanavasena ādāya pattañca aṃsakūṭe laggetvā vihāraṃ gacchati. Nāpi sayaṃ jānātīti “yo evaṃ pabbajati, so theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hotī”ti vā “evaṃ kātuṃ na labhatī”ti vā “evaṃ pabbajito samaṇo na hotī”ti vā na jānāti. Yo evaṃ pabbajati, so theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hotīti idaṃ pana nidassanamattaṃ. Anupasampannakāleyevāti iminā upasampannakāle sutvā sacepi nāroceti, theyyasaṃvāsako na hotīti dīpeti.

'Meals of all sectarians' means meals that are to be given, having been made common to all persuasions and placed in streets, at crossroads, and so on. 'To be managed by the body' means things to be taken care of with the body. 'They go forth' means they go towards. 'By undertaking work' means by doing work such as farming or cattle-herding. 'Taking that very bowl and robes, he goes to the monastery' means having taken the robes as lower and upper garments, and having hung the bowl on his shoulder, he goes to the monastery. 'Nor does he know himself' means he does not know: 'one who goes forth thus is called a fraudulent resident,' or 'it is not allowable to do thus,' or 'one who has gone forth thus is not an ascetic.' The statement 'one who goes forth thus is called a fraudulent resident' is merely an example. 'During the time he is not yet fully ordained'—by this, it is shown that if, upon hearing of this at the time of full ordination, he does not approve, he is not a fraudulent resident.

Sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya…pe… theyyasaṃvāsako na hotīti idaṃ bhikkhūhi dinnaliṅgassa apariccattattā na liṅgathenako hoti, liṅgānurūpassa saṃvāsassa sāditattā nāpi saṃvāsathenako hotīti vuttaṃ. Eko bhikkhu kāsāye saussāhova odātaṃ nivāsetvāti etthāpi idameva kāraṇaṃ [V 3.0235] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Parato sāmaṇero saliṅge ṭhitotiādinā sāmaṇerassa vuttavidhānesupi atheyyasaṃvāsakapakkhe ayameva nayo. Bhikkhuniyāpi eseva nayoti vuttamevatthaṃ “sāpi hi gihibhāvaṃ patthayamānā”tiādinā vibhāveti. Yo koci vuḍḍhapabbajitoti [M 3.0259] sāmaṇeraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Mahāpeḷādīsūti etena gihisantakaṃ dassitaṃ. Sayaṃ sāmaṇerova…pe… theyyasaṃvāsako na hotīti ettha kiñcāpi theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti, pārājikaṃ pana āpajjatiyeva. Sesamettha uttānameva.

'Without renouncing the training...etc....he is not a fraudulent resident'—this is said because, as the sign given by the monks has not been relinquished, he is not a thief of the sign; nor, as he consents to cohabitation that conforms to the sign, is he a thief of cohabitation. In 'a certain monk, though zealous for the ochre robe, wears white,' here too, the same reason should be understood. Furthermore, regarding 'a novice remaining in his own sign,' and so on, this same method applies to the cases mentioned for a novice in the category of a non-fraudulent resident. The statement 'for a bhikkhunī, this is the same method' explains this very point with 'for she too, desiring the state of a householder,' and so on. 'Any adult ordinand' is said with reference to a novice. 'In Mahāpeḷā, etc.'—by this, what belongs to a householder is shown. 'He himself being a novice...etc....he is not a fraudulent resident'—here, although he is not a fraudulent resident, he nevertheless incurs a pārājika offense. The rest here is clear.

Theyyasaṃvāsakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of the fraudulent resident is concluded.

Titthiyapakkantakakathāvaṇṇanā

The commentary on the story of the sectarian apostates

Titthiyapakkantakakathāyaṃ tesaṃ liṅge ādinnamatte titthiyapakkantako hotīti “titthiyo bhavissāmī”ti gatassa liṅgaggahaṇeneva tesaṃ laddhipi gahitāyeva hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Kenaci pana “tesaṃ liṅge ādinnamatte laddhiyā gahitāyapi aggahitāyapi titthiyapakkantako hotī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi “titthiyo bhavissāmī”ti gatassa liṅgasampaṭicchanato aññaṃ laddhiggahaṇaṃ nāma atthi. Liṅgasampaṭicchaneneva hi so gahitaladdhiko hoti. Teneva “vīmaṃsanatthaṃ kusacīrādīni…pe… yāva na sampaṭicchati, tāva taṃ laddhi rakkhati. Sampaṭicchitamatte titthiyapakkantako hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Naggova ājīvakānaṃ upassayaṃ gacchati, padavāre padavāre dukkaṭanti “ājīvako bhavissa”nti asuddhacittena gamanapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Naggena hutvā gamanapaccayāpi dukkaṭā na muccatiyeva. Kūṭavassaṃ gaṇentoti kūṭavassaṃ gaṇetvā saṃvāsaṃ sādiyantoti adhippāyo.

In the story of the sectarian apostates, it is said that one becomes a sectarian apostate as soon as their insignia are adopted, because for one who goes with the intention, 'I will become a sectarian,' their doctrine is considered adopted by the very act of taking the insignia. However, some say, 'One becomes a sectarian apostate as soon as their insignia are adopted, whether their doctrine has been adopted or not.' This should not be accepted. For one who goes with the intention, 'I will become a sectarian,' there is no adoption of doctrine other than the acceptance of the insignia. Indeed, by merely accepting the insignia, one is considered to have adopted the doctrine. Therefore, it is said: 'For the purpose of investigation, regarding the kusa grass robe, etc., [...] as long as one does not accept it, one protects one's doctrine. As soon as one accepts it, one becomes a sectarian apostate.' Going naked to the residence of the Ājīvakas, at every step, there is a dukkaṭa offense—a dukkaṭa is stated on account of going with an impure mind, intending 'I will become an Ājīvaka.' Moreover, on account of going naked, one is by no means freed from a dukkaṭa offense. 'Counting false years'—the intention is that they consent to co-residence having counted false years.

Titthiyapakkantakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of the sectarian apostates is concluded.

111. Tiracchānagatavatthu uttānameva.

111. The case concerning an animal is self-evident.

Mātughātakādivatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The commentary on the stories of matricide and so on

112. Mātughātakādivatthūsu apavāhananti apagamanaṃ, patikaraṇanti attho. Yathā samānajātikassa vikopane kammaṃ garutaraṃ, na tathā vijātikassāti āha “manussitthibhūtā”ti[V 3.0236]. Puttasambandhena mātupitusamaññā[M 3.0260], dattakittimādivasenapi puttavohāro loke dissati, so ca kho pariyāyatoti nippariyāyasiddhataṃ dassetuṃ “janikā mātā”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā manussattabhāve ṭhitasseva kusaladhammānaṃ tikkhavisadasūrabhāvāpatti yathā taṃ tiṇṇampi bodhisattānaṃ bodhittayanibbattiyaṃ, evaṃ manussattabhāve ṭhitasseva akusaladhammānampi tikkhavisadasūrabhāvāpattīti āha “sayampi manussajātikenevā”ti. Cutianantaraṃ phalaṃ anantaraṃ nāma, tasmiṃ anantare niyuttaṃ, taṃnibbattanena anantarakaraṇasīlaṃ, anantarapayojanaṃ vā ānantariyaṃ, tena ānantariyena mātughātakakammena. Pitughātakepi yena manussabhūto janako pitā sayampi manussajātikeneva satā sañcicca jīvitā voropito, ayaṃ ānantariyena pitughātakakammena pitughātakotiādinā sabbaṃ veditabbanti āha “pitughātakepi eseva nayo”ti.

112. In the cases of matricide and so on, 'apavāhana' means 'removal,' and its meaning is 'counter-action.' Just as the act is more severe when harming one of the same species, but not so one of a different species—thus it is said, 'being a human female.' The terms 'mother' and 'father' are designations based on the connection with a child; and even in the world, the term 'son' is seen used in ways such as 'adopted' or 'foster,' but that is only a figurative expression. To show the non-figurative, established meaning, it is said, 'the birth-giver is the mother.' Just as, for one established in the human state, there is the attainment of sharp, clear, and courageous wholesome qualities—as in the production of the threefold enlightenment of the Bodhisattas—so too, for one established in the human state, there is the attainment of sharp, clear, and courageous unwholesome qualities. Thus it is said, 'by one who is himself of human birth.' The result immediately following death is called 'anantara' (immediate). That which is connected to that immediate result, which by its nature produces that result without interval, or which has an immediate purpose, is 'ānantariya' (an act with immediate retribution). By that ānantariya kamma of matricide. In the case of patricide as well, it is said, 'in the case of patricide, the method is the same,' so that all should be understood in this way: when the birth-giving father, who is a human being, is intentionally deprived of life by one who is himself of human birth, this is patricide by the ānantariya kamma of patricide, and so on.

Parivattitaliṅgampi (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.128; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.275; vibha. aṭṭha. 809) mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā jīvitā voropentassa ānantariyakammaṃ hotiyeva. Satipi hi liṅgaparivatte so eva ekakammanibbatto bhavaṅgappabandho jīvitindriyappabandho ca, nāññoti. Yo pana sayaṃ manusso tiracchānabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā, sayaṃ vā tiracchānabhūto manussabhūtaṃ, tiracchānabhūtoyeva vā tiracchānabhūtaṃ jīvitā voropeti, tassa kammaṃ ānantariyaṃ na hoti, bhāriyaṃ pana hoti, ānantariyaṃ āhacceva tiṭṭhati. Eḷakacatukkaṃ saṅgāmacatukkaṃ coracatukkañcettha kathetabbaṃ. “Eḷakaṃ māremī”ti abhisandhināpi hi eḷakaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ manusso manussabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā mārento ānantariyaṃ phusati maraṇādhippāyeneva ānantariyavatthuno vikopitattā. Eḷakābhisandhinā pana mātāpitiaasandhinā vā eḷakaṃ mārento ānantariyaṃ na phusati ānantariyavatthuabhāvato. Mātāpitiabhisandhinā mātāpitaro mārento phusateva. Esa nayo itarasmimpi catukkadvaye. Yathā ca mātāpitūsu, evaṃ arahantepi etāni catukkāni veditabbāni. Sabbattha hi purimaṃ abhisandhicittaṃ appamāṇaṃ, vadhakacittaṃ pana tadārammaṇaṃ jīvitindriyañca ānantariyānānantarabhāve pamāṇaṃ. Katānantariyakammo ca “tassa kammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhissāmī”ti sakalacakkavāḷaṃ mahācetiyappamāṇehi kañcanathūpehi pūretvāpi sakalacakkavāḷaṃ pūretvā nisinnassa [M 3.0261] bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvāpi buddhassa bhagavato saṅghāṭikaṇṇaṃ amuñcanto vicaritvāpi kāyassa bhedā nirayameva upapajjati, pabbajjañca na labhati.

Even if their gender has changed, for one who deprives their mother or father of life, it is indeed an ānantariya kamma. For even with a change of gender, that very same existence-continuum and life-faculty continuum produced by a single kamma persists, and nothing else. However, if a human being deprives of life a mother or father who has become an animal, or if one who has become an animal deprives of life a mother or father who is a human being, or if one who has become an animal deprives of life a mother or father who has also become an animal, that kamma is not an ānantariya, but it is grave; it stands bordering on an ānantariya. Here, the fourfold cases concerning a goat, a battle, and a thief should be related. For, with the intention 'I will kill a goat,' a person who kills their human mother or father standing in the place of a goat incurs an ānantariya kamma, because the object of an ānantariya has been violated with the intention to kill. But one who kills a goat with the intention for a goat and without the intention for one's parents does not incur an ānantariya kamma, due to the absence of the object of an ānantariya. One who kills their parents with the intention for their parents certainly incurs it. This is the method in the other two fourfold cases as well. And as with mothers and fathers, so too with arahants should these fourfold cases be understood. For in all cases, the prior intentional consciousness is not the measure; rather, the consciousness at the moment of killing, its object, and the life-faculty are the measure for it being an ānantariya or not an ānantariya. And one who has committed an ānantariya kamma, even if—thinking, 'I will ward off the result of that kamma'—they were to fill the entire world-system with golden stūpas the size of the Mahācetiya, or give a great offering to the community of monks seated filling the entire world-system, or wander about not letting go of the corner of the Blessed One, the Buddha's, outer robe, upon the breakup of the body, they are reborn in hell and do not obtain ordination.

115. Icchamānanti [V 3.0237] odātavatthavasanaṃ icchamānaṃ. Tenevāha “gihibhāve sampaṭicchitamatteyevā”ti. Saṅghabhedakakathāvitthāro parato āvi bhavissati. Catunnaṃ kammānanti apalokanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ kammānaṃ. Duṭṭhacittenāti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “vadhakacittenā”ti. Vadhakacetanāya hi dūsitacittaṃ idha duṭṭhacittaṃ nāma. Lohitaṃ uppādetīti ettha tathāgatassa abhejjakāyatāya parūpakkamena cammacchedaṃ katvā lohitapaggharaṇaṃ nāma natthi, sarīrassa pana antoyeva ekasmiṃ ṭhāne lohitaṃ samosarati, āghātena pakuppamānaṃ sañcitaṃ hoti. Devadattena paviddhasilato bhijjitvā gatasakkhalikāpi tathāgatassa pādantaṃ pahari, pharasunā pahaṭo viya pādo antolohitoyeva ahosi. Jīvako pana tathāgatassa ruciyā satthakena cammaṃ chinditvā tamhā ṭhānā duṭṭhalohitaṃ nīharitvā phāsumakāsi, tenassa puññakammameva ahosi. Tenāha “jīvako viyā”tiādi.

115. 'Desiring' means desiring to wear white robes. Therefore, it is said, 'merely upon accepting the state of a householder.' The detailed discussion on causing schism in the Saṅgha will become evident later. 'Of the four acts' refers to the four acts such as announcement. 'With a malicious mind' explains the meaning as stated: 'with the mind of a murderer.' Here, a 'malicious mind' means a mind corrupted by murderous intent. Regarding 'produces blood': here, because the Tathāgata’s body is unbreakable, there is no such thing as making an incision in the skin and causing blood to flow through the attack of another. However, blood does collect internally in one place; agitated by a blow, it becomes congested. When Devadatta hurled a rock, a fragment that broke off struck the Tathāgata’s foot, and the foot became just as if struck by an axe, with internal bleeding. Jīvaka, however, by the Tathāgata's consent, cut the skin with a scalpel, drew out the bad blood from that place, and made him comfortable. For him, this was a meritorious act. Hence, it is said, 'like Jīvaka,' and so on.

Atha ye parinibbute tathāgate cetiyaṃ bhindanti, bodhiṃ chindanti, dhātumhi upakkamanti, tesaṃ kiṃ hotīti? Bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ hoti ānantariyasadisaṃ. Sadhātukaṃ pana thūpaṃ vā paṭimaṃ vā bādhamānaṃ bodhisākhaṃ chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Sacepi tattha nilīnā sakuṇā cetiye vaccaṃ pātenti, chindituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Paribhogacetiyato hi sarīracetiyaṃ garutaraṃ. Cetiyavatthuṃ bhinditvā gacchante bodhimūlepi chinditvā harituṃ vaṭṭati. Yā pana bodhisākhā bodhigharaṃ bādhati, taṃ geharakkhaṇatthaṃ chindituṃ na labhati. Bodhiatthañhi gehaṃ, na gehatthāya bodhi. Āsanagharepi eseva nayo. Yasmiṃ pana āsanaghare dhātu nihitā hoti, tassa rakkhaṇatthāya bodhisākhaṃ chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Bodhijagganatthaṃ ojoharaṇasākhaṃ vā pūtiṭṭhānaṃ vā chindituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva, satthu rūpakāyapaṭijaggane viya puññampi hoti.

Then, what of those who, after the Tathāgata has attained Parinibbāna, destroy a shrine, cut down a Bodhi tree, or commit an offense against a relic? It is a grave kamma, similar to an ānantariya kamma. However, it is permissible to cut a Bodhi branch that is damaging a stūpa or an image containing relics. Even if birds perched there drop excrement on the shrine, it is still permissible to cut it. For a shrine of the body is more venerable than a shrine of use. When branches are breaking the structure of the shrine, it is permissible to cut the tree even at its root and remove it. But a Bodhi branch that is damaging the Bodhi-house may not be cut for the sake of protecting the house, for the house is for the sake of the Bodhi, not the Bodhi for the sake of the house. This is also the method in the case of a hall of the seat. But in a hall of the seat where a relic has been placed, it is permissible to cut a Bodhi branch for its protection. For the sake of maintaining the Bodhi tree, it is indeed permissible to cut a branch that is draining its sap or a part that is rotten; and there is even merit in it, as in tending to the Teacher's physical body.

Mātughātakādivatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of Cases Beginning with Matricide is finished.

Ubhatobyañjanakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Topic Concerning Those of Dual Gender

116. Ubhato [M 3.0262] byañjanamassa atthīti ubhatobyañjanakoti iminā asamānādhikaraṇavisayo bāhiratthasamāsoyaṃ, purimapade ca vibhattialopoti dasseti. Byañjananti cettha itthinimittaṃ purisanimittañca adhippetaṃ. Atha ubhatobyañjanakassa ekameva indriyaṃ, udāhu dveti? Ekameva “yassa itthindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa purisindriyaṃ uppajjatīti? No. Yassa vā pana purisindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa itthindriyaṃ uppajjatīti? No”ti [V 3.0238] (yama. 3.indriyayamaka.188) ekasmiṃ santāne indriyadvayassa paṭisiddhattā, tañca kho itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthindriyaṃ, purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisindriyaṃ. Yadi evaṃ dutiyabyañjanakassa abhāvo āpajjati. Indriyañhi byañjanakāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tañca tassa natthīti? Vuccate – na tassa indriyaṃ dutiyabyañjanakāraṇaṃ. Kasmā? Sadā abhāvato. Itthiubhatobyañjanakassa hi yadā itthiyā rāgacittaṃ uppajjati, tadā purisabyañjanaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, itthibyañjanaṃ paṭicchannaṃ guḷhaṃ hoti, tathā itarassa itaraṃ. Yadi ca tesaṃ indriyaṃ dutiyabyañjanakāraṇaṃ bhaveyya, sadāpi byañjanadvayaṃ tiṭṭheyya, na pana tiṭṭhati, tasmā veditabbametaṃ “na tassa taṃ byañjanakāraṇaṃ, kammasahāyaṃ pana rāgacittamevettha kāraṇa”nti.

116. "One who has both characteristics" means a hermaphrodite. This is an external compound with differing subjects, and it also shows the non-elision of the case ending in the first term. "Characteristic" here refers to both the female and male signs. Now, does a hermaphrodite have one faculty or two? Only one, for it is said: "When the female faculty arises in someone, does the male faculty arise in them? No. Or when the male faculty arises in someone, does the female faculty arise in them? No" (Yam 3.188). Since two faculties are denied in a single continuum, the female faculty belongs to the female hermaphrodite, and the male faculty to the male hermaphrodite. If so, does this mean the second characteristic is non-existent? For it is said that the faculty is the cause of the characteristic, and that is not present in this case? It is answered: The faculty is not the cause of the second characteristic for them. Why? Because it is always absent in that role. For when a lustful thought arises in a female hermaphrodite, the male characteristic becomes apparent, while the female characteristic remains concealed and hidden. The same applies conversely to the other. If their faculty were the cause of the second characteristic, both characteristics would always be present. But they are not always present. Therefore, it should be understood that "the faculty is not the cause of that characteristic; rather, the lustful thought, aided by kamma, is the cause here."

Yasmā cassa ekameva indriyaṃ hoti, tasmā itthiubhatobyañjanako sayampi gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, parampi gaṇhāpeti. Purisaubhatobyañjanako paraṃ gaṇhāpeti, sayaṃ pana na gaṇhāti. Yadi paṭisandhiyaṃ purisaliṅgaṃ, yadi paṭisandhiyaṃ itthiliṅganti ca paṭisandhiyaṃ liṅgasabbhāvo kurundiyaṃvutto, so ca ayutto. Pavattiyaṃyeva hi itthiliṅgādīni samuṭṭhahanti, na paṭisandhiyaṃ. Paṭisandhiyaṃ pana indriyameva samuṭṭhāti, na liṅgādīni. Na ca indriyameva liṅganti sakkā vattuṃ indriyaliṅgānaṃ bhinnasabhāvattā. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 632) –

Because there is only one faculty, a female hermaphrodite can both conceive a child themselves and cause another to conceive. A male hermaphrodite can cause another to conceive but cannot conceive themselves. The statement in the Kurundī that at rebirth-linking the presence of either a male sign or a female sign is determined is incorrect. For the signs, such as the female sign, arise only during the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking. At rebirth-linking, only the faculty arises, not the signs. Moreover, one cannot say that the faculty itself is the sign, because the faculty and the signs have different natures. This has been stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī (DhsA. 632):

“Itthattaṃ itthibhāvoti ubhayaṃ ekatthaṃ, itthisabhāvoti attho. Ayaṃ kammajo paṭisandhisamuṭṭhito. Itthiliṅgādi pana itthindriyaṃ paṭicca pavatte samuṭṭhitaṃ. Yathā bīje sati bījaṃ paṭicca bījapaccayā rukkho vaḍḍhitvā sākhāviṭapasampanno hutvā ākāsaṃ pūretvā [M 3.0263] tiṭṭhati, evameva itthibhāvasaṅkhāte itthindriye sati itthiliṅgādīni honti. Bījaṃ viya hi itthindriyaṃ, bījaṃ paṭicca vaḍḍhitvā ākāsaṃ pūretvā ṭhitarukkho viya itthindriyaṃ paṭicca itthiliṅgādīni pavatte samuṭṭhahanti. Tattha itthindriyaṃ na cakkhuviññeyyaṃ, manoviññeyyameva. Itthiliṅgādīni cakkhuviññeyyānipi manoviññeyyānipī”ti.

“Womanhood and the state of being a woman, both are one and the same thing; the meaning is the nature of a woman. This is karmically produced and arises at rebirth-linking. However, the female characteristics and so on arise in the course of existence, dependent on the female faculty.
