187-189. ‘Three things are lost’ means they are lost because latrines and so forth are prohibited for bhikkhunīs. ‘Vāreyya’ means a marriage ceremony. ‘Suttanta’ means one’s own well-practiced discourse. ‘It does not fall apart’ means it is not destroyed, it does not disappear.

Pahiteyeva anujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Discourse on the Allowance Given by the Very Act of Being Sent.

199. Bhikkhugatikoti bhikkhunissitako. So pana yasmā bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ vasati, tasmā vuttaṃ “bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ vasanakapuriso”ti. Sattāhakaraṇīyena gantvā bahiddhā aruṇuṭṭhāpanaṃ [V 3.0258] ratticchedo. Animantitena gantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ettha animantitattā sattāhakiccaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā gacchantassapi vassacchedo ceva dukkaṭañca hotīti veditabbaṃ. Yathāvuttañhi ratticchedakāraṇaṃ vinā tirovihāre vasitvā āgacchissāmīti gacchatopi vassacchedaṃ vadanti. Gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti sattāhakaraṇīyena gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ gacchantena ca antoupacārasīmāyaṃ ṭhiteneva “antosattāhe āgacchissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā gantabbaṃ. Sace ābhogaṃ akatvā upacārasīmaṃ atikkamati, chinnavassova hotīti vadanti. Bhaṇḍakanti cīvaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pahiṇantīti cīvaradhovanādikammena pahiṇanti. Sampāpuṇituṃ [M 3.0283] na sakkoti, vaṭṭatīti ettha “ajjeva āgamissāmī”ti sāmantavihāraṃ gantvā puna āgacchantassa antarāmagge sace aruṇuggamanaṃ hoti, vassacchedopi na hoti, ratticchedadukkaṭañca natthīti vadanti. “Ācariyaṃ passissāmī”ti pana gantuṃ labhatīti “agilānampi ācariyaṃ upajjhāyaṃ vā passissāmī”ti sattāhakaraṇīyena gantuṃ labhati. Sace pana naṃ ācariyo “ajja mā gacchā”ti vadati, vaṭṭatīti evaṃ sattāhakaraṇīyena gataṃ antosattāheyeva puna āgacchantaṃ sace ācariyo upajjhāyo vā “ajja mā gacchā”ti vadati, vaṭṭati, sattāhātikkamepi anāpattīti adhippāyo, vassacchedo pana hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ sattāhassa bahiddhā vītināmitattā.

199. ‘Bhikkhugatika’ means one dependent on a bhikkhu. Since he lives with the bhikkhus, it is said, ‘a man living with the bhikkhus.’ To go on a seven-day matter and have the dawn arise outside constitutes a break of the night. Regarding the statement, ‘It is not permissible to go uninvited,’ it should be understood that for one who, being uninvited, goes having undertaken a seven-day duty, there is both a breaking of the rains-residence and an offense of wrongdoing. For they say that the rains-residence is broken even for one who goes thinking, ‘I will stay in a neighboring monastery and return,’ without a reason for breaking the night as stated. ‘It is permissible to go’ means it is permissible to go on a seven-day matter. And when going thus, one should go only after standing within the boundary of the precincts and making the reflection, ‘I will return within seven days.’ If one crosses the boundary of the precincts without making this reflection, they say that his rains-residence is broken. ‘Bhaṇḍaka’ is said with reference to the robe. ‘Pahiṇanti’ (they send) means they send him on an errand such as washing a robe. Regarding ‘If one is unable to reach it, it is permissible,’ they say that if one goes to a neighboring monastery thinking, ‘I will return today,’ and on the way back dawn arises, there is no breaking of the rains-residence, nor is there an offense of wrongdoing for breaking the night. However, regarding ‘one may go to see one’s teacher,’ one may go on a seven-day matter to see one’s teacher or preceptor, even if they are not ill. Furthermore, if the teacher tells him, ‘Do not go today,’ it is permissible. The meaning is this: if one who has gone on a seven-day matter is returning within the seven days, and his teacher or preceptor tells him, ‘Do not go today,’ it is permissible; even if the seven days are exceeded, there is no offense. However, it should be understood that the rains-residence is indeed broken, because the time was spent outside the seven-day limit.

Antarāye anāpattivassacchedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on No Offense in case of an Obstacle and on the Breaking of the Rains-Residence.

201. Sace dūraṃ gato hoti, sattāhavārena aruṇo uṭṭhāpetabboti iminā vassacchedakāraṇe sati sattāhakaraṇīyena gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti.

201. If he has gone far away, the dawn should be made to rise within seven days. This indicates that when there is a reason for breaking the rains-residence, it is permissible to go for a seven-day task.

Vajādīsu vassūpagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Entering the Rains-Residence in Vajji and Other Places.

203. “Idha vassaṃ upemī”ti tikkhattuṃ vattabbanti satthassāvihārattā “imasmiṃ vihāre”ti avatvā “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti ettakameva vattabbaṃ. Satthe pana vassaṃ upagantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti kuṭikādīnaṃ abhāve “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti vacībhedaṃ katvā upagantuṃ na vaṭṭati, ālayakaraṇamatteneva vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Vippakiratīti visuṃ visuṃ gacchati. Tīsu ṭhānesu natthi vassacchede āpattīti tehi saddhiṃ gacchantasseva natthi āpatti, tehi viyujjitvā gamane pana āpattiyeva, pavāretuñca na labhati.

203. Regarding ‘One should say three times, “I enter upon the rains-residence here,”’ because a caravan is not a monastery, one should not say, ‘in this monastery,’ but should say only this much: ‘I enter upon the rains-residence here.’ However, regarding ‘it is not proper to enter upon the rains-residence in a caravan,’ the meaning is that in the absence of huts and so on, it is not proper to enter by making the verbal declaration, ‘I enter upon the rains-residence here’; it is proper only by the mere act of making it one’s abode. ‘Vippakirati’ (scatters) means they go separately. Regarding ‘In three situations there is no offense in breaking the rains-residence,’ there is no offense only for one who goes together with them. But if one goes separated from them, there is indeed an offense, and one is not permitted to perform the Pavāraṇā.

Vassaṃ anupagantabbaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Places Unsuitable for Entering upon the Rains-Residence.

204. Seyyathāpi [V 3.0259] pisācillikāti ettha pisācā eva pisācillikā, pisācadārakātipi vadanti. Pavisanadvāraṃ yojetvāti sakavāṭabaddhameva yojetvā. Pañcannaṃ chadanānanti tiṇapaṇṇaiṭṭhakasilāsudhāsaṅkhātānaṃ pañcannaṃ chadanānaṃ. Idañca yebhuyyena vuttanti veditabbaṃ rukkhādīsu [M 3.0284] padaracchadanāyapi kuṭikāya vassūpagamanassa vuttattā. Na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabbanti vacībhedaṃ katvā vassūpagamanaṃ sandhāyeva paṭikkhepo, na ālayakaraṇavasena upagamanaṃ sandhāyāti vadanti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana avisesena vuttattā aṭṭhakathāyañca dutiyapārājikasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.84) “vassaṃ upagacchantena hi nālakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannenapi pañcannaṃ chadanānaṃ aññatarena channeyeva sadvārabandhe senāsane upagantabbaṃ. Tasmā vassakāle sace senāsanaṃ labhati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce labhati, hatthakammaṃ pariyesitvāpi kātabbaṃ. Hatthakammaṃ alabhantena sāmampi kātabbaṃ, na tveva asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabba”nti daḷhaṃ katvā vuttattā asenāsanikassa nāvādiṃ vinā aññattha ālayo na vaṭṭatīti amhākaṃ khanti. Nāvāsatthavajesuyeva hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, nāvāya vassaṃ upagantu”ntiādinā sati asati vā senāsane vassūpagamanassa visuṃ anuññātattā “na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabba”nti ayaṃ paṭikkhepo tattha na labbhatīti asati senāsane ālayavasenapi nāvādīsu upagamanaṃ vuttaṃ. Ṭaṅkitamañco nāma dīghe mañcapāde majjhe vijjhitvā aṭaniyo pavesetvā kato mañco. Tassa idaṃ upari idaṃ heṭṭhāti natthi, parivattetvā atthatopi tādisova hoti, taṃ susāne devaṭṭhāne ca ṭhapenti, catunnaṃ pāsāṇānaṃ upari pāsāṇaṃ attharitvā kataṃ gehampi “ṭaṅkitamañco”ti vuccati.

204. Herein, regarding ‘just as a pisācillikā,’ pisācillikā are pisācas themselves; some also say they are young pisācas. ‘Having fitted the entrance door’ means having fitted it, secured with its own door-leaf. ‘Of the five coverings’ means of the five kinds of coverings reckoned as grass, leaves, tiles, stone, and plaster. And this should be understood as a general statement, because entering upon the rains-residence in a hut with a plank roof in a tree and so on has also been stated. Regarding ‘Bhikkhus, one without a dwelling should not enter upon the rains-residence,’ they say that this prohibition refers only to entering upon the rains-residence by making a verbal declaration, not to entering by way of making it one’s abode. However, since it is stated without distinction in the Pāḷi, and since it is stated emphatically in the commentary on the second Pārājika (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.84): ‘Indeed, one entering upon the rains-residence, even if one has undertaken the Nālaka practice, should enter upon it in a dwelling that is covered by one of the five kinds of coverings and has a door that can be secured. Therefore, during the rains-residence, if one gets a dwelling, this is excellent. If one does not get one, one should seek manual labor and build one. Not getting manual labor, one should do it oneself, but one should not enter upon the rains-residence without a dwelling,’ our view is that for one without a dwelling, an abode is not permissible elsewhere, except for a boat and so on. For it is only in the cases of a boat, a caravan, and a cattle-pen that entering upon the rains-residence is separately allowed, with or without a dwelling, by the text beginning, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to enter upon the rains-residence in a boat.’ Therefore, this prohibition, ‘Bhikkhus, one without a dwelling should not enter upon the rains-residence,’ is not applicable there. Thus, in the absence of a dwelling, entering upon the rains-residence in a boat and so on by way of making it one’s abode is stated. A ‘pegged bed’ is a bed made by piercing the middle of long bed-legs and inserting cross-bars. It has no ‘this is the top, this is the bottom’; when turned over and spread, it is just the same. They place it in a charnel ground and in a shrine. A structure made by spreading a stone slab on top of four stones is also called a ‘pegged bed.’

Vassaṃ anupagantabbaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Places Unsuitable for Entering upon the Rains-Residence is concluded.

Adhammikakatikakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Unrighteous Agreements.

205. Tassā lakkhaṇaṃ mahāvibhaṅge vuttanti catutthapārājikasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “yo imamhā āvāsā paṭhamaṃ pakkamissati, taṃ mayaṃ arahāti jānissāmā”ti (pārā. 228) ettha dassitaṃ adhammikakatikavattalakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vadati, paratopi senāsanakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ adhammikaṃ katikavattaṃ āvi bhavissatiyeva.

205. Regarding ‘Its characteristic is stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga,’ he speaks with reference to the characteristic of the practice of an unrighteous agreement shown in the commentary on the fourth Pārājika at the passage (Pārā. 228): ‘Whoever departs first from this residence, him we will know as an Arahant.’ Furthermore, the practice of an unrighteous agreement will become evident later in the explanation of the Chapter on Dwellings.

Paṭissavadukkaṭāpattikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Offense of Wrongdoing through a Promise.

207. Yasmā [M 3.0285][V 3.0260] nānāsīmāyaṃ dvīsu āvāsesu vassaṃ vasantassa dutiye “vasāmī”ti citte uppanne paṭhamasenāsanaggāho paṭippassambhati, puna paṭhameyeva “vasāmī”ti citte uppanne dutiyo paṭippassambhati, tasmā “tassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno purimikā ca na paññāyatī”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭissavassa visaṃvādanapaccayā hontampi dukkaṭaṃ satiyeva paṭissave hotīti āha “tassa tassa paṭissave dukkaṭa”nti. Tenevāha “tañca kho…pe… pacchā visaṃvādanapaccayā”ti.

207. Because for a bhikkhu spending the rains-residence in two residences within different boundaries, when the thought, ‘I will reside,’ arises regarding the second, the taking of the first dwelling is allayed; and when the thought, ‘I will reside,’ arises again regarding the first, the second is allayed. Therefore it is said: ‘For that bhikkhu, bhikkhus, the former is not established.’ Although an offense of wrongdoing occurs conditioned by the breaking of a promise, it occurs only when there is a promise; thus he said, ‘For each promise, an offense of wrongdoing.’ For that reason he said, ‘And that… due to being conditioned by breaking it later.’

Akaraṇīyoti sattāhakaraṇīyena akaraṇīyo. Sakaraṇīyoti sattāhakaraṇīyeneva sakaraṇīyo. Yadi evaṃ “sattāhakaraṇīyena akaraṇīyo sakaraṇīyo”ti ca kasmā na vuttanti? “Akaraṇīyo”ti vuttepi sattāhakaraṇīyena sakaraṇīyākaraṇīyatā viññāyatīti katvā na vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ parato “sattāhakaraṇīyena pakkamatī”ti vāradvayepi “sakaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti ettakameva kasmā na vuttanti? Vuccate – tattha “sattāhakaraṇīyenā”ti avatvā “sakaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti vutte so taṃ sattāhaṃ bahiddhā vītināmetīti na sakkā vattunti “sattāhakaraṇīyena pakkamatī”ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi vutte sattāhassa adhikatattā so taṃ sattāhaṃ bahi vītināmetīti sakkā vattuṃ.

“Not allowable” means not allowable with a seven-day allowance. “Allowable” means allowable only with a seven-day allowance. If so, why was it not also said: “Not allowable with a seven-day allowance, and allowable”? Even when it is said “not allowable,” the state of being allowable and not allowable with a seven-day allowance is understood, so it was not stated. If so, why was it not simply said in both instances: “He departs with an allowance,” instead of “He departs with a seven-day allowance”? It is said: Because if, without stating “with a seven-day allowance,” it were stated as “He departs with an allowance,” it would not be possible to say that he spends that seven-day period outside. Therefore, “He departs with a seven-day allowance” was said. For when it is stated in this way, since the seven days are specified, it can be said that he spends that seven-day period outside.

Ettha ca ādimhi cattāro vārā nirapekkhagamanaṃ sandhāya vuttā, tatthāpi purimā dve vārā vassaṃ anupagatassa vasena vuttā, pacchimā pana dve vārā vassaṃ upagatassa vasena, tato paraṃ dve vārā sāpekkhagamanaṃ sandhāya vuttā, tatthāpi paṭhamavāro sāpekkhassapi sattāhakaraṇīyena gantvā taṃ sattāhaṃ bahiddhā vītināmentassa vassacchedadassanatthaṃ vutto, itaro vuttanayeneva gantvā antosattāhe nivattantassa vassacchedābhāvadassanatthaṃ. “So sattāhaṃ anāgatāya pavāraṇāya sakaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti ayaṃ pana vāro navamito paṭṭhāya gantvā sattāhaṃ bahiddhā vītināmentassapi vassacchedābhāvadassanatthaṃ vutto. Ettha ca “akaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti dutiyavārassa anāgatattā navamito paṭṭhāya gacchantenapi satiyeva karaṇīye gantabbaṃ, nāsatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ime ca satta vārā bahiddhā katauposathikassa vasena āgatā, apare [M 3.0286] satta antovihāraṃ gantvā katauposathassa vasenāti evaṃ purimikāya vasena cuddasa vārā vuttā, tato paraṃ pacchimikāya vasena teyeva cuddasa vārā vuttāti evametesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Here, at the beginning, the four cases are stated with reference to departing without an attachment. Among them, the first two cases are stated with reference to one who has not entered the rains-residence, while the latter two are with reference to one who has entered the rains-residence. Thereafter, two cases are stated with reference to departing with an attachment. Among them, the first case is stated to show the breaking of the rains-residence for one who, though having an attachment, departs on a seven-day allowance and spends those seven days outside. The other case, following the method already stated, is stated to show the non-breaking of the rains-residence for one who departs and returns within seven days. “He departs with an allowance for seven days before the Pavāraṇā has arrived”—this case, starting from the ninth, is stated to show the non-breaking of the rains-residence even for one who departs and spends seven days outside. Here, since the second case, “he departs without an allowance,” has not been stated in this context, it should be understood that even one departing from the ninth case onwards should go only if there is a duty, not if there is none. These seven cases apply to one who has observed the Uposatha outside. Another seven apply to one who has gone inside the monastery and observed the Uposatha. Thus, fourteen cases are stated according to the earlier period. Thereafter, the same fourteen cases are stated according to the later period. In this way, their distinct applications should be understood.

Imehi [V 3.0261] pana sabbavārehi vuttamatthaṃ sampiṇḍetvā dassetuṃ “so tadaheva akaraṇīyotiādīsū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Ko pana vādo dvīhatīhaṃ vasitvā antosattāhe nivattantassāti vassaṃ upagantvā dvīhatīhaṃ vasitvā sattāhakaraṇīyena gantvā antosattāhe nivattantassa ko pana vādo, kathā eva natthīti adhippāyo. Asatiyā pana vassaṃ na upetīti “imasmiṃ vihāre imaṃ temāsaṃ vassaṃ upemī”ti vacībhedaṃ katvā na upeti.

To show concisely the meaning stated in all these cases, it is begun with “On that very day, it is not allowable,” and so on. But what need be said of one who, having resided for two or three days, returns within a week? This means: what need be said of one who, having entered the rains-residence and resided for two or three days, departs on a seven-day allowance and returns within a week? There is simply no issue, is the meaning. But “one does not undertake the rains-residence through lack of mindfulness” means that, having made the verbal declaration, “I will undertake the rains-residence in this monastery for these three months,” one does not truly undertake it.

Komudiyā cātumāsiniyāti pacchimakattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ. Sā hi kumudānaṃ atthitāya komudī, catunnaṃ vassikānaṃ māsānaṃ pariyosānattā “cātumāsinī”ti vuccati. Tadā hi kumudāni supupphitāni honti, tasmā kumudānaṃ samūho, kumudāni eva vā komudā, te ettha atthīti “komudī”ti vuccati, kumudavatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

“On the Komudī Cātumāsinī” means on the full moon day of the later Kattika month. For it is called Komudī because of the presence of white water lilies (kumuda), and it is called Cātumāsinī because it marks the end of the four rainy months. At that time, the white water lilies are in full bloom. Therefore, a multitude of white water lilies, or simply the white water lilies themselves, are called komudā; because these are present there, it is called Komudī, which means “possessing white water lilies.” The rest here is self-evident.

Paṭissavadukkaṭāpattikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Offense of Wrongdoing by Assent is concluded.

Vassūpanāyikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Entering the Rains-Residence is concluded.

4. Pavāraṇakkhandhakaṃ

4. The Chapter on the Invitation

Aphāsukavihārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on an Uncomfortable Dwelling

209. Pavāraṇakkhandhake [M 3.0287][V 3.0262] ādito lāpo ālāpo, vacanapaṭivacanavasena samaṃ lāpo sallāpo. Piṇḍāya paṭikkameyyāti gāme piṇḍāya caritvā paccāgaccheyya. Avakkārapātiṃ dhovitvā upaṭṭhāpeyyāti atirekapiṇḍapātaṃ apanetvā ṭhapanatthāya ekaṃ samuggapātiṃ dhovitvā ṭhapeyya. Samuggapāti nāma samuggapuṭasadisā pāti. Appahariteti aparūḷhaharite, yasmiṃ ṭhāne piṇḍapātajjhottharaṇena vinassanadhammāni tiṇāni natthi, tasminti attho. Tena nittiṇañca mahātiṇagahanañca yattha sakaṭenapi chaḍḍite piṇḍapāte tiṇāni na vinassanti, tañca ṭhānaṃ pariggahitaṃ hoti. Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadassa hi avikopanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ. Appāṇaketi nippāṇake, piṇḍapātajjhottharaṇena maritabbapāṇakarahite vā mahāudakakkhandhe. Parittodake eva hi bhattapakkhepena āluḷite sukhumapāṇakā maranti, na mahātaḷākādīsūti. Pāṇakānurakkhaṇatthañhi etaṃ vuttaṃ. Opilāpeyyāti nimujjāpeyya.

209. In the Chapter on the Invitation, from the beginning, ‘lāpo’ is ‘ālāpo’ (speech), and ‘samaṃ lāpo’ is ‘sallāpo’ (conversation), in the sense of speaking and responding. ‘Should return from the alms-round’ means one should go for alms in the village and then return. ‘Having washed the refuse bowl, one should set it aside’ means after removing the excess almsfood, one should wash a bowl for keeping things and set it aside for storing it. A ‘samuggapāti’ is a bowl similar to a small casket. ‘On a place with little greenery’ means on a place where greenery has not grown, a place where there is no grass that would be destroyed by disposing of almsfood. By this, both a place without grass and a dense thicket of tall grass where, even if almsfood is discarded from a cart, the grasses are not destroyed—such a place is included. This is said for the sake of not violating the training rule concerning living plants. ‘In a place without living beings’ means in a place devoid of life, or in a large body of water free of creatures that could be killed by the disposal of almsfood. For it is only in a small amount of water that tiny creatures die when it is stirred by throwing food into it, not in large lakes and the like. This is said for the protection of living beings. ‘Opilāpeyya’ means ‘to submerge.’

Vaccaghaṭanti ācamanakumbhī. Rittanti rittakaṃ. Tucchanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Avisayhanti ukkhipituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ atibhārikaṃ. Hatthavikārenāti hatthasaññāya. Hatthehi ukkhipanaṃ hatthavilaṅghanaṃ. Tenāha “hatthukkhepakenā”ti. Atha vā vilaṅgheti desantaraṃ pāpeti etenāti vilaṅghako, hattho eva vilaṅghako hatthavilaṅghako, tena hatthavilaṅghakena, aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitahatthenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dve hi janā hatthena hatthaṃ saṃsibbetvā dvīsu hatthesu ṭhapetvā uṭṭhapentā hatthavilaṅghakena uṭṭhapenti nāma. Titthiyasamādānanti titthiyehi samādātabbaṃ.

‘Vaccaghaṭa’ means a water pot for rinsing. ‘Ritta’ means ‘empty.’ ‘Tuccha’ is a synonym for that. ‘Avisayha’ means ‘unable to be lifted,’ that is, ‘too heavy.’ ‘Hatthavikārena’ means ‘by a hand-signal.’ Lifting with the hands is ‘hatthavilaṅghana.’ Hence it is said, ‘by raising the hand.’ Alternatively, ‘vilaṅgheti’ means ‘to convey to another place’; that by which one conveys is a ‘vilaṅghaka.’ The hand itself is the ‘vilaṅghaka,’ thus ‘hatthavilaṅghaka.’ By that ‘hatthavilaṅghaka’ means ‘with hands mutually intertwined.’ For when two people intertwine their hands and, having placed something on their two hands, lift it, they are said to lift by means of ‘hatthavilaṅghaka.’ ‘Titthiyasamādāna’ means ‘what is undertaken by sectarians.’

Aphāsukavihārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on an Uncomfortable Dwelling is concluded.

Pavāraṇābhedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Types of Invitation

212. Dvemā[M 3.0288][V 3.0263], bhikkhave, pavāraṇā cātuddasikā ca pannarasikā cāti ettha purimavassaṃvutthānaṃ pubbakattikapuṇṇamā, tesaṃyeva sace bhaṇḍanakārakehi upaddutā pavāraṇaṃ paccukkaḍḍhanti, atha kattikamāsassa kāḷapakkhacātuddaso vā pacchimakattikapuṇṇamā vā, pacchimavassaṃvutthānañca pacchimakattikapuṇṇamā eva vāti ime tayo pavāraṇadivasāti veditabbā. Idañca pakaticārittavasena vuttaṃ, tathārūpapaccaye pana sati dvinnaṃ kattikapuṇṇamānaṃ purimesu cātuddasesupi pavāraṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, teneva mahāvihāre bhikkhū cātuddasiyā pavāretvā pannarasiyā kāyasāmaggiṃ denti, cetiyagirimahadassanatthampi aṭṭhamiyā gacchanti, tampi cātuddasiyaṃ pavāretukāmānaññeva hoti.

212. “Monks, there are two kinds of Invitation: that of the fourteenth day and that of the fifteenth day.” Here, for those who have completed the earlier rains-residence, the Pavāraṇā is on the earlier Kattika full moon. If those same monks, being harassed by quarrelsome people, postpone the Pavāraṇā, then it is either on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika or on the later Kattika full moon. For those who have completed the later rains-residence, it is on the later Kattika full moon. These three are to be understood as the days for the Invitation. This is said by way of the regular practice. But when such a condition exists, it is allowable to perform the Invitation even on the fourteenth days prior to both Kattika full moons. For this reason, the monks at the Great Monastery perform the Invitation on the fourteenth day and establish communal harmony on the fifteenth day. They also go to see the great sight at Cetiyagiri on the eighth day. That too is only for those who wish to perform the Invitation on the fourteenth day.

Pavāraṇādānānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Authorizing the Giving of the Invitation

213. Sace pana vuḍḍhataro hotīti sace pavāraṇadāyako bhikkhu vuḍḍhataro hoti. Tena ca bhikkhunāti pavāraṇadāyakena bhikkhunā.

213. “But if he is older” means if the monk giving the Invitation is older. “And by that monk” means by the monk giving the Invitation.

Anāpattipannarasakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Fifteen Cases of No Offense

222. Pannarasakesu pavāritamatteti pavāritasamanantaraṃ. Avuṭṭhitāya parisāyāti pavāretvā pacchā aññamaññaṃ kathentiyā. Ekaccāya vuṭṭhitāyāti ekaccesu yathānisinnesu ekaccesu sakasakaṭṭhānaṃ gatesu. Puna pavāritabbanti punapi sabbehi samāgantvā pavāretabbaṃ. Āgacchanti samasamā, tesaṃ santike pavāretabbanti gate anānetvā nisinnānaññeva santike pavāretabbaṃ. Sabbāya vuṭṭhitāya parisāya āgacchanti samasamā, tesaṃ santike pavāretabbanti yadi sabbe vuṭṭhahitvā gatā sannipātetuñca na sakkā, ekacce sannipātetvā pavāretuṃ vaṭṭati, ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā kattabbasaṅghakammābhāvā vaggaṃ na hoti. Uposathepi eseva nayo.

222. “Immediately after the Pavāraṇā” means immediately after the Pavāraṇā. “While the assembly has not risen” means when, after performing the Pavāraṇā, they are conversing among themselves. “While some have risen” means while some remain seated as they were, and others have gone to their own places. “They should perform Pavāraṇā again” means that all should gather again and perform Pavāraṇā. “They come together equally, they should perform Pavāraṇā in their presence” means they should perform Pavāraṇā in the presence of those who are seated, without bringing back those who have gone. “If the entire assembly has risen and they come together equally, they should perform Pavāraṇā in their presence” means if all have risen and gone and it is not possible to assemble them, it is fitting to perform Pavāraṇā having assembled some; because, apart from the motion, there is no Saṅgha act to be done, it is not an incomplete quorum. This same principle applies on the Uposatha day.

Pavāraṇāṭhapanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Discussion of Postponing the Pavāraṇā.

237. “Natthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattā dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi. “Hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā[V 3.0264], na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”tiādinā sassatucchedasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ gaṇhātīti antaggāhikā.

237. “There is nothing given,” etc.—this wrong view, which has ten grounds, proceeds in this manner. “The Tathāgata exists after death,” “The Tathāgata does not exist after death,” etc.—by this, one grasps an extreme known as eternalism and annihilationism; thus, it is a view that clings to extremes.

Bhaṇḍanakārakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Discussion of the Case of the Instigator of Quarrels.

240. Catutthe [M 3.0289] kate suṇantīti catutthe pannarasikuposathe kate amhākaṃ pavāraṇaṃ ṭhapessantīti suṇanti. Evampi dve cātuddasikā hontīti tatiyena saddhiṃ dve cātuddasikā honti.

240. “When the fourth is performed, they hear” means: they hear that when the fourth fifteenth-day Uposatha is performed, their Pavāraṇā will be postponed. “Thus, there are also two Cātuddasikā” means that together with the third, there are two Cātuddasikā.

Pavāraṇāsaṅgahakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Discussion of the Compendium of the Pavāraṇā.

241. Ayaṃ pavāraṇāsaṅgaho ekassa dinnopi sabbesaṃ dinnova hotīti āha “ekassapi vasena dātabbo”ti. Āgantukā tesaṃ senāsanaṃ gahetuṃ na labhantīti sacepi saṭṭhivassabhikkhū āgacchanti, tesaṃ senāsanaṃ gahetuṃ na labhanti. Pavāretvā pana antarāpi cārikaṃ pakkamituṃ labhantīti pavāraṇāsaṅgahe kate antarā pakkamitukāmā saṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā pavāretuṃ labhanti. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyameva.

241. This compendium of Pavāraṇā, even if given to one, is considered given to all; therefore, it is said, “It should be given even by way of one.” “Newcomers are not allowed to take their lodgings” means that even if monks of sixty years' standing arrive, they are not allowed to take their lodgings. “But having performed Pavāraṇā, they are permitted to depart on a journey even in the interim” means that if, after the Pavāraṇā compendium is done, they wish to depart in the middle, they can convene the Saṅgha and perform Pavāraṇā. The remainder here can be easily understood from the Pāli text and the commentary.

Pavāraṇakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Chapter on the Pavāraṇā is concluded.

5. Cammakkhandhakaṃ

5. The Chapter on Leather

Soṇakoḷivisavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Discussion of the Case of Soṇa Koḷivisa.

242. Cammakkhandhake [M 3.0290][V 3.0265] uṇṇapāvāraṇanti uṇṇāmayaṃ pāvāraṇaṃ. Vihārapacchāyāyanti vihārapaccante chāyāyaṃ. Vihārassa vaḍḍhamānacchāyāyantipi vadanti.

242. In the Chapter on Leather, “a woolen cloak” means a cloak made of wool. “In the shade behind the monastery” means in the shade at the edge of the monastery. Some also say it means the increasing shade of the monastery.

Soṇassa pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Discussion of Soṇa's Going Forth.

243. Suttattho pana suttavaṇṇanātoyeva gahetabboti etthāyaṃ suttavaṇṇanā. Sītavaneti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.6.55) evaṃnāmake vane. Tasmiṃ kira paṭipāṭiyā pañca caṅkamanasatāni māpitāni, tesu thero attano sappāyaṃ caṅkamanaṃ gahetvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Tassa āraddhavīriyassa hutvā caṅkamato pādatalāni bhijjiṃsu, jāṇūhi caṅkamato jāṇukānipi hatthatalānipi bhijjiṃsu, chiddāni ahesuṃ. Evaṃ āraddhavīriyo viharanto obhāsanimittamattakampi dassetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tassa vīriyena kilamitakāyassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pāsāṇaphalake nisinnassa yo vitakko udapādi, taṃ dassetuṃ “atha kho āyasmato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āraddhavīriyāti paripuṇṇapaggahitavīriyā. Na anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccatīti “sace ahaṃ ugghaṭitaññū vā vipañcitaññū vā neyyo vā, na me cittaṃ na vimucceyya, addhā pana padaparamo, yena me cittaṃ na muccatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā “saṃvijjanti kho panā”tiādīni cintesi. Tattha bhogāti upayogatthe paccattaṃ.

243. The meaning of the sutta, however, should be taken from the sutta commentary itself, and this is the sutta commentary here. “In the Sītavana” (AN 6.55) means in a forest of that name. In that forest, it is said, five hundred walking paths were constructed in succession. The elder, having chosen a suitable walking path for himself, practiced the ascetic's duties. As he was walking with aroused energy, the soles of his feet cracked; as he walked on his knees, his knees and the palms of his hands also cracked, and they became wounded. Dwelling with such aroused energy, he was not able to see even a mere sign of illumination. As he was sitting on a stone slab at the end of the walking path, his body exhausted from exertion, a thought arose in him. To show this, it was said, “Then to the Venerable…” and so on. Here, “with aroused energy” means with fully exerted energy. “The mind is not freed from the taints without clinging” refers to his conclusion: “If I were one of quick understanding, or one of detailed understanding, or one to be guided, my mind would surely be freed. But I must be one for whom the words are the highest attainment, which is why my mind is not freed.” Having concluded thus, he thought, “There are, however…” and so on. Here, “possessions” is in the sense of individual use.

Pāturahosīti therassa cittācāraṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ soṇo ajja sītavane padhānabhūmiyaṃ nisinno imaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketi, gantvāssa vitakkaṃ sahoḍḍhaṃ gaṇhitvā vīṇopamakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathessāmī”ti sītavane pāturahosi. Paññatte āsaneti padhānikabhikkhū attano vasanaṭṭhāne ovadituṃ āgatassa buddhassa bhagavato nisīdanatthaṃ yathālābhena āsanampi paññapetvāva padhānaṃ karonti[V 3.0266], aññaṃ alabhamānā purāṇapaṇṇāni saṅgharitvā upari saṅghāṭiṃ paññapenti. Theropi āsanaṃ paññapetvāva padhānaṃ akāsi, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “paññatte āsane”ti.

“He appeared” means that, having known the elder's train of thought, he appeared in the Sītavana, thinking: “This Soṇa is sitting today in the Sītavana on his ground for striving, thinking this thought. I will go, grasp his thought along with its origin, and teach him the meditation subject of the lute simile.” “On the prepared seat” means that monks engaged in striving, when the Blessed One, the Buddha, comes to their dwelling place to advise them, prepare a seat for him to sit on with whatever is available and then continue their striving. If they cannot find anything else, they gather old leaves and spread their outer robe over them. The elder also prepared a seat and then engaged in his striving. Referring to this, it was said, “on the prepared seat.”

Taṃ [M 3.0291] kiṃ maññasīti satthā “imassa bhikkhuno avasesakammaṭṭhānena attho natthi, ayaṃ gandhabbasippe cheko ciṇṇavasī, attano visaye kathiyamāne khippameva sallakkhessatī”ti vīṇopamaṃ kathetuṃ “taṃ kiṃ maññasī”tiādimāha. Vīṇāya tantissare kusalatā nāma vīṇāya vādanakusalatā, so ca tattha kusalo. Mātāpitaro hissa “amhākaṃ putto aññaṃ sippaṃ sikkhanto kāyena kilamissati, idaṃ pana āsane nisinneneva sakkā uggaṇhitu”nti gandhabbasippameva uggaṇhāpesuṃ. Tassa –

“What do you think of this?” The Teacher, thinking, “This monk has no need for other meditation subjects. He is skilled and practiced in the art of music; when a topic in his own domain is discussed, he will quickly understand,” said, “What do you think of this?” and so on, in order to teach the simile of the lute. Skill in the sound of the lute's strings means skill in playing the lute, and he was skilled in that. His parents had him learn only the art of music, thinking, “If our son learns another craft, he will tire his body, but this can be learned just by sitting on a seat.” For him—

“Satta sarā tayo gāmā, mucchanā ekavīsati;

Ṭhānā ekūnapaññāsa, iccete saramaṇḍalā”ti. –

“Seven notes, three scales, twenty-one modulations, forty-nine tones—these are the circle of notes.”

Ādikaṃ gandhabbasippaṃ sabbameva paguṇaṃ ahosi. Accāyatāti atiāyatā kharamucchanā. Saravatīti sarasampannā. Kammaññāti kammakkhamā kammayoggā. Atisithilāti mandamucchanā. Same guṇe patiṭṭhitāti majjhime sare ṭhapetvā mucchitā.

—all the musical arts from the beginning were proficient. “Excessively taut” means an overly taut, harsh modulation. “Melodious” means endowed with melody. “Serviceable” means fit for work, suitable for work. “Excessively slack” means a weak modulation. “Established on an even string” means modulated after being established in the middle tone.

Accāraddhanti atigāḷhaṃ. Uddhaccāya saṃvattatīti uddhatabhāvāya saṃvattati. Atilīnanti atisithilaṃ. Kosajjāyāti kusītabhāvatthāya. Vīriyasamathaṃ adhiṭṭhāhīti vīriyasampayuttaṃ samathaṃ adhiṭṭhāhi, vīriyaṃ samathena yojehīti attho. Indriyānañca samataṃ adhiṭṭhāhīti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samataṃ samabhāvaṃ adhiṭṭhāhi. Tattha saddhaṃ paññāya, paññañca saddhāya, vīriyaṃ samādhinā, samādhiñca vīriyena yojayatā indriyānaṃ samatā adhiṭṭhitā nāma hoti. Sati pana sabbatthikā, sā sadāpi balavatīyeva vaṭṭati. Tañca pana nesaṃ yojanāvidhānaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.60-62) āgatanayena veditabbaṃ. Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhīti tasmiñca samabhāve sati yena ādāse mukhabimbeneva nimittena uppajjitabbaṃ, taṃ samathanimittaṃ vipassanānimittaṃ magganimittaṃ phalanimittañca gaṇha nibbattehīti evamassa satthā arahatte pakkhipitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi.

“Excessively aroused” means too strenuous. “Leads to restlessness” means it leads to a state of agitation. “Excessively lax” means too slack. “For laziness” means for the purpose of a state of indolence. “Establish energy and tranquility” means establish tranquility associated with energy; the meaning is: unite energy with tranquility. “And establish the balance of the faculties” means establish the balance, the equilibrium, of the faculties such as faith. There, the balance of the faculties is said to be established by one who balances faith with wisdom, and wisdom with faith; energy with concentration, and concentration with energy. Mindfulness, however, is required everywhere, and it should always be strong. The method of balancing these should be understood according to the approach found in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. I, 60-62). “And there, grasp the sign” means that when that state of balance is present, by which the sign should arise just like the reflection of a face in a mirror, you should grasp and generate that sign of tranquility, sign of insight, sign of the path, and sign of the fruit. Thus the Teacher, having placed him in arahantship, taught the meditation subject.

Tattha ca nimittaṃ aggahesīti samathanimittañca vipassanānimittañca aggahesi. Ekoti asahāyo. Vūpakaṭṭhoti vatthukāmehi ca kilesakāmehi ca kāyena ceva cittena ca vūpakaṭṭho. Appamattoti [V 3.0267] kammaṭṭhāne satiṃ [M 3.0292] avijahanto. Ātāpīti kāyikacetasikavīriyātāpena ātāpo. Ātappati kilesehīti ātāpo, vīriyaṃ. Pahitattoti kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya pesitatto vissaṭṭhaattabhāvo, nibbāne vā pesitacitto. Na cirassevāti kammaṭṭhānārambhato na cireneva. Aññataroti eko. Arahatanti bhagavato sāvakānaṃ arahantānaṃ abbhantaro eko mahāsāvako ahosīti attho.

There, he grasped the sign—he grasped both the sign of serenity and the sign of insight. Alone—without a companion. Secluded—secluded from sensual pleasures and defilements, both in body and mind. Heedful—not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject. Ardent—with the ardor of bodily and mental energy. It is ardor because it burns up the defilements; it is energy. Resolute—because of his disregard for body and life, he had sent forth his self, having relinquished his own being, or his mind was sent forth toward Nibbāna. Not long after—not long after beginning the meditation subject. One—a certain one. An arahant—meaning he became one of the great arahant disciples among the Blessed One’s disciples.

244. Vusitavāti vutthabrahmacariyavāso. Katakaraṇīyoti catūhi maggehi kattabbaṃ katvā ṭhito. Ohitabhāroti khandhabhāraṃ kilesabhāraṃ abhisaṅkhārabhārañca otāretvā ṭhito. Anuppattasadatthoti sadattho vuccati arahattaṃ, taṃ pattoti attho. Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanoti khīṇabhavabandhano. Sammadaññā vimuttoti sammā hetunā kāraṇena jānitvā vimutto. Cha ṭhānānīti cha kāraṇāni. Adhimutto hotīti paṭivijjhitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā ṭhito hoti. Nekkhammādhimuttotiādi sabbaṃ arahattavasena vuttaṃ. Arahattañhi sabbakilesehi nikkhantattā nekkhammaṃ, teheva pavivittattā paviveko, byāpajjābhāvato abyāpajjaṃ, upādānassa khayante uppannattā upādānakkhayo, taṇhāya khayante uppannattā taṇhakkhayo, sammohābhāvato asammohoti ca vuccati.

244. “One who has lived the holy life” means one who has completed the holy life. “Having done what was to be done” means having accomplished what was to be done through the four paths and standing firm. “Laid down the burden” means having put down the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, and the burden of volitional formations, and standing firm. “Reached the true goal” means having attained arahantship, which is called the true goal. “Destroyed the fetters of existence” means having destroyed the bonds of becoming. “Liberated by perfect knowledge” means being liberated by rightly understanding with reason and cause. The six grounds refer to six reasons. “Is fully resolved” means having penetrated and directly realized, standing firm. “Resolved on renunciation” and so on—all these are spoken in terms of arahantship. For arahantship is called renunciation because one has emerged from all defilements; seclusion because of being secluded from them; non-ill will because of the absence of malice; the destruction of clinging because it arises with the destruction of clinging; the destruction of craving because it arises with the destruction of craving; and non-delusion because of the absence of delusion.

Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakanti paṭivedharahitaṃ kevalaṃ paṭivedhapaññāya asammissaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ. Paṭicayanti punappunaṃ karaṇena vaḍḍhiṃ. Vītarāgattāti maggapaṭivedhena rāgassa vihatattāyeva nekkhammasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ paṭivijjhitvā sacchikatvā ṭhito hoti, phalasamāpattivihārena viharati, tanninnamānasoyeva hotīti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

“Merely faith alone” means mere faith unmixed with the wisdom of realization, devoid of realization. “Accumulation” means growth by doing again and again. “Free from lust” means having destroyed lust by realization of the path, thus having penetrated and directly experienced arahantship, which is called renunciation, one stands firm, dwells in the attainment of fruition, and his mind is inclined to that—this is the meaning. The same method applies to the remaining phrases.

Lābhasakkārasilokanti catupaccayalābhañca tesaṃyeva sukatabhāvañca vaṇṇabhaṇanañca. Nikāmayamānoti icchamāno patthayamāno. Pavivekādhimuttoti “paviveke adhimutto aha”nti evaṃ arahattaṃ byākarotīti attho.

Gain, honor, and renown means gain of the four requisites, the good quality of these, and the praising of their virtues. 'Desiring' means wishing and longing for. 'Inclined to seclusion' means declaring arahantship by saying, “I am inclined to seclusion”—this is the meaning.

Sīlabbataparāmāsanti sīlañca vatañca parāmasitvā gahitaggahaṇamattaṃ. Sārato paccāgacchantoti sārabhāvena jānanto. Abyāpajjādhimuttoti [M 3.0293] abyāpajjaṃ arahattaṃ byākaroti. Imināva nayena sabbavāresu attho daṭṭhabbo. Apicettha “nekkhammādhimuttoti imasmiṃyeva arahattaṃ kathitaṃ, sesesu pañcasu nibbāna”nti eke vadanti. Apare “asammohādhimuttoti [V 3.0268] ettheva nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ, sesesu arahatta”nti vadanti. Ayaṃ panettha sāro – “sabbesvevetesu arahattampi nibbānampi kathitamevāti.

Clinging to precepts and vows means the mere grasping of precepts and vows after misapprehending them. 'Returning to the essence' means knowing it as the essence. 'Being inclined toward non-ill will' means one declares arahantship as non-ill will. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances. Furthermore, some say, “'Being inclined toward renunciation' refers to arahantship in this case, while in the other five, it refers to Nibbāna.” Others say, “'Being inclined toward non-delusion' refers to Nibbāna in this case, while in the others, it refers to arahantship.” But the essence here is this: “In all these cases, both arahantship and Nibbāna are spoken of.”

Bhusāti balavanto dibbarūpasadisā. Nevassa cittaṃ pariyādiyantīti etassa khīṇāsavassa cittaṃ gahetvā ṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Kilesā hi uppajjamānā cittaṃ gaṇhanti nāma. Amissīkatanti amissakataṃ. Kilesā hi ārammaṇena saddhiṃ cittaṃ missaṃ karonti, tesaṃ abhāvā amissīkataṃ. Ṭhitanti patiṭṭhitaṃ. Āneñjappattanti acalanappattaṃ. Vayañcassānupassatīti tassa cesa cittassa uppādampi vayampi passati. Bhusā vātavuṭṭhīti balavā vātakkhandho. Neva naṃ saṅkampeyyāti ekabhāgena cāletuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Na sampakampeyyāti thūṇaṃ viya sabbabhāgato kampetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Na sampavedheyyāti vedhetvā pavedhetvā pātetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya.

The mighty ones are powerful, resembling divine forms. They cannot seize and hold the mind of this one whose taints are destroyed. For defilements, when they arise, indeed seize the mind. “Unmixed” means unmixed. For defilements mix the mind with an object; in their absence, it is unmixed. “Steady” means established. “Attained to the imperturbable” means attained to the unshakeable. “And he sees its passing away”—he sees both the arising and the passing away of that mind. A fierce storm—a powerful wind blast. “It would not shake him”—it could not shake him in one part. “It would not make him tremble”—it could not make him tremble entirely, like a pillar. “It would not make him quiver”—it could not make him quiver, causing him to shake and collapse.

Nekkhammaṃ adhimuttassāti arahattaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitassa. Sesapadesupi arahattameva kathitaṃ. Upādānakkhayassa cāti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Asammohañca cetasoti cittassa ca asammohaṃ adhimuttassa. Disvā āyatanuppādanti āyatanānaṃ uppādañca vayañca disvā. Sammā cittaṃ vimuccatīti sammā hetunā nayena imāya vipassanāya paṭipattiyā phalasamāpattivasena cittaṃ vimuccati, nibbānārammaṇe adhimuccati. Atha vā iminā khīṇāsavassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadā kathitā. Tassa hi āyatanuppādaṃ disvā imāya vipassanāya adhigatassa ariyamaggassa ānubhāvena sabbakilesehi sammā cittaṃ vimuccati. Evaṃ tassa sammā vimuttassa…pe… na vijjati. Tattha santacittassāti nibbutacittassa. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

“One intent on renunciation”—one who has penetrated arahantship and stands firm. In the remaining passages, arahantship is also spoken of. “And for the destruction of clinging”—the genitive case is used in the sense of instrumentality. “And the mind free from delusion”—one intent on the mind's freedom from delusion. “Having seen the arising of the sense bases”—having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases. “The mind is rightly liberated”—the mind is rightly liberated with reason and method through this practice of insight, by way of the attainment of fruition, becoming intent on Nibbāna as its object. Or alternatively, the preliminary practice of one whose taints are destroyed is described here. For him, having seen the arising of the sense bases, through the power of the noble path attained by this insight, the mind is rightly liberated from all defilements. Thus, for him rightly liberated... is not found. Here, “peaceful-minded”—one whose mind is extinguished. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Soṇassa pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the story of Soṇa's going forth is concluded.

Sabbanīlikādipaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Prohibition of All Blue Things, and So Forth.

246. Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇāti [M 3.0294] abhinavāriṭṭhaphalavaṇṇā. Udakena tintakākapattavaṇṇātipi vadanti.

246. “The color of a ripe arīṭṭhaka” means the color of a fresh arīṭṭhaka fruit. Some also say it is the color of a crow’s wing soaked with water.

Ajjhārāme upāhanapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Prohibition of Footwear in the Monastery.

248. Abhijīvanti [V 3.0269] etenāti abhijīvanikaṃ. Kintaṃ? Sippaṃ. Tenāha “yena sippenā”tiādi.

248. A means of livelihood (`abhijīvanikaṃ`) is so called because 'they live by this' (`abhijīvanti etena`). What is that? A craft. Hence it is said, “by which craft,” and so on.

Kaṭṭhapādukādipaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Prohibition of Wooden Sandals, and So Forth.

251. Uṇṇāhi katapādukāti uṇṇālomamayakambalehi, uṇṇālomehi eva vā katapādukā. Na, bhikkhave, gāvīnaṃ visāṇesu gahetabbantiādīsu “mokkhādhippāyena visāṇādīsu gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

251. “Sandals made of wool” means sandals made of woolen blankets or simply of wool. “Monks, one should not take hold of cows by their horns,” and so on—in the Ganthipada, it is said that it is permissible to take hold of horns, etc., for the purpose of release.

Yānādipaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Prohibition of Conveyances, and So Forth.

253. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, purisayuttaṃ hatthavaṭṭakanti ettha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, purisayuttaṃ, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, hatthavaṭṭaka”nti evaṃ paccekavākyaparisamāpanaṃ adhippetanti āha “purisayuttaṃ itthisārathi vā…pe… purisā vā, vaṭṭatiyevā”ti. Pīṭhakasivikanti pīṭhakayānaṃ. Pāṭaṅkinti andolikāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

253. Regarding the phrase, 'I allow, monks, a vehicle drawn by a person and a hand-cart,' it is intended that each phrase be completed individually, thus: 'I allow, monks, a vehicle drawn by a person,' and 'I allow, monks, a hand-cart.' It is then said: 'A vehicle drawn by a person, whether by a female charioteer... or by men, is indeed allowable.' 'A seat-litter' means a seat-vehicle. 'A `pāṭaṅki`' is a synonym for a palanquin.

Uccāsayanamahāsayanapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Prohibition of High and Luxurious Beds.

254. Vāḷarūpānīti āharimāni vāḷarūpāni. “Akappiyarūpākulo akappiyamañco pallaṅko”ti sārasamāse vuttaṃ. “Dīghalomako mahākojavoti caturaṅgulādhikalomo kāḷakojavo. “Caturaṅgulādhikāni kira tassa lomānī”ti vacanato caturaṅgulato heṭṭhā vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇoti bhitticchedādivasena vicitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo. Ghanapupphako uṇṇāmayattharaṇoti uṇṇāmayalohitattharaṇo. Pakatitūlikāti rukkhatūlalatātūlapoṭakītūlasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tūlānaṃ aññatarapuṇṇā tūlikā. “Uddalomīti [M 3.0295] ubhatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Ekantalomīti ekatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa”nti dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.15) vuttaṃ, sārasamāse pana “uddalomīti ekato uggatapupphaṃ. Ekantalomīti ubhato uggatapuppha”nti vuttaṃ. “Koseyyakaṭṭissamayanti koseyyakasaṭamaya”nti ācariyadhammapālattherena vuttaṃ. Suddhakoseyyanti ratanaparisibbanarahitaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ panettha “ṭhapetvā [V 3.0270] tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha “ṭhapetvā tūlika”nti etena ratanaparisibbanarahitāpi tūlikā na vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. “Ratanaparisibbitāni vaṭṭantī”ti iminā pana yāni ratanaparisibbitāni, tāni bhūmattharaṇavasena yathānurūpaṃ mañcādīsu ca upanetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpitanti veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca vinayapariyāyaṃ patvā garuke ṭhātabbattā idha vuttanayenevettha vinicchayo veditabbo. Suttantikadesanāyaṃ pana gahaṭṭhānampi vasena vuttattā tesaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ…pe… vaṭṭantī”ti vuttanti apare.

254. “Animal-shaped” refers to artificial animal figures. “A bed and couch crowded with unsuitable figures” is stated concisely in the Sārasamāsa. “‘A large rug with long fleece’ means a black rug with fleece exceeding four finger-breadths. From the statement, “Its fleece is said to exceed four finger-breadths,” some say it is permissible if it is less than four finger-breadths. “A variegated woolen rug” means a woolen rug variegated with patterns like wall sections. “A thickly flowered woolen rug” means a red woolen rug. “A standard mattress” refers to a mattress filled with any of the three types of stuffing: tree stuffing, creeper stuffing, or pod stuffing. “A rug with fleece on both sides” means a woolen rug with fringes on both sides. “A rug with fleece on one side” means a woolen rug with fringes on one side,” as stated in the Dīgha Nikāya commentary. However, the Sārasamāsa says, “A rug with fleece on both sides has raised tufts on one side; a rug with fleece on one side has raised tufts on both sides.” “A covering interwoven with silk” means a covering made of silk cloth, as stated by the Elder Dhammapāla. “Pure silk” means without jewel embroidery. However, the Dīgha Nikāya commentary states, “Except for the mattress, all others like long-fleeced rugs are permissible if embroidered with jewels.” Here, “except for the mattress” indicates that even a mattress without jewel embroidery is not allowed. “Permissible if embroidered with jewels” implies that those with jewel embroidery may be used as floor coverings or on beds as appropriate. In this context, with regard to the Vinaya teaching, because one must stand on what is serious, the decision here should be made in accordance with the principle stated. However, in the Suttanta teachings, since it is also spoken with reference to householders, the phrase “except for the mattress… are permissible” is used to include them, say others.

Ajinacammehīti ajinamigacammehi. Tāni kira cammāni sukhumatarāni, tasmā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbanti. Tena vuttaṃ “ajinapaveṇī”ti. Uttaraṃ uparibhāgaṃ chādetīti uttaracchado, vitānaṃ, tañca lohitavitānaṃ idhādhippetanti āha “uparibaddhena rattavitānenā”ti. “Rattavitānesu ca kāsāvaṃ vaṭṭati, kusumbhādirattameva na vaṭṭatī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Mahāupadhānanti pamāṇātikkantaṃ upadhānaṃ. Ettha ca kiñcāpi dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni aṭṭha. 1.15) “alohitakāni dvepi vaṭṭantiyeva, tato uttari labhitvā aññesaṃ dātabbāni, dātuṃ asakkonto mañce tiriyaṃ attharitvā upari paccattharaṇaṃ datvā nipajjitumpi labhatī”ti avisesena vuttaṃ, senāsanakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 297) pana “agilānassa sīsupadhānañca pādupadhānañcāti dvayameva vaṭṭati, gilānassa bimbohanāni santharitvā upari paccattharaṇaṃ datvā nipajjitumpi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttattā gilānoyeva mañce tiriyaṃ attharitvā nipajjituṃ labhatīti veditabbaṃ.

“By hides of the ajina deer” means hides of the ajina deer. These hides are said to be very fine, so they are stitched together after making them double or triple layered. Hence, it is called “a spread of ajina hides.” “It covers the upper part” means the upper covering, which is a canopy. Here, it specifically refers to a red canopy, as stated: “with a red canopy attached above.” “It is said in the Ganthipada texts that in red canopies, the ochre color is permissible, but red from safflower and so on is not permissible.” “A large cushion” means a cushion that exceeds the proper size. Here, although the Dīgha Nikāya commentary states without distinction: “Even two non-red ones are permissible. If one obtains more than that, they should be given to others. If unable to give them away, one may spread them sideways on the bed, place a covering on top, and then lie down,” in the explanation of the Senāsana Khandhaka, it is said: “For a monk who is not ill, only a head-cushion and a foot-cushion are permissible. For a monk who is ill, it is permissible to spread out cushions, place a covering on top, and then lie down.” Therefore, it should be understood that only a monk who is ill may spread coverings sideways on the bed and lie down.

Uccāsayanamahāsayanapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Rejection of High and Large Beds is concluded.

Gihivikatānuññātādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on What is Allowed Regarding Items Sold by Householders, and so forth.

256. Abhinissāya [M 3.0296] nisīditunti apassāya nisīdituṃ.

256. “To sit depending on” means to sit leaning on.

Soṇakuṭikaṇṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.

257. Papatake pabbateti ettha “pavatte pabbate”tipi paṭhanti, pavattanāmake pabbateti attho. Soṇo upāsakotiādīsu (udā. aṭṭha. 46) nāmena soṇo nāma, tīhi saraṇagamanehi [V 3.0271] upāsakattapaṭivedanena upāsako, koṭiagghanakassa kaṇṇapiḷandhanassa dhāraṇena “koṭikaṇṇo”ti ca vattabbe “kuṭikaṇṇo”ti evaṃ abhiññāto, na sukumārasoṇoti adhippāyo. Ayañhi āyasmato mahākaccānassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā sāsane abhippasanno saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhito papatake pabbate chāyūdakasampanne ṭhāne vihāraṃ kāretvā theraṃ tattha vasāpetvā catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhāti. Tena vuttaṃ “āyasmato mahākaccānassa upaṭṭhāko hotī”ti.

257. “On the Papataka mountain”—here some also read “on the Pavatta mountain,” meaning a mountain named Pavatta. In such texts as “Soṇa the lay follower” (Udāna Aṭṭhakathā 46), his name is Soṇa; he is a lay follower by his declaration of being a lay follower through the three refuges; and though he should have been called “Koṭikaṇṇa” because he wore an ear-ornament worth a crore, he was known as “Kuṭikaṇṇa”—the intention is that this does not mean “delicate Soṇa.” For this man, having heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Mahākaccāna, became deeply devoted to the Teaching. Established in the refuges and precepts, he had a monastery built on the Papataka mountain, in a place abundant in shade and water, and had the elder reside there. He attended to him with the four requisites. Thus it is said, “He was the attendant of the Venerable Mahākaccāna.”

So kālena kālaṃ therassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, thero cassa dhammaṃ deseti, tena saṃvegabahulo dhammacariyāyaṃ ussāhajāto viharati. So ekadā satthena saddhiṃ vāṇijjatthāya ujjeniṃ gacchanto antarāmagge aṭaviyaṃ satthe niviṭṭhe rattiyaṃ janasambādhabhayena ekamantaṃ apakkamma niddaṃ upagañchi. Sattho paccūsavelāyaṃ uṭṭhāya gato, na ekopi soṇaṃ pabodhesi, sabbe vissaritvā agamiṃsu. So pabhātāya rattiyā pabujjhitvā uṭṭhāya kañci apassanto satthena gatamaggaṃ gahetvā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchanto ekaṃ vaṭarukkhaṃ upagañchi. Tattha addasa ekaṃ mahākāyaṃ virūpadassanaṃ bībhacchaṃ purisaṃ aṭṭhito muttāni attano maṃsāni sayameva khādantaṃ, disvāna “kosi tva”nti pucchi. Petosmi, bhanteti. Kasmā evaṃ karosīti? Attano pubbakammenāti. Kiṃ pana taṃ kammanti? Ahaṃ pubbe bhārukacchanagaravāsī kūṭavāṇijo hutvā paresaṃ santakaṃ vañcetvā khādiṃ, samaṇe ca bhikkhāya upagate “tumhākaṃ maṃsaṃ khādathā”ti akkosiṃ, tena kammena etarahi imaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavāmīti. Taṃ sutvā soṇo ativiya saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhi.

From time to time, he would go to attend upon the elder, and the elder would teach him the Dhamma. Filled with a sense of urgency, he lived diligently in the practice of the Dhamma. Once, while traveling with a caravan to Ujjenī for trade, the caravan encamped in a forest along the way. At night, fearing the press of people, he withdrew to one side and fell asleep. At dawn, the caravan arose and departed, but not a single person woke Soṇa; they all forgot and left. When the night had dawned, he awoke, and seeing no one, he took the path the caravan had gone and, walking very quickly, he came upon a banyan tree. There, he saw a large-bodied, ugly, and hideous man eating his own flesh that had fallen from his limbs. Seeing him, he asked, “Who are you?” “I am a hungry ghost, venerable sir.” “Why are you doing this?” “Because of my past kamma.” “What was that kamma?” “Formerly, I was a deceitful merchant living in the city of Bhārukaccha and I consumed the property of others by cheating them. When ascetics came for alms, I insulted them, saying, ‘Eat your own flesh!’ Because of that kamma, I now experience this suffering.” Hearing this, Soṇa was overcome with a great sense of urgency.

Tato [M 3.0297] paraṃ gacchanto mukhato paggharitakāḷalohite dve petadārake passitvā tatheva pucchi, tepissa attano kammaṃ kathesuṃ. Te kira bhārukacchanagare dārakakāle gandhavāṇijjāya jīvikaṃ kappentā attano mātari khīṇāsave nimantetvā bhojentiyā gehaṃ gantvā “amhākaṃ santakaṃ kasmā samaṇānaṃ desi, tayā dinnaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjanakasamaṇānaṃ mukhato kāḷalohitaṃ paggharatū”ti akkosiṃsu. Te tena kammena niraye paccitvā tassa vipākāvasesena petayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā tadā imaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavanti. Tampi sutvā soṇo ativiya saṃvegajāto ahosi.

Going on from there, he saw two young hungry ghosts with black-red blood flowing from their mouths and asked them the same question. They too recounted their own kamma. It seems that in the city of Bhārukaccha, during their childhood, they made a living by trading in perfumes. Their mother, one whose taints were destroyed, had invited monks and was feeding them. They went to her house and scolded her, saying, “Why do you give what belongs to us to the ascetics? May black-red blood flow from the mouths of the ascetics who eat the food you give!” Because of that kamma, they were tormented in hell, and due to the remaining result of that kamma, they were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts and were then experiencing this suffering. Hearing this too, Soṇa became exceedingly filled with a sense of urgency.

So ujjeniṃ gantvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā kuraragharaṃ paccāgato theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā katapaṭisanthāro tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Theropissa pavattinivattīsu ādīnavānisaṃse vibhāvento dhammaṃ [V 3.0272] desesi. So theraṃ vanditvā gehaṃ gato sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā sayanaṃ upagato thokaṃyeva niddāyitvā pabujjhitvā sayanatale nisajja yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhituṃ āraddho. Tassa taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhato te ca petattabhāve anussarato saṃsāradukkhaṃ ativiya bhayānakaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāsi, pabbajjāya cittaṃ nami. So vibhātāya rattiyā sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā theraṃ upagantvā attano ajjhāsayaṃ ārocetvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho soṇo upāsako…pe… pabbājetu maṃ, bhante, ayyo mahākaccāno”ti.

Having gone to Ujjeni and completed that task, he returned to Kuraraghara and approached the elder. After exchanging courteous greetings, he informed him of the matter. The elder, discerning the dangers and benefits in the coming and going of existence, taught him the Dhamma. He paid homage to the elder, went home, ate his evening meal, and having gone to his bed, after sleeping a little, he awoke and sat on his bed, beginning to reflect on the Dhamma as he had heard it. As he contemplated the Dhamma and recalled those former states as a hungry ghost, the suffering of saṃsāra appeared extremely terrifying to him, and his mind inclined toward renunciation. When the night had passed, he attended to his bodily needs, approached the elder, declared his intention, and requested ordination. Thus it is stated: "Then the lay follower Soṇa... Venerable Mahākaccāna, sir, please ordain me."

Tattha yathā yathātiādipadānaṃ ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yena yena ākārena ayyo mahākaccāno dhammaṃ deseti ācikkhati paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttāniṃ karoti pakāseti, tena tena me upaparikkhato evaṃ hoti “yadetaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ ekampi divasaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ, ekadivasampi kilesamalena amalīnaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ, saṅkhalikhitaṃ likhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ caritabbaṃ, idaṃ na sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ…pe… caritu”nti.

Here, the concise meaning of the words "in whatever way" and so on is as follows: In whatever manner the Venerable Mahākaccāna teaches, explains, makes known, establishes, discloses, analyzes, clarifies, and reveals the Dhamma, in that very manner, upon my examination, it occurs to me: "This holy life of the threefold training, to be practiced flawlessly even for a single day so as to reach the final consciousness, is utterly perfect; to be practiced without being stained by the impurity of defilements even for a single day so as to reach the final consciousness, is utterly pure. It must be lived like a polished conch shell, like a scraped conch shell, like a washed conch shell. This is not easy for one living in a household, dwelling in the midst of a home, to practice... to live in this utterly perfect way."

Evaṃ attano parivitakkitaṃ soṇo upāsako therassa ārocetvā taṃ paṭipajjitukāmo “icchāmahaṃ bhante”tiādimāha. Thero pana [M 3.0298] “na tāvassa ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gata”nti upadhāretvā ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno “dukkaraṃ kho”tiādinā pabbajjāchandaṃ nivāresi. Tattha ekaseyyanti adutiyaseyyaṃ. Ettha ca seyyāsīsena “eko tiṭṭhati, eko gacchati, eko nisīdatī”tiādinā nayena vuttaṃ catūsu iriyāpathesu kāyavivekaṃ dīpeti, na ekikā hutvā sayanamattaṃ. Ekabhattanti “ekabhattiko hoti rattūparato virato vikālabhojanā”ti (dī. ni. 1.10, 194; ma. ni. 1.293 a. ni. 3.71) evaṃ vuttaṃ vikālabhojanā viratiṃ sandhāya vadati. Brahmacariyanti methunaviratibrahmacariyaṃ, sikkhattayānuyogasaṅkhātaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ vā. Iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Tatthevāti geheyeva. Buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ anuyuñjāti niccasīlauposathasīlaniyamādibhedaṃ pañcaṅgaṃ aṭṭhaṅgaṃ dasaṅgañca sīlaṃ tadanurūpañca samādhipaññābhāvanaṃ anuyuñja. Etañhi upāsakena pubbabhāge anuyuñjitabbaṃ buddhasāsanaṃ nāma. Tenāha “kālayuttaṃ ekaseyyaṃ ekabhattaṃ brahmacariya”nti.

Having thus informed the elder of his own reflection, the lay follower Soṇa, wishing to undertake that practice, said, "I wish, venerable sir," and so on. The elder, however, considering that "his knowledge has not yet matured," and waiting for the maturity of his knowledge, discouraged his desire for renunciation by saying, "It is difficult," and so on. Here, 'a solitary bed' means a bed without a second person. And here, by the term 'bed,' bodily seclusion in the four postures is indicated—as in 'one stands, one walks, one sits,' and so on—not merely lying down alone. 'One meal' refers to abstaining from eating at the wrong time, as stated: "He eats one meal a day, refraining from eating at night and avoiding food at improper times" (Dī. Ni. 1.10; Ma. Ni. 1.293; A. Ni. 3.71). This refers to abstaining from food at the wrong time. 'The holy life' refers either to the holy life of abstinence from sexual intercourse or to the holy life of the Dispensation, which consists of the application of the threefold training. 'Come now' is a particle of exhortation. 'Right there' means in the home itself. 'Apply yourself to the teaching of the Buddhas' means: apply yourself to the fivefold, eightfold, and tenfold precepts—distinguished as the constant precepts, the Uposatha precepts, the regular observances, and so on—and to the development of concentration and wisdom in accordance with them. For this is what is called the teaching of the Buddhas that a lay follower should apply himself to in the preliminary stage. Hence he said, "Timely, a solitary bed, one meal, the holy life."

Tattha kālayuttanti cātuddasīpañcaddasīaṭṭhamīpāṭihārikapakkhasaṅkhātena kālena yuttaṃ, yathāvuttakāle vā tuyhaṃ anuyuñjantassa yuttaṃ patirūpaṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ, na sabbakālaṃ sabbanti adhippāyo[V 3.0273]. Sabbametaṃ ñāṇassa aparipakkattā tassa kāmānaṃ duppahānatāya sammā paṭipattiyaṃ yogyaṃ kārāpetuṃ vadati, na pabbajjāchandaṃ nivāretuṃ. Pabbajjābhisaṅkhāroti pabbajituṃ ārambho ussāho. Paṭippassambhīti indriyānaṃ aparipakkattā saṃvegassa ca nātitikkhabhāvato vūpasami. Kiñcāpi paṭippassambhi, therena vuttavidhiṃ pana anutiṭṭhanto kālena kālaṃ theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā payirupāsanto dhammaṃ suṇāti. Tassa vuttanayeneva dutiyampi pabbajjāya cittaṃ uppajji, therassa ca ārocesi, dutiyampi thero paṭikkhipi. Tatiyavāre pana ñāṇassa paripakkabhāvaṃ ñatvā “idāni naṃ pabbājetuṃ kālo”ti thero pabbājesi, pabbajitañca taṃ tīṇi saṃvaccharāni atikkamitvā gaṇaṃ pariyesitvā upasampādesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “dutiyampi kho soṇo…pe… upasampādesī”ti.

Here, 'timely' means suitable for the time designated as the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days, and the special observance fortnight; or, it would be suitable, appropriate, and possible for you who are applying yourself at the aforementioned time; the intention is not all the time and everything. All this he says to make him fit for right practice, due to the immaturity of his knowledge and the difficulty of abandoning sensual pleasures, not to discourage his desire for renunciation. 'The impulse to renounce' means the beginning, the effort to go forth. 'It subsided' means it was calmed, due to the immaturity of his faculties and the fact that his sense of urgency was not very keen. Although it subsided, he, continuing to follow the method taught by the elder, approached and attended upon him from time to time and listened to the Dhamma. In the same way as described, the thought of renunciation arose in him a second time, and he informed the elder, and a second time the elder refused him. But the third time, knowing that his knowledge had matured, the elder thought, "Now is the time to ordain him," and he ordained him. And after three years had passed since his ordination, having sought out a chapter of monks, he conferred the higher ordination upon him. With reference to this, it is said, "A second time, Soṇa… and so on… conferred the higher ordination."

Tattha appabhikkhukoti katipayabhikkhuko. Tadā kira bhikkhū yebhuyyena majjhimadeseyeva vasiṃsu, tasmā tattha katipayā eva ahesuṃ[M 3.0299]. Te ca ekasmiṃ gāme eko, ekasmiṃ nigame dveti evaṃ visuṃ visuṃ vasiṃsu. Kicchenāti dukkhena. Kasirenāti āyāsena. Tato tatoti tasmā tasmā gāmanigamādito. Therena hi katipaye bhikkhū ānetvā aññesu ānīyamānesu pubbe ānītā kenacideva karaṇīyena pakkamiṃsu, kañci kālaṃ āgametvā puna tesu ānīyamānesu itare pakkamiṃsu. Evaṃ punappunaṃ ānayanena sannipāto cireneva ahosi. Theropi tadā ekavihārī ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ…pe… sannipātāpetvā”ti.

Here, 'with few monks' means with a small number of monks. It is said that at that time, monks lived mostly in the Middle Country; therefore, there were only a few there. And they lived separately, one in one village, two in one town, thus scattered about. 'With difficulty' means with trouble. 'With hardship' means with exertion. 'From here and there' means from this and that village, town, and so on. For when the elder had brought a few monks, while others were being brought, those who had been brought previously left on some business. After waiting for some time, when they were being brought again, the others left. Thus, because they had to be brought again and again, the assembly took a long time to convene. The elder himself was also living alone at that time. Therefore, it is said, "After three years… and so on… having convened an assembly."

Vassaṃvutthassāti vassaṃ upagantvā vusitavato. Ediso ca ediso cāti evarūpo ca evarūpo ca. “Evarūpāya nāma rūpakāyasampattiyā samannāgato, evarūpāya dhammakāyasampattiyā samannāgato”ti sutoyeva me so bhagavā. Na ca mayā sammukhā diṭṭhoti ettha pana puthujjanasaddhāya eva āyasmā soṇo bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhukāmo ahosi. Aparabhāge pana satthārā saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasitvā paccūsasamayaṃ ajjhiṭṭho soḷasa aṭṭhakavaggiyāni satthu sammukhā aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā atthadhammapaṭisaṃvedī hutvā bhaṇanto dhammupasañhitapāmojjādimukhena samāhito sarabhaññapariyosāne vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā saṅkhāre sammasanto anupubbena arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Etadatthameva hissa bhagavatā attanā saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vāso āṇattoti vadanti.

'Of one who has completed the rains residence' means of one who has undertaken and lived out the rains residence. 'Of such and such a kind' means of this sort and that sort. "That Blessed One has been heard of by me as being endowed with such and such excellence of the physical body and with such and such excellence of the Dhamma body. But he has not been seen by me face to face." Here, the venerable Soṇa desired to see the Blessed One with the faith of an ordinary person. Later, however, having lived with the Teacher in the same fragrant hut, being requested by him at dawn, he recited the sixteen sections of the Aṭṭhakavagga in the Teacher's presence. Having paid attention, taken it to heart, and comprehended it all with his mind, experiencing the meaning and the Dhamma, he recited with joy connected with the Dhamma. Being concentrated, at the end of the melodious recitation, he established insight, and by contemplating the conditioned formations, he gradually attained arahantship. It is said that it was for this very purpose that the Blessed One instructed him to stay with him in the same fragrant hut.

Keci panāhu “na ca mayā sammukhā diṭṭhoti idaṃ rūpakāyadassanameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Āyasmā hi soṇo pabbajitvā therassa santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto anupasampannova [V 3.0274] sotāpanno hutvā upasampajjitvā ‘upāsakāpi sotāpannā honti, ahampi sotāpanno, kimettha citta’nti uparimaggatthāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā antovasseyeva chaḷabhiñño hutvā visuddhipavāraṇāya pavāresi. Ariyasaccadassanena bhagavato dhammakāyo diṭṭho nāma hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ ‘yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.87). Tasmāssa dhammakāyadassanaṃ pageva siddhaṃ, pavāretvā pana rūpakāyaṃ daṭṭhukāmo ahosī”ti.

Some say, "‘It was not seen by me face to face’—this was said referring only to seeing the physical body. For Venerable Soṇa, after going forth, took up a meditation subject in the presence of the elder, and striving and exerting himself, he became a stream-enterer even before full ordination. After ordaining, he thought, 'Lay followers too become stream-enterers, and I am a stream-enterer—what is so special about this?' Developing insight for the higher paths, within that very rains-retreat he became one with the sixfold direct knowledge and performed the Pavāraṇā with the invitation of purity. By seeing the Noble Truths, the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One is said to be seen. For it was said, 'Whoever sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me' (SN 3.87). Therefore, his seeing of the Dhamma-body was already accomplished. But after the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he desired to see the physical body."

Pāsādikantiādipadānaṃ [M 3.0300] attho aṭṭhakathāyameva vutto. Tattha visūkāyikavipphanditānanti paṭipakkhabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhicittavipphanditānanti attho. Pāsādikanti (udā. aṭṭha. 10) vā dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītianubyañjanabyāmappabhāketumālālaṅkatāya samantapāsādikāya attano sarīrappabhāya sampattiyā rūpakāyadassanabyāvaṭassa janassa sabbabhāgato pasādāvahaṃ. Pasādanīyanti dasabalacatuvesārajjachaasādhāraṇañāṇaaṭṭhārasaāveṇikabuddhadhammappabhutiaparimāṇaguṇagaṇasamannāgatāya dhammakāyasampattiyā parikkhakajanassa pasādanīyaṃ pasīditabbayuttaṃ pasādakaṃ vā. Santindriyanti cakkhādipañcindriyalolatāvigamena vūpasantapañcindriyaṃ. Santamānasanti chaṭṭhassa manindriyassa nibbisevanabhāvūpagamanena vūpasantamānasaṃ. Uttamadamathasamathaṃ anuppattanti lokuttarapaññāvimutticetovimuttisaṅkhātaṃ uttamaṃ damathaṃ samathañca anuppatvā adhigantvā ṭhitaṃ. Dantanti suparisuddhakāyasamācāratāya hatthapādakukkuccābhāvato davādiabhāvato ca kāyena dantaṃ. Guttanti suparisuddhavacīsamācāratāya niratthakavācābhāvato ravādiabhāvato ca vācāya guttaṃ. Yatindriyanti suparisuddhamanosamācāratāya ariyiddhiyogena abyāvaṭaappaṭisaṅkhupekkhābhāvato ca manindriyavasena yatindriyaṃ. Nāganti chandādivasena agamanato, pahīnānaṃ rāgādikilesānaṃ apunāgamanato apaccāgamanato kassacipi āgussa sabbathāpi akaraṇato, punabbhavassa ca agamanatoti imehi kāraṇehi nāgaṃ. Ettha ca “pāsādika”nti iminā rūpakāyena bhagavato pamāṇabhūtataṃ dīpeti, “pasādanīya”nti iminā dhammakāyena. “Santindriya”ntiādinā sesehi pamāṇabhūtataṃ dīpeti, tena catuppamāṇike lokasannivāse anavasesato sattānaṃ bhagavato pamāṇabhāvo pakāsitoti veditabbo. Ekavihāreti ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ. Gandhakuṭi hi idha “vihāro”ti adhippeto. Vatthunti vasituṃ.

The meaning of the words "Pāsādika" and so on is stated in the commentary itself. Therein, "visūkāyikavipphanditānaṃ" means the disturbances of opposing views and thoughts. "Pāsādika" refers to that which inspires serenity in people occupied with seeing the physical body, bringing them confidence from every aspect through the perfection of his own physical radiance, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, and the flame-like radiance on his head. "Pasādanīya" refers to that which inspires confidence in those who investigate, being worthy of their confidence, fit to be trusted, or inspiring trust, through the perfection of the Dhamma-body, which is endowed with the immeasurable host of qualities beginning with the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, the six uncommon knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. "Santindriya" means having the five faculties pacified through the removal of craving for the faculties of the eye and so on. "Santamānasa" means having the mind pacified through reaching a state of non-indulgence with the sixth faculty, the mind. "Uttamadamathasamathaṃ anuppatta" means having attained and realized the supreme taming and tranquility, known as the supramundane liberation by wisdom and liberation of mind, and abiding therein. "Danta" means tamed in body due to perfectly pure bodily conduct, from the absence of fidgeting of hands and feet, and from the absence of sportiveness and the like. "Gutta" means guarded in speech due to perfectly pure verbal conduct, from the absence of useless talk and from the absence of shouting and the like. "Yatindriya" means having the faculties restrained in respect of the mind-faculty, due to perfectly pure mental conduct and the absence of unreflective indifference and distraction through the application of noble spiritual power. "Nāga" means one who does not go by way of desire and so on; one for whom there is no returning again to the abandoned defilements of lust and so on; one who does not commit any offense whatsoever towards anyone; and one who does not go to a future existence—for these reasons he is a Nāga. Herein, by "Pāsādika" it shows that the Blessed One is a standard by means of his physical body; by "Pasādanīya," by means of his Dhamma-body. By "Santindriya" and so on, it shows he is a standard by means of the remaining qualities. Thus it should be understood that the Blessed One's status as the standard for all beings without exception in this world, which has these four standards, is revealed. "In a single dwelling" means in a single fragrant hut. For here "fragrant hut" is intended by the word "dwelling." "To stay" means to reside.

258. Ajjhokāse vītināmetvāti (udā. aṭṭha. 46) ajjhokāse nisajjāya vītināmetvā. “Yasmā bhagavā āyasmato soṇassa samāpattisamāpajjanena paṭisanthāraṃ karonto sāvakasādhāraṇā sabbā samāpattiyo [M 3.0301] anulomapaṭilomaṃ samāpajjanto bahudeva rattiṃ ajjhokāse nisajjāya vītināmetvā pāde pakkhāletvā vihāraṃ pāvisi, tasmā āyasmāpi soṇo bhagavato adhippāyaṃ ñatvā tadanurūpaṃ sabbā tā samāpattiyo samāpajjanto bahudeva rattiṃ ajjhokāse [V 3.0275] nisajjāya vītināmetvā pāde pakkhāletvā vihāraṃ pāvisī”ti keci vadanti. Pavisitvā ca bhagavatā anuññāto cīvaraṃ tirokaraṇīyaṃ katvāpi bhagavato pādapasse nisajjāya vītināmesi. Ajjhesīti āṇāpesi. Paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhu dhammo bhāsitunti bhikkhu tuyhaṃ dhammo bhāsituṃ upaṭṭhātu ñāṇamukhaṃ āgacchatu, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇāhīti attho.

258. "Having spent the time outdoors" means having spent the time sitting outdoors. Some say: "Because the Blessed One, while extending a welcome to Venerable Soṇa by entering meditative attainments, entered all the meditative attainments common to disciples in forward and reverse order, spent much of the night sitting outdoors, washed his feet, and entered the dwelling, therefore Venerable Soṇa, understanding the Blessed One’s intention, accordingly entered into all those meditative attainments, spent much of the night sitting outdoors, washed his feet, and entered the dwelling." And having entered, and being permitted by the Blessed One, he spent the time sitting near the Blessed One’s feet, even after making his robe into a screen. "He requested" means he commanded. "Let the Dhamma occur to you, monk, for speaking" means "Monk, may the Dhamma be present to you for speaking, may it come to the forefront of your knowledge; speak the Dhamma as you have heard and learned it"—this is the meaning.

Sabbāneva aṭṭhakavaggikānīti aṭṭhakavaggabhūtāni kāmasuttādīni (mahāni. 1) soḷasa suttāni. Sarena abhāsīti suttussāraṇasarena abhāsi, sarabhaññavasena kathesīti attho. Sarabhaññapariyosāneti ussāraṇāvasāne. Suggahitānīti sammā uggahitāni. Sumanasikatānīti suṭṭhu manasi katāni. Ekacco uggahaṇakāle sammā uggahetvāpi pacchā sajjhāyādivasena manasikaraṇakāle byañjanāni vā micchā ropeti, padapaccābhaṭṭhaṃ vā karoti, na evamayaṃ. Iminā pana sammadeva yathuggahitaṃ manasi katāni. Tena vuttaṃ “sumanasikatānīti suṭṭhu manasi katānī”ti. Sūpadhāritānīti atthatopi suṭṭhu upadhāritāni. Atthe hi suṭṭhu upadhārite sakkā pāḷi sammā ussāretuṃ. Kalyāṇiyāpi vācāya samannāgatoti sithiladhanitādīnaṃ yathāvidhānaṃ vacanena parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanāya poriyā vācāya samannāgato. Vissaṭṭhāyāti vimuttāya. Etenassa vimuttavāditaṃ dasseti. Anelagalāyāti elaṃ vuccati doso, taṃ na paggharatīti anelagalā, tāya niddosāyāti attho. Atha vā anelagalāyāti anelāya ca agalāya ca, niddosāya agalitapadabyañjanāya aparihīnapadabyañjanāyāti attho. Tathā hi naṃ bhagavā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kalyāṇavākkaraṇānaṃ yadidaṃ soṇo kuṭikaṇṇo”ti (a. ni. 1.198, 206) etadagge ṭhapesi. Atthassa viññāpaniyāti yathādhippetaṃ atthaṃ ñāpetuṃ samatthāya.

"All the Aṭṭhakavaggikāni" means the sixteen suttas that belong to the Aṭṭhakavagga, beginning with the Kāma Sutta. "He recited them with his voice" means he spoke them with the voice of sutta recitation; that is, he spoke them in the manner of chanting. "At the end of the chanting" means at the conclusion of the recitation. "Well-grasped" means properly learned. "Well-attended to" means thoroughly borne in mind. Some, even if they learn correctly at the time of learning, later, during the time of attending to it by way of recitation and so on, either misplace the syllables or stumble over the words—but not this one. By him, they were attended to correctly, just as they were learned. Therefore it is said, "well-attended to means thoroughly borne in mind." "Well-penetrated" means thoroughly penetrated as to the meaning. For when the meaning is thoroughly penetrated, it is possible to recite the Pāli text correctly.
