"Endowed with a beautiful voice" means endowed with a refined voice, with well-rounded words and syllables, speaking the lax and tense sounds and so on according to the rules. "Clear" means released. This shows his quality of speaking with release. "Without a dripping flaw" means: 'ela' is called a fault; it does not drip that, thus 'anelagalā'; the meaning is 'faultless.' Alternatively, 'anelagalā' means both 'without fault' (anelā) and 'without stumbling' (agalā); the meaning is 'faultless, with words and syllables not slurred, with words and syllables not deficient.' For the Blessed One placed him foremost, saying: "This is the foremost, monks, among my monk disciples with beautiful voices, that is, Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa" (AN 1.198, 206). "For making the meaning known" means capable of making known the intended meaning.

Kativassoti [M 3.0302] so kira majjhimavayassa tatiye koṭṭhāse ṭhito ākappasampanno ca paresaṃ ciratarapabbajito viya khāyati. Taṃ sandhāya bhagavā pucchīti keci, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ santaṃ samādhisukhaṃ anubhavituṃ yutto, ettakaṃ kālaṃ kasmā pamādaṃ āpannosīti pana anuyuñjituṃ satthā “kativassosī”ti taṃ pucchi. Tenevāha “kissa pana tvaṃ bhikkhu evaṃ ciraṃ akāsī”ti. Tattha kissāti kiṃkāraṇā. Evaṃ ciraṃ akāsīti evaṃ cirāyi, kena kāraṇena evaṃ cirakālaṃ pabbajjaṃ anupagantvā agāramajjhe vasīti attho. Ciraṃ diṭṭho meti cirena [V 3.0276] cirakālena mayā diṭṭho. Kāmesūti vatthukāmesu kilesakāmesu ca. Ādīnavoti doso. Apicāti kāmesu ādīnave kenaci pakārena diṭṭhepi na tāvāhaṃ gharāvāsato nikkhamituṃ asakkhiṃ. Kasmā? Sambādho gharāvāso, uccāvacehi kiccakaraṇīyehi samupabyūḷho agāriyabhāvo. Tenevāha “bahukicco bahukaraṇīyo”ti.

‘How old are you?’ It is said that he was in the third portion of middle age, accomplished in demeanor, and appeared to others as one who had been ordained for a very long time. Some say the Blessed One questioned him with this in mind, but that is without reason. Instead, to inquire why he had fallen into negligence for such a long time, though he was fit to experience the bliss of concentration, the Teacher questioned him, ‘How old are you?’ Therefore, he (the Buddha) said, ‘But why, monk, have you delayed thus for so long?’ Here, ‘why’ means ‘for what reason?’ ‘Have you delayed thus for so long?’ means ‘you have delayed thus’; the meaning is, ‘for what reason did you dwell in the household life for such a long time without undertaking the monastic life?’ ‘Seen by me long ago’ means ‘seen by me after a long, long time.’ ‘In sensual pleasures’ refers to both object-based sensual pleasures and defilement-based sensual pleasures. ‘Danger’ means fault. ‘Moreover’—even though the danger in sensual pleasures was seen in some way, still I was not yet able to leave the household life. Why? Because household life is confining; the state of a householder is beset by various duties and tasks. Therefore, he (Soṇa) said, ‘full of duties, full of responsibilities.’

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti kāmesu yathābhūtaṃ ādīnavadassino cittaṃ cirāyitvāpi gharāvāse na pakkhandati, aññadatthu padumapalāse udakabindu viya vinivattatiyevāti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti pavattiṃ nivattiñca sammadeva jānanto pavattiyaṃ taṃnimitte ca na kadācipi ramatīti idamatthadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

‘Having understood this matter’ means having fully understood in every way this matter: that the mind of one who sees the danger in sensual pleasures as it truly is does not incline toward household life even if it delays, but rather turns away just like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. ‘This utterance’ means that knowing rightly both the round of existence and its cessation, and their causes, he never delights in the round of existence and its causes; he uttered this utterance illuminating this meaning.

Tattha disvā ādīnavaṃ loketi sabbasmimpi saṅkhāraloke “anicco dukkho vipariṇāmadhammo”tiādīnavaṃ dosaṃ paññācakkhunā passitvā. Etena vipassanācāro kathito. Ñatvā dhammaṃ nirūpadhinti sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggattā nirupadhiṃ nibbānadhammaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñatvā, nissaraṇavivekāsaṅkhatāmatasabhāvato maggañāṇena paṭivijjhitvā. “Disvā ñatvā”ti imesaṃ padānaṃ “ghataṃ pivitvā balaṃ hoti, sīhaṃ disvā bhayaṃ hoti, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.271) viya hetuatthatā daṭṭhabbā. Ariyo na ramatī pāpeti kilesehi ārakattā ariyo sappuriso aṇumattepi pāpe na ramati. Kasmā? Pāpe na ramatī sucīti suvisuddhakāyasamācārāditāya suci suddhapuggalo rājahaṃso viya uccāraṭṭhāne pāpe saṃkiliṭṭhadhamme na ramati nābhinandati. “Pāpo [M 3.0303] na ramatī suci”ntipi pāṭho, tassattho – pāpo puggalo suciṃ anavajjaṃ vodānadhammaṃ na ramati, aññadatthu gāmasūkarādayo viya uccāraṭṭhānaṃ asuciṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva ramatīti paṭipakkhato desanaṃ parivatteti.

Here, ‘having seen the danger in the world’ means having perceived with the eye of wisdom the danger and fault in the entire conditioned world, that it is ‘impermanent, suffering, subject to change.’ By this, the practice of insight is described. ‘Having known the Dhamma as free from substratum’ means having fully understood the Nibbāna-Dhamma as it truly is, which is free from substratum because it is the relinquishment of all substrata, having penetrated it with path-knowledge by its nature of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless. The phrases ‘having seen’ and ‘having known’ should be understood in their causal sense, as in examples like: ‘Drinking ghee brings strength, seeing a lion brings fear, and through wisdom, having seen, the taints are destroyed’ (MN 1.271). ‘The noble one does not delight in evil’ means that being far from defilements, the noble and virtuous person does not take even the slightest pleasure in wrongdoing. Why? ‘Because the pure one does not delight in evil’ means that being pure, a pure individual, due to utterly pure bodily conduct and so on, like a royal swan in a refuse heap, does not delight in or approve of evil, defiled things. Alternatively, the reading may be: ‘The wicked do not delight in purity.’ Its meaning is this: the wicked person does not delight in what is pure, blameless, and the cleansing Dhamma. Instead, like village pigs and such, they take pleasure only in impure, defiled things, like a refuse heap. Thus, the teaching is presented from the opposite perspective.

Soṇakuṭikaṇṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa is concluded.

259. Kāḷasīhoti kāḷamukhavānarajāti. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyamevāti.

259. ‘Kāḷasīha’ means a black-faced monkey species. The rest here should be easily understood from the Pāli text and commentary.

Cammakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the chapter on hides is concluded.

6. Bhesajjakkhandhakaṃ

6. The Chapter on Medicines

Pañcabhesajjādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Account of the Five Medicines and So Forth

261. Bhesajjakkhandhake [M 3.0304][V 3.0277] nacchādentīti ruciṃ na uppādenti.

261. In the Chapter on Medicines, 'they do not please' means they do not arouse liking.

262. Susukāti samudde bhavā ekā macchajāti. Kumbhīlātipi vadanti. Saṃsaṭṭhanti parissāvitaṃ. Telaparibhogenāti sattāhakālikaparibhogaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

262. ‘Susukā’ is a type of fish found in the ocean. They also call it ‘Kumbhīlā’. ‘Saṃsaṭṭha’ means strained. ‘By the use of oil’ is said with reference to use permissible for seven days.

263. Piṭṭhehīti pisitehi. Ubbhidaṃ nāma ūsarapaṃsumayaṃ.

263. ‘Piṭṭhehi’ means with ground substances. ‘Ubbhida’ is that which consists of saline earth and dust.

264. Chakaṇanti gomayaṃ. Pākatikacuṇṇaṃ nāma apakkakasāvacuṇṇaṃ. Tena ṭhapetvā gandhacuṇṇaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

264. ‘Chakaṇa’ means cow dung. ‘Pākatikacuṇṇa’ is raw astringent powder. Therefore, they say that all of it is permissible except fragrant powder.

265. Suvaṇṇagerukoti suvaṇṇatutthādi. Añjanūpapisananti añjanatthāya upapisitabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci cuṇṇajātaṃ.

265. ‘Suvaṇṇageruka’ means golden vitriol and so forth. ‘Añjanūpapisana’ means any kind of powder that should be ground for collyrium.

268. Sāmaṃ gahetvāti ettha sappadaṭṭhassa atthāya aññena bhikkhunā gahitampi sāmaṃ gahitasaṅkhameva gacchatīti veditabbaṃ.

268. ‘Sāmaṃ gahetvā’ (having taken by oneself): here, it should be understood that even if something is taken by another bhikkhu for the sake of one bitten by a snake, it still counts as ‘taken by oneself’.

269. Gharadinnakābādho nāma vasīkaraṇatthāya gharaṇiyā dinnabhesajjasamuṭṭhito ābādho. Tenāha “vasīkaraṇapāṇakasamuṭṭhitarogo”ti. Ghara-saddo cettha abhedena gharaṇiyā vattamāno adhippeto. “Akaṭayūsenāti anabhisaṅkhatena muggayūsena. Kaṭākaṭenāti mugge pacitvā acāletvāva parissāvitena muggasūpenā”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

269. ‘Gharadinnakābādha’ is an ailment arisen from medicine given by a housewife for the purpose of subjugation. Therefore it is said, ‘a disease arisen from a subjugating potion’. Here, the word ‘ghara’ (house) is intended to refer to the housewife, being used without distinction. ‘Akaṭayūsena’ means with unprocessed mung bean soup. ‘Kaṭākaṭena’ means with mung bean soup that has been cooked and strained without stirring—as stated in the glossaries.

Guḷādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Account of the Permission Concerning Molasses and So Forth

272. Guḷakaraṇanti [V 3.0278] guḷakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, ucchusālanti vuttaṃ hoti.

272. ‘Guḷakaraṇa’ means the place for making molasses, that is, a sugarcane mill.

274. Avissatthāti sāsaṅkā.

274. ‘Avissatthā’ means suspicious.

276. Appamattakepi [M 3.0305] pavārentīti appamattakepi gahite pavārenti, “bahumhi gahite aññesaṃ nappahotī”ti maññamānā appamattakaṃ gahetvā pavārentīti adhippāyo. Paṭisaṅkhāpi paṭikkhipantīti “divā bhojanatthāya bhavissatī”ti sallakkhetvāpi paṭikkhipanti.

276. ‘Appamattakepi pavārenti’ (they refuse even a small amount) means they refuse even when a small amount is taken, thinking, ‘If much is taken, it will not suffice for others’; they take a small amount and then refuse—this is the intention. ‘Paṭisaṅkhāpi paṭikkhipanti’ (they reject even after reflection) means they reject even after considering, ‘This will be for the daytime meal’.

279. Sambādhe dahanakammaṃ paṭikkhepābhāvo vaṭṭati.

279. In a confined space, it is permissible not to prohibit the act of burning.

280. Ubhatopasannāti ubhayato pasannā. Māghātoti “mā ghātetha pāṇino”ti evaṃ māghātaghositadivaso.

280. ‘Ubhatopasannā’ means pleased in both ways. ‘Māghāta’ means the day proclaimed thus: ‘Do not kill living beings’—that is, the day of the non-killing proclamation.

Yāgumadhugoḷakādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Account of Rice Gruel, Honey-Balls, and So Forth

282. Madhugoḷakanti sakkarādisaṃyuttapūvaṃ. Āyuṃ detīti āyudānaṃ deti. Vaṇṇanti sarīravaṇṇaṃ. Sukhanti kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ. Balanti sarīrathāmaṃ. Paṭibhānanti yuttamuttapaṭibhānaṃ. Vātaṃ anulometīti vātaṃ anulometvā harati. Vatthiṃ sodhetīti dhamaniyo suddhaṃ karoti. Āmāvasesaṃ pācetīti sace āmāvasesakaṃ hoti, taṃ pāceti. Anuppavecchatīti deti. Vātañca byapanetīti sambandhitabbaṃ.

282. ‘Madhugoḷaka’ means a cake mixed with sugar and so forth. ‘Gives life’ means it grants longevity. ‘Complexion’ means bodily complexion. ‘Happiness’ means physical and mental happiness. ‘Strength’ means bodily vigor. ‘Eloquence’ means appropriate and ready eloquence. ‘Regulates the wind’ means it regulates and removes wind. ‘Cleanses the bladder’ means it makes the vessels pure. ‘Digests residual indigestion’ means if there is residual indigestion, it digests it. ‘Provides’ means it gives. And ‘dispels wind’ should be connected.

283. Nanu ca “paramparabhojanena kāretabbo”ti kasmā vuttaṃ. Paramparabhojanañhi pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena nimantitassa taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhuñjantassa hoti, ime ca bhikkhū bhojjayāguṃ paribhuñjiṃsu, pañcasu bhojanesu aññataranti āha “bhojjayāguyā hi pavāraṇā hotī”ti. Yasmā pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ paṭikkhipantassa vuttā pavāraṇā bhojjayāguṃ paṭikkhipantassapi hotiyeva, tasmā bhojjayāgupi odanagatikāyevāti adhippāyo.

283. But why was it said that an offense of successive eating was incurred? For successive eating occurs when one invited to partake of one of the five kinds of food sets that aside and eats another of the five kinds. But these bhikkhus consumed substantial rice gruel, which is one of the five kinds of food—hence it is said, ‘For with substantial rice gruel, there is pavāraṇā’. Because the pavāraṇā stated for one who declines one of the five kinds of food also applies to one who declines substantial rice gruel, therefore substantial rice gruel is considered to be in the same category as cooked rice—this is the meaning.

284. Sukhumojaṃ [V 3.0279] pakkhipiṃsūti “bhagavā paribhuñjissatī”ti maññamānā pakkhipiṃsu.

284. ‘Sukhumojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu’ (they placed fine essence) means they placed it thinking, ‘The Blessed One will partake of it’.

Pāṭaligāmavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Account of Pāṭaligāma

285. Pāṭaligāmoti [M 3.0306] (udā. aṭṭha. 76) evaṃnāmako magadharaṭṭhe eko gāmo. Tassa kira gāmassa māpanadivase gāmaṅgaṇaṭṭhāne dve tayo pāṭalaṅkurā pathavito ubbhijjitvā nikkhamiṃsu. Tena taṃ “pāṭaligāmo” tveva vohariṃsu. Tadavasarīti taṃ pāṭaligāmaṃ avasari anupāpuṇi. Pāṭaligāmikāti pāṭaligāmavāsino. Upāsakāti te kira bhagavato paṭhamadassanena keci saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhitā. Tena vuttaṃ “upāsakā”ti. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti pāṭaligāme kira ajātasattuno licchavirājūnañca manussā kālena kālaṃ gantvā gehasāmike gehato nīharitvā māsampi aḍḍhamāsampi vasanti. Tena pāṭaligāmavāsino manussā niccupaddutā “etesañceva āgatakāle vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatīti ekapasse issarānaṃ bhaṇḍapaṭisāmanaṭṭhānaṃ, ekapasse vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, ekapasse āgantukānaṃ addhikamanussānaṃ, ekapasse daliddānaṃ kapaṇamanussānaṃ, ekapasse gilānānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti sabbesaṃ aññamaññaṃ aghaṭṭetvā vasanappahonakaṃ nagaramajjhe mahatiṃ sālaṃ kāresuṃ, tassa nāmaṃ āvasathāgāranti. Āgantvā vasanti ettha āgantukāti āvasatho, tadeva āgāraṃ āvasathāgāraṃ.

285. Pāṭaligāma (Udāna Commentary, p. 76) was a village of that name in the Magadha country. It is said that on the day that village was being measured out, two or three pāṭala shoots emerged from the ground in the village square. Therefore, they called it ‘Pāṭaligāma.’ ‘Tadavasari’ means he arrived at and reached that Pāṭaligāma. ‘Pāṭaligāmikā’ means residents of Pāṭaligāma. ‘Upāsakā’ means that some of them, it is said, upon first seeing the Blessed One, had become established in the refuges and the precepts. Hence, they are referred to as ‘upāsakā’ (lay devotees). Regarding ‘they approached where the Blessed One was’: it is said that in Pāṭaligāma, the men of King Ajātasattu and of the Licchavi rulers would from time to time go there, evict householders from their homes, and stay for a month or even half a month. Because the residents of Pāṭaligāma were constantly harassed, they thought, ‘When these people come, there should be a place for them to stay.’ So, they designated one side as a place for storing the rulers' goods, one side as a residence, one side for visiting travelers, one side for the poor and destitute, and one side for the sick. Thus they constructed a large hall in the center of the village, sufficient for all to stay without obstructing one another, naming it ‘Āvasathāgāra’ (guest house). Because travelers would come and stay there (`āgantvā vasanti ettha āgantukā`), it was called ‘āvasatha’ (guest house), and that very building (`āgāra`) was the ‘āvasathāgāra.’

Taṃ divasañca taṃ niṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Te tattha gantvā iṭṭhakakammasudhākammacittakammādivasena supariniṭṭhitaṃ susajjitaṃ devavimānasadisaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakato paṭṭhāya oloketvā “idaṃ āvasathāgāraṃ ativiya manoramaṃ sassirikaṃ, kena nu kho paṭhamaṃ paribhuttaṃ amhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya assā”ti cintesuṃ, tasmiṃyeva ca khaṇe “bhagavā taṃ gāmaṃ anuppatto”ti assosuṃ, tena te uppannapītisomanassā “amhehi bhagavā gantvāpi ānetabbo siyā, so sayameva amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sampatto, ajja mayaṃ bhagavantaṃ idha vasāpetvā paṭhamaṃ paribhuñjāpessāma, tathā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghe āgate tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ āgatameva bhavissati, satthāraṃ maṅgalaṃ vadāpessāma, dhammaṃ kathāpessāma, iti tīhi ratanehi paribhutte pacchā amhākaṃ paresañca paribhogo bhavissati, evaṃ no dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā etadatthameva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. Tasmā evamāhaṃsu “adhivāsetu no, bhante, bhagavā [M 3.0307] āvasathāgāra”nti. Tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.297-298; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.22) kiñcāpi taṃ divasameva pariniṭṭhitattā devavimānaṃ [V 3.0280] viya susajjitaṃ supaṭijaggitaṃ, buddhārahaṃ pana katvā na paññattaṃ. Buddhā hi nāma araññajjhāsayā araññārāmā, antogāme vaseyyuṃ vā no vā, tasmā bhagavato ruciṃ jānitvāva paññapessāmāti cintetvā te bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu, idāni bhagavato ruciṃ jānitvā tathā paññāpetukāmā yenāvasathāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Sabbasanthariṃ āvasathāgāraṃ santharitvāti ettha santharaṇaṃ santhari, sabbo sakalo santhari etthāti sabbasanthari. Atha vā santhatanti santhari, sabbaṃ santhari sabbasanthari, taṃ sabbasanthariṃ. Bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesovāyaṃ, yathā sabbameva santhataṃ hoti, evaṃ santharitvāti attho. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ tāva “gomayaṃ nāma sabbamaṅgalesu vaṭṭatī”ti sudhāparikammakatampi bhūmiṃ allagomayena opuñjāpetvā parisukkhabhāvaṃ ñatvā yathā akkantaṭṭhāne padaṃ paññāyati, evaṃ cātujjātiyagandhehi limpetvā upari nānāvaṇṇakaṭasārake santharitvā tesaṃ upari mahāpiṭṭhikakojave ādiṃ katvā hatthattharaṇādīhi nānāvaṇṇehi attharaṇehi santharitabbayuttakaṃ sabbokāsaṃ santharāpesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbasanthariṃ āvasathāgāraṃ santharitvā”ti.

That day, the work reached its completion. They went there and, starting from the gateway, saw the well-finished and well-decorated building, like a divine mansion, perfectly completed with brickwork, plastering, painting, and so on. They thought, ‘This guest house is exceedingly delightful and splendid. Who should be the first to use it for our long-term benefit and happiness?’ At that very moment, they heard, ‘The Blessed One has arrived in the village.’ Filled with joy and gladness, they thought, ‘We might have had to go and bring the Blessed One, but he has come to our dwelling place by himself. Today, we will have the Blessed One stay here and be the first to use it, and likewise the community of monks. When the monastic community arrives, the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha’s word, will also have arrived. We will have the Teacher pronounce a blessing, and we will have him teach the Dhamma. Thus, after it has been used by the three jewels, it will be for our use and that of others. This will be for our long-term benefit and happiness.’ Having made this resolution, they approached the Blessed One for this very purpose. Therefore, they said, ‘Venerable sir, may the Blessed One consent to the guest house.’ Regarding their approach: although the hall was completed that very day and as well-decorated and well-maintained as a celestial palace, it had not yet been designated as suitable for the Buddha. For Buddhas are by nature forest-dwellers, fond of the forest; whether they would stay within a village or not was uncertain. Therefore, thinking, ‘We will prepare it only after knowing the Blessed One’s preference,’ they approached the Blessed One. Now, having learned the Blessed One’s inclination and wishing to prepare it accordingly, they approached the guest house. Regarding ‘having spread out the entire guest house with coverings’: here, `santhari` refers to a covering. `Sabbasanthari` means that the entire place was spread with coverings. This is an expression in the neuter abstract sense, meaning that it was spread so as to be entirely covered. First of all, knowing that ‘cow dung is suitable for all auspicious ceremonies,’ they had the ground, though already plastered, smeared with fresh cow dung. When they knew it was almost dry, they anointed it with the four kinds of fragrances in such a way that footprints would be visible where one stepped. Upon that they spread multicolored mats, and over these they laid out various colored coverings, such as large counterpanes and elephant rugs, over the entire space suitable for furnishing. Therefore, it is said, ‘having spread out the entire guest house with coverings.’

Āsanānīti majjhaṭṭhāne tāva maṅgalatthambhaṃ nissāya mahārahaṃ buddhāsanaṃ paññapetvā tattha yaṃ yaṃ mudukañca manoramañca paccattharaṇaṃ, taṃ taṃ attharitvā ubhatolohitakaṃ manuññadassanaṃ upadhānaṃ upadahitvā upari suvaṇṇarajatatārakavicittavitānaṃ bandhitvā gandhadāmapupphadāmapattādāmādīhi alaṅkaritvā samantā dvādasahatthe ṭhāne pupphajālaṃ kāretvā tiṃsahatthamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭasāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā pacchimabhittiṃ nissāya bhikkhusaṅghassa pallaṅkapīṭhaapassayapīṭhamuṇḍapīṭhādīni paññapāpetvā upari setapaccattharaṇehi paccattharāpetvā sālāya pācīnapassaṃ attano nisajjāyoggaṃ kāresuṃ. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “āsanāni paññapetvā”ti.

‘Seats’ (āsanāni). First, in the central area, against the auspicious pillar, they set up a highly valuable Buddha seat. There, they spread out whatever soft and pleasing coverings there were, placed a comfortable and attractive red cushion on both sides, and hung above a canopy adorned with gold and silver star patterns. They decorated it with fragrant garlands, flower garlands, leaf garlands, and so on, arranged flower nets in the space of twelve cubits all around, and had an area of about thirty cubits enclosed with a cloth screen. Against the western wall, they had couches, stools, chairs with backrests, round stools, and the like prepared for the monastic community, covering them with white spreads. In the eastern section of the hall, they prepared a seating area suitable for themselves. In reference to this, it is said, ‘having prepared the seats.’

Udakamaṇikanti mahākucchikaṃ samekhalaṃ udakacāṭiṃ. Evaṃ bhagavā bhikkhusaṅgho ca yathāruciyā hatthapāde dhovissanti, mukhaṃ vikkhālessantīti tesu tesu ṭhānesu maṇivaṇṇassa udakassa pūretvā vāsatthāya nānāpupphāni [M 3.0308] ceva udakavāsacuṇṇāni ca pakkhipitvā kadalipaṇṇehi pidahitvā patiṭṭhapesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “udakamaṇikaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā”ti.

‘A water vessel’ (udakamaṇikaṃ). This refers to a large-bellied water pot with a girdle. So that the Blessed One and the monastic community could wash their hands and feet as they pleased and rinse their mouths, in various places they filled vessels with water the color of gems, adding various flowers and powdered water-scents for fragrance, then covered them with banana leaves and set them in place. Hence, it is said, ‘having set up a water vessel.’

Telapadīpaṃ āropetvāti rajatasuvaṇṇādimayadaṇḍāsu daṇḍadīpikāsu yonakarūpakādīnaṃ hatthe ṭhapitasuvaṇṇarajatādimayakapallikāsu ca telapadīpe jalayitvā. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti ettha pana te pāṭaligāmikaupāsakā na kevalaṃ āvasathāgārameva, atha kho sakalasmimpi gāme vīthiyo sajjāpetvā dhaje ussāpetvā gehadvāresu puṇṇaghaṭe ca kadaliādayo ca ṭhapāpetvā [V 3.0281] sakalagāmaṃ dīpamālāhi vippakiṇṇatārakaṃ viya katvā “khīrapake dārake khīraṃ pāyetha, daharakumāre lahuṃ lahuṃ bhojetvā sayāpetha, uccāsaddaṃ mā karittha, ajja ekarattiṃ satthā antogāme vasissati, buddhā nāma appasaddakāmā hontī”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā sayaṃ daṇḍadīpikā ādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu.

‘Having lit an oil lamp’ (telapadīpaṃ āropetvā). This means lighting oil lamps in lamp stands with shafts made of silver, gold, and other materials, and in small bowls of gold, silver, and the like, placed in the hands of Yona figures and so on. Regarding ‘they approached where the Blessed One was’: here, the lay devotees of Pāṭaligāma not only prepared the guest house, but also decorated the streets in the entire village, had banners raised, had full pots and banana trees placed at the doors of houses, and made the entire village like a sky strewn with stars with rows of lamps. They had a drum beaten to announce, ‘Give milk to the infants who drink milk, quickly feed the young children and put them to sleep, do not make loud noises—for tonight the Teacher will stay within the village. Buddhas, indeed, desire quiet.’ Then, taking lamp stands themselves, they approached where the Blessed One was.

Atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena āvasathāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamīti “yassa dāni, bhante, bhagavā kālaṃ maññatī”ti evaṃ kira tehi kāle ārocite bhagavā lākhārasena tintarattakoviḷārapupphavaṇṇaṃ surattaṃ dupaṭṭaṃ kattariyā padumaṃ kantento viya, saṃvidhāya timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādento nivāsetvā suvaṇṇapāmaṅgena padumakalāpaṃ parikkhipanto viya, vijjulatāsassirikaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā rattakambalena gajakumbhaṃ pariyonandhanto viya, ratanasatubbedhe suvaṇṇagghike pavāḷajālaṃ khipamāno viya, mahati suvaṇṇacetiye rattakambalakañcukaṃ paṭimuñcanto viya, gacchantaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ rattavalāhakena paṭicchādayamāno viya, kañcanagirimatthake supakkalākhārasaṃ parisiñcanto viya, cittakūṭapabbatamatthakaṃ vijjulatājālena parikkhipanto viya ca sacakkavāḷasineruyugandharamahāpathaviṃ cāletvā gahitanigrodhapallavasamānavaṇṇaṃ rattavarapaṃsukūlaṃ pārupitvā vanagahanato kesarasīho viya, udayapabbatakūṭato puṇṇacando viya, bālasūriyo viya ca attanā nisinnatarusaṇḍato nikkhami.

Then the Blessed One, having put on his lower robe and taken his bowl and outer robe, together with the community of monks, approached the assembly hall. When the time was announced to him by them, saying, 'Venerable sir, it is now the time the Blessed One deems fit,' the Blessed One, having put on a well-dyed, double-layered red robe, the color of a koviḷāra flower dyed red with lac-juice, like one cutting a lotus with shears, and covering the three circles of the body, like one encircling a cluster of lotuses with a golden band, having bound a lightning-streaked girdle, like one wrapping an elephant's forehead with a red blanket, like one scattering a net of coral over a golden base with a hundred jeweled projections, like one putting a red blanket-cover on a great golden stupa, like one covering the moving full moon with a red cloud, like one sprinkling fully ripe lac-juice over a golden mountain peak, and like one surrounding the summit of Mount Cittakūṭa with a net of lightning, and having shaken the great earth with its surrounding world-system, Sineru, and Yugandhara mountains, having donned a superior red rag-robe the color of a newly grasped banyan leaf, emerged from the grove where he had been sitting, like a lion from a forest thicket, like the full moon from the peak of the eastern mountain, and like the newly risen sun.

Athassa kāyato meghamukhato vijjukalāpā viya rasmiyo nikkhamitvā suvaṇṇarasadhārāparisekapiñjarapattapupphaphalasākhāviṭape viya samantato [M 3.0309] rukkhe kariṃsu. Tāvadeva attano attano pattacīvaramādāya mahābhikkhusaṅgho bhagavantaṃ parivāresi. Te ca naṃ parivāretvā ṭhitabhikkhū evarūpā ahesuṃ appicchā santuṭṭhā pavivittā asaṃsaṭṭhā āraddhavīriyā vattāro vacanakkhamā codakā pāpagarahino sīlasampannā samādhisampannā paññāsampannā vimuttisampannā vimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā. Tehi parivārito bhagavā rattakambalaparikkhitto viya suvaṇṇakkhandho, rattapadumasaṇḍamajjhagatā viya suvaṇṇanāvā, pavāḷavedikāparikkhitto viya suvaṇṇapāsādo virocittha. Mahākassapappamukhā pana mahātherā meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupitvā maṇivammavammitā viya mahānāgā parivārayiṃsu vītarāgā bhinnakilesā vijaṭitajaṭā chinnabandhanā kule vā gaṇe vā alaggā.

Then, rays of light emanated from his body like flashes of lightning from a cloud’s mouth, making the trees all around appear golden-yellow, as if sprinkled with streams of golden nectar on their leaves, flowers, fruits, branches, and twigs. Immediately, the great community of monks, taking their bowls and robes, surrounded the Blessed One. Those monks who stood surrounding him were of such a nature: of few desires, content, secluded, not associating, energetic, speakers of Dhamma, patient with speech, reprovers, censurers of evil, accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by them, the Blessed One shone like a mass of gold wrapped in a red blanket, like a golden boat in the midst of a cluster of red lotuses, like a golden palace encircled by coral railings. But the great elders, led by Mahākassapa, dressed in cloud-colored rag robes, surrounded him like great elephants armored with jeweled plates—free from lust, with defilements destroyed, matted hair unraveled, bonds cut off, unattached to family or group.

Iti bhagavā sayaṃ vītarāgo vītarāgehi, vītadoso vītadosehi, vītamoho vītamohehi[V 3.0282], nittaṇho nittaṇhehi, nikkileso nikkilesehi, sayaṃ buddho anubuddhehi parivārito pattaparivāritaṃ viya kesaraṃ, kesaraparivāritā viya kaṇṇikā, aṭṭhanāgasahassaparivārito viya chaddanto nāgarājā, navutihaṃsasahassaparivārito viya dhataraṭṭho haṃsarājā, senaṅgaparivārito viya cakkavattī, marugaṇaparivārito viya sakko devarājā, brahmagaṇaparivārito viya hāritamahābrahmā, tārāgaṇaparivuto viya puṇṇacando asamena buddhavesena aparimāṇena buddhavilāsena pāṭaligāmīnaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji.

Thus the Blessed One—himself without lust, among those without lust; without hatred, among those without hatred; without delusion, among those without delusion; without craving, among those without craving; without defilements, among those without defilements; himself awakened, surrounded by those awakened after him—like a filament surrounded by petals, like a pericarp surrounded by filaments, like the elephant king Chaddanta surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the goose king Dhataraṭṭha surrounded by ninety thousand geese, like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by his army, like Sakka, the king of gods, surrounded by the host of gods, like the great Brahmā Hārita surrounded by the host of Brahmās, like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars—proceeded along the road to Pāṭaligāma with matchless Buddha-bearing and immeasurable Buddha-splendor.

Athassa puratthimakāyato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ghanabuddharasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, pacchimakāyato dakkhiṇapassato vāmapassato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ghanarasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, uparikesantato paṭṭhāya sabbakesāvattehi moragīvavaṇṇā ghanabuddharasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā gaganatale asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, heṭṭhāpādatalehi pavāḷavaṇṇā rasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā ghanapathaviyaṃ asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, dantato akkhīnaṃ setaṭṭhānato, nakhānañca maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānato odātā ghanabuddharasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, rattapītavaṇṇānaṃ sambhinnaṭṭhānato mañjiṭṭhavaṇṇā rasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṃ ṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, sabbatthakameva pabhassarā rasmiyo uṭṭhahiṃsu. Evaṃ samantā asītihatthamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo vijjotamānā vipphandamānā [M 3.0310] vidhāvamānā kañcanadaṇḍadīpikāhi niccharitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandamānā mahāpadīpajālā viya, cātuddīpikamahāmeghato nikkhantavijjulatā viya ca disodisaṃ pakkhandiṃsu. Yāhi sabbadisābhāgā suvaṇṇacampakapupphehi vikiriyamānā viya, suvaṇṇaghaṭato nikkhantasuvaṇṇarasadhārāhi āsiñciyamānā viya, pasāritasuvaṇṇapaṭṭaparikkhittā viya, verambhavātasamuddhatakiṃsukakaṇikārakikirātapupphacuṇṇasamokiṇṇā viya cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇasamparirañjitā viya ca virociṃsu.

Then from the front of his body, golden rays of dense Buddha-radiance arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. From the rear of his body, from his right side, and from his left side, golden rays of dense radiance arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. From the top of his head, from all the hair-whorls, peacock-neck-colored rays of dense Buddha-radiance arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the sky. From the soles of his feet, coral-colored rays arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth. From his teeth, the white parts of his eyes, and the places where his nails separated from the flesh, white rays of dense Buddha-radiance arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. From the places where red and yellow colors mingled, madder-colored rays arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. And everywhere, luminous rays shone forth. Thus, all around, Buddha-rays of six colors—radiant, shimmering, darting—like great lamp-flames rushing into the sky, issuing forth from golden torch-lamps, and like lightning bolts emerging from a great cloud over the four continents, they spread in every direction. By them, all directions shone brilliantly, as if scattered with golden champak flowers, as if sprinkled with streams of golden nectar issuing from golden pots, as if encircled by spread-out golden cloths, as if strewn with the powder of kiṃsuka, kaṇikāra, and kirātaka flowers stirred up by the Verambha wind, or as if completely dyed with Chinese powder.

Bhagavatopi asītianubyañjanabyāmappabhāparikkhepasamujjalaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sarīraṃ abbhamahikādiupakkilesavimuttaṃ samujjalatārakapabhāsitaṃ viya gaganatalaṃ, vikasitaṃ viya padumavanaṃ, sabbapāliphullo viya yojanasatiko pāricchattako, paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitānaṃ dvattiṃsacandānaṃ dvattiṃsasūriyānaṃ dvattiṃsacakkavattīnaṃ dvattiṃsadevarājānaṃ dvattiṃsamahābrahmānaṃ siriyā siriṃ abhibhavamānaṃ viya virocittha, yathā taṃ dasahi pāramīhi dasahi upapāramīhi dasahi paramatthapāramīhīti sammadeva paripūritāhi samatiṃsāya pāramīhi alaṅkataṃ kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni dinnena dānena rakkhitena sīlena katena kalyāṇakammena ekasmiṃ attabhāve samosaritvā vipākaṃ dātuṃ okāsaṃ alabhamānena sambādhappattena [V 3.0283] viya nibbattitaṃ nāvāsahassassa bhaṇḍaṃ ekaṃ nāvaṃ āropanakālo viya, sakaṭasahassassa bhaṇḍaṃ ekaṃ sakaṭaṃ āropanakālo viya, pañcavīsatiyā gaṅgānaṃ sambhijja mukhadvāre ekato rāsībhūtakālo viya ca ahosi.

The Blessed One’s body, adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great man, radiant with the eighty minor marks and a halo extending a fathom, free from defilements like clouds and mist, shone like the sky lit with brilliant stars, like a blossoming lotus grove, like the Pāricchattaka tree spanning a hundred leagues, fully bloomed with all its leaves. It shone as if surpassing the glory of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two wheel-turning monarchs, thirty-two kings of gods, and thirty-two great Brahmās, placed in a row—just as it was adorned with the thirty perfections, fully perfected, namely, the ten perfections, the ten superior perfections, and the ten supreme perfections. The fruits of giving, morality, and wholesome deeds performed for four incalculable periods and more than a hundred thousand aeons, now converging to give fruition in a single existence, were as if produced in a constricted space, unable to find room to ripen, like the time when the cargo of a thousand ships is loaded onto a single ship, like the time when the goods of a thousand carts are loaded onto a single cart, or like the time when the waters of twenty-five Ganges rivers, having converged, are gathered together at one mouth.

Imāya buddharasmiyā obhāsamānassapi bhagavato purato anekāni daṇḍadīpikāsahassāni ukkhipiṃsu, tathā pacchato vāmapasse dakkhiṇapasse. Jātisumanacampakavanamālikārattuppalanīluppalabakulasinduvārādipupphāni ceva nīlapītādivaṇṇasugandhagandhacuṇṇāni ca cātuddīpikamahaāmeghavissaṭṭhā salilavuṭṭhiyo viya vippakiriṃsu. Pañcaṅgikatūriyanigghosā ceva buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttā thutighosā ca sabbā disā pūrayamānā mukharā viya akaṃsu. Devasupaṇṇanāgayakkhagandhabbamanussānaṃ akkhīni amatapānaṃ viya labhiṃsu. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā padasahassehi gamanavaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Tatridaṃ mukhamattaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.22; udā. aṭṭha. 76) –

Even as the Blessed One was illuminated by his radiance, many thousands of torches were raised before him, and likewise behind, to his left, and to his right. Flowers such as jasmine, sumana, champak, forest mālikā, red lotuses, blue lotuses, bakula, and sinduvāra, along with fragrant powders of blue, yellow, and other hues, were scattered like rain showers released from great clouds over the four continents. The sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments and praises associated with the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha filled all directions, making them resound. The eyes of gods, supaṇṇas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and humans received it as if it were a drink of the deathless. Standing in this place, it is fitting to describe his gait in a thousand verses. Here is a mere outline:

“Evaṃ [M 3.0311] sabbaṅgasampanno, kampayanto vasundharaṃ;

Aheṭhayanto pāṇāni, yāti lokavināyako.

“Thus endowed with all features, shaking the earth, harming no living beings, the Leader of the World proceeds.

“Dakkhiṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ, uddharanto narāsabho;

Gacchanto sirisampanno, sobhate dvipaduttamo.

“Lifting his right foot first, the noble bull among men, walking, endowed with glory, the supreme among bipeds shines.

“Gacchato buddhaseṭṭhassa, heṭṭhāpādatalaṃ mudu;

Samaṃ samphusate bhūmiṃ, rajasānupalimpati.

“As the foremost Buddha walks, the soft soles of his feet touch the ground evenly, unsmudged by dust.

“Ninnaṃ ṭhānaṃ unnamati, gacchante lokanāyake;

Unnatañca samaṃ hoti, pathavī ca acetanā.

“Low places rise up as the Leader of the World goes forth; high places become level, though the earth is insentient.

“Pāsāṇā sakkharā ceva, kathalā khāṇukaṇṭakā;

Sabbe maggā vivajjanti, gacchante lokanāyake.

“Stones, gravel, potsherds, stumps, and thorns—all these keep clear of the path when the Leader of the World goes forth.

“Nātidūre uddharati, nāccāsanne ca nikkhipaṃ;

Aghaṭṭayanto niyyāti, ubho jāṇū ca gopphake.

“He does not raise his foot too far, nor does he set it down too close; without striking his knees or ankles together, he proceeds.

“Nātisīghaṃ [V 3.0284] pakkamati, sampannacaraṇo muni;

Na cātisaṇikaṃ yāti, gacchamāno samāhito.

“Not too quickly does he step, the sage accomplished in conduct; nor too slowly does he go, walking mindfully composed.

“Uddhaṃ adho tiriyañca, disañca vidisaṃ tathā;

Na pekkhamāno so yāti, yugamattañhi pekkhati.

“Upwards, downwards, across, and in the cardinal and intermediate directions, he goes not looking about, but watches only a yoke's length ahead.

“Nāgavikkantacāro so, gamane sobhate jino;

Cāru gacchati lokaggo, hāsayanto sadevake.

“He moves with the gait of a lordly elephant, the Conqueror, beautiful in his going; the foremost of the world walks gracefully, gladdening the world with its gods.

“Usabharājāva sobhanto, cātucārīva kesarī;

Tosayanto bahū satte, gāmaseṭṭhaṃ upāgamī”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.22; udā. aṭṭha. 76);

“Shining like a royal bull, like a lion roaming at will; pleasing many beings, he approached the excellent village.”

Vaṇṇakālo nāma kiresa. Evaṃvidhesu kālesu bhagavato sarīravaṇṇe vā guṇavaṇṇe vā dhammakathikassa thāmoyeva pamāṇaṃ. Cuṇṇiyapadehi gāthābandhehi vā yattakaṃ sakkoti, tattakaṃ vattabbaṃ, “dukkathita”nti vā “atitthena pakkhando”ti vā na vattabbo. Aparimāṇavaṇṇā hi buddhā bhagavanto, tesaṃ buddhāpi anavasesato vaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ asamatthā. Sakalampi hi kappaṃ vadantā pariyosāpetuṃ na sakkonti, pageva itarā pajāti. Iminā sirivilāsena alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ pāṭaligāmaṃ pavisitvā bhagavā pasannacittena janena pupphagandhadhūmavāsacuṇṇādīhi pūjiyamāno āvasathāgāraṃ [M 3.0312] pāvisi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena āvasathāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamī”ti.

It is said that this is called the time for praise. On such occasions, regarding the praise of the Blessed One’s physical form or his virtues, the Dhamma speaker’s capacity is the measure. One should speak as much as one is able, whether in prose or verse, and one should not be told, “You spoke poorly,” or, “Your praise was insufficiently expressed.” For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are of immeasurable qualities; even other Buddhas are unable to describe their qualities exhaustively. Even speaking for an entire eon, they could not bring it to an end, how much more so other beings. Adorned with this majestic splendor, the Blessed One entered Pāṭaligāma, and being honored by devoted people with flowers, perfumes, incense, fragrant powders, and so on, he proceeded to the rest house. Thus it is said: “Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, together with the community of monks, approached the rest house.”

Pāde pakkhāletvāti yadipi bhagavato pāde rajojallaṃ na upalimpati, tesaṃ pana upāsakānaṃ kusalābhivuddhiṃ ākaṅkhanto paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanatthaṃ bhagavā pāde pakkhālesi. Apica upādinnakasarīraṃ nāma sītikātabbampi hotīti tadatthampi bhagavā nahānapādadhovanāni karotiyeva. Bhagavantaṃyeva purakkhatvāti bhagavantaṃ purato katvā. Tattha bhagavā bhikkhūnañceva upāsakānañca majjhe nisinno gandhodakena nahāpetvā dukūlacumbaṭena vodakaṃ katvā jātihiṅgulakena majjitvā rattakambalapaliveṭhite pīṭhe ṭhapitā rattasuvaṇṇaghanapaṭimā viya ativiya virocittha. Ayaṃ panettha porāṇānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanamaggo –

“Having washed his feet”—though dust and dirt did not stain the Blessed One’s feet, yet, desiring the increase of merit for those lay devotees and for others to follow his example, the Blessed One washed his feet. Moreover, a body produced by clinging must also be cooled, so for that purpose too, the Blessed One indeed bathes and washes his feet. “Having placed the Blessed One at the forefront”—that is, placing the Blessed One in front. There, the Blessed One, seated amidst both the monks and the lay devotees, having been bathed with fragrant water, dried with a fine cloth, polished with pure vermilion, and placed on a seat wrapped in a red blanket, shone exceedingly like a solid red-gold image. This, however, is the manner of description by the ancients—

“Gantvāna [V 3.0285] maṇḍalamāḷaṃ, nāgavikkantacāraṇo;

Obhāsayanto lokaggo, nisīdi varamāsane.

“Having gone to the pavilion, he whose gait is like a lordly elephant, the foremost of the world, illuminating, sat on the excellent seat.

“Tahiṃ nisinno naradammasārathi,

Devātidevo satapuññalakkhaṇo;

Buddhāsane majjhagato virocati,

Suvaṇṇanekkhaṃ viya paṇḍukambale.

“There, seated, the charioteer of men to be tamed, the god beyond gods, marked with a hundred signs of merit, shines in the middle of the Buddha's seat, like a golden ornament on a pale blanket.

“Nekkhaṃ jambonadasseva, nikkhittaṃ paṇḍukambale;

Virocati vītamalo, maṇi verocano yathā.

“Like an ornament of Jambu-river gold, placed on a pale blanket, the stainless one shines, like a radiant gem.

“Mahāsālova samphullo, merurājāvalaṅkato;

Suvaṇṇathūpasaṅkāso, padumo kosako yathā.

“Like a great sal tree in full bloom, adorned like Meru, king of mountains; resembling a golden stupa, like a lotus in its bud.

“Jalanto dīparukkhova, pabbatagge yathā sikhī;

Devānaṃ pāricchattova, sabbaphullo virocathā”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.22; udā. aṭṭha. 76);

“Shining like a lamp-tree, like a flame on a mountaintop; like the Pāricchattaka tree of the gods, fully blossomed, you shine.”

Pāṭaligāmike upāsake āmantesīti yasmā tesu upāsakesu bahū janā sīle patiṭṭhitā, tasmā paṭhamaṃ tāva sīlavipattiyā ādīnavaṃ pakāsetvā pacchā sīlasampadāya ānisaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ “pañcime gahapatayo”tiādinā dhammadesanatthaṃ āmantesi. Tattha dussīloti [M 3.0313] nissīlo (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.149; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.213; udā. aṭṭha. 76). Abhāvattho hettha du-saddo “duppañño”tiādīsu viya. Sīlavipannoti vipannasīlo bhinnasaṃvaro. Ettha ca “dussīlo”ti padena puggalassa sīlābhāvo vutto. So panassa sīlābhāvo duvidho asamādānena vā samādinnassa bhedena vāti. Tesu purimo na tathā sāvajjo, yathā dutiyo sāvajjataro. Yathādhippetādīnavanimittaṃ sīlābhāvaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya dassetuṃ “sīlavipanno”ti vuttaṃ, tena “dussīlo”ti padassa atthaṃ dasseti. Pamādādhikaraṇanti pamādakāraṇā. Idañca suttaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ vasena āgataṃ, pabbajitānampi pana labbhateva. Gahaṭṭho hi yena yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvikaṃ kappeti yadi kasiyā yadi vaṇijjāya yadi gorakkhena. Pāṇātipātādivasena pamatto taṃ taṃ yathākālaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkoti, athassa [V 3.0286] kammaṃ vinassati. Māghātakāle pāṇātipātaṃ pana adinnādānādīni ca karonto daṇḍavasena mahatiṃ bhogajāniṃ nigacchati. Pabbajito dussīlo pamādakāraṇā sīlato buddhavacanato jhānato sattaariyadhanato ca jāniṃ nigacchati.

The Blessed One addressed the lay devotees of Pāṭaligāma. Since many among these devotees were established in virtue, therefore, first explaining the dangers of moral failure, and afterward showing the benefits of moral perfection, he addressed them with “Householders, these five…” for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Herein, “immoral” (dussīlo) means devoid of virtue (nissīlo). Here, the prefix “du-” conveys absence, as in “unwise” (duppañño) and similar terms. “Morally corrupt” (sīlavipanno) means one whose virtue is ruined, whose restraint is broken. Here, by the term “immoral,” a person’s lack of virtue is stated. This lack of virtue is twofold: either by not undertaking it or by breaking what has been undertaken. Among these, the former is not as blameworthy as the latter, which is more blameworthy. To illustrate the intended dangers resulting from the cause of the lack of virtue with reference to the person, the term “morally corrupt” is used, thereby clarifying the meaning of “immoral.” “Due to negligence” (pamādādhikaraṇaṃ) means caused by heedlessness. This discourse came about with reference to householders, but it also applies to monastics. A householder earns a livelihood through various crafts—whether farming, trade, or cattle-herding. If he is negligent by way of killing living beings and so forth, he cannot accomplish each of those tasks in due time, and thus his work is ruined. Moreover, by engaging in killing, stealing, and other misdeeds, he incurs a great loss of wealth by way of punishment. A monastic who is immoral and negligent suffers loss in terms of virtue, the Buddha’s teachings, meditation, and the seven noble treasures.

Pāpako kittisaddoti gahaṭṭhassa “asuko asukakule jāto dussīlo pāpadhammo pariccattaidhalokaparaloko salākabhattamattampi na detī”ti catuparisamajjhe pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati. Pabbajitassa “asuko nāma satthusāsane pabbajitvā nāsakkhi sīlāni rakkhituṃ, na buddhavacanaṃ uggahetuṃ, vejjakammādīhi jīvati, chahi agāravehi samannāgato”ti evaṃ pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati.

“A bad reputation”—for a householder, a bad reputation arises in the midst of the fourfold assembly when it is said, “So-and-so, born in such and such a family, is immoral, of wicked character, and has abandoned both this world and the next, not even giving a ticket-meal.” For a monastic, a bad reputation arises when it is said, “So-and-so, having gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation, was unable to maintain virtue, unable to learn the Buddha’s teachings, lives by medical work and other means, and is endowed with the six kinds of disrespect.”

Avisāradoti gahaṭṭho tāva “avassaṃ bahūnaṃ sannipātaṭṭhāne koci mama kammaṃ jānissati, atha maṃ niggaṇhissantī”ti vā, “rājakulassa vā dassantī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati, maṅkubhūto pattakkhandho adhomukho nisīdati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti. Pabbajitopi “bahū bhikkhū sannipatitā, avassaṃ koci mama kammaṃ jānissati, atha me uposathampi pavāraṇampi ṭhapetvā sāmaññato cāvetvā nikkaḍḍhissantī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti. Ekacco pana dussīlopi samāno dappito viya vadati, sopi ajjhāsayena maṅku hotiyeva vippaṭisārībhāvato.

“Timidity”—a householder, for his part, thinks, “Surely, in a gathering of many, someone will know my deeds, and then they will reproach me,” or “They will show me to the royal family,” and approaches fearfully, sitting with drooping shoulders, head down, unable to speak confidently. A monastic, too, thinks, “Many monks have gathered; surely someone will know my deeds, and then they will set aside my Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, remove me from the ascetic life, and drive me out,” and approaches fearfully, unable to speak confidently. But even a certain immoral person, though behaving proudly, is inwardly timid indeed due to remorse.

Sammūḷho [M 3.0314] kālaṃ karotīti dussīlassa hi maraṇamañce nipannassa dussīlyakammānaṃ samādāya vattitaṭṭhānāni āpāthamāgacchanti. So ummīletvā attano puttadārādidassanavasena idhalokaṃ passati, nimīletvā gatinimittupaṭṭhānavasena paralokaṃ passati, tassa cattāro apāyā kammānurūpaṃ upaṭṭhahanti. Sattisatena pahariyamāno viya aggijālāya āliṅgiyamāno viya ca hoti. So “vāretha vārethā”ti viravantova marati. Tena vuttaṃ “sammūḷho kālaṃ karotī”ti.

“One dies bewildered”—for when an immoral person lies on the deathbed, the places where they undertook and practiced immoral deeds appear before them. Opening their eyes, they see this world through seeing their children and spouse; closing them, they see the next world through the signs related to their destiny. The four realms of misery appear to them according to their deeds. It is as if they are being struck by a hundred spears or embraced by flames. Crying out, “Stop! Stop!” they die. Thus it is said, “One dies bewildered.”

Kāyassa bhedāti upādinnakakkhandhapariccāgā. Paraṃ maraṇāti tadanantaraṃ abhinibbattakkhandhaggahaṇe. Atha vā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassa upacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cutito uddhaṃ. Apāyantiādi sabbaṃ nirayavevacanaṃ. Nirayo hi saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasaṅkhātā ayā apetattā, sukhānaṃ vā āyassa āgamanassa abhāvā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati, dosabahulatāya vā duṭṭhena kammunā nibbattā gatīti duggati. Vivasā [V 3.0287] nipatanti ettha dukkaṭakārinoti vinipāto, vinassantā vā ettha nipatanti saṃbhijjamānaṅgapaccaṅgāti vinipāto. Natthi ettha assādasaññito ayoti nirayo.

“Upon the breakup of the body”—that is, the relinquishment of the clung-to aggregates. “After death” means the grasping of a new set of aggregates immediately thereafter. Alternatively, “upon the breakup of the body” means the cessation of the life faculty, and “after death” refers to what follows after passing away. “The realms of misery” and so on are all synonyms for hell. Hell is called apāya because it is devoid of “āya” (gain), which is merit, the cause of heaven and liberation; or because there is an absence of the acquisition of happiness. “Duggati” is a destination of suffering; or because it is a destination produced by evil deeds, abounding in aversion. “Vinipāta” is where the wrongdoers fall headlong; or where beings perish, their limbs and minor limbs shattering. “Niraya” is where there is no “āya” (gain) in the sense of enjoyment.

Atha vā apāyaggahaṇena tiracchānayoniṃ dīpeti. Tiracchānayoni hi apāyo sugatito apetattā, na duggati mahesakkhānaṃ nāgarājādīnaṃ sambhavato. Duggatiggahaṇena pettivisayaṃ dīpeti. So hi apāyo ceva duggati ca sugatito apetattā dukkhassa ca gatibhūtattā, na tu vinipāto asurasadisaṃ avinipatitattā. Petamahiddhikānaṃ vimānānipi nibbattanti. Vinipātaggahaṇena asurakāyaṃ dīpeti. So hi yathāvuttenatthena apāyo ceva duggati ca sabbasampattisamussayehi vinipātattā vinipātoti ca vuccati. Nirayaggahaṇena pana avīciādikaṃ anekappakāraṃ nirayameva dīpeti. Upapajjatīti nibbattati.

Alternatively, by the mention of the states of deprivation, the animal realm is indicated. For the animal realm is a state of deprivation because it is devoid of a good destination, but it is not a bad destination since powerful nāga kings and the like exist there. By the mention of the bad destination, the realm of ghosts is indicated. For that is both a state of deprivation and a bad destination because it is devoid of a good destination and is a place of suffering, but it is not a state of utter ruin since it is not utterly ruined like the asuras. Even celestial mansions arise for ghosts of great power. By the mention of utter ruin, the asura realm is indicated. For that is both a state of deprivation and a bad destination for the reasons stated, and it is called utter ruin because of the utter ruin of all attainments. But by the mention of hell, only the manifold hells beginning with Avīci are indicated. “One is reborn” means one comes into being.

Ānisaṃsakathā vuttavipariyāyena veditabbā. Ayaṃ pana viseso – sīlavāti samādānavasena sīlavā. Sīlasampannoti parisuddhaṃ paripuṇṇañca katvā sīlassa sampādanena sīlasampanno. Bhogakkhandhanti bhogarāsiṃ. Sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokanti ettha sugatiggahaṇena manussagatipi saṅgayhati, saggaggahaṇena devagati eva. Tattha sundarā gatīti sugati, rūpādīhi [M 3.0315] visayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo, so sabbopi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti.

The discourse on the benefits should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated. Here, however, is the distinction: “virtuous” means virtuous by way of undertaking precepts. “Possessed of virtue” means one who is possessed of virtue by accomplishing purity and perfection in their precepts. “A mass of wealth” refers to a heap of wealth. In “a happy destiny, the heavenly world,” by the term “happy destiny,” the human state is also included, while by “heavenly world,” only the realm of the gods is intended. There, “happy destiny” means a beautiful destination, and “heavenly world” means the supreme state because of excellence with respect to objects like form and so on. All of it is called “world” in the sense of being subject to breaking up and dissolution.

Pāṭaligāmike upāsake bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāyāti aññāyapi pāḷimuttāya dhammakathāya ceva āvasathānumodanakathāya ca. Tadā hi bhagavā yasmā ajātasattunā tattha pāṭaliputtanagaraṃ māpentena aññāsu gāmanigamarājadhānīsu ye sīlācārasampannā kuṭumbikā, te ānetvā dhanadhaññāni gharavatthukhettavatthādīni ceva parihārañca dāpetvā nivesiyanti, tasmā pāṭaligāmikā upāsakā ānisaṃsadassāvitāya visesato sīlagarukāti sabbaguṇānañca sīlassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato tesaṃ paṭhamaṃ sīlānisaṃse pakāsetvā tato paraṃ ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya pathavojaṃ ākaḍḍhanto viya mahājambuṃ matthake gahetvā cālento viya yojanappamāṇaṃ mahāmadhuṃ cakkayantena pīḷetvā sumadhurarasaṃ pāyamāno viya ca pāṭaligāmikānaṃ upāsakānaṃ hitasukhāvahaṃ pakiṇṇakakathaṃ kathentopi “āvāsadānaṃ nāmetaṃ gahapatayo mahantaṃ puññaṃ, tumhākaṃ āvāso mayā paribhutto, bhikkhusaṅghena paribhutto, mayā ca bhikkhusaṅghena ca paribhutte dhammaratanenapi paribhuttoyeva hoti, evaṃ tīhi ratanehi paribhutte aparimeyyova vipāko, apica āvāsadānasmiṃ dinne sabbadānaṃ dinnameva hoti, bhūmaṭṭhakapaṇṇasālāya vā sākhāmaṇḍapassa vā saṅghaṃ uddissa katassa ānisaṃso paricchindituṃ na sakkā. Āvāsadānānubhāvena [V 3.0288] hi bhave nibbattamānassapi sampīḷitagabbhavāso nāma na hoti, dvādasahattho ovarako viyassa mātukucchi asambādhova hotī”ti evaṃ nānānayavicittaṃ bahuṃ dhammakathaṃ kathetvā –

The lay devotees of Pāṭaligāma spent much of the night in Dhamma discussion, including both miscellaneous Dhamma talk and talk of appreciation for the lodging. At that time, because Ajātasattu was constructing the city of Pāṭaliputta there, he had virtuous and well-conducted householders brought from other villages, towns, and royal capitals. He provided them with wealth, grain, houses, fields, and other necessities, settling them there. Thus, the lay devotees of Pāṭaligāma, recognizing the benefits, held virtue in especially high regard. Since virtue serves as the foundation for all good qualities, the Blessed One first explained the benefits of virtue to them. Then, like one pouring down a celestial river, drawing up the earth’s essence, shaking a great rose-apple tree held aloft, or pressing a honeycomb a league wide to extract the sweetest nectar, he delivered a miscellaneous discourse for the welfare and happiness of the Pāṭaligāma lay devotees. He also said, "Householders, giving lodging is indeed a great merit. Your lodging has been used by me, used by the Sangha of monks, and when used by me and the Sangha, it is also used by the Dhamma jewel. Thus, when used by the Three Jewels, the result is immeasurable. Moreover, in giving lodging, all gifts are given. The benefits of dedicating even a ground-built leaf hut or a branch pavilion to the Sangha cannot be limited. By the power of giving lodging, even when one is reborn, there is no cramped dwelling in the womb. Like a twelve-cubit-wide chamber, the mother’s womb remains unconfined." Having delivered this Dhamma talk in many varied and profound ways,

“Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanti, tato vāḷamigāni ca;

Sarīsape ca makase, sisire cāpi vuṭṭhiyo.

It wards off cold and heat, and likewise beasts of prey, reptiles, and mosquitoes, and also the rains in winter.

“Tato vātātapo ghoro, sañjāto paṭihaññati;

Leṇatthañca sukhatthañca, jhāyituñca vipassituṃ.

Then a harsh wind and heat, having arisen, are warded off; for shelter and comfort, and for meditating and contemplating.

“Vihāradānaṃ saṅghassa, aggaṃ buddhena vaṇṇitaṃ;

Tasmā hi paṇḍito poso, sampassaṃ atthamattano.

The gift of a dwelling to the Sangha is praised by the Buddha as supreme. Therefore, a wise person, considering their own benefit,

“Vihāre [M 3.0316] kāraye ramme, vāsayettha bahussute;

Tesaṃ annañca pānañca, vatthasenāsanāni ca.

Build delightful monasteries, and house the learned there; Provide them with food and drink, clothing, and lodgings.

“Dadeyya ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā;

Te tassa dhammaṃ desenti, sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ;

Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya, parinibbāti anāsavo”ti. (cūḷava. 295, 315) –

One should give to the upright, with a mind serene and clear; They teach him the Dhamma, the dispeller of all suffering. Having understood that Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, without taints.

Evaṃ ayampi āvāsadāne ānisaṃso ayampi āvāsadāne ānisaṃsoti bahudeva rattiṃ atirekadiyaḍḍhayāmaṃ āvāsadānānisaṃsaṃ kathesi. Tattha imā gāthāva saṅgahaṃ āruḷhā, pakiṇṇakadhammadesanā pana saṅgahaṃ na ārohati. Sandassetvātiādīni vuttatthāneva.

Thus, this too is a benefit of offering a dwelling; this too is a benefit of offering a dwelling. He spoke for much of the night, exceeding one and a half watches, on the benefits of offering a dwelling. Here, these verses are included in the compilation, but the miscellaneous Dhamma teachings are not included in the compilation. “Showing” and so on have meanings as stated before.

Abhikkantāti atikkantā dve yāmā gatā. Yassadāni tumhe kālaṃ maññathāti yassa gamanassa tumhe kālaṃ maññatha, gamanakālo tumhākaṃ, gacchathāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmā pana bhagavā te uyyojesīti? Anukampāya. Tiyāmarattiñhi nisīditvā vītināmentānaṃ tesaṃ sarīre ābādho uppajjeyya, bhikkhusaṅghopi ca mahā, tassa sayananisajjānaṃ okāsaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, iti ubhayānukampāya uyyojesi.

“Abhikkantā” means past; two watches have passed. “Yassadāni tumhe kālaṃ maññathā” means: for whatever going you think it is time, it is your time to go, go—this is what is said. But why did the Blessed One dismiss them? Out of compassion. For if they spent the three watches of the night sitting, illness might arise in their bodies, and the community of monks was large, so it was fitting for them to find space for sleeping and sitting. Thus, out of compassion for both, he dismissed them.

Suññāgāranti [V 3.0289] pāṭiyekkaṃ suññāgāraṃ nāma tattha natthi. Te kira gahapatayo tasseva āvasathāgārassa ekapasse paṭasāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā kappiyamañcaṃ paññapetvā tattha kappiyapaccattharaṇāni attharitvā upari suvaṇṇarajatatārakagandhamālādidāmapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ vitānaṃ bandhitvā gandhatelapadīpaṃ āropayiṃsu “appeva nāma satthā dhammāsanato vuṭṭhāya thokaṃ vissametukāmo idha nipajjeyya, evaṃ no idaṃ āvasathāgāraṃ bhagavatā catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuttaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti. Satthāpi tadeva sandhāya tattha saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “suññāgāraṃ pāvisī”ti. Tattha pādadhovanaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya yāva dhammāsanā agamāsi, ettake ṭhāne gamanaṃ nipphannaṃ. Dhammāsanaṃ patvā thokaṃ aṭṭhāsi, idaṃ tattha ṭhānaṃ. Dve yāme dhammāsane nisīdi, ettake ṭhāne nisajjā nipphannā. Upāsake uyyojetvā dhammāsanato oruyha yathāvutte ṭhāne sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi[M 3.0317]. Etaṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavatā catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuttaṃ ahosīti.

“Suññāgāra” means an empty dwelling, but there was no separate empty dwelling there. It seems those householders had a screen of cloth erected around one side of that very guesthouse, prepared a suitable bed, spread suitable coverings there, and above, hung a canopy adorned with gold, silver, stars, fragrant garlands, and other decorations, and set up fragrant oil lamps, thinking, “Perhaps the Teacher, rising from the Dhamma seat, might wish to rest a little and lie down here. Thus, this guesthouse, used by the Blessed One in the four postures, will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.” The Teacher, intending just that, arranged his outer robe there and lay down in the lion’s posture. Referring to this, it is said, “he entered the empty dwelling.” There, from the place for washing the feet up to the Dhamma seat, that much walking was accomplished. Reaching the Dhamma seat, he stood for a short while—this was the standing there. He sat on the Dhamma seat for two watches—that much sitting was accomplished. Having dismissed the lay followers and descended from the Dhamma seat, he lay down in the lion’s posture in the aforementioned place. This place was used by the Blessed One in the four postures.

Pāṭaligāmavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Pāṭaligāma is finished.

Sunidhavassakāravatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Sunidha and Vassakāra

286. Sunidhavassakārāti (dī. ni. 2.153; udā. aṭṭha. 76) sunidho ca vassakāro ca dve brāhmaṇā. Magadhamahāmattāti magadharañño mahāamaccā, magadharaṭṭhe vā mahāmattā, mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgatāti magadhamahāmattā. Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ māpentīti pāṭaligāmantasaṅkhāte bhūmippadese nagaraṃ māpenti, pubbe “pāṭaligāmo”ti laddhanāmaṃ ṭhānaṃ idāni nagaraṃ katvā māpentīti attho. Vajjīnaṃ paṭibāhāyāti licchavirājūnaṃ āyamukhapacchindanatthaṃ. Vatthūnīti gharavatthūni gharapatiṭṭhāpanaṭṭhānāni. Cittāni namanti nivesanāni māpetunti rañño rājamahāmattānañca nivesanāni māpetuṃ vatthuvijjāpāṭhakānaṃ cittāni namanti. Te kira attano sippānubhāvena heṭṭhāpathaviyaṃ tiṃsahatthamatte ṭhāne “idha nāgānaṃ nivāsapariggaho, idha yakkhānaṃ, idha bhūtānaṃ nivāsapariggaho, idha pāsāṇo vā khāṇuko vā atthī”ti jānanti, te tadā sippaṃ jappitvā tādisaṃ sārambhaṭṭhānaṃ pariharitvā anārambhe ṭhāne tāhi vatthupariggāhikāhi devatāhi saddhiṃ mantayamānā viya taṃtaṃgehāni māpenti.

286. Sunidhavassakārāti (Dī. Ni. 2.153; Udā. Aṭṭha. 76): Sunidha and Vassakāra were two brahmins. Magadhamahāmattāti: Great ministers of the king of Magadha, or high officials in the kingdom of Magadha, endowed with great authority—thus they are called Magadha-mahāmattas. Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ māpentīti: They were constructing a city in the area known as Pāṭaligāma. The meaning is that a place previously called “Pāṭaligāma,” they were now making into a city. Vajjīnaṃ paṭibāhāyāti: To ward off the Vajjis, that is, for the purpose of cutting off the revenue of the Licchavi kings. Vatthūnīti: This refers to house-sites, the places for establishing buildings. Cittāni namanti nivesanāni māpetunti: The minds of the architects were inclined toward constructing residences for the king and his great ministers. It is said that through their own expertise, they could discern what was in a place thirty cubits below the ground, knowing, “Here is the domain of nāgas, here of yakkhas, here of spirits; here lies a rock or a stump.” Employing their craft, they avoided such contentious sites and selected non-contentious locations; as if consulting with the guardian deities of those sites, they constructed the various houses.

Atha vā nesaṃ sarīre devatā adhimuccitvā tattha tattha nivesanāni māpetuṃ cittaṃ nāmenti. Tā catūsu koṇesu khāṇuke koṭṭetvā vatthumhi gahitamatte paṭivigacchanti. Saddhānaṃ kulānaṃ [V 3.0290] saddhā devatā tathā karonti, assaddhānaṃ kulānaṃ assaddhā devatā ca. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Saddhānañhi evaṃ hoti “idha manussā nivesanaṃ māpentā paṭhamaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā maṅgalaṃ vadāpessanti, atha mayaṃ sīlavantānaṃ dassanaṃ dhammakathaṃ pañhavissajjanaṃ anumodanañca sotuṃ labhissāma, manussādānaṃ datvā amhākaṃ pattiṃ dassantī”ti. Assaddhā devatāpi “attano icchānurūpaṃ tesaṃ paṭipattiṃ passituṃ kathañca sotuṃ labhissāmā”ti tathā karonti.

Alternatively, deities possessing their bodies incline their minds to construct residences in various places. They drive stakes into the four corners, and once the building site is claimed, they withdraw. For faithful families, faithful deities act thus; for faithless families, faithless deities do the same. Why? The faithful think, “When people build a dwelling, they will first have the Saṅgha of monks sit down and will have them recite blessings. Then we will get to see the virtuous ones and to hear a Dhamma talk, a question-and-answer session, and the rejoicing. And after giving to the humans, they will transfer the merit to us.” The faithless deities also act similarly, thinking, “How shall we get to see their conduct and hear their talk, which is in accordance with our own wishes?”

Tāvatiṃsehīti [M 3.0318] yathā hi ekasmiṃ kule ekaṃ paṇḍitaṃ manussaṃ, ekasmiñca vihāre ekaṃ bahussutaṃ bhikkhuṃ upādāya “asukakule manussā paṇḍitā, asukavihāre bhikkhū bahussutā”ti saddo abbhuggacchati, evamevaṃ sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ vissakammañca devaputtaṃ upādāya “tāvatiṃsā paṇḍitā”ti saddo abbhuggato. Tenāha “tāvatiṃsehī”ti. Seyyathāpītiādinā devehi tāvatiṃsehi saddhiṃ mantetvā viya sunidhavassakārā nagaraṃ māpentīti dasseti.

Tāvatiṃsehīti: Just as in a family, on account of one wise person, and in a monastery, on account of one learned monk, the reputation spreads, “In such-and-such a family, the people are wise; in such-and-such a monastery, the monks are learned,” so too, on account of Sakka, the king of the gods, and Vissakamma, the divine son, the reputation arose, “The Tāvatiṃsa gods are wise.” Hence it is said, “Tāvatiṃsehī.” By the phrase beginning “Seyyathāpīti,” it is shown that Sunidha and Vassakāra built the city as if consulting with the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

Yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatananti yattakaṃ ariyamanussānaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthi. Yāvatā vaṇippathoti yattakaṃ vāṇijānaṃ āhaṭabhaṇḍassa rāsivaseneva kayavikkayaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, vāṇijānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vā atthi. Idaṃ agganagaranti tesaṃ ariyāyatanavaṇippathānaṃ idaṃ nagaraṃ aggaṃ bhavissati jeṭṭhakaṃ pāmokkhaṃ. Puṭabhedananti bhaṇḍapuṭabhedanaṭṭhānaṃ, bhaṇḍaganthikānaṃ mocanaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakalajambudīpe aladdhabhaṇḍampi hi idheva labhissati, aññattha vikkayaṃ agacchantampi idha vikkayaṃ gacchissati, tasmā idheva puṭaṃ bhindissatīti attho. Āyanti yāni catūsu dvāresu cattāri, sabhāyaṃ ekanti evaṃ divase divase pañcasatasahassāni tattha uṭṭhahissanti, tānissa bhāvīni āyāni dasseti. Aggito vātiādīsu ca-kārattho vā-saddo, agginā ca udakena ca mithubhedena ca nassissatīti attho. Tassa hi eko koṭṭhāso agginā nassissati, nibbāpetumpi naṃ na sakkhissati, ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ gaṅgā gahetvā gamissati, eko iminā akathitaṃ amussa, amunā akathitaṃ imassa vadantānaṃ pisuṇavācānaṃ vasena bhinnānaṃ manussānaṃ aññamaññabhedena vinassissati.

Yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatananti: that is, whatever place serves as a resort for noble humans. Yāvatā vaṇippathoti: that is, whatever place serves as a marketplace for traders to buy and sell imported goods in bulk, or as a dwelling place for merchants. Idaṃ agganagaranti: for those noble resorts and merchant paths, this city will be the foremost, the chief, the preeminent. Puṭabhedananti: a place where bales of goods are broken open; it means a place where bundles of goods are untied. For even goods not found elsewhere in the whole of Jambudīpa will be obtained here, and goods that go unsold elsewhere will be sold here. Therefore, it is here that the bales will be broken—this is the meaning. Āyanti: those four at the four gates, and one in the assembly hall—thus, day by day, five hundred thousand will arise there. This shows his future revenues. Aggito vātiādīsu: here, the word “or” (vā) carries the meaning of “and.” It will perish by fire and water and internal dissension—this is the meaning. For one portion of it will perish by fire—they will not even be able to extinguish it. One portion the Ganges will take and carry away. One portion will perish through the mutual dissension of people who have been divided by means of the slanderous speech of those who say of one person to another what was not said, and of the other to the first what was not said.

Evaṃ vatvā bhagavā paccūsakāle gaṅgātīraṃ gantvā katamukhadhovano bhikkhācārakālaṃ āgamayamāno nisīdi. Sunidhavassakārāpi “amhākaṃ rājā samaṇassa gotamassa upaṭṭhāko, so amhe upagate pucchissati ‘satthā kira pāṭaligāmaṃ agamāsi, kiṃ tassa santikaṃ upasaṅkamittha, na upasaṅkamitthā’ti, ‘upasaṅkamimhā’ti ca vutte ‘nimantayittha, na nimantayitthā’ti [V 3.0291] pucchissati, ‘na nimantayimhā’ti ca vutte amhākaṃ dosaṃ āropetvā niggaṇhissati, idañcāpi mayaṃ akataṭṭhāne nagaraṃ māpema, samaṇassa kho [M 3.0319] pana gotamassa gatagataṭṭhāne kāḷakaṇṇisattā paṭikkamanti, taṃ mayaṃ nagaramaṅgalaṃ vācāpessāmā”ti cintetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā nimantayiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho sunidhavassakārā”tiādi. Pubbaṇhasamayanti pubbaṇhakāle. Nivāsetvāti gāmappavesananīhārena nivāsanaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā. Pattacīvaramādāyāti pattañca cīvarañca ādiyitvā kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ katvā, cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ hatthena gahetvāti attho.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One went to the bank of the Ganges at dawn. After washing his face, he sat down, awaiting the time for the alms round. Sunidha and Vassakāra thought, "Our king is a supporter of the ascetic Gotama. When we arrive, he will ask us, 'Has the Teacher gone to Pāṭaligāma? Did you approach him, or did you not?' If we say, 'We approached him,' he will then ask, 'Did you invite him, or did you not?' And if we say, 'We did not invite him,' he will find fault and reprimand us. Moreover, we are building this city in an unsuitable place, and wherever the ascetic Gotama goes, inauspicious influences retreat. Therefore, let us have him pronounce a blessing on the city." Having considered this, they approached the Teacher and invited him. Thus it is said, "Then Sunidha and Vassakāra..." Pubbaṇhasamayanti: in the early part of the day. Nivāsetvāti: having put on the lower robe in the manner of entering a village, and having fastened the waistband. Pattacīvaramādāyāti: taking the bowl and robe, securing them to the body, putting on the outer robe, and holding the bowl in the hand—this is the meaning.

Sīlavantetthāti sīlavante ettha attano vasanaṭṭhāne. Saññateti kāyavācācittehi saññate. Tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādiseti saṅghassa dinne cattāro paccaye tāsaṃ gharadevatānaṃ ādiseyyapattiṃ dadeyya. Pūjitā pūjayantīti “ime manussā amhākaṃ ñātakāpi na honti, tathāpi no pattiṃ dentīti ārakkhaṃ susaṃvihitaṃ karothā”ti suṭṭhu ārakkhaṃ karonti. Mānitā mānayantīti kālānukālaṃ balikammakaraṇena mānitā “ete manussā amhākaṃ ñātakāpi na honti, tathāpi catumāsachamāsantare no balikammaṃ karontī”ti mānenti uppannaparissayaṃ haranti. Tato nanti tato naṃ paṇḍitajātikaṃ manussaṃ. Orasanti ure ṭhapetvā saṃvaḍḍhitaṃ, yathā mātā orasaṃ puttaṃ anukampati, uppannaparissayaharaṇatthamevassa vāyamati, evaṃ anukampantīti attho. Bhadrāni passatīti sundarāni passati.

Sīlavantetthāti: virtuous here, meaning virtuous in this place of dwelling. Saññateti: restrained, meaning restrained in body, speech, and mind. Tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādiseti: when the four requisites are given to the Saṅgha, he should dedicate a share of the merit to those household deities. Pūjitā pūjayantīti: thinking, "These humans are not even our relatives, yet they give us merit," they diligently provide well-arranged protection. Mānitā mānayantīti: honored from time to time by the performance of bali-offerings, they think, "These humans are not even our relatives, yet they perform bali-offerings for us every four or six months," and they remove any arisen dangers. Tato nanti: therefore, that one, meaning that wise person. Orasanti: raised placing (the child) on the breast; just as a mother shows compassion to her own offspring, striving to remove any arisen dangers, so too they show compassion. Bhadrāni passatīti: he sees beautiful things.

Anumoditvāti tehi tadā pasutapuññassa anumodanavasena tesaṃ dhammakathaṃ katvā. Sunidhavassakārāpi “yā tattha devatā āsuṃ, tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādise”ti bhagavato vacanaṃ sutvā devatānaṃ pattiṃ adaṃsu. Taṃ gotamadvāraṃ nāma ahosīti tassa nagarassa yena dvārena bhagavā nikkhami, taṃ gotamadvāraṃ nāma ahosi. Gaṅgāya pana uttaraṇatthaṃ anotiṇṇattā gotamatitthaṃ nāma nāhosi. Pūrāti puṇṇā. Samatittikāti tīrasamaṃ udakassa tittā bharitā. Kākapeyyāti tīre ṭhitakākehi pātuṃ sakkuṇeyyaudakā. Tīhipi padehi ubhatokūlasamaṃ paripuṇṇabhāvameva vadati. Uḷumpanti pāragamanatthāya lahuke dārudaṇḍe gahetvā kavāṭaphalake viya aññamaññasambandhe kātuṃ āṇiyo koṭṭetvā nāvāsaṅkhepena kataṃ. Kullanti veḷunaḷādike saṅgharitvā valliādīhi kalāpavasena bandhitvā kataṃ.

Anumoditvāti: having rejoiced, meaning having given them a Dhamma talk by way of rejoicing in the merit they had acquired at that time. Sunidha and Vassakāra, having heard the Blessed One's words, "One should dedicate the offering to the deities who were there," gave a share of the merit to the deities. Taṃ gotamadvāraṃ nāma ahosīti: that gate of the city by which the Blessed One departed was called the Gotama Gate. However, since he did not descend into the Ganges there for the purpose of crossing, it was not called the Gotama Ford. Pūrāti: full. Samatittikāti: filled to the brim, the water level equal to the shore. Kākapeyyāti: water that could be drunk by crows standing on the shore. With these three terms, it speaks of the fullness equally on both banks. Uḷumpanti: for the purpose of crossing to the far shore, taking light wooden logs and hammering pegs to join them to one another like door panels, it is made in the form of a boat. Kullanti: is made by gathering reeds or bamboo and binding them into bundles with vines or the like.

Etamatthaṃ [M 3.0320] viditvāti etaṃ mahājanassa gaṅgudakamattassapi kevalaṃ tarituṃ asamatthataṃ, attano pana bhikkhusaṅghassa ca atigambhīravitthataṃ saṃsāramahaṇṇavaṃ taritvā ṭhitabhāvañca sabbākārato [V 3.0292] viditvā tadatthaparidīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Udānagāthāya attho pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dassitoyeva. Tattha udakaṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacananti yathāvuttassa yassa kassaci udakaṭṭhānassa etaṃ aṇṇavanti adhivacanaṃ, na samuddassevāti adhippāyo. Saranti idha nadī adhippetā sarati sandatīti katvā. Gambhīraṃ vitthatanti agādhaṭṭhena gambhīraṃ, sakalalokattayabyāpitāya vitthataṃ. Visajjāti anāsajja appatvā eva pallalāni tesaṃ ataraṇato. Kullañhi jano bandhatīti kullaṃ bandhituṃ āyāsaṃ āpajjati. Vinā eva kullenāti īdisaṃ udakaṃ kullena īdisena vinā eva. Tiṇṇā medhāvino janāti ariyamaggañāṇasaṅkhātāya medhāya samannāgatattā medhāvino buddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca tiṇṇā paratīre patiṭṭhitā.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti: having understood this meaning—namely, having known in all respects the inability of the great multitude to cross even the mere water of the Ganges, whereas he and the community of monks had crossed the exceedingly deep and vast ocean of saṃsāra and stood secure—he uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning. The meaning of the inspired verse is as explained in the commentary. Tattha: here, 'aṇṇava' is a term for any body of water, as stated, not specifically the sea; this is the intention. Saranti: here 'saranti' is intended to mean a river, because it flows (sarati). Gambhīraṃ vitthatanti: 'deep and vast' means deep in the sense of unfathomable, and vast in pervading the entire triple world. Visajjāti: without getting stuck in or reaching the marshes, because of not crossing them. Kullañhi jano bandhatīti: people undergo effort to build a raft. Vinā eva kullenāti: such water is crossed without such a raft. Tiṇṇā medhāvino janāti: the wise, endowed with wisdom consisting of the knowledge of the noble path—the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha—have crossed and are established on the far shore.

Sunidhavassakāravatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Sunidha and Vassakāra is concluded.

Koṭigāme saccakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Truths at Koṭigāma

287. Koṭigāmoti mahāpanādassa rañño pāsādakoṭiyaṃ katagāmo, patitassa pāsādassa thupikāya patiṭṭhitaṭṭhāne niviṭṭhagāmoti attho. Ariyasaccānanti ye paṭivijjhanti, tesaṃ ariyabhāvakarānaṃ saccānaṃ. Ananubodhāti abujjhanena ajānanena. Appaṭivedhāti appaṭivijjhanena. Anubodho cettha pubbabhāgiyañāṇaṃ, paṭivedho maggañāṇena abhisamayo. Tattha yasmā anubodhapubbako paṭivedho anubodhena vinā na hoti, anubodhopi ekacco paṭivedhasambandho tadubhayābhāvahetukañca vaṭṭe saṃsaraṇaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “ananubodhā…pe… tumhākañcā”ti. Tattha sandhāvitanti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena bhavato bhavantarupagamanena sandhāvitaṃ. Saṃsaritanti aparāparaṃ cavanupapajjanavasena saṃsaritaṃ. Mamañceva tumhākañcāti mayā ca tumhehi ca. Atha vā sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritanti sandhāvanaṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ mamañceva tumhākañca ahosīti evamettha attho veditabbo.

287. Koṭigāmoti: Koṭigāma was a village built at the corner of King Mahāpanāda’s palace, meaning it was a village established at the place where the pinnacle of the fallen palace was set up. Ariyasaccānanti: 'Of the Noble Truths' refers to the truths which, when penetrated, make those who penetrate them noble. Ananubodhāti: 'without understanding' means through non-comprehension, through not knowing. Appaṭivedhāti: 'without penetration' means through not penetrating. Here, understanding refers to preliminary knowledge, while penetration refers to realization through path-knowledge. Since penetration is preceded by understanding and cannot occur without it, and since understanding is also in some way connected to penetration, and because the absence of both is a cause for wandering in the cycle of existence, therefore it is said: 'Without understanding... and yours.' Tattha sandhāvitanti: here, 'wandered' means having run on from one existence to another through rebirth-linking. Saṃsaritanti: 'transmigrated' means having transmigrated through repeated death and rebirth. Mamañceva tumhākañcāti: 'both mine and yours' means by me and by you. Alternatively, sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritanti: the wandering and the transmigrating were both mine and yours. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

Saṃsitanti [M 3.0321] saṃsaritaṃ. Bhavanetti samūhatāti dīgharajjuyā baddhasakuṇaṃ viya rajjuhattho puriso desantaraṃ, taṇhārajjuyā baddhasattasantānaṃ abhisaṅkhāro bhavantaraṃ neti etāyāti bhavanetti, sā bhavato bhavaṃ nayanasamatthā taṇhārajju ariyamaggasatthena suṭṭhu hatā chinnā appavattikatāti bhavanetti samūhatā.

Saṃsitanti: 'wandered on' means transmigrated. Bhavanetti samūhatāti: 'the conduit to existence is eradicated' means that just as a man holding a string leads a bird tied by a long string to another place, so 'bhavanetti' (the conduit to existence) is that by which volitional formations lead the continuum of beings, bound by the string of craving, to another existence. That string of craving, capable of leading from one existence to another, is well struck, cut off, and made non-occurrent by the sword of the Noble Path. Thus, the conduit to existence is eradicated.

Ambapālīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Ambapālī

288. Yānassa [V 3.0293] bhūmīti yattha sakkā hoti yānaṃ āruyha yānena gantuṃ, ayaṃ yānassa bhūmi nāma. Yānā paccorohitvāti vihārassa bahidvārakoṭṭhake yānato orohitvā.

288. Yānassa bhūmīti: 'the ground for vehicles' means a place where it is possible to mount a vehicle and travel by vehicle. This is called the ground for vehicles. Yānā paccorohitvāti: 'having descended from the vehicle' means having alighted from the vehicle at the outer gatehouse of the monastery.

Licchavīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Licchavīs

289. Nīlāti idaṃ sabbasaṅgāhakavacanaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇātiādi tasseva vibhāgadassanatthaṃ. Tattha na tesaṃ pakativaṇṇo nīlo, nīlavilepanavilittattā panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Nīlavatthāti paṭadukūlakoseyyādīnipi nesaṃ nīlāneva honti. Nīlālaṅkārāti nīlamaṇialaṅkārehi nīlapupphehi ca alaṅkatā.
