Te kira alaṅkārā suvaṇṇavicittāpi indanīlamaṇiobhāsehi ekanīlā viya khāyanti, rathāpi nesaṃ nīlamaṇikhacitā nīlavatthaparikkhittā nīladhajanīlavammikehi nīlābharaṇehi nīlaassehi yuttā, patodayaṭṭhiyopi nīlāyevāti iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Paṭivaṭṭesīti pahari. Kissa je ambapālīti je-ti ālapanaṃ, bhoti ambapāli kiṃkāraṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāhāranti ettha āharanti imasmā rājapurisā balinti āhāro, tabbhuttajanapado. Tena sahitaṃ sāhāraṃ, sajanapadanti attho. Aṅguliṃ phoṭesunti aṅguliṃ cālesuṃ. Ambakāyāti mātugāmena. Upacāravacanañhetaṃ, itthīsu yadidaṃ ambakā mātugāmo jananikāti. Olokethāti passatha. Apalokethāti apavattitvā oloketha, punappunaṃ passathāti attho. Upasaṃharathāti upanetha, imaṃ licchavīparisaṃ tumhākaṃ cittena tāvatiṃsasadisaṃ upasaṃharatha upanetha allīyāpetha. Yatheva tāvatiṃsā [M 3.0322] abhirūpā pāsādikā nīlādinānāvaṇṇā, evamime licchavīrājānopīti tāvatiṃsehi samake katvā passathāti attho.

289. "Blue" is an all-encompassing term. "Of blue color," and so on, is for the purpose of showing its divisions. Here, their natural color is not blue; rather, this is said because they are smeared with blue unguents. "Blue garments" means that their cloths, fine cloths, and silken robes are all blue. "Blue ornaments" means they are adorned with blue gems and blue flowers. It is said that their ornaments, though variegated with gold, appear uniformly blue from the radiance of sapphire gems. Their chariots, too, are inlaid with blue gems, draped with blue cloth, and yoked with blue horses, having blue flags, blue armor, and blue adornments. Even their goads are blue. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances. "He turned back" means he struck. "Why, O Ambapālī?"—here, "O" is a form of address; it means, "Lady Ambapālī, for what reason?" "With its revenue"—here, `āhāra` is that from which the king’s men bring tribute, that is, revenue. It is the district that is enjoyed. `Sāhāraṃ` means together with that; the meaning is 'with its district.' "They snapped their fingers"—they moved their fingers. "By the mango-woman"—by a woman. This is a polite expression, for among women, `ambakā` is used like `mātugāma` (woman) or `jananikā` (mother). "Look"—see. "Look upon"—turn and look, meaning look again and again. "Compare"—bring near. Compare this assembly of Licchavis in your mind to the Tāvatiṃsa devas—draw them near, make them adhere. Just as the Tāvatiṃsa devas are beautiful, pleasing, and of various colors like blue and others, so too are these Licchavi kings—thus, see them as equal to the Tāvatiṃsa devas. This is the meaning.

Kasmā pana bhagavā anekasatehi suttehi cakkhādīnaṃ rūpādīsu nimittaggāhaṃ paṭisedhetvā idha mahantena ussāhena nimittaggāhe niyojetīti? Hitakāmatāya tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yathā āyasmato nandassa hitakāmatāya saggasampattidassanatthaṃ. Tatra kira ekacce bhikkhū osannavīriyā, te sampattiyā palobhento “appamādena samaṇadhammaṃ karontānaṃ evarūpā issariyasampatti sulabhā”ti samaṇadhamme ussāhajananatthaṃ āha. Atha vā nayidaṃ nimittaggāhe niyojanaṃ, kevalaṃ pana “dibbasampattisadisā etesaṃ rājūnaṃ issariyasampattī”ti anupubbikathāya sampattikathanaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aniccalakkhaṇavibhāvanatthañcāpi evamāha. Na cirasseva [V 3.0294] hi sabbepime ajātasattussa vasena vināsaṃ pāpuṇissanti, atha nesaṃ rajjasirisampattiṃ disvā ṭhitabhikkhū “tathārūpāyapi nāma sirisampattiyā vināso paññāyissatī”ti aniccalakkhaṇaṃ bhāvetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇissantīti aniccalakkhaṇavibhāvanatthaṃ āha.

But why did the Blessed One, after having rejected in hundreds of discourses the grasping of signs in forms and so forth, here enjoin the grasping of signs with great effort? Out of a desire for the welfare of those monks, just as he showed heavenly attainments out of a desire for the welfare of the Venerable Nanda. For it is said that some monks were lax in their effort, and enticing them with worldly attainment, he said, "Such sovereign attainment is easily obtained by those who practice the ascetic life diligently," in order to generate enthusiasm for the ascetic life. Or, this is not an injunction to grasp signs, but should be seen simply as a description of worldly attainment in a gradual discourse, like saying, "These kings' sovereign attainment is similar to divine attainment." And he also spoke thus to make manifest the characteristic of impermanence. For before long, all of these will meet with destruction on account of Ajātasattu. Then, the monks present, seeing their royal glory and fortune, will develop the characteristic of impermanence, thinking, "The destruction of even such glory will be perceived," and will attain Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges. Thus, he spoke to make manifest the characteristic of impermanence.

Adhivāsetūti ambapāliyā nimantitabhāvaṃ ñatvāpi kasmā nimantentīti? Asaddahanatāya ca vattasīsena ca. Sā hi dhuttā itthī animantetvāpi “nimantesi”nti vadeyyāti tesaṃ ahosi. Dhammaṃ sutvā gamanakāle ca nimantetvā gamanaṃ nāma manussānaṃ vattameva.

Why did they invite him, even knowing that he had been invited by Ambapālī? This was due to their disbelief and due to custom. For it occurred to them that she, being a cunning woman, might say, 'I have invited him,' even if she had not. Moreover, to invite him at the time of departure after having heard the Dhamma is simply the custom among people.

Licchavīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of the Licchavis is concluded.

Sīhasenāpativatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story of General Sīha.

290. Abhiññātāti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.12) ñātā paññātā pākaṭā. Santhāgāreti mahājanassa santhambhanāgāre vissamanatthāya kate agāre. Sā kira santhāgārasālā nagaramajjhe ahosi, catūsu dvāresu ṭhitānaṃ paññāyati, catūhi disāhi āgatamanussā paṭhamaṃ tattha vissamitvā pacchā attano attano phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Rājakulānaṃ rajjakiccasantharaṇatthaṃ kataṃ [M 3.0323] agārantipi vadantiyeva. Tattha hi nisīditvā licchavīrājāno rajjakiccaṃ santharanti karonti vicārenti. Sannisinnāti tesaṃ nisīdanatthaṃyeva paññattesu mahārahapaccattharaṇesu samussitasetacchattesu āsanesu sannisinnā. Anekapariyāyena buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsantīti rājakulakiccañceva lokatthakiriyañca vicāretvā anekehi kāraṇehi buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. Paṇḍitā hi te rājāno saddhāsampannā sotāpannāpi sakadāgāminopi anāgāminopi ariyasāvakā, te sabbepi lokiyajaṭaṃ bhinditvā buddhādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti.

290. "Well-known" means known, distinguished, evident. "In the assembly hall" refers to a hall built for the great populace to assemble, a hall made for resting. It is said that this assembly hall was located in the middle of the city, visible to those standing at the four gates, so people arriving from the four directions could rest there first before going to their own comfortable places. Some also say it was a hall built for the royal families to conduct state affairs. There, the Licchavi kings would sit and deliberate, conduct, and discuss state matters. "Having gathered" means they sat on seats prepared just for their sitting, which were arranged with valuable coverings and had raised white canopies. "Speaking in many ways of the Buddha’s praises" means that after discussing both royal duties and actions for the world’s welfare, they praised the Buddha for many reasons. For those kings were wise, endowed with faith—some were stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, all noble disciples. Breaking through the world's tangle, they all praised the virtues of the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.

Tattha tividho buddhavaṇṇo nāma cariyavaṇṇo sarīravaṇṇo guṇavaṇṇoti. Tatrime rājāno cariyāya vaṇṇaṃ ārabhiṃsu – “dukkaraṃ vata kataṃ sammāsambuddhena kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni dasa pāramiyo dasa upapāramiyo dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūrentena ñātatthacariyaṃ lokatthacariyaṃ buddhatthacariyaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajantenā”ti aḍḍhacchakkehi jātakasatehi buddhavaṇṇaṃ kathentā tusitabhavanaṃ pāpetvā [V 3.0295] ṭhapayiṃsu. Dhammassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsantā panete “bhagavatā dhammo desito, nikāyato pañca nikāyā honti, piṭakato tīṇi piṭakāni, aṅgato nava aṅgāni, khandhato caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti koṭṭhāsavasena dhammaguṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Saṅghassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsantā “satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddhā kulaputtā bhogakkhandhañceva ñātiparivaṭṭañca pahāya setacchattauparajjasenāpatiseṭṭhibhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānantarādīni agaṇayitvā nikkhamma satthu varasāsane pabbajanti, setacchattaṃ pahāya pabbajitānaṃ bhaddiyamahārājamahākappinapukkusātiādirājapabbajitānaṃyeva buddhakāle asīti sahassāni ahesuṃ, anekakoṭidhanaṃ pahāya pabbajitānaṃ pana yasakulaputtasoṇaseṭṭhiputtaraṭṭhapālaputtādīnaṃ paricchedo natthi, evarūpā ca evarūpā ca kulaputtā satthu sāsane pabbajantī”ti pabbajjāsaṅkhepavasena saṅghaguṇaṃ kathayiṃsu.

Here, the praise of the Buddha is threefold: praise of conduct, praise of the body, and praise of virtues. Regarding this, those kings began praising the conduct: "Truly, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One accomplished what is difficult—fulfilling the thirty perfections: ten perfections, ten higher perfections, and ten supreme perfections over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand more. He reached the pinnacle of conduct for the sake of relatives, the world, and Buddhahood, having relinquished the five great sacrifices." They recounted the Buddha's praise by means of the five hundred and fifty Jātaka stories, taking it up to his dwelling in the Tusita heaven. When speaking the praise of the Dhamma, they said: "The Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One. By collection, there are five Nikāyas; by basket, there are three Piṭakas; by division, there are nine Aṅgas; and by aggregate, there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma." They recounted the virtues of the Dhamma by way of classification. When speaking the praise of the Saṅgha, they said: "Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma, sons of good family with faith, abandoning their mass of wealth and circle of relatives, and disregarding the white parasol, viceroyalty, generalship, the position of a great merchant, treasurership, and other such high offices, went forth in the Teacher’s excellent dispensation. Among those who renounced the white parasol and went forth during the Buddha’s time, there were eighty thousand, including the great king Bhaddiya, Mahākappina, Pukkusāti, and other royal renunciants. As for those who gave up many millions in wealth and went forth—such as the son of good family Yasa, the great merchant’s son Soṇa, the son Raṭṭhapāla, and others—their number cannot be reckoned. Such and such sons of good family go forth in the Teacher’s dispensation." Thus, by way of a summary of the goings-forth, they recounted the virtues of the Saṅgha.

Sīho senāpatīti evaṃnāmako senāya adhipati. Vesāliyañhi satta sahassāni satta satāni satta ca rājāno, te sabbepi sannipatitvā sabbesaṃ manaṃ gahetvā “raṭṭhaṃ vicāretuṃ samatthaṃ ekaṃ vicinathā”ti vicinantā sīharājakumāraṃ disvā “ayaṃ sakkhissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā tassa [M 3.0324] rattamaṇivaṇṇakambalapariyonaddhaṃ senāpaticchattaṃ adaṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “sīho senāpatī”ti. Nigaṇṭhasāvakoti nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa paccayadāyako upaṭṭhāko. Jambudīpatalasmiñhi tayo janā nigaṇṭhānaṃ aggupaṭṭhākā – nāḷandāyaṃ upāli gahapati, kapilapure vappo sakko, vesāliyaṃ ayaṃ sīho senāpatīti. Nisinno hotīti sesarājūnampi parisāya antare āsanāni paññāpayiṃsu, sīhassa pana majjhe ṭhāneti tasmiṃ paññatte mahārahe rājāsane nisinno hoti. Nissaṃsayanti nibbicikicchaṃ addhā ekaṃsena. Na hete yassa vā tassa vā appesakkhassa evaṃ anekasatehi kāraṇehi vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti.

Sīha the general: he was the commander of the army, so named. For in Vesālī there were seven thousand, seven hundred and seven kings. All of them, having gathered together and taken counsel, decided, "Seek one capable of governing the kingdom." Searching, they saw Prince Sīha and concluded, "He is capable." Having made this decision, they gave him a general's parasol covered with a ruby-colored blanket. Regarding this, it is said, "Sīha the general." A disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas means a supporter and attendant of the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta. Indeed, in the land of Jambudīpa there were three chief supporters of the Nigaṇṭhas—the householder Upāli in Nāḷandā, Vappa the Sakyan in Kapilavatthu, and this Sīha the general in Vesālī. "Seated" means that seats were prepared for the other kings in the assembly as well, but for Sīha a place was designated in the middle; thus he was seated on that grand royal seat prepared for him. "Without doubt" means free from hesitation, certainly, unequivocally. For they do not praise someone of little influence in such a way with hundreds of reasons.

Yena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto tenupasaṅkamīti nigaṇṭho kira nāṭaputto “sacāyaṃ sīho kassacideva samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇaṃ kathentassa sutvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamissati, mayhaṃ parihāni bhavissatī”ti cintetvā paṭhamataraṃyeva sīhaṃ senāpatiṃ etadavoca “senāpati imasmiṃ loke ‘ahaṃ buddho ahaṃ buddho’ti bahū vadanti, sace tvaṃ kañci dassanāya upasaṅkamitukāmo ahosi, maṃ puccheyyāsi, ahaṃ te yuttaṭṭhānaññeva pesessāmi, ayuttaṭṭhānato nivāressāmī”ti. So taṃ kathaṃ anussaritvā “sace maṃ pesessati, gamissāmi. No ce, na gamissāmī”ti cintetvā yena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto tenupasaṅkami.

Then he approached Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta. Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, thinking, "If this General Sīha, having heard someone praising the ascetic Gotama, should approach the ascetic Gotama to see him, it will be my downfall," so, anticipating this, first addressed General Sīha, saying, "General, in this world many say, 'I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha.' If you wish to visit anyone, you should ask me first. I will direct you to the appropriate place and steer you away from the inappropriate." Recalling this conversation, Sīha thought, "If he sends me, I will go. If not, I will not." With this in mind, he approached Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta.

Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā nigaṇṭho mahāpabbatena viya balavasokena otthaṭo “yattha dānissāhaṃ [V 3.0296] gamanaṃ na icchāmi, tattheva gantukāmo jāto, hatohamasmī”ti anattamano hutvā “paṭibāhanupāyamassa karissāmī”ti cintetvā “kiṃ pana tva”ntiādimāha. Evaṃ vadanto carantaṃ goṇaṃ tuṇḍe paharanto viya jalamānaṃ padīpaṃ nibbāpento viya bhattabharitaṃ pattaṃ nikujjanto viya ca sīhassa uppannaṃ pītiṃ vināsesi. Gamikābhisaṅkhāroti hatthiyānādīnaṃ yojāpanagandhamālādiggahaṇavasena pavatto payogo. So paṭippassambhīti so vūpasanto.

Having heard his words, the Nigaṇṭha, overwhelmed by intense sorrow as if struck by a great mountain, thought, "He desires to go to the very place I do not wish him to go; I am ruined!" Displeased, he resolved, "I will create a means of opposition for him." Thus speaking, he destroyed Sīha's arisen joy—like striking a moving ox on the snout, like extinguishing a burning lamp, or overturning a bowl filled with food. The term "gamikābhisaṅkhāro" refers to the effort involved in the preparations for travel, such as harnessing elephants and vehicles, and the taking of garlands, perfumes, and so on. "It subsided" means it ceased.

Dutiyampi khoti dutiyavārampi. Imasmiñca vāre buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsantā tusitabhavanato paṭṭhāya yāva mahābodhipallaṅkā dasabalassa heṭṭhā pādatalehi [M 3.0325] upari kesaggehi paricchinditvā dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītianubyañjanabyāmappabhāvasena sarīravaṇṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Dhammassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsantā “ekapadepi ekabyañjanepi avakkhalitaṃ nāma natthī”ti sukathitavaseneva dhammaguṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Saṅghassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsantā “evarūpaṃ yasasirivibhavaṃ pahāya satthu sāsane pabbajitā na kosajjapakatikā honti, terasasu pana dhutaguṇesu paripūrakārino hutvā sattasu anupassanāsu kammaṃ karonti, aṭṭhatiṃsa ārammaṇavibhattiyo vaḷañjentī”ti paṭipadāvasena saṅghaguṇe kathayiṃsu.

For the second time, or the second occasion. And on this occasion, while describing the Buddha's excellence, they recounted the physical beauty of the One with Ten Powers, from the Tusita heaven up to the Great Bodhi seat, delineating it from the soles of the feet up to the tips of the hair, with the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide aura. While describing the excellence of the Dhamma, they extolled the virtues of the Dhamma, saying, "There is not a single syllable or a single consonant misplaced," thus emphasizing its well-spoken nature. While describing the excellence of the Saṅgha, they praised the virtues of the Saṅgha based on their practice, saying, "Having abandoned such fame, glory, and prosperity, those who go forth in the Teacher’s dispensation are not by nature lazy; but fulfilling the thirteen ascetic qualities, they practice the seven kinds of contemplation, skillfully employing the thirty-eight categories of meditation subjects."

Tatiyavāre pana buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsamānā “itipi so bhagavā”ti suttantapariyāyeneva buddhaguṇe kathayiṃsu, “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo”tiādinā suttantapariyāyeneva dhammaguṇe, “suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho”tiādinā suttantapariyāyeneva saṅghaguṇe ca kathayiṃsu. Tato sīho cintesi “imesaṃ licchavīrājakulānaṃ tatiyadivasato paṭṭhāya buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇe kathentānaṃ mukhaṃ nappahoti, addhā anomaguṇasamannāgato so bhagavā, imaṃ dāni uppannaṃ pītiṃ avijahitvāva ahaṃ ajja sammāsambuddhaṃ passissāmī”ti. Athassa “kiñhi me karissanti nigaṇṭhā”ti vitakko udapādi. Tattha kiñhi me karissantīti kiṃ nāma mayhaṃ nigaṇṭhā karissanti. Apalokitā vā anapalokitā vāti āpucchitā vā anāpucchitā vā. Na hi me te āpucchitā yānavāhanasampattiissariyayasavisesaṃ dassanti, nāpi anāpucchitā māressanti, aphalaṃ etesaṃ āpucchananti adhippāyo.

But on the third occasion, as they spoke in praise of the Buddha, they spoke of the Buddha’s qualities in the way of the suttas, saying, “Indeed, the Blessed One is such…” They spoke of the Dhamma’s qualities in the way of the suttas, saying, “The Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One…” and so forth. They also spoke of the Sangha’s qualities in the way of the suttas, saying, “The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well…” and so on. Then Sīha thought: “For three days now, the mouths of these Licchavi princes have not tired of speaking of the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. Surely, that Blessed One is endowed with incomparable qualities. Without abandoning this joy that has arisen in me, today I shall see the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.” Then the thought occurred to him: “What can the Nigaṇṭhas do to me?” Here, “What can they do to me?” means: “What, indeed, can the Nigaṇṭhas do to me?” Whether I ask permission or not—that is, whether I consult them or not—they will not grant me the advantage of vehicles, conveyances, lordship, glory, or special distinction if I ask. Nor will they kill me if I do not consult them. Asking them is pointless—this is the meaning.

Divā divassāti divassa divā majjhanhike atikkantamatte. Vesāliyā niyyāsīti yathā hi gimhakāle deve vuṭṭhe udakaṃ sandamānaṃ nadiṃ otaritvā thokameva gantvā tiṭṭhati nappavattati, evaṃ sīhassa paṭhamadivase “dasabalaṃ passissāmī”ti uppannāya pītiyā nigaṇṭhena paṭibāhitakālo, yathā dutiyadivase deve vuṭṭhe udakaṃ sandamānaṃ nadiṃ otaritvā thokaṃ [V 3.0297] gantvā vālikāpuñjaṃ paharitvā appavattaṃ hoti, evaṃ sīhassa dutiyadivase “dasabalaṃ passissāmī”ti uppannāya pītiyā nigaṇṭhena paṭibāhitakālo, yathā tatiyadivase deve vuṭṭhe udakaṃ sandamānaṃ nadiṃ otaritvā purāṇapaṇṇasukkhadaṇḍakanaḷakacavarādīni parikaḍḍhantaṃ vālikāpuñjaṃ bhinditvā samuddaninnameva [M 3.0326] hoti, evaṃ sīho tatiyadivase tiṇṇaṃ vatthūnaṃ guṇakathaṃ sutvā uppanne pītipāmojje “aphalā nigaṇṭhā, nipphalā nigaṇṭhā, kiṃ me ime karissanti, gamissāmahaṃ satthu santika”nti gamanaṃ abhinīharitvā vesāliyā niyyāsi. Niyyanto ca “cirassāhaṃ dasabalassa santikaṃ gantukāmo jāto, na kho pana me yuttaṃ aññātakavesena gantu”nti “ye keci dasabalassa santikaṃ gantukāmo, sabbe nikkhamantū”ti ghosanaṃ kāretvā pañca rathasatāni yojāpetvā uttamarathe ṭhito tehi ceva pañcahi rathasatehi mahatiyā ca parisāya parivuto gandhapupphacuṇṇavāsādīni gāhāpetvā niyyāsi.

“During the day” means in the daytime, just past midday. “He set out from Vesālī.” Just as in the hot season, when rain falls, the water flows into a river, but after entering, it moves only a little and then stops without continuing, so too on the first day, the joy that arose in Sīha with the thought, “I will see the Ten-Powered One,” was obstructed by the Nigaṇṭha. Just as on the second day, when rain falls, the water flows into a river, but after moving a little, it strikes a sandbank and stops, so too on the second day, the joy that arose in Sīha with the thought, “I will see the Ten-Powered One,” was obstructed by the Nigaṇṭha. Just as on the third day, when rain falls, the water flows into a river, sweeping away old leaves, dry sticks, reeds, and refuse, breaking through the sandbank and reaching the ocean’s slope, so too on the third day, Sīha, hearing the praise of the qualities of the three treasures, was filled with joy and delight. Thinking, “The Nigaṇṭhas are fruitless, the Nigaṇṭhas are useless—what can they do to me? I will go to the Teacher’s presence,” he resolved to go and left Vesālī. As he was leaving, he thought: “For a long time, I have wished to go to the presence of the Ten-Powered One. But it is not proper for me to go in the attire of someone unknown.” So he had it proclaimed: “Let all who wish to go to the presence of the Ten-Powered One come forth!” He had five hundred chariots prepared, stood in the finest chariot, and surrounded by those five hundred chariots and a great assembly, he had perfumes, flowers, powdered scents, and fragrances taken, and then set out.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti ārāmaṃ pavisanto dūratova asītianubyañjanabyāmappabhādvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni chabbaṇṇā ghanabuddharasmiyo disvā “evarūpaṃ nāma purisaṃ evaṃ āsanne vasantaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ nāddasaṃ, vañcito vatamhi, alābhā vata me”ti cintetvā mahānidhiṃ disvā daliddapuriso viya sañjātapītipāmojjo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarontīti bhotā gotamena vuttakāraṇassa anukāraṇaṃ kathenti. Kāraṇavacano hettha dhamma-saddo “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 720) viya. Kāraṇanti cettha tathāpavattassa saddassa attho adhippeto tassa pavattihetubhāvato. Atthappayutto hi saddappayogo. Anukāraṇanti ca so evaṃ parehi tathā vuccamāno. Sahadhammiko vādānuvādoti parehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā tumhākaṃ vādo vā tato paraṃ tassa anuvādo vā koci appamattakopi viññūhi garahitabbaṃ ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ na āgacchati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kiṃ sabbākārenapi tava vāde gārayhakāraṇaṃ natthīti. Anabbhakkhātukāmāti na abhūtena vattukāmā.

“He approached the Blessed One.” As he entered the monastery, seeing from afar the eighty minor characteristics, the aura extending a fathom, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the six-colored dense rays of the Buddha, he thought: “Such a man has been dwelling nearby for so long, yet I have not seen him! Truly, I have been deceived! Alas, what a loss for me!” Filled with joy and delight, like a poor man who has found a great treasure, he approached the Blessed One. “And they explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma”—this means they elaborate on the cause in accordance with what the revered Gotama has said. Here, the word “Dhamma” signifies the cause, as in passages like, “Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma” (Vibhanga 720). The term “cause” here signifies the intended meaning of the word as it has occurred, because it is the reason for its occurrence. For the use of a word is connected with meaning. And “in accordance with the cause” means that others speak in the same way accordingly. “A discussion in accordance with the Dhamma, a reply in accordance with the Dhamma”—whether your own statement is reasoned by what others have said, or a subsequent elaboration of that, no grounds, even the slightest, occur for the wise to criticize. This is said to mean: “Is there in no way any ground for criticism in your statement?” “Not wishing to misrepresent”—this means not desiring to say what is untrue.

291-292. Atthi sīha pariyāyotiādīnaṃ attho verañjakaṇḍe āgatanayeneva veditabbo. Paramena assāsenāti catumaggacatuphalasaṅkhātena uttamaassāsena. Assāsāya dhammaṃ desetīti assāsanatthāya santhambhanatthāya dhammaṃ deseti. Iti bhagavā aṭṭhahaṅgehi sīhasenāpatissa dhammaṃ deseti.

The meaning of “Atthi sīha pariyāyo” and so on should be understood in the same way as explained in the Verañja section. “With the highest assurance” means with the supreme assurance consisting of the four paths and four fruits. “He teaches the Dhamma for assurance” means he teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of assurance, for the purpose of strengthening. Thus, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to General Sīha with these eight factors.

293. Anuviccakāranti [M 3.0327] anuviditvā cintetvā tulayitvā kātabbaṃ karohīti vutta hoti. Sādhu hotīti sundaro hoti. Tumhādisasmiñhi maṃ disvā maṃ saraṇaṃ gacchante nigaṇṭhaṃ disvā [V 3.0298] nigaṇṭhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchante “kiṃ ayaṃ sīho diṭṭhadiṭṭhameva saraṇaṃ gacchatī”ti garahā uppajjati, tasmā anuviccakāro tumhādisānaṃ sādhūti dasseti. Paṭākaṃ parihareyyunti te kira evarūpaṃ sāvakaṃ labhitvā “asuko nāma rājā vā rājamahāmatto vā seṭṭhi vā amhākaṃ saraṇaṃ gato sāvako jāto”ti paṭākaṃ ukkhipitvā nagare ghosentā āhiṇḍanti. Kasmā? “Evaṃ no mahantabhāvo āvi bhavissatī”ti ca, sace panassa “kimahaṃ ete saraṇaṃ gato”ti vippaṭisāro uppajjeyya, tampi so “etesaṃ me saraṇagatabhāvaṃ bahū jānanti, dukkaraṃ dāni paṭinivattitu”nti vinodetvā na paṭikkamissatīti ca. Tenāha “paṭākaṃ parihareyyu”nti. Opānabhūtanti paṭiyattaudapāno viya ṭhitaṃ. Kulanti tava nivesanaṃ. Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsīti pubbepi dasapi vīsatipi saṭṭhipi jane āgate disvā natthīti avatvā desi, idāni maṃ saraṇaṃ gatakāraṇamatteneva mā imesaṃ deyyadhammaṃ upacchindittha, sampattānañhi dātabbamevāti ovadati. Sutaṃ me taṃ bhanteti kuto sutaṃ? Nigaṇṭhānaṃ santikā. Te kira kulagharesu evaṃ pakāsenti “mayaṃ yassa kassaci sampattassa dātabbanti vadāma, samaṇo pana gotamo ‘mayhameva dānaṃ dātabbaṃ…pe… na aññesaṃ sāvakānaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphala’nti evaṃ vadatī”ti. Taṃ sandhāya ayaṃ “sutaṃ me ta”ntiādimāha.

293. “Consider carefully” means it has been said: “Having understood, reflected, and weighed, do what must be done.” “It is good” means it is excellent. For when people like you see me and go to me for refuge, but upon seeing the Nigaṇṭhas, go to them for refuge, criticism will arise: “Why does this Sīha go for refuge to whatever he sees?” Therefore, he shows that careful consideration is good for those like you. “They would carry around a banner”—they say that upon gaining such a disciple, they raise a banner and proclaim through the town: “Such and such a king, minister, or merchant has become our disciple and taken refuge in us.” Why? “Thus, our greatness will become apparent.” And if regret arises in him, thinking, “Why have I gone to them for refuge?” he will dispel it, thinking, “Many know that I have gone to them for refuge; it is difficult now to turn back,” and so he will not retreat. Hence, he said, “They would carry around a banner.” “Like a ready well” means established like a prepared water source. “Household” means your dwelling. “You should consider it fit to be given” means even before, when ten, twenty, or sixty people came, you gave without saying there was nothing; now, just because you have gone to me for refuge, do not cut off giving gifts to them. For it should be given to those who have arrived—thus he advises. “I have heard that, sir”—where was it heard? From the Nigaṇṭhas. They proclaim in the houses of families thus: “We say that gifts should be given to anyone who comes, but the ascetic Gotama says, ‘Gifts should be given only to me… a gift given to the disciples of others is not of great fruit,’ thus he speaks.” Referring to this, he says, “I have heard that,” and so on.

294. Pavattamaṃsanti pakatiyā pavattaṃ kappiyamaṃsaṃ, mūlaṃ gahetvā antarāpaṇe pariyesāhīti adhippāyo. Sambahulā nigaṇṭhāti pañcasatamattā nigaṇṭhā. Thūlaṃ pasunti thūlaṃ mahāsarīraṃ gokaṇṇamahiṃsasūkarasaṅkhātaṃ pasuṃ. Uddissakatanti attānaṃ uddisitvā kataṃ, māritanti attho. Paṭiccakammanti ettha kamma-saddo kammasādhano atītakālikoti āha “attānaṃ paṭicca kata”nti. Nimittakammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ “paṭicca kammaṃ phusatī”tiādīsu (jā. 1.4.75) viya. Nimittakammassāti nimittabhāvena laddhabbakammassa, na karaṇakārāpanavasena. Paṭiccakammaṃ ettha atthīti maṃsaṃ paṭiccakammaṃ yathā “buddhaṃ etassa atthīti buddho”ti. Atha vā paṭicca kammaṃ phusatīti [M 3.0328] pāṭhaseso daṭṭhabbo, svāyaṃ etaṃ maṃsaṃ paṭicca taṃ pāṇavadhakakammaṃ phusatīti attho. Tañhi akusalaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ dāyakassa, upaḍḍhaṃ paṭiggāhakassa hotīti nesaṃ laddhi. Upakaṇṇaketi kaṇṇamūle. Alanti paṭikkhepavacanaṃ, hotu kiṃ imināti attho. Na ca pana teti ete āyasmantā dīgharattaṃ avaṇṇakāmā hutvā avaṇṇaṃ bhāsantāpi abbhācikkhantā na jiridanti, abbhakkhānassa antaṃ na gacchantīti attho. Atha vā lajjanatthe idaṃ jiridantīti padaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na lajjantīti attho.

294. “Available meat” is permissible meat that has come about naturally; the intention is, “Take the money and search for it in the market.” “Many Nigaṇṭhas” means about five hundred Nigaṇṭhas. “A large animal” refers to a creature with a massive body, such as a cow, buffalo, or pig. “Made on purpose” means made having specified oneself—that is, slaughtered. “Action on account of”: here, the word “kamma” is a derivative signifying a past action. Thus it is said: “done on account of oneself.” This is a designation for “action by way of a sign,” as in phrases like “the action touches because of it” (Jā 1.4.75). “Of an action by way of a sign” means of an action to be acquired by way of a sign, not by way of doing or causing to be done. The meat has “action on account of” in it, thus it is “paṭiccakamma,” just as “he has enlightenment, thus he is a Buddha.” Alternatively, the remainder of the passage should be understood as: “the action touches because of it”—meaning that by reason of this meat, that act of killing living beings accrues to one. For they hold the belief that the unwholesome karma is shared half by the giver and half by the receiver. “Near the ear” means at the root of the ear. “Enough” is a word of refusal, meaning “Let it be, what use is this?” “And yet they do not…” means these venerable ones, though long desiring to speak ill and slander, do not become weary—they do not reach the end of their calumny. Alternatively, the word “jiridanti” should be understood in the sense of shame—they do not feel ashamed.

Sīhasenāpativatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of General Sīha is concluded.

Kappiyabhūmianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Allowance of Suitable Ground

295. Abhilāpamattanti [V 3.0299] desanāmattaṃ. Āmisakhādanatthāyāti tattha tattha chaḍḍitassa āmisassa khādanatthāya. Anuppageyevāti pātoyeva. Oravasaddanti mahāsaddaṃ. Taṃ pana avatvāpīti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃvuttanayena avatvāpi. Pi-saddena tathā vacanampi anujānāti. Aṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayenāti sesaaṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayena. “Kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā’ti vā, ‘kappiyakuṭī’ti vā vutte sādhāraṇalakkhaṇa”nti sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaussāvanantikākuṭikaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Cayanti adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Yato paṭṭhāyāti yato iṭṭhakato silato mattikāpiṇḍato vā paṭṭhāya. Paṭhamiṭṭhakādīnaṃ heṭṭhā na vaṭṭantīti bhittiyā paṭhamiṭṭhakādīnaṃ heṭṭhā bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpiyamānā iṭṭhakādayo bhūmigatikattā “kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti vatvā patiṭṭhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭanti. Yadi evaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇitvā patiṭṭhāpiyamānā thambhā kasmā tathā vatvā patiṭṭhāpetuṃ vaṭṭantīti āha “thambhā pana…pe… vaṭṭantī”ti. Saṅghasantakamevāti vāsatthāya kataṃ saṅghikasenāsanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Bhikkhusantakanti vāsatthāya eva kataṃ bhikkhussa puggalikasenāsanaṃ. Mukhasannidhīti iminā antovutthadukkaṭameva dīpitaṃ.

295. “Merely an utterance” means merely a declaration. “For the purpose of eating bait” means for the purpose of eating the discarded bait in various places. “Early in the morning” means in the early morning. “A great noise” means a loud noise. “But even without saying that” means even without saying that, according to the method stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā. The particle “pi” also permits such a statement. “According to the method stated in the commentaries” means according to the method stated in the remaining commentaries. “‘When it is said, “Let us make a suitable hut” or “a suitable hut,” this is the common characteristic’ refers to the characteristic of making a hut with an announcement, as stated in all commentaries. “Foundation” means determination. “Starting from which” means starting from the brick, stone, or lump of clay. “It is not proper below the first bricks, etc.” means that when the first bricks, etc., of a wall are being laid on the ground, since the bricks, etc., placed on the ground are part of the ground, they are not proper to install by saying, “Let us make a suitable hut.” If that is the case, why are posts, when dug into the ground and fixed, proper to install by such a declaration? The answer is given: “But posts... are proper.” “Belonging only to the Sangha” refers to a lodging belonging to the Sangha made for the purpose of residence. “Belonging to a monk” refers to a personal lodging of a monk made for the purpose of residence. “In the presence of the mouth” here indicates only the offense of wrong conduct for one dwelling inside.

Kappiyabhūmianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on the allowance of suitable ground is concluded.

Keṇiyajaṭilavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Matted-haired Ascetic Keṇiya

300. Yena [M 3.0329] āpaṇaṃ tadavasarītiādīsu āpaṇanti ekassa nigamassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmiṃ kira nigame vīsati āpaṇamukhasahassāni vibhattāni ahesuṃ. Iti so āpaṇānaṃ ussannattā “āpaṇa”ntveva saṅkhaṃ gato. Tassa pana nigamassa avidūre nadītīre ghanacchāyo ramaṇīyabhūmibhāgo mahāvanasaṇḍo, tasmiṃ bhagavā viharati. Keṇiyoti tassa nāmaṃ. Jaṭiloti āharimajaṭādharo tāpaso. So kira brāhmaṇamahāsālo, dhanarakkhaṇatthāya pana tāpasapabbajjaṃ samādāya rañño paṇṇākāraṃ datvā bhūmibhāgaṃ gahetvā tattha assamaṃ kāretvā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi vaṇijjaṃ payojetvā kulasahassassa nissayo hutvā vasati. Assamepi cassa eko tālarukkho divase divase ekaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ phalaṃ muñcatīti vadanti. So divā kāsāvāni dhāreti, jaṭā ca bandhati, rattiṃ kāmasampattiṃ anubhavati.

300. In the phrase 'Yena āpaṇaṃ tadavasarīti' and so forth, 'Āpaṇa' is a designation for a certain market town. It is said that in that market town, twenty thousand shop fronts were arranged. Thus, because of the abundance of shops, it came to be known simply as 'Āpaṇa.' Not far from that market town, on the riverbank, there was a dense, shady, delightful area, a great forest grove, where the Blessed One was dwelling. Keṇiya was his name. 'Jaṭila' means an ascetic wearing matted locks. It is said that he was a wealthy brahmin householder, but for the sake of protecting his wealth, he undertook the ascetic's life. Having given a tribute to the king, he took possession of a piece of land, built a hermitage there, engaged in trade with five hundred carts, and lived as the support for a thousand families. They say that in his hermitage there was a palmyra tree that daily yielded one golden fruit. By day he wore ochre robes and tied his hair in a knot, but by night he enjoyed the fulfillment of desires.

Pavattāroti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.285; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.427; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.192) pavattayitāro[V 3.0300], pāvacanavasena vattāroti attho. Yesanti yesaṃ santakaṃ. Mantapadanti mantasadde bahikatvā raho bhāsitabbaṭṭhena mantā eva taṃtaṃatthapaṭipattihetutāya padanti mantapadaṃ, vedavacanaṃ. Gītanti aṭṭhakādīhi dasahi porāṇabrāhmaṇehi udāttānudāttādisarasampattivasena sajjhāyitaṃ. Pavuttanti pāvacanavasena aññesaṃ vuttaṃ, vācitanti attho. Samihitanti samupabyūḷhaṃ rāsikataṃ, iruvedayajuvedasāmavedādivasena tatthāpi paccekaṃ mantabrāhmaṇādivasena sajjhāyanavācakādivasena ca piṇḍaṃ katvā ṭhapitanti attho. Tadanugāyantīti etarahi brāhmaṇā taṃ tehi pubbe gītaṃ anugāyanti anusajjhāyanti. Tadanubhāsantīti taṃ anubhāsanti, idaṃ purimasseva vevacanaṃ. Bhāsitamanubhāsantīti tehi bhāsitaṃ sajjhāyitaṃ anusajjhāyanti. Vācitamanuvācentīti tehi aññesaṃ vācitaṃ anuvācenti. Seyyathidanti te katameti attho. Aṭṭhakotiādīni tesaṃ nāmāni. Te kira dibbacakkhuparibhaṇḍena yathākammūpagañāṇena sattānaṃ kammassakatādiṃ pubbenivāsañāṇena [M 3.0330] atītakappe brāhmaṇānaṃ mantajjhenavidhiñca oloketvā parūpaghātaṃ akatvā kassapasammāsambuddhassa bhagavato vaṭṭasannissitena vacanena saha saṃsanditvā mante ganthesuṃ. Aparāpare pana okkākarājakālādīsu uppannabrāhmaṇā pāṇātipātādīni pakkhipitvā tayo vede bhinditvā buddhavacanena saddhiṃ viruddhe akaṃsu. Rattibhojanaṃ ratti, tato uparatāti rattūparatā. Atikkante majjhanhike yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ nāma, tato viratattā viratā vikālabhojanā. Paṭiyādāpetvāti sappimadhusakkarādīhi ceva maricehi ca susaṅkhataṃ pānaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā.

The term 'Pavattāro' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.285; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.427; A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.5.192) means 'proclaimers,' that is, 'speakers' in the sense of those who recite. 'Yesaṃ' refers to 'whose property.' 'Mantapada' means a 'mantra-word,' that is, a mantra spoken in secret, distinct from ordinary speech, which serves as a cause for the attainment of various purposes; it is a Vedic utterance. 'Gīta' means what was chanted by the ten ancient brahmins, such as Aṭṭhaka, with the excellence of tones like udātta and anudātta, in the manner of recitation. 'Pavutta' means what was spoken to others in the manner of recitation, that is, recited. 'Samihita' means what was gathered and heaped together, that is, compiled and preserved as a collection, referring to the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and so forth, and within those, individually, the mantra and brahmana sections, by reciters and speakers. 'Tadanugāyanti' means that the brahmins of today chant and recite what was previously sung by those ancients, repeating after them. 'Tadanubhāsanti' means they repeat it; this is just another term for the former. 'Bhāsitamanubhāsanti' means they recite what was spoken and chanted by those ancients, repeating after them. 'Vācitamanuvācenti' means they cause others to recite what was taught to others by them. 'Seyyathidaṃ' means 'such as,' that is, 'who are they?' Aṭṭhaka and so forth are their names. It is said that they, endowed with divine vision and knowledge of how beings fare according to their kamma, and knowledge of past lives, observed the ownership of actions of beings and the methods of Vedic recitation of brahmins in past eons, and without harming others, they composed the hymns by comparing them with the words of the Blessed One, Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, which were connected with the cycle of existence. However, later brahmins who arose in the time of King Okkāka and so forth, by inserting practices like killing living beings, split the three Vedas and made them contradict the Buddha's teachings. 'Rattibhojana' means eating at night. 'Rattūparatā' means abstaining from that night meal. Eating after midday until sunset is called 'vikālabhojana' (eating at the wrong time); abstaining from this is called 'viratā vikālabhojanā' (abstaining from eating at the wrong time). 'Paṭiyādāpetvā' means having prepared a well-made drink with ghee, honey, sugar, and spices.

“Mahā kho keṇiya bhikkhusaṅgho”ti kasmā bhagavā punappunaṃ paṭikkhipi? Titthiyānaṃ paṭikkhepapasannatāya. Titthiyā hi “aho vatāyaṃ appiccho, yo nimantiyamānopi na sādiyatī”ti upanimantiyamānassa paṭikkhepe pasīdantīti keci, akāraṇañcetaṃ. Natthi buddhānaṃ paccayahetu evarūpaṃ kohaññaṃ, ayaṃ pana aḍḍhatelasāni bhikkhusatāni disvā ettakānaṃyeva bhikkhaṃ paṭiyādessati, sveva selo brāhmaṇo tīhi purisasatehi saddhiṃ pabbajissati, ayuttaṃ kho pana navake aññato pesetvā imeheva saddhiṃ gantuṃ, ime vā aññato pesetvā navakehi saddhiṃ gantuṃ. Athāpi sabbeva gahetvā gamissāmi, bhikkhāhāro nappahossati. Tato bhikkhūsu piṇḍāya carantesu manussā ujjhāyissanti “cirassampi keṇiyo samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ nimantetvā yāpanamattaṃ dātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti, sayañca vippaṭisārī bhavissati. Paṭikkhepe pana kate “samaṇo gotamo punappunaṃ ‘tvañca brāhmaṇesu abhippasanno’ti brāhmaṇānaṃ nāmaṃ gaṇhātī”ti cintetvā brāhmaṇepi nimantetukāmo bhavissati, tato [V 3.0301] brāhmaṇe pāṭiyekkaṃ nimantessati, te tena nimantitā bhikkhū hutvā bhuñjissanti, evamassa saddhā anurakkhitā bhavissatīti punappunaṃ paṭikkhipi. Kiñcāpi kho bho gotamāti iminā idaṃ dīpeti “bho gotama, kiṃ jātaṃ, yadi ahaṃ brāhmaṇesu abhippasanno, adhivāsetu bhavaṃ gotamo, ahaṃ brāhmaṇānampi dātuṃ sakkomi tumhākampī”ti. Ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasanti ettha taṇḍuladhovanodakampi dhaññarasoyevāti vadanti. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ucchurasanti ettha nikkasaṭo ucchuraso sattāhakālikoti veditabbaṃ.

Why did the Blessed One repeatedly decline, saying, 'Great, Keṇiya, is the community of monks'? Some say it was to inspire confidence in the sectarians by rejecting the invitation. For the sectarians think, 'Ah, this one is indeed of few desires, who, even when invited, does not consent,' and they become pleased when one declines an invitation; but this is without reason. There is no such deceit in Buddhas for the sake of requisites. However, he thought: 'This man will prepare alms-food only for these twelve hundred and fifty monks. Tomorrow, the brahmin Sela will go forth with three hundred men. It would not be proper to send the newly ordained ones elsewhere and go with these, or to send these elsewhere and go with the newly ordained ones. Or if I take them all, the alms-food will not be enough.' Then, while the monks are wandering for alms, people will complain, 'After a long time, Keṇiya invited the ascetic Gotama but could not even provide enough for their sustenance,' and he himself will feel remorse. But if the invitation is declined, he will think, 'The ascetic Gotama repeatedly mentions the brahmins, saying, "You are devoted to the brahmins,"' and he will wish to invite the brahmins as well. Then he will invite the brahmins individually, and those invited will become monks and eat. Thus, his faith will be protected. Therefore, he repeatedly declined. By the words 'But still, Master Gotama...', he indicates this: 'Master Gotama, what does it matter if I am devoted to the brahmins? Let the Blessed One accept. I am able to give to the brahmins as well as to you.' Excluding grain, fruit, and juice—here, they say that even the water used to wash rice is considered the juice of grain. 'I allow, monks, sugarcane juice'—here, strained sugarcane juice is to be known as allowable for seven days.

Imāhi [M 3.0331] gāthāhīti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.400) imāhi keṇiyassa cittānukūlāhi gāthāhi. Tattha aggiparicariyaṃ vinā brāhmaṇānaṃ yaññābhāvato “aggihuttamukhā yaññā”ti vuttaṃ, aggihuttaseṭṭhā aggijuhanappadhānāti attho. Brāhmaṇā hi “aggimukhā devā”ti aggijuhanapubbakaṃ yaññaṃ vidahanti. Vede sajjhāyantehi paṭhamaṃ sajjhāyitabbato sāvittī “chandaso mukha”nti vuttā, sāvittī vedassa pubbaṅgamāti attho taṃpubbakattā vedasavanassa. Manussānaṃ seṭṭhabhāvato rājā “mukha”nti vutto. Ogāhantīnaṃ nadīnaṃ ādhārabhāvato gantabbaṭṭhānabhāvena paṭisaraṇato ca sāgaro “mukha”nti vutto. Candasamāyogena “ajja kattikā, ajja rohiṇī”ti saññāyanato nakkhattāni abhibhavitvā ālokakaraṇato nakkhattehi ativisesasommabhāvato ca “nakkhattānaṃ mukhaṃ cando”ti vuttaṃ. “Dīpasikhā aggijālā asanivicakka”nti evamādīnaṃ tapantānaṃ vijjulatānaṃ aggattā ādicco “tapataṃ mukha”nti vutto. Dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ pana aggattā visesena tasmiṃ samaye buddhappamukhaṃ saṅghaṃ sandhāya “puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānānaṃ, saṅgho ve yajataṃ mukha”nti vuttaṃ. Tena saṅgho puññassa āyamukhaṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvenāti dasseti.

'Imāhi gāthāhi' (Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.400) means 'with these verses,' that is, with these verses agreeable to Keṇiya's mind. Here, it is said, 'Sacrifices have the fire-offering as their foremost,' because without the worship of fire, there is no sacrifice for brahmins—meaning the fire-offering is chief, with the act of offering into fire being primary. For brahmins declare, 'The gods have fire as their mouth,' and thus perform sacrifices preceded by fire-offering. The Sāvitrī hymn is called 'the mouth of the Vedas' because it is the first to be recited by those who chant the Vedas—meaning the Sāvitrī is the precursor to the recitation of the Vedas, since the Vedic study begins with it. The king is called 'the mouth' due to being the foremost among men. The ocean is called 'the mouth' because it is the support for rivers that flow into it, and because it is a destination and a refuge. The moon is called 'the mouth of the constellations' because it is known by conjunctions like 'today is Kattikā, today is Rohiṇī,' and because it illuminates and surpasses the constellations with its light, and due to its exceedingly gentle nature compared to the constellations. The sun is called 'the mouth of radiant things' because it is the foremost among radiant things like lamp flames, fire-brands, and lightning flashes. But for those seeking merit, the Sangha is declared as 'the mouth of those who sacrifice,' referring especially at that time to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, as the Sangha is the foremost field of merit. Thus, it shows that the Sangha is the gateway to merit, being the supreme worthy recipient of offerings.

Keṇiyajaṭilavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Account Concerning the Matted-haired Ascetic Keṇiya is concluded.

Rojamallavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of Rojamalla

301. Rojavatthumhi vihāroti gandhakuṭiṃ sandhāya āhaṃsu. Ataramānoti aturanto, saṇikaṃ padappamāṇaṭṭhāne padaṃ nikkhipanto vattaṃ katvā susammaṭṭhaṃ muttādalasinduvārasantharasadisaṃ vālikaṃ avināsentoti attho. Āḷindanti pamukhaṃ. Ukkāsitvāti ukkāsitasaddaṃ katvā. Aggaḷanti kavāṭaṃ. Ākoṭehīti agganakhena īsakaṃ kuñcikachiddasamīpe koṭehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dvāraṃ kira atiupari amanussā, atiheṭṭhā tiracchānajātikā koṭenti, tathā akoṭetvā majjhe chiddasamīpe manussā [V 3.0302] koṭenti, idaṃ dvārakoṭakavattanti dīpentā vadanti. Vivari [M 3.0332] bhagavā dvāranti na bhagavā uṭṭhāya dvāraṃ vivari, vivaratūti pana hatthaṃ pasāresi. Tato “bhagavā tumhehi anekāsu kappakoṭīsu dānaṃ dadamānehi na sahatthā dvāravivaraṇakammaṃ kata”nti sayameva dvāraṃ vivaṭaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā bhagavato manena vivaṭaṃ, tasmā “vivari bhagavā dvāra”nti vuttaṃ.

301. Regarding the story of Roja, 'vihāro' (dwelling), they said, refers to the perfumed chamber. 'Ataramāno' means not hurrying, unhurriedly, placing the foot slowly in the place of measured steps, having performed the duty, not disturbing the well-swept sand resembling a scattering of pearls, coral, and sinduvāra flowers. 'Āḷinda' means the porch. 'Ukkāsitvā' means making the sound of clearing the throat. 'Aggaḷa' means the door-bar. 'Ākoṭehi' means to strike lightly near the keyhole with the tip of a nail. Explaining, they say that non-humans knock at the very top of the door, animals at the very bottom, and humans knock in the middle near the keyhole—this is the custom of door-knocking. 'Vivari bhagavā dvāraṃ' (The Blessed One opened the door) does not mean the Blessed One got up and opened the door, but rather he extended his hand, as if to say, 'Let it open.' Then, the door opened by itself, as if to say, 'The Blessed One, having given gifts for countless crores of eons, has not with his own hand performed the act of opening a door.' However, since it opened by the Blessed One's thought, it is said, 'The Blessed One opened the door.'

Rojamallavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Roja the Malla is concluded.

Vuḍḍhapabbajitavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Elderly Renunciate

303. Ātumāvatthumhi aññataro vuḍḍhapabbajitoti subhaddo nāma aññataro bhikkhu vuḍḍhakāle pabbajitattā “vuḍḍhapabbajito”ti vutto. Dve dārakāti sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitā dve puttā. Nāḷiyāvāpakenāti nāḷiyā ceva thavikāya ca. Saṃhariṃsūti yasmā manussā te dārake mañjubhāṇine paṭibhānavante disvā kāretukāmāpi akāretukāmāpi kārentiyeva, katakāle ca “kiṃ gaṇhissatha tātā”ti pucchanti. Te vadanti “na amhākaṃ aññena kenaci attho, pitā pana no bhagavato āgatakāle yāgudānaṃ kātukāmo”ti. Taṃ sutvā manussā aparigaṇetvāva yaṃ te sakkonti harituṃ, sabbaṃ denti. Yampi na sakkonti, manussehi pesenti. Tasmā te dārakā bahuṃ loṇampi telampi sappimpi taṇḍulampi khādanīyampi saṃhariṃsu.

303. Regarding the story at Ātumā, 'a certain elderly renunciate' refers to a certain bhikkhu named Subhadda, who was called 'the elderly renunciate' because he had gone forth in old age. 'Two boys' refers to two sons who were in the stage of novices. 'With a nāḷi measure and a bag' means with both a nāḷi measure and a bag. 'They gathered' means that because when people saw those boys, who were charming speakers and intelligent, they had them perform, whether they wished to or not. And when this was done, they would ask, 'What will you take, dear ones?' The boys would reply, 'We have no need for anything else, but our father wishes to make an offering of rice gruel when the Blessed One arrives.' Hearing this, people gave everything they could carry without calculating. Even what they could not carry, they sent with others. Thus, those boys gathered much salt, oil, ghee, rice, and food.

Ātumāyaṃ viharatīti ātumaṃ nissāya viharati. Bhusāgāreti bhusamaye agārake. Tattha kira mahantaṃ palālapuñjaṃ abbhantarato palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā sālāsadisaṃ pabbajitānaṃ vasanayoggaṭṭhānasadisaṃ kataṃ, tadā bhagavā tattha vasi. Atha bhagavati ātumaṃ āgantvā bhusāgārakaṃ paviṭṭhe subhaddo sāyanhasamayaṃ gāmadvāraṃ gantvā manusse āmantesi “upāsakā nāhaṃ tumhākaṃ santikā aññaṃ kiñci paccāsīsāmi, mayhaṃ dārakehi ānītatelādīniyeva saṅghassa pahonti, hatthakammamattaṃ me dethā”ti. Kiṃ, bhante, karomāti? “Idañcidañca gaṇhathā”ti sabbūpakaraṇāni gāhetvā vihāre uddhanāni kāretvā ekaṃ kāḷakaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā tādisameva pārupitvā “idaṃ karotha, idaṃ karothā”ti sabbarattiṃ vicārento satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā bhojjayāguñca [M 3.0333] madhugoḷakañca paṭiyādāpesi. Bhojjayāgu nāma paṭhamaṃ bhuñjitvā pātabbayāgu, tattha sappimadhuphāṇitamacchamaṃsapupphaphalarasādi yaṃkiñci khādanīyaṃ nāma, sabbaṃ pavisati, kīḷitukāmānaṃ sīsamakkhanayoggā hoti sugandhagandhā.

'He dwells at Ātumā' means he dwells relying on Ātumā. 'In a barn' means in a house made of chaff. There, it is said, a large pile of straw was hollowed out from the inside and made into a place like a hall, suitable for the residence of renunciates. At that time, the Blessed One stayed there. Then, when the Blessed One had arrived at Ātumā and entered the barn, Subhadda, in the evening, went to the village gate and addressed the people: 'Lay followers, I do not wish for anything else from you. The oil and other things brought by my children are sufficient for the Sangha. Just give me your manual labor.' 'What should we do, venerable sir?' 'Take this and that,' he said, having them take all the necessary items. Having had hearths prepared in the monastery, and after putting on a blackish-brown robe and similarly covering himself with another, 'Do this, do that,' he instructed all night, spending a hundred thousand, and he arranged for 'eatable gruel' and honey balls. 'Eatable gruel' is a gruel to be drunk after having first eaten; in it, whatever edible items such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flowers, fruits, juices, etc., are all included. For those who wish to play, it is suitable for anointing the head, and it has a fragrant aroma.

Atha [V 3.0303] bhagavā kālasseva sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto piṇḍāya carituṃ ātumagāmanagarābhimukho pāyāsi. Manussā tassa ārocesuṃ “bhagavā piṇḍāya gāmaṃ pavisati, tayā kassa yāgu paṭiyāditā”ti. So yathānivatthapāruteheva tehi kāḷakakāsāvehi ekena hatthena dabbiñca kaṭacchuñca gahetvā brahmā viya dakkhiṇajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā vanditvā “paṭiggaṇhātu me, bhante, bhagavā yāgu”nti āha. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho so vuḍḍhapabbajito tassā rattiyā accayena bahutaraṃ yāguṃ paṭiyādāpetvā bhagavato upanāmesī”ti. Jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchantītiādi vuttanayameva. Kutāyanti kuto ayaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Then the Blessed One, having attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, set out towards the village-town of Ātumā for alms. People informed him, 'The Blessed One is entering the village for alms; for whom have you prepared the gruel?' He, in the very same blackish-brown robes he was wearing, taking a ladle and a spoon in one hand, and like Brahmā, placing his right knee on the ground, paid homage and said, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept this gruel from me.' Therefore it was said, 'Then that elderly renunciate, after the night had passed, had a large quantity of gruel prepared and offered it to the Blessed One.' Even the Tathāgatas, though knowing, ask questions, and so on, as has been stated. 'Kutāyaṃ' means 'kuto ayaṃ' (from where is this). The rest here is clear.

304. Dasabhāgaṃ datvāti dasamabhāgaṃ datvā. Tenevāha “dasa koṭṭhāse katvā eko koṭṭhāso bhūmisāmikānaṃ dātabbo”ti.

304. 'Having given a tenth part' means having given a tenth portion. Therefore it was said, 'Having made ten portions, one portion should be given to the landowners.'

Vuḍḍhapabbajitavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of the elderly renunciate is concluded.

Catumahāpadesakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Great Authorities

305. Parimaddantāti upaparikkhantā. Pattuṇṇadese sañjātavatthaṃ pattuṇṇaṃ. Koseyyavisesoti hi abhidhānakose vuttaṃ. Cīnadese somāradese ca sañjātavatthāni cīnasomārapaṭāni. Pattuṇṇādīni tīṇi koseyyassa anulomāni pāṇakehi katasuttamayattā. Iddhimayikaṃ ehibhikkhūnaṃ puññiddhiyā nibbattacīvaraṃ. Taṃ khomādīnaṃ aññataraṃ hotīti tesaṃyeva anulomaṃ. Devatāhi dinnacīvaraṃ devadattiyaṃ. Taṃ kapparukkhe nibbattaṃ jālinīdevakaññāya anuruddhattherassa dinnavatthasadisaṃ. Tampi khomādīnaññeva anulomaṃ hoti tesu aññatarabhāvato. Dve paṭā desanāmeneva vuttāti tesaṃ sarūpadassanaparametaṃ, nāññaṃ nivattanaparaṃ pattuṇṇapaṭassapi desanāmeneva vuttattā. Tumbāti bhājanāni[M 3.0334]. Phalatumboti lābuādi. Udakatumboti udakukkhipanakakuṭako. Kilañjacchattanti veḷuvilīvehi vāyitvā katachattaṃ. Sambhinnarasanti sammissitarasaṃ. Pānakaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ hotīti ambapānādipānakaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ [V 3.0304] hoti, taṃ vikālepi kappati asambhinnarasattā. Tena tadahupaṭiggahitena saddhinti tena sattāhakālikena tadahupaṭiggahitena saddhiṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

305. 'Parimaddantā' means examining, investigating. 'Pattuṇṇa' is cloth produced in the Pattuṇṇa region. 'A special kind of silk (koseyya)' is indeed stated in the Abhidhānakośa. 'Cīnasomārapaṭāni' are cloths produced in China and the Soma country. The three, beginning with Pattuṇṇa, are suitable as silk (koseyya) because they are made of thread produced by insects. 'Iddhimayika' is a robe produced by the power of merit for the Ehi-bhikkhus. It is one of those like linen, etc., and thus suitable for them. 'Devadattiya' is a robe given by deities. That is produced from a wish-fulfilling tree, similar to the cloth given by the deity-maiden Jālinī to the Elder Anuruddha. That too is suitable as linen, etc., being one of them. The phrase 'two cloths' refers to cloths mentioned by the name of their country; this is solely for the purpose of indicating their nature, not for the purpose of excluding others, since Pattuṇṇa cloth is also mentioned by the name of its country. 'Tumbā' means vessels. 'Fruit tumbā' refers to gourds, etc. 'Water tumbā' is a water-lifting pot. 'Kilañja umbrella' is an umbrella made by weaving bamboo strips. 'Sambhinnarasa' means mixed juice. 'A drink has been received' means a drink like mango juice has been received; it is allowable even at the wrong time because its juice is not mixed. 'With that received that day' means together with that which is allowable for seven days, received that day. The rest here is easily understood.

Catumahāpadesakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Four Great Authorities is concluded.

Bhesajjakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Medicines is concluded.

7. Kathinakkhandhakaṃ

7. The Kathina Chapter

Kathinānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Authorization of the Kathina

306. Kathinakkhandhake [M 3.0335][V 3.0305] sīsavasenāti padhānaṅgavasena. “Kathinanti pañcānisaṃse antokaraṇasamatthatāya thiranti attho”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. “So nesaṃ bhavissatī”ti yujjatīti “so tumhāka”nti avatvā “nesa”nti vacanaṃ yujjati. Ye atthatakathināti na kevalaṃ tumhākameva, ye aññepi atthatakathinā, tesampi bhavissatīti attho. Anāmantetvā caraṇanti cārittasikkhāpade vuttanayena anāpucchitvā kulesu caraṇaṃ. Matakacīvaranti matassa santakaṃ cīvaraṃ. Tatruppādena ābhatanti vihārasantakena khettavatthuādinā ānītaṃ.

306. In the Kathina chapter, 'by way of the head' means by way of the principal factor. 'Kathina' means 'firm' (thira) because of its capacity to encompass the five advantages; so it is said in the Gaṇṭhipadas. The statement, 'it will be theirs,' is fitting; thus, the word 'theirs' is appropriate instead of 'yours.' 'Those who have spread the Kathina' means it will be for them too, not only for you, but also for others who have spread the Kathina. 'Wandering without asking leave' means wandering among families without asking permission, according to the method stated in the training rule on conduct. 'Robe of the dead' means a robe belonging to a dead person. 'Brought by what is produced there' means brought by means of possessions belonging to the monastery, such as fields or land.

Paṭhamapavāraṇāya pavāritāti idaṃ vassacchedaṃ akatvā vassaṃvutthabhāvasandassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ antarāyena appavāritānampi vutthavassānaṃ kathinatthārasambhavato. Teneva “appavāritā vā”ti avatvā “chinnavassā vā pacchimikāya upagatā vā na labhantī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Aññasmiṃ vihāre vutthavassāpi na labhantīti nānāsīmāya aññasmiṃ vihāre vutthavassā imasmiṃ vihāre kathinatthāraṃ na labhantīti attho. Khalimakkhitasāṭakoti ahatavatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dānakammavācāti kathinadussadānakammavācā. Akātuṃ na labbhatīti iminā anādariyena akarontassa dukkaṭanti dīpeti. Kammavācā pana ekāyeva vaṭṭatīti kathinatthārasāṭakassa dānakāle vuttā ekāyeva kammavācā vaṭṭati. Puna tassa aññasmiṃ vatthe diyyamāne kammavācāya dātabbakiccaṃ natthi, apalokanameva alanti adhippāyo.

The phrase 'having been invited at the first Pavāraṇā' is stated to show the status of having completed the rains-residence without a break. This is because the spreading of the Kathina is possible even for those who have completed the rains-residence but have not been invited due to some obstacle. For this reason, instead of saying 'or not invited,' it is simply stated, 'those who have broken the rains-residence or have arrived for the later Pavāraṇā do not receive it.' The statement 'those who have completed the rains-residence in another monastery also do not receive it' means that those who have completed the rains-residence in another monastery with a different boundary do not receive the spreading of the Kathina in this monastery. 'A cloth smeared with clay' is said in reference to new cloth. 'The formal act of giving' refers to the formal act of giving the Kathina cloth. By 'It is not allowable not to do it,' it is shown that for one who does not do it out of disrespect, there is a dukkaṭa offense. However, only one formal act is valid—this refers to the single formal act spoken at the time of donating the Kathina cloth. If another cloth is given later, there is no need for another formal act; a simple announcement suffices—this is the intention.

308. Mahābhūmikanti mahāvisayaṃ, catuvīsatiākāravantatāya mahāvitthārikanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pañcakanti pañcakhaṇḍaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Paṭhamacimilikāti kathinavatthato aññā attano pakaticimilikā. “Kucchicimilikaṃ katvā sibbitamattenāti thirajiṇṇānaṃ cimilikānaṃ ekato katvā sibbanassetaṃ adhivacana”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Mahāpaccariyaṃ kurundiyañca [M 3.0336][V 3.0306] “vuttavacananidassanaṃ byañjane eva bhedo, atthe natthīti dassanatthaṃ kata”nti vadanti. Piṭṭhianuvātāropanamattenāti dīghato anuvātassa āropanamattena. Kucchianuvātāropanamattenāti puthulato anuvātassa āropanamattena. Sāruppaṃ hotīti samaṇasāruppaṃ hoti. Rattinissaggiyenāti rattiatikkantena.

308. 'Mahābhūmika' means having a vast range; it is said to be 'extensive' because it possesses twenty-four characteristics. 'Pañcaka' means five sections. This method applies to the rest as well. 'First small patchwork' refers to one's own usual small patches, different from the Kathina cloth. 'Having made a belly-patchwork, merely by sewing it' – this is a term for sewing together firm, old small patches, as stated in the Gaṇṭhipadas. In the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundī, they say: 'This was done to show that the illustration of the statement has a difference only in the letter, not in the meaning.' 'Merely attaching a back lining (anuvāta)' means merely attaching a lining along its length. 'Merely attaching a front lining (anuvāta)' means merely attaching a lining along its width. 'Suitable' means suitable for a recluse. 'Due to Nissaggiya at night' means because the night has passed.

Kathinānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Account of the Authorization of the Kathina is concluded.

Ādāyasattakādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account Beginning with the Sevenfold Ādāya.

311. Ayanti āsāvacchediko kathinuddhāro. Idha na vuttoti pāḷiyaṃ mātikāpadabhājane savanantikānantaraṃ na vutto. Tatthāti tasmiṃ sīmātikkantike kathinuddhāre. “Sīmātikkantiko nāma cīvarakālasīmātikkantiko”ti kenaci vuttaṃ. “Bahisīmāyaṃ cīvarakālasamayassa atikkantattā sīmātikkantiko”ti ayaṃ amhākaṃ khanti. Sahubbhāre “so katacīvaro”ti pāṭho dissati, evañca sati cīvarapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjatīti viññāyati, idha pana parivārapāḷiyañca “dve palibodhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ chijjantī”ti (pari. 415) vacanato taṃ na sameti, tasmā vīmaṃsitabbamettha kāraṇaṃ.

311. This is the kathina removal that cuts off expectation. It is not stated here, meaning it is not stated in the Pāli text, in the section on the classification of rule headings, immediately after Savanantika. Therein: in that kathina removal that goes beyond the boundary. Some say: 'Sīmātikkantika means one who has crossed the boundary of the robe-making season.' Our understanding is: 'It is called sīmātikkantika because the time for robe-making has passed outside the boundary.' In the Sahubbhāra, the reading 'so katacīvaro' (he has made the robe) is seen. If this were the case, it would be understood that the impediment of the robe is removed first. However, here in the Parivāra Pāli, it does not agree with the statement 'two impediments are removed, neither first nor last' (Parivāra 415). Therefore, the reason for this should be investigated here.

312. “Samādāyavāro ādāyavārasadiso, upasaggamattamettha viseso”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Keci pana “sabbaṃ attano parikkhāraṃ anavasesetvā pakkamanto ‘samādāya pakkamatī’ti vuccatī”ti vadanti. Puna samādāyavārepi teyeva dassitāti sambandho. Vippakatacīvare pakkamanantikassa kathinuddhārassa asambhavato “yathāsambhava”nti vuttaṃ. Pakkamanantiko hi kathinuddhāro niṭṭhitacīvarasseva vasena vutto “bhikkhu atthatakathino katacīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamatī”ti vuttattā, tasmā so vippakatacīvaro na sambhavatīti chaḷeva ubbhārā tattha dassitā.

312. In the Gaṇṭhipadas, it is stated: 'The section on samādāya (taking up completely) is similar to the section on ādāya (taking up); the only difference here is the prefix.' Some, however, say: 'One who departs without leaving behind any of his requisites is said to "depart taking up completely."' Again, in the section on samādāya, the same ones are shown—thus the connection. Regarding an unfinished robe, since the kathina removal at the time of departure is impossible, it is said 'as is possible.' For the kathina removal at the time of departure is stated only in the case of one whose robe is finished—as it is said, 'A bhikkhu who has participated in the kathina departs taking up the finished robe.' Therefore, since that does not apply to one with an unfinished robe, only six removals are shown there.

Tatrāyaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya vāravibhāvanā – ādāyavārā satta, tathā samādāyavārāti dve sattakavārā, tato pakkamanantikaṃ vajjetvā vippakatacīvarassa ādāyasamādāyavāravasena dve chakkavārā, tato paraṃ [M 3.0337] niṭṭhānasanniṭṭhānanāsanantikānaṃ vasena tīṇi tikāni dassitāni. Tattha paṭhamattikaṃ antosīmāyaṃ “paccessaṃ na paccessa”nti imaṃ vidhiṃ anāmasitvā bahisīmāyameva “na paccessa”nti pavattaṃ, tasmā pakkamanantikasīmātikkantikasaubbhārā tattha [V 3.0307] na yujjanti. Dutiyattikaṃ antosīmāyaṃ “na paccessa”nti pavattaṃ. Tatiyattikaṃ anadhiṭṭhita-padena visesetvā pavattaṃ, atthato paṭhamattikena sameti. Anadhiṭṭhitenāti ca “paccessaṃ na paccessa”nti evaṃ anadhiṭṭhitena, aniyamitenāti attho. Tatiyattikānantaraṃ catutthattikaṃ sambhavantaṃ antosīmāyaṃ “paccessa”nti vacanavisesena sambhavati. Tathā ca yojiyamānaṃ itarehi savanantikādīhi aviruddhaṃ hotīti catutthattikaṃ ahutvā chakkaṃ jātanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ tīṇi tikāni ekaṃ chakkañcāti paṭhamaṃ pannarasakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein is the explanation of the sections from the beginning: there are seven sections on ādāya, and likewise on samādāya, thus there are two seven-fold sections. Then, excluding the departure-limit, there are two six-fold sections based on ādāya and samādāya for an unfinished robe. After that, three triads are shown based on completion, non-completion, and the destruction-limit. Among these, the first triad, within the boundary, operates on the basis that 'one will not return' outside the boundary, without considering the rule 'one will return or one will not return.' Therefore, the departure-limit, boundary-crossing, and carrying-beyond-the-limit rules do not apply there. The second triad, within the boundary, operates on the basis that 'one will not return.' The third triad operates by specifying the term 'unestablished' (anadhiṭṭhita); in essence, it aligns with the first triad. 'Unestablished' means unestablished in this way, that is, undetermined, regarding 'one will return or one will not return.' After the third triad, a fourth triad, if it were to arise, would arise within the boundary by the specific statement 'one will return.' And when applied in this way, it would not conflict with the others, such as the hearing-limit and so forth. Thus, it should be understood that the fourth triad does not occur; instead, a six-fold section arises. In this way, three triads and one six-fold section are to be understood as the first fifteen-fold collection.

316-320. Tato idameva pannarasakaṃ upasaggavisesena dutiyaṃ samādāyapannarasakaṃ nāma kataṃ. Puna “vippakatacīvaraṃ ādāyā”ti tatiyaṃ pannarasakaṃ, “samādāyā”ti catutthaṃ pannarasakaṃ dassitanti evaṃ cattāri pannarasakāni veditabbāni. Tattha paṭhamadutiyesu pannarasakesu sabbena sabbaṃ akatacīvaraṃ adhippetaṃ, itaresu dvīsu vippakatanti veditabbaṃ. Tato paraṃ “cīvarāsāya pakkamatī”tiādinā nayena niṭṭhānasanniṭṭhānanāsanaāsāvacchedikavasena eko vāroti idamekaṃ catukkaṃ jātaṃ, tasmā pubbe vuttāni tikāni āsāvacchedikāni tīṇi ca tikānīti etaṃ anāsāyadvādasakanti veditabbaṃ. Tadanantare āsāyadvādasake kiñcāpi paṭhamaṃ dvādasakaṃ labbhati, tathāpi taṃ nibbisesanti tamekaṃ dvādasakaṃ avuttasiddhaṃ katvā visesato dassetuṃ ādito paṭṭhāya “antosīmāyaṃ paccessa”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ dutiyacatukke “so bahisīmagato suṇātī”tiādivacanassa tatiyacatukke savanantikādīnañca okāsakaraṇatthanti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ pana dvādasakaṃ anāsāyavasenapi labbhamānaṃ iminā avuttasiddhaṃ katvā na dassitanti veditabbaṃ. Evamettha dve dvādasakāni uddharitabbāni. Karaṇīyadvādasakepi yathādassitaṃ anāsāyadvādasakaṃ avuttasiddhaṃ āsāyadvādasakañcāti dve dvādasakāni uddharitabbāni.

316-320. Then, this very fifteen-fold collection was named the second 'samādāya fifteen-fold collection' due to the distinction of prefixes. Again, the third fifteen-fold collection is shown with 'taking an unfinished robe,' and the fourth fifteen-fold collection with 'taking up completely.' Thus, these four fifteen-fold collections should be understood. In the first and second fifteen-fold collections, an entirely unmade robe is intended; in the other two, it should be understood as unfinished. Thereafter, in the manner of 'he departs with expectation of a robe,' etc., one section is formed as a tetrad through the modes of completion, non-completion, destruction, and cutting off expectation. Therefore, the previously mentioned three triads and these three triads that cut off expectation are to be understood as the twelve-fold without expectation. In the subsequent twelve-fold with expectation, although the first twelve-fold is obtainable, yet to distinctly show that it is not different, that one twelve-fold is treated as understood without being stated, and from the beginning, it is said, 'one will return within the boundary.' That, in the second tetrad, is to be understood as providing the occasion for the statement 'he, having gone outside the boundary, hears,' etc., and in the third tetrad, for the hearing-limit and so forth. However, this twelve-fold, even though obtainable in the case without expectation, is not shown here, having treated it as understood without being stated. Thus, in this case, two twelve-fold sections should be derived. In the twelve-fold of duties as well, just as shown, the twelve-fold without expectation is understood without being stated, and so is the twelve-fold with expectation—thus, two twelve-fold sections should be derived.

321-322. Yasmā disaṃgamikanavake “disaṃgamiko pakkamatī”ti vacaneneva “na paccessa”nti idaṃ avuttasiddhameva, tasmā taṃ na vuttaṃ. Ettāvatā [M 3.0338] ca āvāsapalibodhābhāvo dassito. Cīvarapaṭivīsaṃ apavilāyamānoti iminā cīvarapalibodhasamaṅgitamassa dasseti. Tattha cīvarapaṭivīsanti attano pattabbacīvarabhāgaṃ. Apavilāyamānoti ākaṅkhamāno. Tassa cīvaralābhe sati vassaṃvutthāvāse niṭṭhānasanniṭṭhānanāsanantikānaṃ vasena ekaṃ tikaṃ, tesaṃyeva vasena antarāmagge ekaṃ, gataṭṭhāne ekanti tiṇṇaṃ tikānaṃ vasena ekaṃ navakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

321-322. Since in the nine-fold section concerning one who is going to a different region, the statement 'one who is going to a different region departs' itself implies 'one will not return,' this is already established without being stated; therefore, it was not stated. By this, the absence of the impediment of the residence is shown. By 'not relinquishing the claim to robes,' it shows his being endowed with the impediment of robes. There, 'claim to robes' means his share of robes that he is entitled to receive. 'Not relinquishing' means desiring. When he obtains robes, for one who has completed the rains residence, one triad is to be understood based on completion, non-completion, and the limit of disappearance from sight; one based on those same categories on the journey; and one at the destination: thus, a nine-fold section in terms of three triads.

324. Tato [V 3.0308] paraṃ niṭṭhānasanniṭṭhānanāsanantikasīmātikkantikasaubbhārānaṃ vasena phāsuvihārapañcakaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyameva.

324. Thereafter, the five-fold comfortable living is stated in terms of completion, non-completion, the limit of disappearance from sight, crossing the boundary, and carrying beyond. The rest here is easily understood from the Pāḷi text and the commentary.

Ādāyasattakādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Account Beginning with the Sevenfold Taking is concluded.

Kathinakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Kathina Chapter is concluded.

8. Cīvarakkhandhakaṃ

8. The Chapter on Robes

Jīvakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Jīvaka

329-330. Cīvarakkhandhake [M 3.0339][V 3.0309] kammavipākanti kammajarogaṃ. Saṃyamassāti ānisaṃsassa, upayogatthe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ.

329-330. In the Chapter on Robes, 'result of kamma' means a disease born of kamma. 'Of restraint' means 'of benefit'; this is a genitive case in the sense of application.

Pajjotarājavatthukathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of King Pajjota and Others

334-336. Vicchikassa jātoti tassa kira mātuyā utusamaye sayanagatāya vicchiko nābhippadesaṃ āruḷho, sā tassa samphassena gabbhaṃ gaṇhi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “vicchikassa jāto”ti. Ussannadosoti sañcitapittādidoso.

334-336. 'Born of a scorpion' means: it is said that when his mother was lying down during her season, a scorpion climbed onto her navel region, and she conceived through its touch. It is with reference to this that it is said, 'born of a scorpion'. 'With excessive humors' means with an accumulation of bile and other humors.

Varayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Requesting a Boon

337. Itarītarenāti itarena itarena. Itara-saddo pana aniyamavacano dvikkhattuṃ vuccamāno yaṃkiñci-saddehi samānattho hotīti vuttaṃ “appagghenapi mahagghenapi yena kenacī”ti. Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavanti hatthipiṭṭhīsu attharitabbatāya mahāpiṭṭhiyanti laddhasamaññaṃ caturaṅgulapupphaṃ kojavaṃ.

337. ‘Itarītarena’ means 'by one and another'. The word ‘itara’, however, is an indefinite term; when repeated twice, it is synonymous with words like ‘yaṃ kiñci’, as stated in 'whether of little or great value, by any means whatsoever'. ‘Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavaṃ’ means a fleece-blanket with a four-finger-breadth floral design, which is designated as ‘mahāpiṭṭhi’ because it is to be spread on elephants' backs.

Kambalānujānanādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Allowance of Blankets and So Forth

340. Upacāreti susānassa āsanne padese. Chaḍḍetvā gatāti kiñci avatvāyeva chaḍḍetvā gatā. So eva sāmīti akatāya katikāya yena gahitaṃ, sova sāmī.

340. ‘In the vicinity’ means in a place close to the charnel ground. ‘Having discarded it, they went’ means having discarded it, they went without saying anything. ‘He is the owner’ means that when no agreement has been made, whoever takes it is the owner.

Cīvarapaṭiggāhakasammutiādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Appointment of Robe-Receivers and So Forth

342-343. Dhuravihāraṭṭhāneti [V 3.0310] vihāradvārassa sammukhaṭṭhāne. Vihāramajjheyeva sammannitabbanti sabbesaṃ jānanatthāya vihāramajjheyeva nisinnehi sammannitabbaṃ. Tulābhūtoti tulāsadiso. Vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ katvāti sabbakoṭṭhāse agghato samake katvā. Tenevāha “same paṭivīse ṭhapetvā”ti. Idanti sāmaṇerānaṃ upaḍḍhapaṭivīsassa dānaṃ. Phātikammanti sammuñjanībandhanādihatthakammaṃ[M 3.0340]. Ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontīti mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Samapaṭivīso dātabboti karissāmāti yācantānaṃ paṭiññāmattenapi samakoṭṭhāso dātabbo.

342-343. ‘In the main monastery’ means in a place in front of the monastery gate. ‘It should be agreed upon in the middle of the monastery’ means it should be agreed upon by those seated in the middle of the monastery itself, for all to know. ‘Like a balance’ means similar to a balance. ‘Having made them of different qualities’ means having made all portions equal in value. Therefore, he said, 'having placed them in equal portions'. ‘This’ means the giving of half a portion to the novices. ‘Work for increase’ means handiwork such as tying brooms. ‘They make an outcry’ means they make a great noise. ‘An equal portion should be given’ means an equal portion should be given even on the mere promise of those asking, “Shall we do it?”.

Cīvararajanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Dyeing Robes

344. Rajanakumbhiyā majjhe ṭhapetvāti antorajanakumbhiyā majjhe ṭhapetvā evaṃ vaṭṭādhārake antorajanakumbhiyā pakkhitte majjhe udakaṃ tiṭṭhati, vaṭṭādhārakato bahi samantā antokumbhiyaṃ rajanacchalli. Rajanaṃ pakkhipitunti rajanacchalliṃ pakkhipituṃ.

344. ‘Having placed it in the middle of the dye pot’ means having placed it inside the dye pot, so that when the circular support is placed inside the dye pot, water remains in the middle, and the dye-bark is all around within the inner pot, outside of the circular support. ‘To put in the dye’ means to put in the dye-bark.

Ticīvarānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Allowance of the Three Robes

346. Uddhaste aruṇeti uggate aruṇasīse. Nandimukhiyāti tuṭṭhamukhiyā.

346. ‘When the dawn has arisen’ means when the head of the dawn has risen. ‘With a joyful face’ means with a delighted face.

Atirekacīvarādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Extra Robes and So Forth

348. Acchupeyyanti patiṭṭhapeyyaṃ. Hatavatthakānanti kālātītavatthānaṃ. Uddharitvā allīyāpanakhaṇḍanti dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ apanetvā allīyāpanavatthakhaṇḍaṃ.

348. ‘Acchupeyyaṃ’ means 'one should establish'. ‘Of ruined cloths’ means of cloths that are out of season. ‘Having removed a piece for patching’ means a piece of patching cloth, after having removed the weak spot.

Visākhāvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Visākhā

349-351. Visākhāvatthumhi kallakāyāti akilantakāyā pītisomanassehi phuṭasarīrā. Gatīti ñāṇagati ñāṇādhigamo. Abhisamparāyoti ñāṇābhisamparāyo ñāṇasahito peccabhāvo.

349-351. In the story of Visākhā, ‘with a healthy body’ means a body that is not weary, a body pervaded by joy and gladness. ‘Destiny’ means the course of knowledge, the attainment of knowledge. ‘Future state’ means the future course of knowledge, a future existence accompanied by knowledge.

Taṃ [V 3.0311] bhagavā byākarissatīti “so bhikkhu sotāpanno sakadāgāmī”tiādinā tassa taṃ ñāṇagatiṃ, tato paraṃ “niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karissatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1004) ñāṇābhisamparāyañca āvi karissati. Sovaggikanti saggasaṃvattanikaṃ. Sokaṃ nudati vinodetīti sokanudaṃ.

‘The Blessed One will declare it’ means that he will make manifest that monk's course of knowledge by saying, “That monk is a stream-enterer, a once-returner,” and so on; and furthermore, he will make manifest his future course of knowledge by saying, “He is certain, destined for enlightenment; having come to this world only once, he will make an end of suffering,” and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1004). ‘Conducive to a good destination’ means conducive to heaven. ‘It removes sorrow’ means it removes and dispels sorrow.

Nisīdanādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on Allowing Sitting Cloths and So Forth

353. Dukkhaṃ [M 3.0341] supatīti nānāvidhasupinaṃ passanto dukkhaṃ supati. Dukkhaṃ paṭibujjhatīti paṭibujjhantopi uttasitvā salomahaṃso dukkhaṃ paṭibujjhati.

353. ‘He sleeps miserably’ means that seeing various dreams, he sleeps miserably. ‘He wakes miserably’ means that even when waking, he wakes miserably, terrified, with his hair standing on end.

Pacchimavikappanupagacīvarādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on Robes and So Forth Not Subject to Subsequent Determination

359-362. Aṭṭhapadakacchannena pattamukhaṃ sibbitunti aṭṭhapadaphalakākārena pattamukhe tattha tattha gabbhaṃ dassetvā sibbituṃ. Aggaḷaguttiyeva pamāṇanti imehi catūhi nikkhepakāraṇehi ṭhapentenapi aggaḷaguttivihāreyeva ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo.

359–362. ‘To sew the opening of the bowl with an eight-paneled covering’ means to sew the opening of the bowl by showing depressions here and there in the shape of an eight-paneled board. ‘The Aggaḷagutti is the standard’ means that the intention is that even when depositing them for these four reasons for depositing, it is appropriate to deposit them in the Aggaḷagutti monastery itself.

Saṅghikacīvaruppādakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on the Arising of Robes for the Community

363. Pañca māseti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Vaḍḍhiṃ payojetvā ṭhapitaupanikkhepatoti vassāvāsikatthāya veyyāvaccakarehi vaḍḍhiṃ payojetvā ṭhapitaupanikkhepato.
