Tatruppādatoti nāḷikeraārāmāditatruppādato. “Vassāvāsikalābhavasena vā matakacīvaravasena vā tatruppādavasena vā aññena vā kenaci ākārena saṅghaṃ uddissa uppannacīvaraṃ, sabbaṃ tasseva atthatakathinassa pañca māse, anatthatakathinassa ekaṃ cīvaramāsaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti avisesato vatvāpi puna vassāvāsikalābhavasena uppanne labbhamānavisesaṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ pana ida”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha idhāti abhilāpamattametaṃ. “Vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa demā”ti vuttepi soyeva nayo. Anatthatakathinassapi pañca māse pāpuṇātīti vassāvāsikalābhavasena uppannattā anatthatakathinassapi vutthavassassa pañca māse pāpuṇāti. Kenaci pana “idha-saddena niyamitattā”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Tathā hi idha-saddena aniyametvāpi “vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa demā”ti vā “vassāvāsikaṃ demā”ti vā antohemante vassāvāsikalābhavasena dinnaṃ cīvaraṃ anatthatakathinassapi vutthavassassa pañca māse pāpuṇāti, teneva [V 3.0312] parato aṭṭhasu mātikāsu “vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa detī”ti imassa mātikāpadassa vinicchaye (mahāva. aṭṭha. 379) “cīvaramāsato paṭṭhāya yāva hemantassa pacchimo divaso, tāva vassāvāsikaṃ [M 3.0342] demāti vutte kathinaṃ atthataṃ vā hotu anatthataṃ vā, atītavassaṃvutthānameva pāpuṇātī”ti vuttaṃ. Tato paranti pañcamāsato paraṃ, gimhānassa paṭhamadivasato paṭṭhāyāti attho.

363. ‘Five months’ (pañca māse) is a term used in the sense of complete connection. ‘From what is deposited after applying interest’ (vaḍḍhiṃ payojetvā ṭhapitaupanikkhepato) means from what is deposited by the stewards after applying interest for the purpose of the rains-residence. ‘From what arises there’ (tatruppādato) means from what arises there, such as in a coconut grove. ‘Any robe-cloth that arises for the Saṅgha—whether on account of the gain of a rains-resident, or on account of the robes of a deceased monk, or on account of its arising in that place, or on account of any other reason—all of it accrues for five months to one for whom the Kathina has been spread, and for one robe-month to one for whom the Kathina has not been spread’—even though it was stated non-specifically, again to show the specific advantage obtainable on account of the gain of a rains-resident, the passage beginning ‘whatever this is’ (yaṃ pana idaṃ) was commenced. Here, ‘this’ (idha) is merely a term of speech. Even if it is said, ‘We give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence,’ the same principle applies. ‘Even for one for whom the Kathina has not been spread, it accrues for five months’ means that because it arises on account of the gain of a rains-resident, it accrues for five months even for one who has completed the rains-residence but for whom the Kathina has not been spread. But some have said that the reason is ‘because it is restricted by the word “this”’; that is not the reason. For even without restricting it by the word ‘this’ (idha), if it is said ‘We give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence’ or ‘We give for the rains-residence,’ robe-cloth given during the winter on account of the gain of a rains-resident accrues for five months even for one who has completed the rains-residence but for whom the Kathina has not been spread. Therefore, later, in the determination of the matrix phrase ‘he gives to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence’ in the eight matrices (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 379), it is said: ‘From the robe-month onwards until the last day of winter, if it is said, “We give for the rains-residence,” whether the Kathina has been spread or has not been spread, it accrues only to those who have completed the past rains-residence.’ ‘After that’ (tato paraṃ) means after the five months, meaning starting from the first day of summer.

“Kasmā? Piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā”ti idaṃ “udāhu anāgatavasse”ti imassānantaraṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gimhānassa paṭhamadivasato paṭṭhāya uppannameva hi piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā “kiṃ atītavasse idaṃ vassāvāsika”ntiādinā pucchitabbaṃ, teneva paratopi vakkhati “gimhānaṃ paṭhamadivasato paṭṭhāya vutte pana mātikā āropetabbā ‘atītavassāvāsassa pañca māsā atikkantā, anāgato cātumāsaccayena bhavissati, kataravassāvāsassa desī’ti. Sace ‘atītavassaṃvutthānaṃ dammī’ti vadati, taṃantovassaṃvutthānameva pāpuṇātī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 379). Potthakesu pana “anatthatakathinassapi pañca māse pāpuṇātī”ti imassānantaraṃ “kasmā? Piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā”ti idaṃ likhanti, taṃ na yujjati. Na hi piṭṭhisamaye uppannaṃ sandhāya “anatthatakathinassapi pañca māse pāpuṇātī”ti vuttaṃ, na ca piṭṭhisamaye uppannaṃ vutthavassasseva pāpuṇāti, sammukhībhūtānaṃ sabbesaṃ pāpuṇāti, teneva parato vakkhati “asukavihāre vassaṃvutthasaṅghassāti vadati, tatra vassaṃvutthānameva yāva kathinassubbhārā pāpuṇāti. Sace pana gimhānaṃ paṭhamadivasato paṭṭhāya evaṃ vadati, tatra sammukhībhūtānaṃ sabbesaṃ pāpuṇāti. Kasmā? Piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 379).

‘Why? Because it arises in the subsequent period’ (kasmā? piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā)—this should be understood as immediately following ‘or in the coming rains-residence.’ For indeed, what arises from the first day of summer onwards arises in the subsequent period, so one should ask, ‘Is this for the past rains-residence?’ and so on. Therefore, it will also be said later: ‘But if it is said from the first day of summer onwards, then the matrix should be applied: “Five months have passed for the past rains-residence, and the future one will be after four months. For which rains-residence do you give it?” If he says, “I give it to those who have completed the past rains-residence,” then it accrues only to those who resided within that rains-residence.’ (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 379). In the books, however, they write ‘Why? Because it arises in the subsequent period’ immediately after ‘Even for one for whom the Kathina has not been spread, it accrues for five months.’ This is not correct. For it was not said with reference to what arises in the subsequent period that ‘even for one for whom the Kathina has not been spread, it accrues for five months.’ Nor does what arises in the subsequent period accrue only to those who have completed the rains-residence; it accrues to all who are present. Therefore, it will be said later: ‘If one says, “For the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence in such-and-such monastery,” then it accrues only to those who have completed the rains-residence up to the time of the removal of the Kathina. But if one says so from the first day of summer onwards, then it accrues to all who are present. Why? Because it arises in the subsequent period.’ (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 379).

Ṭhitikā pana na tiṭṭhatīti ettha aṭṭhitāya ṭhitikāya puna aññasmiṃ cīvare uppanne sace eko bhikkhu āgacchati, majjhe chinditvā dvīhipi gahetabbaṃ. Ṭhitāya pana ṭhitikāya puna aññasmiṃ cīvare uppanne sace navakataro āgacchati, ṭhitikā heṭṭhā gacchati. Sace vuḍḍhataro āgacchati, ṭhitikā uddhamārohati. Atha añño natthi, puna attano pāpetvā gahetabbaṃ. Duggahitāni hontīti ettha saṅghikāneva hontīti adhippāyo. Gahitameva nāmāti “imassa idaṃ patta”nti kiñcāpi na viditaṃ, te pana bhāgā atthato tesaṃ pattāyevāti adhippāyo. Itovāti therānaṃ dātabbatoyeva.

‘However, a fixed share does not remain’ (ṭhitikā pana na tiṭṭhati)—here, if a share is not yet fixed and another robe-cloth arises, and one bhikkhu arrives, it should be divided in the middle and taken by both. But if a share is already fixed and another robe-cloth arises, if a more junior monk arrives, the fixed share is adjusted downwards. If a more senior monk arrives, the fixed share is adjusted upwards. If there is no one else, one should re-acquire one's own share. ‘They are improperly taken’ (duggahitāni honti)—here, the meaning is that they are only Saṅgha property. ‘It is considered as taken’ (gahitameva nāma)—the meaning is that even if it is not known that ‘this belongs to this one,’ those shares have in effect already reached them. ‘From here’ (ito) means it should be given only to the senior monks.

Saṅghikacīvaruppādakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Account on the Arising of Robes for the Saṅgha is concluded.

Upanandasakyaputtavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story Concerning Upananda the Sakyan Son.

364. Sattāhavārena [M 3.0343][V 3.0313] aruṇameva uṭṭhāpetīti etaṃ vacanamattameva ekasmiṃ vihāre sattāhakiccābhāvato. Idanti ekādhippāyadānaṃ. Nānālābhehītiādīsu nānā visuṃ visuṃ lābho etesūti nānālābhā, dve vihārā, tehi nānālābhehi. Nānā visuṃ visuṃ pākārādīhi paricchinno upacāro etesanti nānūpacārā, tehi nānūpacārehi. Ekasīmavihārehīti ekūpacārasīmāyaṃ dvīhi vihārehi.

364. The phrase ‘he makes the dawn rise for a week’ is merely a statement, since there is no seven-day duty in a single monastery. ‘This’ (idaṃ) means a gift with a single intention. In phrases like ‘with various gains’ (nānālābhehi), ‘various’ means separate and distinct gains—these are various gains, referring to two monasteries, with those various gains. ‘With various precincts’ (nānūpacārehi) means that the precinct is defined by separate and distinct walls and so on—these are various precincts, with those various precincts. ‘From monasteries within a single boundary’ (ekasīmavihārehi) means from two monasteries within a single boundary-precinct.

Gilānavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story Concerning the Sick.

365. Palipannoti nimuggo, makkhitoti attho. Uccāretvāti ukkhipitvā. Samānācariyakoti ettha sacepi ekassa ācariyassa eko antevāsiko hoti, eko saddhivihāriko, etepi aññamaññaṃ samānācariyakā evāti vadanti.

365. ‘Palipanna’ means submerged; the meaning is ‘smeared.’ ‘Uccāretvā’ means having lifted up. Regarding ‘samānācariyako’ (having the same teacher): here, they say that even if one teacher has one resident pupil and one co-resident pupil, these are also ‘samānācariyaka’ in relation to each other.

366. Bhesajjaṃ yojetuṃ asamattho hotīti vejjena “idañcidañca bhesajjaṃ gahetvā iminā yojetvā dātabba”nti vutte tathā kātuṃ asamatthoti attho. Nīhātunti nīharituṃ, chaḍḍetunti attho.

366. ‘He is unable to prepare the medicine’ (bhesajjaṃ yojetuṃ asamattho hoti) means that when a physician says, ‘Take this and that medicine, prepare it in this way, and give it,’ he is unable to do so. ‘Nīhātuṃ’ means to remove, the meaning being ‘to discard.’

Matasantakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story Concerning the Property of the Deceased.

367-369. Bhikkhussa kālakateti ettha kālakata-saddo bhāvasādhanoti āha “kālakiriyāyā”ti. Tattha tattha saṅghassāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vihāre saṅghassa.

367-369. Regarding ‘bhikkhussa kālakate’ (when a bhikkhu has died): here, the word ‘kālakata’ is a verbal noun, hence it is said, ‘by the act of dying’ (kālakiriyāya). ‘To the Saṅgha here and there’ (tattha tattha saṅghassa) means to the Saṅgha in that particular monastery.

Saṅghe bhinne cīvaruppādakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story Concerning the Arising of Robes When the Saṅgha is in Schism.

376. Yattha pana dakkhiṇodakaṃ pamāṇanti bhikkhū yasmiṃ raṭṭhe dakkhiṇodakapaaggahaṇamattenapi deyyadhammassa sāmino hontīti adhippāyo. Parasamuddeti jambudīpe.

376. ‘Where the water of dedication is the authority’ (yattha pana dakkhiṇodakaṃ pamāṇaṃ): the meaning is that in whatever country monks become owners of an offering merely by the acceptance of the water of dedication. ‘Beyond the ocean’ (parasamudde) means in Jambudīpa.

378. Matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātīti ettha maggaṃ gacchanto tassa kālakiriyaṃ sutvā avihāraṭṭhāne [V 3.0314] ce dvādasaratanabbhantare aññesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abhāvaṃ ñatvā “idaṃ cīvaraṃ mayhaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti adhiṭṭhāti, svādhiṭṭhitaṃ.

378. ‘He determines a robe of a deceased monk’ (matakacīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti): here, while traveling on a road, upon hearing of that one's death, if he knows there are no other bhikkhus within twelve cubits in a place that is not a monastery, he determines, ‘This robe accrues to me.’ It is validly determined.

Aṭṭhacīvaramātikākathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Story of the Matrix of Eight Robes.

379. Puggalādhiṭṭhānanayena [M 3.0344] vuttanti “sīmāyadāna”ntiādinā vattabbe “sīmāya detī”tiādi puggalādhiṭṭhānanayena vuttaṃ. Parikkhepārahaṭṭhānena paricchinnāti iminā aparikkhittassa vihārassa dhuvasannipātaṭṭhānādito paṭhamaleḍḍupātassa anto upacārasīmāti dasseti. Idāni dutiyaleḍḍupātassa antopi upacārasīmāyevāti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Dhuvasannipātaṭṭhānampi pariyantagatameva gahetabbaṃ. Bhikkhunīnaṃ ārāmappavesanasenāsanāpucchanādi parivāsamānattārocanavassacchedanissayasenāsanaggāhādi vidhānanti idaṃ sabbaṃ imissāyeva upacārasīmāya vasena veditabbaṃ. Lābhatthāya ṭhapitasīmā lābhasīmā. Samānasaṃvāsaavippavāsasīmāsu dinnassa idaṃ nānattaṃ – “avippavāsasīmāya dammī”ti dinnaṃ gāmaṭṭhānaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Kasmā? “Ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcā”ti vuttattā. “Samānasaṃvāsakasīmāya dammī”ti dinnaṃ pana gāme ṭhitānampi pāpuṇātīti.

379. It is stated in terms of the person as the basis: when it should be said, 'the giving of a boundary,' and so on, the statement 'he gives to the boundary,' and so on, is made in terms of the person as the basis. By 'delimited by a place suitable for an enclosure,' it is shown that for an unenclosed monastery, the area within the first clod-throw from the permanent assembly place and so on is the proximity boundary. Now, to show that the area within the second clod-throw is also the proximity boundary, the passage beginning 'furthermore' is introduced. The permanent assembly place should also be taken as having a definite limit. The procedures for nuns—entering a monastery, asking for lodging, reporting probation and mānatta, interrupting the rains-residence, seeking dependence, accepting lodging, and so on—all this should be understood by way of this very proximity boundary. A boundary established for the sake of gain is a gain-boundary. For what is given within the boundaries of common communion and non-separation, this is the difference: what is given with the words, 'I give for the non-separation boundary,' does not reach the village site. Why? Because it is said, 'excluding the village and the village precincts.' But what is given with the words, 'I give for the common communion boundary,' reaches even those standing in the village.

Buddhādhivutthoti buddhena bhagavatā adhivuttho. Ekasminti ekasmiṃ vihāre. Pākavaṭṭanti dānavaṭṭaṃ. Vattatīti pavattati. Paṃsukūlikānampi vaṭṭatīti “tuyhaṃ demā”ti avatvā “bhikkhūnaṃ dema, therānaṃ demā”ti vuttattā paṃsukūlikānaṃ vaṭṭati. Vicāritamevāti upāhanatthavikādīnamatthāya vicāritameva.

'Inhabited by the Buddha' means inhabited by the Buddha, the Blessed One. 'In one' means in one monastery. 'A regular supply' means a cycle of giving. 'It is allowable' means it proceeds. 'It is allowable even for rag-robe wearers' means: because it is said, 'We give to the monks, we give to the elders,' without saying, 'We give to you,' it is allowable for rag-robe wearers. 'It is only administered' means it is only administered for the purpose of a bag for shoes, and so on.

Upaḍḍhaṃ dātabbanti yaṃ ubhatosaṅghassa dinnaṃ, tato upaḍḍhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, upaḍḍhaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ dātabbaṃ. Sacepi eko bhikkhu hoti ekā vā bhikkhunī, antamaso anupasampannassapi upaḍḍhameva dātabbaṃ. “Bhikkhusaṅghassa ca bhikkhunīnañca tuyhañcā”ti vutte pana puggalo visuṃ na labhatīti idaṃ aṭṭhakathāpamāṇeneva gahetabbaṃ. Na hettha visesakāraṇaṃ upalabbhati. Tathā hi “ubhatosaṅghassa ca tuyhañca dammī”ti vutte sāmaññavisesavacanehi saṅgahitattā yathā puggalo visuṃ labhati, evamidhāpi “bhikkhusaṅghassa ca tuyhañcā”ti sāmaññavisesavacanasabbhāvato bhavitabbameva visuṃ puggalapaṭivīsenāti viññāyati, tasmā aṭṭhakathāvacanamevettha pamāṇaṃ. Pāpuṇanaṭṭhānato ekameva labhatīti attano vassaggena pattaṭṭhānato ekameva [M 3.0345] koṭṭhāsaṃ labhati. Tattha kāraṇamāha “kasmā? Bhikkhusaṅghaggahaṇena gahitattā”ti, bhikkhusaṅghaggahaṇeneva puggalassapi gahitattāti [V 3.0315] adhippāyo. Bhikkhusaṅghassa harāti vuttepi haritabbanti īdisaṃ gihiveyyāvaccaṃ na hotīti katvā vuttaṃ.

'Half should be given' means that of what is given to the dual Saṅgha, half should be given to the monks and half to the nuns. Even if there is only one monk or one nun, or even one who is not fully ordained, half should still be given. However, when it is said, 'To the Saṅgha of monks and to the nuns and to you,' the individual does not receive a separate share—this should be taken on the authority of the commentary alone. No specific reason is found for this. For, when it is said, 'I give to the dual Saṅgha and to you,' just as the individual receives a separate share because they are included by both general and specific terms, so too here, in the phrase 'to the Saṅgha of monks and to you,' it would seem that there should be a separate individual portion due to the presence of general and specific terms. Therefore, the statement of the commentary is the sole authority here. 'From the position of attainment, one receives only one' means that from the position one has attained by seniority, one receives only one share. Therein, he states the reason: 'Why? Because one is included by the mention of the Saṅgha of monks.' The meaning is that the individual is also included by the very mention of the Saṅgha of monks. Even when it is said, 'He takes for the Saṅgha of monks,' this is stated on the grounds that this is not a service performed by a layperson, where one would say 'it should be taken'.

Lakkhaṇaññū vadantīti idaṃ sanniṭṭhānavacanaṃ, aṭṭhakathāsu anāgatattā pana evaṃ vuttaṃ. Bahiupacārasīmāyaṃ…pe… sabbesaṃ pāpuṇātīti yattha katthaci vutthavassānaṃ sabbesaṃ pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. akālacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “sace pana bahiupacārasīmāyaṃ ṭhito ‘vassaṃvutthasaṅghassā’ti vadati, yattha katthaci vutthavassānaṃ sabbesaṃ sampattānaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti vuttaṃ. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana “vassāvāsassa ananurūpe padese ṭhatvā vuttattā vassaṃvutthānaṃ avutthānañca sabbesaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi “vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa dammī”ti vutte avutthavassānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Evaṃ vadatīti “vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa dammī”ti vadati. Uddesaṃ gahetuṃ āgatoti tassa santike uddesaṃ agahitapubbassapi uddesaṃ gaṇhissāmīti āgatakālato paṭṭhāya antevāsikabhāvūpagamanato vuttaṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

'Those who know the characteristics speak'—this is a concluding statement. However, since it is not found in the commentaries, it is stated thus. 'Outside the proximity boundary… it reaches all' means it reaches all those who have completed the rains-residence, wherever they may be—this is the intention. For this reason, it is also said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, commentary on the training rule on robes out of season): 'But if, standing outside the proximity boundary, one says, "For the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence," it reaches all who have completed the rains-residence and are present, wherever they may be.' In the Gaṇṭhipadas, however, it is said: 'Because it is said while standing in a place unsuitable for the rains-residence, it reaches all, both those who have and those who have not completed the rains-residence.' That should not be accepted. For when it is said, 'I give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence,' it does not reach those who have not completed the rains-residence. 'One speaks thus' means one says, 'I give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-residence.' 'He has come to receive instruction' means this is said from the time of his arrival with the intention, 'I will receive instruction,' even if he has not previously received instruction from him, because he has become a resident pupil. The rest here is easily understood.

Aṭṭhacīvaramātikākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on the Matrix of the Eight Robes is concluded.

Cīvarakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Robes is concluded.

9. Campeyyakkhandhakaṃ

9. The Campeyya Chapter

Kassapagottabhikkhuvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Story of the Monk of the Kassapa Clan

380. Campeyyakkhandhake [M 3.0346][V 3.0316] campāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tassa hi nagarassa ārāmapokkharaṇīādīsu tesu tesu ṭhānesu campakarukkhāva ussannā ahesuṃ, tasmā “campā”ti saṅkhaṃ agamāsi. Gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīreti tassa campānagarassa avidūre gaggarāya nāma rājamahesiyā khaṇitattā “gaggarā”ti laddhavohārā pokkharaṇī atthi, tassā tīre samantato nīlādipañcavaṇṇakusumapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ mahantaṃ campakavanaṃ, tasmiṃ bhagavā kusumagandhasugandhe campakavane viharati. Taṃ sandhāya “gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre”ti vuttaṃ. Tantibaddhoti tanti vuccati byāpāro, tattha baddho pasuto ussukkaṃ āpannoti attho, tasmiṃ āvāse akataṃ senāsanaṃ karoti, jiṇṇaṃ paṭisaṅkharoti, kate issaro hotīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “tasmiṃ āvāse kattabbattā tantipaṭibaddho”ti, kattabbakamme ussāhamāpannoti attho.

380. In the Campeyya Chapter: in the city named Campā. Indeed, in that city, in various places such as parks and ponds, campaka trees were abundant; therefore, it came to be known as 'Campā.' On the bank of the Gaggarā Pond: not far from that city of Campā, there is a pond known as 'Gaggarā' because it was dug by a royal queen named Gaggarā. On its bank is a large campaka grove, adorned all around with flowers of five colours, such as blue. The Blessed One dwells in that campaka grove, fragrant with the scent of blossoms. With reference to this, it is said, 'on the bank of the Gaggarā Pond.' Bound to duty: 'tanti' is called occupation; 'bound' thereto means devoted, diligent, zealous. The intention is that in that dwelling, he builds lodging that has not been built, repairs what is dilapidated, and is in charge of what has been built. Therefore, he says, 'Bound to duty because of what is to be done in that dwelling,' meaning he is zealous in the work to be done.

Ñattivipannakammādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Formal Acts with Defective Motions, and so on.

385-387. Paṭikkosantesūti nivārentesu. Hāpanaṃ vā aññathā karaṇaṃ vā natthīti ñattikammassa ekāya eva ñattiyā kattabbattā tato hāpanaṃ na sambhavati, anussāvanāya abhāvato pacchā ñattiṭhapanavasena dvīhi ñattīhi karaṇavasena ca aññathā karaṇaṃ natthi.

385-387. When they are objecting means when they are preventing. There is no removal or alteration: because a formal act by motion is to be done with a single motion, removal from it is not possible. Due to the absence of a proclamation, there is no alteration by way of setting aside the motion afterwards and performing it with two motions.

Catuvaggakaraṇādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Forming a Group of Four, and so on.

389. Ukkhepanīyakammakato kammanānāsaṃvāsako, ukkhittānuvattako laddhinānāsaṃvāsako.

389. One on whom an act of suspension has been performed is of different communion with regard to formal acts; a follower of one who has been suspended is of different communion with regard to view.

Dvenissāraṇādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Two Expulsions, and so on.

395. Appatto [V 3.0317] nissāraṇanti ettha nissāraṇakammaṃ nāma kuladūsakānaññeva anuññātaṃ, ayañca “bālo hoti abyatto”tiādinā niddiṭṭho kuladūsako na hoti, tasmā “appatto”ti vutto[M 3.0347]. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sunissārito hotīti? Bālaabyattatādiyuttassapi kammakkhandhake “ākaṅkhamāno saṅgho pabbājanīyakammaṃ kareyyā”ti (cūḷava. 27) vuttattā. Tenevāha “tañcesa…pe… tasmā sunissārito hotī”ti. Tattha tanti pabbājanīyakammaṃ. Esoti “bālo”tiādinā niddiṭṭho. Āveṇikena lakkhaṇenāti pabbājanīyakammassa āveṇikabhūtena kuladūsakabhāvalakkhaṇena.

395. Not liable for expulsion: here, the formal act of expulsion is permitted only for corrupters of families. And this one, indicated as 'foolish and incompetent,' and so on, is not a corrupter of families; therefore, he is said to be 'not liable.' If so, how is he 'well expelled'? Because in the Chapter on Formal Acts it is said, 'If it wishes, the Saṅgha may perform an act of banishment' (Cūḷavagga 27), even for one endowed with foolishness, incompetence, and so on. Therefore, it says, 'And if that one… therefore, he is well expelled.' Therein, the procedure is the act of banishment. 'That one' is the one indicated as 'foolish,' and so on. 'By its specific characteristic' means by the characteristic of being a corrupter of families, which is the specific characteristic of the act of banishment.

Tañce saṅgho nissāreti, sunissāritoti ettha adhippetassa pabbājanīyakammassa vasena atthaṃ dassetvā idāni yadi “tañce saṅgho nissāretī”ti tajjanīyādikammavasena nissāraṇā adhippetā, tadā nissāraṇaṃ sampattoyeva tajjanīyādivasena sunissāritoti byatirekamukhena atthaṃ dassetuṃ puna “tañce saṅgho nissāretī”ti ulliṅgetvā attho kathito. Natthi etassa apadānaṃ avakhaṇḍanaṃ āpattipariyantoti anapadāno. Ekekenapi aṅgena nissāraṇā anuññātāti kammakkhandhake anuññātā. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyameva.

Regarding 'If the Sangha expels him, he is well-expelled': Here, having shown the meaning with respect to the intended act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma), now, if by 'If the Sangha expels him' an expulsion by means of an act of censure (tajjanīya) and so forth is intended, then he has indeed attained expulsion by means of censure and so forth, and he is well-expelled. Thus, in order to show the meaning through the method of contrast, the meaning is explained by again highlighting 'If the Sangha expels him.' Regarding anapadāno: there is no instance, no breaking down, up to the limit of the offense. Expulsion is permitted even by a single factor—it is permitted in the Section on Formal Acts (Kammakkhandhaka). The rest here is easily understood from the Pāli text and the commentary.

Dvenissāraṇādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Two Expulsions and So Forth is concluded.

Campeyyakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Campeyya Section is concluded.

10. Kosambakakkhandhakaṃ

10. The Kosambi Section

Kosambakavivādakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Dispute at Kosambi

451. Kosambakakkhandhake [M 3.0348][V 3.0318] sace hoti, desessāmīti subbacatāya sikkhākāmatāya ca āpattiṃ passi. Natthi āpattīti anāpattipakkhopi ettha sambhavatīti adhippāyenāha. Sā panāpatti eva. Tenāha “so tassā āpattiyā anāpattidiṭṭhi ahosī”ti.

451. In the Kosambi Section, thinking, 'If there is an offense, I will confess it,' he saw an offense due to his docility and desire for training. He said, 'There is no offense,' with the intention that the position of 'no offense' is also possible here. But that was indeed an offense. Therefore, it is said, 'He held the view of no offense regarding that offense.'

453-454. Sambhamaatthavasenāti turitatthavasena. “Akāraṇe tumhehi so bhikkhu ukkhitto”ti vadeyyāti yasmā pubbe vinayadharassa vacanena “sace āpatti hoti, desessāmī”ti anena paṭiññātaṃ, idānipi tasseva vacanena “asañcicca assatiyā katattā natthettha āpattī”ti anāpattisaññī, tasmā “akāraṇe tumhehi so bhikkhu ukkhitto”ti ukkhepake bhikkhū yadi vadeyyāti adhippāyo. Ukkhittānuvattake vā “tumhe āpattiṃ āpannā”ti vadeyyāti yasmā vatthujānanacittenāyaṃ sacittakā āpatti, ayañca udakāvasese udakāvasesasaññī, tasmā sāpattikasseva “tumhe chandāgatiṃ gacchathā”ti adhippāyena “tumhe āpattiṃ āpannā”ti ukkhittānuvattake vadeyya.

453-454. By way of the meaning of flurry means by way of the meaning of haste. 'He might say, “You have suspended that monk without cause”'—the meaning is this: because it was previously promised by this statement of the Vinaya expert, 'If there is an offense, I will confess it,' and now also, by his statement, 'Since it was done unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense here,' he perceives no offense; therefore, if he were to say to the monks who suspended him, 'You have suspended that monk without cause.' Or, 'He might say to the followers of the suspended monk, “You have committed an offense”'—because this offense is intentional, with a mind that knows the matter, and this monk perceives the remaining water as remaining water; therefore, with the intention that the one who is at fault is 'following a wrong course through desire,' he would say to the followers of the suspended monk, 'You have committed an offense.'

455-456. Kammaṃ kopetīti “nānāsaṃvāsakacatuttho ce, bhikkhave, kammaṃ kareyya, akammaṃ na ca karaṇīya”ntiādivacanato (mahāva. 389) sace saṅgho taṃ gaṇapūrakaṃ katvā kammaṃ kareyya, ayaṃ tattha nisinnopi taṃ kammaṃ kopetīti adhippāyo. Upacāraṃ muñcitvāti ettha upacāro nāma aññamaññaṃ hatthena pāpuṇanaṭṭhānaṃ.

455-456. He invalidates the formal act—the meaning is this: from the statement, 'If, monks, a fourth who is of a different communion were to perform a formal act, it is a non-act and should not be done' (Mahāvagga), if the Sangha were to perform a formal act having made him the quorum-filler, this one, even while sitting there, invalidates that formal act. Having left the vicinity—here, 'vicinity' means a place within mutual hand's reach.

457. Bhaṇḍanajātātiādīsu kalahassa pubbabhāgo bhaṇḍanaṃ nāma, taṃ jātaṃ etesanti bhaṇḍanajātā, hatthaparāmāsādivasena matthakaṃ patto kalaho jāto etesanti kalahajātā, viruddhavādabhūtaṃ vādaṃ āpannāti vivādāpannā. Mukhasattīhīti vācāsattīhi. Vitudantāti vijjhantā[M 3.0349]. [V 3.0319] Bhagavantaṃ etadavocāti “idha, bhante, kosambiyaṃ bhikkhū bhaṇḍanajātā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca, tañca kho neva piyakamyatāya, na bhedādhippāyena, atha kho atthakāmatāya hitakāmatāya. Sāmaggīkārako kiresa bhikkhu, tasmāssa etadahosi “yathā ime bhikkhū vivādaṃ āraddhā, na sakkā mayā, nāpi aññena bhikkhunā samagge kātuṃ, appeva nāma sadevake loke aggapuggalo bhagavā sayaṃ vā gantvā attano vā santikaṃ pakkosāpetvā etesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khantimettāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ sāraṇīyadhammadesanaṃ kathetvā sāmaggiṃ kareyyā”ti atthakāmatāya hitakāmatāya gantvā avoca. Tasmā evamāhāti atthakāmattā evamāha, na bhagavato vacanaṃ anādiyanto. Ye pana tadā satthu vacanaṃ na gaṇhiṃsu, te kiñci avatvā tuṇhībhūtā maṅkubhūtā aṭṭhaṃsu, tasmā ubhayesampi satthari agāravapaṭipatti nāhosi.

457. In 'having become quarrelsome,' and so on: the preliminary stage of a conflict is called a 'quarrel' (bhaṇḍana). Those in whom this has arisen are 'quarrelsome' (bhaṇḍanajātā). A conflict that has reached its peak through physical contact such as grasping hands is a 'conflict' (kalaha). Those in whom this has arisen are 'given to conflict' (kalahajātā). Those who have entered into a state of contradictory speech are 'engaging in disputes' (vivādāpannā). 'With mouth-spears' means with word-spears. 'Piercing one another' means striking. 'He told this to the Blessed One' means he spoke the words, 'Here, venerable sir, the monks at Kosambi have become quarrelsome,' and so on. And this was spoken not out of a desire to be agreeable, nor with the intention to cause a schism, but rather out of a desire for their welfare and benefit. It seems this monk was a reconciler. Therefore, it occurred to him: 'The way these monks have started a dispute, it is not possible for me, nor for any other monk, to reconcile them. May the Blessed One, the supreme person in the world with its gods, either go himself or summon them to his presence, and after delivering a discourse on the qualities of cordiality connected with patience and loving-kindness, bring about harmony for these monks.' Out of a desire for their welfare and benefit, he went and spoke. Therefore, he spoke thus because he desired their welfare, not because he was disregarding the Blessed One's word. But those who at that time did not accept the Teacher's word stood silent and dismayed, without saying anything. Thus, on the part of both, there was no conduct of disrespect towards the Teacher.

Kosambakavivādakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Discourse of the Dispute at Kosambi is concluded.

Dīghāvuvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Story of Dīghāvu

458. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesītiādīsu bhūtapubbanti idaṃ bhagavā pathavīgataṃ nidhiṃ uddharitvā purato rāsiṃ karonto viya bhavapaṭicchannaṃ purāvutthaṃ dassento āha. Aḍḍhoti issaro. Yo koci attano santakena vibhavena aḍḍho hoti, ayaṃ pana na kevalaṃ aḍḍhoyeva, mahaddhano mahatā aparimāṇasaṅkhena dhanena samannāgatoti āha “mahaddhano”ti. Bhuñjitabbato paribhuñjitabbato visesato kāmā bhogā nāma, tasmā pañcakāmaguṇavasena mahantā uḷārā bhogā assāti mahābhogo. Mahantaṃ senābalañceva thāmabalañca etassāti mahabbalo. Mahanto hatthiassādivāhano etassāti mahāvāhano. Mahantaṃ vijitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ etassāti mahāvijito. Paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāroti koso vuccati bhaṇḍāgārasāragabbho, koṭṭhaṃ vuccati dhaññassa āṭhapanaṭṭhānaṃ, koṭṭhabhūtaṃ agāraṃ koṭṭhāgāraṃ, nidahitvā ṭhapitena dhanena paripuṇṇakoso dhaññānañca paripuṇṇakoṭṭhāgāroti attho.

458. In 'Then the Blessed One addressed the monks,' and so on: the Blessed One said, 'Once upon a time,' showing what was formerly lived, concealed by existence, as if he were unearthing a treasure buried in the earth and making a heap of it before them. 'Wealthy' (aḍḍho) means a master. Anyone who is wealthy with their own possessions is wealthy. But this one is not merely wealthy; he is said to be 'greatly wealthy' (mahaddhano) because he is endowed with great, immeasurably numerous riches. Sensual pleasures are specifically called 'possessions' (bhogā) because they are to be enjoyed and consumed; therefore, he has great and sublime possessions by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure, thus he is one of 'great possessions' (mahābhogo). He has great strength of army and great physical strength, thus he is one of 'great strength' (mahabbalo). He has great mounts such as elephants and horses, thus he is one of 'great mounts' (mahāvāhano). He has a great conquered kingdom, thus he is one of 'great conquest' (mahāvijito). 'With full treasuries and granaries': 'treasury' (koso) is said to be the inner chamber of a storehouse; 'store' (koṭṭha) is said to be the place for depositing grain; a building that is a store is a 'granary' (koṭṭhāgāra). The meaning is that his treasury is full of deposited wealth and his granaries are full of grain.

Atha [M 3.0350] vā catubbidho koso hatthī assā rathā pattīti. Yathā hi asino tikkhabhāvaparipālako paricchado “koso”ti vuccati, evaṃ rañño tikkhabhāvaparipālakattā caturaṅginī senā “koso”ti vuccati. Tividhaṃ koṭṭhāgāraṃ dhanakoṭṭhāgāraṃ dhaññakoṭṭhāgāraṃ vatthakoṭṭhāgāranti. Taṃ sabbampi paripuṇṇamassāti paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro. Caturaṅginiṃ senanti hatthiassarathapattisaṅkhātehi [V 3.0320] catūhi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ senaṃ. Sannayhitvāti cammapaṭimuñcanādīhi sannāhaṃ kāretvā. Abbhuyyāsīti abhiuyyāsi, abhimukho hutvā nikkhamīti attho. Ekasaṅghātampīti ekappahārampi. Dhovananti dhovanudakaṃ. Parinetvāti nīharitvā. “Anatthado”ti vattabbe da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā “anatthato”ti vuttanti āha “atha vā”tiādi.

Alternatively, the 'treasury' (koso) is fourfold: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. For just as the sheath that protects the sharpness of a sword is called a 'sheath' (koso), so the fourfold army is called a 'treasury' because it protects the king's majesty. The 'granary' (koṭṭhāgāra) is threefold: the treasury for wealth, the granary for grain, and the storehouse for cloth. All of that is full for him, thus he is one 'with full treasuries and granaries.' 'Fourfold army' means an army endowed with the four divisions, namely, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. 'Having armed' means having had them put on armor, such as by fastening leather pieces. 'He marched forth' means he went against; the meaning is he went out to face them. 'Not even a single clash' means not even a single blow. 'Washing' means water for washing. 'Having led away' means having taken away. When anatthado should be said, the letter 'da' is changed to 'ta', and so anatthato is said; this is explained by the phrase 'or alternatively,' and so on.

464. Vaggabhāvena vā puthu nānā saddo assāti puthusaddo. Samajanoti bhaṇḍane samajjhāsayo jano. Tatthāti tasmiṃ janakāye. Ahaṃ bāloti na maññitthāti bālalakkhaṇe ṭhitopi “ahaṃ bālo”ti na maññi. Bhiyyo cāti attano bālabhāvassa ajānanato bhiyyo ca bhaṇḍanassa upariphoṭo viya saṅghabhedassa attano kāraṇabhāvampi uppajjamānaṃ na maññittha nāññāsi.

464. Or, because of being in a group, its sound is great, thus it is a 'great sound' (puthusaddo). Or, its sound is separate and various, thus it is a 'separate sound' (puthusaddo). 'An assembly of people' (samajano) means people with a shared intention for quarreling. 'There' (tattha) means in that group of people. 'He did not think, “I am a fool”' means that even while established in the characteristics of a fool, he did not think, 'I am a fool.' 'And further' (bhiyyo ca): due to not knowing his own foolish state, he did not consider, nor did he understand, that his own state as the cause for the schism of the Sangha—like a further bursting open of the quarrel—was arising.

Kalahavasena pavattavācāyeva gocarā etesanti vācāgocarā. Mukhāyāmanti vivadanavasena mukhaṃ āyāmetvā bhāṇino. Na taṃ jānantīti taṃ kalahaṃ na jānanti. Kalahaṃ karonto ca taṃ na jānanto nāma natthi. Yathā pana na jānanti, taṃ dassetuṃ āha “evaṃ sādīnavo aya”nti, ayaṃ kalaho nāma attano paresañca atthahāpanato anatthuppādanato diṭṭheva dhamme samparāye ca sādīnavo sadosoti attho. Taṃ na jānantīti taṃ kalahaṃ na jānanti. Kathaṃ na jānantīti āha “evaṃ sādīnavo aya”nti, “evaṃ sādīnavo ayaṃ kalaho”ti evaṃ taṃ kalahaṃ na jānantīti attho.

“Whose sphere is speech” (vācāgocarā) means those whose sphere of activity is speech that proceeds by way of quarreling. “Stretching their mouths” (mukhāyāmaṃ) means those who speak, stretching their mouths by way of disputing. “They do not know it” (na taṃ jānanti) means they do not know that quarrel. There is no one who engages in a quarrel and does not know it. Yet, to show how they do not know it, it is said: “Thus full of danger is this” (evaṃ sādīnavo ayaṃ)—this quarrel, by depriving oneself and others of benefit and producing harm, is dangerous and faulty both in this life and the next—this is the meaning. “They do not know it” (taṃ na jānanti) means they do not know that quarrel. How do they not know it? It is said: “Thus full of danger is this” (evaṃ sādīnavo ayaṃ). That is, they do not know that quarrel is “thus full of danger”—this is the meaning.

Akkocchi mantiādīsu akkocchīti akkosi. Avadhīti pahari. Ajinīti kūṭasakkhiotāraṇena vā vādapaṭivādena vā karaṇuttariyakaraṇena vā ajesi. Ahāsīti mama santakaṃ pattādīsu kiñcideva avahari[M 3.0351]. Ye ca tanti ye keci devā vā manussā vā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā taṃ “akkocchi ma”ntiādivatthukaṃ kodhaṃ sakaṭadhuraṃ viya naddhinā pūtimacchādīni viya ca kusādīhi punappunaṃ veṭhentā upanayhanti upanāhavasena anubandhanti, tesaṃ sakiṃ uppannaṃ veraṃ na sammatīti attho.

In such phrases as “He abused me” (akkocchi maṃ): “He abused” (akkocchi) means he reviled. “He struck” (avadhī) means he hit. “He defeated” (ajinī) means he conquered by presenting false testimony, or by winning an argument, or by superior performance. “He robbed” (ahāsi) means he stole something of mine, such as a bowl, etc. And those—whether devas or humans, householders or renunciants—who, concerning the matter of “he abused me” and so on, repeatedly wrap up anger like a cart’s yoke with straps, and like rotten fish with kusa grass, and who harbor it through resentment, for them the enmity once arisen does not subside: this is the meaning.

Ye ca taṃ nupanayhantīti assatiyā amanasikāravasena vā kammapaccavekkhaṇādivasena vā ye taṃ akkosādivatthukaṃ kodhaṃ “tayāpi koci niddoso purimabhave akkuṭṭho bhavissati, pahaṭo bhavissati, kūṭasakkhiṃ otāretvā jito bhavissati, kassaci te pasayha kiñci acchinnaṃ bhavissati, tasmā niddoso hutvāpi akkosādīni pāpuṇāsī”ti evaṃ na upanayhanti[V 3.0321], tesu pamādena uppannampi veraṃ iminā anupanayhanena nirindhano viya jātavedo upasammati.

And those who do not harbor it (nupanayhanti)—either through lack of mindfulness and non-attention, or through reflection on karma and so forth—those who do not apply that anger based on grounds like abuse, thinking, “In a past life, some blameless person was surely abused by you, struck by you, defeated by you after you brought false testimony, or you forcibly took something from someone. Therefore, though blameless now, you experience abuse and the like.” In them, even if animosity arises through negligence, it subsides like a fire without fuel due to this non-harboring.

Na hi verena verānīti yathā hi kheḷasiṅghāṇikādiasucimakkhitaṃ ṭhānaṃ teheva asucīhi dhovanto suddhaṃ niggandhaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, atha kho taṃ ṭhānaṃ bhiyyoso mattāya asuddhatarañca duggandhatarañca hoti, evameva akkosantaṃ paccakkosanto paharantaṃ paṭipaharanto verena veraṃ vūpasametuṃ na sakkoti, atha kho bhiyyo verameva karoti. Iti verāni nāma verena kismiñcipi kāle na sammanti, atha kho vaḍḍhantiyeva. Averena ca sammantīti yathā pana tāni kheḷādīni asucīni vippasannena udakena dhoviyamānāni nassanti, taṃ ṭhānaṃ suddhaṃ hoti niggandhaṃ, evameva averena khantimettodakena yonisomanasikārena paṭisaṅkhānena paccavekkhaṇena verāni vūpasammanti paṭippassambhanti abhāvaṃ gacchanti. Esa dhammo sanantanoti esa averena verūpasamanasaṅkhāto porāṇako dhammo sabbesaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavānaṃ gatamaggo.

“For not by hatred are hatreds ever appeased here”: Just as a place soiled with spit, mucus, or other impurities cannot be made clean and odorless by washing it with those very impurities—on the contrary, that place becomes even more impure and foul-smelling—even so, one who returns abuse for abuse, or a blow for a blow, cannot pacify hatred through hatred; on the contrary, one creates even more hatred. Thus, hatreds are never appeased by hatred at any time, but only increase. “But by non-hatred they are appeased”: Just as those impurities like spit are destroyed when washed with clear water, and the place becomes clean and odorless, even so, hatreds are pacified, calmed, and cease to be through non-hatred—through the water of patience and loving-kindness, through wise attention, reflection, and review. “This is an ancient law”: This ancient principle, known as the pacification of hatred through non-hatred, is the path followed by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and arahants.

Na jānantīti aniccasaññaṃ na paccupaṭṭhāpentīti adhippāyo. Tato sammanti medhagāti tato tasmā kāraṇā medhagā kalahā sammanti vūpasamaṃ gacchanti. Kathaṃ te sammantīti āha “evañhī”tiādi. Tattha evañhi te jānantāti te paṇḍitā “mayaṃ maccusamīpaṃ gacchāmā”ti evaṃ jānantā yonisomanasikāraṃ uppādetvā medhagānaṃ kalahānaṃ vūpasamāya [M 3.0352] paṭipajjanti, atha nesaṃ tāya paṭipattiyā te medhagā sammantīti adhippāyo.

“They do not know” means they do not establish the perception of impermanence; this is the intention. “From that, quarrels cease”: from that reason, quarrels and disputes cease, they go to quiescence. How do they cease? He says, “For thus…” and so on. Here, “For thus those who know”: those wise ones, knowing, “We are approaching death,” thus generate wise attention and practice for the subsidence of quarrels and disputes; then, by that practice of theirs, those quarrels cease. This is the intention.

Tesampi hoti saṅgatīti ye mātāpitūnaṃ aṭṭhīni chindanti, pāṇe haranti, gavādīni ca pasayha gaṇhanti, evaṃ raṭṭhaṃ vilumpamānānaṃ tesampi saṅgati hoti, kimaṅgaṃ pana tumhākaṃ na siyāti adhippāyo.

“For them too there is association”: Even for those who break the bones of their parents, take lives, and forcibly seize cattle and other animals, thus plundering the country, there is association; how much more so should there be for you? This is the intention.

Vaṇṇāvaṇṇadīpanatthaṃ vuttāti “bālasahāyatāya ime bhikkhū kalahapasutā, paṇḍitasahāyānaṃ pana idaṃ na siyā”ti paṇḍitasahāyassa bālasahāyassa ca vaṇṇāvaṇṇadīpanatthaṃ vuttā. Nipakanti nepakkapaññāya samannāgataṃ. Sādhuvihāri dhīranti bhaddakavihāriṃ paṇḍitaṃ. Pākaṭaparissaye ca paṭicchannaparissaye ca abhibhavitvāti sīhabyagghādayo pākaṭaparissaye ca rāgabhayadosabhayādayo paṭicchannaparissaye cāti sabbeva parissaye abhibhavitvā.

It was spoken to illustrate qualities and faults: It was spoken to show the qualities of a wise companion and the faults of a foolish one, with the thought, “Because of their association with a fool, these monks are intent on quarreling, but for those with wise companions, this would not be.” “Discerning” (nipaka) means endowed with discerning wisdom. “A virtuous dweller, wise” (sādhuvihāri dhīraṃ) means a virtuous dweller, a wise person. “Having overcome both manifest and concealed dangers”: having overcome all dangers whatsoever—lions, tigers, and so on are manifest dangers, while the fear of lust, the fear of hatred, and so on are concealed dangers.

Ekakā [V 3.0322] cariṃsūti “idaṃ rajjaṃ nāma mahantaṃ pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, kiṃ amhākaṃ rajjena kāritenā”ti raṭṭhaṃ pahāya tato mahāaraññaṃ pavisitvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā catūsu iriyāpathesu ekakā cariṃsūti attho.

“They wandered alone” means that, thinking, “This kingdom is a great ground for negligence; what use is ruling a kingdom to us?” they abandoned the country, entered the great forest, went forth into the ascetic life, and wandered alone in the four postures. This is the meaning.

Ekassa caritaṃ seyyoti pabbajitassa pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya ekībhāvābhiratassa ekakasseva caritaṃ seyyoti attho. Natthi bāle sahāyatāti cūḷasīlaṃ majjhimasīlaṃ mahāsīlaṃ dasa kathāvatthūni terasa dhutaguṇā vipassanāñāṇaṃ cattāro maggā cattāri phalāni tisso vijjā cha abhiññā amatamahānibbānanti ayaṃ sahāyatā nāma, sā bālaṃ nissāya adhigantuṃ na sakkāti natthi bāle sahāyatā. Mātaṅgo araññe mātaṅgaraññeti saralopena sandhi. “Mātaṅgarañño”tipi pāṭho, araññako mātaṅgo viyāti attho. Mātaṅga-saddeneva hatthibhāvassa vuttattā nāgavacanaṃ tassa mahattavibhāvanatthanti āha “nāgoti mahantādhivacanameta”nti. Mahantapariyāyo hi nāga-saddo hoti “etaṃ nāgassa nāgena, īsādantassa hatthino”tiādīsu (udā. 35).

“A solitary life is better” means that for one who has gone forth, from the time of his going forth, delighting in solitude, the life of one who is alone is better. This is the meaning. “There is no companionship with a fool” means that this companionship—namely, the minor, intermediate, and major moralities, the ten topics of discussion, the thirteen ascetic qualities, insight knowledge, the four paths, the four fruits, the three true knowledges, the six higher knowledges, and the deathless, great Nibbāna—cannot be attained by relying on a fool. Therefore, there is no companionship with a fool. The phrase mātaṅgaraññe is formed by sandhi through vowel elision from mātaṅgo araññe (“an elephant in the forest”). There is also the reading mātaṅgarañño, meaning “like a forest elephant.” Because the state of being an elephant is already stated by the word “mātaṅga,” the word “nāga” is used to emphasize its greatness. He said, “ʻNāgaʼ is a term for the great.” For the word “nāga” is a synonym for great, as in “This is the nāga of a nāga, the elephant with excellent tusks,” and so on (Ud 35).

Dīghāvuvatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Dīghāvu is concluded.

Bālakaloṇakagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Foolish Boy and the Salt Journey

465. Bālakaloṇakāragāmoti [M 3.0353] upāligahapatissa evaṃnāmako bhogagāmo. Tenupasaṅkamīti dhammasenāpatimahāmoggallānattheresu vā asītimahāsāvakesu vā antamaso dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaṃ ānandattherampi kañci anāmantetvā sayameva pattacīvaramādāya anīkanissaṭo hatthī viya yūthanissaṭo kāḷasīho viya vātacchinno valāhako viya ca ekakova upasaṅkami. Kasmā upasaṅkami? Gaṇe kirassa ādīnavaṃ disvā ekavihāriṃ bhikkhuṃ passitukāmatā udapādi, tasmā sītādipīḷito uṇhādiṃ patthayamāno viya upasaṅkami. Atha vā bhagavatā so ādīnavo pageva pariññāto, na tena satthā nibbinno, tasmiṃ pana antovasse keci buddhaveneyyā nāhesuṃ, tena aññattha gamanaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ damanupāyoti pālileyyakaṃ uddissa gacchanto ekavihāriṃ āyasmantaṃ bhaguṃ sampahaṃsetuṃ tattha gato. Evaṃ gate ca satthari pañcasatā bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āhaṃsu “āvuso ānanda satthā ekakova gato, mayaṃ anubandhissāmā”ti. “Āvuso, yadā bhagavā sāmaṃ senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ adutiyo gacchati, tadā ekacārikaṃ [V 3.0323] carituṃ bhagavato ajjhāsayo, sāvakena nāma satthu ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ, tasmā na imesu divasesu bhagavā anugantabbo”ti nivāresi, sayampi nānugañchi. Dhammiyā kathāyāti ekībhāve ānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammakathāya.

465. The village named Bālakaloṇakāra was a prosperous village belonging to the householder Upāli. He approached—without informing the General of the Dhamma, Mahāmoggallāna, or the eighty great disciples, or even the keeper of the Dhamma treasury, the Venerable Ānanda—taking his bowl and robe himself, like an elephant detached from its herd, a black lion separated from its pride, or a cloud severed by the wind, he approached alone. Why did he go? Seeing the drawbacks of living in a group, the desire arose in him to see a monk dwelling in solitude. Therefore, as one longing for warmth when afflicted by cold, he approached. Alternatively, the Blessed One had already fully understood those drawbacks. He was not disenchanted by them, but during that rainy season, there were no individuals there to be trained by the Buddha. Thus, as a means of disciplining those monks, he went elsewhere, heading toward Pālileyyaka intending to encourage the Venerable Bhagu, who dwelt alone. When the Teacher had gone in this way, five hundred monks said to the Venerable Ānanda, 'Friend Ānanda, the Teacher has gone alone. We will follow him.' 'Friends,' he replied, 'when the Blessed One himself prepares his lodging, takes his bowl and robe, and departs without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Saṅgha, going alone without a companion, it is the Blessed One’s intention to wander in solitude. A disciple should act in accordance with the Teacher’s intention. Therefore, the Blessed One should not be followed during these days.' Thus, he restrained them, and he himself did not follow. With a Dhamma talk—a discourse connected with the benefits of solitude.

Bālakaloṇakagamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the story of the journey to Bālakaloṇakāra is concluded.

Pācīnavaṃsadāyagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of the Going to the Eastern Bamboo Grove

466. Yena pācīnavaṃsadāyoti tattha kasmā upasaṅkami? Yathā nāma jighacchitassa bhojane, pipāsitassa pānīye, sītena phuṭṭhassa uṇhe, uṇhena phuṭṭhassa sīte, dukkhitassa sukhe abhiruci uppajjati, evameva bhagavato kosambake bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ vivādāpanne asamaggavāsaṃ vasante, samaggavāsaṃ [M 3.0354] vasante āvajjentassa ime tayo kulaputtā āpāthamāgamiṃsu, atha nesaṃ paggaṇhitukāmo upasaṅkami “evāyaṃ paṭipattianukkamena kosambakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayanūpāyo hotī”ti. Viharantīti sāmaggirasaṃ anubhavamānā viharanti.

466. Why did he approach the Eastern Bamboo Grove? Just as a desire for food arises in one who is hungry, for drink in one who is thirsty, for warmth in one touched by cold, for coolness in one touched by heat, and a delight in happiness arises for one in suffering, so too, while the Blessed One was reflecting on the monks at Kosambi who were living in discord, engaged in mutual disputes, and considering those living in harmony, these three clansmen came into his focus. Then, desiring to support them, he approached, thinking, 'In this way, through the sequence of practice, a means of discipline for the monks of Kosambi will arise.' 'They dwelled' means they dwelled experiencing the taste of harmony.

Dāyapāloti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.325) araññapālo. So araññaṃ yathā icchiticchitappadesena manussā pavisitvā tattha pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā niyyāsaṃ vā dabbasambhāraṃ vā na haranti, evaṃ vatiyā parikkhittassa araññassa yojite dvāre nisīditvā araññaṃ rakkhati, tasmā “dāyapālo”ti vutto. Attakāmarūpā viharantīti attano hitaṃ kāmayamānasabhāvā hutvā viharanti. Yo hi imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvāpi vejjakammadūtakammapahiṇagamanādīnaṃ vasena ekavīsatianesanāhi jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ na attakāmarūpo nāma. Yo pana imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā ekavīsatianesanaṃ pahāya catupārisuddhisīle patiṭṭhāya buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā sappāyadhutaṅgaṃ adhiṭṭhāya aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gāmantaṃ pahāya araññaṃ pavisitvā samāpattiyo nibbattetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ kurumāno vicarati, ayaṃ attakāmo nāma. Tepi tayo kulaputtā evarūpā ahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “attakāmarūpā viharantī”ti.

A grove-keeper (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.325) is a forest protector. He sits at the appointed gate of a forest enclosed by a fence, ensuring that people do not enter wherever they please and take away flowers, fruits, resin, or other materials. Thus, he is called a 'grove-keeper.' 'They dwell with a nature that desires their own welfare' means they abide with a nature that desires what is for their own good. For one who, having gone forth in this dispensation, makes a livelihood through the twenty-one kinds of improper pursuits—such as practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, or running errands—is not called one who desires his own welfare. But one who, having gone forth in this dispensation, abandons the twenty-one improper pursuits, establishes himself in the fourfold purity of virtue, learns the Buddha’s word, undertakes suitable ascetic practices, takes up a meditation subject that suits his mind’s inclination from among the thirty-eight objects, leaves the vicinity of villages, enters the forest, attains meditative absorptions, and practices insight meditation—such a one is truly called one who desires his own welfare. Those three clansmen were of such a nature. Therefore, it is said, 'they dwell with a nature that desires their own welfare.'

Mā tesaṃ aphāsumakāsīti tesaṃ aphāsukaṃ mā akāsīti bhagavantaṃ vāresi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “ime kulaputtā samaggā viharanti, ekaccassa ca gataṭṭhāne [V 3.0324] bhaṇḍanakalahavivādā vattanti, tikhiṇasiṅgo caṇḍagoṇo viya ovijjhanto vicarati, athekamaggena dvinnaṃ gamanaṃ na hoti, kadāci ayampi evaṃ karonto imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ samaggavāsaṃ bhindeyya, pāsādiko ca panesa suvaṇṇavaṇṇo rasagiddho maññe, gatakālato paṭṭhāya paṇītadāyakānaṃ attano upaṭṭhākānaṃ vaṇṇakathanādīhi imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ appamādavihāraṃ bhindeyya, vasanaṭṭhānāni cāpi etesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ nibaddhāni paricchinnāni tissova paṇṇasālā tayo caṅkamā tīṇi divāṭṭhānāni tīṇi mañcapīṭhāni, ayaṃ pana samaṇo mahākāyo vuḍḍhataro maññe bhavissati, so akāle ime kulaputte senāsanā vuṭṭhapessati, evaṃ sabbathāpi etesaṃ aphāsu bhavissatī”ti. Taṃ anicchanto “mā tesaṃ aphāsumakāsī”ti bhagavantaṃ vāreti.

'Do not cause them discomfort' means 'Do not make it inconvenient for them,' and thus he prevented the Blessed One from entering. For it occurred to him: 'These clansmen live in harmony. But a certain kind of person, wherever he goes, stirs up quarrels, brawls, and disputes. He wanders about goring others like a sharp-horned, fierce bull, so that there is no room for two on the same path. Perhaps this one, acting in such a way, might disrupt the harmonious living of these clansmen. Moreover, he is handsome and golden-skinned; I suppose he is greedy for fine tastes. From the moment he arrives, by speaking in praise of his own generous donors and attendants, he might disrupt the diligent abiding of these clansmen. Furthermore, the dwelling places of these clansmen are fixed and limited: just three leaf-huts, three walking paths, three day-quarters, and three beds and benches. But this ascetic seems to be large-bodied and rather old. He might make these clansmen get up from their lodgings at an improper time. Thus, in every way, it would be an inconvenience for them.' Not wishing for this, he prevented the Blessed One, saying, 'Do not cause them discomfort.'

Kiṃ [M 3.0355] panesa jānanto vāresi ajānantoti? Ajānanto. Sammāsambuddho hi nāma yadā anekabhikkhusahassaparivāro byāmappabhāya asītianubyañjanehi dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasiriyā ca buddhānubhāvaṃ dassento vicarati, tadā “ko eso”ti apucchitvāva jānitabbo hoti. Tadā pana bhagavā “māssu koci mama buddhānubhāvaṃ aññāsī”ti tathārūpena iddhābhisaṅkhārena sabbampi taṃ buddhānubhāvaṃ cīvaragabbhena viya paṭicchādetvā valāhakagabbhena paṭicchanno puṇṇacando viya sayameva pattacīvaramādāya aññātakavesena agamāsi. Iti taṃ ajānantova dāyapālo vāresi.

But did he prevent him knowing or not knowing? Not knowing. For when a Perfectly Enlightened One wanders surrounded by many thousands of monks, displaying his Buddha-majesty with his fathom-wide aura, the eighty minor characteristics, and the splendor of the thirty-two marks of a great man, he is to be known without even asking, 'Who is this?' But at that time the Blessed One, thinking, 'Let no one recognize my Buddha-majesty,' concealed all that Buddha-majesty with a psychic determination, as if with the fold of his robe. Like the full moon hidden within a mass of clouds, he took his bowl and robe by himself and went in the guise of an unknown person. Thus, it was without knowing him that the grove-keeper prevented him.

Etadavocāti thero kira “mā samaṇā”ti dāyapālassa kathaṃ sutvā cintesi “mayaṃ tayo janā idha viharāma, añño pabbajito nāma natthi, ayañca dāyapālo pabbajitena viya saddhiṃ katheti, ko nu kho bhavissatī”ti divāṭṭhānato uṭṭhāya dvāre ṭhatvā maggaṃ olokento bhagavantaṃ addasa. Bhagavāpi therassa saha dassaneneva sarīrobhāsaṃ muñci, asītianubyañjanavirājitā byāmappabhā pasāritasuvaṇṇapaṭo viya virocittha. Thero “ayaṃ dāyapālo phaṇakataāsīvisaṃ gīvāya gahetuṃ hatthaṃ pasārento viya loke aggapuggalena saddhiṃ kathentova na jānāti, aññatarabhikkhunā viya saddhiṃ kathetī”ti nivārento etaṃ “māvuso, dāyapālā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

'He spoke thus': The elder, it is said, upon hearing the grove-keeper’s words, 'Do not enter, ascetic!', thought, 'We three people dwell here, and there is no other renunciant. Yet this grove-keeper is speaking as if with a renunciant. Who could it be?' Rising from his day-quarters and standing at the door, looking down the road, he saw the Blessed One. The Blessed One, too, at the very moment of seeing the elder, released the radiance of his body. The fathom-wide aura, resplendent with the eighty minor characteristics, shone forth like a spread-out sheet of gold. The elder thought, 'This grove-keeper does not know he is speaking with the foremost person in the world; he speaks as if with some ordinary bhikkhu, like one stretching out his hand to grasp a hooded viper by the neck.' Preventing him, he spoke the words beginning, 'Do not, friend grove-keeper...'

Tenupasaṅkamīti kasmā bhagavato paccuggamanaṃ akatvāva upasaṅkami? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “mayaṃ tayo janā samaggavāsaṃ vasāma, sacāhaṃ ekakova paccuggamanaṃ karissāmi, samaggavāso nāma na bhavissati, piyamitte gahetvāva paccuggamanaṃ karissāmi. Yathā ca bhagavā [V 3.0325] mayhaṃ piyo, evaṃ sahāyānampi me piyo”ti tehi saddhiṃ paccuggamanaṃ kātukāmo sayaṃ akatvā upasaṅkami. Keci pana “tesaṃ therānaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre caṅkamanakoṭiyā bhagavato āgamanamaggo hoti, tasmā thero tesaṃ saññaṃ dadamānova gato”ti vadanti. Abhikkamathāti ito āgacchatha. Pāde pakkhālesīti vikasitapadumasannibhehi jālahatthehi maṇivaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇesu piṭṭhipādesu udakaṃ āsiñcitvā pādena pādaṃ ghaṃsento pakkhālesi. Buddhānaṃ [M 3.0356] kāye rajojallaṃ nāma na upalimpati, kasmā pakkhālesīti? Sarīrassa utuggahaṇatthaṃ tesañca cittasampahaṃsanatthaṃ. Amhehi abhihaṭena udakena bhagavā pāde pakkhālesi, paribhogaṃ akāsīti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ balavasomanassavasena cittaṃ pīṇitaṃ hoti, tasmā pakkhālesi.

Why did he approach without first going out to meet the Blessed One? It is said that he thought, "We three live together in harmony. If I alone go out to meet him, what is called harmonious living will not exist. Therefore, I will go out to meet him together with my dear friends. Just as the Blessed One is dear to me, so too are my companions dear to me." Thus, desiring to go out to meet the Blessed One together with them, he approached without doing so alone. Some, however, say, "The path by which the Blessed One came was near the door of the leaf-hut and the edge of the walking path of those elders. Therefore, the elder went, as if giving them a signal." "Come forth" means: come here from there. "He washed his feet" means: taking jewel-colored water with his net-like hands, which resembled blooming lotuses, he poured the water over his golden-hued insteps and washed his feet by rubbing one foot with the other. Dust and dirt do not cling to the bodies of Buddhas. Why then did he wash his feet? For the refreshment of his body and for delighting their minds. When they thought, "The Blessed One washed his feet with the water brought by us, making use of it," the minds of those monks were filled with strong gladness. Therefore, he washed his feet.

Āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ bhagavā etadavocāti so kira tesaṃ vuḍḍhataro, tassa saṅgahe kate sesānaṃ katova hotīti theraññeva etaṃ “kacci vo anuruddhā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Anuruddhāti vā ekasesanayena vuttaṃ virūpekasesassapi icchitabbattā, evañca katvā bahuvacananiddeso ca samatthito hoti. Kaccīti pucchanatthe nipāto. Voti sāmivacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kacci anuruddhā tumhākaṃ khamanīyaṃ, iriyāpatho vo khamati, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci vo jīvitaṃ yāpeti ghaṭiyati, kacci piṇḍakena na kilamatha, kacci tumhākaṃ sulabhapiṇḍaṃ, sampatte vo disvā manussā uḷuṅkayāguṃ vā kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ vā dātabbaṃ maññantīti bhikkhācāravattaṃ pucchati. Kasmā? Yasmā paccayena akilamantena sakkā samaṇadhammo kātuṃ, vattameva vā etaṃ pabbajitānaṃ.

The Blessed One addressed Venerable Anuruddha. It is said that since he was the eldest among them, when he was included, the others were included as well. Thus, he spoke these words to the elder himself: "I hope, Anuruddhas..." Alternatively, 'Anuruddha' is said according to the principle of ellipsis, as ellipsis of dissimilar forms is also intended; and by doing so, the plural designation is also justified. `Kacci` is a particle indicating inquiry. `Vo` is a possessive word. This is what is said: "I hope, Anuruddhas, that you are keeping well, that your deportment is agreeable, that you are able to sustain yourselves, that your life is maintained, that you are not wearied by the alms-round, that almsfood is easily obtained for you, and that people, seeing you approach, think to offer a ladle of gruel or a spoonful of almsfood." He asks about the practice of alms-gathering. Why? Because when one is not wearied by requisites, it is possible to practice the duties of a recluse; indeed, this is the practice for those who have gone forth.

Atha tena paṭivacane dinne “anuruddhā tumhe rājapabbajitā mahāpuññā, manussā tumhākaṃ araññe vasantānaṃ adatvā kassa aññassa dātabbaṃ maññissanti, tumhe pana etaṃ bhuñjitvā kiṃ nu kho migapotakā viya aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭentā viharatha, udāhu sāmaggibhāvo vo atthī”ti sāmaggirasaṃ pucchanto “kacci pana vo anuruddhā samaggā”tiādimāha. Tattha khīrodakībhūtāti yathā khīrañca udakañca aññamaññaṃ saṃsandati, visuṃ na hoti, ekattaṃ viya upeti, kacci evaṃ sāmaggivasena ekattupagatacittuppādā viharathāti pucchati. Piyacakkhūhīti mettacittaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā olokanato piyabhāvadīpakāni cakkhūni piyacakkhūni nāma, “kacci tathārūpehi cakkhūhi aññamaññaṃ passantā viharathā”ti pucchati. Tagghāti ekaṃsatthe nipāto, ekaṃsena mayaṃ bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā kathaṃ panāti ettha yathāti nipātamattaṃ, kathanti [V 3.0326] kāraṇapucchā, kathaṃ pana tumhe evaṃ viharatha, kena kāraṇena viharatha, taṃ me kāraṇaṃ brūhīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Then, when that reply was given, he considered: "Anuruddhas, you are royal renunciants of great merit. If people do not give to you who dwell in the forest, to whom else will they think to give? But having enjoyed this, do you live jostling each other like young deer, or is there harmony among you?" Then, asking about the essence of harmony, he said, "I hope, Anuruddhas, you are harmonious?" Here, 'having become like milk and water' means just as milk and water blend together and do not remain separate, becoming as if one – he asks whether you live with minds that have attained oneness in this way through harmony. 'With affectionate eyes' refers to eyes that express affection by looking while establishing a mind of loving-kindness. He asks, "Do you live seeing each other with such eyes?" 'Indeed' is a particle of certainty – it means, "Certainly, venerable sir." 'But how then?' Here, 'yathā' is merely a particle, while 'kathaṃ' is a question about the reason. 'How then do you live thus? By what reason do you live? Tell me that reason,' is what is meant.

Mettaṃ [M 3.0357] kāyakammanti mettacittavasena pavattaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Āvi ceva raho cāti sammukhā ceva parammukhā ca. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Tattha sammukhā kāyavacīkammāni sahavāse labbhanti, itarāni vippavāse, manokammaṃ sabbattha labbhati. Yañhi saheva vasantesu ekena mañcapīṭhaṃ vā dārubhaṇḍaṃ vā mattikābhaṇḍaṃ vā bahi dunnikkhittaṃ hoti, taṃ disvā “kenidaṃ vaḷañjita”nti avaññaṃ akatvā attanā dunnikkhittaṃ viya gahetvā paṭisāmentassa paṭijaggitabbayuttaṃ vā pana ṭhānaṃ paṭijaggantassa sammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma hoti. Ekasmiṃ pakkante tena dunnikkhittaṃ senāsanaparikkhāraṃ tatheva nikkhipantassa paṭijaggitabbayuttaṃ vā pana ṭhānaṃ paṭijaggantassa parammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma hoti. Sahavasantassa pana therehi saddhiṃ madhuraṃ sammodanīyakathaṃ paṭisanthārakathaṃ sāraṇīyakathaṃ dhammakathaṃ sarabhaññaṃ sākacchaṃ pañhapucchanaṃ pañhavissajjananti evamādikaraṇe sammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma hoti. Theresu pana pakkantesu “mayhaṃ piyasahāyo nandiyatthero kimilatthero evaṃ sīlasampanno evaṃ ācārasampanno”tiādiguṇakathane parammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma hoti. “Mayhaṃ piyamitto nandiyatthero kimilatthero avero hotu abyāpajjo sukhī”ti evaṃ samannāharato pana sammukhāpi parammukhāpi mettaṃ manokammaṃ hotiyeva.

"Bodily action of loving-kindness" means bodily action that proceeds from a mind of loving-kindness. "Openly and in private" means both face-to-face and behind their back. The same principle applies to the others. Here, face-to-face bodily and verbal actions are found when living together, while the others are found when living apart; mental action, however, is found in all circumstances. For when living together, if a bed, a bench, a wooden utensil, or an earthenware utensil has been badly placed outside by one of them, another, on seeing it, without showing disdain by thinking, "Who used this?", takes it as if he himself had badly placed it and puts it away, or tends to a place that ought to be tended to—this is called face-to-face bodily action of loving-kindness. When one has departed, for another to put away the lodging requisites badly placed by him, or to tend to a place that ought to be tended to—this is called behind-the-back bodily action of loving-kindness. For one living together, to engage with the elders in sweet, agreeable, welcoming, and memorable talk, in Dhamma talk, chanting, discussion, questioning, and answering—this is called face-to-face verbal action of loving-kindness. When the elders have departed, to speak of their virtues, saying, "My dear companion, the venerable Nandiya, or the venerable Kimila, is so endowed with virtue, so endowed with good conduct"—this is called behind-the-back verbal action of loving-kindness. But for one who reflects, "May my dear friend, the venerable Nandiya, or the venerable Kimila, be free from enmity, free from affliction, and be happy," this is mental action of loving-kindness, whether face-to-face or behind their back.

Nānā hi kho no bhante kāyāti ayañhi kāyo piṭṭhaṃ viya mattikā viya ca omadditvā ekato kātuṃ na sakkā. Ekañca pana maññe cittanti cittaṃ pana no attano viya aññamaññassa hitabhāvena avirodhabhāvena bhedābhāvena samaggabhāvena ekamevāti dasseti. Kathaṃ panete sakaṃ cittaṃ nikkhipitvā itaresaṃ cittavasena vattiṃsūti? Ekassa patte malaṃ uṭṭhahati, ekassa cīvaraṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ hoti, ekassa paribhaṇḍakammaṃ hoti. Tattha yassa patte malaṃ uṭṭhitaṃ, tena “mamāvuso patte malaṃ uṭṭhitaṃ, pacituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte itare “mayhaṃ cīvaraṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ dhovitabbaṃ, mayhaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ kātabba”nti avatvā araññaṃ pavisitvā dārūni āharitvā bhinditvā pattakaṭāhe bahalatanumattikāhi lepaṃ katvā pattaṃ pacitvā tato paraṃ cīvaraṃ vā dhovanti, paribhaṇḍaṃ vā karonti. “Mamāvuso cīvaraṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ, dhovituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti “mama paṇṇasālā uklāpā, paribhaṇḍaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti paṭhamataraṃ ārocitepi eseva nayo.

"Indeed, venerable sir, our bodies are diverse." For this body, like flour or clay, cannot be kneaded and made into one. "But I think our mind is one." This shows that their minds, through mutual benefit, non-opposition, non-division, and unity, were indeed one. But how then did they, setting aside their own minds, act according to the minds of others? For one, rust arises in his bowl; for another, his robe becomes soiled; for another, there is work to be done on his requisites. There, when the one whose bowl has rusted says, "Friend, rust has arisen in my bowl—it needs to be fired," the others do not say, "My robe needs washing," or "My requisites need repairing." Instead, they enter the forest, gather firewood, split it, and having coated the bowl with thick and thin layers of clay in a bowl-kiln, they fire the bowl, and only afterward do they wash the robe or repair the requisites. Similarly, even if one first announces, "Friend, my robe is soiled—it needs washing," or "My leaf-hut is dilapidated—the requisites need repairing," the same principle applies.

Idāni [M 3.0358] tesaṃ appamādalakkhaṇaṃ pucchanto “kacci pana vo anuruddhā”tiādimāha. Tattha [V 3.0327] voti nipātamattaṃ, paccattavacanaṃ vā, kacci tumheti attho. Amhākanti amhesu tīsu janesu. Piṇḍāya paṭikkamatīti gāme piṇḍāya caritvā paccāgacchati. Avakkārapātinti atirekapiṇḍapātaṃ apanetvā ṭhapanatthāya ekaṃ samuggapātiṃ dhovitvā ṭhapeti. Yo pacchāti te kira therā na ekatova bhikkhācāraṃ pavisanti. Phalasamāpattiratā hete pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā vattapaṭipattiṃ pūretvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā kālaparicchedaṃ katvā phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdanti. Tesu yo paṭhamataraṃ nisinno attano kālaparicchedavasena paṭhamataraṃ uṭṭhāti, so piṇḍāya caritvā paṭinivatto bhattakiccaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā jānāti “dve bhikkhū pacchato, ahaṃ paṭhamataraṃ āgato”ti. Atha pattaṃ pidahitvā āsanapaññāpanādīni katvā yadi patte paṭivīsamattameva hoti, nisīditvā bhuñjati, yadi atirekaṃ hoti, avakkārapātiyaṃ pakkhipitvā pātiṃ pidhāya bhuñjati, katabhattakicco pattaṃ dhovitvā vodakaṃ katvā thavikāya osāpetvā pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisati.

Now, asking about their characteristic of heedfulness, he said, “I trust, Anuruddhas…?” and so on. Herein, ‘vo’ is merely a particle, or it is a personal pronoun, meaning ‘I trust you.’ ‘Amhākaṃ’ means ‘among us three persons.’ ‘Returns from the alms-round’ means he returns after having walked for alms in the village. ‘Places the receptacle for leftovers’ means, for the purpose of setting aside excess almsfood, he washes a receptacle and places it. ‘Whoever is last’—it seems these elders do not enter upon the alms-round together. Being devoted to the attainment of fruition, in the morning, having attended to their bodily needs, fulfilled their duties, entered their dwelling, determined the time, and entered upon the attainment of fruition, they sit. Among them, the one who sat down first rises first in accordance with his own determination of time. Having walked for alms and returned, he comes to the place for the meal and knows, “Two monks are behind; I have come first.” Then, having covered his bowl and prepared a seat and so on, if there is just his own portion of food in the bowl, he sits and eats. If there is an excess, he puts it into the receptacle for leftovers, covers the receptacle, and eats. Having finished his meal, he washes the bowl, makes it free of water, places it in its bag, takes his bowl and robe, and enters his own dwelling place.

Dutiyopi āgantvāva jānāti “eko paṭhamaṃ āgato, eko pacchato”ti. So sace patte bhattaṃ pamāṇameva hoti, bhuñjati. Sace mandaṃ, avakkārapātito gahetvā bhuñjati. Sace atirekaṃ hoti, avakkārapātiyaṃ pakkhipitvā pamāṇameva bhuñjitvā purimatthero viya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisati. Tatiyopi āgantvāva jānāti “dve paṭhamaṃ āgatā, ahaṃ pacchimo”ti. Sopi dutiyatthero viya bhuñjitvā katabhattakicco pattaṃ dhovitvā vodakaṃ katvā thavikāya osāpetvā āsanāni ukkhipitvā paṭisāmeti, pānīyaghaṭe vā paribhojanīyaghaṭe vā avasesaudakaṃ chaḍḍetvā ghaṭe nikujjitvā avakkārapātiyaṃ sace avasesabhattaṃ hoti, taṃ vuttanayena jahitvā pātiṃ dhovitvā paṭisāmeti, bhattaggaṃ sammajjati, so kacavaraṃ chaḍḍetvā sammajjaniṃ ukkhipitvā upacikāhi muttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā pattacīvaramādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisati. Idaṃ therānaṃ bahivihāre araññe bhattakiccakaraṇaṭṭhāne bhojanasālāya vattaṃ. Idaṃ sandhāya “yo pacchā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The second one also, upon arriving, knows: “One came first, one is behind.” If there is just a sufficient amount of food in his bowl, he eats. If it is insufficient, he takes from the receptacle for leftovers and eats. If there is an excess, he puts it into the receptacle for leftovers, eats a sufficient amount, and enters his dwelling place like the first elder. The third one also, upon arriving, knows: “Two came first, I am the last.” He too eats like the second elder, and having completed his meal duties, he washes the bowl, makes it free of water, and places it in its bag. He then lifts the seats and puts them away. If there is any water remaining in the drinking-water pot or the utility-water pot, he discards the remaining water and overturns the pots. If there is leftover food in the receptacle for leftovers, he disposes of it in the prescribed manner, washes the receptacle, and puts it away. He sweeps the refectory, discards the sweepings, lifts the broom and places it in a spot free from termites. Then, taking his bowl and robe, he enters his dwelling place. This is the duty of the elders in the dining hall, the place for performing meal duties, in the forest, in an outer dwelling. It is with reference to this that “whoever is last,” and so on, was said.

Yo [M 3.0359] passatītiādi pana nesaṃ antovihāre vattanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha vaccaghaṭanti ācamanakumbhiṃ. Rittanti rittakaṃ. Tucchanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Avisayhanti ukkhipituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ atibhāriyaṃ. Hatthavikārenāti hatthasaññāya. Te kira pānīyaghaṭādīsu yaṃkiñci tucchakaṃ gahetvā pokkharaṇiṃ gantvā anto ca bahi ca dhovitvā udakaṃ parissāvetvā tīre ṭhapetvā aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ hatthavikārena āmantenti, odissa vā anodissa vā saddaṃ na karonti. Kasmā odissa na karonti? Tañhi bhikkhuṃ saddo bādheyyāti. Kasmā anodissa na [V 3.0328] karonti? Anodissa sadde dinne “ahaṃ pure, ahaṃ pure”ti dvepi nikkhameyyuṃ. Tato dvīhi kattabbakamme tatiyassa kammacchedo bhaveyya. Saṃyatapadasaddo pana hutvā aparassa bhikkhuno divāṭṭhānasantikaṃ gantvā tena diṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā hatthasaññaṃ karoti, tāya saññāya itaro āgacchati, tato dve janā hatthena hatthaṃ saṃsibbantā dvīsu hatthesu ṭhapetvā uṭṭhāpenti. Taṃ sandhāyāha “hatthavikārena dutiyaṃ āmantetvā hatthavilaṅghakena upaṭṭhāpemā”ti.

However, ‘Whoever sees,’ and so on, should be understood as the duty within their dwelling. Therein, ‘vaccaghaṭa’ means the rinsing pot. ‘Ritta’ means empty. ‘Tuccha’ is a synonym for the same. ‘Avisayha’ means unable to be lifted, excessively burdensome. ‘By a hand gesture’ means by a hand signal. It is said that they, taking any empty vessel from among the water pots and so on, would go to the pond, wash it inside and out, strain the water, place it on the bank, and then summon another monk by a hand gesture. They do not make a sound, whether directed or undirected. Why do they not make a directed sound? Because the sound might disturb that monk. Why do they not make an undirected sound? If an undirected sound were made, two might come out, thinking, “I first, I first.” Then, for a task to be done by two, the work of a third would be interrupted. Instead, with the sound of restrained footsteps, one goes near the day-dwelling of another monk, and knowing that he has been seen, he makes a hand signal. At that signal, the other comes. Then the two, linking hand with hand, place the vessel on their two hands and lift it. Referring to this, he said: “Having summoned a second by a hand gesture, we assist by linking hands.”

Pañcāhikaṃ kho panāti cātuddase pannarase aṭṭhamiyanti idaṃ tāva pakatidhammassavanameva, taṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā pañcame pañcame divase dve therā nātivikāle nahāyitvā anuruddhattherassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Tattha tayopi nisīditvā tiṇṇaṃ piṭakānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ aññamaññaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanti, aññamaññaṃ vissajjenti. Tesaṃ evaṃ karontānaṃyeva aruṇaṃ uggacchati. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettāvatā therena bhagavatā appamādalakkhaṇaṃ pucchitena pamādaṭṭhānesuyeva appamādalakkhaṇaṃ vissajjitaṃ hoti. Aññesañhi bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhācārapavisanakālo nikkhamanakālo nivāsanaparivattanaṃ cīvarapārupanaṃ antogāme piṇḍāya caraṇaṃ dhammakathanaṃ anumodanaṃ antogāmato nikkhamitvā bhattakiccakaraṇaṃ pattadhovanaṃ pattaosāpanaṃ pattacīvarapaṭisāmananti papañcakaraṇaṭṭhānāni etāni. Tasmā thero “amhākaṃ ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ muñcitvā vissaṭṭhakathāpavattanena kammaṭṭhāne pamajjanaṭṭhānāni, tatthāpi mayaṃ, bhante, kammaṭṭhānaviruddhaṃ na paṭipajjāmā”ti aññesaṃ pamādaṭṭhānesuyeva sikhāppattaṃ attano appamādalakkhaṇaṃ vissajjesi. Imināva etāni ṭhānāni muñcitvā aññattha vihārasamāpattīnaṃ avaḷañjanavasena pamādakālo nāma amhākaṃ natthīti dīpeti.

As for ‘every five days’: the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days are the regular occasions for hearing the Dhamma. Without interrupting that, every fifth day, two elders, having bathed at a suitable time, go to the dwelling place of the Elder Anuruddha. There, the three of them sit together, and concerning one of the three Piṭakas, they ask each other questions and give answers to one another. While they are thus engaged, dawn breaks. It is with reference to this that the statement was made. Thus, when asked by the Blessed One about the characteristic of heedfulness, the elder explained the characteristic of heedfulness precisely in those situations that are occasions for heedlessness. For other monks, the time for entering the alms-round, the time for returning, changing the lower robe, putting on the outer robe, walking for alms within the village, giving a Dhamma talk, giving thanks, leaving the village, performing the duties of the meal, washing the bowl, putting the bowl away, and putting away the bowl and robe—these are occasions for proliferation. Therefore, the elder explained his own characteristic of heedfulness, which had reached its peak, in those very situations which for others are occasions for heedlessness. He showed that even in those places, which are occasions for becoming negligent in one's meditation subject, they do not engage in anything contrary to their meditation subject. By this, he demonstrates: ‘Apart from these situations, there is for us no time for heedlessness, as we do not neglect the attainments of meditative abidings elsewhere.’

Pācīnavaṃsadāyagamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the account of the journey to the Eastern Bamboo Grove is concluded.

Pālileyyakagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of the Journey to Pālileyyaka.

467. Dhammiyā [M 3.0360] kathāyāti samaggavāse ānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammakathāya. Anupubbena (udā. aṭṭha. 35) cārikaṃ caramānoti anukkamena gāmanigamapaṭipāṭiyā cārikaṃ caramāno. Yena pālileyyakaṃ tadavasarīti ekakova yena pālileyyakagāmo, taṃ avasari. Pālileyyakagāmavāsinopi paccuggantvā bhagavato dānaṃ datvā pālileyyakagāmassa avidūre rakkhitavanasaṇḍo nāma atthi, tattha bhagavato paṇṇasālaṃ katvā “ettha bhagavā vasatū”ti yācitvā vāsayiṃsu. Bhaddasāloti pana tattheko manāpo laṭṭhiko sālarukkho. Bhagavā taṃ gāmaṃ upanissāya [V 3.0329] vanasaṇḍe paṇṇasālāya samīpe tasmiṃ rukkhamūle vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “pālileyyake viharati rakkhitavanasaṇḍe bhaddasālamūle”ti.
