467. ‘With a talk on the Dhamma’ means with a Dhamma talk connected with the benefits of living in harmony. ‘Wandering on tour in due course’ means wandering on tour in sequence, in the order of villages and towns. ‘He arrived at Pālileyyaka’ means he arrived, all alone, at the village of Pālileyyaka. The inhabitants of Pālileyyaka village went out to meet him, gave alms to the Blessed One, and since there was a protected forest grove named Rakkhitavana not far from Pālileyyaka village, they built a leaf-hut for the Blessed One there. Requesting, “May the Blessed One dwell here,” they had him stay. Now, the Bhaddasāla was a beautiful, fine sāl tree there. The Blessed One, dwelling dependent on that village, stayed in the forest grove near the leaf-hut at the foot of that tree. Therefore it was said: “He dwells at Pālileyyaka, in the Rakkhitavana grove, at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree.”

Atha kho bhagavato rahogatassātiādi bhagavato vivekasukhapaccavekkhaṇadassanaṃ. Ākiṇṇo na phāsu vihāsinti sambādhappatto ākiṇṇo vihāsiṃ. Kiṃ pana bhagavato sambādho atthi saṃsaggo vāti? Natthi. Na hi koci bhagavantaṃ anicchāya upasaṅkamituṃ sakkoti. Durāsadā hi buddhā bhagavanto sabbattha ca anupalittā, hitesitāya pana sattesu anukampaṃ upādāya “mutto mocessāmī”ti paṭiññānurūpaṃ caturoghanittharaṇatthaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ parisānaṃ attano santikaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanaṃ adhivāseti, sayañca mahākaruṇāsamussāhito kālaññū hutvā tattha upasaṅkamīti idaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ. Nāyamidha ākiṇṇavihāro adhippeto, idha pana tehi kalahakārakehi kosambakabhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekavihāre vāsaṃ vihāsi, tadā vinetabbābhāvato ākiṇṇavihāraṃ katvā vuttaṃ “ahaṃ kho pubbe ākiṇṇo na phāsu vihāsi”nti. Tenevāha “tehi kosambakehi bhikkhūhi bhaṇḍanakārakehī”tiādi.

Then, the words 'the Blessed One, having gone into seclusion,' etc., show the Blessed One's contemplation of the bliss of solitude. 'Crowded, I did not dwell at ease' means, having become overwhelmed, I dwelt crowded. But does the Blessed One have any crowding or association? There is none. For no one can approach the Blessed One against his will. Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are hard to approach and are untainted in every way. Yet out of compassion for the welfare of beings, thinking, 'Freed, I will free others,' in accordance with his declaration, for the purpose of overcoming the four floods, he allows the eight assemblies to approach him from time to time. And he himself, stirred by great compassion, knowing the right time, approaches them—this is the practice of all Buddhas. Here, this dwelling in crowds is not what is meant. Rather, it refers to dwelling in the same monastery with those quarrelsome monks of Kosambi. At that time, because they could not be disciplined, he referred to his dwelling as crowded and said, 'Formerly, I did not dwell at ease when crowded.' Therefore, it is said, 'With those quarrelsome monks of Kosambi,' and so on.

Daharapotakehīti daharehi hatthipotakehi, ye bhiṅkātipi vuccanti. Tehīti hatthiādīhi. Kaddamodakānīti kaddamamissāni udakāni. Ogāhāti ettha “ogāha”ntipi pāḷi. Assāti hatthināgassa. Upanighaṃsantiyoti ghaṭṭentiyo. Upanighaṃsiyamānopi attano uḷārabhāvena [M 3.0361] na kujjhati, tena tā ghaṃsantiyeva. Vūpakaṭṭhoti vūpakaṭṭho dūrībhūto.

Daharapotakehi means by young elephant calves, who are also called bhiṅkā. Tehīti means by the elephants and so on. Kaddamodakāni means waters mixed with mud. Ogāhāti means here 'ogāha' is also the Pāli reading. Assāti means of the great elephant. Upanighaṃsantiyoti means rubbing. Even when being rubbed against, due to his own noble nature, he does not get angry; therefore, they indeed keep rubbing. Vūpakaṭṭhoti means secluded, having become remote.

Yūthāti hatthighaṭāya. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti so kira hatthināgo yūthavāse ukkaṇṭhito taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ paviṭṭho. Tattha bhagavantaṃ disvā ghaṭasahassena nibbāpitasantāpo viya nibbuto hutvā pasannacitto bhagavato santike aṭṭhāsi, tato paṭṭhāya vattasīse ṭhatvā bhaddasālassa paṇṇasālāya ca samantato appaharitaṃ katvā sākhābhaṅgena sammajjati, bhagavato mukhadhovanaṃ deti, nahānodakaṃ āharati, dantakaṭṭhaṃ deti, araññato madhurāni phalāphalāni āharitvā satthu upaneti. Satthā tāni paribhuñjati. Tena vuttaṃ “soṇḍāya bhagavato pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetī”tiādi. So kira soṇḍāya dārūni āharitvā aññamaññaṃ ghaṃsitvā aggiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā dārūni jālāpetvā tattha pāsāṇakhaṇḍāni tāpetvā tāni daṇḍakehi vaṭṭetvā soṇḍiyaṃ khipitvā udakassa tattabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhagavato santikaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhati. Bhagavā “hatthināgo mama nahānaṃ icchatī”ti tattha gantvā nahānakiccaṃ karoti. Pānīyepi eseva [V 3.0330] nayo. Tasmiṃ pana sītale jāte upasaṅkamati. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “soṇḍāya bhagavato pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetī”ti.

Yūthāti means an elephant herd. 'He approached the Blessed One' means: it is said that the great elephant, discontented with life in the herd, entered that forest grove. There, seeing the Blessed One, as if his torment had been extinguished by a thousand water pots, he became calm and stood near the Blessed One with a serene mind. From then on, undertaking his duties, he cleared the greenery from the area around the Bhaddasāla's leaf-hut and swept it with a broken branch; he offered water for the Blessed One to wash his face, brought water for bathing, gave a tooth-stick, and brought sweet fruits from the forest to offer to the Teacher. The Teacher partook of them. Therefore, it is said, 'With its trunk, it provided drinking water and water for use for the Blessed One,' and so on. It is said that with its trunk, it brought wood, rubbed pieces together to kindle a fire, lit the wood, heated stone fragments on it, rolled them with sticks, and threw them into a pool. Knowing the water was warm, it approached the Blessed One and stood by. The Blessed One, understanding, 'The great elephant wishes me to bathe,' went there and performed his bathing. For drinking water also, this was the method. But he would approach when it had become cool. Regarding this, it is said, 'With its trunk, it provided drinking water and water for use for the Blessed One.'

Attano ca pavivekaṃ viditvāti kehici anākiṇṇabhāvaladdhaṃ kāyavivekaṃ jānitvā. Itare pana vivekā bhagavato sabbakālaṃ vijjantiyeva. Imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti imaṃ attano hatthināgassa ca vivekābhiratiyā samānajjhāsayabhāvadīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Attano ca pavivekaṃ viditvāti means knowing his own seclusion—that is, knowing the physical solitude attained by being undisturbed by anyone. But other kinds of seclusion are always present for the Blessed One. Imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti means he uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate the shared inclination toward delighting in seclusion between himself and the great elephant.

Gāthāya pana evamatthayojanā veditabbā (udā. aṭṭha. 35) – etaṃ īsādantassa rathaīsāsadisadantassa hatthināgassa cittaṃ nāgena buddhanāgassa cittena sameti saṃsandati. Kathaṃ sameti ce? Yadeko ramatī vane, yasmā buddhanāgo “ahaṃ kho pubbe ākiṇṇo vihāsi”nti purimaṃ ākiṇṇavihāraṃ jigucchitvā vivekaṃ upabrūhayamāno idāni yathā eko adutiyo vane araññe ramati abhiramati, evaṃ ayampi hatthināgo pubbe [M 3.0362] attano hatthiādīhi ākiṇṇavihāraṃ jigucchitvā idāni eko asahāyo vane ekavihāraṃ ramati abhinandati, tasmāssa cittaṃ nāgena sameti, tassa cittena sametīti katvā ekībhāvaratiyā ekasadisaṃ hotīti attho.

The meaning of the verse, however, should be understood as follows (Udāna commentary 35): The mind of this elephant nāga with tusks like chariot poles meets and corresponds with the mind of the Buddha nāga. How does it meet? Because just as the Buddha nāga, having abhorred his former crowded dwelling, thinking, 'Formerly, indeed, I lived crowded,' now, developing seclusion, delights as a solitary one, without a second, in the forest; even so this elephant nāga, having previously abhorred living crowded with his fellow elephants, now, solitary and without a companion, delights in a solitary dwelling in the forest. Therefore, its mind meets with the nāga’s mind; that is, by its mind meeting with his mind, it becomes similar in its delight in solitude. This is the meaning.

Pālileyyakagamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of the Journey to Pālileyyaka is concluded.

Aṭṭhārasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Eighteen Topics

473. Yo paṭibāheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassāti ettha yo senāsanārahassa senāsanaṃ paṭibāhati, tasseva āpatti. Kalahakārakādīnaṃ panettha “okāso natthī”tiādikaṃ saṅghassa katikaṃ ārocetvā na paññapentassa “ahaṃ vuḍḍho”ti pasayha attanāva attano paññapetvā gaṇhantaṃ “yuttiyā gaṇhathā”ti vatvā vārentassa ca natthi āpatti. “Bhaṇḍanakārakaṃ nikkaḍḍhatīti vacanato kuladūsakassa pabbājanīyakammānuññāya ca idha kalahavūpasamanatthaṃ āgatānaṃ kosambakānampi ‘yathāvuḍḍha’nti avatvā ‘vivitte asati vivittaṃ katvāpi dātabba’nti vuttattā vivittaṃ katvā dentaṃ paṭibāhantasseva āpattī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

473. 'Whoever obstructs incurs an offense of wrong-doing.' Here, an offense is incurred only by one who obstructs a lodging from one who is entitled to it. However, in the case of quarrel-makers and the like, there is no offense for one who, after informing the Saṅgha of the agreement, saying, 'There is no space,' etc., does not assign a lodging. Nor is there an offense for one who prevents someone who, thinking, 'I am senior,' forcibly assigns a lodging to himself and takes it, by saying, 'Take it according to what is proper.' Regarding the statement, 'Expel the quarrel-maker,' and the permission for an act of banishment for a corrupter of families: since it is said, even for the Kosambians who came here to settle the dispute, not 'according to seniority,' but 'if there is no secluded place, it should be given even after making one secluded,' therefore, an offense is incurred only by one who obstructs a person giving a lodging after having made it secluded—this is stated in the knotty passages.

Upālisaṅghasāmaggīpucchāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Upāli's Questions on Saṅgha Concord

476. Na [V 3.0331] mūlā mūlaṃ gantvāti mūlato mūlaṃ agantvā. Atthato apagatāti sāmaggisaṅkhātaatthato apagatā.

476. Na mūlā mūlaṃ gantvāti means not having gone to a root from a root. Atthato apagatāti means gone from the meaning designated as concord.

477. Yena naṃ paccatthikā vadeyyuṃ, taṃ na hi hotīti sambandho. Anapagatanti kāraṇato anapetaṃ, sakāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti.

477. The connection is: 'That by which his enemies might speak of him does not exist.' Anapagatanti means not departed from the cause; thus it is said to be 'with cause.'

Usūyāyāti iminā dosāgatigamanassa saṅgahitattā “agatigamanenā”ti avasesaagatigamanaṃ dassitanti veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhahi dūtaṅgehīti “sotā ca hoti sāvetā ca uggahetā ca dhāretā ca viññāpetā [M 3.0363] ca kusalo ca sahitāsahitadassano ca akalahakārako cā”ti evaṃ vuttehi aṭṭhahi dūtaṅgehi. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyameva.

It should be understood that by 'usūyāya' (by envy), since going on the wrong course through hatred is included, the remaining wrong courses are shown by 'agatigamanena' (by going on a wrong course). 'Aṭṭhahi dūtaṅgehīti' refers to the eight messenger qualities stated as follows: 'He is one who listens, makes others listen, learns, retains, makes others understand, is skilled, discerns what is beneficial and unbeneficial, and is not a quarrel-maker.' The rest here is easily understood from the Pāli text and the commentary.

Kosambakakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Kosambaka Chapter is concluded.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthadīpanī, the subcommentary to the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mahāvagga is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Cūḷavagga-ṭīkā

The Subcommentary to the Cūḷavagga

1. Kammakkhandhakaṃ

1. The Chapter on Formal Acts

Tajjanīyakammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Act of Censure

1. Cūḷavaggassa [M 3.0365][V 3.0332] paṭhame kammakkhandhake tāva “yaṭṭhiṃ pavesaya, kunte pavesayā”tiādīsu viya sahacaraṇañāyena “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”tiādīsu viya nissitesu nissayavohāravasena vā paṇḍukalohitakanissitā paṇḍukalohitakasaddena vuttāti āha “tesaṃ nissitakāpi paṇḍukalohitakātveva paññāyantī”ti. Paṭivadathāti paṭivacanaṃ detha.

1. In the first, the Chapter on Formal Acts of the Cūḷavagga, just as in phrases like 'let the staff enter, let the spear enter,' etc., by the principle of association, or as in phrases like 'the benches make a squatting sound,' etc., by way of the usage of the term for the support for the supported, those dependent on Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka are referred to by the term 'Paṇḍuka-Lohitaka.' Thus he says, 'Those dependent on them are also known as Paṇḍuka-Lohitaka.' 'Paṭivadathāti' means 'give a reply.'

Adhammakammadvādasakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Twelve Unlawful Acts

4. Tīhi [V 3.0333] aṅgehi samannāgatanti paccekaṃ samuditehi vā tīhi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ. Na hi tiṇṇaṃ eva aṅgānaṃ samodhānena adhammakammaṃ hoti, ekenapi hotiyeva. “Appaṭiññāya kataṃ hotīti lajjiṃ sandhāya vutta”nti gaṇṭhipadesu kathitaṃ.

4. 'Endowed with three factors' means endowed individually or collectively with the three factors. For an unlawful act does not arise only from the concurrence of three factors; it can arise from even one. 'It is done without acknowledgment'—this was said with reference to the modest person, as stated in the knotty passages.

Nanu ca “adesanāgāminiyā āpattiyā kataṃ hotī”ti idaṃ parato “tīhi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgatassa bhikkhuno ākaṅkhamāno saṅgho tajjanīyakammaṃ kareyya, adhisīle sīlavipanno hotī”ti iminā virujjhati. Adesanāgāminiṃ āpanno hi “adhisīle sīlavipanno”ti vuccatīti? Tattha keci vadanti “tajjanīyakammassa hi visesena bhaṇḍanakārakattaṃ aṅga’nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pāḷiyā āgatanidānena sameti, tasmā sabbatikesupi bhaṇḍanaṃ āropetvā bhaṇḍanapaccayā āpannāpattivasena idaṃ kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tasmā ‘adhisīle sīlavipanno’ti etthāpi [M 3.0366] pubbabhāge vā parabhāge vā codanāsāraṇādikāle bhaṇḍanapaccayā āpannāpattivaseneva kātabbaṃ, na kevalaṃ saṅghādisesapaccayā kātabba”nti. Apare pana vadanti “adesanāgāminiyāti idaṃ pārājikāpattiṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ, na saṅghādisesaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ‘adesanāgāminiyāti pārājikāpattiyā vā saṅghādisesāpattiyā vā’ti vuttaṃ. Tattha saṅghādisesāpattiyā vāti atthuddhāravasena vuttaṃ, ‘adhisīle sīlavipanno’ti ca idaṃ saṅghādisesaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pārājikaṃ. Tasmā pārājikāpattipaccayā na tajjanīyakammaṃ kātabbaṃ payojanābhāvā, saṅghādisesapaccayā kātabbanti ayamattho siddho hoti. Sukkapakkhe ‘desanāgāminiyā āpattiyā kataṃ hotī’ti iminā virujjhatīti ce? Na ekena pariyāyena saṅghādisesassapi desanāgāminīvohārasambhavato”ti, taṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati.

But does not the statement, 'It is done for an offense that does not require confession,' contradict what follows: 'Bhikkhus, if the Saṅgha wishes, it may carry out an act of censure on a bhikkhu endowed with three factors: he is corrupt in the higher morality'? For is one who has committed an offense that does not require confession called 'corrupt in the higher morality'? Here, some say: 'In the commentary, it is stated that a factor for the act of censure is specifically being a quarrelsome person. This accords with the origin story that comes in the Pāli text. Therefore, in all three types of cases, this act should be performed by attributing quarrelsomeness and based on an offense incurred due to quarrels. Thus, 'corrupt in the higher morality' here also refers to an offense incurred due to quarrels during the initial or subsequent stages, such as accusation or reminding—not solely based on a Saṅghādisesa offense.' Others, however, say: 'The phrase "adesanāgāminiyā" (not requiring confession) refers only to a Pārājika offense, not a Saṅghādisesa. However, in the commentary, it is stated, "adesanāgāminiyā" means "either a Pārājika offense or a Saṅghādisesa offense." Here, "or a Saṅghādisesa offense" is mentioned by way of drawing out the meaning. And the phrase "adhisīle sīlavipanno" (corrupt in the higher morality) refers specifically to a Saṅghādisesa, not a Pārājika. Therefore, the act of censure should not be imposed for a Pārājika offense due to lack of purpose, but it should be imposed for a Saṅghādisesa—this meaning is established. If it is asked, "Does this contradict the statement in the wholesome section, 'It is done for an offense that requires confession'?" No, because in one sense, even a Saṅghādisesa can be spoken of as requiring confession.' This seems reasonable.

Nappaṭippassambhetabbaaṭṭhārasakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Eighteen Topics Not to Be Revoked

8. Lomaṃ pātentītiādi sammāvattanāya pariyāyavacanaṃ.

8. 'Making the hair stand on end,' and so on, is a circumlocution for proper conduct.

Niyassakammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Act of Dependence

11. Niyassakamme “nissāya te vatthabbanti garunissayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na itara”nti kenaci likhitaṃ. Gaṇṭhipade pana “niyassakammaṃ yasmā bālavasena karīyati, tasmā nissāya vatthabbanti [V 3.0334] nissayaṃ gāhāpetabbo”ti vuttaṃ, vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ. Apissūti ettha suiti nipātamattaṃ, bhikkhū api niccabyāvaṭā hontīti vuttaṃ hoti.

11. Regarding the act of dependence, someone has written: "'You should live in dependence' refers to dependence on a senior, not on another." However, in the Gaṇṭhipada it is stated: "Since the act of dependence is performed on account of foolishness, he should be made to take dependence, with the words, 'You should live in dependence.'" The more appropriate interpretation should be adopted after examination. In "apissūti," "su" is merely a particle; what is meant is that bhikkhus are also constantly engaged.

Pabbājanīyakammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Act of Banishment

29. Pabbājanīyakamme tena hi, bhikkhave, saṅgho pabbājanīyakammaṃ paṭippassambhetūti idaṃ tesu vibbhamantesupi pakkamantesupi sammāvattanteyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ.

29. Regarding the act of banishment, the statement "Therefore, bhikkhus, the Saṅgha should revoke the act of banishment" was said with reference to those who, even while disoriented and departing, still conduct themselves properly.

Paṭisāraṇīyakammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Act of Reconciliation

33. Sudhammavatthusmiṃ macchikāsaṇḍeti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tattha kira (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.72 cittagahapativatthu) citto gahapati pañcavaggiyānaṃ abbhantaraṃ mahānāmattheraṃ piṇḍāya caramānaṃ disvā [M 3.0367] tassa iriyāpathe pasīditvā pattaṃ ādāya gehaṃ pavesetvā bhojetvā bhattakiccāvasāne dhammakathaṃ suṇanto sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā acalasaddho hutvā ambāṭakavanaṃ nāma attano uyyānaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kātukāmo therassa hatthe udakaṃ pātetvā niyyātesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe “patiṭṭhitaṃ buddhasāsana”nti udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahāpathavī kampi, mahāseṭṭhi uyyāne mahāvihāraṃ kāresi. Tatthāyaṃ sudhammo bhikkhu āvāsiko ahosi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “āyasmā sudhammo macchikāsaṇḍe cittassa gahapatino āvāsiko hotī”tiādi. Tattha dhuvabhattikoti niccabhattiko.

33. In the story of Sudhamma, in a town named Macchikāsaṇḍa, it is said that the householder Citta, seeing the Elder Mahānāma, who was one of the group of five, wandering for alms, was pleased with his deportment. Taking his bowl, he led him into his house, fed him, and after the meal, while listening to a Dhamma talk, he attained the fruit of stream-entry and became unshakably faithful. Desiring to make his own park named Ambāṭakavana into a monastery for the Saṅgha, he poured water over the Elder’s hands and dedicated it. At that moment, the great earth shook, as if to mark the end of the water-pouring with the words, "The Buddha’s Dispensation is established!" The great merchant then built a large monastery in the park. The bhikkhu Sudhamma was a resident there. It is with reference to this that it is said, "The Venerable Sudhamma was a resident of the householder Citta in Macchikāsaṇḍa," and so on. There, "dhuvabhattiko" means one who regularly receives meals.

Aparena samayena cittassa guṇakathaṃ sutvā bhikkhusahassena saddhiṃ dve aggasāvakā tassa saṅgahaṃ kattukāmā macchikāsaṇḍaṃ agamaṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “tena kho pana samayena sambahulā therā”tiādi. Citto gahapati tesaṃ āgamanaṃ sutvā addhayojanamattaṃ paccuggantvā te ādāya attano vihāraṃ pavesetvā āgantukavattaṃ katvā “bhante, thokaṃ dhammakathaṃ sotukāmomhī”ti dhammasenāpatiṃ yāci. Atha naṃ thero “upāsaka, addhānenāmhā kilantarūpā, apica thokaṃ suṇāhī”ti tassa dhammakathaṃ kathesi. Tena vuttaṃ “ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho cittaṃ gahapatiṃ āyasmā sāriputto dhammiyā kathāya sandassesī”tiādi. So therassa dhammakathaṃ suṇantova anāgāmiphalaṃ pāpuṇi.

On a later occasion, having heard praise of Citta’s virtues, the two chief disciples, along with a thousand bhikkhus, went to Macchikāsaṇḍa, desiring to favor him. Regarding this, it is said, "At that time, many Elders," and so on. Hearing of their arrival, the householder Citta went out about half a league to meet them, led them to his monastery, performed the duties for incoming guests, and requested the General of the Dhamma, saying, "Venerable sir, we wish to hear a brief Dhamma talk." The Elder replied, "Householder, we are weary from the journey, but still, listen a little," and gave him a Dhamma talk. Hence, it is said, "The Venerable Sāriputta instructed the householder Citta, who was seated to one side, with a Dhamma talk," and so on. While listening to the Elder’s Dhamma talk, he attained the fruit of non-returning.

41. Nāsakkhi cittaṃ gahapatiṃ khamāpetunti so tattha gantvā “gahapati, mayhameva so doso[V 3.0335], khamāhi me”ti vatvāpi “nāhaṃ khamāmī”ti tena paṭikkhitto maṅkubhūto taṃ khamāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. Punadeva satthu santikaṃ paccāgamāsi. Satthā “nāssa upāsako khamissatī”ti jānantopi “mānathaddho esa tiṃsayojanaṃ gantvāva paccāgacchatū”ti khamanupāyaṃ anācikkhitvāva uyyojesi. Athassa puna āgatakāle nihatamānassa anudūtaṃ datvā “gaccha, iminā saddhiṃ gantvā upāsakaṃ khamāpehī”ti vatvā “samaṇena nāma ‘mayhaṃ vihāro, mayhaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ, mayhaṃ upāsako, mayhaṃ upāsikā’ti mānaṃ vā issaṃ vā kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Evaṃ karontassa hi icchāmānādayo kilesā vaḍḍhantī”ti ovadanto –

41. He was unable to get the householder Citta to forgive him. So he went there and said, "Householder, the fault is mine alone, please forgive me," but was rebuffed with, "I will not forgive you." Crestfallen, he was unable to get him to forgive. He then returned to the Teacher. Though the Teacher knew the householder would not forgive him, he sent him away without explaining any means of reconciliation, thinking, "Let this arrogant man go thirty leagues and then return." When he came back later, his pride humbled, the Teacher gave him an accompanying messenger, saying, "Go, accompany him and ask the householder for forgiveness," and admonished him: "A recluse should not entertain pride or envy, thinking, 'This is my monastery, this is my dwelling place, this is my male lay follower, this is my female lay follower.' For one who acts thus, defilements such as desire and pride increase."

“Asantaṃ [M 3.0368] bhāvanamiccheyya, purekkhārañca bhikkhusu;

Āvāsesu ca issariyaṃ, pūjā parakulesu ca.

"He might desire a status he does not possess, and prominence among bhikkhus; authority in monasteries, and veneration from other families.

“Mameva kata maññantu, gihī pabbajitā ubho;

Mamevātivasā assu, kiccākiccesu kismici;

Iti bālassa saṅkappo, icchā māno ca vaḍḍhatī”ti. (dha. pa. 73-74) –

"‘Let both householders and the ordained think this was done by me alone; let them be under my authority alone in any matter whatsoever.’ Such is the thought of a fool; his desire and pride increase."

Dhammapade imā gāthā abhāsi.

He spoke these verses in the Dhammapada.

Sudhammattheropi imaṃ ovādaṃ sutvā satthāraṃ vanditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tena anudūtena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ gantvā upāsakassa cakkhupathe āpattiṃ paṭikaritvā upāsakaṃ khamāpesi. So upāsakena “khamāmahaṃ bhante, sace mayhaṃ doso atthi, khamatha me”ti paṭikhamāpito satthārā dinnaovāde ṭhatvā katipāheneva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Hearing this admonishment, the Elder Sudhamma paid homage to the Teacher, rose from his seat, circumambulated him, and went with that accompanying bhikkhu. Having made amends for his offense within the householder's sight, he asked for the householder's forgiveness. And having been asked for forgiveness in turn by the householder, who said, 'I forgive you, venerable sir. If there is any fault in me, please forgive me,' he stood firm in the instruction given by the Teacher and within a few days attained arahantship together with the analytical insights.

Āpattiyā adassane ukkhepanīyakammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Act of Suspension for Not Seeing an Offense

50. Tassā adassaneyeva kammaṃ kātabbanti tassā adassaneyeva ukkhepanīyakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tajjanīyādikammaṃ pana āpattiṃ āropetvā tassā adassane appaṭikamme vā bhaṇḍanakārakādiaṅgehi kātabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

50. The act should be performed only for her non-acknowledgment means that the act of suspension should be performed only for her non-acknowledgment. However, an act such as censure should be performed by charging her with the offense, in the case of her non-acknowledgment or not making amends, or due to factors such as being quarrelsome, and so forth. The rest here is self-evident.

Kammakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Formal Acts is concluded.

2. Pārivāsikakkhandhakaṃ

2. The Chapter on Probation.

Pārivāsikavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of the Probationary Duties.

75. Pārivāsikakkhandhake [M 3.0369][V 3.0336] navakataraṃ pārivāsikanti attano navakataraṃ pārivāsikaṃ. Pārivāsikassa hi attano navakataraṃ pārivāsikaṃ ṭhapetvā aññe mūlāyapaṭikassanārahamānattārahamānattacārikaabbhānārahāpi pakatattaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhanti. Tenāha “antamaso mūlāyapaakassanārahādīnampī”ti. Pāde ghaṃsenti etenāti pādaghaṃsanaṃ, sakkharakathalādi. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tisso pādaghaṃsaniyo sakkharaṃ kathalaṃ samuddapheṇaka”nti (cūḷava. 269) hi vuttaṃ. Saddhivihārikādīnampi sādiyantassāti saddhivihārikānampi abhivādanādiṃ sādiyantassa. “Mā maṃ gāmappavesanaṃ āpucchathā”ti vutte anāpucchāpi gāmaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati. Yo yo vuḍḍhoti pārivāsikesu bhikkhūsu yo yo vuḍḍho. Navakatarassa sāditunti pārivāsikanavakatarassa abhivādanādiṃ sādituṃ.

75. In the Chapter on Probation, 'a newer probationer' means a probationer newer than oneself. For a probationer, indeed, excluding a probationer newer than oneself, others—even those deserving of being sent back to the root, deserving of mānatta, practicing mānatta-conduct, or deserving of rehabilitation—remain in the status of a regular monk. Therefore it is said: 'even those deserving of being sent back to the root, and so forth.' 'That by which one scrubs the feet' is a foot-scrubber, such as gravel, pebbles, and so forth. For it is said: 'Monks, I allow three kinds of foot-scrubbers: gravel, pebbles, and sea foam' (Cūḷavagga 269). 'For one who accepts from co-residents, and so forth' means for one who accepts homage, and so forth, from co-residents. When it is said, 'Do not ask me for permission to enter the village,' it is permissible to enter the village even without asking. 'Whoever is senior' means whoever is senior among the monks on probation. 'To accept from a newer one' means to accept homage, and so forth, from a newer probationer.

Tatthevāti saṅghanavakaṭṭhāneyeva. Attano pāḷiyā pavāretabbanti attano vassaggena pattapāḷiyā pavāretabbaṃ, na pana sabbesu pavāritesūti attho. Yadi pana na gaṇhāti na vissajjetīti yadi purimadivase attano na gaṇhāti gahetvā ca na vissajjeti. Catussālabhattanti bhojanasālāyaṃ paṭipāṭiyā diyyamānabhattaṃ. Hatthapāse ṭhitenāti dāyakassa hatthapāse ṭhitena.

'There, in the same place' means in the place of the most junior of the Sangha. 'One should invite according to one's own turn' means one should invite according to the turn obtained by one's seniority in rains-residence, not, however, after all have invited—this is the meaning. 'But if one does not accept or does not release' means if on the previous day one does not accept it for oneself, and having accepted it, does not release it. 'The meal in the four-hall' means food given in sequence in the dining hall. 'Standing within arm's reach' means standing within the donor's arm's reach.

76. Añño sāmaṇero na gahetabboti upajjhāyena hutvā añño sāmaṇero na gahetabbo. Upajjhaṃ datvā gahitasāmaṇerāpīti pakatattakāle upajjhaṃ datvā gahitasāmaṇerāpi. Laddhasammutikena āṇattopi garudhammehi aññehi vā ovadituṃ labhatīti āha “paṭibalassa vā bhikkhussa bhāro kātabbo”ti. Āgatā bhikkhuniyo vattabbāti sambandho. Savacanīyanti sadosaṃ[V 3.0337]. Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhānaṃ na kātabbanti padhānaṭṭhānaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Kiṃ tanti āha “pātimokkhuddesakena vā”tiādi.

76. 'Another novice should not be taken' means that having become a preceptor, another novice should not be taken. 'Even novices taken after one has given a preceptor' means even novices taken after one has given a preceptor while in the state of a regular monk. One who has obtained authorization, even if commanded, is able to advise regarding the grave rules or other matters; thus it is said: 'Or the burden should be placed on a competent monk.' 'The bhikkhunīs who have arrived should be spoken to'—this is the connection. 'Liable to be spoken to' means faulty. 'The position of a senior should not be taken' means the principal position should not be taken. 'What is that?' He said: 'Or by the reciter of the Pātimokkha,' and so on.

Rajehi [M 3.0370] hatā upahatā bhūmi etissāti rajohatabhūmi, rajokiṇṇabhūmīti attho. Paccayanti vassāvāsikalābhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ekapasse ṭhatvāti pāḷiṃ vihāya bhikkhūnaṃ pacchato ṭhatvā. Senāsanaṃ na labhatīti seyyāpariyantabhāgitāya vassaggena gaṇhituṃ na labhati. Assāti bhaveyya. “Āgantukena ārocetabbaṃ, āgantukassa ārocetabba”nti avisesena vuttattā sace dve pārivāsikā gataṭṭhāne aññamaññaṃ passanti, ubhohipi aññamaññassa ārocetabbaṃ. Yathā bahi disvā ārocitassa bhikkhuno vihāraṃ āgate puna ārocanakiccaṃ natthi, evaṃ aññaṃ vihāraṃ gatenapi tattha pubbe ārocitassa puna ārocanakiccaṃ natthīti vadanti.

'Ground affected by dust' is rajohatabhūmi, meaning ground strewn with dust. 'Requisites' is said with reference to the gains of the rains-residence. 'Standing on one side' means standing behind the monks, having given up one's turn. 'Does not obtain lodging' means one is not able to obtain it by seniority in rains-residence as one who receives a share of the sleeping places. 'Assa' means 'it would be'. Since it is stated without distinction that 'a newcomer should inform, and a newcomer should be informed,' if two monks on probation see each other at a place they have gone to, both should inform each other. Just as for a monk who has been informed after being seen outside, there is no further duty of informing upon his arrival at the monastery, so too, for one who has gone to another monastery, there is no duty of informing again one who was previously informed there—so they say.

81. Avisesenāti pārivāsikassa ukkhittakassa ca avisesena. Obaddhanti palibuddhaṃ.

81. 'Without distinction' means without distinction between a probationer and one who has been suspended. 'Bound' means hampered.

83. Sahavāsoti vuttappakāre channe pakatattena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ sayanameva adhippetaṃ, na sesairiyāpathakappanaṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

83. 'Living together' means specifically sleeping together with a regular monk in the manner stated regarding Channa; it is not intended to mean adopting other postures. The rest here is easily understood.

Pārivāsikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Probation is concluded.

3. Samuccayakkhandhakaṃ

3. The Chapter on Collections.

Sukkavissaṭṭhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Emission of Semen.

97. Samuccayakkhandhake [M 3.0371][V 3.0338] vuttanayena vattaṃ samādātabbanti pārivāsikakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena dvīhi padehi ekena vā samādātabbaṃ. Vediyāmīti cittena sampaṭicchitvā sukhaṃ anubhavāmi, na tappaccayā ahaṃ dukkhitoti adhippāyo. Vuttanayeneva saṅghamajjhe nikkhipitabbanti pārivāsikakkhandhake vuttanayena “mānattaṃ nikkhipāmi, vattaṃ nikkhipāmī”ti imehi dvīhi ekena vā nikkhipitabbaṃ. Tassa ārocetvā nikkhipitabbanti anārocanena vattabhedadukkaṭaparimocanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Dve leḍḍupāte atikkamitvāti bhikkhūnaṃ sajjhāyanasaddasavanūpacāravijahanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, mahāmaggato okkammāti maggappaṭipannabhikkhūnaṃ upacāravijahanatthaṃ, gumbena vā vatiyā vā paṭicchannaṭṭhāneti dassanūpacāravijahanatthaṃ. Anikkhittavattena antoupacāragatānaṃ sabbesampi ārocetabbattā “ayaṃ nikkhittavattassa parihāro”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha nikkhittavattassāti vattaṃ nikkhipitvā parivasantassāti attho. Ayaṃ panettha therassa adhippāyo – vattaṃ nikkhipitvā parivasantassa upacāragatānaṃ sabbesaṃ ārocanakiccaṃ natthi, diṭṭharūpānaṃ sutasaddānaṃ ārocetabbaṃ, adiṭṭhaasutānampi antodvādasahatthagatānaṃ ārocetabbaṃ. Idaṃ vattaṃ nikkhipitvā parivasantassa lakkhaṇanti.

97. In the Chapter on Collections, 'the observance should be undertaken in the manner stated' means it should be undertaken with two phrases or with one, in the manner stated in the explanation of the Chapter on Probation. 'I feel' means: having accepted it with the mind, 'I experience pleasure, and I am not distressed on account of it'—this is the intention. 'It should be laid down in the midst of the Sangha in the manner stated' means it should be laid down with these two phrases, 'I lay down the mānatta,' 'I lay down the observance,' or with one of them, in the manner stated in the Chapter on Probation. 'It should be laid down after informing him' is said for the purpose of being freed from the dukkaṭa offense of breaking the observance by not informing. 'After going beyond two clod-throws' is said for the purpose of abandoning the range of hearing the sound of the monks' recitation; 'stepping off the main road' is for the purpose of abandoning the range of monks traveling on the road; 'in a place concealed by a bush or a fence' is for the purpose of abandoning the range of sight. Since all who have come within the inner range must be informed by one who has not laid down the observance, it is said: 'This is the exemption for one who has laid down the observance.' Therein, 'for one who has laid down the observance' means for one who is living on probation after having laid down the observance. This, in this matter, is the Elder's intention: for one who is living on probation after having laid down the observance, there is no duty to inform all who have come within range; those whose forms are seen and whose sounds are heard should be informed, and also those unseen and unheard who have come within twelve cubits should be informed. This is the characteristic of one who is living on probation after having laid down the observance.

Parivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Probation.

102. “Satiyeva antarāye antarāyikasaññī chādeti, acchannā hoti. Antarāyikassa pana anantarāyikasaññāya chādayato acchannāvā”tipi pāṭho. Averīti hitakāmo. Uddhaste aruṇeti uṭṭhite aruṇe. Suddhassa santiketi sabhāgasaṅghādisesaṃ anāpannassa santike. Vatthunti asucimocanādivītikkamaṃ.

102. There is also this reading: 'When there is an obstacle, one who perceives it as an obstacle conceals it, and it is concealed. But for one who conceals an obstacle with the perception of it as a non-obstacle, is it concealed or not concealed?' 'Without enmity' means one who wishes well. 'When the red has appeared' means when the dawn has risen. 'In the presence of a pure one' means in the presence of one who has not incurred a similar Saṅghādisesa offense. 'Object' means a transgression such as the emission of impurity.

Sukkavissaṭṭhīti [V 3.0339] vatthu ceva gottañcāti sukkavissaṭṭhīti idaṃ asucimocanalakkhaṇassa vītikkamassa pakāsanato vatthu ceva hoti, sajātiyasādhāraṇavijātiyavinivattasabhāvāya sukkavissaṭṭhiyā eva pakāsanato gottañca hotīti attho. Gaṃ tāyatīti hi gottaṃ. Saṅghādisesoti [M 3.0372] nāmañceva āpatti cāti saṅghādisesoti tena tena vītikkamena āpannassa āpattinikāyassa nāmappakāsanato nāmañceva hoti āpattisabhāgattā āpatti ca.

The emission of semen is both the basis and the lineage. The term 'sukkavissaṭṭhi' (emission of semen) is the basis because it reveals the transgression characterized by the emission of impurity, and it is also the lineage because it reveals the nature of the emission of semen, which is common to its own kind and distinct from other kinds. For 'gotta' (lineage) is that which protects (gaṃ tāyati). The term 'saṅghādisesa' is both the name and the offense. It is called 'saṅghādisesa' because it reveals the name of the category of offense incurred through those various transgressions, and it is also the offense because of its nature as an offense.

Tadanurūpaṃ kammavācaṃ katvā mānattaṃ dātabbanti –

Having performed the appropriate formal act, the mānatta should be given—

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu ekaṃ āpattiṃ āpajji sañcetanikaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ ekāhapaṭicchannaṃ, so saṅghaṃ ekissā āpattiyā sañcetanikāya sukkavissaṭṭhiyā ekāhapaṭicchannāya ekāhaparivāsaṃ yāci. Saṅgho itthannāmassa bhikkhuno ekissā āpattiyā sañcetanikāya sukkavissaṭṭhiyā ekāhapaṭicchannāya ekāhaparivāsaṃ adāsi. So parivutthaparivāso. Ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu ekaṃ āpattiṃ āpajji sañcetanikaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ appaṭicchannaṃ, so saṅghaṃ tāsaṃ āpattīnaṃ sañcetanikānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhīnaṃ paṭicchannāya ca appaṭicchannāya ca chārattaṃ mānattaṃ yācati. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dvinnaṃ āpattīnaṃ sañcetanikānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhīnaṃ paṭicchannāya ca appaṭicchannāya ca chārattaṃ mānattaṃ dadeyya, esā ñatti.

“Venerable sir, may the Sangha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has committed one offense—intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day. He requested from the Sangha a one-day probation for that one intentional offense of emission of semen, concealed for one day. The Sangha granted the monk named so-and-so a one-day probation for the one intentional offense of emission of semen, concealed for one day. Having completed the probation, this monk named so-and-so has committed one offense—intentional emission of semen, unconcealed. He requests from the Sangha a six-night mānatta for these offenses—intentional emissions of semen, both concealed and unconcealed. If it is the proper time for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant the monk named so-and-so a six-night mānatta for the two offenses—intentional emissions of semen, both concealed and unconcealed. This is the motion.

Suṇātu me, bhante…pe… so parivutthaparivāso. Ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu ekaṃ āpattiṃ āpajji sañcetanikaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ appaṭicchannaṃ, so saṅghaṃ tāsaṃ…pe… yācati. Saṅgho itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dvinnaṃ āpattīnaṃ sañcetanikānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhīnaṃ paṭicchannāya ca appaṭicchannāya ca chārattaṃ mānattaṃ deti. Yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dvinnaṃ āpattīnaṃ sañcetanikānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhīnaṃ paṭicchannāya ca appaṭicchannāya ca chārattaṃ mānattassa dānaṃ, so tuṇhassa. Yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

“Venerable sir, may the Sangha listen to me… He has completed the probation. This monk named so-and-so has committed an offense—intentional emission of semen, unconcealed. He requests from the Sangha… for these offenses… The Sangha grants this monk named so-and-so a six-night mānatta for two offenses—intentional emissions of semen, both concealed and unconcealed. If it is agreeable to any venerable one to grant this monk named so-and-so a six-night mānatta for two offenses—intentional emissions of semen, both concealed and unconcealed—he should remain silent. If it is not agreeable, he should speak.”

Dutiyampi etamatthaṃ vadāmi…pe… tatiyampi etamatthaṃ vadāmi…pe…

For the second time, I speak on this matter… For the third time, I speak on this matter…

Dinnaṃ saṅghena itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dvinnaṃ āpattīnaṃ sañcetanikānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhīnaṃ [V 3.0340] paṭicchannāya ca appaṭicchannāya ca chārattaṃ mānattaṃ, khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī. Evametaṃ dhārayāmīti –

The Sangha has granted the six-night mānatta to the monk named so-and-so for the two intentional offenses of emission of semen, both concealed and unconcealed. It is agreeable to the Sangha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold it.

Evaṃ [M 3.0373] kammavācaṃ katvā mānattaṃ dātabbaṃ. Ciṇṇamānattassa ca imināva nayena kammavācaṃ yojetvā abbhānaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Having performed this formal act, the mānatta should be given. After the completion of mānatta, reinstatement should be performed by applying the formal act in this very manner.

Aññasminti suddhantaparivāsavasena āpattivuṭṭhānato aññasmiṃ. Dasasataṃ āpattiyo rattisataṃ chādayitvāti yojetabbaṃ.

‘In another’ means in a different instance from the emergence from the offense by way of pure probation. ‘A thousand offenses’ should be construed as having concealed them for a hundred nights.

Parivāsakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Probation is concluded.

Attano sīmaṃ sodhetvā vihārasīmāyāti vihāre baddhasīmameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vihārūpacāratopi dve leḍḍupātā atikkamitabbāti bhikkhuvihāraṃ sandhāya vadati gāmūpacārātikkameneva bhikkhunīvihārūpacārātikkamassa siddhattā. Vihārassa cāti bhikkhuvihārassa. Gāmassāti na vuttanti gāmassa upacāraṃ muñcituṃ vaṭṭatīti na vuttaṃ, tasmā gāmūpacārepi vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo.

Having purified one’s own boundary, “within the monastery boundary” is stated with reference to the established boundary within the monastery itself. And “one must go beyond two stone-throws from the monastery precinct” is stated with reference to a monks’ monastery, since the exceeding of a nuns’ monastery precinct is already accomplished by the exceeding of a village precinct. “And of the monastery” means of the monks’ monastery. “Of the village”—it is not stated that it is allowable to leave the village precinct; therefore, the intention is that it is also allowable within the village precinct.

Tattheva ṭhānaṃ paccāsīsantīti bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ paccāsīsanti. Parivāsavattādīnanti parivāsanissayapaṭippassaddhiādīnaṃ. Yuttataraṃ dissatīti iminā anikkhittavattabhikkhunā viya bhikkhuniyāpi antoupacārasīmagatānaṃyeva ārocetabbaṃ, na gāme ṭhitānampi gantvā ārocetabbanti dīpeti. Tasmiṃ gāmeti yasmiṃ gāme bhikkhunupassayo hoti, tasmiṃ gāme. Bahi upacārasīmāya ṭhatvāti upacārasīmato bahi ṭhatvā. Sammannitvā dātabbāti ettha sammannitvā dinnāya sahavāsepi ratticchedo na hoti.

“There, they expect a place” means they expect a place for the bhikkhus. “Regarding the probation observances, etc.” means probation, dependence, cessation, etc. “A more fitting view appears” indicates that just as with a bhikkhu who has not laid down the observance, so too a bhikkhunī should inform only those who have entered the inner precinct boundary, and not go and inform even those staying in the village. “In that village” means in whichever village there is a bhikkhunī residence. “Standing outside the boundary of the precinct” means having stood outside the boundary of the precinct. “Having agreed, it should be given”—here, even with cohabitation with one given after agreement, there is no break in the nights.

Paṭicchannaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Probation for Concealment

108. Visuṃ mānattaṃ caritabbanti mūlāyapaṭikassanaṃ akatvā visuṃ kammavācāya mānattaṃ gahetvā caritabbaṃ.

108. “To observe mānatta separately” means that, without performing the sending back to the beginning, mānatta should be undertaken and observed by means of a separate formal act.

Sukkavissaṭṭhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Emission of Semen is concluded.

Agghasamodhānaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Probation of Consolidation

134. Ekāpattimūlakanti [M 3.0374][V 3.0341] “ekā āpatti ekāhappaṭicchannā, ekā āpatti dvīhappaṭicchannā”tiādinā vuttanayaṃ sandhāya vadati. Āpattivaḍḍhanakanti “ekā āpatti ekāhappaṭicchannā, dve āpattiyo dvīhappaṭicchannā”tiādinā vuttaṃ āpattivaḍḍhanakanayaṃ sandhāya.

134. “Based on a single offense” refers to the method stated as “one offense concealed for one day, one offense concealed for two days,” and so on. “Increasing the offenses” refers to the method of increasing offenses stated as “one offense concealed for one day, two offenses concealed for two days,” and so on.

Dvebhikkhuvāraekādasakādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Account of the Two Bhikkhus, the Elevenfold Section, and So Forth

181. Thullaccayādīhi missakanti ekavatthumhi pubbabhāge āpannathullaccayadukkaṭehi missakaṃ. Makkhadhammo nāma chādetukāmatā.

181. “Mixed with grave offenses and so forth” means mixed with grave offenses and wrongdoings incurred in a previous part of a single matter. “The quality of denigration” means the desire to conceal.

182. Sambahulā saṅghādisesā āpattiyo āpajjati parimāṇampītiādi jātivasenekavacanaṃ, bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso vā. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyameva.

182. He commits several offenses entailing suspension, whether of a measurable quantity, and so forth. This is a singular expression in terms of class, or a neuter designation in terms of development. The rest here should be easily understood from the Pāli and the commentary.

Samuccayakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Collection is concluded.

4. Samathakkhandhakaṃ

4. The Chapter on Settlements

Sammukhāvinayakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Face-to-Face Procedure

187. Samathakkhandhake [M 3.0375][V 3.0342] saññāpetīti ettha saṃ-saddūpapado ñā-saddo tosanavisiṭṭhe avabodhane vattatīti āha “paritosetvā jānāpetī”ti.

187. In the Chapter on Settlements, regarding `saññāpeti`, it is said that the root `ñā`, when preceded by the prefix `saṃ-`, functions in the sense of an understanding qualified by satisfaction. Thus, it is said, “having fully satisfied, he makes it known.”

Sativinayādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Discipline of Mindfulness and So Forth

195-200. Desanāmattamevetanti “pañcimānī”ti etaṃ desanāmattaṃ. Sativepullappattassa khīṇāsavassa dātabbo vinayo sativinayo. Amūḷhassa dātabbo vinayo amūḷhavinayo. Paṭiññātena karaṇaṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ.

195-200. “Merely the teaching” means that “these five” is merely a teaching. The discipline to be given to one who has attained fullness of mindfulness, an arahant, is the discipline of mindfulness. The discipline to be given to one who is not deluded is the discipline of non-delusion. Doing according to what has been acknowledged is the procedure based on acknowledgement.

212. Tiṇavatthārakasadisattāti taṃsadisatāya tabbohāroti dasseti yathā “esa brahmadatto”ti.

212. The phrase “because of its similarity to covering with grass” shows that this expression is used due to that similarity, just as in the expression, “this is Brahmadatta.”

Adhikaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Disputes

216. Vivādādhikaraṇassa kiṃ mūlantiādīsu vivādamūlānīti vivādassa mūlāni. Kodhanoti kujjhanalakkhaṇena kodhena samannāgato. Upanāhīti veraappaṭinissaggalakkhaṇena upanāhena samannāgato. Agāravoti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.323; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.44) gāravavirahito. Appatissoti appatissayo anīcavutti. Ettha pana yo bhikkhu satthari dharamāne tīsu kālesu upaṭṭhānaṃ na yāti, satthari anupāhane caṅkamante saupāhano caṅkamati, nīce caṅkame caṅkamante ucce caṅkamati, heṭṭhā vasante upari vasati, satthu dassanaṭṭhāne ubho aṃse pārupati, chattaṃ dhāreti, upāhanaṃ dhāreti, nahāyati, uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā karoti, parinibbute [V 3.0343] vā pana cetiyaṃ vandituṃ na gacchati, cetiyassa paññāyanaṭṭhāne satthudassanaṭṭhāne vuttaṃ sabbaṃ karoti, aññehi ca bhikkhūhi “kasmā evaṃ karosi, na idaṃ vaṭṭati, sammāsambuddhassa nāma lajjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte “tuṇhī hohi, buddho buddhoti vadasi, kiṃ buddho nāmā”ti bhaṇati, ayaṃ satthari agāravo nāma.

216. Regarding “What is the root of a dispute?” and so on, the roots of dispute are the roots of contention. “One who is angry” means one endowed with anger characterized by the nature of being angry. “One who is resentful” means one endowed with resentment characterized by the refusal to relinquish enmity. “Disrespectful” means devoid of respect. “Not reverential” means without reverence, of ignoble conduct. Here, a monk who, while the Teacher is present, does not attend upon him at the three times; when the Teacher walks without sandals, he walks with sandals; when the Teacher walks on a low path, he walks on a high path; when the Teacher dwells below, he dwells above; in a place where the Teacher can be seen, he covers both shoulders, carries an umbrella, wears sandals, bathes, or relieves himself of feces or urine; and after the Teacher’s passing, does not go to pay respects at the shrine, but at a place where the shrine is visible, does all that was said regarding a place where the Teacher can be seen—when other monks say, “Why do you act thus? This is not proper. One should feel shame before the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,”—he replies, “Be silent! You speak of ‘Buddha, Buddha.’ What is a Buddha anyway?” Such a one is called disrespectful toward the Teacher.

Yo [M 3.0376] pana dhammasavane saṅghuṭṭhe sakkaccaṃ na gacchati, sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ na suṇāti, niddāyati vā sallapanto vā nisīdati, sakkaccaṃ na gaṇhāti na vāceti, “kiṃ dhamme agāravaṃ karosī”ti vutte “tuṇhī hohi, dhammo dhammoti vadasi, kiṃ dhammo nāmā”ti vadati, ayaṃ dhamme agāravo nāma. Yo pana therena bhikkhunā anajjhiṭṭho dhammaṃ deseti uddisati pañhaṃ katheti, vuḍḍhe bhikkhū ghaṭṭento gacchati tiṭṭhati nisīdati, dussapallatthikaṃ vā hatthapallatthikaṃ vā karoti, saṅghamajjhe ubho aṃse pārupati, chattupāhanaṃ dhāreti, “bhikkhusaṅghassa lajjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttepi “tuṇhī hohi, saṅgho saṅghoti vadasi, kiṃ saṅgho, migasaṅgho ajasaṅgho”tiādīni vadati, ayaṃ saṅghe agāravo nāma. Ekabhikkhusmimpi hi agārave kate saṅghe katoyeva hoti. Tisso sikkhā pana apūrayamāno sikkhāya na paripūrakārī nāma.

One who, when the Dhamma recitation is announced, does not go attentively, does not listen to the Dhamma attentively, either dozes or engages in conversation while sitting, does not learn or recite it attentively, and when told, “Why do you disrespect the Dhamma?” replies, “Be quiet! You keep saying ‘Dhamma, Dhamma,’ but what is this Dhamma anyway?”—this is called disrespect for the Dhamma. One who, without being requested by a senior monk, teaches the Dhamma, recites, or answers questions; who jostles elder monks while walking, standing, or sitting; who sits with his knees bound by a cloth or clasped by his hands; who covers both shoulders in the midst of the Sangha; who carries an umbrella or wears sandals; and when told, “You should be ashamed before the Sangha,” replies, “Be quiet! You keep saying ‘Sangha, Sangha,’ but what is this Sangha, a herd of deer or a herd of goats?”—this is called disrespect for the Sangha. For even when disrespect is shown to a single monk, it is done to the Sangha itself. But one who does not fulfill the three trainings is called one who does not complete the training.

Ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānanti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.325; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.42; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.6.36) ekasmiṃ vihāre dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ uppannavivādo kathaṃ devamanussānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattati? Kosambakakkhandhake viya hi dvīsu bhikkhūsu vivādaṃ āpannesu tasmiṃ vihāre tesaṃ antevāsikā vivadanti, tesaṃ ovādaṃ gaṇhanto bhikkhunisaṅgho vivadati, tato tesaṃ upaṭṭhākā vivadanti, atha manussānaṃ ārakkhadevatā dve koṭṭhāsā honti. Tattha dhammavādīnaṃ ārakkhadevatā dhammavādiniyo honti, adhammavādīnaṃ adhammavādiniyo. Tato ārakkhadevatānaṃ mittā bhummadevatā bhijjanti. Evaṃ paramparāya yāva brahmalokā ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake sabbe devamanussā dve koṭṭhāsā honti. Dhammavādīhi pana adhammavādinova bahutarā honti. Tato “yaṃ bahukehi gahitaṃ, taṃ taccha”nti dhammaṃ vissajjetvā bahutarā adhammaṃ gaṇhanti. Te adhammaṃ purakkhatvā viharantā apāyesu nibbattanti. Evaṃ ekasmiṃ vihāre dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ uppanno vivādo bahūnaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya hoti. Ajjhattaṃ vāti attani vā attano parisāya vā. Bahiddhā vāti parasmiṃ vā parassa parisāya vā. Āyatiṃ anavassavāyāti āyatiṃ anuppādāya.

For the harm and suffering of gods and humans. In one monastery, how does a dispute that arises between two monks lead to harm and suffering for gods and humans? Just as in the Kosambaka chapter, when two monks fall into dispute, their resident pupils quarrel, the community of nuns taking their instruction quarrels, then their supporters quarrel, and the guardian deities of humans split into two factions. There, the guardian deities of those who advocate the Dhamma side with those who advocate the Dhamma, while the guardian deities of those who advocate the non-Dhamma side with those who advocate the non-Dhamma. From there, the friends of the guardian deities—the earth deities—are divided. Thus, in succession, all gods and humans up to the Brahmā world, except for noble disciples, split into two factions. However, those who advocate the non-Dhamma are far more numerous than those who advocate for it. Then, thinking, “What is accepted by the majority is true,” they abandon the Dhamma, and the majority take up the non-Dhamma. Those who live holding the non-Dhamma foremost are reborn in the lower realms. Thus, a dispute that arises between two monks in a single monastery leads to great harm and suffering for many. “Internally” means in oneself or one’s own community. “Externally” means in another or another’s community. “For the non-arising in the future” means for non-production in the future.

Makkhīti [V 3.0344] paresaṃ guṇamakkhanalakkhaṇena makkhena samannāgato. Paḷāsīti yugaggāhalakkhaṇena paḷāsena samannāgato. Issukīti parasakkārādīnaṃ issāyanalakkhaṇāya [M 3.0377] issāya samannāgato. Maccharīti āvāsamacchariyādīhi samannāgato. Saṭhoti kerāṭiko. Māyāvīti katapāpapaṭicchādako. Pāpicchoti asantasambhāvanicchako dussīlo. Micchādiṭṭhīti natthikavādī ahetukavādī akiriyavādī. Sandiṭṭhiparāmāsīti sayaṃ diṭṭhameva parāmasati gaṇhāti. Ādhānaggāhīti daḷhaggāhī. Duppaṭinissaggīti na sakkā hoti gahitaṃ nissajjāpetuṃ. Ettha ca kodhano hoti upanāhītiādinā puggalādhiṭṭhānanayena kodhūpanāhādayo akusaladhammā vivādamūlānīti dassitāni, tathā duṭṭhacittā vivadantītiādinā lobhadosamohā. Aduṭṭhacittā vivadantītiādinā ca alobhādayo vivādamūlānīti dassitāni.

“The contemptuous one” is one endowed with contempt, characterized by disparaging the virtues of others. “The contentious one” is one endowed with contentiousness, characterized by partisanship. “The jealous one” is one endowed with jealousy, characterized by resenting the honors of others and so forth. “The miserly one” is one endowed with stinginess regarding dwellings and so forth. “The fraudulent one” is a cheat. “The deceitful one” is one who conceals his evil deeds. “The one with evil desires” is one of immoral character who desires to be esteemed for virtues he does not possess. “The one with wrong view” is a nihilist, an advocate of causelessness, an advocate of inaction. “The one clinging to his own views” is one who clings to and grasps only his own view. “The one who holds on tenaciously” is one who grasps firmly. “The one who does not easily relinquish” is one who cannot be made to relinquish what he has grasped. Here, by means of the personal designation beginning with “is angry” and “bears hatred,” unwholesome states such as anger and hatred are shown to be roots of dispute. Likewise, by means of “those with corrupted minds quarrel,” greed, hatred, and delusion are shown. And by means of “those with uncorrupted minds quarrel,” non-greed and other wholesome states are also shown to be roots of dispute.

217. Dubbaṇṇoti paṃsupisācako viya jhāmakhāṇuvaṇṇo. Duddassikoti vijātamātuyāpi amanāpadassano. Okoṭimakoti lakuṇḍako. Kāṇoti ekakkhikāṇo vā ubhayakkhikāṇo vā. Kuṇīti ekahatthakuṇī vā ubhayahatthakuṇī vā. Khañjoti ekapādakhañjo vā ubhayapādakhañjo vā. Pakkhahatoti hatapakkho pīṭhasappī.

217. Ugly is like a dust-covered goblin, with a complexion like a burnt stump. Hard to look upon is one whose appearance is displeasing even to the mother who gave him birth. The dwarfish one is a dwarf. The one-eyed is one who is blind in one eye or in both eyes. The crippled is one crippled in one hand or in both hands. The lame is one lame in one foot or in both feet. The paralyzed is one with a paralyzed side, who moves by crawling on a bench.

220. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ kusalaṃ akusalaṃ abyākatanti vivādādhikaraṇaṃ kiṃ kusalaṃ akusalaṃ udāhu abyākatanti pucchati. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusalantiādi vissajjanaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Vivadanti etenāti vivādoti āha “yena vivadanti, so cittuppādo vivādo”ti. Kathaṃ pana so cittuppādo adhikaraṇaṃ nāmāti āha “samathehi ca adhikaraṇīyatāya adhikaraṇa”nti, samathehi sametabbatāya adhikaraṇanti attho. Vivādahetubhūtassa hi cittuppādassa vūpasamena tappabhavassa saddassapi vūpasamo hotīti cittuppādassa samathehi adhikaraṇīyatā pariyāyo sambhavati.

220. The question is asked: "Is a legal issue arising from dispute wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?" The answer is given: "A legal issue arising from dispute may be wholesome," and so on. This is the method for the rest as well. "They dispute by this" — thus, it is called a dispute. It is said: "That mental state by which they dispute is the dispute." But how is that mental state called a legal issue? It is said: "Because it is to be settled by means of settlements, it is a legal issue." The meaning is that it is called a legal issue because it must be resolved through settlements. For by the pacification of the mental state that is the cause of dispute, the pacification of the speech arising from it also occurs. Thus, the designation of the mental state as a legal issue to be settled by means of settlements is appropriate.

222. Āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākatanti ayaṃ vikappo paññattivajjaṃyeva sandhāya vutto, na lokavajjanti dassetuṃ “sandhāyabhāsitavasenā”tiādimāha. Kasmā panettha sandhāyabhāsitavasena attho veditabboti āha “yasmiṃ hī”tiādi. Pathavīkhaṇanādiketi ettha ādi-saddena bhūtagāmapātabyatādipaññattivajjaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ [M 3.0378] saṅgaṇhāti. Yo vinaye apakataññutāya vattasīsena sammuñjaniādinā pathavīkhaṇanādīni karoti, tadā tassuppannacittaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “kusalacittaṃ aṅgaṃ hotī”ti. Aṅgaṃ hotīti ca vattasīsena karontassapi “imaṃ pathaviṃ khaṇāmī”tiādinā vītikkamajānanavasena [V 3.0345] pavattattā taṃ kusalacittaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ, kusalacittaṃ āpattiyā kāraṇaṃ hotīti attho. Na hi vītikkamaṃ ajānantassa pathavīkhaṇanādīsu āpatti sambhavati. Tasmiṃ satīti tasmiṃ kusalacitte āpattibhāvena gahite satīti adhippāyo. Tasmāti yasmā kusalacitte āpattibhāvena gahite sati “natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti na sakkā vattuṃ, tasmā. Nayidaṃ aṅgappahonakacittaṃ sandhāya vuttanti “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākataṃ, natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti idaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhāpakabhāvena aṅgappahonakaṃ āpattiyā kāraṇabhūtaṃ cittaṃ sandhāya na vuttaṃ. Kiṃ pana sandhāya vuttanti āha “idaṃ panā”tiādi. Bhikkhumhi kammaṭṭhānagatacittena nipanne niddāyante vā mātugāmo ce seyyaṃ kappeti, tasmiṃ khaṇe seyyākārena vattamānarūpameva āpatti, na kusalādivasappavattaṃ cittanti āha “asañcicca…pe… sahaseyyādivasena āpajjato (pari. 323 atthato samānaṃ) abyākataṃ hotī”ti. Tasmiñhi khaṇe uṭṭhātabbe jāte anuṭṭhānato tadākārapavatto rūpakkhandhova āpatti.

222. “A legal issue of an offense may be unwholesome or indeterminate”—this distinction is made only with reference to what is blameworthy by rule, not what is blameworthy in the world. To show this, it is said, “by way of speaking with reference to,” etc. But why should the meaning here be understood by way of speaking with reference? It is said, “for in whatever case,” etc. “Digging the earth, etc.”—here, the word “etc.” includes the training rule on what is blameworthy by rule, such as the destruction of plant life. When someone, due to lack of expertise in the discipline, digs the earth, etc., as a matter of duty or by sweeping, etc., then the thought that arises in them is spoken of with reference to that: “a wholesome thought becomes a factor.” “It becomes a factor”—even for one who acts as a matter of duty, because it proceeds with awareness of the transgression, thinking, “I am digging this earth,” etc., that wholesome thought is the legal issue of an offense; the meaning is that the wholesome thought is the cause of the offense. For no offense occurs in digging the earth, etc., if one is unaware of the transgression. “When that exists”—this means when that wholesome thought is taken as the nature of the offense. “Therefore”—because when the wholesome thought is taken as the nature of the offense, it cannot be said, “there is no legal issue of an offense that is wholesome,” therefore— “But this is not said with reference to the thought sufficient for a factor”—the statement, “a legal issue of an offense may be unwholesome or indeterminate, but there is no legal issue of an offense that is wholesome,” is not made with reference to a thought that, by being the originator of the offense, is sufficient for a factor, the cause of the offense. “Then with reference to what is it said?” It is said, “but this,” etc. When a monk, with a mind focused on his meditation subject, is lying down or falling asleep, and a woman lies down with him, at that moment, the offense is solely the physical form continuing in the act of lying down, not a thought proceeding by way of being wholesome, etc. Hence it is said, “unintentionally… by way of lying together, etc., one incurs an indeterminate offense.” For at that moment, when the need to rise has arisen, the offense is simply the form-aggregate continuing in that manner from his not rising.

“Āpattiṃ āpajjanto kusalacitto vā āpajjati akusalābyākatacitto vā”ti vacanato kusalampi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyāti ce? Na. Yo hi āpattiṃ āpajjatīti vuccati, so tīsu cittesu aññataracittasamaṅgī hutvā āpajjati, na aññathāti dassanatthaṃ “kusalacitto vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – pathavīkhaṇanādīsu kusalacittakkhaṇe vītikkamādivasena pavattarūpasambhavato kusalacitto vā tathāpavattarūpasaṅkhātaṃ abyākatāpattiṃ āpajjati, tathā abyākatacitto vā abyākatarūpasaṅkhātaṃ abyākatāpattiṃ āpajjati. Pāṇātipātādiṃ akusalacitto vā akusalāpattiṃ āpajjati, rūpaṃ panettha abbohārikaṃ. Supinante ca pāṇātipātādiṃ karonto sahaseyyādivasena āpajjitabbāpattiṃ āpajjanto akusalacitto abyākatāpattiṃ āpajjatīti.

If it is said that, due to the statement, 'When committing an offense, does one do so with a wholesome mind, or with an unwholesome or indeterminate mind?', a wholesome mind could also be the basis for an offense? No. For when it is said that one commits an offense, it is to show that one commits the offense while endowed with a mind of one of the three types, and not otherwise, that the statement 'with a wholesome mind or...' etc., was made. Here is the meaning in this context: In actions like digging the earth, etc., at the moment of a wholesome mind, because a material form arises by way of transgression, etc., one with a wholesome mind commits an indeterminate offense, reckoned as that arisen material form. Similarly, one with an indeterminate mind commits an indeterminate offense reckoned as an indeterminate material form. One with an unwholesome mind commits an unwholesome offense like killing living beings, etc., but in this case, material form is not conventionally designated. And when one, in a dream, commits killing living beings, etc., or when committing an offense that is to be incurred by way of lying down together, etc., one with an unwholesome mind commits an indeterminate offense.

Kusalacittaṃ [M 3.0379] āpajjeyyāti eḷakalomaṃ gahetvā kammaṭṭhānamanasikārena tiyojanaṃ atikkamantassa paññattiṃ ajānitvā padaso dhammaṃ vācentassa ca āpajjitabbāpattiyā kusalacittaṃ āpajjeyya. Na ca tattha vijjamānampi kusalacittaṃ āpattiyā aṅganti tasmiṃ vijjamānampi kusalacittaṃ āpattiyā aṅgaṃ na hoti, sayaṃ āpatti na hotīti attho. Calitappavattānanti calitānaṃ pavattānañca. Calito kāyo, pavattā vācā. Aññatarameva aṅganti kāyavācānaṃ aññatarameva āpattīti attho. Tañca rūpakkhandhapariyāpannattā abyākatanti iminā abyākatamāpattādhikaraṇaṃ, nāññanti dasseti.

As to 'one might commit it with a wholesome mind': in the case of one who, having taken a tuft of sheep's wool, transgresses a distance of three yojanas while attending to a meditation subject, or of one who, not knowing the regulation, recites the Dhamma word by word, one might commit an offense that is to be incurred with a wholesome mind. And even though a wholesome mind is present there, it is not a factor of the offense—the meaning is that even though a wholesome mind is present in that case, it is not a factor of the offense; it itself is not the offense. 'Of movements and utterances' means of movements and of utterances. Movement is the body; utterance is speech. 'Only one is a factor' means that only one of the two, body or speech, is the offense. And because it is included in the aggregate of form, it is indeterminate—by this, it is shown that the offense-matter is indeterminate, and nothing else.

Yadi [V 3.0346] evaṃ “sāpattikassa, bhikkhave, nirayaṃ vā vadāmi tiracchānayoniṃ vā”ti vacanato abyākatassapi vipākadhammatā āpajjeyyāti? Nāpajjeyya. Asañcicca āpannā hi āpattiyo yāva so na jānāti, tāva anantarāyakarā, jānitvā chādento pana chādanappaccayā aññaṃ dukkaṭasaṅkhātaṃ akusalamāpattādhikaraṇamāpajjati, tañca akusalasabhāvattā saggamokkhānaṃ antarāyakaraṇanti sāpattikassa apāyagāmitā vuttā. Abyākataṃ pana āpattādhikaraṇaṃ avipākadhammamevāti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Teneva porāṇagaṇṭhipadesupi “puthujjano kalyāṇaputhujjano sekkho arahāti cattāro puggale dassetvā tesu arahato āpattādhikaraṇaṃ abyākatameva, tathā sekkhānaṃ, tathā kalyāṇaputhujjanassa asañcicca vītikkamakāle abyākatameva. Itarassa akusalampi hoti abyākatampi. Yasmā cassa sañcicca vītikkamakāle akusalameva hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ ‘natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala’nti. Sabbattha evaṃ abyākatanti vipākābhāvamattaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti likhitaṃ. Yañca āpattādhikaraṇaṃ akusalaṃ, tampi desitaṃ vuṭṭhitaṃ vā anantarāyakaraṃ. Yathā hi ariyūpavādakammaṃ akusalampi samānaṃ accayaṃ desetvā khamāpanena payogasampattipaṭibāhitattā avipākadhammataṃ āpannaṃ ahosikammaṃ hoti, evamidampi desitaṃ vuṭṭhitaṃ vā payogasampattipaṭibāhitattā avipākadhammatāya ahosikammabhāvena anantarāyakaraṃ jātaṃ. Teneva “sāpattikassa, bhikkhave, nirayaṃ vā vadāmi tiracchānayoniṃ vā”ti sāpattikasseva apāyagāmitā vuttā.

If that is so, then from the statement, 'For one who has committed an offense, monks, I declare either hell or the animal realm,' would the nature of having a result apply even to an indeterminate offense-matter? It would not. For offenses committed unintentionally, as long as one does not know of them, are not obstructive. But upon knowing, if one conceals it, then on account of that concealment, one commits another unwholesome offense-matter, reckoned as a dukkaṭa. And because of its unwholesome nature, it becomes an obstruction to heaven and liberation—thus, it is said that one who has committed an offense is destined for the lower realms. However, an offense-matter that is indeterminate is indeed without the nature of having a result; this conclusion should be reached here. Therefore, even in the ancient glosses, it is written: 'Having shown four types of individuals—the ordinary person, the virtuous ordinary person, the trainee, and the Arahant—for the Arahant, the offense-matter is purely indeterminate. Likewise for trainees, and likewise for the virtuous ordinary person at the time of an unintentional transgression—it is purely indeterminate. For the other, it may be unwholesome or indeterminate. And because for him, at the time of an intentional transgression, it is solely unwholesome, it is therefore said, "There is no offense-matter that is wholesome." In all cases, "indeterminate" is said with reference merely to the absence of a result.' And that offense-matter which is unwholesome, when it is confessed or settled, is also non-obstructive. Just as the kamma of disparaging the noble ones, though unwholesome, becomes a kamma that is defunct, having become without the nature of a result because the completion of its application is prevented by confessing the transgression and asking for forgiveness, so too this, when confessed or settled, becomes non-obstructive by becoming a kamma that is defunct due to its nature of being without a result, because the completion of its application is prevented. Therefore, it is said, 'For one who has committed an offense, monks, I declare either hell or the animal realm'—the destiny for the lower realms is stated only for one who has an offense.

Adhikaraṇavūpasamanasamathakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Settlements for Pacifying Legal Questions

228. Vivādasaṅkhāte [M 3.0380] atthe paccatthikā atthapaccatthikā.

228. In a matter reckoned as a dispute, there are opponents and litigants.

229. Sammukhāvinayasminti sammukhāvinayabhāve.

229. Regarding 'in the settlement in the presence,' it means in the state of being a settlement in the presence.

230. Antarenāti kāraṇena.

230. Regarding 'antarena,' it means 'by reason of'.

231. Ubbāhikāya khīyanake pācitti na vuttā tattha chandadānassa natthitāya.

231. In the case of a referendum regarding a complaint, a pācittiya offense is not stated, because in that case there is no giving of consent.

236. Tassa kho tanti ettha kho tanti nipātamattaṃ.

236. Regarding 'tassa kho,' here 'kho' is merely a particle.

238. “Kā [V 3.0347] ca tattha tassapāpiyasikāyā”ti potthakesu likhanti. “Kā ca tassapāpiyasikā”ti evaṃ panettha pāṭho veditabbo.

238. 'And what is the procedure for his further bad character there?' is written in the books. 'And what is the procedure for his further bad character?'—this should be understood as the reading here.

242. Kiccādhikaraṇaṃ ekena samathena sammatīti ettha “kiccameva kiccādhikaraṇa”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.385-86) vacanato apalokanakammādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ vivādādhikaraṇādīni viya samathehi sametabbaṃ na hoti, kintu sammukhāvinayena sampajjati, tasmā sammatīti ettha sampajjatīti attho gahetabbo. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

242. Regarding the statement, 'A procedural matter is settled by one settlement,' here, according to the saying 'a procedure is indeed a procedural matter,' this is a designation for formal acts such as an act of announcement. Unlike matters of dispute and the like, it is not to be settled by the settlements, but is accomplished by the procedure of acting in the presence. Therefore, 'is settled' here should be understood to mean 'is accomplished.' The rest here is easily understood.

Samathakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Settlements is concluded.

5. Khuddakavatthukkhandhakaṃ

5. The Chapter on Minor Matters

Khuddakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on Minor Matters

243. Khuddakavatthukkhandhake [M 3.0381][V 3.0348] aṭṭhapadākārenāti aṭṭhapadaphalakākārena, jūtaphalakasadisanti vuttaṃ hoti. Mallakamūlasaṇṭhānenāti kheḷamallakamūlasaṇṭhānena.

243. In the Chapter on Minor Matters, 'in the form of an eight-square grid' means in the form of an eight-square board; this is said to be like a game board. 'In the shape of the base of a bowl' means in the shape of the base of a spittoon.

245. Muttolambakādīnanti ādi-saddena kuṇḍalādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Palambakasuttanti yaññopacitākārena olambakasuttaṃ.

245. Regarding 'of pearl pendants and so on,' by the word 'and so on' it includes such things as earrings. 'A hanging thread' means a thread hanging down in the manner of a sacrificial cord.

246. Cikkalenāti silesena.

246. 'With mud' means with plaster.

248. Sādhugītanti aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttagītaṃ.

248. 'A good song' means a song connected with impermanence and so forth.

249. Caturassena vattenāti paripuṇṇena uccāraṇavattena. Taraṅgavattādīnaṃ uccāraṇavidhānāni naṭṭhappayogāni. Bāhiralominti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, yathā tassa uṇṇapāvārassa bahiddhā lomāni dissanti, tathā dhārentassa dukkaṭanti vuttaṃ hoti.

249. 'With a perfect style' means with a complete style of recitation. The methods of reciting the 'wave style' and so on are practices that have been lost. 'With the fleece on the outside' is a neuter abstract noun designation; the meaning is that just as the fleece of his woolen cloak is seen on the outside, so for one who wears it thus, it is said to be an offense of wrong-doing.

251. Imāni cattāri ahirājakulānīti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.67) idaṃ daṭṭhavise sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ye hi keci daṭṭhavisā, sabbe te imesaṃ catunnaṃ ahirājakulānaṃ abbhantaragatāva honti. Attaguttiyāti attano guttatthāya. Attarakkhāyāti attano rakkhaṇatthāya. Attaparittaṃkātunti attano parittāṇatthāya attaparittaṃ nāma kātuṃ anujānāmīti attho.

251. 'These four royal serpent families' is said with reference to snakes with venom in their fangs. For whatever snakes have venom in their fangs, they are all included within these four royal serpent families. 'For self-protection' means for the purpose of one's own protection. 'For self-guarding' means for the purpose of one's own guarding. 'To make a self-protection' means 'I allow the making of what is called a self-protection for the purpose of one's own protection.'

Idāni yathā taṃ parittaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “evañca pana bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha [V 3.0349] (jā. aṭṭha. 2.2.105) virūpakkhehīti virūpakkhanāgakulehi. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Sahayoge cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, etehi saha mayhaṃ mittabhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti apādakehīti apādakasattehi. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Sabbe sattāti ito pubbe ettakena ṭhānena [M 3.0382] odissakamettaṃ kathetvā idāni anodissakamettaṃ kathetuṃ idamāraddhaṃ. Tattha sattā pāṇā bhūtāti sabbānetāni puggalavevacanāneva. Bhadrāni passantūti bhadrāni ārammaṇāni passantu. Mā kañci pāpamāgamāti kañci sattaṃ pāpakaṃ lāmakaṃ mā āgacchatu.

Now, to show how that protective chant is to be made, he said, 'And so, monks,' and so on. Therein, 'with the Virūpakkhas' means with the Virūpakkha nāga families. This same method applies to the rest. And this is the instrumental case in the sense of association; the meaning is, 'My friendship is with them.' 'With the footless' means with footless beings. This same method applies to the rest. 'All beings': having previously spoken of specified loving-kindness with this much scope, this is now begun in order to speak of unspecified loving-kindness. Therein, 'beings,' 'living things,' 'creatures' are all just synonyms for an individual. 'May they see good things' means may they see auspicious objects. 'May no evil befall anyone' means may nothing evil or base come to any being.

Appamāṇo buddhoti ettha buddhoti buddhaguṇā veditabbā, te hi appamāṇā nāma. Sesadvayesupi eseva nayo, pamāṇavantānīti guṇappamāṇena yuttāni. Uṇṇanābhīti lomasanābhiko makkaṭako. Sarabūti gharagoḷikā. Katā me rakkhā kataṃ me parittanti mayā ettakassa janassa rakkhā ca parittāṇañca kataṃ. Paṭikkamantu bhūtānīti sabbepi me kataparittāṇā sattā apagacchantu, mā maṃ viheṭhayiṃsūti attho. Sohanti yassa mama etehi sabbehipi mettaṃ, so ahaṃ bhagavato namo karomi, vipassīādīnañca sattannaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ namo karomīti sambandho.

'The Buddha is immeasurable'—here, 'Buddha' should be understood as the virtues of the Buddha, for they are indeed immeasurable. The same method applies to the remaining two. 'Those with measure' means those endowed with measured qualities. 'Uṇṇanābhi' means a spider with a hairy navel. 'Sarabū' means a house gecko. 'Protection has been made by me, a safeguard has been made by me' means that protection and a safeguard have been made by me for this many people. 'May beings retreat'—the meaning is, 'may all beings for whom I have made this safeguard depart; may they not harm me.' Regarding 'So'haṃ' (I, that one): I, who have friendliness towards all these beings, pay homage to the Blessed One; and I pay homage to the seven Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, Vipassī and the others—this is the connection.

Aññamhi chetabbamhīti rāgānusayaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tādisaṃ vā dukkhanti muṭṭhiādīhi dukkhaṃ uppādentassa.

'Another should be cut'—this is said with reference to the underlying tendency of lust. 'Such suffering'—this refers to the suffering of one causing suffering by fists and the like.

252. Jālāni parikkhipāpetvāti parissayamocanatthañceva pamādena gaḷitānaṃ ābharaṇādīnaṃ rakkhaṇatthañca jālāni karaṇḍakākārena parikkhipāpetvā. Candanagaṇṭhi āgantvā jāle laggāti eko kira rattacandanarukkho gaṅgāya uparitīre jāto gaṅgodakena dhotamūlo patitvā tattha tattha pāsāṇesu sambhijjamāno vippakiri. Tato ekā ghaṭappamāṇā ghaṭikā pāsāṇesu ghaṃsiyamānā udakaūmīhi pothiyamānā maṭṭhā hutvā anupubbena vuyhamānā sevālapariyonaddhā āgantvā tasmiṃ jāle laggi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Lekhanti likhitagahitaṃ cuṇṇaṃ. Uḍḍitvāti veḷuparamparāya uddhaṃ pāpetvā, uṭṭhāpetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Oharatūti iddhiyā otāretvā gaṇhatu.

252. 'Having had nets spread around' means having had nets spread around in the shape of baskets, both for the purpose of removing danger and for protecting ornaments and so forth that might slip due to carelessness. 'A lump of sandalwood came and stuck to the net'—it is said that a certain red sandalwood tree, grown on the upper bank of the Ganges, its roots washed by the Ganges water, fell and, breaking apart on the rocks here and there, scattered. From that, a piece the size of a pot, being rubbed against the rocks and pounded by the waves, became smooth and, gradually carried along, covered with algae, came and stuck to that net. This is what is referred to. 'Lekhan' means powder obtained by scraping. 'Uḍḍitvā' means 'having caused it to go up by a series of bamboos'; that is to say, 'having raised it up.' 'Oharatu' means 'let him take it, having brought it down by psychic power.'

Pūraṇakassapādayo cha satthāro. Tattha (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.151-152; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.312) pūraṇoti tassa satthupaṭiññassa nāmaṃ. Kassapoti gottaṃ. So kira aññatarassa kulassa ekūnadāsasataṃ pūrayamāno jāto. Tenassa “pūraṇo”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Maṅgaladāsattā [V 3.0350] cassa kataṃ “dukkaṭa”nti vattā natthi, akataṃ vā “na kata”nti[M 3.0383]. So “kimahaṃ ettha vasāmī”ti palāyi. Athassa corā vatthāni acchindiṃsu. So paṇṇena vā tiṇena vā paṭicchādetumpi ajānanto jātarūpeneva ekaṃ gāmaṃ pāvisi. Manussā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ samaṇo arahā appiccho, natthi iminā sadiso”ti pūvabhattādīni gahetvā upasaṅkamanti. So “mayhaṃ sāṭakaṃ anivatthabhāvena idaṃ uppanna”nti tato paṭṭhāya sāṭakaṃ labhitvāpi na nivāsesi, tadeva pabbajjaṃ aggahesi. Tassa santike aññepi aññepīti pañcasatā manussā pabbajiṃsu. Evamayaṃ gaṇācariyo hutvā “satthā”ti loke pākaṭo ahosi.

The six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa. There (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.151-152; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.312), 'Pūraṇa' is the name of that self-proclaimed teacher. 'Kassapa' is his clan name. It is said that he was born completing a certain family's one hundred slaves. Therefore, they named him 'Pūraṇa.' And because he was an auspicious slave, there was no one to say of what he did, 'This is a wrong deed,' or of what he did not do, 'This was not done.' Thinking, 'Why should I stay here?' he fled. Then robbers stole his clothes. Not knowing how to cover himself even with leaves or grass, he entered a village just as he was born. People saw him and thought, 'This ascetic is an arahant, desireless, there is none like him,' and, bringing him rice cakes and other food, they approached him. Realizing, 'This has arisen because I was not wearing a garment,' from then on, even when he obtained a robe, he did not wear it, taking that very state as his renunciation.
