In his presence, five hundred other people also went forth. Thus, having become a leader of a group, he became known in the world as a 'teacher.'

Makkhalīti tassa nāmaṃ. Gosālāya jātattā gosāloti dutiyanāmaṃ. Taṃ kira sakaddamāya bhūmiyā telaghaṭaṃ gahetvā gacchantaṃ “tāta mā khalī”ti sāmiko āha. So pamādena khalitvā patitvā sāmikassa bhayena palāyituṃ āraddho. Sāmiko upadhāvitvā sāṭakakaṇṇe aggahesi, so sāṭakaṃ chaḍḍetvā acelako hutvā palāyi. Sesaṃ pūraṇasadisameva.

'Makkhali' is his name. Because he was born in a cow-shed (gosāla), his second name was 'Gosāla.' It is said that while he was going along on muddy ground carrying an oil pot, his master said, 'Son, don't slip!' He, through carelessness, slipped and fell, and fearing his master, he began to run away. The master ran after him and seized the edge of his cloak, but he threw off the cloak and, becoming naked, fled. The rest is just like Pūraṇa's.

Ajitoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kesakambalaṃ dhāretīti kesakambalo. Iti nāmadvayaṃ saṃsanditvā “ajito kesakambalo”ti vuccati. Tattha kesakambalo nāma manussānaṃ kesehi katakambalo. Tato paṭikiṭṭhataraṃ vatthaṃ nāma natthi. Yathāha “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ, kesakambalo tesaṃ paṭikiṭṭho akkhāyati. Kesakambalo, bhikkhave, sīte sīto uṇhe uṇho dubbaṇṇo duggandho dukkhasamphasso”ti (a. ni. 3.138).

'Ajita' is his name. Because he wore a hair blanket (kesakambala), he was called 'Kesakambala.' Thus, combining the two names, he is called 'Ajita Kesakambala.' Here, a 'kesakambala' is a blanket made of human hair. There is no cloth more wretched than that. As it is said: 'Just as, monks, of all woven cloths whatsoever, a hair blanket is said to be the most wretched. A hair blanket, monks, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch' (A. Ni. 3.138).

Pakudhoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kaccāyanoti gottaṃ. Iti nāmagottaṃ saṃsanditvā “pakudho kaccāyano”ti vuccati. Sītūdakapaṭikkhittako esa, vaccaṃ katvāpi udakakiccaṃ na karoti, uṇhodakaṃ vā kañjiyaṃ vā labhitvā karoti, nadiṃ vā maggodakaṃ vā atikkamma “sīlaṃ me bhinna”nti vālikathūpaṃ katvā sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāya gacchati. Evarūpanissirikaladdhiko esa.

'Pakudha' was his name. 'Kaccāyana' was his clan name. Thus, combining name and clan, he is called 'Pakudha Kaccāyana.' He was one who rejected cold water. Even after answering the call of nature, he would not perform water ablutions; but having obtained hot water or rice gruel, he would do so. Or he would cross a river or a puddle and, thinking, 'My virtue is broken,' would make a sand mound and reaffirm his virtue before proceeding. Such was his wretched doctrine.

Sañcayoti tassa nāmaṃ. Belaṭṭhassa putto belaṭṭhaputto. “Amhākaṃ gaṇṭhanakileso palibundhanakileso natthi, kilesagaṇṭhirahitā maya”nti [M 3.0384] evaṃvāditāya laddhanāmavasena nigaṇṭho. Nāṭassa puttoti nāṭaputto.

'Sañcaya' is his name. The son of Belaṭṭha is 'Belaṭṭhaputta.' Because of his doctrine—'We have no entangling defilements, no obstructing defilements; we are without the knots of defilements'—he acquired the name 'Nigaṇṭha.' The son of Nāṭa is 'Nāṭaputta.'

Piṇḍolabhāradvājoti [V 3.0351] (udā. aṭṭha. 36) piṇḍaṃ ulamāno pariyesamāno pabbajitoti piṇḍolo. So kira parijiṇṇabhogo brāhmaṇo hutvā mahantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa lābhasakkāraṃ disvā piṇḍatthāya nikkhamitvā pabbajito. So mahantaṃ kapallapattaṃ “patta”nti gahetvā carati, kapallapūraṃ yāguṃ pivati, bhattaṃ bhuñjati, pūvakhajjakañca khādati. Athassa mahagghasabhāvaṃ satthu ārocayiṃsu. Satthā tassa pattatthavikaṃ nānujāni. Thero heṭṭhāmañce pattaṃ nikujjitvā ṭhapeti. So ṭhapentopi ghaṃsentova paṇāmetvā ṭhapeti, gaṇhantopi ghaṃsentova ākaḍḍhitvā gaṇhāti. Taṃ gacchante gacchante kāle ghaṃsanena parikkhīṇaṃ nāḷikodanamattasseva gaṇhanakaṃ jātaṃ. Tato satthu ārocesuṃ. Athassa satthā pattatthavikaṃ anujāni. Thero aparena samayena indriyabhāvanaṃ bhāvento aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Iti so pubbe savisesaṃ piṇḍatthāya ulatīti piṇḍolo. Gottena pana bhāradvājoti ubhayaṃ ekato katvā “piṇḍolabhāradvājo”ti vuccati.

Piṇḍolabhāradvāja (UdA. 36): He is called Piṇḍola because he went forth while seeking and gathering alms. It is said that he was an impoverished brahmin who, having seen the great gains and honor of the Sangha of bhikkhus, went forth for the sake of alms. He would carry a large earthenware bowl, called a 'patta,' and wander about. He drank gruel by the bowlful, ate his meal, and consumed cakes and sweets. Then his great gluttony was reported to the Teacher. The Teacher did not permit him a bowl-bag. The elder would then place his bowl overturned under his bed. When placing it, he would set it down with a scraping sound, and when taking it, he would pull it out with a scraping sound. As time went on, it became worn down by the scraping until it could only hold about a nāḷi of cooked rice. They reported this to the Teacher, and the Teacher then permitted him a bowl-bag. At a later time, the elder, developing his faculties, became established in the supreme fruit of arahantship. Thus, because he had formerly sought alms with special effort, he was called Piṇḍola. By clan, however, he was Bhāradvāja. Combining both, he is called 'Piṇḍolabhāradvāja.'

“Atha kho āyasmā piṇḍolabhāradvājo…pe… etadavocā”ti kasmā evamāhaṃsu? So kira (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.180 devorohaṇavatthu) seṭṭhi neva sammādiṭṭhi, na micchādiṭṭhi, majjhattadhātuko. So cintesi “mayhaṃ gehe candanaṃ bahu, kiṃ nu kho iminā karissāmī”ti. Athassa etadahosi “imasmiṃ loke ‘mayaṃ arahanto, mayaṃ arahanto’ti vattāro bahū, ahaṃ ekaṃ arahantampi na jānāmi, gehe bhamaṃ yojetvā pattaṃ likhāpetvā sikkāya ṭhapetvā veḷuparamparāya saṭṭhihatthamatte ākāse olambāpetvā ‘sace arahā atthi, ākāsenāgantvā gaṇhātū’ti vakkhāmi. Yo taṃ gahessati, tassa saputtadāro saraṇaṃ gamissāmī”ti. So cintitaniyāmeneva pattaṃ likhāpetvā veḷuparamparāya ussāpetvā “yo imasmiṃ loke arahā, so ākāsena āgantvā imaṃ pattaṃ gaṇhātū”ti āha.

Why did they say, 'Then the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja… spoke thus'? It is said (DhpA. 2.180, the story of the Descent from Tāvatiṃsa) that a wealthy man was neither of right view nor of wrong view, but of a neutral disposition. He thought, 'I have much sandalwood in my house—what shall I do with it?' Then it occurred to him, 'In this world, many claim, "We are arahants, we are arahants," but I do not know even one arahant. I will have a bowl fashioned, place it in a net-sling, suspend it sixty cubits high in the air with a series of bamboo poles, and say, "If there is an arahant, let him come through the air and take it." Whoever takes it, I will go for refuge to him along with my wife and children.' Having decided thus, he had the bowl fashioned, raised it with the series of bamboo poles, and declared, 'Whoever in this world is an arahant, let him come through the air and take this bowl.'

Tadā [M 3.0385] cha satthāro “amhākaṃ esa anucchaviko, amhākameva naṃ dehī”ti vadiṃsu. So “ākāsenāgantvā gaṇhathā”ti āha. Chaṭṭhe divase nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto antevāsike pesesi “gacchatha seṭṭhiṃ evaṃ vadetha ‘amhākaṃ ācariyasseva anucchaviko, mā appamattakassa kāraṇā ākāsena āgamanaṃ kari, dehi kira te patta’nti”. Te gantvā seṭṭhiṃ tathā vadiṃsu. Seṭṭhi “ākāsenāgantvā gaṇhituṃ samatthova gaṇhātū”ti āha. Nāṭaputto sayaṃ gantukāmo hutvā antevāsikānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi “ahaṃ ekaṃ hatthañca pādañca ukkhipitvā uppatitukāmo viya bhavissāmi, tumhe maṃ ‘ācariya kiṃ karotha, dārumayapattassa kāraṇā paṭicchannaṃ arahattaguṇaṃ mahājanassa mā dassayitthā’ti vatvā maṃ hatthesu ca pādesu ca gahetvā ākaḍḍhantā [V 3.0352] bhūmiyaṃ pāteyyāthā”ti. So tattha gantvā seṭṭhiṃ āha “mahāseṭṭhi ayaṃ patto aññesaṃ nānucchaviko, mā te appamattakassa kāraṇā mama ākāse uppatanaṃ rucci, dehi me patta”nti. Bhante, ākāsena uppatitvāva gaṇhathāti. Tato nāṭaputto “tena hi apetha apethā”ti antevāsike apanetvā “ākāse uppatissāmī”ti ekaṃ hatthañca pādañca ukkhipi. Atha naṃ antevāsikā “ācariya, kiṃ nāmetaṃ karotha, chavassa dārumayapattassa kāraṇā paṭicchannaguṇena tumhehi mahājanassa dassitena ko attho”ti taṃ hatthapādesu gahetvā ākaḍḍhitvā bhūmiyaṃ pātesuṃ. So seṭṭhiṃ āha “mahāseṭṭhi, ime me uppatituṃ na denti, dehi me patta”nti. Uppatitvāva gaṇhatha bhanteti. Evaṃ titthiyā cha divasāni vāyamitvāpi pattaṃ na labhiṃsuyeva.

Then the six teachers said, 'This is suitable for us; give it to us.' He replied, 'Come through the air and take it.' On the sixth day, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta sent his disciples, saying, 'Go to the wealthy man and tell him, "This is truly suitable for our teacher. Do not make him come through the air for such a trivial matter. Give him the bowl, they say."' They went and spoke thus to the wealthy man. The wealthy man replied, 'Let him who is capable of coming through the air to take it, take it.' Nāṭaputta, wishing to go himself, instructed his disciples, 'I will raise one hand and one foot as if about to leap into the air. You must say, "Teacher, what are you doing? Do not reveal the concealed qualities of an arahant to the multitude for the sake of a worthless wooden bowl!" Then, grabbing me by the hands and feet, drag me and throw me to the ground.' He went there and said to the wealthy man, 'Great wealthy man, this bowl is not suitable for others. Do not desire that I leap into the air for such a trivial matter. Give me the bowl.' The wealthy man replied, 'Venerable sir, take it only by leaping through the air.' Then Nāṭaputta dismissed his disciples, saying, 'Stand aside, stand aside.' He raised one hand and a foot, declaring, 'I will leap into the air!' But his disciples grabbed him, saying, 'Teacher, what is this you are doing? What purpose is there in revealing to the multitude the qualities you have concealed for the sake of a worthless wooden bowl?' They seized his hands and feet, dragged him, and threw him to the ground. He said to the wealthy man, 'Great wealthy man, these ones do not allow me to leap. Give me the bowl.' The wealthy man replied, 'Take it only by leaping, venerable sir.' Thus, after striving for six days, the sectarians still could not obtain the bowl.

Atha sattame divase āyasmato ca moggallānassa āyasmato ca piṇḍolabhāradvājassa “rājagahe piṇḍāya carissāmā”ti gantvā ekasmiṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇe ṭhatvā cīvaraṃ pārupanakāle dhuttakā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “hambho pubbe cha satthāro ‘mayaṃ arahantāmhā’ti vicariṃsu, rājagahaseṭṭhino pana ajja sattamo divaso pattaṃ ussāpetvā ṭhapayato ‘sace arahā atthi, ākāsenāgantvā gaṇhātū’ti vadantassa, ekopi ‘ahaṃ arahā’ti ākāse uppatanto natthi, ajja no loke arahantānaṃ natthibhāvo ñāto”ti. Taṃ kathaṃ sutvā āyasmā mahāmoggallāno āyasmantaṃ piṇḍolabhāradvājaṃ [M 3.0386] āha “sutaṃ te, āvuso bhāradvāja, imesaṃ vacanaṃ, ime buddhasāsanaṃ pariggaṇhantā viya vadanti, tvañca mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo, gacchetaṃ pattaṃ ākāsena gantvā gaṇhāhī”ti. “Āvuso moggallāna, tvaṃ ‘iddhimantānaṃ aggo’ti pākaṭo, tvaṃ etaṃ gaṇha, tayi pana aggaṇhante ahaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti āha. Atha āyasmā mahāmoggallāno “gaṇhāvuso”ti āha. Iti te lokassa arahantehi asuññabhāvadassanatthaṃ evamāhaṃsu.

On the seventh day, the Venerable Moggallāna and the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, having gone to Rājagaha for alms, stood on a stone slab. As they were putting on their robes, some rogues started a discussion: 'Sirs, in the past, six teachers wandered about claiming, "We are arahants." But today is the seventh day since the wealthy man of Rājagaha set up a bowl on a pole and declared, "If there is an arahant, let him come through the sky and take it." Yet not even one has appeared in the sky saying, "I am an arahant." Today, the absence of arahants in the world has become known to us.' Hearing this, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja: 'Friend Bhāradvāja, have you heard what these people are saying? They speak as if they were censuring the Buddha’s dispensation. You are one of great psychic power and might. Go, take that bowl by traveling through the sky.' 'Friend Moggallāna, you are known as foremost among those with psychic powers. You should take it. If you do not take it, then I will,' replied the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said, 'Take it, friend.' Thus, they spoke in this way to demonstrate to the world that it is not empty of arahants.

Tikkhattuṃ rājagahaṃ anupariyāyīti tikkhattuṃ rājagahaṃ anugantvā paribbhami. “Sattakkhattu”ntipi vadanti. Thero kira abhiññāpādakaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā uṭṭhāya tigāvutaṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ antantena paricchindanto tūlapicu viya ākāse uṭṭhāpetvā rājagahanagarassa upari sattakkhattuṃ anupariyāyi. So tigāvutappamāṇassa nagarassa apidhānaṃ viya paññāyi. Nagaravāsino “pāsāṇo no avattharitvā gaṇhātī”ti bhītā suppādīni matthake katvā tattha tattha nilīyiṃsu. Sattame vāre thero piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ bhinditvā attānaṃ dasseti. Mahājano theraṃ disvā “bhante piṇḍolabhāradvāja, tava pāsāṇaṃ gāḷhaṃ katvā gaṇha, mā [V 3.0353] no sabbe nāsayī”ti āha. Thero pāsāṇaṃ pādantena khipitvā vissajjesi. So gantvā yathāṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhāsi. Thero seṭṭhissa gehamatthake aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā seṭṭhi urena nipajjitvā “otara sāmī”ti vatvā ākāsato otiṇṇaṃ theraṃ nisīdāpetvā pattaṃ gahetvā catumadhurapuṇṇaṃ katvā therassa adāsi. Thero pattaṃ gahetvā vihārābhimukho pāyāsi. Athassa ye araññagatā pāṭihāriyaṃ nāddasaṃsu, te sannipatitvā “bhante, amhākampi pāṭihāriyaṃ dassehī”ti theraṃ anubandhiṃsu. So tesaṃ tesaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ dassento vihāraṃ agamāsi. Satthā taṃ anubandhitvā unnādentassa mahājanassa saddaṃ sutvā “ānanda, kasseso saddo”ti pucchi. Tena vuttaṃ “assosi kho bhagavā…pe… kiṃ nu kho so, ānanda, uccāsaddo mahāsaddo”ti.

He circled Rājagaha three times, meaning he went to Rājagaha and wandered around it three times. Some say 'seven times.' The elder, it is said, attained the jhāna that is the basis for supernormal knowledge, arose from it, and, cutting out a piece of the stone slab three gāvutas in size with its edge, lifted it like a cotton tuft into the sky, then circled the city of Rājagaha seven times above it. The stone appeared like a lid covering the three-gāvuta-sized city. The city dwellers, frightened, thinking, 'The stone will fall and crush us!', placed winnowing baskets and other such things on their heads and hid here and there. On the seventh round, the elder broke open the stone slab and revealed himself. The crowd, seeing the elder, said, 'Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, hold your stone firmly, lest you destroy us all!' The elder kicked the stone with the tip of his foot and sent it away. It went and landed right back in its original place. The elder stood on the roof of the wealthy man’s house. Seeing him, the wealthy man prostrated himself on his chest and said, 'Descend, lord.' Then, when the elder had descended from the sky, he had him sit down, took the bowl, filled it with the four sweet foods, and gave it to the elder. The elder took the bowl and set off toward the monastery. Then those who had gone to the forest and had not seen the miracle gathered and followed the elder, saying, 'Venerable, show us a miracle too!' He displayed various miracles to them as he went to the monastery. The Teacher, hearing the loud noise of the shouting crowd following him, asked, 'Ānanda, what is this noise?' This refers to the canonical passage: 'The Blessed One heard… "What is this loud uproar, Ānanda?"'

Vikubbaniddhiyā pāṭihāriyaṃ paṭikkhittanti ettha vikubbaniddhi nāma “so pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā kumārakavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti nāgavaṇṇaṃ vā, vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.13) evamāgatā pakativaṇṇavijahanavikāravasena pavattā [M 3.0387] iddhi. Adhiṭṭhāniddhi pana “pakatiyā eko bahukaṃ āvajjati sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā satasahassaṃ vā, āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti ‘bahuko homī’”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.10 dasaiddhiniddesa) evaṃ vibhajitvā dassitā adhiṭṭhānavasena nipphannā iddhi.

The miracle of transformation was rejected here. In this context, the power of transformation means 'abandoning one's natural form and displaying the form of a youth or a nāga, or showing various military formations' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.13); it is the psychic power that operates by way of abandoning and altering one’s natural appearance. The power of resolve, however, is the psychic power, described as 'naturally being one, one adverts to becoming many—a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand; having adverted, one resolves with knowledge, "May I become many!"' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.10, Section on the Exposition of the Ten Psychic Powers), that is accomplished through the act of resolve.

253-254. Na acchupiyantīti na suphassitāni honti. Rūpakākiṇṇānīti itthirūpādīhi ākiṇṇāni. Bhūmiādhāraketi valayādhārake. Dāruādhārakadaṇḍādhārakesūti ekadārunā kataādhārake bahūhi daṇḍakehi kataādhārake vāti attho, tīhi daṇḍehi kato pana na vaṭṭati. Bhūmiyaṃ pana nikkujjitvā ekameva ṭhapetabbanti ettha dve ṭhapentena upari ṭhapitapattaṃ ekena passena bhūmiyaṃ phusāpetvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Ālindakamiḍḍhikādīnanti pamukhamiḍḍhikānaṃ. Parivattitvā tattheva patiṭṭhātīti ettha “parivattitvā tatiyavāre tattheva miḍḍhiyā patiṭṭhātī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Paribhaṇḍaṃ nāma gehassa bahi kuṭṭapādassa thirabhāvatthaṃ katā tanukamiḍḍhikā vuccati. Tanukamiḍḍhikāyāti khuddakamiḍḍhikāya. Miḍḍhantepi ādhārake ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ādhāraka”nti hi vacanato miḍḍhādīsu yattha katthaci ādhārakaṃ ṭhapetvā tattha pattaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati ādhārake ṭhapanokāsassa aniyamitattāti vadanti. “Pattamāḷo nāma vaṭṭetvā pattānaṃ agamanatthaṃ vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā iṭṭhakādīhi parikkhipitvā kato”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

253-254. 'Not to be touched' means they are not pleasant to the touch. 'Scattered with forms' means filled with female forms and the like. 'Ground support' refers to a ring-shaped support. 'Wooden support' or 'stick support' means a support made from a single piece of wood or a support made from many sticks—this is the meaning. However, one made with three sticks is not suitable. On the ground, however, having overturned it, only one should be placed. Here, some say that if two are placed, the bowl placed on top can be placed with one side touching the ground. 'Porches and small platforms' refers to prominent small platforms. 'Turned over and established right there'—here, it is said in the glosses, 'turned over and established on the small platform on the third occasion.' A 'paribhaṇḍa' is a thin small platform built outside a house to stabilize the wall base. 'On a thin small platform' means on a small platform. It is allowable to place a support even on a small platform, for some say that because of the statement, 'I allow, monks, a support,' one may place a support anywhere on a small platform or the like and place the bowl there, since the location for placing a support is not restricted. In the glosses, it is said, 'A bowl-enclosure is a circular or square area made by enclosing it with bricks or the like to prevent bowls from moving away.'

255. Ghaṭikanti upari yojitaṃ aggaḷaṃ. Tāvakālikaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti sakideva gahetvā [V 3.0354] tena āmisaṃ paribhuñjitvā chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo. Ghaṭikaṭāheti bhājanakapāle. Abhuṃ meti ettha bhavatīti bhū, vaḍḍhi. Na bhūti abhū, avaḍḍhi. Bhayavasena pana sā itthī “abhu”nti āha, vināso mayhanti attho. Chavasīsassa pattanti chavasīsamayaṃ pattaṃ. Pakativikārasambandhe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, abhedepi vā bhedūpacārenāyaṃ vohāro “silāputtakassa sarīra”ntiādīsu viya.

255. "Ghaṭika" refers to a latch placed on top. "It is permissible to use it temporarily" means it is suitable to be taken only once, used to consume food, and then discarded—this is the intention. "Ghaṭikaṭāha" means a potsherd. "Abhuṃ me" here, "bhū" means "to be," growth. "Na bhū" means "not to be," decline. However, out of fear, the woman said "Abhū," meaning "destruction is mine." "The bowl of a skull" means a bowl made of a skull. This is a possessive expression related to natural alteration, or it is a conventional expression using a figurative division even when there is no actual division, as in examples like "the body of the stone statue."

Cabbetvāti khāditvā. Ekaṃ udakagaṇḍusaṃ gahetvāti vāmahattheneva pattaṃ ukkhipitvā mukhena gaṇḍusaṃ gahetvā. Ucchiṭṭhahatthenāti sāmisena hatthena. Ettāvatāti ekagaṇḍusagahaṇamattena. Luñcitvāti tato maṃsaṃ [M 3.0388] uddharitvā. Etesu sabbesu paṇṇattiṃ jānātu vā mā vā, āpattiyeva.

"Cabbetvā" means having eaten. "Taking one mouthful of water" means lifting the bowl with the left hand and taking a mouthful with the mouth. "With a soiled hand" means with a hand that has touched food. "This much" means just by taking one mouthful. "Plucked" means having extracted the meat from it. In all these cases, whether one knows the rule or not, it is still an offense.

256. Kiṇṇacuṇṇenāti surākiṇṇacuṇṇena. “Anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍanti kilañjādīsu karontī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Bidalakanti duguṇakaraṇasaṅkhātassa kiriyāvisesassa adhivacanaṃ. Kassa duguṇakaraṇaṃ? Yena kilañjādinā mahantaṃ kathinaṃ atthataṃ, tassa. Tañhi daṇḍakathinappamāṇena pariyante saṃharitvā duguṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Paṭiggahanti aṅgulikañcukaṃ.

256. "Kiṇṇacuṇṇa" means the powder of liquor ferment. As stated in the glosses: "They prepare kilañja etc., downwind." "Bidalaka" is a term referring to a specific action known as doubling. What is doubled? That large, stiff kilañja etc., which has been spread out. That indeed, having gathered it at the edges to the size of a daṇḍakathina, should be doubled. "Paṭiggaha" means a finger-stall.

257-259. Pāti nāma paṭiggahaṇasaṇṭhānena kato bhājanaviseso. Na sammatīti nappahoti.

257-259. A "pāti" is a specific kind of vessel made in the shape of a receptacle. "Na sammati" means it is not sufficient.

260-262. Nīcavatthukaṃ cinitunti bahikuṭṭassa samantato nīcavatthukaṃ katvā cinituṃ. Arahaṭaghaṭiyantaṃ nāma sakaṭacakkasaṇṭhānaṃ are are ghaṭikāni bandhitvā ekena dvīhi vā paribbhamiyamānaṃ yantaṃ.

260-262. "Nīcavatthukaṃ cinituṃ" means to build a low foundation all around the outer wall. An "arahaṭaghaṭiyanta" is a machine in the shape of a cartwheel, with pots fastened to each spoke, which is rotated by one or two people.

263. Āviddhapakkhapāsakanti kaṇṇikamaṇḍalassa samantā ṭhapitapakkhapāsakaṃ. Maṇḍaleti kaṇṇikamaṇḍale. Pakkhapāsake ṭhapetvāti samantā pakkhapāsakaphalakāni ṭhapetvā.

263. "Āviddhapakkhapāsaka" refers to the side-rafters placed all around the hub-circle. "Maṇḍale" means on the hub-circle. "Pakkhapāsake ṭhapetvā" means having placed the side-rafter planks all around.

264. “Namatakaṃ santhatasadisa”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Cammakhaṇḍaparihārena paribhuñjitabbanti anadhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Ettheva paviṭṭhānīti maḷorikāya eva antogadhāni. Pubbe pattasaṅgopanatthaṃ ādhārako anuññāto, idāni bhuñjanatthaṃ.

264. As stated in the glosses: "Namataka is like a felt rug." "Cammakhaṇḍaparihārena paribhuñjitabbaṃ" means it should be used without formal determination. "Ettheva paviṭṭhāni" means they are entirely contained within the bowl-support itself. Previously, a stand was allowed for keeping the bowl; now it is for eating.

265. Nikkujjitabboti [V 3.0355] tena dinnassa deyyadhammassa appaṭiggahaṇatthaṃ pattanikkujjanakammavācāya nikkujjitabbo, na adhomukhaṭhapanena. Tenevāha “evañca pana, bhikkhave, nikkujjitabbo”tiādi. Alābhāyāti catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ alābhatthāya. Anatthāyāti upaddavāya avaḍḍhiyā.

265. "Nikkujjitabbo" means the bowl should be overturned by the formal declaration for overturning the bowl to refuse the offered alms, not merely by placing it upside down. Hence it is said: "And thus, monks, it should be overturned," etc. "Alābhāya" means for the non-receipt of the four requisites. "Anatthāya" means for harm, trouble, or decline.

266. Pasādessāmāti āyācissāma. Etadavocāti “appatirūpaṃ mayā kataṃ, bhagavā pana mahantepi aguṇe acintetvā mayhaṃ accayaṃ paṭiggaṇhissatī”ti maññamāno etaṃ “accayo maṃ bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca[M 3.0389]. Tattha ñāyapaṭipattiṃ aticca eti pavattatīti accayo, aparādho. Maṃ accagamāti maṃ atikkamma abhibhavitvā pavatto. Purisena madditvā abhibhavitvā pavattitopi hi aparādho atthato purisaṃ aticca abhibhavitvā pavatto nāma hoti. Paṭiggaṇhātūti khamatu. Āyatiṃ saṃvarāyāti anāgate saṃvaraṇatthāya puna evarūpassa aparādhassa dosassa khalitassa akaraṇatthāya. Tagghāti ekaṃsena. Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosīti yathā dhammo ṭhito, tatheva karosi, khamāpesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmāti taṃ tava aparādhaṃ mayaṃ khamāma. Vuḍḍhi hesā, āvuso vaḍḍha, ariyassa vinayeti esā, āvuso vaḍḍha, ariyassa vinaye buddhassa bhagavato sāsane vuḍḍhi nāma. Katamā? Accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaritvā āyatiṃ saṃvarāpajjanā. Desanaṃ pana puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karonto “yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti āha.

266. "Pasādessāma" means we will ask for pardon. He thought, "What I have done is improper, but the Blessed One, without considering even great faults, will accept my transgression," and so he spoke these words: "Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me," etc. Here, "transgression" (accayo) is an offense that occurs by overstepping proper conduct. "Maṃ accagamā" means it has overcome me by transgressing and overpowering me. For even an offense that occurs by crushing and overpowering a person is, in meaning, called one that has occurred by transgressing against and overpowering that person. "Paṭiggaṇhātu" means may you accept it. "Āyatiṃ saṃvarāya" means for the sake of restraint in the future, so as not to commit such an offense, fault, or error again. "Taggha" means certainly. "Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi" means you make amends just as the Dhamma stands—that is to say, you ask for pardon. "Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma" means we accept that transgression of yours. "This, friend Vaḍḍha, is growth in the Noble One’s discipline" means, friend Vaḍḍha, this is what is called growth in the Noble One’s discipline, in the dispensation of the Buddha, the Blessed One. What is it? Seeing a transgression as a transgression, making amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and undertaking restraint for the future. However, when giving a teaching with reference to a person, he said: "One who sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint for the future."

268. Bodhirājakumāravatthumhi (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.324 ādayo) kokanadoti kokanadaṃ vuccati padumaṃ, so ca maṅgalapāsādo olokanapadumaṃ dassetvā kato, tasmā “kokanado”ti saṅkhaṃ labhi. Yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarāti ettha pacchimasopānakaḷevaranti paṭhamasopānaphalakaṃ vuttaṃ tassa sabbapacchā dussena santhatattā. Uparimasopānaphalakato paṭṭhāya hi sopānaṃ santhataṃ. Addasā khoti olokanatthaṃyeva dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhito addasa.

268. In the story of Prince Bodhi (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary 2.324, etc.), "kokanada" is a term for a lotus. That auspicious palace was built displaying a viewing-lotus; therefore, it obtained the designation "Kokanada." "Yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarā," here, "the body of the last step of the staircase" means the first step-plank, because it was the very last part to be covered with cloth. Indeed, the staircase was draped beginning from the upper step-plank. "Addasā kho" means he stood in the door-frame for the very purpose of viewing and saw.

Bhagavā tuṇhī ahosīti “kissa nu kho atthāya rājakumārena ayaṃ mahāsakkāro kato”ti āvajjento puttapatthanāya katabhāvaṃ aññāsi. So hi rājaputto aputtako. Sutañcānena ahosi “buddhānaṃ kira adhikāraṃ katvā manasā icchitaṃ labhantī”ti. So “sacāhaṃ puttaṃ labhissāmi, sammāsambuddho imaṃ celapaṭikaṃ akkamissati. No ce labhissāmi, na akkamissatī”ti patthanaṃ katvā santharāpesi. Atha bhagavā “nibbattissati nu kho etassa putto”ti āvajjetvā “na nibbattissatī”ti addasa. Pubbe kira so ekasmiṃ [V 3.0356] dīpe vasamāno [M 3.0390] samānacchandena sakuṇapotake khādi. Sacassa mātugāmo puññavā bhaveyya, puttaṃ labheyya. Ubhohi pana samānacchandehi hutvā pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, tenassa putto na nibbattissatīti aññāsi. Dusse pana akkante “buddhānaṃ adhikāraṃ katvā patthitaṃ labhantīti loke anussavo, mayā ca mahāadhikāro kato, na ca puttaṃ labhāmi, tucchaṃ idaṃ vacana”nti micchāgahaṇaṃ gaṇheyya. Titthiyāpi “natthi samaṇānaṃ akattabbaṃ nāma, celapaṭikaṃ maddantā āhiṇḍantī”ti ujjhāyeyyuṃ. Etarahi ca akkamantesu bahū bhikkhū paracittaviduno, te bhabbataṃ jānitvā akkamissanti, abhabbataṃ jānitvā na akkamissanti. Anāgate pana upanissayo mando bhavissati, anāgataṃ na jānissanti, tesu akkamantesu sace patthitaṃ ijjhissati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce ijjhissati, “pubbe bhikkhusaṅghassa adhikāraṃ katvā icchiticchitaṃ labhanti, idāni na labhanti, teyeva maññe bhikkhū paṭipattipūrakā ahesuṃ, ime pana paṭipattiṃ pūretuṃ na sakkontī”ti manussā vippaṭisārino bhavissantīti imehi tīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā akkamituṃ anicchanto tuṇhī ahosi. Pacchimaṃ janataṃ tathāgato anukampatīti idaṃ pana thero vuttesu kāraṇesu tatiyaṃ kāraṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Maṅgalaṃ icchantīti maṅgalikā.

The Blessed One remained silent, reflecting, "For what purpose has this great honor been done by the prince?" He understood it was done out of a desire for a son. For that prince was childless. And he had heard, "It is said that by making an offering to the Buddhas, one obtains what is wished for in the mind." So he thought, "If I obtain a son, the Perfectly Enlightened One will step on this cloth. If I do not obtain a son, he will not step on it," and thus he had the cloth spread with this aspiration. Then the Blessed One, reflecting, "Will a son be born to him?" saw, "No son will be born." In the past, it seems, while living on an island, he had eaten fledgling birds with equal delight. If his female companion were meritorious, he might have obtained a son. But since both had committed an evil deed with equal delight, he understood that no son would be born to him. If he stepped on the cloth, the prince might wrongly conclude, "There is a saying in the world that by making an offering to the Buddhas, one obtains what is wished for. I have made a great offering, yet I do not obtain a son. This saying is empty." The sectarians might also complain, "There is nothing the ascetics will not do. They wander around trampling on cloths." Now, when they step on it, many monks are skilled in reading others' minds. Knowing the possibility, they will step; knowing the impossibility, they will not step. But in the future, the supporting condition will be weak. They will not know the future. If they step and the wish is fulfilled, this would be wholesome. If not, people will become regretful, thinking, "Previously, by making an offering to the Sangha, one obtained whatever was wished for. Now they do not obtain it. It seems those monks were fulfillers of the practice, but these are unable to fulfill the practice." For these three reasons, the Blessed One, unwilling to step, remained silent. The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations—this the Elder said, referring to the third reason among those stated. Those who desire blessings are called 'blessing-seekers'.

269. Bījaninti caturassabījaniṃ. Tālavaṇṭanti tālapattādīhi kataṃ maṇḍalikabījaniṃ.

269. A `bījanī` means a four-cornered fan. A `tālavaṇṭa` means a circular fan made of palm leaves and the like.

270-275. “Ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ nāma tālapatta”nti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Kammasatenāti ettha sata-saddo anekapariyāyo, anekena kammenāti attho, mahatā ussāhenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rudhīti khuddakavaṇaṃ.

270-275. "A single-leaf umbrella is called a `tālapatta`," as stated in the Ganthipada texts. "By a hundred deeds"—here, the word "hundred" has many meanings; it means "by many deeds," that is, "by great effort," as it is said. `Rudhī` means a small forest.

278. “Akāyabandhanena sañcicca asañcicca vā gāmappavesane āpatti. Saritaṭṭhānato bandhitvā pavisitabbaṃ nivattitabbaṃ vā”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Murajavaṭṭisaṇṭhānaṃ veṭhetvā katanti bahū rajjuke ekato katvā nānāvaṇṇehi suttehi veṭhetvā murajavaṭṭisadisaṃ kataṃ. Teneva dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.85 pāḷimuttakavinicchaya) vuttaṃ “bahū rajjuke ekato katvā ekena [M 3.0391] nirantaraṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ bahurajjukanti na vattabbaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Muddikakāyabandhanaṃ nāma caturassaṃ akatvā sajjitaṃ. Pāmaṅgadasā caturassā. Mudiṅgasaṇṭhānenāti varakasīsākārena. Pāsantoti dasāmūlaṃ.

278. "Entering a village intentionally or unintentionally with an unfastened waist-band incurs an offense. One should enter or leave after fastening it from the remembered place." This is stated in the Ganthipada texts. A waist-band made by wrapping in the shape of a `muraja` drum's coil is one where many cords are brought together and wrapped with threads of various colors to resemble a `muraja` drum's coil. As mentioned in the commentary on the second Pārājika (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.85, Pāḷimuttakavinicchaya): "Many cords brought together and continuously wrapped with one cord should not be called 'many cords'; that is permissible." What should be said there has already been stated below. A `muddika` waist-band is one prepared without making it square. A `pāmaṅgadasā` is square. "In the shape of a `mudiṅga`" means like the shape of a `varaka` head. `Pāsanto` refers to the root of the tassels.

280-282. Muṇḍavaṭṭīti [V 3.0357] mallakammakarādayo. Pamāṇaṅgulenāti vaḍḍhakīaṅgulaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyameva.

280-282. `Muṇḍavaṭṭī` means wrestlers, laborers, and so on. `Pamāṇaṅgulena` means it is said with reference to the carpenter's inch. The rest here is easily understood from the Pāli text and the commentary.

Khuddakavatthukkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of Minor Matters is completed.

6. Senāsanakkhandhakaṃ

6. The Chapter on Lodgings

Vihārānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Permission for Monasteries

294. Senāsanakkhandhake [M 3.0392][V 3.0358] senāsanaṃ apaññattaṃ hotīti vihārasenāsanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Catubbidhañhi (ma. ni. aṭṭa. 1.296) senāsanaṃ vihārasenāsanaṃ mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ santhatasenāsanaṃ okāsasenāsananti. Tattha “mañcopi senāsanaṃ, pīṭhampi bhisipi bimbohanampi vihāropi aḍḍhayogopi pāsādopi hammiyampi guhāpi aṭṭopi māḷopi leṇampi veḷugumbopi rukkhamūlampi maṇḍapopi senāsanaṃ. Yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamanti, sabbametaṃ senāsana”nti (vibha. 527) vacanato vihāro aḍḍhayogo pāsādo hammiyaṃ guhāti idaṃ vihārasenāsanaṃ nāma. Mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bimbohananti idaṃ mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ nāma. Cimilikā cammakhaṇḍo tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāroti idaṃ santhatasenāsanaṃ nāma. Yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamantīti idaṃ okāsasenāsanaṃ nāma.

294. In the Chapter on Lodgings, the term "lodging not designated" refers to monastery lodgings. For lodgings are of four kinds: monastery lodgings, bed-and-seat lodgings, spread lodgings, and open-space lodgings. Among these, "a bed is a lodging, a seat is a lodging, a cushion is a lodging, a bolster is a lodging, a monastery is a lodging, a half-gabled house is a lodging, a mansion is a lodging, a storied building is a lodging, a cave is a lodging, a tower is a lodging, a pavilion is a lodging, a rock-shelter is a lodging, a bamboo grove is a lodging, the foot of a tree is a lodging, an open hall is a lodging. Or wherever monks retreat—all this is lodging." Thus, according to this statement, a monastery, a half-gabled house, a mansion, a storied building, and a cave—these are called monastery lodgings. A bed, a seat, a cushion, and a bolster—these are called bed-and-seat lodgings. A mat, a piece of hide, a grass spread, and a leaf spread—these are called spread lodgings. "Or wherever monks retreat"—this is called open-space lodging.

Rukkhamūletiādīsu rukkhamūlasenāsanaṃ nāma yaṃkiñci sandacchāyaṃ vivittaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ. Pabbato nāma selo. Tattha hi udakasoṇḍīsu udakakiccaṃ katvā sītāya rukkhacchāyāya nisinnā nānādisāsu khāyamānāsu sītena vātena bījiyamānā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Kandareti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena dārito udakena bhinno pabbatappadeso kandaraṃ. Yaṃ “nitamba”ntipi “nadīkuñja”ntipi vadanti. Tattha hi rajatapaṭṭasadisā vālikā hoti, matthake maṇivitānaṃ viya vanagahanaṃ, maṇikkhandhasadisaṃ udakaṃ sandati, evarūpaṃ kandaraṃ oruyha pānīyaṃ pivitvā gattāni sītaṃ katvā vālikaṃ ussāpetvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ paññapetvā tattha nisinnā te bhikkhū samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Giriguhā nāma dvinnaṃ pabbatānaṃ antarā, ekasmiṃyeva vā umaṅgasadisaṃ mahāvivaraṃ.

In the section on "at the foot of a tree" and so on, a "lodging at the foot of a tree" means any secluded, shady spot beneath a tree. A mountain (`pabbata`) means a rock (`sela`). There, after performing water-related duties at the water channels, they sit in the cool shade of the trees. As the various quarters are scorched and they are fanned by the cool breeze, they practice the ascetic's way of life. A ravine (`kandara`) is so called because `kaṃ` means water; a mountain area split (`dārito`) by water is a ravine. Some also call it a "mountain flank" or "river grove." There, the sand is like a silver sheet, the dense forest canopy above is like a jeweled canopy, and the water flows like a mass of gems. Descending into such a ravine, drinking water, cooling their bodies, piling up sand, spreading out their rag-robes, and sitting there, those monks practice the ascetic's way of life. A mountain cave (`giriguhā`) means the space between two mountains, or a large opening resembling a tunnel in one mountain.

“Vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”ntiādivacanato (vibha. 531) yattha na [V 3.0359] kasanti na vapanti, tādisaṃ manussānaṃ upacāraṭṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitaṃ araññakasenāsanaṃ “vanapattha”nti vuccati. Ajjhokāso nāma kenaci [M 3.0393] acchanno padeso. Ākaṅkhamānā panettha cīvarakuṭiṃ katvā vasanti. Palālapuñjeti palālarāsimhi. Mahāpalālapuñjato hi palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā pabbhāraleṇasadise ālaye karonti, gacchagumbādīnampi upari palālaṃ parikkhipitvā heṭṭhā nisinnā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pañca leṇānīti pañca līyanaṭṭhānāni. Nilīyanti ettha bhikkhūti leṇāni, vihārādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Supaṇṇavaṅkagehanti garuḷapakkhasaṇṭhānena katagehaṃ.

"The term 'vanapattha' is a designation for remote dwellings," as stated in the Vibhaṅga (531). It means a forest dwelling situated beyond the places of human resort, where people do not plow or sow. "Open space" (`ajjhokāsa`) refers to an uncovered area. Here, if they wish, monks may construct a robe-hut and dwell. "On a heap of straw" means in a pile of straw. From a large heap of straw, they pull straw to make dwellings similar to overhanging rock-shelters. They also surround trees, bushes, and so on with straw and, sitting beneath, practice the ascetic's way of life. This is what is meant here. "Five shelters" refers to five places of refuge. Monks take refuge here—thus they are called "shelters," which is a designation for monasteries and so on. "A house shaped like a Supaṇṇa's wing" means a house built in the shape of a Garuḍa's wing.

295. Anumodanagāthāsu sītanti ajjhattadhātukkhobhavasena vā bahiddhautuvipariṇāmavasaena vā uppajjanakasītaṃ. Uṇhanti aggisantāpaṃ, tassa vanadāhādīsu vā sambhavo daṭṭhabbo. Paṭihantīti bādhati. Yathā tadubhayavasena kāyacittānaṃ bādhanaṃ na hoti, evaṃ karoti. Sītuṇhabbhāhate hi sarīre vikkhittacitto bhikkhu yoniso padahituṃ na sakkoti. Vāḷamigānīti sīhabyagghādivāḷamige. Guttasenāsanañhi pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nisinnassa te parissayā na honti. Sarīsapeti ye keci sarante gacchante dīghajātike. Makaseti nidassanamattametaṃ, ḍaṃsādīnampi eteneva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sisireti sisirakālavasena sattāhavaddhalikādivasena ca uppanne sisirasamphasse. Vuṭṭhiyoti yadā tadā uppannā vassavuṭṭhiyo.

295. In the verses of rejoicing, 'cold' refers to the cold that arises due to an internal disturbance of the elements or due to external changes in the weather. 'Heat' refers to the burning heat of fire; its arising can be seen in forest fires and the like. 'It harms' means it afflicts. It acts so that affliction of body and mind does not occur on account of those two. For when the body is afflicted by cold and heat, a bhikkhu with a distracted mind is unable to strive wisely. 'Wild beasts' refers to wild animals such as lions and tigers. For one who enters a guarded dwelling and sits with the door closed, those dangers do not occur. 'Creeping things' means any long-bodied creatures that move by creeping. 'Mosquitoes' is merely mentioned as an example; gadflies and the like should also be understood as included by this. 'Winter' refers to the cold touch that arises due to the winter season and due to a week-long spell of bad weather and so forth. 'Rain' means the rain showers that occur from time to time.

Vātātapo ghoroti rukkhagacchādīnaṃ ummūlabhañjanādivasena pavattiyā ghoro sarajaarajādibhedo vāto ceva gimhapariḷāhasamayesu uppattiyā ghoro sūriyātapo ca paṭihaññati paṭibāhīyati. Leṇatthanti nānārammaṇato cittaṃ nivattetvā paṭisallānārāmatthaṃ. Sukhatthanti vuttaparissayābhāvena phāsuvihāratthaṃ. Jhāyitunti aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu yattha katthaci cittaṃ upanijjhāyituṃ. Vipassitunti aniccādito saṅkhāre sammasituṃ.

'Wind and heat are fierce': this refers to the fierce wind that proceeds by way of uprooting and breaking trees and shrubs, a wind distinguished as being with or without dust, and the fierce heat of the sun that arises during the hot, burning season; both are struck back and repelled. 'For shelter' means for the sake of delighting in seclusion, having turned the mind away from various objects. 'For happiness' means for the sake of a comfortable abiding, through the absence of the aforementioned dangers. 'To meditate' means to contemplate closely upon any of the thirty-eight objects. 'To contemplate' means to thoroughly investigate conditioned phenomena as impermanent and so forth.

Vihāreti patissaye. Kārayeti kārāpeyya. Rammeti manorame nivāsasukhe. Vāsayettha bahussuteti kāretvā pana ettha vihāresu bahussute sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme nivāseyya. Te nivāsento pana tesaṃ bahussutānaṃ yathā paccayehi kilamatho na hoti, evaṃ annañca [M 3.0394] pānañca vatthasenāsanāni ca dadeyya ujubhūtesu ajjhāsayasampannesu kammaphalānaṃ ratanattayaguṇānañca saddahanena vippasannena cetasā.

'He dwells' means in a lodging. 'He causes to build' means he should cause to be built. 'He delights' means in the delightful comfort of a dwelling. 'He should house here the learned' means that, having had them built, he should house in these dwellings those who are learned, virtuous, and of good character. And while housing them, he should give food, drink, robes, and lodgings to those learned ones so that they do not suffer hardship from want of requisites. This he should do for those who are upright and endowed with good dispositions, with a mind made serene through faith in the fruit of kamma and in the qualities of the Triple Gem.

Idāni gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ aññamaññupakāritaṃ dassetuṃ “te tassā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha teti [V 3.0360] te bahussutā. Tassāti upāsakassa. Dhammaṃ desentīti sakalavaṭṭadukkhāpanūdanaṃ saddhammaṃ desenti. Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāyāti so puggalo yaṃ saddhammaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane sammā paṭipajjanena jānitvā aggamaggādhigamena anāsavo hutvā parinibbāyati.

Now, to show the mutual support between householders and renunciants, he states the verse beginning 'They for him.' Therein, 'they' refers to those learned ones. 'For him' means for the lay devotee. 'They teach the Dhamma' means they teach the good Dhamma that removes all the suffering of the cycle of rebirth. 'That he may know the Dhamma here' means that person, having known the good Dhamma in this Dispensation through right practice, becomes free from taints by attaining the highest path and attains final Nibbāna.

So ca sabbadado hotīti āvāsadānasmiṃ dinne sabbadānaṃ dinnameva hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Tathā hi (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.42) dve tayo gāme piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci aladdhā āgatassapi chāyūdakasampannaṃ ārāmaṃ pavisitvā nahāyitvā patissaye muhuttaṃ nipajjitvā uṭṭhāya nisinnassa kāye balaṃ āharitvā pakkhittaṃ viya hoti, bahi vicarantassa ca kāye vaṇṇadhātu vātātapehi kilamati, patissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya muhuttaṃ nipannassa visabhāgasantati vūpasammati, sabhāgasantati patiṭṭhāti, vaṇṇadhātu āharitvā pakkhittā viya hoti, bahi vicarantassa ca pāde kaṇṭako vijjhati, khāṇu paharati, sarīsapādiparissayā ceva corabhayañca uppajjati, patissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nipannassa sabbe parissayā na honti, sajjhāyantassa dhammapītisukhaṃ, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontassa upasamasukhañca uppajjati bahiddhāvikkhepābhāvato, bahi vicarantassa ca sedā muccanti, akkhīni phandanti, senāsanaṃ pavisanakkhaṇe mañcapīṭhāni na paññāyanti, muhuttaṃ nisinnassa pana akkhipasādo āharitvā pakkhitto viya hoti, dvāravātapānamañcapīṭhādīni paññāyanti, etasmiñca āvāse vasantaṃ disvā manussā catūhi paccayehi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahanti. Tena vuttaṃ “so ca sabbadado hoti, yo dadāti upassaya”nti.

‘And he is a giver of all’—this is said because when a dwelling is given, it is considered that all gifts have been given. For it is so (cf. Saṃ. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.42): even for one who, having wandered for alms in two or three villages and obtained nothing, returns and enters a monastery endowed with shade and water, after bathing and lying down for a moment in his lodging, upon rising and sitting, strength is restored to his body as if it had been infused. While wandering outside, the body’s complexion is exhausted by wind and heat; but upon entering the lodging, closing the door, and lying down for a moment, the dissimilar continuity ceases, the similar continuity is established, and the complexion is restored as if it had been infused. While wandering outside, a thorn may pierce his foot, a stump may strike him, and dangers from creeping things and so forth, as well as the fear of thieves, may arise; but upon entering the lodging and closing the door, all dangers cease. For one who recites, the joy and happiness of the Dhamma arise; for one who attends to a meditation subject, the happiness of tranquility arises, due to the absence of external distraction. While wandering outside, sweat pours out and the eyes flicker, so that upon entering the lodging, the bed and seat are not discerned; but after sitting for a moment, the clarity of the eyes is restored as if it had been infused, and the door, window, bed, seat, and so on, become discernible. And seeing him dwelling in this residence, people respectfully attend to him with the four requisites. Therefore it is said: ‘And he is a giver of all, who gives a lodging.’”

296. Āviñchanacchiddanti yattha aṅguliṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ ākaḍḍhantā dvārabāhaṃ phusāpenti, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Āviñchanarajjunti kavāṭeyeva chiddaṃ katvā tattha pavesetvā yena rajjukena kaḍḍhantā dvāraṃ phusāpenti, taṃ āviñchanarajjukaṃ. Senāsanaparibhoge akappiyacammaṃ nāma natthīti [M 3.0395] dassanatthaṃ “sacepi dīpinaṅguṭṭhena katā hoti, vaṭṭatiyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Cetiye vedikāsadisanti vātapānabāhāsu cetiye vedikāya viya paṭṭikādīhi dassetvā kataṃ. Thambhakavātapānaṃ nāma tiriyaṃ dārūni adatvā ujukaṃ ṭhitehi eva veṇusalākādīhi kataṃ.

296. A 'pulling-hole' is that into which one inserts a finger and pulls the door, causing it to touch the door-post; this is its designation. A 'pulling-rope' is a rope that is inserted into a hole made in the door-leaf itself, by pulling which they cause the door to touch the frame. To show that there is no such thing as an unsuitable hide for use in a dwelling, it is said: 'Even if it is made with a leopard's tail, it is allowable.' 'Like the railing at a shrine' refers to a window made on the window-posts with strips and so on, so that it looks like the railing of a shrine. A 'pillar-window' is one made with upright bamboo slats or the like, without adding horizontal pieces of wood.

Vihārānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse concerning the allowance of monasteries is concluded.

Mañcapīṭhādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Allowance of Beds, Chairs, and so forth.

297. Poṭakitūlanti [V 3.0361] erakatiṇatūlaṃ. Poṭakigahaṇañcettha tiṇajātīnaṃ nidassanamattanti āha “yesaṃ kesañci tiṇajātikāna”nti. Pañcavidhaṃ uṇṇāditūlampi vaṭṭatīti etthāpi “bimbohane”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. “Tūlapūritaṃ bhisiṃ apassayituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti keci vadanti, vaṭṭatīti apare. Upadahantīti ṭhapenti. Sīsappamāṇanti yattha galavāṭakato paṭṭhāya sabbasīsaṃ upadahanti, taṃ sīsappamāṇaṃ. Tañca ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato tiriyaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hotīti dassetuṃ “yassa vitthārato tīsu kaṇṇesū”tiādimāha. Majjhaṭṭhānaṃ muṭṭhiratanaṃ hotīti bimbohanassa majjhaṭṭhānaṃ tiriyato muṭṭhiratanappamāṇaṃ hoti. Masūraketi cammamayabhisiyaṃ. Phusitāni dātunti saññākaraṇatthaṃ bindūni dātuṃ.

297. 'Poṭaki-fiber' means the fiber of eraka grass. And the inclusion of 'poṭaki' here is merely an example of types of grass, as he says: 'of any kind of grass.' The five kinds of stuffing, such as wool, are also allowable; here too the word 'for a pillow' should be brought in and connected. Some say, 'It is not allowable to lean on a cushion stuffed with fiber,' while others say it is allowable. 'They place' means they set down. 'Head-sized' is that on which they place the whole head, starting from the nape of the neck; that is a head-sized one. And to show that its maximum limit is a fist-span across, he says: 'whose width at the three corners…' 'The middle part is a fist-span' means the middle part of the pillow is a fist-span across. 'A masūraka' means a leather cushion. 'To make spots' means to make dots for the purpose of identification.

298. Na nibandhatīti anibandhanīyo, na allīyatīti attho. Paṭibāhetvāti maṭṭhaṃ katvā.

298. 'It does not bind': it is not binding; the meaning is, it does not cling.

Iṭṭhakācayādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Allowance of Brickwork and so forth.

300. Rukkhaṃ vijjhitvāti rukkhadāruṃ vijjhitvā. Khāṇuke ākoṭetvāti dve dve khāṇuke ākoṭetvā. Taṃ āharimaṃ bhittipādanti vuttanayena khāṇuke ākoṭetvā kataṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetunti mūlena bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā bhittipādassa upatthambhanavasena ussāpetvā khāṇukehi bhittipādaṃ ussāpetvā ṭhapetunti adhippāyo. Ubhato kuṭṭaṃ nīharitvā katapadesassāti yathā antodvārasamīpe [M 3.0396] nisinnehi ujukaṃ bahi oloketuṃ na sakkā hoti, evaṃ ubhohi passehi kuṭṭaṃ nīharitvā abhimukhe bhittiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā katapadesassa. Samantā pariyāgāroti samantato āviddhapamukhaṃ. Ugghāṭanakiṭikanti daṇḍehi ukkhipitvā ṭhapanakapadarakiṭikaṃ.

300. 'Having pierced a tree' means having pierced tree-timber. 'Having hammered in stakes' means having hammered in stakes two by two. 'That artificial wall-footing' refers to what is made by hammering in stakes in the manner stated. 'To establish on the ground' means to establish it on the ground by its base and to raise it as a support for the wall-footing; the intention is to raise and place the wall-footing with stakes. 'Of the place made by extending the wall on both sides' refers to a place made by extending the wall from both sides and erecting a wall in front, so that those sitting near the inner door cannot look straight outside. 'A surrounding enclosure' means one with a projecting front on all sides. 'A lifting bolt' refers to a wooden bolt that is placed by lifting with poles.

Anāthapiṇḍikavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Anāthapiṇḍika

304. Anāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhivatthumhi (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.242) kenacideva karaṇīyenāti vāṇijjakammaṃ adhippetaṃ. Anāthapiṇḍiko kira rājagahaseṭṭhi ca aññamaññaṃ bhaginipatikā honti. Yadā rājagahe uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍaṃ samagghaṃ hoti, tadā rājagahaseṭṭhi taṃ gahetvā [V 3.0362] sakaṭasatehi sāvatthiṃ gantvā yojanamatte ṭhito attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpeti. Anāthapiṇḍiko paccuggantvā tassa mahāsakkāraṃ katvā ekaṃ yānaṃ āropetvā sāvatthiṃ pavisati. So sace bhaṇḍaṃ lahukaṃ vikkīyati, vikkiṇāti. No ce, bhaginighare ṭhapetvā pakkamati. Anāthapiṇḍikopi tatheva karoti. Svāyaṃ tadāpi teneva karaṇīyena agamāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

304. In the Story of the Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika (Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary 1.1.242): 'On some business' refers to mercantile activity. It is said that Anāthapiṇḍika and the chief merchant of Rājagaha were brothers-in-law to each other. Whenever merchandise was cheap in Rājagaha, the chief merchant would take it and go to Sāvatthī with a hundred carts. Having stopped at a distance of one yojana, he would make known his arrival. Anāthapiṇḍika would go out to greet him, show him great honor, and, having placed him on a single vehicle, enter Sāvatthī. If the goods were sold quickly, he would sell them. If not, he would leave them at his sister's house and depart. Anāthapiṇḍika would also do the same. At that time too, he had gone for the same purpose. This was said in reference to that.

Taṃ divasaṃ pana rājagahaseṭṭhi yojanamatte ṭhitena anāthapiṇḍikena āgatabhāvajānanatthaṃ pesitaṃ paṇṇaṃ na suṇi, dhammassavanatthāya vihāraṃ agamāsi. So dhammakathaṃ sutvā svātanāya buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā attano ghare uddhanakhaṇāpanadāruphālanādīni kāresi. Anāthapiṇḍikopi “idāni mayhaṃ paccuggamanaṃ karissati, idāni karissatī”ti gharadvārepi paccuggamanaṃ alabhitvā antogharaṃ paviṭṭho paṭisanthārampi na bahuṃ alattha. “Kiṃ mahāseṭṭhi kusalaṃ dārakarūpānaṃ, nasi magge kilanto”ti ettakova paṭisanthāro ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa etadahosī”tiādi.

On that day, however, the chief merchant of Rājagaha did not hear the message sent by Anāthapiṇḍika, who had stopped at a distance of one yojana to inform him of his arrival, because he had gone to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. After hearing the Dhamma talk, he invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha for the next day and arranged for the digging of ovens, the splitting of wood, and other preparations at his house. Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, 'Now he will come out to meet me, now he will,' did not receive a welcome even at the door of the house, and even when he entered the house, he received little hospitality. The only greeting he received was, 'Great merchant, are the children well? Were you not weary on the road?' This is why it is said, 'Then it occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika,' and so on.

Buddhoti tvaṃ gahapati vadesīti tassa kira mukhato buddhasaddaṃ sutvā anāthapiṇḍiko pañcavaṇṇaṃ pītiṃ paṭilabhati, sā tassa sīse uṭṭhahitvā yāva pādapiṭṭhiyā, pādapiṭṭhiyā uṭṭhāya yāva sīsā gacchati, ubhato uṭṭhāya majjhe osarati, majjhe uṭṭhāya ubhato gacchati. So pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭo “buddhoti tvaṃ gahapati vadesī”ti evaṃ tikkhattuṃ pucchi. Akālo kho, gahapati, imaṃ kālaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ [M 3.0397] dassanāya upasaṅkamitunti “buddhā nāma durāsadā āsīvisasadisā honti, satthā ca sivathikāya samīpe vasati, na sakkā tattha imāya velāya iminā gantu”nti maññamāno evamāha. Buddhagatāya satiyā nipajjīti aññaṃ kiñci acintetvā buddhagatāya eva satiyā nipajji. Taṃ divasaṃ kirassa bhaṇḍasakaṭesu vā upaṭṭhākesu vā cittampi nuppajji, sāyamāsampi na akāsi. Sattabhūmikaṃ pana pāsādaṃ āruyha supaññattālaṅkatavarasayane “buddho buddho”ti sajjhāyaṃ karontova nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkami. Tikkhattuṃ vuṭṭhāsi pabhātaṃ maññamānoti paṭhamayāme tāva vītivatte uṭṭhāya buddhaṃ anussari, athassa balavappasādo udapādi, pītiāloko ahosi, sabbatamaṃ vigacchi, dīpasahassujjalanaṃ viya canduṭṭhānasūriyuṭṭhānaṃ viya ca jātaṃ. So “pamādaṃ āpannomhi, vañcitomhi, sūriyo uggato”ti uṭṭhāya ākāsatale ṭhatvā candaṃ oloketvā “ekova yāmo gato, aññe dve atthī”ti puna pavisitvā nipajji, etenupāyena majjhimayāmāvasānepi pacchimayāmāvasānepi tikkhattuṃ uṭṭhāsi. Pacchimayāmāvasāne pana balavapaccūseyeva [V 3.0363] uṭṭhāya ākāsatalaṃ āgantvā mahādvārābhimukho ahosi, sattabhūmikadvāraṃ sayameva vivaṭaṃ ahosi, pāsādā oruyha antaravīthiṃ paṭipajji.

Hearing the word 'Buddha' from his mouth, Anāthapiṇḍika experienced five-fold joy. It arose from his head and spread down to the soles of his feet; then rose from the soles back up to his head. Surging from both ends, it converged in the middle, and rising from the middle, it spread to both ends. Filled continuously with joy, he asked three times, 'You say, householder, "Buddha"?' The merchant said: 'It is not the time, householder, to approach the Blessed One for a visit at this hour.' He said this thinking: 'Buddhas are hard to approach, like venomous snakes; and the Teacher resides near a charnel ground, so it is not possible for him to go there at this time.' 'He lay down with his mind fixed on the Buddha' means he lay down with his mind fixed only on the Buddha, thinking of nothing else. That day, no thought arose in him regarding his goods, carts, or attendants. He even neglected his evening meal. Ascending his seven-story mansion, he lay down on a well-prepared, adorned, and excellent bed, reciting 'Buddho, Buddho,' and fell asleep. 'Three times he rose, thinking it was dawn' means that after the first watch of the night had passed, he arose and recollected the Buddha. Then, strong faith arose in him, a light of joy appeared, and all darkness vanished—as if a thousand lamps were lit, or as if the moon or sun had risen. 'I have been negligent, I have been deceived—the sun has risen!' he thought. Standing in the open air, he looked at the moon and realized, 'Only one watch has passed, two remain.' He went back inside and lay down again. In this same way, he rose again at the end of the middle watch and at the end of the last watch, thus rising three times in all. At the end of the last watch, however, he rose in the strong dawn itself, went out into the open air, and faced the great gate. The gate of the seven-story mansion opened by itself. Descending from the mansion, he proceeded along the inner road.

305. Amanussāti adhigatavisesā devatā. Tathā hi tā seṭṭhissa bhāvinisampattiṃ paccakkhato sampassamānā “ayaṃ mahāseṭṭhi ‘buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmī’ti nikkhanto paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ aggupaṭṭhāko hutvā asadisaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ katvā cātuddisassa ariyasaṅghassa anāvaṭadvāro bhavissati, na yuttamassa dvāraṃ pidahitu”nti cintetvā dvāraṃ vivariṃsu. Antaradhāyīti rājagahaṃ kira ākiṇṇamanussaṃ, antonagare nava koṭiyo bahinagare navāti taṃ upanissāya aṭṭhārasa manussakoṭiyo vasanti. Avelāya matamanusse bahi nīharituṃ asakkontā aṭṭālake ṭhatvā bahidvāre khipanti. Mahāseṭṭhi nagarato bahi nikkhantamattova allasarīraṃ pādena akkami, aparampi piṭṭhipādena pahari, makkhikā uppatitvā pakiriṃsu, duggandho nāsāpuṭaṃ abhihani, buddhappasādo tanuttaṃ gato. Tenassa āloko antaradhāyi andhakāro pāturahosi pītivegassa tanubhāve taṃsamuṭṭhitarūpānaṃ paridubbalabhāvato[M 3.0398]. Saddamanussāvesīti “seṭṭhissa ussāhaṃ janessāmī”ti suvaṇṇakiṅkiṇikaṃ ghaṭṭento viya madhurassarena saddaṃ anussāvesi.

305. 'Non-humans' refers to deities who have attained special qualities. For they, seeing firsthand the great merchant's future prosperity, thought: 'This great merchant, having set out thinking, "I will go to attend upon the Buddha," will, upon his very first sight, become established in the fruit of stream-entry. He will become the chief attendant of the Three Jewels, build an incomparable monastery for the Saṅgha, and become one whose doors are open to the noble Saṅgha of the four quarters. It is not right to close the door on him.' Thus thinking, they opened the door. 'It disappeared.' It is said that Rājagaha was crowded with people. Inside the city were nine crores, and outside the city another nine—thus, in and around it, eighteen crores of people lived. Unable to carry out the dead at improper times, they would stand on the watchtowers and throw them outside the gates. As soon as the great merchant stepped outside the city, he stepped on a fresh corpse with his foot, and struck another with the back of his foot. Flies rose up and scattered, a foul stench struck his nostrils, and his faith in the Buddha weakened. Because of this, his light disappeared and darkness appeared, due to the weakening of the force of his joy and the resulting feebleness of the forms that had arisen from it. 'He made a sound heard' means that, desiring to rouse the merchant's effort, he made a sound in a sweet voice, as if striking a small golden bell.

Sataṃ kaññāsahassānīti purimapadānipi imināva sahassa-padena saddhiṃ sambandhitabbāni. Yatheva hi sataṃ kaññāsahassāni, evaṃ sataṃ sahassāni hatthī, sataṃ sahassāni assā, sataṃ sahassāni rathāti ayamettha attho, iti ekekaṃ satasahassaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti. Padavītihārassāti padaṃ vītiharati etthāti padavītihāro. So dutavilambitaṃ akatvā samagamane dvinnaṃ padānaṃ antare muṭṭhiratanamattaṃ. Kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasinti taṃ ekaṃ padavītihāraṃ soḷasa bhāge katvā tato eko koṭṭhāso puna soḷasadhā, tato eko soḷasadhāti evaṃ soḷasa vāre soḷasadhā bhinnassa eko koṭṭhāso soḷasī kalā nāma, taṃ soḷasiṃ kalaṃ etāni cattāri satasahassāni na agghanti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sataṃ hatthisahassāni sataṃ assasahassāni sataṃ rathasahassāni sataṃ kaññāsahassāni, tā ca kho āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā sakalajambudīparājadhītarovāti imasmā ettakā lābhā vihāraṃ gacchantassa tasmiṃ soḷasikalāsaṅkhāte padese laṅghanasādhanavasena pavattacetanāva uttaritarāti. Padaṃ vā vītiharati etenāti padavītihāro, tathāpavattā kusalacetanā, tassā phalaṃ soḷasadhā katvāti ca vadanti. Idaṃ pana vihāragamanaṃ kassa vasena gahitanti? Vihāraṃ gantvā anantarāyena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahantassa vasena gahitaṃ. “Gandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ karissāmi, cetiyaṃ vandissāmi, dhammaṃ sossāmi, [V 3.0364] dīpapūjaṃ karissāmi, saṅghaṃ nimantetvā dānaṃ dassāmi, sikkhāpadesu vā saraṇesu vā patiṭṭhahissāmī”ti gacchatopi vasena vaṭṭatiyeva.

"A hundred thousand maidens"—the preceding words should also be connected with this word "thousand." Just as there are a hundred thousand maidens, so too are there a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, and a hundred thousand chariots—this is the meaning here. Thus, each is shown to be a hundred thousand. Regarding 'the passing over of a step' (padavītihāra): a step is passed over there. This is the interval between two steps when one proceeds without delay, a space the size of a fist-gem. "Not worth a sixteenth part"—this means that if one were to divide that single step-interval into sixteen parts, and then one of those parts again into sixteen, and so on sixteen times, one such part is called a "sixteenth kalā." These four hundred thousands are not worth that sixteenth kalā. This is what is said: a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, a hundred thousand chariots, and a hundred thousand maidens—and they adorned with jewelled earrings, all daughters of the kings of Jambudīpa—all these gains are surpassed by the intention that arises by means of taking a step towards the monastery in that space reckoned as a sixteenth kalā. Alternatively, 'padavītihāra' is that by which one passes over a step, that is, the wholesome intention that has so arisen; and some say its fruit is to be divided into sixteen parts. Now, with reference to whom is this going to the monastery taken? It is taken with reference to one who, upon going to the monastery, is established in the fruit of stream-entry without obstruction. It is also applicable in the case of one who goes thinking, "I will make offerings of perfumes and garlands, I will pay homage to the cetiya, I will listen to the Dhamma, I will make an offering of lamps, I will invite the Saṅgha and give a gift, or I will establish myself in the training rules or in the refuges."

Andhakāro antaradhāyīti so kira cintesi “ahaṃ ekakoti saññaṃ karomi, amanussā ca me anugāmino sahāyā atthi, kasmā bhāyāmī”ti sūro ahosi. Athassa balavā buddhappasādo udapādi, tasmā andhakāro antaradhāyi. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo. Āloko pāturahosīti purimabuddhesu cirakālaparicayasambhūtassa balavato pasādassa vasena uppannāya uḷārāya buddhārammaṇāya pītiyā samuṭṭhāpito [M 3.0399] vipassanobhāsasadiso sātisayo cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhāno āloko pāturahosi. Devatāhi katotipi vadanti, purimoyevettha yuttataro. Ehi sudattāti so kira seṭṭhi gacchamānova cintesi “imasmiṃ loke bahū pūraṇakassapādayo titthiyā ‘mayaṃ buddhā, mayaṃ buddhā’ti vadanti, kathaṃ nu kho ahaṃ satthu buddhabhāvaṃ jāneyya”nti. Athassa etadahosi “mayhaṃ guṇavasena uppannaṃ nāmaṃ mahājano jānāti, kuladattiyaṃ pana me nāmaṃ aññatra mayā na koci jānāti, sace buddho bhavissati, kuladattikanāmena maṃ ālapissatī”ti. Satthā tassa cittaṃ ñatvā evamāha.

"The darkness disappeared": It is said he thought, "I perceive myself as being alone, yet I have non-human followers and allies—why should I fear?" Thus, he became brave. Then, strong faith in the Buddha arose in him, and for that reason the darkness disappeared. This is the method in the remaining instances as well. "A light appeared": Due to powerful faith born from long acquaintance with past Buddhas, a sublime joy with the Buddha as its object arose. Produced by this joy, an extraordinary light appeared, similar to the light of insight, arisen from mind-conditionality and from the season. Some say it was created by deities, but the former explanation is more suitable here. "Come, Sudatta": It is said that as the setthi was walking, he thought, "In this world, many sectarians like Pūraṇa Kassapa and others say, 'We are Buddhas, we are Buddhas.' How then shall I know the Teacher's state of Buddhahood?" Then it occurred to him: "The great populace knows the name that arose on account of my virtue, but my family-given name, no one knows except me. If he is a Buddha, he will address me by my family-given name." The Teacher, knowing his thought, spoke thus.

Parinibbutoti kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto. Āsattiyoti rūpādīsu āsañjanaṭṭhena āsattiyo, taṇhāyo. Santinti kilesavūpasamaṃ. Pappuyyāti aggamaggena patvā. Sesamettha pāḷianusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Yañcettha anuttānamatthaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva.

"He is fully extinguished": He is fully extinguished by the full extinguishment of the defilements. "Attachments": These are attachments, cravings, in the sense of clinging to forms and so on. "Peace": The stilling of the defilements. "Having attained": Having attained by means of the highest path. The remainder here should be understood according to the Pāli itself. And whatever meaning here is not manifest, that has been stated in the commentary.

306. Vayameva veyyāyikanti āha “veyyāyikanti vayakaraṇaṃ vuccatī”ti.

306. Regarding "Expenditure itself is the expender," he said: "The term 'expender' (veyyāyika) is said to mean 'the act of expending.'"

Anāthapiṇḍikavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the story of Anāthapiṇḍika is concluded.

Aggāsanādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Allowing the Chief Seat and So Forth

310-311. Dakkhiṇodakanti aggato upanīyamānaṃ dakkhiṇodakaṃ. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesīti (jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.36 tittirajātakavaṇṇanā) tehi bhikkhūhi attano attano rucivasena aggāsanādirahānaṃ kathitakāle “na, bhikkhave, mayhaṃ sāsane aggāsanādīni patvā khattiyakulā pabbajito pamāṇaṃ, na brāhmaṇakulā, na gahapatikulā pabbajito, na vinayadharo, na suttantiko, na ābhidhammiko, na paṭhamajjhānādilābhino, na sotāpannādayo [V 3.0365] pamāṇaṃ, atha kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane yathāvuḍḍhaṃ abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ añjalikammaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ kattabbaṃ, aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍo laddhabbo, idamettha pamāṇaṃ, tasmā vuḍḍhataro bhikkhu etesaṃ anucchaviko. Idāni kho pana, bhikkhave, sāriputto mayhaṃ aggasāvako anudhammacakkappavattako [M 3.0400] mamānantarasenāsanaṃ laddhuṃ arahati. So imaṃ rattiṃ senāsanaṃ alabhanto rukkhamūle vītināmesi. Tumhe idāneva evaṃ agāravā appatissā, gacchante gacchante kāle kinti katvā viharissathā”ti vatvā atha nesaṃ ovādadānatthāya “pubbe, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatāpi ‘na kho panetaṃ amhākaṃ patirūpaṃ, yaṃ mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ agāravā appatissā asabhāgavuttino vihareyyāma, amhesu mahallakataraṃ jānitvā tassa abhivādanādīni karissāmā’ti sādhukaṃ vīmaṃsitvā ‘ayaṃ mahallako’ti ñatvā tassa abhivādanādīni katvā devapathaṃ pūrayamānā gatā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āharitvā dassetuṃ bhikkhū āmantesi.

310-311. 'Water of dedication' (dakkhiṇodaka) means the water of dedication brought forth first. 'Then the Blessed One addressed the monks': At the time when those monks were speaking according to their own preferences about who was worthy of the chief seat and so forth, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, in my teaching, one who has gone forth from a khattiya family is not the standard for receiving the chief seat and so forth, nor one from a brahmin family, nor one from a householder family; not one who is an expert in the Vinaya, nor in the Suttas, nor in the Abhidhamma; not those who have attained the first jhāna and so on, nor stream-enterers and so on are the standard. Rather, monks, in this teaching, greeting, rising, making an añjali, and proper service should be done according to seniority. The chief seat, the first water, and the first almsfood should be received. This is the standard here. Therefore, a more senior monk is suitable for these. Now, monks, Sāriputta is my chief disciple, one who turns the wheel of the Dhamma in conformity with the Dhamma. He deserves to receive the lodging next to mine. But not getting a lodging this night, he spent it at the foot of a tree. If you are so disrespectful and without deference even now, what will you do as time goes on?' Having said this, in order to give them an exhortation, he said: 'In the past, monks, even animals thought, "It is not proper for us that we should dwell disrespectful, without deference, and with unsuitable conduct towards one another. We should find out who is the eldest among us and perform greetings and so on for him." Having considered well and known, "This is the eldest," they performed greetings and so on for him, and fulfilling the path to the devas, they passed on.' Having said this, he addressed the monks to show them something from the past.

Ye vuḍḍhamapacāyantīti jātivuḍḍho vayovuḍḍho guṇavuḍḍhoti tayo vuḍḍhā. Tesu jātisampanno jātivuḍḍho nāma, vaye ṭhito vayovuḍḍho nāma, guṇasampanno guṇavuḍḍho nāma. Tesu guṇasampanno vayovuḍḍho imasmiṃ ṭhāne vuḍḍhoti adhippeto. Apacāyantīti jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammena pūjenti. Dhammassa kovidāti jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammassa kovidā kusalā. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Pāsaṃsāti pasaṃsārahā. Samparāye ca suggatīti samparetabbe imaṃ lokaṃ hitvā gantabbe paralokepi tesaṃ sugatiyeva hotīti attho. Ayaṃ panettha piṇḍattho – bhikkhave, khattiyā vā hontu brāhmaṇā vā vessā vā suddā vā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā tiracchānagatā vā, ye keci sattā jeṭṭhāpacitikamme chekā kusalā guṇasampannānaṃ vayovuḍḍhānaṃ apacitiṃ karonti, te imasmiñca attabhāve jeṭṭhāpacitikārakāti pasaṃsaṃ vaṇṇanaṃ thomanaṃ labhanti, kāyassa ca bhedā sagge nibbattantīti.

"Those who honor the elders": There are three kinds of elders: the elder by birth, the elder by age, and the elder by virtue. Among them, one accomplished in birth is called an elder by birth; one established in age is called an elder by age; one accomplished in virtue is called an elder by virtue. Of these, one accomplished in virtue and an elder by age is intended as the 'elder' in this place. "Honor": They pay homage with the act of honoring elders. "Skilled in the Dhamma": Skilled, expert in the Dhamma of honoring elders. "In this very life": In this very state of existence. "Praiseworthy": Worthy of praise. "And in the hereafter, a happy destiny": This means that in the next world, to be gone to after leaving this world, their destiny is a happy one. This is the summary meaning here: Monks, whether they be khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, or those gone forth, or even animals—whatever beings are clever and skilled in the act of honoring elders and show respect to those accomplished in virtue and senior in age, they receive praise, commendation, and acclaim in this very state of existence as 'those who honor elders,' and with the breakup of the body, they are reborn in heaven.

Aggāsanādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Allowing the Chief Seat and So Forth is concluded.

Āsanappaṭibāhanādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Obstructing Seats and So Forth

313-4. Uddissakatanti gihīhi saṅghaṃ uddissa kataṃ. Gihivikatanti gihīhi kataṃ paññattaṃ, gihisantakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Atisamīpaṃ agantvāti bhikkhūnaṃ āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ agantvā.

313-4. 'Designated' (uddissakata) means that which is made by laypeople, having designated it for the Saṅgha. 'Made by laypeople' (gihivikata) means made and designated by laypeople; it is said to be 'belonging to laypeople.' 'Without approaching too closely' means without going to a place too near the bhikkhus.

Senāsanaggāhāpakasammutikathāvaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Discussion on the Appointment of a Lodging Assigner

318. Paccayeneva [M 3.0401][V 3.0366] hi taṃ paṭijagganaṃ labhissatīti tasmiṃ senāsane mahātherā tassa paccayassa kāraṇā aññattha agantvā vasantāyeva naṃ paṭijaggissantīti attho. Ubbhaṇḍikā bhavissantīti ukkhittabhaṇḍā bhavissanti, attano attano parikkhāre gahetvā tattha tattha vicarissantīti attho. Dīghasālāti caṅkamanasālā. Maṇḍalamāḷo upaṭṭhānasālā. Anudahatīti pīḷeti. Jambudīpe panāti ariyadese bhikkhū sandhāya vuttaṃ. Te kira tathā paññāpenti. Na gocaragāmo ghaṭṭetabboti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “na tattha manussā vattabbā”tiādinā. Vitakkaṃ chinditvāti “iminā nīhārena gacchantaṃ disvā nivāretvā paccaye dassantī”ti evarūpaṃ vitakkaṃ anuppādetvā. Tesu ce ekoti tesu manussesu eko paṇḍitapuriso. Bhaṇḍapaṭicchādananti paṭicchādanakabhaṇḍaṃ, sarīrapaṭicchādanaṃ cīvaranti attho.

318. For it is only by means of the requisites that he will obtain maintenance: the meaning is that the senior bhikkhus, residing in that lodging, will maintain him for the sake of that requisite, without going elsewhere. 'They will be those who have their goods ready' means they will be those whose goods are taken up; the meaning is that they will move about here and there, taking their own respective requisites. 'The long hall' refers to the walking meditation hall. 'The circular pavilion' is the assembly hall. 'Harasses' means oppresses. Regarding Jambudīpa, this is said with reference to bhikkhus in the noble land. They indeed prescribe it thus. 'One should not intrude upon the alms-village' explains the very meaning stated by 'one should not speak to the people there' and so forth. 'Having cut off the thought' means not giving rise to such a thought as, 'Seeing him going in this manner, they will stop him and give requisites.' 'If among them there is one' means among those people, there is one wise person. 'A covering for goods' means a covering requisite; the meaning is the robe for covering the body.

Paṭijaggitabbānīti sammajjanādīhi paṭijaggitabbāni. Muṇḍavedikāyāti cetiyassa hammiyavedikāya. Hammiyavedikāti ca cetiyassa upari caturassavediyo vuccati. Paṭikkammāti vihārato apasakkitvā. Upanikkhepanti khettaṃ vā nāḷikerādiārāmaṃ vā kahāpaṇādīni vā ārāmikādīnaṃ niyyātetvā “ito uppannā vaḍḍhi vassāvāsikatthāya hotū”ti dinnaṃ. Vattaṃ katvāti tasmiṃ senāsane kattabbavattaṃ katvā.

'To be maintained' means they should be maintained by sweeping and so forth. 'The plain railing' refers to the terrace railing of the shrine. And 'terrace railing' is the name for the four-sided railing above the shrine. 'To step back' means to withdraw from the monastery. 'To deposit' means giving fields, coconut groves and so forth, or money and so forth, to the monastery attendants and so forth, saying, 'Let the income arising from this be for the purpose of the rainy-season residence.' 'Having performed the duties' means having performed the duties to be done in that dwelling.

Puggalavaseneva kātabbanti parato vakkhamānanayena “bhikkhū cīvarena kilamanti, ettakaṃ nāma taṇḍulabhāgaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cīvaraṃ kātuṃ ruccatī”tiādinā puggalaparāmāsavaseneva kātabbaṃ, “saṅgho cīvarena kilamatī”tiādinā pana saṅghaparāmāsavasena na kātabbaṃ. Cīvarapaccayanti cīvarasaṅkhātaṃ paccayaṃ. Vuttanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃvuttaṃ. Kasmā evaṃ vuttanti āha “evañhi navako vuḍḍhatarassa, vuḍḍho ca navakassa gāhessatī”ti, yasmā attanāva attano pāpetuṃ na sakkā, tasmā dvīsu sammatesu navako vuḍḍhatarassa, vuḍḍho ca navakassāti ubho aññamaññaṃ gāhessantīti adhippāyo. Sammatasenāsanaggāhāpakassa āṇattiyā aññena gāhitepi gāho ruhatiyevāti veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhapi soḷasapi jane [M 3.0402] sammannituṃ vaṭṭatīti kiṃ visuṃ visuṃ sammannituṃ vaṭṭati, udāhu ekatoti? Ekatopi vaṭṭati. Niggahakammameva hi saṅgho saṅghassa na karoti, sammutidānaṃ pana bahūnampi ekato kātuṃ vaṭṭati, teneva sattasatikakkhandhake ubbāhikasammutiyaṃ aṭṭhapi janā ekato sammatāti.

'It should be done by relying on individuals' means it should be done by relying on individual consideration, in the manner to be stated later, such as 'The bhikkhus are weary on account of robes; this much of a rice portion is agreeable for making robes for the bhikkhus,' but it should not be done by relying on consideration of the Saṅgha, such as 'The Saṅgha is weary on account of robes.' 'The requisite of robes' means the requisite designated as a robe. 'It is stated' means it is stated in the Great Commentary. Why is it said thus? He says: 'For thus, the junior will have it taken for the senior, and the senior for the junior.' Since one cannot get it for oneself, therefore, when two are appointed, the junior will have it taken for the senior, and the senior for the junior—the meaning is that both will have it taken for each other. It should be understood that even when taken by another on the authority of the appointed lodging assigner, the taking is indeed valid. 'Is it permissible to appoint eight or sixteen people?' Is it permissible to appoint them separately, or all together? It is permissible to appoint them all together. For the Saṅgha does not perform a disciplinary action on the Saṅgha itself, but it is permissible to give an appointment to many at once. Thus, in the Khandhaka of the Seven Hundred, eight people were appointed together for the appointment of the arbitrators.

Maggoti [V 3.0367] magge katadīghasālā. Pokkharaṇīti nahāyantānaṃ pokkharaṇiyaṃ katasālā. Rukkhamūlādayo channā kavāṭabaddhāva senāsanaṃ. Vijaṭetvāti viyojetvā, visuṃ visuṃ katvāti attho. Āvāsesūti senāsanesu. Pakkhipitvāti ettha pakkhipanaṃ nāma tesu vasantānaṃ ito uppannavassāvāsikadānaṃ. Pavisitabbanti aññehi bhikkhūhi tasmiṃ mahālābhe pariveṇe vasitvā cetiye vattaṃ katvāva lābho gahetabboti adhippāyo.

'The path' means the long hall built on the path. 'The pond' means the hall built at the pond for those who bathe. The roots of trees and so forth, when roofed and fitted with doors, are a lodging. 'Having disentangled' means having separated, having made distinct—this is the meaning. 'In the dwellings' means in the lodgings. 'Having put into': here, 'putting into' means the giving of the rains-residence requisites arising from this to those dwelling there. 'Should enter': the meaning is that other bhikkhus, having resided in that monastery of great gain and having performed their duties at the shrine, should then take the gain.

Paccayaṃ vissajjetīti cīvarapaccayaṃ nādhivāseti. Ayampīti tena vissaṭṭhapaccayopi. Upanibandhitvā gāhetabbanti “imasmiṃ rukkhe vā maṇḍape vā vasitvā cetiye vattaṃ katvā gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ upanibandhitvā gāhetabbaṃ. “Kattha nu kho vasissāmi, kattha vasantassa phāsu bhavissati, kattha vā paccayo bhavissatī”ti evaṃ uppannena vitakkena caratīti vitakkacāriko. Araññavihāresu parissayavijānanatthaṃ icchitabbattā “pañca pañca ukkā koṭṭetabbā”ti vuttaṃ.

'He abandons the requisite' means he does not consent to the robe-requisite. 'This one also' means the one by whom the requisite has been abandoned. 'One should have it taken after arranging' means it should be taken after arranging thus: 'Having stayed at this tree or in this pavilion, perform the duty to the shrine and then take it.' 'A wanderer by thought' (vitakkacāriko) is one who moves about with thoughts arising thus: 'Where, indeed, shall I stay? Where will it be comfortable for me to stay? Or where will a requisite be available?' Regarding forest dwellings, because it is desirable to recognize dangers, it is said, 'Five firebrands each should be prepared.'
