352. In the eighteen grounds for causing schism, the ten unwholesome courses of kamma are shown as ‘not the Dhamma’ because they are defiled states and are opposed to states of purification. Likewise for clinging and so forth. There is no state of ‘not the Dhamma’ for the qualities pertaining to enlightenment, since they are entirely blameless. However, to show that speaking by diminishing or adding to the way the Blessed One taught—that is, not speaking in accordance with the Dhamma—constitutes ‘not the Dhamma,’ he said, ‘the three foundations of mindfulness,’ and so on. ‘Leading out’ means it proceeds with wonders and unhindered. ‘Just so’ refers to the meaning stated in phrases such as ‘thus for us.’ An action to be done is called Dhamma because it is done in accordance with the Dhamma; the other is called not the Dhamma, for the opposite reason.

Rāgavinayo…pe… ayaṃ vinayo nāmāti rāgādīnaṃ vinayanato saṃvaraṇato pajahanato paṭisaṅkhānato ca vinayo nāma, vuttavipariyāyena itaro avinayo. Vatthusampattiādivasena sabbesaṃ vinayakammānaṃ akuppatāti āha “vatthusampatti…pe… ayaṃ vinayo nāmā”ti. Tappaṭipakkhato avinayo veditabbo. Tenāha “vatthuvipattī”tiādi. Yāsaṃ āpannassa pabbajjā sāvasesā, tā āpattiyo sāvasesā.

‘The removal of lust… this is called discipline.’ It is called discipline because it is the removing, restraining, abandoning, and reflecting upon lust and so on. The other, for the opposite reason, is non-discipline. He says, ‘the accomplishment of the basis… this is called discipline,’ because all disciplinary acts are unshakeable by reason of the accomplishment of the basis and so forth. Non-discipline should be understood as its opposite. Therefore, he said, ‘the failure of the basis,’ and so on. Those offenses, having been committed, for which the ordination remains with a residue, are called offenses with a residue.

354. Āpāyikotiādigāthāsu (itivu. aṭṭha. 18) saṅghassa bhedasaṅkhāte vagge ratoti vaggarato. Adhammikatāya adhamme bhedakaravatthumhi saṅghabhedasaṅkhāte eva ca adhamme ṭhitoti adhammaṭṭho. Yogakkhemā padhaṃsatīti hitato parihāyati, catūhipi yogehi anupaddutattā yogakkhemaṃ nāma arahattaṃ nibbānañca, tato panassa dhaṃsane vattabbameva natthi. Diṭṭhisīlasāmaññato saṅghataṭṭhena saṅghaṃ, tato eva [M 3.0422] ekakammādividhānayogena samaggaṃ sahitaṃ bhinditvā pubbe vuttalakkhaṇena saṅghabhedena bhinditvā. Kappanti antarakappasaṅkhātaṃ āyukappaṃ. Nirayamhīti avīcimahānirayamhi.

354. In the verses beginning with ‘Bound for the lower world,’ ‘delighting in factions’ means one who delights in the faction known as schism in the Sangha. ‘Established in unrighteousness’ means established in unrighteousness due to unrighteousness, that is, in the unrighteous ground for causing schism, which is the schism of the Sangha. ‘He falls from security from the bonds’ means he declines from what is beneficial. Security from the bonds is the name for arahantship and Nibbāna, because they are untroubled by the four bonds; as for his falling away from that, there is nothing more to be said. ‘Having split the united Sangha’ means having split the Sangha—which is a Sangha due to commonality of view and virtue, and is thus united and harmonious through the application of procedures such as a single formal act—by means of the schism of the Sangha with the characteristics previously stated. ‘For an aeon’ means for the lifespan known as an intermediate aeon. ‘In hell’ means in the Avīci great hell.

Sukhā saṅghassa sāmaggīti (itivu. aṭṭa. 19) sukhassa paccayabhāvato sāmaggī “sukhā”ti vuttā yathā “sukho buddhānamuppādo”ti (dha. pa. 194). Samaggānañcanuggahoti samaggānaṃ sāmaggianumodanena anuggaṇhanaṃ sāmaggianurūpaṃ vā, yathā te sāmaggiṃ na vijahanti, tathā gahaṇaṃ ṭhapanaṃ anubalappadānanti attho. Samaggaṃ katvānāti bhinnaṃ saṅghaṃ saṅgharājippattaṃ vā samaggaṃ sahitaṃ katvā. Kappanti āyukappameva. Saggamhi modatīti kāmāvacaradevaloke aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi abhibhavitvā dibbasukhaṃ anubhavanto icchitanibbattiyā ca modati pamodati laḷati kīḷati.

‘Happy is the unity of the Sangha.’ Unity is called ‘happy’ because it is a condition for happiness, just as it is said, ‘Happy is the arising of the Buddhas.’ ‘And supporting the united’ means supporting those who are united by rejoicing in their harmony, or in a way suitable to their unity; the meaning is grasping, establishing, and giving strength so that they do not abandon their harmony. ‘Having made them united’ means having made a divided Sangha, or one that has developed a fissure, united and harmonious. ‘For an aeon’ means for a life-aeon. ‘He rejoices in heaven’ means, having surpassed other devas in a desire-sphere heaven in ten respects, he experiences divine happiness and, with the fulfillment of his wishes, he rejoices, is glad, plays, and sports.

355. Siyā nu kho, bhante, saṅghabhedakotiādi pāḷianusāreneva veditabbaṃ. “Pañcahi, upāli, ākārehi saṅgho bhijjati kammena uddesena voharanto anussāvanena salākaggāhenā”ti [V 3.0385] evaṃ parivāre (pari. 458) āgatampi saṅghabhedalakkhaṇaṃ idha vuttena kiṃ nānākaraṇanti dassetuṃ “parivāre panā”tiādimāha. Ettha ca sīmaṭṭhakasaṅghe asannipatite visuṃ parisaṃ gahetvā katavohārānussāvanasalākaggāhassa kammaṃ vā karontassa uddesaṃ vā uddisantassa bhedo ca hoti ānantariyakammañca. Samaggasaññāya pana “vaṭṭatī”ti saññāya vā karontassa bhedova hoti, na ānantariyakammaṃ. Tato ūnaparisāya karontassa neva saṅghabhedo na ānantariyaṃ. Sabbantimena hi paricchedena navannaṃ janānaṃ yo saṅghaṃ bhindati, tassa ānantariyakammaṃ hoti, anuvattakānaṃ adhammavādīnaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ kammaṃ, dhammavādino anavajjā. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

355. ‘Venerable sir, should schism in the Saṅgha, and so forth, be understood simply according to the Pāḷi text?’ To show what difference there is between the characteristic of schism in the Saṅgha mentioned in the Parivāra (Pari. 458) thus: ‘The Saṅgha is split, Upāli, in five ways: by a formal act, by recitation, by declaration, by announcement, and by the taking of voting-tickets,’ and what is stated here, the text says, ‘But in the Parivāra…’ Here, when the Saṅgha within a boundary has not assembled, for one who, having formed a separate assembly, makes a declaration, an announcement, or a taking of voting-tickets, or performs a formal act, or recites a recitation, there is both a split and an act with immediate consequence. However, for one who does so with the perception of unity, or with the perception that ‘it is allowable,’ there is only a split, not an act with immediate consequence. Furthermore, for one who does so with an incomplete assembly, there is neither a schism in the Saṅgha nor an act with immediate consequence. For, by the final definition, for one who splits a Saṅgha of nine persons, there is an act with immediate consequence. For the followers who are proponents of non-Dhamma, it is a greatly blameworthy act; the proponents of Dhamma are blameless. The rest here is self-evident.

Upālipañhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on Upāli's Questions is concluded.

Saṅghabhedakakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Schism in the Saṅgha is concluded.

8. Vattakkhandhakaṃ

8. The Chapter on Duties

Āgantukavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties for an Incoming Bhikkhu

356-357. Vattakkhandhake [M 3.0423][V 3.0386] uparipiṭṭhitoti piṭṭhisaṅghāṭassa uparibhāgato, dvārabāhassa uparipadesatoti attho. Vissajjetabbanti sukkhāpanatthaṃ ātape vissajjitabbaṃ. Abhivādāpetabboti tassa vasse pucchite yadi daharo hoti, sayameva vandissati, tadā imināva vandāpito nāma hoti. Nilloketabboti oloketabbo. Yathābhāganti pubbe paññattaṃ padesabhāgaṃ anatikkamitvā. Santānakanti uṇṇanābhisuttaṃ. Ullokāti gehassa uparibhāgato paṭṭhāya, paṭhamaṃ uparibhāgo sammajjitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the Chapter on Duties, 'from above the back' means from the upper part of the back of the outer robe; the meaning is 'from the upper part of the door-frame.' 'It should be put out' means it should be put out in the sun for the purpose of drying. 'He should be made to pay homage' means: when his years in the order are asked, if he is junior, he will pay homage by himself; then he is said to have been made to pay homage by this very act. 'It should be inspected' means it should be looked at. 'According to the portion' means without overstepping the portion of the place previously designated. 'A web' means a spider's thread. 'Looking up' means starting from the upper part of the dwelling; it is said that the upper part should be swept first.

Āvāsikavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of a Resident Bhikkhu

359. Mahāāvāseti mahāvihārasadise mahāāvāse.

359. ‘In a great dwelling’ means in a great dwelling similar to a great monastery.

Anumodanavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of Appreciation

362. Pañcame nisinneti anumodanatthāya nisinne. Upanisinnakathā nāma bahūsu sannipatitesu parikathākathanaṃ.

362. ‘When the fifth one is seated’ means seated for the purpose of giving thanks. ‘Talk while sitting near’ is the name for engaging in conversation when many have gathered.

Bhattaggavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties at the Refectory

364. Manussānaṃ parivisanaṭṭhānanti yattha manussā saputtadārā āvasitvā denti. Hatthadhovanaudakaṃ sandhāyāti bhuttāvissa bhojanāvasāne hatthadhovanaudakaṃ sandhāya. Tenevāha “antarā pipāsitena pana…pe… hatthā na dhovitabbā”ti. Potthakesu pana “pānīyaṃ pivitvā [V 3.0387] hatthā na dhovitabbā”ti likhanti, “hatthā dhovitabbā”ti pāṭhena bhavitabbanti amhākaṃ khanti. Aññathā “na tāva udakanti idaṃ hatthadhovanaudakaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vatvā “antarā pipāsitena panā”tiādinā vuttaviseso na upalabbhati. Atha mataṃ “na tāva therena udakaṃ paṭiggahetabbanti idaṃ kiṃ pānīyapaṭiggahaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, udāhu hatthadhovanaudakaggahaṇaṃ sandhāyāti āsaṅkānivattanatthaṃ ‘idaṃ hatthadhovanaudakaṃ sandhāya [M 3.0424] vutta’ntiādi kathita”nti, tañca na, tattha āsaṅkāya eva asambhavato. Na hi bhagavā “yāva aññe na bhuttāvino honti, tāva pānīyaṃ na pātabba”nti vakkhatīti sakkā viññātuṃ. Yadi cetaṃ pānīyapaṭiggahaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, “na tāva therena udakaṃ paṭiggahetabba”nti udakasaddappayogo ca na kattabbo siyā, aṭṭhakathāyañca “idaṃ hatthadhovanaudakaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vatvā tena nivattitabbamatthaṃ dassentena “antarā pipāsitena pana gale vilaggāmisena vā pānīyaṃ pivitabba”nti ettakameva vattabbaṃ, “pānīyaṃ pivitvā hatthā na dhovitabbā”ti evaṃ pana na vattabbanti. Dhure nisinnā hontīti dvārasamīpe nisinnā honti.

364. ‘The place where people serve’ means the place where people, together with their children and wives, reside and give offerings. ‘Referring to water for washing hands’ means referring to the water for washing hands at the end of the meal for one who has finished eating. Therefore it is said, ‘But if one is thirsty in between… the hands should not be washed.’ However, in the manuscripts they write, ‘After drinking water, the hands should not be washed,’ but it is our preference that the reading should be ‘the hands should be washed.’ Otherwise, having said, ‘“Not yet the water” refers to the water for washing hands,’ the distinction made in the phrase ‘but if one is thirsty in between…’ would not be found. Alternatively, if the view is, ‘To dispel the doubt as to whether “the elder should not yet accept water” refers to accepting drinking water or to receiving water for washing hands, it is explained, “This refers to the water for washing hands,”’ that too is not correct, for there is no possibility of such a doubt there. Indeed, it cannot be understood that the Blessed One would say, ‘As long as others have not finished eating, drinking water is not to be drunk.’ And if this referred to accepting drinking water, the use of the word ‘water’ would not have been made, and in the commentary, having said, ‘This refers to the water for washing hands,’ when showing the meaning to be resolved by that, it should only have been said, ‘But if one is thirsty in between or has food stuck in the throat, one may drink water,’ and not, ‘After drinking water, the hands should not be washed.’ ‘They are seated at the front’ means they are seated near the door.

Piṇḍacārikavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of One Going on Alms-Round

366. Parāmasatīti gaṇhāti. Ṭhapeti vāti “tiṭṭhatha, bhante”ti vadantī ṭhapeti nāma.

366. ‘He touches’ means he takes hold. ‘She makes him stand’ means: one who says, ‘Stay, venerable sir,’ is said to ‘make him stand.’

Āraññikavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties of a Forest-Dweller

367. Kenajja, bhante, yuttanti kena nakkhattena ajja cando yuttoti evaṃ vadantena nakkhattaṃ pucchitaṃ hoti.

367. ‘With what, venerable sir, is it conjoined today?’ means: by speaking thus, ‘With what constellation is the moon conjoined today?’, one has asked about the constellation.

Senāsanavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties Concerning Lodgings

369-370. Aṅgaṇeti abbhokāse. Na vuḍḍhaṃ anāpucchāti ettha tassa ovarake tadupacāre ca āpucchitabbanti vadanti. Bhojanasālādīsupi evameva paṭipajjitabbanti bhojanasālādīsupi uddesadānādi āpucchitvāva kātabbanti attho.

‘In the courtyard’ means in the open air. ‘Not without asking an elder’: here, they say one should ask in his private chamber and in its vicinity. ‘One should act in the same way also in dining halls and so on’: the meaning is that also in dining halls and so on, the giving of appointments and so forth should be done only after asking.

Vaccakuṭivattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties Concerning the Latrine

373-374. Idaṃ [V 3.0388] ativivaṭanti idaṃ ṭhānaṃ gumbādīhi appaṭicchannattā ativiya pakāsanaṃ. Nibaddhagamanatthāyāti attano nibaddhagamanatthāya. Puggalikaṭṭhānaṃ vāti attano vihāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

‘This is very exposed’ means this place is very open because it is not concealed by bushes and so on. ‘For the purpose of regular going’ means for one's own regular going. ‘Or, a personal place’ is said with reference to one's own dwelling. The rest here is easily understood.

Imasmiṃ [M 3.0425] vattakkhandhake āgatāni āgantukāvāsikagamiyānumodanabhattaggapiṇḍacārikāraññika senāsana jantāghara vaccakuṭi upajjhācariya saddhivihārika antevāsikavattāni cuddasa mahāvattāni nāma, ito aññāni pana kadāci tajjanīyakammakatādikāleyeva caritabbāni asīti khandhakavattānīti veditabbāni. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana “imāniyeva cuddasa mahāvattāni aggahitaggahaṇena gahiyamānāni asīti khandhakavattāānī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

In this Chapter on Duties, the fourteen duties that have come down are called the great duties: those for incoming bhikkhus, resident bhikkhus, and departing bhikkhus; and the duties concerning appreciation, the refectory, the alms-round, forest-dwelling, lodgings, the bathhouse, the latrine, the preceptor, the teacher, the co-resident, and the pupil. However, the other eighty duties of the Khandhakas should be understood as needing to be practiced only at certain times, such as when a formal act of censure has been carried out. But in the glosses it is said, 'These same fourteen great duties, when taken up with a wrong grasp, become the eighty duties of the Khandhakas.' This is not to be accepted.

Vattakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Duties is concluded.

9. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhakaṃ

9. The Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha

Pātimokkhuddesayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Request for the Recitation of the Pātimokkha

383. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhake [M 3.0426][V 3.0389] tadahūti (udā. aṭṭha. 45) tasmiṃ ahani tasmiṃ divase. Uposatheti ettha upavasanti etthāti uposatho, upavasantīti sīlena vā anasanena vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho. Ayañhi uposatha-saddo “aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathaṃ upavasāmī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.71; 10.46) sīle āgato. “Uposatho vā pavāraṇā vā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 155) pātimokkhuddesādivinayakamme. “Gopālakūposatho nigaṇṭhūposatho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.71) upavāse. “Uposatho nāma nāgarājā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.246; ma. ni. 3.258) paññattiyaṃ. “Ajjuposatho pannaraso”tiādīsu (mahāva. 168) divase. Idhāpi divaseyeva daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā tadahuposatheti tasmiṃ uposathadivasabhūte ahanīti attho. Nisinno hotīti mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto ovādapātimokkhaṃ uddisituṃ upāsikāya ratanapāsāde nisinno hoti. Nisajja pana bhikkhūnaṃ cittāni olokento ekaṃ dussīlapuggalaṃ disvā “sacāhaṃ imasmiṃ puggale idha nisinneyeva pātimokkhaṃ uddisissāmi, sattadhāvassa muddhā phalissatī”ti tasmiṃ anukampāya tuṇhīyeva ahosi.

383. In the chapter on the suspension of the Pātimokkha, the phrase 'on that day' (Udā. Aṭṭha. 45) means on that very day, on that day. The term 'Uposatha' here means 'where they observe,' that is, 'where they stay.' The meaning is: they dwell, being endowed with virtue or fasting. This term 'Uposatha' occurs in contexts like 'I undertake the Uposatha possessed of eight factors' (A. Ni. 3.71; 10.46), where it pertains to virtue; in phrases like 'the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā' (Mahāva. 155), it refers to Vinaya acts such as the recitation of the Pātimokkha; in expressions like 'the cowherd’s Uposatha, the Nigaṇṭha’s Uposatha' (A. Ni. 3.71), it denotes fasting; in statements like 'Uposatha is the name of a nāga king' (Dī. Ni. 2.246; Ma. Ni. 3.258), it is a designation; in phrases like 'today is the fifteenth, the Uposatha' (Mahāva. 168), it refers to the day. Here too, it should be understood as the day. Therefore, 'on that Uposatha day' means on that day which is the Uposatha day. 'He was seated' means, surrounded by a great Saṅgha of monks, he was seated in the laywoman's Ratanapāsāda in order to recite the Ovāda Pātimokkha. However, while seated, as he surveyed the minds of the monks, he saw one immoral individual and, out of compassion for him, remained silent, thinking: 'If I recite the Pātimokkha while this person is seated here, his head will split into seven pieces.'

Abhikkantāti atikkantā parikkhīṇā. Uddhaste aruṇeti uggate aruṇasīse. Nandimukhiyāti tuṭṭhimukhiyā. Uddhastaṃ aruṇanti aruṇuggamanaṃ patvāpi “uddisatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkha”nti thero bhagavantaṃ pātimokkhuddesaṃ yāci tasmiṃ kāle “na, bhikkhave, anuposathe uposatho kātabbo”ti (mahāva. 183) sikkhāpadassa apaññattattā. Aparisuddhā, ānanda, parisāti tikkhattuṃ therena pātimokkhuddesassa yācitattā anuddesassa kāraṇaṃ kathento “asukapuggalo aparisuddho”ti avatvā “aparisuddhā, ānanda, parisā”ti āha[V 3.0390]. Kasmā pana bhagavā tiyāmarattiṃ tathā vītināmesi? Tato paṭṭhāya ovādapātimokkhaṃ anuddisitukāmo tassa vatthuṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ.

"Abhikkantā" means surpassed, gone beyond, exhausted. "Uddhaste aruṇa" means when the tip of the dawn has risen. "Nandimukhiyā" means with a delighted face. "Uddhastaṃ aruṇa" means even after the rising of the dawn, the elder requested the Blessed One to recite the Pātimokkha for the monks, saying, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the monks." At that time, this was because the training rule, "Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day" (Mahāva. 183), had not yet been laid down. "The assembly is impure, Ānanda" — because the elder had requested the recitation of the Pātimokkha three times, the Blessed One stated the reason for not reciting it by saying, "The assembly is impure, Ānanda," without saying, "Such and such a person is impure." But why did the Blessed One spend the three watches of the night in that way? From that point onward, he wished to not recite the Ovāda Pātimokkha and to make the reason for it clear.

Addasāti [M 3.0427] kathaṃ addasa. Attano cetopariyañāṇena tassaṃ parisati bhikkhūnaṃ cittāni parijānanto tassa purisassa dussīlyacittaṃ passi. Yasmā pana citte diṭṭhe taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo diṭṭho nāma hoti, tasmā “addasā kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno taṃ puggalaṃ dussīla”nti vuttaṃ. Yatheva hi anāgate sattasu divasesu pavattaṃ paresaṃ cittaṃ cetopariyañāṇalābhī pajānāti, evaṃ atītepīti. Dussīlanti nissīlaṃ, sīlavirahitanti attho. Pāpadhammanti dussīlattā eva hīnajjhāsayatāya lāmakasabhāvaṃ. Asucinti aparisuddhehi kāyakammādīhi samannāgatattā na suciṃ. Saṅkassarasamācāranti kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ iminā kataṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ paresaṃ āsaṅkanīyatāya saṅkāya saritabbasamācāraṃ. Atha vā kenacideva karaṇīyena mantayante bhikkhū disvā “kacci nu kho ime mayā katakammaṃ jānitvā mantentī”ti attanoyeva saṅkāya saritabbasamācāraṃ. Lajjitabbatāya paṭicchādetabbassa karaṇato paṭicchannaṃ kammantaṃ etassāti paṭicchannakammantaṃ. Kucchitasamaṇavesadhāritāya na samaṇanti assamaṇaṃ. Salākaggahaṇādīsu “kittakā samaṇā”ti gaṇanāya “ahampi samaṇomhī”ti micchāpaṭiññāya samaṇapaṭiññaṃ. Aseṭṭhacāritāya abrahmacāriṃ. Aññe brahmacārino sunivatthe supārute kusumbhakapaṭadhare gāmanigamādīsu piṇḍāya caritvā jīvikaṃ kappente disvā abrahmacārī samāno sayampi tādisena ākārena paṭipajjanto uposathādīsu ca sandissanto “ahampi brahmacārī”ti paṭiññaṃ dento viya hotīti brahmacāripaṭiññaṃ. Pūtinā kammena sīlavipattiyā anto anupaviṭṭhattā antopūtiṃ. Chahi dvārehi rāgādikilesāvassavena tintattā avassutaṃ. Sañjātarāgādikacavarattā sīlavantehi chaḍḍetabbattā ca kasambujātaṃ. Majjhe bhikkhusaṅghassa nisinnanti saṅghapariyāpanno viya bhikkhusaṅghassa anto nisinnaṃ.

How did he see? By means of his knowledge of others' minds, while discerning the minds of the monks in that assembly, he saw the immoral mind of that man. Since when the mind is seen, the person possessing it is said to be seen, therefore it is said, "Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that immoral person." Just as one who has attained the knowledge of others' minds understands the minds of others that will arise in the next seven days, so too does he understand past minds. "Immoral" means lacking morality, devoid of virtue. "Of bad character" means of base nature due to immorality and ignoble tendencies. "Impure" means not pure, being possessed of impure bodily actions and the like. "Of suspicious behavior" means conduct that should be remembered with suspicion because, on seeing something improper, one might think, "This must have been done by him," thus arousing suspicion in others. Or else, seeing monks discussing some matter, he thinks, "Could they be discussing some deed I have done?"—thus his own conduct becomes suspicious and should be remembered as such. "One of hidden deeds" means one whose actions must be concealed due to being shameful. "No ascetic" means not an ascetic, due to wearing the guise of a corrupt monk. "A false claimant to asceticism" means one who falsely declares, "I too am an ascetic," when counting ascetics for purposes like taking lots, thus making a false claim to asceticism. "Not a celibate" means one who does not live the holy life. Seeing other celibates well-dressed, well-covered, wearing saffron-dyed robes, wandering for alms in villages and towns to sustain their lives, he, though not a celibate, behaves in a similar manner and, appearing at the Uposatha and other occasions, is as if declaring, "I too am a celibate"—thus a false claimant to celibacy. "Rotten within" means inwardly rotten due to bad deeds and the ruin of virtue. "Oozing" means soaked through the six doors by the influx of defilements like lust. "Like rubbish" means one who has become like refuse due to the arising of lust and other defilements and who should be discarded by the virtuous. "Sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks" means sitting within the Saṅgha of monks, as if belonging to the Saṅgha.

Diṭṭhosīti “ayaṃ na pakatatto”ti bhagavatā diṭṭho asi. Yasmā ca evaṃ diṭṭho, tasmā natthi te tava bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekakammādisaṃvāso. Yasmā pana so saṃvāso tava natthi, tasmā uṭṭhehi āvusoti evamettha padayojanā veditabbā. Tatiyampi kho so puggalo tuṇhī ahosīti anekavāraṃ vatvāpi “thero sayameva nibbinno oramissati, idāni imesaṃ paṭipattiṃ jānissāmī”ti vā adhippāyena tuṇhī [M 3.0428] ahosi. Bāhāyaṃ gahetvāti “bhagavatā mayā ca yāthāvato diṭṭho, yāvatatiyaṃ ‘uṭṭhehī’ti ca vutto na uṭṭhāti, idānissa nikkaḍḍhanakālo[V 3.0391], mā saṅghassa uposathantarāyo ahosī”ti bāhāyaṃ aggahesi. Bahi dvārakoṭṭhakā nikkhāmetvāti dvārakoṭṭhakā dvārasālato nikkhāmetvā, bahīti pana nikkhāmitaṭṭhānadassanaṃ. Atha vā bahidvārakoṭṭhakāti bahidvārakoṭṭhakatopi nikkhāmetvā, na antodvārakoṭṭhakato eva. Ubhayathāpi vihārato bahikatvāti attho. Sūcighaṭikaṃ datvāti aggaḷasūciñca uparighaṭikañca ādahitvā, suṭṭhu kavāṭaṃ thaketvāti attho. Yāva bāhāgahaṇāpi nāmāti “aparisuddhā, ānanda, parisā”ti vacanaṃ sutvā eva hi tena pakkamitabbaṃ siyā, evaṃ apakkamitvā yāva bāhāgahaṇāpi nāma so moghapuriso āgamissati, acchariyamidanti dasseti. Idañca garahaṇacchariyamevāti veditabbaṃ.

"You have been seen" means "This one is not of a normal character"; you were seen by the Blessed One. And since you were seen thus, there is no communion for you with the monks in a shared act and so forth. And since there is no such communion for you, therefore, "Rise, friend"—this is how the phrasing here should be understood. For the third time, that person remained silent. Though spoken to repeatedly, he remained silent, perhaps with the intention, "The elder himself, becoming weary, will relent; now I will see their procedure." "Taking by the arm" means: thinking, "By the Blessed One and by me, he has been seen as he truly is. Even when told for a third time, 'Rise,' he does not rise. Now is the time to expel him, lest he become an obstacle to the Saṅgha’s Uposatha," he took him by the arm. "Having expelled him beyond the door-frame" means: having expelled him from the door-hall, beyond the door-frame. The word "beyond" here indicates the place to which he was expelled. Alternatively, "beyond the outer door-frame" means having expelled him even from beyond the outer door-frame, not just from the inner door-frame. In both cases, the meaning is that he was put out of the monastery. "Having applied the latch-pin and bolt" means: having inserted the latch-pin and the upper bolt, that is, having securely fastened the door. "Even up to being taken by the arm" means: upon hearing the words, "Ānanda, the assembly is impure," he should have departed. But instead of departing, that foolish man waited even up to being taken by the arm; this shows how astonishing it was. And this should be understood as a marvel of reproach.

Mahāsamudde aṭṭhacchariyakathāvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Discourse on the Eight Marvels of the Great Ocean

384. Aṭṭhime, bhikkhave, mahāsamuddeti (udā. aṭṭha. 45) ko anusandhi? Yvāyaṃ aparisuddhāya parisāya pātimokkhassa anuddeso, so imasmiṃ dhammavinaye acchariyo abbhuto dhammoti taṃ aparehi sattahi acchariyaabbhutadhammehi saddhiṃ vibhajitvā dassetukāmo paṭhamaṃ tāva tesaṃ upamābhāvena mahāsamudde acchariyaabbhutadhamme dassento satthā “aṭṭhime, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde”tiādimāha. Asurāti devā viya na suranti na īsanti na virocantīti asurā. Surā nāma devā, tesaṃ paṭipakkhāti vā asurā, vepacittipahārādādayo. Tesaṃ bhavanaṃ sinerussa heṭṭhābhāge, te tattha pavisantā nikkhamantā sinerupāde maṇḍapādīni nimminitvā kīḷantāva abhiramanti. Sā tattha tesaṃ abhirati ime guṇe disvāti āha “ye disvā disvā asurā mahāsamudde abhiramantī”ti. Tattha abhiramantīti ratiṃ vindanti, anukkaṇṭhamānā vasantīti attho.

384. What is the connection with the statement: 'Monks, these eight qualities are in the great ocean' (Ud 5.5)? The non-recitation of the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly is an astonishing and marvelous phenomenon in this Dhamma and Discipline. Wishing to explain this along with the other seven astonishing and marvelous phenomena, the Teacher, first showing the astonishing and marvelous phenomena in the great ocean by way of simile, said, 'Monks, these eight qualities are in the great ocean,' and so on. 'Asuras' means: like the gods (devā), they do not shine (na suranti), do not rule (na īsanti), do not radiate (na virocanti); hence they are called asuras. Or, the gods are called suras, and the asuras are their adversaries, such as Vepacitti, Pahārāda, and others. Their abode is in the lower part of Mount Sineru. There, as they enter and exit, they create pavilions and so forth at the base of Sineru, and they amuse themselves and delight. It is because they see these qualities there that they delight; thus it is said: 'The asuras, seeing again and again, delight in the great ocean.' Here, 'delighting' means they find joy; they dwell without longing—that is the meaning.

Anupubbaninnotiādīni sabbāni anupaṭipāṭiyā ninnabhāvasseva vevacanāni. Na āyatakeneva papātoti nacchinnataṭamahāsobbho viya ādito [M 3.0429] eva papāto. So hi tīradesato paṭṭhāya ekaṅguladvaṅgulavidatthiratanayaṭṭhiusabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutaaḍḍhayojanayojanādivasena gambhīro hutvā gacchanto gacchanto sinerupādamūle caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīro hutvā ṭhitoti dasseti.

'Gradually sloping' and so forth are all synonyms for the state of being inclined in succession. 'Not a sheer drop' means it is not a precipice from the very beginning, like a great chasm with an unbroken bank. This shows that, starting from the shoreline, it gradually deepens by one finger-width, two finger-widths, a span, a cubit, a rod, an usabha, half a gāvuta, a gāvuta, half a yojana, a yojana, and so forth, becoming progressively deeper until it reaches the foot of Mount Sineru, where it stands at a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas.

Ṭhitadhammoti ṭhitasabhāvo avaṭṭhitasabhāvo. Kuṇapenāti yena kenaci hatthiassādikaḷevarena. Vāhetīti hatthena gahetvā viya vīcippahāreneva thale khipati. Gaṅgā yamunāti [V 3.0392] anotattadahassa dakkhiṇamukhato nikkhantanadī pañcadhārā hutvā pavattaṭṭhāne gaṅgātiādinā pañcadhā saṅkhaṃ gatā. Tattha nadī ninnagātiādikaṃ gottaṃ, gaṅgā yamunātiādikaṃ nāmaṃ. Savantiyoti yā kāci savamānā sandamānā gacchantiyo mahānadiyo vā kunnadiyo vā. Appentīti allīyanti osaranti. Dhārāti vuṭṭhidhārā. Pūrattanti puṇṇabhāvo. Mahāsamuddassa hi ayaṃ dhammatā – “imasmiṃ kāle devo mando jāto, jālakkhipādīni ādāya macchakacchape gaṇhissāmī”ti vā “imasmiṃ kāle atimahantā vuṭṭhi, labhissāma nu kho piṭṭhipasāraṇaṭṭhāna”nti vā na sakkā vattuṃ. Paṭhamakappikakālato paṭṭhāya hi tīraṃ bhassitvā sinerumekhalaṃ āhacca udakaṃ ṭhitaṃ, tato ekaṅgulamattampi udakaṃ neva heṭṭhā otarati, na uddhaṃ uttarati. Ekarasoti asambhinnaraso.

'Of a stable nature' means having a fixed nature, an established nature. 'Carrion' means any kind of corpse, such as that of an elephant, a horse, and so forth. 'Carries away' means it casts it onto the shore by the impact of the waves, as if taking it by hand. 'The Ganges and the Yamunā' refers to the river that emerges from the southern mouth of Lake Anotatta, which, having become five streams, is known by five names, such as the Ganges and so on, at the place where it flows. There, 'river,' 'downward-flowing,' and so forth, are generic terms, while 'Ganges,' 'Yamunā,' and so forth, are specific names. 'Flowing rivers' means any great rivers or small rivers that flow, stream, and move. 'They reach' means they flow into, they enter. 'Showers' means streams of rain. 'Fullness' means the state of being full. For this is the nature of the great ocean: it cannot be said, 'At this time, the rain is light; let us take nets and so forth and catch fish and turtles,' or 'At this time, there is very heavy rain; will we find a place to stretch our backs?' From the time of the first aeon, the water has stood, having eroded the shore and reached the base of Mount Sineru. From then on, not even a finger's breadth of water descends below or rises above. 'Of a single taste' means of an unmixed taste.

Muttāti khuddakamahantavaṭṭadīghādibhedā anekavidhamuttā. Maṇīti rattanīlādibhedo anekavidho maṇi. Veḷuriyoti vaṃsavaṇṇasirīsapupphavaṇṇādisaṇṭhānato anekavidho. Saṅkhoti dakkhiṇāvaṭṭakatumbakucchidhamanasaṅkhādibhedo anekavidho. Silāti setakāḷamuggavaṇṇādibhedā anekavidhā. Pavāḷampi khuddakamahantarattaghanarattādibhedaṃ anekavidhaṃ. Lohitako padumarāgādibhedo anekavidho. Masāragallaṃ kabaramaṇi. Cittaphalikantipi vadanti. Mahataṃ bhūtānanti mahantānaṃ sattānaṃ. Timi timiṅgalo timitimiṅgaloti tisso macchajātiyo. Timiṃ gilanasamattho timiṅgalo, timiñca timiṅgalañca gilanasamattho timitimiṅgaloti vadanti. Nāgāti ūmipiṭṭhivāsinopi vimānaṭṭhakanāgāpi.

'Pearls' means pearls of many kinds, differing as small, large, round, long, and so forth. 'Gems' means gems of many kinds, differing as ruby, sapphire, and so forth. 'Beryl' is of many kinds, from its form being bamboo-colored, sirīsa-flower-colored, and so forth. 'Conch' is of many kinds, differing as right-spiraled, gourd-bellied, blowing-conches, and so forth. 'Crystal' is of many kinds, differing as white, black, mung-bean-colored, and so forth. 'Coral' is also of many kinds, differing as small, large, red, deep red, and so forth. 'Ruby' is of many kinds, differing as lotus-colored and so forth. 'Masāragalla' is a variegated gem; some also call it 'cittaphalika.' 'Of great beings' means of great creatures. 'Timi, timiṅgala, and timitimiṅgala' are three species of fish. It is said that the timiṅgala is able to swallow the timi, and the timitimiṅgala is able to swallow both the timi and the timiṅgala. 'Nāgas' refers both to those dwelling on the surface of the waves and to nāgas established in celestial mansions.

Imasmiṃ dhammavinaye aṭṭhacchariyakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Discourse of the Eight Wondrous Things in this Dhamma and Discipline.

385. Evameva [M 3.0430] khoti kiñcāpi satthā imasmiṃ dhammavinaye soḷasapi bāttiṃsapi tato bhiyyopi acchariyabbhutadhamme vibhajitvā dassetuṃ sakkoti, upamābhāvena pana gahitānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ anurūpavasena aṭṭheva te upametabbadhamme vibhajitvā dassanto “evameva kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye aṭṭha acchariyā abbhutā dhammā”ti āha. Tattha anupubbasikkhāya tisso sikkhā gahitā, anupubbakiriyāya terasa dhutadhammā, anupubbapaṭipadāya satta anupassanā aṭṭhārasa mahāvipassanā aṭṭhatiṃsa ārammaṇavibhattiyo sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā ca gahitā. Na āyatakeneva aññāpaṭivedhoti maṇḍūkassa uppatitvā gamanaṃ viya āditova sīlapūraṇādīni akatvā arahattapaṭivedho nāma natthi, paṭipāṭiyā pana sīlasamādhipaññāyo pūretvāva arahattappattīti attho.

385. In the same way, indeed, although the Teacher is capable of analyzing and showing sixteen, thirty-two, or even more astonishing and marvelous phenomena in this Dhamma and Discipline, he analyzed and showed only those eight phenomena to be compared, in correspondence with the eight taken as similes, saying, 'In the same way, monks, in this Dhamma and Discipline there are eight astonishing and marvelous phenomena.' Herein, under 'gradual training,' the three trainings are included; under 'gradual action,' the thirteen ascetic practices are included; and under 'gradual practice,' the seven contemplations, eighteen great insights, thirty-eight distinctions of meditation objects, and thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are included. 'The realization of final knowledge is not immediate' means that just as a frog proceeds by jumping, there is no such thing as the realization of arahantship without having first fulfilled virtue and so on from the beginning. The meaning is that arahantship is attained only by successively fulfilling virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

Mama [V 3.0393] sāvakāti sotāpannādike ariyapuggale sandhāya vadati. Na saṃvasatīti uposathakammādivasena saṃvāsaṃ na karoti. Ukkhipatīti apaneti. Ārakāvāti dūre eva. Tathāgatappavediteti tathāgatena bhagavatā sāvakesu desite akkhāte pakāsite. Na tena nibbānadhātuyā ūnattaṃ vā pūrattaṃ vāti asaṅkhyeyyepi mahākappe buddhesu anuppajjantesu ekasattopi parinibbātuṃ na sakkoti, tadāpi “tucchā nibbānadhātū”ti na sakkā vattuṃ, buddhakāle pana ekekasmiṃ samāgame asaṅkhyeyyāpi sattā amataṃ ārādhenti, tadāpi na sakkā vattuṃ “pūrā nibbānadhātū”ti. Vimuttirasoti kilesehi vimuccanaraso. Sabbā hi sāsanasampatti yāvadeva anupādāya āsavehi cittassa vimuttīti attho.

'My disciples' refers to noble individuals such as stream-enterers and the like. 'Does not associate' means does not engage in communion by way of the Uposatha ceremony and so on. 'Suspends' means removes. 'Far away' means indeed distant. 'Taught by the Tathāgata' means taught, declared, and proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, among his disciples. 'There is no decrease or increase in the Nibbāna-element on that account' means that even in countless great aeons when Buddhas do not arise, not a single being can attain final Nibbāna—yet even then, one cannot say, 'The Nibbāna-element is empty.' But during the time of a Buddha, countless beings attain the deathless in a single gathering—yet even then, one cannot say, 'The Nibbāna-element is full.' 'The taste of liberation' is the taste of being freed from the defilements. For all the excellence of the Teaching is only for the mind's liberation from the taints through non-clinging—this is the meaning.

Ratanānīti ratijananaṭṭhena ratanāni. Satipaṭṭhānādayo hi bhāviyamānā pubbabhāgepi anekavidhaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ nibbattenti, pageva aparabhāge. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'Jewels' (ratanāni) are so called in the sense of generating delight (rati). For when the foundations of mindfulness and so on are developed, they produce various kinds of joy and gladness even in the preliminary stage, how much more so in the later stage. For this was said:

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374);

'Whenever one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one obtains joy and gladness. That is the deathless for those who know.'

Lokiyaratananimittaṃ [M 3.0431] pana pītipāmojjaṃ na tassa kalabhāgampi agghati. Apica –

But the joy and gladness occasioned by worldly jewels is not worth even a fraction of that. Furthermore:

Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratananti pavuccati. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33);

'Cherished and of great worth, incomparable, rare to see, enjoyed by superior beings—this is called a jewel.'

Yadi ca cittīkatādibhāvena ratanaṃ nāma hoti, satipaṭṭhānādīnaññeva bhūto ratanabhāvo. Bodhipakkhiyadhammānañhi so ānubhāvo, yaṃ sāvakā sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ, paccekasambuddhā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ, sammāsambuddhā sammāsambodhiṃ adhigacchanti āsannakāraṇattā. Paramparakāraṇañhi dānādiupanissayoti evaṃ ratijananaṭṭhena cittīkatādiatthena ca ratanabhāvo bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ sātisayo. Tena vuttaṃ “tatrimāni ratanāni, seyyathidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādi.

If, then, something is called a jewel by reason of being cherished and so on, then the nature of a jewel truly belongs to the foundations of mindfulness and so on. For such is the power of the factors of enlightenment, by which disciples attain the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, Paccekabuddhas attain Paccekabodhi-knowledge, and Fully Self-Enlightened Ones attain supreme self-enlightenment—because they are proximate causes. For generosity and so on are successive causes as supporting conditions. Thus, the jewel-nature of the factors of enlightenment is preeminent by reason of generating delight and by reason of being cherished and so on. Therefore it is said: "Herein, these are the jewels, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness," and so on.

Ārammaṇe okkanditvā upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ, satiyeva paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Ārammaṇassa pana kāyādivasena catubbidhattā vuttaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti. Tathā hi kāyavedanācittadhammesu [V 3.0394] subhasukhaniccaattasaññānaṃ pahānato asubhadukkhāniccānattabhāvaggahaṇato ca nesaṃ kāyānupassanādibhāvo vibhatto.

They are called "foundations" (paṭṭhāna) by reason of plunging into the object and establishing themselves. Mindfulness itself is the foundation, hence `satipaṭṭhāna`. But because the object is fourfold, as body and so on, it is said, "the four foundations of mindfulness." For thus, in regard to body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, by abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self, and by grasping the nature of ugliness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self, their state as contemplation of the body and so on is distinguished.

Sammā padahanti etena, sayaṃ vā sammā padahati, pasatthaṃ sundaraṃ vā padahananti sammappadhānaṃ, puggalassa vā sammadeva padhānabhāvakaraṇato sammappadhānaṃ, vīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tampi anuppannuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ anuppādanapahānavasena anuppannuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ uppādanaṭhāpanavasena ca catukiccasādhakattā vuttaṃ “cattāro sammappadhānā”ti.

"Right exertion" (sammappadhāna) means striving rightly with this; or one strives rightly oneself; or striving is excellent and beautiful. Alternatively, because it makes a person's exertion truly right, it is called right exertion; this is a designation for energy. And because it accomplishes four tasks—by way of preventing unarisen unwholesome states and abandoning arisen unwholesome states, and by way of arousing unarisen wholesome states and establishing arisen wholesome states—it is said, "the four right exertions."

Ijjhatīti iddhi, samijjhati nipphajjatīti attho. Ijjhanti tāya vā sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi. Paṭhamena atthena iddhi eva pādo iddhipādo, iddhikoṭṭhāsoti attho. Dutiyena atthena iddhiyā pādo patiṭṭhā adhigamupāyoti iddhipādo. Tena hi uparūparivisesasaṅkhātaṃ iddhiṃ pajjanti pāpuṇanti. Svāyaṃ iddhipādo yasmā chandādike cattāro adhipatidhamme dhure jeṭṭhake katvā nibbattīyati, tasmā vuttaṃ “cattāro iddhipādo”ti.

"Accomplishment" (iddhi) means success—it succeeds and achieves its purpose. Or, beings succeed through it, becoming powerful, grown, and exalted—thus, it is `iddhi`. In the first sense, `iddhi` itself is the basis (`pāda`), hence `iddhipāda`; the meaning is a portion of `iddhi`. In the second sense, the basis (`pāda`) of `iddhi` is the foundation, the means of attainment, hence `iddhipāda`. For by it they reach and attain `iddhi`, which is called higher and higher distinctions. And because this `iddhipāda` arises by making the four dominant factors—desire and so on—as the chief and foremost, therefore it is said, "the four bases of accomplishment."

Pañcindriyānīti [M 3.0432] saddhādīni pañca indriyāni. Tattha assaddhiyaṃ abhibhavitvā adhimokkhalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti saddhā indriyaṃ. Kosajjaṃ abhibhavitvā paggahalakkhaṇe, pamādaṃ abhibhavitvā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇe, vikkhepaṃ abhibhavitvā avikkhepalakkhaṇe, aññāṇaṃ abhibhavitvā dassanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti paññā indriyaṃ.

The five faculties (pañcindriyāni) are the five faculties beginning with faith. Herein, the faculty of faith overcomes lack of faith and performs the function of ruling in the characteristic of conviction. The faculty of energy overcomes laziness and performs the function of ruling in the characteristic of exertion. The faculty of mindfulness overcomes negligence and performs the function of ruling in the characteristic of establishing. The faculty of concentration overcomes distraction and performs the function of ruling in the characteristic of non-distraction. The faculty of wisdom overcomes ignorance and performs the function of ruling in the characteristic of seeing.

Tāniyeva assaddhiyādīhi anabhibhavanīyato akampiyaṭṭhena sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvena ca balāni veditabbāni.

These very same faculties, because they are not to be overwhelmed by lack of faith and so on, and by reason of being unshakable and firm in the associated states, are to be understood as powers (balāni).

Satta bojjhaṅgāti bodhiyā, bodhissa vā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā. Yā hi esā dhammasāmaggī, yāya lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhattakilamathānuyogaucchedasassatābhinivesādīnaṃ anekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayavīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsaṅkhātāya dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhati kilesaniddāya uṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikarotīti “bodhī”ti vuccati, tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādayo viya. Yopesa vuttappakārāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvako “bodhī”ti vuccati, tassa bodhissa vā aṅgātipi bojjhaṅgā senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya. Tenāhu porāṇā “bujjhanakassa puggalassa [V 3.0395] aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā”ti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.182; vibha. aṭṭha. 466; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.25), “bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgā”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 2.17) nayenapi bojjhaṅgaṭṭho veditabbo.

The seven factors of enlightenment are called 'bojjhaṅgā' because they are the limbs (aṅgā) of enlightenment (bodhi), or the limbs of the enlightened one (bodhissa). For this is the assemblage of states, by which, arising at the moment of the supramundane path, being the opponent of many obstacles such as sloth and agitation, stagnation, striving, addiction to sensual pleasures, addiction to self-mortification, and adherence to the views of annihilationism and eternalism, and consisting of mindfulness, investigation of the Dhamma, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, the noble disciple awakens, rises from the slumber of defilements, penetrates the four noble truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself—this is called 'bodhi.' The limbs of this enlightenment, which is the assemblage of states, are called 'bojjhaṅgā,' like the limbs of jhāna or the limbs of the path. Or, because the noble disciple awakens by means of this assemblage of states of the aforementioned kind, he is called 'bodhi,' and the limbs of that enlightened one are also called 'bojjhaṅgā,' like the limbs of an army or the limbs of a chariot. Therefore, the ancients said: 'The limbs of the person who awakens are called bojjhaṅgā' (Saṃ. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.5.182; Vibha. Aṭṭha. 466; Paṭi. Ma. Aṭṭha. 1.1.25), and 'They lead to enlightenment, thus they are called bojjhaṅgā' (Paṭi. Ma. 2.17). In this way, the meaning of bojjhaṅgā should be understood.

Ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggoti taṃtaṃmaggavajjhehi kilesehi ārakattā ariyabhāvakarattā ariyaphalapaṭilābhakarattā ca ariyo. Sammādiṭṭhiādīni aṭṭhaṅgāni assa atthi, aṭṭhaṅgāniyeva vā aṭṭhaṅgiko. Mārento kilese gacchati, nibbānatthikehi vā maggīyati, sayaṃ vā nibbānaṃ maggatīti maggoti evametesaṃ satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ atthavibhāgo veditabbo.

The Noble Eightfold Path is called 'noble' (ariyo) because it is far from those defilements that are to be avoided by the path, because it makes one noble, and because it leads to the attainment of noble fruits. It has eight factors, such as right view, or it is simply eight-factored. It goes destroying defilements, or it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna, or it itself seeks Nibbāna—thus it is called 'path' (magga). In this way, the meaning of these, such as the foundations of mindfulness, should be understood.

Sotāpannoti maggasaṅkhātaṃ sotaṃ āpajjitvā pāpuṇitvā ṭhito, sotāpattiphalaṭṭhoti attho. Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannoti sotāpattiphalassa attapaccakkhakaraṇatthāya paṭipajjamāno paṭhamamaggaṭṭho[M 3.0433], yo aṭṭhamakotipi vuccati. Sakadāgāmīti sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena āgamanasīlo dutiyaphalaṭṭho. Anāgāmīti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena kāmalokaṃ anāgamanasīlo tatiyaphalaṭṭho. Yo pana saddhānusārī dhammānusārī ekabījīti evamādiko ariyapuggalavibhāgo, so tesaṃyeva bhedoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

A stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is one who has entered and attained the stream (sota), which is the path, and stands firm; the meaning is, one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry. One who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, for the purpose of personally realizing it, is established in the first path, who is also called the eighth individual. A once-returner (sakadāgāmī) is one who, by way of rebirth, is inclined to come to this world just once; he is established in the second fruit. A non-returner (anāgāmī) is one who, by way of rebirth, is not inclined to come to the sense-sphere; he is established in the third fruit. However, the division of noble individuals such as the faith-follower (saddhānusārī), the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī), and the one-seeder (ekabījī) is a subdivision of these same individuals. The rest is in accordance with what has already been stated.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ attano dhammavinaye matakuṇapasadisena dussīlapuggalena saddhiṃ saṃvāsābhāvasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ asaṃvāsārahasaṃvāsārahabhāvānaṃ kāraṇaparidīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning, namely, the fact of not associating with an immoral person similar to a rotting corpse in one's own Dhamma and Discipline, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna), this utterance illuminating the reasons for those who are worthy and unworthy of association.

Tattha channamativassatīti āpattiṃ āpajjitvā paṭicchādento aññaṃ navaṃ āpattiṃ

There, 'the covered is excessively rained upon' means that having committed an offense and concealing it, he incurs another new offense.

Āpajjati, tato aparanti evaṃ āpattivassaṃ kilesavassaṃ ativiya vassati. Vivaṭaṃ nātivassatīti āpattiṃ āpanno taṃ appaṭicchādetvā vivaranto sabrahmacārīnaṃ pakāsento yathādhammaṃ yathāvinayaṃ paṭikaronto desento vuṭṭhahanto aññaṃ navaṃ āpattiṃ nāpajjati, tenassa taṃ vivaṭaṃ puna āpattivassaṃ kilesavassaṃ na vassati. Yasmā ca etadeva, tasmā channaṃ chāditaṃ āpattiṃ vivaretha. Evaṃ taṃ nātivassatīti evaṃ sante taṃ āpattiṃ āpajjanapuggalānaṃ attabhāvaṃ ativijjhitvā kilesavassanena na vassati na temeti, evaṃ so kilesehi anavassuto parisuddhasīlo samāhito hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sammasanto anukkamena nibbānaṃ pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo.

he incurs another new offense. And from that, the rain of offenses and the rain of defilements pours down excessively. 'The open is not excessively rained upon' means that one who has committed an offense, without concealing it, openly declaring it to his fellow practitioners, making amends in accordance with the Dhamma and Discipline, confessing, and rising up, does not fall into another new offense. For this reason, that openness prevents the rain of offenses and the rain of defilements from pouring down again. And because this is so, therefore, uncover the covered offense. 'Thus, it does not excessively rain upon it' means that in this way, for those who have committed offenses, their being is not pierced through by the rain of defilements, nor is it soaked. Thus, being unstained by defilements, with purified virtue, composed, establishing insight, reflecting step by step, he attains Nibbāna—this is the meaning.

Imasmiṃ dhammavinaye aṭṭhacchariyakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

In this Dhamma and Discipline, the exposition of the eight wonders is finished.

Pātimokkhasavanārahakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on What is Fit for Hearing the Pātimokkha.

386. Atha [V 3.0396] bhagavā cintesi “idāni bhikkhusaṅghe abbudo jāto, aparisuddhā puggalā uposathaṃ āgacchanti, na ca tathāgato aparisuddhāya parisāya uposathaṃ uddisati, anuddisante ca bhikkhusaṅghassa uposatho pacchijjati, yannūnāhaṃ ito paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaññeva pātimokkhuddesaṃ anujāneyya”nti, evaṃ pana cintetvā bhikkhūnaññeva pātimokkhuddesaṃ anujāni[M 3.0434]. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā…pe… pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyāthā”ti. Tattha nadānāhanti na idāni ahaṃ. Uposathaṃ na karissāmi, pātimokkhaṃ na uddisissāmīti paccekaṃ na-kārena sambandho. Duvidhaṃ pātimokkhaṃ āṇāpātimokkhaṃ ovādapātimokkhanti. Tesu “suṇātu me bhante”tiādikaṃ āṇāpātimokkhaṃ, taṃ sāvakāva uddisanti, na buddhā, yaṃ anvaddhamāsaṃ uddisīyati. “Khantī paramaṃ…pe… sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ…pe… anupavādo anupaghāto…pe… etaṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183-185) imā pana tisso gāthā ovādapātimokkhaṃ nāma, taṃ buddhāva uddisanti, na sāvakā. Channampi vassānaṃ accayena uddisanti. Dīghāyukabuddhānañhi dharamānakāle ayameva pātimokkhuddeso, appāyukabuddhānaṃ pana paṭhamabodhiyaṃyeva, tato paraṃ itaro, tañca kho bhikkhū eva uddisanti, na buddhā. Tasmā amhākampi bhagavā vīsativassamattaṃ imaṃ ovādapātimokkhaṃ uddisitvā imaṃ antarāyaṃ disvā tato paraṃ na uddisi.

386. Then the Blessed One thought, 'Now a tumor has arisen in the Bhikkhu Sangha; impure individuals come to the Uposatha, and the Tathāgata does not declare the Uposatha for an impure assembly. And if he does not declare it, the Bhikkhu Sangha's Uposatha is interrupted. What if I were to permit only the bhikkhus to recite the Pātimokkha from now on?' Having reflected thus, he permitted only the bhikkhus to recite the Pātimokkha. Therefore, it is said, 'Then the Blessed One... you should recite the Pātimokkha.' Here, 'nadānāhaṃ' means 'not now I.' In 'I will not perform the Uposatha, I will not recite the Pātimokkha,' the negative particle 'na' is connected with each phrase. The Pātimokkha is twofold: the Āṇāpātimokkha and the Ovādapātimokkha. Among these, the Āṇāpātimokkha begins with 'Suṇātu me bhante,' and this is recited by the disciples, not by the Buddhas—it is recited every fortnight. 'Patient forbearance is the supreme austerity... the non-doing of all evil... not reviling, not harming... this is the teaching of the Buddhas'—these three verses constitute the Ovādapātimokkha, which is recited only by the Buddhas, not by the disciples. They recite it after the passing of six years. For long-lived Buddhas, this Pātimokkha recitation continues while they are living, but for short-lived Buddhas, it is recited only at the time of their first enlightenment, and thereafter the other is recited—and that too by the bhikkhus, not by the Buddhas. Therefore, our Blessed One also recited this Ovādapātimokkha for about twenty years, and seeing this obstacle, he did not recite it thereafter.

Aṭṭhānanti akāraṇaṃ. Anavakāsoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Kāraṇañhi tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti “ṭhāna”nti vuccati, evaṃ “avakāso”tipi vuccati. Yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ. Na ca, bhikkhave, sāpattikena pātimokkhaṃ sotabbantiādi padatthato suviññeyyaṃ. Vinicchayato panettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāya vuttameva. Tattha pure vā pacchā vāti ñattito pubbe vā pacchā vā.

'Aṭṭhāna' means 'it is impossible,' 'without cause.' 'Anavakāsa' is a synonym for that. A cause is called a 'basis' (ṭhāna) because the result stands (tiṭṭhati) upon it, its existence being dependent on that; similarly, it is also called an 'opportunity' (avakāsa). 'Yanti' is a reference to the action. 'And, bhikkhus, one who has committed an offense should not listen to the Pātimokkha'—this and similar terms are easily understood from the meaning of the words. As for the legal decision here, what needs to be said has already been stated in the Commentary. There, 'before or after' means before or after the motion.

Dhammikādhammikapātimokkhaṭṭhapanakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion on the Lawful and Unlawful Suspension of the Pātimokkha

387. Katañca akatañca ubhayaṃ gahetvāti yassa ekantena katāpi atthi, akatāpi atthi, tassa tadubhayaṃ gahetvā.

387. 'Having taken both what has been done and what has not been done': This applies to one who definitely has both what has been done and what has not been done, meaning to take both of these into account.

Dhammikapātimokkhaṭṭhapanakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion on the Lawful Suspension of the Pātimokkha

389. Parisā [V 3.0397] vuṭṭhātīti yasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ pātimokkhaṃ ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ vatthuṃ avinicchinitvā kenaci antarāyena vuṭṭhāti.

389. 'The assembly departs' means that, in regard to a matter for which the Pātimokkha was suspended, the assembly departs due to some obstacle without having resolved that matter.

393. Paccādiyatīti pati ādiyati, “akataṃ kamma”ntiādinā puna ārabhatīti attho.

393. 'Paccādiyati' means to take up again; the meaning is that one begins anew with the thought, 'The act was not done,' and so forth.

Attādānaaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion on the Factor of Taking Oneself as Authority

398. Paraṃ [M 3.0435] codetuṃ attanā ādātabbaṃ gahetabbaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ attādānaṃ. Tenāha “sāsanaṃ sodhetukāmo”tiādi. Vassārattoti vassakālo.

398. 'Attādāna' is a dispute to be taken up by oneself in order to accuse another. Hence it is said, 'desiring to purify the teaching,' and so forth. 'Vassāratto' means the rainy season.

Codakena paccavekkhitabbadhammakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion on the Qualities a Reprover Should Reflect Upon

399. Paṭimāsitunti parāmasituṃ. Palibodhe chinditvā…pe… adhigataṃ mettacittanti iminā appanāppattaṃ mettābhāvanaṃ dasseti. Tenevāha “vikkhambhanavasena vihatāghāta”nti.

399. 'Paṭimāsituṃ' means to grasp. 'Having cut through the hindrances… a mind of loving-kindness has been attained'—by this, it shows the development of loving-kindness that has reached absorption. Therefore, it is said, 'Through suppression, aversion is dispelled.'

Codakena upaṭṭhāpetabbadhammakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion on the Qualities a Challenger Should Establish

400. No dosantaroti ettha cittapariyāyo antara-saddoti āha “na duṭṭhacitto hutvā”ti.

400. 'No dosantaro': here, the word 'antara' is a synonym for 'citta' (mind); therefore he said, 'not being of a hostile mind.'

Codakacuditakapaṭisaṃyuttakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion Connected with the Accuser and the Accused

401. Karuṇanti appanāppattaṃ karuṇajjhānaṃ. Karuṇāpubbabhāganti parikammupacāravasappavattaṃ karuṇaṃ. Mettañca mettāpubbabhāgañcāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sesamettha suviññeyyamevāti.

401. 'Karuṇā' means the jhāna of compassion that has reached absorption. 'Karuṇāpubbabhāga' means compassion occurring by way of preliminary practice and access concentration. The same principle applies here to 'mettā' and 'mettāpubbabhāga.' The remainder here is easily understood.

Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Khandhaka on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha is concluded.

10. Bhikkhunikkhandhakaṃ

10. The Bhikkhunī Khandhaka

Mahāpajāpatigotamīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion on the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī

402. Bhikkhunikkhandhake [M 3.0436][V 3.0398] sakkesu viharatīti paṭhamagamanena gantvā viharati. Mahāpajāpati gotamīti ettha gotamīti gottaṃ. Nāmakaraṇadivase panassā laddhasakkārā brāhmaṇā lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “sace ayaṃ dhītaraṃ labhissati, cakkavattirañño mahesī bhavissati. Sace puttaṃ labhissati, cakkavattirājā bhavissatīti ubhayathāpi mahatīyevassā pajā bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu, tasmā puttapajāya ceva dhītupajāya ca mahantatāya “mahāpajāpatī”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu, idha pana gottena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā “mahāpajāpati gotamī”ti vuttaṃ. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti bhagavā kapilapuraṃ gantvā paṭhamameva nandaṃ pabbājesi, sattame divase rāhulakumāraṃ. Cumbaṭakakalahe pana ubhayanagaravāsikesu yuddhatthāya nikkhantesu satthā gantvā te rājāno saññāpetvā attadaṇḍasuttaṃ (su. ni. 941 ādayo) kathesi. Rājāno pasīditvā aḍḍhateyyasate aḍḍhateyyasate dārake adaṃsu. Tāni pañca kumārasatāni satthu santike pabbajiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ pajāpatiyo sāsanaṃ pesetvā anabhiratiṃ uppādayiṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ anabhiratiyā uppannabhāvaṃ ñatvā te pañcasate daharabhikkhū kuṇāladahaṃ netvā attano kuṇālakāle nisinnapubbe pāsāṇatale nisīditvā kuṇālajātakakathāya (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) tesaṃ anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā sabbepi te sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesi, puna mahāvanaṃ ānetvā arahattaphale. Tesaṃ cittajānanatthaṃ punapi pajāpatiyo sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Te “abhabbā mayaṃ gharāvāsassā”ti paṭisāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Tā “na dāni amhākaṃ paragharaṃ gantuṃ yuttaṃ, mahāpajāpatiyā santikaṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā pabbajissāmā”ti pañcasatāpi mahāpajāpatiṃ upasaṅkamitvā “ayye, amhākaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāpethā”ti āhaṃsu. Mahāpajāpati ca tā itthiyo gahetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami, setacchattassa heṭṭhā rañño parinibbutakāle upasaṅkamītipi vadantiyeva. Pakkāmīti puna kapilapurameva pāvisi.

402. In the Bhikkhunī Khandhaka, 'dwells among the Sakyans' means she went on the first visit and dwelt there. Regarding 'Mahāpajāpati Gotamī,' here 'Gotamī' is her clan name. On the day of her naming ceremony, the honored brahmins, seeing the excellence of her marks, declared, 'If she bears a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a wheel-turning monarch. If she bears a son, he will become a wheel-turning king. In either case, her progeny will be great.' Therefore, due to the greatness of her progeny, both sons and daughters, they gave her the name 'Mahāpajāpati.' Here, however, it is combined with her clan name and stated as 'Mahāpajāpati Gotamī.' 'She approached the Blessed One': The Blessed One went to Kapilapura and first ordained Nanda, and on the seventh day, Prince Rāhula. Then, during the dispute at Cumbaṭaka, when the residents of both cities set out for battle, the Teacher went and reconciled those kings, teaching them the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Pleased, the kings each gave two hundred and fifty young boys. These five hundred youths went forth in the presence of the Teacher. Then, their wives sent messages and stirred up discontent in them. Knowing that discontent had arisen in them, the Teacher took these five hundred young monks to Lake Kuṇāla, sat on a stone slab where he had previously sat in his life as Kuṇāla, and dispelled their discontent by recounting the Kuṇāla Jātaka. He established all of them in the fruit of stream-entry, then brought them back to the Great Forest and established them in the fruit of arahantship. To discern their state of mind, their wives sent messages again. They sent a reply: 'We are unfit for the household life.' Those women thought, 'It is not proper for us now to go to another’s house. We will go to Mahāpajāpati, have her get permission for us to go forth, and then we will go forth.' So all five hundred women approached Mahāpajāpati and said, 'Noble lady, please get permission for us to go forth.' Mahāpajāpati took these women and approached the Blessed One. Some say she approached at the time of the king's parinibbāna, under the lowered white parasol. 'She departed' means she entered Kapilapura again.

Yathābhirantaṃ [M 3.0437][V 3.0399] viharitvāti bodhaneyyasattānaṃ upanissayaṃ olokento yathājjhāsayena viharitvā. Cārikaṃ pakkāmīti mahājanasaṅgahaṃ karonto uttamāya buddhasiriyā anopamena buddhavilāsena aturitacārikaṃ pakkāmi. Sambahulāhi sākiyānīhi saddhinti antonivesanasmiṃyeva dasabalaṃ uddissa pabbajjāvesaṃ gahetvā tāpi pañcasatā sākiyāniyo pabbajjāvesaṃyeva gāhāpetvā sabbāhipi tāhi sambahulāhi sākiyānīhi saddhiṃ. Pakkāmīti gamanaṃ abhinīhari. Gamanābhinīharaṇakāle panassā “sukumārā rājitthiyo padasā gantuṃ na sakkhissantī”ti sākiyakoliyarājāno suvaṇṇasivikāyo upaṭṭhāpayiṃsu, tā pana “yāne āruyha gacchantīhi satthari agāravo kato hotī”ti ekapaṇṇāsayojanikaṃ maggaṃ padasāva paṭipajjiṃsu. Rājānopi purato ca pacchato ca ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahāpetvā taṇḍulasappitelādīnaṃ sakaṭāni pūretvā “gatagataṭṭhāne āhāraṃ paṭiyādethā”ti purise pesayiṃsu. Sūnehi pādehīti tāsañhi sukhumālattā pādesu eko phoṭo uṭṭheti, eko bhijjati, ubho pādā kaṭakaṭṭhisamparikiṇṇā viya hutvā uddhumātā. Tena vuttaṃ “sūnehi pādehī”ti. Bahidvārakoṭṭhaketi dvārakoṭṭhakassa bahi. Kasmā panevaṃ ṭhitāti? Evaṃ kirassā ahosi “ahaṃ tathāgatena anuññātā sayameva pabbajjāvesaṃ aggahesiṃ, evaṃ gahitabhāvo ca pana me sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo jāto, sace satthā pabbajjaṃ anujānissati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. Sace nānujānissati, mahatī garahā bhavissatī”ti vihāraṃ pavisituṃ asakkontī rodamānā aṭṭhāsi. Kiṃ nu tvaṃ gotamīti kiṃ nu rājakulānaṃ vipatti uppannā, kena nu tvaṃ kāraṇena evaṃ vivaṇṇabhāvaṃ pattā sūnehi pādehi…pe… ṭhitāti.

“Having dwelt as long as she wished”—observing the supporting conditions for beings to be enlightened, she dwelt according to her inclination. “She set out on a journey”—gathering a great assembly of people, she set out on an unhurried journey with the supreme majesty of the Buddha and his incomparable Buddha-splendor. “With many Sakyan women”—having taken the appearance of one gone forth in the inner chamber itself, dedicating it to the Ten-Powered One, she also had those five hundred Sakyan women take the appearance of one gone forth. Then, together with all those many Sakyan women, “she set out”—she directed her going. At the time of directing her going, the Sakyan and Koliyan kings thought, “These delicate royal women will not be able to go on foot,” and prepared golden palanquins for them. But they, thinking, “If we ride in vehicles, it would show disrespect to the Teacher,” traveled a distance of fifty-one yojanas entirely on foot. The kings also arranged guards in front and behind, filled carts with rice, ghee, oil, and other provisions, and sent men ahead, saying, “Prepare food at each stopping place.” “With swollen feet”—due to their delicate nature, one blister arose on their feet, one burst, and both feet became swollen as if strewn with splinters. Hence it is said, “with swollen feet.” “Outside the gatehouse”—outside the gatehouse. Why did she stand there thus? It is said that she thought, “I myself took the appearance of one gone forth, having been permitted by the Tathāgata, and this fact has become widely known throughout all of Jambudīpa. If the Teacher grants me the going forth, well and good. If he does not, there will be great blame.” Unable to enter the monastery, she stood there weeping. “What is it, Gotamī?”—“What misfortune has befallen the royal family? For what reason have you come to such a state, with swollen feet… standing thus?”

Aññenapi pariyāyenāti aññenapi kāraṇena. Āpādikāti saṃvaḍḍhikā, tumhākaṃ hatthapādesu hatthapādakiccaṃ asādhentesu hatthe ca pāde ca vaḍḍhetvā paṭijaggikāti attho. Posikāti divasassa dve tayo vāre nahāpetvā bhojetvā pāyetvā tumhe posesi. Thaññaṃ pāyesīti nandakumāro kira bodhisattato katipāheneva daharataro. Tasmiṃ jāte mahāpajāpati attano puttaṃ dhātīnaṃ datvā [M 3.0438] sayaṃ bodhisattassa dhātikiccaṃ sādhayamānā attano thaññaṃ pāyesi. Taṃ sandhāya thero evamāha. Sādhu bhanteti “bahukārā”tiādīhi tassā guṇaṃ kathetvā puna pabbajjaṃ yācanto evamāha.

“Aññenapi pariyāyena” means by another reason. “Āpādikā” means fostering; when your hands and feet were unable to perform their duties, she nurtured and cared for them by developing your hands and feet—this is the meaning. “Posikā” means she nourished you by bathing, feeding, and giving drink two or three times a day. “She gave milk”—it is said that Prince Nanda was a few days younger than the Bodhisatta. When he was born, Mahāpajāpati gave her own son to nurses but herself attended to the duties of nursing the Bodhisatta, giving him her own milk. Referring to this, the elder spoke thus. “Excellent, venerable one”—having praised her virtues with phrases like “of great help,” and so forth, he then requested the going forth for her again, saying thus.

Mahāpajāpatigotamīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is concluded.

Aṭṭhagarudhammakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Eight Weighty Rules.

403. Satthāpi [V 3.0400] “itthiyo nāma parittasaddhā, ekāyācitamatteyeva pabbajjāya anuññātāya na mama sāsanaṃ garuṃ katvā gaṇhissantī”ti tikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipitvā idāni garuṃ katvā gāhāpetukāmatāya “sace, ānanda, mahāpajāpati gotamī aṭṭha garudhamme paṭiggaṇhāti, sāvassā hotu upasampadā”tiādimāha. Tattha sāvassāti sā eva assā pabbajjāpi upasampadāpi hotu.

403. The Teacher, thinking, “Women are of little faith; if they are permitted to go forth after only a single request, they will not take my Dispensation seriously,” refused three times. Now, wishing to make them take it seriously, he said, “Ānanda, if Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts the eight weighty rules, let that be her full admission.” Here, “let that be her full admission” means that this itself should be her going forth and her full admission.

Tadahupasampannassāti taṃ divasampi upasampannassa. Abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ añjalikammaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ kātabbanti mānātimānaṃ akatvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena abhivādanaṃ, āsanā uṭṭhāya paccuggamanavasena paccuṭṭhānaṃ, dasanakhe samodhānetvā añjalikammaṃ, āsanapaññāpanabījanādikaṃ anucchavikakammasaṅkhātaṃ sāmīcikammañca kattabbaṃ. Abhikkhuke āvāseti yattha vasantiyā anantarāyena ovādatthāya upasaṅkamanārahe ṭhāne ovādadāyako ācariyo natthi, ayaṃ abhikkhuko āvāso nāma, evarūpe āvāse vassaṃ na upagantabbaṃ. Anvaddhamāsanti anuposathikaṃ. Ovādūpasaṅkamananti ovādatthāya upasaṅkamanaṃ. Diṭṭhenāti cakkhunā diṭṭhena. Sutenāti sotena sutena. Parisaṅkāyāti diṭṭhasutavasena parisaṅkitena. Garudhammanti garukaṃ saṅghādisesāpattiṃ. Pakkhamānattanti anūnāni pannarasa divasāni mānattaṃ. Chasu dhammesūti vikālabhojanacchaṭṭhesu sikkhāpadesu. Sikkhitasikkhāyāti ekasikkhampi akhaṇḍaṃ katvā pūritasikkhāya.

“On that very day of his full admission”: that is, of one who has received full admission on that very day. “Bowing, rising, joining palms, and proper duties should be performed”: without arrogance or pride, bowing should be done with the five-point prostration; rising means standing up from one’s seat to greet; joining palms is bringing the ten fingernails together; and proper duties, which are considered suitable services such as preparing a seat and fanning, should be performed. “In a residence without bhikkhus”: this is a place where, for a resident bhikkhunī, there is no teacher available to give advice in a location suitable to be approached without obstruction. This is called a residence without bhikkhus; one should not spend the rains retreat in such a residence. “Every half-month”: that is, every Uposatha day. “Approaching for advice”: that is, approaching for instruction. “By what is seen”: that is, seen with the eye. “By what is heard”: that is, heard with the ear. “By what is suspected”: that is, suspected based on what is seen or heard. “A grave offense”: that is, a serious Saṅghādisesa offense. “Fortnightly probation”: that is, a probation of not less than fifteen days. “In the six rules”: that is, in the training rules ending with the one on eating at the wrong time. “One who has trained in the training”: that is, one who has fulfilled the training without breaking even a single training rule.

Na akkositabbo na paribhāsitabboti dasannaṃ akkosavatthūnaṃ aññatarena akkosavatthunā na akkositabbo, bhayupadaṃsanāya kāyaci [M 3.0439] paribhāsāya na paribhāsitabbo. Ovaṭo bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūsu vacanapathoti ovādānusāsanidhammakathāsaṅkhāto vacanapatho bhikkhunīnaṃ bhikkhūsu ovaṭo pihito, na bhikkhuniyā koci bhikkhu ovaditabbo vā anusāsitabbo vā, “bhante porāṇakattherā idañcidañca vattaṃ pūrayiṃsū”ti evaṃ pana paveṇivasena kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Anovaṭo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīsūti bhikkhūnaṃ pana bhikkhunīsu vacanapatho anivārito, yathāruciyā ovadantu anusāsantu dhammakathaṃ kathentūti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panesā garudhammakathā mahāvibhaṅge vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

“One should not abuse or revile”: this means one should not abuse with any of the ten grounds for abuse, nor should one revile with any threat or intimidation. “The range of speech for bhikkhunīs towards bhikkhus is restricted”: the range of speech consisting of advice, instruction, and Dhamma talk is restricted for bhikkhunīs towards bhikkhus; no bhikkhunī should advise or instruct any bhikkhu. However, it is allowable to speak in the way of tradition, such as, “Venerable sir, the senior elders of old fulfilled such and such duties.” “The range of speech for bhikkhus towards bhikkhunīs is unrestricted”: the range of speech for bhikkhus towards bhikkhunīs is unrestricted; they may advise, instruct, or give a Dhamma talk as they like. This is the summary here; but for the detailed explanation, this discourse on the weighty rules should be understood just as it is stated in the Great Analysis.

Ime pana aṭṭha garudhamme satthu santike uggahetvā therena attano ārociyamāne sutvā mahāpajāpatiyā [V 3.0401] tāvamahantaṃ domanassaṃ khaṇena paṭippassambhi. Anotattadahato āhaṭena sītudakassa ghaṭasatena matthake parisittā viya vigatapariḷāhā attamanā hutvā garudhammapaṭiggahaṇena uppannapītipāmojjaṃ āvi karontī “seyyathāpi, bhante”tiādikaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Tattha daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbaññabhāve ṭhito. Maṇḍanakajātikoti alaṅkārasabhāvo. Tattha koci taruṇopi yuvā na hoti yathā atitaruṇo. Koci yuvāpi maṇḍanakajātiko na hoti yathā upasantasabhāvo ālasiyabyasanādīhi vā abhibhūto, idha pana daharo ceva yuvā ca maṇḍanakajātiko ca adhippeto, tasmā evamāha. Uppalādīni lokasammatattā vuttāni. Ito paraṃ yaṃ yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dassitameva.

Then, having learned these eight weighty rules in the presence of the Teacher, and hearing them reported by the Elder, Mahāpajāpatī’s immense sorrow subsided in an instant. As if her head were sprinkled with a hundred pots of cool water brought from Lake Anotatta, her fever of distress was quelled. Filled with joy, she displayed the delight and happiness that arose from accepting the weighty rules, and uttered this inspired saying: “Just as, venerable sir,” and so forth. Here, “young” means youthful. “In the prime of youth” means standing in the state of young adulthood. “Inclined to adornment” means naturally inclined to decoration. In this context, some may be young but not in the prime of youth, like those who are extremely young. Some may be in the prime of youth but not inclined to adornment, like those of a calm nature or overcome by laziness, adversity, and so on. Here, however, the intended meaning is one who is both young, in the prime of youth, and inclined to adornment—hence it is stated thus. “Lotuses” and so on are mentioned because they are esteemed in the world. Beyond this, whatever needs to be explained is shown in the commentary.

Tattha mātugāmassa pabbajitattāti idaṃ pañcavassasatato uddhaṃ aṭṭhatvā pañcasuyeva vassasatesu saddhammaṭṭhitiyā kāraṇanidassanaṃ. Paṭisambhidāpabhedappattakhīṇāsavavaseneva vuttanti ettha “paṭisambhidāpattakhīṇāsavaggahaṇena jhānānipi gahitāneva honti. Na hi nijjhānakānaṃ sabbappakārasampatti ijjhatī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavavasena vassasahassantiādinā ca yaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ khandhakabhāṇakānaṃ matena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.161) pana evaṃ vuttaṃ –

Herein, 'the going forth of a woman' is shown as the reason for the good Dhamma not standing for more than five hundred years, but for only five hundred years. 'It is stated in terms of those taint-exhausted ones who have attained the discriminations': herein, it is said in the Ganthipadas: 'By the inclusion of those taint-exhausted ones who have attained the discriminations, the jhānas are also included. For those without jhāna, success of every kind is not accomplished.' And what is said in terms of taint-exhausted dry-insight practitioners, such as 'a thousand years,' and so on—that should be understood as stated according to the opinion of the reciters of the Khandhakas. However, in the commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.161), it is stated thus:

“Paṭisambhidāpattehi [M 3.0440] vassasahassaṃ aṭṭhāsi, chaḷabhiññehi vassasahassaṃ, tevijjehi vassasahassaṃ, sukkhavipassakehi vassasahassaṃ, pātimokkhena vassasahassaṃ aṭṭhāsī”ti.

“It stood for a thousand years through those who had attained the discriminations, for a thousand years through those with the six higher knowledges, for a thousand years through those with the threefold knowledge, for a thousand years through the dry-insight practitioners, and for a thousand years through the Pātimokkha.”

Aṅguttaranikāyaṭṭhakathāyampi (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.130) –

Also, in the commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya (A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.130):

“Buddhānañhi parinibbānato vassasahassameva paṭisambhidā nibbattetuṃ sakkonti, tato paraṃ cha abhiññā, tato tāpi nibbattetuṃ asakkontā tisso vijjā nibbattenti, gacchante gacchante kāle tāpi nibbattetuṃ asakkontā sukkhavipassakā honti. Eteneva upāyena anāgāmino sakadāgāmino sotāpannā”ti –

“For after the final extinguishment of the Buddhas, they are able to bring forth the discriminations for only a thousand years. After that, the six higher knowledges. Then, being unable to bring forth even those, they bring forth the three knowledges. As time goes on and on, being unable to bring forth even those, they become dry-insight practitioners. By this same method, so too the non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers.”

Vuttaṃ.

It is stated.

Saṃyuttanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.156) –

However, in the commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya (Saṃ. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.3.156):

“Paṭhamabodhiyañhi [V 3.0402] bhikkhū paṭisambhidāpattā ahesuṃ. Atha kāle gacchante paṭisambhidā pāpuṇituṃ na sakkhiṃsu, chaḷabhiññā ahesuṃ, tato cha abhiññā pattuṃ asakkontā tisso vijjā pāpuṇiṃsu. Idāni kāle gacchante tisso vijjā pāpuṇituṃ asakkontā āsavakkhayamattaṃ pāpuṇissanti, tampi asakkontā anāgāmiphalaṃ, tampi asakkontā sakadāgāmiphalaṃ, tampi asakkontā sotāpattiphalaṃ, gacchante kāle sotāpattiphalampi pattuṃ na sakkhissantī”ti –

“Indeed, at the time of the first awakening, the bhikkhus were attainers of the discriminations. Then, as time passed, they were unable to attain the discriminations; they became attainers of the six higher knowledges. Then, being unable to attain the six higher knowledges, they attained the three knowledges. Now, as time continues to pass, being unable to attain the three knowledges, they will attain only the mere destruction of the taints. Being unable to attain even that, they will attain the fruit of non-returning. Being unable to attain even that, they will attain the fruit of once-returning. Being unable to attain even that, they will attain the fruit of stream-entry. As time goes on, they will not even be able to attain the fruit of stream-entry.”

Vuttaṃ.

It is stated.

Yasmā cetaṃ sabbaṃ aññamaññapaṭiviruddhaṃ, tasmā tesaṃ tesaṃ bhāṇakānaṃ matameva ācariyena tattha tattha dassitanti gahetabbaṃ. Aññathā hi ācariyasseva pubbāparavirodhappasaṅgo siyāti.

And since all this is mutually contradictory, it should be understood that the Teacher has, in each respective place, presented only the opinion of those various reciters. Otherwise, the Teacher himself would be faced with the charge of inconsistency.

Tāniyevāti tāniyeva pañca vassasahassāni. Pariyattimūlakaṃ sāsananti āha “na hi pariyattiyā asati paṭivedho atthī”tiādi. Pariyattiyā hi antarahitāya paṭipatti antaradhāyati, paṭipattiyā antarahitāya adhigamo antaradhāyati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Ayañhi pariyatti [M 3.0441] paṭipattiyā paccayo hoti, paṭipatti adhigamassa, iti paṭipattitopi pariyattiyeva pamāṇaṃ. Tattha paṭivedho ca paṭipatti ca hotipi na hotipi. Ekasmiñhi kāle paṭivedhakarā bhikkhū bahū honti, “esa bhikkhu puthujjano”ti aṅguliṃ pasāretvā dassetabbo hoti, imasmiṃyeva dīpe ekavāraṃ puthujjanabhikkhu nāma nāhosi. Paṭipattipūrakāpi kadāci bahū honti, kadāci appā, iti paṭivedho ca paṭipatti ca hotipi na hotipi. Sāsanaṭṭhitiyā pana pariyattiyeva pamāṇaṃ. Paṇḍito hi tepiṭakaṃ sutvā dvepi pūreti. Yathā amhākaṃ bodhisatto āḷārassa santike pañcābhiññā satta ca samāpattiyo nibbattetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā parikammaṃ pucchi, so “na jānāmī”ti āha, tato udakassa santikaṃ gantvā adhigatavisesaṃ saṃsanditvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassa parikammaṃ pucchi, so ācikkhi, tassa vacanasamanantarameva mahāsatto taṃ sampādesi, evameva paññavā bhikkhu pariyattiṃ sutvā dvepi pūreti, tasmā pariyattiyā ṭhitāya sāsanaṃ ṭhitaṃ hoti. Yathāpi mahato taḷākassa pāḷiyā thirāya udakaṃ na ṭhassatīti na vattabbaṃ, udake sati padumādīni pupphāni na pupphissantīti na vattabbaṃ, evameva mahātaḷākassa thirapāḷisadise tepiṭake buddhavacane sati mahātaḷāke udakasadisā paṭipattipūrakā kulaputtā natthīti na vattabbaṃ, tesu sati [V 3.0403] mahātaḷāke padumādīni pupphāni viya sotāpannādayo ariyapuggalā natthīti na vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ ekantato pariyattiyeva pamāṇaṃ.

“'These indeed' means these very five thousand years. The Dispensation has the scriptural learning as its root, as it is said: 'For without the scriptural learning, there is no penetration,' and so on. For when the scriptural learning disappears, the practice disappears; when the practice disappears, the attainment disappears. For what reason? This scriptural learning is the condition for practice, and practice is the condition for attainment. Thus, scriptural learning is the standard even over practice. Herein, both penetration and practice may or may not exist.
