At one time, there are many bhikkhus who accomplish penetration, such that one would have to point with a finger and say, 'This bhikkhu is a worldling,' to show one. On this very island, there was a time when there was not a single bhikkhu who was a worldling. Those who fulfill the practice are also sometimes many, sometimes few—thus, both penetration and practice may or may not exist. But for the stability of the Dispensation, the scriptural learning alone is the standard. For a wise person, having heard the Tipiṭaka, fulfills both. Just as our Bodhisatta, having brought forth the five higher knowledges and the seven attainments in the presence of Āḷāra, asked about the preliminary practice for the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and he said, 'I do not know.' Then, having gone to Uddaka and compared his own special attainment, he asked about the preliminary practice for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He explained it, and immediately after his words, the Great Being accomplished it. In the same way, a wise bhikkhu, having heard the scriptural learning, fulfills both. Therefore, as long as the scriptural learning stands, the Dispensation stands. Just as it cannot be said of a great reservoir with a firm embankment that its water will not remain, and it cannot be said that when there is water, lotuses and other flowers will not blossom; in the same way, when the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka—which is like the firm embankment of a great reservoir—exists, it cannot be said that there are no sons of good family who fulfill the practice, who are like the water in the great reservoir. And when they exist, it cannot be said that there are no noble individuals such as stream-enterers, who are like the lotuses and other flowers in the great reservoir. Thus, scriptural learning is absolutely the standard.”

Pariyattiyā antarahitāyāti ettha pariyattīti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.130) tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ sāṭṭhakathā pāḷi. Yāva sā tiṭṭhati, tāva pariyatti paripuṇṇā nāma hoti. Gacchante gacchante kāle kaliyugarājāno adhammikā honti, tesu adhammikesu tesampi amaccādayo adhammikā honti, tato raṭṭhajanapadavāsinoti tesaṃ adhammikatāya na devo sammā vassati, tato sassāni na sampajjanti, tesu asampajjantesu paccayadāyakā bhikkhusaṅghassa paccaye dātuṃ na sakkonti, bhikkhū paccayehi kilamantā antevāsike saṅgahetuṃ na sakkonti. Gacchante gacchante kāle pariyatti parihāyati, atthavasena dhāretuṃ na sakkonti, pāḷivaseneva [M 3.0442] dhārenti. Tato kāle gacchante pāḷimpi sakalaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkonti, paṭhamaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ parihāyati, parihāyamānaṃ matthakato paṭṭhāya parihāyati. Paṭhamameva hi mahāpakaraṇaṃ parihāyati, tasmiṃ parihīne yamakaṃ, kathāvatthu, puggalapaññatti, dhātukathā, vibhaṅgo, dhammasaṅgahoti.

“'When the scriptural learning disappears': herein, 'scriptural learning' refers to the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, the Pāḷi with its commentaries. As long as that stands, the scriptural learning is said to be complete. As time goes on and on, the kings of the Kali Yuga become unrighteous. When they are unrighteous, their ministers and others also become unrighteous. Then, because of their unrighteousness, the deva does not rain properly. Consequently, the crops do not prosper. When they do not prosper, the donors of requisites are unable to give requisites to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The bhikkhus, being afflicted by the lack of requisites, are unable to take on pupils. As time goes on and on, the scriptural learning declines. They are unable to retain it by way of its meaning; they retain it only by way of the Pāḷi text. Then, as time passes, they are unable to retain even the entire Pāḷi. First, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka disappears. In disappearing, it disappears starting from the top. For first the Mahāpakaraṇa disappears. When that has disappeared, then the Yamaka, Kathāvatthu, Puggalapaññatti, Dhātukathā, Vibhaṅga, and Dhammasaṅgaṇī.”

Evaṃ abhidhammapiṭake parihīne matthakato paṭṭhāya suttantapiṭakaṃ parihāyati. Paṭhamañhi aṅguttaranikāyo parihāyati, tasmimpi paṭhamaṃ ekādasakanipāto…pe… tato ekakanipātoti. Evaṃ aṅguttaranikāye parihīne matthakato paṭṭhāya saṃyuttanikāyo parihāyati. Paṭhamañhi mahāvaggo parihāyati, tato saḷāyatanavaggo, khandhakavaggo, nidānavaggo, sagāthāvaggoti. Evaṃ saṃyuttanikāye parihīne matthakato paṭṭhāya majjhimanikāyo parihāyati. Paṭhamañhi uparipaṇṇāsako parihāyati, tato majjhimapaṇṇāsako, tato mūlapaṇṇāsakoti. Evaṃ majjhimanikāye parihīne matthakato paṭṭhāya dīghanikāyo parihāyati. Paṭhamañhi pāthikavaggo parihāyati, tato mahāvaggo, tato sīlakkhandhavaggoti. Evaṃ dīghanikāye parihīne suttantapiṭakaṃ parihīnaṃ nāma hoti. Vinayapiṭakena saddhiṃ jātakameva dhārenti. Vinayapiṭakañhi lajjino dhārenti, lābhakāmā pana “suttante kathitepi sallakkhentā natthī”ti jātakameva dhārenti. Gacchante kāle jātakampi dhāretuṃ na sakkonti. Atha nesaṃ paṭhamaṃ vessantarajātakaṃ parihāyati, tato paṭilomakkamena puṇṇakajātakaṃ, mahānāradajātakanti pariyosāne apaṇṇakajātakaṃ parihāyati, vinayapiṭakameva dhārenti.

When the Abhidhamma Piṭaka declines, the Sutta Piṭaka declines beginning from the top. First, the Aṅguttara Nikāya declines, and within it, first the Book of Elevens…pe… then the Book of Ones. When the Aṅguttara Nikāya declines, the Saṃyutta Nikāya declines beginning from the top. First, the Great Division declines, then the Division on the Six Sense Bases, the Division on Aggregates, the Division on Causation, and the Division with Verses. When the Saṃyutta Nikāya declines, the Majjhima Nikāya declines beginning from the top. First, the Upper Fifty declines, then the Middle Fifty, and then the Root Fifty. When the Majjhima Nikāya declines, the Dīgha Nikāya declines beginning from the top. First, the Pāthika Division declines, then the Great Division, and then the Division on the Aggregate of Morality. When the Dīgha Nikāya declines, the Sutta Piṭaka is said to have declined. They maintain only the Jātaka together with the Vinaya Piṭaka. For the Vinaya Piṭaka is maintained by the scrupulous, but those seeking gain think, 'Even when the Suttas are recited, no one pays attention,' and so they maintain only the Jātaka. As time goes on, they are not able to maintain even the Jātaka. Then, first the Vessantara Jātaka declines, then in reverse order the Puṇṇaka Jātaka, the Mahānārada Jātaka, and finally the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka declines. They maintain only the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Gacchante kāle tampi matthakato paṭṭhāya parihāyati. Paṭhamañhi parivāro parihāyati, tato [V 3.0404] khandhako, bhikkhunīvibhaṅgo, mahāvibhaṅgoti anukkamena uposathakkhandhakamattameva dhārenti. Tadāpi pariyatti anantarahitāva hoti. Yāva pana manussesu catuppadikagāthāpi pavattati, tāva pariyatti anantarahitāva hoti. Yadā saddho pasanno rājā hatthikkhandhe suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakamhi sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapāpetvā “buddhehi kathitaṃ catuppadikaṃ gāthaṃ jānanto imaṃ sahassaṃ gaṇhatū”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā gaṇhanakaṃ alabhitvā “ekavāraṃ carāpite nāmaṃ suṇantāpi honti asuṇantāpī”ti yāvatatiyaṃ carāpetvā gaṇhanakaṃ alabhitvā rājapurisā [M 3.0443] sahassatthavikaṃ puna rājakulaṃ pavesenti, tadā pariyatti antarahitā nāma hoti.

As time passes, even that declines from the top. First the Parivāra declines, then the Khandhaka, the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, and the Mahāvibhaṅga; thus, in sequence, they retain only the Uposathakkhandhaka. Even then, the scriptural tradition is not yet lost. As long as even a four-line verse is current among people, the scriptural tradition is not yet lost. When a faithful and devoted king has a bag containing a thousand placed in a golden basket on an elephant's back, and has a drum beaten in the city, proclaiming: 'Whoever knows the four-line verse spoken by the Buddhas, let him take this thousand!'—and after having the drum beaten once, thinking, 'It may be that some hear and some do not hear,' he has it beaten up to a third time, but finds no one to take it—then the king's men return the bag of a thousand to the royal palace. At that time, the scriptural tradition is said to be lost.

Ciraṃ pavattissatīti pariyattiyā antarahitāyapi liṅgamattaṃ addhānaṃ pavattissati. Kathaṃ? Gacchante gacchante hi kāle cīvaraggahaṇaṃ pattaggahaṇaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ ālokitavilokitaṃ na pāsādikaṃ hoti, nigaṇṭhasamaṇā viya alābupattaṃ bhikkhū pattaṃ aggabāhāya parikkhipitvā ādāya vicaranti, ettāvatāpi liṅgaṃ anantarahitameva hoti. Gacchante pana kāle aggabāhato otāretvā hatthena vā sikkāya vā olambetvā vicaranti, cīvarampi rajanasāruppaṃ akatvā oṭṭhaṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ katvā rajanti. Gacchante kāle rajanampi na hoti, dasacchindanaṃ ovaṭṭikāvijjhanaṃ kappamattañca katvā vaḷañjanti, puna ovaṭṭikaṃ vijjhitvā kappaṃ na karonti. Tato ubhayampi akatvā dasā chetvā paribbājakā viya caranti. Gacchante kāle “ko iminā amhākaṃ attho”ti khuddakaṃ kāsāvakhaṇḍaṃ hatthe vā gīvāyaṃ vā bandhanti, kesesu vā allīyāpenti, dārabharaṇaṃ karontā kasitvā vapitvā jīvikaṃ kappetvā vicaranti, tadā dakkhiṇaṃ dento jano saṅghaṃ uddissa etesampi deti. Idaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā vuttaṃ “bhavissanti kho panānanda, anāgatamaddhānaṃ gotrabhuno kāsāvakaṇṭhā dussīlā pāpadhammā, tesu dussīlesu saṅghaṃ uddissa dānaṃ dassanti, tadāpāhaṃ, ānanda, saṅghagataṃ dakkhiṇaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ appameyyaṃ vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 3.380). Tato gacchante kāle nānāvidhāni kammāni karontā “papañco esa, kiṃ iminā amhāka”nti kāsāvakhaṇḍaṃ chinditvā araññe khipanti, tasmiṃ kāle liṅgaṃ antarahitaṃ nāma hoti. Kassapadasabalassa kira kālato paṭṭhāya yonakānaṃ setavatthāni pārupitvā caraṇacārittaṃ jātaṃ. Evaṃ pariyattiyā antarahitāyapi liṅgamattaṃ ciraṃ pavattissatīti veditabbaṃ.

It is said that even when the scriptural tradition is lost, the mere appearance will persist for a long time. How so? As time goes on, actions like taking the robe, taking the bowl, bending and stretching, looking ahead and looking aside, are not pleasing. Like the naked ascetics, monks carry bowls like gourds, holding them in their arms as they go about. Even so, the appearance is not yet lost. But as time goes on, they lower the bowl from their arms and carry it by hand or in a string bag. They also do not make their robes properly dyed but dye them the color of lip-rouge. As time goes on, there is not even proper dyeing; just cutting the fringes, making holes for stitching, and making them barely allowable, they use them. Later, they do not even make holes for stitching or make them allowable; instead, they just cut the fringes and go about like wanderers. As time goes on, thinking, 'What use is this to us?' they tie small saffron cloth scraps on their hands or necks, or attach them to their hair. They make a living by supporting families, plowing, and sowing. Then, when people give offerings, they dedicate them to the Sangha, and even these receive them. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: 'Ānanda, in the future, there will be those who are monks in name only, with saffron cloth around their necks—unvirtuous, of evil character. People will give gifts dedicated to the Sangha to those unvirtuous ones, and even then, Ānanda, I declare that the offering to the Sangha is immeasurable, boundless.' Then, as time goes on, while engaged in various tasks, thinking, 'This is a complication, what use is this to us?' they cut off the saffron cloth and throw it away in the forest. At that time, the appearance is said to be lost. It is said that from the time of Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, onwards, it became the practice for the Yonakas to wear white clothes. Thus, it should be understood that even when the scriptural tradition is lost, the mere appearance will persist for a long time.

Aṭṭhagarudhammakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Eight Weighty Principles is finished.

Bhikkhunīupasampannānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Permission for the Higher Ordination of Bhikkhunīs

404-405. Yadaggenāti [M 3.0444][V 3.0405] yaṃ divasaṃ ādiṃ katvā. Tadevāti tasmiññeva divase. Anuññattiyāti anuññāya. Ekāhaṃ, bhante ānanda, bhagavantaṃ varaṃ yācāmīti “evameva kho ahaṃ, bhante ānanda, ime aṭṭha garudhamme paṭiggaṇhāmi yāvajīvaṃ anatikkamanīye”ti paṭijānitvā idāni kasmā varaṃ yācatīti ce? Parūpavādavivajjanatthaṃ. Evañhi keci vadeyyuṃ “mahāpajāpatiyā paṭhamaṃ sampaṭicchitattā bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnañca yathāvuḍḍhaṃ abhivādanaṃ nāhosi, sā ce varaṃ yāceyya, bhagavā anujāneyyā”ti.

404-405. 'From that day onward' means taking that day as the beginning. 'On that very day' means on that same day. 'With permission' means with allowance. 'Venerable Ānanda, I ask the Blessed One for one boon' – if having previously declared, 'Venerable Ānanda, I accept these eight weighty principles for life without transgressing them,' why does she now ask for a boon? It is to avoid criticism by others. For some might say, 'Because Mahāpajāpatī first consented to them, there was no paying respects according to seniority between monks and nuns. If she were to ask for a boon, the Blessed One would have allowed it.'

406. Sarāgāyāti sarāgabhāvāya kāmarāgabhavarāgaparibrūhanāya. Saññogāyāti vaṭṭe saṃyojanatthāya. Ācayāyāti vaṭṭassa vaḍḍhanatthāya. Mahicchatāyāti mahicchabhāvāya. Asantuṭṭhiyāti asantuṭṭhibhāvāya. Saṅgaṇikāyāti kilesasaṅgaṇagaṇasaṅgaṇavihārāya. Kosajjāyāti kusītabhāvāya. Dubbharatāyāti dupposatāya. Virāgāyāti sakalavaṭṭato virajjanatthāya. Visaññogāyāti kāmarāgādīhi visaṃyujjanatthāya. Apacayāyāti sabbassapi vaṭṭassa apacayatthāya, nibbānāyāti attho. Appicchatāyāti paccayappicchatādivasena sabbaso icchāpagamāya. Santuṭṭhiyāti dvādasavidhasantuṭṭhibhāvāya. Pavivekāyāti pavivittabhāvāya kāyavivekāditadaṅgavivekādivivekasiddhiyā. Vīriyārambhāyāti kāyikassa ceva cetasikassa ca vīriyassa paggaṇhanatthāya. Subharatāyāti sukhaposanatthāya. Evaṃ yo pariyattidhammo uggahaṇadhāraṇaparipucchāmanasikāravasena yoniso paṭipajjantassa sarāgādibhāvaparivajjanassa kāraṇaṃ hutvā virāgādibhāvāya saṃvattati, ekaṃsato eso dhammo, eso vinayo sammadeva apāyādīsu apatanavasena dhāraṇato kilesānaṃ vinayanato, satthu sammāsambuddhassa ovādānusiṭṭhibhāvato etaṃ satthusāsananti dhāreyyāsi jāneyyāsi, avabujjheyyāsīti attho. Imasmiṃ sutte paṭhamavārena vaṭṭaṃ, dutiyavārena vivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

406. “For passion” means for the state of passion, for the increase of sensual passion and passion for existence. “For bondage” means for the purpose of fettering within the cycle of existence. “For accumulation” means for the increase of the cycle. “For great desire” means for the state of great desire. “For discontent” means for the state of discontent. “For socializing” means for dwelling in the company of defilements and crowds. “For laziness” means for the state of laziness. “For being difficult to support” means for being hard to nourish. “For dispassion” means for the purpose of detachment from the entire cycle. “For disjunction” means for the purpose of being disjoined from sensual passion and so forth. “For non-accumulation” means for the purpose of diminishing the entire cycle, meaning for the sake of Nibbāna. “For fewness of wishes” means for the complete abandonment of wishes through fewness of wishes regarding requisites and so forth. “For contentment” means for the state of twelvefold contentment. “For seclusion” means for the achievement of seclusion through bodily seclusion, seclusion by substitution, and so forth. “For arousal of energy” means for the purpose of rousing bodily and mental energy. “For being easy to support” means for the purpose of being easily nourished. Thus, the Dhamma of learning, when properly practiced through study, memorization, questioning, and reflection, becomes a cause for abandoning states of passion and so forth and leads to states of dispassion and so forth. This is certainly the Dhamma, this is certainly the Vinaya, as it rightly prevents falling into states of loss, restrains defilements, and is the advice and instruction of the Teacher, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—this you should hold, know, and understand. In this discourse, the first section explains the cycle of existence, and the second section explains liberation from it.

409-410. Vimānetvāti [M 3.0445] aparajjhitvā. Kammappattāyopīti kammārahāpi. Āpattigāminiyopīti āpattiāpannāyopi. Vuttanayeneva kāretabbataṃ āpajjantīti tathākaraṇassa paṭikkhittattā dukkaṭena kāretabbataṃ āpajjanti.

409-410. “Having disrespected” means having offended. “Even if worthy of a formal act” means even if deserving of a formal act. “Even if having committed an offense” means even if having incurred an offense. “They incur the need to be dealt with according to the prescribed method”: this means that because such action is prohibited, one who deals with them incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkata).

413-5. Dve tisso bhikkhuniyoti dvīhi tīhi bhikkhunīhi. Na ārocentīti pātimokkhuddesakassa [V 3.0406] na ārocenti. Na paccāharantīti bhikkhunīnaṃ na paccāharanti. Visesakanti vattabhaṅgaṃ.

413-5. “Two or three bhikkhunīs” means with two or three bhikkhunīs. “They do not inform” means they do not inform the one reciting the Pātimokkha. “They do not report back” means they do not report back to the bhikkhunīs. “A special matter” means a breach of duty.

420. Tena ca bhikkhu nimantetabboti sāmīcidassanametaṃ, na pana animantiyā āpatti.

420. “And that bhikkhu should be invited” indicates proper conduct, but there is no offense if he is not invited.

425. Tayo nissayeti senāsananissayaṃ apanetvā apare tayo nissaye. Rukkhamūlasenāsanañhi sā na labhati.

425. “The three supports” refers to the other three supports, having removed the dwelling support. For she does not obtain a tree-root dwelling.

428. Anuvādaṃ paṭṭhapentīti issariyaṃ pavattenti.

428. “They initiate dispute” means they exercise authority.

430. Bhikkhudūtena upasampādentīti bhikkhuyeva dūto bhikkhudūto, tena bhikkhudūtena, bhikkhudūtaṃ katvā upasampādentīti attho.

430. “They ordain through a bhikkhu messenger”—meaning the messenger is precisely a bhikkhu, a bhikkhu messenger. By means of that bhikkhu messenger, having appointed a bhikkhu as messenger, they ordain—this is the meaning.

431. Na sammatīti nappahoti. Navakammanti navakammaṃ katvā “ettakāni vassāni vasatū”ti apaloketvā saṅghikabhūmidānaṃ.

431. “She is not approved” means she is not capable. “New work” means the donation of Sangha land, after having done new work and having announced, “Let it remain for so many years.”

432. Sannisinnagabbhāti patiṭṭhitagabbhā.

432. “With a settled womb” means with an established pregnancy.

434. Pabbajjampi na labhatīti titthāyatanasaṅkantāya abhabbabhāvūpagamanato na labhati. Idaṃ odissa anuññātaṃ vaṭṭatīti ekato vā ubhato vā avassave satipi odissa anuññātattā vaṭṭati. Sesamettha pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca suviññeyyamevāti.

434. “She does not even obtain the going forth” means she does not obtain it because of her inability to transition from a sectarian creed. “This is allowable, having been specified”—it is allowable because it was specifically permitted, even if there is discharge from one side or from both. The rest here should be easily understood from the Pāli text and the commentary.

Bhikkhunīupasampannānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Permitting the Ordination of Bhikkhunīs is concluded.

Bhikkhunikkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Khandhaka is concluded.

11. Pañcasatikakkhandhakaṃ

11. The Chapter of the Five Hundred

Saṅgītinidānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Origin of the Council

437. Pañcasatikakkhandhake [M 3.0446][V 3.0407] pāvāya kusināranti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.231) pāvānagare piṇḍāya caritvā kusināraṃ gamissāmīti addhānamaggappaṭipanno. Mandāravapupphaṃ gahetvāti mahācāṭippamāṇaṃ pupphaṃ āgantukadaṇḍake ṭhapetvā chattaṃ viya gahetvā. Addasaṃ khoti āgacchantaṃ dūratova addasaṃ. Disvā ca pana “pucchissāmi naṃ bhagavato pavatti”nti cittaṃ uppādetvā “sace kho pana nisinnakova pucchissāmi, satthari agāravo kato bhavissatī”ti uṭṭhahitvā ṭhitaṭṭhānato apakkamma chaddanto nāgarājā maṇicammaṃ viya dasabaladattiyaṃ meghavaṇṇapaṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupitvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā satthari katena gāravena ājīvakassa abhimukho hutvā “apāvuso amhākaṃ satthāraṃ jānāsī”ti āha. Kiṃ pana satthu parinibbānaṃ jānanto pucchi ajānantoti? Āvajjanappaṭibaddhaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ jānanaṃ. Anāvajjitattā panesa ajānanto pucchīti eke. Thero samāpattibahulo rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaleṇamaṇḍapādīsu niccaṃ samāpattiphaleneva yāpeti. Kulasantakampi gāmaṃ pavisitvā dvāre samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhitova bhikkhaṃ gaṇhāti. Thero kira “iminā me pacchimena attabhāvena mahājanānuggahaṃ karissāmi, ye mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ vā denti, gandhamālādīhi vā sakkāraṃ karonti, tesaṃ taṃ mahapphalaṃ hotū”ti evaṃ karoti. Tasmā samāpattibahulatāya na jāni. Iti ajānantova pucchīti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hettha ajānanakāraṇaṃ atthi. Abhilakkhitaṃ satthu parinibbānaṃ ahosi dasasahassilokadhātukampanādīhi nimittehi. Therassa pana parisāya kehici bhikkhūhi bhagavā diṭṭhapubbo, kehici na diṭṭhapubbo. Tattha yehi diṭṭhapubbo, tepi passitukāmāva. Yehipi adiṭṭhapubbo, tepi passitukāmāva. Tattha yehi na diṭṭhapubbo, te abhidassanakāmatāya gantvā “kuhiṃ bhagavā”ti pucchantā “parinibbuto”ti sutvā sandhāretuṃ na sakkhissanti. Cīvaraṃ chaḍḍetvā ekavatthā vā dunnivatthā vā urāni paṭipisantā parodissanti. Tattha manussā “mahākassapena saddhiṃ [V 3.0408] āgatapaṃsukūlikā sayampi itthiyo viya parodanti, te [M 3.0447] kiṃ amhe samassāsentī”ti mayhaṃ dosaṃ dassanti. Idaṃ pana suññaṃ mahāraññaṃ, idha yathā tathā rodantesu doso natthi. Purimataraṃ sutvā nāma sokopi tanuko hotīti bhikkhūnaṃ satuppādalābhatthaṃ jānantova pucchi.

437. In the Pañcasatikakkhandhaka, it is said, “From Pāvā to Kusinārā” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.231). After wandering for alms in the city of Pāvā, he set out on the road, thinking, “I will go to Kusinārā.” Holding a mandārava flower—a flower as large as a great vat—he placed it on a supporting stick and carried it like an umbrella. He saw him approaching from afar. Upon seeing him, he thought, “I will ask him about the Blessed One’s condition.” But then he reflected, “If I ask while seated, disrespect would be shown to the Teacher.” So he rose from his seat, stepped aside, and like Chaddanta, the nāga king with his jeweled hide, he draped his dust-colored rag robe, cloud-colored and given by the Ten-Powered One, over one shoulder, placed his hands together—radiant as ten joined fingernails—on his head, and with deep reverence shown to the Teacher, he faced the Ājīvaka and asked, “Friend, do you know our Teacher?” But did he ask knowing that the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, or not knowing? The knowledge of the arahants is connected with attention. Some say that because he had not directed his attention, he asked without knowing. The elder was often absorbed in meditative attainments, spending his days and nights constantly in the bliss of absorption, whether in caves, pavilions, or other dwellings. Even when entering a village belonging to a particular family, he would enter absorption at the gate and only emerge from absorption to receive food. It is said that the elder thought, “With this final existence of mine, I will benefit many people. May those who give me alms or honor me with garlands and such receive great merit.” Thus he acted. Therefore, due to his frequent absorption, he did not know. Some say he asked without knowing, but this should not be accepted. There is no reason here for ignorance. The Teacher’s passing was clearly indicated by signs—such as the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world system. Among the elder’s assembly, some monks had seen the Blessed One before, while others had not. Those who had seen him still wished to see him again, and those who had not also desired to see him. Those who had not seen him before, eager to see him, upon going and asking, “Where is the Blessed One?” and hearing, “He has attained final Nibbāna,” would be unable to bear it. Casting off their robes, half-dressed or poorly dressed, they would beat their chests and weep. Then people would say, “These rag-robed monks who came with Mahākassapa are wailing like women themselves. How can they console us?” and they would find fault with me. But this is a vast, empty wilderness; here, no matter how they weep, there is no fault. For having heard it earlier, grief becomes lighter. For the sake of the monks’ gain and the arising of mindfulness, he asked while fully knowing.

Ajja sattāhaparinibbutoti ajja divasato paṭilomato sattame ahani parinibbuto. Tato me idanti tato samaṇassa gotamassa parinibbutaṭṭhānato. Avītarāgāti puthujjanā ceva sotāpannasakadāgāmino ca. Tesañhi domanassaṃ appahīnaṃ, tasmā tepi bāhā paggayha kandanti, ubho hatthe sīse ṭhapetvā rodanti. Chinnapātaṃ papatantīti chinnānaṃ pāto viya chinnapāto, taṃ chinnapātaṃ, bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesoyaṃ, majjhe chinnā viya hutvā yato vā tato vā patantīti attho. Āvaṭṭantīti abhimukhabhāvena vaṭṭanti. Yattha patitā, tato katipayaratanaṭṭhānaṃ vaṭṭanavaseneva gantvā puna yathāpatitameva ṭhānaṃ vaṭṭanavasena āgacchanti. Vivaṭṭantīti yattha patitā, tato nivaṭṭanti, patitaṭṭhānato parabhāgaṃ vaṭṭamānā gacchantīti attho. Apica purato vaṭṭanaṃ āvaṭṭanaṃ, passato pacchato ca vaṭṭanaṃ vivaṭṭanaṃ. Tasmā dve pāde pasāretvā sakiṃ purato sakiṃ pacchato sakiṃ vāmato sakiṃ dakkhiṇato samparivaṭṭamānāpi āvaṭṭanti vivaṭṭantīti vuccanti. Vītarāgāti pahīnadomanassā iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu nibbikāratāya silāthambhasadisā anāgāmikhīṇāsavā. Kāmañhi domanasse asatipi ekacco rāgo hotiyeva, rāge pana asati domanassassa asambhavoyeva. Tadekaṭṭhabhāvato hi rāgappahānena pahīnadomanassā vuttā, na khīṇāsavā eva.

Today, the seventh day since the Parinibbāna—today, counting backward from this day, is the seventh day since the Parinibbāna. From that—from the place of the ascetic Gotama's Parinibbāna. Those not free from lust—this refers to ordinary people, stream-enterers, and once-returners. For sorrow has not been abandoned in them; therefore, they stretch out their arms and weep, placing their hands on their heads and crying. They fall as if felled—like the falling of severed things; thus, 'chinnapātaṃ'. This is a neuter designation of state. It means falling from here or there as if cut in the middle. They whirl around—they turn facing towards their object of grief. Wherever they fall, from there they go a short distance by rolling, then return to the place where they fell, again by rolling. They turn away—wherever they fall, from there they turn away, rolling to a different place from where they fell. Furthermore, rolling forward is 'whirling around,' while rolling to the side and backward is 'turning away.' Therefore, even when they stretch out their legs and roll completely around—once forward, once backward, once to the left, and once to the right—they are said to 'whirl around and turn away.' Those free from lust—those who have abandoned sorrow, being unperturbed by the agreeable and disagreeable, like stone pillars—are non-returners and arahants. For even when sorrow is absent, a certain lust may still exist; but when lust is absent, sorrow cannot possibly exist. Because they are of a single nature, by the abandoning of lust they are said to have abandoned sorrow; this refers not only to the arahants.

Sabbeheva piyehītiādīsu piyāyitabbato piyehi manavaḍḍhanato manāpehi mātāpitābhātābhaginīādikehi. Nānābhāvoti jātiyā nānābhāvo, jātianurūpagamanena visuṃ bhāvo, asambaddhabhāvoti attho. Vinābhāvoti maraṇena vinābhāvo, cutiyā tenattabhāvena apunapavattanato vippayogoti attho. Aññathābhāvoti bhavena aññathābhāvo, bhavantaraggahaṇena “kāmāvacarasatto [M 3.0448] rūpāvacaro hotī”tiādinā tatthāpi “manusso devo hotī”tiādinā ca purimākārato aññākāratāti attho. Tanti tasmā. Kutettha labbhāti kuto kuhiṃ kasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne ettha etasmiṃ khandhappavatte yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ…pe… mā palujjīti laddhuṃ sakkā, na sakkā eva tādisassa kāraṇassa abhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā sabbeheva piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo, tasmā dasa pāramiyo pūretvāpi sambodhiṃ patvāpi dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvāpi yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvāpi devorohaṇaṃ katvāpi yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ [V 3.0409] palokadhammaṃ, tañca tathāgatassapi sarīraṃ mā palujjīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, rodantenapi kandantenapi na sakkā taṃ kāraṇaṃ laddhunti.

‘From all that is dear,’ and so on: because they are to be cherished, they are ‘dear’; because they increase affection, they are ‘beloved’—such as mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, and so on. ‘Difference’ means difference of birth, a separate state by passing on according to one's birth; the meaning is a state of being unconnected. ‘Separation’ means separation through death; the meaning is disjunction due to passing away and not returning to that same state. ‘Alteration’ means alteration of existence, a change from a previous form by taking up another existence—such as, ‘a being in the sensual realm becomes one in the form realm,’ or ‘a human becomes a deva,’ and so on—this is the meaning. ‘Taṃ’ means ‘therefore’. ‘How can it be obtained here?’—where, in what place, in this very continuity of aggregates, could it be obtained that what is born... and so on... should not perish? It cannot be obtained, for such a cause does not exist. This is what is meant: Because there is difference from all that is dear and beloved, therefore, even after fulfilling the ten perfections, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dhamma, displaying the twin miracle, and descending from the deva realm—that what is born, come into being, conditioned, and subject to decay, namely the Tathāgata’s body, should not perish—this is not a possible case. Even by weeping and lamenting, it is not possible to obtain that cause.

Tena kho panāvuso, samayena subhaddo nāma vuḍḍhapabbajitotiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ nidānavaṇṇanāyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā) vuttanayameva.

Regarding such phrases as, 'At that time, friends, there was an elderly wanderer named Subhadda,' whatever should be said has already been stated in the same way in the commentary on the introduction (Sāratthadīpanī, Vol. 1, Account of the First Great Council).

Saṅgītinidānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Introduction to the Account of the Council is concluded.

Khuddānukhuddakasikkhāpadakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of the Minor and Lesser Training Rules

441. Samūhaneyyāti ākaṅkhamāno samūhanatu, yadi icchati, samūhaneyyāti attho. Kasmā pana “samūhanathā”ti ekaṃseneva avatvā “ākaṅkhamāno samūhaneyyā”ti vikappavacaneneva bhagavā ṭhapesīti? Mahākassapassa ñāṇabalassa diṭṭhattā. Passati hi bhagavā “samūhanathāti vuttepi saṅgītikāle kassapo na samūhanissatī”ti, tasmā vikappeneva ṭhapesi. Yadi asamūhananaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, tadeva ca icchitaṃ, atha kasmā bhagavā “ākaṅkhamāno samūhanatū”ti avocāti? Tathārūpapuggalajjhāsayavasena. Santi hi keci khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni samādāya vattituṃ anicchantā, tesaṃ tathā avuccamāne bhagavati vighāto uppajjeyya, taṃ tesaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya. Tathā pana vutte tesaṃ vighāto na uppajjeyya, amhākamevāyaṃ doso, yato amhesuyeva keci samūhananaṃ na icchantīti[M 3.0449]. Keci “sakalassa pana sāsanassa saṅghāyattabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ tathā vutta”nti vadanti. Yaṃ kiñci satthārā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ samaṇā sakyaputtiyā sirasā sampaṭicchitvā jīvitaṃ viya rakkhanti. Tathā hi te “khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni ākaṅkhamāno saṅgho samūhanatū”ti vuttepi na samūhaniṃsu. Aññadatthu purato viya tassa accayepi rakkhiṃsuyevāti satthu sāsanassa saṅghassa ca mahantabhāvadassanatthampi tathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi āyasmā ānando aññepi vā bhikkhū “katamaṃ pana, bhante, khuddakaṃ, katamaṃ anukhuddaka”nti na pucchiṃsu samūhanajjhāsayasseva abhāvato, teneva ekasikkhāpadampi apariccajitvā sabbesaṃ anuggahetabbabhāvadassanatthaṃ “cattāri pārājikāni ṭhapetvā avasesāni khuddānukhuddakānī”tiādimāhaṃsu. Evañhi vadantehi “khuddānukhuddakā ime nāmā”ti avinicchitattā sabbesaṃ anuggahetabbabhāvo dassito hoti.

441. ‘Should wish to abolish’ means ‘if one wishes, let them abolish’; this is the meaning. But why did the Blessed One not say definitively, ‘Let them abolish,’ and instead establish it with the conditional phrase, ‘should one wish to abolish’? It was because he saw the power of knowledge of Mahākassapa. For the Blessed One saw that even if it were said, ‘Let them abolish,’ Kassapa would not abolish them at the time of the council; therefore, he established it with a condition. If non-abolition was foreseen, and that very thing was desired, then why did the Blessed One say, ‘should one wish to abolish’? It was due to the disposition of certain individuals. For there are some who do not wish to undertake and practice the minor and lesser training rules, and if the Blessed One had not spoken thus, they might become distressed, which would lead to their long-term harm and suffering. But when it was said thus, they would not be distressed, thinking, ‘This is our own fault, since some among us do not wish for abolition.’ Some say, ‘It was spoken thus for the purpose of making the entire dispensation dependent on the Sangha.’ Whatever training rule the Teacher has laid down, the Sakyan monastics receive it with reverence and guard it as their own life. Indeed, even when told, ‘Should the Sangha wish, let them abolish the minor and lesser training rules,’ they did not abolish them. Rather, even after his passing, they continued to guard them as before. Thus, it should be understood that this was also said to show the greatness of both the Teacher’s dispensation and the Sangha. For Venerable Ānanda and the other monks did not ask, ‘Which, Venerable Sir, is minor, and which is lesser?’ due to the very absence of any intention to abolish. Therefore, without abandoning even a single training rule, to show that all should be embraced, they declared, ‘Excluding the four pārājikas, the rest are minor and lesser.’ For by speaking thus, without determining which were minor and which were lesser, they demonstrated that all should be embraced.

442. Atha [V 3.0410] kho āyasmā mahākassapo saṅghaṃ ñāpesīti ettha pana keci vadanti “bhante nāgasena, katamaṃ khuddakaṃ, katamaṃ anukhuddakanti milindaraññā pucchite ‘dukkaṭaṃ mahārāja, khuddakaṃ, dubbhāsitaṃ anukhuddaka’nti (mi. pa. 4.2.1) vuttattā nāgasenatthero khuddānukhuddakaṃ jāni, mahākassapatthero pana taṃ ajānanto ‘suṇātu me āvuso’tiādinā kammavācaṃ sāvesī”ti, na taṃ evaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Nāgasenatthero hi paresaṃ vādapathopacchedanatthaṃ saṅgītikāle dhammasaṅgāhakamahātherehi gahitakoṭṭhāsesu antimakoṭṭhāsameva gahetvā milindarājānaṃ saññāpesi, mahākassapatthero pana ekasikkhāpadampi asamūhanitukāmatāya tathā kammavācaṃ sāvesi.

442. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Sangha. Here, some say: ‘When King Milinda asked, “Venerable Nāgasena, what is minor? What is lesser?” he replied, “Great king, a dukkaṭa is minor, a dubbhāsita is lesser,” as it is said (Miln 4.2.1). Thus, the Elder Nāgasena knew the minor and lesser rules, but the Elder Mahākassapa, not knowing them, announced the formal motion with the words, “Listen to me, friends.”’ This should not be understood in that way. For the Elder Nāgasena, in order to cut off the arguments of others, took only the final category from the classifications compiled by the great elders who collected the Dhamma at the time of the council and explained it to King Milinda. The Elder Mahākassapa, however, announced the formal motion in that manner because he wished not to abolish even a single training rule.

Tattha gihigatānīti gihipaṭisaṃyuttānīti vadanti. Gihīsu gatāni, tehi ñātāni gihigatānīti evaṃ panettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Dhūmakālo etassāti dhūmakālikaṃ citakadhūmavūpasamato paraṃ appavattanato. Appaññattantiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.136; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.7.23) navaṃ adhammikaṃ katikavattaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ vā bandhantā appaññattaṃ paññapenti nāma purāṇasanthatavatthusmiṃ sāvatthiyaṃ bhikkhū viya. Uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ sāsanaṃ dīpentā paññattaṃ samucchindanti nāma vassasataparinibbute bhagavati [M 3.0450] vesālikā vajjiputtakā viya. Khuddānukhuddakā pana āpattiyo sañcicca vītikkamantā yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya na vattanti nāma assajipunabbasukā viya. Navaṃ pana katikavattaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ vā abandhantā, dhammato vinayato sāsanaṃ dīpentā, khuddānukhuddakampi ca sikkhāpadaṃ asamūhanantā appaññattaṃ na paññapenti, paññattaṃ na samucchindanti, yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya vattanti nāma āyasmā upaseno viya āyasmā yaso kākaṇḍakaputto viya ca.

Here, 'gihigatāni' means 'connected with laypeople,' so they say. The meaning here should be understood as 'gone among laypeople, known by them.' The term 'dhūmakālika' means 'having the time of smoke,' because it does not continue after the cessation of smoke from the funeral pyre. Regarding 'Appaññattaṃ' and so forth, those who establish a new, unlawful agreement or training rule are said to prescribe what is not prescribed, like the monks in Sāvatthī concerning an old felt cloth. Those who expound the Dispensation contrary to the Dhamma and Vinaya are said to abolish what is prescribed, like the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī a hundred years after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. But those who intentionally transgress minor and lesser offenses are said not to conduct themselves having undertaken the training rules as prescribed, like Assaji and Punabbasuka. However, those who do not establish a new agreement or training rule, who expound the Dispensation according to the Dhamma and Vinaya, and who do not uproot even a minor and lesser training rule, are said not to prescribe what is not prescribed, not to abolish what is prescribed, and to conduct themselves having undertaken the training rules as prescribed, like the Venerable Upasena and the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta.

443. Bhagavatā oḷārike nimitte kayiramāneti vesāliṃ nissāya cāpāle cetiye viharantena bhagavatā –

443. When a gross sign was being made by the Blessed One dwelling at the Cāpāla Shrine near Vesālī—

“Ramaṇīyā, ānanda, vesālī, ramaṇīyaṃ udenacetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ gotamakacetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ sattambacetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ bahuputtacetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ sārandadacetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ cāpālacetiyaṃ. Yassa kassaci, ānanda, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, so ākaṅkhamāno kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā. Tathāgatassa kho pana, ānanda, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā [V 3.0411] yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, so ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, tathāgato kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā”ti (dī. ni. 2.166) –

"Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī. Delightful is the Udena Shrine, delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine, delightful is the Sattamba Shrine, delightful is the Bahuputta Shrine, delightful is the Sārandada Shrine, delightful is the Cāpāla Shrine. Ānanda, anyone who has developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a basis of, established, become familiar with, and properly undertaken the four bases of power, could remain for an aeon or the remainder of an aeon, if they wished. Ānanda, the Tathāgata has developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a basis of, established, become familiar with, and properly undertaken the four bases of power. If he wished, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an aeon or the remainder of an aeon."

Evaṃ oḷārike nimitte kayiramāne.

Thus, when such a gross sign was being made.

Mārena pariyuṭṭhitacittoti mārena ajjhotthaṭacitto. Māro hi yassa sabbena sabbaṃ dvādasa vipallāsā appahīnā, tassa cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti. Therassa ca cattāro vipallāsā appahīnā, tenassa māro cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāsi. So pana cittapariyuṭṭhānaṃ karonto kiṃ karotīti? Bheravaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vā dasseti, saddārammaṇaṃ vā sāveti, tato sattā taṃ disvā vā sutvā vā satiṃ vissajjetvā vivaṭamukhā honti, tesaṃ mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetvā hadayaṃ maddati, tato visaññāva hutvā tiṭṭhanti[M 3.0451]. Therassa panesa mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetuṃ kiṃ sakkhissati, bheravārammaṇaṃ pana dassesi, taṃ disvā thero nimittobhāsaṃ na paṭivijjhi.

'With his mind assailed by Māra' means his mind was overwhelmed by Māra. For Māra assails the mind of one in whom the twelve distortions are not completely abandoned. The elder had four distortions that were not abandoned, so Māra assailed his mind. But what does Māra do when assailing the mind? He shows a terrifying visible object or makes a terrifying sound audible. Then beings, seeing or hearing it, lose mindfulness and become open-mouthed. He inserts his hand through their mouths and crushes their hearts, leaving them senseless. But how could he insert his hand through the elder's mouth? He showed a terrifying object, and the elder, seeing it, did not penetrate the sign and its import.

Khuddānukhuddakasikkhāpadakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on the minor and lesser training rules is concluded.

Brahmadaṇḍakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Brahmadaṇḍa

445. Ujjavanikāyāti paṭisotagāminiyā. Rajoharaṇanti rajopuñchanī. Na kulavaṃ gamentīti niratthakavināsanaṃ na gamenti. Kucchito lavo kulavo, anayavināsoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Dhammavinayasaṅgītiyā”ti vattabbe saṅgītiyā vinayappadhānattā “vinayasaṅgītiyā”ti vuttaṃ. Vinayappadhānā saṅgīti vinayasaṅgīti. Sesamettha suviññeyyamevāti.

445. 'Ujjavanikāyā' means 'going against the stream'. 'Rajoharaṇa' means 'a duster'. 'Na kulavaṃ gamenti' means 'they do not cause meaningless destruction'. 'Kucchito lavo' is 'kulavo'; it is said to mean misfortune and destruction. When 'Dhammavinayasaṅgītiyā' (the Recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya) should be said, 'vinayasaṅgītiyā' (the Recitation of the Vinaya) is said because the Vinaya was predominant in the Recitation. A Recitation in which the Vinaya is predominant is a Vinaya Recitation. The rest here is easily understood.

Pañcasatikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Khandhaka of the Five Hundred is concluded.

12. Sattasatikakkhandhakaṃ

12. The Khandhaka of the Seven Hundred

Dasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Topics

446. Sattasatikakkhandhake [M 3.0452][V 3.0412] nikkhittamaṇisuvaṇṇāti rūpiyasikkhāpadeneva paṭikkhittamaṇisuvaṇṇā. Tattha maṇiggahaṇena sabbaṃ dukkaṭavatthu, suvaṇṇaggahaṇena sabbaṃ pācittiyavatthu gahitaṃ hoti. Bhikkhaggenāti bhikkhugaṇanāya.

446. In the Khandhaka of the Seven Hundred, 'nikkhittamaṇisuvaṇṇā' refers to jewels and gold prohibited by the training rule concerning silver. There, by the mention of 'jewels', every matter for a dukkaṭa offense is included; and by the mention of 'gold', every matter for a pācittiya offense is included. 'Bhikkhaggena' means by the count of monks.

447. Upakkilesāti virocituṃ adatvā upakkiliṭṭhabhāvakaraṇena upakkilesā. Mahikāti himaṃ. Dhūmo ca rajo ca dhūmarajo. Ettha purimā tayo asampattaupakkilesā, rāhu pana sampattaupakkilesavasena kathitoti veditabbo. Samaṇabrāhmaṇā na tapanti na bhāsanti na virocantīti guṇapatāpena na tapanti guṇobhāsena na bhāsanti guṇavirocanena na virocanti. Surāmerayapānā appaṭiviratāti pañcavidhāya surāya catubbidhassa ca merayassa pānato aviratā.

447. 'Upakkilesā' (defilements) are so called because, by causing a defiled state, they do not allow one to shine forth. 'Mahikā' means frost. 'Dhūmo ca rajo ca' (smoke and dust) is 'dhūmarajo'. Here, the first three are defilements of non-attainment, but Rāhu should be understood as spoken of in terms of a defilement of attainment. 'Ascetics and brahmins do not burn, do not shine, and do not radiate' means they do not burn with the splendor of virtues, do not shine with the luster of virtues, and do not radiate with the radiance of virtues. 'Surāmerayapānā appaṭiviratā' means not refraining from drinking the five kinds of surā and the four kinds of meraya.

Avijjānivuṭāti avijjāya nivāritā pihitā. Piyarūpābhinandinoti piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ abhinandamānā tussamānā. Sādiyantīti gaṇhanti. Aviddasūti andhabālā. Sarajāti sakilesarajā. Magāti migasadisā. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ visaye bhave vā netīti netti, taṇhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tāya saha vattantīti sanettikā.

'Avijjānivuṭā' means hindered and covered by ignorance. 'Piyarūpābhinandino' means delighting in and being pleased with pleasing and agreeable forms. 'Sādiyanti' means they accept. 'Aviddasū' means blind fools. 'Sarajā' means with the dust of defilements. 'Magā' means like deer. 'Because it leads to this or that sphere or existence, it is called netti'—this is a designation for craving. 'Because they proceed together with it, they are called sanettikā'.

448. Taṃ parisaṃ etadavocāti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.4.362) tassa kira evaṃ ahosi “kulaputtā pabbajantā puttadārañceva jātarūparajatañca pahāyeva pabbajanti, na ca sakkā yaṃ pahāya pabbajitā taṃ etehi gāhetu”nti nayaggāhe ṭhatvā etaṃ “mā ayyā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Ekaṃsenetanti etaṃ pañcakāmaguṇakappanaṃ “assamaṇadhammo asakyaputtiyadhammo”ti ekaṃsena dhāreyyāsi.

448. 'He said this to that assembly': It is said that this occurred to him: 'When sons of good family go forth, they go forth having renounced wives, children, gold, and silver. And it is not possible for them to take up what they have renounced to go forth.' Standing firm in this line of reasoning, he spoke these words beginning with 'Do not, sirs'. 'Ekaṃsena' means you should definitively regard this allowance for the five strands of sensual pleasure as 'not the conduct of an ascetic, not the conduct of a Sakyan son'.

Tiṇanti [V 3.0413] senāsanacchadanatiṇaṃ. Pariyesitabbanti tiṇacchadane vā iṭṭhakacchadane vā gehe palujjante yehi taṃ kāritaṃ, tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā [M 3.0453] “tumhehi kāritaṃ senāsanaṃ ovassati, na sakkā tattha vasitu”nti ācikkhitabbaṃ. Manussā sakkontā karissanti, asakkontā “tumhe vaḍḍhakī gahetvā kārāpetha, mayaṃ te saññāpessāmā”ti vakkhanti. Evaṃ vutte kāretvā tesaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ, manussā vaḍḍhakīnaṃ dātabbaṃ dassanti. Sace āvāsasāmikā natthi, aññesampi bhikkhācāravattena ārocetvā kāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Imaṃ sandhāya “pariyesitabba”nti vuttaṃ.

'Tiṇa' means grass for roofing a dwelling. 'Pariyesitabbaṃ' means that if a house with a grass roof or a tile roof is falling into disrepair, one should go to those who had it built and inform them: 'The dwelling you had built is leaking; it is not possible to live there.' If the people are able, they will repair it; if not, they may say, 'You get carpenters and have it repaired; we will satisfy them.' When this has been said, one should have it repaired and then inform them, and the people will give the carpenters what is to be given. If there are no owners of the residence, it is permissible to have it repaired by informing others also, in accordance with the practice of the alms-round. It is with reference to this that 'pariyesitabbaṃ' is stated.

Dārūti senāsane gopānasiādīsu palujjamānesu tadatthāya dāru pariyesitabbaṃ. Sakaṭanti gihivikaṭaṃ vā tāvakālikaṃ vā katvā sakaṭaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Na kevalañca sakaṭameva, aññampi vāsipharasukudālādiupakaraṇaṃ evaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭati. Purisoti hatthakammavasena puriso pariyesitabbo. Yaṃ kañci hi purisaṃ “hatthakammaṃ āvuso dassasī”ti vatvā “dassāmi bhante”ti vutte “imasmiṃ idañcidañca karohī”ti yaṃ icchati, taṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Na tvevāhaṃ gāmaṇi kenaci pariyāyenāti jātarūparajataṃ panāhaṃ kenacipi kāraṇena pariyesitabbanti na vadāmi.

'Dāru' means that when the wooden parts of a dwelling, such as rafters and so on, are decaying, wood should be sought for that purpose. 'Sakaṭa' means a cart should be sought, either one obtained from a householder or one made for temporary use. Not only a cart, but other implements such as axes, adzes, and spades may also be sought in this way. 'Purisa' means a man should be sought for manual labor. For if any man, when asked, 'Friend, will you offer manual labor?', replies, 'I will, venerable sir,' it is permissible to have him do whatever one wishes, saying, 'Do this and that here.' The phrase 'Na tvevāhaṃ gāmaṇi kenaci pariyāyena' means: I do not say that gold and silver should be sought for any reason whatsoever.

449. Pāpakaṃ katanti asundaraṃ kataṃ.

449. 'Pāpakaṃ kataṃ' means 'unbeautifully done'.

450. Ahogaṅgoti tassa pabbatassa nāmaṃ.

450. 'Ahogaṅga' is the name of that peak.

451. Paṭikacceva gaccheyyanti yattha taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametuṃ bhikkhū sannipatanti, tattha paṭhamameva gaccheyyaṃ. Sambhāvesunti pāpuṇiṃsu.

451. 'Paṭikacceva gaccheyyanti' means one should go first to wherever the bhikkhus assemble to settle that legal issue. 'Sambhāvesuṃ' means they arrived.

452. Aloṇakaṃ bhavissatīti aloṇakaṃ bhattaṃ vā byañjanaṃ vā bhavissati. Āsutāti sabbasambhārasajjitā. “Asuttā”ti vā pāṭho.

452. 'Aloṇakaṃ bhavissatīti' means the food or curry will be unsalted. 'Āsutā' means prepared with all ingredients. Alternatively, the reading is 'asuttā'.

453. Ujjaviṃsūti nāvaṃ āruyha paṭisotena gacchiṃsu. Pācīnakāti pācīnadesavāsino.

453. 'Ujjaviṃsu' means they boarded a boat and went against the current. 'Pācīnakā' means inhabitants of the eastern country.

454. Nanu tvaṃ āvuso vuḍḍho vīsativassosīti nanu tvaṃ āvuso vīsativasso, na nissayapaṭibaddho[V 3.0414], kasmā taṃ thero paṇāmetīti dīpenti. Garunissayaṃ gaṇhāmāti kiñcāpi mayaṃ mahallakā, etaṃ pana theraṃ garuṃ katvā vasissāmāti adhippāyo.

454. 'Nanu tvaṃ āvuso vuḍḍho vīsativassosī'ti means they clarify thus: 'Friend, are you not a senior of twenty years standing and not bound by dependence? Why does the elder dismiss you?' 'Garunissayaṃ gaṇhāmā'ti means the intention is: 'Although we are old, we will dwell having taken this elder as our respected teacher.'

455. Mettāya [M 3.0454] rūpāvacarasamādhimattabhāvato “kullakavihārenā”ti vuttaṃ, khuddakena vihārenāti attho, khuddakatā cassa agambhīrabhāvatoti āha “uttānavihārenā”ti. Suññatāvihārenāti suññatāmukhena adhigataphalasamāpattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

455. Because loving-kindness is merely a form-sphere concentration, it is called 'a small dwelling' (kullakavihārena), meaning a minor dwelling. And its smallness is due to its lack of profundity; hence it is called 'a shallow dwelling' (uttānavihārena). 'Dwelling in emptiness' (suññatāvihārena) is said with reference to the attainment of fruition reached through the gateway of emptiness.

457. Suttavibhaṅgeti padabhājanīye. Tena saddhinti purepaṭiggahitaloṇena saddhiṃ. Na hi ettha yāvajīvikaṃ tadahupaṭiggahitanti “kappati siṅgiloṇakappo”ti ettha vuttasiṅgiloṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi pure paṭiggahetvā siṅgena parihaṭaṃ na tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ. Yāvakālikameva tadahupaṭiggahitanti siṅgiloṇena missetvā bhuñjitabbaṃ aloṇāmisaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Uposathasaṃyutteti uposathapaṭisaṃyutte, uposathakkhandhaketi vuttaṃ hoti. Atisaraṇaṃ atisāro, atikkamo. Vinayassa atisāro vinayātisāro. Taṃ pamāṇaṃ karontassāti dasāya saddhiṃ nisīdane yaṃ pamāṇaṃ vuttaṃ, dasāya vinā taṃ pamāṇaṃ karontassa. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

457. 'In the Suttavibhaṅga' means in the Padabhājanīya. 'With that' means with salt received beforehand. For here, what is for life-long use is not received on that same day; this is said with reference to the horn-salt mentioned where it says, 'The horn-salt allowance is permissible.' For that salt, having been received beforehand and carried in a horn, is not received on that same day. Only what is for temporary use is received on that same day; this is said with reference to unsalted food to be eaten mixed with horn-salt. 'In the Uposatha-saṃyutta' means connected with the Uposatha; that is to say, in the Uposatha Khandhaka. Atisaraṇa is transgression, overstepping. A transgression of the Vinaya is vinayātisāro. 'Of one who makes that the measure' means of one who, without the ten, makes that the measure which was stated for sitting together with ten. The rest here is easily understood.

Sattasatikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of the Seven Hundred is concluded.

Dvivaggasaṅgahāti cūḷavaggamahāvaggasaṅkhātehi dvīhi vaggehi saṅgahitā. Dvāvīsatipabhedanāti mahāvagge dasa, cūḷavagge dvādasāti evaṃ dvāvīsatippabhedā. Sāsaneti satthusāsane. Ye khandhakā vuttāti yojetabbaṃ.

'Collected in two groups' means collected in the two groups designated as the Cūḷavagga and the Mahāvagga. 'Having twenty-two divisions' means there are twenty-two divisions thus: ten in the Mahāvagga and twelve in the Cūḷavagga. 'In the Dispensation' means in the Teacher's Dispensation. It should be connected with 'the khandhakas that are mentioned'.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya sāratthadīpaniyaṃ

Thus in the Sāratthadīpanī, the subcommentary on the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya,

Cūḷavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷavagga is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Parivāra-ṭīkā

The Parivāra Subcommentary

Soḷasamahāvāro

The Sixteen Great Sections

Paññattivāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Designations

Visuddhaparivārassāti [M 3.0455][V 3.0415] sabbaso parisuddhakhīṇāsavaparivārassa. Dhammakkhandhasarīrassāti sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanasaṅkhātadhammakkhandhasarīrassa sāsaneti sambandho. Tassāti “parivāro”ti yo saṅgahaṃ āruḷho, tassa. Pubbāgataṃ nayanti pubbe āgataṃ vinicchayaṃ.

'Of utterly pure retinue' means of one whose retinue is entirely pure, with taints destroyed. 'With the body of the Dhamma aggregates' refers to the body of the Dhamma aggregates, which consists of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the connection is with 'in the Dispensation.' 'Of that' means of that which is included under the term 'Parivāra.' 'The method come before' means the judgment that has come before.

1. Pakatatthapaṭiniddeso ta-saddoti tassa “bhagavatā”tiādīhi padehi samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttatthassa yāya vinayapaññattiyā bhagavā pakato adhikato supākaṭo ca, taṃ vinayapaññattiṃ [V 3.0416] saddhiṃ yācanāya atthabhāvena dassento “yo so…pe… vinayapaññattiṃ paññapesī”ti āha. Tattha vinayapaññattinti vinayabhūtaṃ paññattiṃ.

1. The word 'ta' (that) is an explanation of the established meaning. Showing that the disciplinary rule—by which the Blessed One is established, intended, and well-revealed, and which has the meaning stated in apposition with the words 'by the Blessed One', etc.—has a purpose, together with the request, he said: 'That which… he laid down the disciplinary rule.' Herein, 'disciplinary rule' means the rule that constitutes the discipline.

“Jānatā passatā”ti imesaṃ padānaṃ vinayassa adhikatattā tattha vuttanayena tāva atthaṃ yojetvā idāni suttantanayena dassento satipi ñāṇadassana-saddānaṃ paññāvevacanabhāve tena tena visesena tesaṃ visayavisesapavattidassanatthaṃ vijjattayavasena abhiññānāvaraṇañāṇavasena sabbaññutaññāṇamaṃsacakkhuvasena paṭivedhadesanāñāṇavasena ca atthaṃ yojetvā dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha pubbenivāsādīhīti pubbenivāsāsavakkhayañāṇehi. Paṭivedhapaññāyāti ariyamaggapaññāya. Desanāpaññāya passatāti desetabbadhammānaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ bodhaneyyapuggalānañca āsayānusayacaritādhimuttiādibhedaṃ dhammaṃ desanāpaññāya yāthāvato passatā. Arahatāti arīnaṃ, arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnañca arahattā arahatā. Sammāsambuddhenāti sammā sāmañca saccānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhena. Atha vā antarāyikadhamme [M 3.0456] jānatā, niyyānikadhamme passatā, kilesārīnaṃ hatattā arahatā, sammā sāmaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhenāti evaṃ catuvesārajjavasenapettha yojanā veditabbā.

Regarding 'knowing and seeing'—since the Vinaya is the main topic, having first explained their meaning in the way stated there, now presenting them according to the Sutta method, although the words 'knowledge' and 'vision' are synonyms for wisdom, in order to show the functioning of their specific domains with various distinctions, he connects and shows the meaning in terms of the threefold knowledge, the knowledge of supernormal powers, the unobstructed knowledge, omniscience, the physical eye, and the knowledges of penetration and teaching, saying 'Furthermore...' and so on. Here, 'with past lives, etc.' refers to the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. 'With the wisdom of penetration' means with the wisdom of the noble path. 'Seeing with the wisdom of teaching' means seeing accurately with the wisdom of teaching the things to be taught, the manner in which they should be taught, and the various dispositions, latent tendencies, characters, inclinations, etc., of the individuals to be taught. 'Arahant'—because of having destroyed the enemies (the defilements) and the spokes (of the wheel of existence), and because of worthiness for requisites. 'Perfectly Enlightened'—because of having awakened to the truths correctly and by himself. Alternatively: 'knowing' the obstructive qualities, 'seeing' the liberating qualities; 'Arahant' because of having destroyed the enemies, the defilements; 'Perfectly Enlightened' because of having awakened to all phenomena correctly and by himself. Thus, the application here should also be understood in terms of the four assurances.

Apica ṭhānāṭṭhānādivibhāgaṃ jānatā, yathākammūpage satte passatā, savāsanaāsavānaṃ chinnattā arahatā, abhiññeyyādibhede dhamme abhiññeyyādito aviparītāvabodhato sammāsambuddhena. Atha vā tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇatāya jānatā, kāyakammādivasena tiṇṇampi kammānaṃ ñāṇānuparivattito sammā kāritāya passatā, davādīnaṃ abhāvasādhikāya pahānasampadāya arahatā, chandādīnaṃ ahānihetubhūtāya akkhayapaṭibhānasādhikāya sabbaññutāya sammāsambuddhenāti evaṃ dasabalaaṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhammavasenapi yojanā kātabbā.

Moreover, by one who knows the distinctions of what is possible and impossible, by one who sees beings according to their kamma, by an Arahant through the destruction of the taints along with their latent tendencies, and by the Perfectly Enlightened One who comprehends phenomena that should be fully known and other such distinctions without error. Or alternatively, by one who knows without obstruction in the three times, by one who sees rightly, as the three kinds of kamma (bodily, verbal, and mental) are rightly performed in accordance with knowledge, by an Arahant through the perfection of abandoning defilements such as craving and so on, substantiated by the absence of afflictions, and by the Perfectly Enlightened One through omniscience substantiated by inexhaustible eloquence, which has desire and other factors as the cause of its non-decline. In this way, the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other Buddha-qualities should be applied.

2. Pucchāvissajjaneti pucchāya vissajjane. Etthāti etasmiṃ pucchāvissajjane. Majjhimadeseyeva paññattīti tasmiṃyeva dese yathāvuttavatthuvītikkame āpattisambhavato. Vinītakathāti vinītavatthukathā, ayameva vā pāṭho.

2. 'Question and answer' means answering a question. 'Here' means in this question and answer. The rule is established specifically in the Middle Country, since offenses arise there due to transgression of the stated matter. 'Settled discussion' means discussion of settled matters, or this may also be the reading.

Kāyena pana āpattiṃ āpajjatīti pubbabhāge sevanacittaṃ aṅgaṃ katvā kāyadvārasaṅkhātaviññattiṃ janayitvā pavattacittuppādasaṅkhātaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Kiñcāpi hi cittena samuṭṭhāpitā viññatti, tathāpi cittena adhippetassa atthassa kāyaviññattiyā sādhitattā [V 3.0417] “kāyadvārena āpattiṃ āpajjatī”ti vuccati. Imamatthaṃ sandhāyāti āpannāya āpattiyā anāpattibhāvāpādanassa asakkuṇeyyatāsaṅkhātamatthaṃ sandhāya, na bhaṇḍanādivūpasamaṃ.

"He commits an offense by body"—having made the intention to engage beforehand a factor, he generates the intimation known as the body-door, and thus commits the offense designated as the occurrence of a thought-process. Although the intimation is originated by the mind, because the intended purpose is accomplished through the bodily intimation, it is said, "he commits an offense by the body-door." This refers to the impossibility of reversing an already committed offense, not the cessation of quarrels and so on.

3. Porāṇakehi mahātherehīti sīhaḷadīpavāsīhi mahātherehi. Ṭhapitāti potthakasaṅgahārohanakāle ṭhapitā. Catutthasaṅgītisadisā hi potthakārohasaṅgīti. Ubhatovibhaṅge dvattiṃsa vārā suviññeyyāva.

3. "By the ancient great elders"—the great elders residing in Sri Lanka. "Established"—placed at the time of the compilation of texts. Indeed, the compilation of texts was a council similar to the Fourth Council. The thirty-two sections in the two Vibhaṅgas are easily understood.

Samuṭṭhānasīsavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Chapter on Origins

257. Samuṭṭhānakathāya [M 3.0457][V 3.0418] pana karuṇāsītalabhāvena candasadisattā “buddhacande”ti vuttaṃ, kilesatimirapahānato “buddhādicce”ti vuttaṃ. Piṭake tīṇi desayīti yasmā te desayanti, tasmā aṅgirasopi piṭakāni tīṇi desayi. Tāni katamānīti āha “suttanta”ntiādi. Mahāguṇanti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Evaṃ nīyati saddhammo, vinayo yadi tiṭṭhatīti yadi vinayapariyatti anantarahitā tiṭṭhati pavattati, evaṃ sati paṭipattipaṭivedhasaddhammo nīyati pavattati. Vinayapariyatti pana kathaṃ tiṭṭhatīti āha “ubhatocā”tiādi. Parivārena ganthitā tiṭṭhantīti yojetabbaṃ. Tasseva parivārassāti tasmiṃyeva parivāre.

257. In the discussion of origins, because of the coolness of compassion, being like the moon, it is called “the Buddha-moon”; because of dispelling the darkness of defilements, it is called “the Buddha-sun.” Since they teach the three Piṭakas, therefore Aṅgirasa also taught the three Piṭakas. What are those? He said, “the discourses,” etc. “Of great benefit”—of great advantage. Thus the True Dhamma is led on. If the Vinaya remains—that is, if the Vinaya teaching remains uninterrupted and continues—then the True Dhamma of practice and penetration is led on and continues. But how does the Vinaya teaching remain? He said, “by both,” etc. It should be connected as “they remain, woven with the Parivāra.” “Of that very Parivāra”—in that very Parivāra.

Niyatakatanti kataniyataṃ, niyamitanti attho. Aññehi saddhinti sesasikkhāpadehi saddhiṃ. Asambhinnasamuṭṭhānānīti asaṅkarasamuṭṭhānāni.

‘Fixed’ means determined, regulated; this is the meaning. ‘Together with others’ means along with the remaining training rules. ‘With unconfused origins’ means with unmingled origins.

Tasmā sikkheti yasmā vinaye sati saddhammo tiṭṭhati, vinayo ca parivārena ganthito tiṭṭhati, parivāre ca samuṭṭhānādīni dissanti, tasmā sikkheyya parivāraṃ, uggaṇheyyāti attho.

Therefore, one should train. Since when the Vinaya exists, the True Dhamma endures; and the Vinaya, bound together by the Parivāra, endures; and in the Parivāra, the origins and so on are seen. Therefore, one should train in the Parivāra, meaning one should learn it.

Ādimhi tāva purimanayeti “channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ katihi samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhātīti ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhāti, kāyato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhātī”tiādinā (pari. 187) paññattivāre sakiṃ āgatanayaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

First, regarding the previous method—this was said referring to the method that occurred once in the section on designations (Parivāra 187), beginning with: “From how many of the six origins of offenses does it arise? It arises from one origin; it arises from body and from mind.”

258. Nānubandhe pavattininti “yā pana bhikkhunī vuṭṭhāpitaṃ pavattiniṃ dve vassāni nānubandheyyā”ti (pāci. 1111) vuttasikkhāpadaṃ.

258. ‘Not following a probationer’ refers to the training rule stated as: “Whatever bhikkhunī should not attend on a reinstated probationer for two years…” (Pācittiya 1111).

270. Akatanti aññehi amissīkataṃ, niyatasamuṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti.

270. ‘Unmade’ means unmixed with others; it is said to have a fixed origin.

Antarapeyyālaṃ

Intermediate Ellipsis

Katipucchāvāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section of Questions on 'How Many?'

271. Veraṃ [M 3.0458][V 3.0419] maṇatīti rāgādiveraṃ maṇati vināseti. Etāyāti viratiyā. Niyyānanti maggaṃ. Kāyapāgabbiyanti kāyapāgabbiyavasena pavattaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ.

271. ‘It destroys enmity’ means it destroys, it eliminates the enmity of lust and so forth. ‘By this’ means by abstinence. ‘Leading out’ means the path. ‘Bodily impudence’ means bodily misconduct occurring by way of bodily impudence.

274. Sāraṇīyāti saritabbayuttā anussaraṇārahā addhāne atikkantepi na sammussitabbā. Mijjati siniyhati etāyāti mettā, mittabhāvo. Mettā etassa atthīti mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ, taṃ pana yasmā mettāsahagatacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “mettacittena kataṃ kāyakamma”nti. Āvīti pakāsaṃ. Pakāsabhāvo cettha yaṃ uddissa taṃ kāyakammaṃ karīyati, tassa sammukhabhāvatoti āha “sammukhā”ti. Rahoti apakāsaṃ. Apakāsatā ca yaṃ uddissa taṃ kammaṃ karīyati, tassa apaccakkhabhāvatoti āha “parammukhā”ti. Ubhayehīti navakehi therehi ca. Piyaṃ piyāyitabbaṃ karotīti piyakaraṇo. Garuṃ garuṭṭhāniyaṃ karotīti garukaraṇo. Saṅgahāyāti saṅgahavatthuvisesabhāvato sabrahmacārīnaṃ saṅgahaṇatthāya. Avivādāyāti saṅgahavatthubhāvato eva na vivādāya. Sati ca avivādahetubhūtasaṅgahakatte tesaṃ vasena sabrahmacārīnaṃ samaggabhāvo bhedābhāvo siddhoyevāti āha “samaggabhāvāyā”tiādi.

274. ‘Worthy of recollection’ means it is proper to be recollected, worthy of being remembered, and should not be forgotten even after a long time has passed. ‘One is affectionate through this’ is mettā, loving-kindness; the state of friendship. ‘Loving-kindness is present in this,’ thus it is a ‘bodily action with loving-kindness’; and since it arises from a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, therefore it is said, “a bodily action done with a mind of loving-kindness.” ‘Openly’ means manifestly. The manifestation here means the direct presence of the one for whom that bodily action is done; therefore, he said “face to face.” ‘Secretly’ means unmanifestly. The unmanifestation refers to the absence of direct perception of the one for whom that action is done; therefore, he said “behind one’s back.” ‘By both’ means by new monastics and by elders. ‘It makes one dear’ is that which makes one lovable. ‘It makes one respected’ is that which makes one worthy of respect. ‘For the sake of fellowship’ means for the purpose of gathering together the fellow practitioners, because it is a special basis of fellowship. ‘Not for the sake of quarreling’ means that precisely because it is a basis of fellowship, it is not for dispute. And when there is fellowship, which is the cause of non-dispute, the harmony—the absence of division—among fellow practitioners is certainly established through these things; therefore, he said, “for the sake of harmony,” etc.

Paggayha vacananti kevalaṃ “devo”ti avatvā “devatthero”ti guṇehi thirabhāvajotanaṃ paggaṇhitvā uccaṃ katvā vacanaṃ. Mamattabodhanavacanaṃ mamāyanavacanaṃ. Ekantatirokkhassa manokammassa sammukhatā nāma viññattisamuṭṭhāpanavaseneva hoti, tañca kho loke kāyakammanti pākaṭaṃ paññātaṃ hatthavikārādiṃ anāmasitvāyeva dassento “nayanāni ummīletvā”tiādimāha. Kāmañcettha mettāsinehasiniddhānaṃ nayanānaṃ ummīlanā pasannena mukhena olokanañca mettaṃ kāyakammameva, yassa pana cittassa vasena nayanānaṃ mettāsinehasiniddhatā mukhassa ca pasannatā, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāmā”ti.

‘Speaking with emphasis’ means not merely saying “deva” but saying “venerable deva,” thereby highlighting the firmness of qualities, taking it up and making it high, i.e., speaking. ‘Words indicating possessiveness’ are words expressing “mine.” The face-to-face nature of a completely concealed mental action occurs only by way of originating an intimation. And to show that this is publicly known in the world as a bodily action—without even touching upon gestures of the hand and so on—he said, “opening the eyes,” etc. Although here, the opening of eyes tender with loving-kindness and affection, and looking with a serene face, are indeed bodily actions of loving-kindness, it is in reference to the mind on whose account the eyes are tender with loving-kindness and affection and the face is serene, that it is said, “loving-kindness is a mental action.”

Imāni [M 3.0459][V 3.0420] (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.492; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.6.11) ca mettakāyakammādīni pāḷiyaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vasena āgatāni gihīsupi labbhantiyeva. Bhikkhūnañhi mettacittena ācariyupajjhāyavattādiābhisamācārikadhammapūraṇaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Sabbañca anavajjakāyakammaṃ ābhisamācārikakammantogadhamevāti veditabbaṃ. Gihīnaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya bodhivandanatthāya saṅghanimantanatthāya gamanaṃ, gāmaṃ vā piṇḍāya paviṭṭhe bhikkhū disvā paccuggamanaṃ, pattapaṭiggahaṇaṃ, āsanapaññāpanaṃ, anugamananti evamādikaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Bhikkhūnaṃ mettacittena ācārapaññattisikkhāpana kammaṭṭhānakathana dhammadesanā paripucchana aṭṭhakathākathanavasena pavattiyamānaṃ tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ “cetiyavandanatthāya gacchāma, bodhivandanatthāya gacchāma, dhammassavanaṃ karissāma, dīpamālāpupphapūjaṃ karissāma, tīṇi sucaritāni samādāya vattissāma, salākabhattādīni dassāma, vassāvāsikaṃ dassāma, ajja saṅghassa cattāro paccaye dassāma, saṅghaṃ nimantetvā khādanīyādīni saṃvidahatha, āsanāni paññapetha, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetha, saṅghaṃ paccuggantvā ānetha, paññattāsane nisīdāpetha, chandajātā ussāhajātā veyyāvaccaṃ karothā”tiādikathanakāle mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Bhikkhūnaṃ pātova uṭṭhāya sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīni ca katvā vivittāsane nisīditvā “imasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjā”ti cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ “ayyā sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjā”ti cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma.

These acts of loving-kindness, such as bodily acts of loving-kindness, are found in the Pāli texts in relation to monks but are also found among laypeople. For monks, the fulfilling of the duties of higher conduct, such as those toward teachers and preceptors, with a mind of loving-kindness, is called a bodily act of loving-kindness. And all blameless bodily actions should be understood as included within the duties of higher conduct. For laypeople, going to pay homage at a shrine, to venerate the Bodhi tree, or to invite the Saṅgha; seeing monks who have entered the village for alms and going to greet them, receiving their bowls, preparing seats, and accompanying them—such actions are called bodily acts of loving-kindness. For monks, the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's word, when it is being used with a mind of loving-kindness for teaching the rules of conduct, instructing in meditation subjects, giving Dhamma talks, asking questions, and explaining the commentaries, is called a verbal act of loving-kindness. For laypeople, at the time of saying such things as, “Let us go to pay homage at the shrine, let us go to venerate the Bodhi tree, we will listen to the Dhamma, we will offer lamps, garlands, and flowers, we will undertake and practice the threefold good conduct, we will give ticket-food and so forth, we will offer the rains-residence dwelling, today we will offer the four requisites to the Saṅgha; having invited the Saṅgha, prepare food and other items, set out seats, provide drinking water, go to greet the Saṅgha and escort them in, seat them in the prepared seats, perform services with willingness and enthusiasm”—this is called a verbal act of loving-kindness. For monks, rising early in the morning, attending to their bodies, performing duties like sweeping the shrine courtyard and so forth, and then sitting in a secluded place while thinking, “May the monks in this monastery be happy, free from enmity and affliction”—this is called a mental act of loving-kindness. For laypeople, thinking, “May the venerable ones be happy, free from enmity and affliction”—this is called a mental act of loving-kindness.

Lābhāti cīvarādayo laddhapaccayā. Dhammikāti kuhanādibhedaṃ micchājīvaṃ vajjetvā dhammena samena bhikkhācariyavattena uppannā. Antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampīti pacchimakoṭiyā patte pariyāpannaṃ pattassa antogataṃ dvattikaṭacchubhikkhāmattampi. Deyyaṃ dakkhiṇeyyañca appaṭivibhattaṃ katvā bhuñjatīti appaṭivibhattabhogī. Ettha hi dve paṭivibhattāni nāma āmisapaṭivibhattaṃ puggalapaṭivibhattañca. Tattha “ettakaṃ dassāmi, ettakaṃ na dassāmī”ti evaṃ cittena vibhajanaṃ āmisapaṭivibhattaṃ nāma. “Asukassa dassāmi, asukassa na dassāmī”ti evaṃ cittena vibhajanaṃ pana puggalapaṭivibhattaṃ nāma. Tadubhayampi akatvā yo appaṭivibhattaṃ bhuñjati, ayaṃ appaṭivibhattabhogī nāma. Tenāha “neva āmisaṃ paṭivibhajitvā bhuñjatī”tiādi. Adātumpīti pi-saddena [M 3.0460] dātumpi vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Dānañhi nāma na kassaci nivāritaṃ, tena dussīlassapi atthikassa sati sambhave dātabbaṃ, tañca kho karuṇāyanavasena, na vattapūraṇavasena. Sāraṇīyadhammapūrakassa appaṭivibhattabhogitāya “sabbesaṃ dātabbamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Gilānādīnaṃ pana odissakaṃ katvā dānaṃ appaṭivibhāgapakkhikaṃ “asukassa [V 3.0421] na dassāmī”ti paṭikkhepassa abhāvato. Byatirekappadhāno hi paṭivibhāgo. Tenāha “gilānagilānupaṭṭhāka…pe… viceyya dātumpi vaṭṭatī”ti.

'Gains' means obtained requisites such as robes. 'Lawfully' means arisen through the proper and fair practice of going for alms, having avoided wrong livelihood such as deceit. 'Even the smallest amount, down to what fits in a bowl' means the final limit, what is contained within the bowl, even just two or three spoonfuls of alms-food. One who partakes without dividing is so called because they partake of what is to be given and is worthy of an offering without dividing it. Here, there are two kinds of division: division of material things and division of persons. Therein, dividing with the thought, 'I will give this much, I will not give that much,' is called division of material things. But dividing with the thought, 'I will give to this person, I will not give to that person,' is called division of persons. One who partakes without making either of these two divisions is called 'one who partakes without dividing.' Hence it is said, 'He partakes without dividing the material things,' and so on. For giving is not forbidden to anyone. Therefore, one should give even to an immoral person if they are in need and it is possible; and this should be done out of compassion, not as a way of fulfilling a duty. For one who fulfills the principles of amiability, because of their partaking without dividing, it is said, 'One should give to all.' However, giving specifically to the sick, their attendants, and so on, falls on the side of non-division, because there is no rejection such as, 'I will not give to so-and-so.' For division is primarily characterized by exclusion. Hence it is said, 'To the sick, to those attending the sick... it is proper to give after due consideration.'

Sādhāraṇabhogīti ettha sādhāraṇabhogino idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ – yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ labhati, taṃ taṃ neva lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanamukhena gihīnaṃ deti attano ājīvasuddhiṃ rakkhamāno, na attanāva paribhuñjati “mayhaṃ asādhāraṇabhogitā mā hotū”ti. Taṃ paṭiggaṇhanto ca “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotū”ti gahetvā ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ saṅghasantakaṃ viya passati. Iminā ca tassa lābhassa tīsupi kālesu sādhāraṇato ṭhapanaṃ dassitaṃ. “Taṃ paṭiggaṇhanto ca saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotū”ti iminā paṭiggahaṇakālo dassito, “gahetvā…pe… passatī”ti iminā paṭiggahitakālo. Tadubhayaṃ pana tādisena pubbabhāgena vinā na hotīti atthasiddho purimakālo. Tayidampi paṭiggahaṇato pubbevassa hoti “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotūti paṭiggahessāmī”ti, paṭiggaṇhantassa hoti “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotūti paṭiggaṇhāmī”ti, paṭiggahetvā hoti “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotūti paṭiggahitaṃ mayā”ti evaṃ tilakkhaṇasampannaṃ katvā laddhalābhaṃ osānalakkhaṇaṃ avikopetvā paribhuñjanto sādhāraṇabhogī appaṭivibhattabhogī ca hoti.

Regarding 'one who partakes in common': here, the characteristic of one who partakes in common is this: whatever excellent thing they obtain, they neither give it to householders by way of desiring to conquer gain with gain, while protecting the purity of their livelihood, nor do they partake of it by themselves, thinking, 'May I not be one who partakes exclusively.' And when receiving it, having taken it with the thought, 'May this be common to the Saṅgha,' they strike the bell and regard what is to be consumed as if it were the property of the Saṅgha. By this is shown the establishing of that gain as common in all three times. By the phrase, 'And when receiving it, “May this be common to the Saṅgha,”' the time of receiving is shown. By the phrase, 'having taken it... they regard it,' the time after receiving is shown. But since these two do not occur without such a preliminary part, the prior time is established by implication. This also occurs for one before receiving: 'I will receive it with the thought, “May this be common to the Saṅgha.”' It occurs for one while receiving: 'I am receiving it with the thought, “May this be common to the Saṅgha.”' And having received it, it occurs: 'It has been received by me with the thought, “May this be common to the Saṅgha.”' Thus, one who partakes of a received gain after endowing it with these three characteristics, without violating its characteristic of having been relinquished, is one who partakes in common and one who partakes without dividing.

Imaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.492; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.6.11) pana sāraṇīyadhammaṃ ko pūreti, ko na pūreti? Dussīlo tāva na pūreti. Na hi tassa santakaṃ sīlavanto gaṇhanti. Parisuddhasīlo pana vattaṃ akhaṇḍento pūreti. Tatridaṃ vattaṃ – yo odissakaṃ katvā mātu vā pitu vā ācariyupajjhāyādīnaṃ vā deti, so dātabbaṃ detu, sāraṇīyadhammo panassa na hoti, palibodhajagganaṃ nāma hoti. Sāraṇīyadhammo hi muttapalibodhasseva vaṭṭati. Tena pana [M 3.0461] odissakaṃ dentena gilānagilānupaṭṭhākaāgantukagamikānañceva navapabbajitassa ca saṅghāṭipattaggahaṇaṃ ajānantassa dātabbaṃ. Etesaṃ datvā avasesaṃ therāsanato paṭṭhāya thokaṃ thokaṃ adatvā yo yattakaṃ gaṇhāti, tassa tattakaṃ dātabbaṃ. Avasiṭṭhe asati puna piṇḍāya caritvā therāsanato paṭṭhāya yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ, taṃ taṃ datvā sesaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ.

Now, who fulfills this principle conducive to amiability, and who does not? Firstly, an immoral person does not fulfill it, for the virtuous do not accept what is theirs. But a person of purified morality, not breaking the observance, fulfills it. Herein, this is the observance: one who gives, having specified it for their mother or father, or for their teachers, preceptors, and so on—let them give what is to be given, but for them this is not a principle conducive to amiability; it is called being occupied with an impediment. For the principle conducive to amiability is proper only for one who is free from impediments. Therefore, one who is giving a specified portion should give to the sick, to those attending the sick, to visitors, to travelers, and to one newly ordained who does not know how to take up the outer robe and bowl. Having given to these, what remains should be given out starting from the elders' seat, giving to each as much as they take, not giving little by little. If nothing is left over, one should go for alms again, and starting from the elders' seat, give whatever is excellent and then consume the remainder.

Ayaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammo sāraṇīyadhammapūraṇavidhimhi susikkhitāya parisāya supūro hoti. Susikkhitāya hi parisāya yo aññato labhati, so na gaṇhāti. Aññato alabhantopi pamāṇayuttameva gaṇhāti, na atirekaṃ. Ayañca pana sāraṇīyadhammo evaṃ punappunaṃ piṇḍāya [V 3.0422] caritvā laddhaṃ laddhaṃ dentassapi dvādasahi vassehi pūrati, na tato oraṃ. Sace hi dvādasamepi vasse sāraṇīyadhammapūrako piṇḍapātapūraṃ pattaṃ āsanasālāyaṃ ṭhapetvā nahāyituṃ gacchati, saṅghatthero ca “kasseso patto”ti vatvā “sāraṇīyadhammapūrakassā”ti vutte “āharatha na”nti sabbaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ vicāretvā bhuñjitvāva rittapattaṃ ṭhapeti. Atha so bhikkhu rittapattaṃ disvā “mayhaṃ anavasesetvāva paribhuñjiṃsū”ti domanassaṃ uppādeti, sāraṇīyadhammo bhijjati, puna dvādasa vassāni pūretabbo hoti. Titthiyaparivāsasadiso hesa, sakiṃ khaṇḍe jāte puna pūretabbova. Yo pana “lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me, yassa me pattagataṃ anāpucchāva sabrahmacārino paribhuñjantī”ti somanassaṃ janeti, tassa puṇṇo nāma hoti.

This principle conducive to amiability, however, is easily fulfilled in an assembly well-trained in the practice of fulfilling the principle conducive to amiability.
