For in a well-trained assembly, if one receives something from another, one does not take it. Even if one does not receive anything from another, one takes only what is appropriate, not more. Moreover, even if one repeatedly goes for alms and gives away whatever is obtained, this principle conducive to amiability is fulfilled only in twelve years, not sooner. If, even in the twelfth year, the one fulfilling the principle conducive to amiability places a bowl filled with alms-food in the assembly hall and goes to bathe, and the senior elder of the Saṅgha asks, 'Whose bowl is this?' and is told, 'It belongs to the one fulfilling the principle conducive to amiability,' and then says, 'Bring it here!', has all the alms-food served, eats it, and places the bowl back empty—then if that monk, seeing the empty bowl, becomes displeased, thinking, 'They consumed everything without leaving any for me,' the principle conducive to amiability is broken, and he must fulfill it again for another twelve years. This is like the probationary period for sectarians; once it is broken, it must be fulfilled again. But if one thinks, 'What a gain for me! How well-gained it is for me, that my fellows in the holy life partake of what is in my bowl without even asking!' and generates gladness, for him it is fulfilled.

Evaṃ pūritasāraṇīyadhammassa pana neva issā, na macchariyaṃ hoti, manussānaṃ piyo hoti sulabhapaccayo, pattagatamassa diyyamānampi na khīyati, bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ labhati, bhaye vā chātake vā sampatte devatā ussukkaṃ āpajjanti.

For one who has thus fulfilled the principle conducive to amiability, there is neither envy nor stinginess. He is dear to people and his requisites are easily obtained. Even when what is placed in his bowl is given away, it is not exhausted. He receives the choicest goods in the place where articles are to be shared. When danger or famine arises, the deities are solicitous for him.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – leṇagirivāsī tissatthero kira mahākhīragāmaṃ upanissāya vasati. Paññāsamattā therā nāgadīpaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya gacchantā khīragāme piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci aladdhā nikkhamiṃsu. Thero pavisanto te disvā pucchi “laddhaṃ, bhante”ti. Vicarimha, āvusoti. So aladdhabhāvaṃ ñatvā āha “bhante, yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva idheva hothā”ti[M 3.0462]. Mayaṃ, āvuso, paññāsa janā pattatemanamattampi na labhimhāti. Bhante, nevāsikā nāma paṭibalā honti, alabhantāpi bhikkhācāramaggasabhāgaṃ jānantīti. Therā āgamiṃsu. Thero gāmaṃ pāvisi. Dhurageheyeva mahāupāsikā khīrabhattaṃ sajjetvā theraṃ olokayamānā ṭhitā therassa dvāraṃ sampattasseva pattaṃ pūretvā adāsi. So taṃ ādāya therānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “gaṇhatha, bhante”ti saṅghattheraṃ āha. Thero “amhehi ettakehi kiñci na laddhaṃ, ayaṃ sīghameva gahetvā āgato, kiṃ nu kho”ti sesānaṃ mukhaṃ olokesi. Thero olokanākāreneva ñatvā “bhante, dhammena samena laddho piṇḍapāto, nikkukkuccā gaṇhathā”tiādito paṭṭhāya sabbesaṃ yāvadatthaṃ datvā attanāpi yāvadatthaṃ bhuñji. Atha naṃ bhattakiccāvasāne therā pucchiṃsu “kadā, āvuso, lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhī”ti? Natthi me, bhante, lokuttaradhammoti. Jhānalābhīsi āvusoti? Etampi me, bhante, natthīti. Nanu, āvuso, pāṭihāriyanti? Sāraṇīyadhammo me, bhante, pūrito, tassa me pūritakālato paṭṭhāya sacepi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ hoti, pattagataṃ na khīyatīti. Sādhu sādhu sappurisa anucchavikamidaṃ tuyhanti. Idaṃ tāva pattagataṃ na khīyatīti ettha vatthu.

Herein are these stories: The Elder Tissa, a resident of Leṇagiri, it is said, dwelt near the great village of Khīra. About fifty elders, on their way to worship at the shrine on Nāgadīpa, wandered for alms in Khīra village and, having received nothing, departed. The elder, upon entering, saw them and asked, 'Did you receive anything, venerable sirs?' 'We wandered, friend,' they replied. Knowing they had received nothing, he said, 'Venerable sirs, please remain here until I return.' 'Friend, we fifty persons did not obtain even enough to wet the bowl.' 'Venerable sirs, the residents here are capable; they know what is proper for the alms-round path, even though you received nothing.' The elders returned. The elder entered the village. In the very first house, a great laywoman who had prepared milk-rice stood watching for the elder. As soon as he arrived at her door, she filled his bowl and gave it to him. Taking it, he went to the elders and said to the senior elder, 'Take this, venerable sir.' The senior elder thought, 'We, so many, received nothing, yet he quickly brought this. What could this be?' and looked at the faces of the others. Understanding from their manner of looking, the elder said, 'Venerable sirs, this alms-food was obtained righteously and fairly. Take it without scruple.' He then gave to all of them as much as they desired, and he himself also ate his fill. After the meal was finished, the elders asked him, 'Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma?' 'Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma.' 'Friend, have you attained jhāna?' 'Venerable sirs, I do not have that either.' 'But, friend, is this not a marvel?' 'Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the principle conducive to amiability. From the time I fulfilled it, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the food in my bowl would not be exhausted.' 'Good, good, worthy man! This is fitting for you.' This is the story regarding 'the food in the bowl is not exhausted.'

Ayameva [V 3.0423] pana thero cetiyapabbate giribhaṇḍamahāpūjāya dānaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “imasmiṃ dāne kiṃ varabhaṇḍa”nti pucchi. Dve sāṭakā, bhanteti. Ete mayhaṃ pāpuṇissantīti. Taṃ sutvā amacco rañño ārocesi “eko daharo evaṃ vadatī”ti. “Daharassa evaṃ cittaṃ, mahātherānaṃ pana sukhumā sāṭakā vaṭṭantī”ti vatvā “mahātherānaṃ dassāmī”ti ṭhapesi. Tassa bhikkhusaṅghe paṭipāṭiyā ṭhite dentassa matthake ṭhapitāpi te sāṭakā hatthaṃ nārohanti, aññeva ārohanti. Daharassa dānakāle pana hatthaṃ āruḷhā. So tassa hatthe ṭhapetvā amaccassa mukhaṃ oloketvā daharaṃ nisīdāpetvā dānaṃ datvā saṅghaṃ vissajjetvā daharassa santike nisīditvā “bhante, imaṃ dhammaṃ kadā paṭivijjhitthā”ti āha. So pariyāyenapi asantaṃ avadanto “natthi mayhaṃ, mahārāja, lokuttaradhammo”ti āha. Nanu, bhante, pubbeva avacutthāti. Āma mahārāja, sāraṇīyadhammapūrako ahaṃ, tassa me dhammassa pūritakālato paṭṭhāya bhājanīyaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ pāpuṇātīti. “Sādhu sādhu bhante, anucchavikamidaṃ tumhāka”nti [M 3.0463] vanditvā pakkāmi. Idaṃ bhājanīyaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ pāpuṇātīti ettha vatthu.

That same elder, going to the donation place on Cetiyapabbata for the great Giribhaṇḍa offering, asked, 'What is the choicest item in this donation?' 'Two cloths, venerable sir.' 'These will come to me.' Hearing this, a minister reported to the king, 'A certain young monk speaks thus.' The king said, 'Such is the mind of the young; but fine cloths are suitable for the great elders,' and setting them aside, said, 'I will give them to the great elders.' When he was giving to the Saṅgha, who were standing in order, even when those cloths were placed on the heads of the elders, they did not come into their hands; other cloths did. But at the time of giving to the young monk, they came into his hands. The king, placing them in the monk's hands, looked at the minister's face. He had the young monk sit down, gave the donation, dismissed the Saṅgha, and sat near the young monk. 'Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma?' he asked. The monk, not speaking what is untrue even when questioned indirectly, said, 'Great king, I have no supramundane Dhamma.' 'But, venerable sir, did you not say so before?' 'Yes, great king. I am one who has fulfilled the principle conducive to amiability. From the time that Dhamma has been fulfilled by me, the choicest items come to me in the place of distribution.' 'Good, good, venerable sir, this is fitting for you,' said the king, and having paid homage, he departed. This is the story regarding 'the choicest items come in the place of distribution.'

Caṇḍālatissabhayena pana bhātaragāmavāsino nāgattheriyā anārocetvāva palāyiṃsu. Therī paccūsasamaye “ati viya appanigghoso gāmo, upadhāretha tāvā”ti daharabhikkhuniyo āha. Tā gantvā sabbesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgamma theriyā ārocesuṃ. Sā sutvā “mā tumhe tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ cintayittha, attano uddesaparipucchāyonisomanasikāresuyeva yogaṃ karothā”ti vatvā bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ pārupitvā attadvādasamā gāmadvāre nigrodhamūle aṭṭhāsi. Rukkhe adhivatthā devatā dvādasannampi bhikkhunīnaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ datvā “ayye aññattha mā gacchatha, niccaṃ idheva ethā”ti āha. Theriyā pana kaniṭṭhabhātā nāgatthero nāma atthi, so “mahantaṃ bhayaṃ, na sakkā yāpetuṃ, paratīraṃ gamissāmī”ti attadvādasamo attano vasanaṭṭhānā nikkhanto “theriṃ disvā gamissāmī”ti bhātaragāmaṃ āgato. Therī “therā āgatā”ti sutvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ ayyā”ti pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Sā “ajja ekadivasaṃ vihāre vasitvā sveva gamissathā”ti āha. Therā vihāraṃ āgamaṃsu.

However, fearing Caṇḍāla Tissa, the residents of Bhātaragāma fled without informing the Elder Nun Nāgā. At dawn, the elder nun said to the young nuns, 'The village is unusually quiet; go and investigate.' They went, discovered that everyone had departed, and reported back to the elder nun. Hearing this, she said, 'Do not dwell on their departure. Apply yourselves instead to your recitation, questioning, and wise attention.' Then, at the time for the alms-round, she robed herself and, as the twelfth, stood with her companions at the village gate under a banyan tree. The deity dwelling in the tree offered alms-food to all twelve nuns and said, 'Venerable ladies, do not go elsewhere. Come here always.' Meanwhile, the elder nun’s younger brother, named Elder Nāga, thought, 'There is great danger; it is not possible to carry on. I will cross to the other shore.' Taking himself as the twelfth, he left his dwelling place and, thinking, 'I will see the elder nun before leaving,' came to Bhātaragāma. Hearing that the elders had arrived, the elder nun went to them and asked, 'What is it, venerable sirs?' He explained the situation. She replied, 'Stay in the monastery for one day today and leave tomorrow.' The elders came to the monastery.

Therī punadivase rukkhamūle piṇḍāya caritvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti āha. Thero “vaṭṭissati therī”ti vatvā tuṇhī aṭṭhāsi. Dhammiko tāta piṇḍapāto, kukkuccaṃ akatvā paribhuñjathāti. Vaṭṭissati therīti. Sā pattaṃ gahetvā ākāse khipi. Patto ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Thero “sattatālamatte ṭhitampi bhikkhunībhattameva therī”ti vatvā “bhayaṃ nāma sabbakālaṃ na hoti, bhaye vūpasante ariyavaṃsaṃ kathayamāno ‘bho piṇḍapātika [V 3.0424] bhikkhunībhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vītināmayitthā’ti cittena anuvadiyamāno santhambhituṃ na sakkhissāmi, appamattā hotha theriyo”ti maggaṃ āruhi. Rukkhadevatāpi “sace thero theriyā hatthato piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjissati, na naṃ nivattessāmi, sace na paribhuñjissati, nivattessāmī”ti cintayamānā ṭhatvā therassa gamanaṃ disvā rukkhā oruyha “pattaṃ, bhante, dethā”ti pattaṃ gahetvā theraṃ rukkhamūlaṃyeva ānetvā āsanaṃ paññapetvā piṇḍapātaṃ datvā katabhattakiccaṃ paṭiññaṃ kāretvā dvādasa bhikkhuniyo dvādasa ca bhikkhū satta vassāni upaṭṭhahi[M 3.0464]. Idaṃ devatā ussukkaṃ āpajjantīti ettha vatthu. Tatra hi therī sāraṇīyadhammapūrikā ahosi.

On the next day, the elder nun, having gone on her alms round, approached the elder monk at the foot of a tree and said, 'Please partake of this alms-food.' The elder monk, saying, 'It is sufficient, elder nun,' remained silent. 'Venerable sir, this alms-food is lawfully obtained; partake of it without scruple.' 'It is sufficient, elder nun,' he replied. She took the bowl and threw it into the sky. The bowl remained suspended in the air. The elder monk said, 'Even though it stands at the height of seven palm trees, it is still an elder nun's alms-food,' and then, 'Fear is not always present; but when fear has subsided, and I am speaking of the noble lineage, if I am mentally reproached with, "O alms-gatherer, you have passed the time eating an elder nun's alms-food," I will not be able to remain composed. Be heedful, elder nuns,' and he set out on the path. The tree-deity, thinking, 'If the elder partakes of the alms-food from the elder nun's hand, I will not turn him back; if he does not partake, I will turn him back,' stood waiting. Seeing the elder's departure, she descended from the tree, said, 'Venerable sir, give me the bowl,' took the bowl, brought the elder back to the foot of the tree, prepared a seat, gave the alms-food, had him acknowledge the completion of the meal, and attended to twelve nuns and twelve monks for seven years. This is the story here concerning the deity making an effort. For in that case, the elder nun was one who fulfilled the qualities worthy of recollection.

Natthi etesaṃ khaṇḍanti akhaṇḍāni, taṃ pana nesaṃ khaṇḍaṃ dassetuṃ “yassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha upasampannasīlānaṃ uddesakkamena ādiantā veditabbā. Tenāha “sattasū”tiādi. Anupasampannasīlānaṃ pana samādānakkamenapi ādiantā labbhanti. Pariyante chinnasāṭako viyāti vatthante dasante vā chinnavatthaṃ viya. Visadisudāharaṇañcetaṃ “akhaṇḍānī”ti imassa adhikatattā. Evaṃ sesānipi udāharaṇāni. Khaṇḍanti khaṇḍavantaṃ, khaṇḍitaṃ vā. Chiddantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Visabhāgavaṇṇena gāvī viyāti sambandho. Visabhāgavaṇṇena upaḍḍhaṃ tatiyabhāgaṃ vā sambhinnavaṇṇaṃ sabalaṃ, visabhāgavaṇṇeheva pana bindūhi antarantarā vimissaṃ kammāsaṃ. Ayaṃ imesaṃ viseso.

‘Unbroken’ (`akhaṇḍāni`) means there is no break in them; however, to show a break in them, 'whose,' and so on, is stated. Herein, for the virtue of the fully ordained, the beginning and end should be understood according to the order of recitation. Therefore, it is said, 'in seven,' and so on. For the virtue of the unordained, however, the beginning and end can also be obtained according to the order of undertaking. 'Like a garment torn at the hem' means like a cloth torn at the edge or the end. And this is a dissimilar example because 'unbroken' is what is being referred to. The other examples are also similar. `Khaṇḍa` means having a break, or broken. This same method applies to `chiddā` (perforated), and so on. The connection is 'like a cow of variegated color.' By 'variegated color' (`visabhāgavaṇṇa`) is meant `sabala` (dappled), which is a color mixed in half or a third part; `kammāsa` (spotted), however, is interspersed here and there with spots of different colors. This is the distinction between them.

Bhujissabhāvakaraṇatoti taṇhādāsabyato mocetvā bhujissabhāvakaraṇato. Sīlassa ca taṇhādāsabyato mocanaṃ vivaṭṭūpanissayabhāvāpādanaṃ, tenassa vivaṭṭūpanissayatā dassitā. “Bhujissabhāvakaraṇato”ti ca iminā bhujissakarāni bhujissānīti uttarapadalopenāyaṃ niddesoti dasseti. Yasmā ca taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo serī sayaṃvasī bhujisso nāma hoti, tasmāpi bhujissāni. Suparisuddhabhāvena pāsaṃsattā viññupasatthāni. Aviññūnaṃ pasaṃsāya appamāṇabhāvato viññūgahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhattāti “imināhaṃ sīlena devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti taṇhāparāmāsena “imināhaṃ sīlena devo hutvā tattha nicco dhuvo sassato bhavissāmī”ti diṭṭhiparāmāsena ca aparāmaṭṭhattā. Atha vā “ayaṃ te sīlesu dāso”ti catūsu vipattīsu yaṃ vā taṃ vā vipattiṃ dassetvā “imaṃ nāma tvaṃ āpannapubbo”ti kenaci parāmaṭṭhuṃ anuddhaṃsetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā aparāmaṭṭhānīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sīlaṃ nāma avippaṭisārādipārampariyena yāvadeva samādhisampādanatthanti āha “samādhisaṃvattanikānī”ti. Samādhisaṃvattanappayojanāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni.

'Because it makes one independent' means: by freeing one from the slavery of craving, it makes one independent. And the liberation from the slavery of craving by means of virtue is the bringing about of the condition of being a support for the rolling back of the cycle; thus, its nature as a support for the rolling back of the cycle is shown. And by this phrase 'because it makes one independent,' it indicates that this designation is formed by the elision of the latter word, so that 'those that make one independent' (`bhujissakarāni`) becomes 'independent' (`bhujissāni`). And since a person endowed with it is independent and self-mastered, they are called 'independent' (`bhujisso`); therefore, these virtues are also 'independent.' They are praised by the wise because they are supremely pure and praiseworthy. The term 'wise' is used because the praise of the ignorant is not a valid measure. 'Because they are not grasped at by craving and views' means: because they are not grasped at by the grasping of craving, as in, 'By this virtue, I will become a god or some other divine being,' nor by the grasping of views, as in, 'By this virtue, having become a god, I will be eternal, permanent, and everlasting there.' Alternatively, the meaning should be understood thus: they are 'ungrasped' because it is not possible for anyone to find fault or censure them by pointing out one of the four failings and saying, 'You have this flaw in your virtues,' or 'You have previously fallen into this.' Virtue is for the purpose of accomplishing concentration through the sequence beginning with non-regret; thus, it is said, 'They conduce to concentration.' Those that have the purpose of conducing to concentration are 'conducive to concentration.'

Samānabhāvo [M 3.0465][V 3.0425] sāmaññaṃ, paripuṇṇacatupārisuddhibhāvena majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇassa viya bhedābhāvato sīlena sāmaññaṃ sīlasāmaññaṃ, taṃ gato upagatoti sīlasāmaññagato. Tenāha “samānabhāvūpagatasīlo”ti, sīlasampattiyā samānabhāvaṃ upagatasīlo sabhāgavuttikoti attho. Sotāpannādīnañhi sīlaṃ samuddantarepi devalokepi vasantānaṃ aññesaṃ sotāpannādīnaṃ sīlena samānameva hoti, natthi maggasīle nānattaṃ. Kāmañhi puthujjanānampi catupārisuddhisīle nānattaṃ na siyā, taṃ pana na ekantikanti idha nādhippetaṃ, maggasīlaṃ pana ekantikaṃ niyatabhāvatoti tameva sandhāya “yāni tāni sīlānī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The state of being the same is `sāmañña`. Because there is no break, like in the middle of refined gold, due to the state of fourfold perfect purity, the state of being the same through virtue is `sīlasāmañña`. One who has gone to that, who has reached it, is `sīlasāmaññagato`. Therefore, it is said, 'one whose virtue has attained the state of being the same,' meaning one whose conduct is of a similar nature due to the attainment of virtue. For the virtue of Stream-enterers and others, even of those dwelling in the middle of the ocean or in a deva world, is the same as the virtue of other Stream-enterers and so on; there is no diversity in the virtue of the path. Although for worldlings there may be no diversity in the virtue of fourfold purity, that is not certain, so it is not intended here. The virtue of the path, however, is certain because of its fixed nature. Therefore, it is with reference to this that it is said, 'whatever those virtues are,' and so on.

Yāyanti yā ayaṃ mayhañceva tumhākañca paccakkhabhūtā. Diṭṭhīti maggasammādiṭṭhi. Niddosāti niddhutadosā, samucchinnarāgādipāpadhammāti attho. Niyyātīti vaṭṭadukkhato nissarati nigacchati. Sayaṃ niyantīyeva hi taṃmaggasamaṅgīpuggalaṃ vaṭṭadukkhato niyyāpetīti vuccati. Yā satthu anusiṭṭhi, taṃ karotīti takkaro, tassa, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjanakassāti attho. Diṭṭhisāmaññagatoti saccasampaṭivedhena samānadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ upagato.

`Yā` means: this which has become directly evident to both me and you. `Diṭṭhi` means the right view of the path. `Niddosā` means with faults shaken off; the meaning is that evil states such as greed have been cut off at the root. `Niyyāti` means it goes out, it departs from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth. For it, while itself going forth, is said to lead the person endowed with that path out from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth. One who does that (`taṃ`), the Teacher's instruction, is a `takkaro` (doer of that); the meaning is: of one who practices as instructed. `Diṭṭhisāmaññagato` means one who has attained a state of shared view through the thorough penetration of the truths.

Katipucchāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished.

Chaāpattisamuṭṭhānavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on the Six Origins of Offenses.

276. Paṭhamena āpattisamuṭṭhānenātiādi sabbaṃ uddesaniddesādivasena pavattapāḷiṃ anusāreneva sakkā viññātuṃ.

276. 'With the first origin of an offense,' and so on—all this can be understood simply by following the Pāli text as it proceeds by way of enumeration, explanation, and so forth.

Samathabhedaṃ

The Classification of Settlements.

Adhikaraṇapariyāyavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on the Modes of Legal Issues.

293. Lobho [M 3.0466][V 3.0426] pubbaṅgamotiādīsu pana lobhahetu vivadanato “lobho pubbaṅgamo”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni. Tiṭṭhanti etthāti ṭhānaṃ. Ke tiṭṭhanti? Vivādādhikaraṇādayo. Vasanti etthāti vatthu. Bhavanti etthāti bhūmi. Kusalākusalābyākatacittasamaṅgino vivadanato “nava hetū”ti vuttaṃ. Dvādasa mūlānīti “kodhano hoti upanāhī”tiādīni dvādasa mūlāni.

293. However, in phrases such as 'greed is the forerunner,' it is said 'greed is the forerunner' because disputes arise on account of greed. It is similar for the rest. `Ṭhānāni` means causes. A `ṭhāna` (ground) is that where they stand. What stands there? Legal issues of dispute, and so on. A `vatthu` (basis) is that where they dwell. A `bhūmi` (ground) is that where they come to be. Because disputes arise from those endowed with wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate minds, it is said, 'nine causes.' `Dvādasa mūlāni` (twelve roots) are the twelve roots such as 'one is wrathful and bears malice.'

294-295. Imāneva dvādasa kāyavācāhi saddhiṃ “cuddasa mūlānī”ti vuttāni. Satta āpattikkhandhā ṭhānānīti ettha āpattiṃ āpajjitvā paṭicchādentassa yā āpatti, tassā pubbe āpannā āpattiyo ṭhānānīti veditabbaṃ. “Natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti vacanato āpattādhikaraṇe akusalābyākatavasena cha hetū vuttā. Kusalacittaṃ pana aṅgaṃ hoti, na hetu.

294-295. These same twelve, together with body and speech, are called 'the fourteen roots.' In the phrase 'the seven aggregates of offenses are the grounds,' it should be understood that the offenses previously committed are the grounds for the offense of one who, having committed an offense, then conceals it. Because it is said, 'There is no wholesome legal issue of an offense,' six causes are stated for a legal issue of an offense, by way of the unwholesome and the indeterminate. A wholesome mind, however, is a factor, not a cause.

296. Cattāri kammāni ṭhānānīti ettha “evaṃ kattabba”nti itikattabbatādassanavasena pavattapāḷi kammaṃ nāma, yathāṭhitapāḷivasena karontānaṃ kiriyā kiccādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Ñattiñattidutiyañatticatutthakammāni ñattito jāyanti, apalokanakammaṃ apalokanatovāti āha “ñattito vā apalokanato vā”ti. Kiccādhikaraṇaṃ ekena samathena sammati, sampajjatīti attho. Tehi sametabbattā “vivādādhikaraṇassa sādhāraṇā”ti vuttaṃ.

296. The 'four actions' (cattāri kammāni) are the grounds—here, the Pāli text that proceeds by way of showing what ought to be done, such as 'this should be done,' is called 'action' (kamma). The act of those who act according to the Pāli text as it stands is called 'the legal issue of business' (kiccādhikaraṇa). The 'motion' (ñatti), the 'motion followed by one announcement' (ñattidutiya), and the 'motion followed by three announcements' (ñatticatuttha) actions arise from the motion, and the 'act of proclamation' (apalokanakamma) from the proclamation—thus it is said, 'from the motion or from the proclamation.' The legal issue of business is settled by one settlement, meaning it is accomplished. Because they should be settled by these, it is said, 'common to the legal issue of dispute.'

Tabbhāgiyavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on What Belongs to That Category

298. Vivādādhikaraṇassa tabbhāgiyāti vivādādhikaraṇassa vūpasamato tappakkhikā.

298. Those belonging to the same category as the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇassa tabbhāgiyā) are those who are on the side of the settlement of the legal issue of dispute.

Samathā samathassa sādhāraṇavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Settlements Common to Settlements

299. Ekaṃ [V 3.0427] adhikaraṇaṃ sabbe samathā ekato hutvā sametuṃ sakkonti na sakkontīti pucchanto “samathā samathassa sādhāraṇā, samathā [M 3.0467] samathassa asādhāraṇā”ti āha. Yebhuyyasikāya samanaṃ sammukhāvinayaṃ vinā na hotīti āha “yebhuyyasikā sammukhāvinayassa sādhāraṇā”ti. Sativinayādīhi samanassa yebhuyyasikāya kiccaṃ natthīti āha “sativinayassa…pe… asādhāraṇā”ti. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tabbhāgiyavārepi eseva nayo.

299. When asking whether all settlements, having become one, can settle a single legal issue or not, it is said: 'Settlements are common to settlements, settlements are not common to settlements.' It is said that settlement by majority (yebhuyyasikā) does not occur without a face-to-face procedure (sammukhāvinaya): 'Settlement by majority is common to a face-to-face procedure.' It is said that for the settlement by a verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) and so forth, there is no need for settlement by majority: 'It is not common to a verdict of mindfulness… and so forth.' Similarly for the rest. This same method applies to the section on what belongs to that category.

Vinayavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Discipline

302. Sabbesampi samathānaṃ vinayapariyāyo labbhatīti “vinayo sammukhāvinayo”tiādinā vinayavāro uddhaṭo. Siyā na sammukhāvinayoti ettha sammukhāvinayaṃ ṭhapetvā sativinayādayo sesasamathā adhippetā. Esa nayo sesesupi.

302. Because the mode of discipline is obtained for all settlements, the section on discipline has been set forth with phrases like 'discipline is a face-to-face procedure,' and so forth. In the statement 'it may not be a face-to-face procedure,' here, setting aside the face-to-face procedure, the remaining settlements such as the verdict of mindfulness, and so forth, are intended. This method applies to the rest as well.

Kusalavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Wholesome Section

303. Saṅghassa sammukhā paṭiññāte taṃ paṭijānanaṃ saṅghasammukhatā nāma. Tassa paṭijānanacittaṃ sandhāya “sammukhāvinayo kusalo”tiādi vuttanti vadanti. Natthi sammukhāvinayo akusaloti dhammavinayapuggalasammukhatāhi tivaṅgiko sammukhāvinayo etehi vinā natthi. Tattha kusalacittehi karaṇakāle kusalo, arahantehi karaṇakāle abyākato. Etesaṃ saṅghasammukhatādīnaṃ akusalapaṭipakkhattā akusalassa sambhavo natthi, tasmā “natthi sammukhāvinayo akusalo”ti vuttaṃ. “Yebhuyyasikā adhammavādīhi vūpasamanakāle, dhammavādīnampi adhammavādimhi salākaggāhāpake jāte akusalā. Sativinayo anarahato sañcicca sativinayadāne akusalo. Amūḷhavinayo anummattakassa dāne, paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ mūḷhassa ajānato paṭiññāya karaṇe, tassapāpiyasikā suddhassa karaṇe, tiṇavatthārakaṃ mahākalahe sañcicca karaṇe ca akusalaṃ. Sabbattha arahato vaseneva abyākata”nti sabbametaṃ gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ.

303. When something is acknowledged in the presence of the Saṅgha, that acknowledgment is called 'presence of the Saṅgha' (saṅghasammukhatā). They say that with reference to the mind of acknowledgment, it is said, 'The face-to-face procedure (sammukhāvinaya) is wholesome,' and so forth. There is no unwholesome face-to-face procedure; the threefold face-to-face procedure, consisting of the presence of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the individual, does not exist without these. Here, when it is performed with wholesome thoughts, it is wholesome; when performed by arahants, it is indeterminate. Because these, such as the presence of the Saṅgha, are opposed to the unwholesome, there is no possibility of the unwholesome. Therefore, it is said, 'There is no unwholesome face-to-face procedure.' 'A decision by majority (yebhuyyasikā) is unwholesome when settling with those who speak against the Dhamma; and even among those who speak for the Dhamma, it is unwholesome when a ballot-taker arises on the side of those who speak against the Dhamma. A verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) is unwholesome when intentionally given to one who is not an arahant. A verdict for one who is no longer mad (amūḷhavinaya) is unwholesome when given to one who is not insane; acknowledgment of an offense (paṭiññātakaraṇa) is unwholesome when making one who is deluded acknowledge without knowing; a finding of further guilt (tassapāpiyasikā) is unwholesome when applied to one who is innocent; and covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka) is unwholesome when intentionally applied in a major quarrel. In all cases, by the authority of an arahant, it is indeterminate.' All this is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada.

Samathavāravissajjanāvārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Settlements and the Section on Answers

304-305. Yattha yebhuyyasikā labbhati, tattha sammukhāvinayo labbhatītiādi pucchā. Yasmiṃ [V 3.0428] samaye sammukhāvinayena cātiādi tassā [M 3.0468] vissajjanaṃ, yasmiṃ samaye sammukhāvinayena ca yebhuyyasikāya ca adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammati, tasmiṃ samaye yattha yebhuyyasikā labbhati, tattha sammukhāvinayo labbhatīti evaṃ sabbattha sambandho. Yattha paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ labbhati, tattha sammukhāvinayo labbhatīti ettha ekaṃ vā dve vā bahū vā bhikkhū “imaṃ nāma āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti pucchite sati “āmā”ti paṭijānane dvepi paṭiññātakaraṇasammukhāvinayā labbhanti. Tattha “saṅghasammukhatā dhammavinayapuggalasammukhatā”ti evaṃ vuttasammukhāvinaye saṅghassa purato paṭiññātaṃ ce, saṅghasammukhatā. Tattheva desitaṃ ce, dhammavinayasammukhatāyopi laddhā honti. Atha vivadantā aññamaññaṃ paṭijānanti ce, puggalasammukhatā. Tasseva santike desitaṃ ce, dhammavinayasammukhatāyopi laddhā honti. Ekasseva vā ekassa santike āpattidesanakāle “passasi, passāmī”ti vutte tattha dhammavinayapuggalasammukhatāsaññito sammukhāvinayo ca paṭiññātakaraṇañca laddhaṃ hoti.

304-305. The question is: 'Where a decision by majority (yebhuyyasikā) is obtainable, is a face-to-face procedure (sammukhāvinaya) obtainable there?' and so forth. The answer to that is: 'At the time when a legal issue is settled by a face-to-face procedure and by a decision by majority, at that time, where a decision by majority is obtainable, there a face-to-face procedure is obtainable.' Thus is the connection everywhere. Where acknowledgment of an offense (paṭiññātakaraṇa) is obtainable, there a face-to-face procedure is obtainable. Here, when one, two, or many bhikkhus are asked, 'Have you committed such-and-such an offense?' and they acknowledge it by saying, 'Yes,' then both acknowledgment of an offense and a face-to-face procedure are obtained. In this context, regarding the face-to-face procedure as stated—'the presence of the Saṅgha (saṅghasammukhatā), the presence of the Dhamma and Vinaya, the presence of the individual (puggalasammukhatā)'—if the acknowledgment is made before the Saṅgha, it is the presence of the Saṅgha. If it is confessed there, then the presences of the Dhamma and Vinaya are also obtained. If disputing parties acknowledge it to each other, it is the presence of the individual. If it is confessed in their presence, then the presences of the Dhamma and Vinaya are also obtained. Or, at the time of confessing an offense in the presence of a single individual, when it is said, 'Do you see it?' and the reply is, 'I see it,' then there the face-to-face procedure, designated as the presence of the Dhamma, Vinaya, and the individual, and the acknowledgment of an offense are obtained.

Saṃsaṭṭhavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Association

306. Adhikaraṇānaṃ vūpasamova samatho nāma, tasmā adhikaraṇena vinā samathā natthīti āha “mā hevantissa vacanīyo…pe… vinibbhujitvā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetu”nti.

306. The very settlement of legal issues is called 'settlement' (samatha); therefore, without a legal issue, there are no settlements. Hence, it is said: 'He should not be spoken to in such a way... having analyzed and disentangled, he should make known the distinction.'

Samathādhikaraṇavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Settlements and Legal Issues

309-310. Samathā samathehi sammantītiādi pucchā. Siyā samathā samathehi sammantītiādi vissajjanaṃ. Tattha samathā samathehi sammantīti ettha sammantīti sampajjanti, adhikaraṇā vā pana sammanti vūpasamaṃ gacchanti, tasmā yebhuyyasikā sammukhāvinayena sammatīti ettha sammukhāvinayena saddhiṃ yebhuyyasikā sampajjati, na sativinayādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ tassā anupakārattāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

309-310. The question is: 'Do settlements accord with settlements?' and so on. The answer is: 'There may be settlements that accord with settlements,' and so on. Here, in the phrase 'settlements accord with settlements,' 'accord' means they are accomplished, or legal issues are settled, they come to a cessation. Therefore, in the case of a decision by majority (yebhuyyasikā), it accords by means of a face-to-face procedure (sammukhāvinaya), meaning the decision by majority is accomplished along with a face-to-face procedure, not along with a verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) or other procedures, because they are not helpful to it. This is how the meaning should be understood.

311. “Sammukhāvinayo vivādādhikaraṇena sammatī”ti pāṭho. “Sammukhāvinayo na kenaci sammatī”ti hi avasāne vuttattā sammukhāvinayo [M 3.0469] sayaṃ samathena vā adhikaraṇena vā sametabbo na hoti.

311. The reading is: 'The face-to-face procedure is settled by a legal issue of dispute.' For it is stated at the end: 'The face-to-face procedure is not settled by anything,' meaning that the face-to-face procedure itself should not be settled by a settlement or by a legal issue.

313. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ…pe… kiccādhikaraṇena sammatīti ettha “suṇātu me bhante [V 3.0429] …pe… paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ nikkhipāmī”ti evaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ kiccādhikaraṇena sammatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

313. Here, regarding 'a legal issue of dispute...pe...is settled by a legal issue of business,' it is to be understood that 'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me...pe...I cast the first voting slip'—in this way, a legal issue of dispute is settled by a legal issue of business.

Samuṭṭhāpanavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Origination

314. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ na katamaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti “nāyaṃ dhammo”ti vuttamatteneva kiñci adhikaraṇaṃ na samuṭṭhāpetīti attho.

314. The phrase 'a legal issue of dispute does not give rise to what kind of legal issue?' means that merely by saying 'this is not the Dhamma,' no legal issue whatsoever is given rise to.

Bhajativārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Association

318-9. Katamaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ pariyāpannanti katamādhikaraṇapariyāpannaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ bhajatīti paṭhamuppannavivādaṃ pacchā uppanno bhajati. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ dve samathe bhajatīti “maṃ vūpasametuṃ samatthā tumhe”ti vadantaṃ viya bhajati. Dvīhi samathehi saṅgahitanti “mayaṃ taṃ vūpasamessāmā”ti vadantehi viya dvīhi samathehi saṅgahitaṃ.

318-319. 'In which legal issue is it included?' means 'included in which kind of legal issue?'—or this is the reading. 'A legal issue of dispute is associated with a legal issue of dispute' means a later arisen dispute is associated with a previously arisen dispute. 'A legal issue of dispute is associated with two settlements' means it is associated as if with those saying, 'You are capable of settling me.' 'It is encompassed by two settlements' means it is encompassed by two settlements as if by those saying, 'We will settle it.'

Khandhakapucchāvāro

Section on Questions about the Khandhakas

Pucchāvissajjanāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of Questions and Answers

320. Nidānena [M 3.0470][V 3.0430] ca niddesena ca saddhinti ettha nidānenāti sikkhāpadapaññattidesasaṅkhātena nidānena. Niddesenāti puggalādiniddesena. Ubhayenapi tassa tassa sikkhāpadassa vatthu dassitaṃ, tasmā vatthunā saddhiṃ khandhakaṃ pucchissāmīti ayamettha attho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ upasampadakkhandhake. Uttamāni padāni vuttānīti “na, bhikkhave, ūnavīsativasso puggalo upasampādetabbo”tiādinā (mahāva. 99, 124) nayena uttamapadāni vuttāni. Cammasaṃyutteti cammakkhandhake.

320. Here, in the phrase 'along with the origin and the exposition,' 'by origin' means by the origin designated as the place where the training rule was laid down. 'By exposition' means by the exposition of individuals and so on. By both, the subject matter of each training rule is shown. Therefore, the meaning here is: 'I will ask about the Khandhaka along with its subject matter.' 'Therein' means in that Upasampadā Khandhaka. 'The supreme statements have been spoken' refers to the supreme statements spoken in the manner of, 'Bhikkhus, a person under twenty years of age is not to be given the higher ordination,' and so on (Mahāvagga 99, 124). 'Connected with leather' refers to the Cammakkhandhaka.

Ekuttarikanayo

The Method of Numerical Progression

Ekakavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Chapter on Ones

321. Mūlavisuddhiyā [M 3.0471][V 3.0431] antarāpattīti antarāpattiṃ āpajjitvā mūlāyapaṭikassanaṃ katvā ṭhitena āpannā. “Agghavisuddhiyā antarāpattīti sambahulā āpattiyo āpajjitvā tāsu sabbacirapaṭicchannavasena agghasamodhānaṃ gahetvā vasantena āpannāpattī”ti gaṇṭhipadesu vuttaṃ. Saussāheneva cittenāti “punapi āpajjissāmī”ti saussāheneva cittena. Bhikkhunīnaṃ aṭṭhavatthukāya vasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “aṭṭhame vatthusmiṃ bhikkhuniyā pārājikameva hotī”ti. “Dhammikassa paṭissavassa asaccāpane”ti vuttattā adhammikapaṭissavassa visaṃvāde dukkaṭaṃ na hoti. “Tumhe vibbhamathā”ti hi vutte suddhacitto “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā sace na vibbhamati, anāpatti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Pañcadasasu dhammesūti “kālena vakkhāmi, no akālenā”tiādinā vuttapañcadasadhammesu. Āpattiṃ āpajjituṃ bhabbatāya bhabbāpattikā.

321. ‘An intermediate offense for the purification of the root’ is an offense incurred by one who, having committed an intermediate offense and having undergone the act of being sent back to the root, remains so. ‘An intermediate offense for the purification of worth’ is an offense incurred by one who, having committed many offenses, lives having undertaken an adjustment of worth because they were all concealed for a very long time—this is stated in the glosses. ‘With an eager mind’ means with a mind that is eager, thinking, ‘I will commit it again.’ And this is said with reference to the eight grounds for bhikkhunīs. Therefore, he said, ‘On the eighth ground, it is a pārājika offense for a bhikkhunī.’ Because it is said, ‘for not making good on a righteous promise,’ there is no dukkaṭa offense for breaking an unrighteous promise. For when it is said, ‘You should disrobe,’ if one with a pure mind agrees, saying, ‘Good,’ but then does not disrobe, there is no offense. So it is in all cases. ‘In the fifteen things’ means in the fifteen things stated beginning with, ‘I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time.’ One is ‘liable to an offense’ because of the liability to commit an offense.

Ekakavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Ones is concluded.

Dukavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Chapter on Twos

322. Dukesu nidahaneti ātape aticiraṃ ṭhapetvā nidahane. Vatthusabhāgaṃ desento desento āpajjati, āpannaṃ āpattiṃ na desessāmīti dhuraṃ nikkhipanto na desento āpajjati. Romajanapade jātaṃ romakaṃ. Pakkālakanti yavakkhāraṃ. Anuññātaloṇattā loṇānipi dukesu vuttāni.

322. In the Chapter on Twos, 'burying' means burying after having placed something in the heat for a very long time. While teaching a portion of the subject matter, one commits an offense; by giving up the responsibility, thinking, 'I will not confess the offense I have committed,' and not confessing, one commits an offense. 'Romaka' is that which is produced in the country of Roma. 'Pakkālaka' means alkali from barley ash. Because salt is allowed, salts are also mentioned in the Chapter on Twos.

Dukavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Twos is concluded.

Tikavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Chapter on Threes

323. Tikesu [M 3.0472][V 3.0432] vacīsampayuttaṃ kāyakiriyaṃ katvāti kāyena nipaccakāraṃ katvā. Mukhālambarakaraṇādibhedoti mukhabherivādanādippabhedo. Yassa sikkhāpadassa vītikkame kāyasamuṭṭhānā āpattiyo, taṃ kāyadvāre paññattasikkhāpadaṃ. Upaghātetīti vināseti. Na ādātabbanti “imasmā vihārā parampi mā nikkhama, vinayadharānaṃ vā santikaṃ āgaccha vinicchayaṃ dātu”nti vutte tassa vacanaṃ na gahetabbanti attho.

323. In the Chapter on Threes, 'having performed a bodily action connected with speech' means having performed a respectful gesture with the body. 'The various kinds such as making a mouth-drum' means the different kinds such as playing a mouth-drum. A training rule, in the transgression of which there are offenses originating from the body, is a training rule laid down through the door of the body. 'He harms' means he destroys. 'It should not be accepted' means that when it is said, 'Do not go forth from this monastery, or come to the presence of the experts in the Vinaya to receive a decision,' his word should not be accepted.

Akusalāni ceva mūlāni cāti akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena ekantākusalabhāvato akusalāni, attanā sampayuttadhammānaṃ suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanato mūlāni, na akusalabhāvasādhanato. Na hi mūlato akusalānaṃ akusalabhāvo, kusalādīnaṃ vā kusalādibhāvo. Tathā ca sati momūhacittadvayamohassa akusalabhāvo na siyā.

Unwholesome and also roots: they are unwholesome because they are exclusively unwholesome in the sense of arising from unskillfulness; they are roots because they establish the well-established nature of their associated states, not because they establish unwholesomeness. For the unwholesomeness of unwholesome things does not arise from the root, nor the wholesomeness of wholesome things, and so on. If that were so, the unwholesomeness of the delusion in the two minds accompanied by utter delusion would not exist.

Duṭṭhu caritānīti paccayato sampayuttadhammato pavattiākārato ca na suṭṭhu asammāpavattitāni. Virūpānīti bībhacchāni sampati āyatiñca aniṭṭharūpattā. Suṭṭhu caritānītiādīsu vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Dvepi cete tikā paṇṇattiyā vā kammapathehi vā kathetabbā. Paṇṇattiyā tāva kāyadvāre paññattasikkhāpadassa vītikkamo kāyaduccaritaṃ, avītikkamo kāyasucaritaṃ. Vacīdvāre paññattasikkhāpadassa vītikkamo vacīduccaritaṃ, avītikkamo vacīsucaritaṃ. Ubhayattha paññattasikkhāpadassa vītikkamo manoduccaritaṃ manodvāre paññattasikkhāpadassa abhāvato. Tayidaṃ dvāradvaye akiriyasamuṭṭhānāya āpattiyā vasena veditabbaṃ. Yathāvuttāya āpattiyā avītikkamova manosucaritaṃ. Ayaṃ paṇṇattikathā.

'Misconduct' means that which is conducted badly, that is, not well and not rightly, in terms of conditions, associated states, and mode of occurrence. 'Deformed' means repulsive, because of its loathsome and undesirable nature both at present and in the future. The meaning of 'good conduct' and so on should be understood in the opposite way to what has been said. Both these triads should be explained either by way of designation or by the paths of action. By way of designation: the transgression of a training rule laid down through the door of the body is bodily misconduct; non-transgression is bodily good conduct. The transgression of a training rule laid down through the door of speech is verbal misconduct; non-transgression is verbal good conduct. The transgression of a training rule laid down in both cases is mental misconduct, due to the absence of a training rule laid down through the door of the mind. This should be understood by way of an offense originating from inaction at the two doors. The non-transgression of the aforesaid offense is mental good conduct. This is the explanation by way of designation.

Pāṇātipātādayo pana tisso cetanā kāyadvāre vacīdvārepi uppannā kāyaduccaritaṃ dvārantare uppannassapi kammassa sanāmāpariccāgato yebhuyyavuttiyā tabbahulavuttiyā ca. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā –

But the three intentions beginning with killing, even when arisen at the body door and also at the speech door, are bodily misconduct, because an action arisen at another door does not abandon its own name, and due to its predominant and frequent occurrence. Therefore, the commentary teachers said—

“Dvāre caranti kammāni, na dvārā dvāracārino;

Tasmā dvārehi kammāni, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitā”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. kāmāvacarakusala dvārakathā, kāyakammadvāra);

“Actions proceed through the doors; the doors are not what proceeds. Therefore, actions are distinguished from one another by the doors.”

Tathā [M 3.0473][V 3.0433] catasso musāvādādicetanā kāyadvārepi vacīdvārepi uppannā vacīduccaritaṃ, abhijjhā byāpādo micchādiṭṭhīti tayo manokammabhūtāya cetanāya sampayuttadhammā manoduccaritaṃ, kāyavacīkammabhūtāya pana cetanāya sampayuttā abhijjhādayo taṃtaṃpakkhikā vā honti abbohārikā vā. Pāṇātipātādīhi viramantassa uppannā tisso cetanāpi viratiyopi kāyasucaritaṃ kāyikassa vītikkamassa akaraṇavasena pavattanato. Kāyena pana sikkhāpadānaṃ samādiyamāne sīlassa kāyasucaritabhāve vattabbameva natthi. Musāvādādīhi viramantassa catasso cetanāpi viratiyopi vacīsucaritaṃ vācasikassa vītikkamassa akaraṇavasena pavattanato. Anabhijjhā abyāpādo sammādiṭṭhīti tayo cetanāsampayuttadhammā manosucaritanti ayaṃ kammapathakathā.

Likewise, the four intentions beginning with false speech, even when arisen at the body door and the speech door, are verbal misconduct. Covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—these three states associated with the intention that is mental action are mental misconduct. But covetousness and so on, when associated with the intention that is bodily and verbal action, either belong to their respective sides or are not designated as paths of action. For one who refrains from killing living beings and so on, the three intentions that arise and the abstinences are bodily good conduct, because they proceed by way of not committing a bodily transgression. Moreover, when one undertakes the training rules with the body, there is nothing to be said about that virtue being bodily good conduct. For one who refrains from false speech and so on, the four intentions that arise and the abstinences are verbal good conduct, because they proceed by way of not committing a verbal transgression. Non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—these three states associated with intention are mental good conduct. This is the explanation of the paths of action.

Tikavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Threes is concluded.

Catukkavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Chapter on Fours

324. Catukkesu anariyavohārāti anariyānaṃ lāmakānaṃ vohārā saṃvohārā abhilāpavācā. Ariyavohārāti ariyānaṃ sappurisānaṃ vohārā. Diṭṭhavāditāti “diṭṭhaṃ mayā”ti evaṃvāditā. Ettha ca taṃtaṃsamuṭṭhāpakacetanāvasena attho veditabbo.

324. In the Chapter on Fours, 'ignoble speech' means the speech, conversation, and utterances of ignoble and base individuals. 'Noble speech' means the speech of noble and virtuous individuals. 'Speaking of what is seen' means speaking thus: 'This was seen by me.' Here, the meaning should be understood by way of the intention that originates each instance.

Paṭhamakappikesu paṭhamaṃ purisaliṅgameva uppajjatīti āha “paṭhamaṃ uppannavasenā”ti. Purimaṃ purisaliṅgaṃ pajahatīti yathāvuttenatthena pubbaṅgamabhāvato purimasaṅkhātaṃ purisaliṅgaṃ jahati. Sataṃ tiṃsañca sikkhāpadānīti tiṃsādhikāni sataṃ sikkhāpadāni.

Regarding those of the first eon, he said, 'by way of arising first,' meaning that the male characteristic arises first. 'He abandons the former male characteristic' means he abandons the male characteristic called 'former' because it precedes, in the sense stated. 'One hundred and thirty training rules' means one hundred training rules with an additional thirty.

Bhikkhussa ca bhikkhuniyā ca catūsu pārājikesūti sādhāraṇesuyeva catūsu pārājikesu. Paṭhamo pañhoti “atthi vatthunānattatā, no āpattinānattatā”ti ayaṃ pañho. “Atthi āpattisabhāgatā, no vatthusabhāgatā”ti ayaṃ idha dutiyo nāma.

'In the four pārājikas for a bhikkhu and a bhikkhunī' means in the four pārājikas that are common to both. The first question is this: 'There is diversity of subject matter, but not diversity of offense.' The one called the second here is this: 'There is commonality of offense, but not commonality of subject matter.'

Anāpattivassacchedassāti natthi etasmiṃ vassacchede āpattīti anāpattivassacchedo, tassa, anāpattikassa vassacchedassāti attho. Mantābhāsāti [M 3.0474] matiyā upaparikkhitvā bhāsanato asamphappalāpavācā idha “mantābhāsā”ti vuttā.

Regarding "of a non-offense rainy season break": there is no offense in this rainy season break, hence it is a non-offense rainy season break; of that, meaning of a rainy season break without offense. Regarding "deliberate speech": because it is spoken after having examined it with wisdom, speech that is not frivolous chatter is here called "deliberate speech."

Navamabhikkhunito [V 3.0434] paṭṭhāya upajjhāyāpi abhivādanārahā no paccuṭṭhānārahāti yasmā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bhattagge aṭṭhannaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ avasesānaṃ yathāgatika”nti vadantena bhagavatā bhattagge ādito paṭṭhāya aṭṭhannaṃyeva bhikkhunīnaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ anuññātaṃ, avasesānaṃ āgatapaṭipāṭiyā, tasmā navamabhikkhunito paṭṭhāya sace upajjhāyāpi bhikkhunī pacchā āgacchati, na paccuṭṭhānārahā, yathānisinnāhiyeva sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā abhivādetabbattā abhivādanārahā. Ādito nisinnāsu pana aṭṭhasu yā abbhantarimā aññā vuḍḍhatarā āgacchati, sā attano navakataraṃ vuṭṭhāpetvā nisīdituṃ labhati. Tasmā sā tāhi aṭṭhahi bhikkhunīhi paccuṭṭhānārahā. Yā pana aṭṭhahipi navakatarā, sā sacepi saṭṭhivassā hoti, āgatapaṭipāṭiyāva nisīdituṃ labhati.

Starting from the ninth nun, even the preceptress is worthy of veneration but not of rising. Since the Blessed One, saying, "I allow, monks, that in the refectory, for eight nuns, it is according to seniority, and for the rest, according to their order of arrival," permitted that in the refectory, from the beginning, only eight nuns are to be treated according to seniority, and the rest according to their order of arrival, therefore, starting from the ninth nun, if even the preceptress nun arrives later, she is not worthy of being risen for, but is worthy of veneration, as she is to be venerated by raising the head while remaining seated. However, among the first eight seated, if another, older nun arrives, she may have a more junior nun rise and may then sit down. Thus, she is worthy of being risen for by those eight nuns. But if a nun is more junior than all eight, even if she is sixty years old, she may sit only according to the order of arrival.

Idha na kappantīti vadantoti paccantimajanapadesu ṭhatvā “idha na kappantī”ti vadanto vinayātisāradukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Kappiyañhi “na kappatī”ti vadanto paññattaṃ samucchindati nāma. Idha kappantītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

One who says, "This is not allowable here," while staying in border regions, incurs a dukkaṭa offense of transgressing the Vinaya. For one who says "it is not allowable" when it is allowable, indeed eradicates what has been prescribed. The same principle applies to saying "This is allowable here," and so on.

Catukkavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section of Fours is concluded.

Pañcakavāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section of Fives

325. Pañcakesu “nimantito sabhatto samāno santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā”ti (pāci. 294-297) vacanato akappiyanimantanaṃ sādiyantasseva anāmantacāro na vaṭṭatīti “piṇḍapātikassa kappantī”ti vuttaṃ. Gaṇabhojanādīsupi eseva nayo. Adhiṭṭhahitvā bhojananti “gilānasamayo”tiādinā ābhogaṃ katvā bhojanaṃ. Avikappanāti “mayhaṃ bhattapaccāsaṃ itthannāmassa dammī”ti evaṃ avikappanā.

325. In the section on fives: Because of the statement, "being invited with a meal, without asking a present monk..." (Pācittiya 32), going on a further alms-round is not allowable only for one who accepts an improper invitation. Hence, it is stated, "It is allowable for an alms-gatherer." The same principle applies to group meals and the like. "Eating after having determined" means eating after having made a reflection, such as, "This is a time of illness." "Not assigning" means not assigning thus: "I give my share of the meal to so-and-so."

Ayasato vā garahato vāti ettha parammukhā aguṇavacanaṃ ayaso. Sammukhā garahā. Viyasatīti byasanaṃ, hitasukhaṃ khipati viddhaṃsetīti attho. Ñātīnaṃ [M 3.0475] byasanaṃ ñātibyasanaṃ, corarogabhayādīhi ñātivināsoti attho. Bhogānaṃ byasanaṃ bhogabyasanaṃ, rājacorādivasena bhogavināsoti attho. Rogo eva byasanaṃ rogabyasanaṃ. Rogo hi ārogyaṃ byasati vināsetīti byasanaṃ. Sīlassa byasanaṃ sīlabyasanaṃ, dussīlyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sammādiṭṭhiṃ vināsayamānā uppannā diṭṭhiyeva byasanaṃ diṭṭhibyasanaṃ. Ñātisampadāti ñātīnaṃ sampadā pāripūri bahubhāvo[V 3.0435]. Bhogasampadāyapi eseva nayo. Ārogyassa sampadā ārogyasampadā. Pāripūri dīgharattaṃ arogatā. Sīladiṭṭhisampadāsupi eseva nayo.

From ill-repute or from censure: here, "ill-repute" (ayaso) is speaking of faults behind one's back. "Censure" (garahā) is to one's face. It ruins, thus it is "ruin" (byasana); it throws away, it destroys welfare and happiness—that is the meaning. The ruin of relatives (ñātibyasana) is the destruction of relatives by thieves, disease, fear, and so on. The ruin of wealth (bhogabyasana) is the destruction of wealth due to kings, thieves, and so on. Disease itself is ruin (rogabyasana), for disease indeed ruins health—that is ruin. The ruin of virtue (sīlabyasana) is a name for immorality. A view that arises destroying right view—this is the ruin of views (diṭṭhibyasana). Accomplishment of relatives (ñātisampadā) means the accomplishment, completeness, and abundance of relatives. The same principle applies to the accomplishment of wealth (bhogasampadā). The accomplishment of health (ārogyasampadā) is completeness, a long period of being without illness. The same principle applies to the accomplishment of virtue and views (sīladiṭṭhisampadā).

Vattaṃ paricchindīti tasmiṃ divase kātabbavattaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Aṭṭha kappe anussarītiādinā tasmiṃ khaṇe jhānaṃ nibbattetvā pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ nibbattesīti dīpeti. Ñattiyā kammappatto hutvāti ñattiyā ṭhapitāya anussāvanakammappatto hutvāti attho.

"He determined the duties" means he completed the duties to be performed on that day. By "recollecting eight aeons," etc., it is shown that at that moment he produced absorption and then generated the knowledge of past lives. "Having become subject to the act by the motion" means, the motion having been established, having become subject to the act of proclamation—this is the meaning.

Mandattā momūhattāti neva samādānaṃ jānāti, na ānisaṃsaṃ, attano pana mandattā momūhattā aññāṇeneva āraññiko hoti. Pāpiccho icchāpakatoti “araññe me viharantassa ‘ayaṃ āraññiko’ti catuppaccayasakkāraṃ karissanti, ‘ayaṃ bhikkhu lajjī pavivitto’tiādīhi ca guṇehi sambhāvessantī”ti evaṃ pāpikāya icchāya ṭhatvā tāya eva icchāya abhibhūto hutvā āraññiko hotīti attho. Tenāha “araññavāsena paccayalābhaṃ patthayamāno”ti. Ummādavasena araññaṃ pavisitvā viharanto ummādā cittakkhepā āraññiko nāma hoti. Vaṇṇitanti idaṃ āraññikaṅgaṃ nāma buddhehi buddhasāvakehi ca vaṇṇitaṃ pasatthanti āraññiko hoti.

"Due to dullness and delusion" means he understands neither the undertaking nor its benefits, but because of his own dullness and delusion, he becomes a forest dweller simply through ignorance. "With evil desires, overcome by wishes" means he thinks, "When I dwell in the forest, they will honor me with the four requisites, saying, 'This is a forest dweller,' and they will esteem me for such qualities as, 'This monk is conscientious and secluded.'" Thus, established in this evil desire and being overwhelmed by that very desire, he becomes a forest dweller—this is the meaning. Therefore, it is said, "desiring the gain of requisites through forest dwelling." One who enters and dwells in the forest due to madness becomes a forest dweller because of madness or mental derangement. "Because it is praised" means one becomes a forest dweller because this forest-dwelling practice is praised and commended by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.

Pañcakavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section of Fives is concluded.

Chakkavāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section of Sixes

326. Chakkesu chabbassaparamatā dhāretabbanti padabhājanaṃ dassitaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

326. In the section on sixes, that the maximum is six years should be understood—this is shown by the analysis of terms. The rest is self-evident.

Chakkavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section of Sixes is concluded.

Sattakavāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section of Sevens

327. Sattakesu [M 3.0476] chakke vuttāniyeva sattakavasena yojetabbānīti chakke vuttacuddasaparamāni dvidhā katvā dvinnaṃ sattakānaṃ vasena yojetabbāni.

327. In the section on sevens, the very things stated in the section on sixes should be applied in the manner of the sevens. The fourteen ultimate principles stated in the section on sixes should be divided in two and applied in the manner of two groups of seven.

Āpattiṃ jānātīti āpattiṃyeva “āpattī”ti jānāti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ābhicetasikānanti [V 3.0436] ettha (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.66) abhicetoti pākatikakāmāvacaracittehi sundaratāya paṭipakkhato visuddhattā ca abhikkantaṃ visuddhacittaṃ vuccati, upacārajjhānacittassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Abhicetasi jātāni ābhicetasikāni, abhicetosannissitānīti vā ābhicetasikāni. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānanti diṭṭhadhamme sukhavihārānaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkho attabhāvo vuccati, tattha sukhavihārabhūtānanti attho. Rūpāvacarajjhānānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tāni hi appetvā nisinnā jhāyino imasmiññeva attabhāve asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ nekkhammasukhaṃ vindanti, tasmā “diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānī”ti vuccanti. Nikāmalābhīti nikāmena lābhī, attano icchāvasena lābhī, icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Akicchalābhīti sukheneva paccanīkadhamme vikkhambhetvā samāpajjituṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Akasiralābhīti akasirānaṃ lābhī vipulānaṃ, yathāparicchedeneva vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi lābhīyeva hoti, na pana sakkoti icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ. Ekacco sakkoti tathā samāpajjituṃ, pāripanthike pana kicchena vikkhambheti. Ekacco tathā ca samāpajjati, pāripanthike ca akiccheneva vikkhambheti, na sakkoti kālamānanāḷikayantaṃ viya yathāparicchedeyeva vuṭṭhātuṃ.

He knows an offense—he knows the offense itself as "an offense." The same principle applies to the remaining terms. Regarding "states pertaining to the higher mind": here, "higher mind" refers to an excellent and purified mind, so called because, in comparison to ordinary sense-sphere consciousness, it is superior in beauty and is purified from its opposite. This is a designation for the consciousness of access concentration. States born in, or dependent on, the higher mind are called "states pertaining to the higher mind." Regarding "blissful dwellings in the here-and-now": this means blissful dwellings in the present life. "The here-and-now" refers to one's directly experienced existence; the meaning is states that are blissful dwellings therein. This is a designation for the form-sphere jhānas. For meditators who attain these and sit absorbed, they experience the undefiled bliss of renunciation in this very life. Therefore, they are called "blissful dwellings in the here-and-now." "One who attains at will" means a gainer by wish, a gainer according to his own desire; this means he is capable of attaining absorption at any moment he wishes. "One who attains without difficulty" means he is capable of attaining absorption after suppressing opposing states with ease. "One who attains without trouble" means a gainer of the untroubled, of the abundant; this means he is capable of emerging precisely according to his determination. For one person is a gainer, but is not able to attain at any moment he wishes. Another is able to attain thus, but suppresses obstacles only with difficulty. Another attains thus and suppresses obstacles without difficulty, but is not able to emerge exactly according to his determination, like a water-clock measuring time.

Āsavānaṃ khayāti arahattamaggena sabbakilesānaṃ khayā. Anāsavanti āsavavirahitaṃ. Cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttinti ettha ceto-vacanena arahattaphalasampayutto samādhi, paññā-vacanena taṃsampayuttā ca paññā vuttā. Tattha ca samādhi rāgato vimuttattā cetovimutti, paññā avijjāya vimuttattā paññāvimuttīti veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “yo hissa, bhikkhave, samādhi, tadassa samādhindriyaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.520). Yā hissa, bhikkhave, paññā, tadassa paññindriyaṃ [M 3.0477] (saṃ. ni. 5.516). Iti kho, bhikkhave, rāgavirāgā cetovimutti avijjāvirāgā paññāvimuttī”ti (a. ni. 2.32). Apicettha samathaphalaṃ cetovimutti, vipassanāphalaṃ paññāvimuttīti veditabbāti. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanāyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā, aparappaccayena ñatvāti attho. Sutamayañāṇādinā viya parappaccayataṃ nayaggāhañca muñcitvā paratoghosānugatabhāvanādhigamabhūtāya attanoyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā, na sayambhūñāṇabhūtāyāti adhippāyo. Upasampajja viharatīti pāpuṇitvā sampādetvā viharati.

“By the destruction of the taints” means the destruction of all defilements through the path of arahantship. “Taintless” means devoid of taints. Regarding “mind-liberation and wisdom-liberation”—here, by the word ‘mind’ is meant the concentration associated with the fruit of arahantship, and by the word ‘wisdom’ is meant the wisdom associated with it. In this context, concentration is to be understood as ‘mind-liberation’ because it is liberated from lust, and wisdom as ‘wisdom-liberation’ because it is liberated from ignorance. For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, whatever concentration he has, that is his faculty of concentration. Whatever wisdom he has, that is his faculty of wisdom. Thus, bhikkhus, through dispassion for lust, there is mind-liberation; through dispassion for ignorance, there is wisdom-liberation.” Moreover, here, the fruit of serenity should be understood as mind-liberation, and the fruit of insight as wisdom-liberation. ‘In this very life’ means in this very existence. ‘Having realized it for oneself with direct knowledge’ means having made it manifest through one’s own wisdom, having known it without reliance on another. The meaning is: having abandoned reliance on another, such as knowledge based on hearing, and having relinquished the grasping of methods, one makes it manifest through one’s own wisdom—a wisdom that is an attainment from development following the voice of another, not a wisdom that is self-originated. ‘Having attained, he dwells’ means having reached and accomplished it, he abides.

Sattakavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of Sevens is concluded.

Aṭṭhakavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Chapter of Eights

328. Aṭṭhakesu [V 3.0437] aṭṭhānisaṃse sampassamānenāti –

328. By one seeing the eight benefits in the groups of eight—

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu āpattiṃ āpanno hoti, so tassā āpattiyā anāpattidiṭṭhi hoti, aññe bhikkhū tassā āpattiyā āpattidiṭṭhino honti, te ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhū taṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ jānanti ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā bahussuto āgatāgamo dhammadharo vinayadharo mātikādharo paṇḍito byatto medhāvī lajjī kukkuccako sikkhākāmo, sace mayaṃ imaṃ bhikkhuṃ āpattiyā adassane ukkhipissāma, na mayaṃ iminā bhikkhunā saddhiṃ uposathaṃ karissāma, vinā iminā bhikkhunā uposathaṃ karissāma, bhavissati saṅghassa tatonidānaṃ bhaṇḍanaṃ kalaho viggaho vivādo saṅghabhedo saṅgharāji saṅghavavatthānaṃ saṅghanānākaraṇa’nti, bhedagarukehi, bhikkhave, bhikkhūhi na so bhikkhu āpattiyā adassane ukkhipitabbo”ti (mahāva. 453) –

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has committed an offense. He has the view that it is not an offense, while other bhikkhus have the view that it is an offense. If those bhikkhus know this bhikkhu to be very learned, one who has received the teachings, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, capable, intelligent, modest, conscientious, and desirous of training, and think: ‘If we suspend this bhikkhu for not seeing the offense, we will not perform the Uposatha with this bhikkhu; we will perform the Uposatha without this bhikkhu, and because of that, there will be quarrels, disputes, contention, discord, schism in the Saṅgha, a split in the Saṅgha, a break-up of the Saṅgha, a making the Saṅgha diverse,’ then, bhikkhus, by bhikkhus who see the gravity of schism, that bhikkhu should not be suspended for not seeing the offense.”

Ādinā vuttaaṭṭhānisaṃse sampassamānena. Tena hi saddhiṃ uposathādiakaraṇaṃ ādīnavo bhedāya saṃvattanato, karaṇaṃ ānisaṃso [M 3.0478] sāmaggiyā saṃvattanato. Tasmā ete aṭṭhānisaṃse sampassamānena na so bhikkhu ukkhipitabboti attho.

By one seeing the eight benefits stated beginning with the above. In that case, not performing the Uposatha and other acts together with him is a danger because it leads to division, whereas performing them is a benefit because it leads to harmony. Thus, seeing these eight benefits, that bhikkhu should not be suspended—this is the meaning.

Dutiyaaṭṭhakepi aṭṭhānisaṃse sampassamānenāti –

By one seeing the eight benefits in the second group of eight as well—

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu āpattiṃ āpanno hoti, so tassā āpattiyā anāpattidiṭṭhi hoti, aññe bhikkhū tassā āpattiyā āpattidiṭṭhino honti, so ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu te bhikkhū evaṃ jānāti ‘ime kho āyasmanto bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammadharā vinayadharā mātikādharā paṇḍitā byattā medhāvino lajjino kukkuccakā sikkhākāmā, nālaṃ mamaṃ vā kāraṇā aññesaṃ vā kāraṇā chandā dosā mohā bhayā agatiṃ gantuṃ, sace maṃ ime bhikkhū āpattiyā adassane ukkhipissanti, na mayā saddhiṃ uposathaṃ karissanti, vinā mayā uposathaṃ karissanti, bhavissati saṅghassa tatonidānaṃ bhaṇḍanaṃ kalaho viggaho vivādo saṅghabhedo saṅgharāji saṅghavavatthānaṃ saṅghanānākaraṇa’nti, bhedagarukena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā paresampi saddhāya sā āpatti desetabbā”ti (mahāva. 453) –

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has committed an offense. He has the view that it is not an offense, while other bhikkhus have the view that it is an offense. If, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu knows about those bhikkhus: ‘These venerables are learned, versed in the traditions, upholders of the Dhamma, upholders of the Vinaya, upholders of the Mātikā, wise, articulate, intelligent, modest, conscientious, and desirous of training. They are not capable of going astray due to favoritism, hatred, delusion, or fear. If these bhikkhus suspend me for not seeing the offense, they will not perform the Uposatha with me; they will perform the Uposatha without me. Then, because of that, there will be quarrels, disputes, contention, discord, schism in the Saṅgha, a split in the Saṅgha, a break-up of the Saṅgha, and a making the Saṅgha diverse.’ Then, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who regards schism as serious should confess that offense out of faith in those others.”

Ādinā [V 3.0438] vuttaaṭṭhānisaṃse sampassamānenāti attho.

By one seeing the eight benefits stated beginning with the above—this is the meaning.

Pāḷiyaṃ āgatehi sattahīti “pubbevassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇissa’nti, bhaṇantassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇāmī’ti, bhaṇitassa hoti ‘musā mayā bhaṇita’nti vinidhāya diṭṭhiṃ, vinidhāya khantiṃ, vinidhāya ruciṃ, vinidhāya bhāva”nti (pārā. 220) evamāgatehi sattahi.

By the seven mentioned in the Pāli text: ‘Beforehand, he thinks: “I will speak falsely.” While speaking, he thinks: “I am speaking falsely.” Having spoken, he thinks: “I have spoken falsely”; having laid aside his view, having laid aside his tolerance, having laid aside his liking, having laid aside his disposition.’ Thus, by these seven mentioned.

Abrahmacariyāti aseṭṭhacariyato. Rattiṃ na bhuñjeyya vikālabhojananti uposathaṃ upavuttho rattibhojanañca divāvikālabhojanañca na bhuñjeyya. Mañce chamāyaṃva sayetha santhateti kappiyamañce vā sudhādiparikammakatāya bhūmiyaṃ vā tiṇapaṇṇapalālādīni santharitvā kate santhate vā sayethāti attho. Etañhi aṭṭhaṅgīkamāhuposathanti etaṃ pāṇātipātādīni asamācarantena upavutthauposathaṃ aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgatattā “aṭṭhaṅgika”nti vadanti.

‘Unchastity’ means from ignoble conduct. ‘One should not eat at night, unseasonable food’ means that one who has observed the Uposatha should not eat food at night or unseasonable food during the day. ‘One should sleep on a couch or on a spread on the ground’ means one should sleep either on a permissible couch, or on the ground prepared with plaster and so forth, or on a spread made of grass, leaves, straw, and the like—this is the meaning. ‘This they call the eight-factored Uposatha’ means that the Uposatha observed by one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth, being endowed with eight factors, they call ‘eight-factored’.

“Akappiyakataṃ [M 3.0479] hoti appaṭiggahitaka”ntiādayo aṭṭha anatirittā nāma. Sappiādi aṭṭhame aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Aṭṭhakavasena yojetvā veditabbānīti purimāni aṭṭha ekaṃ aṭṭhakaṃ, tato ekaṃ apanetvā sesesupi ekekaṃ pakkhipitvāti evamādinā nayena aññānipi aṭṭhakāni kātabbānīti attho.

‘It is made unallowable, it is not accepted,’ and so on—these eight are called ‘non-extra’. Ghee and so forth, in the eighth case, become forfeitable at dawn. ‘They should be understood by arranging them as groups of eight’ means that the first eight form one group of eight; then, by removing one and adding another to the remainder, other groups of eight should also be formed in this way—this is the meaning.

Aṭṭhakavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter of Eights is concluded.

Navakavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Chapter of Nines

329. Navakesu āghātavatthūnīti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.340; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.9.29) āghātakāraṇāni. Āghātapaṭivinayānīti āghātassa paṭivinayakāraṇāni. Taṃ kutettha labbhāti “taṃ anatthacaraṇaṃ mā ahosī”ti etasmiṃ puggale kuto labbhā kena kāraṇena sakkā laddhuṃ. “Paro nāma parassa attano cittaruciyā anatthaṃ karotī”ti evaṃ cintetvā āghātaṃ paṭivinodeti. Atha vā sacāhaṃ paṭikkopaṃ kareyyaṃ, taṃ kopakaraṇaṃ ettha puggale kuto labbhā, kena kāraṇena laddhabbaṃ niratthakabhāvatoti attho. Kammassakā hi sattā, te kassa ruciyā dukkhitā sukhitā vā bhavanti, tasmā kevalaṃ tasmiṃ mayhaṃ kujjhanamattamevāti adhippāyo. Atha vā taṃ kopakaraṇaṃ ettha puggale kuto labbhā paramatthato kujjhitabbassa [V 3.0439] kujjhanakassa ca abhāvato. Saṅkhāramattañhetaṃ yadidaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ yaṃ “satto”ti vuccati, te ca saṅkhārā ittarakālā khaṇikā, kassa ko kujjhatīti attho. “Kuto lābhā”tipi pāṭho, sacāhaṃ ettha kopaṃ kareyyaṃ, tasmiṃ me kopakaraṇe kuto lābhā, lābhā nāma ke siyuṃ aññatra anatthuppattitoti attho. Imasmiñca atthe tanti nipātamattameva hoti.

329. In the Nines, ‘grounds for resentment’ means causes for resentment. ‘Removals of resentment’ means causes for the removal of resentment. Regarding ‘How is that to be obtained here?’: How is this wish—‘May he not have done me harm’—to be obtained in regard to that person? By what reason could it be obtained? Reflecting thus: ‘Another person indeed does harm to another according to their own mind's preference,’ one dispels resentment. Alternatively: ‘If I were to get angry in return, how could that act of getting angry be obtained in regard to this person? For what reason should it be obtained, since it is meaningless?’—this is the meaning. For beings are owners of their kamma. By whose preference do they become happy or unhappy? Therefore, it is merely my own getting angry at him—this is the intention. Alternatively, how could that act of getting angry be obtained in regard to this person, since in an ultimate sense there is no one to be angered at and no one who angers? This, which is called ‘a being,’ is merely a formation—the five aggregates. And those formations are of short duration, momentary. Who gets angry at whom? This is the meaning. There is also the reading ‘Kuto lābhā’ (What gain?). If I were to become angry here, what gain would there be for me in that act of getting angry? What gains would there be, other than the arising of harm? This is the meaning. And in this sense, ‘taṃ’ is merely a particle.

Taṇhaṃ paṭiccāti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.103; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.9.23) dve taṇhā esanataṇhā esitataṇhā ca. Yāya taṇhāya ajapathasaṅkupathādīni paṭipajjitvā bhoge esati gavesati, ayaṃ esanataṇhā nāma. Yā tesu esitesu gavesitesu paṭiladdhesu [M 3.0480] taṇhā, ayaṃ esitataṇhā nāma. Idha esitataṇhā daṭṭhabbā. Pariyesanāti rūpādiārammaṇapariyesanā. Sā hi esanataṇhāya sati hoti. Lābhoti rūpādiārammaṇappaṭilābho. So hi pariyesanāya sati hoti. Vinicchayo pana ñāṇataṇhādiṭṭhivitakkavasena catubbidho. Tattha “sukhavinicchayaṃ jaññā, sukhavinicchayaṃ ñatvā ajjhattaṃ sukhamanuyuñjeyyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.323) ayaṃ ñāṇavinicchayo. “Vinicchayoti dve vinicchayā taṇhāvinicchayo ca diṭṭhivinicchayo cā”ti (mahāni. 102) evaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni taṇhāvinicchayo. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhivinicchayo. “Chando kho, devānaminda, vitakkanidāno”ti (dī. ni. 2.358) imasmiṃ pana sutte idha vinicchayoti vutto vitakkoyeva āgato. Lābhaṃ labhitvā hi iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ sundarāsundarañca vitakkena vinicchināti “ettakaṃ me rūpārammaṇatthāya bhavissati, ettakaṃ saddārammaṇatthāya, ettakaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissati, ettakaṃ parassa, ettakaṃ paribhuñjissāmi, ettakaṃ nidahissāmī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo”ti.

“Dependent on craving” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.103; A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.9.23) refers to two types of craving: craving for seeking and craving for what is sought. The craving by which one, having undertaken paths such as goat-paths and stake-paths, seeks and searches for possessions, this is called craving for seeking. The craving that arises for what has been sought, searched for, and obtained, this is called craving for what is sought. Here, craving for what is sought should be understood. “Searching” refers to the pursuit of objects such as forms. This arises when there is craving for seeking. “Gain” refers to the acquisition of objects such as forms. This arises when there is searching. “Judgment,” however, is fourfold, by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought. Among these, “one should know the judgment of pleasure; having known the judgment of pleasure, one should pursue internal pleasure” (Ma. Ni. 3.323), this is the judgment of knowledge. “Judgment is of two kinds: the judgment of craving and the judgment of views,” as stated (Mahāni. 102). Thus, the one hundred and eight movements of craving constitute the judgment of craving. The sixty-two views constitute the judgment of views. “Desire, O lord of gods, has thought as its source” (Dī. Ni. 2.358); in this discourse, what is called judgment here is simply thought. Having obtained a gain, one judges between the desirable and undesirable, the beautiful and the ugly, through thought, thinking: “This much will be for the purpose of form-objects, this much for sound-objects, this much will be mine, this much for another, this much I will enjoy, this much I will store away.” Therefore, it is said, “Dependent on gain, there is judgment.”

Chandarāgoti evaṃ akusalavitakkena vitakkite vatthusmiṃ dubbalarāgo ca balavarāgo ca uppajjati. Ajjhosānanti “ahaṃ, mama”nti balavasanniṭṭhānaṃ. Pariggahoti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena pariggahakaraṇaṃ. Macchariyanti parehi sādhāraṇabhāvassa asahanatā. Tenevassa porāṇā evaṃ vacanatthaṃ vadanti “idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayheva hotu, mā aññassa acchariyaṃ hotūti pavattattā macchariyanti vuccatī”ti. Ārakkhoti dvārapidahanamañjūsāgopanādivasena suṭṭhu rakkhaṇaṃ. Adhi karotīti adhikaraṇaṃ, kāraṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ārakkhādhikaraṇanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, ārakkhahetūti attho. Daṇḍādānādīsu paranisedhanatthaṃ daṇḍassa ādānaṃ daṇḍādānaṃ. Ekatodhārādino satthassa ādānaṃ satthādānaṃ. Kalahoti kāyakalahopi vācākalahopi. Purimo purimo virodho viggaho, pacchimo pacchimo vivādo. Tuvaṃ tuvanti agāravavasena “tuvaṃ tuva”nti vacanaṃ.

“Sensual desire” is when, with regard to an object thought of with unwholesome thought, both weak and strong lust arise. “Clinging” is the strong conviction of “I” and “mine.” “Grasping” is the act of taking possession by way of craving and views. “Stinginess” is the inability to bear things being common to others. Therefore, the ancients explain its meaning thus: “Because it proceeds as, ‘Let this wonder be for me; may it not be a wonder for another,’ it is called stinginess.” “Guarding” is thorough protection, such as by closing doors, guarding chests, and so on. “Because it is a cause,” it is a “ground for dispute”; this is a name for a cause. “The ground for guarding” is a neuter abstract noun, meaning “on account of guarding.” “Taking up the rod” is the taking up of a rod for the purpose of warding off others. “Taking up the weapon” is the taking up of a weapon such as a single-edged sword. “Quarrel” is both a physical quarrel and a verbal quarrel. The former is opposition and dispute; the latter is contention. “You, you” is speech by way of disrespect, saying “you, you.”

Adhiṭṭhitakālato [V 3.0440] paṭṭhāya na vikappetabbānīti vikappentena adhiṭṭhānato pubbe vā

From the time of determination onwards, they should not be disposed of; by one who disposes of them, it should be done either before the determination or...

Vikappetabbaṃ, vijahitādhiṭṭhānaṃ vā pacchāvikappetabbaṃ. Avijahitādhiṭṭhānaṃ [M 3.0481] pana na vikappetabbanti adhippāyo. Dukkaṭavasena vuttānīti “vaggaṃ bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ vaggasaññī ovadatī”tiādinā (pāci. 150) nayena adhammakamme dve navakāni dukkaṭavasena vuttāni.

...it should be disposed of, or the determination having been abandoned, it should be disposed of afterwards. The intention is that what has not had its determination abandoned should not be disposed of. “They are stated by way of wrong conduct”: by the method beginning, “perceiving a faction of the community of nuns to be a faction, he advises them” (Pāci. 150), two sets of nine are stated by way of wrong conduct in an unlawful formal act.

Navakavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Section of Nines is concluded.

Dasakavāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section of Tens

330. Dasakesu natthi dinnantiādivasena veditabbāti “natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paro loko, natthi mātā, natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā, ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī”ti (ma. ni. 2.94, 225; 3.91, 116; saṃ. ni. 3.210) evamāgataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sassato lokotiādivasenāti “sassato lokoti vā, asassato lokoti vā, antavā lokoti vā, anantavā lokoti vā, taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti vā, aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīranti vā, hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.269) evamāgataṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

330. In the Tens, it should be understood by way of what begins with “There is nothing given,” that is, “There is nothing given, nothing sacrificed, nothing offered; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins who have gone rightly and practiced rightly, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known” (Ma. Ni. 2.94, 225; 3.91, 116; Saṃ. Ni. 3.210). This is said with reference to what is found thus. By way of what begins with “The world is eternal,” it includes what is found thus: “The world is eternal,” or “The world is not eternal,” or “The world is finite,” or “The world is infinite,” or “The life principle is the same as the body,” or “The life principle is different from the body,” or “The Tathāgata exists after death,” or “The Tathāgata does not exist after death,” or “The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” or “The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death” (Ma. Ni. 1.269).

Micchādiṭṭhiādayo micchāvimuttipariyosānāti “micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappo micchāvācā micchākammanto micchāājīvo micchāvāyāmo micchāsati micchāsamādhi micchāñāṇaṃ micchāvimuttī”ti (vibha. 970) evamāgataṃ sandhāya vadati.
